“Ānanda! That Tathāgata Samantabhadra further bestowed a prediction upon one bodhisattva, saying that he shall next become a buddha named Candra Tathāgata. Ānanda!”
That Tathāgata Candra further bestowed a prediction upon one bodhisattva, saying that he shall next become a buddha named Puṇḍarīka Tathāgata. Ānanda!
That Tathāgata Puṇḍarīka further bestowed a prediction upon one bodhisattva, saying that he shall next become a buddha named Vimala Tathāgata.
"Ānanda! That Tathāgata Vimala further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying: 'The next one to become a Buddha shall be named Sākṣīkṛtamām (證我如來). Ānanda!"
That Tathāgata Pratyakṣadarśin further bestowed a prediction upon one bodhisattva, saying: "In the future, you shall become a Buddha named Mahāvarṣa Tathāgata.
Ānanda! That Mahāvarṣa Tathāgata further bestowed a prediction upon one bodhisattva, saying: "In the future, you shall become a Buddha named Abhaya Tathāgata."
"Ānanda! That Tathāgata Abhaya further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying: 'In the future, he shall become a Buddha named Svaprabha Tathāgata. Ānanda!"
That Tathāgata Svayaṃprabha further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying: "In the future, he shall become a buddha named Mahābala Tathāgata.
"Ānanda! That Mahābala Tathāgata will further bestow a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying: 'In the future, he shall become a buddha named Sūrya Tathāgata.'"
Ānanda! That Tathāgata Sūrya further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying: "In the future, he shall become a Buddha named Śaradprabha Tathāgata. Ānanda!
That Tathāgata Śaradprabha further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying that he shall next become a buddha named Uṣṇīṣaprabha.
Ānanda! That Tathāgata Uṣṇīṣaprabha further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying that he shall next become a buddha named Lakṣaṇa.
"Ānanda! That Tathāgata Lakṣaṇa further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying: 'In the future, he shall become a Buddha named Anupama-tathāgata. Ānanda!"
That Tathāgata Anupama further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying that he shall next become a buddha named Jinaśreṣṭha.
Ānanda! That Tathāgata Jinaśreṣṭha further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying that he shall next become a buddha named Lakṣaṇaśreṣṭha.
Ānanda! That Tathāgata Lakṣaṇottara further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying: "In the future, he shall become a Buddha named Śālarāja Tathāgata. Ānanda!
That Tathāgata Śālarāja further bestowed a prediction upon one bodhisattva, saying: "The next to become a buddha shall be named Śarīraprabhāsa Tathāgata.
"Ānanda! That Tathāgata Śarīraprabhāsa further bestowed a prediction upon one bodhisattva, saying: 'The next to become a buddha shall be named Aśokabhaya Tathāgata.'"
Ānanda! That Tathāgata Fearless of Any Place further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying that he shall next become a buddha named Transformation (Vikurvaṇa) Tathāgata. Ānanda!
That emanated Tathāgata further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying: "Next you shall become a Buddha named Śāntisamādhi Tathāgata. Ānanda!
That Śāntisamādhi Tathāgata further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying: "Next you shall become a Buddha named Jayendra Tathāgata."
“Ānanda! At the place where that Tathāgata Vijitarāja attained Buddhahood, the kalpa was named Bhadra; there were three hundred Buddhas who all shared the same title, namely, Tathāgata Vijitarāja.”

Ānanda! That Tathāgata Jinarāja was the very last of those Buddhas; he, in turn, bestowed a prediction upon one bodhisattva, saying that the next to become a Buddha shall be named Sarvārthadarśin Tathāgata.
Ānanda! In that world Sarvārthadarśin, the Tathāgata has three hundred million śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are arhats. Ānanda!
The Tathāgata Sarvārthadarśin further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying: "In the future, you shall become a buddha named Aśoka Tathāgata.
Ānanda! That Aśoka Tathāgata further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying: "In the future, you shall become a buddha named Nāgottama Tathāgata."
Ānanda! That Tathāgata Lokottama further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying: "In the future, he shall become a Buddha named Jambūdvīpottama Tathāgata. Ānanda!
That Tathāgata Jambūśreṣṭha further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying that he shall next become a buddha named Nyagrodha Tathāgata. Ānanda!
That Nyagrodha Tathāgata further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying that he shall next become a buddha named Viśvāsa Tathāgata.
Ānanda! That Tathāgata Vistīrṇaprasāda further conferred a prediction upon one bodhisattva, saying: "In the future, he shall become a Buddha named Trāṇamukta Tathāgata. Ānanda!
That Tathāgata Paritrāṇaśūra further bestowed a prediction upon another bodhisattva, saying: "In the future, you shall become a Buddha named Jinaśreṣṭha. "Ānanda!

Those World-Honored Ones, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, each in turn bestowed predictions upon one another until the final Jinaśreṣṭha Tathāgata; I have personally made offerings to and served them all."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"All those Tathāgatas, And Śākyamuni, the Great Lion,
With the Buddha’s pure eye, Behold them all."
Thus the wisdom of the Tathāgata and the inconceivable conduct of the Buddha cannot be known by gods or humans at all. Neither cause and effect nor the Buddha’s wisdom,
nor the manifest characteristics of all phenomena, can be grasped.
This is the realm of the Buddhas alone, which ordinary beings cannot know.
The names of the Buddhas that are spoken and the deeds of the Buddhas that are manifested possess marks of great majestic power; they are seen universally with the Buddha-eye.
"If there be a person of wisdom who desires to seek bodhi, they should read these names of the Buddhas; before long, they shall attain Buddhahood.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have heard what was spoken from the golden mouth of the Buddha; having heard it, I have bound my mind to it, remembering and upholding it without forgetting—namely, that the wisdom of all Buddhas is unimpeded, unequaled, and without obstruction.”
“World-Honored One!
Does the Tathāgata truly know such wisdom?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
“The wisdom of the Tathāgata is fully perfected and all-knowing; therefore, his knowledge and vision are unobstructed and unhindered.
Should the Tathāgata wish to make his sphere of activity broad or narrow, or to contemplate the extent and magnitude of the wisdom of the Buddhas, he attains whatever he desires at will.”
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is just as the Venerable Aniruddha has attained the pure divine eye, which surpasses that of human eyes.”
In this way, the Venerable Aniruddha was able to see a thousandfold world-system with his purified divine eye.
The Tathāgata, however, said:
"I see that which is boundless."
"What is the meaning of this?
At that time, the Buddha remained silent. When he asked a second time, and even a third, only then did the Buddha respond.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do not seek to compare the wisdom of a śrāvaka with that of a Tathāgata. Why is this?

Now, with the pure divine eye which surpasses the human eye, I see within as many Buddha-fields in the eastern direction as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds on the path and planted various roots of goodness."
In some instances, he saw within Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction, immeasurable bodhisattvas receiving their predictions of enlightenment;
or he saw within Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction, various bodhisattvas practicing the bodhisattva path;

or he saw immeasurable bodhisattvas practicing the pure conduct (brahmacarya) in the presence of Buddhas, and subsequently being born in the Tuṣita heaven palace, descending from Tuṣita to enter a mother’s womb.
Some see the Bodhisattva being born from his mother’s right side;
some see the Bodhisattva practicing the ways of a youth;
and some see the Bodhisattva within the palace demonstrating the practice of desire.
In some instances, one sees a bodhisattva renounce the rank of a wheel-turning sage-king to leave the household life and cultivate the Way;
in others, one sees a bodhisattva subdue the four kinds of māras;
and in yet others, one sees a bodhisattva realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi beneath the Bodhi tree.
In some instances, they see the Bodhisattva, having attained awakening, experiencing the bliss of liberation;
in others, they see the Bodhisattva sitting upright in contemplation, engaging in two kinds of discernment;
and in others, they see the Bodhisattva turning the wheel of Dharma.
Some see the Bodhisattva relinquishing his life for the sake of all sentient beings at the moment he is about to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*;

others see the period following the Bodhisattva’s *parinirvāṇa*, during which the True Dharma (*saddharma*) and the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*) abide in the world, observing how long or short, how much or little their duration extends.

Ānanda! In this way, I see that in the eastern buddha-fields, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the various Buddhas attain enlightenment, and after their parinirvāṇa, both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma completely vanish.
"As it is with the lands of the eastern direction, so it is likewise for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda!"

I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and ineffable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a wheel-turning sage king named Sudarśana. He had brought the four quarters under his sway and ruled the world according to the Dharma. All that was governed by that king was abundant and joyful; he did not employ whips or staves, nor was there any killing or harm. Weapons were laid aside, and he transformed people through the Dharma.
Ānanda! The city in which King Sudarśana resided was named Jambūnada; that city was twelve yojanas from east to west, and seven yojanas on each of its north and south sides.

“Ānanda! That city of Jambū is pure, adorned, extraordinary, and exquisite, being entirely embellished with the four precious substances—gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli. Beyond it, there are furthermore seven additional layers of walls.”

Those cities were all seven fathoms high and each three fathoms thick; around the tops of those cities, there were seven tiers of railings on every side. Those railings were exquisitely carved with rare and wonderful beauty, almost peerless, and were likewise composed of the four precious substances: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
If there is a railing of gold, with hooks and pillars of gold and window-sills of silver;
or if there is a railing of silver, with hooks and pillars of silver and window-sills of gold;
or if there is a railing of crystal, with hooks and pillars of crystal and window-sills of lapis lazuli.
If the railings are of lapis lazuli, with hooks and pillars of lapis lazuli and windows and terraces of crystal;

within each of those sevenfold cities, there are sevenfold rows of precious *tāla* trees surrounding them in succession. The branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of those trees are luxuriant, dense, and in full bloom, a sight that people delight to behold.
The roots and trunks of those trees are all composed of the four treasures: gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
The golden tala trees have golden roots and golden trunks, with silver branches and silver leaves, while their flowers and fruits are all silver.
The silver tala trees have silver roots and silver trunks, with golden branches and golden leaves, while their flowers and fruits are all gold.
If it is crystal that constitutes the tala tree, its roots and trunk are of crystal, while its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are of beryl;
if it is beryl that constitutes the tala tree, its roots and trunk are of beryl, while its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are of crystal.

Those tāla trees were all covered with nets; within the spaces of those nets, precious bells were suspended everywhere. All those networks of bells were made of the seven treasures, namely: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musāragalva, agate, coral, and crystal.

Outside those various cities, there are sevenfold moats that encircle them on all sides; these moats are extremely deep and filled to the brim with the water of eight virtues, standing perfectly still.
Various kinds of named flowers—namely, utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka—completely covered the surface of the water.
The bottoms of those moats are all composed of golden sand, and the edges of those moat banks are entirely covered on all sides by nets of the seven treasures spread over them. Ānanda!
On each of the four sides of that city of Jambū, there are sixteen gates; those city gates are composed of the four precious substances: gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
The gates of those cities have silver doors with golden panels, or crystal doors with lapis lazuli panels, or lapis lazuli doors with crystal panels.

Each of those city gates is equipped with defensive watchtowers and battlements, multi-storied pavilions with soaring eaves draped with nets of hanging pearls, all adorned with the seven precious gems; they are so subtle, exquisite, and marvelous that people delight in beholding them.

At each of those city gates, there were sevenfold gate-enclosures made of the four precious substances, which remained firmly established and immovable, opening and closing at will, radiating brilliant light, lovely and delightful—namely, gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.

Those city gates were transparent when viewed from afar; when they were to open, the wind would blow them open of its own accord, and when they were to close, the wind would blow them closed of its own accord.

When the wind opens those sevenfold barriers, each gate aligns with its counterpart so that everything can be seen through them; when the gates are about to close, the wind blows them shut of its own accord, and the sevenfold barrier walls suddenly close back up once more.

“Ānanda! In the center of that city of Jambūnada, there is a great lake named Nandā. That lake is one yojana wide from east to west and half a yojana wide from south to north; its four banks are built with four layers of bricks.”
Those bricks were exquisite, subtle, and pleasing, composed of the four precious substances: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
On all four sides of those ponds were walkways, and those walkways were likewise exquisite and pleasing, also constructed from the four precious substances: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
The golden galleries have silver steps;
the silver galleries have golden steps;
the beryl galleries have crystal steps.
The galleries were made of crystal and the steps of lapis lazuli.

Upon those galleries were battlements, all of which were exquisitely adorned and pleasing to behold, fashioned from the seven treasures: gold, silver, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, and lapis lazuli.
On all four sides of that pond, there are railings, upright and pleasing to behold, likewise composed entirely of the four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
On its eastern side, there was a railing of gold; on its southern side, a railing of silver; on its western side, a railing of lapis lazuli; and on its northern side, a railing of crystal.
There were railings of gold with pillars of gold and window-sills of silver;
railings of silver with pillars of silver and window-sills of gold;
and railings of crystal with pillars of crystal and window-sills of lapis lazuli.
The balustrades are made of lapis lazuli, with pillars of lapis lazuli and windows and platforms of crystal. "Ānanda!

That Lake of Joy is surrounded on all sides by rows of tala trees, seven layers deep. Between those trees there are nets, adorned with the seven precious gems; from within those nets, jeweled bells hang down."
Outside the tala trees, there are seven layers of moats, which are upright and pleasing to behold.
Within those ponds, there are various kinds of flowers, namely the utpala, the padma, the kumuda, and the puṇḍarīka.
On the banks of that pond, there were land-growing flowers, namely the campaka flower, the ātāmra flower, the pāriyātraka flower, and the gandhapāriyātraka flower.
That Lake of Joy is filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities; when the birds are thirsty, they may all drink at their ease.
At the bottom of that lake, golden sand is spread everywhere, and nets of the seven precious gems cover its surface.
Those exquisite nets have bells made of the seven treasures suspended from every joint. "Ānanda!
In that city of Jambū, the streets and lanes are level and even; on both sides of the streets stand tāla trees, and between every pair of tāla trees there is a net."

Within the intervals of that net, at every joint, seven-jeweled bells were suspended; when those seven-jeweled bells were stirred by a gentle breeze, they produced wondrous sounds that were delightful to hear, causing the heart to give rise to joy, like a person performing the five kinds of musical instruments.

Ānanda! All the people in that city of Jambū are entirely upright and honest. When those people wish to enjoy themselves, they have no other sounds; upon hearing the sound of those bells, they immediately rejoice and spontaneously sing and dance, no longer thinking of any other music.

“Ānanda! In that city of Jambū, there are always various kinds of subtle and wondrous music, namely: bells, chimes, conchs, drums, lutes, zithers, harps, flutes, oboes, horns, pipes, biwa lutes, kīṅ lutes, and transverse flutes—such various sounds as these.”

Furthermore, there were immeasurable and subtle sounds of various birds—namely, the jīvañjīvaka, the parrot, the peacock, the kokila, and so forth—countless and boundless in kind; all these diverse birds produced subtle and extraordinary melodies that never ceased for even a moment.
The ground was strewn everywhere with various kinds of exquisite flowers, namely the utpala, kumuda, padma, and puṇḍarīka, as well as various other terrestrial flowers.

Ānanda! In that city there were no sufferings, oppressions, or unpleasant matters; everything was fully provided for, with nothing lacking. Material goods were abundant, food and drink were never in short supply, and all flavors were complete. The entire residential area was filled to capacity with no empty spaces; the population was flourishing, and its majesty and virtue were towering and sublime.
The city where he dwells is, for example, like King Vaiśravaṇa’s city of Alakā in the north; they are exactly alike, without any difference. "Ānanda!
At that time in that world, a Buddha appeared named Ratnagarbha, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles."
Ānanda! Before that Buddha Ratnaśarīra attained the Way, while he was practicing as a bodhisattva, he always delighted in purity, and the people of that city also delighted in purity.

At that time, the Buddha Ratnagarbha resided near the city of Jambūnada. When, at dawn, he wished to go on his almsround and enter the cities and villages, immeasurable thousands of millions of devas would descend to make offerings, surrounding and attending upon the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha.

When he was about to enter the city, his foot touched the city gate; at that time, all the people within the city—due to the supernatural power of being protected by the devas and out of their desire to make offerings to that Buddha of Jewel-Body—cleansed away all filth, sprinkled the ground with fragrant water, smeared the ground with fragrant mud, and scattered various fragrant flowers until they covered the earth. In every place, they set up exquisite incense burners, burned priceless incense, and hung up various kinds of banners, pennants, and canopies.
With such immeasurable articles of offering, he made offerings to the Tathāgata Ratnaśarīra.
At that time, there was a villager from outside the city who, together with people from within the city, had come into the town intending to marry.

That person saw the city, which was so magnificent and exquisite that it was rare in the world; having never beheld such a sight with his eyes since childhood, his heart was filled with great wonder and astonishment, and he asked the inhabitants living within the city:
"What is this city intending to do now?"
The people within that city replied to the villagers:

"A Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Ratnagarbha has appeared in this world; before long he intends to enter this city for alms, and for this reason we are sprinkling water, sweeping, and adorning it."

Furthermore, he spoke extensively to the villagers regarding the immeasurable and boundless merits of the Tathāgata, and he also praised the Buddha’s virtues—how the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha was fully endowed with the ten titles.
In this way, he further extols the virtues of the Jewel of the Dharma, and likewise praises the virtues of the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
Hearing of the merits of the Three Jewels, that person’s heart gives rise to joy; leaping for immeasurable delight, he thinks:
“The Lord of Jewel-nature—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—appears rarely in the world. I should now go to where the Buddha of Jewel-nature dwells.”
After that person had formed this thought in his heart, he immediately went together with the people of the city and various villages to the place where the Buddha Ratnagarbha was.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, he thought to himself:
"If this Tathāgata has attained all-knowledge and perceives my mind, he should first speak with me to comfort and encourage me."
At that time, the Buddha Ratnaśarīra, knowing the thoughts in that man’s mind, spoke first with the villagers of that village.

When the villagers heard the Tathāgata speak first, their hearts were filled with joy and they leaped for immeasurable delight; their wishes being fulfilled, they immediately invited the Tathāgata to receive a meal on the following day. The Buddha then accepted their invitation by remaining silent.
At that time, having received the Tathāgata’s acceptance of their invitation, the villagers were filled with joy; they quickly returned to their homes and prepared various foods and drinks.
Then the Four Heavenly Kings, along with Brahmā, Śakra, and the great assembly of devas, brought forth various celestial offerings and came to present them to the Tathāgata.
Then those villagers returned to their own homes and, during that night, prepared various kinds of fine foods—dishes to be eaten, chewed, licked, and sucked.

Having finished the preparations, they rose early the next morning, swept the ground of their houses until it was pure and clean, smeared the floors with fragrant mud, and repeatedly sprinkled them with exquisite perfumed water. They further scattered various kinds of diverse, wonderful, and beautiful flowers, arranged beds and seats, and immediately sent a messenger to inform the Buddha, saying:
"Tathāgata!..."
"If you know that the appointed time has arrived, I pray that you will come to my home.

Then, at the hour of dawn, the Buddha Ratnakāya donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and, surrounded before and behind by a multitude of one thousand billion śrāvaka bhikṣus, went to the house where he had been invited.
Having arrived at that house, the bhikṣus each sat down in order according to their seniority.
When the villagers saw that the Buddha Ratnagarbha was seated comfortably, they personally took up various kinds of exquisite food and drink, offered them to the Tathāgata, and said:
"World-Honored One!"
"I only pray that the Buddhas, the community of bhikṣus, and the great assembly will eat to their heart's content and be fully satisfied.
After they had finished eating, the food could not be exhausted. That person then thought:
"Since these foods of a hundred flavors cannot be exhausted, it must surely be through the majestic power and virtuous strength of the Tathāgata that they have been made so abundant."
"Since there is such a great abundance of food remaining, I should now summon the lay followers who are attending upon the Tathāgata and give them this food so that they may all eat their fill.
Only then will my heart attain great joy."
Again, this thought arose in him:

"How rare, how rare! This inconceivable Dharma and the majestic power of this Jewel-Body Buddha are so great that my kinsmen have come to assist me of their own accord without being summoned. I have not hired a single person, nor have I expended much effort, yet all matters have been simultaneously accomplished."

Then, after the Buddha Ratnagarbha had finished his meal, he preached the Dharma to those villagers as was appropriate for them, causing them to rejoice and give rise to a sense of wonder. He established those people within the True Dharma, and the entire assembly, having heard the teaching, were all filled with joy; some attained the Path, and eventually they rose and returned to their respective places.

At that time, having heard the Dharma taught by the Buddha Ratnaśarīra for the sake of transforming beings, those villagers listened to and received the teaching. Filled with joy and exultation, they gave rise to a great vow and spoke these words:
"May we, in the future, fully possess all the dharmas attained by the Tathāgata Ratnaśarīra;
furthermore, may we preach the Dharma in this manner within the great assembly, causing all people to rejoice, believe, and accept it."
"Now, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Ratnakāya, leads a community of bhikṣus, walking with serene composure, no different from before.

At that time, having made offerings to the Tathāgata with full respect and a heart of reverence, those villagers followed the Buddha toward the monastery; they shaved off their hair and beards, renounced the secular life, and became bhikṣus.
At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, having dwelt in the world and finished preaching the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, entered parinirvāṇa.
After his parinirvāṇa, immeasurable and boundless multitudes of devas and humans cremated the Buddha’s body and further presented immeasurable articles of offering at the site of the cremation.
At that time, having heard that the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa, that bhikṣu was overcome with great sorrow and distress, and he thought to himself:
"I should now go to the place of cremation; once I arrive there, I shall surely obtain a special Dharma."
At that time, the bhikṣu went swiftly to the place where the cremation was taking place; having arrived there, he immediately obtained extraordinary jewels.
When he first obtained them, he thought those precious gems were not very pure, as they were slightly covered in dust and grime.
"At that time, the bhikṣu carefully scraped and polished it to examine it, and immediately recognized it as a pure, genuine lapis lazuli gem, worth hundreds of thousands of measures of gold.
Wherever that maṇi jewel was placed, there was no difference between day and night; at night it appeared like the sun, so that all the chambers and all the courtyards were filled with radiance."
At that time, the devas and humans, having collected the bodily relics of the Buddha Ratnagarbha, erected a stūpa.
Then that bhikṣu also gave rise to this thought:
"I should now place this maṇi jewel upon the *āmalaka* bowl of the stūpa to serve as a precious vase."
Having formed this thought, he went to the location of the stūpa. Upon arriving there, he thought:

"This maṇi-jewel of mine is worth hundreds of thousands of measures of gold. Now, I shall place this maṇi-jewel upon the stūpa because that Tathāgata was my teacher; for this reason, I now take this maṇi and set it upon the stūpa."

The radiance of that mani-jewel illuminated the top of that stupa for immeasurable thousands of years; furthermore, that bhikṣu lit immeasurable varieties of lamps and lights for a full thousand years, making offerings to that stupa with reverence and respect.
After a full thousand years, his mind never ceased its constant practice of the *nien-fo* samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*).

Because that bhikṣu maintained pure precepts and further made offerings to the Tathāgata’s stūpas, by these causes and conditions, after the end of his life, throughout immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of millions of births within saṃsāra, he experienced the karmic fruits of blissful fortune among humans and devas, never falling into the evil realms.

“Ānanda! After that bhikṣu had passed through more than hundreds of thousands of immeasurable, incalculable, and asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he again encountered a Buddha appearing in the world, named Śakraprabhāsa Tathāgata.”
At that time, that bhikṣu made offerings to the Buddha, maintained the prohibitive precepts, and kept his holy life pure.
Having gone forth as before, he further gave rise to this thought:
"May I, in the future, by virtue of this merit, never be born in the evil realms throughout all my successive lives."
At that time, the Buddha Prabhākara, knowing the aspiration in the mind of that bhikṣu, immediately bestowed upon him a prophecy, saying:
"O worthy one!
In a future age, after the passing of hundreds of thousands of immeasurable, incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, you shall attain Buddhahood as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, named Dīpaṃkara."

When that Dīpaṃkara Buddha was practicing as a bodhisattva, in his final birth, he was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven. From the Tuṣita Heaven, he descended in spirit and entered through the right side, taking up residence in his mother’s womb. Having dwelt there for ten months, when the ten months were complete and he was about to be born with a mind of single-minded right mindfulness, he emitted a radiance that illuminated that buddha-field, filling it entirely.
"At that time, as the Bodhisattva was about to be born, his mother addressed the wise King Jñānendra,
saying: 'Great King,
you should know that I wish to go within the groves to wander and look about.'"
When the King had heard these words from his consort, he immediately issued a decree to the ministers within the city, as well as to the wealthy elders, householders, and merchants, saying:

"My consort now wishes to go to the gardens to view and enjoy herself. You, each from your own households, must adorn the streets and thoroughfares within the city, making them entirely pure. All filth, debris, rubble, and heaps of excrement must be removed. Prepare fragrant water and sprinkle it upon the roads; smear the ground with scented mud; scatter exquisite flowers over it; and at every location, set up fine jeweled incense burners and burn various renowned incenses."

Furthermore, various precious vases were set out, filled with fragrant water and adorned with beautiful, pure flowers—blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (padma), yellow lotuses (kumuda), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka)—which were placed inside the vases.

In every place, plantain trees were set out; according to the size and height of each plantain tree, various banners and streamers of diverse colors were suspended from them. These banners and streamers were interspersed with many hues, and within the interior of each banner-tree, nets made of the seven precious gems and pearl necklaces were further hung. At every knot of these nets, there were jeweled bells.

If it were the night of the pure heavens and the stars had appeared, [the site] would have been adorned with various precious mirrors suspended everywhere, each shining like the sun or moon; or with various multicolored tassels suspended, or golden and silver jeweled bands draped here and there.
The streets and alleys of that city were thus adorned with various kinds of exquisite beauty, equal to the celestial cities of the *gandharvas* and not differing from them in the slightest.

At that time, the king’s consort, accompanied by a thousand attendants, mounted a precious palanquin; led by musicians and surrounded before and behind by various sounds, she filled the streets and alleys as she departed from the palace. Looking about in all four directions, she proceeded with measured grace; her majesty was exceptionally sublime and her power vast, such that among the multitude there was none who could compare with her.

He headed toward that grove; having reached the grove, he gradually approached the riverbank. Once he had reached the bank, he boarded a boat and entered the river. When he had reached the middle of the stream, suddenly a great lamp appeared of its own accord, twelve yojanas in height and breadth.

Within that lamp-light, there was a cluster of *śa* grass, four finger-widths in height; its color was as white as mugwort and it was as soft as *kācilindika* cloth, emitting a wondrous fragrance like that of the *campaka* and *pāriśa* flowers.

Within those groves, various flowers and various fruits emerge, as do various trees; all the trees found in the heavens and among humans, with their famous blossoms and exquisite fruits, completely fill these gardens.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mother looked up toward the sky and, with her right hand, gently grasped a branch of a tree; the branch immediately bent downward.

Then, the royal lady took hold of the branch with her right hand, and from her right side, she brought forth a young boy who was upright, lovely, and pleasing to behold, named Dīpaṃkara (The Lamp-Maker). He was born with his ten fingers naturally joined in the gesture of palms-pressed-together.

When the boy was born, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated and completely filled that buddha-field; then from the heavens there rained down immeasurable flowers, namely: māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers.

Furthermore, they rained down immeasurable powdered incense of candana, which filled and pervaded an area of twelve yojanas; they also rained down various kinds of immeasurable and boundless celestial music that resounded spontaneously without being struck, and from within these sounds issued immeasurable songs of praise, the lyrics of which proclaimed:
"Immeasurable One, you are the Lamp of Light! Immeasurable One, you are the Lamp of Light!"
"This is the auspicious sign and title of that bodhisattva; therefore, he is called Dīpaṃkara.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dīpaṃkara was fully endowed with all his faculties, possessed the perfection of the marks and signs, lacked nothing, and grew day by day. While staying upon a terrace, he enjoyed the pleasures of the five senses.
However, while that youth was enjoying the five sensory desires, although he felt great pleasure, he suddenly had this thought:
"The sensual desires of the world are illusory and temporary; they are destroyed in an instant and will soon perish."
Having reflected thus, he departed from his home, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saṃghāṭī robe, and attained the state of renunciation.
After leaving the household life, desiring to seek bodhi, he gradually proceeded toward the foot of a tree to practice for perfect enlightenment.
After attaining perfect enlightenment, he surveyed all the worlds with his Buddha-eye and immediately gave rise to this thought:
"Who is there who would be most worthy to hear the True Dharma first?
He then saw that the world was empty and devoid of anyone to be transformed.
Observing again through the three contemplations, he likewise saw that in the world there were none who heard the Dharma nor any beings capable of being saved.

That Buddha remained in the world for three thousand years, solitary and without companion; after sitting upright for more than three thousand years, that Buddha Dīpaṃkara—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—had this thought:

"These multitudes of sentient beings are addicted to the five desires and have been negligent for a long time; they are deluded and wild, never reaching satiety. I shall now transform them so that they may attain awakening."
Having formed this thought, he emerged from the city of Dīpāgra and stood in mid-air, where he manifested a city named Jambūnada.

Within that city, he manifested various houses made of lapis lazuli; outside the city, he further manifested various *tāla* trees made of the seven precious gems, arranged in seven rows and adorned with the seven treasures, just as described above regarding the adornments of the city.

The city measured five thousand yojanas from east to west and from south to north; furthermore, the ornaments and furnishings within the city were identical in every respect to those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, without any difference whatsoever.
The people within that city have a lifespan of three thousand years.

All the sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa behold from afar all those inhabitants enjoying themselves and indulging in the five desires; they see them all, know them all, hear of them all, and envy them all.
"At that time, after three thousand years had passed in this manner, Dīpaṃkara Buddha conceived this thought:
'I should now manifest supernatural transformations.'"
"May the people of Jambudvīpa conceive a sense of weary detachment.
At that time, the people of Jambudvīpa saw the city where Dīpaṃkara Buddha resided, with fierce flames blazing from all four walls; struck with great terror, they said to one another:
"Alas! That city is being spontaneously consumed by fire; it will soon be gradually extinguished."

At that time, all the people of Jambudvīpa, whose faculties were matured and who were ready to receive the Buddha’s transformation, saw that illusory city with fires breaking out on all four sides, blazing and burning fiercely. Stricken with fear and alarm, they sought a place of refuge, but there was no one to protect them;

they desired liberation, but there was no one to deliver them. Having uttered these words, they cried: "May this city descend from above, or may this city ascend from below; we shall all extinguish those fires!"
At that time, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, humans, non-humans, and others emerged from that city and said to us:
"Why does this city spontaneously burst into flames?"
At that time, before the city, three stairways suddenly and spontaneously appeared:
one made of gold, one made of silver, and one made of crystal.
Between those galleries, there were rows of various precious *tāla* trees. From those *tāla* trees issued a great voice, saying:

"You people, you should quickly assemble in one place! If you in your hearts desire to see the Buddha Dīpaṃkara—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—that Buddha will before long descend to Jambudvīpa."
At that time, all the people of Jambudvīpa went to the place where the gallery was located; they saw the Buddha Dīpaṃkara emerging from within the city and descending at the foot of the gallery.

At that time, the Brahmās, Śakras, and the Four Great Kings surrounded him from before and behind. When the people of Jambudvīpa had seen that Buddha, they were all filled with great joy and each gave rise to this thought:
"Previously we desired to behold the Tathāgata, and now we have finally seen him."
Again, they gave rise to this thought:
"Each of us should previously have asked the Buddha about this matter: for what reason does this city burn with such fire?
The Tathāgata should explain it for our sake."
When the Buddha Dīpaṃkara had stepped upon the ground, all the people there each thought to themselves:
"I alone shall prostrate my head at the feet of the Buddha and speak these words; may I be the first to worship the Buddha's feet."

"At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara sat upon the lion throne; having sat down, he preached the Dharma for those sentient beings, namely: praising the matter of giving, the matter of maintaining the precepts, the matter of renouncing desire, and the attainment of the dharma of the exhaustion of outflows; he spoke of the benefits and merits of leaving the household life, and assisted them in the dharma of purity."

The Tathāgata beholds these people of Jambudvīpa who, having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, believe with joy and receive it with devotion; their hearts give rise to gladness, their minds become supple, and they attain unimpeded understanding. For them, the Tathāgata further expounds all dharmas, just as the Buddhas of the past, knowing the faculties and capacities of sentient beings, preached the Dharma to bring them joy—namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Now the World-Honored One likewise fully expounds this Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for the people of Jambudvīpa.

At that time, on the first day of Dīpaṃkara Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, he taught and delivered six hundred billion people; they all attained the exhaustion of outflows, realized arhatship, and their minds achieved mastery.

On the second day, he converted five billion people; on the third day, four billion; on the fourth day, three billion; on the fifth day, two billion; on the sixth day, one billion; and on the seventh day, five hundred million. All of them, as mentioned above, attained the state of Arhat.
During the second seven-day period, he taught and liberated one billion and ten million people.

During the final third seven-day period, he further delivered seventy-five billion sentient beings, all of whom attained the supreme benefit of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and mental liberation, becoming Arhats.
That Buddha Dīpaṃkara remained in the world for one kalpa; together with his bhikṣu śrāvaka disciples, he acted for the benefit of the people of the world—thus did the teacher Kāśyapīya speak.

"Ānanda! The Buddhas transmit their predictions of enlightenment to one another in succession. Thus, from the time Dīpaṃkara Buddha first planted the roots of goodness and sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, up until he turned the wheel of Dharma and remained in the world for one kalpa to transform sentient beings—this is how the teachers of the Mahāsāṃghika school have explained it."

“Ānanda! When that Buddha Dīpaṃkara was a bodhisattva, while on a boat, although he experienced the five sensual pleasures, he conceived a deep sense of weary detachment toward the world and thought to himself:
‘I can sit upon this boat and cross to the other shore of the river.’”

As he gave rise to this thought, a single great, pure lotus flower immediately appeared. The youth Dīpaṃkara sat upon that flower in the full lotus posture; once seated, the lotus closed of its own accord, like a lotus on an elephant’s head.
At that time, the palace ladies searched for the youth but did not know his whereabouts, and they immediately informed the Great King.

Thereupon, the Great King dispatched messengers to the four quarters to search and seek him out; yet, in the east, west, south, and north, his location was unknown, and even in the four intermediate directions, his place could not be found.

The Bodhisattva Dīpaṃkara, by virtue of his celestial majesty, spiritual power, and supernormal faculties, sat cross-legged within the lotus pedestal upon that ship; yet his body remained invisible. He immediately attained the five supernatural powers and flew through the air, proceeding until he reached the foot of the Bodhi tree, where he attained all-knowledge (sarvajñā), turned the wheel of Dharma, and preached the teachings, delivering and liberating six billion eight hundred million people, all of whom remained together in the world. This is how the teacher of the Mahīśāsaka school speaks.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
In the latter part of the "Chapter on the Offering of the Arousing of the Mind," at that time,
the World-Honored One was in Śrāvastī and addressed Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda!
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas constantly expound all dharmas day and night, gathering in sentient beings through four kinds of means of integration. What are these four?
First, giving; second, kind speech; third, beneficial action; and fourth, cooperation.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms with ten fingers together, knelt on his right knee, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many Buddhas did the Tathāgata honor in the past while seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Under which Buddhas did he plant the roots of all wholesome merit for the sake of seeking bodhi in future ages?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen attentively and receive it with care!
Reflect upon it well!"
I shall now declare for you the names of those Tathāgatas and the Buddhas, as well as the places where they planted roots of goodness. "Ānanda!

I recall that in the past, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; it was at the side of that Buddha that I planted various roots of goodness, seeking anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi in a future age."

"Furthermore, another Buddha appeared in the world named World-Incomparable; at that time, I made offerings to that Blessed One, planted various roots of goodness, and sought unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment for future lives."

Next, another Buddha appeared in the world named Padmottara; at that time, I made offerings to that Blessed One, planted various roots of goodness, and sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in future lives.

"Next, another Buddha appeared in the world, named Uttaramati; at that time, I made offerings to that Blessed One, planted various roots of goodness, and sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in future ages."

Next, another Buddha appeared in the world, named Guṇottaranāman; at that time, I made offerings to that Blessed One, planting various roots of goodness and seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in future lives.

"Furthermore, another Buddha appeared in the world named Śākyamuni; at that time, I made offerings to that Blessed One, planted various roots of goodness, and sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in future ages."
Next, another Buddha appeared in the world named Diśā; at that time, I made offerings to that Blessed One, planted various roots of goodness, and sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in future ages.

"Furthermore, another Buddha appeared in the world named Puṣya; at that time, I made offerings to that Blessed One, planted various roots of goodness, and sought unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in future ages."

Next, another Buddha appeared in the world, named Sarvārthadarśin; at that time, I made offerings to that Blessed One, planted various roots of goodness, and sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in future ages.

"Furthermore, another Buddha appeared in the world named Vipaśyin; at that time, I made offerings to that Blessed One, planted various roots of goodness, and sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in future lives."

Next, another Buddha appeared in the world, named Śikhin; at that time, I made offerings to that Blessed One, planted various roots of goodness, and sought unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in future lives.

"Furthermore, another Buddha appeared in the world, named Vaiśravaṇa; at that time, I made offerings to that Blessed One, planted various roots of goodness, and sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in future ages."

Next, another Buddha appeared in the world, named Krakucchanda; at that time, I made offerings to that World-Honored One, planted various roots of goodness, and practiced the holy life in order to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in future ages.

"Furthermore, another Buddha appeared in the world named Kanakamuni; at that time, I made offerings to that Blessed One, planted various roots of goodness, practiced the holy life, and sought unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for future lives."

"Furthermore, another Buddha appeared in the world named Kāśyapa; at that time, I made offerings to that Blessed One, planted various roots of goodness, and practiced the holy life in pursuit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in a future age."

“Ānanda! In the presence of Maitreya Bodhisattva, I planted various roots of goodness and sought unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) in a future age. Regarding this, there is a verse that says:
‘This Buddha of great majestic power, Having left desire behind, has attained tranquility;’”
“Śākyamuni Buddha has come, having made offerings to them all.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

With what articles of offering will the Tathāgata worship those Buddhas—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—and plant various roots of goodness to seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in future lives?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable eons, there was a king named Jayasena, of the Kṣatriya caste, who had received the consecration of the royal office."
That king possessed great merit; his lifespan was exceedingly long, he was handsome and pleasing, and his fame was heard afar. Ānanda!
The place where that King Ajātaśatru resided had a great city named Padmāvatī.
That king ruled and transformed this city, establishing his palace therein.

The city measured twelve yojanas from east to west and seven yojanas from north to south. The land was temperate, the rains fell in their proper seasons, the five grains ripened in abundance, and there was no lack of anything.
It was filled to overflowing with many people, leaving no empty space between them.
The gardens and groves were replete with flowers and fruits, while the springs, streams, and ponds had waters that were always clear and still.

On both sides of the streets and alleys, shops and stalls were established; those coming and going for trade never paused for even a moment, just like the city of Vaiśravaṇa named Alakā in the north, which is identical in every respect from east to west and from south to north.
Thus was that city of Padma adorned and fully endowed with every variety of excellence. Ānanda!

That King Ajātaśatru had a wealthy and eminent brāhmaṇa named Sūryapati, who was courageous, powerful, and possessed of abundant riches. He was rich in elephants, horses, servants, and livestock—cows and sheep—and was well-provided with all things, lacking nothing at all.

Within his treasury, there were exclusively various kinds of treasures—gold, silver, pearls, and precious gems, as well as *śaṅkha*, *musāragalva*, coral, and amber—all fully provided, exactly like those of King Vaiśravaṇa in the north.

Ānanda! At that time, the great Brahmin Sūryapati was especially cherished and highly esteemed by that king; they were constant companions, never parting for even a moment, seeing one another every day without ever feeling weary or satiated.
“Ānanda! At that time, King Arindama had a certain matter which he entrusted to the Brahmin Sūrya for adjudication, commanding him to settle it properly.

After Sūrya had rendered a legal judgment, he won the king’s favor; the king felt redoubled joy toward the Brahmin Sūrya, divided half his kingdom and bestowed it upon him, enfeoffing him as a king and charging him with the governance and transformation of that realm.”

At that time, King Aśoka, for the sake of that Brahmin king Sūrya, established another city named Bhūmipati; its streets, lanes, and alleys, as well as its city walls and adornments, were exactly like those of the city of Padmāvatī, without the slightest difference.
Ānanda! King Sūryaprabha had a queen named Candrottarā. Ānanda!

When the Bodhisattva Dīpaṃkara descended from Tuṣita Heaven, at the time of his descent, he entered the womb and sat upright within the right side of Queen Candrāvatī, the consort of King Divākara. From his birth until his attainment of enlightenment and his preaching of the Dharma to transform sentient beings, all attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Regarding the causes and conditions mentioned above, they are explained in the *Dīpaṃkara-bodhisattva-pūrvayoga-sūtra*.
At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara resided in succession in those two cities, preaching the Dharma and delivering sentient beings.
"At that time, his father, King Divākara, constantly provided for that Buddha with the four requisites, honoring and respecting him as the Buddha himself had praised. 'Ānanda!

It gradually came to the ears of King Parājitā that in the royal palace of King Divākara in the city of Jāmbūnada, the chief queen, Candrāvatī, gave birth to a young boy named Dīpaṃkara. He was handsome and pleasing, peerless in the world, endowed with all the marks of excellence, like a statue of gold.'"
Once the boy was born, he was taken to a great wise Brahmin, a master of physiognomy within the kingdom, and instructed to examine the boy’s features and determine what his appearance portended.

The physiognomist said: "This boy is adorned with merit and virtue. If he remains at home, he will become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) who transforms the four continents and acts as the sovereign of the great earth, fully possessing the seven treasures:

first, the golden wheel treasure; second, the divine jewel treasure; third, the jade woman treasure; fourth, the elephant treasure; fifth, the horse treasure; sixth, the minister-treasure of the military commander; and seventh, the minister-treasure of the treasury steward."

Furthermore, he had a thousand sons, all of whom were handsome and possessed the marks of a great man; they were able to crush enemies, their majesty pervaded the great earth, and there was nothing within the four seas, the mountains, or the forests that they did not bring under submission.

The land is peaceful and secure, with rains falling at the proper times; the five grains ripen in abundance, and the people live in peace and happiness, free from suffering and disease. Without the use of weapons or arms, they are governed and transformed according to the Dharma.
If you renounce the world and leave the household life, you shall attain Buddhahood as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with the ten titles, and your fame shall be heard afar.

"Ānanda! That youth will renounce his home to enter the homeless life, and eventually attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). He will then turn the wheel of Dharma, and his fame will spread far and wide, as previously described."
At that time, King Arindama thought to himself:
"How rare is the World-Honored One!
It is extremely difficult for him to appear in the world; to hear his name even once at such a time is rare, and to behold him is even more difficult."
At that time, King Ajātaśatru immediately dispatched an envoy to the Lord of the Sun, saying:
"I have now heard by report that the Queen, the Great Lady, has given birth to a fine boy, endowed with all the marks as described above."
I now wish to invite that Dīpaṃkara Buddha, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, to come to my dwelling in the city of Padma and accept my humble offering.
"If Your Majesty sends him, both sides will benefit;
if you do not release him, I shall go with my fourfold army fully prepared.
Having received these words, the messenger went to King Divākara in the city of Janmanagara and reported everything he had been told to King Divākara.
At that time, having heard these words, King Sūryaprabha was despondent and sorrowful, his heart filled with unhappiness.
King Sūryaprabha then assembled his ministers and related the aforementioned matter to them in full, saying:
"Reflect upon this: he has spoken such words; how should we respond?"
Then the ministers together addressed the king, saying: "Great King!
You should know that regarding such a matter, you ought to consult the Buddha Dīpaṃkara."
"Why is this? Because the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—possesses great compassion.
At that time, King Divākara replied to his ministers, saying:
"I also have such a recollection in my mind.
At that time, King Sūryaprabha, together with his ministers, went in person to the dwelling of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. Thereupon, that Buddha consoled the king, saying:
"Great King, set your mind at ease; do not be startled or afraid!"
Do not give rise to sorrow! Why is this?
I too now wish to travel through other lands to teach and transform the people, out of compassion for all sentient beings.

"At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—traveled toward that land for the sake of transforming sentient beings, proceeding together with an immeasurable and innumerable assembly of hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus."

At that time, King Divākara provided for and made offerings to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara with the four requisites in full, lacking nothing. Following behind the Buddha, he escorted him to his own realm; having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and returned weeping to his own palace.

At that time, King Dharanindhara heard that Dīpaṃkara Buddha had arrived at Padmāvatī City, accompanied by an immeasurable multitude of śrāvaka bhikṣus—all of whom were great arhats whose outflows were exhausted. Having heard this, he was filled with joy; he prepared and repaired the roads, causing all filth and refuse to be cleared away and the way to be adorned and decorated as previously described, until it was identical and indistinguishable from the city of the gandharvas.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru issued a decree, proclaiming:

"Within twelve yojanas of the city, both inside and out, all citizens are forbidden from privately selling any incense, flowers, or garlands. Wherever such items exist, I shall personally purchase them, for I wish to offer them as an act of worship to that Dīpaṃkara Buddha."
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, leading the fourfold army and endowed with great majesty and virtue, emerged from the city to welcome the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.

Chapter Two: Receiving the Prediction of Certainty (*Vyākaraṇa*), Part One. "At that time, on the southern slope of the Snowy Mountains in that country, there was a brahmin named Ratna. His parents were of pure brahmin lineage; tracing back through seven generations of ancestors, they had never been of mixed or impure descent, and no one dared to criticize or disparage them."

Furthermore, his lineage is praised by all the wise and revered by other teachers; he is endowed with the three types of conduct, capable of teaching all the *Veda* treatises, and has fully mastered all four *Vedas*.

Furthermore, he is skilled in the treatises on etymology, phonology, and humor; in the treatises on incantations, prophecies, and the characteristics of the world; and in the treatises on worldly sacrifices and prayers. He is fully endowed with the marks of a great man and is born into a noble family.
Furthermore, there were five hundred youths from noble families who served as his disciples, surrounding and attending upon him.
Ānanda, you should know that the Brahmin Ratna at that time was none other than the present-day Maitreya Bodhisattva.
At that time, those five hundred disciples were constantly following this teacher to study and recite the methods of incantations and sacrificial rites.

Among those five hundred disciples, there was a son of a prominent brahmin family named Megha, who served as the leader within that assembly; he was fully endowed with all virtuous practices and had followed his teacher since childhood.

At that time, he was sixteen years old, upright and pleasing to behold; he was born from virtuous seeds, his parents were pure, and for seven generations back there had been no impurity, such that none could find cause for reproach. His family lineage was fully endowed with the marks of a Great Man, peerless in the world; his body was golden in color, his hair likewise, and his voice was pure, like the sound of Brahmā.

From that precious seer, he received and recited incantations and spells; he was quick-witted and rapid in learning, attaining what was truly authentic, comprehending it upon hearing it once, with eloquent speech and clear articulation of every word and syllable.
He thoroughly mastered all the various incantations, arts, crafts, and skills found within every Brahmin household.
Having mastered them, he said to his Brahmin teacher:
"Great Master, Upādhyāya!"
"I have now completed my training and have mastered all the virtues and skills of my preceptor; I wish to return home.
The preceptor, his heart longing for the youth Megha and unwilling to part from him, spoke to him, saying: "O māṇava!
"I possess a treatise called the Veda, which was spoken by the sages of antiquity; it has never been known or heard of by any of the non-Buddhist Brahmins, much less seen or taught to others."
The māṇava said,
“I only pray that the Upādhyāya will explain this to me.
Then, that Brahmin once again taught that māṇava the secret and essential incantations.
At that time, the māṇava also received them all in full, and spoke again to that brahmin, saying:
"I have now obtained the master’s methods of incantation and understand them completely; what more should I do?"
The brahmin further addressed the māṇava, saying:
"In our brahmin lineage, handed down through generations, there is a family law:
if there is a disciple who studies under a teacher, he must repay that kindness by taking various wealth and goods to offer as alms."
The māṇava said:
"Preceptor, you have explained the family dharma to me; how shall I repay your kindness?
What does the Preceptor now desire?"
The brahmin said: "O māṇava!

If you wish to repay me, you may give me one fine, pure parasol, leather sandals, a golden staff, a golden trident, a golden pitcher, a golden bowl, upper and lower garments, and five hundred gold coins; give these to me."
At that time, the youth said to the brahmin:
"Preceptor, Great Master!
I have none of the aforementioned items to offer to you. I beg you to release me; I shall seek them out in the four directions and bring them back immediately to make offerings to you."
The brahmin replied,
"If you know the time has come, you should follow wherever you go.
Then the youth Megha prostrated at his teacher's feet, circumambulated him three times, took his leave, and departed.

At that time, the youth Megha heard that there was a place five hundred yojanas from this Snowy Mountain; the city was named Śūrpāraka, and within that city lived a great Brahmin of noble lineage named Yajñadatta.
That brahmin was immensely wealthy and possessed abundant assets.

That great brahmin of meritorious sacrifice intended to host a year-long *asaṃvṛta* (unrestricted) assembly for sixty thousand brahmins; he prepared sixty thousand sets of offerings, providing for each individual a complete set of personal requisites: one parasol, one trident, sandals, a water jar, an alms bowl, upper and lower garments, as well as money and other goods—all were fully provided.

For another elder Brahmin, he specially fashioned an exquisite golden-handled parasol, most excellent leather sandals, a staff made entirely of gold with a golden trident tip, a golden water flask, a golden alms bowl, and upper and lower garments.

Each was worth one hundred thousand pieces of gold; five hundred gold coins; and one thousand milch cows, each with its calf, every cow yielding one *dou* of milk at a single milking, their horns all adorned with gold.
There were five hundred young maidens, all adorned with pearl necklaces to grace their bodies;
among them was one maiden named Skillful (Sujātā), who was the foremost leader. The year for the Pañcavārṣika festival had already reached its completion, with only one day remaining.
At that time, the youth Megha descended from the Snowy Mountains and proceeded with composure to the site of the unrestricted assembly at the city of Śūrpāraka.
When those sixty thousand brahmins saw the youth from afar, they raised their voices and cried out:
"Excellent!"
"In this place, we have well prepared this *pañcavārṣika* festival; now that Brahmā has arrived, he comes in person to receive this *pañcavārṣika* offering.
Then, the youth Megha said to those sixty thousand brahmins:
"Do not call me Brahmā; I am a human being and am truly not Brahmā."
The brahmin asked,
"Who are you? The youth Megha replied:

"Have you not heard that on the southern slope of the Snowy Mountains there is a brahmin named Ratna, who is thoroughly proficient in all branches of knowledge and teaches five hundred disciples, even as has been described in the preceding sequence?"

Among that assembly was a preeminent disciple named Yun, sixteen years of age, possessed of wisdom and intelligence, fully endowed with virtue and skill, no different from his teacher, even to the point that his voice was like the sound of Brahmā.
“Did you hear it?
The brahmins and others each replied,
“We heard it.”
The youth Megha replied, "It is this very body.
Once the assembly of brahmins recognized this, they were filled with even greater joy and cried out in a loud voice:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is well-established that this unobstructed assembly has been held, for the youth Megha has come to receive this offering.

At that time, the Brahmin woman Yajñadattā, whose body was skilled in arts, along with her daughters, looked down from the upper story and beheld the youth Megha, whose comely appearance was peerless. Having seen him, she was filled with joy and paid homage toward the four directions to the various devas and spirits, thinking privately to herself:
"May this youth be foremost in debate, surpassing the elder Brahmins; may he cause me to distance myself from these unwholesome people, and never let me become a wife to such unwholesome persons."

Then the youth Megha went to the assembly hall, circumambulated it three times, and having completed the three circumambulations, he approached the foremost Brahmin and addressed him with pleasant words of consolation, asking:
"Virtuous one, what treatise do you recite and uphold?"
Then, these sixty thousand brahmins answered the youth Megha in unison, saying:
"Virtuous one, do not ask me which treatise this elder recites."
"Why is this? For now, this Elder indeed possesses and recites all the mantras, incantations, and treatises of our family’s Brahmin tradition.
Thus spoke the youth Megha.

“O Brahmins! Although this elder of yours recites the medical arts and crafts of the Brahmin household, my own teacher and I study the Brahminical learning which possesses its own distinct dharma; we must inquire of you: do you have a discourse known as the *Pūrva*?”
Then those sixty thousand brahmins each replied together:
"We have never even heard this name before; how much less could we possess it, and how much less could we recite it?"
The youth Megha said:
"In the Dharma of my teacher, he taught me this *Veda* treatise called 'Prior Existence' (*pūrvavat*), which I have also mastered through recitation."
Then the brahmins of that great assembly said, "Please explain it for us; we wish to hear it.
At that time, the youth Megha stood at the place where the high seats were arranged and, with a Brahma-like voice, recited the Vedic treatises that had existed from of old.
At that time, the assembly of sixty thousand brahmins leaped for joy and, with one voice, cried out:
"This accords with our hearts; this accords with our minds! We are filled with great joy!"
He addressed the youth Megha, saying:
"O māṇava! You may now serve as my presiding elder;
sit at the head of my seat, receive from me the most excellent water for the presiding elder, and receive from me the very first food for the presiding elder."
Then the youth Megha pushed the elder down from his superior seat, took the first water for himself at that excellent seat, received the first portion of food, and ate food to his heart's content.

After the meal is finished, one should accept the requisites for alms as needed according to the rules for the senior monk (*upādhyāya*); those items that are not required, one should decline and not accept.
At that time, the great Brahmin Yajñadatta thought to himself:
"I have now established this unobstructed assembly (aviśeṣa-pariṣad), yet it does not rely upon the noble Dharma; all the items offered as gifts do not conform to the noble teachings."
For what reason?
Because in this assembly, regarding all items offered as *dakṣiṇā*, the youth Megha did not accept them in their entirety according to my intention.
Then, the great brahmin Yajñadatta knelt on his right knee and addressed the youth Megha, saying: "Virtuous youth!
You should accept all these things of my offering; do not let me fail to fulfill this act of giving."
Then the youth Megha said to the Brahmin Yajñadatta: "Great Brahmin!

You have practiced excellent giving and are fully endowed with all necessary things; this is not unwholesome. In this *asaṅga-mahāpariṣad* (unrestricted assembly), there is nothing lacking. Only that which I require shall I now accept; that which I do not require would be taken in vain and be of no benefit."
At that time, the thought occurred to that senior elder, the former brahmin:

"For a long time I have prayed for such articles of alms, and I looked forward with certainty to receiving them first. Why is it that now, because of this young māṇava, he has pushed me aside and seized my offerings?"

"By the fruit of all the precepts, diligence, and ascetic practices I have observed since birth, and by the power of that karmic fruit as a condition, may I meet with this youth in every life and at every place of assembly; for the sake of depriving him of his gains and offerings, I shall repay this enmity and never let him go."
"Ānanda, you should know!
At that time, the youth Megha was none other than myself;
the one of virtuous sacrifice was the present-day Dhana-pāṇi."
The elder Brahmin of that time was none other than Devadatta himself. Ānanda!
For this reason, the foolish Devadatta, throughout my past lives from age to age, has always been my enemy, never ceasing his hostility toward me.

At that time, the youth Megha took the various items he had received as offerings and intended to go to the Snowy Mountains to present them to the brahmin. Passing through various villages, towns, kingdoms, and cities—sometimes staying and sometimes traveling—he observed these things, and eventually, in due course, arrived at the city of Padmāvatī.
Entering that city, he saw its adornments were extraordinary, exquisite, and inconceivable, just as previously described; he then had this thought:
"For what reason is this Lotus City now so adorned in such an inconceivable manner?"

Perhaps there is someone who intends to hold an unrestricted assembly (*anavadya-pariṣad*) in this city, or perhaps they are performing sacrifices to the various lunar mansions and deities, or performing rites for auspiciousness, or performing meritorious deeds, or it may be a seasonal assembly of Brahmins. Perhaps the people within this city, having heard my reputation—that I am highly learned and possessed of great knowledge—will say, "He has come here wishing to engage in debate and discuss the meaning of doctrines with the various Brahmins," yet not a single person thinks of me, nor does anyone pay me respect or prostrate before me?
At that time, I immediately asked that person: "Virtuous one!
For what reason is this city adorned so exquisitely and wonderfully?"
At that time, that person replied to me, saying:
"O Greatly Wise Youth!
Have you not heard that the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—will soon come to this city of Padmāvatī to preach the Dharma and transform sentient beings?"
For this purpose, my King has subdued his enemies and issued a decree to the people, commanding each of them to adorn themselves.
At that time, the people, desiring to cultivate meritorious karma, have arranged these various kinds of ornaments, intending to make offerings to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.
"Ānanda! At that time, I had this thought:
'In my Dharma, there is this teaching: if a person is endowed with the thirty-two marks, that person has two possible destinies:'"
If he remains a householder, he will certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King;
if he renounces the world to go forth and cultivate the Noble Path, he will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, his fame will spread far and wide, and his majestic virtue will be sovereign.
"This is beyond doubt.
Ānanda! At that time, I further gave rise to this thought:

"I should now first proceed to this place where the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara resides, to make offerings and pay him homage, and to seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) for the sake of the future; only then shall I separately repay the kindness of my brahmin teacher."
I further gave rise to this thought:
"With what things shall I make offerings to the Buddha?
By what deeds shall I plant various roots of goodness?"
At that time, I thought to myself:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not esteem wealth as an offering; only the offering of the Dharma is praised by the Sages."

"I have not yet attained the Dharma, nor do I hold the view that it is empty; I shall now purchase and seek out exquisite, superior flowers to offer as a tribute, aspiring that in a future age I may become a Buddha."
I then went at once to the house of a garland-maker and said to that person:
"Good sir, would you sell these flowers to me?
At that time, that person replied to me:
"O virtuous youth! Have you not heard?
The Great King Jayasena has issued a decree, proclaiming that no garlands whatsoever are permitted to be sold to others."
"Why is this? Because the king wishes to take it himself to offer to the Buddha.
Having heard those words from that person, I went again to another florist's shop to seek and purchase flowers, but he answered me just as before, no differently.

Thus, being unable to purchase flowers anywhere, he secretly searched through the streets and alleys until he saw a maidservant in blue garments named Bhadrā, who was carrying water; she had discreetly placed seven stalks of *utpala* lotuses inside her water jar and was coming along the road.
Having seen him, my heart was filled with joy, and I immediately said to him:
"What do you intend to do with these flowers?
I shall now give you five hundred coins; you may give me seven stalks of *utpala* lotuses from within your vase."
The woman spoke again:
"Virtuous youth, have you not heard?
The World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, now wishes to enter the city to accept the invitation of this lord of the earth, King Ajātaśatru."

The King, having conceived a heart of deep respect for the Buddha and desiring further to establish all manner of meritorious virtues, issued a proclamation throughout his realm for twelve *yojanas*, decreeing that no one was permitted to privately steal or sell any incense oil, flower garlands, or similar offerings. Should anyone attempt to sell them, the King alone would have the right to purchase them for his own use in making offerings.
"In my neighborhood there is a garland-maker named Vairin; he has a daughter who privately took five hundred coins from me and immediately stole these seven stalks of flowers to give to me."

Since I have transgressed the prohibition and obtained these flowers, I wish to offer them to the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; yet, in truth, I am unable to do so.
Then I spoke further to that woman, saying:
"O virtuous lady, I now understand the causes and conditions you have described.
You may take five hundred gold coins from me; give me five stalks of *utpala* flowers, and I shall return two stalks to you."
At that time, she replied to me, saying:
"O virtuous youth!
Why do you take these flowers? What do you intend to do with them?"
I then replied:

"The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is difficult to encounter and difficult to meet. Having now met him, I wish to purchase these flowers to offer to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, so as to plant various roots of goodness for the sake of seeking Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi in future ages."
At that time, she spoke to me again, saying:
"I observe the youth’s appearance both within and without; his body and mind are courageous, and he is diligent in his love for the Dharma. You shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Māṇava! If you permit me, until I have attained the Noble Path, in every birth and throughout all successive lives, I shall be your wife;
but once you have attained the Path, I shall shave my head and leave the household life to study the Way, seeking Arhatship as your disciple and practicing the conduct of a śramaṇa."
"If it be so, I shall now give you these five stalks of flowers; otherwise, I will not.
At that time, I spoke further to that woman, saying:
"O virtuous woman!..."
"I am now this very person, a Brahmin of pure lineage, who has mastered the four Vedas. Within my Vedas it is said:

'If a person desires to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and practices the bodhisattva path, they should give rise to a heart of compassion and a heart of peace and happiness toward all sentient beings. Toward those who come to them with requests, they should not be stingy; they must even give away their own body and life to others, let alone their beloved wife, children, and other wealth. They must not be miserly or greedy.'"
"Good woman!

I have now made a vow to seek Bodhi for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, out of compassion to rescue and protect them all. If someone comes to demand my wife and children and I give them as alms, and you, with a heart of attachment, create an obstacle, then my resolve to renounce them will not be fulfilled; furthermore, I shall incur immeasurable sin on account of you."
"If you make a vow that, at that time, you will not make any difficulty when I give away all my wealth and precious possessions as alms, I shall grant your request and allow you to be my wife."
At that time, she spoke to me, saying: "Māṇava!
Even if someone were to come before you and beg for my body, I would not give rise to a mind of stinginess or greed; how much less so for a son, a daughter, or any other wealth?"
I said to her: "If you can truly do as you say, according to your wish, I grant that you shall be my wife in a future life.
At that time, she received five hundred coins from me and immediately gave me five stalks of *utpala* flowers, which she held out to me.
"The remaining two stalks I give as an offering to you; let us together create the causes and conditions for our future lives.
He further said to me:
"Wherever you wish to plant roots of goodness, scatter these two flowers upon it, and vow that we may dwell together in every birth and never be parted."
“At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—came from outside and entered the city of Padmāvatī.”

At that time, carrying these seven lotus stalks, I saw the Buddha approaching from afar.
