As he gradually drew near, I beheld his body—exquisite and pleasing to behold, with pure radiance illuminating the world. His faculties were subdued, his mind was tranquil and stable, abiding unmoving; his six sense organs were as clear and still as a pool of lapis lazuli, and his deportment in advancing and halting was like that of a royal elephant.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great assemblies of devas surrounding him from front and back; each scattered immeasurable varieties of celestial flowers, as well as immeasurable celestial powdered sandalwood incense, *utpala* flowers, *padma* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, as respectful offerings to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, King Droṇa, fully prepared with his ceremonial retinue and the fourfold army, went out from the city gate to welcome Dīpaṃkara Buddha.

Then, immeasurable and boundless multitudes of various beings—humans and non-humans, including the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and other spirits—assembled at that place. They took powdered incense and various kinds of flowers and scattered them over the Buddha; not a single flower fell to the ground, but all remained suspended in the air above the crown of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara’s head, forming a great precious canopy. As the Buddha walked, it followed him; as the Buddha stood still, it remained stationary. At that moment, seeing the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, I gave rise to a heart of faith and reverence, and a heart of profound respect. Having developed such reverence, I took these seven stalks of *utpala* flowers and scattered them over the Buddha, making this aspiration:

"If, in a future age, I attain Buddhahood, may it be no different from the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara and his great assembly. May the flowers I scatter remain suspended in mid-air, with petals facing downward and stems facing upward, forming a flower-canopy above the Buddha’s crown that follows him in his walking and standing."
"Seeing such supernatural powers and virtuous strength, my heart gave rise to redoubled faith and reverence. Ānanda!

At that time, those immeasurable and boundless multitudes each took priceless, exquisite garments—namely, fine Kāśika cloth, fine white cotton cloth, fine kṣauma cloth, and exquisite, soft, fine kauśeya cloth, as well as wonderful silken fabrics and kāśyapa woolen robes—and spread them upon the road. Desiring to make offerings to Dīpaṃkara Buddha, they covered the ground until it was completely filled."
Ānanda! At that time, I saw those immeasurable and boundless multitudes of people covering the entire ground with priceless garments.

At that moment, I had only a single deer-skin upon my body; I spread this deer-skin upon the ground, yet wherever my deer-skin covered the earth, it was met with the foul abuse and resentment of those crowds, who dragged my deer-skin and cast it far away to another place.
I had this thought:
"Alas! World-Honored One, Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara!"
"Will you not take pity on me and look upon me with compassion?
Having formed this thought, the Buddha, knowing my mind and out of compassion for me,
then used his supernatural powers to transform a portion of the ground so that it became like thin, loose mud.
At that time, seeing that the road was muddy, the crowd of people each avoided it and walked by; not a single person entered the mud.
As I was traveling, I saw them quickly moving away from the muddy place. Having seen that mud, this thought immediately arose in me:
"O World-Honored One! It is even so!"
"How can I cause him to walk upon this mud?

If he walks on the mud, the mud will soil the Buddha’s feet; I shall now take this foul physical body and make it a great bridge over this mud, so that the World-Honored Buddha may step across my body."

I immediately spread out all my deer-skin, untied my hair and scattered it, and prostrating with my face covered, I served as a bridge for the Buddha. Before any of the people had yet stepped across, the Buddha was the very first to tread upon my hair. It was because I thus made offerings to Dīpaṃkara Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Again, he gave rise to this thought:
"May the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, together with his assembly of śrāvakas, tread upon my body and the hair of my head as they cross over this mud."
He further made this vow:

"I pray that when I attain Buddhahood in a future age, I shall be no different from the present Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara; with such majestic virtue and such power, may I become a Teacher of Gods and Humans."
"Furthermore, I vow that from now until the end of this life, if the Buddha Dīpaṃkara does not grant me a prediction of enlightenment, I shall never rise from this mud.

At the moment the youth spread out his body and hair, the great earth shook in six ways: namely, it surged in the east and subsided in the west; it surged in the west and subsided in the east; it surged in the south and subsided in the north; it surged in the north and subsided in the south; it surged in the center and subsided at the edges; and it surged at the edges and subsided in the center.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll Three;
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on Receiving the Prediction of Certainty, Part Two:

"At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, knowing my mind, came toward me surrounded on all sides by a great assembly of one hundred thousand bhikṣus, as well as tens of billions of devas and nāgas. He walked with steady grace upon my body and over my matted hair like a great dragon king;
looking left and right, he addressed the bhikṣus: 'O you bhikṣus!'"
"You must not travel along the same path as me; no one is fit to tread upon the body or the matted hair of this māṇava, except for the Tathāgata."
"Why is this? Because these are the remains of the Bodhisattva’s body and hair.
Then, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara spoke to me, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!

You, young man (māṇava), have given rise to a vast mind and made vows as great as the ocean. That which you seek is for the sake of bringing benefit to all sentient beings and for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings."

Māṇava! Since you have sought such a great vow for the benefit, peace, and happiness of all the world, out of compassion for immeasurable and boundless beings, and in order to act as a guide for devas and humans, you have given rise to a mind of great diligence and heroic resolve.
“You are indeed able to fulfill such dharmas as these, seeking the vajra with a resolute mind and not begrudging body or life; therefore, you now carry the Tathāgata upon your person and proceed.”
In the future, you shall not begrudge even your own body or life, let alone other wealth. O māṇava!
That you seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is the first sign; that you are able to give rise to such a great vow, you must relinquish all that you possess.
"You, māṇava! In the practice of giving, you must not seek retribution in future lives; seek only the unsurpassed bodhi that transcends the world. Do not give rise to greed;

upon seeing the wealth and possessions of others, do not seize them. You must uphold the prohibitive precepts without deficiency or transgression; do not become defiled or turbid. You should not grasp at signs, nor should you praise yourself, disparage others, or deprecate yourself."

"You should practice patience; even if others come to strike, revile, imprison, or kill you, you must endure it all. Even when your body is being dismembered limb by limb, you should exercise patience toward such enemies and give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion."

One must not kill living beings; one must not plunder the lives or wealth of others; one should always remain far removed from the property of others, and even in seeking for oneself, one should practice contentment.
Do not approach the wives or concubines of others; regarding those who belong to you, you must likewise be free from greed.
Stay far away from false speech; until the end of your life, you must not speak what is untrue to others.
One must not engage in strife or discord, nor cause those who are close to become estranged; upon seeing those who are causing division, one should always teach them to reconcile.
One must not speak with harsh words, but should always employ pleasant speech.
"You must not engage in frivolous speech; rather, you should speak only that which is beneficial, timely, and in accordance with the Dharma.
You should practice right view and abandon all false paths.
You, māṇava!"
If you can shoulder such tasks as these, there shall be nothing among your aspirations that remains unfulfilled.

You should regard all sentient beings as your only child, feeling compassion for them; you must discipline your mind and speech, refraining from flattery and deceit. You should honor and respect those worthy of veneration, and you must not be arrogant or allow your mind to become heedless.
You must constantly abide in the samādhi of tranquil concentration and contemplate the dharma of non-self, so as not to sever the future lineage of bodhi.
You should thus benefit sentient beings and bring peace and happiness to all.
"O Māṇava! If you can accomplish such matters as these, you may yourself proclaim with your own mouth, 'I am able.
At that time, I immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am able.
At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—knowing my mind, immediately smiled.
That Buddha had an attendant bhikṣu who rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition does the Tathāgata smile?
Then, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara addressed the bhikṣu, saying: "Bhikṣu!"
Do you see this māṇava, who, holding seven stalks of flowers as an offering for me, prostrated himself with his hair disheveled and built a bridge upon the mud so that I might cross over?

For this reason, this māṇava shall, after incalculable kalpas have passed, attain Buddhahood, being named Śākyamuni, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he will be fully endowed with the ten titles, no different from me.

"Ānanda! At that time, having heard Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestow upon me the definitive prediction of enlightenment, my body and mind became light and supple; without realizing it, I rose into the air to the height of seven tala trees. With a pure mind, I joined my ten fingers in palms-together salutation and paid homage to the Buddha."
Ānanda! At that time, my entire body was filled with such joy that I could not contain it. Ānanda!
At that time, Dīpaṃkara Buddha addressed me, saying:
"Māṇava! You should observe the world in the eastern direction."
At that time, I immediately beheld all the Buddhas in the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction, who all conferred upon me the definitive prediction: "O Māṇava!..."
"In a future age, after incalculable kalpas have passed, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni, fully endowed with the ten titles.
Just as it is in the eastern direction, so it is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.

“Ānanda! At that time, I descended from the sky, stood firmly upon the ground, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, and withdrew to stand to one side. Thereupon, this thought arose in me:
‘I should now seek to go forth into homelessness in the presence of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.’”
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray, World-Honored One,
that you will allow me to leave the household life and receive full ordination, so that I may practice the holy life under the Buddha."
The Buddha said to me: "O māṇava!
Now is precisely the right time."
He immediately attained the state of a renunciant and shaved off his hair and beard;
once his hair and beard were removed, immeasurable devas took my hair for the sake of making offerings, with ten billion devas together obtaining a single strand of hair.

Ānanda! Since I attained unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, I have never seen a single sentient being who has attained peace and happiness without making offerings to the Buddhas; such a thing is impossible.

Ānanda! At that time, I was still fully bound by all the fetters of affliction, and my greed, hatred, and delusion were not yet exhausted; yet, when immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of sentient beings took my hair and each made offerings to it, they attained liberation.
How much more so today, when I am free from desire, hatred, and delusion—if one performs various meritorious deeds before me and does not attain liberation, such a thing is impossible.
Therefore, Ānanda!
All sentient beings should resolve their minds to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
"Ānanda! [he said].

I have come from there; while practicing the bodhisattva path amidst afflictions, I did not abandon my diligent and courageous resolve, constantly practicing generosity and constantly performing meritorious deeds.

By virtue of such wholesome karmas, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, I attained the position of Brahmā, Śakra, or became a hundred thousand universal monarchs (cakravartin). Through the power of the causal conditions of those roots of goodness, I have now attained Buddhahood as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and have turned the unsurpassed, most wondrous wheel of Dharma.
Ānanda! By the power of my merit and wisdom, all present kṣatriyas, as well as brahmins, householders, śramaṇas, and wise men, now believe and accept my words, and practice according to my Dharma.

Ānanda! Observe that my words are never twofold. Just as the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me the prediction of enlightenment and instructed me, I practiced in accordance with his teaching and have now attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Even if the heavens were to fall to earth, and this great earth were to be destroyed,
all sentient beings would still attain a body of eternal abiding."
"Mount Sumeru, king of mountains, may crumble; the waters of the great ocean may dry up.
Ānanda, you should know this: the Buddhas never speak with double-tongued words.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One further addressed Ānanda:

"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always maintain this practice: although their radiance is immeasurable and boundless, for the sake of all sentient beings, they sustain it at the measure of one fathom;
yet from that single fathom, for the sake of all sentient beings, they further manifest immeasurable and boundless light."

Why is this? It is because they fear that sentient beings do not know the distinctions between day and night, the first and second halves of a month, a year and half a year, or the four seasons and eight seasonal nodes; they fear that these beings might forget or lose track of them.

Ānanda! That Buddha Dīpaṃkara was fully endowed with the ten epithets; his work of illumination was perfected, and his constant radiance was free from darkness. For this reason, that Buddha was named Dīpaṃkara (The Lamp-Lighter), for he constantly possessed a brilliance that illuminated the world. The remaining causes and conditions are as previously described.

"Ānanda! I recall that in the past, there was a Tathāgata who appeared in the world named Sarvābhibhū, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha. I scattered golden flowers over that Buddha and made this aspiration:
'May I, in the future, obtain a subtle and wondrous body, fully endowed with the marks and dharmas, just like the World-Honored One now.'"
At that time, that Buddha, knowing my mind, immediately smiled.
The attendant bhikṣu adjusted his robes and addressed the Buddha, until the Buddha spoke to that attendant, saying: "Bhikṣu!"
"Do you see this person who is about to scatter golden flowers over my head?
At that time, the bhikṣu replied,
"I see him."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"After the passing of one hundred million kalpas, this person shall attain Buddhahood, with the name Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles."
"Ānanda! At that time, having received my prediction, I did not abandon my diligent and courageous resolve; rather, I increased it further and further while cultivating other meritorious deeds."
By virtue of such wholesome causes and conditions, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, I was born in the Brahma Heaven, as Śakra, and as a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
Furthermore, I once acted as a king named Sudarśana.
The city walls, defensive gates, watchtowers, palaces, and halls of that king were made entirely of gold; the gardens, groves, springs, streams, and ponds were all adorned with gold.
"By the causal conditions of those karmas, I have now attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and turn the unsurpassed, pure wheel of Dharma. Ānanda!"
I recall that in the past, there was a Tathāgata who appeared in the world named Padmottara, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; I scattered silver flowers upon that Buddha and made this aspiration.
Then that Buddha said to his attendant:
"Do you see this person who is about to offer silver flowers to me?
The bhikṣu replied:
“I see it,” [the monk replied]. The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“In the future, after more than one hundred thousand kalpas have passed, this person shall attain Buddhahood; his name shall be Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
At that time, having heard the prophecy, I did not abandon my diligent and courageous resolve; rather, I increased it twofold and performed various meritorious deeds.
By virtue of such wholesome karmic retribution, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, I have served as Brahmā, Śakra, and a Cakravartin King.

Furthermore, in the past, I was once a king named Mahāsudarśana; the city where I resided was called Kuśinagara. The watchtowers, battlements, and windows of that city were all fashioned of white silver; its gardens, groves, springs, ponds, and waters were likewise entirely of white silver, magnificently adorned. Even due to the ripening of those karmic causes and conditions, I have now attained Buddhahood as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and have even turned the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma.

"Ānanda! Since ancient times, there has been this law: whenever a Bodhisattva is first born, he walks seven paces toward each of the four directions—east, west, south, and north—without anyone supporting him."

Ānanda! When that Buddha Padmottara was first born, as his two feet touched the ground, lotus flowers sprang up everywhere. He walked seven paces facing each of the four directions—east, west, south, and north—and wherever he stepped, there were lotus flowers. For this reason, this Buddha is named Padmottara.

At that time, immeasurable and boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of beings—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—simultaneously raised a great cry, their voices resounding everywhere, and spoke these words:
"This Great Bodhisattva is named Padmottara."
Because he uttered this sound among the devas and humans, that Buddha, the World-Honored One, was named Padmottara. "Ānanda!
I recall that in the past, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Varaprabhāsa."
At that time, I scattered a handful of golden grains over that Buddha, until that Buddha spoke to his attendant, saying:
"After more than one thousand kalpas have passed, this person shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni."
At that time, having heard the prophecy, I did not abandon my diligence and increased my wholesome karma.
By reason of the causes and conditions of the fruit of those merits, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, I became a Brahmā, a Śakra, and a Cakravartin King.
Furthermore, I once served as a universal monarch named Mūrdhaja.
At that time, within my palace, for seven days there fell a rain of golden grain, reaching up to the knees of the people and filling the entire expanse.
By the power of the causes and conditions of these wholesome karmas, I have now attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, even unto the turning of the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma.
Ānanda! When that Tathāgata of Supreme Conduct wished to go to a village or town to beg for food, his feet moved through the air at a height of six feet from the ground.
At that time, devas, nāgas, humans, non-humans, and others cried out in a loud voice:
"This Buddha, the World-Honored One, is named Uttara-carya (Supreme Conduct).
For this reason, this Tathāgata is titled 'Supreme Conduct. Ānanda!
I recall that in the past, there was a Tathāgata who appeared in the world, named Upariṣṭhanāman, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, I offered a single chamber and the community of bhikṣus to that Buddha and made this aspiration, until that Buddha told his attendant:
"In the future, after five hundred kalpas have passed, this person shall attain Buddhahood, and his name shall be Śākyamuni."

At that time, having received the prediction, because I did not abandon the causal conditions of diligent practice, I passed through immeasurable eons, becoming a Brahmā, a Śakra, and a Cakravartin King.
Furthermore, as a result of that karmic retribution, I was at that time a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Sudarśana.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and Viśvakarman descended and created for me a palace named Sarvārthasiddha.
By reason of the causal conditions of the retribution of these wholesome karmas, I have now attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, even unto turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.

“Ānanda! I recall that in the past, there was a Tathāgata who appeared in the world named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; his name was identical to mine, and his lineage, parents, personal name, and lifespan were in every respect the same as mine.”
Taking a handful of *sumana* flowers, he scattered them over that Buddha. The teacher Kāśyapa said: "Taking a handful of gold, he made such a vow... until that Buddha spoke to his attendant, saying:
'In a full hundred kalpas hence, this person shall attain Buddhahood, and his name shall be Śākyamuni.'"
At that time, having received the prophecy, I did not abandon my diligence; I increased my merit and, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, became a Brahmā, a Śakra, or a Cakravartin King.

By the power of these causes and conditions of wholesome karma, I shall adorn my body with the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma), enabling me to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and even to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
“Ānanda! I recall that in the past, there was a Tathāgata who appeared in the world, named Tiṣya, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
I took a handful of powdered sandalwood and scattered it over that Buddha, until that Buddha addressed his attendant, saying:
"This person, after ninety-five kalpas have passed, shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni."
"At that time, having received the prophecy, I did not abandon my diligence; I increased my merit and, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, became a Brahmā, a Śakra, and a Cakravartin King."
By the power of the causes and conditions of these wholesome karmas, I am named as one who is most excellently endowed with the purity of ethical conduct;

by the causes and conditions of the retribution of these wholesome karmas, I am named as one who is most excellently endowed with the merit of wisdom and vision. Thus spoke the Teacher of the Kāśyapa lineage: "By the power of the causes and conditions of my wholesome karmas, I have attained the merit of most excellent ethical conduct, and my fame has spread far and wide, even unto the attainment of most excellent wisdom and vision, whose merit is renowned afar. I have now realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and have even turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma."
“Ānanda! I recall that in the past, there was a Tathāgata who appeared in the world, named Puṣya, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”

At that time, that Buddha was within a cave of various jewels. Seeing that Buddha, my heart was filled with joy; I joined my ten fingers in palms-together salutation, stood on one foot for seven days and seven nights, and praised that Buddha with this verse, speaking these words:
"Neither in heaven nor on earth is there anyone like the Buddha; In the worlds of the ten directions, there is likewise no peer.
I have seen all that exists in the world, And among them all, none is equal to the Buddha."
“Ānanda! After I had praised that Buddha with this verse, I made such a vow... until that Buddha said to his attendant:
‘This person, after ninety-four kalpas have passed, shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni.’”
At that time, having received the prophecy, I did not abandon my diligence; I increased my merit and, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, served as Brahmā, Śakra, and Universal Monarchs (Cakravartin).

By the power of the causal conditions of these wholesome karmas, I have attained the four kinds of eloquence in full measure; there is not a single person who can debate with me or defeat me. I have realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and even turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
“Ānanda! I recall that in the past, there was a Tathāgata who appeared in the world, named Dr̥ṣṭatattva, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”

At that time, I scattered various kinds of flowers over that Buddha. The teacher Kāśyapa said: "That Buddha was named Sarvārthadarśin (He Who Sees All Principles), and so forth, until that Buddha spoke to his attendant, saying:
'This person, after ninety-three kalpas have passed, shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni.'"
At that time, having received the prediction, I did not abandon my diligent effort; I increased my merit and, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, became a Brahmā, a Śakra, or a Cakravartin King.

By these causes and conditions, I have now attained the name of "Supreme One" and am fully endowed with the practice of the precepts; even to the point of being named as one who possesses all liberations and knowledges, having realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and even turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
“Ānanda! I recall that in the past, there was a Tathāgata who appeared in the world, named Vipaśyin, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
At that time, I took a handful of small beans and scattered them over that Buddha. Thereupon, that Buddha said to his attendant:
"This person, after ninety-one kalpas have passed, shall attain Buddhahood; he shall be named Śākyamuni, fully endowed with the ten titles."
At that time, having received the prediction, I did not abandon my diligence and increased my merit; throughout immeasurable lifetimes, I became a Brahmā, a Śakra, and a Cakravartin King.

By the power of the causes and conditions of these wholesome karmas, I was once a Cakravartin king named Mūrdhaja, who ruled over the four continents and further attained half of Śakra’s throne to sit upon.
By means of this karmic retribution, I have now attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and even turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma. Ānanda!
I recall that in the past, there was a Tathāgata who appeared in the world, named Śikhin, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, I took an invaluable robe and covered that Buddha and the assembly of śrāvakas, making this aspiration. Thereupon, that Buddha said to his attendant:
"After thirty-one kalpas have passed, this person shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
At that time, having received the prophecy, I did not abandon my diligent and courageous resolve, but constantly practiced giving and performed meritorious deeds.

By virtue of such causes and conditions of wholesome karma, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, I have served as the Great Brahmā King, Śakra Devendra, and the Cakravartin King; today, I have further obtained various kinds of garments, namely Kāśika cloth, exquisite kṣauma cloth, exquisite karpāsa cloth, kauśeya silk, and kośamba cloth. Having now attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall even turn the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma.
“Ānanda! I recall that in the past, there was a Tathāgata who appeared in the world, named Viśvabhū Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”

At that time, I presented various excellent foods and drinks of a hundred flavors as an offering to that Buddha and his assembly of śrāvakas, and made this vow. Subsequently, that Buddha said to his attendant:
"After thirty kalpas have passed, this person shall become a Buddha, named Śākyamuni."
At that time, having received the prediction of my future enlightenment, I did not abandon my diligent and courageous resolve, but constantly practiced giving and performed meritorious deeds.

By virtue of these roots of goodness, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, I have become a Great Brahmā King, or a Śakra, or a Wheel-Turning Sage King; now I enjoy various foods and drinks of a hundred flavors, and shall even attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and turn the unsurpassed, pure wheel of Dharma.

“Ānanda! I recall that in the past, in the presence of the Krakucchanda Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, I practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) for the sake of seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in a future age.”

Ānanda! I recall that in the past, in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kanakamuni, I practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) for the sake of seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in a future age.

“Ānanda! I recall that in the past, I practiced the holy life under Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, in order to seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) in a future age.”

“Ānanda! I recall that in the past, at the side of Maitreya Bodhisattva, I brought various kinds of exquisite fourfold offerings to serve, honor, revere, and praise him, offering them freely because I sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in a future life.”

Ānanda! I recall that in the past, wherever I went, I took various kinds of offerings and presented them to the countless Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and assemblies of Śrāvakas of the past, planting all manner of roots of goodness for the sake of seeking Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in future lives.
"Ānanda! In the past, more than a hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
“Ānanda! In this sequence, after the passing of ten billion kalpas, there will appear in the world a Buddha named Sarvābhibhū, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
“Ānanda! In this sequence, after five hundred kalpas have passed, there will appear in the world a Buddha named Uttaraśrī, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
“Ānanda! In this sequence, after the passing of one hundred kalpas, a Buddha appeared in the world named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
“Ānanda! In this sequence, ninety-four kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Puṣya, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
“Ānanda! In this sequence, ninety-three kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Dṛṣṭārtha, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
“Ānanda! In this sequence, during the ninety-first kalpa, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Vipaśyin, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
“Ānanda! In this sequence, during the thirty-first kalpa, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Śikhin, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
Within that same eon, there was yet another Buddha who appeared in the world, named Śrīśruta Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
“Ānanda! At the beginning of this Bhadrakalpa, the first Tathāgata, Krakucchanda, appeared in the world.
The second, Kanakamuni Tathāgata, appeared in the world.”
The third was the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, who appeared in the world.
The fourth is my own self, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, who now exists in the world. Ānanda!
That Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appeared in the world, born into a great brahmin family.
"The Buddha Sarvābhibhū appeared in the world, born into a great Kṣatriya family.
The Buddha Padmottara appeared in the world, born into a great Brāhmaṇa family."
“The Buddha Uttamacārin appeared in the world, born into a great Kṣatriya family.
The Buddha Guṇottaranāman appeared in the world, born into a great Brāhmaṇa family.”
“Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world, being born into a great Kṣatriya family.
Tiṣya Tathāgata appeared in the world, being born into a great Brāhmaṇa family.”
“The Tathāgata Puṣya appeared in the world, born into a great Kṣatriya family.
The Buddha Satyārthadarśin appeared in the world, born into a great Brāhmaṇa family.”
“Vipaśyin Buddha appeared in the world, born into a great Kṣatriya royal family.
Śikhin Tathāgata appeared in the world, born into a great Kṣatriya royal family.”
“The gods have heard that the Tathāgata has appeared in the world, born into a great Kṣatriya family.
Krakucchanda Buddha appeared in the world, born into a great Brāhmaṇa family.”
“Kanakamuni Buddha appeared in the world, born into a family of great brahmins.
Kāśyapa Tathāgata appeared in the world, born into a family of great brahmins.”
“Ānanda! I am now born into a great royal family of the Kṣatriya caste, appearing in the world. Ānanda!”

The Master Niṣaṣya says that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara had a lifespan of eight hundred and forty million billion years, remaining in the world for the sake of benefiting all the worlds.
The teacher Kāśyapīya further said: "The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara remained in the world for one kalpa, together with his assembly of śrāvakas, in order to benefit all the worlds. Ānanda!"
The Sarvāstivādins (Niṣaṇṭhaka masters) say that the Tathāgata Sarvārthasiddha remained in the world for eighty billion years for the sake of benefiting all worlds.
The Kāśyapīya masters further state that the Tathāgata Sarvārthasiddha remained in the world for one kalpa for the sake of benefiting the world.
“The Buddha Padmottara dwelt in the world for eighty thousand years for the sake of benefiting [sentient beings].
The Buddha Uttaramati dwelt in the world for eighty thousand years for the sake of benefiting [sentient beings].”
"The Buddha named Shangming (Supernamed) dwelt in the world for sixty thousand years for the sake of benefiting [beings].
The Buddha Śākyamuni dwelt in the world for eighty thousand years for the sake of benefiting [beings]."
“The Tathāgata Tiṣya remained in the world for sixty thousand years for the sake of benefiting [beings].
The Tathāgata Puṣya remained in the world for fifty thousand years for the sake of benefiting [beings].”
“The Buddha Drumarāja lived in the world for forty thousand years for the sake of benefiting beings.
The Buddha Vipaśyin lived in the world for eighty thousand years for the sake of benefiting beings.”
“The gods have heard that the Tathāgata will remain in the world for sixty thousand years for the sake of benefiting [sentient beings].
The Buddha Krakucchanda will remain in the world for forty thousand years for the sake of benefiting [sentient beings].”
“Kanakamuni Buddha remained in the world for thirty thousand years for the sake of benefiting beings.
Kāśyapa Tathāgata remained in the world for twenty thousand years for the sake of benefiting beings.”
“Ānanda! I, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, now dwell in the world for eighty years for the sake of benefiting [beings].”
And he spoke in verse:
“There are Buddhas who, by means of their supernormal powers, remain in the world to receive offerings;
others, when their supernormal powers and karma are exhausted, enter parinirvāṇa.”
“Ānanda! The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara had an assembly of two hundred and fifty million śrāvaka disciples. After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma remained in the world for seventy thousand years.”

In the final ten years, the bhikṣus will fail to give rise to reverence and faith; lacking a sense of shame and remorse, they will occupy themselves with worldly affairs and take pleasure in various secular occupations. Holding doubts about the teachings, they will not consult one another; each relying on their own abilities, they will harbor mutual arrogance and constantly gather together in unrighteousness.
Taking evil associates and unwholesome people as friends, they become intimate with them, surrounding and following them about.

Because these deluded people act without purity, they cause the Tathāgata’s Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha to swiftly disappear and no longer manifest in the world, and all the sūtras and scriptures will be utterly extinguished.
"The Buddha Sarvābhibhū had an assembly of fourteen thousand śrāvaka disciples; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for a short time."
“The Buddha Padmottara had an assembly of seventy thousand śrāvakas; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for one hundred thousand years.”
“The Tathāgata Ūrdhvagaṃgā had an assembly of sixty thousand śrāvakas; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the True Dharma remained in the world for seventy-seven thousand years.”
“The Buddha Guṇottaranāman had an assembly of twenty thousand śrāvakas; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for five hundred years.”

“Śākyamuni Buddha has an assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty śrāvakas. After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for five hundred years, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain in the world for five hundred years.”
“The Tathāgata Tiṣya had an assembly of sixty trillion śrāvakas; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty thousand years.”

“The Tathāgata Puṣya has an assembly of immeasurable billions of śrāvakas; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there shall be the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, the duration of the Dharma, and even the extinction of the Dharma.”

“In the assembly of the Buddha Sarvārthadarśin, there is a gathering of thirty-two billion nayutas of śrāvakas; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma will exist only for a brief time and will not remain long in the world.”
“Vipaśyin Buddha preached the Dharma in three assemblies to deliver the assembly of śrāvakas:
in the first great assembly, there were one hundred and sixty-eight million people;
in the second great assembly, there were one million people.”
The third great assembly numbered eight hundred thousand people.
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty thousand years.
Śrīgarbha heard that the Tathāgata had only two assemblies for delivering the assembly of śrāvakas:
In the first assembly, seventy thousand people were delivered; in the second assembly, sixty thousand people were delivered.
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for sixty thousand years.
“Kurusondha Buddha had forty thousand śrāvaka disciples; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for five hundred years.”
“Kanakamuni Buddha had an assembly of three million śrāvakas; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty-nine days.”
“Kāśyapa Tathāgata had an assembly of twenty thousand śrāvakas; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for seven days.”

“Ānanda! I, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, have an assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty śrāvakas. After my parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for five hundred years, and the Semblance Dharma shall also remain in the world for five hundred years.”
Now I shall briefly explain the Udāna verses, and thus speak these stanzas:
"Explaining the giving and the number of years, The lineage and the lifespan,
The assemblies of the Śrāvakas, And the True Dharma as well as the Semblance Dharma."
"Those various World-Honored Ones, whether dwelling in the world or having entered Parinirvāṇa—those Great Lions of the Śākya clan—have all been fully described. Chapter 3:

The Lineage of Kings of the Bhadrakalpa. The Mahāvastu-Avadāna, Part Three, Upper Section: The Lineage of Kings of the Bhadrakalpa. At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka-nivāsa Bamboo Grove Monastery in the great city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in accordance with the dharmas of all Buddhas, even to the point of preaching the pure holy life, addressed the bhikṣus:
"O bhikṣus! You bhikṣus!"
"Listen attentively and receive it well!
Just as the World-Honored One has taught.
The bhikṣus said:
“We shall joyfully and with faith uphold this.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“At the beginning of this Bhadrakalpa, once the earth had been established, there was a most honored, eminent, wealthy, and noble great leader of men belonging to the lineage of a Cakravartin king, named Saṃjñāya.”
Once he had been installed, the great assembly addressed the Lord of the Earth, saying:
"O Great Lord of the Earth, you should punish the wicked for our sake and reward the virtuous."
“Virtuous one, you should divide the rice fields and give a portion to us; we shall sow them.
Once we have sown, we shall each harvest our shares and present them to you.

At that time, the landowner accepted the request of the great assembly and immediately conducted a formal inspection according to the law, punishing those who were wicked and rewarding those who were good.
"When people obtain a rice field, each guards it with care; once it has been cultivated and ripened, they enjoy it according to their respective shares.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, that great assembly gathered in such harmony and, together supporting that benevolent man, held him as the lord of the land. Because he was elected by the assembly through mutual consultation, he was called 'the one appointed by the assembly' (Mahāsammata)."

Furthermore, that lord of the land governs and transforms the great assembly according to the Dharma, causing them to rejoice, to be of one mind and to love him, so that they attain harmony and each is assigned their proper place; for this reason, he is called a king.
Furthermore, because he protects all the rice fields and gathers the people together by distributing shares of the rice fields, he is called a Kṣatriya king.
A Kṣatriya king is known as the Lord of the Fields.
"You should know this!
For these reasons, it was from this very lineage that the kings established by the great assembly at the beginning of the eon arose.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, the king established by that great assembly later fathered a son named Satya (Truth). He became a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) who ruled over the four continents, acting as the sovereign lord of the great earth. The seven treasures appeared spontaneously, he was endowed with a thousand sons, and he possessed the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Possessing majestic virtue and valor, he was able to crush his enemies."

During the time that king ruled and transformed the world, the great earth and the oceans were free of thorns, mounds, hills, or uneven terrain; the five grains ripened in abundance, and the people lived in peace and happiness. Free from all terrors and hardships, he did not employ weapons of war, yet all quarters submitted of their own accord as he governed according to the Dharma.

“O monks! Among those thousand sons of that True King, there was an eldest son named Manohara, also called Svayamvṛta. This son also became a Wheel-Turning Sage King, as previously described, possessing the seven treasures and a thousand sons, and even ruling and transforming the great earth according to the Dharma.”
“O bhikṣus! Among the thousand sons of that King Svayambhū, there was an eldest son named Prajñājña, whom the people called Upasaṃpanna.”

That wise king also succeeded to his father’s throne and became a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), as previously described: possessing the seven treasures and a thousand sons, he ruled and transformed the great earth according to the Dharma.

“Monks! Among that wise king’s thousand sons, the eldest, named Mūrdhaja, succeeded to his father’s throne and became a wheel-turning monarch, ruling the great earth with righteous law, just as previously described.”

“Monks! Among the thousand sons of that King Mandhātu, the eldest son was named Mahāsamudra. He also succeeded to his father’s throne and became a wheel-turning monarch, just as previously described.”
"O Bhikṣus!
Among the thousand sons of that Great Ocean King, the eldest son was named Pūrṇa; the multitude also called him Viśāla. He succeeded to the royal throne as previously described."
“Monks! Among the thousand sons of that King Samudravijaya, the eldest son was named Poṣa; he succeeded to the royal throne as previously described.”
“Monks! Among the thousand sons of that King Poṣa, the eldest son was named Puṇyavāhana; he succeeded to the royal throne as previously described.”
“Monks! Among the thousand sons of that King Puṇyavāhana, the eldest son was named Mokṣa; he succeeded to the royal throne as previously described.”
"O bhikṣus! Among the thousand sons of that King Vimukta, the eldest son was named Sudvimukta; he succeeded to the royal throne as previously described."
“Monks! That King Well-Liberated had a son named Viśvantara who succeeded him to the royal throne, as described above. Monks!”
That King Viśvabhū had a son named Mahāviśvabhū, who succeeded him to the royal throne, as previously described.
"O monks! That King Mahāviśvabhū had a son named Ālokakara, who succeeded him to the royal throne, as previously described."
“O bhikṣus! That King Āditya had a son named Mahāditya, who succeeded to the royal throne as previously described.
—From the *Buddhacarita-saṃcaya-sūtra*, Volume Four.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Five,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on the Royal Lineage of the Bhadrakalpa (Part Two).
“Monks! That King Mahāprabha had a son, also named Manojña, who succeeded to the royal throne as previously described. Monks!”
That King Manojña had a son named Sumano, who succeeded him to the royal throne, as previously described.
"Monks! That King Sumano had a son named Pūrṇa, who succeeded him to the royal throne, as previously described."
“Monks! That King Saṃpāti had a son named Mahāsaṃpāti, who succeeded to the royal throne as previously described. Monks!”
That King Mahāsammata had a son, also named Poṣadha, who succeeded him to the royal throne, as previously described.
"O monks! That King Poṣadha had a son, also named Puṇyabala, who succeeded him to the royal throne, as previously described."
“Monks! That King Puṇyavanta had a son named Manujendra, who succeeded him to the royal throne, as previously described. Monks!”
That leader of men, King [Agni], had a son named Agnidatta, who succeeded to the royal throne as previously described.
"O monks! That King Agnidatta had a son named Arciṣmat, who succeeded to the royal throne as previously described."
“Monks! That King Arciṣmān had a son named Supratiṣṭhitamakuṭa, who succeeded to the royal throne as previously described. Monks!”
That King Suprabha had a son named Śūnyaprabha, who succeeded him to the royal throne as previously described.
"O monks! That King Śūnyaprabha had a son named Sudarśana, who succeeded him to the royal throne as previously described."
“Monks! That King Sudarśana had a son named Mahāsudarśana, who succeeded to the royal throne as previously described. Monks!”
"That King Mahāsudarśana had a son named Sumeru, who succeeded him to the royal throne, as previously described.
Monks! That King Sumeru had a son named Mahāsumeru, who succeeded him to the royal throne, as previously described."
“O monks! A Wheel-Turning Sage King governs the four continents, the oceans, and the great earth; he is endowed with the seven treasures and even rules over the people according to the Dharma.”

These kings were all past universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) who fully cultivated immeasurable meritorious deeds and deeply planted roots of goodness. By virtue of this karmic retribution, they all obtained the enjoyment of the entire great earth within these four continents, experiencing various blessings and joys; their lifespans were immeasurable and beyond calculation.
"O Bhikṣus! You should know this!

I shall now further explain the lineage and descendants of those wheel-turning kings, how they have been passed down from generation to generation, as well as other minor kings whose sons and grandsons have succeeded them; I will briefly describe for you their dwellings, names, and their successive numbers. Listen well!"

"O bhikṣus! Since the Great King Sumeru began his reign, through successive generations of sons and grandsons, there have been one hundred and one minor universal monarchs (cakravartin), all of whom resided in the city of Potalaka, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
Among those kings, the last was named Siṃhavāhana.

From King Siṃhavāhana, through successive generations of sons and grandsons, there were sixty-one minor universal monarchs (cakravartin), all of whom resided in the city of Vārāṇasī, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness.
"Among those kings, the last one was named Nārīyāna.

From that King Nārīyāna, through successive generations of sons and grandsons, there were fifty-six minor universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), all of whom resided in the city of Ayodhyā, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
"Among those kings, the last one was named Ugratejas.

From King Ugratejas, through successive generations of sons and grandsons, there were a total of one thousand minor universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), all of whom resided in the city of Kapilavastu, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
"Among those kings, the last one was named Brahmadatta.

From that King Brahmadatta, through successive generations of sons and grandsons, there were twenty-five minor universal monarchs (cakravartin), all of whom resided in the city of Aśvamedhapura, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
"Among those kings, the last one was named Hastidāsa.

From that King Hastidāsa, there were twenty-five minor universal monarchs (cakravartin) in successive generations, from son to grandson, all of whom resided in the city of Takṣaśilā, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
"Among those kings, the very last was named Pālita.

From that King Pālita, there arose a lineage of one thousand two hundred minor universal monarchs (kṣudra-cakravartin), father to son and son to grandson, all of whom resided in the city of Śyānaka, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
"Among those kings, the very last was named Śakrāditya.

From King Śakrāditya onwards, there were ninety minor universal monarchs (cakravartin) in successive generations, from father to son and grandson, all of whom resided in the city of Kanyakubja, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
"Among those kings, the last one was named Vijitāvin.

From that King Vijitāvin, through successive generations of sons and grandsons, there were two thousand five hundred minor universal monarchs who all resided in the city of Campā, ruling over the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
"Among those kings, the last one was named Dragon-Heaven (Nāgadeva).

From that King Dragon-Heaven, through successive generations of sons and grandsons, there were twenty-five minor universal monarchs (cakravartin), all of whom resided in Rājagṛha, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
"Among those kings, the very last was named Kṣema.

From that King Kṣema, through successive generations of sons and grandsons, there arose twenty-five minor universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), all of whom resided in the city of Kuśinagara, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
"Among those kings, the very last was named Maheśvara.

From that King Maheśvara, through successive generations of sons and grandsons, there arose twenty-five minor universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), all of whom resided in the city of Āmrapākapura, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
"Among those kings, the very last king was also named Maheśvara.

That King Maheśvara, through hereditary succession from generation to generation, produced twenty-five minor universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), all of whom resided in the city of Tāṇḍipurī, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
"Among those kings, the very last was named Suyasa.

From that King Suyasa, through successive generations of sons and grandsons, there arose twenty-five minor universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), all of whom resided in the city of Tāmraparṇī, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
"Among those kings, the last one was named Aśokamālā.

From that King Aśokamālā, there arose a succession of eighty-four thousand minor universal monarchs, father to son and grandson to grandson, all of whom resided in the city of Mithilā, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
"Among those kings, the last one was named Viṣṇu.

That King Viṣṇu, through a lineal succession from father to son and grandson, produced one hundred and one kings who all resided in the city of Vaibhāḍra, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
"Among those kings, the very last king was also named Maheśvara.

This King Maheśvara, through successive generations of sons and grandsons, comprised eighty-four thousand kings in total; they continued to rule and transform the people within that city of Maitrāyaṇī, enjoying blessings and happiness."
"Among those kings, the very last was named Matsyarāja (Fish King). Bhikṣus!

You should know that all such minor universal monarchs possessed merit and had planted roots of goodness; they fully experienced worldly rewards of fortune, with none equal to them. The extent of their transformation and influence encompassed the great earth, the oceans, and all the mountains, which they entirely governed."
"Monks! That wheel-turning monarch has various minor kings scattered throughout his realm; I shall now describe them to you. Monks!"
The king of fish had a son named Jāti.
That King Jāti, from his father and grandfather back, had cultivated roots of goodness and thus inherited the kingship; however, because his karmic rewards were exhausted, he lost his royal position.
At that time, seeing that the king’s governance had strayed from the Way and was devoid of merit and virtue, the people said to one another:
"This king is the most wretched among men, the most destitute among men, the most pitiable among men, and the most contemptible among men."
For this reason, all the people of the world called him King Khāṇu.
King Khāṇu had a son named King Samavartana; King Samavartana’s son was named Andhaka;
Andhaka’s son was named Arciṣmat; Arciṣmat’s son was named Suprabha. Suprabha...
For example, there was a prince named Ākāśa; the son of Prince Ākāśa was named Śīlacaryā;
the son of Prince Śīlacaryā was named Aśoka; the son of Prince Aśoka was named Vigataśoka; the son of Prince Vigataśoka was named Śokavinodana;
the son of Prince Śokavinodana was named Jayasena; and the son of Prince Jayasena was named Mahā...
The general’s son was named Garbhaja (Womb-born); the son of Garbhaja was named Tāraka (Star-like);
the son of Tāraka was named Diśpati (Lord of the Quarters); the son of Diśpati was named Reṇu (Dust);
the son of Reṇu was named Sumati (Good Mind); the son of Sumati was named Susthita (Well-established); the son of Susthita...
His name was Nanda; Prince Nanda’s son was named Mahābala; Mahābala’s son was named Mahāprabha;
Mahāprabha’s son was named Mahāyaśas; Mahāyaśas’s son was named Daśaratha;
Daśaratha’s son was named Viṃśatiratha; and Viṃśatiratha’s son was named Citraratha.
The Prince of Wondrous Chariot was named Chariot on Foot; the Prince of Chariot on Foot was named Ten Bows;
the Prince of Ten Bows was named Hundred Bows; the Prince of Hundred Bows was named Twenty Bows;
the Prince of Twenty Bows was named Wondrously Colored Bow; the Prince of Wondrously Colored Bow was named Sinful Bow; [the son of] King Sinful Bow...
His son was named Sāgara-jaya; the prince Sāgara-jaya’s son was named Durjaya;
Durjaya’s son was named Tṛṇa; and Tṛṇa’s son was named Mahātṛṇa.

The Great Māṣa Kings, succeeding one another through the generations from father to son and grandson, comprised a lineage of one hundred and eight kings in total; they continued to reside in that city of Bhaddanagara, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness.
"Among those one hundred and eight kings, the very last was the great king Tṛṇabindu. That king had no son, and he thought to himself:

'Since time immemorial, when the various minor kings of my lineage have seen white hairs grow upon their own heads and beards, they have each consecrated their sons as kings, set aside a most excellent and superior province as a gift, shaved off their hair and beards, renounced the throne, and left the household life to practice the Way. "
"I now have no son; by whom shall I continue the lineage of my royal house?
Who is capable of increasing my clan?
Or have I now brought an end to all the royal dynasties?"
Again, he gave rise to this thought:
"If I do not now leave the household life to cultivate the Way, I shall sever the lineage of all the worthy sages.
Having reflected thus, he immediately entrusted the great kingdom of Kuśa to his ministers.
Surrounded by a great multitude, they escorted the king out of the city; he shaved off his hair and beard and donned the robes of a renunciant.

Once the king had left the household life, he maintained pure precepts with focused and courageous diligence, accomplished the four dhyānas, perfected the five supernatural powers, and became a royal seer (*rāja-ṛṣi*) of exceedingly long life.
When he reached old age, his flesh wasted away and his back became hunched; although he used a staff for support, he could no longer travel far.

At that time, the disciples of that royal seer (rājarṣi), wishing to go here and there to seek food and drink, took fine, soft grass, placed it inside a basket to carry the royal seer, and hung it from the branch of a tree.
Why was this? It was because he feared that insects or wild beasts might disturb the royal seer.
After his disciples had departed to beg for alms, a hunter wandering through the mountains and wilds saw the royal seer from afar; mistaking him for a white crane, he immediately shot at him.
At that time, once the royal seer had been struck by the arrow, two drops of blood fell to the ground and he immediately passed away.

His disciples, returning from their alms round, saw that the royal seer had been shot and died; they also saw the two drops of blood on the ground. They immediately lowered him from the basket, placed the king upon the ground, gathered firewood, cremated the royal corpse, and collected the bones to build a stūpa. They then brought various kinds of exquisite incense and flowers to make offerings at the stūpa, honoring and praising him, and having thus completed their service.

At that time, two drops of blood fell upon that ground, and immediately two stalks of sugarcane sprouted. Their shoots gradually grew tall and large until they reached maturity; when the sugarcane ripened, it split open under the scorching sun. From one stalk of sugarcane emerged a young boy, and from the other stalk emerged a young girl. They were so handsome and lovely that there were no equals to them in the world.
At that time, the disciples thought to themselves: "When the royal seer was in the world, he did not father any sons; these two boys are surely of the royal seer’s lineage.
They raised and cared for them, and informed the ministers of this fact.

At that time, having heard this, the ministers were filled with joy; they went to that grove, welcomed the two boys, and brought them back to the palace. They summoned a great Brahmin skilled in reading physiognomy, commanding him to examine their marks and bestow names upon them.
The physiognomist said:
"Since this boy was born from the opening of a sugarcane that had been ripened by the sun's heat, he is first named Sujāta;
furthermore, because he emerged from a sugarcane, his second name is Ikṣuvāku."
Furthermore, because she was born from sugarcane ripened by the sun, she is also called "Born of the Sun.
Since her origins and circumstances were entirely unique and without peer, she was named Subhadrā, and was also called Jalavāhinī.
Then those ministers took the boy born of the Ikṣvāku lineage; while he was still young and a mere youth, they performed the consecration upon his head and established him as king.
When the maiden Bhadrā reached maturity and was capable of serving him, they appointed her as the king’s chief consort.
"At that time, King Ikṣvāku had a second queen, who was peerlessly beautiful and upright; she gave birth to four sons:
the first was named Flame-Face, the second Golden-Hued, the third Elephant-Host, and the fourth Distinctly-Accomplished."

That Queen Bhadra gave birth to only one son, named Jīvaka; he was handsome and pleasing to behold, with few equals in the world, yet his physical constitution was such that he was unfit to be a king.
At that time, Queen Subhadrā thought to herself:

"The King of the Ikṣvāku lineage has these four sons, Kārakuṇḍala and his brothers, who form a powerful brotherhood. I now have only this one son; although he is exceedingly handsome and without equal in the world, his physical characteristics do not qualify him to be a ruler."
"What skillful means can I employ so that this son of mine may succeed to the royal throne?
He further thought:
"This King of the Ikṣvāku clan now possesses immeasurable respect and affection for me; his heart is deeply attached to me, and he indulges his passions and dissipates his mind."

I shall now further exhaust the methods of feminine adornment—namely, cleansing and rubbing the body, bathing with fragrant water to make the breath aromatic, applying *vela* oil to the hair, smearing the face with cosmetic powders, and adorning myself with various ornaments such as flower garlands and necklaces—so that King Ikṣvāku’s heart may once again give rise to intense attachment, longing, and delight toward me.
"If I obtain my heart's desire, I shall go to a secluded place and offer up my prayer.
Having reflected thus, he adorned his person as previously described, making it exceedingly magnificent, and went before the king.
When the king saw the queen approaching, he conceived a deep sense of love and respect, and his mind became dissolute.
Having seen that the king had given rise to such thoughts, the two lay down together, and the queen said to the king:
"Great King, you should know that I now beg one wish from you; I pray that you grant it to me."
The King said:
"Great Queen!
Do as you wish; I shall not oppose you. I will grant it to you, whatever your heart desires."
Then the consort again addressed the king with renewed earnestness, saying:
"Great King, if you grant me this wish of your own free will, you must not later change your mind or regret it; if you should so change or regret it, I have no need for this."
The king said to the queen:
"I have once granted your heart's desire; if you should later regret it, may my head split into seven pieces."
The queen said:
"Great King!
I pray that you banish your four sons, Jvalanmukha and his companions, from the kingdom, and dispatch my son, Dīrghāyu, to be king."
Then King Ikṣvāku said to his queen:

"These four sons of mine are without fault; they have not sought wealth by improper means, nor do they possess any transgression. How can I, without cause, unjustly drive them away and exile them to another land?"
"Within the realm over which I rule and transform, what inauspicious thing is there that you would not permit to remain?
The consort spoke again, saying:
"The King has already made a vow; if his words are regretted, his head shall split into seven pieces."
The king said to the queen, "I shall grant you your wish as previously stated; if you know the time has come, act according to your own will.
Then, after that night had passed, when the clear dawn arrived, King Ikṣvāku gathered his four sons together and addressed them with these instructions:
“O you four youths!
You must now depart from within my realm of governance; you may no longer reside here, but must go far away to other lands.
At that time, the four youths knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms, and addressed their father, the king, saying:
"Great King!

You should know that we four have committed no crimes and possess no faults; we have not taken the wealth of others through unlawful means, nor have we performed any other evil deeds. Why then has our father, the King, suddenly banished us from the borders of the kingdom?"
The king commanded his sons, saying:
"I know that you are truly without fault and have not taken wealth improperly as described above; it was not my intention that I should banish you."
"This is the intention of the Great Queen Subhaddā.
When that queen made her request, I did not refuse her; therefore, I have caused you to leave the country.
At that time, the mother of the four princes, having heard that King Ikṣvāku intended to banish her sons from the borders of the kingdom, went with great haste to the place where the king was.
Having arrived at the king's location, he addressed him, saying:
"Great King, I have heard that you wish to banish my four sons beyond the borders of the kingdom; is this indeed true?"
The king said,
"I truly did send her.
Each of the consorts then spoke again to the king, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!
We each beg to follow our children."
The King replied to the queens:
"Go as you please.
Then the sisters of the queens spoke again to the King, saying:
"My sister and my nephew have now departed from the kingdom; I too beg to go.
The king replied to each of them, "Do as you wish."
At that time, the various ministers, high officials, and counselors also addressed the king, saying:
"If Your Majesty now banishes these four princes and causes them to leave the country, we, your ministers, also seek to follow them."
The king said,
"As you wish. At that time,
the king's official in charge of the elephants and horses also requested to accompany him, and the king said:

"Your will be done. Furthermore, there were commanders of bows, commanders of crossbows, commanders of prisons, various masters of sheep, cattle, and flocks, as well as the sons of ministers; additionally, there were other treasurers, military commanders, veteran warriors, and masters of archery, along with their slaves, servants, and children. Hearing that King Ikṣvāku wished to exile his four sons beyond the borders of the kingdom, they all addressed the king, saying:
"We all seek to follow the princes as they travel east and west."
The king said, "As you wish. Furthermore,

the bamboo-workers, leather-workers, potters, bricklayers, carpenters, brewers and cooks, barbers, dyers and laundrymen, butchers, masseurs, physicians, pharmacists, fishermen, and other such craftsmen within the kingdom heard that the king intended to banish his four sons from the country.
"Is it truly so? The king replied,
"It is indeed so."
"We seek to depart," they said.
The King replied,
"As you wish."
At that time, King Ikṣvāku commanded his princes, saying: "O princes!

From this day forward, if you wish to marry, you must not take a wife from another lineage elsewhere; rather, you shall take one from within your own family clan, lest the Ikṣvāku lineage be severed."
Then the princes said to their father, the king:
"As the Great King commands.

Having received their father's instruction, each of the princes took his own mother, along with their paternal and maternal sisters, servants, wealth, and various vehicles and mounts, and immediately headed north to the foot of the Snowy Mountains (Himavat). After staying there for a short time, they came to a great river named Vāgīratī; having crossed that river, they ascended to the summit of the Snowy Mountains and remained there for a long period while traveling about.

At that time, the four princes were on the summit of that mountain, hunting and capturing various birds and beasts for food. As they gradually moved forward, they reached the southern face of the mountain and saw that the valley was broad and level, free from pits, hollows, mounds, hills, valleys, ravines, ditches, thorns, dust, and gravel. The ground grew only soft, fine green grass—pure and lovely—while the trees, forests, flowers, and fruits flourished luxuriantly and vibrantly, like black clouds with a shimmering luster.

The forest was densely filled with trees, leaving little open space; namely, śāla trees, tāla trees, nāḍamāra trees, aśvattha trees, nyagrodha trees, udumbara trees, thousand-year jujube trees, kālīra trees, and others, their branches and twigs hanging down, each shading and reflecting upon the other.

Furthermore, there were various kinds of diverse and exquisite flowers, namely: *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *aśoka*, *pāṭala*, *bālasirīṣa*, *kuraṇṭaka*, *kovidāra*, *tānūṣakalikā*, *mucilinda*, *sumana*, and so forth—all these flowers, some already in bloom, some not yet opened, some just beginning to open, and some already fallen after blooming.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable varieties of fruit trees, namely: the *āmra* (mango), *jambu*, *kharjūra*, *panasa*, *tinduka*, *harītakī*, *bibhītaka*, *āmalaka*, and so forth—various kinds of fruits, some of which had first set their seeds, some whose seeds were about to ripen, and some whose seeds were already ripe and fit for consumption.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable varieties of wild beasts, namely: the eṇeya deer, the kṛṣṇasāra deer, the gavaya, the narakas deer, wild oxen, white elephants, lions, and others.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable varieties of flying birds, namely: parrots, kokilas, mynas, peacocks, kalaviṅkas, jīvañjīvakas, cāṣas, mountain pheasants, white cranes, śāmaka birds, and rāma birds, along with all other miscellaneous species of birds.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable waters, ponds, and pools, each filled with various kinds of lotuses—namely, the utpala, the padma, the kumuda, and the puṇḍarīka—which completely cover all the pools and the four sides of their banks.

Furthermore, various flowers hang down and cover the surface of the pond; its water is pure and free from turbidity or filth, serene and overflowing, neither deep nor shallow, easy to cross and easy to traverse, with all kinds of trees surrounding its four sides.
Within the pond there are furthermore various kinds of creatures, namely fish, turtles, alligators, crocodiles, tortoises, sea-turtles, conchs, and bees—every kind of aquatic being.
There are also small birds, namely wild ducks, geese, swans, mallards, egrets, cormorants, mandarin ducks, and so forth—every kind of bird.
However, at that place, there was an ancient seer who resided there, named Kapila.
When the princes saw this location, they said to one another,
"We may build a city here and establish our rule."

"At that time, once the princes had settled down, they recalled their father the king’s words and sought wives from within their own clans; however, being unable to find brides, they each took their maternal aunts and sisters as their wives."

Out of consideration for the proprieties of a wife, she had two motives: first, her desire to comply with the commands of her father, the King; and second, her fear that the Śākya clan would become intermixed through the birth of offspring.
At that time, the King of the Solar Lineage, who was of the Ikṣvāku family, summoned a state preceptor, a great Brahmin, and said to him:
"Great Brahmin!..."
"Where are my four princes now?
The state preceptor replied,
"Great King!"

You should know that the king’s four sons have each taken their own mothers, paternal and maternal sisters, along with their mounts, belongings, and attendants, and have traveled far beyond the borders of the kingdom toward the north, where they have even given birth to handsome sons and daughters.
At that time, King Ikṣvāku, out of love for his own sons, desired to see them; with a heart full of joy, he spoke these words:
"Those princes are capable of establishing statecraft and are excellent at governing and transforming the people."
For that reason, those princes established their clan name as Śākya.
Because they dwelt beneath the lush branches of a great tree, it was therefore called Śākyavardhana.
Because it was originally located at the site of the sage Kapila, the city was named after him; thus, it is called Kapilavastu.

"At that time, after the three sons of King Ikṣvāku had passed away, only one son remained, named Nyagrodha (translated in the Sui language as 'Distinctly Accomplished'). He became king and resided in the city of Kapilavastu, governing the people and enjoying blessings and happiness."
That King Nyagrodha fathered a son named Kulu, who remained in his father the king’s city of Kapilavastu, dwelling there while governing and transforming the realm.
That King Kuru fathered another son named Gokuru, who likewise resided in his father’s city and ruled as king over the realm.
That King Gokuru fathered another son named Siṃhahanu, who also remained in his father’s city and governed the people.
King Siṃhahanu fathered four sons:

the first was named Śuddhodana (translated in the Sui language as "Pure Rice"), the second was named Śuklodana (translated as "White Rice"), the third was named Droṇodana (translated as "Measuring Bowl Rice"), and the fourth was named Amṛtodana (translated as "Nectar Rice"). He also had one daughter, named Amṛtaprabhā (translated as "Nectar Flavor").
King Siṃhahanu’s eldest son, Śuddhodana, succeeded him to the royal throne; he returned to his father’s city, governed the people, and enjoyed blessings and happiness.
"At that time, not far from Kapilavastu, there was another city named Devadṛha.

In that city of Devadṛha, there lived a Śākya, a noble and eminent elder named Suprabuddha. He was immensely wealthy with vast riches, having accumulated various precious gems; his assets were abundant and his majesty and virtue complete. Everything was provided for him naturally according to his wishes, and he lacked nothing; his residence was no different from the palace of King Vaiśravaṇa."
That Śākya elder gave birth to eight daughters:

the first was named Mati; the second, Amati; the third, Sumati; the fourth, Anantamati; the fifth, Cūḍāmati; the sixth, Kālā; the seventh, Piṅgalā; and the eighth, Mahāprajāpatī—which in the language of Sui means "Great Wisdom" (Mahāprajñā) and is also called "Brahmā."
Now, among all these women, this Brahmā-devī was the youngest. On the day of her birth, various Brahmin masters skilled in physiognomy examined her body and prophesied:

"If this girl marries and bears a son, he shall certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), ruling over the four continents; the seven treasures shall appear spontaneously, he shall be endowed with a thousand sons, and he shall govern his subjects without the need for whips or staves."
At that time, the daughter of Sujāta gradually grew up and reached a marriageable age.

King Śuddhodana heard that within his own realm there was a member of the Śākya clan who was exceedingly wealthy; he had fathered eight daughters who were peerless in their beauty and grace. Furthermore, physiognomists had examined the girls and predicted that they would give birth to noble sons.
At that time, having heard these words, King Śuddhodana spoke thus:
"I shall now seek this girl to be my queen, so that the lineage of my Ikṣvāku, the Cakravartin kings, shall not be severed. This is what the Vinaya masters have said.
Furthermore, as for the statement that "Mahāmati is the mother of the Bodhisattvas," this is based on the text of the *Avadāna-sūtra*.
Moreover, the statement that "King Śuddhodana is my father and Lady Māyā is my mother" is as explained in the *Avadāna-sūtra*.
"Upon examining the texts of various sūtras, this meaning is indeed true.

At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately dispatched a messenger to the house of the great elder Suprabuddha to request Mahāprajāpatī—*prajāpati* meaning "the root of livelihood" in the Sui language—to serve as his foster mother.
At that time, Sujāta said to the messenger:
"O good messenger, virtuous one, speak these words to the Great King on my behalf:
'I have eight daughters; the first is named Mati, and so on, up to the eighth, who is named Mahāprajñā.'"
"For what reason, Great King, do you seek the youngest?
Great King, please wait until I have finished arranging my seven daughters; then she shall become the consort for Your Majesty Mahāmati."
At that time, King Śuddhodana again sent a messenger to speak to the elder, saying:
"I cannot wait for you to finish marrying off each of your seven daughters one by one before taking Mahāprajāpatī as my queen; I shall take all eight of your daughters."
Then, Śuddhodana the Śākya replied to the Great King, saying, "If it is so,
I shall comply with Your Majesty’s command and take them away as you wish. Thereupon,
King Śuddhodana immediately dispatched messengers to escort the eight daughters to the palace all at once.
Having arrived at the palace, he immediately took the two women as his consorts; of these two women, the first was named Mati, and the eighth was named Mahāmati.
The remaining six daughters were distributed among his three younger brothers; one brother took two as his consorts and queens.

At that time, King Śuddhodana took the sisters into his palace, where they indulged in pleasures and enjoyed themselves to their hearts' content. In accordance with the laws of kings, he governed and transformed the four quarters.

Chapter Four: Ascending to Tuṣita The Mahāvaipulya Buddhacarita Sūtra: Chapter Four, Ascending to Tuṣita At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having observed the prohibitive precepts under the World-Honored One Kāśyapa Buddha and maintained pure brahmacarya, at the end of his life, was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven with right mindfulness.

Why is this? There are some sentient beings who, on the day their lives end, are dismembered limb by limb by the "wind-blade" [surgical pains], undergoing excruciating agony; or when their breath is about to cease, their gasping is restless. Due to these causes and conditions, they experience great suffering and affliction, lose their original mind, forget their past deeds, and are unable to single-mindedly and correctly settle their minds in meditative concentration.

It is not so for a bodhisattva; as their life draws to a close, they contemplate with right mindfulness, recollecting the circumstances of their previous births, wherein there were such extraordinary and marvelous phenomena.
