Furthermore, there is another quality of bodhisattvas such that, after the end of their lives, they will certainly be reborn in the heavens— whether in higher or lower realms, as no single heaven is fixed—

but those bodhisattvas who are in their last birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha) will mostly be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where their hearts are filled with joy and their wisdom is perfected.

Why is this? Because the gods in the lower realms are often heedless, while the gods in the higher realms possess great power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). Their tranquility is weak, and they do not seek rebirth because they are absorbed in the enjoyment of pleasure; furthermore, they do not give rise to compassion for all sentient beings.
It is not so for the Bodhisattva; rather, it is solely for the purpose of teaching and transforming all sentient beings that he is born in the Tuṣita Heaven.
The devas of the lower realms ascend to the Tuṣita Heaven in order to hear the Dharma and receive its teachings;
likewise, the devas of the upper realms also descend to the Tuṣita Heaven for the sake of the Dharma to hear and receive its teachings.

"Furthermore, this Bodhisattva was also born in Tuṣita; the devas residing in Tuṣita addressed the Bodhisattva by the name 'Pāramitāprabhāsa' (Hùmíng), and for this reason, he was known as Pāramitāprabhāsa."

The devas called out to one another, invoking the name "Guarded Brilliance" (Ratnaprabha), and their voices reached upward through the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa) until they reached the summit of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
At that time, all the devas cried out in unison:
"The Bodhisattva Guarded Brilliance has already been born within the Tuṣita Heaven."
This sound reached down as far as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, extending even to the Cāturmahārājika Heaven, and further penetrated the palaces of the various Asuras, who all said to one another:
"The Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra has already attained rebirth in the Tuṣita Heaven."

From the lowest depths of the Asura palaces up to the highest Akaniṣṭha heaven, they all gathered together in the Tuṣita Heaven, assembling at the residence of the Bodhisattva Mahāprajñāvatī (Huming) to listen to and receive the Dharma.

Once the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra was born in Tuṣita, the celestial palaces of the Tuṣita devas were illuminated with radiance and naturally adorned; furthermore, immeasurable and boundless manifestations of adornment appeared, all resulting from the power of the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s merit and majestic spiritual authority.
The Great Brahmā King and the Asuras of great majesty and virtue all assembled in the Tuṣita Heaven, surrounding the Bodhisattva Prabhāpāla from front and back to protect him.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable and boundless sentient beings who take birth in Tuṣita; having encountered the most excellent and exquisite five desires, their minds become deluded and they forget, failing to remember their original practices or their prior karma.

When the Bodhisattva Dhṛtaprajñā was born in the Tuṣita Heaven, even though he encountered the most excellent and exquisite five desires, his mind was not deluded; he never forgot, but maintained right mindfulness of his original vow. Even for the sake of transforming all sentient beings, he dwelt in the Tuṣita Heaven for a celestial lifespan of four thousand years, preaching the Dharma to those devas, teaching and transforming them, manifesting the characteristics of the Dharma, and causing their hearts to rejoice.
As for the other sentient beings born in that heaven, some are born there due to impure karma from the past, while others die prematurely without completing their full celestial lifespan.

Because Bodhisattva Rakṣaṇaprajña had cultivated causes of pure karma in the past and further acted to transform all sentient beings, he exhausted the entire lifespan of the Tuṣita Heaven; for this reason, it is said that it is rare, rare, and inconceivable. Furthermore, having attained the inconceivable Dharma, Bodhisattva Rakṣaṇaprajña completed his years in that heaven.
"At that time, when the celestial lifespan of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra had reached its full term, the five signs of decay appeared spontaneously.

What are these five? First, the flowers upon his head withered; second, sweat broke out from beneath his arms; third, his garments became soiled and greasy; fourth, his body lost its majestic radiance; and fifth, he no longer took pleasure in his own seat."
At that time, the gods of Tuṣita Heaven, seeing those signs of decline appear in Guhyaprajñā, let out a great cry: "Alas! Alas!
How bitter, how bitter! and said to one another:
"How painful, how painful!"
"Before long, the Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatī will surely abandon this Tuṣita Heaven palace and lose his majestic spiritual power.
How can we remain here any longer?"

At that time, the assembly of Tuṣita devas heard only the sound of wailing; the echoes of this sound reached from the celestial palaces of the various devas all the way to the Akaniṣṭha heaven at the summit of the Form Realm. The assemblies of devas there addressed one another, saying:
"Alas! How tragic!"
"The Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra has now manifested the five signs of decline; before long he will fall and descend from Tuṣita.
This cry of lamentation reached even the palaces of the asuras, its sound filling them everywhere, such that in every place one heard only: "Before long, he shall fall."

At that time, having heard this sound, the devas of Akaniṣṭha, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, and the other heavens of the realm of form and desire all descended to Tuṣita Heaven; likewise, the devas of Yāma and the Cāturmahārājika heavens, having heard this sound, all gathered together and ascended to Tuṣita Heaven.

In this manner, even the dragon kings, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas, and all other terrestrial devas who are included among those of the desire realm belonging to the form realm, all flew up to Tuṣita Heaven and gathered in one place, saying to one another:

"We now see that the Guardian Deva King wishes to descend from Tuṣita to be born in the human world; when the signs of decline appear in Tuṣita Heaven, it corresponds to twelve years in the human reckoning."
At that time, all the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven thought to themselves:
"In the past, we have seen when Bodhisattvas in their final birth descended from Tuṣita to be born among humans; it was no different from this."
"Those devas, seeing now that the Great Being Bodhisattva Varaprabha exhibits the five signs of decline, will certainly know he is descending to Jambudvīpa.
They immediately raised a great cry, proclaiming these words:
"O people, adorn this realm! Before long, the Great Being Bodhisattva shall descend from the Tuṣita heaven to be born here. Cleanse, cleanse! The Buddha desires to descend and be born."
At that time, there were five hundred pratyekabuddhas dwelling in a forest, practicing the path in this Jambudvīpa.
Upon hearing this sound, those five hundred pratyekabuddhas flew up into the air and together proceeded toward the city of Vārāṇasī.

Having arrived at that place, each manifested the five supernormal powers, leaped into the air, emitted smoke and flames, and spoke verses in succession before relinquishing their life-span and entering parinirvāṇa.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Rāhula, seeing those hosts of devas, as well as Brahmā, Śakra, the World-Protectors, the nāgas, the piśācas, and others, observed that their minds were composed, free from fear or alarm, and devoid of doubt or dread; he spoke with gentle words and addressed them, saying:
'O worthy ones!'"
Each of you should know this!
Just as I now see these five signs of decline appear, it will not be long before I descend from Tuṣita Heaven to be born in the human world.
Then Brahmā, Śakra, and the other devas replied, "Venerable Protector of Light!

As you have perceived, since these five signs of decline have appeared, it is certain that before long you shall descend from Tuṣita to be born among humans; you should now call to mind your former original vows."

When those immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas had spoken these words, their entire bodies trembled, the hair on their skin stood on end, and their hearts were filled with great terror; they joined their ten fingers in palms-together salutation and prostrated themselves at the feet of Guṇaratna.
At that time, Vimalaprabha addressed the assembly, saying:
"I shall now certainly descend; of this there is no doubt.

The time has now arrived; therefore, you all should contemplate impermanence and consider the terrors of the future. You must carefully observe how the body is foul and impure, yet the mind is powerfully attached to it, being entangled by these various desires, so that within the cycle of birth and death, one cannot attain liberation."
Such a foul form is utterly loathsome.
All of you, join your palms together and contemplate my body as well as those of all sentient beings; none among us can yet escape this law.
"Therefore, you all should not grieve for me, and you should not suffer on my account.
Those devas replied,
"Venerable Mahāprajāpati!"

I only pray that the Venerable One will cover all with compassion and no longer give rise to other thoughts; rather, reflect upon the causal conditions of your original vows from the past, and how throughout billions of kalpas you have taken birth and likewise experienced the karmic fruits of gods and humans.

"By virtue of the causal conditions of wholesome karma created in the past, I recollect those roots of goodness from giving and the practice of the Dharma, and thus give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings.
Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatī (Hùmíng) replied to the devas, saying:
"You should know this!"
All sentient beings, within the world and in their places of birth, as long as they exist and as long as they are born, cannot avoid separation; how much more so in my case?
"Furthermore, all sentient beings are impermanent; how can one escape from the separation caused by the loss of loved ones?
At that time, the devas spoke again, saying:
"How rare! How rare!"
Venerable Prabhāpāla!
This is inconceivable: that within the realm of impermanence, at the moment of passing away, his mind attained eloquence and a singular, penetrating understanding, free from any variation.
Venerable Prabhāpāla!
Furthermore, when all other gods perceive these five signs of decline appearing, their minds immediately become sorrowful and they lose right mindfulness.
The Bodhisattva Rakṣamati further addressed the assembly of devas once more, saying:

"The bodhisattvas who are in their last birth for enlightenment increase their roots of goodness and understand the nature of all realms of existence. Within these merits, they settle their minds in meditative concentration; even when suffering comes to press upon them, they give rise to no afflictions, nor do they act in accordance with that suffering. They are able to give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings."
Then the devas said: "So it is, so it is!
Venerable Ālokamati!"
All sentient beings who, while in that human realm, planted various roots of goodness, are born in this celestial palace; when their merit here is exhausted, they immediately fall back down.
"Ratnaprabhāsa Bodhisattva again addressed the devas, saying:
'For this reason, I perceive these faults among humans and devas.
I shall now descend from here to be born in the human world to extinguish all suffering for all sentient beings of the world.'"
At that time, there was a certain goddess among them who loved and was deeply attached to the Bodhisattva Guhyaprabha; she further addressed another goddess, saying:
"We should go to Jambudvīpa to observe where our lord, the Bodhisattva Guhyaprabha, will take birth."
The celestial maiden said:
"I too now delight in Jambudvīpa. Why is this?"
"Our mistress wishes to be born in that place; therefore, we also vow to be born there.
Then the two goddesses spoke again to one another:
"It is not for the sake of this mistress alone that we vow to be reborn there."

Why is this? When our great lord went to Jambudvīpa, there were immeasurable and boundless sentient beings who planted various roots of goodness; he taught and transformed them through his faith and acceptance. Furthermore, there were immeasurable and boundless sentient beings who cultivated various meritorious deeds and were reborn here.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Five.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Six.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on Reclining in Tuṣita, Part Two:
"At that time, among the assembly of the Tuṣita devas, there was a son of heaven named Suvarṇapiṇḍa, who had frequently descended to the land of Jambudvīpa since ancient times."
Having understood this, the Protector addressed the deva Suvarṇapiṇḍa, saying:
"Suvarṇapiṇḍa, Son of Heaven!
You descend frequently to Jambudvīpa; you ought to know the royal lineages of the cities, towns, and villages there."
"One who has attained birth as a bodhisattva— into what kind of family should such a person be born?
The devaputra Suvarṇapiṇḍa replied,
"Venerable One!"
"I know this very well; listen attentively, Venerable One, and I shall now speak.
Prajñākūṭa replied, "Very well."
The Golden Ball said:
"In this trichiliocosm, there is a site of the Bodhi-maṇḍala located within the borders of Magadha in Jambudvīpa; it is the place where, in the past, various kings attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Venerable Prabhāpāla!

Within that realm there is a river named Gaṅgā. On its southern bank is a mountain, an ancient dwelling place of sages; it is called Viśāla, also known as Paṇḍavapippala, and Gṛdhrakūṭa, which together surround it as its retinue.
That mountain is firm and solid, its color like that of a green mani-jewel. Within it is a village named Śaila-bahula.
Not far from the mountain is a great city named Rājagṛha.

In that city, there was formerly a royal seer named Udupāli, who had served as a king’s counselor for generations. His queen was of the lineage of the Great King Sudarśana and served as his principal consort; their son became king, named Bāhuka, who currently rules over the kingdom of Magadha, succeeding that royal seer Udupāli.
"Venerable Guardian of Light!
You shall be reborn in Jambudvīpa to serve as the eldest son of that king.
The Bodhisattva Guardian of Light replied to Kintuṇa:

"Although this principle exists, that royal lineage is impure in both father and mother; their city is situated on the periphery, where the terrain is hilly and uneven, consisting entirely of ditches and pits, soil, sand, gravel, stones, thorns, and various weeds. There are few springs or ponds, no flowing rivers, and but meager groves of trees, gardens, flowers, and fruit orchards."
"Therefore, you should now further observe other members of the Kṣatriya caste.
The Devaputra Suvarṇapiṇḍa spoke again:
"Venerable Ālokamati!
In that city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśī, there was a royal seer named King Suprabha who had a son called King Sudhanu; that king would have been a fit father for the Venerable One.
The Bodhisattva Pāramitāprabha replied to Kintuṇa:
"While this reasoning is indeed so, the King of Kāśī, that virtuous man, possesses four qualities by which he is stained and attached to false views."
"Therefore, you should now further examine other royal lineages that are worthy of being my place of birth.
The Devaputra Kinkara then spoke again:
"Venerable Ālokamati!

In the city of Śrāvastī in the kingdom of Kośala, there was a king named Virūḍhaka, who was the sovereign of the great kingdom of Kośala; he possessed great physical strength and a vast population, and you, Venerable One, would be worthy to serve as his son.
The Bodhisattva Pāramitāprabhāsa replied to Kintuṇa:

"While this may be true in principle, the King of Kośala, that lord of the country, is of the lineage of the Mātanga clan; he was born from impure and defiled parents, and furthermore, for generations past, he has not been of royal descent. He is narrow-minded and lowly, lacking in noble bearing;
moreover, his household possesses meager wealth, and though he has the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, agate, and pearl—they are not complete."
"Therefore, you should now separately seek for me another kṣatriya clan worthy of being my place of birth.
The Devaputra Suvarṇapiṇḍa spoke again, saying:
"Venerable Ālokamati!
In the city of Kuśāmbī in the kingdom of Vatsa, there was a king named Sahasrājita; that king had a son named Śatasājita.
That king possessed many elephants, horses, and the seven treasures, and was fully equipped with the fourfold army.
"Venerable One, you are worthy to be the son of that king.
The Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatī (Hùmíng) replied to King Jintuán:
"While this may be the case in principle, the mother of King Batsa is not virtuous; she gave birth to this son by following another man, and thus he is not of the true royal lineage."
"However, that king also constantly preached the doctrine of nihilism.
Therefore, you should look elsewhere for another kṣatriya; where shall I be born?
Thus spoke the Devaputra Suvarṇapiṇḍa.

"In this Vajra Country, there is a city named Vaiśālī, where grain and rice are abundant and free from famine; the people are peaceful and happy, and the land is so magnificently adorned that it is no different from a celestial palace."
The king of that city was the son of the King of Trees; his lineage was pure and beyond reproach.
Within the royal palace and treasuries of that king were many gold, silver, and precious jewels; everything was fully provided, lacking nothing at all.
"The Venerable One is worthy to serve as that king's son.
The Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatī (Hùmíng) replied to Jintuán:
"This is indeed the truth; the lords of Vaiśālī have been of true royal lineage since the most remote antiquity."

However, the people of that country are by nature stubborn and headstrong; each acts according to their own will, claiming, "I am the king. Their arrogance is intense, and they are heedless and self-exalting. They do not intermingle with other classes of beings, nor do they observe the etiquette of honor and humility between superiors and inferiors. They say of themselves, "I understand," and "I know. Although there is a king, they are unwilling to serve him, saying, "Our own dharma is correct; we do not seek it from another."
"Therefore, you should now further observe other places among the kṣatriya royal lineages to see into which family I am born.
The Devaputra Kanthaka then spoke these words:
"Venerable Prabhāpāla!
In that country of Māpābandi, there was a city named Ujjayanī, where a prince of the Mingdeng (Pradīpa) lineage named Pūrṇa resided.
That king’s person possessed great majesty and power; he had many attendants and was able to defeat all enemy nations and adversaries.
"Venerable One, you are worthy to serve as that king's son.
The Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatī (Hùmíng) replied to Jintuán:
"While this may be true in principle, that king possesses not a single dharma of conduct to follow; he is severe, cruel, and violent, and does not believe in cause and effect."
"Therefore, you may now further observe other royal lineages and let me choose my place of birth.
The Devaputra Kanaka-mandala spoke again:
"Venerable Prabhāpāla!"
In that Jambudvīpa, in the city of Mathurā, there was a great king named Subāhu, whose son was known as Svayambhū-vīra.
The Venerable One would have been a worthy son for that king.
The Bodhisattva Rakṣaprabha replied to Kintuṇa:

"While this logic is indeed so, that king was born into a family of wrong views; for this reason, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in his final birth before Buddhahood cannot be born into such a family of wrong views."
"Therefore, you should now further examine other royal lineages to see where I might be born.
The Devaputra Kanaka-mandala spoke again, saying:
"Venerable Protector of Light!

This city of Śvetahastināga belongs to the lineage of King Bimbisāra; its inhabitants are valiant and majestic, handsome and pleasing to behold, peerless in the world, and capable of defeating all powerful neighboring enemies.
"Venerable One, you are worthy to serve as that king’s son.
The Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatī replied to King Kanaṅkamaṇḍala:
"While this may be true in principle, the lineage of King Bimbisāra is pure, yet it has been disturbed by various mixed classes."
Why is this? The eldest son of that king was named Udraka Rāmaputra; he was the son of the Dharma-king Brahmā.
The second was named Vimala-Kāśyapa, the prince of the Wind-gods. The third was named Ārāḍa, the son of Śakra.
Furthermore, there were two other sons born of different mothers: one named Nakula and the other named Sahadeva; these two sons were the offspring of the star-god Aśvinī.
"Therefore, you should now further examine other royal lineages to see where I might be born.
The Devaputra Kanaka-mandala then spoke again:
"Venerable Protector of Light!

In that Jambudvīpa, in the city of Maitilā, there was a king of the Maitila clan named Kalyāṇamitra. He possessed an abundance of elephants, horses, chariots, cattle, and sheep; all necessities of life were fully provided for him. His treasuries were overflowing with immeasurable varieties of jewels, and his stores of gold, silver, and pearls were never lacking. That king had a friend who constantly delighted in diligently practicing the deeds of Dharma.
"Venerable One, you are worthy to serve as that king’s son.
Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatī (Hùmíng) replied to King Jintuán:

"This principle is indeed true; although King Śubhavyūha possesses such complete qualities, that king is now aged and infirm, no longer able to manage the affairs of state, and furthermore, the king already has many sons."
"Therefore, you should now further observe other royal lineages to see where I was born.
The Devaputra Golden Ball (Kandarpa) then spoke again:
"These are all kings of the Central Land; furthermore, there are also kings of outlying regions who hold false views."
On the island of Viṣṇu-sāgara, there was a sovereign of a kingdom belonging to the Brahmin caste, who ruled over the region of Viṣṇu; he was named King Yuezhi (Cīna).
His parents were of pure and complete lineage, and he was further proficient in the rites for sacrificing to the various devas and fully understood all four Vedas.
"Venerable One, you are worthy to be that king’s son.
The Bodhisattva Mahāprajñāpāramitā (Hùmíng) replied to Jintuán:
"While this may be true in principle, when I descend to be born, renounce the world, and attain enlightenment, I must do so as a Kṣatriya; I do not wish to be born into that family of Brahmins."
"Therefore, you should now seek only among the kṣatriyas to see where I was born.
The Devaputra Suvarṇapiṇḍa spoke again:

"Throughout all the kingdoms of Jambudvīpa—in every village, in every place of kings, in every hamlet, in every city, and in every settlement—there dwell kṣatriyas in their respective cities, and these kṣatriyas perform all manner of karmic deeds."

"Venerable sir, throughout the course of my journey, I have experienced immeasurable exhaustion and suffering; my mind is bewildered and my thoughts are disordered, such that I can no longer look about at other places.
Even if I were to observe them, I would not be able to describe them in words as I have done."
The Bodhisattva Rakṣaprabha replied to Kintuṇa:
"It is indeed as you say; however, you must select for me a pure family of the kṣatriya caste that is fit to be my place of birth."
The Devaputra Suvarṇapiṇḍa spoke again, saying:
"As I was a venerable one, tormented by suffering and filled with sorrow, I searched everywhere, yet suddenly I forgot one Kṣatriya family."
The Bodhisattva Rakṣaprabha asked Jintuan,
"What is its name? Jintuan replied:

"There was a Kṣatriya whose lineage from the very beginning has been established through the consensus of the great assembly as the race of the Universal Monarchs (Cakravartin) for generation after generation, even down to the descendants of the Ikṣvāku line. His progeny were born into the Śākya clan in that city of Kapilavastu;
his son was named King Siṃhahanu, and his son was named King Śuddhodana, who possesses great renown among all the devas and humans in the world."
"Venerable One, you are worthy to be that king's son.
Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatī (Hùmíng) replied to Jintuán:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Son of Heaven of the Golden Assembly!
You have skillfully observed the royal lineage; I, too, have long intended to be born into this family, and my profound mind is now exactly as you have described."
"Kintuṇa, you should know!
I shall certainly be reborn in that family as a son. Kintuṇa!"
In the past, the family into which a Bodhisattva in his final birth-place was born was endowed with sixty kinds of merit that filled that household.
What are these sixty?
First, that family has been of pure and noble lineage from the beginning;
second, all the sages constantly observe that family;
third, that family does not engage in any evil deeds.
4. All those born into that family are entirely pure.
5. The lineage of that family is authentic and unadulterated.
6. The ancestral succession of that family is passed down through direct descent without interruption.
Seventh, that family has never interrupted the royal lineage since ancient times.
Eighth, all the kings born into that family have deeply planted roots of goodness in the past.
Ninth, those born into that family are constantly praised by all the noble ones.
10. Those born into that family possess great majesty and virtue.
11. That family has many handsome women.
12. That family has many wise sons.
13. Those born into that family have minds that are disciplined and compliant.
14. Those born into that family are free from frivolity and mischief.
15. Those born into that family have nothing to fear.
Seventeenth, those born into that family are never timid or weak.
Eighteenth, those born into that family are intelligent and possess great wisdom.
Nineteenth, those born into that family have extensive knowledge of the arts and crafts.
19. Those born into that family all fear transgressions and offenses.
20. Those born into that family do not engage in worldly crafts and skills, nor do they covet wealth for the sake of their livelihood.
Twenty-one: Those born into such families always maintain their friendships.
Twenty-two: Those born into such families do not sustain their lives by killing insects or beasts.
23. That family lineage is ever mindful of kindness and righteousness.
24. That family clan is capable of practicing austerities.
25. Those born into that family do not follow after others.
26. Those born into that family never harbor resentment. 27.
Those born into that family do not form deluded thoughts.
28. Those born into that family do not comply with others out of fear.
29. Those born into that family fear harming others.
30. Those born into that family are free from the affliction of sin.
31. Those born into that family obtain much almsfood.
32. Those who go to that house are never sent away empty-handed.
33. That house is stubborn and difficult to subdue. 34.
The laws and customs of that house always issue forth in accordance with ritual and discipline.
35. That family always delights in practicing generosity toward sentient beings.
36. That family establishes the exertion of cause and effect. 37.
Those born into that family are brave and robust in the world.
38. That household constantly makes offerings to all the sages and holy ones.
39. That household constantly makes offerings to the spirits.
40. That household constantly makes offerings to the devas.
41. That family constantly makes offerings to great beings. 42.
Throughout successive generations, that family has never had enemies or rivals. 43.
The fame and majesty of that family resound throughout the ten directions.
That family is the foremost among all families (44).
Those born into that family have been of noble lineage from time immemorial (45).
Those born into that family are the foremost among the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa); this is the forty-sixth [point].
Those born into that family are always of the lineage of the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings (cakravartin-rāja); this is the forty-seventh [point].
Those born into that family are of the lineage of persons of great majesty and power (48).
Those born into that family are surrounded by a vast and immeasurable retinue (49).
Fifty-first: Those born into that family have a retinue that cannot be divided.
Those born into that family have a retinue that surpasses all other people.
Fifty-two: Those born into that family shall all filially support their mothers.
Fifty-three: Those born into that family shall all be filial and obedient to their fathers.
Fifty-four: Those born into that family shall all provide offerings to all śramaṇas.
55. All those born into that family shall provide offerings to all the brahmins. 56.
Those born into that family shall have an abundance of the five grains, with their storehouses overflowing.
Those born into that family possess much gold, silver, mother-of-pearl, and agate; they lack nothing among all their resources and wealth (57).
Those born into that family keep many male and female slaves, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; everything is fully provided (58).
Those born into such families have never served others (59).
Those born into such families possess all such necessities in abundance, lacking nothing within the world (60).
"O Son of Heaven, Jintuan!

Whenever a Bodhisattva who is in his final birth before enlightenment dwells within a mother's womb, that mother must possess thirty-two marks to be capable of sustaining the Bodhisattva in her womb."
What are the thirty-two matters?
First, that mother gives birth to one of upright virtue.
Second, that mother possesses complete limbs and physical faculties.
Third, that mother is one whose virtuous conduct is without flaw.
Fourth, that mother is one who has obtained a favorable place of birth.
Fifth, that mother is one whose actions are nearly perfect.
Sixth, that mother shall be of pure lineage.
Seventh, that mother shall be of incomparable beauty.
Eighth, that mother shall be renowned for her virtuous name.
Ninth, that woman’s physical form and features are well-proportioned from top to bottom.
Tenth, that woman has never given birth before.
Eleventh, that woman possesses great merit.
12. That mother constantly dwells upon matters of happiness.
13. That mother’s mind always accords with all wholesome deeds.
14. That mother possesses no perverse thoughts.
Fifteenth, that mother’s body, speech, and mind were naturally disciplined.
Sixteenth, that mother’s mind was free from fear.
Seventeenth, that mother possessed great learning and dhāraṇī-retention.
18. That mother is extremely skilled in the arts;
19. that mother’s mind is free from flattery and crookedness;
20. that mother’s mind is free from deception and fraud.
Twenty-first: that mother’s mind is free from anger.
Twenty-second: that mother’s mind is free from jealousy.
Twenty-third: that mother’s mind is free from stinginess.
Twenty-fourth, that mother’s mind is not hurried or impetuous.
Twenty-fifth, that mother’s mind is difficult to turn back from its resolve.
Twenty-sixth, that mother’s body possesses the marks of supreme virtue.
Twenty-seventh: that mother is able to harbor patience in her heart.
Twenty-eighth: that mother possesses a sense of shame and a dread of blame.
Twenty-ninth: that mother’s conduct is characterized by a thinning of lust, anger, and delusion.
Thirtieth: That mother conducts herself without transgressing the prohibitions of her husband’s family.
Thirty-first: That mother conducts herself with filial obedience toward her husband.
Thirty-second: That mother gives birth to all virtues; she is fully endowed with all noble qualities and practices.
Such a woman alone is capable of bearing a Bodhisattva in his final birth before attaining Buddhahood.

When the Bodhisattva desires to enter the mother’s womb, he selects the day of the lunar mansion Ārdrā; only then does he enter the womb. Prior to the Bodhisattva’s entry into the womb, the mother must observe the eightfold precepts (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa); only then does the Bodhisattva enter her womb.
The Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatī (Rakṣa-vidyā) spoke again, saying:

"I now take up existence not for the sake of any worldly wealth, the five desires, or pleasures; I descend to the human realm to undergo this one life solely because I desire to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings and out of compassion for those who suffer."
At that time, among the assembly there was a goddess who said to another goddess:
"Our Great Lord, the Bodhisattva Rāhula, will surely descend to the human realm;
we shall be separated from this palace and from the Mahāsattva Rāhula!"
"How can I cause my heart to find joy in this place?
The second heavenly maiden immediately replied to him,
saying, "Alas, alas!"
"What shall we do together now so that we may go to the human world and clearly observe the dwelling place where the Bodhisattva Guhyaprajña has been born?"
A third celestial maiden further spoke, saying:
"We pray that we may now relinquish this celestial lifespan and be reborn in that place.
For what reason?..."
"We also wish to go to that place and be born together with the Bodhisattva Guhmatiprajñā.
A fourth heavenly maiden spoke again:
"Do not harbor any regrets among yourselves."
"Why is this? Even our great lord, the Bodhisattva Mahāprabhāsa, has renounced his celestial lifespan to be born among humans; how much more so should we?
Furthermore, another celestial maiden spoke, saying:
"Venerable Protector of Light!
You are now descending to be born in Jambudvīpa; we pray only that you, Great Being, will not forget us!"
Then the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra addressed those goddesses, saying: "Do not give rise to such great suffering.
Previously, I have already explained to you that all places of existence are entirely impermanent; they are like the trunk of a plantain tree, lacking any solid core;
they are like borrowed goods that must be returned to their owner and do not belong to oneself."
They are like a mirage, an illusion, or a bubble of water;
all places of existence are deceptive,
yet the foolish claim they are born into permanence.
At that time, there was a son of heaven among the assembly who was despondent and sorrowful in heart, and he cried out again:
"Behold the places of birth described by this Bodhisattva; they are impermanent and not true. Alas for us!"
Why should we take pleasure in this place of birth?

We now behold the Bodhisattva Mahāprajñā, whose body is fully endowed with such merit, born in the Tuṣita Heaven; this Tuṣita Palace possesses such a mass of blessings, such beauty, such subtlety, and such magnificence.
"Protector of Light Bodhisattva has abandoned us and descended to be born below;
alas for us! Why are we alone here in this realm of impermanence?
At that time, another second devaputra replied to that first, initial devaputra, saying:
"Excellent, O Son of Heaven!
It is so, it is so, just as you have said.
And he spoke in verse:
"This Great Bodhisattva Guardian of Light, in former times while dwelling within the various realms of existence,
constantly renounced those most dearly loved— wives and children, servants, elephants, horses, wealth, and treasures;
or else he cut away from his own body the flesh and bones, the head, eyes, marrow, brain, blood, and skin."
"In this way, whatever is requested, I shall not refuse; whether it be a hundred or a thousand, I shall give it all.
At that time, another son of heaven among the assembly spoke these verses:
"Alas! Our bodies have been born here in this celestial palace."
I am constantly afraid that I shall now fall; human beings fear death in the same way.
How could there be anyone within the realm of conditioned phenomena whose meritorious karma is not exhausted?
Within these realms of impermanence, all sentient beings must reach the end of their lives.
The Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra addressed the devas, saying:
"O you gods and humans!
You must know that all in the world has separation and birth-and-death as its foundation; for my sake, do not grieve or lament."
Why is this? Since the distant past, I have never committed the karma of an ordinary person; therefore, it is utterly impossible for me to remain in the world for long as I now desire.
In the presence of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha of the past, I planted various roots of goodness, constantly gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, and made great vows.
"Now that you have obtained this favorable retribution and shall attain Bodhi, you ought to rejoice;
why do you suffer in distress? When those devas heard these words, they said to one another: "O you devas!..."
He gazed intently at the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Guhyaprajña, and as he did so, he said: "This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Guhyaprajña will soon descend to the human realm.
He further proclaimed aloud:
"Venerable Guhyaprajña!"
"Venerable One, before long you will be born among humans; all the majesty and splendor of this Tuṣita Palace, as well as the blessings of the devas, you shall take with you.
Venerable One, when you receive a final body in the human realm, how shall we devas serve you?"
The Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatī (Hùmíng) addressed all those hosts of devas, saying:

"Regarding the five signs of decay that appeared before me, and the causes and conditions of impermanence that you have further explained—such a Dharma-gate, you must always keep in mind and never allow it to be forgotten."
"I shall now descend from this place to be born among humans, where I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and turn the unsurpassed, most wondrous Wheel of Dharma."
"You gods! You should each vow to descend to the human realm to receive a body; once you have been born there, you shall attain liberation from all the suffering of the various afflictions."

"At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatī-Abhaya had observed the family of his birth, there was a celestial palace in Tuṣita Heaven named High Banner (Ucchada), sixty yojanas in length and breadth, perfectly equal in all dimensions. From time to time, the Bodhisattva would ascend to that palace and expound the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of the Tuṣita devas."
At that time, the Bodhisattva ascended to that palace; having sat down comfortably, he addressed the devaputras of Tuṣita, saying:
"O you devas!..."
"You should all assemble here.

Before long, my body shall descend to the human realm. I now wish to expound a Dharma-gate of illumination called 'The Expedient Means for Entering the Characteristics of All Dharmas,' which I leave behind to teach and transform you. Because you will remember me at the very end, if you hear this Dharma-gate, you should give rise to joy."

At that time, having heard these words of the Bodhisattva, the great assembly of the gods of Tuṣita, along with their celestial jade maidens and all their retinues, gathered together and ascended to that palace.

When the Bodhisattva Dhṛtaprabha saw that the assembly of devas had finished gathering and desired to preach the Dharma for them, he immediately manifested another celestial palace above the original palace of the High Banner. It was tall, vast, and expansive, covering the four continents; it was delightful, subtle and wondrous, upright and peerless, with majestic and towering splendor, adorned with every kind of jewel. Among all the palaces of the heavens in the realm of desire, there was none to compare with it.
When the devas of the form realm saw that transformed palace, they conceived a perception of their own palaces as being like charnel grounds.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatī (Guiming) had already practiced the true path in the past, planted various roots of goodness, perfected his accumulation of merit, and was fully endowed with virtues; he ascended and sat upon a majestic lion throne that had been prepared for him.

The Bodhisattva Rāhula sat upon that lion throne, which was interspersed with the adornments of immeasurable jewels; various kinds of celestial garments, infinite and boundless, were spread over the seat, and it was perfumed with various exquisite incenses. Immeasurable and boundless jewel censers burned incense, and various subtle and wondrous fragrant flowers were scattered upon the ground.
Surrounding the high seat were hundreds of thousands of millions of various precious jewels, which were adorned with radiating light that illuminated that palace.
Above and below that palace, it was covered by nets of jewels, and from those nets hung many golden bells.
The various golden bells there emitted subtle and wondrous sounds.
From that great jewel palace, moreover, issued forth immeasurable varieties of light.
Above that jeweled palace, ten million banners and canopies of diverse exquisite colors shone forth, covering it completely.
In that great palace, countless, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of canopies were suspended.

Celestial maidens each held various kinds of seven-jeweled musical instruments, performing music and offering praise, recounting the immeasurable and boundless merits of the Bodhisattva from his past lives.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of the Four World-Protecting Kings stood at his left and right to guard that palace;
tens of millions of Śakras prostrated before that palace;
and tens of millions of Brahmās paid reverent homage to that palace.
Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas protect and uphold that palace;
and tens of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas from the ten directions guard and mindfully attend that palace.

Throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, the various pāramitās he has practiced have brought about the fulfillment of their karmic rewards; with all causal conditions complete, his merit increases day and night, and he is adorned by immeasurable virtues—thus it is, thus it is, beyond description, beyond description.
That great and subtle lion throne; the Bodhisattva, having ascended it, addressed all the hosts of devas, saying:
"O you devas!..."

Now, regarding these one hundred and eight dharma-gates of illumination: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is in his final birth before attaining Buddhahood resides in the Tuṣita Heaven and intends to descend to take birth among humans, he must first proclaim and expound these one hundred and eight dharma-gates of illumination before the celestial assembly. He does so to leave them as a reminder for the devas, and only thereafter does he descend to be born.
"You gods! Now listen attentively and receive this with a sincere mind; I shall now speak of it.
What are the one hundred and eight Dharma-gates of Illumination?"
“Right faith is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it prevents the mind from being broken or made unyielding.
‘A pure mind is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it is free from turbidity and defilement.’”
"Joy is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it brings peace to the mind.
Delight is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it purifies the mind."
“‘Purity of physical conduct is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it purifies the three karmas.
‘Purity of verbal conduct is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it severs the four evils.’”
“Purifying mental conduct is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it cuts off the three poisons.
‘Mindfulness of the Buddha is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it contemplates the purity of the Buddha.”
“Mindfulness of the Dharma is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it brings about the purity of observing the Dharma.
Mindfulness of the Sangha is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it results in the firm stability of attaining the Path.”
“Recollection of giving is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it does not look for karmic retribution.
Recollection of precepts is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because all vows are fully fulfilled.”
“Mindfulness of the devas is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it gives rise to the vast mind.
‘Loving-kindness is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it excellently encompasses the roots of goodness in all places of birth.”
“‘Compassion (karuṇā) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it does not harm sentient beings.
‘Joy (muditā) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it relinquishes all things that are unpleasant.’”
“‘Equanimity’ is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it brings about weary detachment from the five desires.
‘Contemplation of impermanence’ is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it contemplates the desires of the three realms.”
“Contemplation of suffering is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it cuts off all cravings.
Contemplation of non-self is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it prevents attachment to a self.”
“‘Tranquil contemplation’ is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it prevents the mind and its thoughts from being disturbed.
‘Shame and remorse’ are gateways to the light of the Dharma, for they bring tranquility to the inner mind.”
“‘Moral shame (hrī) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it extinguishes external evils.
‘Truthfulness (satya) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it does not deceive gods or humans.’”
“‘Truth (satya) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it does not deceive oneself.
‘Dharma-practice (dharmacaryā) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it accords with the practice of the Dharma.’”
“‘The Three Refuges is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it purifies the three evil realms.
‘Knowing gratitude is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it does not abandon roots of goodness.’”
“‘Requiting gratitude is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it does not involve deceiving others.
‘Not deceiving oneself is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it does not involve praising oneself.’”
"To act for the sake of sentient beings is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it does not disparage others.
To act for the sake of the Dharma is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because one acts in accordance with the Dharma."
“Knowing the proper time is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because one does not speak frivolously.
‘Subduing the conceit of self is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because wisdom is thereby fulfilled.’”
“Not giving rise to an evil mind is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it protects oneself and protects others.
‘Being without obstruction is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because the mind is free from doubt and confusion.’”
“Faith and understanding (adhimukti) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it brings definitive resolution regarding the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
‘The meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it abandons the mind stained by desire.’”
“‘Non-contention is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it severs anger and litigation.
‘Non-delusion is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it severs the taking of life.’”
"Delighting in the meaning of the Dharma is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it seeks the meaning of the Dharma.
'Loving the light of the Dharma is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it attains the gateway to the light of the Dharma."
“Seeking much learning is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it leads to the correct contemplation of the characteristics of phenomena.
‘Correct skillful means is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it brings about the perfection of right practice.”
“Knowing name and form is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it removes all obstructions.
‘Removing views of causes is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it leads to liberation.”
“‘The mind free from enmity or affection is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it gives rise to equanimity toward both enemies and kin.
‘Skillfulness regarding the aggregates is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it brings knowledge of all suffering.’”
"The equality of all great elements is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it severs all compounded phenomena.
'The sense bases are a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for they cultivate the true path.'"
“‘The patience regarding non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it realizes the truth of cessation (nirodha-satya).
‘Mindfulness of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for all phenomena are quiescent.’”
“The foundation of mindfulness of feeling is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it severs all feelings.
“The foundation of mindfulness of mind is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it contemplates the mind as being like an illusion.”
“The application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for wisdom is thereby free from obscuration.
“The four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for they sever all evils and bring about the fulfillment of all virtues.”
“The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because body and mind are light.
“The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because one does not follow the words of others.”
“The faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it skillfully attains all forms of knowledge.
“The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it skillfully performs all karmic actions.”
“The faculty of concentration is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it purifies the mind.
“The faculty of wisdom is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it brings about the direct vision of all phenomena.”
“‘The power of faith is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it transcends all demonic powers.
‘The power of diligence is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it is non-retrogressive.’”
“Mindfulness is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it is not shared with others.
Concentration is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it severs all discursive thoughts.”
"The power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it is free from the two extremes.
"The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it is the knowledge of all phenomena as they truly are."
“The factor of awakening of discrimination of phenomena is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it illuminates all phenomena.
“The factor of awakening of diligence is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it brings about thorough knowledge of awakening.”
“The factor of enlightenment of joy is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it brings about the attainment of all meditative concentrations.
“The factor of enlightenment of equanimity is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for that which was to be done has been accomplished.”
“The factor of awakening of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it brings knowledge of the equality of all phenomena.
“The factor of awakening of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it engenders weary detachment from all birth.”
“Right view is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it attains the noble path that brings the exhaustion of outflows.
Right discernment is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it severs all conceptualization and abides in non-conceptualization.”
“Right Speech is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for one knows that all names, sounds, and languages are like echoes.
“Right Action is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for there is neither action nor retribution.”
“‘Right livelihood is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it eliminates all evil destinies.
‘Right conduct is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it leads to the further shore.’”
“Right mindfulness is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it does not give rise to thoughts regarding any phenomena.
Right concentration is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it attains the samādhi of non-distraction.”
“Bodhicitta is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it ensures that the Three Jewels are never interrupted.
‘Reliance is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it does not delight in the Lesser Vehicle.’”
“Right faith is a gate to the illumination of the Dharma, for it attains the most supreme Buddha-dharmas.
‘Progress is a gate to the illumination of the Dharma, for it brings to fulfillment all dharmas of the various roots of goodness.’”

“The perfection of giving is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it brings to fulfillment in every thought-moment the marks and signs that adorn the Buddha-lands and transforms sentient beings who are stingy and greedy.”

"The perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is a gate to the light of the Dharma, for it teaches and transforms those sentient beings who violate the precepts, causing them to distance themselves from the difficulties of the evil realms.

"The perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is a gate to the light of the Dharma, for it abandons all anger, pride, flattery, crookedness, and frivolity, thereby teaching and transforming such evil sentient beings."
“The perfection of vigor is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it fully attains all wholesome dharmas and transforms those sentient beings who are indolent.

“The perfection of meditation is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it accomplishes all meditative concentrations and supernormal powers and transforms those sentient beings who are distracted.”
“Prajñāpāramitā is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it severs the darkness of ignorance and attachment to various views, and brings to spiritual maturity all deluded sentient beings.
‘Upāya is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it manifests and teaches in accordance with the conduct perceived by sentient beings, thereby accomplishing all the Buddha-dharmas.”

“The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for they gather in all sentient beings so that, having attained awakening, one may bestow the Dharma upon all sentient beings.”
"Teaching and transforming sentient beings is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for one does not seek personal pleasure and remains free from weariness.
'Upholding the True Dharma is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it severs all the afflictions of all sentient beings.'"
“‘The accumulation of merit is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it benefits all sentient beings.
‘Cultivating dhyāna is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it fulfills the ten powers.’”
“‘Tranquility (śamatha) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it brings about the fulfillment of the Tathāgata’s samādhis.
‘Insight (vipaśyanā) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, because it brings about the fulfillment of wisdom.’”
"Entering unimpeded eloquence is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it brings about the accomplishment of the Dharma-eye.
Entering all modes of conduct is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it brings about the accomplishment of the Buddha-eye."
“‘The accomplishment of dhāraṇī is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it enables one to hear and uphold all the teachings of the Buddhas.
‘Attaining unimpeded eloquence is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it causes all sentient beings to rejoice.’”
“‘Patience in accordance with reality (anulomikī-kṣānti) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for it accords with all the teachings of the Buddhas.

“‘Attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma, for one thereby receives the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).’”
“The stage of non-retrogression is a gateway to the illumination of the Dharma, for it fulfills all the qualities of the Buddhas of the past.
‘The wisdom that proceeds from one stage to the next is a gateway to the illumination of the Dharma, for it accomplishes the empowerment of omniscience.’”

“The Stage of Empowerment (Abhiṣeka-bhūmi) is a gateway to the illumination of the Dharma, for it leads from the renunciation of worldly life up until the attainment of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).”
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra had spoken these words, he addressed all the hosts of devas, saying:
"Devas, you should know!
These are the one hundred and eight gateways to the illumination of the Dharma (dharmāloka-mukha), which I leave behind for you, the devas."
"You all should receive and uphold this, constantly recollect it in your minds, and do not let it be forgotten.
*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll Six;
*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Five: Descending into the Royal Palace.

At that time, after the winter season had passed and it was the most excellent beginning of spring, all the trees were in full bloom; the weather was clear and bright, with a temperate balance of warmth and coolness. The myriad grasses had newly emerged, glossy, supple, and harmonious, flourishing and radiant as they covered the ground. At the precise moment when the lunar mansion of Mṛgaśiras (the Deer) was in conjunction with the moon, for the sake of those devas, he preached the essentials of the Dharma, causing their hearts to be filled with love, joy, and delight, so overflowing with exultation that they could not contain themselves.

He exhorted and admonished the devas, causing them to practice this Dharma; he taught them to cultivate weary detachment from all conditioned existence—birth, old age, sickness, and death—and to seek the unsurpassed Dharma.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaprabha observed that assembly of devas; like a lion king about to descend to take birth, his mind was tranquil, undaunted, fearless, and unperturbed. He further addressed the assembly of devas once more, saying:
"All you devas, you must know this!
"This is my final birth; it is the last body I shall receive.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, with right mindfulness and a single-minded focus, descended from Tuṣita.

Unlike other devas who, when relinquishing their celestial lifespan, give rise to great sorrow and suffering due to separation from the five desires and lose their right mindfulness; [the Bodhisattva did not].
When the Bodhisattva descends, it is not like this; when the Bodhisattva descends, he is endowed with all inconceivable and rare qualities.
As the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha descended from heaven, the various devas, out of their remembrance of the Bodhisattva, wept all at once, crying:
"Alas! How bitter!"
Alas, how bitter!

Having lost the Bodhisattva Pradīpadāna, from this day forth we shall never again hear the True Dharma; our merit and benefit will diminish, and the very root of birth and death will now increase further.
At that time, the Śuddhāvāsa devas addressed all the hosts of devas, saying:
"Now that you see the Bodhisattva Guhyaprabha about to descend to be born, do not give rise to grief or distress."
Why is this? Because when he descends to be born below, he will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; having attained it, he will return to this celestial palace to preach the Dharma for you.

Just as in the past, the Buddhas Vipaśyin, Śikhin Tathāgata, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa Tathāgata—all those Buddhas departed from here; yet out of compassion for you, they have all returned to this celestial palace to preach the Dharma for you and to take you under their care.
"Now this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, Guardian of Light (Rakṣaprajñā), has come back just as before to gather and transform you, no different from what occurred previously.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, Guardian of Light, descended at night to take birth and was about to enter the womb of Lady Māyā, Lady Māyā addressed King Śuddhodana on that very night, saying:
"Great King!..."

You should know that from this night forth, I wish to undertake the pure eightfold precepts of restraint, namely: not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, not using double-tongued speech, not using harsh words, and not engaging in idle chatter.
Furthermore, I vow not to be greedy, not to harbor anger, not to be deluded, and not to give rise to wrong views.
I shall maintain right view; all such precepts and rules of fasting, I shall receive and uphold.
"I shall now fix my mindfulness and constantly practice with diligence; toward all sentient beings, I shall give rise to a heart of loving-kindness.
At that time, King Śuddhodana replied to Queen Mahāmāyā, saying:
"Whatever your heart desires and delights in, you may act according to your will."
"I shall now also renounce the position of a king and follow wherever you go.
And there is a verse that says:
"The King, seeing the Bodhisattva’s mother, rose from his seat with reverence."
"As toward a mother or a sister, let no thoughts of desire arise in the mind.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatī (Huiming) descended from Tuṣita with single-minded right mindfulness, entrusting himself to the right side of Queen Māyā, the chief consort of King Śuddhodana, entering with calm composure.

When the Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatīputra, with right mindfulness and right awareness, descended from Tuṣita Heaven to enter his mother’s womb, at that time the light of devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—indeed, the light of the entire world—shone everywhere. Furthermore, even those regions outside the world that were dark and gloomy, where the sun and moon, despite their great power and majestic majesty, could not penetrate nor reach with their light, were all fully illuminated by the radiance of this Bodhisattva, whose virtue surpassed them all.
All the sentient beings dwelling in that place said to one another, "How is it that there are suddenly sentient beings here?

At that time, this earth shook in six ways: namely, rising in the east and sinking in the west; rising in the west and sinking in the east; rising in the south and sinking in the north; rising in the north and sinking in the south; rising at the edges and sinking in the center; and rising in the center and sinking at the edges. Thus, even including the signs of trembling, roaring, and so forth, all eighteen kinds of manifestations appeared everywhere.

Next, furthermore, there were a thousand Sumeru Kings of Mountains, all of which shook; a thousand Nimiṃdhara Kings of Mountains, a thousand Dhṛtiparvata Kings of Mountains, a thousand Kālaparvata Kings of Mountains, a thousand Vinataka Kings of Mountains, a thousand Aśvakarṇa Kings of Mountains, a thousand Nimindhara Kings of Mountains, a thousand Sudarśana Kings of Mountains, a thousand Cakravāḍa Kings of Mountains, and a thousand Mahācakravāḍa Kings of Mountains—all such mountains as these shook completely.

Furthermore, all other minor mountains surged, submerged, rose, and fell; they were rugged, jagged, and towering, emitting great clouds of smoke. The four great oceans and other various ponds displayed vast, surging billows as massive waves boiled and surged forth.
The four great rivers—the Ganges, the Sindhu, the Sītā, and the Vakṣu—along with all other waters, all flowed upstream.
All groves, all trees, all medicinal herbs, and all seasonal crops became lush and thick, flourishing and thriving.
Downward even unto the sentient beings suffering in the Avīci hell, all receive happiness.

"For this reason, from the moment the Bodhisattva first descends from Tuṣita, he emits a great light that illuminates all worlds, causing all that is obscure, dark, and hidden to become bright and manifest; this serves as a prior auspicious sign for when, in the future, having attained the Way of the Buddha, he shall universally illuminate all ignorant and deluded sentient beings with the wisdom-light of the Four Noble Truths."

When the Bodhisattva first descended from Tuṣita, the great earth shook in six ways and eighteen manners, and the kings of mountains emitted great clouds of smoke, while the four great oceans surged with boiling waves.
Therefore, for the sake of all evil sentient beings in future ages who have sunk into the mire of the defilements and turbidity of afflictions, the Tathāgata,
having attained the Way, desires to pull them out and place them upon the shore of Nirvāṇa.

"When the Bodhisattva first descended from Tuṣita, all the waters flowed in reverse; therefore, for the sake of sentient beings of evil nature in future ages who follow along with and drown in the current of afflictions, the Tathāgata, having attained enlightenment, preaches the Dharma to deliver all sentient beings, causing them to return to their origin and go against the current of birth and death."
When the Bodhisattva first descended from Tuṣita, he was able to cause all trees, medicinal herbs, and forests to grow; he caused them all to become lush, succulent, and flourishing.

"For the sake of sentient beings of evil nature in future ages who have not yet planted roots of goodness, I shall cause them to plant roots of goodness; for those who have already planted roots of goodness, I shall cause them to attain liberation.
When the Bodhisattva first descends from Tuṣita Heaven, even the sentient beings in the Avīci Hell all experience happiness;
once the Buddha has attained enlightenment, he causes all sentient beings to be liberated from suffering and affliction and to receive happiness."
For these reasons, he first manifested such auspicious signs.
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva descended from Tuṣita, he entered the womb through her right side; other sentient beings enter through the birth canal.

"The Buddha has attained the Way and, for the sake of all sentient beings, preaches the pure Dharma, turning them away from error and leading them into the right path; this is the first manifestation of auspicious signs.
The Bodhisattva, with right mindfulness, descended from Tuṣita Heaven and took up residence in the right side of Queen Māyā, the chief consort of King Śuddhodana."

At that time, while the Great Queen was asleep, she dreamed that a six-tusked white elephant with a vermilion head and seven limbs touching the ground—its tusks adorned with gold—descended through the air and entered her right side.
After the lady had finished her dream, she addressed King Śuddhodana the following morning, saying:

"Great King, you should know that last night I had such a dream: when he entered my right side, I experienced a bliss never before known. From this day forward, I truly have no further need for worldly pleasures."
"Regarding this auspicious dream omen, which master of divination is able to interpret it for me?
At that time, King Śuddhodana summoned a female attendant of the inner palace and addressed her, saying:

"Go quickly to the outer court and proclaim my decree, telling my national preceptor, the son of Dhanamjaya, to urgently summon the eight great Brahmin masters of divination—namely Yajñadatta, Somadatta, Īśvaradatta, Viṣṇudatta, Brahmādatta, and others—and let the three sons of the elder Kāśyapa come at once."
Then that messenger addressed the king, saying:
"As the Great King commands, I dare not disobey.
At that time, the messenger, having received the Great King’s order, went before the palace gate and proclaimed in a loud voice:
"Who is at the gate? Is there any Brahmin who has entered the palace?

At that time, there was a Brahmin youth on duty at the gate, of the Vatsa clan, named Rāyaṇa (which in the language of Sui means "House"); he replied to the palace supervisor’s messenger, saying, "I am here."
The messenger said:
"By the command of the Great King, eight great Brahmins capable of interpreting dreams—namely Yajñadeva, Kāśyapīputra, and the others—are summoned."

The messenger delivered the message, and upon hearing the words of the housekeeper, the state preceptor Mahānāman’s son immediately summoned the eight Brahmin masters of dream interpretation, along with Mahānāman the state preceptor’s son, to enter the palace together.
At that time, King Śuddhodana addressed the Brahmins who were skilled in interpreting dreams, saying:
"Last night, the Queen had this extraordinary dream; what kind of omen is this?"
"What signs or omens are there?

Then those Brahmins who interpreted dreams, having heard the king's words, being well-versed in all physical marks and skilled in divining the auspiciousness of dreams, immediately addressed King Śuddhodana in detail:
"Great King, listen well to the auspicious signs of the dream; we shall explain them fully."
"As I have seen it recorded in the ancient scriptures and texts of the seers and devas,
I shall speak in verse:
'If a woman dreams that the Sun God enters her right side,' " he said.
The son born of that mother will surely become a wheel-turning monarch.
If a woman dreams that the Moon God enters her right side,
the son born of that mother will be the most excellent among all kings.
If a mother sees in a dream a white elephant entering her right side,
the son born of that mother shall be the Most Honored One in the three realms, peerless and infinite.
He shall be able to benefit all sentient beings, treating enemies and kin with equal impartiality.
"Deliver ten million beings from the deep sea of afflictions.
At that time, the Brahmin master who interpreted dreams addressed the Great King, saying:
"The dream the Queen has had is of most auspicious signs!"
"Great King, you should now rejoice; the child born of your lady shall surely be a holy son. In the future, he will certainly attain the Way of the Buddha, and his fame will reach far and wide."
At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the brahmin masters who interpreted dreams, King Śuddhodana was filled with great joy; he leaped for joy immeasurably, unable to contain himself.

At that time, the king prepared immeasurable delicacies and foods of a hundred flavors—things to be sucked, nibbled, licked, and sipped, as well as various cakes, fruits, and other provisions; the brahmin ate them to his heart's content.
When the meal was finished, King Śuddhodana again took immeasurable wealth, money, and precious objects to offer as alms.

At that time, after King Śuddhodana had heard these predictions from the physiognomists regarding the Queen’s dream—that it was an auspicious and fortunate omen—he immediately established great sites for unrestricted assemblies (*anāvaraṇa-mahāpariṣad*) outside the four gates of the city of Kapilavastu, as well as at crossroads, street corners, lanes, alleys, and wherever people traveled. To all who came and required anything, he gave everything: food to those needing food, drink to those needing drink, clothing to those needing clothing, incense to those needing incense, garlands to those needing garlands, as well as unguents, powdered incense, garments, bedding, mats, cushions, houses, dwellings, cattle, sheep, elephants, horses, and carriages; whatever anyone required, he gave it all to them.
He made various offerings such as these, all for the purpose of providing benefit and support to the Bodhisattva.

At that time, there was a seer in that place named Asita, who was able to establish the various doctrines of the non-Buddhists; having renounced the five desires, he possessed great majestic power and great spiritual strength, was endowed with the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and could constantly reach the assembly hall of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, entering it at will.
That rishi mostly resided in the city of Campā in the kingdom of South India; not far from there was a grove called Vardhana, where the rishi practiced the way of the sages within that forest.
All the people of the kingdom of Magadha unanimously said,
"This seer Asita is an Arhat.
All the people of the kingdom of Magadha held that seer in high esteem and respect, honoring and serving him.
At that time, whatever knowledge and understanding that seer possessed, he taught it all to others; having realized and seen it himself, he taught others so that they might see it as well.
At that time, in that village, there was a young boy named Nārada.
As Nārada gradually grew older and reached the age of eight, his mother entrusted him to the seer Asita, intending for him to become his disciple.
At that time, the boy served, honored, revered, and attended upon the seer Asita with the full etiquette of a disciple, never ceasing for even a moment.
At that time, the seer was in the Vardhamāna forest, practicing with diligence day and night, sitting in meditation with his mind composed, together with the youth Nārada;
the attendant youth Nārada stood behind the seer, holding a fly-whisk to drive away mosquitoes and gadflies.

"When the Bodhisattva descended from Tuṣita Heaven with right mindfulness into the palace of King Śuddhodana, entering the womb through the right side of the queen, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated all worlds of humans and devas; furthermore, this great earth shook in six ways and eighteen modes."

At that time, Asita beheld an unprecedented and marvelous phenomenon of diverse radiances; he further saw this earth tremble in six ways, and his heart was struck with great terror such that the hairs on his body all stood erect. He thought to himself:
"By what cause and condition does this great earth now shake?"
"What will be the karmic retribution?

At that time, the seer reflected for a short while and remained silent. Having contemplated with right mindfulness and right concentration until he understood, joy arose in his heart; he leaped for immeasurable delight, unable to contain himself, and uttered these words:
"How rare! A Great Sage, inconceivable, shall appear in the world—a Mahāpuruṣa."

"When the Bodhisattva first descended from Tuṣita and entered his mother’s right side, having completed the entry into the womb, there was a deva named Swift-Gone who went to all the hells and proclaimed in a loud voice:
'All of you people, you must know this: the Bodhisattva is now descending from Tuṣita to enter his mother’s womb; therefore, you should quickly make a vow, wishing to be born in the human world.'"

When the sentient beings in the hells heard these words, all those who had planted roots of goodness in the past but had also created mixed karma—falling into hell because their evil was predominant—each beheld one another’s faces. They grew weary of and detached from the hells, and furthermore obtained light, so that their bodies and minds became peaceful and joyful. Moreover, they heard the sound of the various devas of the world who were swiftly approaching.
Having cast off their bodies as hell-beings, they were immediately reborn among humans.
All the sentient beings within the trichiliocosm who had planted roots of goodness in the past all came to this city of Kapilavastu and took birth on its four sides.
"When the Bodhisattva had finished entering his mother’s womb, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Four Heavenly Kings—Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Vaiśravaṇa—each said to one another:
'O worthy ones, you should know!'"

Since the Bodhisattva has already descended from Tuṣita Heaven and entered his mother’s womb, we must now protect and guard him, ensuring that no other humans or non-humans cause him distress or seek an opportunity to harm him.
"This present Bodhisattva possesses only such supreme majesty and virtue that the devas alone are able to protect him; he is not one whom worldly people can guard.
This is the unprecedented quality of the Bodhisattva. The Tathāgata possesses these four kinds of protection, complete and without deficiency; this is the auspicious sign of prior protection.

“There are beings in the world who, when entering the mother’s womb, are unable to maintain right mindfulness; or while dwelling in the mother’s womb, they likewise cannot concentrate their minds on right mindfulness; or even at the time of birth, they do not maintain right mindfulness.”

There may be sentient beings who, when entering the mother’s womb, are able to maintain right mindfulness; while dwelling within the womb, they are also able to maintain right mindfulness; and at the time of emerging from the womb, they are likewise able to maintain right mindfulness.
There may be sentient beings who maintain right mindfulness upon entering the womb and while dwelling in the womb, yet are unable to maintain right mindfulness at the time of emerging from the womb.

The Bodhisattva, however, maintains right mindfulness upon entering the womb, maintains right mindfulness while dwelling in the womb, and maintains right mindfulness upon emerging from the womb; this is a marvelous and unprecedented quality of the Bodhisattva.

After the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, he teaches the Dharma to transform and guide beings without forgetfulness or loss, speaking in accordance with the faculties and capacities of sentient beings; this is a rare and auspicious omen from the past.
When the Bodhisattva was in his mother’s womb, he remained constantly at her right side and never shifted.
Other sentient beings, because they are not fixed in position, may move to the right side or the left side; for this reason, their mothers suffer pain and undergo immeasurable agony.

While the Bodhisattva was in the womb, he remained on his right side, neither turning nor moving; whether rising, standing, sitting, or lying down, he did not harm the mother’s womb—this is a marvelous quality of the Bodhisattva.
After the Tathāgata had attained the path of Buddhahood and fully accomplished the practice of the Bodhi-dharma, these were the auspicious omens that appeared previously.

"While the Bodhisattva was in the womb, he was neither startled nor terrified; he attained great fearlessness and was untainted by foul things. All impurities—tears, saliva, pus, blood, phlegm, and yellow mucus—could not defile him."
As for other sentient beings, when they are in the mother’s womb, they are defiled by various kinds of impurities.
It is as if a lapis lazuli gem were wrapped in celestial cloth and placed in an unclean place;
it would not be stained or defiled. In this very way, while the Bodhisattva is in the womb, he is not soiled or defiled by any impurity. This is the unprecedented quality of the Bodhisattva.
Once the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, he remains unstained by and unattached to all phenomena; this was a prior auspicious sign from the past.
Furthermore, while the Bodhisattva was in his mother’s womb, his mother experienced great bliss and her body felt no fatigue.
