As for other sentient beings who enter the mother's womb, it may be for nine months or ten months, during which time the mother experiences the burden of heavy weight and her body is ill at ease.

While the Bodhisattva was in the womb, whether his mother walked, sat, slept, or rose, she always experienced peace and happiness, and her body did not suffer any pain; this is a marvelous and unprecedented quality of the Bodhisattva.

Once the Tathāgata had attained the path of Buddhahood, he swiftly realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and correctly acquired all supernormal powers as well as omniscience; these were the auspicious omens from the past.
"When a Bodhisattva is in the womb, his mother observes the prohibitive precepts and constantly maintains the practice of the precepts in her conduct.
As for other sentient beings when they are in the womb, their mothers engage in mixed conduct."
While the Bodhisattva was in the womb, his mother maintained the precepts and did not engage in miscellaneous improper conduct; this is an extraordinary quality of the Bodhisattva.

After the Tathāgata had attained the path of Buddhahood, together with the assembly of Śrāvakas, he was the most excellent in maintaining the precepts, and a great reputation arose throughout the world:
"The Śramaṇa Gautama maintains the precepts without peer; his excellence in the maintenance of the precepts is supreme."
"This was a former auspicious omen.

While the Bodhisattva was in the womb, his mother did not give rise to thoughts of sensual desire, nor was she disturbed by the fire of lust; at that time, the Bodhisattva’s mother constantly practiced the holy life."
As for other sentient beings, when they enter the mother’s womb, it is not long before the mother’s lustful desire becomes intensely fierce, far exceeding what it was before.
When the Bodhisattva is in the womb, his mother feels such weary detachment even toward her own husband that she does not engage in sexual desire; how much less so with any other person?
This is an extraordinary quality of the Bodhisattva.

Once the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, his faculty of the eye is well-subdued, well-concealed, well-guarded, well-covered, and well-perfumed; furthermore, by means of this, he is able to teach the Dharma to others according to what he has known as described above.

In this way, the ear-faculty, nose-faculty, tongue-faculty, body-faculty, and mind-faculty—even when well-perfumed—can likewise cause others to sever [afflictions] by practicing the preaching of the Dharma; this was a prior auspicious sign from the past.
"While the Bodhisattva is in the womb, his mother does not crave unusual flavors.
As for other sentient beings, when they are in the womb, their mothers are greedy and insatiable."

While the Bodhisattva was in the womb, his mother suffered neither from cold nor heat, nor from hunger or thirst; her body remained free from affliction—this is a marvelous quality of the Bodhisattva.
When the Tathāgata attained the state of Buddhahood, he already understood the four kinds of nutriment; this was a prior auspicious sign from the past.
While the Bodhisattva was in the womb, his mother was devoted to practice and aspiration, and she delighted in the performance of *dāna*.
As for other sentient beings, while they are in the mother’s womb, their mothers are stingy and greedy, taking no pleasure in giving and being miserly with their wealth.

When the Bodhisattva is in the womb, however, his mother delights in practicing generosity; her mind becomes open and liberated even while staying within her own home. This is a marvelous quality of the Bodhisattva never before seen.
After the Tathāgata had attained the path of Buddhahood, he preached the Dharma of non-avarice; this was a prior auspicious sign from the past.

While the Bodhisattva was in the womb, his mother constantly practiced loving-kindness and compassion, and was able to feel pity for all sentient beings—indeed, for every class of being possessing consciousness and life.

As for other sentient beings who are in the mother's womb, because their mothers lack benevolence and possess little majestic virtue, they engage in various unwholesome acts, such as speaking harshly and using abusive language.
"While the Bodhisattva is in the womb, his mother constantly maintains a mind of great benefit and peace toward all sentient beings; this is an extraordinary quality of the Bodhisattva."
After the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, he is able to practice a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; this was a prior auspicious sign from the past.
"When a Bodhisattva is in the womb, his mother remains as beautiful and upright as before; all her various features are pleasing to behold.

By contrast, when other sentient beings are in the womb, their mothers become emaciated and thin, their bodies no longer full and robust, and their physical strength becomes weaker than that of ordinary people."

While the Bodhisattva was in the womb, his mother constantly gave rise to a heart of joy; her moral conduct and majestic virtue were such that her physical appearance was most excellent, most wondrous, and most honored—this is a marvelous and unprecedented quality of the Bodhisattva.

Once the Tathāgata had attained the path of Buddhahood, he beheld his own body as majestic and sublime, beyond the reach of ordinary vision; his form was of golden hue, adorned with all the marks of excellence—this was a prior auspicious sign from the past.
"When the Bodhisattva was in the womb, whenever his mother wished to behold him, she would see the Bodhisattva within the womb, his body full and complete, with all his faculties intact."
It is like a bright mirror reflecting the image of a face; when the mother sees it, she leaps for joy with such intensity that it pervades her entire body, and she cannot contain herself.
Other sentient beings dwelling in the womb, however, are shrouded by the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages and thus cannot manifest.
When the Bodhisattva first enters his mother’s womb, his body is fully formed, with all five limbs and five sense organs complete; this is an extraordinary quality of the Bodhisattva.

"While the Bodhisattva is in the womb, if any sentient beings—whether men or women—who are possessed by ghosts see the Bodhisattva’s mother, all demons and all spirits will immediately depart, and they will regain their original minds."

If there are other various ailments already present in their bodies—whether it be the disease of emaciation and jaundice, or wind-epilepsy, or phlegm-disorders, or disorders of the humors in equal proportion, or any other diseases, namely: leprosy, carbuncles, malignant swellings, scabies, consumption, abscesses, ringworm, fistulas, goiters, chills and fevers, or any afflictions that invade and torment the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, throat, or head—if such sentient beings come before the Great Lady Māyā, she will stroke their heads with her right hand; once her hand has stroked their heads, they shall all attain peace and happiness, and all their diseases shall be completely eliminated.

If there is one with a serious illness who is unable to come and see Lady Māyā, Lady Māyā may take a blade of grass, or a tree leaf, or a stalk of grass, and with her right hand stroke it and send it to that patient. When the patient receives these various items—whether by eating them, touching them, or placing them upon his body—he immediately eliminates all illnesses, attains peace and happiness, and his body becomes light and agile.
While the Bodhisattva was in the womb, there were such immeasurable and boundless powers of majestic virtue and unprecedented phenomena. Chapter Six: Birth Under the Tree.

*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Six, Part One: Birth Under the Tree. "At that time, when the Bodhisattva’s holy mother, Māyā, who was carrying the Bodhisattva, had completed ten months of pregnancy and was about to give birth, the elder Suprabuddha—the father of the Great Lady Māyā—sent a messenger to King Śuddhodana of Kapilavastu. As the Mahāsāṃghika masters say, the father of Lady Māyā was named Suprabuddha; he addressed the Great King, saying:"

"As far as I know, my daughter Māyā, the Great Queen of the King, carries a holy embryo within her. Since her majesty and virtue are so great, if she gives birth to him, my daughter’s life will be short and she will surely pass away before long."
It is my wish to welcome my daughter Māyā back to my home, so that she may dwell in comfort within Lumbinī and we may enjoy each other's company, fulfilling the affection between father and daughter.
I only pray, Great King!
Do not create obstacles; out of compassion, please grant me leave to send her to my home to give birth there. Once the delivery is safely completed, I shall immediately escort her back.

When King Śuddhodana had heard these words spoken by the messenger Suprabuddha, he immediately commanded the officials to level the roads between the city of Kapilavastu and Devadaha; to clear away all thorns, pebbles, filth, and mounds of earth; to sprinkle the ground with fragrant water; and to scatter various kinds of exquisite flowers upon it.

Furthermore, they adorned Queen Māyā, embellishing her body with various kinds of incense, various kinds of flower garlands, and various kinds of necklaces, while providing all manner of musical sounds and performing songs and instrumental music.

Relying on the power and majestic authority of the Great King, he sent messengers ahead from all the palace quarters to inform his father, Sujāta, of his arrival, so that he might come out to welcome him.

At that time, the Great Lady Māyā sat serenely and upright upon the great white elephant. Then, the devas on the back of the elephant conjured a subtle and exquisite jeweled canopy; seated within this jeweled canopy, the Great Lady Māyā proceeded toward her father’s home, arriving at the city of Devadaha.

At that time, when Queen Māyā was first about to set out for the city of Devaḍaha, King Śuddhodana prepared ten thousand powerful, fragrant elephants. All were fitted with golden saddles, adorned with the seven treasures, and their bodies were magnificently decorated; they were all exquisite and splendid, prepared to escort Queen Māyā.

Furthermore, there were ten thousand excellent, fine horses, all of a deep blue-black color, with heads as black as crows. They all had full manes and tails that hung down to the ground; they were equipped with pure gold bridles, saddles, stirrups, and halters, all likewise decorated with gold and various miscellaneous jewels that adorned their bodies.

Additionally, there were ten thousand magnificent jeweled chariots, each drawn by four horses; around these chariots were suspended banners, canopies, and clusters of jeweled bells, which chimed together in harmonious resonance.
Having thus made these preparations, they all followed behind Queen Māyā.

Furthermore, there were twenty thousand powerful and heroic warriors, each capable of facing a thousand men; they were fierce, agile, and exceptionally handsome, able to defeat even the most formidable enemies. Clad in armor and holding in their hands bows, arrows, swords, staves, battle-discs, various spears, lances, and all manner of weaponry, they followed behind the Queen.

Furthermore, there were another ten thousand precious chariots, and ten thousand royal consorts all sat within them; wearing various necklaces and diverse garments to adorn their bodies, they surrounded Queen Māyā on her left and right.

At that time, King Śuddhodana again issued strict and urgent commands to the palace supervisors and ministers, ordering them to provide excellent protection. He forbade any non-officials or other wanderers from approaching Queen Māyā’s chariot, and he prohibited the various concubines from mingling with her; he sent only young maidens to pull the chariot and escort it forward.

In this order, Queen Māyā was seated in the center of the elephant carriage, surrounded on all sides by ten thousand precious chariots, each occupied by a queen; she was escorted before and behind, with Queen Māyā herself at the head of the procession.

Outside of that, there were furthermore ten thousand fragrant elephants and ten thousand powerful warriors, all clad in armor, following the lady on her left and right, in front and behind, proceeding in ceremonial procession; each of them sat atop a fragrant elephant.

Furthermore, ten thousand foot-soldier wrestlers, also clad in armor and holding various spears, lances, and weapons in their hands, escorted the Lady; thus adorned, they accompanied Queen Māyā as she proceeded toward her father’s dwelling.
Countless elephants and horses all let out their cries;

furthermore, countless dragon-headed great drums, countless small drums, and various musical instruments produced sublime sounds. Adorned with immeasurable splendor and possessing immeasurable majesty, they proceeded toward the city of Devadaha.
At that time, the minister and elder Sujāta, together with his own retinue, went out from the city to meet Queen Māyā; they carried immeasurable articles of adornment and led the Queen forward.
At that time, the minister Sujāta had a wife named Lumbinī. That woman addressed her husband Sujāta, saying:
"O Great Sage, son of the Śākyas!
If you know it to be the right time, all the clansmen of the Śākya lineage each possess their own groves and orchards; let us go there to roam, observe, and enjoy ourselves together."
"O Great Sage’s Son!
You may now construct a pure grove; we shall together enjoy ourselves with you and experience delight.

Then, Śuddhodana—the father of the noble Queen Māyā—constructed a great grove for his wife near his own domain, between the two cities of Kapilavastu and Devadaha. Because he established this grove for his wife, Lumbinī, it was therefore named the Lumbinī Garden.
The trees in that garden were lush and spreading, peerless in the world; they were adorned with many varieties of flowering trees and fruit-bearing trees.
Furthermore, there were various canals, streams, ponds, and pools, as well as countless and boundless varieties of diverse trees, all filled with mani jewels throughout the gardens.

At that time, on the eighth day of the second month at the beginning of spring, when the lunar mansion of Bharaṇī was in conjunction, the Śākya minister Sujāta accompanied his daughter Māyā toward the Lumbinī Garden, wishing to go and behold that most auspicious site.

Having arrived at that garden, Lady Māyā descended from her precious chariot; she first adorned her body with various exquisite necklaces and ornaments, and further applied and rubbed herself with various kinds of fine incense.

Surrounded before and behind by a multitude of court ladies and the sounds of music and song, he walked slowly and with composed grace, looking about at every place; departing from this grove and proceeding toward that tree, he moved in this manner, circling around in succession.

However, within that garden there was another tree called a *pāṭala*. This tree stood firmly, perfectly symmetrical from top to bottom; its branches and leaves hung down in profusion, half green and half blue, with their emerald and violet hues shimmering against one another like the neck of a peacock. Furthermore, it was exceedingly soft, like *kālinjara* cloth, and its fragrance was exquisite and wondrous, bringing joy to all who smelled it.
Queen Māyā proceeded slowly and steadily toward the foot of that tree.

At that moment, through the power of the Bodhisattva’s majestic virtue, the branches of the tree naturally bent, becoming supple and hanging down low. Queen Māyā then raised her right hand, which was like a magnificent rainbow appearing in the sky; she stretched herself gracefully and grasped a branch of the *pālāśa* tree, looking up into the void.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva’s mother, Lady Māyā, stood upon the ground and reached out her hand to grasp a branch of the *pālāśa* tree, twenty thousand celestial maidens approached the Great Lady Māyā, surrounding her on all sides. Joining their ten fingers in palms-together salutation, they addressed the Great Lady Māyā together, saying:
“Lady, you have now given birth to a son Who can sever the wheel of birth and death;
A teacher of gods and men, high and low, Of whom there shall certainly be no second.”
"He is the embryo of the devas, able to uproot the suffering of sentient beings;
O Lady, do not grow weary, for we shall support you together.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva saw his mother, Queen Māyā, standing upon the ground and grasping a branch of a tree with her hand, he remained in right mindfulness within the womb and rose from his seat.

When all other mothers of sentient beings desire to give birth to their children, their bodies ache throughout; due to this pain, they experience great suffering and distress, repeatedly sitting down and rising up, unable to find any peace for themselves.
The Bodhisattva’s mother was serene, composed, peaceful, and joyful, her body experiencing great bliss.

At that time, Māyā stood upon the ground and, having grasped a branch of a *palāśa* tree with her hand, the Bodhisattva was immediately born. This is a marvelous event of the Bodhisattva, an unprecedented phenomenon.

Once the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, he is without lack or fatigue, without toil or weariness; he is able to uproot all the faculties of affliction and sever all the fetters of affliction, just like cutting off the crown of a tāla tree so that it never grows again—being signless, formless, and devoid of further rebirth. This is the auspicious omen of the Tathāgata’s past.
"Furthermore, while all other sentient beings, being oppressed by the suffering of birth, move about restlessly within the womb, the Bodhisattva is not so;

he enters through the right side and remains there on the right side, never shifting within the womb. When it is time for his emergence, he is born from the right side, unafflicted by any suffering. Therefore, this matter of the Bodhisattva’s is marvelous and an unprecedented phenomenon."

Once the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, he shall practice the holy life until the end of time, forever free from fear, constantly enjoying bliss, and no longer subject to any suffering; this is a prior auspicious sign of the Tathāgata.

"When the Bodhisattva first emerged from his mother’s womb through her right side with perfect mindfulness, he emitted a great radiance that instantly illuminated the entire world—including all devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—so that they all spoke to one another, saying:
'How is it that a sentient being has suddenly appeared here?'"
"This is a rare and extraordinary matter, an unprecedented phenomenon for a bodhisattva.

Once the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, he tears asunder the net of the darkness of ignorance and is able to emit the light of great, pure wisdom; this is a premonitory sign from the past of the Tathāgata."

"When the Bodhisattva first emerged from the right side [of his mother], he was mindful with a composed mind; at that time, the Bodhisattva’s mother’s body remained peaceful and as usual—uninjured, unimpaired, without sores or pain—and the Bodhisattva’s mother’s body was no different than it had been before."

When the Bodhisattva was born, there were various forms of benefit and nourishment; by these causes and conditions, his mother experienced no illness or suffering, and her body, speech, and mind were free from even a single affliction.

For example, suppose there were a sentient being with a massive body, possessing great majesty and great physical strength, who lay upon the ground and rolled about, striking himself; yet the earth would not be damaged, diminished, or broken.
When the Bodhisattva was thus born from the right side of his mother with right mindfulness, his mother remained, by virtue of these causes and conditions, without wound or injury.
At that time, there was a woman there who, with palms joined, addressed the Bodhisattva’s mother, saying:
"O Virtuous Lady!..."
"Upon giving birth to the child, was your body free from pain?
The Bodhisattva’s mother replied, "Because of this Great Being’s majestic spiritual power, my body did not feel even the slightest sensation of pain or itching; my body is now whole and unimpaired."
For this reason, this is a marvelous and unprecedented quality of the Bodhisattva.
Once the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, he practices the Brahma-conduct—unfailing, undiminished, complete, and without deficiency; this is a prior auspicious sign of the Tathāgata.

"When the Bodhisattva first emerges from his mother's womb, he is without suffering or distress and rises up with composure. No impurities can defile him; whether it be feces or urine, phlegm or yellow mucus, pus or blood, none adhere to him in a foul manner."
As for other sentient beings, when they emerge from the mother’s womb, they are accompanied by various evils and impurities.

It is not so for the Bodhisattva; unlike those other classes of beings, he is entirely unstained by any impurity. With a correct mind and correct mindfulness, he emerges from the womb, rising up with steady composure.
For example, when a wish-fulfilling lapis lazuli gem is wrapped in kāśika cloth, neither taints the other.

In this very way, while the Bodhisattva was in his mother’s womb, he remained with single-minded right mindfulness, arose calmly, and was born pure, free from all impurities—even amidst the foul places of pus, blood, excrement, and urine—neither defiled nor stained. This is a marvelous and unprecedented quality of the Bodhisattva.

After the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, while dwelling in the world and abiding within the world, he is neither defiled nor stained by any worldly phenomena or the impurities of the world; this is a previous auspicious sign of the Tathāgata.

"When the Bodhisattva first emerged from his mother’s womb, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, took a fine and exquisite Kāśika cloth, wrapped it around his own hands, and was the first to receive and support the Bodhisattva’s body; this is a marvelous event and an unprecedented quality of the Bodhisattva."

After the Tathāgata had attained the path of Buddhahood and first became the sovereign of the Sahā world, the Great Brahmā King was the first to entreat the Tathāgata to preach the Dharma; this was a prior auspicious sign from the Tathāgata’s past.
"When the Bodhisattva first emerged from her right side, the Four Great Heavenly Kings took him in their arms, led him before his mother, and said to her:
'O Great Lady of the World!'"
"You should now rejoice.
When a woman gives birth to a child and that child has obtained a human body, even the devas rejoice and offer praise;
how much more so should humans?
Therefore, this is a marvelous and unprecedented phenomenon for a Bodhisattva:

once the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, the vast multitude of all bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as well as upāsakas and upāsikās, all turn toward the Tathāgata to listen to and receive the Dharma; they rely upon the Tathāgata’s teachings, neither contravening nor turning away from them. This is a prior auspicious sign of the Tathāgata.
"When the Bodhisattva was born and stood upon the ground, looking up at his mother’s right side, he spoke these words:
'From this day forward, I shall no longer receive such a physical form; I shall not again enter a womb to lie within a mother's side. This is my very last body; I shall become a Buddha.'"
"This is a marvelous and unprecedented quality of a bodhisattva.
After the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, he utters these words:
'For me, the conditions for this life are now entirely exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; I shall not undergo further existence.'"
"This was a prior auspicious sign of the Tathāgata.
*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll Seven;
*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on Birth beneath the Tree, Part Two:
"Once the Bodhisattva was born, without anyone supporting him, he immediately walked four directions, seven paces in each. With every step he raised his foot, a great lotus flower emerged."

Having taken seven steps, he gazed in the four directions with eyes that never blinked, and words issued spontaneously from his mouth. First looking toward the east, he did not speak like an ordinary infant, but according to his own verses, spoke these correct words:
"In this world, I am the most supreme; from this day forth, my births are exhausted."
"This is a marvelous and unprecedented phenomenon for a bodhisattva:
in all other places it is likewise so that, at the time of birth, without anyone supporting him, he walks seven paces in each of the four directions."
After the Tathāgata had attained the path of Buddhahood, he obtained the seven factors of enlightenment that assist the path; these were the auspicious omens of his former life.
"Once the Bodhisattva was born, he gazed in the four directions."
"After the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, he will fully possess the four kinds of fearlessness; this was a prior auspicious sign of the Tathāgata.
When the Bodhisattva was born, he spoke these words himself:
'In the world, I am the most supreme.'"
"Once the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, all the worlds—including gods and humans—will all revere him, honoring and serving him; this is a prior auspicious sign of the Tathāgata."
"Once the Bodhisattva was born, he spoke from his own mouth, saying:
'I have severed birth and death; this is the final limit.
After the Tathāgata had attained the Way of the Buddha, he acted exactly according to his word; this was a prior auspicious sign of the Tathāgata."
"When the Bodhisattva was born, his attendants sought water, running to the east, west, south, and north, yet they could find none.

Suddenly, two pools of water—one cool and one warm—spontaneously welled up in that garden before the Bodhisattva’s mother. The Bodhisattva’s mother took the water from these two pools and used it as she pleased."

Furthermore, from the midst of the sky, two streams of water poured down—one cold and one warm—and with this water they bathed the Bodhisattva’s body; this was a marvelous and unprecedented phenomenon of the Bodhisattva.

After the Tathāgata had attained the path of Buddhahood, he realized śamatha and vipaśyanā; he remained far removed from sensual matters without undergoing any toil, and all his requisites were provided spontaneously—this was a prior auspicious sign of the Tathāgata.
"When the Bodhisattva was first born, the various devas held up a golden couch for the Bodhisattva to sit upon; once seated, the Bodhisattva bathed his body.
Although he possessed a human body, he was supported by the devas—this is a marvelous event and an unprecedented quality of the Bodhisattva."
Once the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, he obtains those four kinds of lotus thrones which support the Tathāgata; this is a prior auspicious sign of the Tathāgata.
"When the Bodhisattva was first born, he emitted a great radiance that eclipsed all other existing lights; this is a marvelous event and an unprecedented phenomenon of the Bodhisattva."

Once the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, there shall be no one capable of surpassing the Tathāgata in discourse according to the Dharma; this was a prior auspicious sign of the Tathāgata.

"When the Bodhisattva was first born, his body emitted a radiance that eclipsed the sunlight, making it like the stars during the day; this is a marvelous and unprecedented quality of the Bodhisattva."

Once the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, he will obtain supreme offerings and supreme renown among the assembly of his śrāvaka disciples; this is a portentous sign from the past of the Tathāgata.
"When the Bodhisattva was first born, all trees and all medicinal herbs blossomed according to their season; this is a marvelous and unprecedented quality of the Bodhisattva."

Once the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, those sentient beings who have not yet attained faith and understanding shall attain it, and those who have already attained faith and understanding shall further increase in it; this is a prior auspicious sign of the Tathāgata.

"When the Bodhisattva was first born, the devas of the upper realms held for him a white parasol with a handle of pure gold, as large as a chariot wheel; this is a marvelous event of the Bodhisattva, an unprecedented phenomenon."

After the Tathāgata had attained the path of Buddhahood, he achieved liberation through non-anger; he obtained wealth and benefits without the toil of exertion—this was a prior auspicious sign of the Tathāgata.
"When the Bodhisattva was first born, he rose into the air above; all the devas each held white whisks, with handles fashioned entirely of various jewels, and fanned the Bodhisattva from above."
"When the Bodhisattva was first born, the void was pure and clear; there were no smoke or clouds, and no dust or mist, yet the sound of thunder was heard.

When the Bodhisattva was first born, in the sky above, free from all clouds and mist, there fell a fine rain of pure fragrant water endowed with the eight meritorious qualities, causing all sentient beings to experience happiness."

"When the Bodhisattva was first born, subtle and wondrous winds arose in the air from the four directions—cool, refreshing, and free from affliction. Throughout all eight directions, there was pure luster, with no smoke, clouds, dust, or obscurations."
"When the Bodhisattva was first born, from the sky above, there spontaneously issued forth a wondrous Brahma-sound, created by no one.

When the Bodhisattva was first born, from the sky above, various celestial musical instruments and various songs spontaneously sounded; various flowers and various incenses rained down, which did not wither even when exposed to the sunlight. This is a rare marvel of the Bodhisattva, an unprecedented phenomenon."

Once the Tathāgata has attained the path of Buddhahood, for the sake of all the worlds, he manifests great supernormal transformations through his various wisdoms and purifies the superknowledges (abhijñā) that are peerless in the world; with the Tathāgata as their foremost, these are the auspicious signs of the Tathāgata’s past.

"When the Bodhisattva was first born, all the devas in the sky above each held immeasurable *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, as well as various other such diverse blossoms; they further held various kinds of subtle and exquisite incenses, and various garlands of many precious jewels, scattering them over the Bodhisattva, scattering again and again, in an unceasing succession."

"When the Bodhisattva was first born, five hundred celestial jade maidens arrived carrying oil perfumed with various heavenly flowers; they stood before the Bodhisattva’s mother, offering words of comfort and inquiry, speaking thus:
'Congratulations on the birth of the Bodhisattva! Are you not weary?'"

"When the Bodhisattva was first born, five hundred celestial jade maidens, carrying heavenly ointments, approached the Bodhisattva’s mother and stood before her. They comforted her and inquired after her well-being, saying:
'Congratulations on the birth of the Bodhisattva; are you not weary?'"

"When the Bodhisattva was first born, five hundred celestial maidens of the devas, holding various kinds of divine and exquisite precious garments, approached the Bodhisattva’s mother and stood before her. They comforted her with greetings, speaking these words:
'Congratulations on the birth of the Bodhisattva; are you not weary?'"

"When the Bodhisattva was first born, five hundred celestial jade maidens, bearing various divine jeweled necklaces and ornaments, approached the Bodhisattva’s mother and stood before her. They comforted her and inquired after her well-being, saying:
'Congratulations on the birth of the Bodhisattva; are you not weary?'"

"When the Bodhisattva was first born, five hundred celestial maidens, holding various kinds of sublime heavenly music, approached the Bodhisattva’s mother and stood before her. They comforted her with greetings and spoke these words:
'Congratulations on the birth of the Bodhisattva; are you not weary?'"
"When the Bodhisattva was first born, this great earth manifested eighteen signs and shook in six ways, and all sentient beings experienced happiness."

At that time, not a single sentient being would give rise to a desire-thought; there would be no more anger or delusion, no pride and no fear, and not a single sentient being would commit an evil deed.
All who are ill shall be healed; the hungry shall obtain food, and the thirsty shall obtain drink, so that all are made full and lack for nothing.

Sentient beings who are昏醉 (stupefied or intoxicated) shall all attain awakening; the insane shall regain their composure; the blind shall gain sight; the deaf shall gain hearing; and those with incomplete faculties shall all become complete.

The poor obtain wealth; those imprisoned and confined all attain liberation; sentient beings in the hells all find rest; sentient beings among the animals are freed from all terrors; and sentient beings among the hungry ghosts all attain sufficiency.
When the Bodhisattva was first born from the right side, there were such immeasurable and boundless rare occurrences and unprecedented phenomena.

Chapter Seven: Returning from the Garden to the City. *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Seven (Part One): "At that time, there was a great minister and state preceptor named Mahānāma, of the Vāsiṣṭha clan. Together with various state preceptors and Brahmins, he went together to the Lumbinī Garden. Having arrived at that garden, he stood outside the gate."
Then Vāsiṣṭha spoke to the brahmin state preceptors, saying:
"Observe this great earth; for what reason does it shake in such a manner?

It is as if one were on a boat upon the water, where the sun and moon are obscured, losing their original radiance and majesty, appearing like stars by day, with only faint forms and shadows remaining."
All the trees blossomed in accordance with the seasons.
In the sky above, it was pure and bright, free from all clouds and obscurations, and one heard only the sound of thunder.
Furthermore, in the void, which was serene, still, and luminously radiant, there fell a rain of exquisite and subtle fragrance, replete with merit and naturally imbued with the eight flavors.

Furthermore, from the eight directions, subtle and wondrous winds arose; these winds were cool and refreshing, with a temperature perfectly balanced between cold and warmth. All quarters became entirely pure, free from smoke, clouds, dust, mist, or any dark gloom.
Furthermore, from within the void of space, there was no one singing, yet naturally the sound of profound Brahma-voices was heard.

Again, from within the void of space, various kinds of celestial music were heard, as well as celestial songs, praises, and chants; celestial fragrant flowers rained down, which, though scorched by the sunlight, could not cause them to wither.
Then the National Preceptor replied to the great minister Vāseṭṭha:
"Although this is so, it is not to be considered strange. Why is that?
"The nature of the earth is such; what inauspiciousness could there be?

Another person said, "Now this great earth quakes in six ways, and the void is so vast and brilliant that it obscures the sunlight, as if one were looking at the stars by day from time immemorial. Furthermore, celestial flowers rain down; though all these lights shine, they cannot alter its appearance—this is truly most rare."
While Vāsiṣṭha was deliberating on this matter with the royal preceptor, a woman from within that park came running out and arrived at the gate.
When that woman reached the gate, she saw Vāsiṣṭha and the royal preceptor; she leaped for joy, unable to contain herself, and said to Vāsiṣṭha and the royal preceptor:
"O sons of the Śākya clan!"
"You should go quickly to the place where the Great King is.
At that time, the high minister and the state preceptor, seeing that woman speak these words, were filled with such joy that they could not contain themselves.
He asked her:
"When you lead us to the presence of the Great King, what should we report?
Shall we announce matters of joy, or of suspicion, wonder, fear, or misfortune?"
She replied: "O son of the Śākyas!
I now announce to you a matter of great fortune and cause for rejoicing."
Then Mahānāman, the royal preceptor, and the others asked her,
"What cause for celebration is there? She replied:

"The Great Lady of the State has given birth to a boy who is handsome and lovely, with few equals in the world; indeed, this boy is truly a deva, for heavenly flowers are scattered everywhere and he emits celestial radiance."
When the ministers heard these words, their hearts were filled with great joy; they leaped for joy so intensely that they could not contain themselves.

At that time, the ministers immediately untied their various precious and exquisite necklaces and bestowed them upon the woman as a reward for hearing such joyful news. Having bestowed them, they further reflected:
"This woman is one who currently enjoys the King's favor within the palace."
When the king saw this woman, he felt great love and reverence for her.
[He thought,] "If I now give away my own body ornaments to her, they may later become a source of trouble.
He immediately took them back; having taken them, he then gave them as a gift to the state preceptor. Having relinquished them, he offered a prayer of blessing, speaking these words:
"I now offer these necklaces to the National Preceptor; whatever merit there is from this, I dedicate it to that woman.
For what reason? Because of the joy I have heard."
Then the minister Mahānāma said to the state preceptor, the brāhmaṇa: "Great brāhmaṇa!
You should now return to the Great King and report this joyful news."
Then, having dismissed that Brahmin, Mahāmaṇava again questioned the woman, saying:
"Regarding the son born to the chief queen of my kingdom whom you previously mentioned—a youth like a deva, emitting a celestial radiance—what other extraordinary signs did you further observe?"
Then that woman replied to the minister, saying:
"Please listen well!

That boy’s appearance transcends that of ordinary men and he possesses great majesty and virtue; when the Great Queen of the country of Māyā stood upon the ground, the boy spontaneously emerged from her right side, yet the Great Queen’s chest, sides, waist, and body remained unbroken and uninjured."

When the youth was born, all the devas from the void took fine and exquisite Kāśika garments and wrapped them completely around the youth’s body; they then brought him before his mother and spoke these words:
"O Great Lady of the Realm, you should rejoice and feel redoubled joy."
For what reason?
Because today, the Great Lady has given birth to a holy son!
When this boy was first about to emerge, he looked up at his mother’s flank and spoke these words:
“From this day forward, I shall no longer receive a womb from a woman; this is my very last body.”
"From this point forward, I shall become a Buddha.

Immediately he stood upon the ground; without anyone supporting him, he walked seven paces. Wherever his feet trod, lotus flowers sprang up. He gazed straight ahead in all four directions with a steady eye, his eyes never blinking, neither startled nor afraid.
Standing upright and facing east, his speech was eloquent and pure, his words and phrases were perfect and not like those of a child, as he spoke these words:
"In all the worlds, I am the most supreme; I shall deliver all beings from the root of birth, death, and afflictions."

At the spot where the youth stood, because of the purity of that youth’s body, two streams of water poured down from the sky—one warm and one cold—and a golden couch was brought forth upon which the youth was seated to bathe his body.

As soon as the boy was born, his body emitted a radiance that eclipsed the sun and moon; the devas of the upper realms held a white parasol with a handle of pure gold, as large as a chariot wheel, suspended in mid-air.
Furthermore, there were devas holding white whisks with handles made of various jewels, waving them over the boy.
Also, from within the void, all manner of music resounded spontaneously without being struck, and the sounds of immeasurable and boundless subtle and wondrous singing were heard.
Furthermore, fragrant flowers rained down, filling every place; even though the sun shone upon them, they remained as fresh and pure as ever, unable to be altered.
At that time, having heard these words, the minister Mahānāma reflected to himself:
"How rare! How rare!"
In this degenerate age, a Great Being has appeared in the world.
I should now go in person to the presence of King Śuddhodana and report such a rare event as this.

Then that minister took a well-trained horse, swift as the wind, harnessed to a precious chariot, and set out from outside the gate of the Lumbinī Garden, proceeding directly toward the city of Kapilavastu. Before even seeing the King, he first beat the drum of joy, striking it with all his physical strength.

At that time, King Śuddhodana sat upon the precious palace, assisted by his ministers who harmonized and administered the affairs of state; surrounded on all sides by his various officials, high ministers, and bureaucratic functionaries—some behind him and some before him—all heard the sound of that drum of joy.
At that time, the king asked his ministers in astonishment: "O you ministers!
Who is this that has suddenly dared to strike the drum of joy of my Ikṣvāku lineage, beating it with all their might and producing such a great sound?"
At that time, the gatekeeper approached and addressed the king, saying:
"Great King!

You should know that the king’s minister, Vāsiṣṭha, whose family name is Mahānāman, has arrived from outside the gate of the Lumbinī Garden, driving a chariot drawn by four horses as swift as the wind."
Suddenly leaping down from the carriage, he exerted all his strength and struck the Great King’s drum of joy; without further words, he spoke directly, saying, "I now wish to see the Great King."
Then King Śuddhodana said to his ministers:
"What joyful news is there?
You should quickly summon that minister of the Śākya clan, Mahānāma of the Vāsiṣṭha lineage, and have him come before me at once."
The minister, having received the king’s command, addressed the Great King, saying:
"I respectfully follow your instructions.
He then went with great haste to summon the Śākya minister Mahānāma, compelling him to arrive at the king's presence with all speed.
At that time, having heard the king’s command, Mahānāma went before the king and cried out in a loud voice:
“May the King always be victorious! May the King always be honored! I now offer these words to increase your physical strength.”
At that time, having heard these words, King Śuddhodana addressed the Śākya minister Mahānāma, saying:
"O Śākya minister!
"Why have you come so hurriedly and swiftly, exerting all your physical strength to beat this drum of joy?
Then the minister Mahānāma replied to the king:

"In the Lumbinī Grove at Devadaha, your majesty’s queen was sporting; there, beneath a tree, she gave birth to a boy whose body is golden in color, whose appearance resembles that of a deva, who is even as handsome as a celestial being, and who radiates divine light."
Then, King Śuddhodana asked again:
"Is it certain that he possesses the marks and signs? What are they like?
At that time, the minister replied to the king once more:
"The ground upon which the lady stood, even down to her right side, did not crack or break.
Once the boy was born, he stood upright by himself. The various devas each took garments of kāśika silk and wrapped his body entirely therein; looking up at his mother’s side, they spoke these words:
'We shall become Buddhas and uproot the very foundation of the suffering and affliction of birth and death.'"

As he bathed, he emitted a radiance that eclipsed the sun and moon; the trees, medicinal herbs, and grasses blossomed according to their season, and the devas in the void held white canopies and whisks, waving them over the boy.

In the void there is the sound of thunder, and a fine rain falls from the heavens; cool breezes come from all directions, yet their forms are not seen. Brahma-sounds and musical tones chant of themselves without being struck by drums; the blossoms shine forth without withering.
As previously described, I have reported each matter in its proper sequence to the King.
Your Majesty,
you should know that because I have witnessed these rare and marvelous events, I now, with great joy, strike the drum of rejoicing and venture to announce this far and wide.
Then that minister, taking the remaining flowers from the offerings made to the devas, respectfully presented them to the Great King and related everything as it had occurred.
Upon hearing these words, King Śuddhodana said to the minister:
"Since you have brought me this joyful news and informed me of it, what wish do you seek from the depths of your heart?"
"I shall give you everything; do as you wish, and I will not go against your intent.
The minister Vāseṭṭha replied:
"Your Majesty, by your grace, I lack for nothing."
At that time, King Śuddhodana again addressed his ministers, saying:
"It is the way of dharma to grant what is requested; I shall certainly give it to you.
The ministers then spoke once more to the king, saying:
"May Your Majesty be pleased; by the King's grace, I have no lack of anything.
Then, King Śuddhodana again addressed the great minister:
"You must not now disobey the King's command; you must certainly request a boon, and I shall grant it to you."
Then the minister Vāsiṣṭha addressed him, saying:
"Great King!
If you are indeed certain to grant my wish, I pray that Your Majesty will allow me to attend upon the Crown Prince, serving him at all times."
Why is this? Since this boy has now been born, he will certainly continue the lineage of the Ikṣvāku solar dynasty, ensuring that the descendants of the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings remain unbroken.
Then King Śuddhodana replied to the minister, saying:
"O you who know the proper time, do as you please.
At that time, King Śuddhodana addressed his ministers, saying:
"O you great ministers!
You should record the auspicious royal laws as they were administered by that minister Vāsiṣṭha, in their proper sequence and in full detail, ensuring that nothing is omitted."
Then King Śuddhodana addressed the great minister, the Śākya Nāma, saying: "Minister!
Come; since such a prince has been born in my kingdom, we must now perform for this most excellent prince the rites pertaining to his birth."

At that time, King Śuddhodana, with his great majestic power and royal majesty, surrounded on all sides by his ministers and officials standing in attendance like a crescent moon, along with the great minister Mahānāma and others, set out for the Lumbinī Garden, desiring to welcome the Bodhisattva.
When they reached the middle of the road, King Śuddhodana addressed Mahānāma and the other ministers, saying: "O ministers!
Having heard that a son has been born to me, and having witnessed such a rare event and an unprecedented phenomenon, how could I not be filled with joy?"
"Why do you cover yourself in grief?
Minister Mahānāma spoke again to the Great King:
"You ought to rejoice and celebrate; there is no need to harbor sorrow."
Why is this? For those born among gods and humans, there are such inconceivable and most marvelous phenomena as these.
Great King, have you not heard that in the past there was a brahmin named Puṣpaka (Flower-Born) who, immediately after birth, did not learn from others but naturally understood the four Vedas?

Furthermore, Great King, have you not heard that in the past there was a king named Mūrdhaja, who was born from his father’s crown? Upon birth, he was just like an infant, but he gradually grew up and ruled over the four continents of the world.
"Furthermore, Great King, have you not heard that in the past there was a king named Vikka, who was born from his father’s palm and did not emerge from a mother’s womb?"
"Furthermore, Great King, have you not heard that in the past there was a king named Rūpa, who was born from his father's thigh?
Furthermore, Great King, have you not heard that in the past there was a king named Kalmāṣapāda, who was born from his father's arm?"
"Furthermore, Great King, have you not heard that among your royal ancestors, from time immemorial, there was one named King Ikṣvāku, who was born from a sugar cane?"
"Although these various kings were born among humans, they are inconceivable.
At that time, King Śuddhodana spoke again to the Śākya minister Mahānāma, saying: "O Mahānāma!..."
"Those kings were all great vidyādharas of immense majesty and power; this [king] does not compare to them.
With a heart full of joy, Mahānāma addressed the king again, saying:
"Great King!..."
"You should know that this prince will certainly surpass all those kings.
King Śuddhodana asked,
"What are his superior marks?"
The minister Mahānāma replied, "Those individuals were born, and this prince was born; when I compared and weighed them, I knew that his marks were far superior."
The king spoke again, saying:
"Do not jest. Why is this?"
Generally, as a father, who would not desire his son to excel above others?

Whether it be through extensive learning and hearing, broad knowledge and understanding, skillful practice, a full mastery of ritual and righteousness, proficiency in the ways of governance, or diligent application of effort—one whose son possesses such qualities will feel joy in his heart.
When King Śuddhodana had finished speaking these words, he gradually proceeded to the Lumbinī Garden.
Upon arriving at that garden, he stood outside the main gate and dispatched a messenger to address the Lady, saying:

"Lady, you possess great merit and have given birth to a noble being. It is fitting that you perform auspicious rites at the place where the Prince was born; prepare the decorations and ensure they are completed with all haste."
"I wish to behold the Crown Prince face-to-face.

Although I previously witnessed various rare, auspicious signs and unprecedented phenomena while this son was in the womb, it is because my heart now cherishes and longs for my son that I wish to go and see him myself."

At that time, Queen Māyā, the Great Consort of the kingdom, having prepared all the various auspicious rites appropriate for a child as practiced by the world, completed them all and immediately dispatched a messenger to inform the King, saying:
"Great King, you should know the proper time; you ought to enter this garden."
At that time, there was a woman who, seeing King Śuddhodana had already entered the park, took up the Bodhisattva in her arms, went to the king's location, and spoke these words:
"Child, you should now pay homage to your royal father."
The King said, "Not so!
First send someone to pay respects to my teacher, the Brahmin, and only then may you see me."
At that time, the woman took the Bodhisattva in her arms and first led him to the place where the brahmin was.
When the state preceptor and the other brahmins saw the Bodhisattva, they addressed King Śuddhodana, offering this benediction:
"We pray only that the Great King..."

"May you always be honored and always victorious, as if seeing your own son prevail! I pray that the Śākya clan may forever flourish like sprouts and leaves; O Great King, this son of yours shall surely become a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
Then King Śuddhodana again asked the royal preceptor, the brāhmaṇa:
"How do you know this to be so?
At that time, the royal preceptor replied to the king:
"According to the characteristics described in the Vidyāraśāstra as I have observed them, when combined with the qualities of this child, this matter is indeed true.
Then King Śuddhodana again asked the National Preceptor, the Brāhmaṇa:
"If it is so, then my Śākya clan, the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, shall surely flourish as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin)."

Why is this? The kings of the present age have all diminished in their merit, asceticism, and diligent application. If this boy were born now possessing such power of merit—endowed with the great strength, valor, and auspicious marks of the kings of the first eon—then our family would surely flourish once more, just like the universal monarchs of the first eon.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mother, Queen Māyā, seeing that King Śuddhodana and the state preceptor, the Brahmin, had cheerful countenances, immediately addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
“Great King!
Show me what the marks and features of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) are like.
Excellent!
Please briefly explain the essentials for me, so that my heart may rejoice.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked the national preceptor, the brahmin:
"Venerable Master!
I pray that you will explain the physical characteristics and marks of a wheel-turning sage king."
Then the State Preceptor and the Brahmin replied to King Śuddhodana and the Queen,
saying: "We pray only that Your Majesty will listen attentively to what we say."

I have received from the transmission of the treatises of former sages that the wheel-turning monarch possesses all sovereign merits in their entirety; when such a wheel-turning monarch governs and transforms the people, he is certainly able to soar through the void while moving and dwelling upon the earth.
If there is a severe drought at any time, rain falls immediately upon his thought.

If within the king’s realm there are sentient beings who are prone to anger and ill will, or who harbor mutual resentment and hatred toward one another, by the power of the Wheel-turning King’s majestic virtue, the sentient beings within the country each become joyful.

The Wheel-Turning Sage King is fully endowed with the seven treasures, namely: the golden wheel, the divine jewel, the elephant, the horse, the jade lady, the treasurer, and the minister of the military; these are called the seven treasures.

The Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses a long life span and never meets an untimely death; he has few illnesses and little affliction, and his physical form is so upright and majestic that it is peerless in the world.
Within his realm, all the people love and revere this king as if he were their only son;
yet the Wheel-Turning Sage King protects his people even more than a mother cherishes her infant.
Then King Śuddhodana again addressed the state preceptor, the Brahmin, saying: "Great Brahmin!
As you have said, all who are Universal Monarchs (Cakravartin-rājas) possess these qualities; yet, is it not so with me?"
"At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mother, Queen Māyā, again addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
'Great King!
This matter is not yet to be considered strange.'"
"Why is this? Because this boy has today been born into a family of the Kṣatriya caste, of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
Then King Śuddhodana spoke these words again:

"How rare is this! That a Wheel-Turning Sage King is born among humans; yet such is the majesty of that Wheel-Turning Sage King, and so great is the ripening of his superior karma—this has caused wonder to arise in my mind."

None of the universal monarchs (cakravartin) of the past possessed such extraordinary marks as these—namely, King Ikṣvāku of the Solar Lineage, King Nyagrodha, King Kokālika, King Gokhali, my father King Siṃhahanu, or even myself—none of them had such extraordinary marks.
"What is the matter?
Furthermore, what is the cause?
At that time, the state preceptor and the brahmins again addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Great King!
You should know that for there to be a before and an after is not at all strange.
Have you not heard, Great King, that in the past there was a king named Yayaṭi, who was fully endowed with every merit, and whose father’s name was Vāyu?"
He had a son named Anavaśyandin.
Anavaśyandin had a son named Tuṇḍu-māra.
Tuṇḍu-māra had a son named Kakṣapuṭa.
Kakravartapuṇya had a son named Arajiṣu.
Arajiṣu had a son named Māndhātṛyani. Māndhātṛyani had a son named Indrabhīra.
Rāvaṇa had a son named Duḥprasaha.
These kings, though possessing great majesty and virtue, were unable to become universal monarchs (cakravartin).
Their last son was Śūraprabha, who fathered a single son named Bharata;
it was this Bharata who first became a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin).
In the past, at the beginning of the kalpa, there was a member of the kṣatriya caste named Mahāsammata who descended from heaven, yet he did not become a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin).

Thereafter, they were handed down in succession from one to another until reaching the Universal Monarch Mūrdhaja, who ruled as far as the Heaven of the Thirty-three. Although the lineage of ancestors, fathers, sons, and descendants continued in this manner, they eventually declined and diminished, such that they could no longer become Universal Monarchs.
At that time, King Śuddhodana spoke again, saying:
"Great Brahmin! These words are excellent."
"For what reason?
I too wish for my son to become like this, and I also pray that my son may be as you have described.
At that time, King Śuddhodana reflected within his own mind:
"Now that I am about to bring the boy into the city, what kind of palanquin shall I use?

King Śuddhodana had this thought, and at that moment, Viśvakarman, the master of craftsmanship, immediately manifested a palanquin made of the seven treasures; it was spontaneously formed without human labor, exquisite and subtle, extraordinary and peerless.

At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately issued a strict decree, ordering the city of Kapilavastu to be repaired; he commanded that all thorns, gravel, pebbles, filth, and mounds of earth be swept away and cleared, ensuring that all impurities and foul odors were completely purified.
That Kapilavastu was adorned with various ornaments, no different from the city of the Gandharvas.

All the various performers of diverse entertainments within that city—musicians capable of singing and dancing, masters of illusion who could either play with pearls or produce water, or adorn themselves as women—all such performers of various transformations gathered there like clouds.

At that time, some in the great assembly leaped up and cast themselves into the air; others tossed their bells aloft, or struck drums; some put on sandals or clogs, while others climbed to the tops of poles; some even walked backward with their heads down and feet up, or threw themselves upside down like revolving wheels.

Some ran along ropes suspended high in the air; some whirled on pikes; others leaped while brandishing sharp blades. There were such limitless and boundless varieties of jesting and displays, some raising their voices with loud shouts and cries, some snapping their fingers, and others playing with their garments.

At that time, the four world-protecting Great Kings each transformed their bodies into those of brahmins; all were of youthful age, upright and pleasing to behold, with their hair tied in spiral topknots, as they personally bore the Bodhisattva’s precious palanquin while walking along.

At that time, Śakra Devendra also concealed his original form and transformed himself into the son of a young brahmin; he was as handsome as before, with hair coiled in a topknot, wearing yellow robes, and holding a golden water-pitcher in his left hand.
Furthermore, with his right hand he held up a precious stand before the Bodhisattva to block the passage of people, and spoke these words:
"O you multitudes! "
"You should each clear the way for the Most Victorious among Beings, who now wishes to enter the city. (The Sanskrit original repeats the last four lines to clarify the gravity of his intention.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King of the Form Realm recited a verse from the past to praise the Bodhisattva, saying:
"In heaven above and on earth below, none is equal to the Buddha; so it is throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Having surveyed all that exists in the world, I find that there is nothing else like the Buddha."
"At that time, when the Bodhisattva was about to depart from the Lumbinī Garden in Devadaha for Kapilavastu, all the devas sprinkled and swept the road."

Furthermore, there were five thousand celestial maidens, each holding a golden pitcher filled with scented water in her hand; they sprinkled this upon the ground and proceeded one after another before the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there were five hundred celestial maidens, each holding a subtle and exquisite celestial broom, sweeping the ground as they proceeded before the Bodhisattva.

Additionally, there were five hundred celestial maidens, each holding a celestial incense burner made of various jewels, burning all kinds of subtle and exquisite incense; they paid homage to the Bodhisattva and led the way as they proceeded.
Furthermore, there were five hundred celestial maidens who, carrying golden jeweled vases filled with exquisite incense, walked before the Bodhisattva leading the way.
Furthermore, there were five hundred celestial maidens, each holding a divine and exquisite fan made of *tāla* leaves, who proceeded before the Bodhisattva to guide his way.
Furthermore, there were five hundred celestial maidens, each holding the tail of a peacock king to serve as a fly-whisk, walking before the Bodhisattva to lead the way.
Furthermore, there were five hundred celestial maidens, each holding a casket made of *tāla* palm leaves, who walked before the Bodhisattva to guide his way.
Furthermore, there were five hundred celestial jade maidens, each holding a celestial folding chair in her hand, walking before the Bodhisattva to lead the way.

Additionally, there were five thousand other celestial maidens, each holding a golden bell; from time to time they shook them, raising their voices to chant auspicious sounds as they walked before the Bodhisattva to lead the way.

"Furthermore, there were twenty-five thousand fragrant elephants, all with golden bridles and reins, golden saddles and housings, and all clad in golden armor; every ornamentation was made entirely of pure gold, and atop these trappings were draped golden nets. They followed behind the Bodhisattva, proceeding one after another."

Furthermore, there were twenty thousand precious horses, all of which were blue in color with heads as black as crows; their manes hung down to the ground, and all their harnesses, saddles, cushions, and stirrups were adorned purely with gold. Nets of celestial gold covered them from above, and they followed behind the Bodhisattva, proceeding one after another in succession.

Furthermore, there were twenty thousand exquisite chariots made of various jewels, yoked with teams of four horses and adorned with banners and canopies; covered above by nets of celestial gold, they followed behind the Bodhisattva, proceeding one after another.

Furthermore, there were forty thousand infantrymen and warriors, all of whom were valiant and robust, each capable of facing a thousand men alone. They were all noble men of great physical strength, able to crush enemies and adversaries. Clad in armor and mail, they held bows and swords in their hands, some grasping iron wheels and others wielding halberds and spears; in this manner, they followed behind the Bodhisattva in succession as his retinue.
Furthermore, immeasurable and boundless hosts of devas from the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) of greatest majesty and virtue proceeded on the right side of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, immeasurable and boundless hosts of devas from the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu) of greatest majesty and virtue proceeded on the left side of the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable and boundless nāga kings, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and others, who manifested half their bodies, each holding various kinds of exquisite flowers that filled the void of space, following the Bodhisattva’s journey.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless billions of tens of millions of deva kings who, filled with joy and leaping for gladness, could not contain themselves. They raised their voices in cries, some snapped their fingers, some danced or sang, producing extraordinary sounds; some played with their garments, some with their hands and feet, performing various acts of merriment.

Some held various kinds of powdered incense, unguents, flower garlands, necklaces, *māndārava* flowers, and other diverse blossoms; each personally bore them aloft above the Bodhisattva and scattered them upon him as they traveled through the void. Having scattered them upon the Bodhisattva, they further scattered them among all the devas. By the power of this Bodhisattva’s majestic virtue, the scent of human beings was not perceived, and although all the people beheld the celestial forms, they were neither struck with wonder nor did they become heedless.

"At that time, all the kinsmen of the Śākya clan, leading the fourfold army—chariots, cavalry, elephants, and infantry—surrounded the Bodhisattva. Whether in front or behind, to the left or to the right, they followed the Bodhisattva’s procession, filling and pervading the city of Kapilavastu."

King Śuddhodana, exercising the power and majesty of a great monarch, struck countless drums—both large and small—and blew limitless, boundless conch shells. With such infinite and boundless sounds of various kinds and diverse natures, he provided entertainment for the Bodhisattva and led him forward into the city of Kapilavastu.

At that time, not far from the city of Kapilavastu, there was a celestial shrine dedicated to a deity named Vaśavartin. Beside that temple, there were always immeasurable members of the Śākya clan—both boys and girls—who would kneel and prostrate themselves while making petitions, always obtaining their heart's desires.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, taking the Bodhisattva back, arrived at that celestial abode and addressed his ministers, saying:
"Now, let my child pay homage to this great deity."
At that time, the wet nurse took up the Bodhisattva and went to that celestial shrine.

Then there was another female deity named Abhayā; the image of this goddess came down from her own hall to welcome the Bodhisattva, joined her palms in reverence, bowed her head to the ground in prostration at the Bodhisattva’s feet, and said to the wet nurse:
"This is a supreme being; do not harbor thoughts of violating or disparaging him. (These two preceding phrases are repeated in the Sanskrit original.)
One should not cause him to kneel and prostrate before me; rather, I should pay homage to him. Why is this?
For the one to whom he pays homage is capable of causing a person's head to split into seven pieces.
