"At that time, there were five hundred ministers of the Śākya clan in the city of Kapilavastu, all of whom were kinsmen and attendants of the Bodhisattva; they once again constructed five hundred vihāras intended for the Bodhisattva’s sitting."
When the Bodhisattva first entered the city, each person stood before their own door and, with a heart of joy, joined their palms in reverence and spoke these words:
"May the God among Gods enter my vihāra;
may the Great Captain enter my vihāra."
May those whose bodies are golden and who purify sentient beings enter my vihāra;
may those who bestow a heart of universal joy enter my vihāra;
may those whose fame is heard afar and who are free from reproach enter my vihāra.
"May the one of most honored virtue, the peerless one, enter my monastery.

At that time, out of compassion for these five hundred kinsmen, King Śuddhodana led the Bodhisattva on a tour, entering their monasteries one after another until he had visited them all; only then did he lead him into his own palace.
"At that time, on the very day the Bodhisattva was born, there were five hundred sons of the Śākya clan born on the same day; yet the Bodhisattva was most eminent and preeminent among them all."
"Furthermore, there were five hundred women of the Śākya clan who were also born on that same day, with Yaśodharā as their leader.
Furthermore, there were five hundred servants of the Śākyas who were also born on that same day in the palace of King Śuddhodana, with Chandaka as their leader."
"Furthermore, there were five hundred Śākya maidservants who were also born on the same day in King Śuddhodana’s palace to serve and attend upon the Prince.
Furthermore, there were five hundred pure white colts who were also born on the same day in King Śuddhodana’s stable, with Kaṇṭhaka as their leader."
"Furthermore, five hundred great fragrant elephant kings appeared suddenly at the gate of the royal palace; their color was white as snow, and each was endowed with six tusks."
"Furthermore, five hundred great and vast hidden treasures appeared spontaneously, surrounding Kapilavastu on all four sides.

Additionally, five hundred exquisite gardens, with flowing springs and bathing pools, and filled everywhere with various flowers and fruits, all manifested around the city of Kapilavastu on its four sides; this was entirely due to the power of the Prince’s majestic virtue."
"Furthermore, five hundred great merchant lords, who had accumulated vast wealth and possessed an abundance of rare treasures, came together to the city of Kapilavastu.
Additionally, five hundred exquisite parasols and five hundred golden jars were sent by the envoys of five hundred minor kings (*kṣudraka-rāja*) to present to King Śuddhodana, with these words:
'We now offer these items to Your Majesty to celebrate the birth of the Prince.'"
"Furthermore, there were five thousand brahmins and kṣatriyas who were great and wealthy householders; each brought his own daughter and presented her to King Śuddhodana."
At that time, King Śuddhodana provided everything that was required.
Then, King Śuddhodana reflected within his mind:
"I have fathered a crown prince; what name shall I now give him?"
He further reflected:
"On the day he was born, all matters were spontaneously accomplished; now I may bestow a name upon the prince, and call him Siddhārtha."
At that time, King Śuddhodana opened his treasury and brought forth ten billion taels of gold to provide for the completion of the offerings and to establish a name for him.
Therefore, the verse says:
"Thus, within the royal palace, All matters were in full abundance."
"Now that we have given the Crown Prince a name, it should be named Siddhārtha.

**Chapter 8: The Examination by the Physiognomists** *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Part One At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately summoned the physiognomists and those skilled in divination, calling them forward to examine the Crown Prince, and spoke these words:
"You physiognomists, Brahmins, and others: examine this Crown Prince; within our clan, will he be auspicious or inauspicious?"
"You all must carefully observe the signs of good and ill fortune.

At that time, the various physiognomists, Brahmins, and others, having heard the king’s command, gazed with single-minded devotion upon the Prince’s appearance and, according to the various treatises of the ancient sages, deliberated together on what was appropriate.
Having completed his assessment of what was appropriate, he addressed the king, saying:
"Great King! You have now attained great benefit for the multitude."
For what reason?
This prince possesses great majestic power and virtue; he is a great being who has now been born into a royal family.
O Great King!

You should know that this prince’s body possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man. Whenever a person is endowed with these thirty-two marks of a great man, there are two possible karmic results in this world that do not fail to manifest, and no other outcome is possible.
What are these two?

First, if one remains a householder and experiences worldly pleasures, one may become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), ruling over the four quarters of the world and protecting the great earth. Endowed with the seven treasures, one governs throughout the seas naturally and in accordance with the Dharma, without the need for swords or staves to transform the people.

If he renounces his royal throne to leave the household life and study the Way, he will attain the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and his fame will spread far and wide, filling the world.
At that time, having heard this prediction, King Śuddhodana asked the brāhmaṇa once more:
"In what parts of the prince's body are the thirty-two marks of a great man?"
The brahmin said:
"As for the thirty-two marks of a great man:
first, the soles of the prince's feet are well-placed and entirely level and full."
Second, beneath both of the Prince’s feet are the marks of thousand-spoked wheels, positioned centrally, beautiful, pleasing, and pure.
Third, the Prince’s fingers are slender and long.
Fourth, the Prince’s heels are full and well-formed.
Fifth, the Prince’s insteps are high and prominent.
Sixth, the Prince’s hands and feet are soft and supple.
Seventh, between the toes of the Prince’s hands and feet, he is fully endowed with webbing.
Eighth, the Prince’s calves are like those of the king of deer.
Ninth, when the Prince stands upright without bending, his two hands reach past his knees.
Tenth, the Prince possesses the mark of the concealed male organ like that of a horse.
Eleventh, each hair on the Prince’s skin grows individually from a single pore and curls upward.
Twelfth, the hairs on the Prince’s body all point upward.
Thirteenth, the Prince’s skin is fine and soft like *tūla* cotton.
Fourteenth, the Prince’s body hair is golden in color.
Fifteenth, the Prince’s body is pure and stainless.
Sixteenth, the Prince’s mouth is deep, beautiful, pleasing, and well-proportioned.
Seventeenth, the Prince’s jaw is square and well-formed, like that of a lion king.
Eighteenth, the Prince’s two calves are broad and expansive.
Nineteenth, the Prince’s body is perfectly symmetrical from top to bottom and side to side, like a nyagrodha tree.
Twentieth, the Prince has seven parts of his body that are full and well-proportioned.
Twenty-first, he possesses forty teeth.
Twenty-second: his teeth are even and closely set. Twenty-third:
his teeth are neither sparse nor missing, nor are they protruding or uneven.
Twenty-fourth: his four canine teeth are white and pure.
Twenty-fifth, his body is pure and of a uniform golden hue.
Twenty-sixth, his voice is like that of Brahmā.
Twenty-seventh, his tongue is broad, long, soft, supple, red, and thin.
Twenty-eighth, all the food he consumes becomes of the finest flavor.
Twenty-ninth, his eyes are deep blue.
Thirtieth, the Prince’s eyelashes are like those of a bull king.
Thirty-first, between his eyebrows is a white tuft of hair that curls to the right, perfectly soft, pure, and brilliantly radiant.
Thirty-second, on the crown of his head is a fleshy protuberance (uṣṇīṣa), high, broad, level, and well-formed.
"Great King!
These are the thirty-two marks of a Great Man possessed by the Prince; he is thus fully endowed with them.
If there is a person who possesses these marks of a Great Man, that person will obtain two kinds of karmic fruition—whether remaining at home or going forth—as previously described."

At that time, when King Śuddhodana heard these words spoken by the physiognomists, his heart was filled with great joy; his entire body leaped with such exuberance that he could not contain himself. He immediately prepared various foods and drinks of a hundred flavors and provided them for those brahmin physiognomists and others, allowing them to eat as much as they desired until they were fully satisfied.
Furthermore, he bestowed upon them various kinds of exquisite garments, diverse jewels, and other material wealth.

At that time, within the great city of Kapilavastu, King Śuddhodana established "unrestricted assemblies" (asaṃvṛta-maṇḍala) at every crossroads, street, and alleyway throughout the city. Whatever was required was provided to all: food to those who needed food, drink to those who needed drink, clothing to those who needed clothing, incense to those who needed incense, bedding and mats to those who needed them, houses and dwellings to those who needed them, wealth and resources to those who needed them, and vehicles and mounts to those who needed them. All such merit was dedicated and transferred for the benefit and nourishment of the Prince’s body.

"At that time, when the Bodhisattva was first born from his mother’s womb in the Lumbinī Garden at the city of Devadṛśa, he was mindful and clearly conscious; he emitted a great radiance that filled the entire world, and this great earth shook in six ways, manifesting eighteen signs."

At that time, the devas and ṛṣis dwelling on earth, having seen this auspicious omen, were filled with joy throughout their bodies; unable to contain themselves, they raised their voices in cries and uttered these great words:

"Today, a Bodhisattva has been born within the Laṇḍīvana grove of Jambudvīpa, to bring great peace and happiness to all the worlds of gods and humans, and to provide great illumination for sentient beings shrouded in the darkness of ignorance."

At that time, when the Four Great Kings heard the loud voices raised by those earth-dwelling devas and sages, the devas residing where the Four Great Kings dwell heard this report and were likewise filled with great joy. They raised their voices loudly, fluttered their garments, and spoke these words:
"Now, among human beings, a Bodhisattva has been born for the sake of peace, happiness, and illumination for all the worlds."
When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven heard the cries of the Cāturmahārājika gods, they too were filled with great joy. In this manner,
it continued until the Yāma gods heard it from the Trāyastriṃśa, the Tuṣita gods heard it from the Yāma,
the Nirmāṇarati gods heard it from the Tuṣita, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods heard it from the Nirmāṇarati.
Successively, it was further heard by the Brahmā gods of the Form Realm from those of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations;
by the Gods of the Retinue of Brahmā from the abode of Brahmā; by the Gods of the Ministers of Brahmā from the Gods of the Retinue of Brahmā;

by Mahābrahmā from the Gods of the Ministers of Brahmā; by the Ābhāsvara gods from that Mahābrahmā; and by the Parīttābha gods from the abode of those Ābhāsvara gods. Thus it reached the Apramāṇa... [gods].
The Ābhāsvara gods heard it from the Parīttābha gods; the Ābhāsvara gods heard it from the Apramāṇābha gods;
the Śubhakṛtsna gods heard it from those Ābhāsvara gods; the Parīttaśubha gods heard it from the Śubhakṛtsna realm; the Apramāṇaśubha gods heard it from the Parīttaśubha gods;
the Śubhakṛtsna gods heard it from the Apramāṇaśubha gods; and the Bṛhatphala gods heard it from those Śubhakṛtsna gods.

From the Vast Heaven (Vaśavartin) to the Limited Vast Heaven (Apramāṇa-vaśavartin), from the Limited Vast Heaven to the Immeasurable Vast Heaven (Aparimāṇa-vaśavartin), from the Immeasurable Vast Heaven to the Fruitful Heaven (Bṛhatphala), from the Fruitful Heaven to the Heat Heaven (Atapa), from the Heat Heaven to the Untormented Heaven (Atapana), from the Untormented Heaven to the Peerless Heaven (Sudṛśa), from the Peerless Heaven to the Good Appearance Heaven (Sudarśana)— in this sequence, in a single instant, he reaches even as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
All the devas each proclaimed:

"Today the Bodhisattva has been born into the world to bring great peace and happiness to gods and humans, and to act as a great lamp of illumination for sentient beings who are shrouded in darkness and blindness."

"At that time, there was an Ṛṣi named Asita who was observing the rains retreat in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Seeing those devas leaping for joy and unable to contain themselves—some tossing their garments and raising their voices as before—he [observed them closely]."
Having seen this, he immediately asked those devas:
"Venerable sirs!

For what reason do the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven now experience such joy and exultation that it pervades their entire bodies, such that they cannot contain themselves, and furthermore, they cry out loudly while clutching at their robes and crowns?"
Having spoken these words, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven replied to the seer Asita:
"Venerable Seer Asita, have you not heard that in this world, on the land of Jambudvīpa, there shall be in the north, beneath the Snow Mountains, a city of the Śākya clan named Kapilavastu?"
In that city there was a king named Śuddhodana.

To the chief queen of that king a son was born, who was exceedingly handsome and most exceptionally lovely; his body was the color of gold, his head was like a parasol, his nose was high, round, and straight, and his two arms hung down [to his knees]. His physical form was dignified and majestic, his six sense faculties were complete, and every part was well-proportioned, like a cast golden statue. He was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and possessed the eighty minor signs of excellence.
"O Great Sage!
That bodhisattva will certainly attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; having attained it, he will certainly turn the unsurpassed, pure wheel of Dharma."
That bodhisattva is able, within all the worlds—including devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—to personally realize the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Having realized these supernormal powers, they proclaim the True Dharma; that Dharma is esoteric, excellent in its beginning, middle, and end, profound and subtle in meaning and flavor, and fully expounds the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*).
When he preached the Dharma, all sentient beings who heard it were such that those subject to the law of birth cut off the law of birth;
those subject to the law of aging cut off the law of aging;
and those subject to the law of illness attained the cutting off of the law of illness.
"One who undergoes the law of death can attain the cessation of the law of death;
sorrow, grief, and affliction shall all be severed and their very roots extinguished.
Having heard this from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the seer Asita conceived deep faith. He immediately vanished from that heaven and descended, appearing in the Nyagrodha Grove.
At that time, there was another who spoke these words:
"In the land of South India, there is a city named Ujjayanī. Not far from the city is a mountain named Vindhya; between them lies yet another mountain named Asita."
At that time, the seer resided on that mountain; because of that mountain, he was known by the name of the seer Asita.

When the seer descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and stayed upon that mountain, the seer Asita, taking a single attendant named Nārada, departed from that mountain, traveled here to the city of Kapilavastu, and stood at a place not far from the city, reflecting thus:
"In the past, in this city of Kapilavastu, I heard various royal preceptors and brahmins say:"
“King Śuddhodana has fathered a son who is a Bodhisattva; he is the teacher of gods, humans, and ourselves, and must not be treated with contempt.
It would be impossible for me to enter the city of Kapilavastu now by manifesting supernatural powers.”
Why is this? The city of Kapilavastu is no longer as it was in the past.
If one were to go there today, other extraordinary signs would surely manifest once more.
"I ought to revere him as I would a supreme deity; I shall rather proceed on foot into that city.

Then, Āsita and his attendant Nārada entered the city of Kapilavastu on foot together, taking a narrow alleyway to approach the residence of King Śuddhodana in secret, until they arrived before the palace gates.

At that time, the people of Kapilavastu were so densely crowded that they filled every place without any empty space; for the sake of the Bodhisattva, they had prepared a magnificent array of ornaments.

When the great multitude saw that seer approaching on foot, entering Kapilavastu and proceeding through narrow alleys toward the palace gate of King Śuddhodana, immeasurable and boundless people gathered like clouds and rain to follow the seer. Witnessing this, they were struck with amazement and, feeling it strange, did not dare to ask why.
For what reason has the seer come here? At that time,

the great assembly and the people within the city— some standing before their own doors, some at the windows, some leaning against the railings, some atop the terraces, and some upon the roofs— all gazed upon the seer and said to one another:
"In the past, when this seer entered the city of Kapilavastu, he traveled through the air by means of great supernormal powers and arrived at the palace of King Śuddhodana."
"We did not know that you had come to the city on foot today.
For what reason have you traveled here on foot?
When Asita had arrived at the gate of King Śuddhodana’s palace, he spoke thus to the gatekeeper:

"I am a brahmin who has long been aged and decrepit, like a grandfather; yet today, walking on foot, I resemble a young child of twenty, arriving here together with the youth Nārada, who is only eight years old. You should inform King Śuddhodana on my behalf."
Then the gatekeeper said to the rishi,
"As the venerable one instructs, I shall respectfully report this.
He immediately entered the palace gates and proceeded gradually until he stood before the king, reporting everything in detail to him.

When King Śuddhodana heard these words, his heart was filled with great reverence and he rejoiced immeasurably. He immediately rose from his seat and said to the gatekeeper who managed the attendants:
"Quickly lead the seer here; do not let there be any delay."
Then the gatekeeper returned to the place where the seer was and spoke these words:
"Great Seer, you know the proper time; you should enter the palace at once.
Having heard those words, Asita immediately entered King Śuddhodana’s palace together with his attendant Nārada.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, standing afar in the palace, saw the seer Asita approaching slowly toward his location. Thereupon, the Great King rose from his seat and went to where the seer was; he attended to him with reverence and welcomed him, supporting him under the armpits. He then brought forth a most excellent, wondrous, and peerless jewel throne, set it out for him to sit upon, and once he was seated, the King prostrated himself and spoke these words:
"I now pay respectful homage to the Venerable One."
At that time, the rishi immediately offered this blessing to King Śuddhodana,
saying: "May Your Majesty always enjoy peace and happiness!"
Then King Śuddhodana said to the seer:
"Venerable sir, for what purpose have you deigned to come here?
Do you require clothing?"
"Do you require food?
Or do you seek anything else?
Speak what you need, and I shall provide it all; I will certainly not refuse you."
Then Asita addressed the king, saying: "Great King!
You should know that my coming here is not for lack of anything; I do not seek food or clothing, nor is there any need for any such things."
Nevertheless, I have now come from afar specifically wishing to see the Great King’s most excellent son.
Out of your compassionate grace, O Great King, I pray that you will show me this most excellent youth.
At that time, the boy was sleeping soundly upon his jeweled throne.
King Śuddhodana said to Asita:
"Venerable Great Seer!..."
‘He has been attentive for but a short time; the boy is now asleep and has not yet awakened. I pray you, wait but a moment.
Then Asita addressed the king, saying:
‘Great King!’
Do not speak such words as to say that the youth is asleep.
Why is this? Although we are awake, we are like those who are sleeping.
"Great King!

For a long time the youth has been free from sleep; day and night he constantly enters meditative absorption for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings and for their great benefit."

At that time, King Śuddhodana, knowing that the moment for the youth’s awakening from sleep was approaching, entered the palace and issued orders to adorn the palaces and halls. He had the floors sprinkled with pure water, swept clean of all filth, and drenched again with scented water; he scattered flowers upon them and placed incense burners everywhere, burning various exquisite fragrances.
Furthermore, various silk banners and canopies were suspended, with hanging tassels and streamers, and great jeweled standards were erected.

Additionally, immeasurable pearl necklaces and pearl nets, along with various jeweled bells, were hung and draped over it; many miscellaneous jewels were suspended, like the radiance of the sun, moon, and stars.
Furthermore, various exquisite garments of precious jewels were hung, resembling celestial beings holding flower garlands in their hands;
additionally, multicolored tassels of vermilion, purple, red, and yellow were suspended in great variety.
All such things were exquisitely adorned and beautifully decorated within the palace, no different from the city of Gandharvas.

Furthermore, he summoned the inner and outer kinsmen of the Śākya clan, including those of the greatest and most eminent majesty and virtue, and had them enter the palace to be together with Lady Māyā.
At that time, Māyā went to where the boy was; having arrived, she took him by the hand and cradled his head, directing him toward the seer as if to pay homage at the seer’s feet.
Then, by the power of the boy’s majestic virtue, his body turned of its own accord so that his feet were directed toward the seer.
Then, King Śuddhodana again supported the boy’s head together with them, intending to have him bow to the seer;
yet by the power of the boy, his feet turned back toward that seer.
At that time, King Śuddhodana again turned the boy so that his head faced the seer, yet he turned his feet back once more; this was repeated three times. From afar, Asita beheld the boy;

at that moment, the boy emitted his usual radiance which illuminated and touched the great earth. The boy’s majestic virtue was upright and lovely; his complexion was pure gold, his head like a precious canopy, his nose straight and rounded, his long arms hanging down, and his limbs and joints perfectly proportioned, complete, and without deficiency, endowed with full adornment.
Then Asita rose from his seat and addressed the king, saying:
"Great King!
Do not offer the noble head of this boy to me."
"Why is this? His head is not fit to prostrate at my feet; rather, my head should prostrate at his feet.
He then uttered these words again:
"How rare, how rare!
A Great Being has appeared in the world; most rare indeed is the appearance of a Great Being in the world!
This very boy is one of whom I have previously heard from the devas!"
"This is indeed the true concentration; it is not different from that.

Then Asita adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, extended both hands, took the boy in his arms, placed him upon his head, and returned to his original seat.
Once the Great Seer had taken his seat, he brought the boy down and placed him upon his knees.
At that time, Queen Māyā addressed the Great Seer Asita, saying:
"O Venerable Master!..."
"Let the boy pay homage at the feet of the Great Sage.
The Seer Asita replied to the Queen,
"O Great Lady of the Realm!"
Do not speak such words.
This youth should not pay homage to me;
rather, I and all the devas, humans, and worldlings should receive his feet and pay homage to this youth.
Then King Śuddhodana took various kinds of diverse and wonderful precious jewels and offered them as a religious gift (*dakṣiṇā*) to the seer Asita.
At that time, Asita took his own water-pitcher, washed his hands with water, accepted these offerings, and having accepted them, immediately took them back and presented them to the boy.
Then King Śuddhodana addressed the great seer Asita, saying:
"Venerable Great Seer!
I offer these things to you; I only pray that you will accept them."
The seer replied, "Great King, you have given this to me;
I now give it back as a gift to the most excellent youth.
King Śuddhodana said:
"I know that because the Great Seer’s field of merit is supreme, I have made offerings to the Great Master.
The seer Asita then replied to the king:
"Because I now perceive these superior causes and conditions, I shall transfer my offering to the youth."
King Śuddhodana said:
"O Great Holy Sage!
I do not now understand this intention of my venerable teacher."
The seer spoke again:
"Great King!
You should know that my body and mind now deeply submit themselves to this youth."
King Śuddhodana said:
"By what cause and by what condition?
I pray that you will explain this for me."
Then Asita replied to the king, saying:
"Great King, with a focused mind, listen well to this meaning; I shall explain its beginning and end for you."
"Great King!

You should know that formerly, while I was dwelling in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven practicing the Path during the summer retreat, I suddenly saw all the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven filled with such joy and exultation that it pervaded their entire bodies; they could not contain themselves, brandishing their robes and headdresses, leaping about in delight."
At that time, I immediately asked them:
"O virtuous devas!
For what cause and for what reason do you leap for joy so uncontrollably, grasping your robes and caps and dancing about with such exuberance?"
After he had spoken these words, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven immediately replied to me, saying:
"O Great Virtuous Seer!
Do you not know now?"
In the northern region of this world, beneath the Snowy Mountains, there is a city of the Śākya clan named Kapilavastu; in that city, there was a king named Śuddhodana.
The king’s principal and most eminent queen gave birth to a boy who was handsome and pleasing, a sight that all people delighted to behold.

His body was the color of gold; his head was well-rounded, his nose straight, his feet full, and his arms long—resembling a golden statue. He was fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics, destined to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and turn the unsurpassed, pure wheel of Dharma.
This youth is now fully endowed with the marks of excellence; of this there is no doubt.

By his own supernatural power, this youth is able to know this world, as well as the past and future worlds, including the devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—all that constitutes the world. Having realized this through his own direct knowledge, he discerns the characteristics of phenomena and, to speak briefly, brings those subject to various sufferings and afflictions to liberation by enabling them to attain liberation.
"Great King, it was because I heard these words at that time that I have come here to observe the boy.
Then, King Śuddhodana replied to the seer, "If this is so, you have shown me great compassion and brought me great benefit; my sorrow is now dispelled."
Furthermore, what dharma is there that surpasses these four modes of practice? Having transcended these four modes, what can be superior and most excellent?
Now, this youth, though born of human parents, shall be able to attain the unsurpassed path in the future.
The seer Asita spoke again to the king, saying:
"Great King, you should know this:
how can all those various brahmins, wherever they may be, attain victory and realize the truth?"
Then, King Śuddhodana again addressed the seer, saying:
"I now stand before the Great Seer; I pray that you will explain for me, so that I may joyfully hear it."
Then Asita replied: "Great King!

According to the oral tradition of my brahmin lineage, as stated in the four Vedas, there was once a brahmin named Meṣa; another brahmin named Bakari; another brahmin named Bakava; another brahmin named Mātaṅga; another brahmin named Kaṭarūri; and another brahmin named Pañcaśikha. They all attained the methods of calculation of the Asura kings, achieving supreme excellence."
Furthermore, there was a rishi named Ātreya, a king named Pramodana, and a king named Janaka; all these individuals attained the skillful means for eliminating physical suffering.
"Great King!
You should know that it is even so; although this youth has been born among humans, he transcends ordinary men and has attained the qualities of a superior being."
"Great King!

In the past there was another king named Bhagīratha. When the great ocean surged with waves as high as mountains, making it exceedingly difficult to cross, he—neither his grandfather nor his father—was the one who personally crossed over."
"Great King!
Although such as these are born among humans, they possess great majesty and virtue; by virtue of this majesty and virtue, they surpass all devas and humans.
At that time, King Śuddhodana replied to the seer, saying:
"If it is as the Venerable Teacher has proclaimed, I have no doubt; however, because my beloved son is narrow-minded and inferior in spirit, he has become terrified."
The seer Asita spoke again to the king, saying:
"Great King, whatever doubts you may have in your heart, you may now inquire about them, and I shall resolve them all for you."
Then King Śuddhodana said:

"Great Master, I truly harbor doubts. Regarding those of the past, such as King Tāmradvīpa, King Tārakṣu, King Jñātiputra, and King Dālabha—men such as these, I have never seen them, nor have I ever heard of them."
"How can this child of mine know and see such a thing?
I pray that you will explain the causes and conditions.
At that time, Asita replied again to the king:
"Great King!
I also know that you have such doubts; one cannot say they do not exist. Why is this? "
Great King, you should merely hear what others have said, examine it with your own mind, deliberate upon it, and thereby resolve your doubts;
for as a general rule, the various kings who have acted before and after [you] do not necessarily possess consistent evidence.
"Great King!
Among those various kings, their sons, fathers, and ancestors differ in terms of superiority and inferiority.

Therefore, Great King, one cannot claim superiority based solely on lineage, nor can one claim superiority based solely on family; one cannot be superior by virtue of being born earlier and later become inferior."
Or there may be those who appear later and surpass those who appeared earlier.
Great King!
It is like at the break of dawn: first the signs of light appear, and only then does the sun rise.
Regarding its luminous appearance, it was not yet able to illuminate; when the sun rose later, it shone universally upon the great earth, destroying all darkness without exception.
"Great King!
Such is the nature of the world that, at times, a son is born who excels his father and his grandfather.
Then, King Śuddhodana addressed the seer, saying:
"O Great Virtuous One, Honored Teacher!
You have skillfully used analogies to clarify this matter and comfort me, enabling me to resolve my doubts and bringing great peace and stability to my mind."
"O Great Sage, Honored Teacher!
Please graciously accept me.
Then Asita spoke again to the king:
"Great King!
You should know that my teeth have decayed and my life is nearly spent.

This youth, however, is still young and in the prime of his years; once he has grown up and reached maturity, he will surely depart for the mountain forests to leave the household life and study the Way."
"I regret that I am so decrepit and aged that I do not behold your compassionate countenance.
Then, King Śuddhodana said to the seer:
"O Great Seer, Honored Teacher!"
"Will this boy now certainly leave the household life?
The seer Asita replied to the king, saying,
"Great King, you need not harbor any doubts at this time."
Then King Śuddhodana turned his head and looked toward the face of the State Preceptor;
at that time, Asita asked the king, "Great King, what do you wish to say within your heart?"
King Śuddhodana said:
"O Great Virtuous Holy Sage!
These brahmins, my national preceptors and others, once spoke to me, saying:"
"This boy shall certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
The seer Asita spoke again to the king, saying:
"Great King!..."
"As it is in my mind, there shall be no falsehood; what I have now spoken is sincere, truthful, and ultimate reality.
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he spoke again:
"O Great Seer, Honored Teacher!"
"If this is indeed so, it causes my heart to feel even greater sorrow; it cuts through my heart and boils with distress within my very liver and entrails.
Then Asita replied to the king, saying, "Great King, you who possess wisdom, do not speak such words."

Great King, because of the causes and conditions of the meritorious deeds performed by your high ancestors in the past, they were able to ferry sentient beings across to the other shore. As such a guide and leader, he has taken birth as your son; it is not merely for the sake of governing and transforming the people and bringing them peace and happiness that he acts as a prince.
Then King Śuddhodana again addressed the seer, saying:
"Great Master!
My mind is likewise; I have reflected in this manner."

Now this youth has been born into my royal lineage to bear the heavy burden and relieve me of my anxieties; when I reach old age, I shall leave the household life to enter the mountains and cultivate the ancient Way.
Then King Śuddhodana again addressed the seer, saying:
"Great Master!
It is my wish that my son may remain forever; what skillful means might there be?"
"And now that he is still in his youth, do not allow him to leave me.
The seer Asita spoke again to the king, saying:
"Great King!
"I truly cannot, with single-minded certainty, declare that these skillful means will create obstacles.
Then King Śuddhodana spoke again to the seer, saying:
"Great Master, listen well!

I shall now employ various skillful means; having established these means, I will not allow my son, from his current youth until he reaches the prime of life, even a moment’s separation, so that he does not abandon me to go forth into homelessness.
The seer Asita then asked the king:
"Great King, for what reason do you speak these words?
At that time, King Śuddhodana replied to the seer Asita:
"Venerable Teacher, you should know that all the physiognomists and brahmins within my kingdom have said to me:
'If this boy remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King.'"
"For this reason, I have spoken thus.
The seer Asita addressed the king again, saying:
"Great King!
You should know that those physiognomists are all uttering great falsehoods. Why is this?
Such superior marks as these are not the marks of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin).
Now this youth possesses the hundred marks of excellence and the eighty secondary characteristics; his extraordinary and sublime beauty is distinct and radiant, fully and completely perfected.
Then King Śuddhodana asked the seer,
"Great Master, what are these eighty minor marks of excellence belonging to this boy?
Thereupon, Asita addressed the king in detail:
“‘Great King, you should know that within the palms of this boy’s two hands there are vajra-marks. ‘Great King!
Now, the nails of this boy’s fingers are thin and soft.’”
“‘Great King!
Now, the color of this youth’s fingernails is a deep crimson, just like copper plates.
Great King!’”
"Now, O Great King, the fingernails of this youth are all smooth and lustrous.
'O Great King!
Now, the fingers of this youth possess a wondrous color.'"
“‘Great King!
Now, all the fingers of this youth are webbed.
‘Great King!’”
"Now, O Great King, the ankle bones of this boy do not protrude.
Furthermore, his two knees are perfectly rounded and possess a great luster."
"O Great King!
Now this youth moves with dignified grace, proceeding calmly and walking at a slow pace.
O Great King!"
"This youth walks like a lion king. 'Great King!
This youth walks like a bull king.'"
"O Great King! This youth's gait is like that of a king of swans. O Great King!"
"This youth walks with a steady and slow gait, like a jeweled earring.
'Great King! This youth walks with such composure that it is as if he were standing still.'"
“‘Great King!
This boy’s body is straight and upright.
‘Great King!’”
"The body of this youth is soft and supple.
'Great King! The body of this youth is smooth and lustrous.'"
"O Great King!
This youth’s body is fully endowed with [these qualities].
O Great King!"
From the body of this youth issues a wondrous incense fragrance. "Great King!
The skin and body of this youth are unsurpassed."
“‘Great King!
This youth’s body is perfectly composed and dignified.
‘Great King!’”
"The limbs and joints of this boy's body are clearly defined, each distinct from the others.
'O Great King! The skin and physical form of this boy appear like those of the Great Brahmā King.'"
"Great King! This youth’s body and skin are free from any deformity. Great King!"
"The body of this youth is pure and free from dark spots or freckles.
'Great King! This youth's body is free from all ailments.'"
“‘Great King!
This boy’s body is perfectly symmetrical.
“‘Great King!’”
"The body of this youth is perfectly proportioned in seven places.
'Great King! This youth's body is endowed with all the marks of excellence.'"
“‘Great King!
This youth’s body is upright and handsome in every part.
“‘Great King!’”
"The physical conduct of this youth is pure.
'Great King! This youth’s body is most excellent and stainless; all his body hairs are pure.'"
“‘Great King!
This youth’s body is free from all defilements and obstructions, and is able to emit pure light.
Great King!’”
The constant radiance of this boy’s body extends one fathom.
"Great King! This boy’s waist is like the belly of a bow. (Note: *bǎiyǎ* is a phonetic transcription for *kodaṇḍa*, meaning "bow").
“‘Great King!
This boy’s abdomen is not broken, meaning his skin is neither wrinkled nor shriveled.
“‘Great King!’”
"The navel of this boy is deep, hidden, and exquisitely beautiful. 'Great King!
This boy's navel is round and does not protrude.'"
“‘Great King!
This boy’s navel is like a chariot wheel.
‘Great King!’”
"The navel of this boy is clearly defined and spirals to the right. 'Great King!
This boy's hands are neither coarse nor rough.'"
“‘Great King!
This boy’s hands are like tūla-cotton.
“‘Great King!’”
"O Great King! The lines and patterns upon the palms of this youth’s hands are deep. O Great King!
The lines and patterns upon this youth’s hands are soft, supple, and lustrous."
“‘Great King! The lines on this youth’s palms are neither broken nor scattered.
“‘Great King!’”
The text on the palm of this youth’s hand is clear and its sequence is distinct:
"O Great King!
The two wrists of this youth are broad and large."
“‘Great King!
This boy’s head is like an ankle bone.
‘Great King!’”
"The lips and mouth of this youth are as red as the *bimba* fruit.
'Great King! The countenance of this youth is serene.'"
"O Great King!
This boy’s tongue is thin and long, and its color is like that of red copper.
O Great King!"
The voice of this youth was deep, clear, and resonant.
*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll Nine;
*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on the Divination of the Physiognomist, Part Two:
“‘O Great King!’”
The voice and speech of this youth are piteous, beautiful, clear, and resonant, vibrating far and wide.
"Great King! This youth’s four canine teeth in his mouth are broad and large."
“‘Great King!
These teeth of the prince are all perfectly sharp.
“‘Great King!’”
"The teeth of this youth are neither missing nor broken. 'Great King!
This youth's nose is upright, round, and straight, like that of a parrot.'"
“‘Great King!
This youth’s eyebrows are level, even, and closely set.
“‘Great King!’”
"This child has his ears pierced with rings that hang down.
"Great King! This child's ears are neither crooked nor distorted."
“‘Great King!
These ears of the youth are neither coarse nor rough.
‘Great King!’”
"The eyes of this youth are without deficiency.
'Great King! The eyes of this youth are without injury or impairment.'"
"O Great King!
The faculties of this youth’s body are serene and composed.
O Great King!"
"The face and forehead of this youth are most excellent and supreme. "Great King!
The hair of this youth is purely deep blue-black in color."
“‘Great King!
This youth’s hair is glossy and lustrous.
“‘Great King!’”
"The hair of this youth is neither coarse nor rough.
'Great King! The hair of this youth is not dense, yet it is thick.'"
“‘Great King!
This youth’s hair is even and fine and dense.
‘Great King!’”
The hair of this youth is neither deficient nor broken. "Great King!
The hair of this youth is curled and spiraled."
"Great King!
This boy’s hair is rounded and curls to the right, its shape like the svastika.
Great King!"
"The crown of this boy's head is like the summit of a mountain with its uṣṇīṣa.
'O Great King!
This boy's skull and forehead are firm and solid.'"
“‘Great King!
No human or non-human can destroy the crown of this boy’s head.
Great King!’”
The crown of this youth’s head is towering and exceedingly high, such that no one can see its base; it is naturally endowed with the three marks of excellence. "Great King!

If there is a person whose body is fully possessed of the thirty-two marks of a great man, and who further possesses these eighty secondary marks, that person will certainly and invariably attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Having attained enlightenment, they shall turn the unsurpassed, most wondrous wheel of Dharma."
At that time, after the venerable seer Asita had finished speaking to the king, he thought to himself:
"When will this boy renounce the world, attain the path of Buddhahood, and turn the most supreme and sublime Wheel of Dharma?"

While he was reflecting in this manner, wisdom arose within his own mind, and he immediately came to know and see that from this day forward, in thirty-five years, this youth will surely attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and turn the unsurpassed, most supreme wheel of the Dharma.
At that time, as the seer was thus focused his mind in contemplation, he again perceived that his own faculties were fully matured; he then reproached himself and uttered this lament: "Alas, alas!
"I am now outside such a teaching for youths; I have not encountered this time.
Having observed this, he wailed and wept, sobbing and choking with emotion, his tears streaming down his face.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, seeing the seer Asita thus weeping and lamenting, unable to restrain himself, was also moved by sorrow and broke into a loud wail;
having seen this, Queen Māyā likewise shed tears, her throat choked with sobs and her voice stammering.
The ministers and retinues of those Śākya clansmen all wailed and shrieked with unrestrained cries;
everyone within the palace, both young and old, likewise wept bitterly, their tears falling like rain.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, with tears streaming down his face and filling it completely, spoke to the great seer Asita:
"O Venerable Master!

When this boy was first about to be born, five hundred Śākya youths were born on the same day; to speak briefly, even five hundred maidens were born on the same day, as well as five hundred male servants, five hundred female attendants, five hundred foals, and five hundred white elephants—all possessing six tusks—gathering simultaneously on the same day outside the palace gates."
Five hundred hidden treasures spontaneously welled up from the earth;
five hundred groves appeared naturally on the four sides of the city of Kapilavastu;

five hundred merchant lords came from all directions to the city of Kapilavastu; and five hundred parasols and five hundred golden jars—along with pearls and jewels from foreign kings and neighboring realms—all came to present to me and prostrated themselves before me.
Furthermore, there were ten thousand celestial maidens who were born into the families of elders, brahmins, and kṣatriyas.
O Great Seer and Honored Teacher!
On the day the boy was born, all my benefits were fully accomplished, and all the desires of my heart were completely fulfilled.
I summoned all the Brahmins within the kingdom who were skilled in interpreting signs and discerning auspiciousness and misfortune, gathering them all together.
Upon seeing the appearance of this boy, they were all filled with great joy; their hearts leaped with such exuberance that they could not contain themselves.
"O Venerable Master alone, now that we see this boy, for what reason do you weep?
For what reason do you shed tears,
causing us, your followers, to fall into doubt?"
"Great Master!
Please explain this matter for me: will there be any calamity or inauspicious event for my son?
Is it due to some personal malevolent spirit?"
"Does it come from without?
At that time, Asita, seeing King Śuddhodana with tears streaming down his cheeks and filled with sorrow and despondency, addressed the king, saying:
"Great King, do not now grieve or be distressed."
Why is this? It is not that I now perceive any calamity or misfortune in the youth, nor do I see any other forms of suffering or affliction; I see no ill omens within his body or without.
"Great King!

You should know that this boy now possesses a long life of great height; he has immense majesty and virtue, is handsome and pleasing to behold, with a complexion like refined gold and silver. His head is shaped like a parasol, his nose like a polished tube, and his body is full and robust, with well-proportioned limbs, resembling a statue made of gold."
"Great King! This youth possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man, and furthermore, Great King, he is endowed with eighty subtle secondary characteristics.
Such marks as these do not belong to the lineage of a wheel-turning sage king."
Great King!
Such signs as these are all the marks of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Great King!

Therefore, seeing this youth, I am certain that he will attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), turn the unsurpassed, pure wheel of Dharma, and preach the Dharma for the sake of the devas, humans, and the world, bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.

That Dharma-treasure is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, even unto its exposition of the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*). If one hears and receives this Dharma, those who are subject to birth shall have the dharma of birth severed; those who are subject to aging shall have the dharma of aging severed; those subject to illness shall have illness severed; and those subject to death shall have death severed. All sentient beings burdened by sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction shall all attain liberation.
"Great King!

I now reproach myself for being advanced in years, my faculties matured, and my body worn out by decrepitude and old age; at that time, I shall not be able to behold it. Having lost this great benefit, I am thus filled with sorrow and lament for my own misfortune;
it is not due to any inauspiciousness on his part."
He then spoke these verses for the sake of the Great King:

"The life span of Queen Māyā was calculated to last for only seven days; therefore, she passed away.
Nevertheless, it has always been the law from time immemorial that as soon as seven days have passed since the birth of a Bodhisattva, his mother takes her final breath."
"Why is this? Because when the Bodhisattvas left home at a young age, their mothers' hearts shattered upon seeing this, and they immediately passed away.
(The Sarvāstivāda masters further said:)

When the Bodhisattva’s mother beheld her newborn son—his body full and robust, upright and lovely, with few equals in the world—and having witnessed such a rare occurrence and unprecedented phenomenon, she was filled with such overwhelming joy and exultation that it pervaded her entire being; unable to bear it, she immediately passed away.
“At that time, after the Great Queen Māyā, the sovereign lady of the kingdom, had passed away, she was immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Having been born in that heaven, she was immediately surrounded on all sides by a multitude of superior, wondrous, and immeasurable celestial maidens who attended upon her from front and back; each holding immeasurable and boundless articles of offering, such as mandārava flowers and the like, they went to the place where the Bodhisattva was and scattered them everywhere.”
Desiring to make offerings to the Bodhisattva, they descended from the void and gradually alighted upon the palace of King Śuddhodana in the human realm.
Having reached the royal palace, they spoke to King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Great King!..."

"You should know this: I have gained a great benefit and been well-born into the human realm. In the past, while I was conceived in the womb of that Great King’s Son, a pure being, I enjoyed happiness for the full ten months; now that I am born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, I again enjoy happiness no different from before. That former joy and this present joy are of one kind, without distinction."
"Great King!
From this day forward, I pray that you do not undergo great sorrow and suffering on my account.
From now on, I shall not be born again."
Then Māyā, with her celestial body, spoke these verses:
"With a mind of equanimity toward all enemies and kin, Vigorous and courageous, never ceasing for a moment;
Skillfully contemplating the true principle of suchness, Mindfulness is without confusion, possessing both beginning and end."
His physical form is radiant with the countenance of pure gold; his faculties are tranquil and well-restrained.
My son is skillful in expounding all dharmas; I prostrate to this most supreme Honored One who practices virtue.
When Māyā had spoken these verses, she immediately vanished from sight and suddenly disappeared, returning to her celestial palace.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, seeing that his chief consort, Queen Māyā, had passed away, immediately summoned the elders among the Śākya clansmen who were his kinsmen and of venerable age and virtue, causing them all to assemble like clouds. He addressed them, saying:

"All of you kinsmen are the relatives of this nation. Now that this infant boy has lost his mother, to whom shall the charge of suckling him be entrusted? Who shall be commanded to raise and nourish him so that he may survive?"
Who can watch over and protect them according to the proper time?
Who can, with a sincere heart, cause their goodness to increase?
Who can feel compassion for them, loving them as if they were born from one's own body, and carry, embrace, and support them?
"Because of a mind of loving-kindness, because of a mind of merit, and because of a mind of joy.
At that time, there were five hundred newlywed brides of the Śākya clan, and each of those brides proclaimed:
"I can nourish him; I can look after him."
Then the Śākya clan said to those women:

"All of you are young and in the prime of your vigor; your minds are addicted to sensual desire. You are unable to nourish and raise [the child] at the proper time, nor can you show him compassionate care according to the Dharma.
Only this Mahāprajāpatī is the true maternal aunt of the youth; therefore, she alone is capable of tending to and raising the youth’s body, and is likewise capable of serving the Great King."
"All the Śākyas united and exhorted Mahāprajāpatī to act as his mother and raise him.
Then, King Śuddhodana took the Prince and entrusted him to his maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī; because she was the Prince’s own maternal aunt, he addressed her, saying:
"Welcome, Lady!"
"In this way, young man, you should nourish him, carefully protect and sustain him, cause him to grow, and bathe him at the proper times.
Furthermore, he selected another thirty-two women to assist in his upbringing: eight women were assigned to hold the Prince, eight to bathe him, eight to nurse him, and eight to amuse him.
"King Śuddhodana begot two sons:
the first was the Crown Prince, named Siddhārtha;
the second was named Nanda."
"That King Śuklodana also had two sons:
the first was named Nandika, and the second was named Upanandika.
That King Droṇodana also had two sons:"
The first was named Ānanda, and the second was named Devadatta.
King Amṛtodana also had two sons:
the first was named Aniruddha, and the second was named Mahānāman.
"The sister of King Śuddhodana was named Amitāmatī (translated in the Sui language as 'Gandharasa'), who gave birth to a son named Tiṣya.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, the paternal aunt of the Prince, addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
'I respectfully abide by Your Majesty's command and dare not disobey it.'"
Then, at the king’s command, Māyādevī raised the crown prince.
Just as the sun and moon, from the first day until the fifteenth day, become pure and full, so too did the raising of the prince proceed; he grew gradually.
Furthermore, it is like the nyagrodha tree: having obtained a fertile soil, it gradually grows until it later becomes a great tree; so it is with the Prince, who grows day by day.

From the time the crown prince was born, all wealth and profit increased daily within the house of King Śuddhodana; gold, silver, and precious gems, as well as bipeds and quadrupeds, were never lacking. Thus, he spoke in verse:
"Grains of the five kinds and material treasures, Gold, silver, and various garments— Whether manufactured or not, They are naturally obtained in abundance."
"The youth and his compassionate mother shall always have an abundance of milk, curd, and butter;
even those mothers who have little milk shall all find it overflowing.

At that time, all the enemies of King Śuddhodana will naturally give rise to a mind of equanimity, and once they possess this equanimity, they will gradually develop feelings of intimacy and affection."

Once they had become close and affectionate, sharing the same mind as the King, they became firmly established; with one heart and one intent, they shared the same aspirations and actions. Consequently, the winds and rains were timely, there were no calamities such as hail, and there was no disturbance.

Sowing little and reaping much, all those crops, medicinal herbs, trees, and groves grow according to their colors and manifest their colors; they abound in fragrances and possess their flavors according to their tastes; they ripen within their allotted time and never exceed it—all this is due to the power of the Prince’s majestic virtue.
Within the entire city, all those who were pregnant gave birth safely and in peace.
Furthermore, among the people, there were no epidemics or calamities, nor was there any premature death, due to the power of this prince’s majestic virtue.

All the people among his attendants—the elders and householders—each maintained their own independence and did not seek to involve one another; there was no such thing as one person asking another, "Let him give to me. Even when matters arose that required some small or large amount to be lent, exchanged, or borrowed, he would not harbor the thought that the other should give more than necessary. Whatever was required, whether it be a certain amount or whatever else, he would simply give that much.
The people within the city each honored one another, filially supported their parents, and reverently served their teachers and elders; this was due to the power of the Prince’s majestic virtue.

Just as in the past, they practiced according to the Dharma; all kings, commoners, and citizens followed the Dharma, fully observing and practicing the ten wholesome paths. Within the kingdom there was no fear, the five grains flourished, and famine and scarcity were far removed.
In this way, within the entire realm of King Śuddhodana’s kingdom, there was neither famine nor scarcity, nor was there any fear.
The five grains were abundant, and all the people acted in accordance with the Dharma, practicing various forms of giving and performing manifold meritorious deeds.
They construct various gardens and groves, and great works such as wells, springs, ponds, and canals, all of which manifest spontaneously.
Celestial dwellings, shrines, halls, offices, bureaus, and government departments likewise appear naturally.
No one suffered injustice or calamity; all the people were filled with joy, just as in the heavens, without any distinction.
By the power of the Prince’s majestic virtue, none of these matters failed to be accomplished.
As it is said in the verse:
“The people follow the Honored One’s teaching; They are neither stingy nor parsimonious.
There is none who does not act according to the Dharma, And with a compassionate heart, they do not give rise to killing.”
"Once hunger and thirst are relieved, Food and drink are fully provided;
All are filled with joy, And together they enjoy celestial bliss.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, having passed the lunar mansion *Jyeṣṭhā* and taken the day of *Viśākhā*, had various precious ornaments made for the Crown Prince—namely bracelets, finger-rings, and anklets, as well as head-ornaments of diverse and exquisite jewels, and flower garlands bound for his neck.

Various kinds of necklaces, pearls, seal-patterned ornaments, rings, armlets, and waist-bands; girdles made of gold thread, golden bells, and jeweled nets; various *maṇi* gems serving as decorative implements; boots and leather sandals adorned with diverse jewels; and their celestial jewel crowns, which are most excellent and exquisite.

Furthermore, there were five hundred kinsmen of the Śākya clan who, for the sake of the Prince, each fashioned a set of various exquisite necklaces and ornaments, adorning them as described above. Having completed these, they went to King Śuddhodana’s presence and addressed the king, saying:
"Excellent, Great King! [We have prepared these for the Prince]."
"We have fashioned this exquisite necklace over seven days and seven nights;
we only pray, Great King, that you will adorn the Crown Prince with it, so that our labor shall not be in vain."

Then, at dawn on the day of the lunar mansion Ārdrā, King Śuddhodana, together with his state preceptor, the Brahmin named Udāyana—the father of the bhikṣu Udāyin—and five hundred other Brahmins, all proclaimed these words:
"How exceedingly auspicious!"
Together they took the Prince to a garden named Vimalaviśuddhavyūha,
which had been held in esteem like a stupa since ancient times.

At that time, within that garden, there were further immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of all kinds of sentient beings—men, women, boys, and girls—who called out to one another and gathered like clouds in that garden, desiring to behold the Prince.

Furthermore, he separately prepared another great carriage, fully equipped with various kinds of necklaces, gold, silver, food, drink, and clothing. Within the city of Kapilavastu, at crossroads, four-way junctions, street corners, and all such narrow alleys, he established a great distribution of alms, proclaiming in a loud voice:
"Whatever is required shall be given to everyone."
Thus the carriage proceeded ahead of the Prince.

Furthermore, there were eight thousand varieties of musical instruments producing all manner of sounds, and from the void there fell a rain of immeasurable and boundless diverse and exquisite flowers.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of women, all of whom adorned their bodies with various precious necklaces and ornaments. They were situated upon the upper galleries, or on high towers, or on the defensive parapets, or at the tops of the city walls and along the battlements; some were atop the city watchtowers, some within the windows, some on the ridges of the halls, and some standing on the roofs. Holding various flowers in their hands, they gazed upon the Prince and scattered them toward him as he passed.
Furthermore, there were eight thousand celestial jewel-maidens, holding brooms in their hands and adorned with physical ornaments, who went before the Prince to sweep and clear the road.
All the Śākya kinsmen and relatives likewise followed in order, walking alongside King Śuddhodana and in front of the Prince.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī held the Prince in her arms, seated him upon her lap, and sat within the palanquin.
Having thus prepared all manner of infinite and boundless adornments, she led the Prince forth to go to that garden.
At that time, the royal preceptor Udāyin’s father, together with those five hundred brahmins, each praised the prince with immeasurable and boundless words of auspiciousness.
They took various necklaces and fastened them upon the Prince’s body.

Once the necklaces were fastened, all the marks of the Prince’s physical form were completely obscured; those necklaces became uniformly dim and lusterless, no longer possessing any brilliant radiance. They were like a mass of ink, unable to shine or illuminate, and devoid of any bright splendor.
It is like placing lumps of charcoal beside priceless Jambūnada gold;

in just such a way, once those various necklaces were fastened upon the Prince, they were like fireflies by day, unable to manifest themselves. All the necklaces, having reached the Prince’s body, were neither visible nor apparent, neither radiant nor brilliant, and it was likewise so.
At that time, the multitude of people, seeing such rare and unprecedented phenomena as these in the Prince, each cried out: "Alas! Alas!"
"How rare! How rare!
they cried, each one laughing joyfully, everyone clapping their hands, singing, dancing, shouting, and whistling, tossing and playing with their garments.
At that time, within that garden, there was a celestial deity named Vimala. That deity, remaining in the void, concealed his body so as not to appear, and spoke these verses:
"Suppose this great earth, along with its cities and villages,
its mountains, rivers, and all its trees, were entirely transformed into Jambūnada gold."
The light from a single pore of the Buddha, complete with majestic and virtuous marks, eclipses those [other lights] like a mass of ink; it is fully adorned with a hundred merits.
The radiance of necklaces and ornaments is extinguished when one possesses all these marks.
"The foremost and most excellent fruit of retribution requires no adornment of necklaces.
Having spoken this verse, the celestial deity took various and immeasurable heavenly flowers, scattered them over the Crown Prince, and returned to his own palace.

At that time, the kinsmen of the Śākya clan took priceless powdered sandalwood and finely ground sandalwood, multicolored ivory mats, and various medicinal herbs, filling many vessels with them; they brought these to the Prince to adorn his body.

Furthermore, he took deer-carts with carriages made of pure gold, various types of boats, and diverse wild beasts, even including foals, all fashioned from miscellaneous jewels; he bestowed these fully upon the Prince, allowing him to play and sport as he pleased.
For eight full years, they entertained and raised the Prince with such joy and delight.

Yet he was unlike the infants of the world who shed impure tears; he had no excrement or filth, nor did he wail, groan, or frown; he neither hungered nor thirsted, and the nurses who raised him were always filled with joy.
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"Now my crown prince is so exceptionally handsome that he has few equals; yet I do not yet know what his strength is like—what exactly is it?"
"Now you may test and examine their strength.

At that time, the Great King sat together with immeasurable youths of the Śākya clan to eat and drink. He took a pure gold bowl, intricately carved and engraved, filled it completely with *mṛdvīkā* (delightful) balls, and further fashioned various golden rings and chains, placing them before all the youths and instructing them to compete for the food.
Furthermore, he gathered many small white elephants and had them compete with the boy for food, saying to all the young boys:
"You should know this!"
"Such white elephants as these shall take away your food.

At that time, the young boys were unable to match the strength of the multitude of white elephants in their struggle; they consequently allowed the elephants to eat, and only then did they inform the Prince, saying: "Prince!"
"Your food has now been seized by another.

At that moment, the prince took the golden bowl with both hands and, exerting a small amount of physical strength, broke the chain, causing the elephant to collapse backward, unable to match the prince.
At that time, King Śuddhodana again gathered many rams for the sake of the Prince and placed them within the palace, intending to bring joy to the Prince.
He provided saddles made of pure gold, adorned with various jewels, and decorated his body with all kinds of necklaces and ornaments, covering him with a golden mesh net.
At that time, the Prince mounted that ram-drawn carriage and proceeded to the grove.
His paternal uncle, Amṛtodana, and the other Śākyas likewise adorned rams for their respective sons, providing them with all the same equipment as before.
Those young princes also rode in goat-drawn chariots, playing as they pleased. Chapter Eleven:

Training in the Arts From the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*, Chapter Eleven: Training in the Arts. "At that time, King Śuddhodana, knowing that the Crown Prince was already eight years of age, immediately assembled his hundred officials, ministers, and counselors, and addressed them, saying:
'You gentlemen should know!'"
"Now within my realm, who possesses the greatest wisdom?
Who is endowed with skill and proficiency in all various arts, such that they are fit to serve as a tutor for the Crown Prince, teaching him to learn writing and other treatises?"
At that time, the ministers replied to the king, saying:

"Great King, you should know that there is now Viśvāmitra, who is well-versed in all treatises and is most excellent and sublime. Such a great master is capable of instructing the crown prince in various scripts and discourses."
At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately dispatched a messenger to summon Viśvāmitra and addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Great Master!..."
"Can you, for my sake, teach this prince all the arts, scripts, and treatises?
Then Maitrāyaṇī replied: "Great King!"
"I respectfully follow Your Majesty’s command; I am now capable of doing so.

At that time, King Śuddhodana was filled with joy. He immediately selected an auspicious day and a favorable moment under a propitious constellation, and together with the elders and virtuous members of the Śākya clan, he ordered all ceremonial rites to be adorned and ensured that every necessary provision was fully prepared.

Furthermore, five hundred youths of the Śākya clan were arrayed, surrounding him on all sides—front, back, left, and right—and there were additionally immeasurable and boundless numbers of other boys and girls who followed the Prince as he was about to ascend to the schoolhouse.

At that time, the great master Viśvamitra, seeing from afar the great majesty and power of the Prince, could not restrain himself; he suddenly rose from his seat, bowed his body to prostrate at the Prince’s feet, and having finished his prostration, looked around in all four directions, feeling profound shame and embarrassment.

At that time, Maitrāyaṇī felt shame and remorse. Then, in the midst of the sky, there was a devaputra named Viśuddhasūkṣma, who, together with immeasurable and boundless great kings of the gods—those who constantly protect this Great Being from the Tuṣita Palace—remained in that void, concealing their forms so as not to appear, and spoke these verses:
“Whatever arts and crafts exist in the world, And all other sūtras and śāstras, This person is able to know them all, And is likewise able to teach them to others.”
This Supreme Being, in order to conform to the ways of the world, has long practiced since ancient times; yet now he demonstrates learning from a teacher.
All the supramundane wisdom, the various truths, and the various powers—
Phenomena born of causes and conditions, once arisen, are then extinguished.
To know them in a single thought—whether name-and-form appears or does not appear—is already a realization;
how much more so regarding mere words and letters!
When the devaputra had spoken these verses, he scattered various flowers over the Prince and immediately returned to his own palace.

At that time, King Śuddhodana took various priceless jewels and used them as alms for the brahmins; he further provided various foods and drinks of a hundred flavors and prepared seats for the assembly of brahmins. He then entrusted the Prince to the great master Viśvāmitra, left behind the wet nurses to attend to the Prince, and returned to the royal palace.

"At that time, when the Prince had first begun his studies, he took a writing tablet made of the finest and most exquisite gośīrṣa-candana sandalwood, its four edges purely adorned with the seven precious gems, and its back smeared with various kinds of extraordinary celestial perfumes. Holding it, he went before the ācārya Viśvamitra and spoke these words:
'Venerable Ācārya, which scripture shall you teach me? There appears to be one scripture missing.'"
Furthermore, there are the books spoken by Brahmā, which are the fourteen phonemes of the current Brāhmaṇa script;
the Kharoṣṭhī script (translated in the Sui language as "Donkey-Lip"); the Puṣkarasārin script spoken by the ṛṣi Puṣkarasārin (translated in the Sui language as "Lotus");
the Akṣara script (translated in the Sui language as "Segmented Parts"); and the Maṅgala script (translated in the Sui language as "Auspicious").
Yamani (Sui: the script of the Great Qin Kingdom), Aṅgulī (Sui:
finger-writing), Yananika (Sui: vehicle-mounting), Sākapūrva (Sui:
female ox), Pālavani (Sui: tree-leaf), and Pāruṣya (Sui: harsh speech).
...the Vitada script (translated in the Sui as "Corpse-Raiser"), the Dhavida script (translated in the Sui as "Southern India"),
the Jirādi script (translated in the Sui as "Naked Person"), the Dugichanabata script (translated in the Sui as "Right-Spiral"),
the Uga script (translated in the Sui as "Fierce Adornment"), the Saṃkhya script (translated in the Sui as "Calculation"), and the A... [script]...
The Brahmi script (Sui: "covering"); the Anuloma script (Sui: "conforming"); the Vidyamishra script (Sui: "mixed");
the Dravida script (Mountains on the Edge of O-chang); the Aparāntaka script (Western Jambudvīpa;
no Sui equivalent); the Khaśa script (Shule); the Cīna script (the Great Sui); the Mana script.

The *doulung* script is for writing [the word] "unmeasured"; the *mucha chara* script is for writing the word "middle"; the *bita xidi* script is for writing the word "cubit"; the *fushu po* script is for writing the word "flower";
the *tipo* script is for writing "deva" (heaven); the *naga* script is for writing "dragon";

the *yaksha* script is for writing "non-Sui" (asura); the *gandharva* script is for writing "celestial music"; the *asura* script is for writing "not drinking wine"; the *kālū* [script is for writing...]
The Rākṣasa script is for the garuḍas; the Kiṃnara script is for non-humans;
the Mahoraga script is for great serpents; the Mṛgacchaka script is for the sounds of various beasts; the Kākatuṇḍa script is for the cries of crows;
the Pūrmadeva script is for the earth-dwelling devas; the Antari-kṣadeva script is for the space-dwelling devas; the Uttara... [script is for the northern devas].
The *Lokulū* script is in the north of Mount Sumeru; the *Pūluba-videha* script is in the east of Mount Sumeru;
the *Utsarpa* script is "lifting"; the *Nisarpa* script is "throwing"; the *Sāgara* script is "ocean"; the *Vajra* script is "diamond";
the *Rigaparatigā* script is "coming and going"; and the *Vikṛti-nirdeśa* script is "transformation."
The *Śeṣāśana* script is the "script of eating remnants"; the *Anubhūta* script is the "script of the unprecedented";
the *Saṃsthānapada* script is the "script of turning like a prostrate one"; the *Gaṇanāpada* script is the "script of counting"; the *Utsarpaṇa* script is the "script of lifting up";
the *Nisarpaṇa* script is the "script of casting down"; the *Pāṭalika* script is the "foot script"; and the *Vikruṣṭa* script...
The Tālapatradhara script is derived from two superior phrases;
the Yavadvīpa script increases by ten phrases or more; the Mūrdhaprasenī script is of medium flow;
the Liśayaṣṭapadavibhakti script pertains to the ascetic practices of the ṛṣis; and the Dhāraṇīpeṣalī script concerns the contemplation of the earth.
The Gaganapeliśani script is for contemplating space; the Sappuṣadiniśanta script is for all medicinal fruits and causes;
the Śaraṅgaheni script is for comprehensive overviews; and the Sarvalūta script is for all varieties of sounds.
At that time, having finished speaking these words regarding the scripts, the Prince further consulted with the Ācārya Maitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
"There are sixty-four kinds of scripts in total; I do not yet know which script you wish to teach me."

At that time, Viśvāmitra, having heard the Prince speak thus regarding this writing, felt joy in his heart; he was glad, delighted, and full of cheer. Secretly harboring a sense of personal shame, he subdued his pride and arrogance and addressed the Prince with these verses:
"O rare one of pure wisdom, Who so skillfully accords with all worldly laws!
Having already mastered all treatises yourself, You have come once more to enter my school."
"I did not know these names of scripts, yet now I have mastered them all through recitation and retention;
you are the great and honored guide of gods and men, and now I wish once more to seek a teacher from you."

At that time, there were also five hundred young sons of ministers from the Śākya clan who entered the school together with the Prince to study writing and recite characters. Because of the power of the Prince’s majestic virtue and the further empowerment of the various devas, diverse sounds issued forth from all the musical instruments.
When pronouncing the syllable A, the sound “All conditioned phenomena are impermanent” issues forth.
When pronouncing the syllable Ī, the sound “All gates of the sense faculties are closed and obstructed” issues forth.
When pronouncing the syllable *u*, the mind attains tranquil concentration; such is the sound that issues forth.
When pronouncing the syllable *ṛ*, because one realizes and knows all the paths of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), such is the sound that issues forth.
When pronouncing the syllable *u*, one should produce this sound: "I shall cross over the great ocean of afflictions.
When pronouncing the syllable *ka*, one should produce this sound: "I shall undergo the karmic retributions of all states of existence."
When pronouncing the syllable Kha, he taught the uprooting of the very root of all afflictions, and such a sound issued forth.
When pronouncing the syllable Ga, he taught that the twelve links of dependent origination are profound and difficult to transcend, and such a sound issued forth.
"When pronouncing the syllable *ṅa*, one should produce this sound: 'May all the extremely thick veils and obscurations of ignorance be purified, removed, and extinguished.

When pronouncing the syllable *o*, one should produce this sound: 'Once the Tathāgata has attained the Way of the Buddha, he shall go to other regions to bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings who are terrified.'"
"When pronouncing the syllable *ca*, one should realize and know the Four Noble Truths; such is the sound that issues forth.
When pronouncing the syllable *cha*, all deceit, crookedness, false delusions, and mental confusion should now be entirely extinguished; such is the sound that issues forth."
"When pronouncing the syllable JA, one should transcend the ocean of birth and death; such is the sound that issues forth.
When pronouncing the syllable DHA, the banners of Māra and the afflictions shall be shattered and overturned; such is the sound that issues forth."
"When pronouncing the syllable *ja*, one should cause the fourfold assembly to all practice in accordance with the teaching; such is the sound that issues forth.
When pronouncing the syllable *ṭha*, all ordinary beings and sentient beings everywhere shall fear and revere these words 'impermanence'; such is the sound that issues forth."

"When pronouncing the syllable *ṭha*, one should bring this syllable *ṭha* to mind; if the faculties are matured, one will realize and know all phenomena without hearing them, and such a sound issues forth."
When pronouncing the syllable *ṭa*, one should attain those four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and be able to fly; such is the sound that issues forth.

When pronouncing the syllable *ṭha*, one forms the *saṃkusumita* flower like the word *ṭha*; as one scatters it, the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and the arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are manifested; such is the sound that issues forth.

"When pronouncing the syllable *ṇa*, it makes this sound: 'When those who have attained the Way receive offerings and sustenance, not even a single atom's worth of afflictions remains without being dispersed and extinguished; they are worthy of receiving the offerings of others.'"
"When pronouncing the syllable *ta*, one should direct oneself toward ascetic practice and utter this sound.

When pronouncing the syllable *tha*, one should observe that the minds of all sentient beings are like axes, while the objects of the various sensory realms are like bamboo and wood; one should utter this sound."
"When pronouncing the syllable *ḍha*, one should practice the conduct of giving and perform various ascetic practices; thus shall harmony be attained—such is the sound that issues forth.
When pronouncing the syllable *ṭha*, there shall be the sound of the Dharma—such is the sound that issues forth."
"When pronouncing the syllable *na*, one must use food and drink to sustain life; thus the sound is uttered.
When pronouncing the syllable *pa*, it is the true reality of suchness (*tathatā*); thus the sound is uttered."
