"When pronouncing the syllable *pha*, one shall attain the Way and realize the sublime fruit; such is the sound that issues forth.
When pronouncing the syllable *bha*, all bonds are liberated; such is the sound that issues forth."
When pronouncing the syllable *ba*, he uttered this sound: "I declare that in this world, one shall no longer undergo further existence.
When pronouncing the syllable *ma*, he uttered this sound: "I declare that all the terrors of birth and death are most fearsome."
"When pronouncing the syllable *ya*, one utters this sound: 'I shall expound for others by opening the gate to all dharmas.
When pronouncing the syllable *ra*, one utters this sound: 'There shall be the Three Jewels.'"
When pronouncing the syllable *la*, one cuts off all branches of craving; such is the sound that issues forth.
When pronouncing the syllable *ba*, one cuts off the fundamental seeds of the entire body; such is the sound that issues forth.
"When pronouncing the syllable *ṣa*, one attains śamatha and vipaśyanā; such is the sound that issues forth.
When pronouncing the syllable *sa*, one should know the six elements; such is the sound that issues forth."
"When pronouncing the syllable *sa*, one shall attain all forms of wisdom; such is the sound that issues forth.
When pronouncing the syllable *ha*, one shall strike away and eliminate all afflictions; such is the sound that issues forth."

"At that time, when those five hundred youths were thus chanting these gateways of letters, by the power of the Prince's majestic virtue, as well as through the sustaining protection bestowed by the devas, there issued forth the sounds of such subtle, secret, and profound Dharma-gates."
At that time, King Śuddhodana again assembled his ministers and deliberated, saying: "O ministers!

Who among you all knows where there is a teacher who is most proficient in martial arts, skilled in military tactics and weaponry, and possesses the strategic wisdom to be able to instruct my son, Prince Siddhārtha?"
Then the ministers reported to the king, saying: "Great King!

You should know that there is a Śākya here named Suprabuddha; his son, Kṣāntideva (translated in the Sui language as 'Endurance-Heaven'), is capable of instructing the prince in the methods of military training."

That which he understands and knows comprises twenty-nine kinds in total; they are skillful and exquisite, their techniques are subtle and refined, their actions are nimble and easy, and they are vigorous, swift, and decisive.
Twenty-ninth: so-called leaping upon elephants and mounting chariots, jumping over ditches and vaulting over horses;
excellence in archery and swiftness of foot; a fierce will and a robust nature; a body that is agile and nimble; acting with careful deliberation; being skilled in training and discipline;
skillfully handling the elephant-hook to secure and position them; and being adept at casting the elephant’s lasso and managing its deployment.
He nourishes and feeds the livestock; he directs and commands with authority; he skillfully manages the troops and horses;
he is thoroughly practiced in discerning right from wrong and in understanding the topography of mountains and rivers; his fists are firmly clenched and his footing is steady on the ground;
his head is wrapped and his hair is tied in a tight knot, secured most securely; he is capable of breaking and opening, of cleaving and hacking, and his arrows never miss their mark.
In archery, he was peerless; hearing the sound from afar, he would shoot and the arrow would hang suspended in mid-air.
Wherever he discharged his shafts, they would penetrate deeply. He was wise and intelligent, with clear speech and swift eloquence;
in counsel and strategy, he was skillful, knowledgeable, and versatile. In discussing antiquity and evaluating the present, he was adept at employing expedient means and stratagems.
He has attained complete mastery in all such secret essentials and divine capabilities of the military arts; only he is fit to instruct the Crown Prince of the Great King in every martial skill.
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, his heart was filled with great joy, and he immediately commanded his ministers to summon Kṣāntideva.
When Kṣāntideva arrived, the king commanded him, saying: "Kṣāntideva!..."
"Are you able to teach Prince Siddhārtha the arts of weaponry?
At that time, the Deva Kṣānti immediately addressed the King, saying,
"I am very capable of teaching him."
The King further commanded, saying:
"If you know the proper time, teach my son well so that he may achieve success.
Then, for the sake of the Prince’s amusement, King Śuddhodana had a park constructed, named *Khema* (Diligence).
At that time, the Crown Prince entered the garden and enjoyed himself in play and merriment, sometimes having himself massaged.
Then those five hundred ministers of the Śākya clan, for the sake of their own children, each constructed gardens intended for amusement, massage, and recreation.
At that time, Śuddhodana led the Prince into the Arāḍa Garden to instruct him in the arts of weaponry;
meanwhile, the other members of the Śākya clan each entered their respective gardens to engage in play and study.
At that time, Arjuna brought several kinds of military weapons and armaments, intending to instruct the Prince.
Upon seeing them, the Prince discarded them all and spoke thus to Arjuna:
"You may teach these to the other Śākya youths; I have already mastered this myself and have no further need to learn it."
At that time, Nandideva immediately instructed the other Śākyas in this martial weaponry and its techniques.
Having completed their training, before long, every individual achieved mastery in twenty-nine types [of weapons] and attained complete proficiency in them all.

Regarding such things as leaping upon white elephants, carriages, and horses, up to and including drawing a powerful bow, he has attained the most supreme wisdom in all these matters; he is most agile and capable, possessing keen intelligence and wisdom.

Furthermore, among these various royal arts, the most excellent and supreme are as follows: namely, writing and arithmetic; understanding all forms of calculation; carving and engraving seals; the musical scales and pitch-pipes (*gong-shang-lü-lǚ*); dancing, singing, and humorous performance; the *yǎn* (a type of acrobatic or dramatic art) and *mán tán* (casual or witty conversation); or the creation of various treasures, rare and extraordinary jewels; dyeing fabrics to produce colors; painting grasses and leaves; and various other tasks such as compounding incense; or handling the brush for calligraphy in both the cursive and regular scripts; being able to compose literary works; and furthermore, being able to move and turn upon the back of a white elephant, or ride with skill upon a saddle-horse. All such skills regarding elephants, camels, heads, necks, tails, and legs, he was able to master entirely.

Furthermore, by the side of the chariot, he was also skillful at performing various feats, mastering the arts of the sword, spear, bow, and arrow; with an air of ease and composure, he engaged in wrestling, twisting arms, testing strength against weights, and the arts of massage, pressing, and kneading, as well as breaking shins and seizing arms.
He was capable of throwing and running, even hitting his mark without fail, as well as shooting by sound; he could draw a heavy bow and discharge arrows in a continuous rain.
Regarding all such martial arts, the Prince abandoned them entirely and refused to learn further, saying:
"I understand these myself; why should I require instruction?"

Furthermore, he wished to instruct the princes in essential arts, namely: astronomy, sacrificial rites, divination, the prediction of future events, the art of eloquent speech and recitation, knowledge of the cries of various beasts, mastery of phonetics (śikṣā), the creation of various crafts, repartee based on those crafts, incantations, and miscellaneous matters—more than ten such categories—as well as the methods of governance and transformation used by ancient sages and all classical scriptures. He taught these to the crown prince, and he likewise instructed his own sons and the sons of others in the same manner.

Furthermore, regarding those things that worldly people study for years and months—whether they succeed or fail—the Prince was able, within four years, to master all those various arts and all treatises, attaining unimpeded penetration and complete mastery alongside the other Śākyas.
At that time, the Deva Kṣānti spoke these verses for the Prince:
"When you were young, you studied with composure;
without requiring great effort, you understood everything in an instant."
"Having studied for but a few days and months, he excels others who have practiced for many years;
the various arts and skills he has acquired are all accomplished beyond those of men.
— *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll Eleven.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Twelve, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve: Sporting and Surveying. Chapter Twelve: Sporting and Surveying.

"At that time, the Prince was raised in the royal palace; during his childhood, he played and had not yet begun formal studies. When he reached the age of eight, he left the inner chambers to visit his teacher and entered the schoolhouse."

From the two great masters Viśvamitra and Kṣāntideva, he received and studied all manner of texts and treatises, as well as military arts and various technical skills; after four years had passed, by the twelfth year, he had thoroughly mastered every kind of craft and ability.
Having attained such mastery, he conformed to worldly ways, delighting his eyes and pleasing his mind; he gave rein to his passions and indulged in dissipation, pursuing sounds and sights.

Once, while at the Garden of Diligence (*Kauśāmbīvana*), he was wandering about and engaged in archery and games; likewise, five hundred other Śākya youths were each amusing themselves and playing within their own respective gardens.
At that time, there was a flock of geese flying through the sky. Then the youth Devadatta drew his bow and shot; he struck one goose.
Wounded by the arrow, the goose fell into the garden of Siddhārtha, still bearing the shaft.

At that time, the Prince saw the goose, wounded by an arrow, fallen upon the ground. Having seen it, he gently took hold of it with both hands; having taken it, he sat cross-legged and placed the goose upon his lap. With his hand—exquisite, smooth, soft, and supple like the ripples of water, marked with the thousand-spoked wheel design, and endowed with merit; its fine texture being like the tender leaf of a plantain—he supported it with his left hand and extracted the arrow with his right, immediately sealing the wound with ghee and honey.
At that time, the youth Devadatta sent a messenger to the prince with these words:
"I shot a wild goose, which has fallen into your garden; you should return it to me immediately and must not keep it there."
At that time, the Prince replied to the messenger, saying:
"If the goose should die, I shall immediately return it to you;
if it does not die, it can never be obtained."
Then Devadatta again sent a messenger with these words:

"Whether he dies or lives, you must certainly return him to me. My hand was first skillfully able to shoot him down; having encountered him and caused him to fall, how can you suddenly leave him behind?"
The Prince replied, "I have already taken this goose under my care.
For since I first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment, I have taken all sentient beings under my care; how much more so this goose, which does not belong to anyone else?"
For this reason, they immediately began to dispute with one another and assembled the elders and wise men of the Śākyas to adjudicate the matter.
At that time, certain devas from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens transformed their bodies into those of elderly elders and entered the assembly of the Śākyas, saying:
"Who was his nurturer?"
"To grasp is to take hold;
to hit the mark is to let go.
At that time, the elders among the Śākyas all gave their assent at once and cried out in a loud voice:
"It is so, it is so, just as you have said.
This was the initial causal connection for the formation of enmity between the youth Devadatta and the Prince.
"Furthermore, on another occasion, King Śuddhodana, together with many young Śākya youths and accompanied by the Prince, went out for an excursion into the fields to observe the sowing of crops."

At that time, all the laborers within that land were working with their bodies bare, toiling diligently at the plowing and tilling. They tethered the oxen to the tips of the plowshares; whenever the oxen walked slowly, they would repeatedly lash and jerk them. As the days grew long and the heavens scorched hot, the animals gasped for breath and sweat flowed; both men and oxen were utterly exhausted by hunger and thirst.
Furthermore, their bodies were so emaciated that only their skeletons remained; beneath the clods of earth turned up by the plow, worms emerged from every spot.
After the people had finished plowing, various birds and sparrows vied with one another to fly down and devour these insects.

The Crown Prince beheld this ox, exhausted and weary, further subjected to lashes; its neck was bruised by the plowshare, its throat constricted by the yoke-strap and bit, blood flowed down from it, and its skin and flesh were torn and wounded.

Again, he saw plowmen whose backs were scorched by the sun; they were naked and bare-bodied, their skin covered in dust and soil, as crows and birds flew toward them, vying with one another to pick up insects for food.
Upon seeing this, the Prince was overcome with great sorrow.
Just as a person would feel profound grief upon seeing their own family members bound in captivity, so too did the Prince feel compassion for all those beings.

Having seen this, he gave rise to great compassion; immediately descending from the horse-king Kanthaka, he walked slowly and composedly, reflecting that all sentient beings were subject to such conditions, and then cried out: "Alas! Alas!"
The sentient beings of the world undergo extreme suffering, namely birth, old age, sickness, and death; furthermore, they endure various afflictions, revolving within them and unable to escape.
Why do you not seek to abandon these various sufferings?
Why do you not seek the wisdom of weariness with suffering and tranquility?
Why do you not contemplate liberation from the causes of birth, old age, sickness, and death?
"Where can I now find a secluded place to contemplate these matters of suffering and affliction?
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having observed the farming work, returned with the youths to enter a garden.
At that time, the Prince walked with composed and steady gait from place to place, seeking solitude.
Suddenly, he saw a Jambu tree in one spot; its trunk and branches were smooth and lustrous, upright and lovely, lush and spreading wide, a sight that delighted all who beheld it.
Having seen this, he immediately said to his attendants: "All of you!
Each of you keep far away from me; I wish to go about in private."
At that time, the Prince dismissed his attendants, ordering them all to disperse, and gradually approached the foot of a tree.

Having reached the tree, he sat cross-legged upon the grass and, with focused mind, contemplated the various sufferings of sentient beings—birth, old age, sickness, and death. He gave rise to compassion and immediately attained mental concentration.
At that time, he immediately became detached from all sensual desires and abandoned all unwholesome states.
By contemplating and discerning the sphere of objects, his outflows regarding the realm of desire were exhausted, and he attained the first dhyāna.
"I too possess such a nature; I have not yet escaped this condition, nor have I crossed beyond this cycle.

While he was reflecting thus, five celestial seers—flying through the void, moving with sovereign ease, endowed with great majesty and power, fully proficient in the Vedas, and skilled in all arts—were traveling from south to north. Passing over that grove of Jambu trees, they were suddenly unable to proceed further.
They said to one another:

"In the past, as we traveled back and forth, we traversed Mount Sumeru at our own will, manifesting various supernormal powers and displaying all manner of transformations, even reaching the palace of the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa. We have also reached the city of Alakāvatī and were able to pass through it; there are many various yakṣas and malevolent spirits there, and we have previously flown over them."
At the tip of this tree, we have also previously crossed over countless times without obstruction and without losing our supernatural powers.
By whose majestic power today has it been caused that we have lost our supernatural powers and are unable to pass through?
Those seers immediately looked at the tree and beheld the Prince sitting cross-legged beneath its shade; his majestic radiance was so towering and brilliant that it was difficult to gaze upon.
Having seen this, they thought to themselves: "Who is seated here?

Could it be that Great Brahmā, the Lord of the World; or perhaps Kaśyapa, the Lord of the Desire Realm; or Śakra, the King of Devas; or Vaiśravaṇa, the Lord of the Great Treasuries; or the Moon Devaputra; or the Sun Devaputra; or perhaps it is a Wheel-Turning Sage King? Or could it be that a Buddha has appeared in the world?"
"However, this person now possesses immense majesty and virtue.
At that time, the deity who protects that forest addressed the sages, saying:

"O sages, this is not Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the World; nor is he Kiṃśana, the Lord of the Desire Realm; nor is he Śakra, the Lord of Devas, nor Vaiśravaṇa, the Lord of the Treasuries; nor is he the Sun or Moon Devas."
This crown prince is named Siddhārtha; he is the son of King Śuddhodana and a youth of the Śākya clan.
O Seers, you should know this!

The majesty and virtue possessed by Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Cāturmahārājika heaven, Śakra Devendra, Vaiśravaṇa the Lord of Treasures, the Moon God, the Sun God, and the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin)—all such majesties and virtues do not equal even a single sixteenth part of the majesty and virtue possessed by Prince Siddhārtha. Even a mere hair’s breadth of his majesty surpasses them all.
"Therefore, you have come to this grove and desired to fly over it, but your supernatural powers are limited and you cannot cross it.
When those seers heard these words from the guardian deity of the grove, they descended from the void and stood before the Prince, each reciting a verse in praise of him.
At that time, a certain seer spoke in verse:
“The fires of affliction blaze fiercely in the world; This can produce the waters of the Dharma-pool.
Having obtained such a subtle and wondrous Dharma, One extinguishes those fires of affliction until not even a trace remains.”
Furthermore, another seer spoke in verse:
"The world is utterly shrouded in the darkness of ignorance; This one can give rise to the light of wisdom.
Having attained such a subtle and wondrous Dharma, He illuminates all those in the world who are blind and deluded."
Furthermore, another seer spoke in verse:
“In the vast wilderness of sorrow and affliction, this great vehicle is capable of bringing one safely through;
having attained such a subtle and wondrous Dharma, one can deliver all sentient beings from the three realms of existence.”
Furthermore, another seer spoke in verse:
"All beings in the world are entangled by afflictions; He is able, through skillful means, to bring about their liberation.
Having attained such a subtle and wondrous Dharma, He is able to release one from all bonds and fetters."
Furthermore, another seer spoke in verse:
"All the maladies of birth and death that exist in the world, This Great Physician is able to cure and heal them.
Having attained such a subtle and wondrous Dharma, He is able to treat all the tumors of birth and death."

When the various seers had each spoken verses in praise of the Prince, they touched his feet in prostration, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then flew up into the void, departing together.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, not seeing the Crown Prince for a brief moment, felt immediately within his heart a sense of displeasure and lack of joy, and asked those around him:
"Where is my Crown Prince now? (These two preceding phrases are repeated in the Sanskrit original).
Suddenly he was gone.
At that time, the ministers galloped hither and thither in the east, west, south, and north, searching for the prince, but none knew his whereabouts.

At that time, a great minister saw from afar the Prince sitting beneath the shade of a Jambu tree, contemplating in meditative concentration; he further observed that while the shadows of all other trees had shifted, only the shade of the Jambu tree remained alone to cover the Prince.

At that time, when the minister saw that the Crown Prince had performed such a rare and inconceivable feat, he was filled with great joy; his elation pervaded him entirely, and he could not contain himself.
Hurrying and galloping with great speed, he went to where the King was; having arrived, he knelt down for a long time and, according to what he had seen, spoke these verses:
"The Great King’s Prince is now present, Sitting cross-legged in deep concentration beneath the shade of a Jambu tree.
He contemplates and has entered into samādhi, His radiance shining forth like a mountain of suns."
This is truly a Great Man; the shadow of the tree stands firm and does not move.
I pray that Your Majesty will observe for yourself: what is the appearance of the Prince as he sits?
Just like the Great Brahmā, Lord of the Devas, or like Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
his majestic power is sublime and his radiance brilliant, illuminating all those groves of trees.

When King Śuddhodana had heard this, he immediately went to the Jambu tree. From afar, he saw the Prince sitting there beneath the tree in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*). He was like a great mass of fire atop a mountain peak seen in the dead of night, emitting fierce and brilliant flames; his magnificent virtue was so prominent and resplendent that it towered aloft. It was as if a bright moon had suddenly emerged from amidst thick clouds, or as if a great, pure lamp were lit within a dark chamber.

When the king saw this, he was struck with a sense of great wonder and marvel; his entire body trembled with awe and the hair on his skin stood on end. He immediately prostrated himself, placing the prince’s feet upon the crown of his head, and leaping for joy, he spoke these words:
“Excellent, excellent!
"This crown prince of mine possesses great majesty and virtue.
He spoke in verse, praising him thus:
"Like a great mass of fire atop a mountain at night, Resembling the bright autumn moon emerging from among the clouds,"
"Now seeing the Prince sitting in contemplation, Unconsciously my hair stands on end and my body trembles.
When King Śuddhodana had finished praising him with this verse, he again prostrated at the Prince's feet and spoke once more in verse:
"I now bow my body for a second time, To prostrate at your supreme and wondrous thousand-spoked feet."
"From the time of my birth until this day, / I have suddenly been able to see you sitting in meditation.
At that time, there were young children carrying fishing weirs and snares who followed the Great King, chattering and laughing.
A certain minister rebuked those children, speaking thus:
"You little children!
Please do not shout and cry out."
Then the children replied to the minister,
"Why do you not allow us to enjoy our clamorous play?
At that time, the great minister answered all those children with a verse:
"Though the sunlight is extremely hot and fierce, it cannot turn back the cool shade of that tree;
furthermore, there is a most wondrous light of one fathom, whose magnificent virtue has no peer in the world."
Contemplating as he sat upright beneath the tree, unmoving and unshakable like Mount Sumeru,
Prince Siddhārtha, with his innermost heart, took delight in this shade of the tree and would not leave it.

Chapter 13: The Contest of Skills and the Struggle for Marriage. *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Thirteen (Part One). "At that time, the Prince gradually grew toward maturity and reached the age of nineteen. Then, King Śuddhodana constructed three seasonal palaces for the Prince:
the first was a warm palace intended for the height of winter;
the second palace was cool, intended for the summer heat."
The third hall was intended for rest during the two seasons of spring and autumn.

The hall designated for winter sitting was consistently warm; the hall designated for summer sitting was consistently cool; and the hall designated for sitting during the two seasons of spring and autumn was temperate, with a moderate climate that was neither cold nor hot.

Furthermore, within the rear garden of the palace, he dammed the flowing channels and constructed ponds and pools, planting various kinds of diverse and famous flowers—namely, *utpala* flowers, *padma* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers—for the sake of bringing joy and delight to the Prince.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable and boundless people, each assigned to their respective duties to attend upon and guard the Prince; some massaged the Prince,
some rubbed him with softness, and some applied various fragrant oils to his body.
Furthermore, there were some who rubbed and wiped the Prince while he was bathing;
others who provided scented bathwater during his ablutions;
and some who dyed his hair and combed his topknot.
Furthermore, some people held mirrors to reflect his image;
some held scented unguents, some eye salves, and others incense for perfuming garments;
some held ox-gall (gorocanā), some flower garlands, and others various kinds of exquisite, multicolored robes; they stood before the Crown Prince, constantly prepared to offer their services.
As for the garments worn by the Prince, they were entirely of Kāśika cloth; having taken them up, he would bow his body and present them immediately to whoever required them.

Regarding the garments worn by the Prince’s father, King Śuddhodana, the inner layer was of Kāśika while the outer surface was made of other materials; the Prince was not so, for the robes he wore were made of Kāśika both inside and out.

He provided his attendants on the left and right, laborers, male and female servants, and all those in his retinue with meals of polished rice, mixed with minced meat, sauces, and condiments, whether as stews or soups.

For the Prince alone, exquisite and fragrant fine rice was set aside, carefully selected; there were various soups and broths, a hundred flavors of fragrant delicacies, all kinds of rare dainties, as well as various cakes and fruits.
In this manner, they constantly prepared these things day after day, both by day and night, each newly constructed for the Prince.

Furthermore, they held a white parasol over the Prince, either fearing that he might be drenched by dew or struck by wind and frost during his nighttime play, or lest he be covered in dust or scorched by the sun during his daytime excursions.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, seeing that the Prince was gradually growing toward adulthood and recalling once more the words of the prophecy given by the seer Asita, assembled the elders of the Śākya clan and the great ministers, and spoke these words:
"O kinsmen!..."
Have you not heard?
When this prince of mine was first born, I summoned those who could interpret signs, as well as the Brahmin Asita and others, and they all prophesied, saying:
"If he remains at home, he will certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King; if he renounces the world and leaves the household life, he will surely achieve the Unsurpassed Way."
"But what expedient means can we now employ so that this youth shall not go forth into homelessness?
The Śākya kinsmen then replied to the King:
"Great King!..."

We should now quickly construct a separate palace for the Crown Prince and provide him with various court ladies for his amusement and diversion; in this way, the Crown Prince will not renounce the world and go forth.
And there is a verse that says:
“What was prophesied by Asita is certain and cannot be altered.
The Śākyas urged the construction of a palace, hoping to prevent him from leaving the household life.
[They thought: "By such expedients, we Śākyas shall attain prosperity; we shall be able to cause everyone to revere and respect us, so that we will not be deceived by the various minor kings."
Then King Śuddhodana spoke again to his kinsmen of the Śākya clan, saying:
"You should consider which Śākya maiden is worthy to be the consort for my Prince Siddhārtha."
At that time, each of the five hundred Śākya clansmen cried out:
"My daughter is worthy to be the consort for the Crown Prince. (In the Sanskrit original, these two phrases are repeated for each; they are abbreviated here.)
At that time, King Śuddhodana again reflected to himself:
"If I do not consult with the Prince today and suddenly take another girl to be his consort, it may prove unsuitable and result in a failure of my duty;
yet if I were to discuss this with the Prince now, his mind is so profound that he would ultimately refuse to speak of it."
"I am now filled with doubt; what expedient means should I employ?
He further reflected:

"I shall now have various kinds of miscellaneous jewels fashioned into a vessel called 'Free from Sorrow' (Aśoka-pātra) and present it to the Prince. I will instruct him to use it to bestow gifts upon the women, while secretly dispatching messengers to observe their intentions. By watching whose side the Prince’s gaze falls upon, I shall immediately betroth her and take her as his consort."

Then King Śuddhodana immediately dispatched craftsmen to fashion various precious playthings for dispelling sorrow, adorned with gold, silver, and diverse ornaments. Once they were completed, he rang a bell in the city of Kapilavastu and proclaimed:

"From this day forth, until the seventh day has passed, my son, the Prince, wishes to see all the women of the Śākya clan. Having seen them, he intends to bestow upon them various precious playthings for dispelling sorrow. All the women within the city should assemble at the gate of my palace."
"At that time, when the six days had passed and the seventh day arrived, the Prince went out as before to the gate of the royal palace and sat down upon the straw mat."

At that time, all the women within the city, having adorned their bodies with various kinds of miscellaneous jewel necklaces, gathered at the palace gate, desiring to see the Prince and also wishing to receive the various precious vessels of sorrowlessness.
At that time, seeing the women approaching, the Prince took various precious vessels and bestowed them upon those women who had come from the four directions to see him.
Because the prince’s majestic power was so great, the maidens were unable to look directly at him; they merely took their precious vessels and each passed by quickly with heads bowed low.

When the precious vessels were all exhausted, last of all there came Mahānāma, a minister of the Śākya clan from the Vāsiṣṭha lineage; his daughter was named Yaśodharā, who arrived surrounded by a vast retinue of maidservants and attendants.

From afar he saw the Prince, towering and majestic; his gaze was fixed, his steps were elegant as he advanced, and he looked straight ahead with a steady stare, his eyes never glancing askance. He gradually drew closer, moving forward toward the Prince.
Like an old acquaintance, he showed no sign of shame and addressed the prince, saying: "Prince!
You should now give me the vessel of various jewels, the 'Free from Sorrow' (Aśoka)."
The Prince replied,
"Since you arrived so late, everything has already been given away.
The woman spoke to the Prince once more:
"What fault have I committed that you now deceive me by not giving me the precious vessel?
The Prince replied:
"I do not deceive you; it is simply that you arrived late and thus could not reach me.
At that time, the Prince took an engraved signet ring from his finger—worth hundreds of thousands—and removed it to give to Yaśodharā.
Yaśodharā said to the Prince,
"May I stop with you at this price for such goods?
The Prince replied:
"As for what I am wearing, as well as my other ornaments, you may take whatever you please.
The girl replied,
"How could I possibly strip the Prince of his garments?"
"It can only serve to adorn the Prince's body.
Having spoken these words to the Prince, he felt no joy in his heart and immediately turned back to depart.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had attained enlightenment, the Venerable Udāyin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Why was it that when the Tathāgata was in the royal palace, although he took all his priceless necklaces and removed them to give as a gift to Yaśodharā, he was unable to cause her heart to feel joy?”
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Udāyin, saying:
"Listen attentively with a sincere mind, Udāyin!"
I shall explain this.

It was not only in this present life that Yaśodharā was made unhappy by being given these necklaces; rather, throughout her past lives, she has once been moved to resentment by even a minor cause, such that she remained displeased despite the gift of many kinds of precious jewels.
Udāyin said: “How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of this?”
"I pray that you will explain this to me.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Udāyin, saying:

"I recall that in the past, immeasurable eons ago, in the city of Vārāṇasī within the kingdom of Kāśi, there was a king who governed and transformed his realm while adhering to false and perverted views."

That king had a son who committed a minor offense; the father-king banished him from the borders of the kingdom. Traveling by stages, he arrived at a certain celestial temple and dwelt there together with his wife.
At that time, the provisions of food the prince had brought with him were completely exhausted. To sustain his life, the prince went hunting and killed various insects and creatures.

While at a place where he was hunting, he saw a crocodile; he pursued and killed it, immediately flayed its skin, and placed it in water to boil. When it was nearly cooked, the liquid suddenly evaporated entirely.
At that time, the prince said to his wife, "The meat is not yet properly cooked; you go and fetch more water.
The prince's wife immediately went to fetch water.

After his wife had departed, the prince was overcome by hunger and could no longer endure it; he immediately ate the crocodile meat until it was entirely consumed, leaving not even a single scrap behind.
At that time, the prince’s wife returned from fetching water and asked her husband,
"Where is the crocodile meat that was here?
The prince replied:
"The crocodile has suddenly come to life; it has now already run away.
His wife did not believe him, asking, "How could this have happened so suddenly?"
"The crocodile has already been cooked thoroughly; how could it possibly run away?
The wife did not believe him, yet she thought to herself:
"It must be my husband who, driven by hunger, ate it all up and deceived me by saying it had run away."
Bearing resentment in his heart, he was constantly unhappy.
Several years later, when his father passed away, the ministers immediately welcomed the prince and consecrated him as sovereign.
Once he had ascended the throne as king, all the various jewels, rare treasures, diverse garments, and priceless objects he had acquired were given entirely to his consort.
Although she had been taken as his consort, her facial expression remained as displeased as before.
At that time, the king said to his consort:
"I have bestowed upon you all my treasures and priceless objects; for what reason is your countenance not joyful, remaining no different than it was before?"
Then his consort immediately spoke in verse to reply to the king:
"O Most Victorious Great King, listen: In the past, while out hunting, Holding arrows or grasping a blade, I shot and killed a wild crocodile until it died."
"Having flayed his skin and nearly finished boiling him, he sent me to fetch water to add to the pot;
he devoured the flesh without leaving a trace, yet deceived me by saying he had run away.
He then addressed Udāyin:
"You should know this!
The king at that time was my own self; the queen was Yaśodharā of today."

At that time, I committed a slight offense against him; subsequently, although I offered him much wealth and treasure in hopes of reconciling our relationship, he still harbored resentment and remained displeased.
It was the same today; even though they presented immeasurable varieties of money and silk, they could not cause his heart to rejoice.

At that time, the secret emissaries sent by King Śuddhodana to observe the Prince watched with single-minded attention the Prince’s eyes and what he gazed upon, as well as his conversations and exchanges with the maidens; those secret emissaries understood everything in full detail.
Having understood this, he immediately went to the king's presence and addressed him, saying:

"Great King, you should know that there is a Śākya minister named Mahānāma; his daughter later conversed with the Prince several times, exchanging words back and forth, smiling as she stood for a short while and engaging in playful banter."
The Prince and the young woman both showed delight on their faces; they exchanged words with one another, their eyes meeting.
When King Śuddhodana heard these words concerning their secret observations, he thought to himself:
"Does the Prince intend to obtain this girl?"
Then King Śuddhodana, having selected an auspicious lunar mansion and a favorable day, summoned the royal preceptor, a Brahmin, and sent him to the home of the Śākya minister Mahānāma, saying:
"I know that you have a daughter; she may now be given to my prince to be his consort."
At that time, having heard the king’s words, the state preceptor went at once to the house of the Śākya minister Mahānāma and spoke thus:
“Mahānāma, the king’s decree is as follows.”
Then the Śākya minister replied to the State Preceptor, saying:
"In our Śākya tradition, the succession has been such that if there is one whose skill surpasses all others, we shall give our daughter in marriage to that person;
if he lacks such skill, we may not give her."

"Great King, the Crown Prince has grown up within the deep palace, indulging in amusements and play; he has never undergone training and possesses no skills. He is unskilled in archery, astronomy, military treatises, weaponry, all forms of combat, or wrestling and boxing. For what reason, then, would I now give my daughter in marriage to one who is not an accomplished artist?"
At that time, having heard these words, the State Preceptor returned to the King’s presence and reported the matter in its entirety to him.
Upon hearing this speech, King Śuddhodana was filled with sorrow and anxiety, and reflected thus:
“Mahānāma’s words are in accordance with the Dharma; he has spoken to me with complete truth, without a single falsehood.”
Although he thought this, the king remained inwardly despondent, silent, and bewildered, appearing as if he were sitting in meditation and contemplation.

At that time, the prince observed his father’s face; its natural color had faded, and he was dejected and unhappy, looking exactly like one engaged in meditative reflection. Having witnessed this, the prince gradually approached the king and asked him:
"I wonder, Father King!"
"For what reason are you sitting here alone, lost in thought with such sorrow and distress?
Having spoken these words, King Śuddhodana replied to the Prince:
"My son, you need not ask me about such matters."
The Crown Prince asked a second time, and the Father King again stopped him.
The Crown Prince asked thus a third time:
"Father King, Great King!"
"You must explain to me the reason for this, so that you may resolve my doubts.
When King Śuddhodana had seen the Prince ask such questions three times, he spoke to the Prince exactly as he had previously described.
Having understood this, the Crown Prince asked his father, the King:
"Does Your Majesty know, O Father King, whether there is anyone within the city who can come forth to compete with me in the arts?"

When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he was immediately filled with great joy; his entire body leaped with exultation such that he could not contain himself. He then questioned the Prince once more, speaking thus:
"Excellent, Prince!"
"Are you truly able to compete in various arts and skills?
The Prince replied,
"Great King, please listen well!"
"I am truly capable of this,
Great King!
You should simply assemble all the young Śākyas at once and compete with me in all the various arts and skills."
Then King Śuddhodana issued an edict throughout the city of Kapilavastu, commanding that at every street, alley, crossroads, and thoroughfare, bells be rung and a loud proclamation made:

"From this day forth, for a period of seven days, my crown prince, Prince Siddhārtha, intends to display all his various skills. Let all those who possess such knowledge gather together so that they may compete and demonstrate their abilities."
When six days had passed and the seventh day arrived, five hundred young Śākya youths, with Siddhārtha at their head, all gathered together.
When they had finished gathering, they went out of the city together to a spacious plain, which was the place where these youths displayed their skills.
At that time, the Śākya minister beautifully adorned Yaśodharā and made her an excellent target, saying:
"Whoever is most proficient in all arts and crafts, being the supreme victor, shall have this girl as his wife."

At that time, King Śuddhodana, together with the elders and venerable elders of the Śākya clan, arrived first. Furthermore, there were immeasurable and boundless men and women, boys and girls of various castes, all of whom gathered at the site of the spacious trial grounds, desiring to witness the Prince and all the Śākya youths competing in their skills to see who was the most excellent.
At that time, there were several young Śākya youths who were proficient in literature; they first competed with the Prince in calligraphy.
Then, some of the Śākyas said to one another, "Now we should appoint Viśvamitra to serve as our examiner."
He then said to him:
"You should examine among these youths whose hand-writing is superior, or who writes with speed and skill, and who understands many types of scripts."
At that time, the Master Viśvāmitra, knowing beforehand that the Prince was the most excellent and supreme among all scholars, spoke these verses with a joyful smile:
"Among all those in the human realm and the heavens, The Gandharvas, Asuras, and Garuḍas—
Regarding all written characters and scriptural canons, The Prince has traversed them all and mastered them completely."
Neither I nor you and your peers know the names of such books;
though all men in the world may try to understand them, they will certainly find that I excel you and you are not my equal.
At that time, those members of the Śākya clan collectively addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
"We now know, Great King, that your son is the most preeminent among those skilled in the scriptures."
"Calculations must be tested to know who is most proficient.
At that time, there was among the assembly a preeminent master of calculation named Aṣvajit, who was the foremost of all in calculation.
Then the Śākyas called Aśvajit and took him away to test him, saying:
"Venerable One!
Observe well among these youths; who is the foremost in calculation?"
At that time, the Prince performed the calculation, ordering a learned youth of the Śākya clan to assist with the counting sticks; yet he could not keep up.
Another youth was brought down to assist, but still it was not enough.
A third youth was brought down, but likewise he could not keep up.
Even when ten youths descended together, he still did not provide them with offerings;
when twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or a hundred descended together, he still did not provide them with offerings;
even when two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred descended all at once, he still did not provide them with offerings.
At that time, the Prince spoke these words:
"You calculate now; I shall play the part of the inferior player.
Then a young Śākya boy called out the numbers, and the Prince played the inferior role, yet he was unable to calculate them all.
The Prince spoke again:
"The two of you have devised a combined plan.
Once more, they were unable to reach him.
The Prince spoke again:
"Even if we count up to one hundred all at once,
it still cannot reach it."
The Prince spoke again:
"Why do you all compete with one another in this manner? Let each of you simply state your own price at once, and I shall provide the lowest."

At that time, five hundred youths of the Śākya clan all shouted at once; the Prince descended simultaneously with them, from the first mentioned up to the last. Without error or confusion, he descended calmly and with discerning composure, following the exact order.
All those young Śākya boys calculated together with all their might, yet they could not reach even a ten-thousandth part of Prince Siddhārtha’s total.
At that time, the great mathematician of the country of Aṭṭhakanāgara was inwardly struck with wonder and extreme joy, and he spoke these verses:
“Excellent! Your quick wit and profound memory are marvelous; You have recited clearly and without error.”
Five hundred Śākya youths, renowned for their mastery of calculation, could not match him when they all challenged him at once.
With such wisdom and a mind of right mindfulness, his reckoning was swift and profoundly subtle;
as such a master of calculation, he could determine the number of drops in the great oceans throughout the world.
"You all should remain silent and restrain your voices; there is no need to contend with him.
Since he already understands such arts, he ought to be able to compare his skill with mine."

At that time, all those members of the Śākya clan were filled with a sense of wonder; they rose from their seats, joined their palms, and prostrated themselves before the Crown Prince, addressing Siddhārtha:
"The Crown Prince is truly victorious; he is truly and supremely victorious."
In unison, they spoke again to King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!
You have gained a great and wholesome benefit!"
He has been born well among humans.
Great King, you have now given birth to such a son of great merit and wisdom—a son of intelligence.
His tongue faculty is likewise light, supple, and smooth, having perfected the karma of speech.”
At that time, King Śuddhodana smiled with a joyful countenance and said to the Prince:
"Excellent, Prince!
Are you now able to engage in calculation with this master of great reckoning, Aṣvajit, regarding the worldly skillful means and wisdom, so that you may reach mutual understanding?"
At that time, the Crown Prince replied to the King, his father, saying:
"Great King, I am able.
Then King Śuddhodana spoke to the Crown Prince, saying:
"If you are able to do so, you should know the time yourself.
Then the great mathematician Aṣvajit said to the prince:
"O noble Prince!..."
"Do you know the calculation of 'one hundred million' (koṭi) and beyond?
The prince replied,
"I know it very well."
Then the mathematician Aśvajit spoke again:
“Do you know how this is so?
Explain it to me.”
The Prince replied:
"All you who enter into the calculations of billions, listen attentively!
I shall now speak of them."
One hundred times one hundred thousand is called a *krośa* (in the Sui language, ten million);
one hundred *krośas* is called an *ayuta* (in the Sui language, ten billion); one hundred *ayutas* is called a *nayuta* (in the Sui language, ten thousand billion);
one hundred *nayutas* is called a *prayuta* (in the Sui language, several hundred trillion); one hundred *prayutas*...
One *khaṅkāra* (Sui: several thousand million billion) is called one *bimbara* (Sui:
several ten quadrillion); one hundred *bimbara* is called one *akṣobhya* (Sui: several ten quintillion); one hundred *akṣobhya* is called one *vibhāsa* (Sui:
several ten million quadrillion); one hundred *vibhāsa* is called one *utkhaṅka* (Sui: several...).
One thousand million *koṭi* is called one *vibhūta*; one hundred *vibhūta* is called one *bahu*; one hundred *bahu* is called one *nāgabala*;
one hundred *nāgabala* is called one *tīkṣṇabala*; one hundred *tīkṣṇabala* is called one *bibhatsanaprajñā*.
(In the Sui system of numeration, these correspond respectively to ten *jing*, one *qian-jing*, ten *qian-jing*, one hundred thousand *jing*, and ten million *jing*.)
One *koti* (京) is a number of several million in the Sui language; one hundred *koṭis* is called a *vibhāsa-tanaprajñāti*, which in the Sui language is a number of several tens of *nayutas*;
one hundred *vibhāsa-tanaprajñātis* is called a *khāroṣṭa*, which in the Sui language is a number of several thousand *nayutas*;
one hundred *khāroṣṭas* is called a *hetudinidra-dha*, which in the Sui language is a number of several tens of hundreds of thousands of *nayutas*. One hundred [of these]...
One *kṣetrendra* is called a *samantānala*; according to the Sui calculation, this is ten million *koṭis*.
One hundred *samantānalas* is called a *gaṇanāgani*; according to the Sui calculation, this is one hundred billion.
One hundred *gaṇanāganis* is called a *nimbaraja*; according to the Sui calculation, this is one trillion. One hundred *nimbarajas* is called a *mukha*.
One *tāpala* is a Sui number of several hundred thousand *qi*; one hundred *tāpala* is called an *aghamuṭa*, which is a Sui number of several ten million *qi*;
one hundred *aghamuṭa* is called a *sappavara*, which is a Sui number of several ten billion;
one hundred *sappavara* is called a *visajapati*, which is a Sui number of several trillion; one hundred *visaja*...
One *pati* is called *sarvasarva*, which in the Sui language is calculated as ten thousand *rang*;
one hundred *sarvasarva* is called *vibudgama*, which in the Sui language is calculated as ten million *rang*;
one hundred *vibudgama* is called *parārdha*, which in the Sui language is calculated as several tens of *gou*. When entering into such numerical calculations, even Mount Sumeru [is included].
If one wishes to calculate and know weights down to the *jin*, *liang*, *zhu*, and *fen*, all can be known.

Beyond this, there is another calculation called *tāpasa-gaṇanī-mana*; beyond this, there is another calculation called *śapana*; beyond this *ni*, there is another calculation called *paranada*; beyond this, there is another calculation called *iṭṭha*; beyond this, there is another calculation called *karoṣaṭapita*; and beyond this, there is another calculation called *sarvanikṣepa*.
As for this calculation, it encompasses and exhaustively includes all reckonings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Beyond this, there is another calculation called *agaśava*; this number takes the count of one hundred thousand million billion Ganges-sands and incorporates them all entirely into it.
"And beyond this, there is yet another calculation known as *paramāṇuvibhāga*.
Then, the great mathematician Aśvalāyana said to the prince:
"This has already been understood."
"Furthermore, how does one calculate the number of atoms within those atoms?
This too must now be understood.
The Prince replied:
"Listen attentively!
I shall now speak of it."

Seven atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute one window-dust particle (*vātāyanaraja*); seven window-dust particles constitute one rabbit-dust particle (*śaśaraja*); seven rabbit-dust particles constitute one sheep-dust particle (*aurabhraraja*); seven sheep-dust particles constitute one ox-dust particle (*goraja*); seven ox-dust particles constitute one nit (*likṣā*); seven nits constitute one louse (*yūka*); seven lice constitute one mustard seed (*sarṣapa*); seven mustard seeds constitute one barley grain (*yava*); seven barley grains constitute one finger-joint (*aṅgulīparvan*); seven finger-joints accumulated constitute half a foot (*vitasti*); two half-feet constitute one foot (*pāda*); two feet are one cubit (*hasta*); four cubits are one bow-length (*dhanus*); five bow-lengths are one staff-length (*daṇḍa*); twenty staff-lengths are called one *krośa*; eighty *krośas* are called one *krośa* (in this context, *krośa* is used as a unit of distance); and eight *krośas* are called one *yojana*.
In this assembly, who is able to know how many atoms constitute one *yojana*—calculated according to the Sui measurement as three hundred eighty-four li and one hundred three thousand paces?
Then the great mathematician Aṣvajit replied to the prince, saying:
"O virtuous and noble one!
I do not even know such numbers; having just heard them spoken, I am already bewildered and distressed—how much more so for others who are of little wisdom, little learning, and foolish?"
"Nevertheless, we pray that the Prince will explain for us: how many atoms constitute one *yojana*?
From the *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha-sūtra*, Volume Twelve;
*Buddhacarita-saṃgraha-sūtra*, Volume Thirteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on Competing in Arts and Contending for Marriage, Part Two:
At that time, the Prince replied to the great master of calculation, Aṣṭana:
"Listen attentively!

As for the number of motes of dust in one yojana, if they were gradually accumulated until they filled one akṣobhya, and likewise another nayuta, and another twenty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands, and another sixty billion hundreds of thousands, and another three billion two hundred million, and another five hundred thousand, and finally another one hundred thousand."
In this manner, the number of such atoms, when fully totaled, completes this one *yojana*.
In this successive order, one calculates the dimensions of *yojanas* by multiplying them against one another.
This Jambudvīpa is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
Aparagoyānī is eight thousand yojanas;
and Pūrvavideha is nine thousand yojanas.
The northern continent of Uttarakuru measures ten thousand yojanas.
This is the number of yojanas for this single trichiliocosm.

Its length and breadth are thus; its dimensions increase and decrease in succession according to these yojanas. Calculating in this manner, one may determine the total by summing up several hundred yojanas, several thousand yojanas, and several hundreds of thousands of yojanas. Furthermore, within each single yojana, there exists a specific number of atoms, which can likewise be calculated in their entirety.

Why is this so? Because this calculation transcends all numbers; therefore it is called "reckoning. It cannot be obtained by counting, nor can it be known by calculation—the number of all such atoms and the like within the entire trichiliocosm.

At that time, the great mathematician Aṣvajit, along with all the clansmen of the Śākya lineage, were filled with immense joy and leaped for boundless delight; it pervaded their entire bodies such that they could not contain themselves. Leaving only a single undergarment upon their persons, they untied all their other clothes and offered them to the Prince.
He further removed immeasurable and boundless necklaces and scattered them as gifts for the Prince, praising him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
The Prince is most profound; he knows and understands with great clarity."
In this manner, as they proceeded through the calculations, the Prince again surpassed them;
for in the profound depths of writing, arithmetic, knowledge, and strategy, the Prince was without equal.
Those Śākyas then spoke these words:
"We already know that this crown prince is currently the most excellent and peerless among those skilled in writing and calculation.
Next, we must test his prowess in weaponry and military strategy; who is the most preeminent in these?"
"Who is the most excellent?
At that time, those clansmen of the Śākya lineage selected a great minister from among their kin named Sahadeva and appointed him as the arbiter, addressing him thus:
"Venerable Upādhyāya!
“May you apply your minds well and observe which youth is most excellent and marvelous among these martial skills—
namely, Akāśagarbha, Śabdavatsa, and the others— who excel in shooting at long distances and shooting with force, drawing powerful bows and wielding their arms.”
"At that time, for the sake of the youth Ānanda, an iron drum was set up and positioned as a target two *krośas* from the shooting range;
for the youth Devadatta, an iron drum was placed at four *krośas*;
and likewise, for the youth Nanda, an iron drum was placed at six *krośas*."
For the great minister Vāsiṣṭha Mahānāman, an iron drum was placed at a distance of eight *krośas*.
Following this sequence, for each of the other youths, targets were set at various distances, both far and near;
however, for Prince Siddhārtha, a sturdy and solid iron drum was installed as the target at a distance of ten *krośas*.
At that time, Ānanda drew his bow and shot at the iron drums placed two *krośas* away; he managed to hit and reach them, but beyond that distance, he could not go further.
The drum placed four *krośas* away, which the youth Devadatta shot, was struck and hit immediately, but he could not go further.
The iron drum placed eight *krośas* away, which the minister Mahānāma shot, was also hit, but he could not go further than that.
Each of these Śākya sons shot their respective iron drums, hitting them all from various distances, yet none could surpass the designated limit beyond which they were placed.

Then, in due order, it was the turn of Prince Siddhārtha to shoot; the official presented him with the bow he had been offered. As the Prince momentarily intended to draw it with his hand, he tested the strength of the bow, pressed upon it, and tried to fix the string firmly, but the bow and its string shattered and snapped at that very moment.
Prince Siddhārtha then asked:
"Within this city, who possesses a fine bow that I might draw and pull, such as would withstand my strength?"
At that time, King Śuddhodana, his heart filled with joy, replied,
"There is. The Prince asked:
"The Great King said it exists; where is it now?
The king replied to the prince:
"Your grandfather was named Siṃhahanu (Lion Cheek). He possessed a bow which is currently kept in the temple; it is constantly worshipped with incense and flowers."
"However, as for that bow, not even all the Śākya kinsmen within the city were able to string it, let alone draw it.
The Prince said, "Great King!"
"Go quickly and fetch the bow!
At that time, the messenger brought the bow and, having arrived among the assembly, first presented it to all the young Śākya boys; yet none who grasped it were able to string it, much less draw it.
Thereafter, it was next given to the minister Mahāmaṇa; at that time, the minister exerted all the physical strength he possessed, yet he could not even string the bow, much less draw it back.
Thereupon, they brought it forward to present to the Prince.

Having taken hold of it, the Prince sat calmly without wavering; exerting only a slight effort, he moved his body not at all. With his left hand he grasped the bow, and with his right hand he stroked the string; drawing it with his finger only slightly, he produced a sound.
That sound filled the city of Kapilavastu, and all the people within the city were struck with terror, each asking one another:
"What is this sound?"
"Or again, there may be someone who hears from another:
'Prince Siddhārtha took the bow used by his grandfather, King Siṃhahanu, and merely drew it and pulled it so that it made a sound.'"
"For this reason, King Śuddhodana will provide immeasurable and boundless quantities of goods as offerings for the Prince.

At that time, the Prince drew the bow with his right hand and grasped the arrow; manifesting such subtle and wondrous physical strength, he pulled the arrow back until it was level with his chest and released it. The arrow passed beyond the drums of the three men—Ānanda, Devadatta, and the minister Mahānāma—and traveled ten *krośas* to the place where it had been aimed, piercing through everything and vanishing into the void.
At that time, the devas in the sky spoke these verses:
"In this most excellent and auspicious place, Seated upon the throne of the Buddhas of the past,
The people of the kingdom of Magadha Now behold the sharp arrow and the skillful, victorious bow."
Having perfected the power of wisdom through the six perfections, one subdues all enemies— whether they be celestial Māras,
afflictions, or the aggregates— and shall thereby attain the cause of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
The true path of non-retrogression toward bodhi forever severs the root-stumps of the suffering of birth and death;
illness, old age, grief, and fear are all eliminated, and one realizes that subtle wisdom of nirvana.
When the devas had spoken these verses, each took various kinds of exquisite celestial flowers and scattered them over the Prince; having scattered them, they suddenly vanished from sight.
At that time, the arrow shot by the Prince was taken up by Śakra, Lord of the Devas, from mid-air and carried toward the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

Once he had reached the celestial realm, for the sake of this arrow, he established the Festival of the Arrow within that heaven; on auspicious days, the devas would assemble and make offerings of various fragrant flowers to it.
Even unto this day, the gods still observe this festival of the arrow.
At that time, the Śākya kinsmen and their retinue spoke again, saying:
"Prince Siddhārtha’s skill in archery is the farthest; he has already surpassed all others."
"Now we must further test the shooting of heavy objects; who among you can surpass them?
At that time, not far from that spot, there was naturally a row of tala trees.
Among them, some of the Śākya youths shot a single arrow, which pierced through one tala tree; some pierced through two tala trees, or three, four, or even five.

At that time, the Prince took up an arrow and shot it, immediately piercing through seven tala trees. Once the arrow had passed through the seven tala trees, it fell to the ground and shattered into a hundred pieces.
At that time, the Śākyas again separately erected iron boars; some Śākya youths among them took up arrows and shot through one iron boar, or two, three, four, or even more than five.
When the Prince took up his arrow and shot once, it passed straight through seven iron boars.

After seven pigs had passed by, the arrow entered the earth and reached the Yellow Springs; the place where the arrow pierced the ground became a well, which people today still commonly call the Arrow Well.

At that time, the Śākya clansmen further set up seven iron water-vats filled with water. Among them, some Śākya youths heated arrowheads until they were glowing fiercely red and used them to shoot through one iron vat, or two, or three, up to four or five.

The Prince, however, took those heated, glowing arrows and shot a single arrow that passed straight through all seven iron water-vats. Not far from the vats was a large śāla grove; once the arrow had passed through, it completely incinerated that forest, reducing it entirely to ashes in an instant.
Then the Śākya clansmen spoke again, saying:
"The Prince has already surpassed us in the skill of archery;
now let him be tested at the axe-throw, and he must sever it with a single stroke."
Among them, there were some of the Śākya clan who, grasping sharp swords in their hands, cut down one *tāla* tree with a single stroke, or two, or three, even up to four or five;
yet when the Prince grasped his sword and struck with a single blow, he cut down seven *tāla* trees, and although those seven *tāla* trees were severed, they did not fall.
Those Śākyas spoke thus:
"The Prince was unable to cut through even a single tree.
At that time, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven in the Form Realm immediately manifested a great and fierce wind that blew the tree down.
Next, Nanda brought a bundle of bamboo to the presence of the Prince; he had secretly placed an iron massage rod inside it and presented it to the Prince.

When the Prince saw this bundle of bamboo, he did not expect there to be an iron rod within it; without using great strength, he grasped his sword with his left hand and sliced through it with a single stroke, just as a strong man wielding a sharp blade might cut down a single stalk of bamboo or a single arrow.

In this manner, when Prince Śama struck that iron mace with his massage-club, thinking it was a bundle of bamboo, he grasped a sword in his left hand and, without exerting much strength, sliced through it in a single stroke, passing clean through it instantly.
Then the Śākyas spoke again, saying:
"We have already tested him with swordsmanship and hacking; the Prince was the most excellent.
Now we must further test his elephant-riding skills, such as leaping and bounding up and down—who else is capable of this?"
Among them were also various Śākya youths who leaped from the tip of the elephant’s trunk onto its back;
some youths leaped up from its feet;
and some leaped up from its tail.
When leaping upward, they may grasp a coarse and massive iron club, or an iron wheel, or an iron shield, or a halberd, or a long sword;
grasping these with their left hands as they leap up, once they have ascended, they receive them with their right hands and immediately hurl them to the ground.

As the Prince leaped, he stood upon the elephant’s back with his feet turned backward as it ran away; he stepped firmly upon its tusks and mounted the top of its head. With his left hand, he grasped various weapons—whether clubs, wheels, spears, lances, or long swords—and whether holding them in his left or right, he hurled them to the ground, tossing them from the left or the right.
When the Śākya clansmen were unable to reach him, they spoke again, saying:
"Now we must test one another on horseback.
Among them, some Śākya youths brandished spears while leaping, or grasped arrows while jumping; they rode from one horse to a second horse, whirling their spears and brandishing their swords.
Or again, some shot arrows at finger-rings; some hit their mark, while others missed.
Some sons of the Śākyas leaped over two horses and mounted the third, continuing until they either hit or missed their mark.
Others leaped over three horses, and having done so, immediately mounted the fourth, hitting or missing their mark.
Sometimes he would leap over four horses and mount the fifth, whether they were stationary or moving.

At that time, the Prince, holding a spear or grasping a bow and arrow, leaped over six horses and mounted the seventh; he shot arrows until they struck as finely as the tips of hair on their heads, hitting them all with perfect precision.
In this sequence, he may manifest lightness while on a chariot, or display great agility.

In such various ways, he may test his vocal skills, or his singing and dancing, or engage in mutual jesting, or engage in casual conversation and playful banter; he may test his skill in dyeing robes, or in crafting precious gems and pearls, or in painting leaves and blending incense; he may demonstrate games of chance such as *chūpú*, *wéiqí*, or *shuāngliù*; or he may show his prowess in *wòshuò*, *tóuhú*, *zhìjué*, or *tiàokōng*—displaying all such diverse arts and skills.
In all such skills that were tested, the Prince was victorious in every instance.
Then the Śākyas spoke again, saying:
"We now know that Prince Siddhārtha is preeminent and superior in all skills."
"Now we must wrestle to see who is capable.
At that time, the prince withdrew to sit to one side, while all the young Śākya boys emerged in pairs and each engaged in wrestling; in this manner, they proceeded through thirty-two bouts.
The young boys ceased their wrestling and withdrew to one side.

Next, Ānanda suddenly stepped forward to face the Prince, desiring to wrestle with him. Just as the Prince was about to seize Ānanda by the hand, the power of the Prince’s physical strength and majestic virtue proved too much for him to withstand; he immediately fell to the ground.

Subsequently, it was the turn of the youth Devadatta to go forward. With a mind of arrogance and self-conceit, he had never once reckoned the Prince Siddhārtha among his peers; desiring to compete with the Prince in prowess and wishing to be ranked as an equal to him, he stepped forth boldly, circled the arena, and facing the Prince, rushed toward him at full speed, intending to pounce upon him.

At that time, the Prince, neither hurried nor slow, with a calm and composed mind, took the boy Devadatta in his right hand and walked; lifting him up, the boy’s feet did not touch the ground as they circled the trial arena three times and spun through the air three times.

Desiring to subdue his arrogance, he gave rise to no thought of malice, but instead cultivated loving-kindness and compassion; then, with calm and steady grace, he prostrated himself upon the ground so that the other’s body would suffer no harm or injury.
The Prince spoke again:
"Ho! You lot! Do not rely on others to wrestle with me; let all of you come together at once and wrestle with me."
At that time, all those young Śākya youths were filled with arrogance; they all rushed forward together toward the Prince, intending to seize and strike him down.
Each of those youths touched him with their hands; by the power of the Prince’s body and his majestic virtue, they were all unable to restrain themselves and fell prostrate to the ground.
At that time, all those Śākyas were filled with a sense of wonder and marveled to one another, saying:
"How extraordinary! How extraordinary!
Having never practiced since birth, he has today produced such various skills as these."
At that time, all the people within the arena who were watching raised shouts and cries, or produced various strange sounds, tossing pearl necklaces, garments, and other such items.
In the immeasurable heavens above the void, all the devas spoke in unison with a single voice, reciting these verses:
"In all the worlds of the ten directions, Even if all the heroic and powerful warriors Were each as strong as Devadatta,
They would not equal a single pore of the Prince’s holy body."
The majestic power of this Great Being is boundless; with a mere touch of his hand, all fall prostrate to the ground.
The holy one’s power of spiritual majesty is so vast—how can you possibly hope to compare yourselves to him?
Even if Mount Sumeru were unshakable, And the great and small Iron Ring Mountains were most solid,
Along with all the mountains of the ten directions, A single touch could crush them into fine dust.
Even iron and other hard substances, vajra-pearls, and all other various jewels, he can grind to powder with his great power of wisdom; how much more so this man of little strength?
When the devas had spoken these verses, they scattered various kinds of flowers over the Prince, then vanished from mid-air and became invisible.
In this manner, Prince Siddhārtha was victorious in every respect.

At that time, King Śuddhodana knew that the Prince’s skills were superior to those of all others; having seen this with his own eyes and confirmed it with his mind, he was filled with such exuberant joy that it pervaded his entire body, and his heart was so delighted that he could not contain himself.
With a most reverent mind, he commanded that the white elephant be summoned and fully adorned with necklaces and ornaments; having prepared everything, he spoke these words:
"My son, the Prince, shall mount this white elephant and enter the city."
That great white elephant, intended for the Prince to ride, emerged from the city gate.
At that time, the youth Devadatta entered the city from outside; seeing this white elephant, he asked the people, "To whom does this elephant belong?"
"Where do you wish to take it?
The man replied,
"I wish to take it out of the city to serve as a mount for Siddhārtha, and then bring it back into the city."

At that time, Devadatta—proud of his Śākya lineage and noble birth, his arrogance flourishing, relying on the strength of his own body, heedless and dissolute, and devoid of all restraint—furthermore being filled with envy, ran a short distance before the elephant, seized its trunk with his left hand, and struck it on the forehead with his right; with a single blow, the elephant fell to the ground, rolled over three times, and then died.
A white elephant lay upon the ground, blocking the city gate so that the passage of people was obstructed and the road was choked with congestion.
After Devadatta had passed by, a youth named Nanda subsequently arrived, following in succession, desiring to enter the city.
Seeing this white elephant lying at the city gate, its massive corpse blocking the road so that the people could not pass,
he immediately asked the people, "Who has done this?"
The people replied:

"This great white elephant was killed by Devadatta; grasping its trunk with his left hand and striking its forehead with his right, he felled it to the ground with a single blow, and after circling three times, it died."
Nanda reflected:

"The youth Devadatta tested his own physical strength by killing a white elephant; however, this elephant's body was so immense and coarse that it fouled the city gate and obstructed people from entering or leaving."
He immediately took the elephant’s tail with his right hand and pulled it away from the gate for about seven paces.
Subsequently, Nanda followed the Prince and came to enter the city; seeing this white elephant at the city gate, he asked the passersby:
"Who has killed this elephant?"
The crowd replied,
"Devadatta killed him with a single blow.
The Prince then said:
“Devadatta, this was unwholesome; why did you kill him?
The prince asked again, “Who dragged him away from the gate?”
The crowd spoke again:
"The youth Nanda took hold of that elephant’s tail with his right hand and pulled it away from the gate for seven paces."
The Prince spoke again:
"Excellent, Nanda! What you have done is well."
The Prince reflected:
"Although those two are able to display their own physical prowess, this elephant's body is exceedingly large and robust; once it decays and rots hereafter, its stench will permeate this city."

Having completed this reflection, he lifted the elephant with his left hand and caught it with his right; from mid-air, he hurled it beyond the city walls, leaping over seven layers of ramparts and crossing seven layers of moats. Once it had been cast away at a distance of one *krośa* from the city, the elephant fell to the ground, creating a great pit.
Even until the present day, people have passed down the tradition of calling this place "The Pit Where the Elephant Fell," which is precisely this very spot.
At that time, immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings all cried out at once:
"How rare! How rare!"
"Such a matter is truly most extraordinary!
Each of them cried out:
"Excellent, excellent!"
O Great Person, O Great Being!
How rare, how extraordinary!
Never before have we heard or seen such a thing.
And he spoke in verse:
“After Devadatta had struck and killed the white elephant, Nanda dragged it seven paces away from the gate;
The Prince held it aloft in the air with his hand, As if throwing a clod of earth beyond the city walls.”
At that time, the minister Mahānāma, seeing that the Prince was preeminent in all arts and possessed of the most excellent and sublime intelligence, spoke these words:
"I pray only this of the Prince!..."
Please accept my repentance.
Previously, I thought that the Prince did not understand various skills and arts, which caused me doubt and led me to refuse to give my daughter in marriage to him.
"I have now understood; I pray that you will accept my daughter to be your consort.

At that time, the Prince selected an auspicious day and a favorable constellation, prepared the necessary provisions according to his family’s resources, and relying on the power of the Great King and employing the majesty of the Great King, he went to welcome and receive Yaśodharā, adorning her body with various necklaces and ornaments.
Furthermore, he went together with five hundred court ladies, escorting her back to the palace where they enjoyed themselves and partook of the pleasures of the five senses.
Therefore, the verse says:
"The daughter of the minister Yaśodharā, Her fame covered the land, known far and near; She was welcomed into the palace, And there she received the delights of the five desires."
Having divined an auspicious day to take her as his consort, he welcomed her into the palace.
There the Prince enjoyed sensual pleasures with her;
in their joy and wantonness, they knew no satiety, just as the Lord of Gods, Kauśika, sports with his consort Śacī.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had attained the Way, the Venerable Udāyin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored Tathāgata!

Why was it that in the past, when you first wished to take Yaśodharā as your wife, you did not take her because she was born of a great family, nor because of her noble lineage, nor because of her wealth and riches, nor because of her beauty and fine complexion? You took her solely on account of her artistic skill, and thus obtained Yaśodharā to be your consort?"
At that time, the Buddha replied to Udāyin: "You, Udāyin!
Listen with a sincere mind."

It was not only today that when I took Yaśodharā, I did not take her because of her noble lineage or high status, nor even for the sake of her physical beauty; I took her solely on account of her skill, and it was the same in the past.
Udāyin said: “World-Honored One!
What is this matter?”
“I pray that you will explain this for me.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Udāyin, saying:

“I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable and boundless eons ago, there was in the city of Vārāṇasī a master smith of exquisite skill. He had a daughter who was upright, beautiful, and pleasing; her body was perfectly proportioned, her face broad and even, and she was rarely equaled by anyone in the world, being loved and revered by many.”
At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī in that kingdom, there was an elder whose son was lovely and handsome, no different from what was previously described.
On one occasion, this son of the elder saw the daughter of a master smith on an upper-story window, showing her face as she looked out.
When that son of a householder saw this woman, he immediately conceived a heart of affection.
Having privately taken note of her in his mind, the son of the householder quickly returned home and addressed his parents, saying:
"In the house of a certain craftsman there is a daughter; my heart is filled with longing for her, and I wish to take her as my wife."
The parents replied to their son, saying:
