"You need not now take this daughter of an iron-smith craftsman to bring disgrace upon our family; we shall seek out another daughter of a householder, or a minister, or a lay devotee to be your wife."
That son of a householder spoke thus:

"I shall never use the daughter of another man as my wife; my heart’s desire is only to take this daughter of the master smith as my wife. If I cannot have this woman as my wife, I will surely take my own life and will certainly not continue to live."
At that time, the parents of the elder’s son were filled with grief, fearing for their child's life; they immediately summoned a skilled iron-smith to their home and said to him:
"The daughter you have, you should now give her in marriage to my son as his wife."
The master smith spoke thus:
"I will not now enter into marriage with one who is not a master smith.
The parents of the elder’s son replied:
"O virtuous one, why would you form a marriage alliance with those who work as craftsmen?
Do not worry that your daughter will suffer from hunger and cold or lack abundant food and clothing.
The smith replied again:
"Although I know this to be so, I am now seeking someone of like kind who understands craftsmanship; if such a person exists, I shall give her to him.
Even if he lacks great wealth or resources, provided he possesses skill in the arts, I will give her to him according to what his household can provide."
When the parents of the elder’s son heard these words, they spoke to their son exactly as had been said before.

At that time, the elder’s son found his mind and will to be in perfect accord with that woman's; moreover, he was sufficiently skilled in the art of craftsmanship. With a refined mind and meticulous attention, he quickly made needles. On another occasion, he manufactured many needles, washed them with oil until they were well-polished and bright, tied them into a large bundle, placed them inside a bamboo tube, and went to the house of a master smith.
Having reached a nearby street, he stood at the head of the road and sang this verse to sell his needles:
"Made of iron that is neither rough nor slippery, Polished bright and thoroughly cleansed,
Crafted by a skilled artisan— Who can buy these needles?"

At that time, the daughter of the artisan’s household was inside a window on the upper floor; hearing the elder’s son reciting the verse as he offered his needles for sale, she immediately replied to him with this verse:
“Alas, you madman! You are utterly devoid of sense.
Having suddenly come to the smith’s house, You cry out that you wish to sell needles.”
Then the son of the elder spoke again in verse, replying to the girl:
"O lovely and upright maiden, I am truly not mad;
by nature I am a man of skill and wisdom, well-able to craft needles."
"If your father knew that I was so skilled in these matters,
he would surely have given you to me as a wife and sent along immeasurable wealth.
At that time, having heard these words from the son of the elder, the daughter of the smith, who was skilled in crafts, went quickly before her parents and spoke thus:
"May my parents listen: there was a person outside who recited a verse as described above.
He related this to his parents, explaining that he had skillfully fashioned needles and had loudly chanted the words.
Then the parents of that master smith immediately summoned the son of the householder to come into their home, where they asked him:
"Excellent, young man!"
"Are you truly skilled at the craft of making needles?
The youth replied,
"I am very capable of doing so."
The smith spoke again:
"Bring out your needle so that I may examine it.
Then the son of the householder drew a needle from within the bamboo tube and showed it to the smith, saying, "This is it."
"Look! Then, having seen the needle, that blacksmith spoke these words:
"Excellent, young man!
"You are skillful at making needles; you are truly able to pierce holes.
Then the boy said to the ironworker:
"This needle did not come from a bamboo tube; there is something else even superior to this."
He then took out another needle and showed it to the ironworker; having examined it, the ironworker again praised him, saying, "You are truly skilled at piercing.
The youth spoke once more:
"This is not the best; there is something even superior.
A third needle was then separately brought out and shown to the smith, who, as before, praised it with flattering words:
"Excellent! It is well-pierced."
The youth spoke again:
"This is not yet refined; there is something even more excellent.
A fourth needle was then produced and shown; after the smith had examined it, he praised it once more, saying:
"It can create great things; it can bore great holes.
The youth spoke again:
"This is still not excellent."
He produced another needle to show him, and after the smith had examined it, he said again:
"Well made! Well pierced!
The youth spoke once more:
"This is not skillful.
For the sixth time, he produced another needle to show him, and the smith spoke again:
"This is truly the most excellent; it is most wonderfully well-pierced."
Then the son of the elder took those needles back, placed them upon his hand, and one by one in succession lowered them into the water; yet all the needles floated.
At that time, the ironworker, beholding this rare and unprecedented event, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he spoke these verses to the son of the elder:
"I have never before heard of or seen one capable of forging such needles;
now, with a heart full of joy, I shall give my daughter in marriage to you."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Udāyin, saying: "Udāyin!
If you wish to know who the son of the elder was at that time, it was my very self."
The daughter of the artisan was none other than Yaśodharā.

At that time, when I took her as my wife, I did not take her because of her family status, nor because of her lineage, nor even because of her physical beauty; rather, she was obtained through the test of her skill in the arts.
Now it is likewise so: Yaśodharā was not obtained because of her lineage or her physical beauty, but rather she was obtained because of her skill in the arts.

Chapter 14: The Constant Adornment for the Reception of the Consort *The Collection of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter 14, Part 1: The Constant Adornment for the Reception of the Consort. "At that time, all the youths of the Śākya clan were handsome, exquisite, and pleasing; they had few equals in the world and were much beloved by the masses. They had all previously mastered every art and craft, and there was none who could surpass them."

He was proficient in all matters such as calligraphy, painting, calculation, and the making of seals; he was skilled in hearing sounds, identifying deities, archery, and so forth. He possessed swift and sharp wit, clever intelligence, and sagacious discernment.
Among those youths, Siddhārtha was the foremost, Nanda was second, and Devadatta was third; with the exception of these three youths, there were none superior to them.
"At that time, within the city of Kapilavastu, there was a minister of the Śākya clan, surnamed Dandapani and named Pāṇi.

That minister was immensely wealthy, possessing an abundance of money and silk, with all manner of assets fully provided; he had acquired them in accordance with the Dharma and sought them without violating principle."

The five grains and seven treasures were accumulated like mountains; two-footed and four-footed creatures—elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep—as well as male and female slaves and servants employed for labor, all matters being fully provided for, everything was completely replete.

Furthermore, there were additionally immeasurable and boundless quantities of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mani-jewels, pearls, musaragalva, agate, coral, and amber; such treasures as these were available for those who needed them according to their hearts' desire, with nothing lacking.
The interior of that minister’s residence was no different from the palace of Vaiśravaṇa.

At that time, Poni had a daughter named Gautamī; she was of exquisite beauty and rare charm, neither short nor tall, neither stout nor thin, neither too fair nor too dark, neither overly large nor overly slender—a jewel of the realm even in her youth.

At that time, King Śuddhodana heard that within his realm there was a daughter of such quality belonging to the Śākya minister Dhānyapāṇi. Having heard this, he selected an auspicious day and immediately summoned the state preceptor and various Brahmins, sending them to the house of Minister Dhānyapāṇi with these words:
"We have heard that you have a daughter named Gopadā; she should now be given as a consort to my crown prince Siddhārtha."

When Nanda’s father heard further that the minister Dandapāṇi had a daughter and intended to seek her in marriage for Prince Siddhārtha as his consort, he too dispatched a messenger to speak thus to the minister Danda:
"O Gautamī!..."
"You may give her to my son Nanda as his wife; if you do not, I shall surely harm you.
Devadatta further heard that the minister Dhana-pāṇi had a daughter whom he wished to seek in marriage for Prince Siddhārtha as his consort. He, too, dispatched a messenger to say to Dhana:
"O Gautamī! [Give her to me]."
"Now you may arrange a marriage for me to take as my wife; if you do not give her to me, I shall bring great calamity upon you.
At that time, the minister Dandapāṇi thought to himself:

"These three youths of the Śākya clan are all handsome and peerlessly pleasing; they are fully endowed with every skill. Siddhārtha the Prince is the foremost, Nanda is second, and Devadatta is third."
I have but one daughter; if I were now to give her exclusively to Prince Siddhārtha, those two youths would surely become my great enemies.
If she were given to Nanda, it would create discord between Siddhārtha and Devadatta.
If she were given to the youth Devadatta, it would instigate enmity and malice between Siddhārtha and Nanda.
At that time, the minister Dandapāṇi was thus displeased; distressed and filled with sorrow, his countenance was not serene as he sat in contemplation, thinking to himself:
"What skillful means should I now employ?"
At that time, Gopadā saw her father sitting thus in silence; she went to his side and spoke these words:
"Father, why do you now sit here unhappy and sorrowful?"
Having spoken these words, her father replied to his daughter Gautamī, saying: "You, Gautamī!
Do not ask about this matter; it is not for you to know."
The daughter asked her father a second time, and her father again replied that it was not for her to hear.
She asked a third time, and he answered as before. Even when she questioned him for the fourth time, her father spoke once more as he had previously. Then the daughter asked again:
"Father must certainly tell you; you must not conceal it.
At that time, because the minister Dandapāṇi questioned his daughter with such earnest persistence, he finally replied to her on the fourth occasion: "Gautamī!..."
"You have asked me three times; listen now attentively, and I shall explain it to you.
King Śuddhodana has sent a messenger to tell me:
'I know that you have a daughter named Gopā; she may be given as a consort to my crown prince.'"
The youth Nanda again sent a messenger to demand Gopadutā to be his wife, saying:
"If you do not give her to me, I shall certainly cause you harm."
Devadatta also sent a messenger to demand Gopikā as his wife, saying:
"If you do not give her to me, I shall surely bring about disaster.
When I heard that those three messengers were demanding you in this manner, I became distressed and thought to myself:
"If one prince is given away, then two youths will become my enemies.
For this reason, I am now despondent and unhappy, sitting here harboring sorrow.
Then Gopadā said to her father,
"Father, do not grieve!
I shall personally employ wise skillful means to ensure that one man becomes my husband."
"Although this is the case regarding principle and fact, Father, please simply grant me leave to act as I wish; I shall marry on my own.

When the minister Dandapani heard these words from Gopikā, he immediately informed the King. Thereafter, at the crossroads of the city of Kapilavastu, he rang a bell and made this public announcement:
"To all people, far and near: from this day until the seventh day, there is a daughter of the Śākya clan named Gopikā who intends to seek a husband for herself."
"Whoever wishes to take [the girl], let us gather together on the seventh day, six days from now.
Having heard these words, on the seventh day, five hundred young Śākya youths, with Siddhārtha at their head, all assembled at the palace gate.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, accompanied by the elders of the Śākya clan, the great ministers, and an immeasurable, boundless multitude of people—men and women, boys and girls—all gathered together at the gate of the royal palace.
At that time, all those who were Siddhārtha’s attendants, as well as the attendants of the other youths, all watched together to see which husband the maiden Gopā would choose.

"At that time, after six days had passed, on the seventh day, during the early morning, the Śākya woman Gautamī bathed herself until she was pure. She took various kinds of exquisite and subtle perfumes and applied them to her body; she put on garments of various colors and adorned her person with various necklaces and ornaments. Furthermore, she donned various garlands of fragrant flowers and was surrounded on all sides by a large retinue of attendants."

Furthermore, there were nurses and various palace attendants who led the way in groups and escorted him from front and back; gradually arriving at the palace gate, he proceeded with composed dignity and entered within the palace gates.

Among those young Śākya youths, Nanda and Devadatta were the foremost; at dawn, they bathed in fragrant water, anointed their bodies with various perfumes, and performed all the acts of adornment as previously described.
Except for Siddhārtha, who did not adorn his body but wore his usual attire, putting on only earrings and a triple-layered, fine golden flower-garland upon his head;
at that time, one of Gautamī’s nurses said to her:
"Daughter, whom do you wish to take as your husband?"
Gautamī examined the five hundred youths one by one and said to her nurse:
"Mother, you should know!

These youths have their bodies so excessively adorned with great necklaces that they resemble women. From the perspective of a woman’s mind, these features appear timid and weak; they do not possess the marks of a manly hero. These are merely the seductive ornaments of women; a true man does not need to adorn his body in such a manner."

The characteristics of a true man naturally possess their own adornments; Prince Siddhārtha’s own personal majesty and radiance do not require necklaces to embellish his body, nor does he rely on external objects for his appearance. He possesses the internal luster of a true man's marks; therefore, my heart delights in Siddhārtha as my husband.

Then Gopikā, holding a *sumana* garland in her right hand, walked through the entire assembly until she reached Siddhārtha. Having arrived, she stood there and fastened this flower garland around Siddhārtha’s neck; having placed it upon him, she embraced his neck and spoke these words:
"Prince Siddhārtha!..."
"I now take you to be my husband.
Siddhārtha replied, "So be it, so be it; it shall be as you say."
At that time, Siddhārtha again took a *sumana* flower garland and tied it around the neck of the maiden Gautamī, speaking these words:
"I now take you to be my consort; you should now become my queen."

At that time, King Śuddhodana, witnessing such a rare and marvelous event, felt a joy arise in his heart; he leaped for joy immeasurably, a rapture that pervaded his entire body, which he could not contain.

At that time, among the multitude, there were some people whose hearts cherished Siddhārtha; they all raised their voices in loud cries, leaping, jumping, and rolling about, shouting and calling out with great joy and exultation, brandishing pearls, necklaces, robes, and ornaments.

The remaining five hundred young brahmins, along with their attendants and those who surrounded them as their retinue, lost their complexion; they were dejected and lusterless, all feeling unhappy. With heads bowed in shame and each harboring regret, they dispersed and returned home.

At that time, Siddhārtha provided all manner of precious jewels and wealth according to his wishes, arranging various extensive rites so that nothing was left unprepared. Furthermore, he adorned and embellished the body of Gopā with various exquisite necklaces and ornaments. He then dispatched messengers to escort five hundred court ladies to surround her as she entered the palace to serve as his consort, where they enjoyed themselves amidst the pleasures of the five senses.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Thirteen;
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Fourteen.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
[This concludes] the section on the constant adornment for receiving the consort, Part II.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had first attained the Way, Udāyin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I do not yet know, World-Honored One!"
What karmic conditions existed in the past between [the Buddha] and Gautamī, the daughter of the Śākya clan,
such that she was able to abandon all other youths and choose the Tathāgata alone as her husband, finding delight in him with all her heart?
"How is it that you have attained such [a state]? Then the Buddha addressed Udāyin, saying: "You, Udāyin!"
Listen with a sincere and attentive mind.

This daughter of the Śākya clan, Gautamī, has not only in this present life rejected other Śākya youths to delight in me; in past lives as well, it was exactly the same—she did not choose those various Śākya youths, but took me as her husband.
Then Udāyin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
I pray that you will explain this for me.”
"What is this matter?
I now wish to hear it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Udāyin, saying:

"I recall that in the past, beneath the Snowy Mountains, there were many various kinds of countless and boundless herds of beasts roaming together, each following the others, freely taking whatever they ate."
At that time, among those beasts there was a tigress, whose beauty was peerless and who had no equal among all animals.
Her fur was so radiant and fresh that countless other beasts sought her out, wishing to take her as their mate, each saying:
"Come and belong to me!"
"Come and belong to me!
Furthermore, there were other beasts who said to one another, "Wait a moment! You all wait!"
"Do not quarrel among yourselves; let that tigress choose for herself whom she will take as her mate. That creature shall be our king.
At that time, among the beasts there was a bull-king who addressed the tigress with these verses:
"All people of the world take my dung, And use it to smear the ground for purification."
"Therefore, you upright and virtuous tigress, you ought to take me as your husband.
At that time, the tigress addressed the bull king with a verse in reply:
"Your neck and hump are exceedingly large; You are fit only for drawing carts and plowing fields."
"How can you, with such an ugly body, suddenly wish to become my husband?
At that time, another great white elephant spoke a verse toward the tigress:
"I am the Great Elephant King of the Snowy Mountains; In battle, there is nothing I do not conquer."
"Since I possess such great power, why do you not now become my wife?
At that time, the tigress replied to the white elephant in verse:
"If you were to see or hear the lion king, your heart would be cowed with terror and you would flee in haste."
"Having left behind a mess of excrement and urine, how could you possibly be my husband?
At that time, among them was a lion, the king of beasts, who addressed the tigress with these verses:
"Behold now this form of mine: The front part is broad and large, while the rear is slender."
Dwelling in the mountains, I live according to my own will, yet I am also able to show compassion and provide for other sentient beings.
I am the king of all beasts; there is none who can surpass me.
Should any see me or hear my roar, all other beasts flee in terror, unable to remain.
I am now thus powerful and robust, my majestic spiritual authority is so great it is beyond description;
therefore, O virtuous tigress, you should know that you may become my wife.
Then, that tigress addressed the Lion King with these verses:
“Possessed of great strength, valor, and majestic power, Your physical form is most perfectly handsome.
Now that I have obtained you as my husband, I shall surely carry you upon my head and serve you.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Udāyin, saying:
"Udāyin, you should understand this:
the lion, the king of beasts at that time, was none other than myself."
The tigress at that time was none other than the Śākya maiden Gautamī;
the various beasts of that time were the present five hundred Śākya youths.
At that time, Gautamī already felt aversion toward the beasts and had no desire for them; yet, upon hearing me recite these verses, she immediately became my wife.
Today it is the same; having rejected five hundred young men of the Śākya clan as being too inferior, she has taken me as her husband.

At that time, King Śuddhodana established three grades of palaces for the sake of housing his crown prince. Within the first palace, all the court ladies were to attend upon the prince during the first watch of the night.
In the second palace, the various court ladies attended upon the Prince at midnight.
In the third palace, the various court ladies waited upon the Prince during the final watch of the night.
In his first palace, Yaśodharā was the foremost, surrounded and attended by twenty thousand court ladies.
In the second palace, Manoharā—which in the Sui language means "Captivating the Mind"—was the foremost.
(The various masters further said:
"As for this Queen Manoharā, we have heard only her name; we have not seen her in the present, nor do we know of her past karmic conditions.
"In the third palace, Gautamī was the foremost."
In this order, the various court ladies who attended upon the Crown Prince numbered sixty thousand in total.
(Furthermore, other teachers say:
"Those who attended the Crown Prince, the various court ladies, numbered one hundred thousand in total, serving as his three palaces; )
"Twenty thousand were all of the Śākya Kṣatriya caste, while the remaining eighty thousand were women of various other lineages.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, mindful of what the seer Asita had said, further constructed within the palace another great and magnificent hall. It was as radiant and lustrous as autumn clouds gathering; its craftsmanship was so exquisite and subtle as to be truly inconceivable. It provided pleasure in harmony with every season, and its railings, pavilions, and walkways were all perfectly symmetrical, without any irregularity.
Why is this? For fear that the Prince might travel about here and there and behold various forms of impurity and filth.
Furthermore, he instructed within the palace that distinct categories of various musical sounds, each numbering in the thousands, should be established.
Among these were one thousand kōng-hou lutes, one thousand zheng zithers, one thousand five-stringed lutes,
one thousand small drums, one thousand zhù instruments, one thousand qin zithers, one thousand pipa lutes, one thousand xigu drums,
one thousand dagu drums, one thousand flutes, one thousand sheng mouth organs, and one thousand [more].
There were one thousand pairs of bronze cymbals, one thousand flutes, one thousand oboes, one thousand transverse flutes,
and one thousand conch shells; all such musical sounds, numbering one thousand distinct varieties,
along with one thousand kinds of songs and one thousand kinds of dances, were performed by their hands and voices constantly within the palace day and night.
It was like the sound of deep, rumbling thunder emerging from within a vast cloud.

Thus, the Prince dwelt amidst hundreds of thousands of most exquisite and supreme court ladies, surrounded before and behind by them as they enjoyed all manner of pleasures; they attended and nurtured him with reverence, all of them adorning their bodies with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments.

Furthermore, with golden bracelets and rings of the seven precious gems strung upon their arms, they produced sounds like those of Śakra, who enjoys the company of celestial maidens; their entertainment of song and dance was most excellent and sublime, as they exchanged charming words, smiled at one another, embraced, caressed, gazed, and cast sidelong glances.

Some lean their bodies to look, while others turn their necks sideways; they are skilled at knitting their brows and adept at casting sidelong glances. Adorned in five-colored silks and possessing four exquisite eyes, they can cause the Prince to experience joy and pleasure without needing to travel far beyond the palace, just as Śakra enjoys the entertainment of his celestial maidens.

In this manner and with these words, the Prince remained amidst the women of the harem, enjoying all manner of delights. Even the various court ladies therein were skilled in the five desires and constantly able to soothe him, causing the Prince to rejoice and preventing him from going further out beyond the palace walls.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, in order to increase the Prince’s various merits, undertook ascetic practices, severed all unwholesome and evil dharmas, practiced every form of goodness, gave away all manner of things, performed manifold meritorious deeds, and fully engaged in austerities; dedicating these roots of virtue to the Prince, he prayed that he would not renounce the world, so that his various merits might flourish.
Therefore, the verse says:
"Because the Great King wished to nurture the Crown Prince, And further, due to the cause of the prophecy concerning Sīta,
He practiced austerities and disciplined himself, abandoning all that is improper, Constantly sitting together with his wise ministers in contemplation."

"In this manner, the Prince remained within the palace of his father the King; being the sole individual there, he was fully endowed with the five desires, enjoying himself in leisure and indulging in play as he pleased for a full ten years, never once going outside."

"At that time, in the southern kingdom of Magadha, there was a great king of the Śāṇḍilya clan named Bimbisāra. Fearing his enemies, his heart was constantly filled with sorrow; he gathered his ministers together and frequently discussed the matter, saying:
'O you ministers!'"

Whether entering or exiting, going or coming, he observed both his inner and outer surroundings, ensuring that no one else surpassed him; for if someone were to surpass him, he feared that person might come and seize his royal throne.
Then the ministers immediately dispatched two men and ordered them to patrol the borders.

Having received the king’s command, the two men traveled through their own territory and the frontiers of neighboring lands, intending to return after completing the circuit. Along the way, they heard someone say:
"To the north of here lies the greatest and most towering Snowy Mountain (Himavat). At the foot of that mountain dwells a distinct clan known as the Śākyas."

Within the clan, a newborn son had recently been born; he was handsome and well-proportioned, born into a noble lineage, and his family name was preeminent and most honored. His kinsmen were powerful and influential, and he was endowed with every excellence. His body possessed the thirty-two marks of a great man, and he was likewise complete with the eighty secondary characteristics.
On the day of his birth, there were Brahmins skilled in the signs of men who gave him this prediction:
"This boy now possesses upon his body the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, all of which are brilliant and clearly manifest."

If he remains at home, he will certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), ruling over the four continents, transforming the people through the ten wholesome paths of action, and being fully endowed with the seven treasures; without the use of weapons, all will naturally submit to him.

If he renounces the world and leaves the household life, he shall attain Buddhahood—becoming a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, complete with the ten titles—and shall even preach the pure holy life (brahmacarya).
Then that messenger, having completed his journey and returned, reported these matters to King Bimbisāra, from the beginning up until the holy life (*brahmacarya*), exactly as described above.
"Therefore, Great King!
While he is still in his youth, you must quickly raise an army to destroy that boy, lest he later seize our position as Great King."
Having spoken these words, King Bimbisāra of Magadha immediately addressed those two messengers, saying:
"You two must not speak in such a manner!"

Why is this? If it be as you say—that this youth, upon renouncing the world, will certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*) who rules and transforms according to the Dharma, then we shall respectfully serve him, bow before him, and follow him; relying upon his majestic power, we shall enjoy happiness and govern with peace and security.
If he renounces his home to become a Buddha, then out of compassion and pity, he will deliver sentient beings, and we shall become his *śrāvaka* disciples, receiving the Dharma from him.
"Now, observing these two kinds of karmic fruits and the causes and conditions of merit, one must not give rise to the thought of harming him.

At that time, King Śuddhodana constructed a separate inner city surrounding the palace courtyard where the Crown Prince resided; it had but a single gate named "Wild Beast. Beneath that gate, a bolt was fitted with a mechanical trigger; when opening or closing it, five hundred men had to support and guard it before it could be opened or shut, and the sound of the gate reverberated for half a yojana.

Next, in the central palace pavilion of the second tier, there was likewise a single gate; its bolts and keys were all equipped with mechanical devices, and when it was opened or closed by three hundred people, the sound could be heard throughout one *krośa*.

Next, he arrived at the inner palace, the hall where the crown prince sat. There was yet another gate, secured by a succession of locks and keys, each fitted with mechanical devices for its operation; two hundred men were required to open and close it, and the defensive preparations were so rigorous that they surpassed anything found in the human world, the sound of which could be heard for half a krośa.

At those three gates, both inside and out, powerful warriors were stationed in defense; they wore armor that was sharp, refined, and sturdy, and held in their hands various weapons of war, namely bows and arrows, battle-axes and long swords, sabers, halberds, tridents, iron mallets and iron clubs, as well as combat wheels, spears, and lances, guarding the palace precincts.
Thus they were on guard, fearing that the Prince would abandon the inner apartments, scale the walls to leave home, and flee into the mountains and marshes.

**Chapter Fifteen: Exhortation to Renunciation by the Voice from Space** *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds* At that time, there was a devaputra in the sky named Kumbhaka. Seeing the Prince, who had remained within the palace for ten years enjoying the pleasures of the five senses, he reflected:

"This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, Pāramitāpradīpa (Hùmíng), though he has spent a vast amount of time within that palace enjoying the various five desires, must not become intoxicated by his mind or lose himself in passion due to attachment to these five desires."
"A hundred years pass in rapidity; time does not wait for anyone. Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatīputra must now exercise vigilance and should quickly renounce secular life to enter the homeless state.
If I do not first manifest signs of world-weariness to him, he will remain immersed in worldly attachments and will not awaken to the resolve to leave the household life."
"I should now praise and assist this matter for the sake of its accomplishment.
Then, at midnight, the Devaputra Kumbhakāra spoke these verses:
"To wish to liberate others while one's own body is bound Is like a blind man leading a multitude of the blind."
Having attained liberation yourself, you shall deliver others, just as one with sight can guide those who are blind.
How excellent, O Benevolent One, that you are in the prime of your years! You should quickly renounce the household life so that your vow may be fulfilled;
thus you shall bring benefit to gods, humans, and all.
Immersed in the realms of the six sense-objects, it is difficult to renounce them;
only through supramundane practice and great wisdom can one truly feel weary of and leave behind these five desires. Therefore, O Benevolent One, you should now cast them aside.

Sentient beings abound with the afflictions of defilement; you, O Benevolent One, should act as their great physician, preaching the various and wondrous medicinal kings of the Dharma, and swiftly lead them to the shore of Nirvāṇa.
Obscured by the darkness of ignorance and entangled in the various nets of views,
quickly kindle the great lamp of wisdom’s light, so that gods and humans may soon attain the pure eye.

At that time, after the Devaputra Ghaṭīkāra had spoken these verses in the air, through the power of his majestic spiritual influence and the causes and conditions of his exhortation, and further by the force of the Prince’s own roots of goodness and merit from past lives, the sounds and songs produced by the palace maidens and musicians within the inner quarters no longer followed matters of the five desires; instead, they transmitted only the subtle sounds of faith, understanding, and the sustaining power of *nirvāṇa*, spontaneously reciting these verses:
"Worldly affairs are impermanent, Just like lightning flashing from the clouds.
The time for the Venerable One has now arrived; You should abandon the home and go forth."
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, Like earthenware vessels made of clay,
Or like borrowed goods used for a time, Or like a city built of dry earth—
Before long they fall into ruin, Just like walls of mud in summer.
Like the sands on both banks of a river, conditioned phenomena cannot endure;
Just as a lamp emits its flame, once born they swiftly pass away;
Like the wind, they do not abide for even a moment, moving with such speed that they never rest.
They are eternally without reality, like the core of a plantain tree;
they deceive the minds of men through illusion, like an empty fist used to lure small children.
All conditioned phenomena arise entirely from causes and conditions.
Each has its own conditions and causes, yet the ignorant do not perceive them.
It is like a person seeking rope: the hands and wood serve as the causal conditions.
Just as a sprout arises from a seed, without the seed the sprout would not grow.
The two cannot be established apart from one another; furthermore, they are neither permanent nor impermanent.
All conditioned phenomena arise from delusion, yet they do not abide within ignorance.
Ignorance, likewise, does not exist within them; their fundamental nature has been empty and quiescent from the beginning.
Because arising and ceasing have no intrinsic nature, they are like a seal producing its impression.
Neither identical to nor separate from that [seal], all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are likewise:
the eye does not exist apart from form, and consciousness arises dependent upon the eye and form.
These three are not separate from one another, yet these three are also not real;
the phenomena of emptiness, purity, and impurity arise from the discrimination of the eye and other faculties.
These inverted discriminations all arise from consciousness.
If there is a person of skillful wisdom who investigates the arising of consciousness,
they will know that it has neither coming nor going; they will know that the self is like a magical illusion,
just as fire is produced from two pieces of wood with the hands as the third cause.
If these three causes do not exist, then the function of fire cannot be obtained.
If one seeks through wisdom, that too has no coming or going;
having searched in all directions, one does not see the fire coming or going.
The aggregates, sense-bases, and elements arise from the karma of greed and delusion;
through the combination of causes there are sentient beings, yet in True Suchness there are no sentient beings.
From the throat, lips, mouth, and tongue, all written characters emerge.
Syllables are not the throat, nor are they apart from it;
because of their conjunction, speech issues forth in accordance with wisdom.
Language does not reside in wisdom, nor does it possess form or shape.
The place of its arising and the place of its cessation— The wise seek them but cannot find them.
That which is observed is entirely empty and quiescent; Speech is like the sound of an echo.
Due to the wood, due to the strings, And through the union of these three with human intelligence, [the sound arises].
The lute produces sound, yet that sound does not exist in any of its three parts.
If a wise person seeks the coming and going of that sound,
searching in all directions, they will find that neither its departure nor its arrival can be apprehended.
Through causes and conditions, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise in this way.
For one who has realized the truth of existence, the contemplation of emptiness should be thus:
the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), both internal and external, are entirely quiescent.
Seeking a self in all places, one finds it is formless like space;
such is the characteristic of all phenomena. You, O Benevolent One, have already realized this in the past under Dīpaṃkara Buddha, and now you proclaim it for the sake of gods and humans.
Because of inverted conceptualization, they are scorched by the fires of desire and the like;
you should raise clouds of compassion and bestow the nectar-rain of the Dharma.
In the past, throughout hundreds of millions of eons, you cultivated mindfulness of generosity and upheld the precepts.
When I have attained the Unsurpassed Way, I shall share the Noble Wealth with all the world.
Venerable One, remember the past: you bestowed the Noble Wealth upon the poor;
having gathered them in through that Noble Wealth, O Tamer, do not be stingy.
In the past, you maintained the pure precepts; even in dire straits, you did not steal another's wealth.
We pray that you open the gate of the nectar of immortality and preach it for the sake of all sentient beings.
Recalling your past conduct, you shall close the gates of hell.
Skillfully opening the path to liberation, the precepts and the heart's aspirations are fulfilled.
Having practiced patience in the past, even when hearing others' insults and abuse,
because he established patience, he contemplated that all conditioned phenomena are entirely empty.
Reflecting on these past deeds, the world is full of hatred;
therefore, teach them to abide in patience and not abandon the power of their vows.
O Benevolent One, practice diligence, and you shall attain my pure wisdom.
Abiding within the ocean of afflictions, you ferry sentient beings to the other shore.
Recalling your vows of the past, you pull them from the river of the four sufferings;
exerting the power of great diligence, you deliver them from calamities and hardships.
In the past, you practiced meditation in order to sever all afflictions,
so as to teach and subdue those whose faculties were untamed.
O Benevolent One, you recalled the past and took pity on beings mired in affliction.
Through the various wisdoms of tranquility and so forth, you have subdued those sense faculties.
O Benevolent One, through the wisdom you cultivated in the past, may you shatter the darkness of afflictions;
out of compassion for beings dwelling in ignorance, reveal the eye of True Suchness.
You, O Benevolent One, remember that in the past, sentient beings were shrouded in the darkness of afflictions;
you opened for them the light free from turbidity and defilement.
With your most supreme wisdom, O Benevolent One, you ought to take pity on all sentient beings and teach them through skillful means so that they may emerge [from suffering].
The fires of birth, old age, and sickness blaze within the three realms; Hunger, thirst, and the heat of affliction never cease.
You should act as a great bridge for the world, To ferry beings across and bring them to the further shore.
Sentient beings wander through the ocean of afflictions, Like bees trapped within the hollows of bamboo;
The three realms of existence revolve like autumn clouds, Ascending and descending, coming and going without rest.
They are like various magical illusions on a theatrical stage, and resemble mountains, rivers, and flowing waters;
so too are the aging, sickness, and death of sentient beings, as they are born among gods, humans, or the three evil realms.
All those possessed by desire and delusion lack self-mastery; Transmigrating through the five realms without awakening, they are like a potter’s whirling fire-wheel.
Everywhere bound by the five desires, they are like flying birds caught in a net, Or like a hunter who has spread sticky glue.
Greedy for the wealth and treasures of others without satiety, Like a fish swallowing bait only to meet the hook;
Competing, quarreling, and enraged, they bind themselves in enmity, Stained by afflictions and attachments, they undergo all manner of suffering.
The faults of the five desires are like a sharp blade, And like a fine vessel filled with poisonous medicine.
One should cast them away like excrement and filth;
for they cause the continuity of existence to arise, increasing the stains of desire that are never severed.
The realms of the six sense objects blaze fiercely, like dry grass consumed by a raging fire.
Arise quickly and renounce the world; go forth into homelessness at once.
It is as terrifying as a pit of blazing fire, like the butcher’s block and cleaver of a meat-carver, like a person suddenly sinking into deep mud, or like licking a sharp blade smeared with honey.

Just as one would touch the head of a snake or stir up a cesspool, so do the noble ones regard sensual desires; they are like arrows, spears, and double-edged swords, like poisoned meat that is difficult to eat.
All enemies have desire as their chief; the merits of the five desires are like the moon reflected in water, like a shadow, and like an echo in a mountain valley;
they are also like a troupe of illusionists on a stage, or like seeing joyful events in a dream.
The objects of the sensory realms are all empty and deceptive; In fear, one cannot attain mastery.
Like a mirage, they possess no reality; They are also like clusters of bubbles upon the water.
All these things arise from conceptual discrimination; The wise should contemplate them in this way.
When ordinary people are young in this world, they are handsome and pleasing, clinging to various desires;
yet when they reach old age and their hair and beard turn white, they are cast aside by the multitude like a dried-up river.
Those who possess wealth and status often become indulgent; such people are greatly attached to sensual desires.
Later, when they lose their wealth and suffer the misery of poverty, they abandon those desires because they no longer have the freedom to enjoy them.
Just as when a tree abounds with flowers and fruit, The multitude comes vying to pluck them;
So it is with one who delights in giving— They seek refuge in him without weariness.
But when that person’s wealth is exhausted and old age arrives, He no longer welcomes others coming to beg from him.
With beautiful form, abundant wealth, and full vigor, people delight in seeing him and gather around in joy;
when his wealth is exhausted and he wanders begging, no one finds him pleasing. When his years have passed and his back is bent as he holds a staff, like a tree broken by hail, no one loves him.
Such is the terrifying dharma of old age; you should swiftly emerge from it to seek perfect enlightenment, and having realized it yourself, speak of it for the sake of others.
Among all people, old age and sickness cause emaciation, like a *mālu* creeper entwining a great tree;
the physical strength of one who has grown old lacks vigor, withered and dry like rotten wood.
Old age robs one of beauty and brings forth ugliness; it makes the cheerful countenance wrinkled.
Old age destroys radiant beauty for a haggard appearance; it robs the joy of desire so that there is no more pleasure.
Old age robs one of power until the end of life; when manifold diseases arrive, one is like a deer falling into a pit.
Having seen the hundred ailments of the world, quickly speak of the means for liberation.
Just as winter winds, snow, and rain break and snap the trees and their tender branches,
so too do old age and many diseases arrive in the world, causing the faculties to wither and decline.
Old age comes and exhausts all one's storehouses; in this world, there is no suffering more deceptive than old age.
The demon of death seizes away a person’s vitality, like the sun setting behind the mountains never to appear again.
The command of death causes loved ones to part; it makes people harbor resentment and dislike meeting again.
Desiring to unite with those one loves, one suddenly loses them like a leaf falling into the great waters.
Death arrives and renders one powerless; life departs like a blade of grass drifting on a current.
When a person reaches the next world, there is no companion; one receives existence according to the conditions of one's own karma.
The demon of death drinks in immeasurable multitudes, like a makara swallowing a sea-going ship,
or as a garuḍa devours great nāgas, or like a fierce fire consuming dry grass and marshes.
Thus oppressed by such suffering and distress, the Great Being recalled his past great vow;
mindful that the power of that vow had now arrived, he should renounce desire and swiftly go forth into homelessness.
Recalling my past practice of giving, My morality, patience, diligence,
And the tranquility of meditative wisdom, All performed for others and not for myself;
Now that these vows have been fulfilled, May I swiftly emerge and liberate others as well.
In the past, you, O Benevolent One, bestowed various treasures—gold, silver, and jeweled necklaces.
You constantly established unobstructed assemblies (amogha-pūjā), granting whatever others desired:
to those who begged for sons, you gave them sons; to those who sought grandsons, you gave them grandsons.
He sought women and gave other women; he begged for rank and relinquished his royal throne;
he begged for wealth and did not refuse it.
He was named Mahāyaśas, and there was also another king of great virtue.
Named Nimiṃdhara, and also named Asita,
and also named Siṃha— these various kings bestowed thousands of kinds of wealth as alms.
Named Constantly Contemplating All Dharmas, and another great virtuous king named True Practice— these ones contemplated the Dharma.
In the past there was a great king, named Diligent Renown-Moon.
Furthermore, there was a prince named Puṇyakarmaprabha,
who possessed great majesty and virtue, and had attained the knowledge of gratitude and righteousness.
In the past, there was a great king named Candraprabha-ṛṣi.
Also named the Valiant and Fierce General; next named Real Increase;
next named Seeking Virtuous Words; next named Possessing Benevolent Intent;
next named Subduer of the Senses—such were these various kings.
Through great diligence in the practice of the Dharma, you have brought this benevolence from the past.
In former times, you were a great king named Candraprabha;
next was the one named Jayamati; and next was the one named Śaśavindu.
The next was named Fangzhu; the next was named Jiānshī;
the next was named the King of Kāśi; the next was named the King Bǎojì.
These various great kings were none other than you yourself.
Various kinds of rare treasures and goods—whenever anyone came to beg, you gave them all as they wished.
You, O Benevolent One, bestowed the wealth of worldly riches in that past life; now I urge you to relinquish the wealth of the Dharma.
In ages past, you beheld Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, you have all made offerings to in the past.
With immeasurable requisites for offering, you gave with no stinginess;
seeking the Way without ceasing, for the sake of the liberation of sentient beings.
Now is precisely that time; quickly depart and do not remain at home.
When you first beheld the Buddha in the past—his name was Akṣayamati—you offered him *viśvaka* flowers with a joyful heart.
In the past, there was a Buddha named Vairocana, who at one time looked upon him with joy.
His name was Subhāṣitaghoṣa; he took a single harītakī fruit, and...
He made offerings to that Blessed One.
In the past, there was a Buddha named White Sandalwood; [the practitioner] stood before that Buddha.
There was a single blade of grass, dark and withered,
called "Connected Rabbit"; when he wished to enter the great city,
he scattered a handful of powdered incense over it.
He preached the Dharma and proclaimed "Excellent! Hearing the Dharma, he spoke of its swift discourse;
the Benevolent One spoke of the immeasurable, and the Honored One was worthy of offerings.
Next, one beheld a Buddha named Universal Manifestation.
You saw him praised as "The Blazing Section"; out of joy,
you contemplated that Buddha’s body and offered him a golden flower garland.
He made offerings to that Buddha.
Now you should call him to mind and not let your heart forget him.
His name was Prabhāketu; he held a handful of small beans.
He used them to make offerings to that Buddha,
whose name was Jñānaketu; the Benevolent One held *śuka* flowers to make offerings to that Buddha.
His name was Taming Vehicle; having seen that Buddha, you stood before him and offered praise.
The next Buddha was named Jewel Victorious; there you lit immeasurable lamps and bestowed sublime, boundless bliss.
The Buddha was named Sarvavijaya; he once offered a necklace of pearls.
Next he saw the Buddha Mahāsāgara; he gave him various lotus flowers.
Upon reaching the Buddha Padmagarbha, he offered a great canopy.
Beside the two Buddhas named Siṃha, he once offered soft grass as a mat;
to the Buddha Sālarāja, he gave all that was required;
before the Buddha Puṣpita, he offered exquisite milk.
At the place of the Buddha Yaśodatta, he offered kuṭaja flowers.
Having truly seen the Buddha and beheld him, he joyfully gave food as an offering.
Formerly, when the Buddha was named Jñānagiri, he bowed his body to pay homage to that Buddha.
There was a Buddha named Nāgaśrī; he gave his own son to that Buddha.
The Buddha Vyomacārin flew high through the air; he once offered powdered sandalwood.
The next Buddha was named Tiṣya; [he received] precious jewels and red flowers.
I once made offerings to that Buddha;
seeing the Buddha Mahāvyūha, I held *campaka* flowers and incense to make offerings to him.
I once saw the Buddha Prabhārarāja and offered various precious jewels as an offering.
In the past, I saw Śākyamuni holding exquisite flowers of silver and making an offering to that Buddha.
Next, I saw the form of Śakra; having seen it, I rejoiced and offered praise.
With a vast face like that of the Sun God, adorned with many held flowers,
he made offerings to that World-Honored One named Jina; holding exquisite and abundant silver flowers, he paid homage.
He adorned that Buddha above.
In the past, there was a Tathāgata named Nāga-jaya; Dīpaṃkara illuminated that Buddha.
At the side of the Tathāgata Puṣya, he once offered a white cotton cloth as a spread.
Beside the Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja, one offers a precious parasol as an offering.
The Buddha’s name is Mahāmuni; furthermore, there is the Lion-like One.
To the World-Honored One of supreme merit, one offers a precious net as an offering.
There was a Buddha named Kāśyapa, whom he honored with various musical sounds.
A former Buddha named Vimukti, whom he honored with various powdered incenses.
To the World-Honored One, Ratnākara, he offered celestial flowers.
To the Buddhas Akṣobhya, I entreat you to mount the palanquin;
To the World-Honored King of Buddhas, I offer garlands of flowers;
To the World-Honored Buddha Śikhin, I renounce my royal throne as an act of giving.
There was a Buddha named Durdharṣa, whom all honored with offerings of incense.
Before the Great Radiant Honored One, he gave his own body as an offering;
before the Buddha Padmottara, he gave various jeweled necklaces.
Above the Tathāgata Dharmadhvaja, I scattered various exquisite flowers and incense;
at the side of the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara, I offered five blue lotuses.
To these and other such Buddhas, as well as countless others beyond measure, [I made offerings].
Inconceivable and difficult to describe are the past ages;
you, O Benevolent One, have offered worship to them all, further providing immeasurable varieties of most exquisite offerings to those Buddhas of the past.
Without a weary heart,
contemplate the Buddhas of the past;
for the sake of bringing about compassionate liberation for all sentient beings, awaken and do not cling to home.
In a past age, when you were in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha,
having made offerings to that Buddha, you attained the supreme non-arising [of dharmas],
acquired the five supernormal powers, and further realized the patient acceptance of the conformity to dharmas (anulomikī-dharmakṣānti).
Thereafter, the Venerable Maitreya made offerings to Buddhas even more excellent than those before—
throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
When all such kalpas had come to an end, those Buddhas also entered parinirvāṇa.
The various bodies you possessed in the past, and the lineages and names received in those worlds—all have likewise utterly perished and ceased to exist.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; the characteristics of the world are unstable.
Quickly abandon these empty and deceptive objects; it is best that you depart from the city at once.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death follow one;
they are difficult to withstand and most terrifying, like the outbreak of the kalpa-fire, its blazing flames consuming the world.
The fire of impermanence is likewise; it consumes the entire world.
Thus oppressed by such sufferings, how could there be even a moment’s respite?
One should observe all sentient beings, submerged in the darkness of afflictions.
Foolish and lacking the eye of wisdom, they cannot awaken to it themselves.
Arouse a mind of great diligence to bring your merits to fulfillment;
for the sake of all sentient beings, depart quickly and do not remain at home.

"At that time, when the various court ladies within the palace produced sounds, from within those sounds there issued forth the sounds of all these dharmas, intended to cause the Prince to grow weary of and detach from the world, so that his mind might attain awakening."

Chapter 16: Meeting an Old Man From the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*, Chapter Sixteen: Meeting an Old Man At that time, the Devaputra Kumbhakāra (Pot-Maker), wishing to lead the Prince out toward the gardens so that he might observe both the beautiful and the ugly and thereby give rise to a mind of world-weariness, gradually instructed him to renounce life within the palace.

At that time, all the court ladies within the palace sang songs with various melodies; as they grew utterly exhausted, they naturally proceeded in succession to further praise the virtues of the grove, their voices proclaiming:
"Listen attentively, O Noble Son!"

The grounds of this grove are exceedingly delightful; that is to say, the ground is covered with soft green grass, the trees are pleasing, their branches and leaves are lush and spreading, and their flowers and fruits are in full bloom, flourishing in dense and verdant abundance.

Furthermore, there were various birds—namely, diverse species of geese, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, as well as kokilas, ruddy sheldrakes, and other such birds—which produced these subtle and exquisite sounds.
At that time, having heard these sounds, the Prince conceived the desire to go forth on a journey; he immediately called his charioteer and said to him:
"O skillful charioteer!..."
"Now you must quickly prepare and adorn a noble, upright, and beautiful chariot; I wish to go to that grove to behold that auspicious place.
When the charioteer heard these words, he addressed the prince, saying, "I shall respectfully follow your instructions and dare not disobey."
At that time, the charioteer quickly addressed King Śuddhodana, saying: "Great King,
you should know that the Prince now wishes to go out toward the gardens to view the beautiful grounds."

Then King Śuddhodana issued an edict, proclaiming throughout the entire city of Kapilavastu, both inside and out, that everyone must sprinkle and sweep the streets, making them pure and magnificent. All mounds of earth, gravel, pebbles, and stones were removed; heaps of filth and excrement were leveled and smoothed. Wondrous fragrant waters were sprinkled upon the ground to extinguish all dust, and fragrant mud was used to coat the surface.
Furthermore, various kinds of fragrant flowers were scattered across the streets and alleys, and in every place, diverse and exquisite incenses were burned.
In all the streets and lanes, at the crossroads and junctions, they placed jars filled with water and set out various flowers, adorning every place with plantain trees.
Between the various trees, multicolored banners were suspended.
Furthermore, upon the trees, they fashioned canopies and standards using either precious materials or silk brocades to adorn them.

Between the trees, true pearl necklaces and nets of the seven treasures were suspended, covering them from above; in every mesh and joint of these nets, golden and silver jeweled bells were hung, which, stirred by a gentle breeze, produced subtle and wondrous sounds.
Or, using the seven precious substances, they fashioned images of the sun and moon as well as the forms of various devas, each holding a necklace, interspersed within the jeweled netting.
Within the lattice of the net, they further suspended white cat tails, ox tails, and various types of plumes.

At that time, King Śuddhodana issued such instructions that the city of Kapilavastu was adorned with various exquisite ornaments, becoming as magnificent and beautiful as a city of the gandharvas, no different in kind.
Having adorned the city, he further embellished the gardens and groves, removing sand, stones, and all manner of filth, even hanging various jeweled necklaces and bells as described above.
Among those trees, those with male names were adorned with male ornaments, and those with female names were adorned with female ornaments.
Furthermore, he instructed that drums be beaten and bells rung to proclaim throughout the city:
"All of you must clear the road; whether you are old or sick, or even dead, or blind, deaf, mute, or deficient in any of the six sense faculties—you must all be driven away."
"However, whatever is unpleasant to the mind and inauspicious must all be cleared away, so that the Prince does not see them on the road.
At that time, the charioteer adorned the carriage, yoked well-trained horses, and having completed all preparations, addressed the Prince, saying:
"Noble Son, you should know!"
"Now that the carriage and horses have already been harnessed, it is precisely the time to travel; you may mount and go forth to view the auspicious grounds.

At that time, the Prince rose from his seat and went to the place where the palanquin stood. Having ascended the precious chariot, he relied upon the majestic spiritual power and towering authority of the Great King. He departed through the eastern gate of the city, leading the way toward the gardens to view the blessed lands.

At that time, the deva Kumbhakāra stood before the street directly in front of the Prince; he transformed his body into that of an old, decrepit man, hunchbacked and with his head bowed, his teeth sparse and missing, his beard and whiskers white as frost, his form blackened and wrinkled, his complexion dark and sallow. He walked with a crooked back and a limp gait, possessing only skin and bone with no flesh remaining; his throat hung loose and sagging like the dewlap of an ox, and his body was withered and collapsed.

Relying solely on the strength of his staff, suffering from labored breathing and a painful cough, his gasping was coarse and his throat rattled like a saw being pulled; his four limbs trembled and shook, his gait was unsteady, and he would fall or require support, using the staff for stability. Bearing such an appearance, he walked along the road before the Prince.

The Prince saw that the old man’s body was trembling in such a manner, exhibiting the inauspicious signs of decay as described above, and that he was crawling along in distress even before the Prince.
Having seen him, the Prince immediately asked his charioteer:
"Who is this person?

His body is wrinkled and shriveled, with little flesh and loose skin; his eyes are bloodshot and tears flow from them. He is exceedingly ugly and uniquely loathsome, unlike any other person, and moreover, his skull is visible as his hair is thin and falling out."
As I see it, others do not perceive him thus.
Furthermore, his eyes are deep-set and exceptionally distinct from those of the multitude; yet his mouth and teeth are broken and decayed, such that he is not fit to be looked upon.
He then addressed the charioteer, speaking in verse:
“O skillful driver, listen now to me: who is this person before me?”
"The body is no longer upright and the hair is thinning; is this how it was from birth, or has old age arrived?
At that time, the charioteer, through the supernatural power of the Devaputra Kumbhakaraka, replied to the Prince, saying:
"O Great Holy Prince!..."
"A person such as this is what the world calls 'old.
" The Prince again asked the charioteer,
"In this world, what is it that is called 'old'?"
The charioteer then reported the matter to the Prince, saying:

"Generally, one who is called 'old' is a person oppressed by decrepitude; their faculties gradually decay until they have no further perception, their strength becomes feeble, and their body grows emaciated. Having reached such a state of suffering, they are driven away by their kinsmen because they are incapable of anything, and thus know not whom to rely upon.
Furthermore, this person will not last long; whether morning or evening, their life is about to end."
"For these reasons, it is called decay and ruin.
He then spoke a verse for the Prince:
"This old age is called a great suffering; It robs one of beauty and of pleasure."
"The faculties are ruined and his mindfulness lost; his limbs and movements no longer obey his will.
When the Prince had heard this verse, he asked the charioteer:
"Is it the law of this man's family alone that has caused him to be thus?"
"Is it the case that all the characteristics of the entire world are exactly like this?
At that time, the charioteer replied to the Crown Prince:
"Noble Son!"
You should know that it is not only this person’s own family dharma that causes them to be thus; rather, all sentient beings in the world possess this same dharma.
The Prince again asked the charioteer:
"Must this body of mine also undergo the law of old age in this same way?
The charioteer replied:
"It is so, it is so, Great Holy Prince!

Though there be distinctions between the noble and the lowly, all who have come into existence have not yet transcended this law of aging; even now, the human body possesses such signs of decay and infirmity, though they have not yet become manifest."
The Prince again asked the charioteer:

"If this body of mine cannot escape this law of aging, and has not yet transcended these marks of ugliness and decay, then I shall not go to that grove for pleasure, play, or amusement; you should quickly turn the carriage back and enter the palace, so that I may contemplate what means might be found to escape this suffering."
At that time, the charioteer replied to the Prince, saying,
"As the noble son commands, I dare not disobey.
He immediately turned the carriage and returned to the city.
At that time, the Prince entered his palace and sat upon his original seat, contemplating with right mindfulness:
"I too shall grow old; I have not yet transcended the law of aging.
Why do I indulge in negligence and allow my body and mind to run wild?"
Then King Śuddhodana asked the charioteer, saying:
"O skillful charioteer!
Having followed the Prince from within the palace to the park to roam, observe, and enjoy himself to his heart's content, was he filled with joy?"
The charioteer knelt and reported to the king, saying:
"Great King!
You should know that when the Prince went out on an excursion, he turned his carriage back halfway along the road and did not reach the park."
Then King Śuddhodana asked the charioteer,
"For what reason has the Prince not gone to the park, but returned from mid-way?
The charioteer replied:
"Great King!

You should know that the Prince, wishing to go to the park for recreation, had barely reached the halfway point when he suddenly saw an old man by the side of the road; his body was trembling as he leaned on a staff, now falling and now rising, unable to walk upright."
When the Crown Prince had thus seen that person, he immediately ordered the chariot to turn back and returned to the palace, where he sat cross-legged and contemplated with right mindfulness.
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"How extraordinary! How extraordinary!"
These physical characteristics and the words of the prophecy given by the seer Asita must certainly be true; I fear that the Prince will surely renounce his home and become a monk.

I should now further increase the Prince's five sensual pleasures for him; if he witnesses these five desires extensively, his eyes and mind will be satisfied, and becoming infatuated with attachment, he will not renounce his home to become a monk—this would accord with my wishes.

At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately provided Siddhārtha with all manner of sensory pleasures and luxuries, increasing them all the more, so as to cause the Prince’s heart to become attached to these delights and prevent him from leaving home.
And there is a verse that says:
"Within those palaces he enjoyed much pleasure, But wishing to go out for recreation, he saw an old man;
Returning to the palace, his heart was filled with sorrow: 'Alas! I have not yet escaped this aging.'"
When the father-king heard these words, his mind was filled with fear that his son would abandon him to go forth into homelessness;
he increased the five sensual pleasures and the number of palace women, seeking to bind him with affection so that he might succeed to the throne.

"At that time, the Prince remained within the palace, fully indulging in the pleasures of the five desires, sporting and enjoying himself without any hindrance; he was the sole individual held in honor and esteem by those of noble and superior rank."
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds,
Volume Fourteen and Volume Fifteen,
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta during the Sui Dynasty.

Chapter Seventeen: King Śuddhodana’s Dream At that time, the devaputra Kumbhakarṇa, wishing by means of his supernormal powers to inspire in the Prince the resolve for renunciation, appeared that very night to King Śuddhodana with seven types of dream omens.
At that time, King Śuddhodana was lying upon his bed when, within a dream, he beheld these signs:

first, he dreamed of a great banner of Śakra, the Lord of Devas, surrounded on all sides by immeasurable and boundless people, who were lifting it up and exiting through the eastern gate of Kapilavastu.
The second dream was that the Prince mounted ten great elephants, drove a multitude of chariots, and departed through the southern gate of Kapilavastu.
The third dream was that the Prince, seated upright in a carriage drawn by four horses, departed through the western gate of Kapilavastu.
The fourth dream was that he saw a single wheel adorned with various jewels emerge from the northern gate of Kapilavastu.
The fifth dream was that he saw the Prince, standing in the middle of the great thoroughfare within the city of Kapilavastu, holding a mallet in his hand and striking a large drum.

In the sixth dream, he saw that in the center of this city of Kapilavastu there was a lofty tower; the Prince sat upon it and scattered immeasurable treasures in the four directions, while from the four quarters came immeasurable and boundless billions of sentient beings who took those treasures away.

In the seventh dream, he saw that not far outside this city of Kapilavastu, there were six men who raised their voices and wailed loudly, weeping and shedding tears; each used both hands to pull out his own hair, rolling about upon the ground.

At that time, King Śuddhodana saw such a vision in his dream; his heart was filled with great terror, his hair stood on end with fear, his entire body trembled, and overcome by agitation and wonder, he suddenly awoke.
Having awakened, he immediately summoned the various ministers of his inner palace and commanded them, saying: "Do you know?
Tonight, I saw such a terrifying dream; I shall describe all seven successive events exactly as they were previously listed."
He further commanded them, saying:
"You must carefully retain these various dreams and not allow yourselves to forget them.
Tomorrow, when you are seated in the hall, report them to me within the assembly so that I may know of them."
When the ministers had heard the king’s decree, they immediately addressed the king, saying:
"We respectfully obey the king's command and truly dare not disobey.
At dawn, as the king sat among his assembly, they reported the night's dream in full detail for the king's information.
At that time, having heard the minister’s report, King Śuddhodana immediately summoned all the brahmins within the kingdom who were skilled in interpreting dreams and addressed them, saying:
"O you of great wisdom!..."
"Interpret my dream; what will be its fruit and retribution?
My dream was such as previously described.
Having heard the king's command, those highly wise brāhmaṇas deliberated together, weighing the propriety and feasibility of the matter, and addressed the king, saying:
"O Great King!
You should know that we have never heard of such a dream before. Having heard it, our minds are bewildered and distracted; we do not know what karmic retribution this dream will bring."
When King Śuddhodana heard these words from the Brahmins who interpreted his dreams, his heart was filled with renewed sorrow, and he thought to himself:
"Perhaps my son will not become a Wheel-Turning Sage King; or having already attained it, might he fall back down from the rank of a Wheel-Turning King?"
"Now, within my heart, there is extreme sorrow and anxiety; who can resolve such a knot of doubt for me?

At that time, the Devaputra Kumbhakarṇa, while within his palace in the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, saw King Śuddhodana thus grieving and unhappy. Having seen this, he suddenly departed from that celestial palace and came here, concealing his divine form. He manifested as a Brahmin of the Brahmā class, with a spiral topknot on his head and a garland as a crown; he was wise and intelligent, handsome and in the prime of youth, wearing black antelope skin as his garment.
Standing outside the gate of King Śuddhodana’s palace, he proclaimed these words: "I am well able to interpret King Śuddhodana’s dream and resolve whatever doubts you have."
At that time, having heard these words from the brahmin, the gatekeeper quickly went to King Śuddhodana, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Great King!..."
"You should know that there stands outside the gate a brahmin who declares:
'I am well able to interpret all dreams.

At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately issued an order to summon this brahmin to enter the palace. Once he had entered, the king was filled with joy and issued a decree to question the brahmin, speaking as follows:"
"O skillful and wise Great Brahmin!
Do you now know?
Last night at midnight, I saw these seven kinds of dream-omens."

First, he saw a banner of Śakra, immeasurable and boundless, surrounded on all sides by hundreds of thousands of people who were lifting it together. As they emerged from the eastern gate of Kapilavastu, not far from the city, he saw six men wailing aloud and tearing out their hair with their hands.
"I am now terrified and my mind is distraught; since the signs in my dream are thus, I do not yet know whether they portend good or evil.
You should explain each of them for me.
Having spoken these words, King Śuddhodana remained silent and waited for the interpretation.
At that time, the devaputra Kumbhakāra addressed the king, saying: "Great King, you should know that as for the dream you saw—

of a single banner of Śakra surrounded on all sides by immeasurable and boundless multitudes who together lifted this banner and were carrying it out through the eastern gate of the city— this refers to Prince Siddhārtha, the Great King’s son, who, surrounded on all sides by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas, shall renounce the crown princehood and depart from the palace chambers to leave the city and become a homeless wanderer."
"This dream is a premonitory sign of that which is to come.

Furthermore, Great King, as for what you saw—the Prince riding upon a ten-fold fragrant elephant, driving a multitude of chariots, and departing through the southern gate of the city—once he has renounced the world, he will immediately realize *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) and the ten powers;
this dream is a premonitory sign of that."

"Furthermore, Great King, as for what you saw—the Prince riding in a carriage drawn by four horses and departing through the western gate of the city—once he has gone forth, he will realize *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) and fully attain the four fearlessnesses;
this dream is a prior auspicious omen of that."

"Furthermore, Great King, as for the dream of a wheel adorned with various jewels exiting through the northern gate of the city: after he has gone forth and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he will turn the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous Wheel of Dharma before gods and humans;
this dream is a prior auspicious omen of that."

"Furthermore, Great King, regarding the dream you had of the Prince standing in the middle of the crossroads within the city of Kapilavastu, holding a mallet in his hand and striking a great drum: after he has gone forth and realized *bodhi*, when he turns the wheel of Dharma, the various devas will each raise their voices in proclamation; that sound will penetrate upward as far as the Brahma-heaven, being passed along and made known until its resonance pervades the entire realm of form (*rūpadhātu*);
this dream is a premonitory sign of that event."

"Furthermore, Great King, as for the dream in which the Prince sat upon a central pavilion in the city of Kapilavastu and scattered various kinds of jewels in all four directions: after he has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he shall scatter such wondrous jewels of the Dharma before the assembly of devas, humans, and the eight classes of beings—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold path, and various other dharmas.
This dream is a premonitory omen of that event."

"Furthermore, Great King, regarding the dream you had: not far outside this city of Kapilavastu, you saw six men weeping aloud with raised voices and pulling out their hair; this signifies that the Prince will renounce the household life and shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Once he has attained enlightenment, at that time there will be the six heretical teachers whose minds shall give rise to great sorrow and distress—namely, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarī Gośālīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, Sañjayī Vairaṭīputra, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra;
this dream is a premonitory omen of this for them.
"At that time, after the devaputra Kumbhakāra had explained the dream to King Śuddhodana, he addressed the Great King, saying: 'Great King!
You should give rise to joy in your heart; do not harbor fear, anxiety, or distress.'"
"Why is this? This dream is auspicious and shall yield a favorable result; you must rejoice at heart and take care not to harbor any anxiety.
Having thus comforted King Śuddhodana, he suddenly vanished.

At that time, having heard the Brahmin’s interpretation of the dream as foretelling auspicious and virtuous results, King Śuddhodana further increased the Prince’s provisions of the five sensory pleasures, hoping to cause the Prince’s mind to become stained with attachment and longing so that he would not leave the household life.
At that time, the Prince remained within the palace, indulging his will in the affairs of the five desires in an inconceivable manner.
Chapter 18: Seeing a Sick Man on the Road From the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*, Chapter Eighteen: Seeing a Sick Man on the Road. "At that time, the Devaputra Kumbhakarṇa again reflected:
'This Great Being, the Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatī’s Son (Guiming), remains within that palace, attached to the five desires; he has been dissolute and unrestrained for a long time.'"
"The world is impermanent, and the prime of youth is easily lost; Bodhisattva Guhmatiprabha ought to renounce his palace and leave home at an early date.
I should now first manifest signs for him, exhorting him toward enlightenment and causing him to quickly feel weary of and detached from worldly life."

Having thought thus, by the supernatural power of the Devaputra Ghaṭīkāra and also through the causal conditions of the past merit of the Great Being Bodhisattva Mahāprajñāpāramitā, while seated within the palace, he suddenly conceived the desire to go out to the gardens to view and enjoy himself.
At that time, the Prince summoned his charioteer and addressed him, saying:
"O skillful charioteer!
You should quickly prepare a fine carriage; I wish to go out of the city toward the gardens to roam about, delight my eyes, and observe the groves."
At that time, the charioteer addressed the Prince, saying:
"As the Noble Son commands, I dare not disobey.
Having heard these instructions from the Prince, the charioteer immediately went to report them to King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Great King!
You should know that the Prince now wishes to go out toward the gardens to view the auspicious grounds.
