At that time, King Śuddhodana issued a decree and proclamation to the people within the kingdom, ordering them all to adorn and sweep the city of Kapilavastu until it was pure and clean. He further dispatched messengers to remove all weeds, gravel, thorns, rotten wood, mounds of earth, filth, and foul-smelling places, ensuring that everything was made level and smooth.
Furthermore, all those trees within the garden that were named after women were adorned with female ornaments, while those trees named after men were decorated with male ornaments.
Furthermore, along the road, they did not allow any who were old or sick to appear before the Prince, lest the Prince, upon seeing them, should conceive thoughts of world-weariness and renunciation.
At that time, the charioteer, having finished adorning the chariot, addressed the Crown Prince, saying:
"The chariot is now fully prepared; I pray only that the Holy Son will know the proper time himself."

At that time, the Prince immediately mounted the precious chariot; having done so, he took up the majestic majesty and profound virtue of the Great King and gradually departed through the southern gate of the city, intending to go toward the gardens to gaze upon and enjoy the sights.

At that time, the Devaputra Kumbhakāra immediately manifested before the Prince’s path a sick man who was emaciated and distressed, with his ribs showing, suffering from abdominal dropsy, and enduring great agony. His body was wasted away, his arms and legs were thin and frail, he was jaundiced and lacked luster, his breathing was weak, and his life hung by a thread.

Lying amidst excrement and filth, writhing and groaning, unable to lift himself up; wishing to speak, he opens his mouth, and as soon as he produces a sound, he cries out, "I prostrate myself! I beg you to help me sit up!"
At that time, the Prince saw that sick man, who even spoke with his own voice, crying out, "Support me and help me up!
Having seen that afflicted person, the Prince asked the charioteer:
"O skillful charioteer!..."
"Who is this person?

His belly is so enormous it is like a great cauldron; as he pants, his entire body trembles; his arms and shanks are thin and limp, his frame is emaciated and frail, and he is jaundiced and colorless.
Or perhaps he cries out: 'Alas, Mother!'"
Or again, they cry out, "Alas, my father!
Their grief is so piercing and bitter that it is unbearable to see or hear; they must rely upon another's body before they can rise or move.
Then, the devaputra Kumbhakaraka, by means of his supernormal powers, instructed the charioteer to report to the Prince, saying:
"May the Noble Son listen!
This is called a sick person."
The Prince again asked the charioteer:
"What is the meaning of the term 'sick person'?
The charioteer replied:
"O Great Holy Prince!
This person’s body is no longer at ease; his majestic virtue has been exhausted, he is debilitated and powerless, and the hour of death is approaching, yet there is nowhere to turn for refuge.
Both parents have passed away, leaving him with no one to whom he may appeal."
Having no refuge and no one to whom he may appeal, this person will before long naturally meet his end.
Though he seeks to remain alive, he is subjected to extreme suffering and will certainly not survive;
there is no possibility of finding a day of recovery, for he can only await his time.
"O Great Holy Prince!
It is for these reasons that it is called 'sickness.
As it is said in a verse:"
“The Crown Prince asked the charioteer, ‘For what reason does this person undergo such suffering?
The charioteer replied to the Crown Prince, ‘Because the four great elements are out of harmony, illness arises.’”
The Prince again asked the charioteer:
"Does this person alone possess this dharma of his family,
or do all sentient beings in the world possess this dharma?"
The charioteer replied:
"This law of illness is not unique to this single family; all classes of beings, including devas and humans, cannot escape it."
The Prince spoke again:
"I too have this illness; I have not yet passed beyond it, nor am I yet liberated from it. In time, I shall surely become like him and undergo such a fate—alas, how terrifying!"
The Prince then said to his charioteer: "O charioteer!

If this body of mine cannot escape this sickness, being possessed of the nature of disease and difficult to deliver from, then I shall not go to that grove to play and enjoy myself. Turn back the carriage and return to the palace; I shall reflect upon this."
The charioteer replied,
"As the Prince commands.
Having received these instructions, the charioteer then turned the carriage back toward the palace.
At that time, the Prince returned to the inner palace and sat upright in contemplation, thinking:
"I too shall fall ill; since the nature of illness has not yet manifested in me, how can I indulge my passions?"
Then King Śuddhodana asked the charioteer,
"Did the Prince enjoy himself while wandering in the park?
The charioteer replied:
"Great King!

You should know that the Prince intended to go outside the city to travel and view the ponds; however, midway he encountered a sick man, who even spoke with his own mouth, saying, 'I pray you, help me up.'"
Having seen this, he immediately gave the command to turn the chariot back.
He sat in quietude within the palace, contemplating and fixing his mind upon this thought.
At that time, having heard these words, King Śuddhodana reflected within his heart on the prophecy given by the seer Asita, concluding it to be certain and true.

"Prince, do not abandon your home and go forth into homelessness again. I shall now provide the Prince with even greater objects of the five desires to increase his pleasure, so that he becomes attached to these five desires and does not renounce them to go forth."
At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately increased the Prince’s provisions for the five sensual pleasures, doubling them once more.
There is a verse that says:
“The Prince has long dwelt within the palace chambers; Desiring to go forth to the garden to enjoy the five sensual pleasures, He now seeks to experience the delights of the senses.”
Seeing on the road a man emaciated, frail, and ill, he immediately conceived a sense of weary detachment from desire and turned back.
Sitting upright, he contemplated the causes of old age and sickness: "How can I find joy when I have not yet transcended these?"
Forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and all such tactile objects— most exquisite, most supreme, and never wearisome—
are experienced now in peerless, ultimate bliss, due to the causes and conditions of the virtuous deeds performed by the Great Being in the past.
"In this manner, while the Prince was within the palace, he fully enjoyed the merits of the five desires without interruption, day and night."

Chapter Nineteen: Encountering a Corpse on the Road From the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*, Chapter Nineteen: Encountering a Corpse on the Road. "At that time, the Devaputra Kumbhakāra again had this thought at one point:
'This Great Being, the Bodhisattva Guhyaprabha, remains within his palace, indulging in the utmost pleasure and amusement.'"
"The time has now arrived; the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra should leave the household life early.
For the sake of that Great Being, I shall now exhort him to renounce the five desires and depart from his home to become a renunciant."
At that time, because the devaputra Kumbhakāra wished to inspire and encourage Guhyaprajña, he resolved to lead him out from within the palace toward that garden to behold the auspicious grounds.
At that time, the Prince said to the charioteer:
"O skillful charioteer!
You may quickly harness the precious chariot drawn by four horses; I wish to go out of the city to the park for recreation."
At that time, having heard the Prince’s command, the charioteer immediately went in haste to report to King Śuddhodana,
saying: "Great King,
you should know that the Prince wishes to go out to view the gardens."

Then, King Śuddhodana issued a command to adorn the city of Kapilavastu; he ordered the streets and alleys to be swept and sprinkled, and all thorns, gravel, debris, rotten wood, mounds of earth, filth, tiles, and stones were completely cleared away.
Furthermore, throughout the park, all the trees were adorned with ornaments named after women for those who were female, and with ornaments named after men for those who were male.
Again, bells and chimes were shaken, and this proclamation was made:
"Let there not be even a single inauspicious person before the Prince—whether old or sick—for once the Prince has seen them with his own eyes, he will conceive a sense of weary detachment."
At that time, the charioteer immediately prepared a fine carriage for the Prince; having finished, he presented it and addressed the Prince, saying:
"Noble Son!
Listen well!"
"Once the carriage has been prepared, I pray you will let me know when it is ready.
The Prince ascended the carriage; endowed with majestic spiritual power and great virtue, he departed through the western gate of the city to go outside and view the gardens and groves.
At that time, the devaputra Kumbhakāra manifested a corpse before the Prince, lying upon a bed and being carried by a multitude of people.
Furthermore, he spread various beautifully colored straw garments over it, fashioning them into a canopy.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable and boundless kinsmen surrounding him on all sides—left, right, front, and back—wailing and weeping; some had disheveled their hair, some beat their breasts, and others struck their heads while crossing their arms; some took up dust with both hands and scattered it over their faces and heads; others uttered various sounds of piteous sobbing, their tears falling like rain as they wailed and lamented with such bitter anguish that it was difficult to hear.
When the Prince saw this, his heart was filled with compassion and he asked the charioteer, saying: "O skillful driver!
Whose body is this lying upon the bed?"

Adorned and surrounded by various flowers, even with multi-colored robes of kusha grass fashioned into a canopy, it was carried along on the shoulders of men, while a great multitude surrounded them, wailing and crying out in lamentation.
He spoke in verse, asking:
“The Prince’s wondrous form is upright and handsome; I ask the skillful driver, who is this?
Lying upon a bed, carried by four men, Surrounded by kinsmen who wail and weep.”
At that time, the devaputra Kumbhakaraka, by means of his supernatural powers, caused the charioteer to reply to the Prince:
"O Great Holy Prince!
This is called a corpse."
The Prince again asked the charioteer,
"What is this corpse?
The charioteer replied:
"O Great Holy Prince!
This man has already abandoned his worldly life and possesses no majestic virtue; he is now like stone or wood, just like a wall or a partition, with no distinction remaining."
Having abandoned all kinsmen and acquaintances, the spirit alone proceeds toward the next world.

From this day forward, one shall no longer see parents, brothers, wives, or children; such relatives are separated by the cycle of birth and death, never to be seen again. Therefore, it is called a "corpse."
He addressed the Crown Prince with these verses:
"Having already abandoned mind, intention, and all the sense faculties, The corpse is devoid of consciousness, like wood or stone.
Relatives wail and briefly surround it; Here, love and affection are parted forever."
The Prince again asked the skilled charioteer:
"O skilled charioteer!
Do I too possess this nature of death?"
Furthermore, regarding this law of death, have I already transcended it or not?
The charioteer replied, “Great Sage, Prince! [I have not yet.]”
The noble body of the Prince, too, cannot escape this law of death.

Among all beings in the world—whether gods or humans—all those who have kin, relatives, and acquaintances must each experience such matters of separation; there, one does not see the other, and here, the other does not see this one.
And he spoke in verse:
"All sentient beings exhaust their karma here; Whether gods, humans, noble, or base, all are equal and uniform.
Though they dwell in various worlds of good or evil, When the time of impermanence arrives, there is no difference."
At that time, having heard these words, the Prince replied to the charioteer:

"If this body of mine is likewise subject to death, and has not yet transcended the law of mortality; and if I cannot now see the gods or any of their retinues in heaven, nor can they see me—why should I now go toward those gardens for pleasure and amusement?"
"You may quickly turn the chariot back and enter the palace; I shall reflect upon this.
At that time, having heard these words from the Prince, the charioteer immediately turned the carriage and drove back toward the palace.
At that time, having entered the palace, the Prince sat upright and reflected:
"I must certainly die, for I have not yet attained transcendence over the law of death.
Fixing his mindfulness, he remained silent and contemplated thus:
"The rewards of the world ultimately return to impermanence.

Now, when the Prince was first about to enter the palace, there was an ignorant and foolish physiognomist standing outside the gate of the Great King’s palace. He gazed intently at the Prince’s face, observing his features from top to bottom and his masculine marks, and cried out in a loud voice:
"All of you people, you must know this!..."
"From this day forward, within seven days, these seven treasures shall spontaneously appear and arrive for this Prince.
Then King Śuddhodana asked the charioteer,
"O skillful charioteer!"
"Did you lead the Crown Prince to the grove and succeed in making him as pleased as he desired, so that he might enjoy himself?
The charioteer knelt and replied to the King:
"Great King!"
"You should know that the Prince has gone out today, but he has not reached the pleasure grove.
Then, King Śuddhodana asked the charioteer,
"For what reason has the Prince not reached the pleasure grove?"
The charioteer replied:
"Great King,
listen well!

As the Prince departed from the palace, along the way he saw a dead man lying on a bed, carried by four men, while his kinsmen surrounded him weeping. Having seen this, he immediately turned back and entered the palace, reflecting with a sense of unease.
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he reflected within his mind:
"The prediction of the seer Asita must surely be true.

Let not the Prince abandon me again to go forth into homelessness; I shall now further increase the Prince's indulgences in the five desires so that he becomes attached to them and does not leave the household life."
At that time, King Śuddhodana provided his crown prince with an abundance of clothing, ornaments, and various articles of luxury.
There is a verse that says:
"Through the meritorious practices of an ocean of immeasurable kalpas, The Crown Prince, having seen those who have met their end,"
His heart was deeply despondent and filled with sorrow; returning to the inner palace, he thought only of death.
"In the past, this city’s palaces were magnificent; the Prince, in the full bloom of youth, was most exceptionally handsome.
With his five desires satisfied, he took great delight, as if dwelling in the Joyful Garden of the Thousand-Eyed One."
"In this manner, the Prince remained within the palace, fully enjoying the five sensual pleasures to his heart's content and delighting in them. Chapter 20:

Yaśodharā’s Dream, from the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*, Part One. "At that time, the Devaputra Kumbhakāra saw that the Prince had gone out to observe the corpse and had turned away from worldly sensual pleasures in weary detachment; he returned to his seat within the palace, and after six days had passed, it happened once more in this same way."
He reflected deeply again, saying:
"This Great Being, the Bodhisattva Guhyaprabha, is so attached to the five desires that his mind is deluded and dissolute; he is unwilling to renounce them."
"The time has now arrived; the Bodhisattva Mahāprajāpatī-putra must quickly renounce his home and leave the world. I shall now act as the occasion for his exhortation.

At that time, because the son of the *kumbhanda* deity wished to inspire the Prince’s mind toward leaving the world, and also moved by the karmic conditions of the son of the *kumbhanda* deity’s past merit, he himself caused the Prince to conceive the intention to go and stroll within the park.
"At that time, the Prince summoned his charioteer and commanded him, saying:
'O skillful charioteer!
Quickly prepare the carriage; I wish to enter the garden.'"
The charioteer, having received these instructions, immediately went to inform King Śuddhodana,
saying: "Great King,
you should know that the Prince now wishes to go out toward the gardens to roam and observe."
At that time, King Śuddhodana issued an order to thoroughly purify and adorn the city of Kapilavastu, exactly as before. He even had a bell struck to proclaim throughout the city:
"Let not a single person—whether old, sick, or dead, or one with impaired faculties—be allowed to stand before the Prince, lest he see them and give rise to a mind of weary detachment."

The charioteer, having received these instructions, advanced the fine and noble carriage. Knowing the proper time, the Prince immediately sat upon the carriage; majestic and dignified in his presence, he drove forth from the northern gate of the city.

At that time, the devaputra Kumbhakāra, by means of his supernormal powers, not far from the chariot, manifested before the Prince a man who had shaved off his hair and beard, was wearing a saṃghāṭī robe with one shoulder bared, held a mendicant’s staff in his hand, and carried an alms bowl in his left palm as he walked along the road.
Having seen him, the Crown Prince asked the charioteer, saying:
"O skilled charioteer! Who is this person?"

Standing before me, his deportment was dignified and solemn; he walked with measured and steady steps, gazing straight ahead for the distance of a fathom without looking to the left or right. His mind was focused and his conduct restrained, unlike that of others;

his hair and beard were shorn, and his robes were a pure crimson dyed from tree bark, differing from those of the white-robed laity; the bowl he held emitted a dark-blue luster, like the pigment of stone collyrium.
At that time, the deva Kumbhakarṇa, by means of his supernormal powers, instructed the charioteer to say to the Prince:
"O Great Holy Prince!
This man is called one who has gone forth from the household life."
The Prince again asked the charioteer:
"Regarding what is called 'leaving home,' what kind of practice is this?
The charioteer replied:
"O Great Holy Prince!

This person constantly practices wholesome dharmas and remains far removed from unwholesome conduct; he practices with equanimity, practices generosity well, skillfully disciplines his faculties, and skillfully subdues himself. He skillfully bestows fearlessness, gives rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings, does not fear sentient beings, does not harm sentient beings, and skillfully protects and cherishes all sentient beings."
"Prince! It is for this reason that it is called 'leaving home.
The Prince again asked the charioteer:
"O skillful charioteer!
This person is well able to perform various karmic actions. Why is this?
As for what is called "practice of the Dharma," this is wholesome conduct, up to and including being able to refrain from harming sentient beings.
Therefore, you should now take your carriage toward those renunciants.
The charioteer, having received the command, said to the Prince:
"As the Prince has instructed.
He then drove the carriage toward the place where the renunciant was.
At that time, having arrived, the Prince questioned those renunciants, speaking thus:
"Venerable Great Beings! Who are you?"
Then the deva Kumbhakāra, by means of his supernormal powers, instructed that man who had gone forth and shaved his hair, saying to the prince: "Prince!
I am now one who has gone forth."
The Prince asked again:
"Virtuous one!
For what reason is one called a 'renunciant'?"
He replied again:
"Prince! I see that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in the entire world are entirely impermanent."
Having contemplated in this way, he abandoned all worldly affairs and distanced himself from his kinsmen; seeking liberation, he left the home life for homelessness and reflected thus:
"By what means can one sustain the lives of all beings?"
"In this matter, I am content; I practice the Dharma well and, furthermore, am well able to refrain from taking the lives of any living beings.
Prince! It is for these reasons that I am called one who has gone forth."
The Prince spoke again:

"O Benevolent One, the work you perform is most virtuous. If you can contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as impermanent dharmas, and if you know them thus, extending even to being one who grants fearlessness to all sentient beings, and if your mind does not give rise to the intent to harm any living being, and furthermore, if you sustain their lives and bestow upon them peace and security."
And there is a verse that says:
“Observing that the world is subject to cessation, Seeking the state of inexhaustible nirvana,
Having cultivated a mind of equanimity toward enemies and kin, One does not engage in worldly desires and such matters.”
Whether dwelling among mountains and forests, beneath trees, or in cemeteries and open spaces,
having renounced all conditioned things, one lives by begging while contemplating true suchness with clarity.

At that time, out of reverence for the Dharma, the Prince descended from his chariot and proceeded on foot toward the place where the renunciant was. He prostrated himself before the renunciant with his head at the other’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and then returned to sit upon his chariot. He immediately commanded the driver to turn back and return to the palace.
At that time, there was a woman within the palace named Mṛgajā. Seeing from afar the Prince returning and entering the palace, she spoke these verses out of desire:
"The Great King Śuddhodana enjoys happiness; Mahāprajāpatī is free from sorrow.
The court ladies within the palace are most beautiful; Who could ever rival this Noble Son?"

At that time, having heard the sound of these spoken verses, the Prince’s entire body trembled and his tears fell like rain. With his heart inwardly delighting in the state of Nirvana, his faculties purified, and inclining toward Nirvana, he spoke these words:
"I must now attain that Nirvana; I must now realize that Nirvana; I must now practice that Nirvana; I must now abide in that Nirvana."

"At that time, King Śuddhodana was within the palace, surrounded on all sides by his ministers and officials. Suddenly, the Prince entered the presence of the King, joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation, stood with his body bowed, and addressed his father, the King, saying:
'I pray only this of Your Majesty!'"
I pray that you will now grant me leave; I wish to renounce the household life and seek nirvana with all my heart.
Great King!
You should know that all sentient beings are subject to separation.

At that time, having heard these words from his son, the Crown Prince, King Śuddhodana’s entire body trembled like a tree shaken by an elephant; his joints loosened, tears filled his eyes, and his voice was choked with sobs as he replied to the Crown Prince:
"O my son, the Crown Prince!"
Let us set this matter aside for now; it is not the time for you to go forth from home.

I too, when I was young and my faculties were still agitated, had not yet seen the manifold sufferings of the world, nor did I practice the holy life. Furthermore, I had not yet encountered the various evil desires before I undertook ascetic practices.
"Son, you have conceived this thought, which is truly unbearable.
My son, while still a youth, your mind is not yet settled and your faculties are not yet subdued; you wish to dwell in that araṇya, yet you cannot endure ascetic hardships."
"My son, young man!
Wait until I am old; when my time has come and I wish to practice the holy life, I shall renounce the kingdom, entrust the royal throne to you, and enter the wilderness to practice asceticism."
My son, young man! If a son is rebellious,
does not obey my heart, and acts contrary to my words while practicing the path of Dharma,
that son will acquire unwholesome dharmas in this present life because he has disobeyed the words of his superior.
"Therefore, my son!
You must quickly abandon this mind of diligence; remain within the palace, settle your mind at home, and practice the ways of the world."
"My son, young man!
All people of the world must first experience the pleasures of the five desires, and only then resolve their minds toward the aspiration for renunciation.
The Prince replied:
"Great King!
At this time, you cannot obtain the mind for renunciation as a monk through a partitioned wall. Why is this?
For example, suppose there were a person who wished to run out from that burning house of fierce and blazing flames; this would be a courageous man, and he must not be obstructed.
"Great King!
For all who are born, there will inevitably be separation.
If a person perceives that within this world there is universal separation, yet cannot relinquish the nature of separation, this is not a true benefit."
"Furthermore, it is like a person who fails to accomplish their task when the time of death is approaching; because they do not act with urgency, they lack wise discernment.
He then spoke these verses for his father, the King:
"If one perceives that all things are certainly impermanent, And that all conditioned phenomena ultimately disintegrate,..."
"It would be better to endure separation from all one's worldly kin; when the moment of death approaches, the task must be accomplished.
Then King Śuddhodana spoke again with great earnestness to the Prince:
"O my son, my child!
"You must by no means abandon me to go forth into the homeless life.
Furthermore, the various ministers, relying on the treatises of ancient sages and each speaking from their own perspective, exhorted the Prince, saying:
"O Great Holy Prince!..."
Have you not heard?

Since the beginning of the eon, according to the Vedas, when kings of old were young, they each ruled their own realms in accordance with the Dharma; when they reached old age, they passed the succession to their legitimate heirs, sending their crown princes to inherit the royal throne, and only then retired to the mountains to practice the path of the Dharma.
"For this reason, O Great Holy Prince!
You must not alone contravene the law of your late father.
When King Śuddhodana heard these words from the ministers, tears fell from him like rain; with single-minded attention, he gazed intently at the face of his son, his eyes blinking not once.
At that time, the Crown Prince felt doubt within his heart; filled with sorrow and finding no joy, he returned to the palace.

When the prince arrived at the palace, the various court ladies saw him from afar and were all filled with delight. They rose from their seats, some joining their palms, some displaying graceful expressions, some dancing or singing, and some attending to him with their bodies.

Seeing the Prince seated, each woman, with lustful hearts and overflowing seductive gestures, surrounded him and took pleasure together with him; like the Lord Īśvara within his palace, his majestic virtue was towering and his various marks were brilliant, and their joy was likewise so.
"At that time, the Prince, together with those who shared his marks and secondary characteristics and were equal to him in every respect, was constantly adorned and played day and night."
Furthermore, seeing that the Prince’s various marks were so vividly manifest and brilliant, he conceived this thought of wonder: "This is the Moon Deity himself descending to earth."

When those court ladies beheld the Prince’s appearance in such a manner, they were filled with intense envy; some raised their eyebrows, some gazed at him with their eyes, some whispered words, and some beckoned with their hands. Yet, due to the power of the Prince’s majestic spiritual authority, their lustful desires could not blaze forth, nor could they laugh; meanwhile, the Prince also emerged from his father the King’s presence.
At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately summoned his charioteer and addressed him, saying:
"O skillful charioteer!
Has the Prince not gone to that grove?"
The charioteer replied,
"Great King! You should know this!"

The Prince, wishing to proceed toward that grove, saw a man on the way who had shaved off his hair and beard, wore dyed robes, and carried a staff and an alms bowl; having seen that man, he turned his chariot back to the palace and sat upright in meditation.
At that time, having heard these words, King Śuddhodana reflected thus:

"The great seer Asita’s words are not false; it is certain that the prince will renounce his home and go forth into homelessness. I shall now further increase the five sensual pleasures so that he becomes attached to them and does not leave the household life."

At that time, King Śuddhodana further provided the five sensory pleasures and instructed him to remain within the palace to experience happiness, forbidding him from leaving home. He spoke these verses again:
"The Prince saw on the road a man who had left home, His body clad in garments dyed with tree bark;
Having beheld him, he resolved to seek the Unsurpassed Way, His profound heart finding joy only in leaving home."
Observing that the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death are boundless, And seeing those who have left the home life to live by begging for food,
He grew weary of and detached from the world, abandoning the three afflictions, Longing for liberation and seeking the unconditioned.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death are like various sores and ulcers;
the Prince, wishing to be free from such sufferings, saw that renunciant on the road and felt great joy in his heart, thinking, "This one is truly real."
"Desiring to abandon the roots of affliction such as greed and anger, I ought to shave my head and enter the mountain thickets;
since the Prince seeks the Dharma of ultimate truth, he feels great joy upon seeing that śramaṇa."
Mounting a chariot drawn by well-trained, excellent steeds, he set out from the Garden of Contemplation to depart from the triple world;
seeing him on the way casting off his worldly robes, his heart rejoiced, for this was the supreme Bodhi.
At that time, King Śuddhodana further prepared all the merits of the five desires for the Prince on a grand scale, increasing every item and making them all more abundant.

Furthermore, beyond the walls and moats of the old palace city, on all four sides, they established a secure defense by constructing another massive and lofty rampart encircling the old compound. The ditches and moats were exceedingly deep, and atop the battlements and parapets, various nets made of the seven precious gems were installed; at every knot of these nets, tinkling bells were suspended. The gates and doors of the palace chambers were strictly guarded.
At the times of entering and exiting, or opening and closing, during morning and evening, let there be a great sound that reaches far and wide outside the gate.

Furthermore, station immeasurable war chariots, elephants, and horses, along with groups of men holding one another, all equipped with saddles and armor, ensuring they are entirely robust and well-prepared.

Furthermore, outside the palace compound, he stationed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of warriors, whose appearances were upright and peerlessly handsome, all of whom were capable of defeating every enemy.

Wearing armor upon their bodies and holding tridents, bows, arrows, long swords, halberds, spears, barbed darts, and clubs in their hands—armed with various weapons such as these—they guarded the prince at both the inner and outer city gates.

Furthermore, he instructed those within the palace to issue strict orders: let the various court ladies perform all kinds of music and manifest every form of entertainment, day and night without ceasing.
All the powers of female enchantment were manifested, binding him with the shackles of desire to make his mind attached to lust, so that he would not abandon them to go forth [into homelessness].

Chapter on Yaśodharā’s Dream, Part Two:
"At that time, the National Preceptor had a son named Udāyin (in the Sui language, 'Eloquent'), who was intelligent and wise, possessing skillful eloquence in all discourses."
At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately dispatched a messenger to summon Udāyin. Once he had arrived, the king spoke to him as follows:
"Udāyin, you are quick-witted and possess great wisdom.

You must now go to attend upon Prince Siddhārtha; using skillful means, instruct my son so that his mind may be at peace and he may take delight in the palace, ensuring that he does not grow weary or renounce desire to leave the home life."
Then King Śuddhodana again summoned all his Śākya kinsmen and retinue to assemble, and spoke to them, saying:
"O members of my clan!
My mind is filled with apprehension; Siddhārtha will certainly not remain living at home."
"Now that you all assist me, by what means can we ensure he does not depart?
Then the Śākyas replied to the Great King:
"We shall together guard the Prince with great care; what power could there be that would enable him to leave home by force?"

"At that time, King Śuddhodana and the various members of the Śākya clan stationed five hundred valiant youths outside the eastern gate of the city of Kapilavastu. These youths were skilled in the use of weapons, adept at divine archery, possessed of many expedient means, and all were of great strength, like mighty warriors whose power was nearly peerless.
Each youth was surrounded by five hundred chariots;
beside each chariot, there were furthermore five hundred swift and sturdy men, each surrounding his respective vehicle."
In this same sequence, it was likewise at the southern, western, and northern gates, each guarded by five hundred men as previously described.
Furthermore, the elder Śākya ministers all took their positions at the crossroads and four-way junctions, collectively guarding Prince Siddhārtha in turn.

At that time, King Śuddhodana specially appointed five hundred of the most excellent and robust Śākya officials as attendants; all of them were equipped with armor and rode upon elephants and horses, surrounding the palace of King Śuddhodana on all four sides, each stationed inside and outside the gate-towers to keep watch throughout the night.
"At that time, the Great Queen Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī was within the palace; she gathered her ladies-in-waiting together and said to them:
'You all should know!'"
From this day forward, do not sleep by day or night. Take various luminous jewels and place them atop high banners so that the night is not dark.
Furthermore, light ghee-oil lamps, incense lamps, and wax candles in every location; constantly tend to the fires and ensure they are never extinguished.
Securely lock all the gates and keys; do not allow anyone to open them at improper times.
Adorn your bodies with necklaces and ornaments, and each holding hands like a chain of hooks, stand together surrounding the Prince so that he may not wander about at will.

If you hold bows and swords, or carry tridents and clubs, or lean upon spears and lances—whether sitting or standing, grasping or facing them—with all manner of weapons, you must apply your minds day and night so as not to fail to perceive the Prince’s movements.
"If he were to leave the household life, my palace would be empty and devoid of anything for entertainment.

At that time, Udāyin, the son of the state preceptor and attendant to the Prince, entered the inner quarters of the crown prince and saw him sitting in meditation within the hall, while all the palace ladies remained silent.
Having seen this, he spoke to those women, saying:

"All of you are skilled in discourse and conversation, playful and humorous, adept at anticipating the wishes of others, and capable of turning sorrow into joy. You are beautiful and lovely, peerless in this world; each of you possesses such talents as these. Why do you all remain silent today?"
How could such a functional capacity be forgotten?
It should be understood as being like the matters of adornment performed in the northern continent of Uttarakuru.
Furthermore, you all!
She is worthy to be the queen consort of Vaiśravaṇa, the Great King Who Guards the World in the northern quarter; how much less could she not be fit for the palace of a human being?
You ladies-in-waiting!
"How could we allow this prince to remain free from desire?

If even people like you can cause those who follow the teachings of the truly holy ones to practice the five desires, how much more so today, when we cannot prevent this Śākya prince from becoming stained by and attached to the world?"

"You ladies! You are able to speak sweet words, turn away anger and bring about joy, and skillfully capture the hearts of others. Given all the expedients and illusory arts possessed by the female body, even if a woman were capable of practicing lust, how much more so would a man not be captivated by you?"
"If worldly people were to dwell in the same place as you all, it would be impossible for them not to engage in lust.
And he spoke in verse:
"You ladies of the court, Possess great power of skillful means; [If worldly men were to dwell with you, They could never remain free from desire.]”
Skilled at enchanting others, you well display your realm;
even if those who are free from desire— true sages and the like—
were to behold you, they would surely give rise to lustful thoughts.
"How much less could this prince, observing your amusements, ever engage in the five desires? Such a thing is utterly impossible.
"Thus it is for you!"

"You are all skillful in means within your own spheres of influence; I see that you all possess such means, yet you have still been unable to cause the Prince to develop a lustful attachment toward yourselves, which greatly displeases me."
Each of you should further apply yourselves with diligence and employ skillful means so that, upon seeing you, Prince Siddhārtha may develop a distinct desire for you and not feel weary or detached.
"You ladies! Have you not heard?
Formerly, in the kingdom of Kāśī, there was a rishi named Tīṣyayana (translated in the Sui language as Shansheng), who was deceived by the courtesan Sundarī."
Yet that seer was no different from a deva; even the devas could not do anything against him.
Because he was deluded by the courtesan Sundarī, he followed her on foot and entered the city.
Furthermore, in the past, there was a rishi named Ekasṛṅga-putra (Son of the One-Horned Rishi), who from his very birth had never experienced sexual desire.

At that time, there was a courtesan named Śāntā (translated into Chinese as *Jìdìng*, "Tranquil Stability") who deceived that rishi, causing him to lose his meditative concentration and his five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

Furthermore, in the past there was a rishi named Viśvamitra (translated into the Sui language as Huazhi), who practiced asceticism for a long time; after ten years had passed, he had consumed nothing at all.
At that time, there was a courtesan named Mṛgānā (in the language of Sui, meaning "The One"), who was exceedingly beautiful; even that seer was deceived and deluded by her.

Even such great seers and sages as these were frequently deceived and deluded by lustful women, who enticed them and led them to engage in worldly desires; how much more so, then, is it for Prince Siddhārtha today, who is in the prime of his youth and possesses a body of such delicate softness?

The Prince, the son of the Great King, is skilled in all matters; you should serve and attend upon him with a sincere heart, causing him to develop a sense of attachment toward you, so that he does not sever the royal lineage.

After those court ladies heard these words from the state minister’s son, Udāyin, they displayed various forms of artful seduction and enchantment toward the Prince, causing him to give rise to an even more intense and sublime desire.

Some of the court ladies manifested dancing forms; some produced subtle and exquisite sounds to chant hymns and songs of praise; some performed music; some displayed laughable and extraordinary facial expressions; and some composed hundreds of kinds of speech and phrases.

Some further displayed graceful and elegant gait before the Prince; some brought various kinds of diverse, exquisite, and fresh flowers to offer to the Prince; some applied various hundred-fold blended incenses to the Prince’s body; some blew whistles into their mouths to produce the sounds of various birds;
and others addressed him with these words: "O Prince of Noble Lineage!"
"May you grant us leave to engage in various worldly expressions of sensual desire, jesting, and flirtation.
While the Crown Prince was within the palace, he heard these various playful words of desire and reflected thus:

"In this world, beings are oppressed by suffering—namely birth, old age, sickness, and death. Since such afflictions exist, they do not know how to cultivate weary detachment to abandon those sufferings, nor do they seek a place of refuge."
"How may I now skillfully employ expedient means to abandon these various worldly sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death?

Furthermore, although those court ladies displayed for him many kinds of song, dance, music, and various exquisite sensual pleasures, when Prince Siddhārtha saw them, he felt no sense of wonder or attachment.
At that time, among the palace women, there was a certain lady-in-waiting who took a garland of *mallikā* flowers in her own hand and stepped forward to fasten it around the Prince’s neck.

However, the Prince gazed at the woman with a steady, unblinking eye; he then immediately untied the *mallikā* garland himself, and having done so, held it in his hand and threw it out through the window.

At that time, the royal preceptor’s son, Udāyin, saw the Prince sitting upright in right mindfulness, contemplating and remaining unattached to the conditioned realms of the world, nor stained by love for exquisite forms, sounds, or fragrances. Having seen this, Udāyin—who was clever, wise, and skillfully versed in various excellent discourses on diverse methods—addressed the Prince, saying:
“O Great Holy Prince!...”

"I have been sent here by the Great King's command to serve as a companion and delight for the Prince. I now submit this request; may the Prince deign to listen: my mind remains unmoved regarding worldly affairs because of the Prince."
And he spoke in verse:

"I have briefly described the characteristics of a friend: One who offers harsh admonition for one's own good, Who encourages virtuous conduct, And provides relief in times of calamity— Such a person is called a true and virtuous friend."
When Udāyin had spoken this verse, he further said:
"O Great Holy Prince!
Since I am now a friend of the Noble Son, we must deliberate together upon all matters, whether good or bad."
Seeing me silently depart as if you were indifferent and wishing to abandon me, one cannot truly be called a friend.
Therefore, I now wish to address the Prince with what I have to say; relying upon the heart of a friend, I pray that you will graciously accept it.

"Prince! You are currently in the prime of your youth; yet as I observe your mind now, you do not perform virtuous deeds but instead wish to abandon these court ladies and harbor resentment toward them—what is there about them that is so loathsome?"
Whatever binds the mind follows this principle: the sentiment of attachment has the state of desire as its root, and the body of a woman finds joy solely in being respected by a man.

If the Prince’s heart is such that he will certainly not be attached to the affairs of the five desires, then worldly wealth, status, and splendor are difficult to attain; one should instead use pleasant words and kind speech to console and encourage the palace women, causing their hearts to be gladdened.
And he spoke in verse:
“Women find joy in respect; respect is the highest form of joy.
Without respect, there is only physical beauty, like a tree that has no flowers.”

At that time, having heard these words from the royal preceptor Udayin, the Prince immediately employed various skillful words and a voice of compassion—like the subtle rumbling of thunder amidst gathering clouds, or like a beautiful, harmonious, and soft sound—and replied to Udayin, saying: "O Udayin!..."
I also know that you are my good companion and my virtuous friend; you have opened my mind with a kind heart and exhorted me to understand my own purpose.
I now likewise recognize that your intention toward me is intimate and profound, and I shall not now oppose your heart.

"You now see that I have such faults; I shall now comply with you. However, it is not that I am ignorant of the pleasures of the five worldly desires. I have clearly and thoroughly understood all matters of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); because the world is impermanent and subject to decay, for this reason, I find this place fearful and my mind finds no joy therein."
And he spoke in verse:
"Though worldly glory brings pleasure, It is subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death.
If these four were not present, Who would not find joy in my heart?"
At that time, having spoken these verses, the Prince further addressed Udāyin again:
"Udāyin! You should observe these palace women;

since their youthful vigor has been snatched away by old age, they look at one another with hearts devoid of joy. How much less could a deluded person wish to give rise to a mind of love and delight toward such a state?"
And he spoke in verse:
"Birth, old age, sickness, and death are the nature of things;
To dwell amidst this birth, old age, and sickness, If one dwells with a mind attached to the pleasures of life, One is no different from birds and beasts."
"At that time, while the Prince was engaged in conversation with the royal preceptor’s son, Udāyin, and others, as they went back and forth, the sun eventually set."
Once the prince had seen the sun set, he entered the palace and, together with his court ladies, indulged in the pleasures of the five desires; they gathered together and remained surrounding him.
On that very night, the Crown Prince’s consort, Yaśodharā, perceived that she was pregnant.

Furthermore, during that same night, the Prince’s maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, saw in a dream a white bull-king within the city, bellowing loudly as it walked with steady gait; not a single person was able to stand before it or create an obstacle.

Furthermore, during that night, King Śuddhodana also dreamed that in the center of the city, a banner of Śakra was erected; adorned with many varieties of diverse jewels and further embellished with various necklaces, it was magnificent and splendid, like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, which rose up from the earth and stood in the sky.

From that banner of Śakra, a great radiance further issued forth, illuminating all around in the four directions. Furthermore, great clouds arose from the four directions and gathered together above Śakra’s banner, pouring down heavy rain that drenched and washed the banner of Śakra with a torrential deluge.
Furthermore, from the sky there fell a rain of various, immeasurable, and boundless exquisite flowers.
Around that banner of Śakra, there were also immeasurable varieties of subtle and wondrous sounds, resonating spontaneously without being struck.

Furthermore, there was another bright white parasol, with a shaft made of various jewels and a handle of gold; it was upright and pleasing to behold, and it spontaneously covered the top of Śakra’s banner.
Furthermore, from the four directions, the Four Great Heavenly Kings and their retinues came toward the city, opened the gates, and brought forth that banner of Śakra.

At that time, during that night, Yaśodharā was sleeping in utter exhaustion, unconscious of her surroundings; as she lay dreaming, she beheld twenty kinds of terrifying things. Her heart trembled and her body shook; filled with dread and unease, suspicious, strange, and panicked, she suddenly awoke.
At that time, the Prince asked Yaśodharā: "O Yaśodharā!
For what reason are you so terrified and trembling, panting and agitated at heart, as to have suddenly risen?"

Why is this so? You, Yaśodharā! Now you are no longer in the Śītavana cemetery, nor are you surrounded by corpses; you are not on the mountains, nor do you dwell in the wilderness. Now, within this city, protected by immeasurable and boundless weaponry, you are in the royal palace. This place is secure and firm; you need not fear wild beasts, nor do you have cause for concern regarding thieves coming to alarm you. Herein lies peace and happiness; this is a place free from fear.
Now that I have seen you, Yaśodharā, my heart is filled with great terror, my heart is filled with great sorrow, and doubt and fear arise within me; I have suddenly awakened.
What is the cause of this?
At that time, the Crown Prince’s consort Yaśodharā shed tears like rain; terrified and sobbing with grief, she addressed the Crown Prince, saying:
“O Great Holy Crown Prince!
"Tonight, I have seen twenty such omens in a dream; I pray that you will listen attentively as I describe them.
'Noble Son! I recently dreamed that the entire earth shook and trembled on all sides.'"
“‘Noble son! Furthermore, in a dream you saw the banner of Śakra collapse to the ground.
“‘Noble son!’”
Next, he again dreamed that the sun, the moon, and all the constellations in the sky fell down.
"O Noble Son!

Next, I dreamed of a great, fresh, and pure parasol, which has been my place of refuge from of old, my protector, and my compassionate guardian; yet that son of a slave-woman, Chandaka, suddenly used his strength to seize it from me and depart."
“‘Noble son!
Furthermore, I dreamt that my hair, bound in a topknot and adorned with various jewels, was cut off by a sword and taken away.
Noble son!’”
Next, I again dreamed that all the necklaces and ornaments upon my body were swept away by water. "Noble son!
Next, I again dreamed that my physical form, which was subtle, exquisite, and upright, suddenly became ugly."
“‘Noble son!
Furthermore, I next dreamed that all the hands and feet upon my body fell off naturally.
“‘Noble son!’”
"Furthermore, next I dreamed that this body of mine suddenly became naked. 'Noble Son!
Furthermore, next I dreamed that the bed upon which I have always sat since my birth—when I sit upon it to serve the Noble Son—that bed suddenly collapsed onto the ground of its own accord.'"
“‘Noble son! Furthermore, I next dreamed that the bed upon which I always slept and enjoyed pleasure with you, noble son, had all four of its legs broken off.’”

"Noble Son! Furthermore, he next dreamed of a great mountain composed of various jewels, with sharp, slender edges and four corners, immeasurably high and steep, which was consumed by fire and collapsed, falling to the ground."
“‘Noble Son! Furthermore, in a dream, I saw a magnificent tree within the palace of Great King Śuddhodana being blown down by the wind. Noble Son!’”
Next, he again dreamed that a bright full moon, surrounded by a multitude of stars, was suddenly swallowed up within this palace.
"O Noble Son!
Next, he again dreamed that a pure sun, illuminating with a thousand rays of light and surrounded by them, was suddenly swallowed up within this palace."
"After he has vanished, the world will be shrouded in darkness, devoid of light. "O Noble Son!
Furthermore, next I saw in a dream that within this palace city, there was a torch which went out toward the exterior of the city."
“‘Noble Son! Furthermore, next in my dream, I saw the tutelary deity who has protected this city from of old, his entire body adorned with various kinds of necklaces, lovely and handsome.’”
He suddenly broke into lamentation, raising his voice in a great cry as he stood outside the gate: "O Noble Son!
Furthermore, I have dreamed that the city of Kapilavastu has suddenly become a desolate wilderness, as terrifying as the night, where my heart finds no place of joy."

“‘Noble Son! Furthermore, in my dream I saw that all the ponds within the city of Kapilavastu had become turbid; all the trees in the groves—with their flowers, fruits, branches, and leaves—had fallen and were strewn across the ground, so that nothing remained beautiful to behold.’”

“‘Noble son! Furthermore, in my dream I saw all the warriors, holding swords and staves in their hands and wearing armor and spears on their bodies, galloping to and fro in every direction around me.’”
"Noble Son!
I have seen these twenty kinds of dreams, and my heart is filled with great terror; I am startled, doubtful, and ill at ease. What are these omens?
Are they inauspicious or auspicious?"
What is this karmic retribution?
Is it that my own life span is about to end,
or is it that I am to be separated from the noble son with whom I share such affection?
"Therefore, my heart is now like that of one being beaten with a pestle; it trembles, is frantic with fear, and cannot be restrained. In the midst of sleep, I suddenly woke up in alarm.
When the Prince heard these words, he reflected within his mind:
"It will not be long before I renounce the world and leave the household life; for this reason, Yaśodharā has seen such a dream of great terror."
At that time, the Prince replied to his consort Yaśodharā, saying:
"Consort Yaśodharā!
Although you have seen those thousand Indras' banners collapse and lie prostrate on the ground, what harm does it do to you?"
Furthermore, even if you were to see a thousand suns, moons, and stars fall to the ground, why would you suffer?

Though you see a thousand parasols, though the servant-born Channa has forcibly lifted them and is departing—since this is a dream-deprivation and not a reality of the day, why is your mind so disturbed?
Do not harbor grief, O virtuous Great Queen!
Do not be startled, do not be afraid!
Do not engage in conceptual discrimination.
Within the phenomena of the world, such illusory dreams naturally occur; there is no need to harbor sorrow, but you should simply rest in peace and sleep as usual.
O virtuous Great Queen!
"You are still young in years, your body is tender and soft; for this reason I am filled with anxiety and fear, worrying that you will become exhausted.
Having heard these words from the Prince, Yaśodharā—who possessed a body accustomed to pleasure and had never before experienced hardship—lay back down and fell asleep.
In order to comfort, console, and bring peace to Yaśodharā, the Prince indulged in the pleasures of the five senses with her, and they slept together.
At that time, during the night, the Prince himself had five great dreams:
first, he dreamed that he took this great earth as his couch and placed Mount Sumeru as a pillow for his head.
The eastern great ocean, he places his left arm;
the western great ocean, he places his right arm;
the southern great ocean, he places both feet.
"In the second dream, I saw a stalk of grass named 'Establishment' (Pratiṣṭhāna) emerge from my navel, its tip reaching as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven."
"In the third dream, four birds of various colors came from the four directions and, beneath the Prince’s two feet, spontaneously transformed into a uniform, pure white."
"In the fourth dream, he saw four white beasts with black heads; from their feet upward, as far as their knees, they licked the Prince’s feet."
"In the fifth dream, I saw a mountain of excrement, towering, steep, and vast; the Prince himself was upon that mountain, walking to and fro all around it, yet remained unsullied by that excrement."

Chapter Twenty-one: Leaving the Palace and Renouncing the World. *The Mahāvastu-Avadāna*, Chapter Twenty-one, Part One: Leaving the Palace and Renouncing the World. "At that time, while the Prince was sleeping within the palace at night, a chamberlain who served as his guard addressed all those on watch duty, saying: 'O you men!'"

When performing the ritual of *saṃkramaṇa*, one should each call out as follows: "Kumbhīra, Kumbhīra" (Kumbhīra means "The Terrifying" in the Sui language); or "Muktila, Muktila" (Muktila means "Liberation" in the Sui language); or "Aṅgana, Aṅgana" (Aṅgana means "Falling Inside" in the Sui language).
"You people! Are you already here? They replied:
"We are here. At that time, the minister spoke again to those people, saying:
"All of you must remain vigilant while on watch; all of you must remain vigilant while on watch."

The night is now deep; all beings—whether dwelling in the water, residing on land, perched in trees, staying in caves, by the sides of mountain valleys, or within houses—are utterly exhausted and overcome by sleep.
"You all! Tonight, while keeping watch, you must each take up your weapons and guard the gates and chambers together; you should remain vigilant and exercise great care in your duties.
As for the others on duty keeping watch at the various stations, do not allow yourselves to fall asleep."
"Your Majesty is most solemn and has issued such a decree. Why is this?

It is because we fear that the Crown Prince might abandon this city and shave his head to leave the household life. If he is protected within the palace, this holy prince will surely attain the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) and rule over the four quarters of the world."
"The Great Seer, the National Preceptor, has thus bestowed this prophecy.
When these words were spoken, the first watch of the night had passed and it was now midnight; the keeper of the water-clock cried out loudly, "O Great Holy Lord!"
Ever supreme and honored!
May my great master enjoy long life and auspicious peace!

The first watch having passed and it being the middle watch, when the hourglass had not yet reached its midpoint, at that time the various devas of the Form Realm and the Śuddhāvāsa heavens descended to the city of Kapilavastu.

At that time, all the people within the city were utterly bewildered and fell into a deep, heavy sleep; King Śuddhodana, along with his attendants, the various ministers in charge of the Prince’s stables, and the palace women and maidservants, were all likewise confounded and sank into a profound slumber from exhaustion.

At that time, there was a son of heaven within the assembly named Dharmacārin, who came into the palace and, by means of his supernormal powers, caused the bodies and garments of the court ladies to become disarrayed and ill-fitted, or even bared and exposed, so that they were unable to maintain their composure.
Some of the ladies-in-waiting slept with their hands supporting their chins;
some ladies cast aside their *konghou* lutes and set them to one side before lying down to rest;
and some ladies slept while cradling drums with both arms.
Some had both hands thrust through the lattice windows, their upper bodies exposed as they slept; some lay with each embracing the other with both arms;
some ladies slept with their eyelids closed but their pupils wide open, gazing fixedly as they slumbered;
and some ladies slept leaning against various necklaces, which hung down and dangled upon them.

There may be palace women whose features are upright and beautiful, who have always maintained proper deportment and possessed a full sense of shame, and who were complete in every skill; yet now, entangled by the conditions of deep sleep, they emit sounds as they pass wind—whether large or small, coarse or fine—with foul odors billowing forth, all of which they do not perceive at all.

Some cast off their various necklaces and ornaments; some threw away their diverse flower garlands; others discarded their garments and lay with eyes wide open, no different from a corpse, so that bystanders looking on could not conceive the thought that they were alive.
Some lie on their backs with their hands and feet fully extended, sleeping with their mouths agape;
some toss their hands and feet about, sleeping with them crossed over one side;
and some sleep with their arms and thighs clenched and drawn up, their limbs twisted and contorted.
Some lie down standing or leaning against a wall, their bodies swaying like those who are intoxicated;
some sleep with their heads covered while snoring;
others sleep crouching with their necks drawn in.
Some lay there with faces turned pale blue and drained of color, appearing utterly hideous;
some ladies-in-waiting slept with small waist-drums suspended from their necks, draped across their armpits;
some ladies slept with lutes resting upon their shoulders; and some ladies slept with their teeth gnashing, emitting grating and clamorous sounds.
Some slept with their heads hanging down and snoring;
some slept with their faces buried, like corpses in a cemetery;
and some slept while losing control of their excrement and urine.

At that time, the Prince suddenly awoke and beheld within the palace wax candles and lamps, some as thick as fists and others as large as arms, blazing and radiant with extreme brilliance. He saw the palace women thus sleeping, some holding bronze gongs, flutes, lutes, pipes, transverse flutes, zithers, *zhu*, *pipa* lutes, *yu* organs, reed pipes, conch shells, and oyster shells; their mouths were frothing white and mucus and saliva flowed from their noses.
Seeing these various appearances, the Prince reflected: "The physical forms of women are merely like this; what is there to be craved in such impure and foul secretions?"

With external adornments of powder and ointment, necklaces, garments, flower garlands, hairpins, and bracelets, they falsely embellish their bodies; yet ignorant people do not realize this, being perversely deceived and deluded, giving rise to false desires toward the realm of form.

If there is a wise person who observes the body of a woman with right mindfulness, seeing that its essential nature is thus empty and without a master, like a dream or an illusion, then within it there should be no room for indulgence or the arising of greed; yet, due to perverse thoughts, one is bound by ignorance.
And he spoke in verse:
“The world is deluded by impure and manifold afflictions; Nothing surpasses the nature of a woman’s body.
Because it is adorned with garments and necklaces, The ignorant give rise to lustful craving toward her.”

If there are those who can contemplate in this way—seeing that all is like an illusion or a dream and not real—they will swiftly abandon ignorance and remain heedful; they will surely attain the body of liberation and merit.
At that time, the Prince again focused his mind and reflected thus:
"Alas, this world!
Such great afflictions exist."
"Alas, how terrifying!
What is there to crave?
Thinking thus with a heart of compassion and pitying all sentient beings, he raised his voice and wept aloud.
"In this place of bondage, the foolish person is like a butcher severing all lives;
in this place of impurity, the foolish person falsely gives rise to attachment and delight, like a painted jar filled with excrement;
in this place of falsehood, the foolish person is submerged and stagnated, like a weak mud that swallows elephants."
This place is foul and impure, yet foolish people regard it as fragrant and delicious, like a pig in a latrine;
this place is empty and deceptive, yet foolish people perversely give rise to attachment, like a dog embracing a bone devoid of flesh;
this place is harmful, yet foolish people vying with one another cast themselves into it, like moths rushing toward a lamp.
This place is poisonous, yet foolish people crave and delight in it, like fish and turtles swallowing baited hooks;
this place is withered and pale, yet foolish people take pleasure in and frequent it, like moisture-born flowers separated from water and scorched by the sun;
this place is precarious and fragile, yet foolish people walk and traverse it, like an old ox sinking into deep mud.
This place is perilously precipitous; the foolish fall into it and sink away, like a blind man tumbling down a steep cliff.
This place is one of cyclic revolution; the foolish transmigrate through birth and death, like a potter’s spinning wheel.
This place is one of entanglement; the foolish are bound by its fetters, like a dog wearing a collar that deprives it of freedom.
In this place there is no moisture; the foolish person is scorched and withered, like parched grass in the intense heat of summer.
In this place there is decay and exhaustion; the foolish person daily diminishes, like the waning moon approaching its end.
In this place there is no profit; the foolish person’s roots of goodness are spent, like one who loses his wealth at gambling.
At that time, the Prince observed the bodies of the court ladies in this manner and further reflected:

"I have now clearly seen such signs; I ought to rejoice, exert myself with vigor and diligence, arouse a mind of *vīrya*, increase my merit and virtue, and give rise to great vows to rescue and deliver the world. For those beings who have no savior, I shall act as their protector; for those who have no nurturer, I shall act as their refuge; for those beings who have no shelter, I shall act as their dwelling."
The task I have set for myself has now appeared before me; before long, this resolve shall surely bear its fruit. Why is this?
For these women have all cast aside their modesty and shame, and are overcome by a deep sleep.
"At that time, the devaputra Kumbhakaraka, having seen that the Prince had awakened from his sleep at midnight, approached him calmly and addressed the Prince, saying: 'Prince!'"
In the past, he accomplished and perfected matters of ultimate truth.
Furthermore, Prince!
Formerly, while among humans, he gave rise to this thought:
"I vow that upon casting off this body, I shall be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven. "Prince!
That time for your vow has already passed."
Furthermore, in the past, while in the Tuṣita heaven, he made the vow to be born among humans and take up residence in a mother’s womb; that vow was fulfilled.
While in the womb, he vowed to emerge early; that vow was also completed.
Having been born and having grown up, while residing within the palace, he experienced the pleasures of youth and sported with sovereign ease; those vows were likewise transcended.
In my early youth, I desired to apply myself with diligence and learn various arts and crafts; that wish has now been fulfilled.
In my prime, I gave rein to my heart and desired to enjoy worldly pleasures; that wish has now been realized.
"It is not fitting to remain indulgent for long; today, all you devas and humans, I pray that you cause the Prince to renounce the world and go forth to cultivate the Noble Path.

At that time, having heard these words from the Deva Kumbhakarṇa, the Prince immediately put on his leather sandals, which were crafted from various jewels worth eight thousand *koṭis* of gold. Having fastened them upon his feet, he wished to rise and look back at the precious couch where he sat.
Then, he spoke these great words: "This is the last place where my body shall experience the five desires; from this day forward, I shall never again receive them."
"This is my body, the final place where I shall experience the five desires; from this day forward, I shall never again receive them.

At that time, the Prince raised his right hand, drew aside the canopy and lattice-work made of various jewels, and emerged from the palace. He proceeded with steady, slow steps, having walked but a short distance, he stood facing the east within the hall, joined his ten fingers in palms-together gesture, and with a sincere heart, brought to mind all the Buddhas.
Having reflected thus, he raised his head and gazed upward at the void and the various constellations.

At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings who protect the world and Śakra, Lord of Devas, knowing that the time for the Prince’s renunciation had arrived, each prepared according to their own power, intending to come.

At that time, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, leading his entire retinue of gandharvas and hundreds of thousands of followers, preceded and followed him while performing various musical performances. Coming from the east, he circumambulated the city of Kapilavastu three times, descended to the ground, and withdrew to stand in his quarter. Joining his ten fingers in palms-together salutation, he bowed his head and bent his body, facing toward the Prince.

At that time, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, leading his entire retinue of kumbhāṇḍas and others under his command—a multitude of hundreds of thousands—preceded and followed him. Carrying precious vases filled with various kinds of exquisite fragrant water, he came from the south, circumambulated the city of Kapilavastu three times, descended to the ground, and withdrew to stand in that direction. With palms joined, head bowed and body inclined, he faced toward the Prince.

At that time, the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa, leading all his retinues—the various dragon kings under his command—accompanied by hundreds of thousands of millions of followers in front and behind, held in his hands various exquisite strings of pearls and carried diverse kinds of miscellaneous precious jewels. Simultaneously, he raised various clouds of incense, flowers, and jewels, and further produced a subtle, exquisite, and soft fragrant wind. Coming from the western direction, he circled the city of Kapilavastu three times, descended to the ground, and stood aside in that quarter with his ten fingers joined in palms-together salutation, bowing his head and bending his body as he faced the Prince.

At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, leading all his retinues of yakṣas under his command—a multitude of hundreds of thousands—preceded and followed him. Holding fire-jewels, or lamps and candles, or torches of blazing and fierce flame, they were clad in armor. Carrying bows, swords, arrows, spears, and other weapons such as halberds and tridents, they came from the north, circumambulated the city of Kapilavastu three times, descended to the ground, and stood at that quarter with their palms joined, bowing their heads and bodies toward the Prince.

At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, together with his retinue of all the devas—preceded and followed by a multitude of hundreds of thousands of millions—brought celestial flower garlands, powdered incense, and unguents; some carried banners, pennants, and precious parasols, while others held various exquisite necklaces. Coming from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, they circled the city of Kapilavastu three times, then withdrew to stay above, joined their ten fingers in palms-together salutation, bowed their heads and bodies, and faced the Prince.

At that time, the Prince surveyed all directions, gazing upward at the void and the various constellations, and beheld the four world-protecting Great Heavenly Kings. Their bodies were adorned with various exquisite and supreme necklaces; they wore celestial crowns upon their heads and proceeded in succession, walking with calm and slow steps. Accompanied by Gandharvas, Kumbhāṇḍas, all the Nāgas, and Yakṣas, they were surrounded on their left and right by hundreds of thousands of attendants. Each coming from their respective quarters—east, south, west, and north—they arrived here and took their positions according to their directions.

Furthermore, he saw Śakra Devānām Indra, the Lord of Devas, leading a retinue of hundreds of thousands of devas, filling the space before and behind him as they gathered together in the void on all sides.
Furthermore, seeing that the lunar mansion of the Ghosts (Ārdrā) had already conjoined with the moon, the devas cried out in a great voice:
"O Great Sage, Prince!
The constellation of the Ghosts has already joined; the time has now arrived. If you wish to seek the supreme Dharma, do not remain here."
"The Lion among Kings, when the time has come, will swiftly renounce his home and go forth.
Thus did the devas further assist him, proclaiming these words:
"Go forth quickly; do not remain!"
At that time, the Prince looked up at the void and reflected thus:

"Now the midnight is still and the constellation of Mṛgaśiras has already joined; the great assembly of devas, the earth, and the void all provide assistance. It is certain that my time has now arrived without fail; it is fitting that I go forth into homelessness."
Having reflected thus, the Prince immediately summoned his slave Caraka, who was born on the same day as he, and said to him:

"Caraka! Come quickly; do not disobey me. Swiftly saddle my royal steed Kanthaka, born on the same day as you, and bring him here before my kinsmen—the sons of the Śākyas—can hear the sound of that horse."
At that time, having heard these words from the Prince, Chandaka looked up at the sky and reflected thus:
"It is now only midnight."
His heart was immediately filled with doubt; his entire body trembled, the hairs on his skin stood on end, and he was so terrified and uneasy that he addressed the Prince, saying:
"O Great Holy Prince!
"Why did you send me out in the middle of the night with the horse-king Kaṇṭhaka?
What terror is there?
What enemy is there?"
"What urgent matter is there?
Is there something good or bad either outside the city or now within the city?
At that time, the Prince spoke to Chandaka, saying:
"O Chanda! I am now in great haste, terrified by my enemies and oppressed by manifold sufferings; how could you possibly know this?
Quickly saddle my noble steed Kanthaka, born on the same day as I, and bring him here with all speed!"
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Sixteen;
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Seventeen.
Translated by the Sui Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta.
Chapter on Leaving the Palace and Becoming a Monk, Part Two:
At that time, having heard these words from the Prince, Chandaka reflected within his own mind:
"The Noble Son now definitely intends to leave the household; he is unwilling to remain."
Having thought thus, he intentionally raised a loud voice, spoke with great words, and addressed the Prince, hoping that the palace attendants would take notice:
"O Noble Son, Prince!..."
"You always know the tasks to be performed at each season and always act in accordance with the time. What time is it now that you call for horses?
If the Noble Son wishes to go to the park to view the beautiful grounds and enjoy himself, this is not the right time; what use have you for horses?"

"Noble Son, today you have no enemies, nor are there any who oppose or rebel against you. The four quarters are peaceful and quiet; there is no one causing turmoil or disorder. Throughout the borders, there are none who have fled, and neighboring states likewise do not attempt to invade or seize. As for those who wish to fight with the Noble Son, you, Noble Son, cover the entire earth alone and without peer. Why, then, do you now need the horse-king Kaṇṭhaka?"

"Noble Son, today here within this palace, you are surrounded by all these court ladies, enjoying yourself in pleasure and delight, just as Śakra-devānām-indra is surrounded by the celestial maidens in the Nandana Grove.
Noble Son is likewise; seated here upon this jeweled couch within the palace, what need have you for a horse?"
"Only wish for peace of mind; among these hundreds of thousands of maidens, remain here enjoying the sounds of music.

At that time, Chandaka spoke thus with his mouth, and furthermore, he used his hands to pull the hair of the maidens to wake them, and he also stepped upon their bodies with his feet; yet those maidens neither perceived nor knew it, due to the supernatural power of the higher devas.
At that time, the Prince felt doubt within his heart, fearing that the multitude might perceive him; he spoke these verses in a private, low voice to Chandaka:
"Chandaka, born of the same womb, you should know:
I view the inner palace as a cemetery, No different from a den of maggots, Like dwelling together with rākṣasas."
Lying in disarray toward the east, west, south, and north, they resemble embryos floating in the waters at the beginning of conception.
Chanda, I have seen the suffering of the five desires; my mind has no wish to remain in this palace.
Even if I were to travel to various lands, I would find no joy, for I have beheld old age, sickness, and the corpse.
“Chanda, bring Kaṇṭhaka quickly; I am now determined to go forth into homelessness.
At that time, having heard these words from the Prince, Chanda was like a fierce beast struck by a poisoned arrow; overcome with great anguish, he wept aloud and addressed the Prince, saying:
“Noble Son!...”
"Now may you depart, O noble ones?
The Prince replied,
"Well done, Chandaka!"
I now wish to seek a supreme state; I would rather abandon all my present kinsmen and relatives than allow myself and my retinue in the future to fall into the mouths of the Lord of Death.
He spoke further in verse to Chandaka:
"For the sake of seeking Nirvāṇa, I would rather abandon my kinsmen and go forth into homelessness.
In the future, the ghost of Death will plunder men; Once life enters its mouth, it devours them all."
At that time, having heard these words of the Prince once more, Chandaka addressed the Prince again with great earnestness:
"O Great Holy Prince!..."
All the people of the world say:
"The Prince will certainly become a great Wheel-Turning King.
Why do you wish to renounce it?
The Prince again interrupted Chanda with these words: "Ho, Chanda!
Do not speak such words!"

In the past, when I was in the Tuṣita Heaven—which is superior to this place—I served as the Heavenly King and governed all those Trāyastriṃśa gods; even at that time, I did not find delight in the pleasures of that realm.
Why is this? Because one perceives the affliction of impermanence within birth and death; how much more so now in this human realm?

To dwell for a short time within this human sphere is to be beset by many troubles and turbidities. Though one occupies this royal throne and governs the world with temporary sovereignty, one cannot escape the fear of illness and death.
"However, within this world, there are realms governed by the Lord of Death (Mṛtyu), where even those kings cannot attain sovereign peace and happiness.
Chandaka spoke again to the Prince, saying:
"O Great Holy Prince!"

Although the Prince does not desire the position of worldly sovereignty, King Śuddhodana is now advanced in years while the Prince is in the prime of his youth; let not the Great King’s heart be filled with distress.
The Prince replied:
"O Chandaka, born of noble birth!

My heart now feels love and reverence toward my great grandfather king; as he loves me, I love him all the more. The Great King is extraordinary in his affection for his kin, and I too do not wish to abandon my relatives; nor do I harbor any other thoughts toward my kinsmen."

However, I am greatly terrified, deeply fearful, and profoundly alarmed by the suffering of birth and death within the realms of existence.
