Because I now wish to seek the Dharma of liberation, I temporarily abandon those whom I hold dear and cherish; this is so that I may compassionately protect my kinsmen in future lives, and so that we shall not be separated in the ages to come.
At that time, Chandaka addressed the Crown Prince, saying:
"Great Sage, Crown Prince, is your mind resolved?
Must you truly renounce the secular world and seek the life of a renunciant?"
The Prince replied,
"Welcome, Chandaka!
I have already made my resolve."
Chanda spoke again:
"For what purpose?
The Prince replied:
"I have seen the faults of impermanence in the world, and thus I intend to seek that supreme state exclusively.
Chandaka asked again,
"For what reason do you seek that supreme state?"
The Prince replied:

"If it were so that in this world there were neither birth nor death, neither old age nor sickness, neither separation from the beloved nor union with the hated; if, having attained the royal throne, one were to enjoy all merits without impermanence, if the realms of experience were truly real, and if, being born once among humans, there were no defilement or impurity—if it were thus, then my heart might find delight in this place."
"You are a good Chandaka!
Do not oppose my heart; I have already commanded you to quickly saddle my horse-king Kanthaka, who was born on the same day as I.
Chandaka replied:
"As the Prince has commanded, we dare not disobey.

Having heard these words of command from the Prince, Chandaka understood the deep intent of the Prince's heart; he was also well aware of King Śuddhodana’s strict prohibitions and heavy restrictions, yet, through the empowerment of the various devas, he resolved to take Kaṇṭhaka and bring him before the Prince.
And there is a verse that says:
"Because Chandaka was empowered by the divine strength of the devas, He endured the violation of the Great King’s command;
Furthermore, as the Bodhisattva’s former vows were fulfilled, He resolved his mind and proceeded to adorn the horse."

At that time, Chandaka went immediately to the stable and, from among the troughs and stalls, seized Kanthaka. He then fashioned a golden bridle adorned with the seven precious gems and fastened it through the horse’s mouth.

He led him out from the stall and tied him to another stake; he scraped and brushed his back, first applying a soft, light, and fine substance to his spine, then saddling him with a saddle and crupper adorned with the seven treasures made of gold, and covering it with a golden net.
Having thus fully equipped and saddled the horse, he led him forth toward the presence of the Prince.
At that time, the horse-king Kanthaka, born together with the Prince, saw from afar that the Prince’s physical strength was robust; his entire body was filled with joy, and he let out a great neigh.
At that time, when the horse-king Kaṇṭhaka let out his neighing cry, it could be heard for half a yojana;

however, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, through their supernatural power, caused the sound of the horse to vanish so it could not be heard, fearing that someone might obstruct the Prince and prevent him from leaving home.

At that time, the Prince was filled with such joy and exultation that it pervaded his entire body. He then took the right hand—its fingers soft, webbed, and marked with lines like lotus petals, and its nails as red as purple lac—and stroked the back of the horse-king, Candaka, who had been born on the same day as himself, and commanded him, saying:
"O Candaka, horse-king, born on the same day as I!"
I now wish to seek the Dharma of the Deathless; you must exert yourself in such virtuous conduct so that no one may create obstacles for me.
You, excellent Kanthaka!
Even during times of battle, one exerts the utmost strength for the sake of desiring victory over others; today, you must assist me well as I seek the bliss of transcendence from the world.
The pleasures of the world bring joy for a fleeting moment, yet before long they are lost, giving rise to great sorrow and distress.
To exert oneself for the sake of the Dharma is an exceedingly difficult task; therefore, desiring to seek liberation for all the world, I now wish to leave the household life and cultivate the Way.
Exert yourselves well; apply your heroic strength and move with swift agility.
I am now going forth into homelessness to bring great benefit to all the world and to you all.
At that time, the Prince stood upon the ground with right mindfulness and made a great, far-reaching vow, speaking these words:
"This is my final carriage while remaining in the household; from this day forward, I shall never again ride in such a vehicle."
Having made this vow, he fastened the reins and mounted the horse Kanthaka; once mounted, he spoke again to the horse Kanthaka, saying: "O Kanthaka!"
"May you carry me with diligence; this is the final burden. It is for the sake of bringing benefit to the world of devas and humans that I have now resolved to leave the home life.

At the moment the Prince sat upon the saddle of the horse-king Kanthaka, all the immeasurable hosts of asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, rākṣasas, piśācas, the earth-dwelling devas, and those of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, followed after the horse-king Kanthaka.

At that time, the various devas held white parasols, whose handles were adorned all around with various kinds of precious jewels; nets of pearls made of many gems were suspended above them, and between the meshes of these nets, golden bells were hung, which they held aloft to cover the Prince.
At that time, the Prince mounted the horse Kanthaka and gradually approached the palace gate.

As Kanthaka walked, the sound of his hooves could be heard for one *krośa*. The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, through their supernormal powers, concealed that sound so it would not be heard from afar, fearing it might create an obstacle to the Prince’s renunciation.

"At the time when the Prince renounced the household life, there was a yakṣa in the sky named Pāda; that yakṣa Pāda and his host of yakṣas remained in the sky, each supporting the four hooves of the horse with their hands, proceeding slowly and steadily."
When the Prince first intended to set out for his renunciation, a certain devaputra proclaimed these words:
"May the Great Dharma-Captain, who brings forth auspiciousness and welfare, now deliver immeasurable sentient beings across the ocean of afflictions."
Again, another deva proclaimed these words:
"May the Great Sage, the World-Honored One, who is free from all obstacles, now go forth into homelessness to cross the ocean of birth and death."
At that time, the Prince said to Chandaka:
"O well-born Chandaka!
You should now walk before me and show me the way."
As he was exiting through the inner palace gate, when the bolt and key of that gate were about to be opened, the sound would have been heard for one *krośa*.

Non-human beings arrived at the gate and opened the bolt and key; at the moment of opening, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, by means of their supernormal powers, concealed that sound so as not to let anyone hear it, fearing that there might be obstacles when the Prince went forth into homelessness.
At that time, Chandaka addressed the Crown Prince, saying:
"O Great Sage, Crown Prince!
The palace gates have already been opened."
The Prince replied, "The gates have already opened;
my mind is resolved upon the benefit I seek, and it shall certainly be accomplished without any doubt."
Then Chandaka addressed the Crown Prince, saying:
"O Great Holy Prince!
How rare and extraordinary this is!"
"This palace gate, when it was opened previously, could only be opened with great exertion of strength; yet now that the Noble Son has arrived, it has opened immediately.
Then the Great Holy Prince reached the side of the gate, just as a fierce wind blows against a mass of clouds, scattering them to both sides.
At that time, having exited from the inner palace gate into the outer world, the Prince made this proclamation:
"This is my final departure from the palace gates; from this day forward, I shall never emerge again."

At that time, having departed from the palace, the Prince proceeded calmly to the gate of Vaiśālī. Beside the gate stood a yakṣa general named Suviveśa, together with his retinue of five hundred yakṣas. Seeing the Prince approaching the gate, walking slowly and steadily, they each spoke to one another:
"Now this Great Holy Prince Siddhārtha has come to the gate at midnight, an improper time. Should we now do something for him?"
Then the host of yakṣas said to one another:

"We should open the gates for the Prince so that he may move freely as he pleases to the east or west; should his heart's desire be fulfilled and his aspirations realized, he shall attain the Path of Ambrosia."
"Having realized this for myself, I shall further bring great benefit to the world of devas and humans.
At that time, the yakṣa general Sunetra quickly opened the gate of Vaiśālī.
Whenever that gate was opened or closed before him, its sound resounded and reached for half a yojana.

At that time, the Śuddhāvāsa devas, using their supernormal powers, concealed the sound of the gate so that no one could hear its resonance, fearing it might create an obstacle to the Prince’s renunciation.

"When the Prince first departed from this city of Kapilavastu through the Vaiśāla gate, all the generals who served as gatekeepers there—some of whom were holding the keys—either fell asleep and did not notice the Prince leaving the palace, or they were deluded by those yakṣa deities, or deluded by the supernatural power of the devas;
even those most vigilant and skilled sentries were all overcome by deep sleep and failed to perceive anyone departing."

"At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, the King of the Desire Realm, seeing that the Prince had first gone forth into homelessness, sought to terrify him by means of his supernormal powers. He conjured various sounds, namely: great clouds appearing in the sky, and from within those clouds, further thunderous roars and the crashing of lightning bolts."
Furthermore, he again manifested various great rivers, blowing upon massive boulders as they surged, submerged, and flowed forth.
Before the Prince, he further created a great mountain, its peaks steep and lofty, displaying vast precipices and cliffs.
Furthermore, he further manifested a great mass of fierce fire, blazing with intense flames.

At that time, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, by means of their supernormal powers, concealed that great cloud, as well as all sounds of thunder, lightning, and peals of thunder; they caused that great mountain, the river stones, the high and precipitous cliffs, and the fierce fire to all disappear from view.
"Cast the Māra Pāpīyān beyond hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*, so that he does not obstruct the Prince’s renunciation.
At that time, having exited through the city gate and reached the outskirts, the Prince turned his body to look back at the city of Kapilavastu and uttered this lion’s roar:
"I would rather cast away my own body, falling from a great rocky precipice, or drink various poisons to bring about the end of my life, than eat or drink [if I am hindered]."
"If I have not yet attained the power to deliver sentient beings from the ocean of birth and death according to their heart's desires, I shall never enter the city of Kapilavastu.
When the various devas heard the Prince’s lion’s roar, they all rejoiced with him.

"At that time, when the Prince uttered this lion’s roar, all the spirits and deities who guarded the city of Kapilavastu—whether they were guarding the city gates, the walls, or the watchtowers—all cried out with a great voice: 'So it is! So it is! "
"May your lion’s roar of fearlessness, just as it has issued forth from you, Prince, be fully accomplished.
With hearts full of joy, they each raised both hands and said to the Prince:
"O great hero, valiant one!"
Having emerged, he looked back toward the city of Kapilavastu.
At that time, having heard these words, the Prince was neither startled nor terrified; with a heart full of joy, the hairs on his body all stood on end, and he spoke further:

"I shall never again enter this city. Only when I have attained the nectar-like state praised by the sages, severed the stream of birth, death, and afflictions, and realized the path to Nirvana, shall I then enter."

After the Prince had gone outside the city and uttered this lion’s roar as a solemn vow, vowing that he would realize true *tathatā* and *bodhi*, and only then return to the city to teach and transform others, his followers built a stūpa at the spot where these words were spoken, naming it "The Place Where the Prince Uttered the Lion’s Roar."
Now, at that place there was a very large nyagrodha tree, which had a deity residing within it. That deity addressed the Prince in verse, saying:
"If a person wishes to cut down trees, They must certainly exhaust them to their very roots;
Just as when chopping an object, the head must be severed, And when crossing water, one should reach the further shore."
"Once words have been spoken, they cannot be made void; once enmity has been created, one must not rejoice in it again.
At that time, the Prince replied to the tree-guardian deity with these verses:
"The Himalayan mountains might be moved from their place, And the waters of the ocean might be made to dry up,"
"Though the void might be made to collapse to the ground, the words I utter shall never be in vain.
At that time, the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens spoke in verse:
"In this place now appears the Great Medicine King, Who shall cure the poison of the afflictions of sentient beings."
If there are those pierced by the arrows of craving, this Master can now extract them all.
Herein has now appeared the Honored Great Physician, who skillfully cures the ailments of all sentient beings;
if people suffer from the maladies of old age, sickness, and death, he provides the treatment that can heal them all.
Now, from this place, a great torch of wisdom emerges, illuminating those deluded sentient beings who are subject to inversion;
wherever they dwell in the darkness of ignorance and blindness, they shall all behold the light of the Great Radiance.
Now, here emerges one of great majesty, who can act as a great illumination for the world;
with the eye of wisdom and the light of insight perfectly complete, he shines universally upon all realms throughout the ten directions.
In this place now appears a great captain, who shall ferry across those beings yet to be crossed;
having firmly rigged the vessel of the wisdom of skillful means, he will deliver immeasurable billions of devas and humans.
Now there emerges from this place a great caravan leader, Who desires to instruct all beings to cross the vast desert;
To all the countless crowds who are deluded, He shows the way and leads them to travel upon the correct path.
In this place now appears the Great King, the supreme sovereign of the world’s Dharma;
he raises the banner of Dharma and the great signs of the Dharma, causing all to know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
Now this Great Guide has appeared here, Who can subdue all the worlds;
Those gods and humans who have not yet been tamed, He shall be able to skillfully tame them all.
In this place now appears this Great Lord, the Lord of the World’s Dharma, the Unsurpassed Lord;
he shall turn the subtle and wondrous Great Wheel of Dharma, subduing all those of external paths.
In this place, now there has appeared a Great Awakened One, who shall awaken those in the world who have not yet awakened;
for those who are entangled by various afflictions, he can sever all bonds and bring them to liberation.
Now, in this place, the Great Imperial Banner has arisen; it shall rain down the boundless rain of the Great Dharma.
Endowed with the ten powers, peerless in the world, he is able to subdue all those of external paths.
Now, mounting this great white elephant, he shall cross the vast and distant desert of ignorance;
grasping the sharp vajra-pestle of wisdom, he shall shatter all the heterodoxies of the outsiders.
Now, the Great Brahmā King appears here, out of compassion for all beings in the world;
for the benefit of the ignorant and deluded masses, he shall sound the great Dharma bell, conch, and drum.

Now from this place emerges a great dragon; It shall rain down the great Dharma-rain upon the world, Moistening and benefiting all sentient beings of the three realms, And removing their feverish afflictions and all perverse maladies.
At that time, after the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens had spoken these verses, they cried out with their voices:
"Homage to the Venerable One, the Great Being!
They prostrated before the Prince and followed him as he walked.

At that time, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, each possessing a subtle body obtained as the fruit of their prior karma—endowed with majestic virtue and valor, and characterized by resolute diligence that had accomplished what is difficult to do—emitted bodily radiance for the sake of the Prince to dispel the darkness and reveal the path; it was just like the sun emerging from amidst thick clouds and emitting a great radiance, even so.
The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens likewise emitted various rays of light from their bodies to manifest a path for the Prince.

At that time, the sons of the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) each transformed themselves into the forms of handsome and pleasing *māṇava* youths, leading the Prince along a level road before him.
“Mahābrahmā, together with the assembly of Brahma deities and his retinue, walked on the right side of the Prince.
Śakra, King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, together with the assembly of Śakras and the retinue of the thirty-three gods, walked on the left side of the Prince.”

"The Four Great Heavenly Kings each adorned their bodies with various exquisite necklaces and crowned their heads with wonderful celestial tiaras; with these necklaces hanging down, they were further surrounded on all sides by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of gandharvas, kumbhāṇḍas, nāgas, and yakṣas."

Wearing various kinds of firm armor upon their bodies, they held bows and arrows in their hands, or sharp swords, or long blades, or iron clubs, or spears and halberds, or tridents; some held lances and hooks, while others carried shields and bucklers. They walked before the Prince, leading the way, and addressed him, saying:
"O Great Holy Prince!"
"Proceed along this path swiftly; do not linger!

From above in the void, there were again immeasurable and boundless multitudes of hundreds of thousands of billions of devas, who leaped for joy with such overwhelming rapture that it filled their entire bodies, and they could not contain themselves.

They scattered flowers grown on both land and water from the Tian-shui region over the Prince, as well as sandalwood, various exquisite aloeswood, *tagara*, and other celestial powdered incenses; furthermore, there were various miscellaneous perfumes which they scattered over the Prince. Moreover, there were unguents, powdered incenses, and burning incenses, each held in their hands as the Prince walked, scattering them over him as an offering to the Prince.
"At that time, all the court ladies within the Prince's palace awoke from their sleep and suddenly cried out:
'We do not see the Prince!
We do not see the Prince!'"
When Yaśodharā saw that she was alone upon the bed and did not see the Prince, she cried out loudly, saying: "Alas! Alas!"
"We have now been deceived and enticed by this noble son!

They cried out in great lamentation, throwing themselves upon the ground; they seized handfuls of dust and scattered it over their heads, raised both hands to pull out their hair, and snapped and broke the various necklaces adorning their bodies, casting them to the ground. With the nails of their fingers, they tore at their four limbs, their skin, and their flesh, and they tore apart and destroyed all the garments they were wearing.
He raised his voice and wept bitterly, uttering various words of poignant sorrow, while further manifold afflictions pressed upon and entangled his own body and limbs.
"At that time, the palace ladies and attendants addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
'Your Majesty, you should know that tonight, upon waking from sleep, we do not see the Prince.'"
The groom who was in charge of the horse, having lost Bālāha, likewise addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Your Majesty, please be informed that tonight, the king of horses, Bālāha, is also nowhere to be seen in the stable."
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he cried out in a loud voice, exclaiming:
"Alas! Alas! My beloved son!"
Having spoken thus, he fainted and fell to the ground; a courtier took sandalwood water in his hand and sprinkled it upon him, whereupon after a short while he revived and returned to his senses.
Thereupon, he summoned the generals who guarded the city and commanded them, saying:
"You all must quickly array the fourfold army and properly don your armor; seek the Prince with all haste so that his location may be known."

At that time, the general who guarded and protected the city, having heard the king’s thus solemn and severe command, emerged from the palace and proclaimed throughout to the other great generals, saying:
"You generals, each of you should know this!
King Śuddhodana issued this decree:

"Throughout all the realms within my domain, let all the officials and great ministers who receive sustenance from my fiefs and livelihoods who depend upon me gather together; such people as these must swiftly go out in separate groups to search for the Prince."
"If you find him, comfort him with kind words and do not allow him to remain in those mountain forests and ravines; instead, escort him back here.

At that time, having heard these words from the city-guarding general, the various ministers and officials immediately rang bells at every street and thoroughfare inside and outside the city of Kapilavastu, proclaiming:

"All you subjects and citizens who receive stipends from the domain of Great King Śuddhodana, and all those who depend upon the Great King for their livelihood—ministers and officials alike—must all quickly depart from the city of Kapilavastu to seek the Prince."
‘If you find him, comfort and persuade him to turn back, and he shall return to the palace.

At that time, the ministers and officials of the Śākya clan, as well as all the inhabitants of the city of Kapilavastu—both those who received stipends and those who did not—all emerged from the city to search for the Prince.

At that time, the city-guarding minister, having finished addressing all the people he encountered in this manner, proceeded gradually to the residence of the minister in charge of the prince’s horses and spoke to him as follows:
"By the command of King Śuddhodana, seek out the prince immediately; he has departed from the city."
The minister replied,
"I may not go to the place where the crown prince resides.
Then the city-guarding minister spoke again, saying these words:
"King Śuddhodana has issued this strict command:
'All those who serve as attendants to the Prince on his left and right must be bound and imprisoned.
The horse-attendant replied accordingly:"

"Virtuous One, if you wish to bind me, first bind all those who are your own kin—your wife, children, brothers, sisters, paternal and maternal aunts, and uncles—and have them all imprisoned and bound."
At that time, the great multitude of people within the city all went out to search for the Prince.
However, because the Prince was shielded by the majestic power of the various devas, they were unable to find him despite their efforts to seek him out.

Chapter 22: Shaving the Hair and Donning the Robes. *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Twenty-two, Part One: "Shaving the Hair and Donning the Robes. "At that time, after the Prince had departed from the gate of Kapilavastu, he commanded his charioteer, Chandaka, saying: 'O Chandaka!'"
"I now tell you: before me, guide [the horse] and proceed directly toward the village of Rāma.
At that time, Chandaka addressed the Prince, saying:
"As the Prince commands, I dare not disobey."

Leading him forward directly toward the vicinity of Rāmagrāma, the horse Kaṇṭhaka moved with lightness and speed, his steps steady and secure; traveling from midnight until the appearance of the morning star, they covered twelve yojanas.
“The Mahāsāṃghika masters speak thus:
‘A horse travels twelve yojanas in half a night.
Alternatively, other masters speak as follows:”
"From midnight until the appearance of the morning star, he traveled one hundred yojanas.
Arriving at a village named Mṛgadāva, by the time the sun rose, he reached the dwelling place of the seer Bhārgava.
Having arrived at that place, he asked Chandaka: "O Chandaka!
What is this location?"
At that time, Chandaka replied to the Prince, saying:
"O Great Holy Prince!
This place is not far from the village of Rāma."

At that time, the Prince beheld this forest grove, the dwelling place of sages, as well as the various birds and beasts, flowing streams, wells, springs, ponds, canals, and rivers; knowing that Chandaka and the horse Kanthaka were already exhausted from their journey, he addressed Chandaka, saying:
"O virtuous Chandaka!
"Now, if you know the time has come, you should halt here and rest.
At that moment, the Prince dismounted from his horse-king Kanthaka and uttered these words of a great, solemn vow:
"This is now the place where I have for the last time mounted and dismounted; this is now the place where I have for the last time mounted and dismounted."
At that time, having dismounted from Kanthaka, the Prince comforted Chandaka with kind words, speaking thus: "Chandaka!
Among those who serve in this world, though their hearts may be devoted and loyal toward their masters, they possess no autonomy."
Furthermore, there are servants whose minds, though free, lack filial piety.
There are also servants whose minds lack filial piety and who moreover are devoid of strength.
Furthermore, there are servants whose hearts are filial and obedient, and who possess great strength.
Well-born Chandaka!
Just as you today have attained that which is rare and difficult to find—reverently and filially devoted, with a good heart toward me, and possessing great strength.
"Chanda! I am now greatly pleased with you because of such deeds; you have been profoundly filial toward me, and you have loved and revered me with great affection—thus have you loved me."
"You now serve me not for the sake of seeking profit.
Generally, in worldly affairs, those who are wealthy and noble still have attachments and thus seek to serve others;
your service to me now is not of that nature."

Furthermore, there are people in this world who seek to serve others when they are wealthy and noble for the sake of obtaining material goods, yet turn their backs and abandon them as soon as they see them become poor and lowly;
you, however, are not like this.
And he spoke in verse:
"Raising children is for the sake of establishing a household; Serving one's father is to repay his upbringing;
Cultivating fields is for the sake of profit— All these are done for the purpose of seeking recompense."
At that time, having heard this verse, Chandaka asked the Prince:
"O Great Holy Prince!
Whenever a servant intends to perform any task for a person of wealth and status, they cannot inquire about every single reason for doing so."
But today, having seen the Holy Son enter this mountain, I venture to inquire of the Holy Son: for what reason have you conceived such a mind as to come here?
At that time, the Prince replied to Chandaka, saying:
"O good Chandaka!
I wish to speak to you, but what need have you now to know it?"
Candaka spoke again:
"O Great Holy Prince!
Although I am lowly, I was born on the same day as the Holy Son; I am the Prince’s servant, following him in accordance with his will and never opposing his intent."
At that time, the Prince said to Chandaka:
"O good Chandaka!
I now speak to you: can you do this for me?"
Chandaka replied,
"O Great Sage, the Crown Prince!
Since I am now the servant of the Noble Son and have personally attended upon him, how could I dare not do as you command?"
The Prince spoke again:
"O excellent Chandaka!
I now renounce the throne of a noble king not out of fear of others, but solely to seek liberation and to be free from all bonds."
"Chanda! I am now joyful in my heart because I do not accept such a royal throne. Chanda!"
"All royal thrones are a source of great terror;
I now see this clearly within my own heart, Chanda!"

I have seen that there are such benefits in leaving the household life; therefore, I have severed those ties and come into the mountain forests so that I shall no longer be constrained by birth and death. I now wish to seek liberation from birth and death.
"O good Chandaka!
You may now turn back and take the horse Kanthaka to return to the royal palace; I have now resolved my mind to leave the household life.
And he spoke in verse:
"No further words need be spoken; know that my heart loves you.
Since I have come here having severed all ties of kinship, you must now quickly take Kaṇṭhaka away."
At that time, Chandaka addressed the Prince, saying:
"O Great Holy Prince!
When ordinary people renounce the household life, they do so after having seen four kinds of things."
What are these four? They are:
being advanced in years; being afflicted by illness; being solitary and friendless; or lacking material resources.
Yet, among these four conditions, none are currently present in you, O Noble Son.

Furthermore, at the time of the Noble Son’s birth, there were Brahmins skilled in interpreting signs and other experts in divination who, having read many scriptures and being well-versed in various treatises, had previously made this prophecy:
"This boy shall surely become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), ruling over the four quarters of the world as a sovereign of the great earth, endowed with the seven treasures."

Those seven treasures are as follows: the wheel treasure, the jewel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the woman treasure, the minister-treasure of the treasury, and the minister-treasure of the military. Furthermore, one thousand noble sons were born, all of whom were brave and robust, capable of defeating the enemies of others.
That Wheel-Turning King shall rule over this entire great earth, including all its oceans, having subdued them in accordance with the Dharma, thereby attaining governance and transformation.

Noble son, when he obtains the precious wheel-treasure, this jewel-wheel is not made by humans; it is upright and pleasing, and it travels ahead through the air. The King shall ride through the sky, following that precious wheel, while his kinsmen and retinue surround him on the left and right as they fly through the air. At that time, he shall occupy the station of a Wheel-Turning King and receive great merit.
At that time, O Noble Son!
By means of the moon-bright maṇi jewel, during the darkness of night, it illuminates seven yojanas, so that the surrounding ground is bathed in light.
At that time, O Noble Son!
Thus, for immeasurable [eons], he enjoyed the pleasures of the royal throne,
O Great Holy Prince!

If you, O Benevolent One, were now to mount a white elephant, its seven limbs would all touch the ground; its six white tusks would all be adorned and inlaid with gold, draped with golden saddles, cruppers, and halters, and its back would be decorated with golden necklaces and garments, further covered by a fine mesh net. Possessing supernatural powers, it would soar and leap with ease; having mounted such an elephant, you would be able to travel everywhere across this great earth.
"At that time, O Noble Son, you shall receive the royal throne and experience supreme happiness.
Furthermore, O Noble Son!

In a future age, you shall mount that horse-king, whose entire body is deep blue-black, whose head is jet black, and whose mane and tail are exceedingly long; who is adorned with a golden saddle-cloth, jeweled stirrups engraved with precious gems, and pure gold necklaces adorning his body, all covered above by a golden mesh net."

That horse possesses supernormal powers, acting with sovereign mastery and without obstruction; it is well able to leap and travel through the void. When he wishes to travel, the Noble Son mounts him and traverses this great earth, reaching everywhere in its entirety.
"Noble son, at that time, you will receive this royal throne and experience supreme happiness.
Furthermore, noble son!

In a future life, when you obtain the Woman-Jewel (strī-ratna), she will have beautiful eyes and a lovely countenance; her gait will be composed, most excellent and sublime, like a celestial maiden, and she shall appear of her own accord."
"Noble son, at that time, you will fully receive and enjoy the five sensory pleasures at will; the position of a Wheel-Turning King will be exceedingly vast, prosperous, and joyful.
Furthermore, noble son!"

If, in a future age, one should obtain the treasure of the Lord of the Treasury, that minister who is the Lord of the Treasury, by virtue of having attained the divine eye, will be able to bring forth from the earth all manner of treasures, such as hoards of gold and silver, and present them to the noble son.
At that time, he shall experience the five sensory pleasures endowed with all merit.

Furthermore, noble son, if in a future life he should obtain the treasure of the military commander, that minister of the army—being skillful, highly wise, intelligent, of sharp faculties, and well-versed in strategy—will be able to lead the fourfold army. In a single moment, he will know the Prince’s mind and ensure they are all clad in armor, fully equipped and lacking nothing; he will divide them and lead them to the Prince’s side for him to employ as he pleases.
"Noble son, at that time, you shall receive the royal throne and experience great happiness.
Furthermore, noble son!

If in a future age you should fully obtain these seven kinds of treasures, then at that time, this entire great earth, along with the four oceans, all mountains and rivers, forests and springs, and so forth, shall have nothing that does not belong to you."
All his enemies throughout the entire world came to submit and surrender; once they had been completely subdued, there was no place where he felt fear and no place where he felt doubt.

All the people were entirely prosperous and sufficient; there were none who did not submit as subjects. Even in places of peril and difficulty, there was no need for swords, staves, or weapons of war. They acted in accordance with the Dharma, and having acted according to the Dharma, they governed and transformed the world.
"At that time, the Prince shall receive the throne of the Holy King, and his happiness shall be boundless.
Having heard these and other such words, the Prince then replied to Chandaka, saying:
"O good Chandaka!"
"Those physiognomists and brahmins gave me only such a prediction; is there perhaps another prediction yet to be given?
At that time, Chandaka replied to the Prince, "There is indeed another distinct prediction."
The Prince asked,
"What is this prediction?
Chandaka replied:
"Those fortune-tellers and Brahmins further gave this prediction:

'If this youth renounces his royal throne and leaves the household life, he will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; having attained Bodhi, he will immediately turn the unsurpassed, subtle, and wonderful Wheel of Dharma.'"
At that time, the Prince said to Chandaka: "O Chandaka!
Be careful not to speak falsely; you must be truthful."

At that time, the seer Asita gave a definitive prophecy, declaring that this boy would certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and he gave a definitive prophecy that he would turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
At that time, having heard these words, Chandaka’s heart was struck with alarm and terror, and his hair stood on end; he addressed the Crown Prince, saying:
"O Great Sage, Crown Prince!..."
"Do you remember these words of prophecy?
These attendants, Śreṣṭhin and the others, heard this prophecy in secret; do not let the Noble Son learn of it, for we fear he might resolve to attain bodhicitta."
At that time, the Prince said to Chandaka: "Chandaka!

From the time I descended from Tuṣita Heaven and entered my mother’s womb, as well as all the events while I was within the womb, I have held them in my mind and have not forgotten them; how much less could it be that after being born, I would forget the prediction [of my enlightenment]—such a thing is simply impossible."
"Chanda! The devas spoke to me again, saying:
'O noble Prince!'"
If you go forth into homelessness quickly, you will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; having attained *bodhi*, you will definitively turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
"Chanda! For this reason, I know that I shall certainly attain the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and I shall certainly turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma."
"Chanda! I now speak to you with words of truth. Chanda!

I would rather have my body cut by a blade, I would rather die from eating poison, I would rather enter a great fire, I would rather throw myself from a high precipice, or I would rather commit suicide by strangulation; I shall never return home until I have attained the Dharma that brings liberation from birth and death."
"Why is this? Such worldly objects of the five desires are all impermanent; they do not endure for long and are of a nature to perish.
— *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Volume Seventeen.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume XVIII,
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Sui Dynasty.
Part II of the Chapter on Shaving the Hair and Dyeing the Robes.
"At that time, the Prince took from his celestial crown and topknot a priceless celestial maṇi jewel and gave it to Chandaka, saying these words:
'Chandaka!'"
"I now give you this maṇi jewel; take this jewel back to my father, the Great King Śuddhodana, and once you have reached him, pay him infinite prostrations."

"You know my intention; I entrust this to you. You should believe me: I now command you to take this treasure back to your father the King, and inform him so that he may have all his sorrow and suffering removed."
Furthermore, please respectfully petition my father, the King, on my behalf, saying these words:

"I do not now abandon the presence of my father, Your Majesty, because I have been deceived by others; nor is it out of a heart of anger or resentment, nor for the sake of seeking wealth and resources, nor because of a lack of fief or emoluments, nor do I wish to seek birth in the heavens.
It is only because I see all sentient beings upon the wrong path, wandering in confusion through the darkness of deviant ways."

Desiring to produce radiance, desiring to eliminate such phenomena of birth and death, desiring to seek the words that benefit the world—the state free from sorrow—and desiring to sever impermanent and out-flowing conduct, he seeks to go forth into homelessness.
"Greatly Compassionate Father-King, seeing that I thus delight in leaving the household life, you should not grieve.
And he spoke in verse:
"Even if those bound by affection dwell together for a long time, When the time arrives, there will inevitably be separation."
"Seeing this impermanence in an instant, I therefore now seek liberation.
Having spoken this verse, the Prince then said:
"Because I now wish to leave behind this sorrow and suffering, I shall renounce the world and go forth. Therefore, I inform my father, the Great King: you need not grieve."
If there are people in the world who, due to sorrow, become bound and attached to the five desires, those people ought indeed to grieve. Why is that?
In this world, there are many people whose fathers raise their sons for the sake of seeking wealth;
however, those who repay their parents by bestowing the wealth of the Dharma are rare indeed.
If it is Your Majesty’s intention, and you harbor such a thought as, "It is not the time for my son to leave the household life," I pray only this of the King, Father:
do not think thus. For those who seek the Dharma, there is no fixed season.

Why is this so? Because human life in the world has no fixed limit; knowing this, the wise person must resolutely abandon [worldly pursuits] and seek the state of supreme practice—this is my definitive word.
For example, it is impossible for someone who dwells in the same room as a mortal enemy destined for death to claim that his life is long. Chanda!
When you reach my father, King Śuddhodana, speak these various words to him so that the king’s mind may find peace.
When you arrive at that place, skillfully employ such expedient means to console them so that they do not remember me. Chanda!

Nevertheless, I further tell you this: when you reach my father, King Śuddhodana, speak only of my wicked and rebellious deeds, of how I lack virtue and conduct, and how the Great Prince is thus devoid of gratitude and righteousness and lacks a heart of affection; do not speak of my filial piety.
"Why is this? Because he has already abandoned craving, he has likewise abandoned all recollections and sorrows.

At that time, having heard these and other such words from the Prince, Chandaka’s entire body was consumed by burning distress, and tears flowed down his face as he joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation toward the Prince and spoke thus:
“O Great Sage, Prince! We shall do as the Prince instructs.
However, regarding what was said previously concerning our kinsmen and the King, Father, it has caused us great sorrow; my heart is displeased and my spirit is broken.”
"Just as a great elephant king sinks into deep mud and cannot emerge by himself—
having heard these words, who would not shed tears?
He spoke further, saying:

"When others hear speak of this spirit of diligence, they are still greatly startled; how much more so for me, Chandaka, who from my youth have shared the same days and times as the Noble Son, growing together with a heart of love and respect that never ceases its mutual delight."
And he spoke in verse:
"Even if one were to forge a heart from iron, Upon hearing such words of oath and vow, Who would not feel the piercing agony of sorrow?
How much more so for me, who shared my very birth with her?"
At that time, having spoken these verses, Chandaka addressed the Noble Son, saying:
"I brought the King of Horses for the Noble Son to ride; it was by the supernatural power of those devas that my mind was compelled to deliver him here, not of my own volition."
"How can I now sever my connection with the Noble Son’s renunciation?

Since I am a slave born on the same day as he, and this horse-king is of one kind with no difference between us, how could I possibly part from the Noble Son for even a moment and return alone to the palace?"
This can never be.
Noble son!

It is also improper for you to let my Kanthaka go toward our home, and furthermore, to cause me to convey these words of sorrow, grief, and the pain of separation to speak such matters to the Great King, my grandfather.

Furthermore, it is not fitting for the Holy Son now to abandon his aged father, the King, and go forth into the homeless life on his own; that dharma is not right, nor is there any other dharma more sublime, extraordinary, or transcendent than this—namely, the ability to excel in filial support of one's biological parents—and one ought likewise not to forsake the wet-nurse, Mahāprajāpatī.
Judging by this, the Noble Son has also become a person devoid of gratitude and righteousness, for he does not recall the time when we nurtured him in his youth.
Noble Son!
Your principal consort Yaśodharā is a woman of pure virtue, endowed with every excellence; it is likewise not fitting that you should abandon her and depart from her.
Although the Noble Son now abandons all his kinsmen of the Śākya clan, I am a slave born on the same day as he; thus, it would be improper for me to be released.
Nevertheless, wherever the Noble Son sets foot, I shall always follow him in accordance with his will and may not turn back or abandon him.
O Great Holy Prince!

Therefore, my heart now cannot bear to turn back toward the city with a mind scorched by these blazing fires of grief and sorrow, and release the Noble Son here alone in this desolate forest wilderness while I return to the city myself. What words will King Śuddhodana have for me when he rebukes me?

Furthermore, since the noble son has not returned home and I am departing alone, what shall I say when the noble son’s friends and acquaintances, as well as the palace ladies, court ladies, and queens, question me?
The Noble Son spoke to me again, saying:
"Now you must take these wicked words of mine—this act of defamation and unrighteousness—and speak of them to my kinsmen, so that they may forget me and come to detest me."
"How could I dare to utter such slanderous words?

Would my heart not feel self-reproach, shame, remorse, and disgrace? If I were to speak ill of the Noble Son with my mind and tongue, even if I were to utter such falsehoods regarding him, who would believe my words?"
"Noble son!
Suppose there were a person who spoke various evil things and words of insult against the Moon God; would anyone who heard such matters be able to believe them?"
"However, Noble Son, you have always practiced a mind of loving-kindness and compassion; therefore, it is not fitting for you to speak these words of entrustment.
Since you have performed great deeds of compassion and have always comforted sentient beings with pleasant words, to now abandon all your kinsmen is not good."
"Therefore, how excellent it would be, noble son!
Turn your mind toward home and enjoy its pleasures.
At that time, the Prince, having seen Chanda uttering such words of sorrow, grief, and distress, and having heard them, replied to him again:
"Chanda! You must now relinquish the suffering of separation; do not be distressed. Why is this?
All sentient beings undergo birth and old age, and all experience separation. Chanda!

All that sentient beings possess—their hearts of attachment, craving, and delusion; those who are nurtured within the womb—all of these are empty and false, for there will inevitably be separation. They are not me, and I am not they.
And he spoke in verse:
"Just as a great tree where flocks of birds gather, Each coming from various directions to roost together,
Then on the following day they fly apart and go their separate ways— The separation of sentient beings is likewise so."
Just as a great cloud arises in the height of summer, gathering for a moment before dispersing once more, so too is the nature of all beings' partings:
they meet for a brief instant and then are separated again.
Since we have come to be born here together, now each shall return to their own origin;
do not say that there is any difference between you and me, nor harbor feelings of attachment regarding who stays and who goes.
All that comes and goes has no basis; it is only through the attachment of sentient beings that one forcibly creates the mental constructs of "self" and "other.
Each possesses a distinct physical form and appearance, yet these conditions are fundamentally free from defilement.
How much more so for the class of impermanent sentient beings,
who fall away as their time of ripening arrives; the length of human life is likewise,
whether long or short, yet death ultimately leaves none.

I constantly speak of such matters of impermanence; even if one’s lifespan were eight great kalpas, when the time comes for this impermanent body to decay and perish, death is certain—of this there is no doubt.
Just as people from various directions each come To a river, desiring to drink its water together,
Or board a boat to cross to the other shore, Once they have reached the shore, they part ways once more.
It is the same for parents giving birth to children, as well as for kinsmen and all circles of associates;
though they may dwell together from childhood, in a mere moment of growth they must part from one another.
Though they share the same household through the commonality of karmic fruits, their experiences of suffering and joy are not equal;
yet when the matter of impermanence urges them on, each abandons the other, with no distinction between kin and stranger.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the Prince addressed Chandaka, saying:
"O well-born Chandaka!
Therefore, do not distress your own heart now; you must certainly return."
Why is this? If you now cease because of your attachment to your great family and cannot abandon it, yet upon reaching home you return to seek me out;
or if you return to the city of Kapilavastu and see my kinsmen grieving for me, you should speak to them as follows:
"O you, my attendants!
You ought to sever and abandon all hearts of attachment toward the Prince. Why is this?
"I now know that he has made a solemn vow.
At that time, the Prince spoke this verse and addressed Chandaka, saying:
"Even if it were my own body's flesh and blood, And even my limbs, sinews, veins, and skin,"
All things will be ground down, extinguished, and utterly perish; Or perhaps my very life will not be fully preserved.

If I do not cast off this heavy burden, Cross over all sufferings, and reach the ultimate source, Attaining liberation and sitting upon the seat of enlightenment, I shall never return to see you again in vain.

At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the Prince, Chandaka immediately prostrated himself on the ground with his four limbs outstretched; taking both hands, he placed them before him to clasp the Prince’s two feet and spoke these words:
"Excellent, Noble Son!"
I now beg you for joy; do not utter such bitter and cutting vows.
Great Sage, Great Prince!
What power do I possess, what divine virtue do I have, that could cause the Holy Son to return to his own palace?
"But from now on, if I go home alone, the noble son’s kinsmen will surely beat me; or perhaps the noble son’s father, King Śuddhodana, and his maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī, will surely ask me:
'My son of wondrous Brahma-voice and great wisdom, where have you brought him from now? "
At that time, the Prince replied to Chandaka, saying: "Chandaka!
Do not speak such words!"
Do not speak such words!
When my parents and all my kinsmen see you returning here alone, they will never strike you. Why is that?
All my kinsmen and attendants likewise cherish and love you.
Chandaka!
Arise quickly, arise quickly!

In what has been discussed above, there is such a principle: if anyone in the world addresses their beloved person with words and expressions directed toward that [other] person, they will certainly receive a reward.
"You must certainly and swiftly return home; once my father, the king, sees that you have returned, his mind will find relief.
However, when my father, the king, saw me renounce my home to hear the Way and leave the household life, he was overcome with great anguish."

The person of our father-king and his entire retinue are all wailing and weeping with choked sobs; likewise, all the people within the city, both great and small, have given rise to profound suffering and distress on my account. If they were to see you returned, their hearts would find at least a little joy.
At that time, Chandaka rose from the ground, joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation, and with tears flowing like a stream, he raised his voice and wept aloud, saying to the Prince:
"For this reason, I now wish to take the Noble Son back home, so that the lineage of the Great King shall not be severed."

At that time, having risen from the ground, the horse-king Kaṇṭhaka knelt with his front knees on the earth; he extended his tongue to lick the two feet of the Prince, while tears flowed from both his eyes.
At that time, Chandaka addressed the Prince, saying:
"O Great Sage, Prince!
Although this horse possesses the body of a mere beast, he still sheds tears out of compassion; how much more so must the hearts of Your Holiness’s kinsmen feel? What calamity will they not witness?"

I pray only that the Noble Son will look upon this horse-king, Kaṇṭhaka! Seeing now that the Noble Son does not wish to return home, he kneels on his hind legs, bends his two fore-knees, opens his mouth, extends his tongue, and licks the feet of the Noble Son; with a heart of compassionate sorrow, tears fall from both his eyes.

At that time, the Prince—whose thousand-spoked wheel-mark on the soles of his feet was adorned with myriad marks of merit, whose inner heart was as soft as a plantain tree, and whose golden right palm possessed webbed fingers—stroked the crown of the horse-king Kaṇṭhaka’s head and spoke to him, saying:
“Kaṇṭhaka!...”
"You have now fully performed the duties of a horse and have successfully carried this great burden; from this day forward, you, my horse Kanthaka, shall return home and support yourself."
"This is now my very last task involving riding from home; I must travel a great distance, and it is thanks to you today that I shall reach my destination.
Kaṇṭhaka!"

"Do not now give rise to grief or distress; do not weep or lament. What you have carried for me shall bring me great reward. I now seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and when I realize it in the future, I shall distribute the nectar of immortality to you."
And there is a verse that says:
"The Prince, with his right hand— its fingers webbed like a net, marked with the *svastika* and the thousand-spoked wheel,
golden-hued, supple, and pure— used it to stroke the head of the horse-king Kaṇṭhaka."
It is as if two people were conversing face to face:
"Kaṇṭhaka, you who were born on the same day as me, do not weep excessively or give way to distress; you have already fulfilled your duty as a horse."

If I should realize the taste of the deathless nectar, I shall repay those who have entrusted me with their burden by discerning and explaining the profound and secret teachings; my debt to them shall never be in vain.
At that time, Chandaka addressed the Crown Prince, saying:
"O Great Holy Prince!

Today you have already attained the vast sovereignty of a king; Your Holiness is endowed with all the marks of excellence and the treasure of a jade-like woman. The palace adorned by her is everywhere manifest, filled with various kinds of the five desires—most excellent and most wondrous, difficult for the human world to procure—which you have now obtained."
For what reason, Noble Son, do you abandon this exquisite pleasure to take delight in the wilderness filled with various beasts and birds?
Furthermore, this place is full of dangers from wicked bandits; how can your heart find joy in wandering and sitting alone, far removed from all pleasures?
The Prince replied,
"O excellent Chandaka!
What you have said is not false."
Although this is the principle, listen attentively now as I shall explain it for you.

The five desires of the world ultimately lead to impermanence; they are not ultimate dharmas and do not accord with peace of mind. If obtained, they are soon lost, flowing away as swiftly as a current without pausing even for a moment. They are like dew upon the grass, vanishing before long;
they are like an empty fist used to deceive a small child.
Like the core of a plantain tree, it possesses no reality;
like autumn clouds arising, they spread for a moment and then vanish;
like flashes of lightning, they suddenly appear and then extinguish.
"Like foam upon the water, it has no permanence or stability;
like a shimmering mirage in the heat, it deceives and deludes people.
And he spoke these verses:
“The various matters of the five desires are like the butcher’s block,
like a blade smeared with honey, like borrowing another’s utensils for use,
like the wailing over a newly deceased, and like seeing pleasure in a dream.”
After waking, one seeks but finds nothing returned;
It is like a man who has been impaled, Or like the fruit of a tree when ripe, Which will soon fall to the ground;
Like a wicked man with sword and staff, Who slays his enemy without a heart of compassion.
It is like slicing off pieces of flesh, which brings great suffering;
it is like grasping a great flaming torch, which burns the body through lack of care.
Having long enjoyed the bliss of the fruits of human and celestial realms of exquisite form, [one must eventually face their end].
The mind has no sense of weary detachment; having already attained, it seeks yet more.
It is like a person parched with heat and thirst who drinks salt water again and again;
seeking after the five desires and the like, one likewise feels no weary detachment.
Therefore, if a wise person wishes to be free from the five desires,
which are like the heads of venomous snakes, and seeks a long life,
they should distance themselves from them as if from poison or a great mass of fire.
If there is a person of wisdom, they should distance themselves and abandon it.
All things subject to birth and death are entirely without solidity;
not a single moment does anything remain still—such is the nature of worldly phenomena.
"Life has no autonomy; one is inevitably headed toward the Lord of Death.
Having reflected thus, do not remain in this world.
When the Prince had spoken this verse, he addressed Chandaka, saying:
“Chanda! The matters of the five desires possess many such various faults and calamities. Chanda!”
The royal throne is likewise so, being filled with various sufferings, afflictions, and turmoil.

Seeing such terrifying signs as these, I would rather dwell here in this wilderness—a place of fear shared by birds, beasts, and bandits—living alone and traveling alone, far removed from sensual pleasures.
This is my intention; it is not what he desires. Chandaka!
Having heard these words of mine, do not again oppose me in this great matter.
“Chanda! Within these dharmas and practices, I shall open the Dharma-eye; you must rejoice in this and not obstruct me.
At that time, Chanda addressed the Prince, saying:
"O Great Sage Prince!
If the Prince is indeed resolved upon this intention, I now dare not disobey the command of the Noble Son; as the Noble Son has instructed, I shall return home."
At that time, the Prince praised Chandaka, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
O great and virtuous Chandaka!"
"Since you have now thus complied with my wishes, you have obtained great and wholesome benefit; well done for what you have done.
At that time, the prince untied all the precious necklaces and ornaments upon his body and spoke these words of a great vow:
"This is the very last adornment of my body while I am still at home; this is the very last adornment of my body while I am still at home."
Having understood this, he took them in his hands and handed them over to Chandaka; having handed them to Chandaka, he spoke these words again: "Chandaka!
Take these various precious necklaces and ornaments and return them to my kinsmen."
At that time, Chandaka took those various precious necklaces; having received them, he further asked the Prince:
"Noble Son! When I arrive at home and present these necklaces to your noble son’s kinsmen, should they happen to ask me: [what shall I say?]"
“Chanda! For what reason have you now taken my Prince and sent him to another land, while you abandoned him and come back alone?”
"Chanda! What further matters did Prince Siddhārtha entrust to us?
If they ask me such things, how should I answer?"
The Prince spoke again: "Chanda!
When you arrive home, prostrate on my behalf before King Śuddhodana and my maternal aunt Mahāprajāpatī, and inquire after the health of all the other venerable members of my family."
"Chanda! Report this to King Śuddhodana on my behalf, saying:
'I truly recognize that my father, the Great King, has shown me profound kindness; however, it was for the sake of realizing *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* that I have departed from him.'"
"Once I have attained realization, I shall immediately return home to pay my respects to the Great King.
Furthermore, on my behalf, please inform my maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the Queen Mother:
"Do not give way to great sorrow on my account; the Noble Son will surely achieve supreme and great benefit, and shall return to be joyfully reunited with his mother."
Furthermore, all the ladies of my inner court, my kinsmen, the youths of the time, and the other Śākyas spoke these words:
"We now wish to shatter the dark net of ignorance and attain the light of wisdom;
having attained the light of wisdom, we shall return to enter Kapilavastu."

At that time, the Prince took from Chandaka the seven-jeweled handled sword, adorned with various mani-gems, and grasping it with his right hand, he drew it from its scabbard. He then seized with his left hand the blue-black, *utpala*-colored spiral topknot, and using the sharp blade held in his right hand, he cut it off. Holding it aloft with his left hand, he cast it into the air.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, with a sense of rare wonder, gave rise to great joy; he cupped the Prince’s topknot in his hands so as not to let it fall to the ground, receiving and supporting it with a celestial, exquisite robe.
At that time, the various devas made offerings to him with the supreme celestial articles of worship belonging to the higher heavens.
At that moment, among the great assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa devas, not far from and yet not too close to the Prince, there was a flower garland named Sumana.
That *sumana* flower descended and transformed into a barber, who took up a sharp razor and stood not far from the Prince.
Having seen him, the Prince spoke these words: "O barber!"
"Are you able to shave my hair for me?
The barber replied to the prince,
"I am quite capable of doing so."
The Prince replied,
"If you are able to do so, now may you know it is time. At that moment,
the master who had transformed into a hair-cutter immediately used a sharp blade to shave the Prince’s hair— his invisible crown-mark (uṣṇīṣa) and his dark-blue, right-spiraling locks.

When his head was being shaved, Śakra, King of the Devas, gave rise to a sense of wonder; he ensured that not a single hair fell to the ground, but received each one upon a celestial robe, and having taken them, he carried them toward the Heaven of the Thirty-three to offer them in worship.
From that time forward, the various devas established a festival in his name, making offerings on the "Festival of the Bodhisattva’s Topknot Crown," which continues uninterrupted to this day.

At that time, the Prince himself untied all the necklaces and the celestial crown from his body and shaved off his hair and beard. Once the cutting was finished, he observed that there were still celestial robes upon his body; seeing this, he thought:
"These garments are not the attire of one who has left the household life. For a person who has gone forth dwelling among the mountains, who can provide me with a saffron-colored robe?"
"According to the dharma of renunciation, one who dwells in mountain forests must possess robes in accordance with the Dharma.

At that time, the Śuddhāvāsa devas, knowing the Prince’s thoughts, immediately manifested themselves in the form of a hunter, wearing dyed saffron-colored robes and holding a bow and arrows in their hands; they gradually approached until they were not far from the Prince, where they stood in silence.
At that time, the Prince saw the hunter wearing a *kāṣāya* robe and holding a bow and arrows in his hands; having seen him, he spoke these words:
"O benevolent one of the mountains and forests!
"Will you be able to give me this saffron-colored robe?

If you give it to me, I shall give you a Kāśika garment; this garment is worth hundreds of thousands of millions of gold pieces and has been perfumed with various types of sandalwood and other fragrances."
"What use have you for these coarse and inferior garments of the saffron robe color?
You should take such kāśika cloth instead.
And he spoke in verse:
"This is the noble robe of liberation; it is not fitting to wear it while holding a bow and arrows.
Give it to me with a joyful heart; do not begrudge it as you trade it for a celestial garment."
At that time, the hunter replied to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, O virtuous one!
I truly do not begrudge giving this to you now."

At that time, the emanated person immediately gave the Bodhisattva his monastic robe (kāṣāya) and took from the Bodhisattva his Kāśika garment, which was worth hundreds of thousands of gold pieces and had been perfumed with various kinds of sandalwood.

At that time, the Bodhisattva felt great joy in his heart as he accepted the monastic robe; deeply grateful for this blessing, he immediately removed the kāśika garment from his own body and gave it to the hunter.

Then, the person emanated by the Śuddhāvāsa devas took the exquisite Kāśika cloth from the Bodhisattva and, by means of supernatural power, flew up into the air from that spot. In the space of a single thought-moment, he returned to the Brahma Heaven; wishing to make an offering to that wondrous garment, he traveled through the air by means of celestial supernatural powers before the Bodhisattva.

Upon seeing this, the Bodhisattva gave rise to great joy and a sense of rare, supreme, and extraordinary wonder; regarding these dyed robes of the *kāṣāya*, he further developed a heart of even greater reverence and profound joy.

"At that time, having finished shaving his head and having obtained and donned the dyed robes of a monk, his appearance transformed; once he was fully and solemnly attired, he uttered these words of a great vow:
'From this day forward, I am truly called one who has left the home life.'"
At that time, the Bodhisattva sent Chandaka back; with tears streaming down his face, he saw him off.

Once their parting was complete, he stood alone and peerless. Having already donned the saffron-colored robes upon his body, he proceeded with calm and measured steps toward the dwelling place of the seer Bhārgava.
At that time, Chandaka bowed his body and prostrated at the two feet of the Bodhisattva, circumambulated him three times, and then turned back.

Having seen that the Bodhisattva had resolved to leave and would not return home, and moreover seeing that his body was clad in the *kāṣāya* robe, his head was bare of the celestial crown and his hair and beard were all shorn, and his body was further devoid of various precious necklaces as well as exquisite Kāśika garments—seeing that all such things were entirely absent—he raised both hands from afar, cried out with his full voice, wailed to heaven, and threw himself prostrate upon the ground; his mind became faint and he lost consciousness, only reviving after a long while.

Having regained consciousness, he rose and gazed intently at the ground where he stood; looking toward the place where the Bodhisattva had gone, he raised his voice once more, wailing in grievance and weeping, as he clasped the nape of Kaṇṭhaka’s neck with both hands, sobbing with a choked throat and crying out in lamentation.

After weeping for a long while, he beheld that the Bodhisattva’s mind was not to be turned back and there was nothing left to hope for; taking the various necklaces and garments, and leading the horse-king Kaṇṭhaka, he turned back and intended to return home. This was a retreat of the body, but truly not a renunciation of the heart.

As he traveled along the road, at times he would reflect deeply, at times he would raise his voice and weep, and at times he would faint and fall prostrate upon the ground; or he would stand upright in one place, unable to move forward.
At times he brooded with longing and sat without joy; thus, with his mind filled with sorrow and manifesting various signs of suffering, Chandaka gradually made his way to the city of Kapilavastu.
The horse Kanthaka repeatedly turned his head to look back at the Bodhisattva, neighing and calling out as he followed after Chandaka, shedding tears as he went.

Previously, the horse had possessed great strength and moved with joyful vigor; however, because he saw the Bodhisattva renounce his home to leave the household life and shave his hair and beard, he was now oppressed by suffering and filled with sorrow, constantly distressed until his body became emaciated and his strength was utterly exhausted.

Even though this horse was adorned with jeweled necklaces, because his heart was separated from the Bodhisattva, he lacked majesty and lacked splendor; looking back and gazing repeatedly at the Bodhisattva, he let out a great cry, his face covered in tears, and proceeded with mournful neighing.

While on the road, he did not eat grass or drink water; oppressed by hunger and thirst, his gait became feeble and weak, and his power and majesty were entirely diminished so that he could no longer proceed.
The tears in his eyes remained constantly unceasing.

When the Bodhisattva first mounted [the horse], he traveled until midnight at every destination; however, now because his body was emaciated and weakened by the intensity of his suffering, it took eight days for him to return home.
And there is a verse that says:
"The Bodhisattva first set out at midnight; Chandaka took leave and led Kaṇṭhaka away.
Overwhelmed by grief and his strength failing, He returned home only after eight days."

Chapter 23: The Return of Chandaka and Others. *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Twenty-Three, Part One: "The Return of Chandaka and Others. "At that time, Chandaka, leading the horse Kanthaka, took his leave of the Prince and returned to the city of Kapilavastu."

When he first entered, it was as if someone had entered an empty house; within and without the city of Kapilavastu, on all four sides, the groves, the springs and ponds, the canals and rivers, and the parks were all withered, parched, and desolate because the Prince had abandoned his worldly life to go forth into homelessness.

Within the city of Kapilavastu, all the inhabitants, both great and small, saw from afar that Chandaka was returning leading the royal steed Kanthaka; yet they did not see the Prince. Because they did not see him, they all followed behind Chandaka and Kanthaka, proceeding in succession and asking Chandaka:
"Where is Prince Siddhārtha now?"
At that time, Chandaka’s face was drenched with tears; weeping and sobbing, he was unable to speak.

Then all the people within the city wailed and lamented, following after Chandaka and Kanthaka. As they walked, they followed along, their hearts filled with doubt, and they questioned Chandaka, saying these words:
"Where is the Prince now?"
"Great joy has arisen within our kingdom; where have you come from now, having abandoned him?
At that time, Chandaka, as he traveled along, replied to those people, saying:

"I truly did not dare to abandon or turn my back on the Noble Son. It was the Noble Son himself who, renouncing his own palace and casting off his secular robes and appearance, sent me and the horse Kaṇṭhaka back here, while the Prince remained alone in the mountains to enter the homeless life."
At that time, all the people within the city, having heard these words, felt a sense of wonder at such a marvelous and unprecedented event, and they praised and supported him, saying:
"This is a phenomenon never before seen!"
Facing one another, they said to each other:
"Prince Siddhārtha is capable of performing what is difficult to perform.
At that time, although all the people within the city spoke these words with their mouths, tears fell from them like flowing streams; furthermore, each reproached themselves, saying:

"Come now, let us follow him together into the homeless life; let us go to that place to behold the Man-Lion walking on foot. It would be better for me to go there and follow him than to live my life for a single day separated from the Noble Son."
Why is this so? Because this city is now devoid of that noble son, it lacks majesty and lacks power; because it is without the Crown Prince, it is desolate, no different from a wilderness.
Yet wherever he dwells, by the majestic spiritual power of the Crown Prince, mountains, marshes, and forests are transformed back into inhabited settlements.
And there is a verse that says:
“The people within the city, hearing these words, Exclaimed with their mouths, ‘How rare is such a thing!
This wilderness has become the city of Siddhārtha, And there, where the prince resides, is like a kingdom-city.”

At that time, the horse-king Kaṇṭhaka neighed; all the people within the city were each in their own homes, and having heard his voice, all the people as well as the various court ladies within the two palaces thought to themselves: "The Prince is returning and entering the city."
At that time, the people and all the court ladies within the palace either opened their windows or drew back their door-curtains, gazing at the Prince from afar with hearts full of joy.

At that time, the people and the palace ladies saw only the Horse-King and Chandaka returning alone after being separated from the Prince; having seen this, they each closed their windows and doors, retreated into their homes, and wailed aloud, crying out in grievance.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, his body tormented by the suffering of love, thought longingly to see Prince Siddhārtha. He immediately entered the hall of fasting, purified his precepts and cleansed his mind, and practiced asceticism. Overwhelmed with sorrow and despondency, he sought day and night within his heart the protection of all devas and spirits, further employing various skillful means and conditions in his desire to see his son and find solace for his heart.

At that time, Chandaka was afflicted with bitter grief and sorrow, his tears falling like rain. Holding Kaṇṭhaka by the hand, as well as the Prince’s body-ornaments and priceless jeweled crown, he carried them and entered King Śuddhodana’s palace; it was just as when a prince is slain by an enemy on the battlefield, and his attendants carry the horse and the ornaments into the royal palace—just so it was.

The servant Chandaka, having been separated from the Crown Prince, took the horse and the royal regalia and entered the Great King’s palace with tears falling like rain, just as [the Prince] had done.

When Chandaka entered, the horse Kanthaka stood outside the gate of King Śuddhodana’s palace; wishing to enter the gates to gaze upon the Crown Prince and look toward the places where he had moved, walked, sat, and lain, he did not see him. His tears flowed like a stream, and he pawed the ground and neighed loudly, like a person recounting a tale of bitter suffering amidst a great crowd.

At that time, all the various birds within King Śuddhodana’s palace—peacocks, parrots, mynas, jīvañjīvakas, kokilas, and other such diverse birds—hearing the sound of Kaṇṭhaka, also thought, "The Prince is returning home. They were filled with joy and each let out its own voice, warbling in harmonious and elegant tones.

When Kaṇṭhaka had thus made this sound, all the other horses remaining in the Great King’s stable, hearing the sound of Kaṇṭhaka, also thought that the Prince was returning home; they were all filled with joy and began to neigh and call out.

King Śuddhodana’s palace contained many hundreds of thousands of court ladies, including Mahāprajāpatī and others; furthermore, there were over sixty thousand court ladies within the Prince’s own quarters, as well as his chief consort Yaśodharā and her attendants. Because they were thinking of the Prince, they were overcome with great sorrow and distress. With faces covered in tears and dust, each left her natural appearance as it was, no longer washing or combing their hair. Their bodies and garments were all soiled and greasy, and they had cast aside all their exquisite necklaces and ornaments. Dejected and despondent, their minds were ill at ease; some wept and wailed, while others sat lost in thought.
Hearing the sound of Kanthaka’s neighing, they said to one another:
"Since Kanthaka makes such a sound, it is certain that our Prince is returning home; there is no doubt about it."
Having heard the sound of Kaṇṭhaka, they were filled with great joy because of their longing to see the Prince.

Mahāprajāpatī, Yaśodharā, and many thousands of court ladies, each from their own chambers—whether on upper stories, within palaces, or inside rooms—suddenly rose up in eager longing to see the Prince. They ran together in haste toward Chandaka and Kaṇṭhaka.

Those palace ladies saw only Chandaka and the horse Kanthaka returning toward the palace after their separation from the Prince; having seen them, they each raised both hands, wailing and weeping loudly with tears streaming down their faces, as they sang aloud of the various virtues of the Prince.
And there is a verse that says:
"The hearts of those court ladies were pierced with grief;
Thirsting and longing to see the Prince’s return, They suddenly beheld Chandaka and the horse returning empty-handed; Tears fell covering their faces as they wailed and wept."
They cast off their exquisite necklaces and fine garments;
with disheveled hair and emaciated bodies, each raised both hands in despair, wailing and unable to sleep until the break of dawn.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume XVIII.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume XIX.
Translated by the Indian Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of the Sui Dynasty.
In the chapter on the Return of Chandaka and Others:

"At that time, Mahāprajāpatī and Gautamī, having seen the bright pearl from the crown of the Prince’s hair, the parasol, the crosswise sword, the fly-whisk adorned with *maṇi* jewels, and his other ornaments, as well as the horse-king Kaṇṭhaka and Chandaka—having seen these things, their hearts were filled with great terror.
Each raised both hands and beat their bodies, and in deep sorrow they asked Chandaka: 'Where now is our beloved son, Siddhārtha?'"
"You may return on your own," Canda replied,
"O Great Queen of the Nation!"

Prince Siddhārtha, having renounced the five desires for the sake of seeking the Way, left the household life to enter the mountains; distancing himself from his kinsmen, he shaved his hair, donned dyed robes, and contemplated ascetic practices.
At that time, having heard these words from Chandaka, Mahāprajāpatī was like a cow that had lost its calf; she wept and wailed with such grief that she could not control herself.
When Mahāprajāpatī heard Chanda’s report of the Prince’s words, she was likewise overcome; she immediately raised both hands, her heart shattered with shock and terror, and cried out loudly:
"Alas, my son!"
"Alas, my son!

he cried, his face drenched with tears, his entire body trembling. Suddenly he fell into a swoon, collapsing and prostrating himself, writhing in the dust like a fish cast out from the water onto dry land, leaping about in agony.
Mahāprajāpatī was likewise; she fell to the ground and rolled about, speaking with choked sobs as she asked Channa: "Channa!..."

I have not seen any fault in myself, nor any lapse in my mind or speech; I have been carrying you with me, so why do you now suddenly take my son and cast him away in the wilderness like a piece of wood being tossed about?
