"You have taken my child and placed him within that forest, leaving him to dwell alone amidst various fearsome insects and beasts; you have abandoned him and come away, showing no pity for my child—have you turned your back on me?"
Chanda replied, "O Great Lady of the Realm!
This slave does not dare to abandon the Prince."
"O Lady! The Prince himself abandoned the slave.

The Prince entrusted me with the horse-king Kanthaka and various necklaces, instructing me to return quickly to the palace out of fear that his noble lady’s heart would give rise to sorrow and anxiety, so as to ensure she remains peaceful and free from distress."
At that time, the various court ladies within the palace each wept and cried out,
"Alas, our father!
or they cried out again:
"Alas, my brothers!
some cried out again,
"Alas, our great master!"
Or again, they cry out:
"Alas, my husband!
With these various words of love-lorn lamentation, rooted in the defilement of passion, they wail as their bodies suffer.

Some of the court ladies wept with rolling eyes; some wept while gazing at one another; some wept turning their bodies away; some wept with heads held high; some wept looking into each other’s faces; some wept beating their bellies with both hands; some wept clutching their hearts with both hands; some wept with their two arms crossed; some wept raising both hands to strike their heads; some wept scattering ashes and dust over their heads; some wept with disheveled hair covering their faces; some wept pulling out their sideburns and hair while bowing their heads; and some wept with both hands raised toward the heavens.
Some palace ladies, out of grief and suffering, ran hither and thither in the four directions like wild deer struck by poisoned arrows;
some covered their faces with their robes and wailed and wept;
others trembled all over their bodies as they wept, rising and falling like banana leaves swaying in the wind.
Some fell to the ground in a swoon, unconscious and unaware, yet possessing a sliver of remaining life, barely managing to utter cries of weeping;
some ladies-in-waiting were like fish cast out from water onto dry land, writhing as they lay there, with only faint breaths and a meager remnant of life, sobbing in their exhaustion;
others lay prostrate upon the earth like uprooted trees, rolling about and wailing.
Afflicted by all such various sufferings and distresses that oppressed his very body, he wailed for the Prince.
At that time, the sounds of weeping from Chandaka, the horse Kanthaka, and those countless hundreds of thousands of court ladies were so great that they could not be heard [by others].
Mahāprajāpatī, weeping and fainting, revived slightly and then wailed loudly for the Prince, crying out these words:
"Alas, my son!"
Alas, my son!
Your body was formerly anointed, rubbed, and cleansed with various kinds of perfumes, and adorned with majestic power and great virtue;
how is it that you now dwell in the mountain valleys, enduring the bites of mosquitoes, gadflies, and minute venomous insects upon your body, remaining thus in the wilderness?
Alas, my son!
Your body was always covered with Kāśika garments and perfumed incense;
how can you now endure wearing these coarse, rough, and foul-smelling clothes?
Alas, my son!

When you were at home, you partook only of pure, exquisite fragrances and various soups and stews made from the hundred flavors, as well as clean, white foods; other coarse or mixed things never entered your mouth.
How can you now endure eating such coarse, harsh, and bland food and drink—whether it be rice, parched grain flour, roasted grain, or thin gruel—and how can you swallow this empty sustenance?
Alas, my son!

While within the palace, you rested upon fine and smooth bedding, soft woolen rugs, or were covered with celestial garments; with pillows placed at both sides for support, you lay or reclined as you pleased in total ease.
How is it that you now must lie and sleep upon bare, red earth, or upon thickets of thorns and coarse grass? How can you endure such a bed?
Alas, my son!

When you were at home, there were servants and attendants who constantly served you; with hearts of compassion, some leaned against your body, some knelt on one knee, and some stood upon the ground, gazing toward your face as they attended to you, lacking for nothing.
Now, why do you look upon those who are angry, or those who are poor, or those who are tormented by suffering, with no mercy? How can you observe them and seek to grasp their spirit?
"Alas, my son!
When you were within the home, with the exquisite complexion of a fine flower, lovely and handsome, surrounded on all sides by a retinue of maidens, you enjoyed every pleasure;
how is it that you now dwell in the vast wilderness like a wild beast, constantly terrified, sitting alone and walking alone, yet finding delight in your heart?"
Alas, my son!

Your well-formed webbed feet are long and straight; your toes are soft and supple, and your ankles, calves, and shanks are like those of a king of deer. The soles of your feet are as tender as lotus petals, adorned with the two wheels clearly and distinctly marked.

How can you now bear to walk about on foot, treading upon the earth where there may be thorns and needles, or grit and pebbles, or where it is sometimes frozen cold and sometimes scorching hot? How can you endure traveling here and there in this manner?

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, having wept for the Prince with such immeasurable and boundless words of various kinds, her heart was somewhat revived; she regained her original composure, rose from the ground, and asked Chandaka: "Chandaka!"
This being so, what instructions did my son Siddhārtha give to you when he set out on his journey? Chanda!
And who was it that cut off all the soft, blue-black hair of my son?
"Chanda! Where now are my son's locks of hair?
Chanda replied:
"The Great Lady of the Nation, the Queen, and Prince Siddhārtha have entrusted me with these words:
'Candaka! When you arrive at my home, on my behalf, bow deeply and respectfully inquire after the health of my mother, Mahāprajāpatī. Once you have bowed, speak as follows:'"
"I address my request to the Great Mother: I pray that you do not grieve excessively, do not give rise to suffering, and do not think of me;
before long, your son shall attain what his heart desires, and having attained it, he will return to pay his respects to you, O Great Mother."

The noble son then drew the sword from its scabbard with his own hand; holding his topknot with his left hand and grasping the sword in his right, he severed it himself and cast it into the air. The devas caught it and carried it back to their celestial palaces for the purpose of making offerings.
At that time, having heard these words from Chandaka, Mahāprajāpatī wept even more bitterly for the Prince’s topknot, crying out, "Alas, my son!"

Your hair is very long, soft, and curled in a topknot; it is exceedingly well-formed, with a single hair growing from each pore, spiraling upward without being disordered or broken—fit to wear a royal crown and receive the throne. How can you now bear to cut it off and cast it away?
Alas, my son!
Your two arms are exceedingly long, and your gait is composed and dignified like that of a lion king;
your two eyes are perfectly round, like those of a bull king.
His body is golden in color, his chest and shoulders are broad and expansive, and his voice is deep and resonant, like a drum or thunder.
How could a person such as this endure leaving the household life to dwell in the mountains and wilds?

"Now this place of mine lacks the marks of merit; if this person were to practice the Dharma as it truly is, once this ground had collapsed, he would not be able to rise again to become a lord of the world."
I vow that all virtuous persons, endowed with every merit, may encounter the appearance of a Dharma King in the world, bringing peace, security, and happiness to the great assembly.
And there is a verse that says:
"If this land were devoid of merit, Such a person of wisdom would not have been born here.
Since such a body of wondrous virtues has appeared, He shall surely become a holy sovereign for the world."
At that time, Yaśodharā cried out in a loud voice, alternately expressing anger and cursing, using various kinds of speech to rebuke Chandaka, saying these words:
"Chandaka!..."
My wife is young; at midnight, she sleeps soundly and is unconscious of anything. Where are you now taking my beloved, wish-fulfilling, noble husband?

"Chanda! How far from here is my noble Lord, that Great Being? He traveled with you and the horse, these three in equal company; yet now, Chanda and Kanthaka alone have come before me. Not seeing my noble Lord, who was so dear to my heart, my body and mind are now trembling."
"Chanda! You are no good man; you have brought me no benefit.
"Chanda! [he said.]

I speak these essential words now: even a cruel, violent, and extremely wrathful enemy could not cause such harm as you have today brought upon me by bringing me to this state of exhaustion and distress.
"Chanda!

Since you are one who should be my refuge, you ought to have protected me and nurtured me; why is it that now, seeing me sleeping in confusion at midnight, you have secretly and stealthily taken away my noble Lord—where have you placed him?"
"Chanda! You yourself are now my greatest enemy; since the task you were assigned has already been accomplished, why do you continue to weep in such distress?"
"You should wipe your face; why do you force yourself to grieve and shed tears in vain?
Chandaka!
Your unwholesome task is now finished; there is no need for lamentation."

"Chanda! Because you have been my noble attendant and good friend, you have restrained my entry and exit; when it was appropriate to go, you permitted me to go, and when it was not, you restrained me.
Now you have acted contrary to this, allowing my noble lord to depart at his own will."
"Chanda! What use are you?
Having now committed such an unwholesome deed, you ought to rejoice; I know that you have now gained a great karmic fruit and attained vast merit."
"Chanda! Among people in the world, it is better to take one who possesses wisdom as an enemy than to make friends with one who is foolish. Chanda!"
"Although you were a friend to my husband, you have never reflected upon your actions.
Why is this so, Chanda?"
"You have now brought about what is disadvantageous for my household; you should, therefore, feel great joy.
Chandaka!
These palaces, lofty and majestic, like a mass of clouds, filled with various necklaces and brimming with wealth and treasures—all of these are now utterly empty for your sake."
He then addressed Chandaka with these verses:
"It is better for a man to rely on a wise enemy than to take a fool as a friend.
Because you acted without careful reflection, you have caused my entire household to be tormented by suffering."
Then, having spoken this verse, Yaśodharā addressed Chandaka once more, saying: "Chandaka!
How could my heart not be filled with grief now?"

If my husband had been facing me just now, these various ladies of the court—whose complexions are as white as snow, whose lips are as red as vermilion, who are peerlessly lovely, and foremost in their exquisite beauty—would have been present.
She untied the necklaces from her body and removed her exquisite garments, thinking that they should have enjoyed all manner of sensual pleasures together.

Who would have known that one morning she would suddenly become a widow? Because she has no husband, her tears flow day and night like a stream; her wailing and lamentation are constant and never ceasing.
"Chanda!

Furthermore, this Kanthaka has been my constant adversary throughout the long night, bringing me no benefit; seeing that I was sleeping at midnight, he did not inform me as I was carrying away the Lord who is dear to my heart from the city."
This horse’s actions were extremely wicked; for what reason does it now stand before me, neighing in such agony that its sound fills the entire royal palace?
When my noble son was first led out, why did this ill-behaved horse remain silent and proceed with its breath suppressed?
Had it neighed loudly at the time of departure, everyone would have heard the sound and awakened; thus, I would not now be witnessing such great suffering.
This untrained horse, even if it were pierced through the body with arrows or slain with a staff, ought not to have been allowed to go out toward the mountain forests.

Therefore, this horse has brought no benefit to my household; yet, out of mere fear and because of a few lashes of the whip, it has led forth from me the innermost beloved, the supreme holy Lord and Great Man, toward the mountain thickets.

This palace of mine is now without a master; its halls, pavilions, chambers, villages, city walls, kingdoms, towns, streets, towers, windows, gates, balconies, railings, curved rulers, and agate ornaments—its crescent-shaped palaces, so subtle, exquisite, supreme, and magnificent—are now entirely empty and void because of this evil horse-king, Kaṇṭhaka. Thus my royal inner apartments have become like a desolate wilderness; wherever one looks or where one treads, there is nothing to be desired.
When Yaśodharā uttered these various words, so bitter, painful, sorrowful, and choked with sobs, they were unbearable to hear or behold; she became faint and motionless for a moment.
Having heard these words from Yaśodharā, Chandaka lowered his head, held his breath, and with palms joined, wept aloud with tears streaming down as he replied to the noble son’s consort, Yaśodharā:
"Your Highness, you should not now reproach Kaṇṭhaka, nor should you scold or revile me."
I am without fault; neither I nor Kaṇṭhaka are truly guilty.
On the night when the noble husband of the Queen first departed, I created many kinds of obstacles for him, such as by raising a loud cry.
At that time, I called out loudly to my consort with various words, speaking thus:
"Great Consort, rise quickly!
Great Consort, awaken quickly!"
"Tonight, in this palace, the husband beloved by the Queen intends to take me and Kaṇṭhaka away.

Grasping the hair, he showed each strand to Yaśodharā, saying, "This hair was plucked by me at that time from such-and-such a lady; this is the hair of such-and-such a lady; this is the hair of such-and-such a lady."
Each called out their own names, addressing him;
at that time, they were unaware that all the other court ladies were doing the same.
This horse, Kanthaka, also created an obstacle when the Noble Son departed; more than a thousand times he neighed and cried out, stamping the earth with his hooves, refusing to move forward.
Furthermore, with its jaws and nostrils wide open, it roars and bellows.
When this horse neighs, its sound can be heard for half a yojana, and the sound of its hooves can be heard for one krośa.
At that time, I spoke to the queen, saying:
"That which you love has departed this very night.
Yet the queen and her other court ladies were not aware of such voices; furthermore, through the supernatural power of the devas, these sounds were concealed so that they could not be heard.
"O Great Queen, you must know!
Neither I nor Kaṇṭhaka truly dare to take the Holy Son away.
Do you think, by such reasoning, that the Queen and the Holy Lord will accept my words?"
"Noble Son, if you act according to my words, such a thing shall never come to pass.
She then addressed the Prince with these verses:
"I can no longer bear these tears that flow; With palms joined and head bowed, I pray you further: "
"Your Majesty, it was truly not right for you to rebuke the horse, nor should you harbor anger toward me. 'Great Queen!
I have long known that King Śuddhodana had issued a strict command that all those around him must apply themselves with great care to protect the Prince.'"

Although I previously knew that such a teaching existed, I was not free; the power of the devas was so strong that it deluded my mind and heart, so that whatever I wished to do could not be carried out according to my will.
"The conduct of the Noble Son is through the power of the devas; it is fitting that he go forth into homelessness.

At that moment, as he thought this, the city gates opened of their own accord. Previously, those palace gates had been guarded by many thousands of people who remained vigilant and did not let their guard down.
They were all overcome by sleep and did not awaken.
When the Noble Son first departed from the palace gate, he was like the rising sun, emitting a great, pure radiance that shattered all darkness.
"At that time, I knew for myself that this was the work of the devas.
Great Queen!
At that time, when the noble son went out of the city and traveled along the road, I was at the very front, running on foot."
At that time, O Great Queen, my body felt no fatigue.
As this horse Kanthaka traveled along the road, his hooves did not touch the ground; it was as if someone were carrying him along, and when he made a sound, it could not be heard from afar.
"Great Queen!
At that time, in my private thoughts, I also knew that this was the work of the devas.
'Great Queen!'"

At that time, O Noble Son, in accordance with the Dharma, I delighted in the saffron-colored robes of a śramaṇa; having begged them from others, I gave away my own clothes to another, and when I cut off my topknot hair, it was cast into the air without falling to the ground, where the devas received it.
At that time, I knew in my mind that this was the work of the devas.
Great Queen! For this reason, you should not give rise to anger or resentment toward us.
"Why is this? It was not because of me, nor was it due to the horse, that they took the Noble Son away.
At that time, Queen Yaśodharā lay upon the ground; after reflecting for a short while, she lamented and wailed with various words, speaking thus:
"Alas, my lord!
Why have you now abandoned me—who has practiced according to the Dharma and been devoted and filial toward you—and departed?
As for those who seek to practice the Dharma, they possess no true Dharma, because they are unable to act in accordance with it."
"Alas, my Lord!
Have you not heard how those kings of old, when they desired to seek the Dharma in the mountain forests, took their wives and children with them as they departed?"
Those kings will not be hindered from the Noble Path and shall likewise attain accomplishment.
Alas, my Lord!
How could he not know that such a Dharma exists?

Even these people shave their heads together with their wives, leave the household life to practice the Way, and apply themselves diligently to asceticism; they intend to bring fine horses to sacrifice to the various heavens and hold an unrestricted assembly (paṇḍaka-mahāpariṣad), so that in future lives, the two shall together receive supreme and wondrous karmic rewards.
If you know the teachings expounded in the Vedas, why do you now act with such stinginess toward me alone, withholding the practice of the Dharma?
Alas! To have come here in vain is to have been born among humans in mere futility.
If one knows that the world collectively possesses affection and attachment toward women, how can one abandon them?
Desiring to be born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three and craving celestial maidens—when I now observe such matters as these, what is there in those celestial maidens to crave?
"What is so beautiful?
What are these matters of pleasure and delight among the five desires?

If one does not crave such pleasures, and having renounced this royal throne, its majesty, and its merits—along with all of us maidservants—and having thus cast them aside, goes forth to dwell in the empty forests and mountains wishing to practice asceticism; if I were now not to seek the fruit of rebirth in heaven, nor envy the body of a celestial maiden, my mind being content, and possessing such strength that while remaining here I have no need for birth in heaven, but instead practice asceticism in this very place, I would beg for such a vow."

"Whether in the human realm or in the heavens, we wish only to serve a master such as you. Our resolve is firm; even if you were to abandon us and enter the empty mountains and secluded forests, our minds would likewise remain steadfast and unshakable, no different from solid rock—most secure and most true."

"If I, like this wife of mine who now has no husband, were to see my own master depart from the house and travel into the mountain forests, leaving me alone and solitary in an empty room, how could my heart not shatter?"
He then spoke in verse:
"My body and mind are now exceedingly rigid, No different from iron or stone.
The Lord has abandoned me to enter the mountains while the palace remains empty; For what reason does my heart not break?"
At that time, due to these circumstances, Yaśodharā was so overwhelmed by grief and distress on account of the Prince that her mind became bewildered and she suddenly collapsed to the ground.

In a brief moment she rose again; sometimes she raised her voice, wailing with grief and lamentation; sometimes she remained silent, bowing her head in contemplation; and sometimes she was suddenly startled, speaking wildly and incoherently:
"Where has that husband of mine gone now?"
"Where does my noble lord now reside? He has left me solitary and alone within the palace;

he has abandoned me, cast me aside, and turned his back on me. From this day forth, having lost my noble son, I shall not lie upon my usual bed, nor shall I bathe with fragrant water. I shall no longer adorn my person, nor rub it with ointments, nor apply cosmetics, nor wear garments of variegated colors."

From this day forward, I shall not wear various kinds of mixed ornaments; I shall not perfume or adorn my body with incense or flowers; I shall not eat fine foods, nor drink fine beverages; I shall not drink any kind of alcohol whatsoever; I shall always eat superior food, and from now on, I shall no longer [eat ordinary food].

The white hair upon his head was no longer groomed; though he remained at home, he constantly maintained the perception of being in a mountain forest and practiced asceticism. Even before he beheld that most supreme and noble Great Being, I saw all the gardens, groves, ponds, springs, and palaces entirely filled with dust, appearing exactly like a desolate wilderness, no different at all.
"Because the Holy Son of Kapilavastu is gone, all the palace chambers and all the towers have lost their luster, appearing like a desert of sand.

Due to this sorrow and mental anguish, she could not sustain herself and lost her right mindfulness; devoid of shame and lacking any sense of modesty, Yaśodharā lay upon the ground, tossing and turning in such agony and uttering these frantic words. At that time, all the court ladies within the palace raised their voices in unison, wailing and weeping until their faces were covered in tears.
And there is a verse that says:
"Thus tormented by suffering and distress, the maidservants and Queen Yaśodharā each looked at one another as their tears flowed like heavy rain falling in the height of summer."
At that time, seeing Yaśodharā thus undergoing such various afflictions, Chandaka admonished her, saying:
"Great Queen!
Do not give rise to such bitter and piercing anguish; do not suffer with such great sorrow. You must pause for a moment and do not dwell upon the Noble Son."

When the Holy Son emerges, although he is among humans, he is no different from the gods; his majestic spiritual power and physical strength are not distinct from those of the gods. When the Holy Son emerges, he is surrounded by the various devas:

to his right are the Brahmā Kings and their retinues, and to his left is Śakra along with the retinues of the Thirty-three Gods. To his east is the Gandharva King Dhṛtarāṣṭra; to his south is Virūḍhaka, the King of the Kumbhāṇḍas; to his west is Virūpākṣa and the various Dragon Kings; and to his north is Vaiśravaṇa, leading the Yakṣas, surrounding him on both sides.

Their bodies were all clad in adamantine armor; some held bows and arrows, some held halberds and spears, some appeared before the Noble Son to show him the way, some stood behind to guard the Noble Son, and some followed along at his left or right.

In the void above, there were always immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial jade maidens, all filled with great joy that pervaded their very bodies, such that they could not contain themselves; they took various celestial flowers and scattered them over the Son of the Sage, scattering them again and again after each initial scattering.

At that time, when the Noble Son beheld those celestial maidens, his inner mind was neither joyful nor delighted; he felt no attachment, no aversion, no grasping, and no contact. Thus, the Noble Son’s heart remained unattached to their charms.
O Great Queen, Mother of the Nation!

When the Holy Son was born, the various devas manifested such supernatural powers and performed every kind of service to honor the Holy Son; it would be difficult for me now to describe each and every detail in full.
When these words had been spoken, the second consort, the noble lady Gopī, was like a great tree branch that has broken and hangs down, unable to lift itself up.

For the sake of the Prince, the noble lady Gopī suffered great anguish; her heart was tormented by poison, scorched by the fire of grief for him, and her entire body trembled as she lay upon the ground, rolling about and weeping bitterly, crying out these words:
"Alas, my Lord!"
My heart is constantly filled with joy.
Alas, my Lord!
Your face is like the full moon.
Alas, my Lord! Your physical perfection is peerless. Alas, my Lord!
Most supreme and most excellent, endowed with all marks.
Alas, my Lord!
Your pure body is peerless in the world; its limbs and joints are complete, well-formed in their proper order, like a statue of gold.
Alas, my Lord!
Your merit is most supreme.
Alas, my Lord!
Possessing great kindness and great compassion, you are honored by devas and humans. Alas, my Lord!
You are courageous, robust, and possessed of great strength like Nārāyaṇa; you have no enemies, for you are able to subdue them all.
Alas, my Lord!
Your Brahma-voice is subtle and wondrous; the sound you utter is like that of the kalaviṅka bird.
Alas, my Lord!
His fame is heard afar.
Alas, our Lord!
A gathering of merit adorned with a hundredfold ornaments, there is none equal to you in the world of devas and humans.
Alas, our Lord!
Your merit is perfected; all the sages who behold you are filled with joy.
Alas, our Lord!
Your fame resounds throughout the zenith, nadir, cardinal directions, and intermediate points; you are a gathering place for all who offer supreme and universal veneration, like a forest of wisdom.
Alas, my Lord!
Within this world, your sense of taste is unsurpassed.
Alas, my Lord!
Your lips are crimson-red, like the *bimba* fruit.
Alas, my Lord!
His two eyes are a deep blue flame, like blue lotuses.
Alas, my Lord!
His forty teeth are pure and white, like milk, like fine silk, like snow, and like frost.
"Alas, my Lord!
Your nose is high, prominent, and straight, like a cast golden pillar.
Alas, my Lord!"
The white tuft of hair between his eyebrows abides in perfect purity.
Alas, my Lord!
Your two shoulders are rounded and thick, broad and level; your waist is slender and long, like the grip of a bow, and your hands and feet are soft and supple.
Alas, my Lord!
Your thighs, shanks, arms, and elbows are like the trunks of elephants; your hands and feet are perfectly symmetrical, and your nails are all crimson.
Alas, my Lord!
"This necklace was crafted under an auspicious sun, with favorable planets and constellations; when the Great King Śuddhodana commissioned its creation, he experienced great joy.
Why is it that we must now be parted from it?"
"I now likewise take no pleasure in seeing these kinds of necklaces.

At that time, Gopikā, with a heart of bitter anguish, was repeatedly terrified and repeatedly agitated, like a wild deer being pursued by others and driven into an enclosure; with hands grasping swords, spears, or bows and arrows, they shot at her body. She suffered great pain as she ran hither and thither, looking toward the four quarters for anyone who could provide protection or enable her escape.

At that time, Gopadā’s mind was likewise so; her speech was incoherent as she searched throughout the palace and within the halls, from east to west and south to north, but could not find him. Weeping and wailing with tears streaming down her face, and finding no one to protect her, she suffered great anguish and cried out once more:
"O Noble Son, you are here!"

This place is just like the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa devas, identical and without difference, with all things complete; it was also like Śakra’s majestic and towering splendor, its radiance blazing intensely.
Now all has utterly vanished. Because the Noble Son has suddenly and without cause departed, this city is now like a śītavana cemetery, or like a mountain marsh, or like a vast wilderness.
"While I was within this palace, together with the Noble Son, I experienced incomparable bliss and gave rise to great joy, never feeling weary or detached;

now that the Noble Son is gone, my mind finds no delight. It is like a fish or a turtle that has emerged from the water and dwells upon dry land—it finds not even a moment’s pleasure, let alone true happiness."
I am just like this: since the noble son is gone, what joy can there be?
It is just as when spring has passed and the bees find no pleasure; because the flowers are gone, they do not settle in that grove nor do they crave those trees.
I am now the same: because the noble son is gone, what delight can there be within these inner chambers?
"Alas, my Lord!
Wherever you sat or rose, there was always the sound of music; the palace ladies would perform great songs and dances with hearts full of joy.

Now, though this palace remains exactly as it was without any difference, it causes me to suddenly give rise to sorrow and suffering, and my heart is no longer glad—how much more so in the presence of musical performances?"
Alas, my Lord!

Adorned with various exquisite fragrant flowers, graced by necklaces and self-adorned with ointments and powdered incense, you were provided with all necessities at all times without lack; you should have been enjoying sublime pleasures and rejoicing to your heart's content—why then have you suddenly abandoned us and departed?
Just as when great masses of clouds arise in the sky, flashing lightning and rolling thunder release a torrent of hail and rain, yet they suddenly vanish;
so it is with the Noble Son: having succeeded to the royal throne, he ought to enjoy pleasures without any lack, yet he has cast them all aside and departed.

"Surely in the past, after having given exquisite gifts, my mind gave rise to regret. Because of that regretful mind, I have now received this retribution. Although I have experienced immeasurable and profound merit as a karmic fruit, it has suddenly been lost again due to the karma of regret; thus I have now become widowed. I am currently of meager fortune, having lost such a supreme and most excellent person."
Alas, this affection will not last long; it is lost in an instant, just as in a theater where great joy is experienced only for a moment before everyone suddenly disperses.

The present facts are thus; furthermore, it is heard that in the past there were royal sages (*rājarṣi*) who practiced tranquility, subdued their sense faculties, and realized meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Having gone to those empty forests, they abstained from all killing, devoted themselves exclusively to asceticism, consumed various medicinal herbs and sweet fruits, and dwelt in secluded mountain thickets, practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) together with their wives.
For what reason does he now go alone into the mountains and wilds to exert himself so diligently?
Then, Gopikā embraced the head of Kanthaka and wailed aloud at the top of her voice: "Alas, Kanthaka!
You horse devoid of compassion, with whom I shared the same moment of birth as the Holy Son—where are you now?"
"For what reason did you depart at midnight without informing me?
Thus he rebuked Chandaka, saying: "Ho, you Chandaka!"
"You truly have no heart of compassion; since I was already asleep, why did you not wake me?
This one was beloved in my heart, and now she has suddenly departed; for what reason did you not inform me?"
"It is a truly great suffering for me to remain here alone, sleeping and sitting for so long.
Ho, you, Chandaka!
For my sake, tell me: when the Noble Son departed, how did he go?"
Furthermore, who will lead them forth?
While they are in this palace, who will guide them out?
Toward which direction will they travel?
"Where have you gone now?
Having thus rebuked and scolded Chandaka, Queen Gopadā spoke to him again with gentle words:
"Since things have come to this, you, Chandaka, my good man!"

"You brought us here in person and know the whereabouts of the Noble Son; lead us to that place. We shall follow the Noble Son in body, practicing austerities and seeking the Way with single-minded devotion, hoping that in a future life we may be born together with the Noble Son in the heavens."

At that time, having heard these various words of both anger and joy from Gopā, Chandaka felt despondent; his grief and distress redoubled, and a fierce pain pressed upon his body. With tears streaming down his face, he forcibly restrained himself and composedly consoled Gopā’s heart, speaking thus:
"May the Queen listen well!..."
"Do not grieve!
Nor is it necessary to weep in this manner; you shall soon behold the noble son. Why is this so?"
When the Noble Son sent me back, he spoke to me, saying: "Chanda, go!

Upon reaching the palace, inquire after the welfare of all my kinsmen, including my queens and all the young Śākya relatives who are my acquaintances. I have sent you back toward the palace to console them; speak to them on my behalf, saying these words:"

"I have now cast off the net of greed, hatred, and delusion; before long, I shall achieve the perfect enlightenment of wisdom. Once I have attained it, I shall return once more to enter the city of Kapilavastu."

"I know, O Noble Son, that you will certainly attain keen wisdom and fulfill your heart's desire; there is no doubt you will return. I am certain that such a most excellent being as you does not speak falsely."

"At that time, King Śuddhodana, thus afflicted with grief and distress, performed sacrifices to the various deities within his palace. When he had finished what was to be done, he heard from afar the sound of loud wailing and weeping within the prince’s inner chambers, and the king immediately emerged from his own palace."

At that time, Chandaka took the Prince’s necklaces, parasol, and the horse Kanthaka, led them before the King, and displayed each one. Having received the Prince’s command and being bound by his earnest instructions, he prostrated himself at the feet of King Śuddhodana, his tears flowing freely and his face drenched with sobs, as he reported everything in full detail.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, beholding his crown prince’s various precious necklaces, as well as the parasol and the horse Kaṇṭhaka, and furthermore hearing the kind and compassionate words with which the prince had entrusted him, suddenly let out a great cry and wailed aloud, weeping so bitterly that he lost his voice, saying:
"Alas, my son!"
"Who would have expected such a thing regarding that which is most cherished by our hearts?

At that time, King Śuddhodana, because he was thinking of the Crown Prince, felt a grief so piercing it cut through his very body; he fell to the ground in a swoon, unconscious and unable to regain his senses.
And there is a verse that says:
"The King, hearing of the Bodhisattva’s solemn vow, And seeing Chandaka return with Kanthaka,
Suddenly fell into a swoon and threw himself down, Like Śakra’s banner of joy snapping in two."

"At that time, all the Śākya kinsmen and relatives within the palace of King Śuddhodana, seeing King Śuddhodana’s body prostrate upon the ground, were all seized by great sorrow and suffering; their hearts found no moment of joy, and each raised their voice, wailing and weeping, uttering various words of lamentation and crying out loudly as described above."

At that time, all the people within the city of Kapilavastu, both great and small, because they were separated from the Noble Prince, each cried out in grievance, weeping with loud voices as they longed for the Prince.
In this manner, the various kinsmen and attendants together offered consolation to King Śuddhodana.

At that time, because King Śuddhodana was constantly mindful of his crown prince, his heart of grief and distress could not be laid to rest for even a moment; among his relatives, some spoke words to comfort and persuade the king, while others supported him to help him rise from his seat.

Although the King sat up for a short while, he fell back over again, losing consciousness and remaining unconscious; at times he briefly regained his senses, his face drenched with tears, and he commanded Chandaka, speaking these words:
"O Chandaka! You, Chandaka!"
"Why did you not send the Crown Prince back to the palace?
At that time, Chandaka immediately addressed the King, saying:
"Great King!"

You should know that I also exerted great and earnest effort through skillful means, wishing to persuade the Noble Son to change his mind and return; yet, because the Noble Son’s mind was unstained by any worldly or mundane dharmas, he had renounced everything and felt no desire for pleasure. He then said to me: "Do not admonish me;
I now have no use for any of the five desires. I have renounced all my kinsmen, kingdom, and cities, and I delight only in the quietude of mountain forests, springs, and streams."

When King Śuddhodana had again heard these words from Chandaka, and moreover saw the Prince’s various jeweled ornaments lying upon the ground, he immediately prostrated himself; with tears streaming down his face, he wept aloud and said to Chandaka:
"I am now exhausted of strength and devoid of spirit; my limbs are all broken, like a withered stump."

Because I am now separated from this beloved son, I am like a tree stripped of its branches, with only the roots and trunk remaining; thus, in foreign lands, I am now seen as one who is despised and mocked.
Furthermore, being alone and unable to do anything, I am like a tree struck by hail, being toyed with by children.
Alas, my son!

You who are most supreme and most excellent, a subtle and wondrous man of lovely appearance and peerless comeliness, a tender youth—why have you departed against my heart’s desire? Why have you gone forth into homelessness, abandoning the five sensual pleasures that the mind delights in, and leaving me behind?
Alas, my son!
You are endowed with all the marks of excellence, adorned by a hundred merits; within each and every mark, they are all fully present.
Alas, my son!
All the physical marks of excellence were completely and fully manifested upon his body.
"Alas, my son!
While the court ladies slept without awakening, you suddenly departed."
Alas, my son!
When you were within the palace, I had not a single sorrow.
Alas, my son!
The royal families are most excellent. Alas, my son!
Since time immemorial, you have always been born into the superior lineages of various kings.
Alas, my son!
Why have you suddenly forsaken the royal throne to become a renunciant?
Alas, my son!
He is always pleasing to behold for many people—whether men or women, old women or men—and when they gaze upon him with their eyes, there are none who are not filled with joy.
Alas, my son!
Skillful and possessed of great wisdom! Alas, my son!
Having abandoned the four quarters, all the seven treasures, and your entire retinue, you have gone forth alone into the homeless life.
Alas, my son!
Like a white elephant breaking through a great tree, you have left the palace to go forth into homelessness.
Alas, my son!

When you departed from the palace, all the city gates were difficult to open and difficult to close; even when they were opened or closed, their sound reached far and wide. Why is it that now you do not let me hear them?
The gods must surely have concealed that sound. Alas, my son!
Now, in this place, the city of Kapilavastu, there is nothing left to hope for among the Śākya clan, because you, Siddhārtha, have abandoned them to go forth into homelessness.
Alas, my son!

You have been able to renounce all the wealth of the Śākya clan in the city of Kapilavastu—gold, silver, precious gems, granaries of grain and barley, and all other possessions—casting them aside as if they were phlegm or spittle, and have gone forth from home.
Alas, my son!

I thought you had constructed various seasonal palaces for the spring, summer, autumn, and winter; why do you now abandon them and go forth to find delight in the wilderness and uninhabited places, taking pleasure only with wild beasts and the mountain forests?
Alas, my son!

In the past, the various sages bestowed two kinds of prophecies upon you; because of these causes and conditions, I was filled with such joy that it pervaded my entire body, and I could not contain it.
At that time, I unconsciously prostrated at my son’s two feet. Alas, my son!
Now that you have gone forth, all the guardian deities of the city have abandoned this city and departed.
Alas, my son! Your face is as round as the moon. Alas, my son!
Your teeth are pure white, and your eyes are like those of a bull king.
Alas, my son!
Hearing your words in the past brought joy to my heart; yet today, as I recall them, they instead turn into sorrow and suffering.
Alas, my son!

Your body was once constantly anointed with exquisite tagara incense, sandalwood, aloeswood, and gośīrṣa sandalwood; it was adorned with various necklaces and embellished by powdered incense, perfumed incense, and burning incense. That supple body is now suddenly nowhere to be seen.
Alas, my son!
Your heart of love and longing has permeated my skin, flesh, sinews, veins, marrow, and bones, dwelling within me; yet now you have suddenly abandoned it and departed for the mountain forests.

Chapter on the Return of Chandaka and Others, Part Two:
At that time, King Śuddhodana spoke again, saying:
"I now pray that all the World-Protecting Devas of the Four Quarters, who protect all sentient beings, will now constantly provide assistance for the sake of my son’s accomplishment of benefit."

The Great Lord of Heaven, Śakra, the Thousand-Eyed Lord of Devas, the husband of Śacī, the Great Powerful Heavenly King, together with the hosts of devas surrounding him on all sides, we pray that you become our sons and provide assistance for whatever our hearts desire.

Furthermore, the various deities of the world—the wind deity, the water deity, the fire deity, and the earth deity, as well as those in the four cardinal and four intermediate directions—all such deities shall provide assistance.
O Most Excellent One, Supreme among Men, for what reason have you abandoned the four great continents?

This son of mine has now left the household life, aspiring toward the unsurpassed, most sublime, and holy fruit; whatever he seeks, may he swiftly accomplish the path of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and quickly realize its realization.
King Śuddhodana lay upon the ground and, with various words of reproach, addressed Kaṇṭhaka, saying:
"You are an unskilled horse, having long performed many kinds of services for me in matters of my pleasure;
for what reason today have you suddenly failed to benefit me, thus bringing such harm to the Śākya clan?"
"My crown prince has always loved you, his heart was in harmony with mine, and he constantly brought me joy; since you have now acted in such a manner, you must be destroyed."

"You may take me to the place where the Prince is; there I shall practice asceticism together with my beloved son. Because I am now separated from my beloved son, my life remains but a moment; I shall not survive for long."
And he spoke in verse:
“Kaṇṭhaka, you swift horse, run quickly; Carry me back to that place.
Without my son, my life is hard to sustain, Like a gravely ill man who finds no physician.”

When King Śuddhodana had spoken these words, he was overcome by the intensity of his grief for his son; prostrating himself upon the ground, he underwent such torments of suffering, wailing aloud with a voice choked with sobs, now collapsing and now rising up.

At that time, a wise minister together with the state preceptor, a Brahmin, and others, saw King Śuddhodana rolling upon the ground, falling to the left and being supported from the right; their hearts were filled with great sorrow and poison, they were oppressed by grief and suffering, their minds found no moment of joy, and both body and mind simultaneously gave rise to great feverish affliction.
Wishing to open the King’s understanding and resolve his mind, they displayed countenances free from sorrow and spoke together to the King:
"Great King!

You should now abandon all grief, lamentation, and distress; steady your own heart and maintain a sense of fortitude. You ought not to faint and throw yourself down in this manner, weeping and shedding tears like an ordinary man."
Why is this so? Great King!
You should know this!
"Just as in the past there were many kings who cast aside their royal thrones like withered flower garlands and retreated into the mountains,
so too, Great King, Prince Siddhārtha’s past karmic conditions dictate that he shall receive such a retribution."
"Great King!
You should now recall the prophecy formerly granted by the seer Asita, who said to the Great King:
'That boy cannot be constrained by the retributions of humans or devas, nor can he be expected to remain in this world through attachment to the rank of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.'"
"Great King!
If you now truly desire to summon the Crown Prince back, simply command us two to go; we shall follow the King's command and never dare to disobey."
Then King Śuddhodana replied to them, saying:
"If you two know the proper time, you may go quickly to the side of the Prince; if not, my life will now lack auspiciousness, as I am beset and oppressed by various sufferings."

At that time, the great ministers, along with the state preceptor and the brahmins, having heard King Śuddhodana’s command, immediately set out together for the Prince’s dwelling and spoke these verses:
“The Prince ought to accept such a destiny; O King, you should recall the words of Asita:
He was prophesied not to crave the heavens or the wheel-turning kingship, But rather to delight in the five sensual pleasures of the human world.”

"When those ministers and the state preceptor had finished speaking these words, they departed together. Having heard such bitter and reproachful words in various places, the horse Kaṇṭhaka became deeply sorrowful and gave rise to great anguish."
Because of this burning affliction, there is not even a moment of joy;
since the mind is no longer joyful, life comes to an end.
Upon the end of life, one is reborn at that very moment in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

Having been born in that heaven, he later learned that the Tathāgata had attained enlightenment; he immediately departed from that heaven and descended to be born in the kingdom of Central India at the city of Nāpā. In that city, there was a family of the Brahmin caste who fully practiced the six duties; he became a son to that household, and as he gradually grew up, he went into the presence of the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata knew that in a former life he had been born as a horse, and upon the end of his life there, he was reborn in heaven; at that time, the Buddha immediately explained the causal conditions of that horse, and having heard the Dharma, his outflows were exhausted, he attained liberation, and entered parinirvāṇa.

Chapter 24: Observing the Various Heretical Paths from the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra* "At that time, the Prince took a blade in his own hand, cut off his topknot, shaved away his beard and hair, and donned the kāṣāya robe. Immediately, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas were filled with great joy; it pervaded their entire bodies so that they could not contain themselves. With hearts full of delight, they raised their voices in unison, singing loudly and whistling, tossing their garments about, and cried out:
'Prince Siddhārtha!'"
Now he has gone forth!
Prince Siddhārtha!
Now he has gone forth!

He shall certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; having attained it, all sentient beings subject to birth shall obtain liberation from that state of birth, and even those sentient beings who ought to undergo suffering, affliction, and separation shall all obtain liberation from these bonds.
“At that time, where the Bodhisattva cut his topknot, a stūpa was later erected called the Topknot-Cutting Stūpa;
where the Bodhisattva’s body was clothed in the kāṣāya robe, a stūpa was later erected known as the Receiving-the-Kāṣāya Stūpa;
and where Chandaka and Kaṇṭhaka took their leave and returned toward the palace, a stūpa was later erected called the Stūpa of Chandaka and Kaṇṭhaka’s Return.”
As the Bodhisattva traveled along the road, he gazed steadily and walked slowly; when people questioned him, he remained silent and did not answer.
Those people spoke among themselves, saying:
"This seer must surely be a son of the Śākyas."
"For this reason, he was named Śākyamuni.
At that time, the Bodhisattva gave rise to this reflection within his own mind:

'Since I have now already renounced the royal throne and abandoned my own kin, realm, kingdom, and city, I must not give way to regret; once this matter is accomplished, it is a phenomenon characterized by cessation.'"
Having reflected thus, his mind became even more resolute.

At that time, as the Bodhisattva gradually journeyed from the village of Animiṣa toward Vaiśālī, there was along the way the dwelling place of a seer; that ancient seer’s name was Vāgava (translated in the Sui language as "Potter").

When the Bodhisattva entered that hermitage of the sages, his radiance shone brilliantly, illuminating those mountain forests. Having already removed all his jeweled ornaments and cast off all his Kāśika garments, the majesty of his very body still emitted light, dazzling the eyes of the sages throughout the mountain forests.
And there is a verse that says:

“The Bodhisattva, like an elephant king or a lion in his stride, Cast off his exquisite robes and jeweled ornaments, And directly donned the coarse dharma-garment of the kāṣāya; His body still outshone all those sages.”

“At that time, all the brahmin sages practicing austerities within that grove—whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, or holding objects in their hands—remained there according to their respective dignified postures.”
All of them turned their faces toward the Bodhisattva, giving rise to a mind of reverence, loving him with respect; some, however, were filled with doubt as they gazed up at the Bodhisattva.

Yet, within that forest there were elder brahmin sages who had gone out to gather flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, tree roots, or grasses, and others who were away on various errands and had not yet assembled. They did not see him and thus did not conceive any doubts; rather, from afar they heard the voice of the Bodhisattva, and having heard it, their hearts were startled and they quickly returned to their original dwellings within the forest.

That which was to be done shall no longer be done; that which was to be grasped shall no longer be grasped. As for the remaining flowers, fruits, and medicinal roots, even those already taken shall all be relinquished; one’s mind should only desire to come swiftly before the Bodhisattva.

"At that time, all the birds within that forest—namely the cranes, herons, geese, ducks, parrots, mynas, mandarin ducks, kalaviṅkas, peacocks, as well as the kalingas, kuśīlavas, and all other species of birds—upon seeing the Bodhisattva enter the forest, each produced its own harmonious and elegant notes, making subtle and wondrous sounds."
Furthermore, all the insects and beasts within that forest, having completely abandoned their water and grass, neither eating nor drinking, came joyfully before the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the brahmins of that forest, for the sake of performing a sacrifice, milked the female cows to take their milk.
Although those female cows had already been milked, their milk continued to flow naturally just as before.
At that time, all those brahmins said to one another, "We have heard of eight Vasava deities; could this person perhaps be one of them?"
Or again, some might say:
"The Kṛttikā devas—this is one such group. Why is that? Because..."
"Ever since he came and entered this grove, this grove has emitted light that is entirely radiant, like the rising sun illuminating the world.
And he spoke in verse:
"Whether it be eight Vasus, or this one [Vasu], Or two [of the] Seven Ṛṣis, or one of the Devas,"
"If it were not for this forest, why would it be radiant, like the sun first shining upon the world?

At that time, those brahmins who practiced the dharma of rishis and resided in that forest took whatever offerings the forest produced and, with these various articles of worship, invited the Bodhisattva. With single-minded devotion, they prostrated themselves at his feet in unison and spoke together:
"Welcome, O Noble One!"

"We, the various seers, wish to invite the Noble One to dwell here; whatever flowers, fruits, groves, medicinal roots, stalks, and leaves there are, as well as the flowing springs and cold water, are all suitable for your acceptance and use at any time."
"This is the dwelling place of the ancient seers; for those seeking liberation, it is easy to find peace of mind. This place is secluded and empty, and its walking paths are tranquil.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, with words of subtle beauty, elegant in diction and phrasing, and with a voice deep and resonant like thunder or a drum, responded to the greetings according to what was appropriate for his listener.

At that time, among the assembly of sages, there was a brahmin sage who was highly skilled in the methods of forest-dwelling and ascetic practice. Having observed the Bodhisattva’s excellent appearance and deportment, he addressed another brahmin, saying:
"Do you not know, O worthy one?"
This divine youth thoroughly understands the minds of others and is skilled in expedient means. Why is this?
For all people in the world say to one another:
"I have fathered these sons; I ought to nurture them. Once they have grown up, they will be able to establish a household for me, seeking wealth through trade and establishing a livelihood."
"At that time, as I sought wisdom and the Way, if I had incurred debts to others, I would have repaid them all in full.
Thinking thus, out of affection for his children, he raised and nurtured his sons.
"This is not so; for the sake of others he seeks the Way, disregarding his own death and seeking no personal benefit.
At that time, from within that assembly, there was yet another brahmin who addressed the aforementioned brahmin, saying:
"O worthy one, O worthy one!"
"It is so, it is so; it is just as you have said.

People of the world do not awaken to this themselves, nor do they discern it for themselves; they are constantly insatiable, merely saying, 'I must perform such a rite today,' and 'Tomorrow I must again perform such a rite. Even when the time for me to practice the Dharma has arrived, they still say it has not yet come."
Thus, all people in the world, because of their delusion, fail to discern what is beneficial for themselves in this life, and likewise fail to achieve any benefit in future lives.
"At that time, when the Bodhisattva descended from Tuṣita Heaven and entered the womb of a member of the Śākya clan,
intending to take birth, two golden trees spontaneously sprang up at the dwelling place of the seer Bhārgava in the forest."
At that time, those two trees were lofty, steep, and massive; yet on the very night the Bodhisattva renounced the world, they suddenly sank into the earth and vanished all at once.

When the seer Bhārgava saw that those two trees had both vanished and disappeared during the night, his heart was filled with great distress and sorrow. With a dejected countenance and head bowed low, he reflected and thought:
"Surely my time of decline has arrived, as indicated by these signs; or perhaps yet other evil omens are coming?"
Seeing that the seer Bhārgava was thus sorrowful, with his head bowed and his mind despondent, finding no joy, the Bodhisattva gradually approached him and addressed the seer, saying:
"Venerable One!..."
"Why is it that your countenance is so sorrowful and you sit with your head bowed?
At that time, the seer replied to the Bodhisattva,
"O noble youth!..."
"In this dwelling place of mine, from time immemorial, there have been two golden trees that sprang forth from the earth; those trees are lofty and majestic, beautiful and worthy of being beheld."
"I saw that tree, yet now it has suddenly vanished; because it has disappeared, I am now filled with sorrow and my mind finds no joy. Thus, with my head bowed, I sit here lost in thought."
The Bodhisattva then asked that seer:
"Venerable One!
How long has it been since those two trees emerged?"
The seer replied,
"From that time until now, twenty-nine years have passed.
The Bodhisattva asked again:
"How long has it been since that tree vanished?
The seer replied,
"It was only at midnight last night that it first disappeared and became invisible."
The Bodhisattva then spoke to that seer, saying:
"Those two trees grew as the fruit of my own merit; had I been to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, I would have established them here as a virtuous grove and park.
Now that I have renounced the world and left the household life, for this reason, those trees vanished last night and no longer appear."
"For this reason, Venerable One, do not give rise to further sorrow within yourself.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, surrounded on all sides by all those sages, proceeded ahead toward their dwelling place. There he wandered at will, observing the various sites where they sat, rose, practiced meditative concentration, engaged in asceticism, and strove diligently in their quest for the Way.
At that time, there was a rishi within that forest who constantly practiced asceticism; he followed behind the Bodhisattva as he walked.

When the Bodhisattva had entered the forest and reached the place where the rishis sat, he looked toward the east, west, south, and north, observing their dwellings for walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—their sites of ascetic practice—desiring to seek out the most excellent among them. He then addressed those various rishis, saying:
"I have only just entered here and have not long sought the Way; therefore, I wish to inquire of you, O rishis!"
I only pray that you will explain this for me in accordance with the Dharma.
This practice of yours is something I have never known before;
may you reveal it and proclaim it to me, so that having heard it, I may practice it according to the Dharma.
"Those who seek the true practice of profit in this place shall follow my own conduct, just as you all perform your ascetic practices.
Those seers replied to the Bodhisattva, "Venerable sir,
regarding all the ascetic practices and the methods for seeking the Way that you ask us about, we shall explain them to you in due order."

In all their practice of asceticism, within this assembly, some ate vegetables, some ate young shoots, some ate the branches of the nyagrodha tree, some ate the branches of the tṛṇaśūnya tree, some ate the branches of the kaṇikāra tree, and others ate the branches of only a single tree.
Some eat cow dung; some eat sesame dregs mixed with fruits and lotus roots; some eat the tender branches of various kinds of trees; and others sustain their lives by drinking water.
Some sustain their lives like dung beetles; others sustain their lives by eating grass like deer or gazelles.
Some find contentment by standing on the ground, while others find satisfaction by sitting on the ground; some sustain their lives by eating only four mouthfuls of food.

Furthermore, there are those who wear garments made of hemp, or those who wear garments made of black sheep’s wool; some wear garments made of grass, or garments made of wild silkworm silk; some use dragonwhisk fern to make garments, or use *śaṣpa* grass to make garments; some wear garments made of deer skin, or garments made of old, worn-out skins; some wear garments made of matted hair, or garments made of coarse hair; some wear garments made from the shrouds of the dead, or rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*).
Alternatively, they lie naked upon thorns, or lie upon wooden planks, or lie upon tree stumps, or lie upon pestles.
Or again, they dwell in śmaśāna charnel grounds, or dwell on ant-hills like snakes, or dwell in the open air, or enter into water.
Some again worship fire, or revolve with the sun;
some stand upright with both hands raised, while others squat on the ground; some do not wash or comb their hair, leaving their bodies covered in dust and dirt.
Some shave their hair into topknots, some pluck out their hair, and some pluck out their beards and whiskers.
Yet we, by means of such practices, maintain ourselves; subsequently, we may observe the proper time and act with deliberate reflection.

Furthermore, some may wish to seek rebirth in the heavens, while others may wish to seek rebirth among humans; only through the practice of asceticism does their body subsequently attain peace and happiness.
"Why is this? Because seeking the Dharma is extremely difficult; one must take the practice of asceticism as its very foundation.
And he spoke these verses:
"When one practices asceticism in this manner, there is naturally the retribution of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
through the diligence of ascetic practice, one subsequently attains happiness. Therefore, suffering is the cause of all forms of happiness."

At that time, although the Bodhisattva heard of such ascetic practices from the sages, his eyes had not yet seen the ultimate limit of their Dharma; thus his heart did not rejoice, and knowing these words were not truly excellent, he replied to those sages in a gentle voice:
"I have now observed that although your Dharma exists, suffering must be extinguished, yet its subsequent retribution leads nowhere else but to rebirth in heaven."

Furthermore, all the celestial palaces of the various devas and their resultant rewards are impermanent phenomena. Because they practice such minor rewards as described above, these ascetic practices require the abandonment of beloved kinsmen and the relinquishment of all worldly pleasures. By practicing asceticism and distancing oneself from all pleasures in order to seek happiness, one instead enters a great prison.
And he spoke in verse:
“You have abandoned your beloved kin and worldly pleasures, Practicing austerities with the desire to be born in heaven;
Though you claim this is the path to transcendence, You fail to realize that in the future you will return to hell.”
At that time, having spoken these verses, the Bodhisattva further said:

"If there should be someone whose body is oppressed by suffering who seeks a superior state, desiring to be born in the heavens because they enjoy the five sensual pleasures therein, yet remains ignorant of the need for wearying detachment, such a person will not escape the afflictions and harms of future lives."

Those sages, by means of asceticism, seek yet greater suffering! When these sentient beings reach the end of their lives, they encounter great terror and thus seek a favorable rebirth; yet because they seek birth, they remain once more inseparable from that impermanence.

Why is this? Because wherever there are terrors in the world, they return again to become attached to those very places; for, being oppressed by the harshness of this world and desiring to be born in heaven to experience pleasure, they long with thirsty aspiration, wishing to be born there. Yet, their task remaining unfinished, they fall back into states that are of no benefit, nor do they seek weariness with suffering through ascetic practice, nor do they seek the Dharma of a body free from suffering, though they desire to find a superior place that surpasses the pleasures of the heavens.

If there is a wise person who has abandoned these five desires, they must gradually seek a superior state, advancing step by step like one walking forward; having realized that superior state, they must further seek a state even more supreme than that.
If one torments the body to obtain the Dharma, this practice of tormenting the body is called non-Dharma.
If one obtains happiness in the heavens by tormenting the body, it is because through the practice of such a method one has obtained what is not the Dharma.
"However, this body moves and acts because of the mind; therefore, one should first discipline the mind and not torment the body.
And he spoke these verses:
"When this body moves, it is driven by the mind; One should first discipline the mind and not torment the body."
"The body is like wood or stone, possessing no consciousness; for what reason does it weary itself by following the mind?
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke again:
"If, as previously stated, one should obtain merit through fasting, then wild beasts and the like ought to obtain great merit."

Furthermore, because the poor person’s prior karmic fruits are slight and not deeply planted, they lack material wealth; this is just like a person in the world who lacks merit and constantly seeks the meritorious waters of all the deities upon the earth to bathe their body, hoping thereby to obtain their heart's desires, yet such a thing does not come to pass.
At that time, those practitioners of asceticism said to the Bodhisattva:
"O wise and virtuous one!
What faults do you perceive in this place?"
The Bodhisattva replied to those ascetics, saying:
"By practicing these austerities now, you will return in the future to enter this realm of existence.
The ascetics then questioned the Bodhisattva again in detail, saying:
"I have such a practice of the Dharma here.
The Bodhisattva replied,
"How can you know that such asceticism leads back to the realm of existence?"
"Your current practice is not the ultimate entry, nor is it the state of fearlessness.
At that time, the ascetic teacher spoke again to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Virtuous One! O Noble One!"
I only pray that you, O Benevolent One, do not speak thus.

This dwelling of mine and the path upon which I travel are places free from fear and possess great merit; if anyone follows this path, they shall cast off this wretched form and attain a superior, sublime body.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Although one may abandon an evil form and subsequently obtain a sublime body, this is in truth not yet the dharma of transcending existence.
Because of this present body of suffering, one obtains a future body; yet that future body, too, has not escaped suffering."
"Why is this? Although one may practice many kinds of asceticism, though one seeks happiness through such desires, one does not escape suffering.
The teacher of asceticism, further adhering to his own reasoning, addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:

"Virtuous one, it is not so; one does not undergo suffering in a future life merely because of present asceticism. Rather, because we cause this body to suffer now, we will certainly attain happiness in future lives."
The Bodhisattva replied again:
"Such words as these are likewise ignorant. Why is this?"
For example, suppose there is a person who desires to seek profit, yet does not realize that within it lies a great loss.
Because they do not recognize this loss, one who seeks profit in such a manner is not a wise person.
At that time, there was a certain brahmin among the assembly who cried out in a loud voice:
"Rare indeed, rare indeed!
This prince possesses true wisdom."
For example, if there were a person who obtained delicious food mixed with poison, who would desire to eat it?

In the same way, although one may obtain happiness in this matter later on, one has not yet escaped the phenomena of conditioned birth, aging, sickness, and death; is this not merely seeking rebirth once again?
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke again, saying:
"The world is suffering and suffering; though one loathes the ghost of the Lord of Death, one still seeks rebirth—this is the height of deluded folly."
The ascetic said: "Excellent, Prince! You must not scrutinize this practice too deeply.

In the past, immeasurable beings of great virtue practiced this very path; at this very dwelling place, in former times, countless kings and sages—by the hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, and millions—practiced this asceticism together in their quest for the happiness of future lives."
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"That you now speak of ten million years is a rare instance of great delusion!
Alas, what a falsehood!"

Venerable sirs, because of their ascetic practices, these people discriminate within their spheres of experience and seek happiness in future lives; yet they undergo existence through birth and death in the future, never finding contentment. Amidst the afflictions, they fail to perform what ought to be done, transmigrating back and forth therein; because they seek happiness through worldly means, they instead obtain much suffering.
At that time, the ascetic spoke again:
"O virtuous Prince!

This lord of the realm resides in the city of Śrāvastī. That king intends to hold an unobstructed assembly (aviśeṣa-pariṣad) to sacrifice to the various devas; he slaughters living beings in no small number, seeking to receive happiness in the future."
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"Can that which is obtained through killing and harming be called the practice [of the Dharma]?
The ascetic master replied once more:
"We have inherited this tradition from our predecessors; such is the ritual procedure for sacrificing to the various devas.
The Bodhisattva replied, "How can that which involves causing suffering to others be called the Dharma?"
If one's body is covered in dust and one uses dust to wipe it away, can it ever become clean?
If one's body is smeared with blood and one washes it with more blood, how could it ever become clean?
"It is impossible that one who practices what is not the Dharma should attain the Dharma.
The ascetic replied, "Indeed,
such a thing is possible."
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"What is the cause and condition for this?
The ascetic replied:
"According to the Vedas, this was spoken by the ancient seers.
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"What is the meaning of this?"
The ascetic replied,
"If there are people who perform sacrifices to the various devas, this is what is called the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva spoke again:

"Let me first ask you about a mundane, proximate matter: if a person slaughters a sheep and performs a sacrifice to the gods and thereby attains what is in accordance with the Dharma, why does he not slaughter his own beloved kinsmen to sacrifice to the gods?"
"Therefore, I know that sacrificing sheep has no merit.
You practice a mixed dharma with such an intention.
At that time, the Bodhisattva saw from afar, not far from his seat, a grove of trees like a śītavana cemetery; having seen it, he addressed those teachers practicing austerities, saying:
"Venerable sir, merely look at that place: what kind of asceticism is this?
Beneath that grove, there are corpses being devoured by various birds;
there are also corpses where white bones are heaped together, which we can see for ourselves now."
There may be corpses that are cremated by fire until they become a heap of bones;
there may be corpses suspended from trees;
or there may be corpses that have been slain by their own kinsmen, whose seats are adorned and buried according to the rites, after which the survivors feel shame and remorse.
"Or there may be a corpse surrounded by its kinsmen, who escort it toward the Śītavana forest, place it upon the ground, and then return home.
The ascetic further spoke again:
"O noble Prince!..."

However, as for that Śītavana charnel ground, it is common to all four classes of followers; there is no discrimination, and bodies are offered equally upon this ground of merit, which is thus called the Wilderness.

In this place, those who give their bodies do so without the exertion of painful labor; they are swiftly reborn in the heavens, and seeking the superior realms of the world, they quickly attain the enjoyment of bliss.
"Or there may be benevolent persons who cast themselves from a precipice, or burn themselves, or give themselves as offerings, and thereby are reborn in the heavens.
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"If those who practice in such a manner later seek wealth and status, alas, how great is their folly!"
Alas, impermanence!
Yet one seeks the next life; many harbor enmity and resentment. One seeks future wealth and nobility—alas, what great suffering!
To seek such things is to return to great suffering!
"Those who are deluded and devoid of wisdom enter a great mass of fire; they enter the mouths of great serpents.
With such eloquence, the Bodhisattva addressed the sages with words of liberation, speaking these subtle and exquisite words. As he spoke thus, the sun was about to set.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva returned to the place where that seer resided; he stayed there overnight, and when dawn broke on the following day, he traveled to another location."
Those sages followed behind the Bodhisattva, proceeding one after another.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva had walked for a short while, he saw those sages following behind him.
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva sat down beneath a tree. Those various sages surrounded the Bodhisattva, some sitting and some standing.
At that time, among those many sages, the eldest sage conceived a sense of wonder toward the Bodhisattva and addressed him, saying:
"O Noble Prince!
Ever since you arrived at my dwelling place, this region has been spontaneously adorned.
Now that you have departed, O Noble One, it has become a wilderness just as it was before. For this reason, I pray only that you, Noble One, [remain].
Do not abandon the place where I sit.
Why is this? If ordinary people wish to be swiftly reborn in the heavens, those who practice here in this land of merit will, before long, be born and face the celestial realms.
"Therefore, O Benevolent One!
You should not abandon this subtle, pure path practiced by the former sages to travel elsewhere.
And he spoke in verse:
“‘When you, O Benevolent One, came to my forest, it was majestic with your awesome virtue; now that you depart, it suddenly becomes a desolate wilderness.
Therefore, you should not abandon me, just as one who loves life does not cast off their own body.’”
At that time, after the seers had spoken these verses, they further addressed him, saying:
"O benevolent Prince!
While staying here now, have you not encountered those base and evil people who lack gratitude and righteousness?"
Do you see people who have fallen into mixed conduct, or perhaps those who practice impurity?
If it were not so, why, O Venerable One, do you not take pleasure in the place where I dwell?

"We, the various sages, wish to become your virtuous friends, following you in harmony without opposition, and practicing in accordance with your instructions. We wish to seek a supreme and wondrous place together with you; even if the planet Jupiter were to dwell with you, it would still attain a superior state, let alone we, the ascetic sages."

At that time, the Bodhisattva, having received the request from those sages and their leaders to seek liberation together, and having perceived their intention, immediately spoke of the vows originally made by his own mind and further praised all those sages for their ascetic practices, saying to them:
"O worthy sages!..."

Now that you have attained unimpeded eloquence and have long practiced in accordance with the Dharma, because your inner mind is pure, you are able to give rise to a heart of profound reverence and respect even toward those whom you have never known before.
Now, if you wish to renounce them as if they were your own dear kin, you will give rise to great sorrow.
Although that may be so, the Dharma sought by you, O virtuous ones, is for the sake of the fruit of rebirth in heaven; I do not hold such a view.
I now wish to seek liberation with all my heart and have no desire to take up existence. Such is my firm resolve.

Having observed these signs within my own mind, I see that the place where you dwell is not one I find pleasing; I am driven by two opposing impulses—one wishing to return and one wishing to depart—and these two are far apart.

Yet it is not that I do not delight in this place, nor do I harbor hatred or resentment toward others, nor do I perceive the faults of others; nevertheless, I do not remain here, but depart from it with equanimity.
However, you all! You all abide in the Dharma;
following what was spoken by the sages and saints of old, you have all already attained the Dharma of the Great Sage.
At that time, those seers, seeing the supreme excellence of the liberation sought by the Bodhisattva, conceived an even more profound sense of affection and reverence toward him.

"At that time, among that assembly there was a brahmin seer who constantly lay upon ashes or on a thatched roof; he wore a corpse as clothing and rags from a dust-heap, his ears and eyes were blue and yellow, his nose was long and his body white, and he held a *kamaṇḍalu* in his hand."
Having heard these words spoken by the Bodhisattva, he turned toward the Bodhisattva’s face and, with great joy, replied to him in praise:
"The words you have spoken, O Benevolent One, are exceedingly subtle and sublime; they are the most supreme of vows."

That you, at such a young age and before having experienced the five desires, have already perceived their faults and perils—if you do not thirst for rebirth in heaven, how could you know of the subsequent sufferings in the celestial realms? Having contemplated thus and sought liberation, such a person will, before long, attain liberation.
If you, O Benevolent One, possess such an intention and are determined to seek that liberation, you should now proceed with all haste.
Not far from here is the dwelling place of a seer named Guhānuja; there dwells a seer named Ārāḍa, who has already attained the definitive, right knowledge of the pure eye.
"Virtuous one, you may go to that border to inquire; there you shall hear of the true expedient means for traveling the path.
If you hear these expedient means, you will surely reach that truth. As I observe from my own perspective, what you have seen must surpass even that."

"Now, O Virtuous One, with your mind, thoughts, and body, and all their characteristics, you shall certainly cross to the further shore of all wisdom; you have now attained everything that surpassed the former sages and was never realized by them."
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied to those brahmin seers and others,
saying, "I am willing to accept what you, virtuous ones, have described. Then,
