the Bodhisattva set aside the earnest entreaties of those seers and turned away from them, intending to go toward the place where Ārāḍa resided.
And there is a verse that says:
“The noble prince of the great Śākya clan, With skillful and beautiful words, comforted the sages;
As he resolved to proceed toward Rāhula, All the sages returned to their own abodes.”

Chapter Twenty-five: The Return of the King’s Messengers. *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Twenty-five, Part One. "At that time, the State Preceptor, a great Brahmin, and a high minister—these two together, having received the King Śuddhodana’s command given amidst tears of grief and lamentation, immediately prepared a noble and excellent chariot and stood ready to drive it. Upholding the majesty and power of the Great King, they departed from the city of Kapilavastu where he resided. Having left, they followed the tracks of the Bodhisattva’s feet, traveling with great speed until they gradually reached the dwelling place of the seer Bhārgava."
When Bāhuka saw the messenger approaching from afar, he rose to meet him as he drew near, saying aloud:
"Welcome, O worthy one!"
"How is it that you have suddenly condescended to come here?
I pray that you will rest for a moment and stay awhile; please sit and take a brief respite upon this grass mat. I shall prepare sweet fruits and cool water for you to eat and drink as you please."

Then the two messengers immediately prostrated themselves at the feet of the seer Bhārgava; having paid their respects, they withdrew and sat to one side. Once they were seated comfortably, Bhārgava offered various words of consolation to the king’s two messengers.
At that time, the minister immediately intercepted Bāhuka and addressed him, asking:
"O Great Seer and Honored Teacher!
We have come now by the command of that Great King Śuddhodana of the Ikṣvāku lineage; I myself am the minister of that king."
Pointing to the National Preceptor, he said:
"This is the venerable teacher of that king’s realm, a great Brahmin.
That King Ikṣvāku has a crown prince named Siddhārtha."

Out of fear of birth, old age, sickness, and death, he sought liberation; having abandoned his palace and entered the mountains, we have heard that he has arrived at this place, and so we have come here seeking him.
Having spoken these words, the seer Bhārgava replied to those two messengers:

"It is indeed true that a man of superior excellence, endowed with the merit of long arms, once came to this place. Having arrived here, he asked me about the dharma I practice; I explained it to him according to reality. Once he had understood it, he said:
'Although this is superior to the human realm, in the end one returns again into the cycle of birth and death; it is not the place of ultimate liberation.'"
Having departed in dissatisfaction, desiring to seek liberation and escape from birth and death, he now proceeds toward the dwelling place of the seer Arāḍa.
He then spoke these verses:
“The long-armed Great Man, endowed with all virtues, Has come here and heard that my Dharma is not the truth.”
"Seeking the ultimate Great Nirvana, he has turned his back on me and gone toward the abode of Ārāḍa.

At that time, the two messengers—the great minister and the state preceptor brāhmaṇa—having heard the words of the seer Bhārgava, were driven by their filial devotion and their profound reverence for King Śuddhodana. Unaware of fatigue and free from weariness, they neither ate sweet fruits nor drank water; following the instructions of the seer Bhārgava, they immediately set out together to search for the Bodhisattva.

They gradually approached the Bodhisattva and saw him from afar in the forest, sitting upon a bed of grass beneath a tree. Having removed all his precious necklaces and ornaments, his body emitted light, majestic and brilliant, naturally adorning him.
It was as if the sun had suddenly emerged from amidst thick clouds, its radiance illuminating the world and filling the spaces between the trees.

Having seen this, they descended together from their chariots and proceeded on foot with composed dignity toward the Bodhisattva. Upon reaching him, they prostrated at the Bodhisattva’s feet and spoke in unison:
"We pray, O Noble Son!"
"May all be ever victorious!
Having said this, he stepped forward again and stood near the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Bodhisattva comforted them, greeting them with words of thanks and inquiry according to their respective capacities and needs.
The Bodhisattva commanded them to sit nearby; once the two messengers were seated, they addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Great-Wise Prince!
Because your father, the Great King Śuddhodana, loves and reveres you, O Noble Son, he suffers great anguish."

Why is this? On the day the noble son departed from the palace, when the Great King heard of it, he fell to the ground and struck himself; he fainted and lost consciousness, remaining entirely unconscious for a long while until water was sprinkled upon him and he finally revived.
Having returned to his original state of mind, his face was covered with tears as he remembered the Noble Son in such a manner.
Now we have been sent to the side of the Noble Son; we pray only that the Noble Son [will grant us his presence].
With a focused mind, he listened as the King issued this command:
"I know that your true aspiration is for the Dharma; I know that you will not remain in my palace, but must surely go forth to seek the unsurpassed path."
Although that may be the principle, now is not the time for you to enter the mountains.
Since I have seen you enter the mountains at an improper time, I am now filled with sorrow and bitter anguish; my entire body is ablaze, like a great forest consumed by a fierce fire.
"You should now set aside your resolve for a moment and return to enter my palace; for a while, relinquish your heart that loves the Dharma and accept my affectionate regard.
If you do so, this shall constitute your practice of the Dharma."
If you do not return to my presence, the suffering I now endure will continue to increase.
It is like a great river flowing for a long distance; in a single moment, both its banks collapse, the water is choked by the debris, and it suddenly ceases to flow.

Furthermore, it is like a fierce wind blowing through a great mass of clouds; like a fire in a hot day burning dry grass; like the parching heat of a drought month drying up all springs; and like hail destroying the lush crops of spring.
"O virtuous son!
My mind is now just like this; because I am mindful of my affection for you, my heart is greatly agitated, scorched, and shattered.

Therefore, you should first return to the palace, enjoy the royal throne, and govern the world. Later, if you perceive any matters of good or evil, you may then follow your own heart and enter the mountains to seek the Dharma."
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Twenty;
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Twenty-One.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on the King’s Messenger Returning, Part Two:
At that time, King Śuddhodana spoke again in this manner:
"My wise son!..."
Although you now feel no attachment toward your kinsmen, simply follow my wishes and return home; do not cause me to meet my end through grief and anguish on account of you.
"Good son!

When ordinary people practice the Dharma, they give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings; it is only in this way that one may be called a practitioner of the Dharma. How could it be that one is called a practitioner of the Dharma merely by entering deep mountains alone?"

Why is this so? I have heard that in the past, there were those who, while remaining in their own homes, did not remove their necklaces or various ornaments for adorning the body, and allowed their hair and beards to grow, yet—being fully endowed with merit and seeking liberation—they were able to attain the Dharma of liberation even while within the household.
In practicing the dharmas of the path to liberation, one requires only wisdom and diligence; these alone are the true causes of liberation.
That you now disregard my words and enter the mountains is merely an act of fleeing from the dharma of fear regarding the five desires.
Nevertheless, as for those individuals who, while remaining at home and adorning themselves with various necklaces and ornaments, attain liberation—I shall now briefly explain this to you.

In the past, there was a benevolent one named Suichang (Following Constancy); a benevolent one named Jin'gangli (Vajra Power); a benevolent one named Duoyou (Possessing Much); a benevolent one named Liuxing (Flowing); a benevolent one named Dafu (Great Wealth); and a benevolent one named Biantian (Border Heaven). Furthermore, there was the King of Videha named Nengsheng Yeyadi (Capable of Producing Ya-yati; Sui: "Practicing Practice"), a benevolent one named Jingxian (Pure Immortal), and also King Rama (Sui: "Creating Joy"). There were such immeasurable and boundless lay kings who all attained liberation.
"You should know now that one may attain the Dharma of liberation even while remaining at home; it is not necessarily required to renounce the world.
Therefore, you should return home quickly to fulfill two kinds of wishes:
first, that you may enjoy the pleasures of the five desires."
Second, it causes my mind to be constantly joyful.
Among all people in the world, one who attains a royal throne and possesses the power to make their mind achieve its wishes is called a true king.
I can now fulfill this wish for you; though the royal throne is difficult to relinquish, for your sake I am able to renounce this which is so hard to give up and pour it over your head.
"If you establish such causes and conditions, I shall rejoice; I will then take my leave, renounce the world to go forth, and enter the mountains to seek the Way.
He then spoke in verse:
"The royal throne and close kinships are truly difficult to abandon; Now I sever them all completely and entrust them to you."
"Because I see that you are capable of governing the world, I have given rise to joy and entered the mountains.

At that time, the ministers, along with the state preceptor and the brahmins, having fully and exhaustively reported the verses spoken by King Śuddhodana’s oral decree to the Bodhisattva, further admonished the Bodhisattva with three additional points, saying:
"O Greatly Wise and Holy Son!
These are the bitter words of command that our noble son’s father, King Śuddhodana, has uttered to us with tears and sobs.
Therefore, noble son!
Having now heard such a painful command from your father, you ought to honor and revere your father’s command; you must not disobey it.

"O Noble Son, our father the King has now sunk into the depths of a great river of suffering; no one is able to pull him out to the shore of wisdom except you, Noble Son. You alone can provide protection and are capable of rescuing him from that misery."

Just as one who has fallen into the deepest water can only be pulled out by a great master mariner, even so, O Noble Son, your father the King has now sunk into a deep sea of great suffering and affliction; there is no one else capable of pulling him out but you, Noble Son.

Furthermore, O Noble Son, when you were but a small infant, it was Kautamī alone who nurtured and raised you; moreover, she is your maternal aunt. Do not let her be left desolate and widowed, nor cause her life to end.
Now, because we long for our noble son, we undergo great suffering and distress, just as a cow, having lost her calf, bellows piteously.
In this very way, because her eyes cannot see her noble son, that Gautamī wails with grief and sorrow, constantly weeping; therefore, noble son, you should not abandon us.
Furthermore, due to the grace of his past nurturing, just as that ox yearns for its calf, so too do the women and retinues within the palace likewise undergo suffering.
Furthermore, within the city of Kapilavastu, all the Śākya men and women, both great and small, were tormented by the fire of suffering because their hearts were parched with love for the Noble Son.
Therefore, noble son!
You may now return home to see them; just as when the great earth is scorched by fire, the gods above send down a great rain of sweet nectar to extinguish that fierce and agonizing heat.

At that time, having heard these words from his father the King’s messenger, the Bodhisattva reflected for a short while. Having composed his body, mind, and speech and stilled his breath, he replied to the messenger:

"I have long known that fathers toward their sons always possess a heart of love; I know that my father, the Great King Śuddhodana, feels a heart of extreme affection, longing, and attachment toward me."
I now do so merely because I am terrified by the birth, aging, sickness, and death of the world; seeing myself submerged, how could I save those who are sinking?
Desiring liberation, I have therefore abandoned those kinsmen.
Who, indeed, would delight in abandoning such beloved kin? Who would not wish to see them constantly?
If there were no separation from those one loves within this world, who would not find joy in it?

Although one may dwell for a long time together with one's circle of kinsmen, one must inevitably part from them; therefore, I now renounce all beloved relatives as well as my father and mother, resolving to seek Bodhi.
If it is as you say— that because of my love for me, my father the King has been brought to great suffering—
having heard these words, I truly have no attachment to such affection.

Why is this so? It is like a person who, while asleep, dreams of being reunited with loved ones, only to find them separated again upon waking. If such an ordinary person does not understand the skillful means [to transcend this], their mind gives rise to suffering; these are ignorant and deluded sentient beings.

If there is a wise person who can reflect for themselves: the gathering of those one holds dear is like travelers on a road who join as companions and travel together; as they follow one another for near or far distances until reaching their destination, they each disperse and return to their own origins.
For this reason, since even beloved kin and retinues that have gathered must eventually part, why should one feel grief and distress?
Furthermore, in previous lives, those who were once one's kin have been left behind as one came here;
likewise, the kin of this life will be left behind when one reaches the next world.
After they have been abandoned in one lifetime, they are again abandoned in a subsequent lifetime;
as they thus pass from one to another in mutual abandonment, from where does this heart of affection for these kinsmen arise?
Wherever one goes,
for all people in the world from the moment of conception until they reach every destination, at every single thought-moment and instant, the ghost of death pursues them.
What is it like this?
It is the timely and the untimely.
Now you speak thus to me:
"My son, this is not the time for you to enter the mountains to seek the Way;
how much less so while living at home and indulging in the five desires?
If you were to ask me whether this is the right or wrong time, I shall now briefly address it."

Why is this? That demon of death seizes all sentient beings at all times; there is no time when it does not seize them. Therefore, I now seek to escape that cycle of birth, old age, sickness, and death. For this reason, there is no time that is not the right time [to act].
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"If my father were to call for his son and simply say, 'Come,' I would certainly grant the son the consecrated rank of a universal monarch.
My father must possess a most great and expansive vow; that he could so easily grant me such a difficult task is a pity, as it prevents me from cultivating the Path."
However, I do not wish to accept this royal throne; attachment to loved ones is a bond, not the path to liberation.
Just as a sick person has no thought for fine food, how could a wise person crave such worldly pleasures?
Because that body of ignorance, false perception, and delusion is fraught with great suffering and affliction, one is thus able to accept this royal throne.

Yet once established upon the throne, one becomes heedless and self-indulgent, wallowing in wine and sensual pleasures without being able to renounce them; it is like a golden palace engulfed in a raging fire, like delicious broth mixed with various poisons, or like a lotus pond inhabited by a dragon.
"Even so, even so; the pleasures of sovereignty and the enjoyments of the mind are pursued by all manner of afflictions, yet one neither perceives nor knows them.
For these reasons, I now find no joy in them, nor do they accord with the Dharma."
And he spoke in verse:
"Just as a golden house ablaze with fierce fire, Like delicious food mixed with deadly poison,
Or like a lotus-filled pond inhabited by a dragon— The enjoyment of royal power brings great suffering later."
At that time, having spoken this verse, the Bodhisattva further said:

"For this reason, in the past, when various kings had attained the throne, they governed and enjoyed pleasures during their youth; later, upon reaching old age, they grew weary of and detached from the five desires, abandoning their palaces to enter the mountain forests."

An ordinary person would rather dwell in the mountain forests, sustaining life by eating grass, than reside in palaces to enjoy the pleasures of the five desires, which is like raising a black snake only to suffer its calamity later.
When first experiencing pleasure, one does not recognize its harm; later, when anger arises, it will bite one.
It is better to abandon the household life and enter the mountain forests than to abandon the mountain forests and return to the household life.
Why is this? Because [such conduct] was censured by the former sages.
Now that I have been born into a noble family, I ought to cultivate wholesome dharmas; I must not, like a deluded person, practice unwholesome dharmas and allow my own mind to run wild.
Having shaved off their hair and beard and donned the kashaya robes, they dwell in mountain forests to cultivate the Way and study.
Yet, later on, they cast off those kashaya robes and harbor no sense of shame; such are called shameless and foolish people.
Whether out of greed, or out of anger, or out of delusion, or out of fear of others, one thus regresses.
I do not now envy the palace of Śakra, Lord of Devas, much less would I wish to return to my own home.
For example, suppose there is a person who has obtained fine food; after having eaten it, they vomit it out and discard it on the ground. Would they then be able to eat it again?

It is just so, just so. If a person abandons those five desires and leaves the household life, yet for various reasons wishes to return to the household, it is exactly like this—just as if someone who has already left a burning house wishes to enter it again.
"In this way and that way, having seen the perils of the mundane world, one abandons the form of a layperson and enters the mountains to practice the Way; yet the returning is likewise so.
And he spoke in verse:
"Just as a person flees from a burning house, Only to suddenly turn back once again at a later time,"
"Having seen the afflictions of worldly life, one leaves home; to return from the forest back to the world is likewise so.
When the Bodhisattva had spoken this verse, he addressed the two messengers, saying:

"As for what you previously cited regarding your father the King’s words—that in the past there were kings who practiced the Dharma while remaining at home and attained liberation—this is not the case."
Why is this? These two matters have causes and conditions that are contradictory, being vastly separated from one another. Why is that so?
One who seeks liberation must have a mind that is tranquil and settled; only in such a subtle and sublime state can one find rest.

If one dwells within the palace, the passions of the five desires will be turbulent; if one goes out to govern the people, one must resort to whipping, beating, anger, reprimand, and punishment. For one to seek liberation amidst such mental states is impossible.
If a person’s inclination is toward the unconditioned tranquility, they will not crave worldly sovereignty; even if they should hold such a position, they must renounce it.
If one delights in sovereignty, that person’s mind cannot attain tranquility.

If one delights in tranquil concentration yet craves worldly affairs, these two are diametrically opposed and as far apart as heaven and earth; they cannot coexist, just as water and fire cannot dwell together.
In this very way, it is impossible for one who seeks the Dharma of liberation to remain attached to the five desires.
Therefore, I now know for certain that those kings of the past attained the Dharma of tranquil concentration only after they had relinquished their royal thrones.

While they were still on the throne and engaged in governing, their wisdom was not yet perfected; at that time, they merely practiced the application of the mind to manage the people, rather than focusing exclusively on seeking the Dharma of liberation.
Although that may be so, those various kings each followed their own inclinations, seeking either liberation or indulging in the five desires;
I am not like them now, for I do not emulate them, nor have I ever given rise to such a thought.
"I have now severed the shackles of desire for the household life and attained liberation; I no longer crave the five worldly desires. How could I return home?
At that time, the two messengers, hearing these words of the Bodhisattva—words free from attachment, focused, decisive, and truly authentic—again addressed the Bodhisattva in detail:
"O Great Sage, Prince!..."
The vow I have now made to seek the unsurpassed Dharma is true and not without reason;
however, to act in this manner at present is not yet the right time.
Why is this? Your father, the Holy King, now endures such grief and affliction;
therefore, O Noble Son, to act contrary to his heart is not in accordance with the True Dharma.
And he spoke in verse:
"Now seeking the treasury of the Dharma is truly beneficial; yet though there be right principle, it does not accord with the timing.
My father, the King, is tormented by grief that cuts through his heart; if filial virtue is thus neglected, what kind of path is this?"
"Then, after the two messengers had spoken these verses, they addressed the Noble Son again, saying:
'O Great Holy Prince!
As we perceive it, this intention of yours is not a subtle contemplation of the Dharma; regarding worldly wealth and the five desires, it is not a skillful means.'"
Why is this? Noble son, you have not yet seen the cause; how can you seek the fruit?
Having obtained the present retribution, you now abandon it to seek that which lies in the future.
O Great Sage, Prince!
Regarding all the various scriptures in the world, each possesses its own *siddhānta*. Some people say:
"There is a future world."
Some may say: "There is no future world.
Yet, regarding this matter, many people harbor doubts.
"Therefore, O Noble Son!
Since you have attained the retribution of the fruit and are currently experiencing it, if there were no future life, why would you need to strive diligently for that liberation?
Furthermore, some people say:
"To determine that there is good and evil in the world, and that one will experience their results in future lives"—
to diligently practice for the sake of seeking the path to liberation based on this principle is called delusion (*moha*).

If the sense faculties were destined to perish, if separation from loved ones and encounter with those one hates were inevitable, and if contact with sensory objects led naturally to their abandonment, then why would it be necessary to exert effort through skillful means against birth, old age, sickness, and death?
One should know that this principle has no reality.
Furthermore, while in the womb, the hands, feet, chest, back, abdomen, hair, nails, joints, and network of channels are all spontaneously formed.
Furthermore, there may be someone who, having attained the formation of a body, has it subsequently destroyed; or there may be someone who says:
"Once it has been destroyed, it naturally forms again."
Therefore, in the ancient scriptures, there is this saying:
"The sharp point of a thorn—who whetted it?
The variegated colors of birds and beasts—who painted them?"

This principle is spontaneous and not created by anyone; furthermore, it cannot be made to succeed simply because one desires it, for worldly phenomena cannot be turned at will according to one's mind.
And there is a verse that says:
"Who sharpened the point of the thorn?
Who painted the variegated colors of birds and beasts?"
Each transforms according to its own karma; there is no creator within the world.
Furthermore, some say:
"The creator of the world is entirely the work of Īśvara. If things were produced spontaneously, why would people need to exert themselves in labor?"
"It is not that one comes by means of this cause of transmigration, nor that when departing, one departs by means of that same cause of transmigration.
"Furthermore, some say: 'Because of discrimination, the mark of self arises; therefore one undergoes existence (bhava), and the exhaustion of existence is likewise so.'"
If sensation has a time of arising, it arises spontaneously without depending on diligent seeking;
if it has a time of ceasing, it ceases spontaneously, nor does it depend on extinction.
"Furthermore, some say:

'When one is about to receive a human body in this world, if one's father has not incurred debts to others, then one may be born; this applies equally to birth in the heavens or as a celestial being (ṛṣi), in all such cases.'"
If one is free from debt in these three places, this person need not exert effort, but will attain liberation in those places spontaneously, just so.
In the various sūtras in succession, each according to its own *siddhānta* (established tenet) declares this very thing, and each attains liberation.
When a wise person diligently seeks a superior state, they will inevitably cause their mind to suffer.

Therefore, I know that if you, Noble Son, desire to seek liberation, you should seek the path to liberation by relying on reason and relying on the Dharma, just as it is fully explained in the established conclusions (siddhānta) of the ancient scriptures.
If it is thus, you will certainly attain it; there is no doubt.
For the sake of the noble son, his compassionate father, King Śuddhodana, who has endured the suffering of attachment, shall surely find healing.
"Noble Son, when you now return to the palace, if you should find the sight of the palaces within your mind to be a source of weariness or aversion, you need not dwell upon it. Why is this?"
In the past, there were various royal sages who, having renounced their homes and gone into the mountain forests, later returned to their own palaces.
It is said that those kings each had their own distinct names.

The so-called King Āmrapālīśa—translated into the Sui language as "Space-Arrow"—having renounced his home to dwell among the mountains and forests, was exhorted and enlightened by his ministers and officials; those to his left and right, and before and behind him, surrounded him and returned [to the city].

King Rāma—translated into the Sui language as "Capable of Delighting"—having seen that the great earth had been ravaged by wicked men, who were seizing one another's property and killing each other in turn, could not bear to look upon it. He emerged from the mountains and protected [the land] in accordance with the Dharma.

Furthermore, in the past, in the city of Vaiśālī, there was a great king named Tuluomo (translated in the Sui language as "Tree"), who also came down from the mountain forests to his own kingdom to protect and sustain the world.

Furthermore, in the past, there was a king of brahmanical seers named Śakrāditya (translated in the Sui language as "Leaving Words"), a king of brahmanical seers named Rājyadatta (translated in the Sui language as "Delighting in Heaven"), and a king of brahmanical seers named Dharmayaśas (translated in the Sui language as "Dharma Renown"). Countless and boundless kings such as these, having each abandoned the mountain forests, returned to their original palaces to pacify and govern the great earth.
"Therefore, O Noble Son!
Having heard these accounts of the former deeds of the kings of old, you shall have no further suffering or affliction upon returning to the palace.
And he spoke in verse:

"Kings of such renown as these, each having abandoned their court ladies to enter the mountain forests, later all left the mountains to return to their own palaces; what fault is there now in the Noble Son’s return?"
At that time, having heard these words from the two messengers, the Bodhisattva addressed the great minister and the state preceptor, the Brahmin, saying:
"As for the meaning of existence and non-existence, whether there is doubt or no doubt, I know it myself."
As for these two meanings and all truths therein—whether hidden or manifest—I accept them;
yet as for those things merely heard by report, since they lack any causal basis, how can they be trusted?

If there is a wise person, they should not act in reliance upon the false speech of others; it would be like a blind person wishing to travel a road who, having no guide and not seeing the reality, how could they proceed?
My mind cannot decide for itself whether this is good or not; that blind and foolish person, even if confronted with pure phenomena, perceives them as impure because of his lack of wisdom.

Therefore, I would rather now arouse a heart of diligent effort; though I have not yet attained the goal, I am willing to undergo long-term suffering as its retribution. Truly, I cannot bear to be mired and submerged in the mud of the five desires, only to be rebuked by the noble ones for the sake of a momentary pleasure.
Furthermore, as for your claim that in the past, both the Arrow King of Space (Gaganasara-rāja) and the One Who Brings Joy (Ratnakara) departed from the mountain forests and returned home.
I do not take those kings as witnesses for the Dharma of liberation. Why is this?
Because those kings have exhausted their supernatural powers through what they have studied and possess no further methods of ascetic practice; therefore, they returned to their palaces.

"You all must not harbor such thoughts. I shall now make a vow: even if the sun and moon were to fall to the earth, or this King of Snow Mountains were to shift from its original place, it would be impossible for me—were I not yet to have attained the treasure of the True Dharma—to return to my own palace in my ordinary body out of a craving for worldly affairs."
"It would be far more fitting for me now to enter a great pit of blazing, fierce, and scorching fire than to return to the palace without having attained self-benefit;
such a thing is impossible. Having made this vow, the Bodhisattva rose from his seat, left the grove, turned away from the two men, and proceeded alone.

At that time, having heard these words of the Bodhisattva and seeing his firm resolve to renounce all kinsmen and make such a vow, the two messengers knew he would certainly not turn back. They threw themselves to the ground, rose up again with tears streaming down their faces, and wailed aloud as they followed the Bodhisattva’s path, desiring to draw near to him.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s majestic power was so immense that those two were unable to approach him; just as the sun’s radiance dazzles their eyes, they could not behold the Bodhisattva’s body.
At that time, the messengers once again addressed the Bodhisattva with these words:
"We pray, O Noble Son!
Do not harbor such a rigid and stubborn resolve. Please settle our hearts of longing; as we have not yet severed our affection, we cannot bear to abandon you, the Noble Son, and depart."

Because those two loved the Bodhisattva and also held great affection for King Śuddhodana, for these reasons they followed behind the Bodhisattva, moving here and there, sometimes stopping or watching, and sometimes walking or running.
Then those two men further instructed four others to follow behind the Bodhisattva, moving to his left and right while remaining hidden from view, saying:
"You people!..."
"Do not leave the Noble Son; see where he goes.
Having been thus instructed, the two men were filled with grief and poison in their hearts, suffering great anguish as they wept and wailed, each asking the other:
"How shall we now reach the city and behold the face of the Great King?"
"Because of his noble son, the Great King’s heart suffers great anguish; how can we present these words of ours?
If we go before the King, what further speech could we offer that might soothe his mind?"
And there is a verse that says:
"The two messengers knew that the Noble Son Would certainly not return to his own palace;
They dispatched four others to follow behind him, While they themselves returned to see the King and report what had been said."

Chapter Twenty-Six: Questioning Ārāḍa. Part One of the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*. "At that time, when the Bodhisattva had parted from his father the king, his ministers, his messengers, and the state preceptor who was a brahmin, they both shed tears. Having thus taken their leave, he proceeded forward by degrees, moving with steady composure toward the city of Vaiśālī."
Before reaching that city, along the way, there was a place where a rishi practiced the Way; his name was Ārāḍa and his clan name was Kālāma.

At that time, the seer had a disciple who saw from afar the Bodhisattva approaching him. Having seen him, he was struck with a sense of great wonder, for he had never before in his life witnessed such a thing.

Having seen this, he quickly ran to the place where his teacher was seated; upon arriving, he called out the names of his fellow students, the māṇavas, in a loud voice, addressing each one individually: "O worthy Bāhuka! "O worthy Bāhuka! and so forth.
"O virtuous Maitrāyaṇīputra!
O virtuous Śāriputra!
To all such young brahmins as these, he addressed them, saying:"
"O you all, you should now each rejoice; you ought to abandon the practice of sacrificial rites. A virtuous guest of great merit from afar has arrived here, and he must be welcomed."

Yet this benevolent one has already been able to weary of and detach from all fetters and afflictions, seeking the most supreme and ultimate true liberation; he is none other than the son of King Śuddhodana, the Lord of the Śākyas!

His various marks were dignified and majestic, like pillars of gold; his body was radiant and brilliant, lofty and grand. His long arms hung down, reaching past his knees; upon the soles of his feet appeared wheels with a thousand spokes. His gait was steady and composed, and he looked about like a bull king. With a halo of light and majestic virtue like the orb of the sun, his body was like refined gold, and he wore the robes of a *kāṣāya*.
"Our supreme benefactor, the Most Honored One, is gradually approaching us.
We must now prepare offerings and services according to our means, ensuring nothing is lacking; we shall pay him homage with reverence and respect, receiving him with heads bowed."
At that time, the young brahmin praised the Bodhisattva with these verses:
"Your gait is composed and skillful; your glance is like that of a great bull-king.
Your body is adorned and perfected with all the marks; every hair upon it points upward."
The soles of your feet possess wheels with a thousand spokes; between your brows, a wondrous white tuft curls gracefully.
Your long arms are thick, straight, and hang down naturally; you are the Great Lion among men.
At that time, after that young brahmin had praised the Bodhisattva by reciting these verses, he addressed those young brahmins once more, saying:
"All of you, young brahmins!
"Let us go together to the teacher's place and inquire about this matter.

Thereupon, those young brahmins followed him and went to their teacher Ārāḍa; having arrived, they related the matter in detail to the teacher exactly as it had occurred, and when they had finished speaking.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva proceeded with composed grace and suddenly arrived before Ārāḍa.
When the seer Ārāḍa saw the Bodhisattva approaching from afar, and having seen him draw near, he could not help exclaiming in a loud voice:
'Welcome, noble son!'"
The Bodhisattva proceeded to the place where Ārāḍa was; when the two men faced each other, they exchanged greetings:
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you at ease?"
After they had finished greeting one another, Ārāḍa invited the Bodhisattva to sit upon a bed of grass.
There is a verse that says:
"The two men, having seen each other, were filled with great joy; Each inquired after the other’s health and freedom from affliction."
"Hardly had we finished our conversation when he immediately spread out a pure seat of grass.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva had sat upon the grass mat, Ārāḍa Kālāma observed the Bodhisattva’s body with a concentrated mind; having surveyed it from top to bottom, he was filled with great joy at this rare occurrence. He then addressed the Bodhisattva with eloquent words, engaging him in conversation and praising him, saying:
"Venerable Gautama!..."
I have long heard, O noble gentleman!
that you were able to renounce the royal throne, scale the city walls to leave the household life, and sever the defiled web of affectionate attachment.
It is like a great elephant that breaks its sturdy iron chains or thick leather thongs; once they are suddenly severed, it strides forth with freedom, proceeding wherever its heart desires.

It is so, it is so! O worthy one, today you have been able, with a resolute mind, to leave your palace and enter the mountains; in all circumstances, you are contented and free from desire, and possess great wisdom.
"O Venerable Gautama!

Having attained such rare things as worldly wealth, honor, and the power of karmic fruition, yet being able to renounce them and shave your head to dwell in the mountain forests—this is truly difficult to accomplish."

In the past, although various kings possessed the full karmic retribution of their royal status and fully experienced the five sensory desires, when they reached old age, they would summon their crown prince, entrust him with the throne, and consecrate him as king; only thereafter would they renounce the palace and depart for the mountain forests to seek the Way.
This is not difficult for him, nor is it rare. As I see it, you are young in years;

yet, having not succumbed to the five desires, you have renounced these matters of wealth, honor, and merit, being able to cultivate such a resolve as to come here to seek the Way. Having already attained such an inconceivable sovereign rank of a Great Sage and this most supreme state, at the very height of your youth, you are able to withdraw your mind and thoughts, remaining unattached to all desires. You are determined to seek liberation, neither bound nor fettered, untainted by the objects of the sense-faculties, and capable of knowing all the afflictions within existence, remaining unentangled by the realms of becoming.

Why is this? In the past there was a king named Mūrdhaja. Although that king had already brought the four continents under his dominion, he remained unsatisfied; he ascended to the Heaven of the Thirty-three and sat upon half the throne of Śakra. Because his inner mind was insatiable, the realms of the five desires were instantly lost, and he fell back to earth.

"Furthermore, there was another king named Nahuṣa who also ruled over the four continents and ascended as far as the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where he governed and transformed the various devas; yet even this was not enough for him, and he lost his royal throne and fell back to earth."

All such as these—King Rāma, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, King Aśoka, and others, as well as many universal monarchs (cakravartin)—because they were never satisfied with attaining their royal thrones, all lost their realms; their wealth, nobility, and royal positions were entirely extinguished.
"In this world, there is no one who, having attained their objective, finds contentment in their mind; they are like a great fire that blazes even more fiercely upon obtaining fuel.
After Ārāḍa had spoken these words, the Bodhisattva replied:
"O Great Seer, worthy sir!"
Having observed such characteristics in the world, I further perceive that all things are like the plantain tree: their inner nature is not solid, and they eventually disintegrate.
Because one encounters sensory objects, there is a fear of never knowing contentment; thus, one seeks no self-benefit and becomes weary of and detached from the affairs of desire.

Having realized this, I sought the true path and wandered from place to place, just like a person traveling through a vast wilderness who has lost his companions and become disoriented, unable to find a guide; seeking such a guide, he wanders everywhere—and so it is with me now.
When the Bodhisattva had spoken these words, Ārāḍa again addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Venerable Gautama!"
"I have long observed the mental disposition of this Great Being; you are inclined toward liberation and are fit to be a great vessel.
At that time, there was among the assembly a young brahmin who was a disciple of the seer Ārāḍa. Joining his palms, he addressed his teacher and praised the Bodhisattva, saying these words:
"How rare is this person! He is inconceivable, for he is able to accomplish such a resolve."

In the past, when various kings were young, they sat within their palaces enjoying the five sensory pleasures; later, when they reached old age with white hair, each summoned his crown prince, entrusted him with the royal throne, and consecrated him as king. Thereafter, they renounced their homes and entered the mountain forests, practicing the path step by step until they attained the state of a royal seer (*rājarṣi*).

This is not so; for one in the prime of youth and vigor is precisely at the time when one may enjoy the five sensory pleasures to one’s heart's content, having little illness or affliction, with physical strength fully sufficient, hair black, body supple, endowed with valor, and lacking nothing.

The father king, being advanced in years, did not crave the royal throne; weary of and detached from the world, he had no desire for karmic rewards, and was thus able to leave the household life, enter the mountains, and seek the Way.
Then Ārāḍa addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Virtuous One, having resolved your mind, what do you seek?
What path do you wish to accomplish?"
"It is because you have been able to resolve your mind [for enlightenment] that you have come to this place.
The Bodhisattva replied,
"O Venerable Great Master!"

Having observed that the sentient beings of this world are entangled by birth, old age, sickness, and death, and are unable to escape on their own, I have now resolved to arouse such a mind of diligent effort.
Then Ārāḍa spoke again: "Venerable Gautama!
You have been able to give rise to such an eye of wisdom and conceive such a thought; this principle is indeed true."
Why is this so? He spoke in verse:
“The supreme among all phenomena is only practice; Purity, tranquility, and concentration do not transcend the mind.”
"Attachment to affection is the greatest enemy; all terrors are old age and death.
When Ārāḍa had spoken these words, there was among that assembly a young brahmin who was a disciple of the seer Ārāḍa. He addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Benevolent One, having now abandoned your beloved kin and followers, what is the purpose of your coming here and turning your back on them?"
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Whatever gatherings and assemblies exist in the world must inevitably end in separation.
Knowing this to be so, I have conceived this intention, desiring to seek the Ultimate Truth."
Then the seer Ārāḍa spoke again to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Virtuous One, you have now attained liberation. Why is this so? Because—"

Sentient beings are submerged in this mud that is difficult to cross; they are bound by the world with these firm and strong ropes. You, O Benevolent One, have already been able to master this mind alone; I shall now expound for you this Dharma-gate of liberation.

That which is called "affection" must be abandoned by the benevolent. This so-called affection is a great and evil dragon within the world that dwells and resides within the waters of the mind, causing one to lose all benefit.

For this reason, I now observe that the people of the world do not practice correctly; only those who are wise are able to grasp the Dharma of correct practice. Having distanced themselves from the defilement of craving, they should resolve to abandon the perception of signs and cultivate signlessness.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Great Seer and Honored One!
I accept these words; it is as you have said."
The seer Ārāḍa asked the Bodhisattva again,
"How do you accept it?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"People of the world are bound by the perception of signs (*nimitta*).

As for those bound by signs, whenever parents give birth to and raise children, it is for the sake of establishing a household; they nurture their offspring with the thought, 'They will be able to increase and bring success to our family. For this reason, parents raise their children.
Yet, if there were no such causal conditions, even one's own permitted kinsmen would not be approached, let alone others."
"In all cases of associating with others, if one does so out of a greedy pursuit of profit, such intimacy will ultimately be nowhere to be found.
The seer Ārāḍa further praised him, saying:
"Excellent, O virtuous one!"
“O Śramaṇa Gautama! You have now understood all phenomena in the world;
you have thus clearly realized all-knowledge.
At that time, there was among that assembly a young brahmin who was also a disciple of the seer Rāma. He addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Venerable Gautama!
You have now attained this supreme bliss. Why is this so?"
One who can gradually detach from all marks of craving will immediately attain the various dharmas of non-affliction in the world. Why is this so?

I observe the world and see that there are few people who are able to refrain from grieving for their wives and children, from seeking wealth and property, and from raising both hands in lamentation within the world.

I have often seen people who, because they do not practice fewness of desires and lack knowledge of contentment, cherish their wealth and constantly give rise to greed; being stained by attachment to worldly profit, every household raises its hands and weeps bitterly.
And he spoke in verse:
“In this world, those who know contentment are rarely seen; Having few desires and no seeking, they do not suffer.
Those who weep for the sake of affection and love Are mostly those greedily attached to amassing wealth.”
Then Ārāḍa addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"How extraordinary, O worthy Gautama!

Such is your vast wisdom; therefore, you have now prepared this valor, subduing the sense faculties so that they do not increase their attachment to desires, nor allow yourself to be led astray by them."
At that time, the Bodhisattva asked the Venerable Ārāḍa:
"Great Sage, Venerable One!
For what reason are your faculties so unsettled?"
As for those who wish to subdue [them], what are the skillful means?
I only pray that the Venerable One will explain this for me.
The seer Ārāḍa replied:
"O Great Being, Śramaṇa!
For those who dwell in the world and desire to become weary of and detached from birth, I shall now briefly explain for you, Great Being, the characteristics of the skillful means."
"Great Being, listen attentively.
And there was a verse that said:
"The Great Honored Seer Ārāḍa Inspired the Bodhisattva’s mind of divine wisdom."
"Within the *siddhānta* of my own doctrine, I shall explain it by distinguishing its essential points in brief.
"O Great Being Gautama!
Those who wish to eliminate the essential characteristics of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) as well as the objects of those faculties (*viṣaya*) must reflect and discern in this manner."
Why is this? Because all these sense faculties and their respective objects, once they have been discerned and known, must all be relinquished.
Furthermore, within the range of the sense faculties and their objects, there exist various attachments; being stained by such attachment, one becomes bound by it.

Because of this attachment, sentient beings are submerged in the world and cannot escape; all ordinary persons undergo the sufferings of being bound by craving and so forth, and all such matters arise solely because of objective spheres (*viṣaya*).
"O Great Being, you should know!
For what cause and condition is this so?
He then spoke in verse:
“The goat is killed because it bleats; the moth falls into the lamp because of its love for the flame’s color;
the fish on the hook is caught because it swallows the bait; so too, worldly people hasten toward death, led astray by sensory objects.”
At that time, having heard this verse, the Bodhisattva asked again:

"Venerable One, you have now described the characteristics of the skillful means for subduing the sense faculties: they arise through common causes and conditions, their essential nature is empty, they are deceptive and without reality, like a pit of fire, like a dream or an illusion, and like dew upon the grass."
"I now contemplate with my mind and know it to be thus.
Then, the seer Ārāḍa again asked the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva:
"Virtuous one, for what reason do you say that within all objective realms there is no perception of benefit?"
The Bodhisattva replied:

"If an ordinary person wishes to dwell upon various sense objects to receive their karmic retribution, it is like someone building a house, desiring to shield themselves from the sunlight or to avoid the wind and rain."

It is like a person who, because of thirst, seeks water; or like a person who, because of hunger, searches for food; or like a person with filth and impurity who desires to bathe their body; or like a person who, being naked, seeks clothing to cover their form; or like a person who, because of exhaustion, seeks a vehicle; or like one who, wishing to dispel cold, seeks warmth; or like one who, wishing to dispel heat, seeks coolness; or like one who, wishing to remove fatigue, sits upon a bed or a mat.
Regarding such matters as these, all who seek them do so because they are oppressed by suffering within their own bodies; thus they investigate and search for them.
It is like a patient who, because their ailment is grave, seeks out a skilled physician.
"Everyone in the world has such expectations.
At that time, Ārāḍa praised him, saying: "Gautama!"
How rare is this mind!
Venerable sir,
how is it that within the world you are able to act with such swiftness as to immediately give rise to the perception of impermanence?
"How rare, how rare!
You are able to see reality.
Your faculties are sharp and your great benefit is such that you are quick-witted and easily awakened; if one can perceive with such clarity as this, it is called true seeing."
If one holds a different view, it is called deception.
As you have said, because people seek food when hungry and avoid wind and rain, they give rise to the perception of pleasure when cold and heat are temporarily relieved.
Again, he uttered this praise:
"O worthy Gautama!
You are truly a bridge of Dharma, upholding the great vessel. Although I have heard of you by report, I first observed your disciples to see whether they were capable of receiving the Dharma."
If you are able to receive [this teaching], I shall thereafter expound for you various discourses.

As I perceive it, you today are no longer as you were; your deportment and conduct are profoundly refined, such that there is no need for further observation. Within my treatises, there are truths of ultimate meaning; I shall explain them all to you.
At that time, having heard these words from the seer Ārāḍa, the Bodhisattva was filled with great joy and asked again:
"Venerable Great Seer!

Today, unaware of my filial devotion, you have suddenly delivered such a sublime discourse for my sake; I recognize these signs that, though no immediate benefit has yet been realized, I have already obtained great profit.

Why is this? It is like a person who, wishing to see forms, obtains light; or like a traveler going a long distance who requires a skilled guide; or like one crossing to the other shore who requires a boatman. The Venerable One’s manifestation of my mind today is likewise so.
"I only pray, Venerable One!
Please explain further for my sake that which you know: how does one transcend and escape birth, old age, sickness, and death?
— *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll Twenty-one.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll Twenty-Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Part Two of the Chapter on Questioning Ārāḍa.
At that time, the Venerable Seer Ārāḍa, who well understood the supreme virtue within the Bodhisattva’s mind, further expounded the definitive *siddhānta* of his own treatise, speaking in verse:
“Śramaṇa Gautama, listen attentively; I shall explain the general *siddhānta* within my treatise.
Although you are currently amidst the afflictions, In the future, you will naturally attain liberation.”
At that time, after Ārāḍa had spoken this verse, he said:
"Regarding all sentient beings, there are two aspects:
first, their fundamental nature; second, their manifestations. These two combined are collectively termed 'sentient beings.'"

What is called "original nature" refers to the five great elements; these five great elements are namely earth, water, fire, wind, and space. Together with the self and the signless, these are termed the "original essence-nature."

What is called "transformation" refers to the sensory faculties and their objects, the hands and feet, speech, movement, coming and going, as well as the mind and consciousness; these are termed "transformations."

If one knows these various objects in this manner, it is called "knowing the objects. To say that one who can know those various objects is "I who am able to know," and to contemplate such an "I," is what is spoken by wise people.
And he spoke in verse:
"If one is able to recognize all sense faculties and objects, This is called knowing their spheres well.
To say that one knows all spheres of experience Is what the wise call knowing through reflection."
At that time, Ārāḍa spoke these words:

"The one who contemplates me is the seer Kapila and his disciples; they too, by measuring this realm of the mind for themselves, hold the same view as the son of the seer Vasiṣṭha, named Gambhīramati."
Just as one repeatedly undergoes birth, old age, sickness, and death, experiencing various bitter sufferings, so too, having deeply and truly understood this, one explains it for others.
Mindful of its transcendence and contemplating this principle, one should realize that all things are signless (*animitta*).
Furthermore, it is said:
"That which is caused by afflictions refers to ignorance and attachment to various karmas.
Such karmas as these belong to the cause of afflictions."
These causes of affliction are fourfold; because this person has not yet abandoned these various afflictions, they are unable to be liberated from birth and death.
What are these four?
First is a lack of faith; second is attachment to the self; third is the presence of doubt; and fourth is a lack of stability.
Because these remnants remain, one lacks skillful means, becomes deeply attached to the world, and constantly falls into decline.
For this reason, one undergoes birth in various places.
"To speak of 'lack of faith' means that one constantly acts in a perverted manner; one should know it as such, yet instead fails to know it—this is called lack of faith."
"To speak with attachment to a self is to say, 'This is mine,' or to designate that as 'not mine,' or to say, 'I speak thus,' 'I experience thus,' 'I act,' or 'I abide.'"
To perceive the marks of a self and a body, thinking "this is called a self," and failing to realize this for oneself—this is called attachment to a self.
As for what is called "having doubt," it refers to being confused by all things because one does not understand them; it is merely a single phenomenon.
It is like a lump of clay; this is called doubt.

To say that there is no certainty—claiming "it is thus and thus," "this is so," "that is also so," or "this is not so"—and regarding all mental conceptions and karmic actions as "this is the multitude, this is I," "this is that, this is this"—this is called lack of certainty.

"Furthermore, as for the 'residue': because they have not yet known the superior states, have not awakened to initial awakening, and have not realized their own nature, but are now beginning to realize and know it, this is called 'residue'."

"Furthermore, it is said that one who lacks skillful means is one who lacks wisdom; because they lack wisdom, they do not understand skillful means, and because they lack skillful means, they are unable to manifest them."
For this reason, it is called "lacking skillful means.
Furthermore, as for those who are stained by attachment, they are people without wisdom; upon seeing, hearing, touching, or cognizing, they immediately give rise to attachment.

At times, the mind becomes attached to the body, to speech, or to words; or the mental karma becomes attached to all objective spheres. That which should not be the object of attachment yet is deludedly attached to—that is called "attachment."
"Furthermore, as for 'falling away': if one thinks and contemplates, 'I am that place' or 'that place is I,' such a state of mind is called falling away."
By these causes and conditions, one falls into afflictions; this is called lacking virtue and lacking wisdom.
These are called the five states, which are characterized by suffering and distress and devoid of joy—these are places where there is no joy.
What are called darkness, delusion, and great delusion have two types of cohabitation;
these are known as the five bases. "Darkness" refers to indolence;
"delusion" refers to birth and death.
What is called "great delusion" refers to the practice of sensual desire. Why is this so?
Because even if there were a person of great virtue in such a state, they would still remain confused and fail to awaken; therefore, it is called great delusion.
The second form of dwelling in confusion is what is called ill-will;
furthermore, there is a second form of dwelling in confusion, which is called indolence.

Beings obscured by ignorance do not practice in this way; they become deluded, submerged, and attached to these five locations, remaining within the ocean of afflictions and suffering, following the current of birth and death.

"I have seen, I have heard, I have realized, I have done, I have taught others to do; I have arrived at such a state because of such a mind and such an intention. Thus, one wanders in saṃsāra, submerged in the ocean of afflictions.
These four kinds of things entangle, envelop, and bind one within afflictions, asserting that there is neither cause nor effect.
Venerable Gautama!
You should understand these matters as they truly are.
And he spoke in verse:
"If a person desires to attain right view and knowledge, The pure state of liberation of the four dhyānas,
If their mind awakens to and understands that wisdom, They will know those who are true sages and those who are not."
As analyzed above, this should be proclaimed; therefore, it is called the liberation of the four dhyānas.
Being able to relinquish all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) as well as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), this is precisely knowing the name of the wordless phrase.
Therefore, there in that place the Great Brahmā Heaven Expounds the various brahma-faring practices of the world;
If one can practice these brahma-faring practices, One shall immediately attain rebirth in the Brahma palace.
At that time, having heard these words from Ārāḍa, the Bodhisattva questioned him once more:

"Regarding those skillful means, the destination reached by practicing those skillful means, as well as the cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya) and the dharmas to be practiced in the course of such practice—Venerable Sir, please explain all of this to me."
At that time, Ārāḍa, relying upon the principles, categories, and essential tenets of his own compendium, addressed everything toward the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O worthy Gautama!..."

Those who wish to practice the path should abandon their palaces and homes, follow the rites of renunciation, sustain their lives by begging for alms, make great and vast vows, cultivate the practice of the precepts, and abide in contentment.
Providing himself with whatever clothing, food, bedding, and secluded dwellings he can manage, he dwells alone in walking and sitting.

Just as described in the various treatises, having perceived through wisdom the faults of greed, hatred, and delusion, he distances himself from them; loathing all sensual desires, he experiences the highest bliss, subdues his sense faculties, and enters into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
At that time, being secluded from sensual desires and secluded from unwholesome states, he gave rise to the first dhyāna in a solitary place, free from discursive thought.
Having attained the first dhyāna, he again reflects and discriminates in this manner, gradually attaining bliss; having attained bliss, he abides in this tranquil concentration.

Relying further on the power of this tranquil concentration, the mind develops a profound sense of weary detachment toward desire, anger, and the like; having repeatedly cultivated such detachment, the mind becomes increasingly joyful; with this increased joy, wisdom grows, and at that time, one attains rebirth in the palace of Mahābrahmā.

Having been born in that place, they again reflect and discriminate in this way: "This disturbs my wisdom," and they abandon it once more; having abandoned it, they attain the second dhyāna and experience great joy.
Having attained joy, seeing that his mind was overwhelmed by great rapture, he sought an even more excellent state and immediately reached the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Upon reaching the Ābhāsvara Heaven, he beheld the place where bliss is experienced; having arrived there, he grew weary of and detached from that joy and bliss.
Having already departed from joy and pleasure, one immediately attains the third dhyāna.
Upon reaching the third dhyāna, one surpasses the gods of the Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna) realm below, experiencing exclusively bliss.
If one can thus attain such bliss and then relinquish it—neither receiving nor clinging to it—one departs from all states of suffering and pleasure and attains the fourth dhyāna.
Having already departed from suffering and pleasure, as well as the攀緣心 (攀緣心; *ālambana-citta*, the mind that grasps at objects), one relinquishes everything.

Furthermore, there are those who, due to their own conceit, seek the marks of liberation and desire to transcend the retributive fruits of the four dhyānas. Therefore, they internally contemplate these dharmas of the four dhyānas and the retributive fruits received within the Bṛhatphala Heaven; this is the contemplation of coarse wisdom.

Furthermore, as it is said: after that person has contemplated such matters, they arise from samādhi and perceive that their physical form possesses various defects and afflictions; desiring to relinquish the physical body and seek supreme, transcendent wisdom, they give rise to this thought.

Having thus abandoned all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), that person advances to seek a superior state and gives rise to this thought as previously described: having abandoned all sensual matters and likewise having relinquished the coarse physical body, they give rise to a mind of weary detachment (*nirveda*).

At that time, one immediately attains the boundless discrimination of all space within the body. Regarding all these forms, as well as the objects within those forms—such as trees and other things—one discriminates them all as boundless space. Having clearly and thoroughly discriminated all such locations of form as boundless space, one then realizes the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
And there is a verse that says:
"In this such subtle and wondrous abode of Great Brahmā, All is signless and eternally beyond words;
The wise declare it the cause of liberation, And this itself is named the fruit of Nirvāṇa."
At that time, having spoken these words, Ārāḍa addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Venerable Gautama!
This is the very place of my liberation, along with its expedient means; I have now finished revealing it to you."
"If you, O Benevolent One, find joy in this Dharma, you may accept it as I have explained.
Then he spoke in verse:
"This pure Dharma of liberation, I have now realized and shall proclaim further; I have now realized and shall proclaim further;"
“If your mind, O Benevolent One, is pleased, I only wish that you would accept and take this up. Then Ārāḍa spoke again:

“In times past, the Ṛṣi Gīṣpati (translated in the Sui as ‘Seeking Victory’), the Ṛṣi Vītaśoka (translated in the Sui as ‘Free from Sorrow’), the Ṛṣi Parāsara (translated in the Sui as ‘Other’s Arrow’), and all other such sages, all together proclaimed this Dharma of liberation; they likewise mounted this very Dharma of liberation and thereby attained liberation.”
“Virtuous one, since you are a man of great wisdom, you are capable of practicing this Dharma;
having practiced this Dharma, you will be able to obtain the fruit of liberation in a favorable rebirth.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, having heard the Dharma of the holy life as taught by the seer Ārāḍa, accepted and practiced it. Desiring the conduct of a śramaṇa and seeking the fruit of a śramaṇa, he practiced this Dharma and immediately realized it through direct knowledge.

Then, having heard the Dharma preached from the mouth of Ārāḍa, the Bodhisattva practiced this teaching with faith, neither contradicting nor turning away from it; yet he did not say, "I already knew this myself. Rather, having received and upheld it, he contemplated this Dharma with increasing progress, further giving rise to a mind of firm wisdom, seeking a superior state.
Having seen this superior state, he did not give rise to pride or disparage that seer;

rather, he reflected to himself: "It is not only Ārāḍa who possesses such faith and practice; I too now possess such faith and practice. It is not only Ārāḍa who possesses diligence, right mindfulness, samādhi, and various forms of knowledge; I too possess them, even up to those knowledges. I should now seek the Dharma known and realized by Ārāḍa, explain it to others, analyze and reveal it, and establish it as a supreme state."
“At that time, the Bodhisattva fully realized all the teachings and practices taught by Ārāḍa; he practiced with knowledge and vision.

Yet, having heard those various dharmas from him, he mastered them entirely in a mere moment without much exertion; his ability to practice, explain, propagate, and demonstrate them was in every way identical to his teacher’s.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva again approached Ārāḍa and spoke these words: "Venerable Ārāḍa!
You are able to personally realize such knowledge of the Dharma and explain it to others, namely, seeking rebirth in the realm of non-perception."
Having spoken these words, Ārāḍa replied to the Bodhisattva:
"Venerable Gautama!
This Dharma-knowledge, having been personally realized by me, I have proclaimed, disseminated, and revealed it to others."
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"Having heard this Dharma from the Venerable One, and having practiced as the Venerable One has taught, I have faith and know that I have realized this Dharma."
If there is one who possesses wisdom and understands the sphere of practice, they likewise should not abandon such a teaching.
However, from my own perspective, although this teaching is sublime, it has not yet reached the ultimate consummation.

Why is this? It is because when I observe and contemplate with such an intention, I see that these phenomena still undergo change; yet the nature of this realm is simply thus. Having known this through wisdom—which, though it is itself non-wisdom—I further desire to give rise to a distinct understanding of all other phenomena.

However, the Venerable One has said: although one may say, "I have attained pure liberation," if one analytically contemplates this as being subject to dependent origination, then upon encountering conditions, it will arise again; thus, it is not true liberation. It is like sowing seeds out of season: though they are buried in the earth, if the time is not favorable and there is no water or rain, the sprouts will not grow.
But if they are sown at the proper time, moistened and made suitable, and all conditions are fully present and harmonized, then they will grow.

Now this is likewise; merely because of a lack of wisdom, one clings to the karma of craving. Having abandoned such phenomena as these through discrimination, one says, "I am liberated," yet there remains only the clinging to a self, which must all be relinquished.

Even if one abandons these [states] such as ignorance, craving, and karma where there is no basis for their conjunction, once these have been abandoned, although one attains something superior to before, one has not yet reached the true state; one merely continues to function within a realm of conceptualization that posits a self.

Those three subtle matters exist together; because of those subtle afflictions, there is yet another distinct state of non-existence where their lifespan is extremely long. Due to this discrimination, they say, "I have attained liberation."
And he spoke in verse:
"Because the various afflictions are subtle, One receives a body in the Place of Non-perception;
Since the duration of one's lifespan is exceedingly long, One then claims, 'I have attained liberation.'"
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"As you have said before, I have already abandoned the self; yet, since I have declared that I have abandoned the self, this cannot be called the true abandonment of the self."
If one relies on conceptual discrimination, those who are not yet liberated cannot be said to be free from affliction and entanglement.

By this, it should be known that where there is affliction and entanglement, one cannot say that liberation has been attained; nor can the state of non-self be said to be distinct from the affliction of a self.

It is like the color and heat of fire: heat is not separate from color, and color is not separate from heat. Since these two do not each exist as distinct entities prior [to their conjunction], it is impossible for them to exist as a composite.
As it is with me, so it is with all afflictions;
once liberated from these, one reaches that state only to be bound again, because one grasps at objects through the intellect.
Once that form has been extinguished, there remains only consciousness; he perceives "I have consciousness," and this is precisely what is called existence.
Because of this existence, it is not called liberation.

This is my own established tenet (*siddhānta*): regarding the magnitude of the spheres of experience, one who knows them as they are will likewise attain such [realization] and seek the superior state.
For this reason, what need is there for further discrimination?
"This self is not-self; it is like wood, like a wall—layer upon layer, mutually relinquished.
Since each is layered and yet exists through wisdom, I therefore contemplate that one must completely relinquish all objective realms in order to attain self-benefit."
And he spoke in verse:
"Layer upon layer, all are completely relinquished; This is what is called 'abandoning the sphere of objects.
Because all faculties and their objects are entirely released, This is called benefiting oneself and benefiting others."
"At that time, among the followers of Ārāḍa, there was a disciple who addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
'Venerable Gautama!
Now that you have come here to our dwelling place, it has become entirely a worthy vessel, and furthermore, we have attained the eight kinds of mastery.'"
The Bodhisattva replied,
"How can there be mastery in this place?
Then, Ārāḍa addressed his disciples, saying:
"Do not, for now, deliberate upon this matter. Why is this?

One who is called 'sovereign' is able to exercise decisive power over all matters; being peerless and without equal, they give rise to joy because they have personally realized internal tranquility and concentration."
The Bodhisattva replied, "This is not so. Ārāḍa said:
"What is its meaning? The Bodhisattva replied, "It is so, it is so."
Ārāḍa said: "Virtuous one, please speak; do not withhold these words.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"If it is as the Venerable One says— that this practice has no turning back"—
Ārāḍa said, "Virtuous one,
for what reason do you pose this question?"
"Where is there any doubt?
The Bodhisattva replied,
"Since my mind is now weary of and detached from birth, I wish to ask about what is truly authentic."
Āḷāra said: "Venerable Gautama!
If you wish to hear it, I shall explain it for you."

Whoever wishes to transform and enlighten the world is none other than I; I exist only as a name, neither born nor aging, neither declining nor returning, without limit or center, without beginning or end—this is what is called "I."

He possesses sovereign mastery to enter and revolve within the cycle of birth and death, yet does not dwell therein even for a moment. Regarding that which is Dharma and that which is non-Dharma, those gods and humans, and all realms of existence—he can travel afar; he can act as a vehicle. Those who mount his vehicle can cross the deep ocean of existence. He can cause the flow of coming and going, create birth and death, and manifest transformations. Sovereign, most excellent, most wondrous, and greatest, he can act as the Lord of the World, gathering and transforming all beings.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"Does such a transformation as this truly exist? Ārāḍa replied:
"I observe the sound of your inquiry, O Benevolent One, and it seems you certainly do not wish to accept such a meaning; perhaps your mind does not find delight in this?
The Bodhisattva replied, "I have no affliction."
Ārāḍa said: "Venerable Gautama! Do not harbor doubt; follow what you find pleasing.

Simply discourse upon the meaning toward which you are directed, enter into it through careful reflection, and illuminate it for yourself. If you see and know this for yourself—neither deceived by others, nor dependent on the teachings of others, nor following the doctrines of others—one who realizes it in this way is said to have attained self-benefit, which others cannot do."
If one’s mind is not settled, one will grasp the meaning according to various masters, and thus one’s wisdom will diminish.

You, O virtuous ones, having heard this, should engage in correct reflection, recite it individually, contemplate its profound meaning, and examine it until you realize it for yourselves through direct knowledge.
"Knowing that you have doubts, ask me as you wish, and I shall explain it for you.
The Bodhisattva asked again:
"Regarding what the Venerable One has said—that one who can manifest transformations of the world and has attained mastery—within this meaning, my mind harbors a doubt."
Ārāḍa said, "According to your honorable intention, this principle is not so.
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"I see it thus. Ārāḍa said: "For what reason do you see it thus?"
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"This condition is singular. Why is this so?"

If Īśvara were the creator of this world, then it would not be possible for things to arise and appear according to a sequential order as we observe them; the wheel of afflictions would not revolve in such a sequence, and sentient beings should obtain what they desire without their minds even seeking it.

A single sentient being should not suffer from manifold afflictions; he should be worthy of the offerings of all people in the world with sovereign respect, like a father or a mother, such that no other deities receive such veneration.
That poor person should not be said to possess any karma of defilement, honor, good, or evil; all such karma should reside in that [other].
All sentient beings should have no place of attachment, should seek nothing, and should have nothing to do.
People of the world should not think in this way, that Īśvara exists or that Īśvara does not exist.

People of the world thus discriminate between existence and non-existence, performing various karmas—both those they ought to do and those they ought not to do—and thereby naturally receiving their retributive fruits.
If that Lord (Īśvara) attains sovereignty by practicing asceticism, then the world should also collectively undergo this karma, and everyone should likewise be called "Sovereign."

If that which is causeless were to act as the Sovereign (Īśvara), there would be no place and no person who is not sovereign; if it were not established as being sovereign, it could not even be called existent—how, then, could one say it is established as the Sovereign?
Ārāḍa praised the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Venerable Gautama!

Your wisdom is profound and far-reaching; you are skillfully able to manifest it and uphold all treatises. You comprehend general principles and essential natures, discerning and knowing them all through the power of your intellect."

"Therefore, please show me the path of truth regarding all *siddhāntas* through your impartial vision; I pray you do not decline my request out of weariness or stinginess regarding the jewel of the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"I should now make offerings to the Venerable One."
Ārāḍa said: "The teachers are many;
how could you, O Noble One, possibly provide for them all?
However, since you are now the leader, you are certainly capable of making offerings to them as well."
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"Venerable One, you should simply explain such meanings as these for me. Ārāḍa said:
"They are truly superior; they have never existed before in any world, and they were born first.
O virtuous one, reflect deeply with a well-intentioned mind: does karma come first, or does the body come first?"
The Bodhisattva replied,
"What is the meaning of this? Ārāḍa said:
"This is a great affliction. Why is this so?
If karma were prior and not preceded by the body, one would not receive a body; the body would be without karma, and karma itself would not arise. Who, then, would create this karma?"
If the body existed prior to karma and was not preceded by karma, then there would be no karma;
if there were no karma, for what reason would sentient beings still receive bodies?
Furthermore, who would be able to transform and guide the world?
That [self] should be indestructible and eternally existent.
