As that which binds the three realms and serves as the fundamental source for the birth of all sentient beings, it should produce its own body.
If it were not sovereign, then every person’s cherished body would have to be produced by something else.
"If it were already possessed by oneself, it should naturally exist in all places.
The Bodhisattva replied, "I am like a sick person seeking a physician for treatment; I do not find this principle difficult to understand."
At that time, there was among the assembly an ascetic who was a disciple of the seer Ārāḍa; he addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, Gautama!
"O Venerable One! We pray that you do not find fault with this meaning. Such a meaning as this need not be disputed.
If one were to dispute it, it would be of no benefit; you should simply accept it as the Venerable One has taught."
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I find it no difficulty; I merely wish to ask about the lineage from which this has been transmitted, for I must understand its meaning.
The seer said:
"Following these causes and conditions, you, O virtuous one, should uphold them and grasp their true meaning;
if you wish to give rise to doubt or engage in internal debate, this is a great violation of the Dharma and will result in transgression in the future."
Then the disciple of that ascetic seer spoke in verse:
"When an ordinary person listens to and receives instruction, their mind must not be distracted for the meaning to be settled.
If one harbors doubt or a crooked, deceitful heart, they will instead engage in contention, seeking out the faults of others."
Second, when one seeks out another's faults, enmity is formed; when two enemies contend, their speech becomes malicious.
The wise wish to sever the transgressions of verbal karma, and thus they speak according to principle without harboring a competitive mind.
Seeking victory in debate is called greed; vying for fame and subduing others brings shame upon men.
Excessive speech reveals one's faults—this is a great affliction; listening to the meaning with a sycophantic mind leads to self-conceit.
Arrogance and malice increase their transgressions; each speaks of right and wrong while mutually reviling one another.
What should be done is left undone, and what should not be done is performed; because these two aspects compete with one another, they constitute a great enmity.
At that time, having heard these verses, the Bodhisattva said to the seer: "It is indeed so;
there is such a fault as mutual contention, yet you claim it does not exist on the Path."
"However, I wish to seek the matters of the original lineage and its accomplishments; it is not that I intend to exhaustively investigate them.
Having spoken these words, the mind of that seer was still unable to bear it, and Ārāḍa said:
"Venerable Gautama!..."
"Do you, O Benevolent One, detest the path of liberation?
Such circumstances as these are not original.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"If one wishes to seek that liberation, one must seek it in this manner.
At that time, the disciples of the seer Ārāḍa spoke again, saying:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
"O Benevolent One, if you seek liberation while remaining apart from this [body], you will merely waste your physical form in vain.
The Bodhisattva replied,
"If people who seek the impermanent pleasures of the world still experience lack and insufficiency, how much more so for one who seeks the liberation that does not return?"
Then the disciple of the seer Ārāḍa spoke again, saying:
"Virtuous One, since you have now said that you will not return, you may practice as you please forever."
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Since this place where I am now traveling is one that accords with my own inclinations, once I have reached that destination, why would I ever return? Ārāḍa said:
"Do not go there, and do not return here; would that not be possible?
The Bodhisattva replied, "This is most extraordinary!
The Venerable One previously stated that one receives existence later, yet why do you now say that one shall not return again?"
Ārāḍa replied: "It is indeed so, O worthy one! This is truly marvelous.
That essence of True Suchness (tathatā) is quiescent; it is without beginning and without end, without limit, without first or last, its course is not fixed, and it cannot be fully exhausted."
"However, it was established by the Master of Signlessness, the Lord of Dhyāna; that is the Great Brahmā Heaven.
The Bodhisattva spoke again:

"I now ask further, O Great Sage and Honored One: when the kalpa comes to an end, this entire great earth, its forests, Mount Sumeru and the like, and even the palaces of Śakra, will all be consumed by the fires of the kalpa."
At that time, where was that deity dwelling?
What were his name and what was his surname? How did he speak?
"How does the fruit of merit abide?
Furthermore, when the kalpa comes to an end and all things are consumed, why is that [merit] not burned?
At that time, Rāhula smiled silently.
At that time, a disciple of the seer Ārāḍa addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Benevolent One, your wisdom is now most supreme.
Could you not know for yourself that all the seers of the past attained the Right Path? That is to say, the Honored One..."
The rishi Parāśara, the rishi Phalada, the rishi Āśvalāyana,
the rishi Bhadanta, the rishi Kātyāyana, the rishi Dhanadatta,
the rishi Dattilyāyana, the rishi Pañcālāda, and the rishi Aṣāḍha.
The Ṛṣi Dhā, the Ṛṣi Varmadatta, the Ṛṣi Jayanti son of King Nahuṣa,
the Ṛṣi Śābarī, the Ṛṣi Parāvañcana, the Ṛṣi Bhadrika, the Ṛṣi Janaka,
the Ṛṣi Deva of Āpaṇḍu and Rohitaka, and the Ṛṣi Ja...
The Ṛṣi Kāśyapa, the Ṛṣi Tivira, the Ṛṣi Vidahavya,
the Ṛṣi Vāsu, the Ṛṣi Devayaṇa, the Ṛṣi Saṃjātayana,
the Ṛṣi Yajñadatta, the Ṛṣi Nyagrodha, and the Ṛṣi Hārīti.
“...and the Ṛṣi Vajrapāhu— indeed, all such Ṛṣis as these entered the sunlight and thereby attained the right path.
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied to those Ṛṣis, saying:
"Now that you have said that those who enter the light of the sun seek liberation, what is the meaning of this?
I should now pay homage to all those beings; I truly have no need for such sovereignty."
At that time, having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva reflected within himself:

And there is a verse that says:
"The King beheld the Bodhisattva like Śakra; His body’s radiance shone forth, and his heart was filled with joy.
He inquired after his well-being and whether the four elements were in harmony, Asking if he had little illness or distress, and no physical ailment."

At that time, with a subtle and gentle voice like the sound of Brahmā, his eloquent words and phrases were untainted and unattached as he addressed King Bimbisāra of Magadha, greeting him with these words:
"O Great King, who governs so well!
Great good fortune and auspiciousness!
From where have you come so far?
Please sit and rest.
"What matter do you seek that you have come here?

At that time, King Bimbisāra, having heard these words of the Bodhisattva, approached the Bodhisattva and sat down comfortably upon a stone. Desiring to gauge the Bodhisattva’s intention, the king addressed him, saying:
"O Virtuous One, if you do not decline it out of weariness, I wish to inquire about a doubt within my mind; I only pray that you, O Virtuous One, will resolve it for me."
He then asked: "Virtuous one, who are you?
Are you a deva or a nāga?"
"Are you Brahmā or Śakra?
Are you a human or a deity?
At that time, the Bodhisattva, free from pride, greed, and anger, having severed all thorns of affliction and speaking without guile or crookedness, replied to King Bimbisāra of Magadha:
"Great King!
You should know that I am not a deva, nor a nāga, nor a Brahmā;
I am a human being, Great King!"
"I have gone forth from home for the sake of seeking tranquility.
Then King Bimbisāra of Magadha said to the Bodhisattva,
"O worthy bhikṣu!"

Now that I behold you, I am filled with great joy; therefore, I now wish to pose a question. Out of my affection and reverence for you, I desire to speak a single word; I pray only that you will listen and receive it.
Why is this? You are currently young and in the prime of your life; you are peerlessly handsome and your physical form is exquisite, a time fit for pleasure, play, and indulgence.
Why now do you conceive such an intention as to become a śramaṇa, renouncing the royal palace to sit alone in the empty mountains?
Furthermore, O Benevolent One, with a physical appearance such as yours, it would be fitting only to apply red sandalwood paste; you ought not to wear these robes of the *kāṣāya*.

Your two hands should rather be used to guide and transform the world; with a hundred flavors set before you, to be enjoyed at will, how could you possibly hold a vessel and go about begging from others?
And he spoke in verse:
“Your noble body should be anointed with red sandalwood powder; you ought not to wear this tattered kāṣāya robe.
Your fingers are fit to point out the world; how could it be appropriate for you to live by begging food from others?”
Then, after King Bimbisāra had spoken these words, he addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:

"If you, O Benevolent One, out of love and respect for your father, do not accept the royal throne but instead renounce it to go forth into homelessness, I now entreat you to remain within my realm and enjoy the five sensory pleasures and all that you require; I shall comply with your every wish."
"I shall provide you with wealth, treasures, and female attendants.
If you assist me, I shall grant you half the kingdom to rule; you may dwell within my domain and receive my royal throne. I shall serve you and ensure that you lack for nothing."
For what reason?
O worthy śramaṇa!
Your body is so delicate that you should not dwell in a secluded araṇya; if you sit upon a bed of grass on the bare ground, it will injure your body and I fear you may fall ill.
"However, after a short time, my noble father will decline and pass away, and you shall once again receive the royal throne of your own kingdom.
Therefore, if you now love me and have compassion for me, accept this royal throne of mine and dwell within my realm."

Since you, O Benevolent One, are known as one of great lineage, yet find my realm narrow and my land impure and mixed, I and my ministers and all the various officials shall further open up other countries for you, making them vast and spacious so that we may rule them together with you.
"Furthermore, I wish that you, a member of a noble family, and I may together create the conditions for a close and affectionate kinship.
Do not give rise to doubt, thinking this to be untrue.
And he spoke in verse:
“If you, O Benevolent One, claim to be of great lineage and loathe my realm as being too narrow to stay,
I shall join with my ministers and officials to further annex territories and make it vast.”
When King Māgadha had spoken these words, he addressed the Bodhisattva once more, saying:

"I have feelings of affection and respect for you, as well as a heart of veneration. Since you, O Benevolent One, now seek alms to sustain your life, you should simply exert yourself to cultivate a broad and expansive mind, accepting the Dharma, accepting wealth, and enjoying the pleasures of the five senses."

Why is this? By receiving these three kinds [of offerings], while staying within the palace and enjoying the pleasures of the company of court ladies, one can cause others to obtain rewards in the present life, and likewise in the future.

If a person does not accept these three kinds of dharmas but abandons even one of them, that person will ultimately be unable to obtain the full fruit of retribution, whether in the present life or in the future;
even if they do accept them, there will necessarily be deficiencies.
Therefore, O virtuous one!

If you broaden your mind, you ought to fully experience these three kinds of happiness. By experiencing these three joys, you shall utilize the youthful years and the karmic fruit of physical beauty to receive the Dharma, receive wealth, and receive all manner of desires.
When a man of the world experiences desire, he fathers a son who succeeds him; this is a great wealth.
Therefore, O virtuous one, do not let it pass in vain.
“Furthermore, worthy one!
These arms and shoulders of yours are capable of drawing bows and crossbows; do not let them go to waste for the sake of this single lifetime alone.
Furthermore, in the past, King Mūrdhagata, by virtue of his valor and strength, ruled over the four continents as well as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.”
Thus, O worthy one, you are capable of undertaking this task. Why is this?
I now offer this exhortation out of compassion for all sentient beings; I do not exhort you for the sake of my own royal throne.

Now that I behold your noble person, with such upright and graceful form, tears of sorrow flow from my eyes and my heart cannot bear it; for this reason, I have conceived a redoubled sense of longing and thus earnestly entreat you with such bitter persistence.

"You are currently in the prime of your youth; for now, pursue worldly desires. Wait until you are old and decrepit, when it is time to practice the Dharma, and only then may you leave the household life.
"Furthermore, O worthy one!"

Since the time of our ancestors, within this very lineage, when one reaches old age, one first entrusts the affairs of royal governance to the crown prince or a great minister according to the laws of the land, and only then relinquishes the throne to go forth from home and enter the mountains.
"Furthermore, worthy one! In the past, the sages spoke thus:

'In youth, one should first engage in sensual pleasures; in middle age, one should seek wealth to support oneself; and when one reaches old age and infirmity, only then may one abandon [worldly concerns] to practice and study the Dharma. In this way, one can establish everything.'"

Furthermore, when a person is young, they do not indulge in various desires nor seek after wealth; this is an enemy to the body and is also called a thief, for it ruins the sense faculties and makes them difficult to control.
"Furthermore, worthy one!

Even if one is young and desires to seek the Dharma, yet is dragged away by the sense faculties toward the five desires, when one reaches old age, one may contemplate within the mind, sever all worldly affairs, be able to restrain the sense faculties, give rise to a sense of shame and remorse, and attain tranquility of mind."
"Furthermore, O worthy one!
When young people in this world are in the midst of heedlessness, they do not perceive the distant path and thus commit many transgressions.
By the time they reach middle age, their vital energy gradually weakens and their period of heedlessness has already passed."
It is like a person traveling across a vast wilderness who, coming to a halt, sighs and says, "I have already crossed over this place.
Therefore, O virtuous one, while you are now in the prime of youth and at a time of indulgence, as much as you desire, I pray that you may enjoy sensual pleasures for the time being.
"Furthermore, O worthy one!

When one is young, the faculties are difficult to turn back. If you, worthy one, wish to practice the Dharma and take delight in the Dharma, you may follow the family traditions of your house to perform sacrifices to the various devas; by means of these sacrifices, you shall also attain birth in the heavens."
While staying within the household, he adorns his own person, with his two arms embellished by gold, silver, and various jewels; these many jewels emit light like bright lamps.
"Furthermore, O virtuous one!

In the past, various kings wore jeweled crowns upon their heads and adorned their bodies; they constantly remained within their palaces, making offerings to the devas, practicing the path of Dharma, and establishing unrestricted assemblies (*amogha-mahāpariṣad*). Alternatively, some entered the mountains to practice the conduct of great sages (*maharṣi*) in order to seek liberation.
"O Benevolent One, having now studied under them, you should act in accordance with the times.
Thus, King Māgadha, through various metaphors and words, employed skillful means to exhort the Bodhisattva.

At that time, having heard these words from King Māgadha, the Bodhisattva was neither afraid nor startled, neither astonished nor amazed; like the king of mountains, his body and mind remained unmoved, dwelling in tranquil composure. Guarding and collecting his sense faculties, he gave rise to no other thoughts; with the three karmas purified, he replied to the king:
And there is a verse that says:
“The King of Magadha admonished the Bodhisattva, Just as friends advise one another for their mutual benefit;
But the Bodhisattva’s pure conduct of the three karmas Was like a flower that does not cling to water, and he requited him thus.”
“‘Great King of Magadha! Your words are unwholesome;
this speech is like the talk of an ignorant person and does not accord with the principles of kingship for the world.’”
If Your Majesty possesses a sincere heart toward me, and these words are truly honest—yet fail to bring deep benefit or show compassion for me—they will cause me great harm.

In this world there are evil people who lack a heart of compassion, like those who, though wealthy and noble, are cowardly and weak. If one wishes to benefit the world, one should instruct them by teaching the matters handed down from the past; such a person is called a friend, and such an act is called growth.
If, when ordinary people encounter hardship and calamity, one does not abandon them but remains united with them in body, speech, and mind, such a person is called a true friend;
this is my view. At a time of wealth and honor, who cannot act as a friend or a companion?
If a person acquires wealth and manages it according to the Dharma so that it is not dissipated, they are called a wise friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

When such a person later wishes to utilize their treasures and instructs them, the other does not heed their words; yet, whether due to past karma or by losing the wealth themselves, they do not feel regret later on.
‘If Your Majesty intends to be my friend and regards me with love and respect, please reveal this matter; I may then either praise Your Majesty or not praise Your Majesty.
Having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva further addressed the king as follows:
‘Great King!’
You should know that I now seek the Way solely out of fear of birth, old age, sickness, and death; for this reason, desiring liberation, I have assumed this form.

One's kinsmen and relatives are truly dear and beloved, worthy of respect and difficult to part with; their faces are drenched with tears as they weep in anguish, and some may even give up their lives for my sake.
"I have already turned my back on them and come to this place; yet, regarding the matters of the five worldly desires, greed, attachment, and clinging are mostly due to unwholesome states.
"Furthermore, Great King!"

I do not truly fear those venomous snakes, nor do I fear the thunderbolts of heaven, nor do I fear the fierce flames of a wildfire driven by the great wind that burns the marshes and forests; I only fear being oppressed by the realm of the five desires.
For what reason?

Great King, you should know that all sensual desires are impermanent, like bandits who plunder all merits; they are as empty and without reality as illusions manifested in the world, which appear real when observed, yet their essence is nothing but deception.
"The people of the world do not understand this, yet they stubbornly cling their minds to them; how much more so for those who actually practice the five desires?
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke these verses:
"The five desires are impermanent and harm merit; The six sense objects are empty and illusory, injuring sentient beings."
The worldly fruits of retribution are fundamentally deceptive; what wise person could remain stationary for even a moment?
If the foolish find no satisfaction even in the heavens, how much less can they find contentment in the human realm?
One does not perceive the defilement and attachment of desire, which is like a fierce fire burning dry grass.
In the past, the noble King Māndhātṛ, sovereign of the four realms, brought them under his control as his golden wheel flew;
he even attained half of Śakra’s seat, yet when greed suddenly arose, he fell.
Even if one were to rule this entire great earth, the mind would still desire to encompass other lands;
the worldly crave their desires without knowing satiety, like the vast ocean receiving all flowing streams.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva had spoken these words, he further addressed him, saying:

"Great King, you should know that in the past there was a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Nahuṣa. He ruled over the four continents as well as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and though his transformation encompassed both devas and humans, he still knew no satisfaction."
For this reason, he fell back into the world.

"Furthermore, King Ilāvarta, the Wheel-Turning Monarch, was also like this; though he ruled over the four continents and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, because he lacked contentment, his life came to an end."
"Furthermore, once the Asura King Bali had attained the throne, he was defeated in battle against Śakra and consequently had it seized from him."
After Śakra had obtained it, he in turn was deprived of it by that Cakravartin King Nahuṣa.
Once King Nahuṣa had obtained it, he was again deprived of it by Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
In this way, the realms of gods and humans are subject to reversal and are entirely impermanent; who, then, possesses superior merit?
When one reaches that state, if there is a wise person capable of such reflection and observation, they will realize: "The realm of impermanence changes in an instant; how can it be trusted?"

There are only those seers dwelling in the mountain forests who subsist on various medicinal roots, tubers, fruits, flowers, and leaves; they wear tree bark or the fur and hides of deceased animals; their bodies are so emaciated that only skin and bone remain; and they desire to attain deliverance and transcend all the sufferings of the world, seeking liberation in the unconditioned state of nirvāṇa.
If one is entangled and oppressed by the indulgence of the five desires, one will fall back into the cycle of rebirth; what wise person would delight in craving this?
To be attached to the five desires is like seeking out an enemy for oneself.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further spoke in verse:
“The various sages who dwell in mountain valleys, Eating fruit, drinking water, and wearing tree bark—
Though their hair is matted and their bodies are emaciated, It is because they seek liberation and detachment from desire.”
They cannot restrain themselves, being still dragged away by the five desires;
such are these impermanent enemies of desire—those of wisdom should not be attached to them.
At that time, having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva further addressed him, saying:
"Great King, you should know that within the realm of desire, one seeks union for the sake of savoring its flavors; yet once that has been obtained, one knows no satisfaction."

If one lacks wisdom, though they experience various desires in the present, because they do not know contentment, they undergo great suffering and affliction; furthermore, they will suffer its calamities in future lives as well.
For this reason, a wise person does not grasp at the notion of desire.

Therefore, the wise person, seeing that those who practice unwholesome deeds undergo great suffering and desiring their own peace and security, should not engage in nor delight in any sensual desires, but must abandon them.
If there is a gathering, one should know that separation is certain.

Even if one indulges in desires and lets one's passions run wild, the mind becomes negligent; when negligence increases, one commits unwholesome deeds. Once unwholesome deeds are accomplished, one falls into hell.

In past lives, one performed great ascetic practices and presently obtained various desires; yet after obtaining those desires, despite striving to maintain them, one was unable to guard them and they were inevitably lost.
"Furthermore, Great King!
Regarding these various desires, if a wise person reflects thus:
'The people of the world, both gods and humans, are like borrowed goods; since they are not permanent things, why does the mind covet them?'"
All the karmic fruits of these gods and humans are like dew upon the grass, like the head of a venomous snake, or like the skeletal remains of corpses in a desolate forest.
Furthermore, they are like a mass of flesh in a woman’s first pregnancy, like a dream, like an illusion, and like a mass of fire.

"Such various things involve many calamities and misfortunes; they are constantly oppressed by all manner of suffering and affliction. Therefore, a wise person should not harbor a mind of attachment or delight toward them.
Furthermore, Great King!"
As various treatises state, in times past, in the city of Maitrīla, there was a blind king within that city named Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Although the king was blind, he raised many sons, numbering one hundred, all of whom possessed talent and wisdom.
The king’s younger brother also had five sons of his own; thus, including uncles and brothers, there were one hundred and five in total.
When their respective fathers passed away, they vied with one another to become kings; driven by the conditions of their desires, they slaughtered and destroyed each other until none remained.
"Furthermore, Great King!
It was just as when the vast wilderness of Dandaka was consumed by fire, and Aśvatara slaughtered all manner of creatures."
"Furthermore, it is like those asuras beneath Mount Sumeru; their brothers, each out of greed, desired the same jade maiden, and as they vied with one another, they fought and killed each other."

"Furthermore, just as in the world at the site of a butcher or meat-seller, where various wooden stakes are erected and the forms of diverse kinds of livestock are hung there for slaughter, so it is with the objects of desire;
how could a wise person find delight in them with their mind?"
He then spoke in verse:
"In the past, two brothers of the asuras Slew each other for the sake of a single jade maiden.
Through affection for their own flesh and blood, they were stained by attachment and hatred; The wise man observes and knows this, and thus does not crave desire."
The Bodhisattva spoke again: "Great King,
you should know that there may be people who, for the sake of the five desires, or wishing to be born in heaven, or wishing to be born in the human realm [practice such deeds]."
Once born, because of attachment to the five desires, one throws oneself into water or rushes into fire.
Such is impermanence and the delusive realm; for the sake of the five desires, one seeks out one's own enemies—what meaning is there in such longing and pleasure?
Furthermore, he spoke in verse:
"Because of their craving for desire, foolish people are impoverished; Bound, wounded, and killed, they undergo all manner of suffering.
In their minds, they hope that these desires will accomplish their many aims, Yet they do not realize that their strength is exhausted and they will suffer calamity in the next life."
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"O King of Magadha!
I know that these five desires possess such various and manifold faults and afflictions; Your Majesty should not now attempt to entice me with these five desires."
I now wish to travel the path of fearlessness; if Your Majesty is truly my good friend, you should repeatedly exhort me, saying:
"May the great vows and sublime aspirations you have set forth be swiftly fulfilled, and may you quickly be liberated from afflictions."

"Why is this? It is not that I have entered the mountain forests because I was pursued by others, nor have I been driven out by enemies, nor have I fled because my royal throne was seized by another, nor do I seek to emulate the ancient seers of old by withdrawing from the world; therefore, I shall not accept the king's words."
"Furthermore, Great King!
If someone were to grasp the head of a venomous snake and, having let it go, wished to seize it once again—would that be possible?"
It is like a fierce torch: having released it because it burned one's hand, would one then seize it again?
In just this way, I have already abandoned those five desires and gone forth; for me now to take them up again would be exactly the same.
"Furthermore, Great King!
For example, would a person with clear vision and eyes ever envy one who is blind?
For example, would a person who is liberated and free from affairs ever envy one who is bound in prison and burdened by worldly concerns?"
For example, would a person of immense wealth and great riches ever envy one who is poor, starving, cold, and begging?
Or would a person of clear understanding and sharp wisdom ever envy one who is mad and deranged?
"Yet even they still have things to envy; I, however, have now departed from such five desires and have nothing left to crave.
Furthermore, Great King!"
"As the Great King previously stated: 'Dwell within my realm, enjoy my five sensory pleasures, and amuse yourself as you wish; I shall provide you with abundant wealth as well as female attendants.
O Great King!"
"You should know that I do not now take up the five worldly desires, nor any of the matters previously described.
Furthermore, Great King!
While I was in my former palace, amidst an abundance of the five desires, I was already able to renounce sixty thousand court ladies to leave the home life and enter the mountains."
"Great King!

You should know that all sensual desires are like this: they possess immeasurable and boundless harms and afflictions, dragging people directly toward the great hells; as for their subsequent retribution, one returns to the realms of animals and hungry ghosts; in this present life, they further sever all roots of goodness and are not praised by the noble ones."
"Furthermore, Great King!
The various desires of the world are like floating clouds, having no momentary stability;
they are like a fierce wind arising, which does not rest for even an instant."
It is like the flow of mountain waters, where the surging waves rush with great urgency.
Furthermore, Great King!

If a person is foolish and addicted to the five desires, they do not know the original limit (pūrvakoṭi) and sink into the cycle of birth and death. Bound by afflictions, they cannot attain liberation; they are like a traveler far from home who, exhausted by hardship and fatigue, drinks salt water, which only increases their thirst even further.
"In this way, and in this way, it is likewise with those who experience the five sensual pleasures and do not recognize their peril.
Furthermore, Great King, I shall now speak of what must be said:
suppose there were a person who obtained the five sensual pleasures of the devas as well as the most exquisite five sensual pleasures of humans, possessing them all in pure abundance."
"Having obtained these various desires, a single person does not know contentment; they increase further still and seek them out in all places.
Furthermore, Great King!
As Your Majesty previously stated, we shall rule the kingdom of Magadha together, and I shall cede half of my share to govern the rest of the world;

or again, you may say that I shall accept your royal throne and you will relinquish it all to me, and I shall serve you; or perhaps we shall raise an army to expand our territory, making it pure, vast, and magnificent.
"Furthermore, Great King!

I have now renounced those four continents, which were entirely abundant and lacked nothing, along with the seven treasures I previously possessed; I have abandoned them all to go forth into homelessness."
"How could I now again covet the petty position of a minor king over this single kingdom?
Furthermore, Great King!

It is like the fruit of the merit of the Sāgara Dragon King of the great ocean: having obtained the vast and expansive waters of the great ocean as his palace, fully adorned with the seven treasures, how could he ever again covet the water in a cow's hoofprint?"
"Great King!

You should know this: just so, just so. Since I have now already aroused a courageous mind, renounced the four continents, the seven precious palaces and towers, dyed my robes, shaved my hair, left the household life, and entered the mountains—if I were now to again covet the worldly throne of kingship, it would be exactly the same."
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds,
Scroll Twenty-three and Scroll Twenty-four,
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on Encouraging the Acceptance of Worldly Benefits, Part Two:
At that time, the Bodhisattva again addressed the king, saying:

"As you previously stated, O King: 'A benevolent bhikṣu has a body of such softness that he should not dwell in the empty and secluded forests of the araṇya, nor sleep, lie down, sit, or rest upon mats spread of grass.'"

"Great King, you should know that while I was in my own palace, seated upon a couch made of various exquisite jewels, I became weary and disenchanted; having thus renounced, I left the household life."

Why is this so? Great King, you must recognize that this body is fragile and brittle, subject to decay and impermanence; it is not a solid form, but a phenomenon destined for disintegration, which one must leave behind wherever one goes.
It is just like a lump of clay; they are of one kind and no different.
Furthermore, Great King!
If a wise person has already cast away a corpse, would he ever pick it up again?
"If you wish to take it back again, such a thing is ultimately impossible.
"Furthermore, Great King!
As Your Majesty previously stated, if you feel compassion for me, you ought to rejoice; yet to suddenly find fault with my living by begging for alms is not right."
"O Great King!
You should know that those who love me should not harbor such thoughts. Why is this?"

I now wish to cross the ocean of the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death; I practice the various deeds to enter the Path, and for this reason I have assumed this form of a bhikṣu. It is for the sake of seeking the state of quiescent peace and bliss that I must accept this appearance of wearing shabby robes; furthermore, it is because I desire to eliminate all faults and calamities in future lives.
"Great King!
You should know that if there is another person who, in this present life, experiences the fruit and reward of those five sensual desires and becomes deeply attached to craving."
Those people must be pitied.
If there is anyone who, in this present life, does not attain a mind of tranquil stability and peace, they will certainly undergo various sufferings in their future births.
"You should feel compassion for those sentient beings.
Furthermore, Great King!
Because I am now terrified by the suffering of the afflictions (*kleśa*), I have renounced the world to seek the true reality of quiescent nirvāṇa."
"Even if I were to obtain the palace of Śakra, Lord of Devas, my mind would find no pleasure; how much less so for the coarse and inferior retributions of the human realm?
He then spoke in verse:
"I have been pierced by the arrows of affliction, Seeking the medicinal ointment of nirvāṇa to apply."
"Even if one were to obtain the palace of Śakra, Lord of Devas, the mind would still not be greedy for it, much less for a royal throne.
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"Great King!..."

You should know that, as the King previously stated, regarding all people in the world who must seek benefit across the three periods of time, from my perspective, such words do not constitute true benefit.
Why is this so? Seeking wealth may yield much, yet all meetings must inevitably end; seeking desire only increases desire, for there is never a time of satiety.
If one speaks of seeking the Dharma, this is true benefit. Though benefits vary in depth, they must necessarily be sought; in seeking them, there are five kinds of efficacious power.
And he spoke in verse:
“If one is free from the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death, This person is a true Great Man (mahāpuruṣa).
The pursuit of wealth and the indulgence in desires are entirely worldly sentiments; I renounce these two pursuits and seek only the Dharma.”
The Bodhisattva spoke again: "Great King!

You should know that as for what Your Majesty said previously—that you should merely rule the people and assume the royal throne, and while still in the prime of youth and not yet old, enjoy those five sensual pleasures—that is also not so."
Why is this? If youth were something permanent, all sentient beings would never grow old; and in every place, they would not be led away moment by moment by that ghost of death.

Because the lifespans of sentient beings are not fixed, a wise person who seeks the dharma of tranquil concentration and liberation must not seek to obtain the worldly throne or the pleasures of the five desires.

Therefore, whether one is in youth, middle age, or even old age, one must quickly seek to accomplish what ought to be done and ensure it is completed early. If you wish to seek liberation or seek meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), do not allow it to be delayed; you should act with great urgency.
"Furthermore, Great King!

As Your Majesty previously stated—that one must rely on family tradition to perform sacrifices and practice giving in order to seek whatever fruits and rewards one desires in future lives—Great King!"
You should know that I do not now take such pleasure as this.
If pleasure is sought and obtained because suffering has come to press with urgency, this is not true pleasure.
When ordinary people seek rewards in future lives by performing sacrifices to various deities and the fire god, they must inevitably take the lives of other sentient beings; this is irrational.

Why is this so? If a person practices loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they should not harm the life-faculties of others. Even if one were to sacrifice all the various devas and the fire-god (*agni-deva*), and by killing sentient beings obtain the fixed fruit of eternal bliss, it would still be improper to take life for the sake of such a sacrifice;
how much more so when all fruits obtained are impermanent, subject to destruction and extinction, and not a solid dharma?
"Furthermore, Great King!

When an ordinary person wishes to practice the Dharma of liberation, even if they possess no special benefits, or lack diligent practice, or lack the observance of precepts, or lack meditative concentration, they still must not harm the lives of others while seeking future beneficial rewards."
Furthermore, when ordinary worldlings in this world obtain the fruit of peace and happiness by means of killing living beings, this too is unwholesome. Why is that?
"Because they lack compassion, it is absolutely impossible for them to hope for a good retribution in the future.
He then spoke in verse:
"Even if a person were born into this world, And obtained happiness by killing the lives of others,"
"The wise declare this to be not good; how much less, then, for seeking rebirth as a human or deva in future lives.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha, having heard these words of the Bodhisattva, conceived a sense of rare and extraordinary wonder.
Before the Bodhisattva, out of compassion, he spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent!
Śramaṇa Gautama!"
He possesses the virtue of great asceticism and difficult practices, and is able to renounce all desires within the world.
O venerable bhikṣu!
From what direction have you suddenly come?
In which village was he born?
Of what lineage is he?
Where are his parents from?
"Who are you by name?
Having spoken these words, he listened with a sincere and attentive mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, with a composed mind and a steady gaze, replied to the king in a gentle tone:
"Great King!
You should know that to the north of here, beneath the Snowy Mountains, there is a great settlement called the Śākya clan.

There is a city there named Kapilavastu (translated in the Sui language as 'Abode of the Yellow-Headed'), where a king of the Śākya clan resides, known by the name Śuddhodana; he is my father, and I am his son. My mother’s name is Māyā (translated in the Sui language as 'Illusion'), and my name is Siddhārtha (translated in the Sui language as 'Accomplished Benefit')."
When King Bimbisāra heard these words, he wept and wailed in grief. After a short while, having wiped his tears from his face, he addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
“How extraordinary, O Bhikṣu! Having been born into such a great family of noble lineage, why do you wander alone within this forest?”

The various beasts here are fierce and evil, terrifying and fearsome; this forest is not auspicious. How can you dwell, sit, and rise alone in self-comfort, without any companion, merely seeking your own amusement?
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied to Bimbisāra:

"Great King, you should know that I now have no fear of any wicked beasts; nor am I startled, terrified, or cowed. Even if they were to come here, they would not be able to move so much as a single hair on my body."
"Great King!

You should know that I now fear only being oppressed by birth, old age, sickness, and death; therefore, I have come here to this forest of terrifying wild beasts, where I enjoy myself alone and without a companion."
"Great King!
You should know that old age is most fearsome. Why is this? Because—"

When old age approaches, it can seize one's youth; it carries away one’s vigor and strength, breaking down the physical form until the waist and spine are bent and one can no longer walk. Like a withered tree, who would take pleasure in looking upon such a sight?
"This is most terrifying.
Furthermore, Great King!
That which is called 'the arrival of disease' is what is truly terrifying."

Why is this so? During times of health and vigor, one neither knows nor perceives [the coming end]; yet when a single day of excruciating pain arrives, one wallows and moans. What was once radiant and flourishing suddenly withers and fades; beset by distress, resentment, and agonizing torment, one finds no peace whether lying down or sitting up. At such a time, who could take one’s place?
"Lying upon a bed and pillow, one's physical condition does not follow one's will.
For this reason, illness is most fearsome.
Furthermore, Great King!"
Death is most fearsome. Why is this?

On the day death arrives, it diminishes my lifespan and suddenly seizes me away; even if one possesses the power to govern the four continents, with a golden wheel subduing all and the seven treasures leading the way, neither sharp blades nor strong armies can obstruct it, nor can it be contested or reclaimed.
"For this reason, death is the most terrifying thing for human beings.
At that time, King Bimbisāra again questioned the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Great Holy Prince!
"What do you seek now, O Benevolent One?
The Bodhisattva replied,
"Great King Māgadha!"
What I now seek is solely anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; having attained it, I shall turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma. It is for this reason that I seek it.
Then King Bimbisāra addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Great Holy Prince!

As I see it, your mind is courageous and you are diligent and persevering; there is no doubt that you will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and you will surely be able to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma."
Excellent, Prince!
I have now beheld your virtue.
Excellent, Prince!
I have heard your name, O virtuous one!
Excellent, Prince!
You have well renounced the world.
"O virtuous son of the Śākya lineage, from this day forward, I shall constantly serve you.
Great Sage Prince!

I now invite you to come to my palace every single day; I pray that you will see me frequently. Whatever four kinds of requisites you require, I shall provide them so that you never lack for anything."
When King Bimbisāra had spoken these words, the Bodhisattva replied:
"Great King,
you should know that before long I shall depart from here and proceed to another region."
When King Bimbisāra heard these words, he joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Great Holy Prince!
Regarding that which Your Benevolent Heart seeks, I pray only that there be no obstacles from Māras; may that which You intend to achieve be swiftly accomplished."
O virtuous son of the Śākya lineage!

I pray that when you attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I may reverently make offerings to you; having beheld your person, I shall immediately become your *śrāvaka* disciple in accordance with the Dharma.
Thereupon, he spoke a verse in praise, saying:
"I, King Bimbisāra, join my palms in praise: I pray only that the Prince may swiftly accomplish the Way.
If you have achieved your purpose, please remember these words now and grant compassion to all sentient beings."
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva immediately replied to the king, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!
May it be as you have said; may the vows we have made be auspicious for both of us."
Then King Bimbisāra, joining his ten fingers in palms-together salutation, bowed his head with single-minded devotion and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, Prince!
You should now accept my repentance on my behalf."
"Out of ignorance, I have troubled and disturbed the Great Sage.
The Prince has transcended desire and regards it as impure, whereas my mind is stained by desire and takes it to be pure."
"I only pray that you will show me leniency and pardon this offense of mine.
At that time, the Bodhisattva smiled with joy and addressed King Bimbisāra, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!"

"So be it, so be it. Having accepted the King’s pure confession, I pray that you may abide in peace and happiness, with little illness and little affliction; that you guard your body and mind with vigilance, never again succumb to negligence, always practicing wholesome dharmas and abandoning what is unrighteous."
"If it be so, Your Majesty shall attain peace and security, and receive much prosperity.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, by means of teaching the Dharma and its meaning, consoled King Bimbisāra, causing him to rejoice; having exhorted, instructed, elucidated, and proclaimed [the truth], he rose from his seat and gradually departed for another place.

Then King Bimbisāra immediately went forward and prostrated at the Bodhisattva’s two feet; having circumambulated him three times, he stood upon the ground facing the Bodhisattva, gazing at him for a short while, and then returned from that place back to his palace.
And there is a verse that says:
"The Bodhisattva confirmed the words of Bimbisāra: 'When I have attained the Way, I shall deliver the King.
Reflecting upon the conduct of the Great Sage with joy, He did not realize he had returned from the mountain to his own country."

Chapter 29: The Chapter on Austerities and Asceticism. *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Twenty-nine, Part One: "Austerities and Asceticism. "At that time, the Bodhisattva emerged from the forest of Paṇḍava Hill and proceeded on foot with steady composure toward the city of Gayā. Having arrived there, he ascended Mount Gayāśīrṣa (translated in the Sui language as 'Elephant-Head') in order to collect his mind and body and to eliminate all evils."
Having ascended that mountain, he chose a level spot and sat upon a spread of grass beneath a tree.
At that time, the Bodhisattva contemplated within his mind three similes, all of which were rare occurrences in the world, never before heard, never before seen, and never before realized.
What are these three?

First, there are those śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, although their bodies do not engage in sensual desires, yet within all those desires, their minds still possess desire-love, desire-affliction, desire-fever, and desire-attachment; these are not extinguished, nor have they attained right concentration. Still harboring the notion of a self, they seek deliverance for their own bodies alone.

Such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas constantly experience suffering and affliction; their minds are not joyful and their hearts find no delight. They are unable to know or see, nor do they attain the Dharma of the Supreme Benevolent One, nor can they realize the state of fearlessness.
However, although they lack the notion of a self and do not merely cross over themselves nor undergo suffering and affliction,
and although they do not experience mental states of joy or delight, they are still unable to know, realize, and witness the Dharma and the state of fearlessness.
"It is as if there were a person who took fresh, wet wood and wet dung, placed them upon the water, and tried to churn out fire from within.
Then, another person intentionally came from the opposite bank and begged him for fire."
However, if such a person were to take wet wood, wet dung, and water, and exert effort to rub them together to produce fire, would they be able to obtain fire?
If they could, it would be utterly impossible.
Since the fire does not emerge, from what could that person obtain it by seeking it?
In this very way, if there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, though they do not practice sensual desire, are nevertheless unable to know, realize, and witness the Dharma.
"This is the first analogy, which has never existed nor been heard of in the world.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further engaged in a second reflection, thinking:

'If those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, though they restrain their bodies and do not engage in sensual desire, still possess within them the feverish affliction and attachment of mental craving for desires, which they have not extinguished; they have not attained right concentration, yet still maintain the notion of a self, saving only themselves, and in vain undergo suffering and distress, neither joyful nor at ease, unable to know, witness, or realize the state of the fearless Dharma of the Supreme Sages.'"

Furthermore, although they lack the notion of a self, they do not merely liberate their own bodies from suffering; yet, because they do not experience joy in their minds, they are unable to know, witness, realize, and attain the Dharma of the Noble Ones and the state of fearlessness.
It is like a person who takes fresh, damp wood and places it on the ground, wishing to produce fire by friction.
Then another person comes to him and begs for fire.
Suppose one were to take moist wood and, by rubbing it together, seek to produce fire; would that person be able to obtain fire?
If they could obtain it, such a thing is impossible.
In this very same way, although these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas do not practice sensual desire, they are nonetheless unable to know, see, realize, or witness the Dharma.
"This second analogy has not been heard of in the world.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further engaged in a third reflection, thinking:

"If there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, though restraining their bodies and abstaining from sensual desires, still possess within those very desires mental craving, feverish affliction, and attachment—such that these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, despite having attained self-benefit and the benefit of others, and despite the joy and pleasure in their hearts, are unable to know or see the Dharma of the Supreme Sage or to realize the state of fearlessness."
It is like a person who takes dry wood and dry dung, places them upon the ground, and wishes to rub them together to produce fire.
There is also another person who comes from this shore and begs him for fire.
And that person, with little effort, immediately obtains fire and gives it to the other person.

In this very way, if there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who practice free from desire, their mental afflictions of craving and fever within desire are extinguished, and they even attain the Dharma of the Supreme Noble One and realize the state of fearlessness.
"This is the third parable of the Bodhisattva, arising from his own reflection; all of it has never before been heard or seen in the world.
At that time, the Bodhisattva descended from Mount Gayāśīrṣa and proceeded toward the village of Magadha, walking step by step and asking people:
"What meritorious practices are there in this place that may be performed?"
"What unrighteousness is there that must be severed?
I now seek the most supreme tranquility and the most wondrous speech.
Having proceeded thus, he arrived south of Gayā at a village named Uruvilvā.
When he arrived at that place, it was time for the midday meal.

The Bodhisattva put on his robes and entered the village, going to a potter’s house where he begged for a ceramic vessel. Having obtained one, he held it in his hand and proceeded through the village, begging for food in due order, until he reached the home of a village headman, an elder named Nandika (translated in the Sui language as "Self-pleased").
Having arrived at that house, he stood to one side and remained there in silence.

Now, the village headman Nandika had a virtuous daughter named Sujātā (translated in the Sui language as "Well-Born"), who was of such exquisite beauty and peerless charm that she was a delight for all people to behold.
The daughter of Sujātā saw from afar the Bodhisattva standing silently with an earthenware bowl in his hand, wishing to beg for food; upon seeing him, milk spontaneously flowed from her two breasts.
At that time, the daughter of Sujāta asked the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O most excellent and benevolent one!
Whose son are you?"
What is his caste?
What is his name?
Where are his parents from?
"What do you seek now?
O Benevolent One, what is your nature, and what divine wonders do you possess?
By merely seeing you once, you have caused the milk from both my breasts to flow naturally."
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied:
"Good sister!
My name is Siddhārtha; this is the name established for me by my parents. I now wish to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and having attained it, I shall turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma."

When the maiden Sujātā heard these words, she took the earthenware vessel from the Bodhisattva’s hand, entered her own home, and filled it to overflowing with fragrant, delicious, and sweet foods, as well as various cakes, fruits, soups, and stews. She then came out, knelt on her right knee, offered the vessel to the Bodhisattva, and spoke these words:
"O Most Excellent and Benevolent One!"
I vow to constantly provide for you, O Venerable One, with the four requisites—robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal elixirs—ensuring that all your needs are fully satisfied.
I only pray, O Venerable One!
I accept you with compassion.

As I observe the name bestowed upon you by your parents, and see your diligence, valor, and single-minded devotion, I am certain that you will surely achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and will definitively turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma; this is the truth, beyond doubt.
"O Benevolent One, when you have accomplished the path to Bodhi, you should come to my home to receive my offerings; deliver me from suffering, and I shall become your disciple as a śrāvaka."
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied:
"Good sister!
May it be as you wish."
Having accepted the food, he then departed from there.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva had received the alms-food from the girl Sujātā, he ate it according to the Dharma in a secluded and quiet place.

Having finished eating, he set out and gradually arrived at a certain place where the ground was level, pure, and delightful; his heart rejoiced at the desire to behold it. There, the forest was lush and dense, with branches and twigs flourishing profusely, abounding in flowers and fruits. Purely flowing canals and fragrant, beautiful waters—rivers, ponds, springs, and marshes—reflected one another in a crisscrossing array; all manner of things were abundant, lacking nothing.

Those waters are neither shallow nor deep, clear and limpid, easy to cross and easy to draw from; within them there are no poisonous or malevolent insects, and they are surrounded on all sides by excellent birds and beasts.
He departed from the village, neither too near nor too far, so that he might go and return for alms without weariness or exhaustion;
the roads and paths between were level and even, neither low nor high, easy to travel and easy to traverse.

If there should be someone who desires to seek the unsurpassed, most supreme benefit—which is easy to obtain and easy to accomplish, swiftly realized and swiftly attained—and which is moreover free from mosquitoes, gadflies, and various insects and scorpions; which is not noisy, with few people passing to and fro during the day to cause disturbance, and where at night all sounds are cut off, being peaceful, quiet, and secluded; where the temperature is harmoniously balanced and wind and rain follow their proper seasons—such a place is fit for practicing the path of meditative concentration and cultivating the mind.
Furthermore, in the past there was a royal seer named Gaya—translated in the Sui language as "Elephant"—who resided there; this was the site of that royal seer’s former city-dwelling.
At that time, having seen this ground, the Bodhisattva reflected thus:
"The terrain here is excellent, well-proportioned, and level; it is pleasing to the eye at first sight and even suitable for practicing the path and cultivating dhyāna."
If there is a man who seeks the unsurpassed and most supreme benefit and would sever all evils, this ground is fully capable of providing a place for him to dwell securely.
Since I now desire to subdue all evils and cultivate all roots of goodness, I ought to halt here, sit in this place, and seek bodhi, ensuring that it is surely accomplished.
"Having reflected thus in his mind, the Bodhisattva immediately took some grass and spread it upon the ground to sit, intending to practice dhyāna.
Once he was seated in meditation, he thought to himself:
'May all sentient beings who seek liberation perform every kind of various and manifold ascetic practices.'"
It refers to certain classes of sentient beings who remain suspended with both hands raised, having renounced all worldly affairs because they are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Such practitioners of asceticism may, when begging for food, not accept food from the mouth of a jar;
or they may not accept food from the small opening of an alms bowl.
Some do not accept food from between two sheep;
some do not accept food from among human excrement;
and some do not accept food from those carrying staffs or poles.
Or he does not accept almsfood from those who carry swords or staves;
likewise, in such intervals, and when he knows that a woman has reached her period of impurity, he does not accept food from them;
nor does he accept food from a woman when she is pregnant.
Or, knowing that a household has impure karma, one does not accept food from them;
or there may be cases where one does not accept food from someone who is intoxicated by wine;
or when two people are eating together, one likewise does not accept food from their side.
When receiving food, if a dog comes before one, one shall not accept the food;
furthermore, when receiving food, if mosquitoes, gadflies, or the like should alight upon it, making it impure and foul, one shall likewise not accept it from such a person;
nor shall one accept food from someone who calls out or shouts while offering it to you.
If someone calls out, "Stay here and I will give you food," he does not accept it;
or if someone calls out, "I am preparing food as an offering, you should wait and take it," he likewise does not accept it;
nor does he accept food that has been intentionally prepared for him.
"Furthermore, there may be someone who does not accept food that is the remains of offerings made to the various devas;
nor does he accept food containing sugar or rock honey;
nor does he accept food containing ghee, oil, and so forth."
If there are items such as milk or curd within the food, one should not accept it;
if there are fish, mixed meats, or the like within the food, one should not accept it;
or if there are asafoetida, pungent scents, various spices, or similar flavors within the food, one should not accept it.
Alternatively, one may accept food from only one household and stop after a single mouthful;
or accept food from two households and stop after two mouthfuls;
and so on, up to accepting food from seven households and stopping after consuming exactly seven mouthfuls.
Or again, one may eat at only one mealtime in a day;
or again, one may eat at two mealtimes in a day;
or one may begin eating food only after half a day has passed.
Sometimes they would eat only once every three days;
sometimes they would eat a small amount on one day;
and sometimes they would eat a small amount on every second day.
Even for up to seven days, he takes only a small amount of food;
sometimes he eats only vegetables,
or sometimes he eats only millet.
Or again, some eat only the tender branches and twigs of trees;
or they eat only curd;
or again, some eat only the branches and twigs of the *kaniṅkala* tree.
At times they eat nothing but sheep dung;
at other times they eat nothing but cow dung, or sesame dregs,
or they eat the kernels of fruits.
Some eat various kinds of all root-herbs;
some eat lotus roots;
some eat various tender branches and twigs of grasses.
"Furthermore, there are some who sustain their lives by drinking only water;
some who sustain their lives with whatever they happen to obtain in small or large measure;
and others who sustain their lives by imitating wild beasts in eating grass."
At times they stand upright upon the ground;
at other times they sit in a fixed posture without moving;
and at yet other times they support themselves on four legs planted upon the earth, taking food with their mouths.
Some wear only garments made solely of pure grass;
some wear only tattered rags from charnel grounds;
and others wear various kinds of grass garments.
Some wore garments made of *kauseya* silk;
some wore garments made from white peach bark;
and some wore garments made from dragon-whiskers.
Furthermore, some used the skins of various animals to make robes;
some used old animal skins to make robes;
and some made robes from various types of hair and wool.
Some tear the hides of various animals into strips to make garments;
others again make robes from refuse rags.
Some are even naked.
Some lie upon thorns;
some lie upon wooden planks;
and others again lie upon mani-jewels.
Some lie upon rafters;
some lie among graves;
some dwell within ant-hills, just as snakes take up residence there.
Some lie on the open ground;
some again serve water;
others again serve fire.
Some turn about day by day;
some remain standing with both arms raised;
some remain crouching.
Or again, some smear their bodies with sand, soil, smoke, and dust and stand upright;
or they do not wash their heads, faces, or eyes, remaining with hair coiled like conch-shells;
or again, they pluck out their hair.
Some pluck out their beards and whiskers.

"Furthermore, some serve the deities of springs, ponds, wells, rivers, canals, and sources; the earth deities, tree deities, forest deities, mountain deities, and stone deities; or the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and asura kings such as Rāhu (translated in the Sui language as 'Speech'), Bali (translated in the Sui language as 'Hook'), and Vemacitra (translated in the Sui language as 'Subtle Mechanism') Śambara, and others;
or they serve the planet Jupiter."
Some worship the seer Bhiṣaj-rāja;
some worship the seer Parāśara;
and others again worship the seer Gautama.
Some worship the King Vaiśravaṇa;
some again worship the deity Kumāra, or Maheśvara, or worship the Sun, or worship the Moon;
some again worship Nārāyaṇa, or Śakra, or worship Brahmā, or worship the four world-protecting devas.
"Having thus brought each of them joy through their respective practices, he granted them the boons they requested; having obtained what they desired, each sought liberation.

Having observed that they were thus seeking liberation through erroneous means, the Bodhisattva, upon seeing this, resolved to practice the formidable and most arduous asceticism. Regarding this, there is a verse that says:
"When the Bodhisattva reached the Nairañjanā River, He sat upon its bank with a pure mind."
"Is it because those who seek the Way are not yet true in their practice that you wish to undergo great suffering to transform them?

At that time, the Bodhisattva, having observed thus with focused and upright contemplation, sat down, closed his mouth, pressed his teeth together, placed his tongue against the upper palate, and concentrated his mind in a single thought.

Maintaining such mindfulness and subduing both body and mind, he focused his attention by pressing his teeth, tongue, and palate together; while practicing in this manner, sweat flowed from beneath his armpits.

When the Bodhisattva saw that sweat was flowing in this manner, he once again gave rise to courageous and vigorous diligence; his mind was without attachment, neither erring nor confused, abiding in a state of tranquility, steadfast and unmoving. Thus, in this supreme manner, his body, mind, and speech were entirely unmoved by suffering.
At that time, he further thought to himself:
"I shall now enter the Immovable Samādhi.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva completely ceased all breathing from his mouth as well as the air from his nostrils.

Once the mouth and nose had ceased their activity, there immediately issued from the two ear canals a great sound of wind; the sound and force of that wind were like the great noise produced when fresh butter is churned within a large vat, as if stirring curdled milk.
In this very way, when the Bodhisattva closes the breath of his mouth and nose so that it does not exit, the sound of wind emerging from his two ear canals is likewise the same.
The Bodhisattva further reflected:
"I have now resolved upon a mind of diligence, free from all attachments and having abandoned indolence, even to the extent of such supreme asceticism and most excellent hardships."
He reflected again:
"I shall further enter the Immovable Samādhi.
At that time, having brought his body, speech, and mind to perfect stillness, the Bodhisattva ceased the breath of his mouth, nose, and ears, closing them all entirely.
Once the mouth, nose, and ears have all become completely stilled, the internal wind becomes powerful; because it cannot escape, the breath strikes the crown of the head.
It is like a brave and strong man of great strength who takes a fine, sharp axe and strikes another’s skull with it.

In this way, indeed, as the Bodhisattva held his breath so that it did not exit through his mouth, nose, or ears, because of the intensity of the internal wind, the sound of it striking his brain was likewise.
The Bodhisattva further reflected:
"I have now resolved to exert diligence, free from all attachments, having abandoned indolence, even unto such supreme and most excellent ascetic practices."
Having reflected thus, he immediately entered the *āniñjya-samādhi* (the immovable samādhi).

At that time, the breath from his mouth, nose, ears, and crown of the head all ceased; he did not allow it to exit, even to the point of blocking it so that it could not emerge. Consequently, the internal wind grew powerful, churning and surging within the space between his two ribs.
It is, for example, like a butcher or a butcher’s son who is skilled at slaughtering oxen; those butchers, grasping either a sharp sword or a keen blade, tear open the ox's belly or break its ribs.
"In this way, and in this way, even as the Bodhisattva’s internal winds became so powerful that they produced a sound like the piercing of his two ribs, it was likewise.
Having reflected upon this, he further resolved to exert himself with even greater vigor and supreme asceticism, thinking: 'I shall now re-enter the Immovable Samādhi.'"
"At that time, the Bodhisattva closed his mouth, nose, and ears so that no breath escaped; because the internal wind was forceful, it caused his body to become feverish and distressed.
It was as if two most powerful, great wrestlers were to seize a weak man by each arm and lead him toward a massive conflagration, either tormenting or roasting him."
In this way, just as it was said, because the Bodhisattva did not exhale his internal breath, his body suffered from the distress of heat; it was exactly like that.

Having reflected upon this, he further gave rise to a mind of intensified diligence, becoming entirely free from attachment and having abandoned all indolence. He attained right mindfulness, his mind was undistracted, and everything became tranquil. His body, speech, and mind all attained meditative absorption (*samādhi*); such was his supreme and most excellent asceticism.
"At that time, various devas from the higher realms came and, seeing the Bodhisattva engaged in such ascetic practices, said to one another:
'Now this Prince Siddhārtha of great wisdom has already met his end.'"
Furthermore, among that assembly, there were other sons of gods who said to one another:
"This Prince Siddhārtha’s life has not yet come to its end, yet he now wishes to bring it to its conclusion."
Furthermore, some other sons of the gods said:
"This Great Holy Prince Siddhārtha neither dies now, nor will he come to an end hereafter."
Why is this? This crown prince is an arhat.
As for those who are arhats, they possess such conduct; there is no need to find it strange.
"At that time, while the Bodhisattva was practicing asceticism in that forest hermitage (*araṇya*), he achieved the state of the greatest asceticism.
At that moment, all the people from the neighboring villages surrounding the place where the Bodhisattva sat came to see him performing such asceticism and spoke thus:
'Since this śramaṇa practices such great asceticism, let us therefore give him the name "The Great Śramaṇa" (*Mahāśramaṇa*')."
"The title 'Great Śramaṇa' originated from that proclamation; for this reason, he has this name.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflected thus:
"In the world, there may be śramaṇas or brahmins who establish their practice by restricting their food, each maintaining purity."
They subsisted by eating only barley, or boiled barley, or barley flour, or various foods made from barley to sustain their lives.

In this manner, they further subsisted by eating either sesame seeds, or non-glutinous rice, or small beans, or large beans; even consuming nothing but large bean porridge, or large bean broth, or large bean flour, or various foods made from large beans, using these to sustain their lives.
"There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who sever all food and establish pure conduct.
I too may now sever all food and practice asceticism."
Thus the Bodhisattva reflected within his mind.
At that moment, various devas suddenly appeared there, concealing their forms so as not to be seen; they approached the Bodhisattva and addressed him, saying:
"O Great Sage, O Benevolent One!
I pray that you do not entertain such thoughts or maintain this intention of wishing to completely sever all food and abstain from eating. Why is this?

If you, O Venerable One, now wish to practice by severing all food, we, the various devas, shall each take all manner of celestial nectar and descend into the pores of your body, thereby enabling you to sustain your life.
"Furthermore, O virtuous one!
Do not harm your body.
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva reflected thus:
"I have now declared to all people that I do not consume any food whatsoever.
Yet, the various devas have now concealed their bodies and brought celestial nectar to enter my pores, thereby sustaining my life."
"This would be my greatest falsehood, deceiving all beings.
Having thought thus, he addressed those devas, saying: "O you devas!..."
"Even though you have such a thought, this matter is not so.

At that time, having severed the minds of those devas in this way, the Bodhisattva restricted his daily intake to a single grain of black sesame, or a single grain of non-glutinous rice, mung beans, soybeans, green gram, red beans, barley, or wheat—thus consuming exactly one grain of each respectively every day.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflected:
"I may now sustain my life by taking a small amount of liquid in the palm of my hand to drink, such as a soup of small beans, red beans, peas, or mung beans."
“At that time, not far from that village, there was a preeminent brahmin of the highest lineage named Senāyani (translated into Chinese as Jiāngbīngjiāng, ‘General-Commander’).”
That brahmin received a cluster of villages as a fief from King Bimbisāra of Magadha; that village was situated near the village of Uruvilvā.
After that brahmin had received his fief, he established the name Senāyana for it.

Furthermore, there was another brahmin named Deva (translated in the Sui language as "Heaven"), whose birthplace was the city of Kapilavastu. While engaged in a certain business, he gradually traveled until he reached the village of Senāyana and stayed there for a few days as a guest.
At that time, the brahmin Tiṣya was attending to other affairs when he gradually made his way to the forest where the Bodhisattva was dwelling.
Upon seeing the Bodhisattva performing great austerities in the forest, the brahmin Tiṣya recognized him immediately and spoke these words:
"This is my country’s Prince Siddhārtha; he is indeed capable of performing such great austerities."
Seeing the Bodhisattva practicing such asceticism, he was filled with great joy.
At that time, having seen the brahmin Tiṣya, whose heart was inclined toward the Bodhisattva and who had conceived such joy, the Bodhisattva addressed the brahmin Tiṣya, saying:
"Great Brahmin!..."
"Can you prepare a small amount of food for me? Would it suffice to sustain my life?
If there were a soup made of small beans, large beans, mung beans, red beans, or the like, and I were to eat it, I could use it to maintain my life."

Because that brahmin was narrow-minded and inferior, possessing little insight and limited knowledge, he lacked a broad perspective; yet, wishing to practice giving, he agreed with these words and replied to the Bodhisattva:
"O Great Holy Prince!..."
"I am capable of preparing such food.
Thus, for six years, that brahmin daily provided the Bodhisattva with the aforementioned necessary provisions.
Day after day, the Bodhisattva accepted this food and consumed it according to the Dharma to sustain his life.
At that time, the Bodhisattva received it with his palm each day, eating only a small amount as he obtained it to maintain his life—such as a thin soup of small beans, red beans, and the like.

At that time, as the Bodhisattva’s intake of food was so meager—limited only to what his palms could hold, such as the various bean soups mentioned above—after he had consumed that food, his body became emaciated and his breath grew exceedingly weak. He was like a decrepit old man of eighty or ninety years, entirely devoid of physical strength, with his hands and feet no longer under his control.
In this way, and in this manner, the joints and skeletal members of the Bodhisattva were likewise affected.
As the Bodhisattva thus reduced his food and drink and practiced asceticism with diligent effort, the skin of his body became entirely wrinkled and shriveled.

It is like a bitter gourd that has not yet fully ripened; if its stem is severed and it is placed in the sun, it will be scorched and wither to a yellowish hue. Its color appears ripe, its flesh dries up, and its skin wrinkles until the pieces fall away of their own accord, like a withered skull.
In this way, indeed, the skull of the Bodhisattva remains no different.
Because the Bodhisattva had consumed so little food, his two eyeballs were deeply sunken, like water at the bottom of a well from which one can only see the stars.
In this way, in this manner, as soon as they appear before the Bodhisattva’s two eyes, they are likewise perceived.
Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva eats so little, his ribs stand far apart from one another, covered only by skin; it is like a cowshed or a sheepfold with rafters laid upon them.

At that time, all the lambs, calves, and foals in that village, while wandering in that forest, saw the Bodhisattva practicing such asceticism; having seen him, they each gave rise to great joy and a sense of wonder, and they constantly attended upon and made offerings to the Bodhisattva.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds,
Volume Twenty-Four and Volume Twenty-Five,
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on Diligent Asceticism, Part Two:

"At that time, when the peak of spring had arrived, King Śuddhodana went out for recreation and sightseeing. He saw that in the various groves, new branches and leaves had emerged, and all manner of diverse herbs and flowers were in full bloom, pure and magnificent, filling the entire area."
Within the waters, geese, wild ducks, swans, cranes, and mandarin ducks abound in the various ponds.

Upon the trees, there are further jays, parrots, and *kūṭāhala* birds, as well as peacocks, *kalaviṅkas*, and *jīvajīvaka* birds, who delight one another or call out to one another with exquisite sounds.
At that time, having heard these words, King Śuddhodana heaved a long sigh, wiped away his tears, and said:
"Alas, my son, Prince Siddhārtha! Suddenly you have abandoned me, and already six years have passed."
Since he has gone forth from home and I am unable to see him, alas! Why do I live alone now? What purpose is there in knowing this?

Because I no longer see my son Siddhārtha, I remain here surrounded on all sides by these court ladies; though day and night we produce various sounds—lutes, biwangs, harps, cymbals, drums, and flutes, and all manner of music—I now enjoy these supreme and exquisite five desires. Yet how is it that my son remains all alone there in the mountains, forests, and wilderness, amidst a place devoid of human crowds, surrounded by all kinds of wild beasts—tigers, wolves, lions, white elephants, and every other beast—or perhaps those beasts, each with their own claws and fangs, are harming one another and devouring one another?
"Who else could know whether you are there—whether dead or alive?
There is no news at all; it is silent.
King Śuddhodana’s heart was thus; he brooded with sorrow and distress, finding no joy.

"At that time, while the Bodhisattva was practicing austerities in the village of Uruvilvā, he became emaciated and exhausted. When he wished to rise and move, his strength could not support his body, and he fell to the ground as soon as he stood up."
At that time, the gods dwelling on earth who were present there, having witnessed this event, said:
"The Bodhisattva’s life is about to end.
Distressed in their hearts, they passed the word among themselves:
"Prince Siddhārtha has now suddenly passed away.
At that time, among the host of devas dwelling on earth, there was a certain son of heaven who quickly went to King Śuddhodana; having arrived there, he addressed King Śuddhodana, saying these words:
"Great King!..."
