"Know this, Great King: the noble Prince Siddhārtha, having renounced the four continents along with the seven treasures, left the household life to enter the mountains; while practicing austerities, he has now passed away."
Within that assembly of devas, there was yet another terrestrial deva who quickly went to the king’s presence and addressed him, saying:
"Great King!
You should know that although Prince Siddhārtha has not yet passed away, his remaining life will not exceed seven days."
At that time, having heard these words from the various devas, King Śuddhodana, out of concern for his son, was overcome with grief and distress that pierced his heart, and he cried out loudly:
"Alas, my son!"
"Why did you die alone in this empty forest?
Though you have obtained a human body, you did not enjoy the five desires, nor did you realize the supreme flavor of the Dharma.
Having spoken these words, his body and mind became bewildered and confused; he fell to the ground in a faint.

At that time, King Śuddhodana and all the members of the Śākya clan heard this sound; having heard it, they all hurried together to the palace of King Śuddhodana. Upon arrival, they comforted King Śuddhodana’s heart and spoke these words:
"Great King, do not be so distressed."
"Furthermore, Great King, your body is currently extremely emaciated; do not let this matter cause you to meet your end.
King Śuddhodana said, "Today, in this city of Kapilavastu, how many members of my own kinsmen and retinue reside here?"
At that time, all those Śākyas addressed the king, saying: "Great King!
You should know that the total number of Śākyas now amounts to ninety-nine thousand."
Then, King Śuddhodana spoke again, saying: "O my kinsmen!
If you wish to preserve my life, quickly show me the place where Prince Siddhārtha resides."
At that time, all the Śākyas replied together, saying: "Great King!

You should know that it would indeed be possible for Your Majesty to seize this great earth, the mountains and forests, the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa), the great oceans, and Mount Sumeru, and lift them with a single hand to hurl them to another realm."
If one wishes to bring the Prince back home by assembling all the beings of the heavens and the world while his afflictions are not yet exhausted, such a thing can never happen.
At that time, the son of the Śākya national preceptor named Udāyin addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Great King!..."
"You should know that I can now go to the place where Prince Siddhārtha has gone forth into homelessness, comfort his mind, and lead him back to the palace.
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he immediately replied to the National Preceptor, saying:
"Excellent, Udāyin!"
"If you can go to the Prince's side, and if the Prince should take your words to heart, then return home; once you have been together with him for a while, come back here quickly."
If the crown prince is unwilling to come, you shall never again set eyes upon my face for the rest of your life. Why is this?
Although your words were intended to comfort me, if my son does not come and I must look upon your face, my sorrow will only increase all the more because of the hope I place in you.
"At that time, the state preceptor’s son Udāyin prepared his carriage and departed immediately from Kapilavastu, traveling directly toward the Nairañjanā River at the village of Uruvilvā."
Having arrived there, Udāyin first saw from a distance the five men, including Kauṇḍinya, and upon seeing them, he asked Kauṇḍinya:
"Venerable Kauṇḍinya!"
"Where is Prince Siddhārtha now?
Then Kauṇḍinya immediately replied to Udāyin,
"Prince Siddhārtha has already entered the forest to practice asceticism."
Then Udāyin asked again,
"What is the name of his personal attendant?
At that time, Kauṇḍinya replied to him:
“O Udāyin! If you wish to know, that person’s name is Aśvajit, which in the language of Sui means ‘Tamer of Horses.
Thereupon, Udāyin immediately approached Aśvajit and spoke these words:
"Aśvaka, you must now go to where the Prince is and, as I have instructed, announce my arrival for me:
'Your father has sent an envoy who has arrived here and wishes to see you.'"
Then the horse-tamer replied to Udāyin, "I truly did not dare to convey these words to the Prince. Why was that? Because—"
The Prince had already practiced austerities for six years; since his renunciation, he had never once turned his face toward his birthplace or sat facing the city of Kapilavastu.
Why is this? Because of the weariness with the affliction of birth. You, Udāyin!
"You may enter the forest yourself and meet the Prince face-to-face to discuss the words sent by our father, the King.

At that time, Udāyin entered the forest and saw the Bodhisattva lying upon the ground; from head to foot he was covered in dust, devoid of majestic radiance, his color matching that of the earth. His body was emaciated and skinless, with only bones and skin remaining to envelop his frame.
His eyes were sunken deep, like stars at the bottom of a well; his entire body was bent and contorted, with every joint dislocated.
Seeing the Bodhisattva’s body in such a state, Udāyin raised both hands, cried out loudly, and wailed: "Alas! Alas!"

"I, a scion of the Śākyas, have suddenly fallen into such calamity today. Once possessing such upright and pleasing form, and such wondrous beauty, my body has now become no different from the earth; yet, since I cannot attain liberation and peace, I have merely exhausted myself in harming such a wondrous body."
At that time, having heard the sound of Udāyin’s wailing, the Bodhisattva immediately asked:
"Who is this? Why is his inner heart so filled with sorrow and distress, as if burning with fire, speaking while weeping?"
Then the upāsikā replied to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Great Holy Prince!
I am the son of the National Preceptor of Your Majesty’s own kingdom; he whose name is Udāyin is none other than myself."
"The Great King Śuddhodana, the father of the Prince, has sent me here to welcome the Prince.
The Bodhisattva replied, "You, Udāyin!"
"I now have no need for these messengers of affliction; I desire only to obtain the messenger of Nirvāṇa, and do not wish for this messenger of birth and death from my father, the King.
At that time, Udāyin again addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Great Holy Prince!
“O Benevolent One, what kind of vow have you now established that it is so firm?
The Bodhisattva then replied to Udāyin:

“I pray only that my body may be shattered upon this ground like sesame seeds, white powder, or fine dust; yet if I do not attain self-benefit and benefit for others, I shall never relinquish this mind of diligence to give rise to indolence.”
"I now vow thus with my body and mind.
At that time, Udāyin addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Great Holy Prince!"
"I received this solemn oath from the presence of the Prince’s father, the King, which compelled me to follow the Prince into the city with absolute resolve.

If today the Prince has made such a grave vow, and should his life come to an end before he has attained self-benefit or benefited others, how could I dare abandon him, violate my original oath, and enter the city of Kapilavastu alone?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke again to Udāyin: "O Udāyin!
While I am here in this place of ascetic practice, should I not yet achieve my own self-benefit and pass away midway, then you, Udāyin!"
Take my remains and, following the path by which I originally departed, carry me on a litter into the city of Kapilavastu.
Furthermore, on my behalf, speak thus to all the people, both within and without the city of Kapilavastu:
"This is the body of bones belonging to that man of diligence, who spoke no falsehoods, and who stood firm in his vows with upright intention and a pure mind."
"You, Udāyin! Once again, answer for me my father the King’s words of greeting; inquire after my father and speak these words to him:
'Great King!'"

You should know that because the prince has already exerted diligent effort, his current relinquishing of life is not due to indolence; as one who speaks according to reality, his present relinquishing of life is not a falsehood.
"O Udāyin! Although it is so, while I was here in this forest, last night in a dream, immeasurable devas came to my side, concealing their forms, prostrated at my feet, and said to me:
'Prince Siddhārtha, you should now give rise to great joy; from this day forth, within seven days, you will surely achieve the greatest benefit.'"
"O Udāyin! This dream that I have received shall never be in vain. O Udāyin!"
"You may now return home; I have no need for you as my friend.
When Udāyin heard the Bodhisattva’s vow, he no longer harbored any hope regarding the Bodhisattva and immediately departed alone from the grove where the Bodhisattva was seated.
Having departed, he returned to the city of Kapilavastu and saw King Śuddhodana. Upon arriving, he addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Great King, you should know that Prince Siddhārtha is safe, courageous, and alive."
King Śuddhodana said,
"If my prince remains safe and does not die, why should I have any further sorrow?
Having heard these words, his heart was filled with great joy.

"At that time, Māra Pāpīyān of the desire realm, wishing to cause disturbance to the Bodhisattva, remained constantly and secretly near the Bodhisattva’s side throughout those six years of ascetic practice, seeking an opportunity; yet he could find not even the slightest fault."
He then spoke in verse:
“The hermitage is both pure and excellent, With trees and groves most beautiful to behold.
To the east of the village of Uruvilvā, Beside the banks of the Nairañjanā River.”
Having selected and attained that ground, he firmly bound his vows and sat in the full lotus posture;
with a mind of great diligence and heroic resolve, he declared: "I shall now certainly attain liberation."
The Māra Pāpīyān came to him and, with deceitful sweet words, addressed him thus:

"May you, O Benevolent One, have a long life; only with a long life can one practice the Dharma, and only through a long life can one achieve self-benefit, after which there will be no cause for regret."
Your body is now extremely emaciated; it is certain that the end of your life will come before long.
Truly, you are now a thousand parts toward death, with perhaps only one part of merit remaining.
Merely by practicing much generosity and serving the devas, and by performing sacrifices to the various fire-gods, [you may yet find relief].
If one may thus attain such great merit, what is the use of practicing meditative concentration?
It is extremely difficult to seek the supreme path of renunciation, and to tame one's own mind is likewise not easy.
The Māra-king thus addressed the Bodhisattva with various words of praise, but the Bodhisattva then responded to him with subtle speech, his voice skillful and profound:
"Pāpīyan, you are unwholesome and negligent; you wander through the world seeking only your own self-interest."
Regarding this merit and mind of yours, you have never sought even so much as a speck of dust.
If you truly desire to seek merit, how could you utter such words?
I contemplate the suffering of death as if it were birth; truly, for a single thought-moment, I have no fear of extinction.
Even if all sentient beings were to perish and vanish, my mind would never turn back for even a moment.
Now, spanning the ocean of desire, I build a great bridge; with diligence and valor, I cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Thus, when a wind-disaster arises in the world, it can even dry up all flowing waters;
how much more so the fluids within this body? How could its juices not wither and parch?
The fat and marrow, which provide moisture, will first be exhausted, and only thereafter will the skin and flesh become dry.
The flesh wastes away, the skin stands out, and physical strength becomes feeble; yet the mind can attain tranquil concentration.
For those who increase all forms of diligence, there is only the entry into the gateway of samādhi.
Now that I wish to practice this conduct, I hope to reach that supreme state of awakening;
therefore, I do not begrudge this body or life—may you know my inner pure heart.
In my heart now lies this utmost sincerity, Adorned with wisdom, it is exceedingly firm;
Among the people of the world, I have yet seen none Who are capable of severing this diligence of mine.
I would rather have my life taken by death than live for many years at home;
a man of honor would rather die in battle than remain alive while submitting to another.
Since the hero has already subdued you, what more is there to fear?
Only the brave can destroy all enemies; before long, I shall subdue you, O Māra.
In your army, the first is sensual greed; the second is named lack of joy;
the third consists of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and the like; attachment is called the fourth army;
the fifth is that sleep and drowsiness; and fear and dread are the sixth.
The seventh is doubt and uncertainty; the eighth army is hatred and anger.
The ninth consists of vying for profit and contending for fame; the tenth is ignorance and folly.
The eleventh is self-praise and arrogance; the twelfth is the constant disparagement of others.
Pāpīyān, such are you and your retinue; your armies and horses all move through the darkness.
Those who fall into these evil ways are those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas whom your host constantly traverses throughout the world, deluding all gods and humans.
I now behold those armies and horses of yours;
with sublime wisdom as your formidable weapon, you are able to subdue them all without exception.
Having utterly shattered your great host, they shall be dispersed like water breaking a clay vessel; the dissolution of your army shall be just so.
My mind is settled in right mindfulness, stable as a mountain; wisdom and skillful means are both perfected.
I practice my conduct with a mind free from negligence—how could you possibly find any flaw in me?
At that time, the Bodhisattva again reflected and thought:

"If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, in past times, for the sake of seeking their own benefit, underwent great suffering—whether it was mentally unpleasant, or both physically and mentally unpleasant—even though they underwent such things, those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas did not transcend this suffering."

Just as I now undergo these sufferings of body, mind, and mental displeasure for the sake of seeking my own benefit, so too, in future lives, whatever physical and mental sufferings any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas may undergo for their own benefit shall not exceed this.

Just as I now undergo suffering of body and mind for the sake of seeking my own benefit, yet have not yet realized the state of a superior person, have not yet attained knowledge and vision, and have not yet realized further progress—by what other path could I attain Bodhi?
The Bodhisattva further reflected in this way:

"I recall that formerly, while within my father the king’s palace, I observed the plowing of the fields. At that time, I encountered the cool shade of a Jambu tree. Having seen it, I sat beneath that shade, abandoned all defiled minds of desire, grew weary of and disparaged all unwholesome dharmas, gave rise to a mind of discernment, delighted in tranquil concentration, and produced joy and bliss, thereby realizing the first dhyāna."
"I should now return to mindfulness of that meditative concentration; this path should lead toward the way of enlightenment.

Having thus reflected and contemplated, the Bodhisattva practiced right observation according to the Dharma and entered that tranquil concentration with a single-minded focus, hoping to reach enlightenment by means of this path.
He then spoke in verse:
"This dharma is neither free from desire, nor is it the correct path toward Bodhi;
furthermore, it is not the supreme cause for liberation, but merely the root of suffering for body and mind."
If I now wish to practice and train, I should do as I did of old when viewing the cultivation of fields;
sitting beneath the shade of that Jambu tree, free from defilement, I attained the realization of the four dhyānas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva again reflected and thought:

"That bliss consists solely in being far removed from all desires and unwholesome states. How could I not know that bliss? It is precisely so that I may realize that bliss that I now seek to achieve all-knowing vision."
The Bodhisattva further reflected in this way:

"I wish to achieve the bliss of knowledge and vision; I ought to attain that bliss, yet I am emaciated and devoid of physical strength. How can I possibly attain that bliss by virtue of my body being thin and lacking power?"
"Now, for the sake of seeking strength for my body, I shall eat coarse food—either boiled beans, or parched grain, or flour, or oil, or ghee—and then I shall seek warm water to bathe this body."
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to his attendant Brahmin:
"Venerable Deva!
From this day forward, I shall no longer sustain my life with food and drink as I did before; I intend to seek a superior sustenance than this food to maintain my life."
"Or [food such as] parched grain, roasted flour, boiled beans, and the like; or ghee and oils for anointing this body, as well as bathing in warm water.
Are you able to provide these things for me?"
At that time, Deva said to the Bodhisattva:

"I do not currently possess such things; moreover, my family is poor and cannot afford to provide these various items. Furthermore, even if I were to give them to you right now, I would not have them immediately at hand. You should simply make a vow, and I shall seek them out for you by every possible means."
The Bodhisattva asked,
"What vow do you now wish me to make?
At that time, Deva addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:

"When you have completed your ascetic practices and your heart's desire is fulfilled, at that time, when it is your turn and your portion of the Dharma, please come to my home again and accept my food."
The Bodhisattva replied, "It shall be as you wish.

At that time, the brahmin Trapuṣa, having heard the Bodhisattva’s confirmation of his request, took his leave of the Bodhisattva and departed. He returned to the home of the brahmin Snāyana, and upon arrival, spoke to that brahmin, saying:

"Virtuous one, it is to be hoped that you will once again take pleasure in the practice of the Dharma. Not far from this village, there is a śramaṇa who practices great asceticism; he has not eaten for many months and years. Now, as he seeks food—perhaps rice, flour, parched grain, ghee, fat, or honey—or perhaps boiled beans and oil for anointing his body, as well as the need for bathing—you, virtuous one, may now provide these things for him."

"At that time, in the house of the Brahmin Senāyana, the general, there were two daughters: the first was named Nanda (translated in the Sui language as 'Joy'), and the second was named Balā (translated in the Sui language as 'Power')."
Now those two daughters were exceedingly beautiful and peerlessly lovely, with few equals in the world.

Those two girls had previously heard that to the north of here, beneath the Snowy Mountains, there was a settlement of the Śākya clan called Kapilavastu. Within that city lived a Śākya king named Śuddhodana. That king’s foremost and principal queen was named Māyā, and from that queen was born a crown prince who was extremely handsome, most exceptionally pleasing, and of extraordinary countenance; his body was golden in color, the crown of his head was rounded like a parasol, his nose was like a parrot’s beak, his arms reached down to his knees, and every part of his body was perfectly proportioned.

His faculties were fully developed, like a golden statue; he was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man that adorned his body, and was further perfected by the eighty secondary characteristics.
When the prince had been born, he was taken to a Brahmin soothsayer to have his fortune told. The latter’s prediction was as follows:

"If this prince remains at home, he will surely become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), ruling over the four continents as the sovereign lord of the great earth; at that time, he will possess the seven treasures and govern the world with the True Dharma.
If he renounces the world and leaves the household life, he will certainly become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, whose fame will be heard afar."
When those two maidens heard these words, they recalled what they had previously discussed with their father, saying:
"Now that we have heard it said that the son of this Śākya clan is handsome and peerlessly lovely, let that prince be our husband."
At that time, the general Senāyana, having received this news concerning the Bodhisattva from the Brahmin Tiṣya, said to the two daughters:
"Sisters, your heart's desire shall be fulfilled."
Why is this? You should now go quickly to where that greatest of śramaṇas practices austerities.
For what reason?

Once you have arrived there, request that the śramaṇa provide alms and food; honor and make offerings to him, presenting oil and ghee for him to anoint his body, and afterwards separately provide warm water for him to bathe.
"By such causes and conditions, your heart's desires shall later be fulfilled.

At that time, having heard their father’s command, the two daughters of the general took whatever food, oil, ghee, and other provisions were available at home and went to the place where the Bodhisattva was practicing austerities.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva, presented the food he had brought, and spoke these words:
"O Great and Virtuous Honored One!"
"I pray that you will partake of this food offered by me.
At that time, the Bodhisattva accepted the food from the two women and ate it as he pleased; he took ghee and oil to anoint his body, and afterwards bathed with warm water.
At that time, the Bodhisattva used that ghee and oil to anoint and rub his body; they entered his entire frame through each and every pore.
It was as if one were pouring ghee and oil onto a mound of earth or loose sand: they all soaked in completely and no longer remained visible.
In this way, and so it was, the ghee and oil applied to the Bodhisattva’s body were entirely absorbed and no longer visible.
At that time, the Bodhisattva had not yet recovered his original physical form and features.
"At that time, having finished his meal, the Bodhisattva addressed those two women, saying:
'O sisters! By virtue of this merit, what wish do you seek to fulfill?'"
Then those two women said to the Bodhisattva:
"O Great and Virtuous Honored One!
We have heard in the past that there was a member of the Śākya clan who begot a crown prince, lovely and handsome, peerless in the world; we wish for that man to become our husband."
The Bodhisattva replied:
"O sisters! I am that very Prince of the Śākya clan.
From this day forward, I vow no longer to experience the pleasures of the five desires. In the future, I wish to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and I vow to turn the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma."
At that time, having heard these words, the two sisters said to the Bodhisattva:
"O Great Sage, O Benevolent One!

If this is so, you will certainly attain that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). Once you have attained it, you should come to our home; we pray to see you, for we shall become your śrāvaka disciples."
The Bodhisattva replied to the two women:
"So be it, so be it; it shall be as you sisters have wished.

From that time forward, the two women sent food to the Bodhisattva every day. They would first take ghee and oil to anoint the Bodhisattva’s body, and then separately use warm water to bathe his body, until gradually they restored him to his original physical appearance and adornment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva addressed the two women, saying:
"O sisters! From this day forward, do not harbor any other thoughts; as for the method of nourishing the body, simply provide me with food."
Why is this? From this day forward, it would be impossible for me to come into physical contact with the female organ of a woman;
my mind does not delight in such a thing, nor is it my intention.

At that time, there was a shepherd’s son who saw the Bodhisattva; because of his ascetic practices, the Bodhisattva’s body was greatly emaciated. Seeing the Bodhisattva thus exerting himself with such great diligence and austerity, the shepherd’s son felt joy in his heart toward the Bodhisattva and, immediately kneeling on his right knee, addressed him, saying:
“O Great Sage, Honored One!
"I now wish to serve, honor, and respect the Venerable One; I do not yet know whether the Venerable One will accept this.
The Bodhisattva replied, "If you know the proper time, then prepare what you intend to do accordingly."
At that time, the lamb immediately rubbed its body for the Bodhisattva and offered him goat’s milk to serve as his food.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva broke off a branch of a great nyagrodha tree and planted it in the ground to provide shade.

At that time, by the power of the Bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual authority (*ṛddhibala*), the broken nyagrodha branch immediately sprouted from the earth, further developing branches, twigs, leaves, flowers, and fruit, all of which were fully complete.
When the people of that time saw this, they called that tree "the Nyagrodha planted by the Shepherd Boy.
At that time, while the Bodhisattva was eating coarse food, those five sages said to one another:
"Prince Siddhārtha has now lost his meditative concentration and returned to his ordinary nature; how much more so must he have lost his observance of the precepts?"
"Thus, this person has now become one who is indolent; he does not attain tranquil concentration, and his mind is agitated.
Having deliberated in this manner, they conceived feelings of weariness and contempt toward the Bodhisattva, abandoned him, and went elsewhere.
Gradually approaching the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, he entered the Deer Park and practiced meditative concentration.
There is a verse that says:
“Those five ascetic sages, seeing the Bodhisattva eating coarse food, [were filled with contempt].”
"It is said that there is no practice of meditative concentration, But only indulgence and self-nourishment of this five-element body.

Chapter 30: Approaching the Bodhi Tree, Part One. From the *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha-sūtra*, Chapter Thirty, "Approaching the Bodhi Tree," Part One: "At that time, when the Bodhisattva desired to seek coarse food, it was only to allow his body to regain a small measure of physical strength."

At that time, from the very moment she first saw the Bodhisattva, Sujātā, the daughter of the village headman, began on that day to provide the Bodhisattva with cooked food and vessels for his alms, rather than giving them to anyone else.

Furthermore, before noon has arrived, if he sees a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa coming for alms, he gives away all the cooked food he has begged as well as his eating utensils. Then, with both mind and mouth, he makes this aspiration:

"By virtue of all the merit from this gift of food, may it be transferred to that Great Son of the Śākya clan who practices austerities; may he achieve success and quickly attain the various supernormal powers; may he swiftly realize the wondrous fruit of Bodhi; and may his austerities be fulfilled exactly according to his heart's desire."
"In this manner, he practiced the giving of food along with vessels for six years.
At that time, when the six years were complete and it was the sixteenth day of the second month of spring, the Bodhisattva reflected within his own mind:
'I should not now realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by consuming such food.'"
From whom else shall I now seek exquisite food?
Who is able to provide me with such excellent food that, having eaten it, I may immediately realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

At that time, while the Bodhisattva was reflecting in his mind in this way, a certain devaputra, knowing the Bodhisattva’s thoughts, quickly went to the two daughters of the village headman Sujāta. Having arrived there, he addressed them, saying:
"O daughters of Sujāta!..."

If you know the time has come, the Bodhisattva now desires excellent food; the Bodhisattva now requires the most supreme food, for having eaten this excellent food, he then intends to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"You all should now prepare for him sixteen portions of excellent, fine milk-rice.

At that time, the two daughters of the village headman Sujāta, having heard this announcement from the deity, were filled with such joy and exultation that it pervaded their entire bodies, which they could not contain.

He quickly gathered one thousand cows and milked them; he then took that milk and fed it to five hundred cows. On another day, he milked these five hundred cows and took the milk to feed two hundred and fifty cows. On the following day, he milked these two hundred and fifty cows and fed the milk to one hundred and twenty-five cows. On the next day, he milked these one hundred and twenty-five cows and fed the milk to sixty cows. On the subsequent day, he milked these sixty cows and fed the milk to thirty cows. On the following day, he milked these thirty cows and fed the milk to fifteen cows. On the final day, he milked these fifteen cows and placed the milk with a portion of pure, high-quality non-glutinous rice to cook the supreme milk porridge for the Bodhisattva.
When those two women were boiling the milk gruel, various signs appeared: sometimes the sign of a vase filled with flowers emerged;

sometimes the sign of a deep pool of the river of merit; at times the sign of the *svastika* (万字); or the sign of the thousand-spoked wheel of merit; or again, the sign of a humped bull; or the sign of an elephant king or a dragon king; or the sign of a fish; at times the sign of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) appeared; or again, the form of Śakra; and at times the form of Brahmā appeared.
Alternatively, he may manifest milk-rice surging upward and boiling over, reaching as high as half a *tāla* tree before descending again in an instant;
or he may manifest the milk-rice rising upward to the height of one full *tāla* tree before finally descending;
or he may manifest it rising to the height of a man, yet it returns into that vessel without a single drop leaving the vessel to fall elsewhere.

While the milk-rice was being cooked, another diviner skilled in the ocean of calculation and the interpretation of signs arrived at that place. Seeing the various kinds of omens appearing in the milk-rice, he observed them well through his expertise in divination and spoke these words:
"How marvelous! How marvelous!"
"Who will obtain this milk-rice and eat it?
Once that person has eaten it, they will before long realize the sublime medicine of the Deathless.

Then, on the twenty-third day of the second month, at the time of dawn, the Bodhisattva adjusted his robes properly and set out toward the village of Uruvilvā to beg for alms, gradually arriving at the village of Nandika.
Having arrived at that village, he stood silently outside the main gate of the village headman’s house, desiring to seek alms.

At that time, the daughter of the village headman, Sujātā, saw the Bodhisattva standing by her gate seeking alms in silence. Upon seeing him, she immediately took a golden bowl, filled it with milk-rice mixed with honey, and holding it in her own hands, approached the Bodhisattva. Having arrived, she stood before him and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"I pray only that you, O Venerable One!"
"Please accept this bowl of honeyed milk-rice from me out of compassion for me.
At that time, when the Bodhisattva saw that the milk-rice had been prepared with honey, he thought to himself:
"I have now obtained an excellent medicine for healing my wounds; therefore, I must now exert myself with vigorous diligence in order to realize the nectar of immortality and the True Dharma."

Furthermore, having long since lost this essence of the Dharma and its practice, I must today give rise to the path; therefore, I now manifest this sign of a vow and resolve my mind thus: "Just as I have today prepared this honey-mixed milk-rice porridge of merit and, according to the proper time, partaken of this solid food in accordance with the Dharma, so too, having eaten, I must cross over the realm of the Lord of Death, subdue the hosts of that army of the Lord of Death, and reach the further shore."
"Having reflected and contemplated thus, the Bodhisattva accepted the milk-rice and asked Sujātā, the daughter of the village headman:
'Sister, O virtuous one!'"
"After I have finished eating this milk gruel, to whom shall I entrust this bowl?
The daughter Sujātā replied,
"Entrust it to you, O Noble One!"
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"Such a vessel as mine has no use.
The maiden Sujātā said:
“O benevolent one, act according to your own intention; furthermore, since I have always been giving food to others, I have constantly prepared it along with the vessels for offering.
At that time, having accepted that food, the Bodhisattva departed from the village of Uruvilvā with right mindfulness and, proceeding slowly and steadily, reached the banks of the Nairañjanā River.
Having arrived, he immediately took the food he had obtained, placed it on a clean spot to one side, removed his clothes, and entered the river to bathe, thereby clearing away the heat from his body.

When the Bodhisattva bathes his body, the devas in the void space mix various kinds of subtle and exquisite celestial powdered incense with the water and rain it down upon the water in a variety of blended showers.
"At that time, the Nairañjanā River there was filled with various powdered incenses and diverse flowers, flowing together in a mingled stream.

Having bathed in those waters, the Bodhisattva took his kāṣāya robe, washed it, wrung it out, and spread it to dry; he then put it on his body and intended to cross the river. However, the current was swift and turbulent, and his body was so emaciated and weak that he could not get across. Furthermore, due to six years of diligent and ascetic practice, his physical strength was so depleted that he was unable to reach the opposite bank."

"At that time, there was a great tree by that river named Aśvattha (translated in the Sui language as 'Now'), and a deity of that tree named Karkoṭaka (translated in the Sui language as 'Small Peak') dwelt depending upon it."
Then that tree deity, with arms adorned with various necklaces and ornaments, led him toward the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Bodhisattva took the hand of the tree deity and was able to cross over that river.

Within the river where the Bodhisattva bathes, the fragrant water is taken by each of the various devas and carried back to their palaces; because it is this merit-bestowing and auspicious water, they sprinkle it throughout their own abodes.

"At that time, there was a nāga girl named Nairañjanā (translated in the Sui language as 'Not Widow') belonging to the Lord of the Nairañjanā River. She leaped forth from the earth, holding in her hands a magnificent and celestial casket adorned with ornaments, and offered it to the Bodhisattva."
Having accepted it, the Bodhisattva sat upon it.
Once seated, he took the milk-gruel offered by Sujātā, the daughter of the village headman, and ate his fill according to his desire, consuming it all until nothing remained.

Once the Bodhisattva had consumed that milk gruel, by virtue of the power of the karmic maturation of his practice of giving (*dāna*) in past lives, the marks and signs of his body were restored as they were before—upright, pleasing, perfectly complete, and without any deficiency.
"At that time, when the Bodhisattva had finished eating the gruel, he cast the golden bowl into the river.

Then, the Naga King of the Ocean gave rise to a heart of great wonder and rarity; furthermore, because a Bodhisattva is difficult to encounter in the world, he took up that golden vessel, intending to make an offering of it, and set out for his own palace."

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, the Lord of Devas, immediately transformed his body into that of a garuḍa with a beak made of vajra-jewels; he snatched the golden bowl from the dragon in the ocean and carried it toward the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven in the Tuṣita Palace, where he constantly made offerings to it himself.

Nowadays, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three establish a festival there called the Festival of Offering the Bodhisattva’s Golden Bowl; from that time until now, it has continued without interruption.

At that time, having finished eating the congee, the Bodhisattva rose from his seat and proceeded slowly and calmly toward the Bodhi tree. Meanwhile, the Naga princess took back her own raft and returned to her own palace for the purpose of making offerings.
And there is a verse that says:
"The Bodhisattva partook of the milk-rice according to the Dharma, Offered by that daughter Sujātā;
Having finished eating, he joyfully proceeded toward the Tree of Enlightenment, Resolutely desiring to realize and attain Bodhi."
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll Twenty-Five;
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll Twenty-Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
In the chapter on "Approaching the Bodhi Tree," it is said:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva bathed in the river, consumed the milk-rice, and his physical form and radiance were restored to their original state, with sovereign power and majesty."

When he proceeded calmly toward the Bodhi tree, his manner of walking was like that of all bodhisattvas of antiquity; that is to say, he moved with gradual refinement and gentleness, his steps were taken with a joyful mind, he bestowed gifts upon those who approached, and his gait was steady and composed.

He walks like Sumeru, the king of mountains—walking loftily, walking without fear, walking without turbidity or confusion, walking with a mind of contentment, walking neither too fast nor too slow, and walking without stumbling or falling.

He walks with his two feet perfectly aligned so as not to rub against one another; he walks without encroaching upon others; he does not walk too quickly; he does not walk with a swaying body; he walks with composure, he walks with purity, he walks with sublime grace, he walks without harm or affliction, he walks like a lion king, he walks like a great dragon king, and he walks like a great bull king.

He walks like a king of geese; he walks like a king of elephants; he walks without timidity; he walks without hesitation or obstruction; he walks without error or confusion; he walks with vast and expansive strides; he walks with the gait of Nārāyaṇa; he walks without touching the ground; he walks with the thousand-spoked wheels on his soles imprinting the earth; he walks with his toes webbed and his nails possessing the luster of red copper; he walks making the entire great earth tremble; and he walks making sounds like the echoes from great mountain valleys.
When walking, all pits and uneven ground become perfectly level and he proceeds naturally;
all soil, sand, pebbles, and stones upon the earth are cleared away as he walks;
from the webbed membrane between his toes he emits radiance that touches sentient beings who are subject to transgressions, causing them to abide in stillness as he proceeds with virtuous conduct.
Their gait is pure, and they are born upon exquisite lotus flowers, treading upon the calyxes of those lotuses as they walk;
they attain this conduct because they practiced pure and wholesome deeds in the past.
In the past, the Buddhas sat upon high lion thrones and proceeded with steadfast conduct;
their minds were firm, proceeding with a resolve like adamant;
they blocked off the dense forest of all realms of existence and proceeded with majestic dignity.
They are able to bring about peaceful and blissful conduct for all sentient beings across all realms of existence;
they proceed by crushing the banners of all Māras and proceeding by destroying all the powers of Māra.
They proceed by trampling down all demonic influences;
they proceed by shattering all demonic majesty;
they proceed by diminishing all demonic activities.
They proceed by dispersing all hosts of Māra;
they proceed by falling away from all the power of Māra;
they proceed by relinquishing all the activities of Māra.
They proceed by slaying all demonic armies;
they proceed by severing all demonic nets.
They subdue all heterodox assemblies that act contrary to the Dharma, and they proceed by gathering in those of external paths in accordance with the Dharma.
They proceed by illuminating the cataracts of affliction;
they proceed by dispersing and subduing the companions of affliction;
and they proceed fearlessly, their majestic power eclipsing Śakra, Brahmā, Maheśvara, and the world-protecting devas.
In this trichiliocosm, he alone is uniquely honored as he proceeds;
not learning from others, he has personally realized the Way and proceeds with clarity;
he proceeds with the desire to realize all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
With right mindfulness and right intention, one practices with contentment and right conduct;
one practices desiring to extinguish birth, old age, sickness, and death;
one practices desiring to proceed toward that subtle, supreme, and fearless state of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; one practices desiring to enter the city-gate of Nirvana.
Possessing such conduct, the Bodhisattva proceeded, facing directly toward that Bodhi tree, walking with a steady gaze.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflected and thought:
"Now that I have arrived at this site of enlightenment, what kind of seat shall I use to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
He then realized for himself that he should sit upon the grass.
At that time, the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens addressed the Bodhisattva, saying: "So it is, so it is."
O Great Sage, O Benevolent One!
All the Tathāgatas of the past who sought to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* sat upon a spread of grass and attained perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva again reflected thus:
"Who can provide me with such grass?
Having reflected in his mind, he looked around him in all four directions—left, right, front, and back.

At that time, Śakra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, having known the Bodhisattva’s mind through his celestial wisdom, immediately transformed his body into that of a grass-cutter. Standing to the right, neither too near nor too far from the Bodhisattva, he began to cut the grass.

The grass was greenish-blue, its color like that of the neck of a peacock king; it was soft, supple, and lustrous. When touched by the hand, it felt like fine Kāśika cloth. Its form was thus: exquisite in color, fragrant, and curling to the right.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva saw that person not far away, on his right side, mowing such grass as this. Having seen him, he gradually approached the man's side; having arrived, he calmly asked the man:
'O virtuous and benevolent one!'"
"What is your name? The man replied,
"My name is Kṣema."
Once the Bodhisattva had heard that person's name, he reflected thus:

"I now desire to seek my own auspicious welfare, and I also do so for the sake of others seeking their auspicious welfare. This one named 'Auspicious' stands before me; I shall certainly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
After the Bodhisattva had reflected thus in his mind, he produced yet another exquisite and wondrous sound, speaking to that person and saying:

"His speech is like the subtle and wonderful voices of all the Bodhisattvas of the past—namely, words of truth, not uttered falsely, but using genuine speech; it is a clear and resonant voice, a moist and lustrous voice, a wondrous voice, a joyful voice, a voice heard with reverence, a voice heard without contradiction, a flowing and graceful voice, a transformative voice, a guiding voice, a voice free from stammering, a voice free from contraction or groaning, a voice free from harshness, a voice free from double articulation, a soft and smooth voice, a sweet and refined voice, a distinct and clear voice that reaches the ear from afar, and a voice which, when heard, brings joy to the heart, mouth, and mind."

Having heard it, they eliminate desire, delusion, hatred, strife, and anger, causing them all to attain a pure voice—a voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird, the jīvajīvaka bird, and the rumbling sound of thunder.

It is like the sounds of various musical instruments, songs, and hymns—sounds that are deep and far-reaching, loud and resonant, unobstructed, not emitted from the nose, pure, authentic, and truthful.
It was like the voice of Brahmā, like the sound of ocean waves, like the roar of a mountain collapsing—a thunderous sound.

It was the voice of praise from all the celestial kings, the beautiful singing of the asuras, a deep sound difficult to fathom that severs the power of Māra, and a voice that subdues all non-Buddhists.

The voice of a lion, the sound of a swift wind, the roar of a king of elephants, the sound like the grinding of clouds, a voice that can reach the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, and a voice that addresses all the beings being transformed.
It is not a hurried voice, not a sluggish voice, not a halting voice, not a deficient voice, and not a turbid or impure voice; it accords with all voices and enters into the sound of all sounds.

The sound of liberation; the sound of non-bondage; the sound of non-attachment; the sound of speech that accords with meaning; the sound of speech appropriate to the occasion; the sound of speech that does not exceed the proper time; and the sound skillfully proclaiming eight quadrillion *koṭis* of Dharma gates.
It is a voice without obstruction, a voice that never ceases, a voice capable of discerning all sounds.

It is a voice that can fulfill all vows according to one's mind, a voice that can produce all peace and happiness, a voice that manifests all forms of liberation, and a voice that circulates through all paths.
When speaking amidst the assembly, he does not do so outside of it, producing a sound that causes all the great multitude to rejoice;
when this sound issues forth, it accords with the Dharma-sound of all Buddhas.
"Then, with these various voices, the Bodhisattva addressed the grass-cutter, saying:
'O worthy one!
Will you give me some grass?'"
The emanated person replied,
"I can give it to you. Thereupon,
the person created by Śakra immediately mowed the grass and presented it to the Bodhisattva.
The grass was pure and exquisite; the Bodhisattva then took a handful of it and held it himself in his hand.
At the moment the Bodhisattva took that grass, the earth immediately shook in six ways.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, intending to take this grass, proceeded calmly toward the foot of the Bodhi tree.

As the Bodhisattva was walking while holding the grass, five hundred bluebirds suddenly appeared from the ten directions; having circumambulated the Bodhisattva three times clockwise, they followed behind him as he walked.
Furthermore, five hundred *kucīra* birds came from the four directions and surrounded him as before;

additionally, five hundred peacocks came, and so on, briefly stated: five hundred white geese, five hundred cranes, five hundred white gulls, five hundred *kalaviṅka* birds, along with five hundred *jīvajīvaka* birds, and five hundred white elephants, all of which had six tusks.

There were five hundred white horses with heads and ears black as ink, their manes and tails entirely vermilion, long and flowing; and there were five hundred bull-kings, all with dewlaps reaching to their chests, resembling dark clouds.

At that time, there were also five hundred boys and five hundred girls, each adorning their bodies with various kinds of exquisite necklaces; there were five hundred sons of gods and five hundred daughters of gods, along with five hundred precious vases filled with various fragrant flowers.
Furthermore, various kinds of exquisite perfumed waters were filled [in vessels], which moved through the air spontaneously without anyone holding them.

Moreover, all auspicious things in the world came from the four directions like clouds raining down; each remained on the right side of the Bodhisattva, and after circling him three times, they followed his path.
"Furthermore, among all the trees and every kind of medicinal herb in the world, when the Bodhisattva walks, they all bow down from their very roots toward the Bodhisattva."
Furthermore, from the four directions, subtle, cool, and harmonious breezes blew away all obscurations, rendering everything completely pure, free from clouds and mist, and devoid of smoke and dust.

In the space above, there were again immeasurable thousands of myriads of devas who followed along as the Bodhisattva proceeded toward the Bodhi tree. All of them simultaneously experienced such joy and exultation that it pervaded their entire bodies; they could not contain themselves, singing and shouting, or whistling with their mouths, making all manner of sounds, and playing with their celestial robes and precious necklaces.
Again, a voice resounded, speaking these words:
"Now, in this Jambudvīpa, a Buddha, a World-Honored One, has appeared in the world.
Furthermore, immeasurable devas from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens came to stand at the Bodhisattva’s left, right, front, and back; they prostrated themselves before the Bodhisattva and addressed him thus:
"O Great Holy One!
For a long night in the past, you have constantly made aspirations; today, those aspirations have been fulfilled. All the devas in the world are worthy of performing rites of auspiciousness for you."
"Those who can bring about auspicious signs for you, O Benevolent One, and who can further fulfill your heart's aspirations—all of them have come before the Bodhisattva.
As the Bodhisattva turned his face toward the Bodhi tree and proceeded forward, at the moment he was about to reach the foot of the Bodhi tree, the earth shook in six ways.

"Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva walks, his gait is like that of a lion, like that of a dragon king, like that of a bull king, like that of a white goose king, and like that of an elephant king. He walks without fear, walks without obstruction, and walks without attachment. He walks having extinguished all causes for the hair on his body to stand on end; he walks with the virtuous conduct of one who cannot be defeated by others; he walks with the true, supreme, and most excellent state of meditative concentration; he walks with the highest and most wondrous subduing of all enemies; and he walks having severed all unbeneficial actions."

He practices because he wishes to take up the unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma; he practices because he wishes to take up and embrace unsurpassed bliss; he practices because he wishes to take up the supreme, tranquil concentration.

When he walks, all sentient beings upon the earth who hear the sound of the ground shaking—including the gods dwelling on earth, asuras, all nāgas, gandharvas, all birds, quadrupeds, humans, and others—all hear that sound of the earthquake. Their minds are filled with doubt and wonder as they look about everywhere, asking: "What strange event is occurring? What cause and condition is there for the great earth to surge, subside, and tremble in this way?"

"At that time, there was a nāga king in that land named Kāṭa (translated in the Sui language as 'Black'), who was long-lived and had lived through many kalpas, having previously seen many Buddhas come in the past."

Furthermore, for the dragons, days and nights are exceedingly long; before they have slept for very long, they perceive the great earth shaking and hear a thunderous roar, whereupon they immediately awaken in alarm.
Having awakened, he suddenly rose and quickly emerged from his own palace.
As he went outside to look toward the four quarters, the Naga King Kāta, after surveying the four directions, saw a Bodhisattva walking with composed grace not far from his own dwelling.

At that time, the Dragon King, seeing this Bodhisattva and the auspicious omens that preceded him, perceived them to be no different from those of the great Bodhisattvas of the past who had resolved to proceed to the foot of the Bodhi tree.

Having seen these signs, he was no longer doubtful; he knew with certainty that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva would surely realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Filled with great joy, he immediately spoke a verse, joining his palms with single-minded devotion and praising him, saying:
“O Great Benevolent One of towering majesty, Just as I have seen in the past, When various Bodhisattvas came here, So too are you now, without any difference.”
Now that I see you, O Benevolent One, come to this place, I am certain you will become a Buddha; there is no doubt.
The World-Honored One’s gait is most composed and serene; First raising the right foot, he moves forward.
Observing all directions with a steady gaze, You shall surely become a Buddha, a World-Honored One.
"O Benevolent One, now from this auspicious place, you shall beg for a handful of grass and hold it in your hand;
facing directly toward the Bodhi tree, you will certainly become a Samyaksambuddha this very day."
From the four directions and all sides, cool and refreshing breezes blow, sounding like the lowing of a bull-king;
various birds also come to attend him, surrounding him on all sides—front, back, left, and right.
The world is shrouded in darkness, obscure by day and night, covered by the ignorance and folly of *avidyā*.
Having perfected the virtues of a benevolent and sagacious man, you shall surely emit a great light that shines everywhere.
Furthermore, various wondrous beasts shall come, with hundreds of thousands of millions surrounding you before and behind, circling to the right like the turning of a wheel;
thus, O Benevolent One, you will certainly become a World-Honored One.
Furthermore, elephants, horses, and various other animals, along with banners, garlands, and the like,
arrived and rushed swiftly toward the Bodhisattva, clearly knowing that he would become a Buddha, a World-Honored One.
Furthermore, all the gods of the Pure Abodes, bearing their pure and adorned bodies,
bow with heads lowered in prostration before you, O Benevolent One, knowing that you will certainly become a Buddha, a World-Honored One.
O Benevolent One, you now possess this mind with outflows, yet it is further oppressed by all manner of afflictions;
now that those fetters and delusions have been extinguished, you will surely attain supreme and unsurpassed Bodhi.
You, O Benevolent One, are now fully endowed with the subtle and wondrous Dharma, profound, unfathomable, and inconceivable;
having realized it, your gait is steady and your stride is broad, and for this reason my mind is free from doubt or hesitation.
O Benevolent One, all that you have now performed is in accordance with the Dharma; what you have taught is supreme and beyond reproach.
Among all devas and humans, there is none equal to you; therefore, my mind is free from doubt or hesitation.

At that time, after the Black Dragon King had praised the Bodhisattva with these verses, his heart was filled with great joy and he leaped for immeasurable delight. Joining his ten fingers in palms-together salutation, he prostrated himself before the Bodhisattva, bowing his head to the Bodhisattva’s feet.
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to the Dragon King:
"Excellent, Great Dragon King!
It is so, it is so, just as you have said; I shall now certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
And he spoke in verse:
"O Great and Virtuous Dragon King, as you have said, This shall increase my diligence;
I shall now surely accomplish the Unsurpassed Way, Peerless and without equal in all the world."
Adorned with the marks seen by others, may great auspicious omens assist me;
now, within this ocean of afflictions, I shall certainly cross to the other shore without doubt.

At that time, the Black Dragon King had a dragon queen named Golden Light (*Suvarṇaprabhā*), who was surrounded on all sides by immeasurable dragon maidens. Each of them held in her hands exquisite fragrant flowers, powdered incense, unguents, various colored garments, precious banners, flags, canopies, and diverse necklaces, while celestial music was performed.
Within those musical sounds, various songs and hymns were performed in praise of the Bodhisattva.
Following the Bodhisattva’s movements, such verses emerged from the melodic tones, extolling him thus:
“The World-Honored One’s body and mind are eminent and immovable; Free from alarm and fear, he dwells in steadfast composure.”
Rejoicing and leaping for joy, free from all desires, having utterly abandoned anger and delusion, you have no place for craving;
O Honored One, you are able to act as a physician for the world, and for this reason I now prostrate with my head at your feet.
The world’s various latent tendencies and afflictions are thick; none are able to liberate themselves from those entanglements.
You have naturally subdued your own faculties and further subdue others; you can pull out the poisonous arrows of sentient beings.
To those who have no refuge or protection, you provide refuge and protection; in the darkness of the world, you act as a guide.
The Lamp of Illumination for the Three Realms, You alone are supreme; therefore, we now prostrate to You.
World-Honored One, no one can subdue You, for You have exhausted greed, hatred, and ignorance;
having abandoned all afflictions and the passions of desire, I now bow my head in worship.
The thorns of affliction pierce the minds of sentient beings, and no one is able to extract them;
now the World-Honored One acts as the Great Physician, capable of curing their great suffering and distress.
Where there is no refuge, you act as the refuge; where there is no guide, you act as the guide.
Amidst the darkness that pervades the three realms, the World-Honored One’s radiance shines everywhere.
As I now behold the hosts of devas, Holding exquisite incense and flowers that fill the void,
Dancing with necklaces and scattering their robes— Having seen these preliminary signs,
I have weighed the matter and found it free from error; O Benevolent One, you shall now become a Buddha, and my heart rejoices.
Go swiftly to the foot of the Bodhi tree of virtue, Subdue those hosts of the four Māras,
Tear asunder the leather net of afflictions, And quickly attain unsurpassed, tranquil Nirvāṇa.
Just as the wise ones of old attained perfect enlightenment upon reaching this place, so too have you, O Benevolent One, now arrived here;
I know that you will certainly become a Buddha, without any doubt.
When the World-Honored One was formerly on the path of practice, he performed deeds for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas;
with diligent toil and austerity, he never rested for a moment, aspiring to attain perfect enlightenment and realize True Suchness.
The time has now arrived; I pray you do not delay. Quickly go and sit beneath the tree of the Way.
With a focused mind relying upon that King of Trees, you will surely realize Bodhi; of this there is no doubt.
At that time, having heard these verses, the Bodhisattva proceeded with composed dignity toward the Bodhi tree. Along the way, he thought to himself:

"Within this realm of desire, Māra the Evil One is the sovereign ruler who exercises power and authority. I must now speak to him so that he may know; if I were to attain the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without informing him, I would not truly be called a Great Awakened One."
Why is this? It is because he wishes to subdue Māra Pāpīyān and to bring him under his influence; furthermore, it also serves to encompass and subdue all the devas of the desire realm.

Within that palace of Māra, among the hosts of Māra, there were furthermore immeasurable and boundless celestial beings who were kinsmen of Māra; these had already planted various roots of goodness in the past.

If they hear me utter the lion’s roar, or if they see me realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), then they shall all come toward me and resolve to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, having reflected thus, the Bodhisattva emitted from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows a single ray of light named "Able to Subdue and Disperse the Multitudes of Mara’s Armies."
Having emitted this light, it immediately reached the palace of Māra at that very moment, eclipsing all the light of the ancient palaces and the karmic power of all the māras.
Furthermore, this light spread laterally throughout the trichiliocosm, creating a great radiance that filled everything entirely.
At that time, within that radiance emitted by the Bodhisattva, Māra Pāpīyān spontaneously heard the sound of these verses:
“In the world there is a Great Being, Who has fulfilled his practices through many kalpas;
The crown prince of King Śuddhodana Has renounced the royal throne and gone forth into homelessness.”
He wishes to open the gate of the deathless nectar; now he approaches the Bodhi tree.
If you possess great physical strength, you may go beneath the tree and test him together.
Having now reached the further shore himself, he desires to ferry others across to that same place;
having already awakened through self-realization, the Bodhisattva now further wishes to awaken others.
Furthermore, having personally attained that tranquil meditative concentration, one further desires to teach others to become serene;
having oneself traversed the path free from bondage, one wishes to lead others toward the city of liberation.
He shatters and disperses the three evil realms until they are entirely empty, filling the paths of humans and devas until they are full;
manifesting the powers of dhyāna and the five supernatural faculties, he establishes beings so that they may know the palace of ambrosia.
Before long he shall realize great illumination; he will surely empty your realm.
Your companions—foolishness, darkness, and hatred—along with all your factions, shall be destroyed without remainder.
Once crushed and shattered, with no place to flee, what plan would the mind devise at that moment?
If one were to realize the Dharma of Ambrosia, there would be eternal bliss, selfhood, purity, and profound tranquility.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, the King of the Desire Realm, having heard these verses from within the radiance, was suddenly startled in his sleep; he naturally saw in a dream thirty-two kinds of inauspicious omens.
What are the thirty-two dreams? They are as follows:
one dreams that all the palaces claimed by the various celestial realms have become entirely dark, devoid of any light.
He saw his own palace filled with sand, gravel, filth, and excrement;
he saw his own body as terrifying and unpleasant, devoid of any sense of joy.
He saw himself running hither and thither in all directions;
he saw himself with the crown upon his head suddenly falling off, having lost his leather sandals, walking barefoot.
"I see my own throat, lips, and palate parched, and my body afflicted by cold and heat.
I see all the trees in my garden, with their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, completely withered and dried up."
He saw that all the flowers in the ponds and springs had completely withered away.

He saw that in his own garden, all the birds—the parrots, mynas, peacocks, ruddy geese, swans, cranes, cormorants, as well as the *kokila* and *jīvañjīvaka* birds—had their feathers and plumage entirely molted and fallen off.

He saw that all the musical instruments within the palace—the conch shells, drums, lutes, harps, *konghou*, flutes, and reed organs—everything belonging to the five types of sound, had been completely shattered, broken, destroyed, and ruined, lying in utter disarray upon the ground.

He saw that those whom he had previously loved—his attendants and followers—had all spontaneously departed from his side; filled with sorrow and distress, they stood apart at one side, lying alone upon the ground.
He saw that beautiful and lovely jade-like woman, naked and writhing, raising both her hands to pull out her hair as she lay upon the ground.
He saw all the sons of Māra, who were skilled in wisdom and eloquence, proceeding toward the foot of the Bodhi tree and prostrating at the feet of that Bodhisattva.
He also saw his four beloved daughters, each raising both hands and wailing aloud with these words:
"Alas, alas!"
"Alas, alas! He saw that the garments he was wearing were soiled and impure.
He saw his own body covered all over with dust and filth."
He saw his own body suddenly become emaciated and debilitated, devoid of any luster.
He saw his own palace—with its city walls, doors, windows, watchtowers, gates, parapets, battlements, and skylights—all utterly collapsed, ruined, and fallen into decay.

He saw all the great generals, yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, or even nāga kings; they all hung down their two arms, or at times raised them, beating their heads and striking their chests, each experiencing extreme suffering.

He saw all the lords of the desire realm, including the four world-protecting kings, Śakra, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin, all of whom were wailing and weeping until their faces were covered with tears; they rushed toward the Bodhisattva, gazed upon his face, and stood before him.

"Seeing him within the field of battle, amidst swords, staves, arrows, and blades, he himself, along with his attendants and retinue, has completely abandoned the Māra King and fled in all directions."
"He saw that the auspicious crests from which he had come were all shattered and destroyed;
he saw the celestial seer Nārada chanting inauspicious words."
"I saw a deity named Nandika standing at the gate making a sound and proclaiming thus: 'I am not joyful.
I also saw the void filled everywhere with dust, mist, smoke, and clouds."
The Great Deity of Merit, Guardian of the Māra Palace, raised his voice and wept aloud:
"Behold how that which was once his realm of sovereignty has now become a place of lack of sovereignty."
"I see my own friends, all of whom have become enemies;
I see the various palaces of Māra, some turned into darkness, others set ablaze, all of them utterly consumed by fire."
He saw all the palaces of the various Māras trembling and becoming unstable;
he saw all their trees and groves being cut down by others or falling to the ground on their own.
"Observing all his thoughts and deliberations, or the schemes he devises, and weighing them throughout the entire day, he does not obtain even a single mouthful; there is only mental agitation."

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, the King of the Desire Realm, having seen these thirty-two inauspicious dreams, awoke from his sleep; his entire body trembled, his mind was restless, and he harbored fear within.

He summoned all the kinsmen of Māra’s household to assemble, as well as those within his palace, his attendants and ministers, and the great generals and gatekeepers who guarded the various city gates, and spoke to them of what he had seen in his night dream.
"O you all! Last night I saw various strange omens in a dream, as previously described.
Having seen such inauspicious dreams, I was struck with great terror; my body and mind were ill at ease, and because of this, doubt arose within me, and I suddenly woke up."
"I shall surely lose this place before long; I fear that someone of great majesty and power of merit may come to be born here to take my place."
And he spoke in verse:
"Last night, a radiance appeared spontaneously; Within that radiance, these verses were spoken:
'The Prince of the Śākya clan now goes forth into homelessness, His body adorned with the thirty-two marks.'"
Having completed six years of asceticism as a renunciant, he now gradually approaches the Bodhi tree;
having awakened himself and awakened others through bodhi, if you have the strength, go and test him.
Having planted roots of goodness for a thousand billion eons, he has now attained Bodhi and realized the True and Right.
He shall shatter your realm until it is entirely empty;
if you cannot subdue him, he will realize the nectar of immortality and abide in the eternal body, seeking to destroy this demonic palace of yours.
Therefore, I tell you, O Māras: if you possess great power, go forth toward him at once!
That śramaṇa sits alone beneath a tree; quickly shatter him and do not let him remain whole.
If you would heed my loving words, prepare for me a fourfold army.
There are many Pratyekabuddhas in the world; having now emerged, they have entered Nirvana.
I hope to become the Dharma King alone, so that the lineage of the Tathāgatas shall not be severed.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān’s eldest son, named Śreṣṭhidāra, immediately addressed his father in verse:
“O Father King, why is your face colorless? Your heart trembles and your body lacks its majestic luster.
Beholding this form, it seems you are greatly alarmed; I wonder what you have seen or heard?”
"I only pray that you will speak truly to my sons, discussing each thing exactly as you have heard and seen.
Then Māra Pāpīyān, in turn, addressed his son Śreṣṭhin with these verses:
"My son, you should now listen well and attentively; last night I had a dream most extraordinary."
"If I were to explain it fully within my assembly, the great multitude upon hearing it would all fall to the ground in despair.
Then, Māra Pāpīyān’s eldest son, Śreṣṭhin, further addressed his father in verse:
"The great multitude falling to the ground is not what I dare refuse; to retreat from the fray is a great suffering."
"If you see such signs in a dream, it is better to stay and not fight, lest you be pursued by others.
Then, Māra Pāpīyān again addressed his son in verse:
"A man who has resolved to seek victory in battle may stop fighting even before he has been defeated."
"What can that lone śramaṇa possibly do? When I reach the foot of the tree, I shall rise and run away.
At that time, the merchant leader again addressed his father in verse:
"Whether one possesses great strength, the strength of the multitude, or the strength of the weak, it is the single individual with wisdom who triumphs in combat over others."
Though fireflies may fill the three thousandfold world system, a single sun appearing in the world can outshine them all.
If a person is arrogant and lacks reflection, haughty and deceitful toward others, and does not inquire extensively;
when wise people come to offer counsel and admonition, if they do not accept these words, they are difficult to cure.
"At that time, as the Bodhisattva was heading toward the Bodhi tree but had not yet reached its location, he saw a mango tree along the way and thought to himself, 'This is the Bodhi tree.'"

When the Bodhisattva arrived beneath that tree and wished to sit, regarding it in his mind as the Bodhi tree, at that moment the ground, due to the power of the Bodhisattva’s physical majesty and virtue, could not support its own weight and was about to sink downward.
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflected thus:

"There are two kinds of people whose ground sinks down when they walk or sit. Who are these two? [The text continues: ... those who have abandoned their preceptors and teachers, and those who have committed the five heinous crimes."
"First, there is the total severance of all roots of goodness; second, there is the vast accumulation of merit and virtues.
I am certainly not one whose roots of goodness have been completely severed; therefore, this must not be beneath the Bodhi tree."

At that time, the devas of the Pure Abodes in the Form Realm, in order to mark the true Bodhi tree, suspended exquisite silk banners upon it; furthermore, all the trees within that place had their branches and trunks incline toward the Bodhi tree.

At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately recognized that this was the true Bodhi tree; he then left behind the former mango tree and turned his steps with composed grace, gradually approaching the vicinity of the Bodhi tree.
"At that time, as the Bodhisattva was proceeding toward the Bodhi tree, there was a yakṣa named Gandhamādana who guarded that Bodhi tree and stayed there not far from it."
Seeing the Bodhisattva approaching, he was seized with urgency and immediately informed another companion named Rakta-akṣa, saying to that yakṣa:
"O worthy one, come here!"
I now speak to you; you must take heed and understand. Quickly go for my sake to the presence of Māra, the Lord of the Desire Realm, and deliver these words to him:
"In the past, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa—the great seers and sages—attained supreme perfect enlightenment at the very spot where they dwelt upon this ground."

Now there is yet another person of diligent effort, whose merit is perfected and whose bodhisattva practices are complete; having fully attained the thirty-two marks, he has encroached upon the realm where the Lord of Māra dwells.

This is the son of King Śuddhodana of the Śākya clan, named Siddhārtha; having abandoned ascetic practices and attained right mindfulness, he has arrived at this most excellent place, desiring to take up residence here.
"May Your Majesty know the time.
Having heard these words from the Gandharva Yakṣa, Red-Eye quickly went to the abode of Māra Pāpīyān; having arrived there, he related everything exactly as he had been told.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, the King of the Desire Realm, having heard these words from the red-eyed yakṣa, immediately summoned all the devas of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin, Nirmāṇarati, Tuṣita, Trāyastriṃśa, and Cāturmahārājika heavens, as well as the earth-dwelling devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and the entire great assembly, and commanded them, saying:
"All of you, assemble!"
"Listen to my instructions.
There is a son of the Śākya clan who desires to attain bodhi.
Let us go together to that place and sever such a courageous resolve, so that he does not realize the fruit of enlightenment."
At that time, the elder son of the Māra King, Śreṣṭhin, addressed his father, King Mārapāpīyān, saying:
"Father King, such as this is, my heart finds no joy."

Why is this? Because now our father, the King, wishes to become an enemy of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siddhārtha; we only fear that later on, when the king’s heart feels regret, it will be too late to remedy.
Having spoken these words, Māra Pāpīyān addressed his son Śreṣṭhidāraka, saying: "Ho, you child!
You are ignorant, deluded, shallow, and limited;
you have never known my transformative supernatural powers, nor have you ever beheld my sovereign majesty."
At that time, the merchant leader said to his father:
"Father King, you should know!

I am not a foolish son to my father king, nor am I ignorant of the sovereign power and spiritual majesty of your supernatural faculties. It is simply that you have not yet fully understood the spiritual powers of Prince Siddhārtha, nor have you yet seen the strength of Siddhārtha’s virtue."
"Although that may be so, O Father King!
When you arrive there, you shall see for yourself and know for yourself his supernormal powers.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān of the desire realm did not heed the words of his son, the Merchant Leader. Having heard this, he suddenly equipped four kinds of elite and formidable troops, ordering them all to assemble, clad in armor and bearing weapons. He was like a powerful and most valiant general leading a terrifying army of various kinds of men; those who beheld it would have their hair stand on end—it was something never before seen or heard of in the world.

In this way, there were immeasurable hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, and millions of celestial deities and ghostly armies; that is to say, a single body could manifest many hundreds of thousands of faces, and from each individual face could emerge immeasurable varieties of snake bodies, with hands and feet contorted and twisted, their appearance utterly terrifying.

They all held various weapons such as bows, arrows, spears, lances, mallets, clubs, axes, chisels, knives, and swords, as well as the supreme vajra implements; some had bodies, heads, eyes, hands, and feet of diverse and strange forms; some had great fires blazing upon their heads, or emitted extremely fierce flames from their bellies; some spoke with harsh voices and shrieked, while others held plows or carried pestles and other such objects.
Their eye sockets are terrifying; some have eyes that are askance, gazing with a sidelong, flickering glance up and down.
Some have mouths that are crooked and slanted, and they possess many teeth.
Their tongues are vast and manifest in various shapes; sometimes the tongue hangs downward, or it is curled and shriveled like a pebble.

Some emit light from their eyes, resembling black snakes filled with venom; some have their necks entwined by various serpents; and some hold great pythons in their hands and devour them, just as the garuḍa takes dragons from the ocean and eats them.

Or again, they may take human flesh, bones, blood, heads, eyes, limbs, and joints in their hands and devour them; or they may take human internal organs, intestines, stomachs, and excrement in their hands and eat them.
Some had blue eyes like those of the lion king, wide and terrifying;
some had eyes that were uneven, opening and closing while emitting light; others rode upon great mountains of fierce fire, coming through the air.
Some bore flaming fires upon their two shoulders, blazing as high as mountains;
others, upon the ground, uprooted trees with both hands, including their roots, and carried them into the midst [of the assembly].
Some have ears like those of a ram, some like winnowing baskets, some like oysters or clams, some like elephant ears, some like pig ears, and some have drooping lobes.
Some have bellies like those of people suffering from dropsy, with thin and weak calves and emaciated bodies.

Some have flat noses, some have bellies like jars, and some have feet like overturned bowls; their skin is as dry as dried meat, their flesh is parched, and their blood and veins are completely withered away.
Some have their hands and feet cut off and hung up; others have their heads severed, which they hold in their hands.
Some have blood flowing from their bodies, drinking it from one another; having drunk it, they vomit it back up, or they spit out white foam, or drink molten copper, or swallow iron balls.
Some have their hands, feet, elbows, or knees severed and must crawl along; some possess only skeletons, devoid of skin or flesh.

Some take the form of pigs; others take the forms of donkeys, mules, elephants, horses, camels, oxen, sheep, rams, rhinoceroses, wild oxen, water buffaloes, foxes, rabbits, gayals, *śarabhas*, crocodiles, whales, cormorants, lions, tigers, wolves, bears, brown bears, jackals, monkeys, jackals, leopards, wild dogs, raccoon dogs, and dogs.
With all such various appearances, creating great terror and inspiring great dread, this host of troops was fully prepared and stood solemnly in attendance, awaiting orders to set forth.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds,
Volume Twenty-Six and Volume Twenty-Seven,
