translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on Approaching the Bodhi Tree, Part Two:
At that time, the Māra King addressed his messenger, the yakṣa Red-Eye, saying:
"O Red-Eye, do you now see this host of troops?"
"Who is it that dares to invade my domain?
At that time, the yakṣa messenger Red-Eye addressed King Mārapārśva, saying:
"Great King!"

You should know that this is the son of King Śuddhodana of the Śākya clan, named Siddhārtha; like a bull-king, he let out a great roar before Sujātā, the daughter of the village headman, and from Kṛṣṇa, the grass-cutter, he begged for a handful of grass.

There was a tree named Eḍakajaṅgha Nyagrodha that gradually approached, surrounded by five hundred blue jays. In the month of early spring, all the lovely trees put forth flowers and fruit; their branches hung down of their own accord, and even those trees devoid of consciousness bowed their heads in lowly worship. The great earth trembled as they moved toward the foot of that Bodhi tree.
At that time, when Māra saw that the Bodhisattva was about to proceed toward the foot of that Bodhi tree, he thought to himself:
"I pray that this Śākya may go to the foot of another tree to spread grass and sit; let him not sit beneath this Bodhi tree."
Having reflected and contemplated thus in his mind, he addressed all those hosts of yakṣas, saying:

"All you yakṣas, you should each take a small number of your own yakṣa followers and go quickly to lie in wait beneath that Bodhi tree; take care not to let this son of the Śākya clan approach that spot under the Bodhi tree."
The yakṣas addressed the Māra king, saying,
"We respectfully obey the strict commands issued by Your Majesty.
Thereupon, the yakṣas immediately withdrew a small portion of their host and remained hidden at a short distance from the Bodhi tree.

When the various yakṣas of Māra’s host saw from afar that the Bodhisattva was approaching the Bodhi tree, his body blazed with brilliance like a mountain of gold emitting light, beyond all comparison.
When that host of yakṣas had seen him, they immediately spoke in verse:
"This must be the new sun of a thousand rays, Its majestic virtue shining like a mountain of gold.
Out of compassion for all devas and humans, He approaches the king of trees like a lion."
Then the deity who protects that grove replied to those yakṣas in verse:
“The World-Honored One has perfected his merit over a thousand kalpas;
Fully complete in the six perfections—giving, morality, patience, Vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom— He is endowed with every form of adornment.”
Now he gradually approaches the King of Trees, desiring to realize the path of unsurpassed Bodhi;
the devas, humans, and the eight classes of beings, reflecting thus, all follow him.
At that time, having heard these verses, the hosts of yakṣas who were the kinsmen of those Māras all departed from the side of the Bodhi tree and fled in every direction like scattered stars.
At that time, the Bodhisattva gradually arrived at the stage where the qualities of the sixteen marks are fully perfected.
What are these sixteen marks?

That is to say, when that land is consumed by the conflagration at the end of the kalpa, it is the very last to be burned away; yet when the kalpa first begins to be established, it is the very first to be formed.
Furthermore, the various grasses that grow upon that land are the most excellent and most wondrous.
That is to say, there are blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (padma), yellow lotuses (kumuda), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka), in abundance and not few.
Furthermore, that land is situated at the very center of Jambudvīpa.
"Furthermore, that land does not dwell upon dull-witted or ignorant sentient beings; it is only where those of noble lineage and great merit practice and reside.
Moreover, that land is free from pits and hollows, being spacious on all four sides and a place of level terrain."
"Furthermore, that ground is neither low nor high, pure, vast, and level like the palm of a hand.
Moreover, many flowers grow there spontaneously—blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (padma), yellow lotuses (kumuda), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka)."
"Furthermore, that ground is universally known by all the sages.
Furthermore, that ground manifests spontaneously.
Furthermore, at all times, that ground is constantly inhabited by sages and is never empty or vacant."
"Furthermore, on that ground, no one will ever be able to subdue him.
Moreover, the fame of that ground shall be heard afar, being called the Lion’s Most Exalted Seat."
"Furthermore, in that stage, even if one were to search with a mind seeking for faults, none could be found—namely, those of Māra or the retinues of Māra.
Moreover, that stage is the most central and balanced among all stages."
"Furthermore, that ground is composed of vajra.
Moreover, the various grasses growing upon that ground are exactly four finger-widths high, soft and green, like the neck of a peacock."
When touched, it is like Kāśika cloth—its color is exquisite, its form is lovely and upright, its fragrance is fragrant, and its hair curls entirely to the right.
In the past, there were various Wheel-Turning Sage Kings who all heard of this delightful and rare occurrence; for this reason, they constantly came and went to observe this place.

"At that time, as the Bodhisattva was about to reach the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, the ground spontaneously swept clean, becoming pure, magnificent, and beautiful. It was sprinkled with fragrant liquids, lovely and upright, inspiring a joyful and contemplative mind to behold it. Furthermore, it was entirely free of all sand, gravel, tiles, stones, thorns, briars, and various weeds."

At that time, the Bodhisattva first held the grass in his left hand as he walked; later, having arrived beneath the tree, he took a handful of that grass from his left hand with his right hand—whose five soft fingers were adorned with webbing and whose reddish hue was like that of vermilion applied—and intended to place it securely beneath the Bodhi tree.
Facing east, he held some grass and cast it upon the ground; its roots immediately turned toward the tree.
The Bodhisattva made this aspiration in his heart:
"Having sat here in this place, I shall now transcend the ocean of afflictions and cross over to the other shore."

Then the Bodhisattva threw that handful of grass onto the ground; it lay like a flower placed within a basket, or like a whirlpool in a river, or like the figure of a thousand-spoked wheel (*svastika*).
At that time, seeing that the grass he had grasped had fallen randomly upon the ground yet remained naturally unscattered, and observing such auspicious signs, he spoke these words:

"Just as this grass I have thrown today should have been scattered but remains unscattered—this auspicious sign portends that although I shall be amidst a world of disorder, I will certainly realize the Dharma that is not disordered."
When the Bodhisattva had thus cast down the grass and spread it out, at that moment the earth shook in six ways.
Then Māra Pāpīyān, the Lord of the Desire Realm, approached the Bodhisattva and spoke these words:
"O son of the Kṣatriya caste!
It is not appropriate for you to sit here beneath this tree with grass spread out as a seat. Why is that?
Because at midnight, many immeasurable piśāca demons, pūtana spirits, yakṣas, and rākṣasas frequently and constantly come here to devour human flesh.

"To the north of this tree, there is another grove where the Great Seer dwells; that location is called the village of Uruvilvā. It is delightful, beautiful, and pleasing to behold. You, son of the Śākyas, should go to that place and sit as you please."
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied to Māra with these words:
"O Māra Pāpīyān! Do you not know?
I dwell in mountain hermitages, in empty and secluded marshlands, or beneath trees, or among burial mounds, or within groves; at midnight I am peaceful and secure, my mind free from fear.
Furthermore, it is not that I am currently lacking wisdom, nor am I devoid of the power of skillful means, such as an ordinary person who has arrived at this place.
Rather, I have long known that in the past, all Buddhas attained the Noble Path beneath this tree in this place of fearlessness.
"It is for this reason that I have come here.
At that time, there was another yakṣa standing to the right of Māra Pāpīyān, who spoke to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O son of the Śākya clan!
"Why do you now suffer by sitting beneath this tree?
Outside here on all four sides, there are many other trees; you should quickly move elsewhere.
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied to the yakṣa, saying:
"I have a heart's desire that cannot be fulfilled under any other tree;
my wish lies solely beneath this tree, and it shall certainly be accomplished here, nowhere else."
Then, that yakṣa addressed the Māra king, saying:
"Great King!
Have you now heard what he said?"
"What further action can be taken to cause him to depart?
Māra Pāpīyas replied to that yakṣa:
"I must now employ various skillful means and exert diligent effort to sever his path, so that he is not permitted to sit here."
At that time, seeing Māra Pāpīyas speak thus, the Bodhisattva spread the grass and sat down, reflecting within his mind and making this vow:
"I now sit upon that adamantine site where all the Buddhas of the past and future have sat; having sat here, I shall subdue the Māra King Pāpīyas."
Having sat here now, I shall eradicate all afflictions such as desire, hatred, and delusion.
Having sat here now, I shall realize the subtle, wondrous, ambrosial, and cooling Dharma.

At that time, the grass spread by the Bodhisattva had its roots pointing inward and the tips all facing outward. Having finished spreading it, he circumambulated the Bodhi tree three times to the right, then sat down cross-legged with body and mind upright and straight, like a coiled serpent, standing firm and motionless.
He uttered three times with his voice:
"I have realized the Deathless!
I have realized the Deathless!"
"I shall now certainly realize the deathless nectar.
Then the Bodhisattva’s mind gave rise to this great vow:
"Seated here, if all outflows are not completely eliminated, or if my mind does not attain liberation, I shall never rise from this seat."
A verse says:
"The Bodhisattva sat cross-legged beneath the tree, as if coiling a great serpent around his own body;
having given rise to such a heart of great resolve, he would not rise from his seat until the task was accomplished."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān vanished from that spot and remained unseen; after a short while, he manifested his form again with disheveled hair and his body covered in dust.

Wearing coarse hair-cloth garments, his lips parched and his appearance like one suffering from hunger and thirst, he came swiftly holding a large bundle of books in his hands. Approaching the Bodhisattva, he stood before him and cast the books he held toward the Bodhisattva, speaking these words:

"This first letter is sent by your kinsman Mānava; this one is sent by Nīladha; this one is sent by Nandika; this one is sent by Bhaṭṭika; this letter is sent by Nanda; and this one is sent by Ānanda."
"Furthermore, these various other books, each containing the seeds of their respective commentaries, have been sent to you.
At that time, upon one of the books, there was a forged copy containing false and deceptive words, which spoke thus: "Devadatta!"

Now he is here in this city of Kapilavastu; having assumed the royal throne, he has entered your palace and taken all your queens and consorts as his own. He has seized your father, the Great King Śuddhodana, and cast him into prison. Furthermore, your other uncles—Śuklodana, Droṇodana, and Amṛtodana—as well as all the elder Śākya kings, have been driven out and banished beyond the city walls.
"Upon seeing this letter, you must come at once; what is the use of your staying there in that āraṇya?
When the Bodhisattva heard these words, three thoughts arose in his mind:
"Because of these court ladies, a desire has been aroused; yet my queen-consort, Devadatta was truly able to take her."
Because Devadatta gave rise to a mind of contention, could he truly have seized my kingdom and my father’s royal throne?
Because of the Śākyas, I conceived a murderous intent; why did they each cherish their own bodies and fail to protect my father?
The Bodhisattva further reflected in this way:
"The realms of the world are entirely impermanent, defiled and impure, arising and ceasing from moment to moment, without even a brief moment of abiding."
"Reflecting that all things are of a nature to disintegrate and perish as soon as they arise"— by reflecting in this way, one severs the mind of desire,

gives rise to the mind of renunciation, calms the mind of contention, arouses the mind of loving-kindness and compassion, abandons the mind of killing and harming, and generates a mind of sorrowful pity.
"Such matters as these I have long since cast away.
Having reflected thus, he immediately gave rise to a mind of renunciation.

Chapter 31: The Demon’s Terror of the Bodhisattva The Mahāsāṃghika-buddhacarita-sūtra, Chapter Thirty-one (Part One): The Demon’s Terror of the Bodhisattva "At that time, the Bodhisattva had already sat beneath the Bodhi tree."

At that time, the deity who protects the Bodhi tree was filled with great joy; his heart leaped with exultation, pervading his entire being until he could not contain himself. He immediately untied all the necklaces from his body and loosened his topknot, then quickly approached the Bodhisattva and praised him with words of most supreme and wondrous auspiciousness.
With profound sincerity in their hearts and inspired by great wonder, they summoned all their kinsmen and retinues to protect the Bodhisattva, remaining reverent and solemn.

At that time, from every direction, the tree spirits dwelling in the groves—regardless of whether their trees were large or small—each emerged from their respective trees and approached the spirit who protected the Bodhi tree, asking:
"O Great and Virtuous Tree Spirit!..."
Who is this person who now sits beneath your tree?
We have never before heard of or seen anyone so wondrous and supreme, whose body is adorned with all the marks of excellence, like a god among gods.
Having spoken these words, the deity who protects the Bodhi tree addressed the other tree deities, saying:
"O you deities, you should know!

This is the son of King Śuddhodana, of the Ikṣvāku lineage. In the beginning of past kalpas, he was selected by the great assembly and established as king; through hereditary succession from generation to generation, he has come down to this day, and he is now their scion."
Then the tree spirits spoke again to the Bodhi-protecting spirit, saying:
"O Bodhi-tree spirit!

You have now truly attained the greatest benefit and the most excellent meritorious karma, for you have caused such a supreme being—one who is the most honored and wondrous being in the triple world—to dwell in your abode. Such a being is as difficult to appear in the world as the Udumbara flower."

At that time, all those tree deities each took aloeswood, ox-head sandalwood, and various powdered incenses, as well as many kinds of exquisite and wonderful fragrant flowers, and scattered them over the Bodhisattva; scattering them again and again, they were filled with such joy and exultation that it pervaded their entire bodies, which they could not contain.
Raising their hands and bowing their heads, they joined their palms in reverence toward the Bodhisattva and each proclaimed in unison:
"O Foremost among all beings, we pray that you, O Benevolent One, may quickly fulfill this vow and swiftly realize Bodhi."

Next, the various devas dwelling in the Four Heavenly Kings’ realms, as well as the Four Great Kings themselves, followed by immeasurable devas of the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens—in short, all the infinite and boundless devas, including the Brahmā devas—each brought various kinds of exquisite celestial flowers: māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, divine kumuda, as well as padma and puṇḍarīka flowers; they further took various kinds of powdered incense and unguents and scattered them like rain upon the Bodhi tree.
That Bodhi tree was like a chariot wheel, filling the entire area within one *yojana* with various fragrant flowers piled up to the knees.
"At that time, when the Bodhisattva sat beneath that Bodhi tree, not a single ant or termite made a sound, much less any large beast."
All birds likewise ceased their cries, and even if there were wind, all the trees remained unmoved.

When the Bodhisattva sat beneath that Bodhi tree, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens were filled with such exultation that it pervaded their entire bodies; unable to contain themselves, they prostrated before the Bodhisattva, each making this vow within their hearts:
"O Foremost among Beings, may your noble resolve soon reach fulfillment, and may you swiftly attain Bodhi."
"At that time, when the Bodhisattva sat beneath that Bodhi tree, he made this solemn vow:
'I shall not rise from this seat until I have attained the Way.'"
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān felt great terror arise within his heart and spoke these words:
"This son of the Kṣatriya Śākya clan intends to destroy my realm and intends to cause me to depart from this realm."

If that Victorious One were to stand before me, he would surely instruct all people so that they might attain nirvāṇa, and he would preach to them the means for attaining nirvāṇa, thereby causing my realm to become as empty space.
Yet he has not yet attained the pure eye; while he remains within my domain, I must now employ diligent and skillful means to cause his practice to falter and for him to flee.
And he spoke in verse:
"If he now attains enlightenment, he will extensively proclaim the True Dharma to others,
and shall thereby diminish my realm."
Once the multitude has found the opening of the true path, my realm will naturally become empty; with the realm empty, I shall become a widow.
Since they have not yet attained the eye of purity, they remain within my realm;
I should swiftly go to their side, first creating obstacles to thwart their purpose.
"Just as when the river water has not yet arrived, one must nevertheless prepare a bridge in advance.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān had a full thousand sons; among them, five hundred sons assisted the Bodhisattva, with Sārthavāha at their head, sitting on the right side of Māra Pāpīyān.
Among them, there were also five hundred who assisted Māra Pāpīyas; the foremost leader was named Duṣkha, and he sat on the left side of Māra Pāpīyas.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān addressed his sons, saying: "O you, my sons!

I now wish to deliberate with you on our advance and retreat, seeking to ascertain your individual intentions and wisdom so that we may devise a plan together: by what means might we be able to subdue the Bodhisattva?"
At that time, the eldest son on the right, the merchant leader, spoke a verse to his father, Māra Pāpīyān, saying:
“If a person dares to touch the great sleeping serpent, And can further turn back a mad, intoxicated elephant,
And has once fought with the fierce King of Beasts— Only such a one can subdue that śramaṇa.”
At that time, the second son on Māra Pāpīyān’s left side, named Durvaca, spoke again to his father in verse:
“If people seeing my heart broken and wounded cause all the trees to uproot themselves and fall to the ground,
how much more so when that śramaṇa beholds me— would he not run far away in one breath and hide?”
At that time, there was a son of Māra on the right side named Subhāṣita, who addressed his father in verse, saying:
“If a person were to float across the great ocean, And then desire to drink it all until it is completely dried up— Father King, such a feat would not be cause for alarm;
But if one were to behold the face of the Bodhisattva, that would be truly strange.”
At that time, another son of Māra on the left side, named Śata-yuddha, again addressed his father in verse, saying:
"A hundred arms have grown upon my shoulders; Each single arm can shoot three hundred arrows.
Father King, go forth without sorrow or distress; I alone am able to defeat that śramaṇa."
At that time, there was a son of Māra on the right side named Sujñāta, who again addressed his father in verse:
“If one possesses strength like that of an elephant or a horse, or even like that of Viṣṇu or Vajrapāṇi—
none of those powers can equal the power of a person’s latent karma, patience, and majesty.”
At that time, another son of Māra on the left side, named Ugratejas, further addressed his father in verse,
saying: "I shall rain down water, fire, and wind from the sky, Until I can shatter the body of that bhikṣu,
Reducing his body to a single heap of ashes, Like fierce flames consuming dry grass."
At that time, there was a son of Māra on the right side named Sunetra (Good Eyes), who spoke again to his father in verse:

"Even if the most excellent Mount Sumeru were to crumble, And all the celestial palaces were utterly destroyed, If the waters of the great ocean were to dry up completely, And the sun and moon were to fall from the sky— [Even so, he could not be moved. "
He can cause the sunlight to become as cold as ice, and make the celestial palaces fall to the earth;
once the Bodhisattva has sat beneath the tree, he will not move until he has attained perfect enlightenment.
At that time, another son of Māra on the left side, named Vairapratyarthika, again addressed his father in verse:
"I can grasp the sun and moon, The stars and all the celestial bodies in the void;
I can seize all those gods, And hold the waters of the four oceans within my palm."
How much more so this śramaṇa, a single son of the Śākyas—having now been flung to the edge of the foreign lands!
Quickly dispatch these various armies and hasten toward that place where the śramaṇa is.
At that time, another son of Māra on the right side, named Guṇaprasāda, addressed his father in verse, saying:
"The sun and moon move across the sky without seeking companions; The Wheel-Turning King appears through transformation without equal peers.
The various sages and bodhisattvas do not rely on a multitude; They alone are able to shatter the great army of Māra."
At that time, another son of Māra on the left side, named Guṇadūṣaka, spoke again to his father in verse:
"Among weapons for combat, none surpasses the sword; Clad in armor, the heart knows no fear.
With such an army, we shall surely slay him; Father King, do not fear that śramaṇa."
At that time, another son of Māra on the right side, named Puṇyālaṃkāravibhūṣaṇa, spoke again to his father in verse:
“His body is as firm as Nārāyaṇa, The essence of the Four Truths is difficult to destroy;
With the armor of patience and the sword of the three liberations, He wields the arrows of wisdom to subdue us.”
At that time, another son of Māra on the left side, named Anivartin, again addressed his father in verse:
"Just as dry grass ignites instantly when touched by fire, Just as a skilled archer’s divine arrow surely hits its mark,
And just as a thunderbolt penetrates a mountain upon striking it— Upon seeing my hand, the Śākya son shall surely be subdued."
At that time, there was a son of Māra on the right side named Dharmakāya, who addressed his father once more in verse:
"If someone were to paint figures in the sky with colors, Or create all sentient beings with a single mind,
Or entangle the Moon God and the Wind Deity in a net— Even such things could not move the Bodhisattva’s place of enlightenment."
At that time, another son of Māra on the left side, named Constantly Committing Evil, addressed his father once more in verse:
“I drink poison as if it were food; my fingers turn weapons to ash upon touching them.
If I do not crush his body into dust, I shall never again hold these two hands.”
At that time, there was a son of Māra on the right side named Sārthavāha, who again addressed his father in verse:
“The three-thousandfold world system is filled with poison, yet the World-Honored One gazes upon it without fear;
since he has utterly extinguished those terrifying three poisons, why should we return to our palace to fight?”
At that time, another son of Māra on the left side, named *Lolita* (Greedy Play), further addressed his father in verse:
“I shall take tens of billions of musical sounds and hundreds of thousands of adorned jade maidens;
by means of these illusions, I will delude and confuse his mind, causing him to lose his tranquil meditation and fall prey to various desires.”
At that time, there was a son of Māra on the right side named Dharmakrīḍa, who addressed his father in verse, saying:
“He takes the dharma of meditative concentration as his play; He constantly enters and dwells in the nectar of liberation.
Using the various means of attraction and joy, he uproots the calamities of the masses; He does not take the five desires as his pleasure.”
At that time, another son of Māra on the left side, named Jaitri (Swift), spoke again to his father in verse:
"My strength is so swift that I can seize the sun and moon; I can also cut through fierce fire and wind.
I shall grab this śramaṇa and place him before you, Like crushed barley awns scattered by the wind."
At that time, there was a son of Māra on the right side named Siṃhanāda, who addressed his father once more in verse:
"In the vast wilderness, countless jackals howl, Yet they have not yet heard the roar of the Great Lion.
If all the beasts were to hear the lion’s roar, They would scatter in all directions, fleeing in every quarter."
Thus we, all the māras, had never heard the Great King of Dharma proclaim his voice;
each spoke according to our own intent and refused to desist, until we reached the presence of that [Buddha] and naturally came to rest.
At that time, there was a son of Māra on the left side named Duṣcintin, who spoke again to his father in verse:
"I, Duṣcintin, now wish to seize him; how could he not see this army of Māras?
His mind is truly deluded and devoid of intent; why does he not flee and quickly take flight?"
At that time, there was a son of Māra on the right side named Suvicintita, who spoke again to his father in verse:
"He is neither foolish nor powerless; it is you yourselves who lack human discernment.
You do not yet know his skillful means; later, he shall subdue you with wisdom."
You sons of Māra, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, though you possess such eloquence that fills the three thousandfold world-system, cannot harm even a single hair on his body;
how much less could you kill him or cause him to rise [from his state]?
Direct your pure minds toward that place; with words of praise and bodies bowed low, do not harbor malice or harm your own army, for he shall surely become the Lord of the Three Realms.

"In this manner, up until one thousand sons of Māra, during that interval, some assisted the white side while others assisted the black side, each speaking their own opinions according to their own inclinations."
"At that time, Māra Pāpīyān had a chief military minister named Bhadra-senāpati.
Then, Māra Pāpīyān spoke to that minister, the great Bhadra-senāpati, saying:
'Come here, Bhadra-senāpati!'"

Follow me. Here is a son of the Śākya clan who desires to attain unsurpassed bodhi; I shall now go with you to that place to sever his path of the Dharma, so that he may not be permitted to realize unsurpassed bodhi.
Then the General Subāhu immediately addressed his Great King Mārapāpīyān in verse,
saying: “The Four Heavenly Kings whom Your Majesty commands, The Asura kings, the Kiṃnaras, The Garuḍas,
and the Mahoragas— With their ten fingers joined upon their heads, they take refuge in him.”
Moreover, all the Brahma worlds— the Ābhāsvara, Bṛhatphala, and Śuddhāvāsa heavens—
as well as the gods dwelling on the earth and in the Desire and Form Realms, all together prostrate themselves at his feet.
Furthermore, the king’s sons possessed superior wisdom and valor beyond compare in the world;
within their hearts, they constantly paid homage to that Honored One.
Although the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and various ghosts remained upon the ground before the king, [they were surpassed by the sons].
With a mind constantly mindful of that faultless man, he joins his ten fingers in palms-joined salutation and bows his head in worship.
When the myriad hosts of Māra’s army behold that Sage, they privately scatter fragrant flowers from afar upon him.
Seeing these clear signs, I know that the Bodhisattva will surely triumph over the multitudes of Māra’s army.
In the dwelling places of Māra’s armies, there are many cries of owls and starlings;
or again, the sounds of hooting owls, crows, and magpies, along with the harsh noises of donkeys, foxes, and various other beasts.
I see beneath that Bodhi tree auspicious birds of various kinds making their sounds—
ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, and *kīra* birds, starlings, parrots, and peacocks;
surrounding him with holy and subtle voices, such a sublime sign indicates he will surely be powerful.
Furthermore, where the camps of Māra’s hosts reside, there is a constant rain of sand, gravel, dust, and soil;
yet at the holy seat beneath the Bodhi tree, the heavens shower down various kinds of exquisite fragrant flowers.
The ground where the hosts of Māra dwell is uneven; it is full of high and low places, pits, hollows, mounds, and hillocks, abounding in gravel, thorns, and filth.
But the ground surrounding the foot of the Bodhi tree is adorned with the seven treasures, gold, and silver. Seeing such signs as these, [he knew that he would attain enlightenment].
If wise people have the intention [to seek enlightenment], upon seeing these signs they should turn back.
Such adornments covering the earth shall surely bring about the attainment of the Unsurpassed Way.
Great King, if you do not follow my admonition, that which was seen in the dream will not be in vain.
Thus, this seer must not be provoked; you should turn your troops back toward their original location.
Because a king of old offended the seers, his kingdom was incinerated by their spells and reduced entirely to ashes.
In the past, there was a King Brahmadatta who offended the sage Viśvāmitra.
The king possessed a magnificent garden filled with various flowers and fruits; however, through the sage’s curse, fire broke out and consumed it entirely.
For many years, not even a blade of grass grew in that garden, let alone trees, flowers, or fruits.
When he performed all the many austerities of the world, severing all evils and practicing the holy life, the kings all came to prostrate at his feet; we may now return to our own homes.
In the past, Your Majesty must have heard the Vedas, which clearly state that a person possesses the thirty-two marks;
such a person leaves the household life to seek the Way, and will surely sever all the entanglements,
nets, and fetters to attain the unsurpassed, true, and perfect enlightenment, emitting from between his eyebrows a ray of white light.
It universally illumines billions of lands throughout the ten directions;
how much more so these hosts of Māra’s armies—how could they not be subdued?
If Your Majesty wishes to fight, you shall not be victorious.

Just as the crown of his head reaches the highest heavens, such that millions of devas cannot behold it, he shall surely attain that subtle and wondrous fruit; what the world has never heard before, he now hears.
Just as Mount Sumeru and the Iron Ring Mountains, the sun, moon, Śakra, and Brahmā,
the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and all the forest trees— all bowed their bodies toward the Bodhi tree.
Undoubtedly, this great mass of merit—through the power of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom—has practiced these deeds throughout successive kalpas;
now it shall surely cause my demonic armies to retreat and disperse.
Like an elephant trampling broken pottery shards, like the lion, king of beasts, letting out its roar,
like the sun eclipsing the light of all fireflies— so too does the World-Honored One destroy Māra.
The lion alone scatters all beasts and insects; a venomous snake kills many with a single sting.
By the power of the roots of goodness cultivated by the Bodhisattva, he alone is able to destroy all my māras.

At that time, having heard these verses from his ministers, Māra Pāpīyān felt terror arise within him; he was consumed by feverish distress and lacked peace, his body and mind were filled with sorrow and grief, and he found no joy. Overcome with shame and humiliation, he did not know what to do.
Yet in his inner heart, he still harbored pride; he was unwilling to turn back, nor did he flee.
He spoke again to the rest of the army, saying:
"All of you, unify your minds! Do not be startled, do not be afraid!"
"Do not fear! Do not run away!
This was merely my testing of his mind.
Now, with sweet words, I shall further console him to see whether he will rise and depart from the Bodhi tree."
"Do not let such a jewel among sentient beings suddenly encounter great calamity.
At that time, the eldest son of the Māra King, Śreṣṭhidāraka, said to his father:
"O Great King, Lord of Māras!"
In my heart, I do not wish for our Father the King to become an enemy with these scions of the Śākya clan. Why is this?

Even if hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Māras were to come before these Śākyas, brandishing swords and blades in their hands, intent on creating obstacles, they would ultimately be unable to do so; how much less so could Father the King alone, by himself?
"O Father King!
Behold this son of the Śākyas, seated here beneath the Bodhi tree upon the lion throne, neither startled nor terrified.
O Father King!"
"Behold this seed of Śākyamuni; it does not waver or move.

"Furthermore, when the immeasurable hosts of devas in the void joined their ten fingers in palms-pressed salutation and prostrated before him—and when such devas were thus prostrating, making offerings, and offering praise—he did not feel joy."
Seeing that his father, the king, harbored evil thoughts and a malicious intent to come and slaughter him, he felt no anger.
"Father, King!
You should know that even if someone were to take various exquisite colors and attempt to paint the void;"
Suppose that a person were able to lift up and carry away that great King of Mountains, Sumeru, with a single finger;
this might be possible. Or suppose there were someone who could float across the great ocean and reach the other shore; this might also be possible.
Or suppose there were someone who could suddenly bind and restrain the greatest wind-gods as they blow from the four directions; this too might be possible.
One may also take the sun, moon, and stars and place them upon the ground;
one may also cause all sentient beings to act with a single mind;
and one may also relocate all sentient beings to various places.
"In the end, this son of the Śākyas shall not be subdued by me.
Then, Māra Pāpīyān addressed his eldest son, Sārthavāha, in verse, saying:
"You are truly my enemy, not my son; Do not turn your face toward me again."
"Since your heart is now set upon the śramaṇa, you should go to where that son of the Śākyas is.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān did not heed the counsel and admonition of his eldest son, Saṃjaya, but addressed his daughters, saying:
"You daughters!..."
"Each of you should listen to my words together and act accordingly. You must go to that son of the Śākyas and observe his mind: does he have any desire or passion?
Having heard their father's command, the māra-maidens proceeded together with composed grace toward the Bodhisattva.
Having arrived there, she stayed at a distance from the Bodhisattva, neither too near nor too far, manifesting various forms of feminine allure, flattery, and guile.

That is to say, she would cover her head, or perhaps leave it bare; she would show half her face, or reveal her entire countenance; she would smile, displaying her white teeth, and she gazed and looked toward the Bodhisattva again and again.

Some prostrated themselves with their heads at the Bodhisattva’s feet; some looked up at his face; some lowered their heads and covered their faces while gazing at the ground; some moved their eyebrows; some opened and closed their eyes; and some loosened their topknots, combing their hair with their hands.
Some clasp both arms, some raise both hands to reveal their armpits, or again, they grasp and fondle their breasts with their hands;
some expose their chests and backs, revealing the space between their bellies and breasts.

Or again, they may strike their navels with their hands; or repeatedly loosen their garments; or repeatedly tie their clothes back together; or repeatedly lift up and pull aside their undergarments, exposing their buttocks and thighs.

Some untied their necklaces and threw them upon the ground; some removed their earrings, while others put them back on again; some toyed with infants, or played with various birds; others walked about, glancing here and there to their left and right.

Or again, they may yawn and stretch, sighing and heaving long exhalations; or they may draw figures on the ground with their toes, or sing, or dance, or move their waists and bodies, or assume airs of pride; or they may recall the times of past indulgence in acts of affection, desire, laughter, sleep, and amorous dalliance.

Alternatively, they may manifest in the form of a young girl, or at times manifest in the form of a woman, or manifest as a newlywed bride, or manifest as a middle-aged woman; in such ways, they display various forms of feminine artifice, seduction, and attachment.

Again, they took fragrant flowers and scattered them over the Bodhisattva; furthermore, they used various objects of the five desires to entreat the Bodhisattva, observing his face and examining his state of mind to see whether he possessed any signs of desire or not.
Does he now observe us with a mind of desire, or does he observe us without a mind of desire?

Those māra-daughters saw that the Bodhisattva’s profound mind was tranquil and settled, fundamentally pure, unturbid and stainless; his countenance was as pure as the full moon emerging from the grasp of Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, clear and free from defilement.
Like the sun first rising, its radiant flames are brilliant;
like a bar of molten gold, it is pure and unstained;
just as a lotus flower emerges from the water yet remains unsullied by it.
Like the flame of a fire;
like Mount Sumeru, firm and immovable;
like the Cakravāḍa mountains, rugged and towering high.
Having well-restrained their sense faculties and subdued their minds, they all felt shame and remorse upon seeing the Bodhisattva in such a manner.
*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll 27;
*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll 28.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
From the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Fear of Māra":
At that time, those daughters of Māra, who were well-versed in the deceptive arts of women, further employed other methods of seduction to entice and disturb the Bodhisattva, speaking in verse:
“The fine season of early spring is beautiful and auspicious; the fruit trees and forest groves are all in bloom.
Such a magnificent sight is fit for joy.
Now that you are young, your spirit is free and unrestrained; this is precisely the time for a man to enjoy himself.”
To seek the path to enlightenment is extremely difficult; you, O Benevolent One, should turn your mind and enjoy worldly pleasures.
Behold us, the celestial maidens, with our lovely forms and supple bodies, adorned with various necklaces and ornaments—now who could obtain such a body?
Having been moved by your benevolence, why do you not accept me?
My body is as fragrant and pure as a lotus flower; why do you abandon such a person of merit and virtue in this world and refuse to employ me?
The hair is radiant and deep blue-black, constantly perfumed with various kinds of fragrant oils;
a precious wreath of extraordinary maṇi jewels is fashioned, and flowers are held to be inserted upon it.
Our foreheads are broad and our heads are perfectly round; our brows and eyes are level, upright, and remarkably elongated.
Pure as the blue lotus, our noses all resemble those of the parrot;
our lips are radiant with the color of vermilion, or shaped like the *bimba* fruit.
They resemble coral and vermilion; her teeth are as white and pure as conch shells.
Her tongue is thin like a lotus petal, and her speech and songs produce wondrous sounds like the voice of a kinnarī.
Her two breasts possess a hundred charms, all exquisite and sublime.
Furthermore, her waist is supple and slender like the grip of a bow;
her back is broad, smooth, and level. Her hips are soft, white, large, and straight, resembling the forehead of a king of elephants;
their shape is as elegant as the trunk of an elephant.
His two calves are perfectly symmetrical, slender and rounded, pure like those of the king of deer;
the soles of his feet are level and full, without slope or depression, glowing with a crimson-and-white luster like that of a lotus flower.
Our bodies possess a lovely appearance, adorned with such various marks and features;
we are fully endowed with every skill and are swift at producing all kinds of sounds.
Furthermore, we are adept at song and dance to delight the hearts of the multitude; when the devas see us, they all rejoice.
Everyone envies my birth and desires me; it is not that we do not delight in you, O Benevolent One.
Why, now that you see us, do you not feel desire?
You have abandoned us and fled far away, not knowing that wealth and goods are the causes of pleasure.
The intention of your benevolence is likewise so: you do not recognize the joy of the five desires, remaining in silent concentration and meditative stillness, refusing to grasp at a self.
Perhaps you, O Benevolent One, are greatly deluded; why do you not accept worldly pleasures? The path to Nirvana is exceedingly remote.

At that time, the Bodhisattva gazed intently at the māra-daughters with a steady mind, his eyes never wavering for a moment. With right mindfulness and a gentle smile, he restrained his sense faculties and remained in meditative concentration. His body was free from shame or embarrassment; neither hurried nor sluggish, he stood upright and composed like Mount Sumeru, his mind unshakable.

Through the remaining gateways of skillful means and wisdom, which have already subdued all afflictions and ailments in the past, he addressed those māra-maidens with verses, his compassionate voice surpassing the resonance of Brahmā and like the song of the kalaviṅka bird:
“Those five desires of the world are full of suffering, many faults, and entangled in manifold vexations;
because of these afflictions, one loses supernormal powers and falls into the darkness of ignorance.”
Sentient beings receive these things and know no contentment;
I have long since abandoned all the prisons of affliction, like a pit of raging fire or a casket of poisonous medicine, having long ago departed from them since the distant past.
Having already drunk the nectar-water of wisdom, if one has awakened to it within one's own mind and seeks to awaken others,
one should preach the subtle and secret dharma-gate; if one now indulges in such defiled desires,
one will ultimately never be able to attain this path.
This is what is called great folly; having been unable to achieve even one's own benefit, how much less could one benefit all beings? Therefore, my mind now does not indulge in it.
The five desires of the world burn sentient beings, Just as the fire at the end of an eon destroys all things.
The five desires are like bubbles on water, And like illusions or mirages, lacking even a single atom of reality.
They are false and deceptive for ordinary people; What wise person would take pleasure in such matters?
Just as ignorant children play amidst their own excrement, so do deluded,
foolish, and witless people see various necklaces and become attached to them; having observed them,
they immediately give rise to thoughts of desire.
Foul, filthy, and loathsome, like a severe ulcerous sore; the teeth grow long as if drinking from it;
the lips, mouth, ears, nose, and eyes—all are like bubbles upon the water.
The waist, hips, spine, back, and buttocks are foul-smelling and impure, arising from blood.
The belly is a sack for excrement and urine, filled within with all manner of impurities;
these karmic results all arise from craving.
Just as one constructs a wheel to serve as a millstone, so too do the ignorant pursue pleasure.
If there are any wise people who discern these various calamities and misfortunes, they will not accept such pleasure in this place.
Their bodies constantly bleed day and night; this foul-smelling place is unpleasant even to the eye.
With both thighs, both shins, and the two feet, tendons and bones bind one another to keep them standing.
I observe you now in this way: like illusions, like transformations, like dreams;
all things arise entirely from causes and conditions. The five desires possess no true merit;
they can cause one to lose the various noble paths and lead people away into the evil realms.
The five desires are like a great pit of fire, And like vessels filled with various poisons;
They are like the head of a wrathful serpent, not to be touched.
To forcibly conceive pure thoughts and give rise to craving— The five desires are like a hired laborer.
Serving as slaves to women,
and departing from wisdom, tranquility, and dhyāna; dwelling amidst confusion and clamor,
abandoning the sublime Dharma to pursue sensual play— such a person will fall into hell without doubt.
When these various illusions appear before my eyes, I take no pleasure in them within my mind;
desiring the ultimate bliss of sovereignty, I also teach others to join me in this.
Having liberated myself from that world, I am like the wind in space, which cannot be bound.
"O demonesses, even if you were as numerous as all the sentient beings in the world, my mind would never discriminate among them; for a moment, I would enjoy the five desires with you all."
I have long since eliminated anger and resentment; folly, greed, and desire are all absent.
The Buddhas, the Greatly Wise Holy World-Honored Ones, possess minds free from obstruction, like the very nature of space.

At that time, the daughters of Māra Pāpīyas, who were well-versed in the arts of feminine enchantment, further displayed their affectations and accentuated their coquettish charms. Adorning their bodies and manifesting exquisite voices and skillful words, they came to seduce the Bodhisattva.
And there is a verse that says:
"The Māra Pāpīyān has three daughters, Lovely, delightful, and peerless in their beauty;
The most noble and magnificent among all maidens, They were finely adorned at the command of the Māra King."
She swiftly went to where the Bodhisattva was, manifesting various illusory charms and assuming a coquettish air;
she made her body like the branch of a weak tree, swaying and fluttering gently with the wind.
Standing before the Bodhisattva, they sang and danced, chanting these words:
"O virtuous son of the Śākyas, you shall become a king; why do you sit beneath that great tree?"
This is the magnificent and sublime season of spring; men and women meet in union, giving rise to joy, just as various birds delight one another.
Once the desire-mind has been stirred, it is difficult to restrain;
the time has come, so let us together enjoy pleasure. Why do you guard your heart and not look upon me?
We have now come together once more; it is fitting that we proceed together in harmony.

That Sage is like the sun first rising; having practiced all manner of deeds and accumulated merit for billions of kalpas, his mind is as immovable as Mount Sumeru, and his wondrous voice is as clear and resonant as the roll of thunder.
His gait is steady and composed like that of a lion; his speech is beneficial and accomplishes much.
The beings of the world do not reflect upon this; they constantly give rise to strife for the sake of various desires, and once strife has arisen, they engage in disputes and litigation.
Thus, those who lack wisdom and the like are constantly tormented by such sufferings.
The wise, knowing this, do not follow after them; they renounce the world and depart, dwelling in mountain forests to find their own delight.
The time has now arrived before me; desiring to realize the eternally abiding Dharma of ambrosia, I must first subdue those hosts of Māra, and thereafter I shall become a Honored One of Ten Powers.
Then Māra Pāpīyān’s daughters addressed the Bodhisattva once more, saying:
“O Benevolent One, your countenance is like a pure flower; we pray you will listen to our words.
Please accept for now the sovereignty of the world, as a most supreme, exalted, and noble lord of absolute power.”
Whether lying down, sitting, or rising to walk, you produce wondrous sounds without interruption.
The supreme fruit of Bodhi is exceedingly difficult to attain; how much more so the wisdom-body of all Buddhas?
The path to liberation is difficult to traverse—O Benevolent One, whom do you see who can reach it?
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied to him:
"The Sovereign Lord among gods and humans, who turns the unsurpassed, wondrous Wheel of Dharma;
endowed with the ten powers and fearlessnesses, he stands alone, towering high above the triple world."
The assembly of disciples, both those in training and those beyond training, numbering in the billions, surround me;
with their mouths they constantly offer this praise: "The Great Sage has appeared, removing the doubts of the world."
When I preach the Dharma for them, I travel everywhere according to my will;
therefore, within this world, I take no pleasure in any of the delights of the five desires.
The demoness spoke again to the Bodhisattva:
"The time for decay and old age has not yet arrived; while your physical strength and vigor are at their peak, indulge yourself.
Only when you have become emaciated and can no longer endure it should you abandon this upright body."
We, the Flower-Faced Ones, are all thirty-five; we are truly your virtuous and excellent companions.
Our play in the five desires is most exquisite; for what reason, then, do you thus feel weary of us and seek to leave?
"If you, O Benevolent One, will not now grant us your acceptance, we shall follow you and never turn back.
The Bodhisattva spoke again to them:
"Exert yourselves to distance yourselves from all hardships, and strive diligently to enter that gate of ambrosia."
When one is able to abandon the hardships and calamities of the world, Then one leaves behind all the difficulties of humans and devas.
While old age, sickness, and death have not yet arrived, And while various evils and strife have not yet arisen,
We should practice with swift diligence, To quickly depart from these places of hardship.
"Abiding eternally in the state of tranquility and fearlessness—this is that true city of Nirvāṇa.
At that time, the demoness spoke again in verse:
"You are like Śakra among the gods, with beautiful celestial maidens at your side."
In Yama, Tuṣita, and Nirmāṇarati, as well as in Paranirmita-vaśavartin and the palace of Māra, all sensory delights are fully present without deficiency;
there, one experiences the five desires alone, without entering into nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied in verse:
"The five desires are like frost, not remaining for long; They are also like autumn clouds and rain, lasting but a moment.
Your daughter is as fearsome as an angry serpent; Even Śakra, Yama, Tuṣita, and the rest [cannot withstand her]."
"All are subject to the King of Māras and lack self-mastery; how can one crave sensual pleasures that harbor a hundred enmities?
At that time, the māra-daughters again spoke in verse:
"Virtuous One, do you not see the flowers upon the trees, And the various songs and calls of the bees and birds?"
The earth produces soft, green grass, and various wondrous groves emerge;
the Kinnaras and devas play musical sounds—such a sublime time is fit for enjoying delight.
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied in verse:
"When trees bear flowers and fruit according to the season, Bees and birds, driven by hunger and thirst, take their fragrance;
When the sun's heat reaches its peak, the earth dries of itself— Yet the nectar of the former Buddhas can never be exhausted."
At that time, the demoness spoke again in verse:
"O Benevolent One, your facial complexion is like the new moon; Behold my countenance, which resembles a lotus flower.
Your teeth and gums are white and pure; A woman as wondrous as this is rare even among the gods."
"Moreover, O Benevolent One, you have already attained this in the world; your body and mind are supple and compliant, without mutual conflict.
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied with a verse:
"I observe that your body is a flow of impurity, with millions of pores surrounded by various worms."
All manner of evils, unstable and pervasive, fill my body; birth, old age, sickness, and death constantly follow me.
I seek the most supreme and difficult path in the world: the way of the wise person who truly does not retreat.
Seeing those sixty-four kinds of arts— the movement of her hands, her necklaces, and her earrings—
she was struck by the arrows of desire and said with a smile:
"Noble son, why are you not deluded?"
"O Great Benevolent One, those who perceive the peril of existence see the five sensual desires as beautiful yet like poisonous thorns;
they are like a sharp blade smeared with honey that wounds the tongue when it cuts.
Desire is like the head of a serpent or a pit of fire, and like a man-eating lion whose movement stirs the wind, causing trees, mountains, and cliffs to all collapse."
Now, amidst my majesty and power, free from desire, I have cast you aside just as he did.
Though those demonesses displayed a hundred arts to seduce him, they could not move the Bodhisattva even slightly.
Like an elephant or a lion king, like Mount Sumeru, he remained unmoved.
When they could no longer deceive or mislead him, their hearts were filled with shame and remorse, and each bowed his head low.
With reverence and joy, they praised him, saying:
"He is like the finest clarified butter and the autumn moon; his towering radiance shines like a mountain of gold."
"May that which the mind seeks be fulfilled, so that he may deliver himself and millions of others.

At that time, Māra’s daughters, being unable to delude the Bodhisattva through their powers of illusion, felt shame in their hearts; each was filled with modesty and, bowing together, they prostrated at the Bodhisattva’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew. They returned calmly to the side of Māra Pāpīyān, and upon arrival, they addressed their father thus:
"O Father King!..."
One should not give rise to the intention of creating enmity toward those sentient beings. Why is this?
Because since time immemorial, we have never seen such sentient beings within the desire realm who could display such seductive gestures and charms that would cause us to waver for even a moment.

Furthermore, when we engage in the act of desire, we invariably wither the minds of all people, just as all grasses and trees are surely scorched and destroyed during a drought; it is like placing clarified butter in the sun during springtime, where it naturally melts away.
"For what reason does this man alone act thus?
Therefore, O Father King,
I pray that you do not harbor enmity toward him."
He then addressed his father with these verses:
"His form surpasses the color of the campaka flower; His boundless majesty and fame are preeminent.
Immovable like the king of great mountains, Having completed his prostrations, he has now arrived."
I shall explain the matter in full detail.
He smiled and observed my mind, which remained unshakable; his countenance was pure, his gaze unwinking, free from anger, resentment, or desire.
Even if Mount Sumeru should topple to the ground, If the stars, the moon, and the sun should all fall,
And the great ocean should dry up until its waters are utterly extinguished— One who perceives the affliction of desire will not turn back their mind.
Your speech is subtle and brings joy to others; observe my compassion and freedom from desire, see that I harbor no thoughts of anger, and reflect that my nature is not like that of a fool.
Examine my mental conduct and my physical body, and contemplate with discernment the afflictions of women.
Therefore, the mind does not engage with the five desires.
Free from desire and without craving—who could know this?
It is not something that can be measured by humans or devas.
If that mind possesses desire, the mental faculty is extinguished like dry wood;
yet we observe that our minds are free from desire, dwelling as firmly as a mountain king.
Adorned with the merit of a hundred blessings and endowed with wisdom, they have fulfilled the perfection of generosity and perfected their conduct in the precepts.
Having practiced the Brahma-conduct for ten billion kalpas, You are a pure being of great majestic power;
we prostrate to you, O Golden One. Without doubt, you shall subdue our Māras and surely realize the Bodhi of Perfect Enlightenment.
"We do not wish to form enmity; this battle is difficult to strike and we are difficult to defeat.
To subdue him would likewise be a great hardship. Father King, simply look into the void:
many hosts of Bodhisattvas have arrived from other directions, their bodies adorned with various necklaces and ornaments, paying homage to that Honored One with deep reverence."
Clouds of rain showering down *mandārava* flowers and the like, they offer exquisite verses in praise of him;
the Buddhas of the ten directions all dispatch messengers bearing various kinds of wondrous ambrosial food.
All classes of sentient beings come together, as do insentient mountains and diverse trees.
The deity of Mount Sumeru and Śakra prostrate themselves toward the Forest of Merit.
Therefore, O Father King, this is not the right time; we ought to return to our own abodes.
At that time, the Māra spoke in verse:
"When a person crosses a river to the other shore, If they wish to dig up something, they must cut its roots;
If one forms an enmity, it must be carried through to the end— In all matters one undertakes, there can be no regret."

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān did not accept the exhortations of his eldest son, the merchant leader, nor did he heed the words of admonition from his own daughters; he went in person to the site of the Bodhi tree and approached the Bodhisattva.
Having arrived, he addressed the Bodhisattva with these words:
"O Śākya śramaṇa!

For what purpose have you come here to this place of many poisonous and evil dragons, clouds, rain, and wild beasts—a terrifying and startling location in the dead of night—and why do you sit alone beneath the trees of this forest?"
"O Bhikṣu, do you not fear all those enemies, thieves, and robbers?
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied to Māra Pāpīyas, "Māra Pāpīyas!"

I now seek the tranquil nirvāṇa, the domain traversed by the Buddhas of the past, the supreme state of fearlessness where all existence is exhausted; for the sake of seeking this, I sit alone here beneath a tree in this araṇya.
At that time, Māra immediately addressed the Bodhisattva in verse, saying:
“O Śramaṇa, you dwell alone in the forest hermitage; That which you seek through asceticism is exceedingly difficult.
The aged seers, though endowed with skillful means, Have lost their meditative concentration and have all fallen back.”
"Moreover, you are young and in the prime of your vigor; for what reason do you seek this supreme excellence?
At that time, the Bodhisattva again replied to Māra Pāpīyas in verse:
"The sages of antiquity who practiced austerities, though their diligence and valor were great, were not yet so profound."
The power of his merit and virtue is not strong; my past observance of the precepts was firm and steadfast.
Pāpīyan, if I do not realize the Way, I shall never leave this forest grove.
At that time, Māra spoke again in verse:
"I am the most honored in the realm of desire; Śakra and the World Protectors all depend upon me.
Asuras, kiṃnaras, nāga kings, and others—from the Avīci Hell upward, they have all been my subjects."
"You too are within my realm; arise quickly and remember yourself, then leave this tree.
At that time, the Bodhisattva again replied to Māra Pāpīyas in verse:
"Though you may be autonomous within the realm of desire, you have no mastery over the definitive realm of phenomena."
"You know only of the hells and the hungry ghosts;
yet I am not one of the three realms of existence. Once I have attained the Way, I shall surely shatter your demonic palace and cause you to lose your sovereignty forever."
Then Māra Pāpīyas again spoke to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Son of the Śākyas!

Arise quickly and leave this place; you shall certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), ruling over the four continents as a sovereign of the great earth, endowed with the seven treasures, and even commanding all mountains and rivers."
"Son of the Śākyas!
Do you not remember how the sages of truthful speech spoke thus in the past,
prophesying that you would become a king?"
"You should quickly arise to become a sovereign lord of the world.

If you do so, your majesty will be supreme and peerless according to the Dharma; as you abide in the governance and transformation of others, all the people of every kingdom will come to look up to you with longing, honoring and making offerings to you."
Furthermore, O son of the Śākyas!

Your body is delicate and supple; having been nurtured since childhood within the deep seclusion of the palace, you now stand alone without companion in this desolate forest where there are few people but many fierce and terrifying beasts. I fear for your safety and am constantly filled with anxiety.
"O son of the Śākyas!

Depart from this place at once and return to your own palace. You have already attained what is difficult to obtain: the subtle and exquisite five desires that delight the eyes and satisfy the mind; take heed that you do not reject them."

"Although you now wish to seek that unsurpassed path so difficult to attain, O son of the Śākyas, it remains unknown to you; yet that Bodhi is exceedingly difficult to achieve, and you shall only weary yourself in vain."
Having spoken these words, he remained silent.
Then, the Bodhisattva replied to Māra Pāpīyān, saying: "Māra Pāpīyān!..."
"You need not speak such words now.
Why is this? It is because my mind finds no pleasure in the affairs of the five desires."
Māra Pāpīyān!
I have long since known the various afflictions of the five desires; once one is addicted to them, there is no satisfaction, for they yield pleasure only for a moment and cannot endure for long.

Impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, they are not solid; they are like dew upon the grass, or like a snake’s tongue—fearsome and difficult to touch; they are like a heap of bones, foul and impure; they are like a piece of meat that various beasts greedily covet, contending with one another and killing each other.
They are like ripe fruits upon a tree that will not long remain upon their branches;
they are like dreams, like bubbles, like illusions, and like mirages, devoid of reality.
They are like fire covered by sheep dung, which suddenly burns a person.
Māra Pāpīyān!
I now wish to realize the state of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Pāpīyān!
"You know that I have already renounced the prosperous and joyful regions of the four continents as well as the seven treasures.
Furthermore, Māra Pāpīyān!
It is like a person who, having eaten a delicious meal, vomits it back up; for that person to wish to eat it again—such a thing is impossible."
"It is so, it is so; I have now renounced the aforementioned rewards, which is a difficult matter. Just as that man who has vomited will not eat again, how could I return to the palace?"
Māra Pāpīyān!
It will not be long before I definitively attain bodhi; I shall become a Buddha and bring an end to the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death. Pāpīyān!
"Return to the place from which you came; do not remain here. You speak much at random, uttering words that are without benefit—the speech of a foolish person.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān again thought to himself:
"This man cannot be deceived by the matters of the five desires; I shall not be able to win him over."
"I shall now employ another expedient, using pleasant words to console his mind and send him away.
Having thought thus, Māra Pāpīyān addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Śramaṇa, scion of the Ikṣvāku clan, rise quickly, rise quickly!"
"Since your childhood, you have never seen combat; the weapons of war are truly terrifying.
O Benevolent One!
Simply carry out your own royal law; this matter of opposing an enemy's army is not something you can endure."

Furthermore, O Benevolent One, do not form enmity with others; for if one harbors resentment and aversion, the mind and consciousness will remain turbid and defiled by long-lasting anger, desire, ignorance, and greed, making it impossible to attain liberation from the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"O Benevolent One, quickly turn back this unwholesome mind and this body of wrong views!
O Śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas!

Return home and hold an unrestricted assembly; rule the world according to the royal law, govern the realm, and receive the station of a Golden Wheel-turning King. Do not remain attached to these things, for they are the wounds of battle."

"Your Majesty has returned to your palace as a son of great majesty and merit. This royal path is delightful and upright, praised by all kings of the past; the realm is vast, governing the four quarters of the world, with everything in abundance and no lack in any matter."
Since you were born within the deep palace of a great king, it is not fitting for you to become a mendicant by shaving your hair today.
Why do you assume the form of a śramaṇa and live a life of poverty?
O Śākya son of royal lineage!
It was out of compassion for you that I spoke these words; I did not intend to force you to rise and depart from here, but merely could not bear the thought of you committing evil.
And he spoke in verse:
“O Kṣatriya, the Lord of Death is fearsome; you should abandon this quest for liberation and return to your palace.
Establishing justice with bow and arrow, govern the world; enjoy happiness now and be reborn in heaven hereafter.”
This path is known as that which pervades all; it is one traversed by all kings of antiquity.
Since you have now been born into a royal lineage, it is not fitting for you, O Benevolent One, to live your life as a mendicant śramaṇa.
When Māra Pāpīyas had spoken thus, the Bodhisattva gazed at him intently and remained firm, refusing to comply; neither did he move his body nor shift from his seat, but thought to himself:
"Alas, Pāpīyas!..."
"You seek your own self-interest; you do not act for my sake.
Having thought thus, he spoke to Pāpīyān:
"O Māra, King Pāpīyān!"
I am now seated upon the adamantine firmness, bound in the full lotus posture, which is exceedingly difficult to destroy, for the purpose of realizing that nectar-like Dharma.
O Māra Pāpīyān!
"Whatever you wish to do, do it according to your will; whatever you are able to accomplish, accomplish it according to your will.
Then, Māra Pāpīyān, provoked to anger and filled with resentment, spoke to the Bodhisattva:
"O Śākya bhikṣu!"
"Why do you now sit alone here beneath this tree in the forest hermitage?
Māra uttered such a hollow roar as this: "What do you think? Am I sitting at ease?"
Some may say it is like sitting within a city, saying to oneself that one is securely defended by the surrounding four walls.
But now, O Bhikṣu!

Do you not see the fourfold army I have led forth—elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry; various miscellaneous troops with banners, flags, standards, and streamers, and canopies and ensigns? There are many yakṣas who all eat human flesh, who are skilled in divine archery, each grasping strong bows and wielding sharp arrows, spears, lances, hooks, halberds, swords, clubs, vajra-wheels, axes, battle-axes, and all manner of weapons. They ride upon thousands of millions of elephants, horses, and chariots, letting out a great roar that fills the void of space.
Beyond that, there were further immeasurable dragons, each riding upon a great mass of black clouds, emitting flashes of lightning and hail that fell down in a swirling, chaotic mist.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas drew a sharp sword from his waist; grasping it with swift hands, he rushed toward the Bodhisattva, shouting these words:
"O Śākya Bhikṣu!..."
"This sword of mine shall now sever your body, just as a strong man cuts a bundle of bamboo.
He then spoke in verse:
"This precious sword of mine is most firm and sharp; Behold it well, for it is now in my hand."
"O śramaṇa, if you do not flee in haste, I shall cut your body as if it were a bundle of bamboo.
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied to Māra, saying:
"Even if Māras filled this entire earth, each holding a blade as vast as Mount Sumeru, [I would remain unmoved]."
They cannot move even a single hair of mine, much less cut through my body.
O Māra, if you possess great power, and if you wish to obstruct me as I now seek to realize Bodhi, do not listen [to my plea];
act quickly and do not linger, following your own will!
At that time, having spoken these verses, the Bodhisattva further addressed the Māra, saying: "O Māra Pāpīyān!

Even if there were thousands of millions of sentient beings, all exactly like you in body, who came here with all their might to create obstacles for me, wishing to hinder my enlightenment so that I might not realize the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I would never rise from this place to sit beneath another tree."
Then Māra Pāpīyas said to the Bodhisattva:
"O Bhikṣu of the Śākya clan!

Formerly, while you were at the place of the village of Uruvilvā by the banks of the Nairañjanā River, you gave rise to a mind of diligence and practiced austerities for six years, not sparing even your own body or life; yet you still did not realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor did you attain the supreme liberation."
"How much less so now, when you abandon that intent for diligence, fall away from meditative concentration, and give rise to a mind of indolence—how can you hope to attain it?
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied to Māra Pāpīyān, saying: "Māra Pāpīyān!..."
Because I first gave rise to the mind of diligence in the past, I sat in that forest hermitage (*āraṇya*) to subdue my own mind; thus, I have now achieved courageous diligence.
Furthermore, during my six years of ascetic practice in the past, I quickly became weary and exhausted, but today it is not so.
"You, Māra Pāpīyān!
To offer such counsel to me now is not out of compassion;
if you were truly compassionate, would you speak in such a manner?"
Since you have already given rise to such a mind, I shall now certainly attain liberation for myself, and I shall also cause others to attain liberation.
O Māra Pāpīyān!
"I shall certainly realize that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; I shall certainly attain that subtle and wondrous liberation.
When Māra Pāpīyas heard these words of the Bodhisattva, his heart was filled with great sorrow and distress. He abandoned all his diligent efforts and thought to himself once more:
"I cannot cause him to rise from beneath this tree of enlightenment by means of pleasant words and gentle speech."

Since his vow is so grave that it cannot be moved by pleasant words, you should now strictly constrain him with threats, rebukes, and combat, and by inflicting cuts and wounds, cause his heart to be startled so that he will rise in haste and flee.
When Māra Pāpīyān had thought thus, he spoke to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Śākya bhikṣu!

Since I have spoken these words of truth to you, if you do not accept such good counsel from me and do not quickly arise and depart for another region, you must surely be deluded; today you will certainly encounter misfortune."
Then the Bodhisattva spoke to Māra Pāpīyan, saying: "Māra Pāpīyan!
Even when I was formerly in my mother’s womb, you were still unable to create any obstacles for me; how much less so today!"
Māra Pāpīyān!
Return quickly to the place from which you came.
Since time immemorial, we have not feared you, and now we remain fearless.
At that time, the Bodhisattva addressed Māra Pāpīyān, speaking in verse:
"Though swords and staves rain down upon my body from the void, And my limbs be severed inch by inch and joint by joint,
If I do not cross over the sea of birth and death, This Bodhi tree shall never be moved."
Then Māra Pāpīyān said to the Bodhisattva:
"O Śākya Bhikṣu! If it is as you say, it is because you have not yet seen the hosts of my army."
Why is this? My demonic armies wear firm and sturdy armor upon their bodies and hold various weapons and implements in their hands, raining them down upon your person.
At that time, O Bhikṣu of the Śākya clan!
You should quickly rise from beneath this tree yourself, come to where I am, and surely utter these words:
"O Māra King, you should take refuge in me."
"O bhikṣu! You have not yet awakened to, nor do you yet know, the supernormal powers I have exercised; therefore, you sit upon that lion throne and utter the lion's roar.
O bhikṣu of the Śākya clan!"
"Rise at once! Why must you today vainly utter empty words and roar the lion's roar yourself?
He then spoke in verse:
"I have an army of soldiers, elephants, and the like, And divine generals skilled in the art of battle."
Clad in armor and grasping weapons in hand, you may flee for your life now;
it will be most difficult to seek my protection later, for though I wish to save you, I cannot.
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to Pāpīyan: "O Māra Pāpīyan!
The waters of the four great oceans and this great earth may be moved elsewhere; [but you cannot move my resolve]."
The sun, moon, and constellations may fall from the sky to the earth;
the great Mount Sumeru may be split into a hundred pieces;
and both the great earth and Mount Sumeru may be lifted up into the heavens.
One might even overturn the great earth and Mount Sumeru;
one might dam the waters of the Ganges with dry soil and prevent their flow.
Yet this mind of mine cannot be restrained, nor can it be shifted or moved away from this place.
For what reason?
O Māra Pāpīyān!
Just as when I was practicing my former conduct, and by means of the various powers such as my own physical strength, meditative concentration, and moral discipline—just so it is, Pāpīyān!

Whether among devas or nāgas, there is none who surpasses me and none who excels me; through my practice of the bodhisattva path over hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, I have attained full accomplishment.
Then the Bodhisattva addressed Māra Pāpīyas with these verses:
“The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens are my host; The power of wisdom is my arrow, and skillful means my bow.
It will not be difficult for me now to subdue you, Just as a rutting elephant tramples dry bamboo.”
Then, having heard these words from the Bodhisattva, Māra Pāpīyān’s anger intensified; his rage filled his entire being as he cried out to the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and others:
“O Mahāsena, Saṃmardaka, and Lohitākṣa!”
"Come quickly!

Take up mountain rocks, trees, bows and arrows, swords, vajras, clubs, mallets, spears, halberds, pikes, axes, and various other weapons, and rain them down upon the head of this Kṣatriya son of the Śākyas, so that they all fall like a shower of hail."

At that time, having heard these words of Māra Pāpīyān, the yakṣas such as Mahāsena and the others immediately arrayed their fourfold army; all donned their armor, took up their weapons, and came forth with great speed.

There were immeasurable thousands of myriads of yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others, with various forms, various appearances, various colors, and various implements; they manifested terrifying transformations, with their bodies and heads inverted, uttering various cries and emitting loathsome sounds and odors.

Some have the faces of elephants, some the heads of horses, or the heads of camels, oxen, and water buffaloes; some are like donkeys or dogs, or like sheep, pigs, and wolves; others resemble lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, bears, brown bears, rhinoceroses, and wild oxen; or like water otters, gayals, monkeys, foxes, jackals, cats, rabbits, and deer—having such forms as these, as well as the faces of various birds.

Furthermore, there were those with heads like makaras, turtles, and fish; some with snake heads and various insect bodies; elephant heads with horse bodies, horse heads with elephant bodies, camel heads with ox bodies, and ox heads with camel bodies; some with buffalo heads and donkey or mule bodies, or again, donkey heads with buffalo bodies; and dog heads with pig bodies, or pig heads with dog bodies.
Some had the heads of black sheep with the bodies of jackals and wolves; some had the heads of jackals and wolves with the bodies of black sheep;
some had the heads of lions with the bodies of tigers and leopards; some had the heads of tigers and leopards with the bodies of lions;
some had the heads of wildcats with the bodies of bears and *pī*; some had the heads of bears and *pī* with the bodies of wildcats; and some had the heads of rhinoceroses with the bodies of otters.
...bodies with the heads of otters or rhinoceroses; bodies with the heads of gayals or monkeys;
bodies with the heads of monkeys or gayals; bodies with the heads of apes or jackals; bodies with the heads of jackals or monkeys;
bodies with the heads of cats and the bodies of birds; bodies with the heads of birds and the bodies of cats; or [bodies] of the *mā*...
There are those with the bodies of *makara*, turtles, and tortoises, yet with the heads of turtles and tortoises and the bodies of *makara*;
those with fish heads and snake bodies, or snake heads and fish bodies; those with animal heads and human bodies, or human heads and animal bodies.
"Or again, some were headless with only empty bodies; some had half-faces, or half-bodies; or some had two heads on a single body."
Furthermore, there were some with a single body and three heads, or a single body and many heads.

Some had heads but no faces; some had faces but no heads; some had half-heads but no faces; some had half-faces but no heads; some had two heads but no faces; some had three heads but no faces; and some had many heads but were entirely without faces.
"Some have no eyes at all, or have only one eye, two eyes, three eyes, or even many eyes.
Or again, they have no ears, or have one ear, two ears, three ears, or even many ears."
Some were without hands, some without arms, some with one hand, two hands, or three hands, even up to many hands.
Some were without feet, some with only one foot, two feet, or three feet, even up to many feet, as well as those who were footless.
