"Some have their heads inverted, or else their heads are pulled upward; some have their heads facing downward and their feet facing upward, with hands and feet inverted, having been cut to pieces and hung up."
Some have inverted eyes, some have protruding eyes, blue-black and terrifying; some have red eyes, some have eyes that emit light, or eyes that dart and roll.

Some have drooping ears, or ears like those of a goat, or ears like those of a donkey; some have ears like trees, or ears like those of a monkey, or ears like those of a fish; or they may have many kinds of ears while still possessing human bodies.
Some have swollen noses and coarse, ugly bodies; some have hanging mouths, or hanging tongues; some have thick and large tongues, or tongues that emit light.
Some have teeth that are exceedingly long and large while their bodies are short; some have teeth that protrude unevenly; some have teeth like swords, or tongues shaped like swords.

Some had their bellies hanging down, or were without bellies; some had disheveled hair, or were without knees; some had knees like jars, or were without thighs; their feet were shaped like overturned bowls, or like pestles and mortars.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds,
Volume Twenty-Eight and Volume Twenty-Nine,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
The Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Fear of Māra, Part Two:

"At that time, the hosts of Māra, assuming such various forms—some riding white elephants, others mounted on horses, or riding camels, water buffaloes, rhinoceroses, and various chariots—gathered like clouds from the four directions."

Some resemble asuras such as the kinnaras; others are like mahoragas, as well as kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas, yakṣas, piśācas, and the Kālamukha spirits; or again, their bodies are emaciated and tall, resembling those of hungry ghosts.

Some have various strange forms and appearances; some have countenances of immense majesty; some have heads like ropes, or very large heads; some have small faces, or wrinkled faces; some have deformed shapes that cause those who see them to lose their own dignified luster.

Some were seen snatching away the souls, spirits, and consciousness of others; some had faces that were blue, while others had bodies the color of red copper. Some had red heads and blue bodies, or yellow heads and smoke-colored bodies; some had heads like smoke and yellow bodies, or red heads and black bodies, black heads and red bodies, white heads and green bodies, or green heads and white bodies.

Some have the left side of their heads white while the right side is green; some have the right side white while the left side is green; or again, the same occurs throughout the body and face on both sides.

"Or again, some have their entire bodies manifesting only skeletons; or heads that are skulls while the bodies are plump with flesh; or faces and heads covered in flesh while the bodies expose bare bones;
or human hands and feet on the bodies of animals; or animal legs on human bodies."

Some have body hairs that are all like needles piercing the skin; some have body hairs resembling the bristles of a boar; some have body hairs similar to the mane of a donkey; some have hair like that of a bear, a monkey, or a weasel; and some have body hairs that emit flames of light.
Some have disheveled hair, some have hair growing upward, some have topknots, and some are bald with no hair.
Some wear red garments, and their waistbands are of various colors.
Or again, they wear garlands of skulls upon their heads;
some have hair on a single head that is mixed with shades of gray, blue, yellow, red, white, and smoke-colored, using these skulls as crowns—such figures gathered like clouds and came forth.

Some held in their hands a *khāṭvāṅga*—the Sui translation of which is "one-fourth of a bed"—consisting of a single leg of a bed together with its frame; others wore waistbands from which hung various bells that made a loud noise as they moved, while in their hands they carried human skulls.

Some wear human skeletons as flower garlands; some hold the hands and feet of the dead; others hold bells, shaking their hands to make them ring. Some have bodies as tall as a *tāla* tree, holding in their hands spears, swords, knives, arrows, lances, bows, or crossbows; some hold halberds, tridents, clubs, or wheels; others carry long blades, sharp axes, iron pestles, or iron mallets and white staves, lifting stones as large as mountains, with fierce flames erupting from their heads.

Some wore garments made of various skins—blue, yellow, red, white, or black; some were naked with snakes coiled around their bodies; and from their eyes, ears, and noses issued forth various snakes, which were black in color. They seized them with their hands and, before the Bodhisattva, devoured them with their mouths.
Some ate human flesh, while others drank blood.

Some emitted thick, smoky fumes from their bodies and torches from their mouths; some had all manner of fire issue from their pores, while others had fire burst forth from their palates and scatter across the ground.
"Or great black clouds emerge from the void; or within the void, whirling winds scatter rain, flashing lightning appears, and the sound of thunder resounds."
Hail fell from the sky, raining down various mountain rocks or fragments of stone, while thunderbolts struck great trees.
Some had their bodies severed limb by limb;
others drew their bows or clapped their hands, shouting and hollering in an attempt to incite terror.
Some raised a great cry, shouting aloud:
"Arise quickly and flee!
Do not remain in this place!"
Or again, he may manifest as the body of an old woman, raising both hands and wailing aloud:
"Alas, my son! Alas, my brother!"
Some laughed loudly, while others were filled with panic and ran hurriedly toward the east, west, south, or north.
Some fled backward and then turned to come forward again; some suddenly rose up, while others suddenly flew through the air, sporting with ease and mastery.

Some even climbed trees and walked while suspended from them; others danced with swords, leaped about, or sported with spears, long blades, tridents, axes, battle-axes, halberds, and the like, their hands and feet never ceasing their movements.
Some were like bull-kings bellowing in the height of summer; others made sounds like those of the śiśumāra beast.

Furthermore, in the air, they produced such sounds as *ha-ha*, *ṭa-ṭa*, *hu-hu*, *si-si* (pronounced with the *qi* rhyme), *ṇṛ-ṇṛ* (pronounced with the *ju* and *qi* rhymes), and *ṛ-ṛ*; they whistled with their mouths while simultaneously playing with their garments.
Thus, these hosts of yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, and others—immeasurable, boundless, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions—crowded and choked the area before the Bodhi tree.
Extending southward to the sea, the demonic armies filled it entirely, leaving not even a space as small as the eye of a needle between them.
Their transformed appearances were terrifying; they sought to seize the Bodhisattva and sought to kill the Bodhisattva.
They waited only for a single command from the Māra Pāpīyān, and they all turned their faces directly toward him to look upon him.
All such spirits and deities as these pressed around the Bodhi tree, tormented by hunger, thirst, and exhaustion, their minds intent solely on slaying the Bodhisattva.
"On the three sides of that Bodhi tree—the east, west, and north—countless devas from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens were stationed, filling the space.
Furthermore, countless devas from the Rūpadhātu joined their ten fingers in palms-together salutation and prostrated to the Bodhisattva, speaking thus:
'O worthy ones, look!'"
"Now you should realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Or some devas proclaimed thus:
"O Great Kṣatriya clan!"
“O seed of sugarcane!
Depart quickly from this place; this place is terrifying, for there are various such weapons here that will harm your body.
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied to them, saying:
"I shall soon surely shatter those factions and cause them all to disperse, just as the wind blows away the fine flowers upon a cotton cloth.

When all those hosts of devils and spirits had thus assembled, it was exactly midnight; the void was devoid of light, and although there were both the moon and the many stars, their radiance did not appear at all. It was a profound and great darkness such that even one with eyes could see nothing, perceiving only the rising of a great fire and the sound of a swift, fierce wind, which was most terrifying. The earth shook violently, and the four oceans all boiled over.
And he spoke these verses:
“The four great oceans boil and the earth quakes; Flames erupt from the ten directions and an evil sound is heard.
The stars and moon in the void are obscured and lack luster; In the pitch-black darkness of midnight, nothing can be seen.”

"At that time, within that assembly, there was a dragon king named Dharaṇīdhara. In his inner heart, he desired the Bodhisattva’s victory and conceived a mind of resentment toward Māra. Because of this malicious intent, he glared at Māra Pāpīyān with both eyes and exhaled a foul vapor from his mouth that struck the body of the Māra king, causing him to writhe in constant distress."

At that time, the devas of the Pure Abodes in the higher realms, desiring the Bodhisattva’s victory, conceived a heart of compassion toward Māra; because they were free from outflows, they harbored no further anger.

At that time, all the devas present there who had faith and reverence for the Bodhisattva, seeing this host of Māras filling the ground and disturbing the Bodhisattva at the Bodhi tree, all rose into the air and cried out with one voice:
"Alas! Alas!"
And there is a verse that says:

"Under the Bodhi tree, the assembly of devas gathered; Seeing the hosts of Māra wishing to harm the Bodhisattva, Because they believed in the Dharma and its liberation for the world, They cried out with a great voice, 'Alas!'"
At that time, the Bodhisattva contemplated only the Dharma; his mind was undisturbed, and he harbored no other thoughts or intentions.
Then the Bodhisattva spoke to Māra Pāpīyas, saying:
"Son of Heaven of the Desire Realm!
Since I am of the Kṣatriya caste, my lineage has never uttered falsehood; there is only the vow of truth.
What must you do? Do it quickly; do not delay.
Then Māra Pāpīyas said to the Bodhisattva:
"As you have spoken, I now wish to shatter your body into a hundred pieces."
"Are you here before me, wishing to fight with me?
Or have you placed me before you so that I might harm you?
Then the Bodhisattva spoke to Māra Pāpīyas:
"I have no bows, arrows, swords, or staves with which to strike or shoot you; although this is so, I shall first subdue you right now, and only after that will I become a Buddha."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān immediately commanded his own host, saying:
"Each of you must exert your full physical strength with valor; do not remain in fear, but manifest great upheavals and terrifying sights before this son of the Śākya clan."
Then the hosts of Māra, having received the command, said to the Māra King:
"As the Great Deva commands, we shall not disobey.
Thereupon, each manifested their own power, displaying terrifying forms in order to frighten the Bodhisattva.

Among these hosts of Māras, there were some spirits who protruded long tongues from their mouths and moved their jaws back and forth; their teeth were extremely sharp as they sought to bite the Bodhisattva.
Their eyes were round and bulging like those of a lion, and their ears were curled like iron hooks; their appearance as they sought to harm the Bodhisattva was most terrifying.
They approached the Bodhisattva, manifesting such terror; some stood with mouths agape, gazing upward and straight ahead as if wishing to swallow the Bodhisattva.
There was a verse that said:
"The hosts of Māra thus approach in a fearsome manner, Yet that Sage stands tall and unshaken."
"Just as one of great wisdom views the play of small children, so too does the Bodhisattva regard Māra.

At that time, another ghost within that assembly gave rise to a heart of malice and hatred; he took a long sword and hurled it at the Bodhisattva, but the sword stuck to his hand and would not come loose.
Some lifted mountains and large boulders and hurled them at the Bodhisattva; yet those mountains and stones remained stuck to their hands and did not fall to the ground.
Others, remaining in mid-air, hurled mountains, stones, trees, mallets, axes, halberds, spears, and lances at the Bodhisattva; these likewise stayed suspended in the air without descending.
Some, as they came down, spontaneously shattered into hundreds of pieces and scattered to other places.

Or, as if in the sky like the sun-god, he rains down a great rain of fire from blazing clouds; yet by the power of the Bodhisattva, that rain of fire is immediately transformed into a rain of red *kumuda* flowers that falls down.
Furthermore, some may come before the Bodhisattva and spit forth various snakes to bite him; yet those snakes, upon reaching the ground, will stand motionless as if bound by a spell, unable to stir.

"Or they may manifest as great clouds, emitting lightning and thundering with great peals of thunder, raining down hailstones and stones upon the Bodhi tree; yet by the power of the Bodhisattva, those rains, upon reaching the ground, transform into various showers of flowers."
Some took up bows and arrows to shoot at the Bodhisattva, yet all those arrows returned to their bowstrings and did not fall.
Others simultaneously released five hundred arrows, and those arrows likewise remained suspended in the air and did not descend.
Some, grasping long swords and raising them toward the Bodhisattva, rushed forward; yet before they could reach him, they themselves fell prostrate, face down upon the ground.

At that time, there was a rākṣasī whose body was pitch black and who held a skull in her hand; wishing to come and delude the Bodhisattva by stirring his mind, she ran swiftly toward him, intending to draw near. However, from the place where she set out, she moved in ever-widening circles and could not advance to reach the Bodhisattva’s side.

"Or there were those whose two eyes emitted great, blazing, and fierce flames of fire, wishing to burn the Bodhisattva; they ran swiftly toward him until they reached his side, yet suddenly the Bodhisattva’s body was no longer to be seen."

Furthermore, there were some spirits who took up massive boulders and rushed toward the Bodhisattva; however, they were unable to reach the foot of the Bodhi tree as they fled from the direction from which they had come, becoming utterly exhausted and distressed.
And there is a verse that says:
“The hosts of Māra, their bodies and minds utterly confused and deluded, Employed various skillful means wishing to harm the Sage;
Yet they could not shake him from his seated place, Because his power of wisdom and the strength of his vows were firm.”

"Furthermore, some may let out the roar of a lion, or produce the sounds of tigers, wolves, bears, brown bears, jackals, leopards, and various other wild beasts; and if any hear those sounds, immeasurable sentient beings will all be struck with terror."
Some ghosts made this sound:
"Slay, slay this son of the Śākyas!
Other ghosts made this sound:
"Seize him! Seize this son of a kṣatriya!
Or some ghosts made such sounds as: "Strike him dead!
Strike this son of a śramaṇa to death!"
Some ghosts uttered these words:
"Harm him! Harm this descendant of Gautama!
Other ghosts uttered these words:
"Cut, cut this Ikṣvāku lineage!
Or some spirits made such a sound:
"Grind, grind this Kṣatriya lineage!"
Some ghosts made this sound:
"Shatter, shatter this son of the Śākyas!
Other ghosts made this sound:
"Destroy, destroy this son of a kṣatriya!
Some ghosts made such a sound as:
"Quickly extinguish, quickly extinguish this son of a śramaṇa!"
Some ghosts made this sound:
"Joint by joint, dismember this son of the Gautamas!
Other ghosts made this sound:
"Act as you please, act as you please; do whatever is convenient.
Or there were some ghosts who made such a sound:
"Do as you wish, do as you wish; act quickly and do not linger."
Thus, such clamor and commotion cannot be endured; when these sounds are heard, even the void might fall to the ground, and the entire great earth might shatter into pieces.

When these sounds are heard, all wild beasts let out great cries and scatter in all directions; and as for all the birds, at the moment they hear this roar, they all throw themselves from their trees down to the ground.

At that time, among all those hosts of Māras and ghosts, some made sounds of mocking laughter; others made the sound "ri-li" (𭈢梨); some whistled; some cried "chua-chua" (斫斫); some cried "duan-duan" (斷斷); some cried "sha-sha" (殺殺); some cried "ge-ge" (割割); some cried "po-po" (破破); some cried "jie-jie" (節節); and some cried "jie-jie" (解解). Such evil sounds were beyond counting.
Then Māra Pāpīyān immediately drew his sharp sword, grasped it in his hand, and rushed forward, intending to intimidate the Bodhisattva; he advanced with swift strides, shouting aloud:
"You, Śākya bhikṣu!"
"If you dare not rise from this seat once I am seated here, I shall surely harm you!
Yet that Māra King, though he moved back and forth from east to west, wishing to approach the Bodhisattva, was unable to come forward.
At that time, the elder son of the Māra King, Śreṣṭhin, immediately took hold of the Māra King with both hands and spoke these words:
"O Father King, O Father King!"
"Do not wish it! Do not wish it!
Your father, the King, will certainly be unable to kill the Śākya son Siddhārtha, nor will he be able to move this seat; moreover, he will incur immeasurable and boundless transgressions."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān did not accept the admonition of his son Sārthavāha; he rushed toward the Bodhisattva and refused to turn back.

Then, a certain devaputra from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, remaining invisible in mid-air, saw Māra Pāpīyān running with a distracted mind to harass the Bodhisattva. With a concentrated mind, the deva produced a sublime voice and said to Pāpīyān:
"O you, Māra Pāpīyān!..."
Do not set limits for yourself; you must not now disturb this noble one.
Quickly abandon these delusive and evil thoughts and return to your own realm; you shall never be able to shake this noble one.
"Why is this? It is because he is like Mount Sumeru, which cannot be moved by a violent wind.
Then, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven spoke a verse to Māra Pāpīyān:
"May fire lose its nature of heat, may water lose its moisture and cease to flow,
may earth lose its solidity and fail to support, and may wind lose its blowing motion and become utterly still;
yet throughout immeasurable kalpas of practicing meritorious deeds, I shall never abandon this heart of vow."
Seeing sentient beings in this world afflicted by suffering and distress, burdened by the heavy illnesses of stinginess, greed, desire, and ignorance, he gives rise to compassion and pity for them;
thus, wishing to manifest as a holy physician with the medicine of wisdom.
Why do you now create such difficulty?
He now wishes to open the eye of right view; he is the Great Sage, the King of Liberation, and the guide for merchants who have lost their way.
This desire is to kindle the lamp of wisdom; this noble one desires to enter the city of Nirvāṇa, grasping a torch to shatter the darkness of the world.
With the flower-leaves of faith and the trunk of intention firmly rooted, the tree of wisdom can provide the sustenance of the fruit of Dharma.
You should not now uproot and cause him to fall.
Furthermore, you are currently bound by the ropes of delusion; since he desires to untie your fetters, how could you possibly give rise to an evil mind toward him?
He seeks liberation and desires to teach others; your creating obstacles is but a wearying exertion in vain.
Sentient beings are submerged in the great ocean of afflictions—who in this world understands how to act as their helmsman?
He wishes to establish a great bridge; why do you now give rise to such evil?
Having cultivated various paths of practice throughout past kalpas, the time has now come for their fruits to ripen.
Therefore, he sits cross-legged beneath this tree, just like all the sages of antiquity.

At that time, having heard these words from the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, Māra Pāpīyān gave rise to overweening pride and his heart of malice redoubled; he then hurried back toward the Bodhisattva’s location, desiring to harm him.
"At that time, there were eight devas guarding the Bodhi tree at that place:
first, Guṇa; second, Vardhana; third, Abhaya; fourth, Karmavicitra; fifth, Tejas; sixth, Mahābala; seventh, Satyavādī; and eighth, Suvinīta."
Those eight deities gazed up at the Bodhisattva, their eyes never blinking, and simultaneously praised him with sixteen kinds of marks, speaking these words:
"O Benevolent One, you are now the most supreme and pure among sentient beings; your radiance shines forth like the sun and moon in the sky."
“‘O Benevolent One, you are now an exceptionally eminent and pure being, resplendent and blazing like the sun-god first rising in the sky.
‘O Benevolent One, you are now a bright, pure, and stainless being, with all your marks fully blossomed, like a red lotus blooming within a green pond.’”
“O Benevolent One, you now dwell fearlessly among pure sentient beings with sovereign power and vigor, like a lion king within a great forest.
O Benevolent One, you now abide in tranquility among pure sentient beings, unmoving and unshaken, like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, rising out from the midst of the ocean.”
“Virtuous One, you are now pure and all-encompassing, manifest and standing firm like the Great Iron Ring Mountains, solid and immovable.
Virtuous One, you are now profound, grave, and discerning, endowed with the manifold virtues of sentient beings, like the great ocean filled with all manner of treasures.”
“‘Your magnanimity and breadth of mind are now vast and increasing day by day, like space which has no boundaries.
‘Your present sincerity and lack of crookedness, with a mind fixed in right concentration, are like the great earth that nurtures all living beings.’”
“Virtuous One, your mind is now fully endowed with freedom from defilement and turbidity, just as the pure waters of Lake Anavatapta possess the eight meritorious qualities.
Virtuous One, you have now severed all fetters and your mind is unstained, just as a great wind is not attached to anything in the world.”
“‘O Benevolent One, your majesty is now so sublime that it is difficult to behold your face; you are like a fierce, blazing fire, far removed from all the heat of afflictions.
‘O Benevolent One, you are now a courageous and steadfast being among sentient beings, possessing great power like that of Nārāyaṇa, whom no one can subdue.’”
“‘O Benevolent One, your diligence has been cultivated through kalpas, and your mind is difficult to turn back, like the vajra released by Śakra.

“‘O Benevolent One, you have now attained the foremost and most excellent benefit; as the preeminent leader among all sentient beings, you are endowed with the ten powers and shall before long realize unexcelled bodhi.’”
"At that time, the various divine kings who guarded that Bodhi tree praised the Bodhisattva with sixteen kinds of marks; the verses were as follows, though one praise was originally missing."
"At that time, the devas of the Pure Abodes in the Form Realm again collectively used sixteen kinds of signs to revile and humiliate King Māra, crushing his power."
"What are these sixteen?
'Pāpīyān! You now possess no majesty or power; you are like a weakling who, having been subdued by a strong man, falsely claims, "I am the victor. "
“Pāpīyān! You now stand alone, solitary and without companion, like a person cast out into the wilderness. Pāpīyān!”
"All you hosts of troops now have your various powers shattered and broken, like an old, emaciated ox burdened by a heavy load. 'Pāpīyan!
You are now foolish, blind, foul, and impure, like an arrow shot at night falling upon impure ground.'"
“Pāpīyan! You now wander aimlessly here and there like a lame and blind donkey, fallen onto a perilous and evil path like a lost merchant. Pāpīyan!”
"Your retinue is now scattered and your body lacks its luster, like a destitute beggar burdened with straw.
'Pāpīyan! Your majesty and virtue have truly declined; having nowhere to rely upon, you force yourself to act with such craftiness, like a fool devoid of shame.'"
“Pāpīyan! The karma you have now created is impure and heavily defiled, like that of a person devoid of gratitude, righteousness, filial piety, and virtue. Pāpīyan!”
"You are now being driven away by others, just as a jackal pursued by a lion finds no freedom. 'Pāpīyān!
All your armies will soon retreat and scatter, like birds blown away by a fierce wind.'"
“‘Pāpīyan, you are now deluded and obscured by darkness; you do not know the proper time, like a dead man arriving at the home of a lonely, poor child. “‘Pāpīyan!
Your followers have now been defeated and scattered, like medicinal powder leaking out from a porous vessel with holes.
"Pāpīyan! Before long you shall be restrained and punished, just as one who understands the principle pursues a foolish man."

“Pāpīyān! This very moment, all the strength of your body shall be severed, just as a criminal has his hands and feet cut off and placed in different locations, thus lacking two of his original limbs.”
"Then all the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, having thus reviled Māra Pāpīyas with these sixteen kinds of signs, destroyed his power."
At that time, the eight deities who protect the Bodhi tree again collectively reviled Pāpīyān with sixteen characteristics.
What are these sixteen? "O Pāpīyān!..."
1. "Before long, you shall be subdued by the Bodhisattva, just as a valiant warrior is slain by an enemy. 2. 'Pāpīyān!
You have now been struck down by the Bodhisattva, just as a timid, weak, and emaciated man is beaten by a great athlete.'"
“Pāpīyān! You are now overwhelmed and eclipsed by the light of the Bodhisattva, just as the rising sun obscures the light of a tiny firefly. 3.
“Pāpīyān! You have now been naturally driven away by the majesty of the Bodhisattva, just as a handful of crushed barley flour is scattered in all directions by a great wind.”
“Pāpīyan! You are now terrified by the Bodhisattva and flee with stumbling feet, like a small beast pursued by a lion.
“Pāpīyan! [he said].
6. "Pāpīyan! You are now uprooted by the Bodhisattva, like a śāla tree blown down to the ground with its roots by a fierce wind. 7. 'Pāpīyan!
You are now destroyed by the Bodhisattva, like the city of an enemy thief crushed and annihilated by a king of great power.'"
“Pāpīyan! You are now exhausted by the Bodhisattva, like the water in a cow’s footprint dried up by a scorching sun.
“Pāpīyan! [he said.]
"Now you have been repulsed by the Bodhisattva; bowing your head, you flee straight away like a criminal who has suddenly escaped after being on the verge of execution by another.
9. "O Pāpīyān!..."
10. "Pāpīyan! You are now being harassed by the Bodhisattva, like a flock of birds in a wild marsh that is suddenly terrified by a great conflagration. 11. 'Pāpīyan!
Your mind is now subdued by the Bodhisattva, and you harbor inner grief, like a king of a subordinate generation who has suddenly lost his power due to failing in the practice of the Dharma.'"
“Pāpīyan! Before long you shall be stripped bare by the Bodhisattva, just like an old, sick swan or crane without wings.
“Pāpīyan! [he continued].
13. "Pāpīyan! Before long you shall be diminished by the Bodhisattva, like a person traveling through a wilderness without provisions.
14. 'Pāpīyan! Before long you shall be plundered by the Bodhisattva, like a man whose ship is lost and sinks in the great ocean.'"
“Pāpīyan! You are now being scorched by the Bodhisattva, just as all the dense forests and trees are consumed by fire at the end of an eon.
“Pāpīyan! [he said].
"You shall soon be toppled by a Bodhisattva, just as a diamond shatters a mountain of stone.
Thus did these celestial deities rebuke the Māra Pāpīyas in sixteen ways.

When Māra Pāpīyān heard the various devas thus reviling him and offering such exhortations, he rushed toward the Bodhisattva, desiring to kill him; having failed in his exhortations and being reviled by the devas, his mind remained unrelenting, and instead of returning to his own palace, he further increased his fury and commanded his host of soldiers, saying:
"Arise quickly! You all!"
Strike this seer down quickly and crush him; do not let him live!

This man has now crossed over to the other shore by himself, and within my realm, he further teaches immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to escape from my domain. I will not release you—if you think you can escape my hands, you are truly a śramaṇa indeed!
"Arise quickly and flee far away from beneath this Bodhi tree; then you shall live long and not encounter such suffering.
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied to Pāpīyas:

"Even if this Sumeru, King of Mountains, were to collapse and leave its original place, even if all sentient beings were to cease to exist, even if all the stars, the sun, and the moon were to fall to the earth, and even if the great ocean were to dry up."
"I am now seated beneath the Bodhi tree; I cannot be moved.
Māra became even more enraged and uttered harsh and evil words:

"Seize this Gautama, son of the Śākyas! Lift him up and fly away with him! Do not kill him for now, but take him quickly to my exquisite palace. Bind him with the fivefold bonds and fetters, place cangues upon his hands, and send him to guard my gates, so that I may repeatedly see him in such suffering and various calamities, like a wretched slave."
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied to Pāpīyas:
"It might be possible to paint various forms of exquisite colors upon this empty space, or even for the empty space, the stars, the sun, the moon, and the devas to fall to the earth."
"You hosts of Māras, you have filled the three thousandfold world-system and terrify me; yet even here beneath this tree, it is impossible for you, Māra, to intimidate me.

Chapter 32: The Bodhisattva’s Subduing of Māra. *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Thirty-Two, Part One. "At that time, the host of Māras exerted all their power to threaten the Bodhi tree, yet they could not cause even a single hair of the Bodhisattva to tremble."
There is a verse that says:
"The host of Māra’s celestial armies suddenly assembled; everywhere drums were beaten, shaking the earth with their clamor.
Conchs and shells were blown with various sounds, as they cried out:”
"What do you intend to do?
Now that you see this great host of Māra’s army, why do you not rise and flee from here?
Your exquisite form now is like cast gold; your pure countenance is looked up to by gods and humans."
Such a body will soon perish; this great host of Māras is difficult to withstand.
Behold the earth and the sky, filled with all manner of transformations;
if we must fight them, I fear we shall not prevail, and in our rage, we might even harm our own bodies.
With a Brahma-voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird, he addressed the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and others:
"Those who, out of folly, wish to vex the nature of space—those who now come to terrify me are likewise like this.
One might be able to shatter the king of mountains with a vajra, or dry up the great ocean by blowing upon it with one's mouth,"
Some fierce, wrathful nāgas seize him by the hand; thus they are able to move my mind.
The hosts of Māra, in their fury, release mountains of fire; they uproot trees along with their roots and hurl them in chaotic confusion;
molten copper, blazing crimson, pours down like scattering stars; some grasp wicked, venomous serpents in their hands.
Some have heads like camels, horses, or white elephants; some have heads like cats, jackals, or monkeys.
Some are wrathful snakes or dragons with tongues that spit fire; others fly as thunderbolts and lightning.
They rain down a mixture of earth, stones, hail, and vajras, or pour forth iron balls and various weapons.
Lances, spears, long swords, and tridents, Or manifesting vajra-teeth and venomous snakes,
They fell to the ground, shattering tree branches and twigs; Various armaments let out great roars,
Some with a hundred arms shot a hundred arrows, While snake mouths spat forth fierce flames of fire.
Some brandish iron balls as large as Mount Sumeru; others rain down terrifying, blazing fires that strike the ground and split it open all the way to the subterranean springs.
Some flee forward and backward while being hemmed in from all sides;
others appear at their left and right or by their feet. Upside down, they emit smoke and flames from their hands and feet.
Suddenly, he broke into a great laugh once more.
Seeing that these were like illusory transformations, the Bodhisattva realized that such demonic power might well have taken his life;
yet he viewed it as being like the moon reflected in water, neither truly male nor female in form.

There is no self, no life-principle, and no sentient being; the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, and mind, as well as internal and external causes and conditions, each exist of their own accord. All these phenomena are thus produced without a person;
my words that "I act" are not false. If you do not believe this, you should further make a vow.
Just as I now see them coming toward me with the intent to terrify me,
so too the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and my own body are entirely empty and devoid of reality.

"At that time, when the hosts of yakṣas from Māra’s army, with their various forms and diverse bodies, sought to terrify the Bodhisattva in this manner, the Bodhisattva was then neither startled nor afraid; he remained unmoved and unshaken."
Then that Māra Pāpīyān further increased his heart of anger; harboring grief and anxiety within, it pervaded his entire body so that he could not find peace.
As a verse says:
"The family and retinue of Māra are most fearsome, Each assuming various forms of terror."
"Seeing that Bodhisattva without alarm, Pāpīyān’s heart was filled with intense grief and resentment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflected:
"This Māra Pāpīyān does not accept the counsel of others; he commits various deeds without realizing it himself. I shall now use words in accordance with the Dharma to sever all his evil practices."
Having reflected thus in his mind, the Bodhisattva spoke to Māra Pāpīyān, saying: "Māra Pāpīyān!
Listen well and attentively."
I originally came here to the foot of the Bodhi tree; at the very beginning, I took a handful of grass, spread it out, and sat down. Why was that?
I fear that in the future you will become an enemy with Māra Pāpīyān, engaging in strife, contention, and malicious abuse.
You, Māra Pāpīyān!
You have committed various evil deeds and possess no virtuous mind; I now wish to sever all your enmity, Māra Pāpīyān, and I wish to extinguish all your evil karma.
"You, Māra Pāpīyān!
If you wish to give rise to a heart of resentment, you should think thus:
'For what reason does this Bodhisattva sit beneath this tree, making a mat of grass and wearing robes of discarded rags?'"
"You harbor such envy and jealousy toward these matters, you Māra Pāpīyān!
Compose yourself for a moment;
if I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall later take all such things as these and entrust them to you. I pray that you will turn your mind and give rise to great joy."
Māra Pāpīyān! Within your own mind now there is also this vow:
"We must certainly terrify the Bodhisattva, causing him to abandon this seat and flee without stopping."
"Furthermore, I have this vast and great vow:

'As long as I remain seated upon this seat, should any cause or condition arise such that my body here is shattered like fine dust and my life-span extinguished, if I do not attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, my body shall never rise from this place.'"
"O Māra Pāpīyān!
Let us observe this sequence: who possesses the strength of courageous vow-power?
Whether it be I, or you, O Māra, along with your hosts, whoever is able to first fulfill this vow."
"If the power of my meritorious deeds and roots of goodness is strong, I shall surely fulfill this vow without fail.
At that time, the Bodhisattva addressed Māra Pāpīyas with these verses:

"You once held a single *asaṃkhyeya* assembly, And now you have obtained such great majesty and authority; If you can grant me the fulfillment of my wish, Then I shall bestow upon you the fruit of my merit."
"For immeasurable billions of eons, I have bestowed various gifts upon all sentient beings.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān again addressed the Bodhisattva in verse:
"In the past, I performed the Unrestricted Sacrifice; now you have verified that it was no falsehood."
"Who would believe your words that you have practiced the perfection of giving for so many kalpas, and now wish to subdue me?
After Māra Pāpīyān had spoken this verse, at that time the Bodhisattva was neither afraid nor startled; he was neither timid nor weak, remaining focused and undisturbed.

With a supple mind, he cast off all fears; his body hairs were smooth and supple, and his blinking was calm and composed. He extended his right hand, the nails of which were red like vermilion copper.

Furthermore, adorned with all manner of marks and signs in complete perfection, produced by the roots of goodness and the merit of his various practices throughout immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, he raised his hand and stroked [the child’s] head.
Having rubbed his head with his hand, he then rubbed his feet; having rubbed his feet, with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, like a dragon king wishing to look about, he raised his head.
Having raised his head, he carefully observed the host of Māras; having observed them, he pointed to the great earth with his right hand, adorned with millions of merits, and spoke this verse:
"This earth can give birth to all things, It is without marks and acts with equanimity.
This shall bear witness that my vow is not in vain; I pray that you speak truly before me."

At that time, after the Bodhisattva had pointed to this earth with his finger and spoken these words, the Earth Deity who supports this earth, adorned herself with various precious jewels—namely, exquisite celestial crowns, earrings, bracelets, armlets, and rings—and decorated her body with all kinds of necklaces and ornaments. Furthermore, she filled seven-jeweled vases with various fragrant flowers and held them in both hands. Moving neither too close nor too far from where the Bodhisattva sat, she suddenly surged forth from beneath the earth, manifesting half her body. Bowing low in reverence toward the Bodhisattva, she addressed him, saying:
"O Great Man!..."
"I bear witness to you; I know you.
In a past age, ten trillion kalpas ago, you offered an unobstructed assembly (anāvaraṇa-pariṣad).

Having spoken these words, at that moment the earth throughout the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, producing a great sound like the ringing of a bronze bell struck in the kingdom of Magadha—resounding, roaring, and so forth, as previously described, possessing the eighteen characteristics.

"At that time, all the hosts of Māra's armies and Māra Pāpīyas himself, having thus gathered together, were completely routed and dispersed; their strength was broken and they were no match for him. Each fled in haste, their battle arrays shattered; overcome by natural terror, they could find no peace of mind and ran hither and thither, stumbling at every step."
At that time, some white elephants suddenly stumbled and fell, some horses lay exhausted, and some chariot axles broke, leaving them strewn about in utter disorder.

Some troops were so bewildered and dazed they could not move; others found their crossbows, spears, bows, arrows, long swords, lassos, scimitars, discus-weapons, tridents, halberds, fans, small axes, battle-axes, and hatchets spontaneously dropping from their hands to the ground.
Furthermore, their various sturdy armor shattered and fell away from their bodies.

Thus, they scrambled for refuge in all four directions; some covered their faces and lay prostrate on the ground, while others fell backward, tossing and turning from left to right like shifting corpses.

Some fled to the mountains, some entered underground caves, some leaned against trees, and some entered dark forests; others turned their hearts back toward the Bodhisattva, entreating him for protection and care. Those who relied upon the Bodhisattva did not lose their original resolve.

At that time, Pāpīyān heard the sound of the great earth; his heart was filled with great terror, and he fell to the ground in a swoon, losing all sense of direction. From the air above, he heard only this voice:
"Strike him! Grasp him! Seize him! Hack him! Kill him! Cut him asunder! Let the dark practices be utterly extinguished; do not let Pāpīyān escape!"

The Bodhisattva’s Subduing of Māra, Part Two:
At that time, there was another earth-dwelling goddess present who took a flask of cool water and sprinkled it over the King of Māras, saying to him:
"O Māra Pāpīyān!..."
Arise quickly! Run back to your own palace!
For your sake, various weapons shall now appear, intending to come and harm your body, dismembering you limb by limb.

Then that host of Māras, having manifested themselves by assuming various forms and extraordinary bodies according to their original natures, and having arrived brandishing all kinds of weapons and implements, were so terrified that they could no longer maintain their shapes.

Returning in this manner, they reached their original place, yet each was lost to the others; after seven days had passed, some among them were able to see one another while others could not, and those who did meet one another questioned each other about their circumstances.
Some wept for their mothers, some for their fathers, some for their elder brothers, some for their younger brothers, and some for their elder sisters or younger sisters, saying to one another:
"We have now encountered this great calamity; it is our own misfortune. That we have now returned with our very lives is truly beyond the power of thought for us."
And there is a verse that says:
“The Bodhisattva’s right hand is adorned with a hundred blessings; The fingers are joined by webs and the nails are crimson;
Within the palm, the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel shines brightly, Filled with the wondrous color of Jambu-river gold.”
With hands composed and gentle, he stroked his head and feet; thus, from beneath his palms, there appeared clouds and lightning.
He spoke these words:
"I have never failed anyone who has come to beg; this is attested by the deities of water, fire, and wind."
Brahmā, Śakra, and the sun and moon, as well as all the Buddhas of the ten directions,
fully perceive and know that I have sought bodhi through ascetic practices— through the six perfections of giving,
ethical discipline, diligence, patience, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as the four immeasurables and the various supernormal powers.
Thus, through these successive causes that aid the path, I have fully realized all practices of cultivation;
throughout the ten directions, I have performed every merit— both the Pañcavārṣika festivals and acts of giving—
and you, O Māra, possess not even a ten-thousandth part of it.
The sound of the earthquake was like the tolling of bells; the ocean waves surged and subsided in six ways.
When Māra beheld this, he fell to the ground, fainting and unable to recover. Some voices in the air cried out, "Bind him! Seize him!
Though he had descended, his face lost its luster; he knew for himself that he could not match the majestic power of the Bodhisattva.
Beating their breasts, they wail and cry out; their bodies are exhausted and they have no place of refuge.
They run hither and thither across the east, west, south, and north; their minds are bewildered and they fall into a swoon, devoid of feeling.
The power of elephants, horses, chariots, and soldiers is utterly crushed, as are the kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, and rākṣasas.
Stricken with natural terror, they all scattered in every direction; retreating and fleeing, they sought their way about in confusion.
Like birds in a marsh caught in a fire, they flew away;
fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, and daughters, seeking one another in pairs, could not find their way, each asking, "Where have you gone now?"
Even if they were to meet one another and harbor mutual disdain, saying that calamity has arrived and their lives are in peril,
those countless hosts of Māras would suddenly vanish like scattered clouds.
Thus he suffered for seven days; later, when they encountered one another, they cried out, "He lives!
and our hearts were filled with great joy.
At that time, the Great Deity of the Bodhi Tree, with a compassionate heart, took a flask of cold water and sprinkled it upon Māra, saying these words:
"Arise quickly! Do not linger; go wherever your heart desires. If you do not heed my words now, you shall find bitter suffering when you encounter calamities in the future.
Whether it be a Mahoraga or a Piśāca—whatever terrifying forms exist in this world—"
The Demon King led his hosts down from the tree, Desiring to terrify the Bodhisattva.
With a countenance of perfect beauty and all marks complete, His merit was like that of the thousand-rayed sun;
His mind was unshakable like Mount Sumeru, And he viewed those demonic hordes as mere illusions.
All phenomena are without difference or distinction, like stars, dew, and floating clouds;
when one correctly contemplates the nature of phenomena in this way, the mind rests securely in the full-lotus posture.
If there is a sense of "self," then hearing and seeing arise; such false thoughts give rise to craving.
When foolish people harbor such attachments to a self, they perceive terrors due to their mental conceptions.
Śākyamuni, the Great Honored One, observes that all phenomena are equal in their suchness;
that the twelve links of dependent origination arise in continuous succession; and that the realms of mind and consciousness are empty and devoid of reality.

Seeing the deceitful Māra, they are not startled; though exhausted, without gain, and their bodies weary, they cast aside wood, stone, swords, and staves; their kinsmen flee, leaving them without refuge.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān’s eldest son, named Śreṣṭhidāraka, prostrated with his head at the feet of the Bodhisattva, seeking forgiveness and repentance, and spoke these words:
“O Great and Virtuous Noble Son!
I pray that you will grant my father leave to confess his transgressions and offer his apologies. He is but a foolish and shallow man, like a small child, devoid of wisdom.
It was he who suddenly came here to disturb the Holy Son, leading a host of māras and manifesting various forms to terrify him.
Previously, I consulted my father with a loyal and upright heart, saying:
"Even a wise man well-versed in all arts would still be unable to subdue Prince Siddhārtha, let alone someone like me."
"Only I pray, Noble Son!
Please forgive my father.
My father is ignorant and does not understand the Way; how could he possibly give birth to such a terrifying Great Holy Prince?"
"O Great Sage, Prince!
May the vow you have sworn be swiftly fulfilled, and may you quickly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, all the devas who had conceived faith in the Bodhisattva—whether in the air, upon the earth, or in any other direction—all experienced a great joy that filled their entire bodies, such that they could not contain themselves. With hearts full of joy, they cried out these words:
"Li li, ba ba, li li.
The sound filled the void of the four directions, its resonance shaking and piercing through as it fluttered his robes: "Alas, how rare is this Bodhisattva!"
"Now he has already subdued all Māras and their hosts.
Thus they played celestial music and sang celestial songs to praise the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, they took celestial flowers—Mandārava, Mahāmāndārava, Mañjūṣaka, Mahāmañjūṣaka, Utpala, Kuvalaya, Padma, and Puṇḍarīka—as well as fine powdered sandalwood incense from the heavens, and scattered them over the Bodhisattva.
Having scattered [the flowers], they scattered them again; having rained them down, they rained them down once more.
A verse says:
“When the Bodhisattva had already subdued the Māra King, This great earth shook in six ways.”
Sentient beings are submerged in the darkness of ignorance, yet the Great Sage’s divine light shines everywhere.
Heaven and earth are opened wide as the sun and moon radiate their brilliance;
it is like a woman adorning her face, while from the void fall rains of various flowers—mandārava blossoms and others besides.

At that time, there were again immeasurable and boundless other devas, numbering in the thousands of myriads of koṭis—such as the Lord of the Sahā World, the Great Brahmā King, Śakra, and others—who all rejoiced greatly. Their entire bodies could not contain their exuberance; they pressed their ten fingers together in palms-joined salutation, prostrated before the Bodhisattva, and spoke these words:
"O Holy One! Now, this Sage!"
"You shall certainly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, not far from that spot beneath the Bodhi tree, there was a nāga king named Kāla, who immediately praised the Bodhisattva in verse:
"Just as I formerly beheld the Sun of the Buddha arise, he has now returned to this very place beneath the Bodhi tree."
Performing great supernormal powers and rare feats, he skillfully subdued the King of Māras.
The World-Honored One now does likewise: spreading grass and sitting cross-legged in tranquility, his mind does not cling to objects but dwells in right mindfulness;
for even a single thought-moment, he has never been startled.
With such valor and great diligence, this most supreme Muni Buddha is certain [to attain enlightenment].
Thus the great earth shakes in six ways, its roar thundering like the sound of a bell;
surging and subsiding in the east, west, south, and north, he will before long surely achieve the Great Supreme Awakening.
The hosts of devas, numbering hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas, fill the void;
raising subtle voices with joyful hearts, they proclaim: "O Benevolent One, you shall surely become a Great and Wondrous Sage."
Myriads of billions of devas, beyond counting, each brandishing garments that fill the void;
such preliminary signs as these are boundless: you, O Benevolent One, shall now become a Buddha and a Great Sage.
Tens of millions of nayutas of devas, standing in the sky with palms joined in reverent salutation, could not have fully described this prior omen:
"O Benevolent One, you shall now become a Buddha, a Great Honored Awakened One."
Tens of billions of celestial youths, filled with joy, hold exquisite celestial flowers in their hands;
they rain down clouds of blossoms upon you, O Benevolent One, for you shall now become a Buddha, a World-Honored One, most supreme.
The branches of the surrounding Bodhi tree all bend low toward the Honored One;
these auspicious signs are not of a single kind—O Benevolent One, you shall now become a Buddha, the most supreme and great Honored One.
Since you, O Benevolent One, have already subdued the hosts of celestial Māras— with their fearsome voices and strange forms—
having fully gathered and transformed them through the power of your compassion, you now become the Buddha, the one of great and honored renown.
After the Naga King Kāla had praised the Buddha, his heart was filled with joy and great delight. Chapter 33:

Attaining the Unsurpassed Way From the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*, Chapter Thirty-three: Attaining the Unsurpassed Way. "At that time, having already subdued all demonic adversaries, having extracted the thorns of poison and erected the banner of victory, and having sat upon the Vajra-seat, the Bodhisattva extinguished all worldly minds of internal strife."

Having extinguished strife and conflict, with inner and outer self-mastery and pure mental conduct, he acts for the benefit of all sentient beings in the world, for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings in the world, for the sake of causing all wicked sentient beings to give rise to a mind of compassion, and for the sake of severing the fetters and defiled practices of all wicked sentient beings.

Having personally eliminated the hindrance of drowsiness and torpor, his mind attained purity, luminosity manifested before him, and right mindfulness became perfected; he also taught sentient beings, causing them to sever all obscurations of sleep.

Having personally severed all frivolous speech, one attains a pure mind free from turbidity and confusion; furthermore, one teaches sentient beings to extinguish all frivolous thoughts and cause them to attain purity.

Having severed for oneself all hearts of doubt and regret, and having departed from dark and defiled conduct, one becomes free from hesitation regarding all phenomena, both wholesome and unwholesome, thereby attaining a pure mind.
"At that time, once the Bodhisattva has severed these five kinds of mental states, his afflictions gradually thin out. Why is this?
Because these five dharmas can act as obstructions to wisdom, fail to assist wisdom, and block the subtle, excellent path to Nirvana."

Having completely relinquished all these things, free from thoughts of desire and unwholesome states, distinguishing between the internal and external, reflecting and examining with a mind concentrated and tranquil, desiring to realize joy, he enters and dwells in the dharma of the first dhyāna.
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflected thus:

"I have now realized the first stage of the superior mind (*adhicitta*), having presently attained the subtle and wondrous Dharma of peace and bliss; with a mind free from negligence, I ought to rightly remember to depart from the village and fully master all the practices of one who relies upon the forest hermitage (*āraṇya*)."

At that time, the Bodhisattva, wishing to abandon all conceptual observations and purify his inner mind so as to be entirely free from discrimination, gave rise to joy and bliss born of samādhi and proceeded to practice within the dharma of the second dhyāna.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflected thus:
'I have now given rise to these two increased states of mind; having abandoned all evils and perfected the various practices, I have entered the second dhyāna.'"

At that time, the Bodhisattva felt weary of and detached from [sensual desires], experiencing joy; his conduct was pure, and with right mindfulness and right wisdom, he experienced physical bliss as praised by the Noble Ones, having abandoned all evils.
Having attained such superior peace and happiness, he dwells practicing within the dharma of the third dhyāna.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflects:
"This is my third increase of the mind, even as I practice in the araṇya."

At that time, the Bodhisattva, wishing to relinquish pleasure and wishing to relinquish pain, just as he had previously relinquished the discrimination between suffering and pleasure, became free from both suffering and pleasure; with equanimity and pure mindfulness, he realized the Dharma of the fourth dhyāna and proceeded therein.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflected:

'This is my fourth stage of mental cultivation, the practice of dwelling in happiness through direct realization in this very life; it has already been attained and realized, and the mind is free from negligence.'"
“Good son!
You should practice with right mindfulness and single-mindedness, dwelling in the tranquility of an araṇya.

At that time, the bodhisattva, thus single-minded, pure and stainless, without obstruction or obscuration, had all suffering and affliction completely extinguished; being harmonious, supple, and fit for all tasks, he abided in certainty.

During the first watch of that night, desiring to accomplish the supernormal power of the body, he experienced various realms of supernatural faculties: namely, being able to manifest as many bodies from a single body, and then merging those many bodies back into one; having become a single body, he would vanish from above and appear below in the midst of space, or vanish from below and appear above, moving freely between concealment and manifestation, and likewise traversing horizontally across all directions.
He passes through mountain cliffs and stone walls without obstruction, proceeding according to his thought; he enters a wall and emerges, and having emerged, he re-enters.
It is like being in a mist: having vanished, one immediately appears; having appeared, one vanishes again.
He entered the earth as if it were water and walked upon water as if it were solid ground; he emerged from and submerged in the void like a flying bird.
At times he emitted smoke and fumes, and at times he produced blazing flames like a great mass of fire.
The sun and moon possess the greatest majesty and loftiness; yet [the Bodhisattva] can touch them with his palm and manifest a vast body reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven.
It is like a skilled master craftsman or his disciple who takes pure gold and fashions various vessels, which are completed at will.
He also discriminates and knows the high or low value of those objects.

Just as a potter or a potter’s apprentice, having prepared a lump of clay and placed it upon the wheel, can produce whatever vessel he desires and immediately knows its value; or just as a master carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice, having felled a tree that is neither rotten nor withered, can produce whatever object he desires and immediately knows its value.
Just as an ivory worker or an ivory worker’s apprentice, upon obtaining fine ivory, is able to fashion whatever object he desires and also knows its value—so it is with the Bodhisattva.

Having thus accomplished a pure mind, a mind free from turbidity and defilement, a mind free from obstruction, a mind free from affliction and entanglement, a gentle and supple mind, a mind perfected in action, and a mind of true tranquility and meditative concentration.

During the first watch of the night, he cultivated and performed various supernormal powers, perfected the mind of wisdom, and manifested various realms of supernormal power; that is to say, he made one body into many bodies, and so on, briefly described, until his body reached the Brahma Heaven.
When the Bodhisattva’s mind attains such tranquil concentration, such purity, such stainlessness, and such clarity, it eliminates all afflictions, troubles, and burdens.
Having performed these various deeds, his mind attained tranquility.

At that time, during the first watch of that very night, the Bodhisattva further desired to realize the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) and to perfect his mental cultivation, wishing to know within his own mind the various thoughts and mental states of others.

That is to say: the place where one receives a body for one lifetime, two lifetimes, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, one hundred, two hundred, one thousand, ten thousand, immeasurable hundreds of millions, half-eons, small eons, intermediate eons, great eons, and immeasurable small, intermediate, and great eons.

"In the past, at such-and-such a place, I had such-and-such a name, such-and-such a clan, such-and-such a lineage, such-and-such food and drink, such-and-such pleasures, and such-and-such a lifespan; having died there, I was reborn in that other place, where I was born again and died."
"At that time, by means of such signs and such knowledge, the Bodhisattva knew his various past lives; as it was with his own person, so it was with others.

Furthermore, he knew his various past existences just as, for example, a person who has left his own village and traveled to another village, walking along the road, knows where he sat, where he walked, where he slept, where he spoke, and where he remained silent."

Upon reaching this village, he knows the duration of the journey and the distance between that village and the present one; he knows where to walk, where to sit, and even where to lie down or remain silent until he reaches that village, and having reached it, returns to his own village.
Furthermore, he reflects in this way, contemplating and fully knowing: "From this village, after a certain period of time, I shall reach that village.

Again, at a certain place, I shall stay for a certain period of time; for a certain period of time I shall walk, for a certain period of time I shall sit, for a certain period of time I shall speak, and for a certain period of time I shall remain silent; after another certain period of time has passed, I shall again arrive at a certain town."

Furthermore, he knows that at that place, for a certain duration of time, he has walked, sat, stood, slept, lain down, spoken, remained silent, or stayed put, until finally reaching his own village; all such things he knows completely.
The Bodhisattva is likewise.

With such a concentrated mind, a pure mind, a stainless mind, such a supple mind, a mind free from affliction and distress, and a mind capable of action, during the first watch of the night, he attains the knowledge of past lives; through right mindfulness he realizes and knows them, his mind having accomplished its practice.

"At that time, having reflected and known the places where his own self was born as well as the places where others were born—namely, the lands of a single lifetime up to the places born during immeasurable and boundless billions of kalpas—the Bodhisattva [proceeded]."

At that time, the Bodhisattva, in accordance with reality and as taught, heard the successive explanations and came to know the places where his own self had been born, as well as the various places of birth of other beings, which he also recollected.

“Once the Bodhisattva has recollected such births, he is able to develop a mind of loving-kindness toward all classes of sentient beings throughout their various rebirths, thinking: ‘This one was my relative; this one was a stranger to me. Having abandoned those relatives, I have been born again in such-and-such a place; thus, from this world to that world, I have transmigrated without ceasing.’”
Like a windmill, like a plantain tree, they are certainly devoid of substance; the impermanence of afflictions is a certainty—thus should the mind know it.

"At that time, with his mind thus concentrated, thus purified, thus stainless, thus free from affliction, and thus supple, fit for the practice of tranquility, the Bodhisattva, in the middle of that night, desiring to achieve and realize the divine ear, gave rise to this thought:
'By means of the divine ear, which is thoroughly purified, it surpasses the human ear.'"
They hear various sounds, namely: the sounds of hell-beings, the sounds of animals, the sounds of devas, and the sounds of humans; sounds from afar and sounds from nearby.
For example, suppose in a village, town, city, or kingdom, or perhaps in a marketplace, there is a person who has ascended to a high hall or a multi-storied tower and is staying therein.

Furthermore, there is another person who, with pure ears, hears various sounds; that is to say, they may hear the sound of blowing conch shells, or the sound of large drums, or small drums, or *mṛdaṅga* drums; or the sound of the *vīṇā*, or the lute, or the flutes, pipes, reed organs, and zithers—various such musical sounds.

They may hear the sound of singing, or the sound of dancing, or the sound of laughter, or the sound of weeping; they may hear the voices of women, or the voices of men, or the voices of boys, or the voices of girls.

In this way, in this manner, the Bodhisattva thus pacifies his mind, making it pure and stainless, free from affliction and turbidity, and supple in its activity; then, at the middle of that night, he hears various sounds, even the sounds of all the hells and so forth.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva was tranquil, concentrated, pure, stainless, and free from affliction. In the middle of that night, he achieved the realization of the divine eye, which surpasses the human eye and perceives all things: whether beings who have passed away and fallen, or those being born; beings in the higher realms or the lower realms; beings of handsome appearance or of ugly appearance; or all beings who have fallen into the evil destinies, or all beings who are born into the good destinies."
Whether they be practitioners, those who abide [in the path], or those who perform actions, he is able to see through his eyes all the actions they have performed.

Furthermore, he knows that such sentient beings have committed impure physical actions and impure mental actions; they slander their teachers and the Sangha, or cling to false views. Because of these false views, they create such evil karma; by reason of these causes and conditions, they cast off this life and are born within the hells of the evil realms, where they undergo various sufferings and afflictions.
Such sentient beings, due to their verbal karma, undergo various sufferings in the evil realms.
These beings, with impure verbal karma, commit all manner of evil speech; by these causes and conditions, they are born among animals and endure manifold afflictions.

These sentient beings perform evil deeds of body and are possessed of evil deeds of body; by these causes and conditions, they create evil deeds of mind and are possessed of evil deeds of mind. Even going so far as to revile all the noble ones and holding various wrong views, because of those wrong views and the causal conditions of wrong views, at the end of their lives and upon casting off the body, they fall among the hungry ghosts and undergo the sufferings of hungry ghosts.

Such sentient beings practice pure deeds of body and pure deeds of speech; they do not disparage the noble ones, and by practicing right view, they create karma of right view. By these causes and conditions, at the end of their lives and the casting off of the body, they are reborn in the heavens.

Some sentient beings, having cultivated pure bodily and verbal conduct that is complete in every respect—neither transgressed nor deficient—and not slandering the noble ones, possess right view; by reason of such karma and conditions of right view, at the end of their life and the casting off of the body, they are reborn among human beings.

In this way, the Bodhisattva, with the purified divine eye that surpasses that of humans, perceives all sentient beings—whether at the time of falling away or at the time of taking birth—be they beings of the higher realms or those of the middle and lower realms, those who are handsome or ugly, those whose bodies are fragrant or whose bodies reek of foul odors, and whether they have reached evil destinies or good destinies; he knows them all truly, according to the karma they have created.

It is, for example, as if there were a person who, from atop a great platform or high tower in a kingdom, city, village, or marketplace—a place of clamor and bustle—sits and beholds people with the pure divine eye. He sees them coming from the east or coming from the west; some facing west and going east, others facing east and going west; some facing south and going north, others facing north and going south; some coming from the south, others coming from the north; whether they are coming or going, standing or sitting, moving back and forth among one another, or traveling in reverse or in regular order.

In this way, in this manner, the Bodhisattva, being thus tranquil, concentrated, pure, stainless, and free from affliction, with actions that are gentle and supple, at the middle of that night, perceives all sentient beings receiving their retributions according to their karma, whether good or evil.
And there is a verse that says:
"In the hells, one undergoes the extreme calamity of karmic suffering; Among animals, each devours the other;
Hungry ghosts constantly suffer from hunger and thirst; In the human realm, people are beset by distress as they seek wealth and resources."
When the retribution in the heavens is exhausted, one suffers the pain of separation from loved ones; this suffering is most heavy and beyond all comparison.
As it passes from one to another among all classes of sentient beings, there is nowhere a time of true joy.
This is called the abyss of the ghost of death, And also the very bottom of the ocean of afflictions;
Sentient beings drown within it with no way out, Circling back and forth, coming and going.
Observing in this way within the five realms of existence, one perceives them all with the divine eye:
the beginning and end of afflictions have no reality, just like the layers of a plantain tree when split leaf by leaf.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mind was thus tranquil, thus pure, and stainless; having thus distanced himself from all evils, his mind was disciplined and supple, capable of performing its task, and had already attained stillness and concentration."

At that time, as the latter part of the night drew to a close, because he desired to realize and know the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*), he exerted himself; having thus aroused his knowledge, he further knew the minds of others—from what source they arose and what matters they contemplated—penetrating them all completely and knowing them as they truly are.
If there are sentient beings who give rise to a mind of desire and wish to engage in sensual acts, they know this truly as it is.
If they leave behind the mind of desire and distance themselves from desire, they realize and know it according to reality.
If the mind is full of hatred and is incited by hatred, one understands this as it truly is.
One feels weary of and detached from the hateful mind, and remains far removed from hatred, understanding this as it truly is.
If there is a mind of delusion, one truly understands that it has arisen from a mind of delusion.
Having become weary of and detached from the mind of delusion, one understands it as it truly is.

Thus, in brief, he understands as they truly are: those with craving and those free from craving; up to the conditioned and the unconditioned; those who flow downward and those who flow upward; the tranquil and the agitated; the broad and the narrow; the great and the small; the finite and the infinite; the surpassable and the unsurpassable; those who have attained meditative concentration and those who have not; and those who are liberated and those who are not.

For example, suppose there is a man or a woman in the prime of youth who always delights in adorning their body; having adorned themselves, they might at times look at their own facial features in a clear mirror or in clear water, seeing them all completely.

In this way, in this way, the Bodhisattva thus calms his mind; thus it becomes pure, thus stainless, thus free from affliction, supple and harmonious, and fit for action. Having attained such tranquility, returning during the latter part of the night, with a pure mind he desires to realize the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives, and likewise for his own mind and the minds of others.
From where the mind is generated and from where it arises, he understands them all as they truly are, throughout their entirety.
Whether there is a mind of desire or a mind free from desire, he understands them as they truly are.
"Up to liberation, he understands that the mind is not liberated. Thus he knows.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva attains such a concentrated mind, a pure mind, a stainless mind, a mind free from all evil, a supple mind capable of performing its function, and one that has already attained tranquility.

Returning during the latter part of the night, desiring to realize the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), he internally gave rise to a mind of wisdom and thought thus:

"These sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of afflictions; that is to say, they repeatedly undergo birth, old age, sickness, and death. Having passed away from this life and reached another place, when they receive their subsequent birth, they again encounter all such manifold sufferings. They are unable to know how to leave behind these various sufferings, namely the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death."
Thus he reflected:
"By what skillful means should I now act? How may I be freed from these various sufferings?
What course of action should I undertake, and how may I abandon birth, old age, sickness, and death to cross over to the further shore?"
And he spoke in verse:
“In the ocean where the world is submerged in birth and death, Having died again and again, one undergoes rebirth;
Bound by the manifold sufferings of old age and illness, The deluded and ignorant cannot find escape.”
At that time, having spoken these verses, the Bodhisattva further reflected:
"From where does this old age, sickness, and death come?
By what causes and conditions do this old age, sickness, and death exist?"
When the Bodhisattva contemplated and reflected in this way, he knew that old age, sickness, and death exist because of birth; since there is birth, old age, sickness, and death follow accordingly.
The Bodhisattva further reflected:
"From what does this birth arise? By what causes and conditions does it come to be?"
"Can there be this birth?
Having reflected and contemplated thus, the Bodhisattva knew that because of existence (*bhava*), there is this birth.
The Bodhisattva further reflected again:
"From what does this existence arise?
By what causes and conditions is this existence obtained?
Having reflected and contemplated in this way, the Bodhisattva knew that this existence exists because of grasping.
The Bodhisattva further reflects:
"From what does this grasping arise?
By what causes and conditions does this grasping come to be?"
After the Bodhisattva had reflected and contemplated in this way, he knew that because of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), there is grasping (*upādāna*).
The Bodhisattva further reflected:
"From what does this craving arise?"
"For what cause and condition does this craving exist?
Having reflected and contemplated in this way, the Bodhisattva knew that craving exists because of sensation.
The Bodhisattva further reflected again:
"From what does this feeling arise?
By what causes and conditions does this feeling come to be?
Having reflected and contemplated in this way, the Bodhisattva knew that it is because of contact that this feeling exists.
The Bodhisattva further reflected:
"From what does this contact arise?
By what causes and conditions does this contact come to be?"
After the Bodhisattva had reflected and contemplated in this way, he knew that because of the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), there is this contact (sparśa).
The Bodhisattva further reflected again in this manner:
"From what do these six sense bases arise?"
"By what causes and conditions do these six sense bases arise?
Having reflected and contemplated in this way, the Bodhisattva knew that the six sense bases exist because of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The Bodhisattva further reflected again in this manner:
"What are the causes and conditions for this name-and-form?
From what does it arise?
Having reflected and contemplated thus, the Bodhisattva knew that name-and-form exists because of consciousness.
The Bodhisattva further reflects in this way:
"By what causes and conditions does this consciousness exist?
From what does it arise?"
Having reflected and contemplated in this way, the Bodhisattva knew that this consciousness exists because of the various formations (*saṃskāra*).
The Bodhisattva further reflected again:
"By what causes and conditions do these various formations exist?"
“From what do they arise?
Having reflected and contemplated in this way, the Bodhisattva knew that volitional formations exist because of ignorance.
The Bodhisattva further reflected again in this manner:

"Conditioned by ignorance, there are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations, there is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness, there is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form, there are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases, there is contact; conditioned by contact, there is feeling; conditioned by feeling, there is craving; conditioned by craving, there is clinging; conditioned by clinging, there is becoming; conditioned by becoming, there is birth; conditioned by birth, there are old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and various forms of suffering and affliction."
"Thus these various sufferings arise, each conditioned by the other.
Never before had the Bodhisattva heard this from another, nor had he seen it for himself; yet from the Dharma, there arose in him vision, knowledge, intention, wisdom, and clarity."
The Bodhisattva further reflected in this way:
"In the absence of what are there no sickness, old age, and death?
Through the cessation of what do sickness, old age, and death cease?"

The Bodhisattva, reflecting and contemplating in this way, realized that because there is no birth, there is no aging, illness, or death; and because birth is extinguished, aging, illness, and death are extinguished.
The Bodhisattva further reflected in this manner:
"By the absence of what does this birth not exist?"
"By the cessation of what does this birth cease?
Thus the Bodhisattva reflected and understood: "When existence is absent, there is no birth; by the cessation of existence, this birth ceases."
The Bodhisattva further reflects in this way:
"Due to the absence of what do all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) become non-existent?
Due to the cessation of what do all conditioned phenomena cease?"

The Bodhisattva, reflecting and contemplating in this way, understood that because there is no ignorance (*avidyā*), there are no formative forces (*saṃskāra*); because ignorance is extinguished, formative forces are extinguished.
The Bodhisattva further reflected thus:

"Because ignorance is extinguished, formative forces are extinguished; because formative forces are extinguished, consciousness (*vijñāna*) also follows in being extinguished; briefly stated, even down to birth, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, all are extinguished."
"In this way, all these sufferings and their origins are completely extinguished.

To the Bodhisattva, who had never heard such a thing before, within these teachings there arose vision, there arose knowledge, there arose intention, there arose clarity, there arose light, and there arose wisdom.

At that time, the Bodhisattva attained such a concentrated mind, such purity, and such stainlessness; having thus attained a supple mind free from all afflictions, it was a mind capable of performing its function.

Having attained a tranquil mind, one knows truly that "this is ignorance," and likewise knows how the cause of ignorance arises and how the condition of ignorance ceases; having understood this with true clarity, this is the characteristic of the total extinction of ignorance.
