Having attained the right path, one knows it truly; in brief, one knows as they really are consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sickness, death, and so forth.
"This is the origin of all old age, sickness, and death; this is the cessation of all old age, sickness, and death; having ceased, the path is attained"—thus he knows it all.
"This is the noble truth of suffering; this is its origin, he knows it as it truly is;
this is the cessation of the noble truth of suffering, he knows it as it truly is;
this is the path leading to the cessation of the noble truth of suffering, having brought about its cessation, he knows it as it truly is."
One truly knows these outflows;
one truly knows the origin of these outflows, the cessation of these outflows, and how, once these outflows have ceased, the path is attained.
"This is the outflow of sensual desire; he knows it as it truly is.
This is the outflow of existence; this is the outflow of ignorance; he knows them as they truly are.
In this state, all outflows are extinguished without remainder, and all forms of existence are severed."

“Suppose, for example, there were a village, or perhaps a city, or a town, not far from one another, where there was a pond. Its water was cool, sweet, pure, and free from any filth or turbidity; it was always full, level with its banks.”
Furthermore, on all four sides of the bank, many trees surround and adorn it.

Within the pond there are also various kinds of insects, such as oysters and snails, as well as soft-shelled turtles, crocodiles, tortoises, and turtles—many aquatic creatures. There are also stones or sand, and various fish such as eels, trout, bream, sea-bass, and catfish, as well as makara fish; these move to and fro across the water in the east, west, south, and north, seeking food and drink, some remaining still while others pursue one another.

Yet there is a person on the shore with pure eyes who sees all those insects clearly and distinctly; he knows that these are oysters, conchs, tortoises, crocodiles, and turtles, and that these are sand, stones, fish, insects, makaras, and so forth—some seeking food, some hibernating, some scurrying east, west, south, or north, and some pursuing one another.

In this way, in this way, the bodhisattva thus brings the mind to tranquility; it is thus purified, thus stainless, thus free from affliction, and thus supple, such that it is capable of performing all activities and has already attained serenity.
"This is ignorance; he knows it as it truly is.
This is the origin of ignorance, this is the cessation of ignorance, and this is the path leading to the cessation of ignorance; he knows these as they truly are."
To speak briefly, all outflows (*āsrava*) in this place are completely extinguished without remainder.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind attains liberation from the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), his mind attains liberation from the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and his mind attains liberation from the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).

Having attained liberation, he develops wisdom-liberation; having developed it, he immediately knows: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence in future lives."

When two-thirds of the night had passed and it was the fourth part—the latter portion of the night—just as the morning star was about to appear, the night was still tranquil, and all sentient beings, whether moving or stationary, were not yet awake.
At that time, the Bhagavān gave rise to wisdom and insight, and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
There is a verse that says:
"Three-quarters of this night have already passed, And the final quarter remains as the light is about to appear."

The various classes of beings do not all remain unmoved; at that time, the Great Sage, the Unsurpassed Honored One, having extinguished all sufferings, attained Bodhi and was immediately named the All-Knowing One of the World.
“At that time, when the Blessed One attained wisdom and vision, this world—including the palaces of Brahmā and Māra, the devas, humans, śramaṇas, and brahmins—was all brilliantly illuminated.”
Between the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains and the Great Iron Ring Mountains, it has been perpetually dark from time immemorial, never having seen light;
yet even with such virtue, such radiance, and such power as these suns and moons possess, they are ultimately unable to cause that place to be illuminated or made resplendent.
Now, all have spontaneously become vast and clear, and everyone beholds the radiance; all sentient beings therein see one another, recognize one another, and speak to one another, saying:
"Are there other sentient beings here as well?"
"Are there any sentient beings here as well?
Immediately, all the trees produced flowers and fruits, which ripened and fell to the ground.

By the power of the World-Honored One, the void became pure, free from dust and mist, and devoid of smoke or haze; suddenly clouds arose spontaneously, sending down a fine rain to sprinkle the earth, while a cool breeze blew, perfectly temperate in its warmth and cold, so that all directions became clear and serene, appearing with distinct clarity.

Furthermore, in the midst of the void, all the devas played celestial music and sang celestial hymns of praise, raining down various kinds of immeasurable flower showers, namely mandārava flowers and mahāmandārava flowers.

Furthermore, they rained down celestial robes such as *kauśeya* and other silks; they rained down treasures such as gold, silver, and lapis lazuli; they rained down *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses; and they rained down various kinds of powdered incense and unguents, scattering them over the Buddha. Scattering again and again, these various rains of flowers, powdered incense, and unguents filled an area of one *yojana* all around that ground, piling up to the height of the knees.
At that time, this great earth shook in six ways, and all sentient beings experienced nothing but the most sublime bliss, untroubled by any suffering.

During that period, not a single sentient being harbored desire, nor anger, nor greed or delusion; furthermore, they gave rise neither to prideful thoughts nor to the mind of self-conceit (*māna*). They were free from fear, committed no transgressions, and were without disease; all ailments were cured, and none were ever to recur.
Sentient beings suffering from hunger and thirst all attained full satisfaction; those intoxicated by wine all regained their sobriety and ceased drinking wine thereafter.

Those who were deranged and insane all recovered their original minds; those who were blind and sightless all gained the ability to see forms; the deaf heard sounds; and those whose bodies and sense faculties were incomplete all became fully endowed with them.

All impoverished sentient beings shall obtain the ground of wealth; all emaciated sentient beings shall become full and robust; and those bound and imprisoned in jails shall all be liberated, with their shackles and fetters naturally dissolving.

The sentient beings in the hells were all freed from suffering and affliction; the sentient beings among the animals had their terrors entirely extinguished; and the sentient beings among the hungry ghosts were relieved of the pains of hunger and thirst, all attaining full satiation.
And there is a verse that says:
"At that time, sentient beings were free from anger and the like; They extinguished all suffering and experienced great bliss.
Those intoxicated by wine or deranged regained their original nature, And all who were terrified obtained peace."
At that time, after the World-Honored One had attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he uttered this lion’s roar and spoke in verse:
“The merit and benefits cultivated in the past, And all matters contemplated by the mind, have now been fulfilled.
I have swiftly realized that state of meditative concentration, And have further reached the shore of *nirvāṇa*.”
All enemies whatsoever, and even Māra Pāpīyān, the sovereign of the desire realm, cannot afflict me;
they all take refuge in me.
If one can exert oneself with courageous diligence, it will not be difficult to attain the state of a noble sage.
"Having attained this, one immediately reaches the end of all suffering, and all transgressions are utterly extinguished.
At that time, when the Tathāgata had first attained Buddhahood, he spoke these verses on verbal karma for the very first time.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Thirty;
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Thirty-One.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Sui Dynasty.
34. Chapter on Competing with Māra in the Past, Number Thirty-Four.
"At that time, during the first watch of the night, the Bodhisattva pointed to the earth with his finger and subdued the host of Māras and the retinue of Pāpīyān."
At that time, this earth shook in six ways, even unto great trembling, like the striking of a bronze bell.

At that moment, all the people dwelling in the villages, towns, and kingdoms saw the great earth quake and heard the sound of its thunderous roar; their minds were filled with doubt, and each went to the side of a physiognomist, a diviner, an astronomer, or a seer, or to a master skilled in divination, and asked them all:
"What does this mean?"
For what reason does the great earth shake in this manner and produce such a great sound?
Between Māra and the śramaṇa, who is superior and who is inferior?
"Each of you is well-versed in divination and observation; we pray that you will explain this matter for us.
At that time, all those seers, astronomers, and masters of the stars each replied to the person who had questioned them, saying:

"In the village of Gayā in the kingdom of Magadha, there were two men of great power who contended with one another. One sought the greatest Dharma King of the world beyond, while the other sought a king of unrighteousness within the world. As they vied and fought, the one who sought the Dharma King overthrew the one who sought the king of unrighteousness."
"When his task is completed, in the middle of the following night he will become a Great Dharma King, and before long he will turn the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma.
And there is a verse that says:
"All people, hearing of the earthquake, Each went in person to the side of the diviners."
They asked the master diviner, saying:
"O you who are sages and knowers of the world, for what reason does this great earth tremble?
We pray that you will examine it with careful discernment and skillful observation, and quickly resolve this doubt of ours."
All those teachers replied: "The Dharma King and the Non-Dharma King are both there;
the two shall compete in their majestic spiritual power, each testing their virtuous strength to see who is the more exalted."
The Bodhisattva and the celestial Māra contend with one another; through the practice of the Dharma, he crushes and subdues that demonic host.
Having achieved such victory, he attains Bodhi and becomes a Buddha, a King of Dharma, alone and fearless.

"At that time, when the morning star appeared during the latter part of the night, the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. At that moment, a supreme radiance spontaneously arose in the world, and the earth shook in six ways."

Then, after that radiance and the earthquake had occurred, King Śuddhodana was awakened from his sleep within the palace; he summoned the various physiognomists, as well as the Brahmins and astrologers, and commanded them, saying: "O Brahmins!..."
"What is this matter?
Please explain it to me.
Having spoken these words, the astrologers, diviners, and astronomers immediately addressed the king, saying:
“‘We pray only that Your Majesty will wait a short while; we shall divine and observe first, and then inform the King.

At that time, the Buddha’s mother, Lady Māyā, having already attained a celestial body and assumed the form of a jade maiden, descended from the heavens and addressed King Śuddhodana, Yaśodharā—the mother of Rāhula—and the others, speaking these words:”
"Great King!
You should know that this very night Prince Siddhārtha has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it is because of this sign that the great earth trembles."
"Once the Tathāgata has attained perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), having subdued all Māras and being without enemies, there is nothing in the world that he fears.
At that time, the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven in the form realm still harbored doubts as to whether or not the Tathāgata had indeed attained perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those devas, soared into the void and, for the sake of severing their doubts, uttered this lion’s roar:

"I have now severed all fetters of sensual desire; my mind regarding desire is settled. I have dried up the waters of all afflictions so they flow no more; I shall not undergo further existence, nor shall I again enter into the midst of afflictions. Having reached the end of suffering, there is nothing further remaining."
At that time, having heard these words, all those devas each thought to themselves:
"The Tathāgata has already attained *samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Filled with joy and exultation, his entire body was so overcome that he could not contain himself; taking celestial wonderful flowers, unguents, powdered incense, celestial sandalwood incense, and the fine powder of ox-head sandalwood, as well as *māndārava* and *mahāmāndārava* flowers, he scattered them over the Tathāgata, scattering them again and again after each initial offering.

When Māra Pāpīyas saw the hosts of devas offering such articles of worship to the Tathāgata, he immediately sat upon the ground not far from the Tathāgata’s presence. Dejected and unhappy, his heart filled with great sorrow, he drew figures on the ground with a single reed splinter and thought to himself:
"How truly rare is this world!"
"How inconceivable!
I am able to turn back the ascetic practices of all the sages, and I can instill desires in the hearts of Śakra and all the other devas;
how is it that now this śramaṇa of the Śākya clan, through a single-minded samādhi for but a brief moment, has caused my entire army and horses to be thus subdued?"
Afterwards, when the Tathāgata was extensively performing Buddha-activities and preaching the Dharma through his secret teachings, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!"

“World-Honored One, how is it that by the power of diligence one attains supreme enlightenment (sambodhi), accomplishes the seven factors of awakening (bodhyaṅga), and fulfills the treasure of the Dharma?
Having spoken these words, the Buddha immediately addressed those bhikṣus, saying: “You bhikṣus!...”

Now you should know this: it is not solely by the power of my diligence in this single lifetime that I have attained supreme enlightenment and the seven factors of awakening; rather, it is through the power of my diligence in former times that I obtained the maṇi jewel.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is this matter?"
"We pray that you will analyze and explain this for us.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!..."
Listen attentively with a sincere mind.

I recall that in the past there was a merchant leader who entered the sea to gather treasures. Within the sea, he obtained a precious maṇi jewel, worth exactly one hundred thousand taels of gold; having obtained it, it suddenly fell back into the sea.

At that time, the merchant leader took up a single ladle and, generating a heart of great diligence and courageous resolve, began to scoop out the waters of the great ocean, desiring to dry it up in order to seek the maṇi jewel.
At that time, the deity of the ocean, seeing that person attempting to scoop up the seawater with a ladle and place it on dry land, thought to himself:
"This person is foolish and lacks wisdom; the waters of the great ocean are immeasurable and boundless—how can this person hope to scoop them up with a ladle and place them on dry land?"
Then that sea deity spoke in verse:
“In this world there are many beings who act in various ways out of greed for wealth and profit;
yet now I see your great folly, and there is no one who surpasses you.”
The ocean is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep; now you wish to scoop it dry with a ladle.
In your exhaustion, you will merely waste your life, for before much has been scooped out, your life will come to an end.
The water you have drawn out is but a single hair-tip; this great ocean is vast and exceedingly deep.
Now, lacking wisdom and failing to reflect, you wish to take the earrings and fashion them into Mount Sumeru.
At that time, the merchant leader again addressed the sea deity with these verses:
"O Celestial Deity, these are not auspicious words, For you wish to prevent me from emptying the ocean.
Deity, simply fix your mind and contemplate me correctly; Before long, I shall drain the sea until it is void."
Since you, O Benevolent One, have remained here for this long night, my heart should indeed be filled with great sorrow;
yet I vow to exert myself with undaunted resolve, until I have surely exhausted the great ocean and caused it to dry up.
My priceless treasure has fallen within this; therefore, I must drain the waters of the great ocean.
Once the water is exhausted to the bottom and I have recovered my treasure, I shall return home.
When the sea deity heard these words, fear arose in his heart, and he thought to himself:
"This man is so diligent and courageous that he drains this seawater; it will surely be exhausted."
At that time, having thought thus, the sea deity immediately returned the priceless jewel to the merchant leader. Having returned it, he spoke these verses:
"An ordinary person must cultivate a courageous mind; Do not complain of weariness when bearing the burden of hardship.
Seeing such power of diligence, One loses the jewel but regains it and returns home."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Diligence brings fulfillment in every circumstance; Laziness always leads to great suffering.
Therefore, one should vigorously arouse a courageous mind; By this, the wise person attains Bodhi."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that great caravan leader was at that time, it was I myself.
At that time, the caravan leader entered the sea; having obtained an invaluable jewel, he lost it upon his return. With a courageous mind, he sought the jewel and recovered it."
"It is the same today; by means of diligence, one attains the path of the seven factors of enlightenment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Then the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!"
"How rare and extraordinary!
How inconceivable! A single person alone is able to subdue all these hosts of Māras.
Having spoken these words, they each became silent.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You bhikṣus! Listen with a sincere and attentive mind."
It is not only now that I alone have thus subdued the hosts of Māra; in past lives as well, I likewise alone subdued those hosts of Māra.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the matter?”
"I only pray that you will analyze and explain this for me.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Listen well!

I recall that in the past, immeasurable eons ago, there were two brother śuka parrots; one was named Maṇikīri (in the Sui language, "Mañjūṣaka-parvata" or "Girimañjarī"), and the other was named Gandhārī (in the Sui language, "Tadāgiri" or "Parvatatadā").
At that time, two parrots were perched upon a tree when, suddenly, a hawk came swooping down with great speed, seized one of the smaller ones, and flew off into the air.
Thereupon, the elder brother spoke this verse to his younger brother:
"To suffer alone is also misery; To rejoice alone is also joy."
"Peck at that hawk's vital spots; when he is pained and exhausted, he will release you.
Now that your body is small and my strength is slight, rely solely on your own diligence and do not be indolent."
Having heard his elder brother’s words, the younger brother, wishing to display acts of courageous power,
exerted all the strength of his body and, after deliberating to the utmost, immediately pecked at the hawk’s vital parts.
Afflicted by physical suffering, the hawk quickly released the parrot;
because his body was tormented by pain, he ran swiftly here and there seeking refuge.
That clever parrot bird escaped from its bonds; by pecking at the eagle’s most vital joint, it left the eagle exhausted with no place to hide, while the fierce parrot bird soared through the sky.
When the hawk saw the parrot flying after it, it abandoned its pursuit and fled far away to seek a way to survive;
that parrot which was pecked by the hawk at that time is now my very self, Śākyamuni,
and that hawk was none other than Māra Pāpīyas.
Since he was already able to subdue him and bring him under control, how much more so now that he is fully endowed with merit?
How could he not subdue that Māra-king?
You bhikṣus, you should know this.
At that time, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that Māra Pāpīyas repeatedly deceives the Tathāgata yet is unable to prevail over him, while the Tathāgata always escapes his calamities?”
Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "You bhikṣus!
Listen with a sincere and attentive mind; I shall speak for you."
It is not only now that I have been deceived by the Māra Pāpīyān and escaped his grasp, nor have I ever been disturbed or troubled by him;
in past lives as well, when the Māra Pāpīyān sought to delude me, he was likewise unable to afflict me.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the matter?”
"I only pray that you will analyze and explain this for me.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I recall that in the past there was a river named Pāriyātra—translated in the Sui language as 'Crossing Beyond the Joints'."
At that time, there was a man on the riverbank who was a garland-maker; he had a garden situated by the side of that river.
At that moment, a tortoise emerged from the water and entered the flower garden, wandering about in search of food and trampling the flowers as it went along.

At that time, the owner of the garden saw that turtle wandering about seeking food and trampling his flowers; thereupon, the garden owner devised a stratagem to capture the turtle, and having seized it, placed it inside a basket, intending to kill and eat it.
At that time, the tortoise thought to himself:
"How may I now escape this peril?
What skillful means might I employ?"
"What clever stratagem can I employ?
He then gave rise to this thought:
"I should now deceive this owner of the garden."
Having formed this thought, he immediately addressed the owner of the garden with these verses:
“Since I have emerged from the water, my body is covered in mud; Please set aside the flowers and wash my limbs.
As my body is already defiled by impure mud, I fear it might soil your basket and the flowers.”
Then the owner of that garden thought to himself:
"Excellent is this tortoise!
His good words have instructed me!"
"I must now accept his words.
I shall wash his body so that the mud does not soil my flower basket.
Having thought this, he immediately took the tortoise in his hands and led him toward the water, intending to wash the tortoise's body.
At that time, the man immediately lifted the turtle out and placed it upon a rock, intending to wash it by scooping up water.
Then, the turtle exerted great strength and suddenly plunged back into the water.
At that time, seeing the tortoise submerged in the water, the florist thought to himself:
"How marvelous is this tortoise!
It has been able to deceive me in such a way; I shall now likewise entice and deceive this tortoise to cause it to emerge from the water."
Then the florist spoke this verse to the tortoise:
"O wise tortoise, listen attentively to my intention: You have many kinsmen and friends;
I shall make a flower garland and tie it around your neck, So that you may go home at will and enjoy yourself."
At that time, the tortoise thought to himself:
"This garland-maker is deceiving me with false words.

This garland-maker’s mother is ill and confined to her bed; his sister gathers flowers to make garlands for sale in order to earn a living. His making such a statement now is surely a deception intended to lure me out so that he may eat me."
At that time, the tortoise spoke these verses to the garland-maker:
"You have prepared wine at your home to host a gathering for your kin, And you have prepared various kinds of flavorful foods.
When you arrive inside your house, speak these words: 'The tortoise meat has been boiled; its fat shall season the rice.'"
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!
If you wish to know who that turtle was that entered the water at that time, it was I myself."
The garland-maker was Māra Pāpīyān.
At that time, he sought to deceive me but could not succeed; how could he possibly succeed now as he seeks to deceive me once again?
Then, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
Truly inconceivable.”
"Even though Māra Pāpīyān possesses sovereign power and authority over the realm of desire, and employs all manner of deceptions and delusions, he was still unable to move this seat.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!..."
Now you should know that it is not only today that this Māra Pāpīyān has sought to deceive me by employing his power and influence;
it was the same in the past, and he could not find an opportunity to deceive me.
Then, those bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent,
World-Honored One!"
"What are these matters?
I only pray that you will analyze and explain them for me.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I recall that in the past, within the great ocean, there was a large *nāga* king. This *nāga* had a wife who was pregnant; suddenly, she conceived a craving to eat the heart of a monkey."
Due to these causes and conditions, her body became emaciated, jaundiced, and haggard; she trembled and was ill at ease.
When the *ṛkṣa* saw that his wife’s body was thus wasted away and devoid of color, he asked her:
"O virtuous and kind lady!"
"What is your ailment?
What food do you desire to eat?
I have not heard you ask me for food; why is this so?"
At that time, the female nāga remained silent and gave no reply.
Her husband asked again:
"For what reason do you not speak to me now?"
The wife replied to her husband:
"If you can grant me my heart's desire, I shall speak;
if you cannot, why should I even bother to speak?"
The husband replied again, "Just speak it;
if it can be made consistent with reason, I shall employ skillful means to seek it out so that you may obtain it.
The wife then said:
"I now intend to eat the heart of a monkey; can you obtain it?
The husband replied, "That which you require is a most difficult matter."
"Why is that? I dwell within the waters of the great ocean, while the monkey is upon the trees in the mountain forests; by what means could it be obtained?
The wife said:
"What shall I do now? My mind is set upon such food; if I cannot obtain such things, this fetus will surely miscarry, and I fear my own life will soon come to an end."
At that time, her husband spoke again to his wife:
"O virtuous and benevolent lady!
Please be patient for a while; I am now seeking to depart."
"If this matter is accomplished, it would be beyond words how profound it would be; then both you and I would share in great joy.
At that time, the dragon immediately emerged from the sea and came onto the shore.
Not far from the shore, there was a great tree named Udumbara (in the Sui language, "Seeking Wishes").
At that time, a large monkey was at the top of the tree, eating its fruit.

At that time, having seen the monkey sitting atop the tree eating its fruit, the crocodile gradually approached the foot of the tree. Upon arrival, he immediately comforted him with kind words, inquiring after the monkey’s well-being:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Vasiṣṭha, what are you doing up in this tree?
Are you not suffering greatly from the hardship of your labor?
Is it not easy for you to find food, and are you not weary?"
The monkey replied,
"It is so, O virtuous one!
I am not currently experiencing great suffering."
The dragon spoke again to the monkey, saying:
"While you are here, what do you eat?
The monkey replied:
"I am upon an udumbara tree, eating its fruit.
At that time, the dragon spoke again to the monkey, saying:
"Now that I have seen you, I am filled with such great joy that it pervades my entire body and I cannot contain it; I wish to take you as a virtuous friend, that we may love and respect one another."
Take my words; why must you remain here?
Furthermore, there are few seeds from this tree and not many; how can you find such delight in this place?
You may come down and follow me; I shall take you across the sea. On the other shore, there is a great forest where all kinds of trees abound with flowers and fruit in great abundance.
These are the so-called amra fruits, jambu fruits, lakuca fruits, panasa fruits, tinduka fruits, and various other such trees in immeasurable numbers.
The monkey asked, "How can I now reach that place?
The ocean waters are deep and vast, making them extremely difficult to cross; how shall I be able to swim across?"
At that time, the crocodile replied to the monkey, "I shall carry you on my back across to the other shore; you should now simply come down from the tree and mount my back."

"At that time, because the monkey’s mind was unsettled, being narrow-minded, base, foolish, and of little insight or knowledge, he felt joy upon hearing the dragon’s pleasant words. He descended from the tree, climbed onto the dragon’s back, and desired to follow the dragon away."
Within his heart, the dragon-king gave rise to this thought:
"Excellent, excellent!
My vow has been fulfilled."
He then intended to take him with him to his own dwelling, but both he and the monkey sank into the water together.
At that time, the monkey asked the nāga,
"Good friend!"
"Why have you suddenly submerged yourself in the water?
The dragon replied, "You do not know."
The monkey asked,
"What is this matter?
What do you intend to do?"
The dragon replied, "My wife is pregnant;
she has conceived a desire to eat your heart. For this reason, I have brought you here."
At that time, the monkey thought to himself:
"Alas! I am now most inauspicious;
I shall bring about my own destruction."
"Alas! What expedient means can I now employ to escape this urgent calamity and preserve my life?
He further thought thus:
"I must deceive the naga."
Having formed this thought, he said to the dragon:
"O virtuous friend!
My heart remains left behind, deposited upon the Udumbara tree; I have not brought it with me."
"O Benevolent One, why did you not speak the truth at that time, saying 'I know now that I must have your heart'?
Had you done so, I would have followed you immediately.
When you, Good Friend, turned back, you released me to fetch the heart; having obtained it, I shall return."
At that time, having heard these words from the monkey, the crocodile emerged from both ends.

Seeing the crocodile about to emerge onto the shore, the monkey exerted himself with great vigor and leaped with swift agility, using all his strength to spring down from the crocodile’s back and climb up onto a great Udumbara tree.
The dragon stayed below for a short while waiting, and seeing that the monkey lingered and did not descend, he said to him:
"Dear and close friend!
Descend quickly; I shall accompany you to my home."
The monkey remained silent and refused to descend from the tree.
Seeing that the monkey had not come down for a long time, the dragon spoke this verse:
“O good friend monkey, having attained your heart’s desire, I pray you will quickly descend from the tree.”
"I shall escort you to that forest, a place abundant with all kinds of fruits.
At that time, the monkey thought to himself:
"This dragon is without wisdom."
Having reflected thus, he immediately addressed that nāga with these verses:
“Though your nāga’s calculations may be broad, your mental discernment is exceedingly narrow and inferior.
You should simply examine and reflect upon this yourself: among all classes of beings, who is without a mind?”
Although that forest abounds in seeds and various wondrous fruits such as the *āmra*, my mind now truly does not dwell upon them; I would rather eat this *udumbara* myself.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus,
you should know that the great monkey at that time was none other than myself."
The dragon at that time was none other than Māra Pāpīyān.
Even then, he sought to deceive and delude me, yet he could not succeed; now he again wishes to entice me with the five worldly sensual desires, but how could he possibly move me from this seat?
When he had spoken these words, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
It is extraordinary, World-Honored One!”
This is truly inconceivable.

How can this be? The Māra Pāpīyān has brought this host of hideous and heterogeneous beings to the place where the Tathāgata resides, yet the Tathāgata is able to perceive and know each and every one of them.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!
You should know that it is not only today that the Māra Pāpīyān has brought this host of great māras with their hideous forms to my side; I have observed and known this before."
Then the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
What is this matter? We pray that you will explain it for us; we long to hear it.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I recall that in the past there was a hunter who knew of a forest abounding in many birds and would frequently descend upon it."
Having arrived there, he constructed a grass hut, covering its top with branches from various trees; he then entered within it and sat down, concealing his body.
At that time, those birds, thinking it was a tree branch, flew down and perched upon his hut.
When the hunter saw the birds perched above, he gradually killed them, either by shooting or by seizing them with his hands.
At that time, there was a bird which, having seen this hut, thought to itself:
"This hut moves from place to place, while all other trees remain fixed in one spot;
beneath this hut, it will surely not be empty."
Having understood this, he left that hermitage so as not to be seized by the hunter, and spoke these verses:
"I see all the trees in the forest— The aśvattha and the viśāla, The āmalaka and the jambu, The nirguṇḍī and the tinduka."
It remains firmly established in one place, unmoving since its birth;
yet this tree wanders and shifts from place to place. It must surely not stand there in vain;
if there were something evil within it, I would quickly abandon this grove.
Great doubt has arisen within my mind: "Perhaps this is an evil-doer devoid of compassion, fearing that he might kill me there.
Furthermore, in the past, in other lands, I have already been torn apart and fled from nets; therefore, the wise, knowing this, should abandon such a place."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should know, O bhikṣus, that the flying bird was none other than my own self."
That hunter was Māra Pāpīyān.
At that time, he assumed a terrifying form, wishing to kill me; I perceived and knew this then.
Now again, he has brought this army of Māra’s hideous and fearsome hosts to my side; I have known this for a long time.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If the world does not engage in profound reflection, How could it attain the qualities of a superior person?
Now, by means of supreme reflection, I have been liberated from bondage and attained the unconditioned."

35. The Two Merchants Present Food. *The Sutra of the Collection of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Thirty-Five, Part One: "At that time, the World-Honored One had first attained the Way of Bodhi and sat beneath the tree for seven days and nights without rising from his cross-legged posture, taking the joy of liberation as his sustenance."

At that time, after seven days had passed, the World-Honored One, with a single-minded and correct mindfulness, arose from samādhi and sat upon the lion throne. During the first watch of the night, he correctly contemplated the twelve links of dependent origination, observing from the bottom to the top and from the top to the bottom. He contemplated them with skillful mindfulness and skillful observation, without loss or deviation. Because of this, that arises; because of the existence of that, this again comes to be. That is to say: conditioned by ignorance there are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations there is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness there is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form there are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases there is contact; conditioned by contact there is feeling; conditioned by feeling there is craving; conditioned by craving there is grasping; conditioned by grasping there is becoming; conditioned by becoming there is birth; and conditioned by birth, there arise old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and other forms of suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having realized this Dharma, spoke in verse:
“If one who practices the holy life contemplates all dharmas, One will see that such characteristics of dharmas arise.
If one sees that all dharmas arise from characteristics, One will know that all dharmas exist through causes and conditions.”

At that time, during the middle of that very night, the World-Honored One contemplated the twelve links of dependent origination from beginning to end; he contemplated them in reverse order with a focused mind, observing them skillfully and reflecting upon them skillfully, without loss or confusion.

Because that does not exist, this is naturally non-existent; because that ceases, this naturally ceases. That is to say: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, and so on, until birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair—all are completely extinguished.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having realized this Dharma, spoke these verses:
"If one who practices the holy life contemplates all dharmas, One will see the arising of such characteristics of dharmas;
If one sees that all dharmas arise from conditions, One will know that all dharmas are extinguished through causes and conditions."

At that time, during the latter part of the night, the World-Honored One contemplated the twelve links of dependent origination, observing from the beginning to the end and from the end to the beginning; he contemplated them well and reflected upon them well, without loss or confusion.
That is to say: when that has arisen, this arises; because that exists, this exists; because that is absent, this is also absent; and when that ceases, this also ceases.

That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; conditioned by volitional formations, and so forth, all the various sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, and affliction come into being.
When that [ignorance] is absent, this [volitional formation] is also absent; when that is extinguished, this is also extinguished.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having understood this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one who practices the holy life contemplates the world, They will see the arising of signs and even their cessation;
Having dispersed all Māras and established themselves in stability, They will be like the sun, shining through the void."

At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his lion throne and, not far from the Bodhi tree, sat cross-legged once more. For seven days he remained motionless, dwelling in the bliss of the practice of liberation.
For seven days he gazed intently at the Bodhi tree, his eyes never turning away for a moment, and further thought to himself:
"In this place, I have brought an end to boundless suffering and have laid down my heavy burden."
At that time, after seven days had passed, the World-Honored One, with right mindfulness and right awareness, arose from samādhi.
Subsequently, someone erected a stūpa at the place where the Tathāgata had gazed upon the Bodhi tree, naming it the Animiṣa Stūpa (The Unblinking Stūpa).
And he spoke in verse:
"In this place of enlightenment, all sufferings are exhausted; sitting again at this very spot, I behold that seat.
Having crossed over all vows and reached the further shore, I shall realize bodhi at that place."

At that time, the World-Honored One rose from the site of the Animiṣa (Unblinking) Stūpa and proceeded slowly and steadily toward the place of walking meditation known as Māriṣā (in the language of Sui, "Heat-Mirage").
Having finished his walking meditation, he sat cross-legged and remained for another seven days experiencing the bliss of liberation.
Then, after those seven days had passed, the World-Honored One, with right mindfulness and right awareness, arose from samādhi.

At that time, the Naga King Kāla—translated into the Sui language as "Black"—approached the place where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the Buddha's presence, he prostrated at the Buddha's feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Having stood to one side, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This palace of mine was previously offered by me to all the Buddhas of the past; having accepted it, each of those Buddhas dwelt herein out of compassion for me."

As for those Buddhas—namely the World-Honored One Krakucchanda, the World-Honored One Kanakamuni, the World-Honored One Kāśyapa, and the World-Honored One of today—it is well that you know the proper time!
Out of compassion for me, please remain here for a short while. Why is this?

I have already offered this palace to the three Buddhas of the past; today, the World-Honored One is the fourth to accept this palace for my sake. Thus, it shall be known as "The Palace Accepted by Four Buddhas," endowed with complete merit.

At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the palace of the Dragon King Kāla; having accepted it, he entered within and sat cross-legged. After another seven days had passed, he remained in a single concentration without rising, experiencing the bliss of liberation.
At that time, after seven days had passed, the World-Honored One, with right mindfulness and right awareness, arose from samādhi and addressed the great nāga king Kāla, saying:
"Nāga king, come to me and receive the three refuges equal to those of a Buddha, as well as the five precepts; you shall enjoy great peace and happiness for a long night."
Then the Nāga Kāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I shall respectfully follow the Buddha's teaching; my heart dares not disobey, just as the World-Honored One has commanded.

Having heard the Buddha's words, the Nāga Kāla joined his palms toward the Buddha and immediately received from the Buddha the three refuges—taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Saṃgha—and further received the five precepts. Thus, he was the very first in the world to receive the name of an upāsaka.
Among the animals, he repeated the Three Refuges; having received the Three Refuges, he was none other than the Dragon King Kāla.
At that time, there was yet another dragon king named Mucilinda, who approached the place where the Buddha was, and having arrived, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Having stood to one side, the dragon king then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This palace of mine was previously offered by me to all the Buddhas of the past; having accepted it, they dwelt therein."
These are the World-Honored One Krakucchanda, the World-Honored One Kanakamuni, and the World-Honored One Kāśyapa!
Excellent,
World-Honored One!
"Now you too should accept this palace for my sake; since I have received this palace from four Buddhas, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, I have obtained a great benefit.

At that time, having accepted the palace from the Dragon King Mucilinda, the World-Honored One sat cross-legged and remained seated for seven days without rising, desiring to experience the bliss of liberation.

At that time, within those seven days, clouds arose in the sky and rain poured down, and a great cold wind blew; throughout the seven days, the rain did not cease for even a moment, resulting in freezing cold.

At that time, the Dragon King Mucilinda emerged from his palace and, with his great body, encircled the Buddha’s body in seven layers, shielding it from view; furthermore, he draped his seven heads over the World-Honored One like a grand canopy and remained there, majestic and steadfast.
He thought thus:
"May the body of the World-Honored One not be afflicted by cold, wind, dampness, or dust; may mosquitoes, gadflies, and other insects not touch the body of the World-Honored One."
At that time, after seven days had passed, the World-Honored One saw that the sky was free of clouds and mist and had become pure; with right mindfulness and right awareness, he arose from samādhi.

At that time, the Dragon King Mucilinda withdrew his dragon body, coiled it seven times around [the Buddha], and concealing his dragon form, transformed himself into the body of a young brahmin. Standing before the Buddha, he joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

It is not out of fear or a desire to disturb the Tathāgata that I have coiled my dragon body seven times around the Buddha and covered the World-Honored One with my seven heads, remaining there in tranquility; rather, it is only because I fear that cold, wind, dust, dirt, water, gruel, mosquitoes, or gadflies might touch the body of the World-Honored One.
“World-Honored One!
Having reflected upon these matters at that time, I covered the body of the World-Honored One.
Then, for this reason, the World-Honored One immediately spoke a verse in self-praise, saying:
“Contentment and tranquil concentration are the supreme bliss; With contentment, one contemplates the profound nature of all phenomena.
Such bliss brings no affliction to the world, Nor does it involve the harming of any living beings.”
If one attains worldly peace and happiness, remaining far removed from all desires and greed,
and abandoning the arrogance of self-conceit— this happiness is the most supreme and wondrous joy.
Whatever sensual pleasures humans possess, if one can completely abandon them so that craving ceases entirely,
then when those pleasures are compared with this [bliss], they do not equal even a sixteenth part.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Dragon King Mucilinda, saying:
"O Great Dragon King!
Come and receive the Three Refuges as well as the Five Precepts, so that you may obtain peace and happiness throughout the long night."
Then Cūḍapanthaka addressed the Buddha, saying,
"As the World-Honored One has instructed, I shall not dare to disobey.
Having heard the Buddha's teaching, Cūḍapanthaka immediately received from the Buddha the three refuges and the five precepts.

"At that time, there was a shepherd boy at that place who, during the six years of the Bodhisattva’s ascetic practices while he was with the World-Honored One, made offerings to the World-Honored One with a pure heart, honoring and respecting him; furthermore, he offered milk to the World-Honored One and additionally broke off branches from a nyagrodha tree to provide shade."
At that moment, the branches of that tree immediately became a great tree.

Then, according to the causes and conditions of his various degrees of faith, meritorious karma, and roots of goodness, after the life of that lamb ended, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, becoming a deity of great virtue and power with sovereign supernormal powers.
At that time, after that devaputra had been born in the heavens, he reflected thus:
"By what karma did I originally obtain this body as a result of its retribution?
He then further thought:

"In the past, when the World-Honored One was a bodhisattva, I performed such deeds with my own body: I offered breast milk during the Bodhisattva’s ascetic practices; while the Bodhisattva was there, I took a branch from a nyagrodha tree and planted it in the ground to provide shade for him."
"By virtue of this wholesome karma, I have now obtained this subtle and wondrous retribution.
He further thought:
"It is because I personally made offerings to the World-Honored One while he was in the body of a bodhisattva that I have obtained this retribution."
I planted those tree branches to provide shade; for this reason, I have now obtained this karmic fruit and, moreover, attained such unimpeded supernormal powers.
How much more so, World-Honored One, since you have now realized unsurpassed Bodhi—should you not now return to that tree for my sake and receive its shade?

At that time, that devaputra emitted from his body a magnificent light of supreme color, which shone resolutely upon that tree at midnight. Having illuminated himself with this celestial radiance, he approached the place where the Buddha was; having arrived there, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then that devaputra addressed the Buddha,
saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
"I only pray that you will accept this tree from me for your own ease and comfort as you please, out of compassion for me.

At that time, wishing to show compassion to that devaputra, the World-Honored One accepted the nyagrodha tree planted by the former sheep-butcher; having accepted it, he sat cross-legged beneath the tree.
He remained seated for seven days without moving, dwelling in liberation and experiencing bliss.
Then, after those seven days had passed, the World-Honored One, with right mindfulness and right awareness, arose from samādhi and addressed the devaputra, saying:
"Come, O devaputra!"
"You may receive from me the three refuges and the five precepts, so that you may attain peace and happiness for a long night.
Having received the three refuges and the five precepts, that devaputra became, at that time, the very first lay follower (*upāsaka*) among the gods in this world.
Because the Buddha spoke of the three refuges a second time— stating that the son of the sheep-herder attained a celestial body by giving trees,
milk, and other things as alms— the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*,
scroll thirty-one, and scroll thirty-two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Part Two: The Offering of Food by the Two Merchants.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having risen from the grove of trees planted by the sheep-herder, proceeded slowly and gradually until he reached the foot of another grove of trees. That grove was named Khalatika, which in the language of the Sui means "the grove that exudes milk."
Having reached that grove, he sat down cross-legged and remained thus for seven days, desiring to experience the bliss of liberation.
Then, after those seven days had passed, the World-Honored One, with right mindfulness and clear comprehension, arose from his samādhi.
Thus, World-Honored One, for seven weeks you remained continuously in the power of samādhi.
Yet that daughter of the village headman Sujāta, having offered the milk-rice, has not eaten anything else since that single meal, and yet she remains alive to this day.

"At that time, there were two merchant leaders from North India who came to that place: the first was named Tiṅgali-puṣa (translated in the Sui language as 'Gourd'), and the second was named Bhārika (translated in the Sui language as 'Golden Staff')."

Those two merchant leaders were possessed of great wisdom, meticulous in mind, and upright in intention. Those two merchant leaders, having obtained various goods produced in the land of Central India and filled five hundred carts with them, had gained a great profit and were now returning from there to the kingdom of Northern India. At that time, they were traveling by stages along a road not far outside the Kāliṅgavana forest.

Those caravan leaders had another pair of tamed oxen that always went at the head; whenever there was a place of terror ahead, that pair of well-trained oxen would refuse to move, as if they were tied to a tethering stake.
At that time, the forest deity who protected the Khadiraka grove there remained invisible and secretly seized those two tamed oxen, holding them so that they could not proceed further.

The two caravan leaders each took a stalk of an *utpala* lotus and struck the two well-trained oxen, yet they still refused to move; furthermore, the five hundred oxen yoked to the other carts all remained motionless.

The wheels of those chariots no longer turned; their leather straps and reins all snapped of their own accord. Furthermore, the poles, yokes, axles, pins, hubs, spokes, boxes, rims, sideboards, breastbands, thongs, and heart-pieces were either broken, shattered, crushed, or split asunder—such were the various strange portents and ill omens.
"At that time, Dṛḍhalipta and the others were struck with terror; they were all deeply distressed, and the hairs on their bodies stood on end. They said to one another:
'What strange calamity have we encountered now?'"
"What calamity or misfortune have we encountered?

Each person stepped back from their chariot two or three paces, joined their ten fingers above their heads in *añjali* and prostrated themselves before all devas and all spirits. Standing there with single-minded devotion, they spoke these words:
"We pray that all present disasters, anomalies, misfortunes, and terrors may be swiftly extinguished, and that we may enjoy peace, security, and auspiciousness."
At that time, the deity who protects that forest manifested his own physical form and comforted those caravan leaders, saying: "O merchants!..."
Do not give way to fear!
For you all, there is no calamity here, nor is there any misfortune; you need not be terrified.
O caravan leaders!
In this place dwells only the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who has for the first time attained unsurpassed bodhi and now resides within this grove.
However, since the Tathāgata attained the Way, forty-nine full days have now passed, and he has never yet received food.
O caravan leaders!

If you know it is the right time, you should go together to where that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is. It is most fitting that you go first and offer him ground meal, curd, and honey balls; thus you shall obtain long-lasting peace, security, happiness, and great benefit.
When the two merchant leaders heard these words from the forest deity, they immediately addressed the deity, saying:
"We shall not disobey what the deity has instructed."
Then those two merchants each took a ball of parched grain mixed with curd and honey, and together with the other merchants, they went to where the Buddha was.

Having arrived there, the two merchant leaders saw the World-Honored One from afar—delightful and upright, peerless in the world, even like the multitude of stars adorning the void; his body was adorned with all the [major and minor] marks. Upon seeing him, their hearts were filled with great reverence and pure faith. They approached the World-Honored One, prostrated themselves at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then the two merchant leaders addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Out of compassion for us, we pray that you will accept this pure offering of parched grain, curd, and honey balls."
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Did all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Arhats, and Samyak-saṃbuddhas of the past all accept and maintain alms bowls?"

At that time, the World-Honored One gave rise to internal wisdom and vision, and immediately knew that all past Buddhas—Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—had all without exception accepted and maintained the alms bowl.
At that time, the World-Honored One again thought thus:
"By what vessel should I now receive the meal of parched grain, curd, and honey balls from the two merchants?
The World-Honored One wishes to accept it."

Once he had formed this thought, the Four Heavenly Kings each came from one of the four directions, swiftly carrying four golden bowls together; they went to where the Buddha was, and upon arrival, each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then the Four Heavenly Kings, having stepped back and stood aside, presented four golden bowls to the World-Honored One and spoke these words:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One [accept them]!"

"By using this bowl to receive the portions of parched grain, curd, and honey from the two merchant leaders, out of compassion for us, we shall for a long night obtain great benefit, great happiness, and great peace."
The World-Honored One did not accept them, for it is not fitting for one who has left the household life to keep such vessels.
Those Four Heavenly Kings then set aside the four golden bowls and presented four silver bowls to the World-Honored One, speaking thus:
"World-Honored One!"
"You may receive food in this vessel," he said, "and so on, briefly stated, until: 'it shall bring me great benefit and great peace.
Yet the World-Honored One did not accept it.
In this manner, he further brought four crystal bowls, but the Buddha still did not accept them.
In this manner, he further presented four lapis lazuli bowls, but [the Buddha] would not accept them.
In this manner, he further presented four red pearl bowls, but [the Buddha] would not accept them.
Next, he further presented four agate bowls, but [the Buddha] would not accept them.
Next, he again brought four carnelian bowls to offer to the World-Honored One, but the Tathāgata likewise did not accept them from him.
At that time, Vaiśravaṇa, the King of the North, addressed the other three Heavenly Kings, saying:
"I recall that in the past, the deities of the blue realm brought four stone vessels to offer to us and said to us:"
"O virtuous ones! You may take this stone vessel and eat from it.
At that time, another devaputra named Vairocana addressed us, saying:
“O Deva Kings!
Be careful not to receive food and eat from within these stone vessels; you should simply receive and hold them together as offerings, regarding them as if they were stupas.”
Why is this? In the future, there will be a Tathāgata who appears in the world, whose name shall be Śākyamuni.
O virtuous ones!
"You should offer these four stone alms bowls to that Tathāgata.
"O Heavenly Kings! Now the time has come;
you may take these stone bowls and present them to the World-Honored One."

At that time, the four Great Kings who guard the quarters each led their respective retinues and attendants, swiftly proceeding to their own palaces. Each held a stone almsbowl—upright and pleasing to behold, its color a deep azure like a mass of clouds—filled to the brim with celestial flowers. They anointed those bowls with all manner of perfumes and offered them all kinds of exquisite music as an offering, then quickly departed for the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, they together offered the four bowls to the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will accept these stone bowls; within these bowls, please accept the balls of parched grain, curd, and honey from the two merchant leaders."
"Out of compassion for us, please grant that each of us may obtain great benefit, peace, and happiness throughout the long night.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought again:

"These four Heavenly Kings, with hearts of pure faith, offer me four alms bowls. It would not be appropriate for me to accept and keep all four. If I were now to receive them from one person alone, then the hearts of the other three would each harbor resentment."
If I receive two bowls from two people, those two will harbor resentment;
if I receive three bowls from three people, one person will harbor resentment.
I should now accept all four bowls at once and, through my supernormal power, transform them into a single bowl.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having accepted the bowl from the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, spoke these verses:
“By giving this fine almsbowl to the World-Honored One, you shall certainly become a sublime vessel of the Dharma.
Since you have offered this pure bowl to me, your wisdom and right mindfulness will surely increase.”
At that time, having received the bowl from the Deva King Virūḍhaka, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“I contemplate True Suchness: who has offered this bowl? May they attain right mindfulness and increase their resolve;
May they be able to nourish and sustain the world to bring it peace, And swiftly perfect a wondrous, blissful, and pure body.”
At that time, having received the bowl from the Deva King Virūpākṣa, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"You have offered this pure bowl with a pure mind; With a clear and sincere heart, you have presented it to the Tathāgata.
In the future, you shall swiftly attain a pure mind, And find fulfillment among humans and devas in the world."
At that time, having received the bowl from the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The Buddha, the World-Honored One, who maintains pure precepts, Has well subdued his faculties and bestowed this complete bowl.
With an unimpaired mind and with profound reverence you have given; In a future age, you shall obtain a field of purity.”

At that time, having accepted the four bowls, the World-Honored One placed them one upon another in succession; having received them with his left hand, he pressed them down with his right hand, and by means of his supernormal power, they were merged into a single bowl with four rims on the outside.
And he spoke in verse:
"My past merits have brought their fruits to fulfillment;
Through the arousal of a compassionate and pure mind, The Four Great Heavenly Kings now, with purity and firm resolve, Bestow upon me this alms-bowl."
And there is a verse that says:
"At that time, when the World-Honored One desired to receive food, The devas from the four directions brought vessels and each offered them to the Buddha, the Tathāgata;
Having accepted them, he used his supernormal powers to transform them into a single bowl."

At that time, within the newly purified alms-bowl offered by the deva, the World-Honored One [received food] from that Northern Heavenly King, Tiriṭivisa (formerly translated as Tiwei Bolili; this is likely a phonetic transcription of a Brahmin name, though it is uncertain which version is correct).

In this sutra, it is said that the two merchant leaders did not commit a grave offense by accepting from the two merchants a ball of parched grain mixed with curd and honey; out of compassion, he accepted it and ate it in accordance with the Dharma.
Having finished eating, he immediately addressed those two merchant leaders and the rest of the people, saying: "O merchant leaders!

Come and receive from me the refuges in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and further receive the five precepts; this shall cause you to attain peace and happiness for a long night and secure great, wholesome benefits."
When the two merchant leaders and their retinues heard the Buddha’s words, they immediately addressed him together, saying:
"In accordance with the Holy Teaching of the Buddha, we shall not disobey."
They immediately together received the three refuges.

Those two merchant leaders were the very first in the human world to receive the name of *upāsaka*—one who observes the five precepts and the three refuges—namely, the two merchant leaders, Trapuṣa and Bhallika.
At that time, because the two merchant leaders had given rise to sympathetic joy, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The gift bestowed was perfect in both color and flavor; Having received it, they skillfully departed from afflictions.
Because various ingredients were blended therein, It is therefore called *saktu-ghṛta-maṇḍa* (the gruel-and-curd beverage).”
Having finished eating, the body becomes moist and radiant; the complexion shines like a flower and the countenance is clear.
Physical strength is fully restored and benefits are gained; hunger and thirst are eliminated, and the mind attains peace.
Thus did these two merchant lords offer the gruel-balls to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, so that all those of holy life might be fully satisfied;
now that I have received them, my meal is complete.
Born of the Solar Clan, the lineage of Ikṣvāku, they praise such a person as supreme;
by virtue of this merit of giving, they shall reach the ultimate fruit of noble wisdom and further attain the exhaustion of all outflows.
Thereafter, as one continues to progress further and further, there is no fear; gradually, one attains liberation from the fetters of all realms of existence.
Having entered the state of outflowlessness, one attains pure coolness.
The seeds, grain, and sprouts are all excellent, and rain and wind provide nourishment in accordance with the seasons.
The grain crops grow and become naturally abundant;
having sprouted, they gradually increase in lushness and vigor.
All varieties of grain overflow in double measure, and the harvest of seed cannot be measured.
One who can extensively bestow various foods and drinks will later obtain a fruition so vast it is difficult to describe;
this is because they achieved benefit in the past.
If one hopes to further attain fruits of great profit, there is only one way: to make offerings to the Benevolent and Wise Honored One.
When one attains the fruition of the wondrous Bodhi, And achieves the state of the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World;
Having personally realized manifold benefits for oneself, One is further able to bestow Dharma-benefits upon others.
Because they enable others to gain self-benefit and benefit sentient beings, They are therefore called the Great Wise Ones.
Desiring to benefit oneself and all others, And desiring to seek the Way to guide the world,
One should, toward the Triple Gem— the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha— Resolve the mind and give rise to right faith and practice.
Through the power of faith, one attains the fruit of retribution;
having extensively and skillfully reached the limit of faithful practice, one immediately attains inconceivable conduct of the precepts and the most supreme, unsurpassed path.

Through giving, one can obtain this supreme retribution; by observing the world as it truly is, one further attains the fulfillment of the wisdom of the Path. Thus do the noble ones possess right view.

Having attained this vision, it is called right mindfulness; it scatters all defilements, fetters, and afflictions, realizes the great nirvana of fearlessness, and liberates one from all suffering in the world.
Thus endowed with all dharmas, the noble ones praise this as most supreme.
Since birth, old age, sickness, and death no longer exist, the suffering of grief and separation is utterly extinguished.
The World-Honored One of Ten Powers praises this bliss; one shall attain the eternal state beyond birth and death.
At that time, the two merchant leaders, Trapuṣa and Bhallika, along with all the other merchants, addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We are currently on our way; we only pray that the World-Honored One [will grant us this favor]."
"For our sake, please make auspicious aspirations so that we may reach our own country swiftly and without any obstacles.
At that time, the World-Honored One made auspicious aspirations for the two merchant leaders and all the merchants, speaking these verses:
"May there be great prosperity for bipeds, And may all quadrupeds also be at peace. May all beings be free from calamity, And may all who travel be safe."
May there be much auspiciousness wherever you travel; may all directions you face accord with your wishes.
May day and night, whether walking or sitting, be filled with joy and comfort; may everything be favorable wherever you are at midday.
May your every endeavor be fulfilled according to your heart’s desire, and may both the merchant leader and his merchants remain in good health.
Hoping for their offspring, parents till the fields; having finished sowing the seeds, they look forward to a bountiful harvest.
All merchants travel in search of profit; entering the perilous seas, they gather precious gems.
You all journey forth with high expectations, wishing that the gains you plan to acquire may be swiftly realized.
I have now attained the Way with great joy; wherever you go, may all be auspicious.
May you obtain every benefit your heart desires, and may your wishes be swiftly fulfilled.
As you travel toward whatever lands you reach, may there be no obstacles whatsoever.
At that time, the merchant leader addressed the Buddha together with his companions, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that you grant us one object to serve as a reminder. When we reach our native land and can no longer see the World-Honored One, we shall build a stupa with that object and pay it homage, thereby manifesting our remembrance of the Great Sage, the World-Honored One, and we shall all offer worship and respect for as long as our lives endure.”
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately gave the merchants hair and nail-clippings from his own body for them to use as objects of mindfulness, and addressed them, saying:
"O caravan leaders!..."
"I now give these hairs and nails to you so that you may keep them in mind; when you see these objects, they shall be no different from me.
Hereafter, another stone shall descend from the sky to your location; when you see it, you should build a stupa for it and pay it honor and respect."
At that time, the two merchant leaders, Trapusa and Bhallika, having received the hair and nail-clippings from the Buddha, thought to themselves:
"These hair and nail-clippings are discarded items from the body; they are not sublime by nature and are not worthy of veneration."
They had no intention of making an offering.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts of all those merchants, addressed them, saying:
"O leaders of the merchants, do not harbor such a thought."

I recall that in the past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable eons ago, there appeared in the world a World-Honored One named Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, I was a young brahmin (*māṇava*) fully proficient in the four Vedas.
During that period, I saw that Blessed One entering a city named Padma.
At that time, I scattered five stalks of blue utpala flowers over that Buddha and immediately gave rise to the mind of enlightenment.
Then, that World-Honored One bestowed upon me this prediction: "O māṇava!..."
In a future age, after a period exceeding incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he shall attain Buddhahood, with the name Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, within the Dharma of that Blessed One, I abandoned my home, shaved off my hair and beard, and went forth as a renunciant.
After I had gone forth, all the devas took my hair; for every single hair, there were ten billion devas who divided it up and carried it away, making offerings to it together.

From that time until now, since I have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I have observed those sentient beings with the Buddha-eye; there is not a single sentient being who, while remaining by the side of a Buddha, has not attained the realization of Nirvana.

At that time, although I had not yet escaped or been liberated from greed, hatred, and delusion, immeasurable sentient beings numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions attained nirvāṇa by making offerings to my hair and nails; how much more so today, when I have exhausted all afflictions and the fetters of delusion, greed, anger, and ignorance have all been utterly extinguished? For what reason do you not show greater reverence for these pure and undefiled hairs and nails of mine?

At that time, the merchant leader and the multitude, having heard the World-Honored One speak of these past causes and conditions, conceived a sense of wonder toward his hair and nails. They gave rise to a heart of great reverence and respect, and with single-minded devotion, they prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times, and then withdrew.
There is a verse that says:
"A group of merchants was traveling through various regions when a tree deity perceived them and addressed them, saying:
'Here is one who has attained self-benefit, the World-Honored One; you should prostrate yourselves and offer him food.'"
"Thus, World-Honored One, for forty-nine days you received no food or drink; it was only from those merchants that you first obtained this meal.
After the World-Honored One had eaten, due to the power of past karma, he suddenly suffered from abdominal distress and indigestion."

"At that time, there was a medicinal deity dwelling in the mountains who took some freshly harvested, exquisite, sweet, and delicious harītakī fruits and went to where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the Buddha's presence, she prostrated at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and said:
'World-Honored One!'"
"If there is anyone suffering from abdominal ailments, this *harītakī* fruit—freshly harvested, subtle, sweet, and delicious—is what I have now brought to offer to the World-Honored One.
If the Buddha knows it is the right time, please accept this *harītakī* for my sake; having accepted it, may you eat it out of compassion for me."
After the World-Honored One had eaten this harītakī, the ailment within his abdomen was immediately cured.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted that harītakī out of compassion for that medicinal deity; having received it, he immediately addressed the medicinal deity, saying:
"Come, you medicinal deity!"

"Take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha; you shall receive the five precepts, and through this, you will attain great benefit and much peace and happiness for a long night.
Having heard these words of the Buddha, that medicinal deity immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent!"
“World-Honored One!
I do not oppose the Buddha.
He then received the three refuges along with the five precepts.

At that time, among all the medicinal goddesses and female deities, those who for the second time received the three refuges along with the five precepts became the first upāsikās; they were the great medicinal goddesses who surrounded the female deity dwelling on that mountain.

At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the *harītakī* fruit offered by the goddess Yakṣiṇī and immediately ate it. Having eaten it, he took the seed and planted that *harītakī* seed in that very spot. By the power of the Buddha’s sovereign spiritual authority, on that very day it sprouted, developed roots and stems, grew into a great tree with branches and twigs, produced leaves and flowers, and its fruit ripened.
The World-Honored One’s internal ailment was immediately cured, and he no longer suffered from distress.

Chapter Thirty-Six: The Brahmā’s Exhortation. *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Thirty-Six, Part One: "At that time, the World-Honored One emerged from that Śālavana grove and proceeded slowly back to the foot of the Bodhi tree."

At that time, if there were men or women within the kingdom who were gravely ill, confined to their beds, emaciated by severe disease, incurable, and unlikely to recover—such that they would soon meet their end—and yet their breath had not yet ceased, they would immediately be sent to the forest to be buried there.

While the Bodhisattva was engaged in ascetic practices, there was in that forest a woman named Rāṣṭrapālī whose breath had not yet ceased; she stood before the Bodhi tree, not far from it, while her attendants had abandoned her and left her lying on the ground.

Then that woman, seeing from afar the Bodhisattva practicing austerities beneath the tree of enlightenment, felt a great sense of reverence and faith arise within her heart. Having conceived this reverence and faith, she removed her garments from her body, set them aside, and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Great Sage, Honored One!"

If you, O Benevolent One, arise from these ascetic practices and cross to the further shore of the ocean of afflictions, fulfilling your own vow, at that time—when you are freed from fear and have no clothing—you may take this rag-robe of mine for whatever use you please, out of compassion for me.

At that time, after the woman had lived out her days until the end of her life, because she had directed her mind toward the Bodhisattva and given rise to right faith, following the cessation of her breath, she relied upon those roots of goodness to immediately attain rebirth in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. There she became a celestial jade maiden, possessing great majesty and virtue, with radiant and brilliant features; having attained a celestial body, her supernormal powers were sovereign and free.
Having been born in that heaven, she thought to herself:
"By what karmic fruit have I come to achieve such a body as this?

As she reflected, she recognized her own past lives: "In the past, when I was among humans, I was in the form of a woman; I gave rag-robes to the World-Honored One for his use as he pleased. By virtue of that wholesome karma, I have now achieved such a retribution."
He further thought:

"If even I can still obtain such power of supernatural fruit as this, despite the World-Honored One not yet having accepted my rag-robe for use, how much more so for the World-Honored One—having accepted my robe for use—how could he not obtain a fruit superior to this?"

At that time, that deva, in the form of a jade maiden, emitted a supreme radiance and went to the Buddha’s dwelling at midnight. Her light shone everywhere throughout the grove of trees; having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, she prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
That goddess of the jade maidens then addressed the Buddha,
saying: "Excellent,
World-Honored One!"
"Please accept this rag-robe I have offered; use it as you wish out of compassion for me.
And the World-Honored One accepted that rag-robe out of compassion for the goddess Ratnajālinī.
Having accepted them, the Tathāgata addressed that goddess, saying:
"Come, Goddess of the Jade Maidens!
