Take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha; furthermore, receive the five precepts, and you shall obtain great benefit and great peace and happiness for a long night."
Having heard the Buddha’s words, that celestial jade maiden immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has instructed, I shall not dare to disobey.
She then received the Three Refuges as well as the Five Precepts.

At that time, the celestial maiden Yum-nu (Vasudhārā) saw the World-Honored One accept her rag-robe; for this reason, her heart was filled with great joy and immeasurable exultation, which pervaded her entire body so completely that she could not contain herself.
That goddess of the jade maidens prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and then vanished from that place, her body no longer visible.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Now that I have these robes made of discarded rags, where shall I wash them?"
Having given rise to this thought, Śakra, King of the Devas, for the sake of the Tathāgata, manifested a river not far from the grove; its waters were pure and free from any impurity.

Śakra, King of the Devas, further manifested three large boulders by the riverbank; the first stone was intended for the World-Honored One to sit upon, and the second stone was for washing the refuse-rag robes, which Śakra, King of the Devas, personally drenched with water from his own hand.
As for the third stone, after the washing was finished, it was intended to be spread out to dry.

At that time, by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the stone used for drying clothes flew through the air to Northern India, where it became a stūpa for the sake of making offerings to the merchant leader Trapuṣa and others.
"The Mahāsāṃghika masters state this:
'In this manner, one recites for seven periods of seven days in succession.
Alternatively, other masters say:"
"This matter lasted for two weeks," or again, as some masters say:
"This matter lasted for three weeks."
Furthermore, some teachers say:
"This matter took four seven-day periods.
During the first seven days, he remained beneath the Bodhi tree with a concentrated mind; during the second seven days, he gradually moved to the Animiṣa-caitya."

At that time, the World-Honored One rose from that Animisa-cetiya; having risen, he went to the foot of a Rājāyatana tree. Having reached the foot of the tree, he sat cross-legged for seven days, experiencing the bliss of liberation, remaining in meditative concentration without rising.
"At that time, after seven days had passed, the World-Honored One, with right mindfulness and right awareness, arose from samādhi.

At that moment, the two merchant leaders, Trapusa and Bhallika, set out from the city of Kāpota and gradually arrived at the place where the Buddha was. Having reached the Buddha's presence—and so on, as briefly described—they circumambulated him three times and followed behind the Buddha."

At that time, the World-Honored One rose from beneath the Rājāyatana tree and, proceeding slowly and composedly, arrived at the foot of the Mucilinda tree and sat down; having arrived, he proceeded to speak these verses.
At that time, after seven days had passed, the World-Honored One dressed in the morning, took up his bowl, and went to the home of Nandika, the village headman.
Having arrived at that house, he stood silently to one side for the sake of seeking alms.

When the village head’s daughter saw the World-Honored One standing silently by the door, desiring to beg for food, she took the bowl from the World-Honored One’s hand, brought it into her home, filled it with various excellent foods of a hundred flavors, and came out to offer it to the World-Honored One, saying these words:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One..."
"Accept this food from me out of compassion for me.
Having accepted the food offered by the woman, the village headman Sunīdhā, the World-Honored One addressed her, saying:
"Come, Sunīdhā!"
"Having received the three refuges along with the five precepts, you shall obtain great benefit and great peace for a long night.
When the girl Sujātā heard the Buddha’s words, she said to him:
"World-Honored One!"
"As the World-Honored One has taught, I dare not disobey.
She then received the Three Refuges along with the Five Precepts.
At that time, Sujātā—the daughter of the village headman—became the first among human beings to receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts once again, thus becoming an upāsikā.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted food from the daughter Sujātā; having finished eating, he sat beneath that Bodhi tree and experienced the bliss of liberation for another seven days.
At that time, after seven days had passed, the World-Honored One, with right mindfulness and right awareness, arose from samādhi.

In the early morning, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and proceeded slowly and steadily to the house of the brahmin Sāṇāyana. Having arrived, he stood to one side at the entrance of the house and remained silent, seeking alms.

When Sīyana saw that the World-Honored One was standing outside the gate, silently seeking alms, he immediately requested the Buddha’s bowl from him. Having taken it, he led him into his own home and filled the bowl with various kinds of food of a hundred flavors and various soups and stews. Holding it forth to offer to the Buddha, he further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray, World-Honored One!"
"Please accept this food from me out of compassion for me.
Having received the food from the brahmin Sona, the World-Honored One then addressed him, saying:
"Come, brahmin!"
"You should even receive the three refuges and the five precepts.
Having heard the Buddha's words, that brahmin, following the Buddha's instruction, received the three refuges up to the five precepts.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having received the food and drink from the brahmin Suyāna, proceeded gradually and composedly toward the Maṇḍa Stūpa (the "Churning Butter" Stūpa in the language of Sui). Having finished his meal, he adjusted his robes according to the Dharma and returned to the foot of the Bodhi tree, where he sat cross-legged for seven days, experiencing the bliss of liberation.

At that time, after seven days had passed, the World-Honored One, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, arose from samādhi. In the early morning, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and proceeded gradually to the place where the four sisters, his kinswomen and relatives, Sāyanāyikā, were staying.

As for the four sisters: the first was named Bharā (in the Sui language, "Strength"); the second was named Mahābharā (in the Sui language, "Extreme Strength"); the third was named Sundarī (in the Sui language, "Beautiful Woman"); and the fourth was named Kumbhakārī (in the Sui language, "Potter").
Having arrived at their home, he stood to one side and remained silent for the purpose of begging for alms.

When the four sisters saw the World-Honored One standing there in silence, they immediately approached him and requested his bowl; entering the house, they filled it with food of a hundred flavors, possessing exquisite color and form, as well as various kinds of soups and stews. Having placed these fully within the bowl, they took it and offered it to the Buddha.
Again they spoke these words:
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will accept this food of ours out of compassion for us."
Then the World-Honored One, out of compassion, accepted those four sisters' hundred kinds of food and drink; having accepted them, he immediately addressed the sisters, saying:
"Come, sisters!"
"Because you have received from me the three refuges and the five precepts, you shall obtain benefit, peace, and happiness for a long night.
Having heard the Buddha's words, the four sisters immediately addressed the Buddha,
saying, "As the World-Honored One has instructed, we shall not disobey."
They immediately received together the three refuges and the five precepts.
At that time, having accepted the offerings from those sisters, the World-Honored One proceeded slowly and steadily toward the Maṇḍana Stūpa.
Having arrived, he ate to his heart's content according to the Dharma and returned to sit beneath the Bodhi tree, experiencing the bliss of liberation for one full week.
"At that time, when the seven days had passed, the World-Honored One, with right mindfulness and right awareness, arose from samādhi."

In the early morning, having dressed and taken up his bowl, he proceeded slowly and steadily toward the nyagrodha tree planted by the sheepherder's son. Before reaching the vicinity of the tree, halfway between the Bodhi tree and that spot, he saw a cowherd woman churning curds to extract butter.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually approached the place where the cowherd woman was; having arrived, he stood silently not far from her for the purpose of seeking food.

At that time, having seen the World-Honored One standing silently not far away, the woman immediately requested his almsbowl from the World-Honored One, filled it with curd, and offered it to the World-Honored One, saying to the Buddha:
"O Great Sage, Honored One!"
"Please accept this curd from me out of compassion.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having received the curd from the woman, addressed her, saying:
"Come, sister!"
"If you receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, you will surely obtain great benefit and attain peace and happiness throughout the long night.
At that time, the woman followed the Buddha's teaching and received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.

At that time, the World-Honored One ate his fill according to his desire; having finished washing his bowl, he gradually proceeded to the spot beneath the nyagrodha tree planted by the sheepherder’s son and sat there, experiencing the bliss of liberation for seven days.
At that time, after seven days had passed, the World-Honored One, with right mindfulness and right vision, arose from samādhi.

At that moment, a certain deceitful and fault-finding brahmin suddenly approached the Buddha; having arrived, he exchanged greetings and pleasantries with the Buddha, spoke various words, and then withdrew to stand to one side.
And he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
What is it that constitutes a brāhmaṇa?"
"What is the function of the dharma practiced by a brāhmaṇa?
How many dharmas are there in total?
Having known this, the Tathāgata immediately let out such a lion’s roar and spoke these verses:
"Having eradicated all sinful karma, he is therefore called a brāhmaṇa;
pure and free from a crooked mind, he dwells constantly in right concentration, both internally and externally."
Practicing the holy life according to the Dharma, with speech and thought likewise so;
being able to remain free from craving in all circumstances—this is called the lineage of a brāhmaṇa.
"Thus, during this interval, for a total of eight seven-day periods, he did not eat at all during the first three seven-day periods.
It was only during the remaining five seven-day periods that he finally sought food."

"At that time, the World-Honored One sat in a samādhi called 'Universal Observation of the World. As the World-Honored One observed the world with his unsurpassed Buddha-eye, he saw that among the beings in the world, there were some sentient beings who, having emerged from hell, fell back into hell;
some sentient beings who, having emerged from hell, were born in the bodies of animals;
and some sentient beings who, having emerged from hell, received the bodies of hungry ghosts."
There are some sentient beings who, having emerged from hell, receive a human body;
there are some sentient beings who, having emerged from hell, receive a celestial body.
“Some sentient beings, having escaped from the animal realm, receive a body in hell;
some sentient beings, having escaped from the animal realm, are reborn again as animals;
and some sentient beings, having escaped from the animal realm, receive a body as a hungry ghost.”
There are some sentient beings who, having escaped from the animal realm, are born among humans;
there are some sentient beings who, having escaped from the animal realm, are born in the heavens.
"There are some sentient beings who, having escaped from the realm of hungry ghosts, fall into hell;
there are some sentient beings who, having escaped from the realm of hungry ghosts, return to receive the state of a hungry ghost;
and there are some sentient beings who, having escaped from the realm of hungry ghosts, fall into the realm of animals."
There may be sentient beings who, having escaped from the realm of hungry ghosts, are born among humans;
or there may be sentient beings who, having escaped from the realm of hungry ghosts, are born in the heavens.
“Some sentient beings die in the human realm and fall into hell;
some sentient beings die in the human realm and fall among the animals;
some sentient beings die in the human realm and fall among the hungry ghosts.”
There are some sentient beings who, dying from the human realm, receive another human body;
there are some sentient beings who, dying from the human realm, are born in the heavens.
"There are some sentient beings who, falling from the heavens, are born in the hells;
there are some sentient beings who, falling from the heavens, fall among the animals;
and there are some sentient beings who, falling from the heavens, receive the body of a hungry ghost."
There are sentient beings who descend from the heavens to be born among humans;
there are also sentient beings who die in the heavens and are reborn within the heavens.

At that time, the World-Honored One saw that all sentient beings were attached to various views; some sentient beings had their bodies scorched by the fire of desire, while others had their bodies heated and burned by the fire of hatred or the fire of delusion. Attached to sensual objects, they gave rise to joy and pleasure because of the affliction caused by those desires; it was the same for all [those afflicted by] hatred, delusion, and so forth.
Then the World-Honored One, seeing that all sentient beings were being consumed by the fires of the three poisons, uttered this lion’s roar:
“In this world, these multitudes of sentient beings, entangled by various attachments, diligently create karma and thereby obtain such forms; thus the body is a great affliction.”
Wherever one is attached through mindfulness, the wrong thoughts that arise therein constantly increase; as they increase, they constitute this very existence (*bhava*).
Because of attachment, there are sentient beings within the various worlds;
because of attachment, one continues to contemplate existence, thereby constituting existence.

And wherever all those sentient beings may be, in whatever state of existence they suffer the pains of existence—if one can extinguish those various pains of existence by entering into this Dharma and practicing the holy life (brahmacarya), this is called the holy life.

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, recognizing that existence is afflicted with suffering, know the transcendence of all existences, they are all said to be "unattached to all existences. Having known this, they are able to transcend all existences; thus do I speak.
Furthermore, if there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who speak of existence while desiring to be liberated from all forms of existence, I declare that none of them are truly liberated from existence.
Such a person falls into a false path; I declare that this is called undergoing great suffering.
By abandoning all false paths in the world and exhausting all those fruits of karma and suffering, once all suffering is exhausted, it is termed "non-existence."

This is the world, where sentient beings, through the view of self, are each deceived by ignorance; they take pleasure in and cling to various states of existence, and having clung to these states of existence, they are unable to attain liberation from all suffering.

Furthermore, if there is a person who observes all states of existence in every respect, yet remains not free from existence in every respect and abides in existence everywhere—since they dwell in existence, this is called impermanence, this is called suffering, and this is called unreality.
Regarding phenomena that lack substantial reality, one should observe and know them as they truly are through such-and-such correct wisdom (*yathābhūta-samyagjñāna*).

If one can observe with such correct wisdom, then all states of existence (*bhava*) will be exhausted; and once craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is exhausted, even the state of non-existence will not be mentally conceived. This is called attaining cessation (*nirodha*).

Once the bhikṣu has attained cessation, he will no longer arise in future existence, nor will he receive a future body; he is then able to subdue all Māras, achieve victory over all battles, and obtain great benefit in every respect, remaining without thought or reflection regarding any state of existence.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds,
Volume Thirty-Two and Volume Thirty-Three,
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Brahmā’s Exhortation Chapter, Part Two:
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
"The Dharma I have realized is profound; it is difficult to see and difficult to know. It is like fine dust, beyond perception, beyond the sphere of deliberation, and an inconceivable path."
I have no teacher, nor is there any skillful master capable of instructing me to realize this Dharma.

However, because sentient beings are attached to the *ālaya*—the "place of attachment" in the language of the Sui—they delight in the *ālaya*, dwell in the *ālaya*, and take pleasure in that place of attachment; for their minds are full of craving, this place is difficult to see. This place is what is called the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). These twelve links of dependent origination arise from one another in succession; yet in this very place, all sentient beings are unable to perceive it, and only a Buddha can know it.

Furthermore, in all places, the difficulty of abandoning doubt regarding the Path is overcome; all false paths are extinguished without remainder, and in every place where craving taints, one is entirely free from desire, attaining the tranquility of Nirvana.
Although I now expound such teachings as these to others, those sentient beings have not yet realized this Dharma; they merely cause me weariness and waste my words in vain.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having reflected thus, regarding this matter—which he had never heard before, had not obtained from another, and had never been spoken of by anyone—his mind discerned it spontaneously, and he spoke these verses:
"I have now attained this Dharma through arduous effort; It must not be proclaimed hastily.
Bound by the fetters of desire, delusion, and hatred, All sentient beings face this difficulty."
Only the subtle mind and wisdom that flow against the current can perceive them as something like a mote of dust;
they are difficult to see and know because they are shrouded by the darkness of ignorance.
"Because of this, after the Tathāgata had perceived this profound matter, his mind desired to dwell in an araṇya (forest hermitage), and he did not wish to preach this Dharma to others."
And there is a verse that says:
"Seeing that sentient beings have heavy afflictions, And that the paths of the heterodox and their errors and faults are many,
While the Dharma of liberation is exceedingly profound and difficult, I know this, and thus wish to dwell in an araṇya."
"At that time, Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world, while in his Brahma palace, saw from afar that the World-Honored One had conceived such a thought. Having known this, he immediately reflected:

'The sentient beings in this world have suffered much ruin and loss. Today, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, having realized such an unsurpassed jewel of Dharma and attained its fulfillment, does not yet let the world know of it; instead, his mind has suddenly turned toward delighting in the forest hermitage (araṇya), showing no desire to preach the Dharma.'"

At that time, the Brahma King, like a strong man extending or contracting his arm, vanished from the Great Brahma Palace and descended before the World-Honored One. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, addressed him, saying:
"Excellent!..."
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings in this world currently have no refuge; their goodness has been utterly ruined and lost.

Now that the World-Honored One has attained such an unsurpassed jewel of the Dharma and realized its true nature, upon seeing it, his mind suddenly desires to enter an araṇya, and he takes no pleasure in preaching the Dharma.”
I now entreat the Unsurpassed World-Honored One for the sake of all sentient beings: do not abide in quiescent stillness.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will, out of compassion, preach the Dharma; I pray that the Sugata will, out of pity, preach the Dharma.

Nowadays, there are many beings who have little dust and defilement, whose faculties are matured, whose fetters and compulsions are thin, and who possess sharp faculties and are easily transformed; yet because they do not hear the Dharma, they naturally decline.
"If the Tathāgata were to expound the essentials of the Dharma, sentient beings would be enabled to realize and know the characteristics of the World-Honored One’s teachings.
At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, having spoken these words, further requested the Buddha in verse:
"The World-Honored One now resides in the kingdom of Magadha, Expounding the various causes of sentient beings."
First he opens the wondrous Dharma-gate of the nectar of immortality, And then explains it in its pure sequence.
If a person does not ascend to the summit of Mount Sumeru, How could they ever see the limits of the world?
The Great Sage has perfected the path to Bodhi; Swiftly ascending the Dharma Hall, his eye of wisdom shines.

Guiding the blind masses to leave suffering behind, Out of compassion for all sentient beings, World-Honored One, quickly depart from beneath this tree; Wander throughout the world to bring universal salvation.
Having attained their own benefit, they are supreme among devas and humans; with all sufferings exhausted, they have attained coolness.
The Buddha neither increases nor diminishes any roots of goodness, having reached the further shore of the pure Dharma.
The Tathāgata has no peer in the world; how much less could there be anyone superior?
Walking alone through the three realms, he is called the World-Honored One; the asuras are not the equal of the King of Mountains.
You show compassion for this world of suffering; O Benevolent One, you must not now abandon sentient beings.
You who possess all virtues, powers, and fearlessness—only the Honored One can deliver all conscious creatures.
Sentient beings have long been pierced by the poisoned arrow—namely, those in the worlds of devas and humans;
having encountered the World-Honored One, they should have it extracted. May you act as their place of refuge.
Devas and humans, throughout their successive births in the world, have resolved to hear this secret Dharma-gate;
since that wish of theirs has now been fulfilled by the World-Honored One, please speak swiftly so as not to let them turn back.
O World-Honored One, if sentient beings were to know this matter as I now see it—
whether they hear it from others or hear it themselves— they would immediately come to prostrate at the feet of the World-Honored One.
Even if one's parents, children, or others should die, with their bones scattered and hair strewn about,
one does not grieve at the time of their passing, nor does one weep for those people.
They do not know that the Honored One, pure and sublime, has descended from Tuṣita Heaven;
therefore, I now entreat the World-Honored One to guide those who have long been lost on the path.
Having not heard the True Dharma for immeasurable eons, I am like a emaciated person who has obtained fat and marrow, or like parched land that receives the irrigation of water;
I only pray that the World-Honored One will let fall the rain of the Dharma.
The Buddhas have no stinginess regarding the Dharma; the sages of the three periods of time delight in practicing *dāna*.
Since the past Buddhas entered *nirvāṇa*, there has been none who did not preach this true and correct Dharma.
The Honored One is likewise of the Koliya clan, capable of delivering immeasurable sentient beings;
being no different from those Buddhas, the time has now come to teach the multitude of wholesome dharmas.
Opening the pure eyes of all sentient beings, you cause them everywhere to see the path of the True Way;
for those who have entered the thorny forest of false views, you should show the pure and direct path that leaves the treacherous trails behind,
so that by traveling this road, they may attain the nectar of immortality.
No other person is able to rescue and deliver us; the World-Honored One alone can guide us through this great peril.
Furthermore, he is able to skillfully teach us to resolve our minds [for enlightenment]; now that the time has come, we pray you will not decline.
To encounter the Sage together is impossible to expect even over many kalpas; it is as rare as the appearance of the udumbara flower.
Since the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is so difficult to meet, today we have suddenly encountered the Great Teacher.
O Benevolent One, your power of diligence is boundless; your body is adorned and complete with all the marks.
It has never happened that anyone failed to resolve their mind [on enlightenment] after hearing you speak; for from your golden mouth, words of contradiction never issue.
The accomplishment of the three periods of time has now arrived; thus today I have completed my own deliverance.
To deliver others, one must arouse the power of diligence; the vow of truthful speech should be fulfilled in a timely manner.
The World-Honored One has extinguished the darkness and kindled all lights; O Buddha, may the great Dharma-banner be swiftly raised.
The time has come; speak the True Dharma with wondrous words, roaring like a lion or the sounding of a celestial drum.
I entreat the Tathāgata to launch the Dharma-ship, so that in future ages he may guide immeasurable multitudes;
the World-Honored One has already crossed the ocean of afflictions, yet sentient beings remain submerged and must be rescued.
Just as a person who discovers a hidden treasure Holds it to enrich others rather than using it alone, So the World-Honored One has attained the inexhaustible treasury of Dharma;
I pray that you will analyze and proclaim it for the sake of all sentient beings.

At that time, having heard the verses of exhortation from the Brahma King, the World-Honored One gave rise to a heart of compassion for the sake of all sentient beings and, with his Buddha-eye, surveyed all worlds.
Having observed with the Buddha-eye, he saw that sentient beings are born into the world and grow within it; some possess sharp faculties while others possess dull faculties.

Among these sentient beings, some may easily realize the Path through their accomplishments, while others, seeing all the perils of future lives, give rise to fear and do not become negligent, for they too shall attain the Path in a future life.

For example, suppose there were ponds of blue utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka lotuses. Within them, all the various flowers—whether utpala, padma, kumuda, or puṇḍarīka—that have already sprouted from the earth but have not yet emerged from the water remain submerged and unmanifest therein; they must be nurtured through the harmony of the four great elements before they can emerge from the water.
Or there may be utpala, puṇḍarīka, and so forth, which have surged up from the pond and stand level with the surface of the water.
Or there may be utpala, puṇḍarīka, and so forth, which have emerged from the water and blossomed, yet do not cling to the water.

In this way, in this way, the World-Honored One, with his Buddha-eye, beholds all sentient beings in the world: those born into the world and growing within it, some possessing sharp faculties and some dull faculties, some easily transformed and some easily attaining the Way.
Having understood this, he addressed the Great Brahmā King with these verses:
"Great Brahmā King, listen well and attentively; I now wish to open the gate of the Deathless Nectar.
If there are those who would come with joy to hear it, Listen with a sincere heart to the flavor of my Dharma teaching."
At that time, having heard this verse, the Brahmā deity reflected thus:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, shall preach this Dharma; the Sugata intends to preach this Dharma."
"The World-Honored One has compassionately accepted my invitation because he wishes to preach the Dharma.
For this reason, joy arose in his heart, pervading him with such exuberance that he could not contain himself.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and then vanished from the Buddha’s side, his body no longer visible.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"In this place where I first preached the Dharma, who is there who can not oppose me, but instead act exactly according to my intention, understand the essence of my Dharma, and having realized it, cause me no distress?"
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"That Udārakalāmaputra possesses a mind skilled in wisdom and is discerning and intelligent; he has achieved these qualities through the long night. Although his mind still bears a slight amount of dust and defilement, his various latent tendencies and fetters are thin, his faculties are matured, and his wisdom is sharp."
"I should now first teach the Dharma before Udraka Rāmaputra; he will be able to quickly realize and understand the Dharma I have taught."
After the World-Honored One had reflected and contemplated thus, there was at that time a deva in the air who, concealing his body so as not to appear, approached the Buddha and spoke these words:
"Son of Kālāma, seven days have already passed since his death."
The World-Honored One further used his internal wisdom and vision to perceive that Udāyin had indeed been dead for seven days.
The World-Honored One then reflected:
"After Udāyin’s death, where will he be reborn?"
Then the World-Honored One’s mind again gave rise to wisdom and insight: "The son of Udumbara, having passed away, has been reborn in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
At that time, the World-Honored One further reflected thus:
"What is the lifespan in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception?"
"Is there a limit?
At that time, the World-Honored One gave rise to knowledge and vision, [realizing] that the lifespan in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception is eighty-four thousand great kalpas.
"Then, the World-Honored One again thought thus:"
“Udraka Rāmaputra, having been born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, where will he be reborn after his life there ends?
At that time, the World-Honored One gave rise to wisdom and insight, knowing that Udraka Rāmaputra was currently in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.
Having passed away from that place, they will later fall back down and be born here, receiving the body of a flying weasel (*śvāvidh*).
Once they have obtained the body of a flying weasel, they shall constantly kill the lives of those sentient beings who are born in the water, or dwell on land, or fly through the air.
Or again, having engaged in sexual acts with those various sentient beings, when his retribution was exhausted, he died of starvation.
At that time, the World-Honored One further reflected in his mind:
"After Udraka Rāmaputra abandoned his life as a flying fox, what kind of rebirth did he undergo?"
At that time, the World-Honored One gave rise to a wisdom-insight by which he knew that after Udraka Rāmaputra’s life had ended following his existence as a flying fox, he had been reborn in hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One again thought and reflected thus in his mind:
"Alas, alas! You, Udāyī Kālāma-putra, have received this body in vain; you have lost a great benefit and shall not obtain the wondrous, excellent, and wholesome retribution of the human realm."
Yet Udāraka Rāmaputra has not been able to hear such wholesome teachings as these from me.
If Udāraka Rāmaputra were to hear such wholesome teachings, he would immediately and swiftly realize this Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One again thought thus:
"For whom should I first preach this Dharma now?
When I preach the Dharma, who will not contradict my Dharma, will not trouble me, and will be able to swiftly realize my Dharma?"

At that time, the World-Honored One reflected thus within his mind, knowing that Ārāḍa Kālāma was one of extremely skillful wisdom, intelligent and subtle-minded, who had achieved perfection over a long night; although he possessed a slight degree of defilement, his fetters were thin and his faculties sharp.
"I should now go to the presence of Ārāḍa Kālāma and first teach this Dharma to him; if he hears the Dharma I preach, he will surely and swiftly realize it."
After the World-Honored One had reflected and contemplated thus, a certain deva, concealing his form so as not to appear, went to where the World-Honored One was and spoke aloud:
"That Ārāḍa Kālāma of the Kāśyapa clan passed away yesterday."
At that time, the World-Honored One gave rise to wisdom and vision, knowing that Ārāḍa Kālāma had passed away yesterday.
Then the World-Honored One further reflected thus:
"Having passed away from this life, where has the lineage of Ārāḍa been reborn?"
At that time, the World-Honored One gave rise to knowledge within his mind, knowing that Ārāḍa had ended his life in this place and was reborn in the Sphere of Nothingness (Ākiṃcanyāyatana).
Then the World-Honored One further thought:
"What is the lifespan of the devas in the Sphere of Nothingness?"
"Is there a limit to its extent?

At that time, the World-Honored One, through his internal wisdom and vision, knew that the lifespan in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is finite, being sixty-three thousand great kalpas in duration.
At that time, the World-Honored One again thought thus:
"After Ārāḍa has passed away from the Heaven of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, where will he be reborn?

Then, through the wisdom and vision of his inner mind, the World-Honored One knew that after Ārāḍa had passed away from the Heaven of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, he would fall back here to this world, being born in a remote borderland where the Dharma is unknown, and there he would become a king.
At that time, the World-Honored One again thought thus:
"As for Ārāḍa, after he passed away from his life as the king of the borderland of the ignorant, what kind of rebirth did he receive?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, through his internal wisdom and vision, knew that Ārāḍa, after the death of the King of the Borderland, had fallen into the great hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself: "Alas, alas!
You, Ārāḍa Kālāma, have received a human body in vain; you have lost much and failed to obtain wholesome benefit, for you did not hear such a sublime Dharma as this."
"If they were to hear this Dharma of mine, they would immediately and swiftly realize it.

**Chapter 37: Turning the Sublime Wheel of Dharma** *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Thirty-Seven, Part One: "Turning the Sublime Wheel of Dharma" At that time, the World-Honored One reflected thus:

"Among all beings in the world, which sentient being has pure body and speech, possesses little dust and little defilement, has thinned the fetters (*saṃyojana*), has mature faculties and sharp wisdom, and who, when I first preach the Dharma, will not trouble me but be able to swiftly realize my Dharma, without hindering my turning of the wheel of Dharma?"
At that time, the World-Honored One thought thus:
"There are five sages; those five sages were of great benefit to me in the past, for while I was practicing austerities, they attended upon me."

Those five sages are all pure, with little defilement and little dust; their fetters are thin and their wisdom is sharp. They are capable of receiving the sublime Dharma spoken by me when I first turn the wheel of the Dharma, and they will not oppose me.
"I should now go to those five seers and preach the Dharma to them first.
At that time, the World-Honored One again thought thus:
"Where are those five seers now?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure divine eye which surpasses that of humans, beheld those five sages who were currently wandering through the Deer Park in the city of Vārāṇasī.
"At that time, after the World-Honored One had dwelt by the Bodhi tree for as long as was necessary, he gradually proceeded toward the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
There is a verse that says:
'The World-Honored One, wishing to speak of Rāmaputra, Resolved his mind to observe his place of birth.'"
"Knowing now that my life has ended and I am in heaven, my mind yearns for the five sages and desires to go there.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān saw the Buddha wishing to leave this Bodhi tree and depart; his heart was filled with anguish, so he hurried to the Buddha's location. Having arrived, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent! [May you remain!]"
World-Honored One!
We only pray that the World-Honored One will not depart from this place, but remain seated without moving; with the World-Honored One here, we shall proceed as you please.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pāpīyān, saying:
"Māra Pāpīyān! You are shameless and devoid of modesty.
Previously, when you sought to disturb and confuse me, I still possessed all defilements such as greed, hatred, and delusion, which were not yet exhausted; even so, you were unable to disturb me."
How much more so today, when I have already realized the unsurpassed, most true, and equal path of awakening, having completely abandoned all deviant paths and attained right liberation?

"At that time, the World-Honored One, having risen from beneath the Bodhi tree, proceeded slowly and steadily until he reached the village of Caṇḍāla (translated in the Sui language as 'Fierce Heat').
From Caṇḍāla, he proceeded slowly and steadily to the hamlet of Caṇḍaprastha (translated in the Sui language as 'Hornless Mound')."
On the road, he encountered a wandering brahmin named Upaka (translated in the Sui language as "Coming to Meet"), whom he met face-to-face. Upon seeing the Buddha, the brahmin addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Gautama!..."
The skin of your body is quickly becoming healthy and pure, free from any impurities or oiliness.
O worthy one!
Your countenance is perfectly adorned, and your sense faculties are tranquil and composed.
"Venerable Gautama!
Who is your teacher?
Under whom have you gone forth?"
"Whose dharma is this joy of the mind that you delight in?
At that time, as he walked along, the World-Honored One spoke these verses in response to that begging brahmin:
"I have already subdued all the worlds, And have fully accomplished manifold wisdom."
Unstained by attachment among all phenomena, forever liberated from the snare of all craving,
able to manifest various supernormal powers for the sake of others— for this reason, one is called "Omniscient."
I am now worthy to receive the offerings of the world; having attained sovereign mastery, I have become the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Within all the realms of devas and humans, I alone am able to subdue the hosts of Māras.
I have no teacher; I am self-awakened within. In this world, there is no one equal to me as my peer.
Among gods and humans, I alone am the most honored. My body and mind are pure, and I have attained liberation.
I have attained mastery over all spheres of penetration; I have realized what is to be realized;
I have found rest in that which is fit for rest; Therefore, I am called the World-Honored One, supreme.
Just as a *puṇḍarīka* lotus in the water, though it remains within the water, is not defiled by the water;
so too am I in this world, unsullied by anything in the world. Therefore, I am called a Buddha.
At that time, the brahmin Upaga again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Gautama!
Where do you intend to go now?"
The World-Honored One replied to that brahmin, saying,
"I now wish to go toward the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
That brahmin again asked the Buddha:
“Venerable Gautama!
What is it that you, sir, intend to do upon reaching there?
The World-Honored One further replied to the brahmin Upaka with a verse:
"I now wish to turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma; therefore, I have come to that place of Vārāṇasī.
To bring all sentient beings from the darkness of ignorance to full awakening, I shall beat the drum of the Gate of Ambrosia."
At that time, the brahmin Upaka again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In my view, Elder Gautama!
Regarding your claim that you have personally attained arhatship and have subdued all afflictions—what is the meaning of this?"
The World-Honored One further answered that Brahmin Upaka with another verse, saying:
"You should know that I have subdued all enemies, And forever exhausted all outflows (āsrava).
All evil dharmas of the world have been extinguished; Therefore, I am called the Truly Honored One."
And there is a verse that says:
"What is so strange about gaining profit for one's own nourishment, Yet being unable to increase the benefit for others?
Seeing the masses in deep darkness, you show no compassion; Having attained the Way, you should share it with others."
Having crossed to the other shore oneself, yet seeing others drowning—if one cannot pull them out, one is no true person of virtue.
Having personally attained the treasury of the earth, yet seeing others in poverty—if one does not bestow it upon them, one lacks wisdom.
Holding the medicine of ambrosia in one's own hand, If seeing a sick person, one does not treat them;
Like traveling on a path through a fearsome wilderness, Upon seeing those who have lost their way, one should instruct and guide them.
Just as a lamp in great darkness produces light, yet its brilliance does not cling to my mind,
so too the Buddha creates the light of the Dharma, and remains unattached even to these causes and conditions.
At that time, the brahmin Upaka called out,
"Venerable Gautama!
He struck his thigh with his hand, stepped off the path to avoid the Buddha, and proceeded toward the east.

At that time, there was a deva who had previously been an old friend of the brahmin Upaga. Desiring to bring benefit, peace, and liberation into a state of fearlessness for the brahmin Upaga, the deva addressed him in verse:
"Now you have encountered the unsurpassed Teacher of gods and men, Yet you do not recognize the World-Honored One, the Truly Awakened One.
With wrong views and naked body, where do you wish to go? You shall suffer until the end of time."
If one encounters such a Teacher who tames others, yet abandons him without offering worship, what merit do your hands and feet possess?
You ought to give rise to faith in this life.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded slowly and steadily from Cūḍāmaṇivardhana (which means "The Hornless Mound") to Kalandakapura (the Sui translation for which is "Ear City");
from the village of Kalandakapura he proceeded slowly and steadily, gradually reaching Śālāstamba (the Sui translation for which is "Taming City");
and departing from the village of Śālāstamba, he arrived at Rohitaka-sūkta (the Sui translation for which is "City of Obstruction").
From the city of Saṃkassa to the bank of the Ganges River, having reached the riverbank, he approached the boatman; having arrived, he spoke to that boatman, saying:
"Excellent, O worthy one!"
"I beg you, ferryman, to deliver me to the other shore.
The ferryman replied,
"Venerable One!"
"If you would give me the fare for crossing, then I shall ferry the Venerable One across.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the boatman,
"Where could I possibly have the fare for crossing?"

I have severed all attachment to wealth and treasures; even if I were to see them again, I would regard them no differently than shards of pottery, stones, or clods of earth. If someone were to cut off one of my arms, and another were to smear sandalwood paste upon my other arm, my mind would remain equanimous toward both individuals.
"For this reason, I have no fare for crossing.
The boatman spoke again:
"Venerable One!"
"If you can provide me with the fee for crossing, I shall ferry the Venerable One across this very moment.
For what reason?
It is solely by means of this that I maintain my livelihood and support my wife and children."

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure divine eye which surpasses that of humans, saw a flock of five hundred geese flying through the air from the south bank of the Ganges River toward the north.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One addressed the boatman and spoke in verse:
"The flocks of geese crossing the Ganges Never asked the boatman for a fare;
Each exerting its own strength to carry itself, They fly through the air with ease wherever they wish."
I should now, by means of my supernormal powers, soar through the void like a wild goose;
when I reach the southern bank of the Ganges River, I shall remain securely established and steadfast as Mount Sumeru.
At that time, having seen the Buddha pass by, the boatman felt great remorse in his heart and thought to himself:
"Alas, alas! Having beheld such a Great Sage, a field of merit, I did not know to offer alms so as to cross over to the further shore."
"Alas, alas! I have lost a great benefit.
Having thought thus, he fainted and fell to the ground.

Then that boatman, having been dazed for a short while, regained his composure; rising from the ground, he immediately hurried to King Bimbisāra, the lord of Magadha, and reported these matters to him.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha, having heard this matter, spoke as follows:
"How can ordinary people know whether one possesses supernatural powers or lacks them?"

Therefore, from this day forward, whenever any person who has left the household life comes seeking ordination, do not inquire as to their right or wrong; provided they have come, do not accept any fee for ordination, but ordain them immediately according to their wish.
At that time, the World-Honored One flew across the Ganges; having reached the other shore, he again performed a supernatural feat, soaring through the air toward the city of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, there was a dragon pond in that place, and its dragon king was named Śaṅkha (translated into Chinese as *shéngqié*, meaning "conch").
The World-Honored One arrived at the edge of that pond and descended.
Wherever the World-Honored One set foot, the Dragon King erected a stūpa; because of this, the stūpa was named Miciga (translated in the Sui language as "Earth Stūpa").
The Tathāgata stayed there for one night, awaiting the time for his subsequent meal.
At that place where he had waited for the time, another stupa was erected, which was named the Stupa of Waiting for the Time.
There is a verse that says:
"The Buddhas do not enter among humans at night; They must wait for the time of the meal to beg for food."
"One who acts at the improper time has great afflictions; therefore, the noble ones wait for the right time.

At that time, the World-Honored One, relying on the *samaya* [the occasion] when the Magadhan fast was about to begin, entered the city of Vārāṇasī through the western gate and went on his almsround in due order.
Having received alms-food by begging in Vārāṇasī, he departed calmly through the eastern gate of the city.
Once outside the city, he sat upright by the side of a body of water and ate his meal.
Having finished eating and washed his hands, he proceeded northward, moving with steady composure toward the Deer Park.
There is a verse that says:
"The birds and beasts of the Deer Park raise their voices in chorus; This is the dwelling place of the sages of old."
“The World-Honored One’s body emits a brilliant radiance, gradually approaching that grove like the sun-god.
At that time, the five seers saw the World-Honored One from afar as he drew near; having seen him, they said to one another:
“Elders, we have made a solemn vow: this person who is coming toward us is that śramaṇa Gautama of the Śākya clan.”
"This indolent person has lost his meditative concentration; because of his indolence, his entire being is shrouded in bondage.
We have no need to show him respect, no need to pay him homage, no need to go out to meet him, and no need to offer him a seat."
"Nevertheless, let us follow our own inclinations and sit according to our own preference.
Only Kauṇḍinya alone had a mind that did not agree with this vow, yet his mouth did not dissent; he sat facing them and spoke these verses:
"Gautama has now suddenly arrived, indolent as he is; we five sages have each reached a mutual agreement."
"None among us shall pay him respect or prostrate; this man has broken his vow and is not worthy of being welcomed.

At that time, as the World-Honored One gradually drew near the five sages, once he was close by, those five sages each sat so restlessly that they suddenly broke their own vow and each desired to rise.
For example, it is like a śakuni bird inside an iron net while someone outside sets a great fire ablaze;
because the net is hot, the bird cannot remain at ease, but desires to fly away and leap about.
In this way, as soon as those five sages saw the World-Honored One, they involuntarily rose from their seats all at once.

Among the five sages, some were arranging and setting out seats; some were holding water, intending to wash his feet; some were bringing the foot-washing stone and leather sandals; others were bringing forward basins filled with water; some, having finished washing his feet, were bringing wooden stands intended for him to place his feet upon;
and others were receiving his three robes and alms bowl, while exclaiming aloud: "Welcome, Elder Gautama!"
"Sit comfortably upon this mat.
And there is a verse that says:
"Either receiving the bowl and the three robes, Or else prostrating at the Buddha's feet,"
"Or they may have prepared a seat in advance, or brought water vessels and bathing flasks.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat down calmly upon the prepared seat.
When the Buddha had finished sitting, he reflected thus:
"All of these are deluded people; although each has made such a vow, they act in contradiction to it and do not abide by it."
At that time, when the five sages saw the Buddha seated, they addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Gautama!
Your physical complexion and skin are exceptionally beautiful and pure; your countenance is full and radiant, and your faculties are tranquil and composed."
“Venerable Gautama!
You must have encountered the exquisite nectar of immortality, or perhaps attained the noble path of the pure nectar of immortality.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those five sages, saying:
"O you seers! Do not address the Tathāgata as 'Elder. Why is this? "
"You, O sages! In the long night of the future, you shall encounter suffering and affliction. Why is this?"
I have now realized the Dharma of the Deathless; I have now attained the Path to the Deathless.
Follow my instruction and listen to my words; I am able to teach and guide you all.

Follow my words and do not deviate from them; if you act in accordance with my instructions and practice with purity, then that son or daughter of good family who, with right faith, has left the home life, shaved off their hair and beard, and gone forth seeking the unsurpassed holy life (brahmacarya), shall reach the source of the holy life, perceive all phenomena directly, attain mastery in supernormal powers, and realize the fruits of practice. They will be able to declare for themselves: "Birth and death have been severed; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence in future lives."
"You each should know for yourselves in this way.
And there is a verse that says:
"Those five seers called out the Buddha’s clan name, And the World-Honored One, out of compassion, taught them, saying:"
"Do not harbor arrogance in your minds; abandon self-conceit and pay homage to me.
I am equal toward those with pride and those without pride. I wish to transform the karmic causes of you all;
having already attained Buddhahood as the World-Honored One, I act for the benefit of all sentient beings."
Having spoken these words, the five sages addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Gautama!

In the past you practiced this practice; in the past you sought this path; in the past you underwent this austerity, yet you never attained the state of a superior person, nor did you attain the wisdom and vision shared by the noble ones, nor did you achieve any further progress."
"How much more so today, when you have become indolent, lost your meditative concentration, and are bound by sloth?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again to those five sages, saying:
"You sages, do not speak such words."
The Tathāgata does not engage in the conduct of indolence, nor has he lost his meditative concentration; I, too, am not bound by the fetters of indolence. O you seers!
I have now become an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha; I have now realized that nectar and know the path to nectar.
"You, O sages!
You should receive my instruction and listen to my Dharma.
If you now accept my teaching and guidance, I shall be able to instruct and admonish you."
"Rely upon my teaching; do not contradict my teaching; practice my dharma-teaching, and you shall eventually attain the state where there is no further existence.
At that time, the five seers again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Gautama!"

In the past, I practiced in such a manner and sought the Way in such a way; I underwent such austerities, yet I did not realize the supreme Dharma, nor did I share the same wisdom and vision as the noble ones, even falling into indolence which entangled my own person.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those five sages three times, saying: "O you sages!
Do you yourselves know whether I have ever previously spoken false words when among people?"
The five sages replied,
"No, Venerable One!"

At that time, the World-Honored One extended his tongue from his mouth until it reached both ear canals and both nostrils. Having used his tongue to block both nostrils, he then used his tongue again to lick his own tongue, covering his entire face. Having covered it, he withdrew it and returned it to its original position at the base of the tongue.
Once it was settled, he addressed the five sages, saying: "O you sages!..."
"Have you ever seen with your own eyes, or heard with your own ears, that a person who speaks falsely possesses such supernatural power of the tongue?
Those sages replied, "No."
"Venerable ones!
Therefore, you must not call the Tathāgata indolent; nor has the Tathāgata lost his meditative concentration. However, I am not bound by the fetter of indolence."
"O Sages!

You should know that I have now become an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha; I have realized the Deathless (amṛta) and know the path to the Deathless. You should receive my teaching and instruction, listen to my teaching, and practice according to my teaching. If you do not go against it, those sons of good family and daughters of good family who seek liberation, having left their homes to renounce the world, shall ultimately not undergo further existence."
At that time, the World-Honored One instructed those five seers with such teachings.

All the externalist appearances, externalist intentions, and externalist treasuries possessed by those seers were entirely extinguished and vanished from sight. The robes they wore upon their bodies immediately became the three dharma-robes (trīcīvara), and they held alms-bowls in their hands. Their hair, beards, and whiskers fell away naturally, as if seven days had passed since they had been shaved. Their majestic deportment was perfected; their appearance was like that of a bhikṣu of a hundred summers. Their dignified bearing, their walking, sitting, rising, and moving about, were all established in this manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those five bhikṣus, saying:
"O bhikṣus! Each of you, according to your respective capacity, observe the eastern direction."
At that time, the five bhikṣus, wishing to look toward the east, saw the west.
The World-Honored One spoke again: “You, bhikṣus!
"Each of you should observe the western direction to the best of your ability.
When those bhikṣus wished to look toward the west, they saw only the east.
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"O bhikṣus! Observe the northern quarter.
Those bhikṣus, wishing to observe the northern quarter, instead saw the southern quarter.
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"O bhikṣus! Observe the southern direction."
He immediately saw the northern direction.
The World-Honored One spoke again: "You bhikṣus!"
"Observe the zenith.
He immediately saw the nadir.
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"O bhikṣus! Observe the region below.
Those bhikṣus, wishing to observe the region below, instead saw the region above.
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"O bhikṣus! Observe the other directions, each according to your own capacity."
Those bhikṣus, wishing to look toward another direction, then saw the cardinal directions.
The World-Honored One spoke again: "You bhikṣus!"
"Observe the cardinal directions.
Those bhikṣus, wishing to observe the cardinal directions, instead saw the other directions.

At that time, the World-Honored One skillfully instructed those five bhikṣus, causing joy to arise within each of their hearts, leading them to realization, bringing them into accord with the True Principle, and filling each of them with gladness.

At that time, the five bhikṣus’ minds were opened and their intentions were liberated; they followed the World-Honored One, consulted with him, and received his teachings. They conformed to the World-Honored One’s mind and did not deviate from the Dharma he taught. Having heard his words, they accepted them with sincerity and attended upon the World-Honored One without ceasing for even a moment.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll Thirty-three;
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll Thirty-four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on Turning the Sublime Wheel of Dharma, Part Two:
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
"In what place did the Buddhas of the past—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—turn the unsurpassed, subtle, and sublime wheel of Dharma?"
At that time, once the World-Honored One had formed this thought, the earth immediately and spontaneously surged upward, distinct from all other regions.
Then, the World-Honored One again reflected thus:
"In what manner did the Buddhas of the past—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma?"
"Should I turn [the wheel] while seated, or should I turn it while lying down?
At that moment, as soon as the World-Honored One had formed this thought, five hundred high lion-thrones immediately appeared in that place.

When the World-Honored One saw these five hundred seats, he immediately gave rise to a heart of reverence; out of respect for the past World-Honored Ones, he circumambulated the three high seats three times, then approached the fourth seat, ascended it, and sat cross-legged, like a lion who is neither fearful nor perturbed.
Then the five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare indeed, World-Honored One!
Since so many Buddhas have now come together to preach the Dharma, why are there so many high seats?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed the five bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
You should now know this!"
Within this Bhadrakalpa, five hundred buddhas have appeared in the world; three buddhas have already passed away into parinirvāṇa, and I am now the fourth to appear in the world.
"The others shall continue to flourish and manifest in the future.
At that time, the World-Honored One again thought thus:
"Did the Buddhas of the past—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—turn the golden wheel, the silver wheel, the crystal wheel, or the lapis lazuli wheel?"
Will you turn the wheel of red pearls, the wheel of agate, the wheel of musaragalva, the wheel of amber, the wheel of coral, the wheel of the seven jewels, or will you turn the wooden wheel?

At that time, as the World-Honored One was reflecting thus, there arose within his mind a vision born of his own wisdom, whereby he knew that past Buddhas—Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—had turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma by means of the twelve aspects of dependent origination through the sequential three turnings based upon the Four Noble Truths.

And within this world, there is no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, nor any among the devas, māras, or the Brahmā world—no single sentient being—who is able to thus turn the wheel of Dharma with such sovereignty and fearlessness.

"At that time, during the fifteenth day of the month of the lunar mansion Jyeṣṭhā, when more than half of the twelfth day had passed and the shadow was cast, at such a moment called Vijaya (translated in the Sui language as 'Difficult to Conquer'), facing north and coinciding with the conjunction of the lunar mansions Mūla and Rohiṇī, the World-Honored One turned the unsurpassed, pure Wheel of Dharma."

Among all those in the world—whether śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, celestial māras, or brahmās—none are able to turn such a wheel of Dharma as this. One turns the wheel on the day of the lunar mansion Abhijit (Háng), preaching the Dharma without obstruction; it is for worldly reasons that this particular day is used.

"At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the five bhikṣus with a voice such as this: the Tathāgata possesses a voice that is well able to instruct and well able to console; it teaches without deficiency and teaches with reverence; it is neither crooked nor sycophantic, neither ornate nor coarse, neither flowery nor plain, but gentle, compliant, and harmonious."

It is skillfully executed, neither lax nor hurried, free from obstruction, truly sublime, artfully distinct, flowing with sweetness, pleasing to the hearts of all, unturbid and stainless, and indestructible.

Peerless, free from defilement and pure, having long since practiced constant relinquishment, it is neither lost nor diminished; without fetters and without bonds, it is liberated and radiant, neither impoverished nor insatiable, and likewise not weak.

It can bring happiness to all sentient beings; it can provide moisture to the bodies of all sentient beings; it can awaken the minds of all sentient beings; it can sever the mind of desire, sever the mind of hatred, and sever the mind of delusion; it can subdue all Māras, destroy all transgressions, and completely overcome all non-Buddhists.
“The World-Honored One’s voice is well able to instruct others; it is like the sound of a drum, like the voice of Brahmā, and like the song of the kalaviṅka bird.”

It was like the voice of Śakra, like the sound of ocean waves, like the sound of an earthquake, like the resonance of Mount Kunlun, and like the calls of the peacock, the kokila bird, and the kalaviṅka bird.

It is like the voice of a king of geese, like the cry of a crane, like the roar of the lion, the king of fierce beasts; it is like the sound of the *vīṇā*, the lute, the five-stringed zither, the *kinnara* lute, the flute, and other such instruments—those who hear it are able to bring all to joy.

The instructions are clear and distinct; those who hear them do so with joyful intent. They are subtle and profound, lacking nothing in any respect, capable of causing sentient beings to cultivate all roots of goodness, so that for those who hear them, it is not in vain.

The characters are distinct and radiant; the phrases and sentences are clear and manifest; the meanings and functions are profound and subtle; the treasury of Dharma is true and real. It accords with the proper time and occasion, conforms to the *samaya*, and bestows [teachings] without missing the right moment. It knows the faculties and dispositions of all beings, follows the words of the Dharma, and is adorned with various kinds of giving. Its precepts are pure, its patience is receptive, its diligence is courageous and fierce, its meditations are tranquil and stable, its supernormal powers are swift and powerful, and its wisdom discerns the good and evil of the world. Through loving-kindness it accomplishes happiness, through compassion it is free from weariness, and through sympathetic joy and equanimity it brings about renunciation.

He establishes the three vehicles, perpetuates the lineage of the Triple Gem, distinguishes the three groups of beings, and purifies the three gates of liberation. His speech is truthful and instructive, praised by the wise and approved by the sages; it is immeasurable and boundless like space, reaching everywhere and endowed with all excellent marks.
With such a voice, the World-Honored One addressed the five bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
Those who have left the household life must always renounce two worldly matters."
What are these two?
First, the enjoyment of sensual pleasures: whatever activities involve dependence upon a village, which are praised by worldlings—these must be abandoned.

Regarding the second type of relinquishment: that which causes one's own person distress, being a place of suffering not praised by the Noble Ones, wherein one neither attains self-benefit nor benefits others—such phenomena must be relinquished.
And he spoke in verse:
"Quickly abandon that which harms one’s own body; One must relinquish all sensory realms.
If one can relinquish these two kinds of things, One will immediately attain the nectar-like, true, and correct Path."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should know this!

Having thus abandoned those two extremes, I have taught the Middle Way, which I myself have realized through direct knowledge. It is for the sake of opening the eyes, for the sake of producing wisdom, for the sake of tranquility, for the sake of the superknowledges, for the sake of full awakening, for the sake of being a śramaṇa, and for the sake of nirvāṇa; it is by means of this that one achieves fulfillment."
"O bhikṣus!

If you wish to know the middle way leading out of existence, as I have realized it—for the sake of opening the eye, for the sake of generating wisdom, and for the sake of tranquility, even unto nirvāṇa—it is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."
"O bhikṣus! This is the middle way, which I have realized and known;

it is for the sake of opening the eye, for the sake of generating wisdom, for the sake of tranquility, for the sake of developing the various supernormal powers, for the sake of full awakening, for the sake of being a śramaṇa, and for the sake of nirvāṇa—it shall be brought to fulfillment."
And he spoke in verse:
“By these eight kinds of causes for the right path, The terrors of birth and death are entirely extinguished.
Once all karmic actions have been extinguished, One shall never again undergo any further rebirth.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You bhikṣus! Listen with a sincere and attentive mind!"
There are four noble truths.
What are the four?

They are the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering; these are called the four kinds of noble truths.
“Monks, what characteristics are called the Noble Truth of Suffering? They are:

the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of sorrow and lamentation, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of encountering the hated, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.”
Because of these various sufferings, it is called the Noble Truth of Suffering. "Monks,
what is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering?

"That which is this craving, which causes the mind to fluctuate repeatedly, gives rise to thoughts of desire, and dwells upon objects everywhere—this is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering. "O Bhikṣus!"
What is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering?

It refers to the detachment from and relinquishing of that craving, its total eradication and extinction without remainder, and the complete stillness and tranquility of both mind and mental formations; this is what is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.
“Monks! What is called the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the cessation of suffering?

It is the attainment of this Eightfold Noble Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is called the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the cessation of suffering.”

"This is the noble truth of suffering; regarding this, from time immemorial, I have not heard it from another, but within all phenomena, I have spontaneously given rise to vision and knowledge, I have given rise to intention, I have given rise to clarity, I have given rise to resolve, and I have given rise to wisdom."
"This is the noble truth of suffering; it must be known thus. ... [omitted] ...

"In regard to these dharmas unheard before, vision, wisdom, and so forth arose; that noble truth of suffering has already been fully illuminated and known. (The Sanskrit original repeats this phrase; here, only the essential portion is extracted.)

"Thus, regarding this noble truth of the origin of suffering, through hearing it from no other, vision and knowledge arose among all phenomena; that dharma of the origin of suffering must be entirely extinguished."
In this way, even up to the noble truth of the origin of suffering, it has been completely extinguished.
"Thus, regarding the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, through no other's hearing, there arose within me vision and knowledge concerning all phenomena."
"That noble truth of the cessation of suffering must now be realized.
Thus, until wisdom has arisen, one attains the realization and full knowledge of the exhaustion of the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.

"In this way, having ceased the noble truth of the origin of suffering, one attains the noble truth of the path; without hearing it from another, within all phenomena, there arises the eye and wisdom."

Regarding that suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the realization of the path to its cessation—up to the arising of wisdom and the return to the extinction of that suffering—the four preceding chapters all repeat this path.

“O Bhikṣus! As long as I had not yet realized these four noble truths through their three turnings and twelve aspects according to reality, I had not attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor could it be said that I had awakened to them.”

“O monks! It was by realizing these Four Noble Truths through three turnings and twelve aspects according to reality that I attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it is only then that one may say, ‘I have awakened.’”
“Monks! At that time, I gave rise to knowledge and vision; with a mind undistracted, I attained liberation. Monks!”
"This is my final birth; I shall no longer undergo further existence.

When the Buddha had spoken these words concerning the characteristics of the Dharma, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya, while sitting right there, became free from dust and defilement, cast off all fetters, and purified all afflictions.
Regarding all phenomena, one attains the wisdom of the pure eye; all conditioned formations that have arisen are completely extinguished.
Having known the extinction of phenomena, one realizes it as it truly is.

Just as a clean cloth, free from stains and without black threads, takes on whatever color it is dyed with, even so, at that very seat, Kātyāyana’s defilements were all removed and his afflictions utterly extinguished; he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye and knew things as they truly are.
At that time, sixty thousand devaputras in the assembly were distanced from dust and freed from defilement; they also attained the pure eye of wisdom regarding all phenomena.
Then, the World-Honored One let out a lion’s roar and spoke these verses:
“The ineffable Dharma is profoundly deep; True Suchness is tranquil and nameless.”
"The most excellent Kauṇḍinya has realized it first; the path I sought has not been attained in vain.
And there is a verse that says:
"When this most profound Dharma was being taught, the most excellent World-Honored One acted out of compassion."
"Kauṇḍinya has attained the pure Dharma-eye, and there are further billions of devas.
At that time, all the devas dwelling on earth, having heard the World-Honored One speak such characteristics of the Dharma, simultaneously raised a great cry, saying:
"O worthy ones, each of you should know!"

Today, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park, the dwelling place of the sages of old, turning the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous Wheel of Dharma.
"Whether they be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, Brahmā, or Māra, none in truth are able to turn such a wheel of Dharma.
And he spoke in verse: "How excellent!
The World-Honored One perceives true thusness, And for the sake of the multitude turns the ambrosial wheel of Dharma."
With morality and meditative concentration as its spokes, rim, and hub-nut;
with shame, remorse, and diligence as its axle, linchpin, and hub—this wheel of profound, non-dual, and perfectly true teaching was established by the Honored One of the Three Realms.
It now stands at the outskirts of the city of Vārāṇasī, and is thus turned within the Deer Park.

At that time, after the gods dwelling on earth had uttered these words, the sound ascended to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. Having heard it, the Four Kings in turn proclaimed the sound, and within that sound they spoke thus:
"Today, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī, turning the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous Wheel of Dharma."
"In all the worlds, whether among śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, or among Brahmā or Māra, there is truly no one who can turn it back.

When the Four Heavenly Kings made this sound, the Trāyastriṃśa gods heard it; when the King of the Trāyastriṃśa made this sound, the Yāma gods heard it; when the Yāmas made this sound, the Tuṣita gods heard it; when the Tuṣitas made this sound, the Nirmāṇarati gods heard it; when the Nirmāṇaratīs made this sound, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods heard it; and when the Paranirmita-vaśavartins made this sound, the Brahmā kings heard it.
Then Brahmā, King of the Gods, spoke these words:
"Today, the World-Honored One—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—is in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, turning the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous Wheel of Dharma."
"In all the worlds, no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, Māra, or Brahmā can truly turn it back.

In this manner, in the space of a single thought-moment, the news was passed from one deity to another among the gods above until the sound filled everywhere, reaching even as far as the realm of Mahābrahmā.
At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, having heard the sound, again uttered such a Brahma-voice, proclaiming:
"Today, the World-Honored One, the Buddha, the Bhagavat, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is turning the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous Wheel of Dharma in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī."
In all the world—whether among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, māras, or brahmās—there is truly no one who can turn [the wheel] in such a manner according to the Dharma.
"In this manner, [the light] proceeded in succession up to the Heaven of the Summit of Existence.

At that time, when the World-Honored One was about to turn the Wheel of Dharma, all the devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, as well as the entire world, were universally illuminated by a great radiance."
Between the Cakravāḍa Mountains and the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, there is a realm of profound darkness and gloom where all sentient beings undergo extreme suffering.
Yet these sun and moon, with such radiance, such great virtue, such supernormal powers, such majesty, and such sovereignty, are unable to illuminate or bring light to that place.

By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, that region is universally illumined; because the sentient beings therein obtain this light, they are able to see one another, recognize one another, and say to one another:
"Furthermore, there are sentient beings here as well"—these two phrases are repeated in the Sanskrit original.

"At that time, all the trees, hundreds of species of herbs and medicinal plants upon the land of that world, all followed their proper seasons; according to their respective kinds, large or small, each produced its own stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits. Once produced, the flowers spontaneously rained down upon the Buddha as an offering."

The sky was pure and clear, free from dust, mist, smoke, or clouds; a light cloud briefly arose, sending down a fine rain that sprinkled the earth—the rainwater was cool and possessed the eight meritorious qualities.

After the rain had ceased and the sky cleared, a gentle breeze arose again; it was cool and temperate, and all four directions were pure, appearing with vivid clarity and free from any dust or obscuration.

The devas of the upper realms gathered in the void, performing celestial music and singing sublime heavenly songs; they rained down various kinds of *mandārava* flowers, as well as *mahāmandārava* flowers.

Furthermore, there rained down exquisite celestial garments, and seven-jeweled lotuses made of heavenly gold, silver, and lapis lazuli; there also rained down immeasurable *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, which fell upon the Tathāgata.
Moreover, there rained down immeasurable varieties of mixed incense, powdered incense, and unguents, which were scattered over the Tathāgata, scattering again and again after each scattering.
In the area surrounding the Tathāgata’s seat for one *yojana* on all four sides, various kinds of flowers completely filled the space without any gaps.
