Furthermore, this great earth shook in six ways: it moved, moved everywhere, and moved equally everywhere; it trembled, trembled everywhere, and trembled equally everywhere; it surged, surged everywhere, and surged equally everywhere; it roared, roared everywhere, and roared equally everywhere; it quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere; and all sentient beings experienced nothing but great bliss.

At that time, there was not a single sentient being who suffered from desire, hatred, delusion, pride, or arrogance; they were neither startled nor terrified, and not a single sentient being committed any transgression.
If sentient beings are afflicted by illness, they shall immediately be cured;
if sentient beings suffer from hunger and thirst, they shall immediately be satiated;
if sentient beings are intoxicated by wine, they shall immediately regain their sobriety.
Sentient beings who were deranged all regained their original minds;
the blind gained sight, and the deaf gained hearing;
those whose six sense organs were incomplete all became fully endowed with them.
May all sentient beings who are poor, cold, and naked become wealthy and abundant;
may all emaciated sentient beings become full and robust;
and may all sentient beings who are imprisoned and bound attain liberation.
Sentient beings bound by stocks, manacles, fetters, and shackles shall naturally be released;
sentient beings in the hells shall immediately have their afflictions extinguished;
and sentient beings among the six domestic animals shall be free from fear and alarm.
As for the sentient beings who are hungry ghosts, they attain meditative concentration through hunger and thirst.
By such causes and conditions, Kauṇḍinya received the name "One Who Has Realized Wisdom.

At that time, the Elder Kauṇḍinya perceived all dharmas as they truly are, knew all dharmas as they truly are, and realized all dharmas as they truly are. He truly crossed the perilous path of afflictions, crossed the shoals of afflictions, and reached the ground beyond doubt. His mind was resolute and free from obstruction; having attained fearlessness, he no longer relied on the teachings of others.

At that time, Kauṇḍinya, understanding his practice of the Dharma, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent!
“World-Honored One!
I have entered the Buddha’s Dharma; may the World-Honored One deliver me, ordain me as a śramaṇa, and grant me the full precepts, so that I may become a bhikṣu.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kauṇḍinya, saying:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!
Enter my Dharma; practice the holy life (brahmacarya) so as to bring an end to suffering.
At that moment, the Elder Kauṇḍinya immediately went forth and attained full ordination.
The other four bhikṣus each expounded the essentials of the Dharma and instructed them according to their individual capacities.
Among that assembly, three bhikṣus had gone out to beg for food, so only two bhikṣus received the teachings;
later, when those three returned with their alms-food, there were six people in total who sat together to eat.

Having received the Dharma teachings and instructions of the Tathāgata and accepted them, at that time, next there was an elder named Badarikā (translated in the Sui language as "Lesser Sage"), and the elder following him was named Vappa (translated in the Sui language as "Arisen Spirit"). These two, while still seated, became free from dust and defilement; they exhausted all fetters and delusions, purified the realm of afflictions, and attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena. All their fetters and delusions were entirely extinguished, and they realized and understood, according to reality, the impermanent nature of all things.
Just as a clean cloth, free from black threads and free from grease, takes on whatever dye it is intended for and perfectly receives its color;

even so, while the Elder Bāṭikā and the Elder Vāṣpa were seated there, they became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye. Briefly stated, they then achieved renunciation and received full ordination.
"In this manner, as they proceeded in succession, those who came later to beg for alms were taught according to the Dharma and gathered in according to the Dharma.

When the World-Honored One had thus manifested the Dharma, the elder Mahānāma (translated in the Sui language as 'Great Name') and the elder Aśvajit (translated in the Sui language as 'Horse-Tamer'), while sitting right there, became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena."
In this very way, the Elder Mahānāma and the Elder Aśvajit, while sitting right there, exhausted the defilements of affliction and realized it as it truly is.

Having personally realized the characteristics of all phenomena for themselves and transcended those characteristics, they were free from further doubt and reached the stage of fearlessness, no longer relying on what was heard from others.

Having attained knowledge and realization within the Buddha’s Dharma, they rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined before the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“We pray only that the World-Honored One [grant us this].”
“Grant me permission to leave the household life and bestow upon me the full precepts.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the two bhikṣus, saying: “You, bhikṣus!”
"Welcome! Enter my well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, practice the holy life, and bring an end to suffering.
At that time, the two elders immediately became renunciants and received full ordination.
And there is a verse that says:
“Kauṇḍinya of lesser wisdom who has aroused his energy, Mahānāma, and Aśvajit—
these were the first to realize and see this Dharma-door of the Tathāgata’s drum of ambrosia.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those five bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
Because I have constantly practiced right mindfulness day and night, and having practiced with right conduct, I have attained and fully realized and known unsurpassed, perfect, and true liberation."
"You, bhikṣus!
You should learn from me to form such a thought and practice right conduct; you too shall attain this unsurpassed, true, and perfect liberation, and you shall realize it for yourselves."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas went to where the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying. Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, he addressed the Buddha in verse, saying:
“Gautama, you are entangled by sensual desire—by all the desires of devas and humans alike.
Now that you have entered this great bondage, I shall certainly not release you, O śramaṇa.”
At that time, the World-Honored One reflected and knew that this was the Māra Pāpīyān speaking. Having thus reflected and known it, the World-Honored One immediately replied to Pāpīyān in verse:
"I have long been liberated from the entanglements of craving; I am entirely free from both celestial and human desires.
Since I have already escaped these great bonds, How much more so you, who were previously defeated by me?"
At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the Buddha, Māra Pāpīyān remained silent and thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama!..."
"You know my thoughts and conduct,
O Śramaṇa son of the Śākyas!
You see the state of my heart."
Immediately, he became despondent and distressed, finding no joy; in that very place, his body vanished and was no longer seen.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the five bhikṣus, saying:
"O bhikṣus! You all..."

If one knows that all forms are without self, then those forms will not manifest the characteristics of affliction and destruction; one shall not undergo suffering. One should see them thus, and one should know them thus.
Thus, there is form; because form is without self, all form can give rise to vexation and form can give rise to suffering.
Although it gives rise to suffering and vexation, one cannot find a fixed nature in form.
Since form is not fixed, one cannot wish that form be thus, nor can one say that one wishes it to be otherwise.
As it is with form, so it is with feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

“O bhikṣus! You should know that within consciousness (vijñāna) there is likewise no self (ātman). If consciousness were to have a self, this consciousness would not cause affliction nor cause suffering; for the essence of consciousness is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.”
How could one possibly bring about such existence?
Nor can one wish for such non-existence.

Because consciousness is without self, consciousness is able to produce affliction and suffering; since consciousness is fundamentally non-existent, one cannot wish for consciousness to be thus existent or thus non-existent.
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think? Is consciousness permanent?"
"Is it then impermanent?
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This consciousness is impermanent.
The Buddha asked again:
"Since consciousness is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?"
The bhikṣus said:
"World-Honored One!
This consciousness is suffering."
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Since consciousness is suffering, impermanent, and subject to destruction, it is not the true Dharma and is not eternally abiding.
If one can perceive consciousness in this way, then one may engage in such reflection:"
"Is that mine, or am I that, or do I see 'I' as being mine?
The bhikṣus replied, "No,
World-Honored One."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should know this!
Regarding all forms—whether past, present, or future; internal or external; coarse or subtle; superior or inferior; near or far—one must never entertain such thoughts toward them as follows:"
"This is mine, this am I, this is my self"— in such a manner, one must apply right knowledge according to reality as it is,
to all feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, whether past, future, or present; internal or external.
Regarding coarse and subtle, superior and inferior, distant and near consciousnesses, they do not form such thoughts: "I am this, that is mine," or "I am I."
"In this way, in this way; through such true and right vision, you should understand it thus.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "You should know!"
If there is a learned śrāvaka who is able to contemplate and perceive in this way, they will cultivate weary detachment toward form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
having become weary and detached, they will find no pleasure in anything;
and with a mind that finds no pleasure, they will attain liberation.

Having attained liberation, one should give rise to this knowledge: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence after this. Thus do I know.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this Dharma, the five bhikṣus, amidst conditioned phenomena, extinguished all outflows (āsrava) and their minds attained liberation.
At that time, there were six arhats in this world: one was the World-Honored One, and five were bhikṣus.
Later, the Tathāgata bestowed this prediction upon them: "O bhikṣus!..."

If one knows that at the time I first turned the wheel of Dharma and preached the teaching, he who was foremost in not contradicting my instruction was the leader of the five seers—namely, the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare it is, World-Honored One!
What roots of goodness did the elder bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya cultivate?"
"For this reason, those who do not contradict the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma that the Tathāgata has first turned shall be so.
Having spoken these words,
the Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"O bhikṣus! Listen with a sincere and attentive mind.
I recall that in the past, here in this very city of Vārāṇasī, there was a potter."
At that time, there was a pratyekabuddha who was afflicted by an illness. Desiring to cure his ailment, he entered a village.
As the summer retreat was about to begin, the pratyekabuddha went to a potter for the sake of medical treatment; having arrived there, he spoke to the potter, saying:
"O virtuous potter!"
"If you do not decline, I would like to entrust myself to your home for the duration of this summer retreat, so that I may rest and recover from my illness.
Then, with a pure heart, that potter addressed the Pratyekabuddha, saying:
"Excellent, Great Sage!"
"This statement does not contradict [my intent]; you may stay as you please.
I shall provide for the Great Sage according to my ability, offering the four requisites.
Then that potter, for the sake of the Pratyekabuddha, constructed a small dwelling not far from his home and gave it to him to sit in, providing bedding and mats, a fly-whisk, and lamp oil.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha entered the fire-samādhi during that very night.
When the potter saw the great blaze of light, he thought to himself:
"Why does this lamp burn so fiercely and bright, yet does not go out for so long?"
“Has that grass hut not been consumed by fire?

At that time, the potter, with slow, steady, and light steps, approached the grass hut and secretly observed it from a distance. He saw the Pratyekabuddha sitting cross-legged, like a great mass of fire emitting blazing light, yet his body remained solemn and was not scorched or burned.
Upon seeing this, the potter quickly looked back, ran away in haste, and returned home; thereafter, his faith doubled and he felt a sense of rare wonder.

That Pratyekabuddha Arhat remained in the potter’s house, dwelling in such tranquility for the duration of one summer retreat, maintaining himself during the *anvaya* (rainy season). The potter provided him with all four requisites, serving and honoring him with everything he required.

Furthermore, he took physicians and sent them to treat his illness; whatever medicines were required for his cure, he provided them all, yet he was unable to alleviate or heal the physical ailment of that Pratyekabuddha.
That Pratyekabuddha, having fallen ill due to his physical condition, subsequently passed away.

At that time, the potter saw the body of that venerable Pratyekabuddha enter parinirvāṇa; having seen this, he was despondent, sorrowful, and unhappy, weeping and shedding tears, crying out in lamentation and calling it a grievance.
At that time, immeasurable and boundless people, having heard the sound of the potter’s wailing, went to him and asked: "O potter!
For what reason do you thus cry out 'Alas' and weep?"
Then that potter explained to those people the causes and conditions for the pratyekabuddha’s supernormal powers:
"This seer was so diligent and so observant of the precepts, constantly practicing the sublime Dharma, that even when I brought a physician to treat him, he could not be cured."

“At that time, there were another group of pratyekabuddhas—fewer by one than five hundred—who, carrying sandalwood, flew through the air by means of their supernatural powers and arrived there. Having completed the cremation of that pratyekabuddha’s body, they consoled the potter, saying:
‘O virtuous potter!’”
Your heart should give rise to joy and exultation that pervades your entire body.
Why is this? Since you have made offerings to this rishi’s person, by this merit you shall obtain great and wholesome benefit in future lives.
"Have you seen our supernatural powers?
The potter replied, "I have."
At that time, those pratyekabuddhas spoke again to the potter, saying:
"Just as the supernatural powers we have displayed, so too are the supernatural powers of this rishi; among us, he is the eldest."
Then that potter immediately asked those pratyekabuddhas, saying,
"Venerable ones, where do you currently reside?
The pratyekabuddhas replied to the potter, saying:
"From here, there is a village named Rājagṛha. Not far from that city is a mountain called Ṛṣipatana, where we dwell and reside."
At that time, the potter addressed those Pratyekabuddhas, saying:
"Welcome, O Sages!
Accept my household meal; when you have finished, depart as you please."
At that time, all those pratyekabuddhas accepted his offering of food. Having finished eating, they said to the potter:
"In a future age, a Buddha will appear; you should, before him, resolve your mind and make a vow, relying upon this merit and pure heart."
Having heard this, he immediately addressed those sages, holy ones, and pratyekabuddhas, saying:
"O venerable sages!

My former teacher was the eldest and most senior among us; may I likewise, in a future age, encounter the Tathāgata Śākyamuni and, upon entering the monastic order within his teaching, become the most senior elder when I have grown old."
The seers replied,
"May this vow of yours be surely fulfilled. Then,
having made this vow to the potter, those pratyekabuddhas departed from that place, flying through the air.

Having seen the Pratyekabuddhas and others soaring through the air and traveling by means of their supernormal powers, the potter, with a pure mind, observed their conduct, joined his ten fingers and palms together, and prostrated before them.

At that time, the potter, seeing that the body of the Venerable Pratyekabuddha had entered parinirvāṇa, collected his relics and erected a stūpa. He adorned the stūpa, affixing an exquisite *cakra* (wheel) on top; within the wheel he suspended bells, and with silk banners and streamers, as well as various flowers, he offered incense—burnt incense, powdered incense, and ointment incense—as an act of worship.
He made this vow:

"By means of these roots of goodness, may I, in a future age, encounter that Tathāgata Śākyamuni; may I realize and know the Dharma he teaches, and may I become the greatest and most senior śrāvaka among his followers."
"O monks, you should know!
The potter of that time is none other than this Venerable Mahā-Kauṇḍinya, the bhikṣu.
Because of the power of the roots of goodness from his past offerings to that pratyekabuddha, he has now attained realization upon hearing the very first teaching from me."
I further grant this prediction: among all the members of the Saṅgha, he shall be the first to realize the Dharma and act in accordance with my mind; he who went forth first is the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya.

Chapter 38: The Causes and Conditions of Yaśodharā The Mahāvastu-Avadāna, Chapter Thirty-Eight (Part One): The Causes and Conditions of Yaśodharā At that time, not far from the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a nyagrodha tree. Its branches spread wide and its foliage grew thick and luxuriant. All the people within and outside the city—including princes, ministers, and the various officials—would all, at the proper times, offer sacrifices, serve, and make offerings to that tree.
Whenever anyone comes to that tree to make a request, they say:
"May this wish of mine be fulfilled exactly as desired; may whatever I undertake be successfully accomplished."
"If I accomplish such a matter, I shall perform a sacrifice to repay this debt of gratitude.

Those people, whether their karmic seeds from previous lives were pure, or because their power of merit was strong and they had accomplished those causes, or seeking immediate retribution, followed their own thoughts and said, "This tree can grant me my wish. When that person arrived, they made a great offering to repay the favor.
Furthermore, there are other individuals who come to make requests; their wishes are likewise fulfilled.
If, moreover, someone comes to that tree and begs for a son or daughter, they shall obtain a child through the causal conditions of their own prior karma and merit.
Those people each thought to themselves,
"Those trees can grant us sons and daughters. Thus,
they came and each performed great sacrifices and made grand offerings to repay those trees.
All the people of that forest gave the trees a name, calling them "divine trees that grant every wish upon being petitioned.
At that time, there was a most eminent and wealthy elder in that city named Sujāta.

That elder possessed vast wealth and resources, with power and influence at his command. He owned countless livestock—namely elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, camels, as well as donkeys and mules—of which he lacked nothing. His stores of the five grains were abundant, and he had many servants, slaves, musicians, and concubines, as well as merchants and laborers. He was fully endowed with pearls, amber, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, agate, white jade, conch shells, gold, silver, copper, and coin; all things were complete, and there was no deficiency whatsoever.
The house of that elder was just like the palace of Vaiśravaṇa, the Great King of the Northern Quarter, without any difference whatsoever.
At that time, the elder had no sons or daughters, and all his kinsmen and visitors spoke thus:
"O worthy elder!..."

If you, O benevolent one, know for yourself that your family is immensely wealthy and possesses great power—briefly stated, everything is fully provided—and yet within your household there is no offspring;
however, outside this city, there is a divine tree named "Granting All Wishes," such that if any man or woman comes to it to beg for a son or daughter, they shall obtain one.
"Elder, why do you not go to that tree and beg for sons and daughters?
If you were able to beg for them, you would surely obtain sons and daughters without doubt; do not allow the lineage of your noble family to be severed."
Then, that elder replied to all his kinsmen, saying:
"How could such a thing be possible?
Those trees are without consciousness and without feeling; it is impossible for them to grant the wish for a son or daughter."
Generally, whether one obtains a son or a daughter is due to the karmic causes and conditions of the parents' prior deeds, or perhaps through the power of merit.
Yet those people say:

"We each personally made earnest prayers by that tree and thereby obtained a son or a daughter. Because our wishes were fulfilled, we go to that tree and perform great offerings to repay its kindness."
Then the relatives and kinsmen of that householder, for a second and even a third time, earnestly entreated him, saying:
"O Great Householder!..."
"You must not disbelieve this. That tree is truly able to grant such wishes; it has already provided sons and it has already provided daughters.

Householder, simply go there. That tree can fulfill the heart's desires of those who seek them: if you seek a son, you shall obtain a son; if you seek a daughter, you shall obtain a daughter. This is certain and beyond doubt."
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll 34;
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll 35.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on the Causes and Conditions of Yaśodharā, Part Two:

"At that time, the great wealthy elder Sujāta, having repeatedly and earnestly exhorted his kinsmen to reason with her, even up to the third time, offered bitter and urgent admonitions. Yet, the elder’s resolve remained unyielding; he then took his household servants and brought along large axes, winnowing baskets, shovels, hoes, as well as spades, mattocks, and various kinds of knives and saws. He went to the location of the tree, and upon arriving, stood before it and spoke these words:
'O Tree, you must know!'"

"I have heard from others that you are a divine tree, named 'The Attainment of All Desired Vows,' such that if anyone comes to beg for a son or daughter, their wish is always fulfilled. Yet I have not had a single child; though my heart longs for one, my desire remains unfulfilled."
"I now beg of you: if you allow me to give birth to a fine son, I shall come to provide such offerings and repay you in this way.
If you cannot grant me a son, I shall take this great axe, spade, and pickaxe to hew and dig up your tree—roots, branches, and all—and I will never let you go."

Even down to leaving behind only remnants like the roots and fibers of *mārga* grass; if you dig into the earth to take your roots and stalks, I shall chop them into pieces; if I take your branches and twigs, I shall mince them bit by bit. Having thus hacked, severed, and sliced you, I shall dry you out thoroughly in the sun, then carry you to a fire and burn you to ashes.
Once you have become dust and ash, I shall either cast your ashes into a swift, rushing river against the current, or blow your ashes apart in all directions with a fierce, mighty wind.
“At that time, there was a deity dwelling in that tree. Upon hearing these words, the deity was seized with great terror; distressed and unhappy, he thought to himself:
‘I truly do not produce sons or daughters for others. Rather, when people come here, they obtain sons and daughters through their own karmic causes and their own power of merit.’”
Those people said, "This tree can grant us sons and daughters; once we have obtained our wish, we shall later come to repay the tree's kindness.
Then that tree deity, weeping with streaming tears, spoke these words:
"This is the tree where I have dwelt since birth. Because that elder has failed to obtain a son, he will surely destroy this tree of mine."
That tree spirit, who constantly served Śakra Devānām Indra, then quickly went to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the palace of Śakra Devānām Indra.
Having arrived, he knelt down and addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying: "O Great and Virtuous Heavenly King!
Regarding the words spoken by the elder previously when he sought his son—concerning the fortune or misfortune, the good or evil that might result—"

I only pray that Great Heaven, through your skillful wisdom and expedient means, will act with such diligence and swiftness as to provide this upright young man for the elder, lest he perish beneath this tree of mine.
At that time, Śakra, the Great King and Lord of the Devas, addressed the tree spirit, saying: "O tree spirit!
Do not speak such words."
Why is this? Even I am currently unable to definitively grant sons or daughters to those in the world; rather, such people obtain sons and daughters through their own causes of merit.
Although this is the case, O tree deity!
Be patient for a moment and do not give rise to distress; I shall examine whether that householder possesses the necessary conditions.
At that time, there was a certain son of heaven among the Trāyastriṃśa gods who manifested the five signs of decay; it was certain that he would soon fall back into the world.
What are these five signs of decay?
First, the exquisite flowers upon his head suddenly withered and turned yellow.
Second, sweat flows from beneath the armpits of those devas;
third, the garments worn by those devas become soiled and impure;
fourth, the majestic radiance of the bodies of those devas naturally undergoes transformation.
Fifth, that celestial being, who constantly resided upon a subtle and exquisite jeweled couch, suddenly became displeased and moved hither and thither.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, the Lord of Devas, spoke to that son of heaven, saying:
"Well done, O son of heaven!"

If you recognize the proper time, you possess virtuous conditions and have planted many roots of goodness; you are constantly diligent, cautious and fearful of transgression, free from all faults and calamities, and do not commit any wrongs. Furthermore, since you have never committed grave evil karma, it is solely due to jealousy that you must now fall away from this place and be reborn among humans in a favorable realm.
Then the devaputra said to Śakra:
"I wish to hear of that place.
Śakra replied:

"Now, in this world below, on the land of Jambudvīpa, there is a great city named Vārāṇasī. In that city, there is a great elder named Suprabuddha; that elder’s household is immensely wealthy and possesses abundant resources and great power, lacking nothing whatsoever, yet he has no son."
"You have now resolved to go to Vārāṇasī and become a son for him.

At that time, this devaputra had attained the body of a deva in past lives, having planted various roots of goodness as the causes and conditions for liberation from birth and death. He was oriented toward nirvāṇa and turned his back on afflictions; he did not grasp at the various realms of existence and did not crave birth within any conditioned phenomena. Throughout that single life, he desired to attain the exhaustion of outflows and to realize the Noble Path.
Then that devaputra addressed Śakra, saying:
"Great and Virtuous Lord of Devas!
I now do not wish to dwell in a household to enjoy worldly pleasures."

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra will, before long, descend from that Tuṣita heaven and take birth by descending his spirit into the womb of the chief queen of King Śuddhodana within the Śākya clan at Kapilavastu; he shall enter the womb through her right side and be born when the months are complete."

Having been born, he will renounce the royal throne and leave the household life; he shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), and having attained it, he shall turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
I intend to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of that bodhisattva.

However, that householder possesses great wealth and precious treasures at home, along with many powers and all manner of abundance; yet, as for that householder’s place of indulgence and negligence, it is not my intention to go toward him or arise there.
At that time, Śakra, the Great King and Lord of Devas, spoke thus to that son of heaven:

"Simply make a vow to seek birth in that family; before long, the Bodhisattva Guptamati shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), and having attained it, he shall turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma."
"At that time, I shall personally bring about the conditions for your renunciation and also assist you in the matter of leaving the household life.
Then, that deva-son replied to Śakra,
saying, "Excellent, O Heavenly King!"

"If at that time, the King is able to assist me in such a way regarding the causes and conditions for my resolve to attain enlightenment, so that it may be fulfilled, I shall be born into that family.
At that time, Śakra, the Great King of Devas, replied to the tree deity of the Nyagrodha tree, saying:
"O virtuous tree deity!
If you know the time has come, you should quickly inform that householder and say to him:
"Excellent, householder!
The son for whom you have prayed shall soon be born, and he will be handsome."
“Not long after his birth, he will leave the home life to become a renunciant and act as a śramaṇa.
At that time, having heard these words from Śakra, the tree deity was filled with great joy; she leaped for joy so completely that she could not contain herself.
He went quickly to the house of that great elder; having arrived, he remained in the air, concealing his body so as not to appear, and spoke to the elder, saying:
"O Great and Virtuous Elder!"

"You shall certainly give birth to a son who will be wise, handsome, and possessed of merit; however, as soon as he is born, he will surely leave his home and renounce the world to become a śramaṇa before long."
At that time, the elder replied to the tree deity, saying:
"Excellent, O celestial being!
I only pray that as long as I live, I may employ skillful means so that I do not abandon my home to become a śramaṇa."

At that time, the devaputra descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and entered the womb of the elder’s wife. Once he had entered the womb, the woman immediately became aware of it and said to the elder:
"O great and virtuous elder!..."
"You should rejoice, for I have conceived.

When the elder heard these words, he immediately established for his wife the most excellent methods of nursing, providing her with the finest bedding, the finest ornaments, the finest attendants, the finest food and drink, and the finest clothing, so as to provide for her and allow her to enjoy herself.

"At that time, the householder established an unobstructed assembly outside the four city gates of Vārāṇasī at a crossroads where many people gathered. To those who came seeking anything, he gave food to those who sought food, drink to those who needed drink, garlands to those who desired garlands, incense to those who asked for incense, and even ointments to those who required ointments."
To those who required bedding and mats, he immediately provided bedding and mats; to those who required the necessities of life, he gave them all in full.
At that time, all the wealth and property within his household were collected into the inner treasury, and all wine shops and slaughterhouses were completely abolished.

At that time, the householder’s wife, having reached either nine or ten months, her fetus fully matured, gave birth to a son who was exceedingly handsome and rare to behold. His body was golden in color, like a pillar of gold; his head was perfectly round like a parasol; his nose was like that of a parrot; his long arms hung down; his limbs were well-proportioned and straight; all his faculties were complete; and his flesh was soft and supple, like a mass of fresh butter.
Once that son was born, a subtle canopy made of the seven precious jewels spontaneously manifested above him; and all those people of the world who saw it cried out in unison:
"How rare! How extraordinary!"
"Never before have we seen such a sight.
At that time, the elder appointed four nurses for the boy:
the first to hold him, the second to bathe him, the third to give him milk, and the fourth to play with him.
After the boy was born, the elder constantly established an unrestricted assembly (*anivārita-pūjā*) outside the four city gates and at the crossroads, just as he had previously arranged.
Furthermore, he gathered his inner and outer kinsmen and said to them:
"I have now fathered such a son; you all must bestow a name upon him."

His kinsmen deliberated together: "From the moment this son was first born, a precious canopy appeared spontaneously above him. Because of these causes and conditions, his fame has spread throughout all lands; therefore, this son should be named Upacāru (The One with the Canopy Above)."
Thereupon, later generations collectively called him Yaśodharā; "Yaśodharā" means "Umbrella of Excellence" (*śreṣṭhacchatra*) in the language of Sui.

To his parents, Yaśodharā was their only son; they loved and cherished him so dearly that he never left their hearts. They desired to gaze upon him constantly, raising him before their very eyes so that he might grow up easily observed and easily nurtured.
And there is a verse that says:
“The person of merit grows swiftly, Just like fruit trees planted in fertile soil;
One of meager fortune, little aid, and lacking auspicious marks, Is like planting various trees at the edge of a road.”

As that boy gradually grew up and became able to walk, he was later instructed in various skills according to family tradition and taught the practice of crafts, namely writing, arithmetic, and the making of seals and marks.

He dispenses wealth to others, receives and accepts goods from abroad, engages in trade and commerce, dyes various colored silks, tailors clothing, distinguishes between different types of incense, identifies the five grains, and discerns the seven treasures as well as all manner of precious objects.

All such things as these he had thoroughly trained in; there was nothing he did not understand deeply. He was skilled in arts, quick in eloquence, sharp-witted and intelligent, having achieved complete mastery such that no one could equal him.
When he reached adulthood, his father wished to have him live separately.
At that time, his father built three halls for the youth:
one intended for the winter retreat, one for the spring and autumn seasons, and one for the summer retreat.
If one intends to sit in the hall during winter, it will be consistently warm;
if one intends to sit during summer, it will be consistently cool with a breeze;
if one intends to sit during the two seasons of spring and autumn, it will be neither hot nor cold, but harmonious and moderate.
Within those three halls, all utensils and garments are composed of a mixture of various precious jewels; all food and drink are most excellent and sweet, such as the heart delights to behold.

His various garments and manifold ornaments, as well as diverse powdered incenses and ointments, were all arranged in their proper places. He stationed beautiful and charming court ladies to provide him with entertainment. Within his palace, before the halls and pavilions, various stairways were established; at each stairway stood five hundred men carrying five hundred precious tables, which they set out as soon as the sun rose and withdrew after sunset.

"Surrounding that hall, five hundred men stand guard and keep watch; their bodies are all clad in sturdy armor, and they hold swords and clubs, or carry iron wheels, tridents, and other weapons, prepared for defense.
Each of the three types of halls is likewise so equipped."

Fearing that the youth Yaśoda might suddenly abandon his home to go forth into homelessness, they made all the doors and bolts inside and outside the hall secure; the sound of those gates opening and closing could be heard for half a yojana.
At that time, Yaśodharā was in that palace hall, fully enjoying the pleasures of the five senses and sporting at her ease.

Then, after the World-Honored One had first turned the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma in Vārāṇasī, Śakra, King of the Devas, descended from the heavens and arrived within Yaśodharā’s palace. Having arrived, he awakened Yaśodharā, saying:
"O virtuous Yaśodharā!"
"The time for your benevolence has now arrived; you must surely, before long, renounce the household life to become a monastic.
When Yaśodharā heard these words from Śakra Devendra, she accepted them in silence.
Having silently accepted [the invitation], at daybreak he sought a carriage drawn by four horses, intending to go to the park to inspect the auspicious site.

At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One donned his robes and took up his alms bowl, entering the city of Vārāṇasī in a composed manner, desiring to beg for food, with the Elder Aśvajit serving as his attendant.

Yaśodharā saw from afar the Tathāgata approaching; his deportment was upright and dignified, his gait was steady and composed, his body was complete, and he was adorned with all the marks of excellence, like the sky filled with stars.

Having seen him, his heart was filled with joy and purity; with that inner heart of joyful purity, he descended from his chariot, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and having finished the circumambulation, returned to the chariot and proceeded on his way.
Not long after Yaśodharā had seen the Tathāgata return, the Buddha, knowing her pure heart, let out a subtle snort and emitted a radiance.

At that time, the Elder Aśvajit adjusted his robes and stood upright; baring his right shoulder, placing his right knee upon the ground, and joining his palms in reverence toward the Tathāgata, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"
"For what cause and condition do you smile and emit light?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Aśvajit, speaking these words:
"O Bhikṣu! Do you see this youth Yaśoda?
He came to my side, prostrated at my feet, circumambulated me three times, and then withdrew to mount his carriage."
Aśvajit immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
I have already seen it."
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Listen attentively now!
This great son of good family, Yaśodharā!"
Tonight he will certainly renounce his home to enter the homeless life; he will come to me and beg to become a śramaṇa, and having become a śramaṇa, before long he will attain the fruit of arhatship.
Then Yaśodharā entered the park, surveyed the auspicious grounds, and began to walk back and forth in meditation.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, by means of his supernormal powers, immediately conjured the corpse of a dead woman; her body was bloated and on the verge of rotting away, with flies, maggots, and various insects feeding upon it in every place.
At that time, Yaśodharā saw that corpse so foul and putrid; having seen it, a sense of loathing arose in her heart, and she thought to herself:
"In this foul and putrid body, what is there to find pleasure in or to give rise to attachment, such that one would become self-indulgent?"
"Furthermore, within this, how could one give rise to the perception of pleasure?
It is now already festering with pus.
Thereupon, he cried out:
"I no longer take pleasure in this foul and loathsome enjoyment," he thought, wishing to return home.

As the youth emerged from the grove and re-entered his own hall, and while he was about to fall asleep during the first watch of the night, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, used his supernormal powers to cause all the court ladies to fall into a deep sleep. Within the house, lamps were lit everywhere, each as large as an arm, illuminating everything with a magnificent and brilliant light that left no darkness.
"At that time, during that night, the World-Honored One had this thought:
'During this very night, the great son of good family Yaśodhara will, with resolute courage, renounce his home to leave the household life and seek to become a śramaṇa.'"

Having reflected thus, he went to a river named Pārāṇa (translated in the Sui language as "Elimination"), crossed over to the other bank, gathered grass himself and spread it out; having spread the grass, he sat down cross-legged, intending to sleep for one night out of compassion for the young man Yaśoda.

At that time, Yaśodharā, who was fast asleep, suddenly woke up of her own accord and saw that lamps the size of an arm were placed everywhere within the hall, and she saw that all the court ladies were fast asleep.

Some of the court ladies had small drums suspended from their necks; some court ladies held lutes (vīṇā) under their arms; some court ladies held five-stringed instruments; some court ladies embraced kōṅhōu harps; some court ladies held drums against their arms; and some court ladies held flutes, pipes, and various other musical instruments in their hands.
Some of the court ladies slept with half their bodies exposed and panting;
some slept with their hair disheveled and their heads tilted to one side;
and some slept with impurities such as flowing tears and saliva.
Some of the court ladies slept with their teeth clenched together, making a sound;
some slept with their faces covered;
and some slept with their faces turned upward.

When Yaśodharā saw all the court ladies within the hall sleeping thus, covering the floor like corpses with no difference whatsoever, she immediately conceived a sense of revulsion and a sense of great affliction.
In her heart, she desired to seek the thought of nirvāṇa, and she wished to establish her mind upon the path toward nirvāṇa.
And he forms this thought:
"This so-called 'great' is a place of terror!
Alas, this so-called 'great' is a place of disturbance, unrest, resentment, and aversion!"

When Yaśodharā had seen this, she suddenly rose from her bed, put on leather sandals adorned with various jewels—their value being two hundred thousand [pieces of gold]—and having done so, she thought to herself as she was about to descend from the hall: "I have reached the edge of the hall's foundation, yet there is no staircase."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately brought forth a staircase and set it before him; his body emitted a radiance, and this light shone everywhere throughout the palace.

When Yaśodharā saw this brilliance, she emerged from the hall and gradually approached her father’s quarters where the ladies-in-waiting were gathered. Upon arrival, she saw that within the hall where her father lay, lamps made of fine fragrant oil had been prepared; their wicks were as thick as an arm, and they were placed all around the floor and the pillars.

Seeing all the court ladies fast asleep, with their musical instruments still suspended as described above, appearing just like corpses in a cemetery, he conceived a sense of weary detachment upon seeing them, and even gave rise to extreme terror.
At that time, Yaśodharā emerged from her father’s hall and gradually approached the outer gate. She saw that the outer gate was bolted and its locks were very secure;
yet when she opened the door, the sound resounded so far as to be heard for half a yojana.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, swiftly opened the gate, making it vanish so as not to produce a sound, fearing that obstacles might arise at the moment Yaśodharā went forth into homelessness.
Then Yaśodharā, having departed from her home, arrived at the great city gate named Bhadravatī—which means "Noble Lord" in the language of Sui.
When she reached that Bhadravatī city gate, it was closed and its bolt was very firm; the sound of it could be heard from as far as half a yojana.
At that moment, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, opened that gate in the space of a single thought-instant and concealed that sound so that others would not hear it.
He thought to himself:
"Let no one obstruct Yaśodharā’s karmic conditions for renunciation."
Then, Yaśodharā emerged from the city gate and gradually reached the Pārā river.

At that moment, the waters of the river suddenly surged in a violent flood, rising until they levelled with the banks and filled them completely, so that all the birds had to drink by lowering their heads into the water.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately caused that radiance to vanish.
When Yaśodharā reached this bank of the river, she stopped there and cried out:
"What a great affliction! Alas, what a great terror!"
At that time, the World-Honored One was walking up and down on the open ground on the far bank of the river.
Out of compassion for Yaśodharā, the World-Honored One emitted light from his body and extended his golden arm toward her, saying these words:
"Welcome, welcome!"
"O Yaśodharā! This place is free from affliction;
this place is free from fear; this place is peaceful and blissful; this place is one of sovereignty.
And there is a verse that says:
“Having perceived his mind, the Tathāgata spoke these words aloud:
‘Come, come, Yaśodharā! Take this path to fearless nirvāṇa.’”
There is nothing the World-Honored One does not see; there is nothing the World-Honored One does not know.
Therefore, he is able to know that other’s mind; thus it is said that the World-Honored One is endowed with all clear insights (vidyā).
At that time, having heard these words from the World-Honored One, Yaśodharā was immediately freed from all mental distress and sorrow, and she attained concentration of mind.

It is like a person traveling on a road during the late spring who, afflicted by the heat and suffering from extreme exhaustion, hunger, and thirst, suddenly encounters a pond. Its water is cool and refreshing; entering within it, he bathes and drinks, thereby extinguishing all the sufferings of his feverish afflictions.

In this way, indeed, when the great son of good family Yaśoda heard these words of consolation from the Buddha, all the distress and affliction in his mind were extinguished, and his heart attained tranquil stability.
At that time, the great son of good family Yaśoda felt joy arise in his heart; he leaped for joy immeasurably, and this rapture filled his entire body so completely that he could not contain it.
He cast off those leather sandals made of various precious gems, worth two hundred thousand [pieces of gold], and proceeded on foot toward the Pārāṇaka River.
It was as if a person were to discard phlegm or saliva and walk away without further thought.
"It is even so, it is even so. Yaśodharā’s casting aside of her leather sandals was likewise; she entered the river and crossed over, at which time the waters of that river became shallow for her."
At that time, Yaśodharā, having successfully crossed the river and reached the opposite bank, arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was.

From afar, Yaśodharā beheld the World-Honored One, whose dignified deportment was perfectly composed and whose appearance was worthy of admiration; his faculties were tranquil and his mind was fixed in right concentration. His body was further adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, like the stars filling the expanse of space. Having seen him, she gave rise once more to pure joy. Having experienced this joy, she gradually approached the Buddha’s presence. Upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, she prostrated herself at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

"At that time, having seen Yaśodharā standing to one side, the World-Honored One immediately preached the Dharma to her in successive order: namely, he spoke of the practice of giving, the practice of observing the precepts, and further, the practice of the causes and conditions for rebirth in heaven; he described the faults and afflictions of the five desires, how the outflows are not yet exhausted and defilements still remain, and he praised the pure Dharma of renunciation."

The World-Honored One knew that Yaśodharā’s heart had already given rise to joy, had already conceived a sense of wonder, and that her mind was now supple, unimpeded, and capable of receiving the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One, employing the Buddha’s words that gladden others and lead them to attain the Way, preached the Dharma to him—namely, the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. As he was thus speaking to Yaśoda, at that very seat, Yaśoda became detached from dust and defilement, exhausting the realm of afflictions.
Having become free from afflictions, the pure Dharma-eye arises regarding all phenomena; all fetters and delusions are completely extinguished, and they are realized and known as they truly are.

Just as a clean cloth, free from all black threads, takes on the dye immediately upon immersion, even so, at that very seat, the mind of the noble son Yaśodhara was freed from dust and defilement; he exhausted all afflictions and realized everything exactly as it is.
At that time, when the wife of the noble son Yaśodhara awoke from her sleep, she suddenly found her husband Yaśodhara nowhere upon the bed.
Because his mind was preoccupied with Yaśodharā, and he was further filled with longing, yearning, and deep affection for her, he went at once to his mother’s side; having arrived, he said to her:
"O Noble Mother!..."
Do you know now whether the Holy Mother loves her son Yaśodharā?
Last night, when the bride woke from sleep and sought him out, he was suddenly nowhere to be seen; we do not know where he has gone.

At that time, having heard these words, the Holy Mother, out of pity, remembrance, and love for Yaśodharā, wept with distress and hurried to the side of Yaśodharā’s father, the great householder. Upon arriving, she addressed the great householder, saying:
"Householder!..."
"Do you now know where your beloved son Yaśoda is?
Each [of them] replied exactly as the bride had described.

At that time, having heard that Yaśodā was missing from the palace, and because he was preoccupied with the memory of his son Yaśodā, the elder dispatched messengers in haste to the wise men, the astrologers, the gamblers, and the brothels, telling them: "Go and search for him."
"O you people!
You should go with all haste to such-and-such a place to seek out my son Yaśodhara and bring him here.
At that time, the messengers went to the four crossroads of the city of Vārāṇasī, shook their bells, and proclaimed as follows:

"If there should be anyone who can tell me of Yaśodharā’s sight, who knows the place where Yaśodharā is located and the path she has traveled, such that they may let me see her and let me hear from her."
"I shall beg from that man an object worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
Then, during the latter part of the night, he ordered the city gates to be opened and dispatched messengers to gallop forth, proclaiming everywhere:
"All of you, go swiftly outside the city and search for my Yaśodharā!"

"At that time, during the night when the sky was about to dawn, Yaśoda’s father, the elder, filled with grief and despondency, weeping and shedding tears, quickly went toward the city gate of Bhadrāvatī; having arrived, he immediately emerged."

Gradually proceeding, he saw the tracks of Yaśodharā’s leather sandals; having seen them, he followed the traces of the sandals until they ended. At the riverbank, he saw leather sandals worth two hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. Regaining some measure of his composure, he immediately thought:
"My beloved son Yaśodhara must not yet be dead."
He let out a great sigh and thought to himself:
"If his body has died, these leather sandals should long since have ceased to exist.
Then, having seen the leather sandals, the householder neither touched them nor took heed of them; he cast them aside and departed.
Just as a person, seeing the tears or spittle of another, neither looks at it nor takes note of it, but passes by having cast it aside;
even so, the father of the noble son Yaśoda, seeing those sandals made of the seven precious gems, cast them aside and passed by, immediately crossing the Pārana River to search for his son.
At that time, from afar by the riverbank, the World-Honored One saw the father of the noble son Yaśoda approaching toward the Buddha. Having seen him, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"This father of the noble son Yaśoda has come seeking his son; out of affectionate concern, he may perhaps act impulsively and, without regard for propriety, embrace the body of the noble son Yaśoda."

"I should now manifest my supernormal powers; for if I perform such feats of supernatural transformation while the noble son Yaśodhara’s father is here, he will only be able to see the face of the noble son Yaśodhara with his own eyes, and I shall then cease [the manifestation] so that we do not come into contact."

At that time, the father of the noble son Yaśodhara saw from afar the World-Honored One, whose majestic deportment was perfectly composed and who was upright and pleasing to behold—indeed, like the sun and moon adorned by the stars in the sky. His heart was filled with joy, and with a joyful mind, he went to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived at the Buddha's dwelling, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Great Virtuous Śramaṇa, have you perhaps seen my son Yaśodhara come here?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed the elder, saying:
"O wealthy elder!
If you know the proper time, sit down for a moment in tranquility; before long, you shall behold Yaśodharā."
At that time, the householder thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa should not speak falsely; what he says must be true."

Having heard these words, his heart was filled with joy; he leaped for joy so intensely that he could not contain himself. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and having stood there, [he remained].

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately taught the householder the Dharma through successive skillful means as was appropriate, namely, the practice of giving (*dāna*), and how all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and afflictions (*anuśaya*) are completely extinguished, which he then realized through direct knowledge according to reality.

Just as a clean cloth easily takes dye, even so, at that very seat, the householder was freed from dust and defilement; he realized the truth as it is, attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, crossed the ocean of afflictions, transcended all hindrances, became free from doubt, reached the state of fearlessness, and no longer relied on what was heard from others.
Having heard the Dharma teachings from the Blessed One, he took refuge in the Buddha, took refuge in the Dharma, and took refuge in the Saṅgha, and further received the five precepts.

At that time, among the humans there, that great householder was the very first to become a lay follower (upāsaka); he was one who, within his human existence, accomplished the three refuges through the "three declarations," namely, the father of the young man Yaśoda.

At the time of the preaching of the Dharma, Yaśoda’s son, the noble youth, thus realized and thus practiced, attaining the path and seeing that all outflows were exhausted; his mind attained liberation amidst all phenomena.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"The father of the young man Yaśoda has heard the Dharma and attained insight; having realized the exhaustion of outflows as they truly are, his mind has attained liberation. He ought not to remain at home and experience the five desires as he did formerly when he was a householder."
"I shall now withdraw my supernormal powers.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One immediately withdrew his supernormal powers. Having withdrawn them, Yaśoda’s father sat right there and beheld his son; having seen him, he addressed Yaśoda, saying: "Son Yaśoda!"
"Your mother remembers you and suffers great anguish; she weeps for you and grieves for you. Do not cause her to lose her life on your account!
You may go there and restore her life."
Having spoken these words, the noble son Yaśoda immediately gazed upon the face of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Yaśoda’s father, saying:
"O Great Householder!
"What do you think?

If there is a trainee who has already studied the various knowledges and has already studied the vision of the Dharma, and upon hearing the Dharma, realizes the exhaustion of the outflows and attains liberation of mind—could such a person, were they to turn their mind back toward their former home, ever again experience the five desires?"
The householder replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the elder, saying:
"That noble son Yaśoda has now studied wisdom and insight, and has realized all dharmas; he is no different from you."
"Now, Yaśoda, upon hearing the Dharma being preached, has realized the fruit of the path; his outflows are exhausted, and his mind is pure and liberated.
The Buddha said to the elder, "This good man Yaśoda!"
"Now I should not return home to dwell within the household and experience the five objects of desire as I did formerly when living at home.
At that time, the elder addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent!"
"Bhagavān!
Yaśodharā has now been born among humans; she has well attained great benefit and is well-born into this world, for all her outflows are extinguished and her mind has attained liberation."
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing the body of the young man Yaśoda adorned with various necklaces and ornaments, spoke these verses:
“With his body adorned by various necklaces, He has attained the Dharma through a mind of tranquil concentration;
His faculties are fully tamed and utterly pure, And he gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.”
If one can practice such truth and reality, this is called true brahmacarya;
it is also called being a son of the Śākya-śramaṇas, and it is also called being a bhikṣu-saṃgha.
Then the father of the young man Yaśoda addressed the Buddha,
saying: "Excellent,
World-Honored One!
"I pray that you will accept my invitation to receive offerings of food and drink, together with the noble son Yaśoda and the others.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation from the elder in silence, out of his desire to show compassion for the elder.

At that time, having seen that the World-Honored One had accepted his invitation by remaining silent, the elder rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, took his leave of the Buddha, and departed.
Not long after the elder had departed, the great son Yaśoda rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent!...”
"World-Honored One!
I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me the going forth and confer upon me full ordination."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Yaśodharā, saying:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!
Now, within the Dharma taught by me, practice the holy life (brahmacarya) so as to bring all outflows (āsrava) to their complete end."
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the body of the elder Yaśoda immediately became that of one who has gone forth, he received full ordination, and became a great śramaṇa.
At that time, there were seven arhats in this world:
one was the World-Honored One himself, along with the five bhikṣus, Yaśoda, and the others.
At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and commanded Yaśodharā to serve as his attendant as they proceeded toward his father’s home.
Having arrived at that house, he spread out a seat and sat down.

At that time, the elder Yaśodharā’s mother and the elder Yaśodharā’s wife came toward the Buddha; having reached the Buddha’s presence, they prostrated at his feet and withdrew to sit to one side. Once they had withdrawn to one side, [the Buddha spoke].

The World-Honored One taught the Dharma to them in successive order, namely by preaching on the practice of giving, up to its ultimate purity. The Tathāgata fully knew all of them; their minds were filled with joy, pure and supple, and free from all hindrances.

"At that time, the World-Honored One taught for them the Dharma that brings joy to all Buddhas—namely, the Truth of Suffering, the Truth of the Accumulation of Suffering, the Cessation of Suffering, and the Path leading to its cessation. When the World-Honored One preached this Dharma to them, they sat there, far removed from all dust, attaining pure wisdom; the realm of their afflictions was exhausted, and regarding all phenomena, they attained the pure Dharma-eye."
Having fully known all defiled phenomena and all phenomena that are subject to cessation, he has brought them all to total extinction and realized this through direct knowledge as it truly is.
It is like a clean cloth free from stains and grease: whatever dye it is immersed in, it takes on that color.

In this way, in this manner, those attendants sat upon their seats; having become free from dust and defilement, and with all defiled phenomena completely extinguished, they realized and knew it as it truly is.

Having seen all phenomena, those women attained profound realization and reached the limit of all phenomena; they crossed over the wilderness of afflictions, attained freedom from doubt and fear, and no longer relied on the teachings of others for their realization.
Having attained knowledge and vision within the teaching of the Blessed One, they took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and immediately received the five precepts.

At that time, on that very day, these were the first among humans in the world to receive the precepts through the three refuges and become upāsikās: namely, the elder Yaśodharā’s mother, the elder Yaśodharā herself, and all their various kinsmen and attendants.

"At that time, the great wealthy householder Sujāta, having heard the World-Honored One preach the Dharma appropriately for his retinue, was filled with joy upon hearing it; he immediately rose and prepared food."
The elder, together with his wife and his new daughter-in-law, personally took various kinds of fine foods and offered them as alms to the Buddha and Yaśodharā.
These included foods to be licked, sucked, chewed, bitten, and nibbled; the food they bestowed was entirely sufficient, and they ate to their heart's content until fully satiated.

At that time, the elder Yaśoda’s father Sujāta, the householder’s wife, and the new bride, seeing that the Buddha had finished his meal, put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, and was thus pure and seated at ease, each brought a small mat for themselves and followed one after another to the presence of the Buddha, sitting according to their seniority.

At that time, when the World-Honored One saw that the kinsmen of the householder Sujāta had arrived according to the Dharma and were seated before him, the Tathāgata, out of compassion and wishing to deliver them so they might be freed from suffering and affliction, preached the Dharma to them as was appropriate.
Having heard the Dharma, their hearts were filled with joy; their faith blazed forth and their majestic virtue increased.
At that time, having listened to the Dharma, all of them experienced such joy in their hearts, and they understood it thus.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat, and Yaśodharā followed after the Buddha.

Chapter Thirty-nine: Yaśodharā’s Past Causes.
"At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī in India, there were four householders who were great and wealthy elders, the most eminent among the ranks of good sons."
What are these four?

The first is named Vimala, translated in the Sui language as "Undefiled"; the second is named Śubhāhu, translated as "Good-Armed"; the third is named Pūraṇaka, translated as "Complete"; and the fourth is named Gavampati, translated as "Lord of Cows."
Having heard from others that the noble youth Yaśoda had gone to the side of the śramaṇa to practice the holy life (brahmacarya), they immediately reflected thus:
"How extraordinary this is!"

Within the practice of the Dharma of that Great Śramaṇa, the holy life (brahmacarya) should be firm and unshakable; it should surpass others, and its assembly of teachings should surely be the foremost.
Why is this? Because the great virtuous son Yaśodhara has gone to the side of the śramaṇa to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) and has thereby attained renunciation.
We, too, should now go to that Great Śramaṇa to seek the cultivation of the holy life.

Having thus deliberated together, they went to Yaśodharā. Upon arriving, they conversed with her face to face using elegant words and skillful speech; each spoke from the depths of their hearts, exchanging pleasant words and greeting her with respectful inquiry.
Having comforted one another, they each sat to one side.
Once seated, those four elders addressed Yaśodharā together, saying:
"Venerable Yaśodharā!..."
"This holy life must surely be steadfast; it is certain to surpass others.
Such an assembly of the Dharma is worthy of reverence and delightful.
Just as you, Venerable One, are now practicing the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa, we too now wish to seek the practice of the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa."
At that time, the Elder Yaśoda, together with the four great householders of the city of Vārāṇasī, went to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, they prostrated at his feet; having paid homage at his feet, they withdrew to sit to one side.
Then Yaśodharā addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Greatly Awakened World-Honored One!
These four elders were each my friends when we lived as householders; they were the most excellent among the sons of good family!"
Those known as Vimalabāhu-paripūrṇa, Govinda,
and the others have come here today specifically to take refuge in the World-Honored One.
Excellent!
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will preach the Dharma for these four great elders, instructing, exhorting, and guiding them as is appropriate.

At that time, the World-Honored One, giving rise to great compassion and out of pity for them, immediately preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to those four great elders through successive skillful means—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, and patience—and even expounded various essential points of the Dharma.

When those elders heard the World-Honored One preach such characteristics of the Dharma, they immediately, while still seated, became free from dust and defilement; they fully understood all phenomena of origination and likewise knew, as they truly are, the phenomena of cessation.
Just as a clean cloth, free from stains and grease, takes on the color of the dye it is placed in,
even so, those four elders, while still in their seats, came to know the nature of the arising and ceasing of all fetters and afflictions, realizing them as they truly are.

Those four elders each likewise perceived the characteristics of all dharmas, attained the characteristics of all dharmas, realized the characteristics of all dharmas, and entered into the characteristics of all dharmas. They crossed the desert of afflictions; their minds were without obstruction; they transcended the net of doubt; they extinguished the fetters and latent tendencies; they attained the state of fearlessness; they did not rely on the knowledge of others, but practiced in accordance with the Buddha-dharma.
Rising from his seat, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with his right knee on the ground before the Buddha, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Greatly Enlightened World-Honored One!"
"We now seek ordination from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and wish to receive the full precepts according to the Buddha’s teaching and Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those four elders, saying: "You bhikṣus!"
“Come, O pure ones! Enter my Dharma and practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) for the sake of extinguishing all suffering.

When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, the hair of those four great householders of Vārāṇasī fell off of its own accord; their beards and mustaches appeared as if shaved seven days prior, and their bodies were naturally clothed in the three robes. Holding alms bowls in their hands, the four householders immediately became renunciants and received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

At that time, the four elders, having not long since left the household life and having only recently received full ordination, stayed in a certain place. Abandoning all worldly affairs, they were careful with body and speech, not daring to be negligent. Diligent and energetic, they practiced wholesome conduct in secluded places; sitting alone and rising alone, they never ceased their efforts, dwelling within the *araṇya* as if their very heads were on fire.

At that time, those sons of good family, having left the household life out of right faith for the sake of seeking the Way, soon attained the unsurpassed holy life (*brahmacarya*). Having personally perceived the characteristics of phenomena and realized the various supernormal powers and fearlessnesses, they proclaimed:
"Birth and death have been severed; the fruit of the holy life has been obtained; what was to be done has been accomplished; there shall be no further existence in future lives."
Having known this for himself and realized it through his own direct experience, those four elders all simultaneously became arhats with minds well-liberated.
At that time, there were eleven arhats accomplished in the world: first, the World-Honored One;
second, the five bhikṣus; third, Yaśoda; and fourth, the four sons of noble family who were the most excellent lay friends among the elders.

"At that time, the Elder Yaśoda had fifty friends from his former life as a householder who had gathered from various countries. Among them were some young men who had been raised together since childhood. Upon hearing that the young man Yaśoda had gone to the Great Śramaṇa to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*), they said to one another:
'That holy life must surely be of supreme excellence, a firm and powerful assembly of the Dharma, for the young man Yaśoda serves that Great Śramaṇa and practices the holy life.'"
"We too should now go to that Great Śramaṇa and seek to practice the holy life.

Having thus deliberated together, they went together to Yaśodharā. Upon arrival, they spoke face-to-face with Yaśodharā; their words were elegant and refined, and they engaged in various conversations, exchanging greetings and showing mutual respect. When this was concluded, they withdrew to stand to one side. Having stood to one side, they...
"At that time, those fifty friends—each being a preeminent elder from a different country and former close companions from his lay life—addressed Yaśodharā together, saying:
'O virtuous Yaśodharā!'"
"This holy life must surely be excellent, for it surpasses that of others, and the Elder practices this holy life in the presence of the Great Śramaṇa.
Our inclinations are the same as yours; we wish to go to that Great Śramaṇa and practice the holy life there."

Then Yaśodharā immediately went with those fifty former lay friends to the place where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, she prostrated herself at his feet; having paid homage at his feet, she withdrew and sat to one side.
Yaśodharā then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Great and Virtuous World-Honored One!

When I formerly lived at home, I had these fifty friends and acquaintances, some of whom were before me and some behind me; all of them were sons of noble family, and their hearts all delighted in taking refuge in the Tathāgata."
"Only we pray, World-Honored One!
Out of great compassion and pity, please preach the essentials of the Dharma for us, providing instruction and guidance.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately preached the Dharma to them in accordance with their needs.
When those elders had heard what the Buddha taught, they came to know everything exactly as it is.
Those elders all became Arhats whose outflows were exhausted, their minds well-liberated.

At that time, there were sixty-one Arhats in the world: namely, the Buddha, the World-Honored One; the five bhikṣus; and Yaśoda. Regarding Yaśoda, he had four virtuous friends in the city of Vārāṇasī—Vimala, Subāhu, Pūrṇa, and Govinda. Among Yaśoda’s lay friends, there were fifty great householders who had all been summoned from various countries; these sons of good family arrived one after another, both before and after him.
"At that time, after the World-Honored One had converted these people in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, he desired to travel elsewhere and addressed the Elder Yaśoda, saying: 'You, Yaśoda!'"
Return and remain here; do not follow after me.
Why is this? O Yaśodharā!
Since childhood you have never suffered physical hardship; moreover, your skin is soft and delicate, unaccustomed to coarse clothing or poor food.
Stay here and receive the offerings required by your parents, enjoying whatever superior food and clothing you desire at your own will.
"Your parents are able to provide for you.
At that time, Yaśodharā received these instructions and stood respectfully, then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the World-Honored One has commanded, I dare not disobey."
Upon hearing the Buddha’s command, Yaśodharā remained in Vārāṇasī, steadfast and unmoving.

At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī in India, there were five hundred merchants and elders who had also been friends with Yaśodharā during her lay life. Having gone to sea to gather treasures, they returned home all at once and each inquired after the whereabouts of Yaśodharā.
Having asked this, they heard that Yaśodharā was now practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) under that great śramaṇa. Upon hearing this, they said to one another:

"That holy life must surely be sublime and its teaching superior to others; for if it were not so, how could the noble son Yaśodharā have turned his mind toward that great śramaṇa to practice the holy life?"
"We too should now go together to the Great Śramaṇa and seek to practice the holy life (brahmacarya).
At that time, those five hundred merchants and great elders gathered together and approached the Elder Yaśoda. Having arrived, they addressed Yaśoda, saying:
"Venerable Yaśoda!..."
"It has been a long time since we last met; we entered the sea and have only now returned.
Having heard that you have left the household life, we have come to inquire after you: Are you at ease, free from affliction, and living in happiness?"
Having thus exchanged various kinds of kind words and pleasant speech as a mutual greeting, and once they had finished their conversation, each showed respect and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the five hundred merchant elders addressed the Elder Yaśoda, saying:
"Venerable Yaśoda! This is truly excellent."
Then Yaśoda replied to him, saying, "So it is, so it is;
this is now most excellent.

At that time, those five hundred elder merchants immediately sought ordination as renunciants under the Elder Yaśoda and requested full admission to the precepts. After many years had passed, they were still unable to attain the Way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having traveled through other countries, returned to the city of Śrāvastī and stayed within the Jetavana Monastery.
Then the Elder Yaśoda, after a long period had passed and the summer retreat was concluded, departed accompanied by a community of five hundred bhikṣus.
Hearing that the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove Monastery and wishing to go there to see the Tathāgata, those visiting bhikṣus arrived at the Jeta Garden.
At that time, the resident bhikṣus there were taking up their alms bowls or folding their robes and placing them inside the rooms, making a great clamor and a noisy commotion.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the answer] yet asking on purpose, addressed the Elder Ānanda, saying: "Elder Ānanda!
What is this great and lofty sound here, so tumultuous and distracting?"
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored Tathāgata!
It has just been announced that five hundred visiting bhikṣus have arrived here, with the Elder Yaśoda at their head."

When we saw that visiting bhikṣus had arrived, the resident bhikṣus there greeted them with mutual consolation and inquiries after their well-being; yet, when they received the visitors' robes and bowls and placed them inside the rooms, they raised this loud clamor.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Elder Ānanda!
If you know the proper time, summon those visiting bhikṣus of such a kind to come to me."
At that time, having heard the World-Honored One’s command, Ānanda immediately went to where those visiting bhikṣus were and said to all the visiting bhikṣus: "O elders!..."
"The World-Honored One now summons all of you guest bhikṣus.
When the bhikṣus heard Ānanda speak these words, they said to him,
"As the Elder intends, we dare not disobey."

At that time, having heard Ānanda’s instruction, the five hundred visiting bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was. Upon arriving at the Buddha’s presence, they prostrated at his feet; having completed their prostrations, they withdrew to stand to one side.
When the visiting bhikṣus had taken their places to one side, they stood there in silence.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those visiting bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
Why do you raise such a great clamor?
It is like the shouting and laughing that arises when worldly people engage in disputes; it is like fishermen competing with one another as they pursue various fish, each calling out to the others.
"O bhikṣus! Return each to your own original places; you must not dwell here together with me. I am driving you out.
At that time, those five hundred newly arrived visiting bhikṣus, having heard these words from the Buddha, each addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has commanded.
