Having heard these words from the Buddha, those five hundred visiting bhikṣus prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, took their leave, and departed. Carrying their robes and bowls, they emerged from the vihāra.

He arrived at the bank of a river named Varadrumavatī, which in the language of Sui means "Exquisite Beauty Sovereign. He dwelt there on the bank of that Exquisite Beauty river, practicing with diligence day and night without ceasing.
During the first and last watches of the night, they do not lie down nor sleep; with fierce diligence, they cultivate the path, aspiring to seek and realize the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Therefore, they apply their minds. Applying their minds without ceasing or resting, before long, the task they have undertaken is accomplished.

Those sons of good family, having each attained right faith, left the household life for homelessness; they were able to accomplish that unsurpassed holy life (brahmacarya) and brought it to fulfillment.
Having personally realized the Dharma and realized the various supernormal powers (abhijñā), they immediately severed all fetters (saṃyojana). They themselves proclaimed: "Birth and death have ended;
the fruit of the holy life has been attained; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence in future lives. Thus they realized and knew for themselves.
"All those elders had become arhats; their minds were well-liberated, and they were free from all fear.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying for a short while at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, and having resided there, he wished to travel further through other villages.
Traveling from that village to another village, proceeding by degrees, he arrived at Vaiśālī.
Having reached that city, he went to the Markaṭahrada Lake; on the shore of that lake was a grass hut, where he immediately took up residence.

At that time, when the sun had set in the west, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi, emerged from the grass hut, and proceeded toward an open space where he spread out his seat and sat down, surrounded on all sides by the assembly of bhikṣus who stood to his left and right and before and behind him.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Elder Ānanda!
I see that at the place where the bhikṣus reside along the river Varakalyāṇī, there is great radiance; on the banks of that Varakalyāṇī, there dwell five hundred bhikṣus."
Thus he spoke three times.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"You may now summon those bhikṣus and have them come to see me."
At that time, having heard these instructions from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Ānanda went to a young bhikṣu and, upon arriving, addressed him, saying:
"Excellent, Elder!
"Go quickly to the banks of the Brahmāyus River; there are currently many bhikṣus at that place. Speak thus to those elders:
'The World-Honored One now wishes to see you, venerable ones. If you know it is the right time, you should go quickly to see the World-Honored One.'"
When that young elder bhikṣu had heard these words from Ānanda, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
“As the Venerable One instructs, I shall not dare to disobey.”
Then that young elder bhikṣu moved with great speed; it was as if a strong man were to extend his bent arm, or so it was.

At that time, the young elder bhikṣu, from Vaiśālī, quickly vanished from sight and arrived at the bank of Brahmāgupta. There he manifested himself and went to where the resident bhikṣus were, and having arrived, he addressed all those bhikṣus, saying:
"Excellent, Elders!"
If you now perceive that it is the right time, and if you know well that the World-Honored One desires to see you elders, you should quickly go to where the World-Honored One is.
At that time, the bhikṣus there addressed the young messenger bhikṣu, saying:
"As the Elder instructs, we dare not disobey."

At that time, having heard these words, those bhikṣus, like a strong man bending and extending his arm, vanished from their place by the Pārāvatagomātī River and appeared instantly at the base of the Kuśa-hermitage on the shore of the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī.

At that time, as the World-Honored One was entering the Immovable Samādhi, the Elder Yaśoda also entered the Immovable Samādhi, and those five hundred bhikṣus who had come likewise entered the Immovable Samādhi.
When the first watch of the night had passed, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, adjusted his robes, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"May the World-Honored One take note that one watch of the night has passed; it would be well for the World-Honored One now to console those visiting bhikṣus."
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and said nothing.
When this had been repeated, and the middle watch of the night had passed, Ānanda requested yet again, until the World-Honored One remained silent and said nothing.
At that time, when the night had reached its third watch, Ānanda again made his request, but the World-Honored One remained silent.

As the final watch of the night passed and it was time for the drum to be struck, just as the morning star was about to appear, the Elder Ānanda rose once more from his seat, bared his right shoulder, adjusted his robes, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"May the World-Honored One take note!"
It is now the latter part of the night; before long the drums will be beaten and the morning star is about to appear.
The Blessed One may now instruct the bhikṣus to welcome those visiting bhikṣus, for these bhikṣus have already sat for a long time and their bodies are weary and exhausted.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Elder Ānanda!
You do not yet understand this principle."
Why is that? Venerable Ānanda!
If you understood the principle, you should not have asked this question.
This samādhi now is not within your domain.
Why is this so? Ānanda!

I have entered this Samādhi of Immovability, and these five hundred bhikṣus have also entered the Samādhi of Immovability, with the Elder Yaśoda at their head; all have entered the Samādhi of Immovability, and I now know this principle for myself.
At that time, wishing to speak in verse, the World-Honored One uttered this lion’s roar:

“Having already crossed the mire of afflictions and desires, And having further extinguished all thorns of the aggregates, He has reached the place where greed and delusion are utterly exhausted; Therein, he no longer dwells upon suffering or pleasure.”
Having already crossed over to the further shore, he is called truly brave and steadfast;
he is also termed a bhikṣu who has skillfully shattered evil, and is further named a person of perfect liberation.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, those five hundred bhikṣus felt a sense of wonder at such an unprecedented event. Because they had experienced this rare and unprecedented occurrence, they said to one another: "O Elders!..."
"How rare is this!

This elder Yaśoda possesses great supernormal powers, such that he has enabled these five hundred bhikṣus—all of whom likewise possess great supernormal powers—to have been his friends in the past, each resembling him; even their parents are all endowed with virtue."

At that time, those five hundred bhikṣus each conceived doubts in their minds; wishing to ask the World-Honored One to resolve their uncertainties, they spoke together to the World-Honored One, saying:
"What roots of goodness did this elder Yaśoda plant in the past?"

Now, within this very body, you are thus able to possess a household so prosperous, such abundant wealth, such manifold treasures, and such a full complement of bipeds and quadrupeds; yet, though born into such a family, at the moment of your birth, a precious canopy was spread over you from above.
Furthermore, his parents constructed three types of pavilions for Yaśodharā; by what past karma did she obtain such a karmic retribution?
Moreover, why was it that he could perceive those among the court ladies as being like a cemetery?

Having encountered the Buddha, they left the household life and received full ordination, becoming arhats. Their parents and wives all attained the noble Dharma. Furthermore, their lay friends, those from various kingdoms, merchant leaders, court officials, and the five hundred bhikṣus by the banks of the Brahmāgupta River all attained the fruit of arhatship.
Having spoken these words, they all remained silent.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed those bhikṣus, saying: "You bhikṣus!
Listen attentively with a sincere mind.
I recall that in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a man who wished to undertake a certain task. He thought to himself:

"Once this matter of mine is accomplished, I shall perform another; once that is finished, I shall do yet another. When all these matters of mine are completely concluded, I will subsequently prepare various kinds of fine foods and drinks—solid foods, chewables, bites, sips, and suckables—and having prepared each of these, I shall give them as alms to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, so that they may all be fully satisfied, satiated, and filled."

"At that time, by virtue of the causes and conditions of his courageous mind and wholesome karma, and further moistened by a multitude of merits, all the undertakings he engaged in were successfully accomplished."
Having seen that his task was accomplished, that man rose at dawn, prepared various kinds of abundant food and drink fit for consumption, and taking them all with him, went to the city gate.
Having arrived and settled there, he formed this thought:
"Whoever shall be the first to see this city gate—whether a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa—I shall offer them these various kinds of food and drink, even down to the dregs, as a gift."

"At that time, outside the gate of that city, there was a Pratyekabuddha named Nāgārṣi (translated in the Sui language as Chéngjì, 'Accomplished Topknot'), who constantly resided in the city of Vārāṇasī."

Then that venerable Pratyekabuddha, at the time of dawn when the sun was in the east, put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and walked slowly, intending to enter the city of Vārāṇasī to beg for food.

From afar, this person saw that Pratyekabuddha, whose dignified deportment was orderly and composed; his movements were upright and balanced, his steps steady and without deviation; he looked to the left and right while walking slowly with a direct gaze; his every action was deliberate, neither hurried nor lax; when standing still, he gazed upward, a sight that people delighted to behold; his physical form and robes were in perfect harmony, and both his inner and outer demeanor were solemn and majestic.
Having seen him, that person attained a pure mind and gave rise to great joy; he immediately took the food and offered it to the pratyekabuddha.
At that time, the pratyekabuddha thought to himself:

"I have now received various kinds of delicious food as an offering, yet the time for my meal has not yet arrived. For the time being, I shall collect my mind and practice dhyāna meditation with focused mindfulness."

Having reflected thus, he stepped back to one side, went to the riverbank, and sat cross-legged beneath a tree. With his mind set on right intention and fixed in concentration, his body remained upright; silent and single-minded, he stayed there without wavering or moving.
"At that time, there was a king in the city of Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta (translated in the Sui language as 'Brahma-Virtue'), who set out from the city gate with his fourfold army in full array."

At that time, outside the city, there was suddenly a man coming from a village who, holding a parasol in his hand, encountered the king head-on. Seeing King Brahmadatta approaching before him, the man thought to himself:
"I should now avoid King Brahmadatta so that he does not see me."
Having formed this thought in his mind, the man immediately left the road and headed toward a different path; that path led to the Pārā river.

Following the current downstream from the riverbank, before he had traveled far, he suddenly beheld that Pratyekabuddha sitting cross-legged beneath a tree on the bank, with right mindfulness and right reflection, his body unmoving.
As that Pratyekabuddha’s body was touched by the rays of the sun, he broke into a sweat.
Seeing this, the man thought to himself:
"This seer must be pure in his observance of the precepts; he has surely attained realization of the true Dharmas."
"Now that this sunlight has already shone upon his body, he may suffer from the affliction of heat.
Having formed this thought, [he reflected]: "I should now take this parasol and cover his body with it, providing him with shade and coolness."
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha, knowing that the time for his meal had arrived, thought to himself:
"The time for my meal has come; it is fitting that I should arise from this samādhi."

At that time, the Pratyekabuddha emerged from samādhi and saw that person holding a parasol over his body. Having seen this, out of compassion for that person, he leaped into the air and performed the eighteen transformations. In mid-air, he moved about, coming and going; he knelt, stood, lay down, and sat. He further emitted smoke and flames, or released firelight, or at times produced water. He manifested such immeasurable varieties of supernatural powers as emerging and submerging, appearing and disappearing.

"At that time, that person immediately conceived pure faith toward this Pratyekabuddha Nāgaśikhi; joining his ten fingers in palms-together salutation, he prostrated with utmost sincerity and made this aspiration:
'May I, in a future life, encounter a holy one such as this, or even one superior to him;
having encountered him, may I be able to swiftly realize and know the Dharma he teaches; and may I never fall into the evil realms in the future.'"
He further requested that the Pratyekabuddha accept his food from his own hands, and inquired, saying:
"Venerable One, where do you currently reside?
The Pratyekabuddha then replied to him:
"I dwell in such-and-such a place; I travel to such-and-such a place.

At that time, the man went to the vicinity of the grass hut where that pratyekabuddha resided. Having arrived, he swept the earthen floor inside and out and cleared away all the weeds. Once this was finished, he invited the pratyekabuddha, saying:
"I wish to provide you with the four requisites for sustenance. Whatever you may require, I am able to procure all food and clothing for you."
Having thus served that Pratyekabuddha, he returned to his own home and spoke as before to his parents, wife, children, kinsmen, and countless other people, saying:

"I have now seen such a seer, with such ascetic conduct, such purity, and one who has realized the sublime Dharma. If you know it to be the right time, go to his dwelling and pay him honor and respect."

At that time, the man’s parents, wife, children, as well as his friends and acquaintances, having heard this, all went to where the Pratyekabuddha Nāgāraka was and, with pure hearts, paid him respectful homage and made offerings.
"At that time, after a short while had passed, that person formed this wholesome thought: 'Living at home is a great affliction, entangled by defilements;

going forth is a great joy, characterized by liberation and the unconditioned. It is difficult for one at home to accomplish this; it cannot be attained in its entirety without stain, nor can it be attained in its entirety without defilement. Even if one desires to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) with purity and freedom from stain throughout the duration of one's entire life, in the end, it cannot be achieved.'"
"I should now go to that seer and beg for permission to renounce the world.
Having thought thus, the man went to where the Pratyekabuddha Śikhin was and addressed him, saying:
"Excellent, Great Seer! [I wish to renounce the world]."
"Please allow me to go forth.
But the Pratyekabuddha did not grant permission for his going forth.
That man petitioned him a second time, and even a third time:
“Excellent, Great Seer!
Grant me permission to leave the household life.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha Śikhin, feeling compassion for that person after he had thus requested three times, addressed him and spoke these words:
"O son of good family!
If you now wish to seek renunciation, not far from here there are various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) named Pārivrajaka—translated in the Sui language as 'Going and Going Again. "

In that place, you should first cultivate and discipline your body and mind; then, in a future life, within the True Dharma, you shall create the causes for renunciation. Furthermore, you should make this aspiration: "In a future age, there will be a Buddha appearing in the world named Śākyamuni Tathāgata; I pray that I may behold that Buddha, and having encountered him, may I never be lost or fail. Having gone forth into homelessness within the teaching of that Tathāgata, I vow to abandon all suffering."
At that time, that person took the words of the Pratyekabuddha Kāla to heart and followed them without deviation.
He immediately invited the Buddha for as long as he lived and provided him with all manner of offerings to serve the Pratyekabuddha.
"At that time, the Venerable Pratyekabuddha Nāgārasiṃha, having lived in the world for as long as his conditions permitted, entered parinirvāṇa."

All the kinsmen and retinues of those people gathered together; seeing the Pratyekabuddha enter parinirvāṇa, they immediately took up the Pratyekabuddha’s body and made offerings according to the Dharma, performing the rites of enshrinement and cremation. Specifically, they constructed stūpas for his relics, upon which they fashioned inverted basins and *cakra* wheels, hung precious bells, and offered banners, canopies, incense, flowers, powdered incense, and burning incense, as well as lighting lamps to maintain a continuous illumination as an act of worship.
"At that time, after that person had made such offerings and the period of time had passed, he went forth into homelessness within the Dharma of Pāṭaliputra.
Having gone forth, he continued to dwell and reside in that forest, rising and sitting there; at the time of dawn, he would frequently enter the city of Vārāṇasī to beg for food to sustain his life."

Once, on a certain day while entering Vārāṇasī for alms, he saw the corpse of a woman on one side who had died of a terminal illness; her body was turning blue and decaying, with maggots boring through her flesh and feeding upon it everywhere. Having seen this, he stood near it, gazing and observing intently, and within his mind, the perception of impurity arose; having abandoned it, he departed.

Thus he focused his mindfulness on the impurity of the body; recollecting it without abandoning it, and reflecting upon it again and again, he achieved diligent effort and attained the mind of the fourth dhyāna. He then once more made this vow:
"May I, in a future age, encounter Śākyamuni Buddha appearing in the world."
"At that time, may my vows be fulfilled.
On the day I encounter him, may I leave the household life as a youth under that Buddha and practice the holy life."
"May I, having heard the Dharma taught by that Buddha, the World-Honored One, quickly be able to realize and know it.
After that person has remained in the world for a certain period of time, they eventually pass away.
After his life ended, he was reborn in the Brahma palace.

Then that person descended from heaven and was again born in the human world; proceeding in this manner through successive kalpas, in his final existence, he returned to be born into the family of a most wealthy and eminent elder in this city of Vārāṇasī. That elder possessed abundant wealth, assets, clothing, and ornaments, such that there was nothing he required that was lacking.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"There is another causal connection which I shall explain in full.
Recall the past, when I was still in this very city of Vārāṇasī; there was the kingdom of Kāśi, and its king was named Reṇu (in the Sui language, 'the King Wasted')."

After the Parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, that Nṛsiṃha collected the relics and erected a stūpa made of the seven precious substances—namely gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, agate, coral, amber, and other such jewels—which he placed inside the structure. Furthermore, he encased the exterior of this jeweled stūpa with stone, making it one yojana high from the ground and half a yojana in width.

"At that time, the stupa erected by King Nṛga of that country was named Daśalakṣaṇa (Sui: 'Ten Marks'). Regarding the tiers of its parasol: the first bowl-shaped cover was made by King Nṛga; the second bowl-shaped cover was made by the King’s chief queen; the third bowl-shaped cover was made by the King’s eldest son; the fourth bowl-shaped cover was made by the King’s daughter, named Mālinī (Sui: 'Small Garland'); the fifth bowl-shaped cover was made by King Nṛga’s second son; the sixth bowl-shaped cover was made by King Nṛga’s third son; and the seventh bowl-shaped cover was made by King Nṛga’s fourth son."
"O bhikṣus, you should know!

At that time, the third son of King Nṛga, who constructed the sixth-tier *āvaraṇa* (roofing bowl) for the stupa of the relics of Kāśyapa Buddha—the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—was none other than the present bhikṣu Yaśoda."
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"Furthermore, he who at that time held a parasol in his hand to provide shade for the Pratyekabuddha Kālaśikhi was none other than this very Yaśoda, the bhikṣu."

As for Yaśodharā, she once held a parasol over a Pratyekabuddha with her hand to provide him shade; and she once adorned the *stūpa* of the relics of Kāśyapa Tathāgata by covering its bowl and making its *cakra* (wheel) radiant. Because the fruit of these karmic conditions has now ripened, at the time of her birth, a precious parasol spontaneously appeared upon her head.

Furthermore, in the past, when he was a Nāgila pratyekabuddha, he constructed a grass hut and, taking various necessities, went to the place of the pratyekabuddha Śikhin, making offerings of various garments, food, and drink through these causal conditions.

Due to that karmic retribution, he has now obtained birth in a wealthy household with all its requirements; in the prime of his youth, his parents have constructed three mansions for him, wherein he enjoys various kinds of sovereign blessings and rewards.

"Furthermore, in the past, he once saw the corpse of a dead woman in a forest and gave rise to the perception of impurity; as these thoughts continued in succession, he relied upon that wholesome karma of binding the mind for its fruit and reward."
In this present life, while living as a householder, he conceives the perception of a cemetery within the bodies of his various female attendants.

Furthermore, because he previously made a vow before the Pratyekabuddha Śikhin, saying, "May I, in future lives, never fall into the evil realms," by the power of the fruit of this virtuous cause, wherever he may be, he does not pass through the woeful states; he passes from heaven to the human realm and from the human realm to heaven, experiencing the retribution of happiness.
Furthermore, in the past, before that Pratyekabuddha Śikhin, he made this vow:

"In a future life, may I encounter such a Great Sage and Honored One, or one even more sublime than him; whatever subtle and secret essential teachings that World-Honored One may speak, may I be able to hear and retain them all entirely, and having heard them, may I swiftly attain realization and realization-knowledge."
"By virtue of the causal conditions of that merit and its karmic fruition, he encountered me, the most supreme World-Honored One.
Furthermore, within the teachings I have proclaimed, he left the household life and attained the state of an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted."

"Furthermore, in the past, when he first heard of that Pratyekabuddha Śikhin, his heart was filled with joy. Having experienced such joy, he immediately went to his home and spoke to his parents, wife, children, six types of relatives, and other kinsmen, describing the various merits of the Great Sage Nāgārāja Śikhin, praising and extolling him."

Having heard this from him, those attendants conceived a heart of even greater faith, reverence, and solemnity; filled with joy and exultation, they immediately led one another to prepare various articles of offering and went there to pay homage, presenting offerings so that the four requisites were fully provided.

By virtue of the causes and conditions of that wholesome karma and its karmic reward, in this present life, the elder bhikṣu Yaśoda, along with his parents, wife, concubines, and all his kinsmen, have all attained the noble Dharma within my teaching.
Furthermore, the elder Yaśoda had lay acquaintances, as well as five hundred bhikṣus who had long resided on the banks of the Brahmāyus River; all of them had fully realized the fruit of arhatship.

At that time, they encountered Pratyekabuddhas and each made the same aspiration; with one mind, they together made such great vows and planted various roots of goodness under these sages and saints, thereby obtaining this karmic retribution.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"By making such offerings to the various holy and true ones, One obtains immeasurable and great fruits of retribution:
The Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddha Śikhin, And all Arhats who have exhausted their outflows."
Furthermore, those who make offerings to the Honored One of Ten Powers— He who is fully endowed with fearlessness, perfected in all marks,
possessed of great loving-kindness and great compassion, and the source of all correct wisdom— shall attain fruits of retribution that are inexhaustible.
By making offerings to the fields of the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as to the assembly of Śrāvakas who have attained liberation,
one receives the fruit of reward in the present among humans and devas, and later attains the great nirvāṇa of quiescence.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Thirty-Six;
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Thirty-Seven.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter 40: The Ordination of Pūrṇa At that time, not far from the city of Kapilavastu in the kingdom of Kośala, there was a village on a crossroads.

In that village lived a great brāhmaṇa who served as the royal preceptor to King Śuddhodana. His family was immensely wealthy, possessing abundant riches and treasures; even his residence was no different from the palace of Vaiśravaṇa in the northern quarter.

That brahmin had a son named Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (in the Sui language, "One Whose Compassion is Fulfilled"), who was exceedingly handsome and lovely, with few equals, and whom all people delighted to behold.

He was skillful, wise, and intelligent, possessing subtle discernment and a refined mind. He was able to recite all the Vedas and treatises thoroughly; having mastered them himself, he could also teach others.

He possessed a complete understanding of the three Vedas, the ancient commentaries on the Nirgrantha doctrines, the Nārāyaṇīya treatises, and the *Akṣara-bhañjana* (Letter-Destruction) treatises. Furthermore, he could expound upon the treatises of the five sciences concerning past events, distinguishing every single word, half-word, verse, or half-verse. He also thoroughly understood the treatises on prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*). Among worldly dialectics, he fully mastered sixty types of subjects and possessed the marks of a great man.
"On the very day that Prince Siddhārtha was born to King Śuddhodana, the son of Mitrā also came into the world at the same time.

By nature, that man feels weary of and detached from the world; he is resolved to seek liberation, constantly harbors fear within the midst of afflictions, and his mind is ever tranquil and concentrated."

In the past, they have already beheld various Buddhas appear; at the feet of those Buddhas, they planted roots of goodness, performed manifold meritorious deeds, and perfumed their minds, setting their will upon the gate of Nirvana and taking no pleasure in afflictions.

Within all forms of existence and throughout the cycle of birth and death, they have completely distanced themselves from them; having performed their practice, their fetters are shattered and decayed; taking causal conditions as their strength, they reach the stage of maturation and arrive at the noble Dharma.
At that time, Pūrṇa sat alone in contemplation, thinking:

"My father serves as the royal preceptor to King Śuddhodana; he must manage many affairs and possess various skills, presiding over the royal administration and adjudicating legal matters on behalf of the king."
Furthermore, this son, Prince Siddhārtha, is certainly no different from King Śuddhodana himself; he shall surely become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin).
"If my father were not alive, I would certainly have become the state preceptor to that Cakravartin King Siddhārtha.

Since my father was already the state preceptor to a minor king, he had no leisure even then; how much less could he now serve as the preceptor to a great kingdom as a Cakravartin King? To have any leisure while attending to affairs throughout the entire realm is simply impossible."
"What should I do now beforehand? What plan should I devise?
At this moment, I have only one recourse:
to renounce my home and go forth into homelessness."

"Then, after Pūrṇa had thought thus, at the time when the Bodhisattva went forth into homelessness during the night, he departed from his home in silence at midnight without consulting his parents. Accompanied by thirty friends, he went directly to the system of the Pārivrajakas, requested ordination, and dwelt in the Snowy Mountains, seeking the Way through ascetic practices."

Those individuals were courageous and diligent, never resting for even a moment; those thirty people simultaneously achieved perfection, attaining the four dhyānas as well as the five supernormal powers.
At that time, the ascetic seer Pūrṇa thought to himself:
"I should now inwardly examine whether the time has arrived for Prince Siddhārtha to accept the position of a holy wheel-turning monarch."

Then Pūrṇa, observing with his divine eye, beheld the World-Honored One in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), and having already turned the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous wheel of Dharma, expounding the teaching for the sake of devas and humans.
Having seen this, he immediately went to his friends and said to them:

"You all should now give rise to a heart of joy and leap for great exultation; that Great Holy Prince Siddhārtha has now left the household life, has already realized unsurpassed Bodhi, and having realized Bodhi, has already turned the unsurpassed, pure Wheel of Dharma."

"Today the Blessed One is present here in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, teaching and revealing the Dharma to gods and humans. You should now accompany me to his presence and practice the holy life there."
At that time, those friends replied with joy, "Your words are excellent; we shall comply.

Then, the ascetic seer Pūrṇa, together with his thirty companions, descended from the Snowy Mountains and traveled through the air like a king of geese soaring in the sky, arriving at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī to approach the Buddha.

Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, grasping the World-Honored One’s feet with both hands to rub and press them against his head; then, raising his head, he kissed the Tathāgata’s feet and knelt with his right knee on the ground before the Buddha, praising him with these verses:
“In the past, while in the Tuṣita Heaven, With right mindfulness, you manifested the form of a white elephant.
Entrusting yourself to enter the womb of Māyā, You came to the house of the Śākyas to become their son.”
Like a wondrous lotus that is not defiled by water, his body remained unstained while dwelling in the mother’s womb;
his mother experienced immeasurable joy and bliss, neither craving the five desires nor seeking anything but the Dharma.
Practicing only virtuous deeds and abandoning all evils, he beheld the Honored One in the womb like cast gold;
with joyful exultation, he never grew weary, gazing upon him without satiety as if looking again and again.
While dwelling within the womb, the Honored One constantly preached the Dharma; all devas and humans gave rise to hearts of compassion and joyfully drank the essence of the Dharma.
Having liberated sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, he emerged from his right side and took seven steps.
Fearless like the lion king, I am the Tathāgata who shall bring an end to suffering.
When the World-Honored One was first born, the waters of the bathing pool were neither cold nor warm, and the banks were level all around.
Having finished his bath, he adorned his body with fragrant ointments; spontaneously, canopies and fly-whisks appeared in the air.
"Such a rare sight as this has never been seen in the world; therefore, we prostrate ourselves before the Honored One.
Having spoken these verses, Pūrṇa and the various other seers raised their voices and requested ordination from the Buddha, addressing him thus:
"We only pray, World-Honored One!"
"Have compassion for us!
It is our heart's desire to leave the household life; out of your loving-kindness and pity, please deliver and liberate us.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Pūrṇa, saying:
“Pūrṇa! Arise quickly now; I shall grant you and your companions whatever you desire, according to your wishes.
When Pūrṇa had received the Tathāgata’s permission to leave the household life, he requested full ordination (*upasampadā*), together with his twenty-nine friends.

Not long after those elders had gone forth and received full ordination, each applied themselves with diligent effort; they slept alone, walked alone, sat alone, and stood alone. With courageous vigor, they practiced in secluded forest hermitages (*āraṇya*), dwelling apart from others, mindful and prudent, never being negligent, and constantly abiding in solitude for no great length of time.

If a son of good family, for the sake of seeking the great benefit, with a right mind and right faith, leaves the home life to go forth from the household; desiring to seek the unsurpassed holy life (*brahmacarya*), having exhausted the limits of desire and perceived the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); desiring to cultivate the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and immediately realizing those dharmas; having severed all further births, attaining the fruit of the holy life, having completed what was to be done, and no longer undergoing future existence.

Having realized this for themselves, all those elders became arhats; with their minds having attained perfect liberation, they all became great virtuous ones, each capable of performing great deeds to benefit sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "You should know!
Among those who preach the Dharma, this Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra is the foremost."
And there is a verse that says:
“The World-Honored One was in Vārāṇasī, Addressing the multitude with subtle and wondrous words:
‘This is the truly fulfilled bhikṣu, The foremost among all those who preach the Dharma.’”

“At that time, there were ninety-one Arhats in the world in total: namely, the Buddha, the World-Honored One; the five bhikṣus; the Elder Yaśoda; and the four most excellent friends born at the same time as Yaśodā in the city of Vārāṇasī—those sons of good family who were the most eminent among the eminent, namely Vimala, Subāhu, Pūrṇa, and Gavāmpati;
furthermore, the fifty friends of Yaśodā, who was a householder merchant and trader;
and next, the son of good family, the Elder Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, along with twenty-nine old acquaintances.”

Chapter 41: The Renunciation of Nārada. *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Forty-one, Part One: "The Renunciation of Nārada. "At that time, in the southern region of Jambudvīpa, there was a kingdom named Aparāntaka. Within that kingdom, there was a village named Markaṭahāra."

Within that village, there was a very wealthy Brahmin of the Mahākātyāyana clan; his household possessed abundant wealth and treasures, as well as male and female slaves, livestock, grain, wheat, beans, and sesame, along with houses and gardens—all so plentiful that they were no different from the palace of Vaiśravaṇa.

That brahmin was intelligent and wise; he had read, recited, and mastered the three Vedas, and was extensively learned in all things, such as the ten names for a single object like *nīdhruva* and others, as well as treatises on grammar, phonology, and etymology. He possessed knowledge of all matters of the past and the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*), understanding even half-verses and distinguishing the various prophetic treatises concerning the world. He was fully endowed with the sixty marks of a great man, having read, recited, and thoroughly understood them all, serving as the royal preceptor to King Ugratejas.

At that time, the eldest son of the royal preceptor, the great Brahmin, took leave of his family to travel to other lands to study, never knowing contentment. He sought out teachers everywhere until he had mastered all the treatises; having perfected his skills, he returned to his native home.
Having paid his respects to his father, he immediately addressed him, saying:
"Excellent, Father!

I have now mastered various fields of learning and attained thorough proficiency. Please assemble all the great assembly for me; I wish to recite the Vedas and other treatises, as well as demonstrate my various skills."
Upon hearing this, the father was filled with joy and immediately assembled the crowd.
Seeing the people gathered, the son stood before them and, without concealing anything, recited aloud all the Vedic treatises he had memorized as well as all his various skills.

Thereupon, that great assembly together honored the lion of that country, elevating him to the position of the senior elder (sthavira); his father then immediately presented him with various kinds of rare jewels as offerings.
"At that time, the royal preceptor, the great Brahmin, had another second son named Nārada (translated in the Sui language as 'Not Crying'). His father said to that second son:
'You, Nārada!'"
"Now you should leave home and go to another country to study and recite the Vedas and various treatises, so that you may become like your elder brother.
When Nārada’s elder brother was reciting all the Vedic treatises, Nārada would grasp them all immediately upon hearing them once.
At that time, having heard these words, Nārada immediately said to his father:
"Excellent, Father!
I have already mastered all the Vedas and incantations; you may now gather the entire assembly for me, so that I may recite the various Vedas and display my skills before them."
When the father heard these words from his son, a sense of wonder arose in his heart;
he immediately gathered a great assembly, and having gathered them, he made various arrangements.
At that time, Nārada stood before the great assembly and recited all the Vedas, treatises, and other scriptures.
Having heard this, the members of the assembly each felt joy in their hearts and praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Child of Great Wisdom!
You have skillfully mastered the recitation of the various Vedic treatises.
His father then provided him with various kinds of wealth and treasures as offerings.
At that time, when the eldest brother heard that his younger brother had mastered all the treatises through recitation, he was filled with distress and thought to himself:

"For immeasurable years I have traveled through various countries, studying and learning the various incantations and treatises; only through such mental toil and exertion have I finally succeeded in mastering these spells and arts."
How is it that Nārada, having heard this, was able to receive and uphold it in its entirety and purity within such a short time?
Since even a youth can achieve such a feat, if he were to grow up, he would certainly become the royal preceptor.
For this reason, I must employ skillful means to eliminate his very existence; in this way, I shall achieve a great benefit.
Otherwise, he will ultimately seize my throne.
At that time, the father, perceiving the inner thoughts of his eldest son—who had thus conceived an evil intent toward Nārada—realized this and reflected:
"This boy of mine is wise and pitiable; let him not be deprived of his life by his elder brother."
Having had this thought, he reflected: "I must employ skillful means so that he does not know.
At that time, there was a city in the south named Ujjayinī; not far from the city was Mount Vinataka, and within that mountain lived an old seer named Asita.
That seer had mastered all the Vedas as well as various treatises; having attained the four dhyānas, he was endowed with the five supernormal powers.
He was the maternal uncle of the youth Nārada.
At that time, the state preceptor, the great Brahmin, together with his wife, took their son Nārada and went to that mountain, where they entrusted him to the seer Asita to be his disciple.
Once Āsita had received Nārada, he instructed and guided him; before long, he achieved perfection, attaining the four dhyānas and possessing the five supernormal powers.
"At that time, the brahmin seer Asita, taking his disciple Nārada with him, departed from the mountain toward the city of Vārāṇasī. Outside the city, he constructed a grass hut and dwelt therein."
During the six periods of day and night, he gave such instruction, proclaiming in a loud voice:
"Excellent, excellent!
You, Nārada, the Buddha has now appeared in the world"—thus he spoke three times.

"You should go to him, shave your hair and beard, leave the household life for homelessness, and practice the holy life; you will surely gain great benefit and great happiness for a long night, and having benefited yourself, you should further benefit others."
At that time, after the aged seer Asita had spoken these words and instructed his disciple Nārada, he passed away before long.
After the death of the seer Asita, all the worldly gain and fame formerly possessed by that brahmin seer Asita were entirely obtained by his disciple Nārada.

At that time, because Nārada possessed such abundance of worldly gain, offerings, and fame, his mind became greedily attached; lacking right mindfulness, he no longer conceived the aspiration to seek what is superior, nor did he believe in the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha.

At that time, the Naga King Elapatra—translated in the Sui language as "Huoxiangye" (Corydalis Leaf)—having received his naga body, felt a sense of weary detachment and desired liberation. Disliking those defiled and evil perceptions, he thought to himself:
"In the past, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, personally bestowed this prediction upon me:
'O Great Dragon King!'"

From this day forward, after the passing of several years, several hundred years, several thousand years, several hundred thousand years, and several hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of years, there shall appear in the world a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Since such immeasurable, boundless billions of hundreds of thousands of myriads of years have now passed, has that Buddha, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, appeared in the world or not?"
“At that time, there was yet another dragon king named Śaṅkha (translated in the Sui language as ‘Conch’). In the palace of that dragon king, immeasurable hosts of dragons were constantly gathered.”
At that assembly site, many hundreds of thousands of nāga kings gathered like clouds, and the nāga king Elāpattra was also present in that palace.
At that time, there was a yakṣa king named Suvarṇa who was a close friend of the nāga king Elāpattra; he too sat among that assembly of nāgas.
At that time, the Naga King Elapatra, amidst the assembly, addressed the Yaksha King with these words:
"O Virtuous One!
Do you know whether the Tathagata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha Shakyamuni has appeared in this world?"
At that time, the yakṣa replied to the Dragon King:
"O Great and Virtuous Dragon King!
I truly do not know whether the Tathāgata Śākyamuni has appeared or not."
Nevertheless, O Dragon King!

I now know that within that wilderness there is a city; this city was originally the palace of a yakṣa, named Arakapaṇḍa—which in the Sui language means "Palace of the Wilderness. Long ago, there were two verses in that city, which said:
"If no Buddha appears in the world, no one will ever be able to read these verses."
Even if there were those who read it, they would still be unable to understand the meaning of these verses.

Only when a Buddha appears in the world will they be able to read and know them; yet no one else can explain their meaning, for only the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha can expound this meaning, or perhaps someone might hear it from the Buddha and thereby attain understanding.
At that time, the Naga Erāvaṇa addressed the Yakṣa King with these words:
"O Benevolent One!
Can you now go there, read and take those verses, and return?"

At that time, the yakṣa king Suvarṇacakra, having received these words from the nāga king Elāpattra, immediately went to the palace of Aruṇavanta; there he received and recited those verses, and having mastered them, he quickly returned to the presence of the nāga king Elāpattra.
Having arrived, he immediately addressed Airāvaṇa, saying:
"O Great and Virtuous Nāga King!
Today you should give rise to a heart of joy."
Why is this? Because the Great Sage Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni has now appeared in the world.
How is this known?

It is because he was able to cause me to read that verse; I have already received and retained that verse to bring back with me. If there is anyone who can understand the meaning of this verse and further proclaim it, one should know that this person is truly a Buddha.
At that time, the Naga King Elāpattra was filled with great joy; his entire body leaped for joy, and he could not contain himself. He then received those verses from the Yakṣa King Suvarṇa-śṛṅga.

At that time, the Naga King Śaṅkha had a daughter named Nityābhaktā, who was beautiful and pleasing to behold, possessing the most excellent complexion; she was beloved by all people, and her like did not exist in the world.
At that time, the various dragon kings in that assembly had this thought:

"On the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, or the twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth days of the month, we should take fine golden vessels filled with silver grain and silver vessels filled with golden grain; we shall take this dragon girl, adorn her body, and embellish her with various exquisite necklaces and ornaments. We will then depart from this dragon palace, place her on the bank of the Ganges River in an open space, and recite these two verses to show them to all people."
"In what does sovereignty reside? What is called 'defilement,' and how is it purified?
How does one receive the name 'delusion'?"
Why do deluded people wander in confusion?
What constitutes a wise person?
When one has realized that meeting is inevitably followed by separation, it is called the exhaustion of causes and conditions.
When that Dragon King had spoken this verse, he addressed all the worlds, saying:

"If there is anyone who can understand and recite this verse, we shall immediately take these gold and silver vessels filled with millet and other grains, along with this dragon maiden, and offer them as a gift; we shall then regard that person as a Buddha."
"If there should be someone who has heard it from another and reports it to me, I shall likewise give this gift.

At that time, King Śaṅkha and the various nāga kings, such as Elāpattra, desiring to see the World-Honored One, thirsting for and yearning for the World-Honored One, and constantly longing for him, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both the bright and dark fortnights, took fine golden vessels filled with silver grain and silver vessels filled with golden grain, along with their nāga daughters adorned in various ornaments, and went to the bank of the Ganges River, where they set them down upon the dry land.
Those two dragon kings spoke these two verses to one another:
"In what does sovereignty reside? ... up to ... the exhaustion of causes and conditions.
They further said:
"If there is anyone who can explain the meaning of this verse, we shall offer these two vessels of gold and silver, as well as this beautiful and charming nāga girl, as a gift."

As that Dragon King spoke these words, his voice resounded throughout the eight directions. All those in the mountains and forests, whether in the water or on the land—be they brahmins or householders—said to one another:

"On the sixth day of both the waxing and waning moon, those two Dragon Kings emerge from the water, carrying two vessels filled with gold, silver, and grain, as well as a dragon maiden adorned with necklaces and ornaments. They emerge from the Ganges and stand upon the land in such-and-such a direction on the bank, reciting these two verses:
'In what state of mastery does it abide? ... until the exhaustion of causes and conditions.'"
They spoke these words:
"If there is anyone who can read and explain this verse, we shall give these two vessels along with our daughter as a gift.

At that time, the brahmins and householders, having heard these words from the two nāga kings, all came flocking together from the eight directions to the place where the nāga kings were, each proclaiming:
"I am able to read and interpret these two verses.
When he arrived before the nāgas, however, he was unable to read the verses, nor could he understand their meaning.
Alternatively, there may be someone who, having read these verses, turns back and asks those two nāga kings:
"What is this verse? he asked again, inquiring what its meaning was.

At that time, the young seer Nārada dwelt in the kingdom of Magadha, serving as a guide for the people. The men and women of that country respected, served, praised, and sang hymns in honor of the seer Nārada, saying to one another:
"This young brahmin, having known it himself, further teaches others to know; having seen it himself, he further teaches others to see.
At that time, all the people within the kingdom of Magadha thought to themselves:

"This holy youth, the seer Nārada, having known and seen it himself, teaches others to know and see. We heard these two verses from the side of those two dragon kings, yet no one was able to recite them or answer regarding them. We should now go to the presence of the seer youth Nārada, and upon arrival, we ought to speak of this matter."

Having formed this thought, the brahmins and elders of the kingdom of Magadha immediately went to the place where the young seer Nārada was staying. Upon arrival, they respectfully addressed the young seer Nārada, saying:

"Venerable sir, if you know the time has come, there are two nāga kings on the banks of the Ganges—one named Śaṅkha and the other named Elāpattra—who regularly, on the sixth day of both the waxing and waning moon, emerge from the waters of the Ganges onto dry land. Carrying vessels of gold and silver filled with grain and women, they proclaim: 'Whoever can explain the meaning of these verses, we shall bestow these gifts upon them.
They recite these two verses: 'By what does one attain mastery? ... [and so on] ... until the exhaustion of causes and conditions.'"
At that time, the young seer Nārada thought to himself:

"Since I have now become the honored teacher for the people within this kingdom of Magadha, these people all make offerings to me, honoring and serving me with deep reverence. Furthermore, they believe that having attained self-knowledge and vision myself, I am now able to teach others."

If I were now to say before these people that I do not understand the meaning of these two verses, these people would immediately disparage and insult me; all my gains, offerings, and reputation would diminish, and I would lose them all.
Having formed this thought, he immediately addressed the brahmins and great householders of the kingdom of Magadha, saying to them:
"I shall [act] together with you!"
"At one time, he went to the side of the two dragon kings, requested them to recite two verses, and immediately sought their meaning.

At that time, the youth Nārada the Seer, surrounded on all sides by the elders, people, and brahmins of Magadha, with the youth Nārada the Seer placed at the head as the foremost leader, proceeded toward the two dragons.
Having arrived, he said:
"O two great dragon kings!
I pray that you will recite two verses for us; having heard them, I shall contemplate and grasp their meaning."
At that time, the two dragon kings Śaṅkha and others immediately spoke these two verses for that seer:
"In what state does one attain mastery? ...until the exhaustion of causes and conditions."
At that time, the youth Nārada the Seer addressed those two nāgas, saying:
"I have now received these two verses from you, O two Nāga Kings; from this day forward, after seven days have passed, I shall come before you to explain the meaning of these verses."
Then those two nāgas said to the youth-sage Nārada:
"We shall do as you, O worthy one, have instructed.
Having received the verses from the two nāga kings, Nārada then returned to his original dwelling place.

At that time, all the people of Magadha, all the people of Kośala, and the various people of Kuru and Pañcāla heard by report that the youth Nārada, having received two verses from the two dragon kings Śaṅkha and Elāpattra, would return here seven days from now to explain the meaning of those two verses.
The people there, mounting various vehicles—namely elephant-carts, horse-carts, ox-carts, and those on foot—assembled together like a gathering of clouds.
At that time, on both banks of the Ganges, eighty-four thousand beings of diverse kinds gathered in a great throng, all desiring to hear the Nārada Seer and the two Dragon Kings explain the verses.
At that time, there were six teachers residing in the city of Vārāṇasī, each of whom claimed for himself:
"I am the Honored One.
They were Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarī Gośālīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra.

Then, the young seer Nārada immediately approached those six teachers with the intention of inquiring about the meaning of the verses; having arrived, he asked them for the meaning of these two verses.

Since those six teachers were unable to understand the meaning and intent of these two verses, they became even more arrogant and gave rise to a mind of malice toward the seer; they then turned back to question the seer Nārada, saying:
"What is the meaning of these two verses?"
"At that time, the World-Honored One, having newly realized perfect enlightenment, was dwelling in the Deer Park within the Forest of the Ancient Seers at the city of Vārāṇasī.
Then the young seer Nārada thought thus to himself:
'This śramaṇa is staying in the Forest of the Ancient Seers in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī; I should now go to him and inquire about the meaning of these two verses.'"
He reflected again:

"Other śramaṇas and brahmins of advanced age and great virtue, who are worthy to serve as teachers to all kings and have long been ordained—such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, and even Nirgrantha Jñātiputra and others—even when I went to them and asked these two verses, they were unable to explain them. How much less so this young śramaṇa, who has been born but a short time ago and has only recently left the household life?"
"I asked about the meaning of these two verses; how could he possibly have answered?
He then reflected further:
"One must not hastily disparage a young śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa."
Why is this? For there may be young śramaṇas or brahmins who are also clever and possess swift wisdom; I should now simply go to that Great Śramaṇa and inquire about the meaning of these verses.

At that time, the youth Nārada the Seer went to the Buddha’s side; having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he gazed upon the Buddha, exchanged greetings and kind words, and after engaging in various skillful and pleasant conversation, he withdrew to sit to one side.
Once the young brahmin seer Nārada had sat down to one side, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir! Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"I wish to consult the Venerable One on a certain matter; I do not yet know whether the Venerable One will grant me permission.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the māṇava, saying: "You, māṇava!"
"Whatever questions you may have, I shall explain them for you.
Then, having received the Buddha’s permission, the young brahmin seer Nārada spoke in verse, asking the Buddha:
"In what does the sovereign king reside? What is called 'defilement' that brings about attachment?"
How is that purity attained?
How does one receive the name "deluded"?
For what reason is the deluded person confused?
"What is it called to be a wise one?
When one has experienced separation from all associations, it is called the 'exhaustion of causes and conditions.
At that time, having heard what he said, the World-Honored One immediately replied to the young brahmin Nārada with a verse:
"Because of mastery over the sixth [sense], the king is called 'defiled' when he is defiled;
though undefiled, he appears defiled—therefore, this is termed delusion."
"Because he has submerged himself in the great waters, he is named 'One Who Has Exhausted Expedient Means.
Because all expedient means have been exhausted, he is called a 'Wise One.

At that time, having heard these verses from the Buddha, the youth Nārada the Seer’s mind was opened and liberated; he gave rise to great joy, his entire body leaping with rapture, unable to contain himself.
Having heard this, he immediately ran and went to where the two nāga kings Śaṅkha and Elāpattra were; having arrived at the side of those two great nāga kings, he addressed them, saying:
"O you nāga kings!"
"Speak a verse to question me.
Then the two dragon kings, relying upon two verses, addressed the youth-sage Nārada, saying:
"In what does sovereignty reside? ... [and so on] ... until the exhaustion of causes and conditions."
At that time, the youth, the seer Nārada, replied to the dragon king with two verses:
"Because of mastery over the sixth [sense], it is called 'knowledge' (jñāna)."
At that time, having heard this verse, the Naga King Elāpattra thought to himself:

"I have now obtained the unsurpassed World-Honored One; I have now obtained the supreme Sugata. I now know that the World-Honored One has appeared; I know the Sugata, the Great Sage, the World-Honored One, who has been born for my sake, has appeared in the world for my sake, and has awakened for my sake"—thus he spoke these words a second time.
Then the two great nāga kings, Elapattra and Airāvata, having thought thus, addressed the māṇava Nārada, saying:
"O venerable māṇava!..."
"Please tell me truly: is this the power of your own eloquence and wisdom, or did you understand this meaning by hearing it from another? O Māṇava!

Truly, I do not see anyone in this world or in the heavens—whether śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, or humans—who could, through their own eloquence, master these two verses and speak them themselves; such a thing is impossible."
"Only from the Tathāgata, the Unsurpassed World-Honored One, or from a Buddha’s śramaṇa, could one hear this and then explain it.
At that time, the youth Nārada the Seer addressed the two dragon kings, Elāpattra and his brother, in verse:
"As the Dragon Kings have said, this is not my own eloquence; The Great Sage, the World-Honored One, has already appeared in the world."
"One whose body is adorned with all the marks of perfection can speak with such eloquence.
At that time, the Nāga King Elāpattra addressed the young seer Nārada in verse:
"If what the Great Seer says is the word of the Buddha, did you perhaps hear it while sleeping in a dream?"
"If this is indeed clearly manifest before our eyes, I pray that you, O Benevolent One, will now explain it further.
At that time, the youth Nārada, based on what he had witnessed, replied to the Dragon King with these verses:
"The Great Man, sovereign of devas and humans, now dwells within the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī."
"Having already turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, he roars like a lion in the forest.
At that time, the Nāga King Elāpattra again addressed the youth-sage Nārada in verse:
"Regarding the Buddha, the World-Honored One, whom you have now spoken of—I have not heard of him for a long time; today I hear his name mentioned."
Having heard that you and the Benevolent One were coming together, I have come to behold that rare and inconceivable sight.
Having seen them in the past, I now behold them once more—the various marks and signs of the Perfectly Awakened Tathāgata.
Today they appear in the world for the first time again; as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower, they are hard to meet.
Arising only once after the passage of many eons, pure like the moon in the sky,
with a body adorned and complete in all marks— this is the supreme, most excellent enlightenment of Perfect Awakening.
For a vast and long time, no sound has been heard; its clarity and resonance are like the voice of Brahmā.
If any sentient beings should hear it, they shall enter the gate of liberation through the Buddha.
At that time, after the Naga King Elāpattra had praised the World-Honored Buddha with these verses, he addressed the seer Nārada once more, saying:
"O Seer Nārada!"
"O Benevolent One, you are the Buddha!
At that time, the youth-sage Nārada replied to the Dragon King, saying:
"I say you are the Buddha. [In the Sanskrit original, this question and answer are repeated.]
The Dragon King spoke again: "Narada Rishi!
Such a roar as this is extremely rare in the world; it refers to that Buddha, the World-Honored One."
"Narada! Where is that Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha, now located?
Then the young seer Narada adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in reverence toward the direction where the Buddha was, and pointed it out to the Dragon King, saying:
"O Dragon Kings!
If you wish to know, that Buddha, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is currently in such-and-such a direction."

At that time, having learned of the Buddha’s location, the Naga King Elāpattra adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and facing the direction where the Buddha was, joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation and uttered these words three times:
“Homage to the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Thus he spoke three times.
Then the Naga King Elapatra addressed the young seer Narada, saying: "O Brahmin seer!
Let us go together to that Blessed One, the Tathagata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha, to pay him homage and make offerings."
Then Nārada replied to the Dragon King, saying:
"Excellent, Dragon King!
Let us go together."

"At that time, the two great dragon kings Elāpattra and Śaṅkha, along with their immeasurable retinues of other dragons, the seer Nārada, the māṇava, and eighty-four thousand other sentient beings, desired to go to where the Buddha was."
At that time, the Naga King Elāpattra thought to himself:
"If I were now to see the Buddha with a manifested body, it would be unwholesome for me; I should now go to see the World-Honored One with my own promised reward-body."
"At that time, the Nāga King Elāpattra went to his own nāga palace and, assuming his natural form, desired to see the Buddha.

From the city of Takṣaśilā in Northern India to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, the distance was approximately three hundred and sixty yojanas. When the Nāga King set out to see the Buddha, his head had already reached the place where the World-Honored One resided, yet his tail still remained in his original palace."

That dragon-king’s head was shaped like a single tree trunk; his neck was like an elephant’s trunk pouring forth water; his eyes and ears were like bronze bowls from the kingdom of Kośala; from his mouth issued flames of light like lightning flashing from heavy clouds; his breath produced sounds like the rumbling of thunderclouds, making the sound "gaṭa gaṭa."
Those eighty-four thousand beings all followed Elapatra.

When Elapatra saw the Tathāgata from afar—extremely handsome, with a radiance and countenance of extraordinary beauty—joy arose in his heart; he was as if adorned by the brilliant splendor of stars in the void. Having beheld him, he conceived a pure mind and a mind of right faith toward the Buddha; leaping for joy, he proceeded toward the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing from afar the Naga Erāvaṇa approaching gradually, spoke upon seeing him:
"Welcome, welcome!"
"King Elāpattra! It has been a long time since we last met. Is your body now at ease, O King?
Are you free from illness and affliction, and are all your kinsmen likewise free from disease?"
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds,
Scroll Thirty-Seven and Scroll Thirty-Eight,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
The Chapter on Nārada’s Renunciation:
At that time, the Dragon King Elāpattra thought to himself,
"The World-Honored One already knows my name."
Furthermore, he redoubled his joy toward the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One; attaining a pure mind, he gave rise to a heart of love and reverence.

At that time, Elāpattra immediately concealed his original form and transformed himself into the body of a māṇava; approaching the presence of the World-Honored One, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Having stood to one side, he again personally recited those two verses and asked the Buddha once more:
"In what does the Sovereign King abide? What is called 'defilement' through attachment?
How is he purified?"
How does one acquire the name "deluded"?
For what reason is a deluded person confused?
And how is one called a wise person?
"When one has completely parted from them, it is called the exhaustion of causes and conditions.
At that time, the World-Honored One again replied to the Dragon King in verse:
"Because of mastery over the sixth [consciousness], the king is defiled; this is called 'defilement'."
To be unstained yet appear stained—this is therefore called delusion.
Because one is submerged in the great waters, it is called the exhaustion of skillful means;
when all skillful means are exhausted, one is therefore called a wise person.
At that time, the Naga King Elāpattra again addressed the Buddha in verse,
saying: "By upholding what precepts and practicing what conduct, and by performing what further karmic causes,
can one receive a superior body among humans and devas, and cultivate the most supreme and boundless benefit?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the Dragon King with these verses:
"Honor the elderly and do not disparage others; when wishing to see your elders, observe the proper timing.
Always cherish virtuous conduct and Dharma-discourse, and frequently listen to true and beneficial teachings."
Delighting in the Dharma, they deeply contemplate right enlightenment; with wisdom they discern and reflect upon its meaning.
Speaking truthful words, they practice the holy life with diligent austerity, and constantly exercise the generosity of giving toward others.
Be upright and honest, thorough and discerning, with a diligent mind; in laughter, weeping, and speech, always avoid evil;
stay far away from flattery, crookedness, and arrogance, and do not harbor enmity toward others.
Wholesome speech resides within right mindfulness; whether hearing or knowing, one’s mind is concentrated.
If a person constantly engages in heedless conduct, such individuals neither hear nor possess right reflection.
If one can practice the causes of the noble path, this is called purifying verbal karma through conduct;
such persons possess patience and right mindfulness, abiding within extensive learning and vast wisdom.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, the youth-sage Nārada immediately became detached from the phenomena of desire.
At that time, the dragon Elāpattra, having seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance; moved by a mingling of sorrow and joy, his tears fell like rain.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Great Dragon King Elāpattra, saying:
"O Great Dragon King!
For what reason do you suddenly gaze upon my face, smiling yet sorrowful, with tears falling like this?"
Having spoken these words, the Naga Elapatra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Tathāgata, World-Honored One!

I recall that in the past, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Kāśyapa, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. At that time, within the Dharma of that Buddha, I practiced the holy life as a renunciant."
“‘World-Honored One!

At that time, I saw a blade of grass named Ira; I then cut that grass with my hand, took hold of it, and went to where the Buddha Kāśyapa was. Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, I addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”’”
"If there were a bhikṣu who cut this grass, what karmic fruit would he obtain?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to me, saying:
"You, bhikṣu, should know!"
“If a person intentionally cuts this grass with a blade, that person shall fall into the Firm牢地獄 (Dṛḍha-naraka).
“World-Honored One!
At that time, having heard these words from that Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, I did not believe them in my heart, nor did I conceive of them as something rare or marvelous.”
Because I did not accept those words of the Buddha, I failed to receive the instructions of that Tathāgata; furthermore, I thought to myself:
"What karmic retribution could there possibly be for my merely cutting this *ilā* grass?"
He thought to himself:
"World-Honored One!

At that time, having committed that *pāyattika* offense, I did not believe in the retribution for a *pāyattika*, nor could I abandon this wrong view. After my life ended, I was consequently reborn among the long-lived nāgas; for this reason, they gave me the name Elāpattra at that time."
At that time, I returned to the presence of that Buddha Kāśyapa and asked him:
"Great Sage, World-Honored One!
When shall I be able to escape this form of an evil dragon?"
"When shall I ever again obtain a human body?
Having spoken these words, he remained silent.
At that time, the Buddha Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, addressed me, saying:
“O Great Dragon King!
You should now know this:

after the passing of several years, several hundreds of years, several thousands of years, and after the passing of several hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years, there shall be a Buddha appearing in the world named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. That Buddha Śākyamuni shall grant you the prediction that you will regain a human body.”
“‘World-Honored One!
At that time, I had this thought:

“Because I now rejected and did not believe the Dharma and precepts taught by Kāśyapa Buddha, I have received this dragon body; yet, due to a slight root of goodness, I have now encountered the World-Honored One, and still do not uphold the precepts.”’”
“World-Honored One!
Because I have seen such faults and transgressions of my own, I reproached myself and wept with tears streaming down my face like rain;
yet, seeing the World-Honored One, I was filled with joy and smiled for this reason.”
I thought thus:
"How rare, how rare! This is an unprecedented matter;
that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are able to act in such a way regarding such a Dharma, without any double-tongued speech."
"Just as that Tathāgata, the World-Honored One Kāśyapa, bestowed this prediction upon me:
'O Great Dragon King!
After a certain number of years, even up to a hundred million years, a Tathāgata shall appear in the world hereafter.'"
"It is exactly as that Buddha said; there is no difference.
World-Honored One!
For this reason, I now ask the Buddha, the World-Honored One once more: when shall I be liberated from this dragon body?"
"When shall I ever again obtain a human body?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Great Dragon King Elāpattra, saying:
"O Great Dragon King!

From this day forward, after the passing of several years, even as many as hundreds of millions of years as previously mentioned, there shall appear in the world a Buddha named Maitreya, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; at that time, you shall obtain a human body.
"At that time, that Blessed One will lead you forth from the household life into homelessness; by practicing the holy life, you shall bring an end to all suffering.
Then, the Blessed One further preached the Dharma for Elāpattra, causing him to rejoice, and exhorted and instructed him, saying:
"Come, O Dragon King!"
Take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha; by upholding the five precepts, you shall obtain benefit for a long night and attain great peace and happiness.
Having heard these words from the Buddha, the nāga Elāpattra immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In accordance with the World-Honored One’s instruction, I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and shall uphold the five precepts."
At that time, the World-Honored One further instructed Elāpattra, saying:
"O Great Dragon King!
You should now know that the time has come."
Then Elapatra said to the young brahmin Nārada:
"Come, young brahmin!
Whatever amount of gold, silver, or precious jewels you require, ask for them from me as you wish; I shall give them to you."
Yet this dragon girl is of no use to you, O Benevolent One.
Why is this? Because with a single breath from her mouth, she can reduce all people in the world to ashes and dust.
Then Nārada replied to the Dragon King, saying: "O Great Dragon King!
I do not require gold, silver, or precious jewels, nor do I require the daughter of the Dragon King."
"Why is this? Having now heard these verses from the Buddha, I have conceived a sense of weary detachment toward all sensual desires.
At that time, the Naga King Elāpattra prostrated at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, took his leave, and returned.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those eighty-four thousand assemblies, with Nārada as their foremost leader, teaching them in successive order. That is to say, he taught the practice of giving and maintaining the precepts to attain rebirth in the heavens; he further spoke of the many faults and afflictions within desire to inspire in them weary detachment and the realization of the exhaustion of outflows; and he instructed them on renunciation, praising its merits to assist them in achieving liberation.

The World-Honored One knew that among that great assembly, Nārada and the others were the foremost; each of them gave rise to a heart of joy, a heart of exultation, a heart of pliancy, and attained a heart free from hindrance.

"At that time, all the teachings of the World-Honored One were the true and essential core that caused others to rejoice—namely, the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path."

The World-Honored One, having used various skillful means to explain, reveal, instruct, establish, analyze, proclaim, teach, and train [others] in these Four Noble Truths—namely, that such is suffering, such is the origin of suffering, such is the cessation of suffering, and such is the path leading to its cessation.
The Blessed One, through various causes and conditions, revealed, proclaimed, and even taught the practice of these four noble truths.
Thereupon, while still seated, that assembly was freed from all dust and defilement, exhausted the realm of afflictions, and attained the pure eye of wisdom regarding all phenomena.
All phenomena that arise are entirely extinguished; one knows and sees them as they truly are.
It is like a clean cloth, free from grease and free from black fibers, which, when dyed as desired, takes on all colors.

In this way, indeed, that great assembly, including Nārada and the others, in their respective seats, became free from afflictions, brought all accumulations to an end, realized all phenomena, established fearlessness, crossed over the net of doubt, and no longer followed the words of others; knowing the teaching of the World-Honored One, they took refuge together in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and received and upheld the five precepts.

At that time, those eighty-four thousand members of the assembly rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and took their leave to return to their own abodes.

Then the youth Nārada, having seen all dharmas, attained all dharmas, realized all dharmas, and entered into all dharmas; having crossed over all doubts and crossed over all delusions, being free from the net of doubt and having attained fearlessness, he no longer followed the words of others. Knowing the subtle and profound mystery of the World-Honored One’s teaching, he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray, World-Honored One!"
"Grant me the going forth and the full ordination.
Then, the Buddha said to that youth:
"Welcome, bhikṣu!"
"Enter into my Dharma and practice the holy life (brahmacarya) so as to rightly exhaust all suffering and reach its end.
At that time, the elder immediately became a renunciant, fully endowed with the precepts and conduct.

At that time, the Elder Bhikṣu Nārada, having already gone forth and being fully accomplished in the precepts, before long practiced alone in walking and sitting, shunning the clamor of crowds. He was circumspect in body and speech, never indulging in negligence, but was diligent, courageous, and free from indolence.

Before long, that son of good family—who had gone forth for the unsurpassed holy life—advanced to the further shore, directly perceived all phenomena, and personally realized the various supernormal powers. Having realized them, he knew them by himself; having seen and awakened to them himself, he proclaimed aloud:
"Birth and death are ended; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence hereafter. Thus did he understand.
Then that elder immediately became an Arhat, with his mind well-liberated and his wisdom well-liberated.
Once the elder bhikṣu Nārada had attained the fruit of Arhatship and was free from attachment, he dwelt alone in a secluded place and thought to himself:
"I should now go to where the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is, and question the Buddha in verse."

At that time, the Elder Bhikṣu Nārada rose from his dwelling early in the morning and went to where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
