Once seated to one side, Nārada immediately addressed the Buddha with verses, asking about the meaning of the Dharma:
"Now I have finally verified what Sita said of old; It is clearly understood that his words were not untrue.
Now, furthermore, I have heard the World-Honored One’s teaching, And shall cross over to the further shore of all dharmas."
Having already renounced the household life and being able to go forth, you further sustain your life by begging for alms;
what fruit do you obtain by practicing this way?
I now inquire of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the Elder Nārada with these verses:
"You ask about the fruits and retributions of practice; This matter is impermanent and difficult to verify.
I shall now explain it to you in detail; You should arouse firm and steadfast diligence."
Whenever a practitioner enters a village, they should maintain an equanimous mind toward both praise and blame;
wherever there is distraction, one must guard against it, and thus attain the unsurpassed fruit of tranquil concentration.
The practitioner constantly contemplates the sound of wailing, Like a fierce fire burning with intense flames.
Seeing a woman of upright appearance, One must abandon her and not give rise to defilement.
By remaining undefiled by the phenomena of desire, Neither party will have a cause for mutual defilement.
Being free from defilement is the absence of conditions for conflict.
My body and their bodies are no different; my life and their lives are equal and common.
Contemplating and reflecting with such careful discernment, when anger arises, do not kill and do not harm one another.
One should abandon the objects of pride, such as greed;

all ordinary beings are defiled by attachment to the body, yet those with vision can distance themselves from this enemy, just as one who has consumed poisonous medicine dies regardless of whether it is taken equally.
If you enter a village to beg for food, do not look about with a distracted mind;
if you abandon all objects of greedy attachment, you shall be liberated through non-attachment.
When sitting alone at night, do not think of requesting alms; stay far from inhabited villages and do not dwell on them either.
Only when dawn approaches and you wish to beg for food, enter the village with right mindfulness and right attention.
Upon reaching the village, remain silent and proceed through the houses one by one to collect alms.
Wandering through villages, do not treat them with neglect or derision; when speaking to others, do not be coarse or harsh.
Holding your alms bowl, go forth to beg for food; though you possess eloquence, remain silent.
Even if you receive but a small amount of food, do not harbor resentment; if there is one who gives you alms-food, do not revile or abuse them.
If you obtain [alms], it is most excellent; if you do not obtain them, do not give rise to anger.
Maintain a mind of equanimity toward both extremes.
Having finished eating, return to the forest and sit cross-legged beneath a tree.
Standing upon the platform like a seer, with body, mind, and speech all fully restrained,
casting away all fear and exerting the will, do not think of other matters, but contemplate only the forest.
Staying beneath a tree, one should observe well; pressing the tongue against the palate, gradually exhale the breath.
All other sense-faculties must be fully subdued; the mind and its intentions must not cling to external conditions.
Banish all sensory objects and let the mind dwell upon nothing; all defiled and turbid states must be abandoned.
One should practice the pure, true mind and cultivate the Brahma-faring life;
one must receive instruction from those who are widely learned and possess great wisdom.
Those who are tranquil and free from desire—such persons as these should be approached; having gone before them, one should follow them with a faithful heart.
Having gained faith, one should revere [the teacher] as if they were the World-Honored One.
Do not disparage others or praise yourself; when speaking, do not raise your voice too loudly, so that it may be heard from afar like a fierce fire.
This is called the dharma of a monk who has gone forth:
having completely detached from both actions performed and those not performed, if one can remain at peace wherever contact occurs, the practice of the Noble Ones should be thus.
Know that karma revolves like a wheel: when the Noble Dharma is taught to one person, another may contemplate it and realize it immediately.
With senses subdued, dwelling in solitude, with senses subdued and the mind perfected, his fame shall later spread throughout the ten directions.
This practice is found only in secluded forests, or sitting among the mountains and beneath trees, or by the banks of rivers and beside ponds and springs; in such places one sits and reflects.
Lacking wisdom, one is perpetually asleep; when perfected in tranquil concentration, one is always awake.
Like a spring, a pond, or the great ocean, so too is it with those who possess tranquil concentration.
The foolish person is like a half-filled jar of rinse-water; the wise person is like a full pool of water.
Though the wise person may speak much, they do not lose the proper timing of their speech despite its abundance.
Some possess eloquence and much speech; others speak little yet with careful discernment.
Such sparing speech is also called wisdom; these are named sages and holy ones.
This is called the practice of the true Middle Way; this is called attaining liberation through tranquility.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, Nārada’s mind was opened and understood; he leaped for joy with great delight.
(Furthermore, other teachers say:
"As for this Elder Nārada, his original clan and lineage was Kātyāyana; because of his original surname, people called him Mahākātyāyana.")
Furthermore, the Buddha once declared concerning the Elder Mahākātyāyana:
"O bhikṣus! You should now know this!"

Within this great assembly of my śrāvakas, there is one who is swift and sharp in grasping the meaning; when he hears a brief teaching, his intelligence enables him to fully comprehend it, or even upon hearing only a little, he is able to explain it extensively for others. The foremost among them is this very bhikṣu Mahākātyāyana.
At that time, having heard these words, those bhikṣus were struck with wonder and said to one another:
"How truly extraordinary is this Venerable Mahākātyāyana!"
Doubt arose in his mind: "There is no one else capable of resolving my doubts; the Buddha, the World-Honored One alone, is the one who understands the meaning of all sūtras!"
He immediately went to where the Buddha was, and having arrived, he addressed the Buddha together with the others,
saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”

What roots of goodness did this Elder Mahākātyāyana plant in the past, such that he has now come to the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, immediately gone forth from home, received full ordination, and realized the fruit of Arhatship?
The World-Honored One further declared:

"Among the assembly of śrāvakas, he who possesses swift and sharp wisdom—who can provide a detailed explanation of what is briefly stated and can summarize what is extensively spoken—is foremost of all; this refers to none other than the bhikṣu Mahākātyāyana."
"We wish to hear it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"O bhikṣus! You all..."
Listen with a sincere and attentive mind.
I recall that in the past, during this Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of sentient beings was twenty thousand years,
there appeared in the world a Tathāgata named Kāśyapa, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha.

At that time, after that Buddha, Kāśyapa Tathāgata, had turned the wheel of Dharma and raised the banner of the Dharma, his former vows were fulfilled; he possessed sovereign benefit, accomplished all the deeds of a Great Man, and having transformed those to be transformed, he delivered eight thousand *koṭis* of various classes of beings, such as the assembly of lotuses, causing them to be reborn in the heavens.

At that time, after that Buddha had entered nirvana and established the dharma-gate of liberation, he resided in this city of Vārāṇasī, within the Deer Park at the abode of the sages, dwelling there while preaching the Dharma.
"At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a virtuous upāsaka who followed the path of faith and observed the five precepts.
That upāsaka was well-versed in the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), proficient in worldly treatises (*lokavāda*), and capable of explaining their meanings."
That upāsaka went to the Deer Park and briefly asked the bhikṣus about the meaning [of the teaching].
Having asked thus, the bhikṣus then explained it to him in detail.
Having heard those bhikṣus extensively explain such meanings for him, that upāsaka felt a sense of admiration and made this aspiration:
"Excellent and rare indeed!"

"May I, in a future life, obtain a Dharma even more excellent than this, and may I likewise be able to analyze and explain it to others in successive order, just as these bhikṣus do, without any difference."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should know!
That upāsaka who observed the five precepts at that time was none other than this Mahākātyāyana."

Having received and upheld the five precepts from that Buddha as an upāsaka, he was well-versed in the subtle meanings of the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) and was further able to analyze and explain them for others.
At that time, he made this vow:
"May I, in a future life, accomplish all these dharmas and be able to explain them extensively and in various ways for the sake of others."
"Furthermore, monks!

You should know that this monk Kātyāyana planted such roots of goodness in the past with a joyful heart. By reason of these causes and conditions, he came into my presence, immediately went forth as a renunciant, and attained the fruit of Arhatship."
I now bestow this prediction: among my assembly of śrāvakas, the foremost in being able to expand upon concise meanings and condense extensive meanings is the bhikṣu Mahākātyāyana.

"At that time, there were ninety-two Arhats in the world: first the World-Honored One, then the five bhikṣus, as well as the body of the Elder Yaśoda, and furthermore the sons of good family who were the most eminent among the eminent—the wealthy friends of Yaśoda, such as the elders Vimala, Subāhu, Pūrṇa, Gavāmpati, and others."
Furthermore, Yaśodharā had fifty friends who were leading merchants, as well as various good sons who had come from other regions.
Additionally, there was the Elder Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra with twenty-nine of his friends, along with the Elder Kātyāyana and others.

Chapter 42: The Ordination of Sāṃkṛtyāyana. From the *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha-sūtra*, Chapter Forty-two, Part One: "At that time, there was a city in Northern India named Takṣaśilā, which in the language of the Sui means 'Chiseled Stone.'"
At that time, there was a certain family within that city, and the women of that household suddenly gave birth to twins—a boy and a girl.
The parents immediately summoned a skilled physiognomist and ordered him to examine them.
At that time, the physiognomist immediately performed a divination and declared, "This girl has poor marks;
there is nothing auspicious about her. When the girl's parents heard these words, they thought to themselves:
"Since this girl now lacks any favorable marks, she is not auspicious. When she reaches maturity, who will take her as his wife?"

After the parents had thus deliberated together, they sought out the wife of a learned non-Buddhist ascetic named Pārivāja (translated in the Sui language as "Practitioner of Conduct"). They spoke to her as follows:
"We now beg you for this daughter of ours; please nurture and instruct her in the Dharma so that she may grow in it. Whatever provisions or requisites she may require, we shall provide them all."

At that time, the non-Buddhist Pāṭimātṛ immediately took her in and raised her, caring for her in this manner. As the girl gradually grew with the passing of time, she reached the age of maturity, and her intellect and understanding were fully developed.

At that time, when the daughter of that non-Buddhist Pārilava had grown up, his wife taught her various incantations and various skills, all of which she mastered; she became clear-minded and intelligent in various treatises until she reached full maturity.

He was handsome with few equals, pleasing to many to behold; his body was supple, his countenance surpassed others, his joints were well-developed, and his physique was perfectly proportioned without any deficiency.

At that time, she wore a single *śāṭī* garment below her waist and another *śāṭī* draped over her shoulders; holding a three-pronged stand for a water jar in her hand, she traveled from place to place through villages, cities, market towns, kingdoms, and royal palaces to perform ablutions.
Seeking out various non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*) with the intent to debate and subdue them, he traveled by stages.
Along the way, he encountered a Pāśupata ascetic named Paramasvatantra-paravijaya, who was wandering from place to place, traveling from South India to North India.
At that time, that practitioner was likewise pleasing; he was handsome with few equals, in the prime of his youth, and a joy for all to behold.
His countenance was even more distinguished than others, his body was well-proportioned, and his limbs were lovely to look upon. Among all the masters of treatises, he was most renowned.

At that time, the practitioner saw this daughter of the Pārivājaka, so pleasing, upright, and beautiful that others delighted in beholding her; having seen her, he conceived a heart of attachment toward that woman of the Pārivājaka.
At that time, the daughter of Pārivājaka likewise conceived a lustful mind toward the ascetic Pārivājaka; they became mutually infatuated with one another, their private longing never ceasing.
At that time, the visiting parivrājaka ascetic spoke thus to the parivrājaka woman:
"O virtuous lady, O noble one!
"I now earnestly desire and take pleasure in your accompanying me in worldly affairs.
At that time, the woman also replied:
"In my heart, I too long for you and wish to be in one place with you."
Then that Pārivrajaka practitioner replied to the woman, saying:

"We two are both renunciants who practice the Way. If we were to engage in worldly affairs while in the midst of such dharma-practice, and if people were to see us doing such things, they would immediately reprimand and revile us."
"We should now debate before these people and establish a solemn oath: whoever is defeated shall be made to serve the victor.
At that time, the woman spoke thus:
"If I am victorious and you, on the other hand, are defeated, this would be unwholesome and contrary to propriety; how could it be right for a man to serve a woman?"
"If a woman does not excel her husband but instead serves him, this is indeed good; this is in accordance with principle.
Then that Pārivrajaka practitioner replied to the woman, saying:
"Excellent, virtuous lady!"
"The meaning of these words of yours is most reasonable, just as you have said.
At that time, the Pārivrajaka ascetic immediately struck the drum of debate amidst the assembly and announced:
"Is there anyone here who is able to engage me in a question-and-answer discussion?"
"Whether it be a male parivrājaka or a female parivrājika, who among you is able to engage me in dialogue and debate?
Whoever is so able shall do well."
This was repeated three times.
Then, having heard these words in the midst of the assembly, that woman Pāribhājā cried out:
"I am now quite capable of engaging with you in debate, coming and going, asking and answering!"
At that time, the woman, with a composed and dignified bearing, posed questions regarding their meaning within the great assembly; the Pārivrajaka practitioners were able to explain them correctly.
Then, the Pārivrajaka practitioners questioned the woman in turn, and she likewise explained them correctly.
Thus they repeated this process twice more, each questioning the other and each communicating with the other.
When they reached the third round, that Pārivrajaka ascetic questioned the woman on the meaning of the doctrine; she possessed great power and was able to explain and communicate it to him.
However, because she protected that Pārivājaka out of affection for him in her heart, she appeared to be unable to respond and remained silent without answering.
Then, that Pārivājika practitioner immediately subdued her in the midst of the assembly.
"At that time, having been subdued by the Pāṛśva ascetic, she immediately took from his hands the leather sandals and the trident, and holding them, she walked away before the assembly."
Once those two had manifested their intentions, they engaged in such defiled union without avoiding one another, moving together in one place.
Because of that union between the two practitioners, the woman immediately became pregnant.
Since the woman had become pregnant, she deviated from her original practice; consequently, she lost her natural complexion and was no longer beautiful.
When that Pārivrajaka ascetic saw that her body had lost its original color, he immediately felt revulsion and contempt, and said to her:
"I can no longer dwell or stay in the same place with you."
Then that woman replied to the Pārivrajaka practitioner with these words:

"The two of us were both practicing the Way, yet both have lost our way. Now, this fetus has already formed within me because of you; if you now see that I am without beauty or charm and suddenly abandon me, I shall die on the spot, and if I do not die, I will surely suffer great agony."
At that time, the Pārivrajaka ascetic, having made his resolve firm, gave the woman a single gold ring as a token and further told her:
"If you give birth to a daughter, use this ring to trade for wealth, and with it provide for her upbringing."
"If you give birth to a son, you should give him this signet ring as a token so that he may seek me out.
Having given her the ring, she left her behind and turned her back on her, traveling south toward South India.
"At that time, the woman Pāṭalī, carrying her pregnant body, traveled from place to place, journeying along until she gradually arrived at the village of Mathurā."
At that time, in that village, there was a frontier district named White Cloud; situated within a certain county there, he gave birth to a son.

Once the child was born, all the men and women residing within that district conceived feelings of affection, love, and compassion; some gave him ghee, some gave him oil, and they also bestowed upon him whatever else he required.
Then that woman, Pāṭalīvaśā, thought to herself:

"This son of mine was born within the jurisdiction of a district; now I shall establish his name according to the designation of that place. Therefore, this son's name shall be Sāvitra (Sui: County Official)."
"At that time, the woman Pṛṣadhā raised her son Sāvitra according to the Dharma, nourishing him with milk and food so that he might grow."

As the youth Sāṃkṛtyāyana grew up, his intelligence gradually matured; meanwhile, that woman Pāribhājī instructed her son in writing, painting, arithmetic, seal-marking, incantations, and all other treatises, teaching him until he was fully accomplished in them.
That youth was quick-witted and intelligent; whatever he studied, he mastered completely, and there was nothing he did not know.
At one time, Sāvitrī asked his mother:
"Mother, Mother!..."
"Who was my father?
Where is he now?
At that time, his mother replied to her son, saying:
"Son Sāvitra! Your father is currently in the kingdom of South India; you should now go there to seek him out and find your father.
At that time, the mother took the signet ring previously left by her husband as a token, gave it to her son, and addressed him, saying:
"Take this prediction and seek out your father.
Then Sāṃkṛtyāyana replied to his mother,
"I shall act exactly as my mother has instructed."

Then, having received the prediction, Sāvitra gradually set out toward South India, traveling from village to village, from one settlement to another, and from city to city, proceeding step by step toward the land of South India.
Wherever he went, he defeated all those who engaged him in debate.
Gradually arriving at his father’s location, he neither recognized his father nor asked for directions; upon reaching him, he immediately struck the drum of debate and spoke these words:
"Is there anyone here—whether a *pārivrajaka* ascetic or a *pārivrajakī* female ascetic—who is capable of engaging me in such a dialogue and debate?"
At that time, when the father of the youth Sāvitrī saw his son, love for his child naturally arose within his heart; then the Pārivrajaka ascetic asked the youth:
"O virtuous youth!..."
"Who are you now,
and from where have you come?
At that time, the youth spoke at length to the ascetic Pāṭimātṛ regarding the causes and conditions of his arrival, taking a finger-ring out to show it to him.
When that Pārivājaka ascetic saw the ring, he said to the youth, "You are my son.

Having thus regained his son, the Pārivājaka ascetic further advanced his instruction in various incantations and skills; for the Pārivājaka had previously cultivated and attained various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and so he taught these methods of concentration to his son in due order.
Not long thereafter, that Pārivrajaka practitioner passed away. After Sāvitrī’s father had died, he gradually made his way toward the seashore;

having arrived there, he constructed a grass hut and dwelt in that place, sitting in silent contemplation. Before long, he attained the four dhyānas and simultaneously realized the five supernormal powers.
Having realized this, he thought to himself:
"Among all those in the world who are Arhats, or those who claim for themselves, 'I have attained the path of an Arhat,' I am also called an Arhat in their company; we are of one kind, no different."
“At that time, the mother of the youth Sāvitra had already passed away and was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

At this time, after the World-Honored One had realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and turned the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma in the Deer Park, the various gods dwelling on earth each proclaimed the news to one another; their voices were passed from one to another until they reached the Heaven of the Thirty-three.”
At that time, having heard this sound, the Trāyastriṃśa goddess who was the mother of the youth reflected within her mind:
"Where does my son dwell today?
Observing with right mindfulness, she saw her son dwelling on the seashore.

At that time, a certain deity, whose bodily radiance surpassed all others, released a celestial light at the very hour of midnight, illuminating the dwelling place of his son as far as the limits of where Udraka Rāmaputra was practicing his austerities, and addressed Udraka, saying: "O Udraka!
"You are not an Arhat, nor have you yet entered the path of an Arhat or the dharma of an Arhat.
Regarding the method for seeking the path of an Arhat, you have not yet attained the proper sequence."
Then Sāvitrī asked that deva,
"Who is this deva? Is he now an arhat?"
"Is there a dharma for entering the path of arhatship?
Is there perhaps anyone who knows the teachings of the arhat-dharma and can cause others to train so as to attain arhatship?
At that time, that deva immediately replied to Sāvitrī, saying:

"O Sāṃjīya! There is now a World-Honored One, a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, currently residing at the Abode of the Rishis in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī. That World-Honored One is himself an Arhat; having entered the path of an Arhat and attained self-knowledge, he is further able to teach others so that they may attain the Dharma of an Arhat."
Then Sāvitra again asked the deva, saying: "O Great Deva!
I am currently lacking wisdom; by what skillful means can I come to know that he is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha?"
At that time, that deity instructed Sāṃbhūti to speak as follows:
“Pārīvāja! When you inquire about the principles of the Dharma, it should be done in this manner:”
Since you have received such a name as "bhikṣu," how do you discipline yourself?
How do you practice virtue?
And what constitutes being a Buddha?
What is a bhikṣu?
What is a śramaṇa and a brāhmaṇa? What is purity?
What is meant by wisdom and knowing the field of merit?
What is called skillful mastery of expedient means?
And what is called a "seer" (ṛṣi)?
What is meant by renown?
What is meant by compliance?
What is meant by diligence?
What is meant by "dragon"?
What is meant by "feeling"?
What is meant by "noble"?
How does one practice the practices?
How does one seek the Way?
You, Sāṃkṛtyāyana!
If you see someone to whom you may ask about this matter, and that person explains it to you point by point, bringing you joy, you should practice the holy life under them.

Then, having heard these words from that deity and having taken them to heart, Sāvitrī Pārilavāja traveled through all the kingdoms, cities, towns, and villages, beating drums everywhere to seek out those with whom he might debate.
Again, he proclaimed aloud:
"Is there any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who can explain the meaning of this question I have asked?
At that time, wherever he went, there was not a single person capable of explaining such a discourse.

At that time, wherever Sāṃkṛtyāyana traveled, there were people who had been there before, either sitting in contemplation of the Dharma or engaged in debate; upon hearing that Sāṃkṛtyāyana had arrived at their side, they each fled in different directions, and in the end, no one dared to engage him in discussion, conversation, or discourse.
"At that time, Sāvitrī Parivrājaka traveled by stages and gradually arrived at the city of Vārāṇasī.
At that moment, there were six great masters in that city, each proclaiming:
'I am the foremost in the world.'"
This refers to Pūraṇa, along with the three Kāśyapas, Nigaṇṭha, and others.

At that time, Sāvitrī immediately went to where Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and the others were; having arrived, he exchanged greetings and polite inquiries with Pūraṇa face-to-face, and once their conversation was concluded, he withdrew to stand to one side.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume 38 and Volume 39.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
The Chapter on the Renunciation of Śveta, Part Two:
At that time, Śveta the Parivrājaka questioned Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and the others regarding the meaning as previously described: "What is a bhikṣu?"
"How, furthermore, is it called 'seeking the Way'?
After Upatiṣya had thus questioned Kāśyapa, Kāśyapa and the others, having received the meaning of his words, were bewildered in mind and unable to provide an answer.

Because he could not grasp the meaning and intent of that [teaching], his frown deepened further; his brows and forehead contracted into three furrows, resentment arose in his heart, and with anger and indignation, he cried out pointlessly.
At that time, Sāṃkṛtyāyana Pārilava had this thought:

"This elder, when questioned by me regarding the meaning of atoms and such, was unable to provide an answer. Furthermore, he misunderstood my intent, responding with errors and inconsistencies; he could not grasp the meaning, his phrasing was stilted and halting, and he became even more deeply ashamed, giving rise to resentment and anger, shouting out for no reason."

At that time, Sāvitrī Pārilavaśa, having conceived a sense of weary detachment toward Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, turned away from him and departed, going instead to the presence of Maskarī Gośālīputra and the Nirgranthas.
Having arrived there, he even exchanged mutual greetings and comforting words with the Nirgrantha, and after completing his polite inquiries regarding their affairs, he withdrew to stand to one side.
Then Sāṃjīva Pāripājaka questioned the Nirgranthas and others as previously described: "In what sense is one called a bhikṣu, and so on, up to the seeking of the Way?"
When those Nirgranthas had been thus questioned by Sāṃkṛtyāyana, their minds were thrown into confusion and they were unable to provide an answer.
At that time, Sāṃkṛtyāyana thought to himself:

"These elders are ultimately unable to explain even such matters as the nature of atoms; yet when I questioned them, their minds became bewildered and disordered, and they failed to comprehend, instead increasing their anger and shouting as before."
Then Sāvitrī thought to herself:

"Is there perhaps another person in this world—whether a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa—who is renowned throughout the world as a truly omniscient Arhat? If such a one exists, I shall go to him and ask about my doubts; if I attain understanding, I shall serve, make offerings to, and prostrate before him, never departing from his side day or night."
Then, Sāvitra thought to himself once more:

"The Great Śramaṇa is now at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī, the abode of the sages. People of the world say that the wise Arhat is one of great intelligence; I shall now go to that Śramaṇa and inquire about my doubts."
He further reflected:

"In this world, there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are elderly and of long-standing virtue, having practiced the holy life for many years. Each of them is capable of serving as a teacher to various kings; they are each spoken of in the world as being clever, wise, and great arhats—namely, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and others, as well as the Nirgranthas."
Even I do not know the answer to my own questions; how much less could this śramaṇa, who has been a renunciant for only a short time since his youth, understand what I have now asked?
He further reflected again:
"That śramaṇa must not be treated with contempt, nor may he be deceived or insulted. Why is this so?"

"As for those śramaṇas, although they may be young, some might be intelligent and possess great wisdom that cannot be easily discerned; I shall now simply go to that Great Śramaṇa and ask about what I doubt in my mind."

Then, Sāvitrī Pārilavāja went to where the Buddha was. From afar he saw the World-Honored One, who, like the sky adorned with a multitude of stars, was proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma amidst the assembly.
Having seen him, a thought of faith and practice arose in his mind:
"This must certainly be that Tathāgata, World-Honored One, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha whom I have previously heard of; there is no difference."
He then proceeded to where the Buddha was.

Upon arriving at the Buddha’s presence, he exchanged pleasant words with the World-Honored One, offering skillful speech and consolation through various discourses. Having finished speaking, he withdrew and sat to one side.
Then Sāṃkṛtyāyanapārileya immediately addressed the Buddha in verse:
“I am the practitioner Sāṃkṛtyāyana; I have come from afar from another region.
In my heart there is a doubt I wish to ask of the Great Wise One; I only pray that you will explain it to me in detail.”
If you can sever the doubts in my mind, reflect upon each one and explain them for me;
interpret them according to the sequence of my words and meanings, clarifying each point individually without any inconsistency.
When Sāṃbhīya had spoken this verse, he remained silent.

Now, it is the nature of all Buddhas that they possess three gateways of supernormal power (*abhijñā*) through which they teach; if there is anyone who can be transformed, they immediately transform them.
What are these three?
The first is called the supernormal power of manifestation; the second is named the supernormal power of instruction; and the third is named the supernormal power of instruction in practice.
Then the World-Honored One, knowing the doubts that had arisen in the mind of Sāvitrī Parivrājaka, addressed Sāvitrī with these verses:
“Sāvitrī, you have come from afar, wishing to ask about the doubts in my heart.
You may now speak, and I shall explain; I will attend to whatever you ask.”
Just as you have intended, let there be no deviation; you, Subhūti, should speak forthwith.
With every heart you desire to request this, do not harbor doubt; according to each question, I shall proclaim it in detail.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, Sāvitrī Parivrājaka thought to himself:

"In all the places I have previously visited, there were various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who were elderly and of long-standing virtue, who had been ordained for a long time and were worthy of serving as royal preceptors; they were regarded by the world as great arhats, wise and intelligent."
I questioned them regarding the points they doubted, yet they were all entirely mistaken and unable to answer me.

Because they could not respond to the meaning of my questions, they harbored shame within their hearts; with their faces split into three parts, frowning their brows and wrinkling their foreheads, they gave way to resentment and cried out pointlessly.
At that time, Sāvitrī felt a sense of wonder, thinking:

"This Great Śramaṇa, when questioned by me, did not become angry or resentful; his appearance became even more pure and serene, without any change in expression, but rather grew increasingly radiant. He consented to explain what I asked him. In this person, whose faculties are so tranquil, I see no fault whatsoever."
Having understood this, Sāvitrī Parivrājaka was filled with great joy; his heart leaped with exultation so intensely that he could not contain himself.
Having attained joy, he immediately addressed the Buddha with verses, asking about the meaning of the Dharma:
"Great Sage, what is meant by the name 'bhikṣu'?
What is meant by the 'subduing' of those who are subdued by the noble ones?"
"What must be known and seen to be called awakening?
I pray only that the World-Honored One will explain this for me.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Pāṭimāṣya Sāvitrī with these verses:
“Seeking enlightenment through unimpeded asceticism, crossing over all doubts toward the shore of Nirvana,
having utterly abandoned both existence and non-existence— one whose taints are exhausted through the holy life is called a bhikṣu.”
Practicing right mindfulness in all states of relinquishment, Within this world of non-violence, one attains a pure and untainted body; Being liberated from all fetters is called "taming."
If one can restrain all the sense faculties both internally and externally, such subduing is called "straightforwardness.
To feel weary of and detached from this world and the world beyond, awaiting the time for *nirvāṇa*, is called "virtuous conduct."

Having practiced with diligent effort throughout all kalpas, Experiencing the two extremes of birth and death according to karma, One becomes stainless in the world and free from all fetters; This is called awakening to the exhaustion of birth and death.
At that time, Sāvitrī Pāripājaka, hearing these words, was filled with joy and further questioned the Buddha in verse, saying:
"What is it called that constitutes the cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya)?"
How is a śramaṇa pure?
How does the Buddha, who possesses great wisdom, discipline himself?
Now I ask the World-Honored One to explain this for me.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Pārileyyaka Sāṃjaya with these verses:
"Having abandoned all transgressions and being free from the taints of defilement, Having well attained meditative concentration and abiding in the ground of right practice,
One who alone is able to transcend the ocean of afflictions— Such a person is called a holy practitioner of the Brahma-faring."
Accumulating merit and abandoning all that is non-virtuous, knowing no affliction in this world or the next,
and because all birth and death have been extinguished— one who attains such realization is called a śramaṇa.
All karmic retributions are entirely eliminated; throughout all worlds, both internal and external, no devas or humans can defile it—this is what is called a pure form.

All fetters are exhausted and there is nothing that binds; from all internal and external spheres of the world, one is completely liberated from greed, delusion, and hatred—the Buddha says such a person is called one of great wisdom.
At that time, having heard these words, Sāvitrī Parivrājaka again questioned the Buddha in verse, saying:
"What do the Buddhas take as the field of merit?"
How does one skillfully know the excellent expedient means?
What is it that is called a Great Sage (Maharṣi)?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Pārikṣita Sāṃjīya with these verses:
"One who discerns and knows each of all the lands, Who is worthy of offerings from all Brahmās and devas,
Who understands the bondage of attachment to karmic retribution and is liberated from it— Such a person is called a field of merit."
From what karma, faculties, retribution, and seeds do they arise? All the Brahmās and devas distinguish these;
one who can sever their roots through various patiences is called one who possesses skillful wisdom.
Each chooses for themselves the pure cause; whatever exists within or without all worlds is not grasped by a self and has no fixed location—such skillful means are called "expedient wisdom."
Knowing the existence and non-existence of all phenomena, seeing that all worlds have neither interior nor exterior,
and being honored by gods and humans in this world— one who is unimpeded and uniquely liberated is called a *ṛṣi*.
At that time, having heard these words, Sāṃkṛtyāyanapārāśarya again questioned the Buddha in verse, saying:
"By what means is one said to have 'heard' [the Dharma]?"
What is meant by "conformity" and "diligence"?
What is it that is called being a "great nāga"?
We pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for us.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Pārīśarāśvīya with these verses:
"All dharmas are heard and known; Regarding all transgressions and merits alike, One transcends them without further thorns of doubt;
To be unattached to anything at all—this is called 'hearing' (śruta)."
Name-and-form are both causes of delusion; the internal faculties and external objects are the root of affliction.
Having attained liberation from all such bases, the Buddha calls this "conformity with the mind."
Having abandoned all bonds of sin, one must be courageous in leaving behind the suffering of hell;
being liberated from them without further attachment—such a person is called one of diligence.
One who distances themselves from all worldly craving, severs both bondage and liberation,
has exhausted all outflows and is free from the thorn of suffering— such a person as this is called a Nāga.
At that time, having heard these words, Sāvitrī Parivrājaka again questioned the Buddha in verse, saying:
"For what reason is it called 'feeling' (vedanā)?"
How are the noble ones and their practices described?
For what reason are they called "those who seek the Way"?
Now I ask the World-Honored One to explain this for me.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Pārāśarya Sāvitrī with these verses:
"Whatever Vedas have been selected one by one, Or from the side of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas,
Having understood and realized them, I have received each and every one from them."
Having severed and cut through the net of false views, that wisdom no longer undergoes rebirth in a womb;
having already removed the mire of the three types of conceptual signs, one who does not engage in discrimination is called a noble one.
Having fully attained all supernormal powers, knowing all phenomena with equanimity,
and being able to penetrate all worlds of the Sugata— one who understands in this way is called a practitioner of practice.
Regarding the retribution of suffering inherent in all phenomena— whether superior, inferior, or intermediate—
one who can fully comprehend the sphere of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is such a person as seeks the Way.

"At that time, all the points of inquiry posed by Sāvitrī Parivrājaka to the World-Honored One were entirely in accord with his own mind. Having rejoiced, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation, and gazing up at the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he praised him, saying:
'Excellent!'"
"Bhagavān!
All sixty-two views existing in the world are of no use; within the world, all such things are merely false dharmas."

I now take refuge in the Unsurpassed World-Honored One. Only the World-Honored One can discern and know all things; he alone is a Great Man. Only the World-Honored One can skillfully explain the Dharma; only the World-Honored One can know all paths. Only the World-Honored One can ferry others across the ocean of suffering; only the World-Honored One can eternally exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*). Only the World-Honored One possesses the greatest majesty and virtue; only the World-Honored One uniquely possesses abundant wisdom. Only the World-Honored One is able to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
And he spoke this verse of praise:
"I now prostrate to the Great Being, Who, through the practice of truth, radiates light that shines everywhere;
Within the world of devas and humans, He skillfully opens the gate of the drum of nectar."
All the doubts and uncertainties I previously held, only the World-Honored One can resolve for me.
Since the World-Honored One is a Great Sage who has awakened, all defilements are exhausted without remainder;
he shall never again receive a physical body, and all causes of birth have been utterly extinguished.
The World-Honored One has attained the state of coolness; with a pure mind of contentment, he always practices the truth.
Thus the World-Honored One is like a dragon; what this Great Man speaks from his golden mouth is that which Śakra, all the devas, and all the seers and sages delight to hear.
The World-Honored One is one who has attained true awakening; the World-Honored One is skilled at instructing sentient beings;
the World-Honored One is able to subdue the hosts of Māra; the World-Honored One is able to sever all latent tendencies and fetters.
Having liberated oneself, one further liberates others; equal toward both demerit and merit, one transcends and is without attachment to anything, clearly understanding the worlds of gods and humans.
Only the Buddha, the Truly Real and Unsurpassed Honored One, Has transcended all erroneous paths;
All outflows and their causes have been utterly extinguished.
Just as the moon is bright on the fifteenth night, Surrounded by stars filling the sky, So does he illuminate the world within.
Consciousness, name-and-form, life-span, and so forth—
the people dwelling in the royal capital of Rājagṛha have a mountain named Vipula, which is the most excellent and supreme of all.
Furthermore, as among all dragons, the Snowy Mountain is supreme; among those who fly, the sky is highest;
among all streams, the ocean is deepest; and among all stars, the moon is foremost.
If one wishes to take refuge in the Tamer, one should take refuge only in the Unsurpassed One.
I take refuge in the Most Victorious One of the world; I take refuge in the Supreme among Men, the Righteous Charioteer;
I take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One, the Sugata; I take refuge in the Peerless, the Truly Perfected One.
Just as fire is most honored among sacrifices, and incantations are supreme among discourses,
as the king is the most sovereign among men, and the great ocean is the widest among rivers,
as the moon is the most luminous among the stars, and the sun is the most radiant among all lights—
Throughout the six realms above and below, the good and evil destinies— namely, all the worlds of the three realms—
including every sentient being with form, whether deva or human— the World-Honored One alone is supreme. Therefore,
I now join my ten fingers together and prostrate my head at the feet of the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Then, after Sāvitra had spoken these verses in praise of the Tathāgata, he addressed the Buddha again,
saying: "Excellent,
World-Honored One!"
“I only pray that the World-Honored One,
out of compassion and pity, will grant me permission to leave the household life and bestow upon me the full precepts.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Sāvitrī, saying:
"Welcome, welcome! You, Sāṃjīva!
Because you have attained liberation through the complete exhaustion of all suffering within my own teaching of the Dharma and its practice."
At that time, the Elder Sābhiya’s body immediately became that of a bhikṣu, fully endowed with the complete precepts.

Not long after Sābhiya had left the household life and received full ordination, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he remained solitary without companion. He was never defiled by attachment; he was prudent in body and speech, never daring to be heedless, and for the sake of seeking the Way, he acted as if his head were on fire.

Not long after practicing in this manner, that son of good family, with right faith and heroic vigor, left his home to go forth into homelessness, desiring to seek the unsurpassed, pure brahmacarya. Directly perceiving all phenomena, he realized them within his own mind and declared:
"I have exhausted all birth and death; I have attained the fruit of brahmacarya; there is no further existence for me; what was to be done has been accomplished. Thus did he know for himself.
When Sāṃkṛtyāyana had thus realized this state and attained the fruit of arhatship with a mind well-liberated, there were then ninety-three arhats in the world:
from the First World-Honored One down to the very last, including Sāṃkṛtyāyana.

"At that time, after the World-Honored One had attained enlightenment, he was at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī. Including himself, there were eight people who entered the summer retreat on the sixteenth day of the sixth month. On the fifteenth day of the ninth month, a total of ninety-three people concluded the summer retreat."

Chapter Forty-three: Training the Soldiers and Generals. *The Sutra of the Collection of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Forty-three, Part One: Training the Soldiers and Generals. "At that time, there were groups of people from various other regions—coming from different towns, villages, and kingdoms—who called out to one another. With a shared aspiration and joy, they desired to seek renunciation and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
They came to Vārāṇasī, approached the Buddha, and said to the World-Honored One: 'Grant us renunciation and bestow upon us full ordination.'"
"For this reason, the senior bhikṣus must attend to them, becoming weary and exhausted.
Those people, desiring to go forth, create a clamorous noise; because of this, they disturb the World-Honored One, preventing him from finding quietude."
At that time, on one occasion, the World-Honored One was sitting alone in a quiet chamber and reflected thus:
"Now these people have come from various distant regions, villages, and kingdoms to this place, thinking in their minds: 'May the Tathāgata grant us the going forth and the full ordination.'"
For these reasons, those people have come from afar with the intention of seeking [me], yet they are weary; furthermore, they cause me disturbance.

I should now dispatch the bhikṣus to various other villages and cities to teach and transform all beings there. If there are those who wish to leave the household life and receive full ordination, I shall grant it to them according to the Dharma.
At that time, having formed this thought, the World-Honored One rose from his chamber at dawn and, for this reason, assembled the entire community of bhikṣus.
Once they had assembled, he addressed them, saying:
"O bhikṣus! You should now know this!"

While staying in a secluded and quiet room, I engaged in this reflection as previously described, up to the point where I said: "You all should go elsewhere to grant them the going-forth and the full ordination; do not let them come here, for they would both exhaust themselves and cause disturbance to others."
Having spoken thus, he further addressed them again:

"I now charge you, monks: when you arrive in other regions, villages, towns, or cities, if there are those who come seeking to go forth and receive full ordination, you should grant them the going forth and the full ordination."
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"When that person comes wishing to go forth from the household life, you must perform these actions: first, you should shave off his hair and beard;

once they have been shorn, you should instruct him to put on the saffron-colored robes. As he puts on the robes, ensure his attire is neat and orderly, and have him bare his right shoulder. Instruct him to stand before the assembly, place his right knee on the ground, and instruct him to prostrate at the feet of the bhikṣus."
Having completed the prostration, he rises and kneels before the bhikṣu. The bhikṣu instructs him to join his palms together and speaks these words:
"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha."

"O bhikṣus! From this day forward, in accordance with my instructions, if anyone comes seeking to leave the household life and receive the precepts and the three refuges, they shall immediately obtain full ordination."
At that time, the World-Honored One was still staying at the Deer Park in the city of Vārāṇasī for the summer retreat, and he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"O bhikṣus! You all..."

If you should know that I have attained liberation, you ought to practice your conduct among all devas and humans for the sake of bringing benefit to many people, for the sake of bringing happiness to many people, and for the sake of seeking future benefit and happiness for the world.
If you wish to travel to another village, you may go alone; there is no need for two people.
Furthermore, monks!

If you go to another village, out of compassion for many people and for the sake of gathering them in, you should preach the Dharma that is good in the beginning, middle, and end—subtle in meaning, complete, and flawless.
"O bhikṣus! You should preach the holy life (brahmacarya).

There are sentient beings who have little dust and defilement, whose fetters are thin, and whose faculties are matured; yet they fear that if they do not hear the True Dharma, they will be unable to know the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa)."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I shall gradually depart and travel toward the village of Uruvilvā, going to the village of Senāpati in order to teach the Dharma to them."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“O Bhikṣu, I have now crossed over all sufferings; Having accomplished my own benefit, I further benefit others.
Since the suffering of many people remains undispelled, I must now act with compassion for them.”
Therefore, you monks, each of you should proceed alone;
I too shall now depart from here, intending to go to the village of Piṇḍola.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān secretly approached the place where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, he immediately addressed the Buddha in verse:
“You are bound by all manner of fetters, Just as all gods and humans are likewise bound;
Since you are entangled by every cord, O Śramaṇa, you have not escaped the net.”
At that time, having heard this verse, the World-Honored One immediately reflected and thought:
"These are the words of Māra Pāpīyān."
Having understood this, he replied to Māra Pāpīyān with these verses:
“I have long since been liberated from all bonds; I possess nothing whatsoever that belongs to gods or humans.
Since these bonds of mine have already left my body, what more can you say, O Pāpīyān, after having been defeated?”
At that time, the World-Honored One once again reproached the Māra Pāpīyān with these verses, saying:
"All forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tangibles— These are the five desires that defile humanity.
I have now eliminated them all; I have already subdued you, evil Māra Pāpīyān."
At that time, having heard this verse, Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind.
He was overcome with great anguish and deep remorse, and suddenly vanished from that place.
At that time, all the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha together,
saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
If someone were to come to me and ask me:
"Venerable Bhikṣu!
What are the names for a śramaṇa and a brāhmaṇa?"
"Once we bhikṣus have heard this from him, how should we respond to him?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If someone asks, 'What is a śramaṇa and what is a brāhmaṇa?'"
"Monks, when a renunciant is in such a state, you, monks, should know it for what it is when you recognize the time;
having known it, you should observe it with a correct mind."
At that time, for this reason and on this occasion, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to the bhikṣus:

"Having forever eliminated flattery, crookedness, and ego-conceit, With greed and anger exhausted, free from all desire— One whose nature is thus eternally pure: Such a person is a śramaṇa, a bhikṣu."
Those whose various sins and outflows are exhausted are called brahmins; those who practice diligence and asceticism are named śramaṇas.
When their defilements are exhausted and they have emerged from worldly toil, they are truly renunciants who have destroyed all evils.
At that time, having heard these verses, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha,
saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
When we bhikṣus go on our alms-round, what words should we speak?
Should we say, "Please give me food," or should we simply say, "Please give alms-food"?
"How should we employ skillful means when begging for alms?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!..."
One should not rely on what you have said in this manner.
Why is that? Because one must protect the minds of sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the bhikṣus in verse:
"The wise man who begs for alms remains silent; He does not point and say, 'Give me food.
The noble one stands to the side in silence and contemplation; This is called a true bhikṣu who begs for alms."
If there is one who is wise, when begging for food, he should simply stand gazing intently at one side;
when others see him in such a manner, they will immediately know him to be a mendicant śramaṇa.
Then the bhikṣus again asked the Buddha:
"If there is another person who, having conceived faith, begs us for food and shows us respect, what further words should we, the bhikṣus, speak?"
Should one say to him,
"May you have great good fortune," or should one say to him...?
"Are you greatly at ease?
Or should one say to him:
"Do you possess great merit?"
Should one say to him:
"I have now accepted it; you shall gain great merit"?
Or should one say: [no]?
"Do you have no merit?
How should we bhikṣus respond?
We only pray that you will instruct us.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
You should not rely upon what you have thus spoken."
"I now provide you with skillful instruction; you should act in this way.
He spoke in verse, saying:
"Generosity increases great merit; Through patience, all enemies and enmity cease."
The virtuous person abandons all that is non-virtuous; free from desire, they naturally attain liberation.
By cultivating merit, they always obtain peace and happiness; their aspirations are easily fulfilled and abound in manifold benefits.
In this present life, they swiftly attain a mind of tranquil concentration, and thereafter realize the state of Nirvana.
“At that time, the World-Honored One briefly spoke this verse to instruct the bhikṣus on the ritual method for receiving food and offering prayers of blessing.
Then, having received such instruction from the Buddha, the assembly of bhikṣus rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed as they pleased.”

At that time, after those various bhikṣus had each departed, there were forest-protecting deities, tree-protecting deities, and walking-path-protecting deities in that place. Seeing the forest empty, seeing the spaces beneath the trees empty, and seeing the walking paths empty, they felt private longing for the bhikṣus and went to the Buddha’s dwelling to speak this verse, inquiring of the Buddha:
"We deities are filled with great longing; We see these forests and trees all empty.
Where has that assembly of many-learned bhikṣus gone? O Gautama, son of the Śākyas, where have they now departed?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to those deities who protect the forest with these verses:
“Having brought all sense faculties under control, you shall travel abroad to teach and transform sentient beings;
some shall go to Kośala, and others shall head toward the city of Vaiśālī.”
Some go to the land of Ayodhyā, while others proceed to the region of Vajrapāṇi;
resolving the doubts and delusions of others, they preach the Dharma according to their capacities and inclinations.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had completed his summer retreat in the city of Vārāṇasī and remained there for some time, he again addressed the bhikṣus, instructing them to travel through various regions to teach and transform beings according to their conditions.
Then the World-Honored One, traveling from the city of Vārāṇasī, gradually arrived at the village of Uruvilvā, which was the place where the Tathāgata had formerly practiced austerities.
In that village there was a great brahmin named Senāpati; he reached that village and proceeded along the ancient, well-trodden path for the sake of teaching and transforming beings.

At that time, as the World-Honored One was traveling along the old road, he saw a grove by the side of the path that was lush and lovely. Thereupon, the World-Honored One left the road and entered deep into that forest; moving from tree to tree, he saw a tree that was upright and pleasing, and he sat beneath it to rest for a day.
At that time, there were thirty men in that forest, including companions and friends; twenty-nine of them all had wives, while only one man was alone and without a wife.
At that time, those twenty-nine friends together sought a wife for this one man who was without a spouse, yet they were unable to find one who met with his approval.

Suddenly, he hired a courtesan and brought her back to enjoy himself with her. That courtesan then engaged in pleasure with him as they pleased, attending to worldly affairs. She waited until those thirty men were all fast asleep; she then selected all the fine goods and fled with them.
"At that time, that man and his friends sought after that courtesan together; they traversed the entire grove, yet were unable to find her."

From afar he saw the World-Honored One sitting beneath a tree, lovely and upright, a sight that all people delighted to behold; his faculties were subdued and his mind was tranquil. He had attained the most supreme and excellent Dharma, like an elephant king who is most well-trained and exquisite; like a great pond filled with pure, cool water; with a fathom-wide radiance like a bar of gold; his physical marks were fully perfected, like a *śāla* tree covered in blossoms, even as the stars filling the void of space.
"At that time, those people, having seen this, went to where the Buddha was; having arrived at the Buddha's presence, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
'Venerable One!'"
"Have you seen such a woman here?
The Buddha replied to them, saying,
"O you people!..."
"Who is this woman whom you ask about?
For what reason has this woman come here?
At that time, they all answered the Buddha together, saying:
"O Great and Virtuous One!
We are thirty friends in all, all of us being upright and good, dwelling together in this forest. Twenty-nine of us have wives, and only one among us is single and without a wife."

We all hired a courtesan together to be our wife for a time so that we might enjoy ourselves; however, seeing us in the height of our pleasure and sleeping soundly at our ease, that courtesan chose our finest belongings and fled with them.
"We have also come into this grove for the sake of this friend, and furthermore, each for our own respective purposes, seeking that courtesan.
At that time, the Buddha addressed those men, saying: "O men!..."
I now ask you: what do you think?
Between these two matters—seeking your own welfare now, or seeking out that harlot—which would you consider superior?
Those men replied together to the Buddha,
saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
"If we now seek our own selves, this is the most excellent; it would be better not to seek those women.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again, saying:
"O sons of good family!
"If it be so, sit down comfortably; I shall now preach the Dharma for you.
At that time, those thirty men, his friends and companions, together addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
"We shall rely solely upon the holy teaching and dare not venture to contravene it.
At that time, those thirty friends prostrated at the Buddha's feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to him in due order as was appropriate, namely: generosity, ethical discipline, and the practice of patience; up to: all conditioned phenomena are of the nature of cessation. Having observed this according to reality and realized it for himself, he was like a clean cloth, free from black threads and free from grease and grime, which takes on whatever color it is dyed with.

In this way, indeed, those thirty male friends, right there on their seats, distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement; immediately, all afflictions were extinguished, and they attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, perceiving and knowing that all defiled phenomena possess the nature of cessation.

"At that time, those men, having thus seen the characteristics of all phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), attained these characteristics, realized these characteristics, entered these characteristics, and mastered these characteristics; they eliminated their doubts, were no longer deluded or attached, reached the stage of fearlessness, and no longer followed others."
Having understood the noble teaching of the World-Honored One, he rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
"We pray that you will allow us to go forth from the household life and receive the precepts.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these words to those men: "Come, O men!"
"Enter into my teaching and instruction, practice the holy life (brahmacarya), and bring about the complete exhaustion of the accumulation of suffering, reaching the end of suffering.
At that time, those elders immediately became renunciants and were fully ordained with the precepts.
"At that time, the World-Honored One further expounded the essentials of the Dharma for them, instructing and admonishing them with earnest care.

When the Buddha had thus further taught and exhorted them with the Dharma, before long, those sons of good family, out of right faith, abandoned their homes to go forth into homelessness. Having completed the pursuit of the supreme holy life and having personally realized and witnessed supernatural powers, they declared with their own mouths:
'I have now attained the fruit of the holy life; what was to be done has been accomplished; I shall no longer undergo future existence. Thus did they know."
Those elders all became arhats, their minds well-liberated.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had instructed those thirty elder friends and they had attained realization, he traveled on his journey, passing through the White Cottonwood Forest. Upon reaching that forest, he entered deep within it and saw a tree that was exquisite and pleasing; he sat beneath it and rested for a day.

"At that time, sixty men of the Meghiya clan happened to pass by along the forest path. From afar, they saw the World-Honored One sitting beneath a tree—exquisite and pleasing, a sight for all to delight in, even like the sky adorned with a multitude of stars."
Having seen him, his mind attained purity and right faith; he was filled with great joy, and because of that joy, he went to where the Buddha was.
Upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and having sat down, remained there in silence.

"At that time, the Buddha taught the Dharma in successive order for those sixty people of the Meghiya clan, namely: instruction on the practice of giving and maintaining ethical discipline, up to the realization and knowledge [of the fruits of the path]."
All those elder bhikṣus attained the fruit of arhatship and their minds were well-liberated.
At that time, having instructed those sixty elder bhikṣus of the Meghiya clan and inspired them toward enlightenment, the World-Honored One departed and traveled to other regions.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds,
Volume Thirty-nine and Volume Forty,
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on the Conversion of the Soldiers and Generals, Part Two:

At that time, the World-Honored One gradually proceeded until he reached the bank of the Ganges River. Having arrived there, he saw a boatman on the riverbank who, seeing the World-Honored One approaching from afar, rose quickly from his seat and hurried forward to welcome him.
Having arrived before the Buddha, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Welcome, World-Honored One!
From where have you come so far?"
And yet, you have suddenly arrived here.
World-Honored One!
Out of compassion for me, I pray that you will board this boat; I shall ferry the World-Honored One to the other shore and shall not take any payment.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately ascended the boat. Having sat upon the boat, he instructed and exhorted the boatman with these verses:
“Now you must thoroughly dry this boat in the sun; In this way, the vessel shall become light and swift.
If you can abandon these desires, anger, and afflictions, You will certainly and swiftly reach Nirvana.”
Dry this boat with a heart of loving-kindness, so that it may become light and swiftly cross over;
if you can now abandon desire and anger, you will certainly and quickly attain Nirvāṇa.
By drying this boat with a heart of compassion, you shall make it light and swift to cross;
if you can now renounce desire and hatred, you will surely and quickly attain Nirvana.
Dry this boat with a joyful mind, so that it may become light and cross swiftly;
if you can now abandon desire and anger, you will certainly and quickly attain Nirvana.
You should dry this boat with a mind of equanimity, so that it may become light and easily cross over;
if you can now abandon desire and anger, you will certainly and swiftly attain Nirvana.
If there is a bhikṣu who practices a mind of loving-kindness, And is able to have faith in the Buddha’s teachings,
He will swiftly realize the state of tranquil concentration, And before long attain unshakable nirvāṇa.
If there is a bhikṣu who practices compassion, And can have faith in the Buddha’s teachings,
He will swiftly realize the state of tranquil concentration, And before long attain unshakable nirvāṇa.
If there is a bhikṣu who practices a mind of joy, And is able to have faith in the Buddha’s teachings,
He will swiftly realize the state of tranquil concentration, And before long attain unshakable nirvāṇa.
If there is a bhikṣu who practices the mind of equanimity, And is able to have faith in the Buddha’s teachings,
He will swiftly realize the state of tranquil concentration, And before long attain unshakable nirvāṇa.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the boatman, saying:
"O son of good family!
Sprinkle water upon the ship."

Having spoken these words, the lay appearance of that boatman vanished entirely; his left hand naturally held a ceramic bowl, and his beard and hair were as if shaved seven days prior, like those of a bhikṣu. His gait and deportment were no different from those of a senior elder of a hundred summer retreats. Having thus attained such perfection, he immediately became a renunciant and received full ordination.
"At that time, the World-Honored One, desiring to cause him to give rise to joy, further increased his teaching of the Dharma for him.
And before long, son of good family!..."

Having completed the holy life and realized the Dharma for himself through direct experience, he attained the various supernormal powers; desiring to cast off birth and death, he cultivated pure conduct, and having accomplished what was to be done, he declared: "I shall not undergo further existence."
That elder had attained arhatship, with a mind well-liberated.
At that time, after the Elder had been instructed by the Buddha, he was sent to travel to other regions to transform and guide sentient beings.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had instructed the elder bhikṣu Nāvika and sent him on his way, he remained alone with no second companion, gradually proceeding toward the village of Uruvilvā.
"At that time, Śakra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, had this thought:
'Where is the Tathāgata now?
He looked about for himself and saw that the Tathāgata was alone, without anyone else, proceeding toward Uruvilvā."

Having observed this, Śakra immediately concealed his own form and manifested himself in the guise of a brahmin youth (*māṇava*), handsome and upright, whom all people delighted to behold. With a conch-shell topknot upon his head serving as a crown, he wore yellow robes; in his left hand he held a pure golden water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and in his right hand he carried a staff adorned with various jewels. Standing before the Tathāgata, he took the three robes and the alms-bowl from the Buddha and walked ahead of him.

At that time, Śakra was traveling along the road in front; whenever he encountered a prefecture, a commandery, a village, or a capital city, he would immediately use his supernatural powers to fly up into the air, circumambulate each prefecture, commandery, village, or town three times, and having completed these three circumambulations, he would hover above it.
“At that time, the body of that emanated māṇava was so upright, so pleasing, and possessed such majestic virtue that it was a sight for all people to behold.
Having seen him, a multitude of hundreds of thousands gathered like clouds and rain, and each asked him: ‘O māṇava!’”
From what place do you come?
To what family lineage do you belong?
What are your brothers' names?
"How have you come?
At that time, the māṇava replied to those people in verse, saying:
"The man of the world who knows contentment, Who has awakened by himself and is peerless in the world,"
Named Arhat, skilled in solitary wandering, I am now his disciple.
Sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of afflictions; oppressed by suffering, they cannot reach the further shore.
He now acts as their captain of the Dharma-ship; having already crossed over himself, he desires to ferry others across.
If there is one in this world who can cross over, I shall follow behind as his attendant;
since he has been able to exhaust desire, greed, and anger, and has shattered the darkness of ignorance,
having utterly extinguished the outflows of the world, I shall serve him as his disciple.
The most wondrous and peerless pair in the world—how could there be anyone superior?
Now the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has appeared; I serve him personally, following him wherever he goes.
Such a supreme Honored One in the world intends to come here this very day.

When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had spoken this verse, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, arrived before them. The assembly beheld the Tathāgata as so exceedingly pleasing and extraordinary that people delighted in gazing upon him; even his body was like the void adorned with the many stars. Having seen him, the great multitude said to one another:
"A teacher such as this is worthy of such a disciple; a disciple such as this is worthy of such a teacher."
Then the World-Honored One, for the sake of those people, expounded the meaning of the Dharma through subtle, skillful, and esoteric teachings.

At that time, among all those people, some who heard the Tathāgata preach this sublime Dharma conceived the aspiration to leave the household life; others attained the fruit of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhatship.

Furthermore, some act as the causal conditions for the seeds of the Śrāvaka Vehicle in future lives; some act as the causal conditions for the seeds of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle in future lives; and some act as the causal conditions for the seeds of the Bodhisattva Vehicle in future lives. Among them, there are those who receive the three refuges and the five precepts.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had sent away Śakra, Lord of the Devas, it was time for him to go on his almsround; he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and proceeded alone, wishing to beg for food, gradually arriving at the village of Mahāsena.
Having entered that town, he went straight to the house of the brahmin general; upon arriving at the house, he entered through the doorway and sat down on a prepared seat.
At that time, the great Brahmin Senāpati had two daughters, one named Nandā and the other named Parā.
Then those two daughters went toward the Buddha; having arrived at the place where the Buddha was, they prostrated at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing their mental dispositions and inclinations and that their fetters were already attenuated, and having understood the various elements (*dhātu*) and the sense bases (*āyatana*), taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
When he had spoken thus, those two women, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, shattered the mountain of twenty layers of views and immediately realized the fruit of *srotāpanna*.

Having perceived the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), those women followed the Buddha and requested to receive the three refuges and the five precepts. Once they had received the precepts, they took the alms bowl from the Buddha’s hand, filled it with various foods and drinks endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor, and offered it to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having accepted the food, departed from the village.
Then, the great Brahmin Deva heard from others that the Great Śramaṇa had arrived there; having heard this, he immediately thought to himself:
"In the past, I invited that Great Śramaṇa and promised to provide him with food and drink. Now, my wealth is meager, I am poor and destitute; what plan should I devise?"
When the great Brahmin Deva heard these words, he returned with great haste toward his own home. Upon arriving at his house, he spoke thus to his wife:
"Formerly, when the Great Śramaṇa was practicing austerities in the village of Uruvilvā, I vowed to offer food to that Great Śramaṇa;
now that he has arrived here today, what plan should we make?"
Then his wife replied to her husband Deva:
"Please listen to what I have to say; will you not consider it?
I recall when I was young, at that time the military commander, the Great Brahmin, once toyed with me, desiring worldly intimacy. I did not consent to him then, yet he briefly touched me."
Now this noble man will engage me and him in worldly affairs; whatever amount of money or goods he may request from them, I shall obtain it to provide as a food offering for that great śramaṇa.
At that time, the great Brahmin Deva replied to his wife, saying: "This is not so;
it is not within the proper conduct for us Brahmins to engage in such an act."
However, after the great Brahmin Deva had reflected further, he went to the Brahmin Senāpati; having arrived at his location, he addressed him, saying:
"Excellent, Senāpati!
"I only pray that you will lend me five hundred coins. If I am able to repay them, this would be most excellent!
Should I be unable to repay them, my husband and I, both together, shall enter your household and work for you."
At that time, the general, the great Brahmin, gave five hundred coins to the Brahmin Tiṣya and said to him:
"Take these now and use them as you please. When the matter is concluded, you must not borrow from others; instead, use this [money] to repay me."
"Whatever you require, I shall exert my own strength to seek out money and give it to you.
At that time, the great Brahmin Deva received five hundred coins from the military officer in accordance with the law; having returned to his own home, he gave them to his wife and said to her:
"You should prepare a fine meal with the utmost care."
He then went forth from his own body into the forest outside and proceeded toward the Buddha.

Having arrived at the Buddha’s location, he faced the Buddha face-to-face, exchanged words of consolation and greeting, and after completing the inquiries concerning his well-being, stood to one side, desiring to invite the Tathāgata.
At that time, the great brahmin Deva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, O Great Virtuous One!
Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"I only pray that you will accept my meal tomorrow.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Then, the great brahmin Deva, knowing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation through silence, rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, took his leave of the Buddha, and departed for his own home.
At that time, all the streets and alleys within the city were selling cooked food.

Then, during that very night, the great Brahmin Deva prepared many kinds of sweet and delicious meals—such as those to be chewed, bitten, sucked, and sipped—and throughout the night he prepared all such flavors. When the night had passed and dawn broke, he swept and cleaned his house, arranged the beds and seats, and then went before the Buddha. Kneeling with long knees, he addressed him, saying:
"O Great and Virtuous Śramaṇa!"
"If you know the time has come, the food and drink are prepared; we pray that you will visit our home.

At that time, when it was mealtime, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and proceeded gradually until he reached the house of the brahmin Tiṣya. Having arrived at the house, he sat down upon the seat that had been spread out.

At that time, having seen the Buddha seated, Deva and his wife personally lifted various kinds of exquisite, pure foods and drinks with their own hands, stood before the Buddha, and offered them to the World-Honored One, saying:
"We only pray that the Tathāgata..."
"Eat as you please.

At that time, after Deva had finished serving the Buddha his meal, he prepared a seat apart from the Buddha and sat down. Once seated, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to the great Brahmin Deva as was appropriate, providing instruction and guidance until he was filled with joy.
Rising from his seat, he departed as he pleased.
