At that time, the great brahmin Deva escorted the Buddha out; meanwhile, Deva’s wife had borrowed a garment from another to wear while serving food to the Buddha. Having made her offering, she saw the Buddha returning and immediately removed her garment, set it aside, and began sweeping the ground.
At that time, a thief suddenly came and stole his robe and took it away.
Because her husband’s robe was lost, Devadatta’s wife was deeply distressed in heart.
When Devadatta returned home after escorting the Buddha, he saw that his wife was greatly agitated and immediately asked her:
"Why are you now so distressed?
The wife replied to her husband,
"Noble husband, you should know this!"
"The garment I borrowed has suddenly vanished; I do not know who has stolen it.
Upon hearing these words, Devadatta’s heart was filled with confusion and distress, and not knowing what to do, he spoke as follows:
"I borrowed five hundred coins from another to provide for the ritual requisites; you now borrowed a robe from another to wear, yet suddenly lost it.
My family is poor and destitute—how shall we provide for its repayment?"
"What plan should I make?

At that time, Deva, wishing to seek his own death, went immediately to the Śītavana cemetery, climbed to the top of a great tree, and intended to throw himself to the ground; however, he was unable to fall and became greatly distressed once more.

However, those thieves took his clothes and went to the Śītavana cemetery; they suddenly returned and, beneath the tree where Deva had been, they dug into the ground and buried him, covering him with earth and defecating upon it before departing.
At that time, Deva was in the tree; seeing this from afar, he descended from the tree after the thieves had departed, dug up the garment, and returned with it to his home.

At that time, Devadatta’s wife was cleaning the interior of the house, clearing away debris everywhere. Suddenly, one corner of the house collapsed of its own accord. Looking down at the ground beneath, she saw a red copper jar filled with gold. To speak briefly, she saw a second jar, a third, and a fourth—all were jars. Looking further down, she saw yet another red copper vat, likewise filled with gold.
Upon seeing the gold, she cried out in great alarm and pointed it out to her husband, saying:
"Noble husband, noble husband!
Come quickly, come quickly!"
"I have already obtained it.
At that time, having heard his wife's voice, Devadatta thought to himself:
"This woman is pitiable; why has she lost her mind so as to speak such a lie?"
"What do you mean by 'I have obtained it'?
What thing have I obtained?
Previously, I borrowed a robe from another place and lost it; now I have obtained it, and the robe is right here."
"For what reason do you proclaim, 'I have attained it'?
At that time, Deva took his robe and entered the house, asking his wife:
"O virtuous mistress of the household!"
"What have you obtained?
The woman immediately pointed to the gold and said to her noble husband,
"I have obtained this."
At that time, Deva spoke again to his wife, saying,
"The garment you lost, I have also found. Thereupon,
the woman took the clothing and returned it to its owner at the place from which it had been borrowed.
At that time, the great Brahmin Deva thought to himself:
"I cannot now consume so much gold by myself.
He immediately took five hundred coins and went straight back to the military commander, the Brahmin, to repay his debt.
Having arrived, he said to that great military commander:
"I borrowed five hundred coins from you, noble sir; here they are returned to you.
At that time, the military commander spoke to Deva:
"I told you before that you must not repay me by borrowing money from others; you must repay me only with the labor of your own body.
Devadatta replied again, "I did not borrow this object from anyone else."
The military commander asked again,
"From where did you obtain it? Deva replied:
"I obtained this treasure of gold from the earth," he said,
but they did not believe him.
Thereupon, Deva immediately took his soldiers and went to his own home, showing them the treasure of gold.
At that time, the military commander saw that what was a storehouse of gold was actually a heap of charcoal;
he said to Deva, "What madness is this? Why do you tell me that this charcoal is gold?"
At that time, Deva spoke again to the military commander, saying:
"This is indeed genuine gold; it is not charcoal.
Thus he repeated this a second and a third time, touching the hoard of gold with his hand and proclaiming:
"This is gold, not charcoal.
He then made this vow:
"If it is by the power of the causes and conditions of my own wholesome karma that I have obtained this gold, I pray that you show me the military general, the Brahmin."
When he had spoken these words, the charcoal immediately turned into gold.
At that time, the general saw that this entire hidden treasure was gold; having seen it, he asked Deva again:
"Virtuous one, whom do you now worship?"
Are you a deva, a rishi,
or perhaps a virtuous person?
You and he have thus made such a vow of requital.
Devadatta replied:
"Today, my family has made offerings solely to this Great Śramaṇa who came to our home; it must be by virtue of the karmic fruit and retribution of that act that this has come to pass."
At that time, the military commander replied to Deva:

"This treasure of gold you have now obtained has arisen entirely as a result of the causes and conditions of your own virtuous karma; no one can seize it, and no one can destroy it. Do not harbor any doubts; enjoy it in peace."
At that time, Devadatta thought to himself:
"By giving food to the Great Śramaṇa, I have produced such a reward of great merit."
His heart was filled with joy, and he leaped for immeasurable delight; this gladness pervaded his entire body so completely that he could not contain himself.

He approached the Buddha once more, and upon arrival, engaged in pleasant conversation with the Buddha, offering words of consolation and inquiry. Having spoken in various ways, he withdrew and sat to one side.
At that time, Deva addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"I pray, Great Śramaṇa!
Accept my further offering of food tomorrow."
The World-Honored One remained silent and accepted his invitation.

At that time, having seen that the Buddha had silently accepted his request, Devadatta rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, took his leave, and returned home. Once he arrived at his own house, he found that throughout all the streets and alleys of the city, there were five kinds of cooked food being sold, as previously described. After providing food for the Buddha’s meal, he and his two wives sat upon seats spread before the Buddha, desiring to listen to the Dharma.

The Buddha, knowing the nature of their mental activities and that their underlying propensities (*anuśaya*) were slight, taught them the gateway to the characteristics of the four immeasurables and other dharmas.
Having heard this, they cast down the twenty-layered mountain of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and immediately realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
Having perceived the true nature of phenomena, they immediately took the three refuges and undertook the observance of the five precepts.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and proceeded as he pleased.
At a later time, the bhikṣus, with doubts arising in their minds, each reflected and asked one another:
"What karma did that great brahmin Deva and his wife previously perform, such that having created that karma, they obtained this retribution?"
"Having gone before the Tathāgata, how did he realize the various noble dharmas?
Furthermore, what karma did he perform such that he was poor in this life, yet subsequently became immensely wealthy?
When the bhikṣus had spoken thus, they immediately went to where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the Buddha's presence, they addressed him with these questions:
“Excellent,
World-Honored One!
What karma did that great Brahmin Deva and his wife and others perform in the past, such that having created that karma, they have now obtained this retribution?”
"Furthermore, how did he come to the presence of the Buddha and attain the various noble dharmas?
What further karma did he create such that he was poor at first and later became wealthy, suddenly becoming like this?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"O bhikṣus! If you wish to hear, you should now listen attentively.
That great brahmin Deva also had past karma and present karma."
What is called past karma?

Monks, you should know that I recall in the past, during this Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of sentient beings was twenty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.

At that time, Kāśyapa Buddha had already turned the wheel of Dharma, crossed over to the far shore of birth and death, erected the banner of the Dharma, fulfilled his ancient vows, and become a supreme great man. Having enlightened and transformed immeasurable billions of sentient beings so that they dwelt in the wholesome paths, he returned to reside here in the Deer Park at the site of the ancient sages in the city of Vārāṇasī.
"At that time, back in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a certain person who received the three refuges and the five precepts from the Buddha.
Throughout his life, he did not practice giving; however, at the moment of his death, he made this aspiration:

'The Tathāgata Kāśyapa bestowed a prophecy upon a bodhisattva named Mahāpratibhāna, declaring that this bodhisattva shall attain Buddhahood in a future age when the lifespan of sentient beings is one hundred years, under the name Śākyamuni, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. May I encounter that World-Honored One.'"
"For this reason, you should know!
At that time, the upāsaka who had received the three refuges and the five precepts but did not practice giving was none other than this brāhmaṇa Trapuṣa."

At that time, having received these three refuges and upheld the five precepts as an upāsaka, he made a vow at the end of his life, wishing to meet me; by virtue of these causes and conditions, he has now met me.
Furthermore, because one did not practice giving at that time, one now receives the retribution of poverty; this is karma created in the past.
"Bhikṣus, you should know!
What is called karma of the present life?

In the past, during my six years of ascetic practice, that Deva offered me food as was appropriate; now that I have attained unsurpassed enlightenment, he has again invited me to his home and offered me food.
By these causes and conditions, one obtains retribution in the present life.

Therefore, you bhikṣus, should give rise to a mind of reverence and wonder toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; you shall then obtain such fruits of merit and reward, just as the brahmin Tisya received his blessings in his very own body. Those who do not receive such retribution are people of stinginess and greed who refuse to practice giving; they now suffer the afflictions of poverty, lowliness, and hardship.
"You monks! You should train yourselves in this way.

"World-Honored One, from the time you departed from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī until you arrived at the village of Uruvilvā, during that interval, eighty thousand people received the Buddha’s transformative teaching and entered into all dharmas."

Chapter 44: The Three Brothers of the Kāśyapa Clan, Part One. *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Forty-four, Part One: The Three Brothers of the Kāśyapa Clan. "At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
'I should now first convert one person who has attained supernatural powers, causing him to rejoice. Once he has rejoiced, I shall gradually and extensively convert many others.'"

At that time, in the village of Uruvilvā, there resided three brahmin seers with matted hair (*jaṭila*). The first was Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, who led five hundred disciples with matted hair, teaching them the methods of the seers; he was their master and guide, walking at the very head of the procession.
The second was named Nadī-Kāśyapa, who likewise led three hundred disciples with matted hair as their leader and guide.
The third was named Gayā-Kāśyapa, who led two hundred disciples with matted hair as their leader and guide.
"There were about a thousand people who followed those brothers to practice the methods of the seers.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Now this Uruvilvā Kāśyapa’s fame fills the entire kingdom of Magadha; all the people, both inside and outside that region, claim that he is an Arhat."
I should first convert that Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and cause him to rejoice; once he has rejoiced, many people will receive his teaching.
The Buddha further reflected:
"What do these various sages hold as most important?"
"What is that practice?
Having thought this, he immediately knew that they held asceticism alone as supreme, and next, they considered leading a community as important.

At that time, when all those sages saw the manifested assembly, they were each filled with urgency and ran hither and thither; some prepared mats for seating, some washed their feet, some entered the grass huts to sweep and tidy them, some gathered grass to fashion mats for spreading, and some fetched water in preparation for bathing.

"From where have you all suddenly come to arrive here?
You did not inform us."
"Why did you not previously send a messenger to inform us that you wished to come? Had we known beforehand, we would have made preparations in advance.

The World-Honored One, knowing that all the sages had conceived this aspiration and were fully aware that he was the Buddha,

At that time, when those sages saw that the World-Honored One had shaved off his hair and beard and was wearing saffron-colored robes, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa!..."
"He possesses great majestic power and great majesty; yet he has not attained the fruit of arhatship, remaining here as I do today.
This was the first supernatural feat manifested by the Tathāgata.
At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Great Śramaṇa!
Why have you come here from so far away?"
"Excellent, Great Śramaṇa!

"This is a grass hut; this is a grass hall. Choose whichever you please.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, saying:
"Excellent, Kāśyapa!"
"If you do not decline and can show me respect, I wish to enter your place for the fire sacrifice and dwell there.
At that time, one of Uruvilvā Kāśyapa’s disciples had long suffered from the ailment of dysentery; because of this diarrhea, he had defiled the grass hut with excrement.
All the other disciples, seeing the filthy grass hut, were filled with anger and resentment at its impurity, and they drove him out.
At that time, as the sick māṇava was being expelled, he thought to himself:
"This hermitage was built for all those with conch-shell crests; why is it that upon seeing me, a sick man suffering from diarrhea, you drive me out?"
"May I, upon casting off this life, obtain such a body as this to repay them for their deeds in this manner.
Having formed this thought, the patient then passed away.

After his life ended, he immediately received the body of such a great venomous dragon; having been born within that grass hut, whenever anyone or any beast came there, they were all bitten and killed by him.
Due to these causes and conditions, that hall immediately became empty, with no one dwelling there.
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"What countermeasure is there capable of subduing this venomous dragon?"
"Only fire should be able to overcome it.
Having formed this thought, he immediately installed the Fire Deity within that grass hut and constantly made offerings according to the Dharma at the proper times.
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha,
saying: "O Great Śramaṇa,
I truly do not refuse, nor do I begrudge this grass hut."

However, in that grass hut dwells a most wicked and fierce dragon king; this dragon possesses great supernormal powers, possesses great and evil venom, and possesses violent poison—not only will it harm you, but it will also injure me.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke thus a second time to Kāśyapa:
"If you do not decline nor show disrespect toward him, you should simply allow me to dwell in your grass hut."
Kāśyapa replied:
"In my mind, I do not wish for you, O Venerable One, to dwell in this fire hall. Why is that? Because—"
"At that place there is currently a great venomous dragon, fierce, cruel, and blazing; I fear it may inflict poisonous harm upon you, O Virtuous Great Śramaṇa, as well as upon my own person."
"This hall was originally abandoned long ago by us, master and disciples; no one is able to enter it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa for a third time, saying:

Even if all the venomous nāgas were to come and fill this hall to dwell therein, they would not be able to harm even a single hair of mine, let alone a single dragon.
Venerable Kāśyapa!
"If it pleases your mind, I shall enter by myself; I pray that you do not decline, nor regard that hall with such weight, for in the end it will be unable to harm me.
At that time, because the Buddha had thus urged him three times without ceasing, Upavāna Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, Great Śramaṇa!"
I do not decline, nor do I hold them in high regard; I speak thus to you so that, if your mind has no doubt, you may dwell as you please, always employing skillful means so as not to suffer harm.

At that time, having received the approval and permission of Kāśyapa, the World-Honored One took a handful of grass in his own hand and entered the hall of the fire deity. Having entered, he spread out the grass, folded his saṃghāṭī robe into four layers, laid it upon the grass, and sat cross-legged upon the saṃghāṭī.

He stood with his body upright, unmoving in right mindfulness, having cast off all internal and external fears; the hairs on his body did not stand on end as he remained in tranquil meditative concentration.

At that time, the venomous dragon left the hall to search for food, wandering here and there until, being fully satiated, he returned to the fire-hall. Seeing the Tathāgata from afar sitting within the hall, he thought to himself:
"While my own body still lives, who is this person who has suddenly entered my hall?"
His intent being thus evil, he immediately gave rise to poisonous malice, and smoke and flames issued from his mouth;

The Buddha and the venomous dragon each emitted fierce flames; at that time, the hall was ablaze with intense and violent fire, and because of those fierce flames, the grass hut became crimson, like a great mass of fire.
At that time, the World-Honored One again thought thus:

"I shall now perform such a supernatural power; having performed this power, I must not harm the life-faculty of that dragon king, but shall only burn his skin, flesh, tendons, and bones until they are entirely consumed."

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately performed such supernatural transformations; by means of his supernormal powers, he ensured that the life of the dragon king was not harmed, while causing all other parts of his body to be consumed by flames.
When this was concluded, there again issued from his body various kinds of multicolored light—
namely, blue, yellow, red, white, and black— which, having emerged, illuminated the ground for only a fathom’s distance, manifesting it to that nāga.

"At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, not far from the hall where the fire sacrifice was being performed, saw from a distance a great, fierce flame issuing from within the hall. Having seen it, he immediately thought to himself:

At that time, there was among that assembly a young brahmin named Arāḍa Kālāma (translated in the Sui language as "Wet Tree-Bark Robe"). "Namely: Kaṭhamuni (translated in the Sui language as 'Ascetic Sage'), Yamakinī (translated as 'Twin Fire'), Harinivisayanā (translated as 'Fire-Erected'), Viraprabhāsa (translated as 'Light of the Hero'), Śamalanayana (translated as 'Variegated-Eyed'), Pārayana (translated as 'Able to Cross to the Other Shore'), Kaṭayanā (translated as 'Leading Loving Conduct'), Gautama (of the Gautama clan, translated as 'Dark Ox'), Maudgalyāyana (of the Maudgalyāyana lineage, translated as 'White Staff'), Vāsiṣṭha (of the Vāsiṣṭha clan, translated as 'Transformation-Abiding'), and Bhāradvāja (translated as 'Heavy Banner. "Come quickly! Come quickly!
This great śramaṇa is now being scorched by the fire spat forth by a venomous dragon; we must go to assist him in extinguishing it.
At that time, having heard these words, those young brahmins hurriedly came running, some carrying water jars and others carrying ladders.

Having arrived, he set up a ladder and climbed onto the great hall of that fire deity; once atop it, he took water with the intent to extinguish the fire, but by the power of the Blessed One, those flames grew even more intense and blazing.
Then all those young brahmins immediately descended from that hall of the Fire God and stood to one side, each saying to the others:
"This great śramaṇa is handsome and pleasing to behold, yet he has been tormented by a venomous dragon. (In the Sanskrit original, the term *śramaṇa* is repeated for each instance of his arrival.)
At that time, among the assembly, the young brahmin seer clad in moist tree-bark garments spoke these verses in sorrow, weeping for the Buddha:

"Alas! Your subtle, wondrous, and upright body, With hair most azure and fingers like a webbed net, With the seven parts perfectly full and eyes so upright— Now shrouded by the dragon’s canopy, like the sun and moon eclipsed."
At that time, there was yet another māṇava who, once again, wept piteously before the Buddha and spoke in verse:
"Alas! Born into a lineage of victorious kings, Of the Ikṣvāku clan, the most excellent among men— There is no birthplace in this world superior to this;
Yet now your body is consumed by the fire of a venomous dragon."
At that time, there was yet another māṇava who again wept with sorrow before the Buddha, speaking in verse:
“Your body adorned with the thirty-two marks, Who attained liberation for yourself and could liberate others;
One who could subdue anger and whose person was free from harm— Now you are extinguished by the venomous fire of the poisonous dragon.”
At that time, there was yet another young brahmin who again wept with sorrow before the Buddha and spoke in verse:
“Your limbs and joints are long and short in perfect symmetry; Born of the Ikṣvāku royal lineage, you have brought prosperity to all kings.
Your body is like a pillar of Jāmbūnada gold, Yet now it is consumed by the fire of the venomous dragon.”
At that time, there was yet another young brahmin who again wept with sorrow before the Buddha and spoke in verse:
"The seers hear his voice and their hearts rejoice; In generosity and upholding the precepts, he is the supreme field of merit.
His body is supple and he is of great auspiciousness; Alas! He has now been slain by the dragon's fire."
At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa also came and gathered with his followers, standing at a short distance from the fire hall.
Then, a certain young brahmin approached Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and addressed him thus:

"Preceptor, please examine and perform divination for that great śramaṇa once more; observe the birth constellation of that great śramaṇa to see if he has been afflicted by any other malevolent stars."

At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, having looked up at the stars in the sky, replied to that māṇava, saying:
"O māṇava! [Which star is it?]"
"You should know now!
This great śramaṇa was born under the constellation Mṛgaśiras, and that Mṛgaśiras is not affected by any other stars.

O māṇava, this constellation of the great śramaṇa is exceedingly bright and clear. According to the appearance of the constellations as I see it, the manner in which the great śramaṇa is currently contending for victory with the dragon’s horn is certain."
"This great śramaṇa will certainly subdue that dragon; there is no doubt about it.

"This Great Śramaṇa possesses great supernormal power!"
"His majestic authority is great!
Although his spiritual transformations are thus, he still has not attained the fruit of Arhatship as I have now," so said the Niśāsa school.
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa held an annual great assembly in his residence, known as the Nakṣatra Festival of the Aśvinī Constellation.

On the day of that assembly, several tens of millions of people from the kingdom of Magadha gathered there; furthermore, there was a marketplace at the assembly where people could purchase whatever goods they required.
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"If a śramaṇa comes here tomorrow morning, all the people will go to watch him and will not prepare a meal for us."
Having reflected thus, he went to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Śramaṇa!

Tomorrow morning, at my forest hermitage for practicing the Way, a great assembly shall be held; many sentient beings, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, will gather there in great clamor. And yet, Great Śramaṇa!"
"Delighting in tranquility, you should always frequent pure and secluded places. Śramaṇa!
You should move from this spot and seek another quiet place to dwell. This is what was said in the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya.

At that time, the World-Honored One departed from that dwelling and proceeded to the Kāliṅga Forest. Having arrived at that forest, he brought to mind those four Kāla-rāja kings named Saṃsparśa; furthermore, he called to mind the four Dhṛtarāṣṭra nāga kings, the four water-spirit nāgas, the four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devendra, and all other gods of the desire realm, as well as Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world, and others—all of whom he likewise called to mind.

At that time, those four *kṣatriya* kings, the *garuḍas*, and others, having perceived such thoughts within the Buddha’s mind, produced a great wind and soared from the dwelling place of Uruvilvā Kāśyapa into the void, immediately proceeding to the Cālikā forest.
Having arrived there, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and withdrew to stand to one side; gazing afar at the World-Honored One, he paid homage toward the Buddha.

"The four Dragon Kings, headed by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and the four Water Deity Kings, also knowing the Buddha's mind, produced great clouds and rain; from the dwelling of Upavartana Kāśyapa, they flew toward the Cālikā Forest."
Having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, joined his palms, and withdrew to stand to one side, paying remote homage toward the Buddha.

At that time, the Four Great Kings of the Four Quarters, also knowing the Buddha’s mind, assumed forms of great beauty and charm that were pleasing for all to behold; with brilliant and majestic radiance illuminating their own bodies, they all mounted white elephants and surged forth from the earth, proceeding from the abode of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa to the Kalandaka Grove.
Having arrived, they prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and even joined their palms, paying homage to the Buddha from afar.

At that time, Śakra, King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and Mahābrahmā, Lord of the Sahā World in the Desire Realm, knowing the Buddha’s thoughts, emitted a majestic radiance from their bodies that illuminated the entire ground. Flying through the air from the dwelling place of Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, they simultaneously proceeded to the Khalatika Forest. Having arrived, they prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and even bowed their bodies, paying homage to the Buddha from afar.

At that time, all the people there, seeing such a multitude of devas, nāgas, and others, felt fear in their hearts; their hair stood on end, and they immediately asked Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and the others:
"Venerable Upādhyāyas!..."
What deity is this that creates such a strange and monstrous transformation?
Is it not a calamity?
Perhaps there will be an epidemic, or great terror, or great strife; or perhaps the kaṭapūtana demons and the dark spirits intend to come?
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This must surely be the power of that great virtuous śramaṇa, manifesting such supernatural transformations."
He then addressed that great assembly, saying: "All of you!
Do not fear; do not be terrified!"
"Do not fear, do not be alarmed!

This is neither a calamity nor an epidemic, nor have demons or malevolent spirits come to cause strife. There shall be fearlessness; there shall be abundance; there shall be no portents of ill omen. You need not be terrified, for there will be no disease."
"You need only comfort yourselves with peace of mind; there is no cause for suffering in this matter. All these signs are entirely auspicious.
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"I should now go to that Great Śramaṇa to gauge the situation. I must know for myself what the reason and what the transformation are that have caused this to happen."

Having formed such thoughts and reflections, he immediately went to where the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying. As he approached the presence of the Buddha, the Tathāgata suddenly employed his supernormal powers to manifest a high and steep great mountain right before him; unable to pass over it, he reached that mountain and then turned back to return.
After that night had passed, he returned to where the Buddha was staying. Having arrived at the Buddha's location, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Śramaṇa!
What kind of such strange and miraculous phenomenon occurred yesterday?"
“I have resided here since time immemorial, yet I have never before witnessed such an event.
At that moment, the World-Honored One then explained the preceding events to him in detail. Having heard this account, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa was struck with great wonder and thought:

“How extraordinary and marvelous! For many years I have lived here, constantly performing sacrifices to the fire deity, yet not even a whiff of a whirlwind has ever reached me, much less any other deity.”
"But now, Śramaṇa Gautama!
This place possesses great majesty and power, such that all the devas come toward his side.
Having formed this thought, he immediately conceived a heart of faith and a sense of wonder toward the Buddha.
Thereupon, with his mind, he invited the Buddha, the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray that the Great Śramaṇa will accept my humble offering from me once again at the time of the morning meal tomorrow; if the Buddha is truly the All-Knowing One, he should know my heart."
Having formed this thought, the Tathāgata, knowing the mental reflection of Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, silently accepted his invitation.
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa returned to his dwelling and addressed all the māṇavas, saying:
"Go to the Great Śramaṇa and observe him; see what the Great Śramaṇa is doing."
"Should we seek food and go out to beg for alms, or should we remain silent and sit in quietude?

At that time, having heard these words from Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, those young brahmins immediately went to the Cālikā forest. Upon arrival, they saw the Buddha sitting there beneath a tree in the grove, meditating in profound stillness. His body emitted a radiance that illuminated that place; content with whatever food was offered, he did not go begging and remained there in silence.
Having seen this, they went to where the Buddha was; having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Śramaṇa!
For what reason do you not now seek alms?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed all those māṇavas, saying: "Māṇavas!
I have already been invited."
They asked, "Venerable Śramaṇa!
By whom were you invited?"
The Buddha replied,
“Your preceptors have already invited me.
At that time, those māṇavas felt a sense of wonder.
"How most extraordinary and marvelous!
Rare, indeed, are these rare qualities!
This great śramaṇa, though he speaks no word, knows the minds of others from afar."
They were immediately filled with great joy and exultation, which pervaded their entire bodies such that they could not contain themselves.
At that time, they quickly returned to the presence of Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, and upon arrival, they said to him:
"Venerable Upādhyāya!..."
I know with certainty that this Great Śramaṇa is omniscient.
When my preceptor silently entreated him with his mind, he immediately knew my preceptor’s thoughts and spoke to me, saying:
“I have already understood the silent request from your preceptor’s mind.”
At that time, having heard those words, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa immediately prepared a seat of great value.
Once it was prepared, he thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama!..."
"If you, O Benevolent One, are now the All-Knowing One, you should appear upon this seat immediately in accordance with my thought.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing what Uruvilvā Kāśyapa was thinking in his mind, manifested his body upon that seat at that very moment.

At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, seeing the World-Honored One sitting upright upon his seat, was filled with joy. He immediately took various kinds of excellent delicacies and food and offered them to the Buddha with his own hands—abundant and at his disposal, consisting of what is chewed, eaten, sucked, and drunk.
Furthermore, he thought: "How rare! How rare!"
This great śramaṇa!
He possesses great majestic power!
He possesses great spiritual strength!
"You are indeed able to know what is in my mind;
yet, despite such majestic power, you have still not attained the fruit of Arhatship as I have now.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished receiving food from Upatiṣya Kāśyapa, returned to the Cālikā Forest and stayed there while walking in meditation.

At that time, the saffron robes worn upon the body of the World-Honored One were all completely torn. Now, in a certain household of a brahmin village belonging to those military commanders, a member had passed away and was being buried in the forest. At that moment, the World-Honored One saw this in the forest and immediately picked up those discarded rags (*pāṃśukūla*).
Having taken them, the World-Honored One thought to himself: "Where now might I wash such discarded rags so as to make them clean?"

At that time, Śakra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, having understood the intention in the World-Honored One’s mind, immediately at that spot dug into the earth with his hand and fashioned a pond. Its water was pure and clear; having finished it, he then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent! [...]”
“World-Honored One!
I pray that you will use this water to wash your rag-robe.
At that time, having seen the pool water, the World-Honored One again thought thus:
"Although we have now obtained water, upon what shall we wash and rinse these robes?
At that time, Śakra, knowing the Buddha’s thoughts, brought a large stone from Mount Cakravāḍa, placed it before the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One [accept this]."
"I shall wash and beat this robe upon this rock.
At that time, the World-Honored One further thought to himself:
"Now that I have obtained the rock, upon what else shall I lean while washing and beating this robe?"
At that time, there was an old tree on the bank of that pond named Kakubha (translated in the Sui language as "Peak").
Within that tree resided a tree deity who, knowing the Buddha’s intention, pressed down a branch of the tree so that it hung downward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray, World-Honored One!"
"By climbing this tree branch, I shall wash and tread upon these rag-robes.
At that time, the World-Honored One further thought to himself:
"Once I have finished washing my robes, upon what shall I hang them out to dry?"
At that time, Śakra, knowing the Buddha’s thought, immediately took a most massive and broad stone from between the Iron Ring Mountains and placed it before the Buddha.
Having arranged it thus, he immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray, World-Honored One,
that you will use this stone to dry your robes."
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately spread out his refuse-rag robe (pāṃsukūla) upon the stone to dry it.
Then, after the night had passed, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa went to where the Buddha was; having arrived at the Buddha’s location, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Śramaṇa! ”
"The time for the meal has arrived and everything is prepared.
He then addressed the Buddha again:
"Virtuous Śramaṇa!..."
Previously there was no such pond in this place; for what reason has it suddenly appeared today?
Furthermore, these two stones were not here before; from where have they come?
"Previously, the branches of this Kakubha tree did not hang down; for what reason today have they drooped so?
I do not know by what cause it has suddenly become like this."
Having spoken these words, he remained silent and said no more.
The Buddha addressed Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, saying:
"Venerable Kāśyapa!..."
At this place, I obtained a *pāṃsukūla* (rag-robe), and at that time I had this thought:
"With what shall I wash this rag-robe?
Then Śakra, knowing my thought, dug a pond with his hand, brought forth water from that pond, and said to me:
“World-Honored One!
Now you may wash the *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) with the water of this pond.
For this reason, it has been passed down to the present day as being called “The Pond Dug by the Hand of Śakra.”
Having obtained this water, I further reflected thus:
"Upon what shall I tread upon my rag-robe?
At that time, Śakra, knowing my thoughts, took a great stone from Mount Cakravāḍa, brought it to this spot, and said to me:
“May the World-Honored One please wash his robes upon this rock. For this reason,
it is called “The Rock Thrown by a Non-human Being.”
At that time, I thought to myself:
"Upon what shall I grasp with my hand to step upon this cloth?
Then, the deity of that Kakubha tree, knowing my thoughts, pressed down a branch of the tree with his hand so that it hung down, and said to me:
“May the World-Honored One please grasp this branch with his hand and step upon the robe with his foot.
By reason of these words, the branch of this tree thus hung down.
Having obtained the branch, I thought to myself:
"Upon what now shall I spread these robes?
At that time, Śakra, knowing my thoughts, took this broad stone from Mount Cakravāḍa, cast it before me, and said to me:
“May the World-Honored One please spread out the washed robes upon this stone.
For this reason, this stone is named “Thrown by Non-Humans.”
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa possesses truly great power!"
"He possesses great supernormal powers!
He is thus able to cause Śakra, Lord of the Devas, to come and serve him;
yet, despite such transformations, the Great Śramaṇa has not, in truth, attained the fruit of Arhatship as I have now."
At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his meal at the dwelling of Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, returned to the grove and stayed there walking in meditation.
Then, after the night had passed, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa went to where the Buddha was; having arrived, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Śramaṇa!..."
"If you know the time has come, the meal is prepared.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, saying these words:
"Venerable Kāśyapa!
"You go on ahead; I shall follow immediately.
At that time, having sent Uruvilvā Kāśyapa away, the World-Honored One immediately mounted his supernormal powers and proceeded toward Mount Sumeru.
At that time, there was a Jambu tree on that mountain; it was because of this Jambu tree that the name "Jambudvīpa" was obtained.
Having taken a fruit from that tree, he went first to the fire temple where Uruvilvā Kāśyapa resided and sat down upright.
Then, when that Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa arrived later and saw the Tathāgata sitting within the fire-hall, he was struck with wonder and astonishment; having seen this, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Śramaṇa!..."
"By what path have you come to this place?
You were originally in the forest, setting out after me; why have you suddenly appeared before me now, sitting at ease within this hall of the Fire God?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa, saying: "Kāśyapa!
After I had previously sent you forth, you reached Mount Sumeru. There is a tree there named Jambu; because of that tree, this world has now received the name 'Jambudvīpa'."
"The fruit from that tree, I have now brought here into this hall.
Pointing it out to Kāśyapa, he said:
"That jambu fruit is this very one; its color is exquisite, its fragrance and flavor are subtle and wonderful, and it is most delicious when eaten. You may now take this sweet fruit and eat it."
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Virtuous Śramaṇa! This is not so;
you yourself should eat these sweet fruits, and I ought not to eat them."
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This Great Śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers!
He possesses great majesty!"
Only after he had first dispatched me did his body arrive at Mount Sumeru, where he took a jambu fruit and came here to this Fire God Hall, sitting before me;
nevertheless, he still has not attained arhatship as I have now.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his meal at the dwelling of Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, quickly returned to the grove to practice walking meditation.
Then, after the night had passed, when morning dawned, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa went to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
"Virtuous Śramaṇa!
"If you know the time, the meal is ready.
Then the World-Honored One said to Kāśyapa, "Kāśyapa, you go on ahead for now; I shall follow after you."
At that time, after the World-Honored One had first sent Kāśyapa away, he immediately returned toward Mount Sumeru. Not far from the Jambu tree, there was another tree named Āmra.
Taking a fruit from an *āmra* tree, he arrived first at the fire-hall where Kāśyapa resided and sat down.
When Kāśyapa arrived later, he saw the World-Honored One sitting peacefully in the fire-hall; having seen him, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Śramaṇa!..."
“From which path did you come?
You arrived here before me at this shrine of the Fire God.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"After I have sent you away, go to Mount Sumeru, obtain some of these amra fruits, bring them here, and first exhort Kāśyapa to eat them."
Kāśyapa replied,
"It is not fitting for me to eat.
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa thought to himself thus:
"This great śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers!
He possesses great majesty!
For he was able to dispatch me first to Mount Sumeru to fetch fruit and bring it back, so that I might sit down before him."
"Nevertheless, even so, he has not yet attained arhatship as I have now.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his meal at the dwelling of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, returned to that grove and walked there in meditation.
At that time, after the night had passed and at the break of dawn, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa went to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Śramaṇa!..."
"If you know the time has come, the meal is ready. ...

[He traveled] until he was not far from the location of that Jambu tree; there was a Harītakī tree nearby, from which he took some fruit and arrived first at Kāśyapa’s fire-hall. He said, "The śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers; nevertheless, even so, he has not yet attained arhatship as I have now."

"At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his meal, returned to that grove to practice walking meditation. Eventually, he came near the Jambudvīpa tree; there was another tree named Viśāla, from which he took a fruit and brought it back, arriving first at the hall."

"Furthermore, as previously mentioned, this great śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers; he first sent my body away and only afterwards took the fruit. Nevertheless, even so, he has not yet attained arhatship as I have now."

"At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his meal, returned to that grove to practice walking meditation. He went as far as a jambu tree, and beyond that was another tree named āmalaka; he took fruit from that tree, brought it back first, and sat in the Agniśālā Hall."
"Even a śramaṇa of great supernatural power who sent me on ahead and brought fruit to the Fire God Hall after me still cannot attain arhatship as I have now."
"At that time, having finished his meal, the World-Honored One returned to that grove to practice walking meditation.
Then, after the night had passed, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa went to where the Buddha was."
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Śramaṇa!
If you know it is the time, the meal is prepared.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa, “You go on ahead; I shall follow later.
At that time, having sent Kāśyapa away, the World-Honored One went to Aparagoyānī. Upon arriving there, he begged for milk until his bowl was full and proceeded ahead to the Fire God Shrine.
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, having seen him, addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Śramaṇa!
By which path have you come?"
"He is before me, having arrived inside this hall.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"After I sent you away, you went to Aparagoyānī, where you obtained this milk by begging and filled this bowl; you are sitting here."
"Kāśyapa!
This milk is of exquisite color, its fragrance sweet and delicious; if you so desire, take this milk and drink it.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
"I cannot drink it; let the śramaṇa drink it himself.
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa possesses immense power!"
He possesses great supernormal powers!
He first sent me, and afterwards he went himself to the country of Aparagoyānī to beg for milk until his bowl was full, returning here first to this hall of the Fire God;
nevertheless, even so, he has not yet attained the state of an Arhat as I have now.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll 41;
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll 42.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Sui Dynasty.
The Chapter on the Three Brothers of Kāśyapa, Part Two:
"At that time, having finished his meal, the World-Honored One returned to that grove to practice walking meditation.
Then, after the night had passed, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa went to where the Buddha was; having arrived, he addressed the Buddha:"
"Venerable Śramaṇa, if you know the time has come, the meal is ready.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "You go on ahead; I shall follow after you."

At that time, after the World-Honored One had first sent Kāśyapa away, he proceeded directly to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Having arrived at that heaven, he took a flower named Pārijātaka—which in the language of Sui means "Born on the Other Shore"—and having taken it, he went first to the Hall of the Fire Deity.
Kāśyapa arrived later and saw that the Buddha was already seated.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Śramaṇa!"
"From which path did he come?
He was before me, having arrived at the temple of Agni.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:

"I previously sent you to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven palace; now bring these pārijāta flowers to this divine hall. These pārijāta flowers are lovely in color and possess a most excellent fragrance; if it pleases your mind, you may take these flowers and smell their scent."
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha:
"Virtuous Śramaṇa!
The fragrance of these flowers is subtle, exquisite, and refined; as a Śramaṇa, you carry them yourself, so it is not fitting for me to smell them."
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This Great Śramaṇa possesses great majesty!
He possesses great supernormal powers!"
"Only after I have first been dispatched and you have subsequently arrived in the heavens to gather those pāriyātraka flowers, and then come to sit first within the Fire God’s Hall;
even so, you still shall not attain the physical and mental tranquility of an arhat such as I possess now."

At that time, at the dwelling of Kāśyapa, the various brahmins with spiral-topknots were unable to break the bundles of firewood; if they stood leaning against them, they could not bend their bodies; when they lowered their waists, they could not stand upright; and when the axes struck the wood, they could not pull them out.
At that time, those jaṭila brahmins thought to themselves:

"This supernatural power must surely be the work of that great śramaṇa; there is no doubt of it. It is for this reason that we are unable to split these firewood today, despite our extreme toil and hardship."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed all those, including Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, saying:
"Kāśyapa of the Conch-Curls!
Do you now wish to split firewood?"
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha:
"Virtuous Śramaṇa!
I truly wish to split this firewood, yet I am unable to do so."
When the Buddha had spoken these words, those brahmins were immediately able to break their firewood at will.
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This Great Śramaṇa possesses great majesty and great supernormal powers."
"Nevertheless, even so, you have not yet attained arhatship as I do now.
At that time, having finished his meal, the World-Honored One returned to that grove and performed walking meditation.
At that time, at the dwelling place of Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, the fire he wished to kindle would not ignite.
Then those ascetics with matted hair thought to themselves:
"This supernatural power must surely be the work of that great śramaṇa; there is no doubt about it. It is because of him that we have undergone such hardship, for the fire will not burn."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed all those including Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, saying: “Kāśyapa!
Do you wish to kindle a fire?”
At that time, those Kāśyapas replied,
"Venerable Śramaṇa!
We wish to kindle a fire."
When the Buddha had finished questioning him, those five hundred fires immediately blazed up.
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This Great Śramaṇa possesses great majestic power!"
He possesses great supernormal powers!
He is able to prevent the fire in that combustible material from burning, yet when he wishes for it to burn, it immediately ignites;
even so, he still cannot attain Arhatship as I have now.
"At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his meal, returned to that grove to practice walking meditation.
At that moment, those jaṭila brahmacārins wished to extinguish the fire, but they were unable to do so."
At that time, those jaṭila brahmins thought to themselves:
"This is the power of the śramaṇa’s supernormal faculties (ṛddhi) that causes our flames, which were about to be extinguished, to remain unextinguished."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Kāśyapa: "Kāśyapa!
Do you now wish to extinguish these flames?"
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha:
"O Great Virtuous Śramaṇa!
I now wish to extinguish these flames, yet I am unable to do so."
When the Buddha had finished questioning him, the five hundred flames were immediately extinguished.
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This Great Śramaṇa possesses great majestic power!"
He possesses great supernormal powers!
His strength is such that he can extinguish fire at will and ignite it at will;
even so, he still has not attained arhatship as I have now.
“At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished eating, he returned to that forest and stayed there walking in meditation.

At that moment, those jaṭila brahmins, during the height of the bitter winter, at midnight or even the latter part of the night, amidst severe cold and heavy wind and snow, entered the waters of the Nairañjanā River, submerging and emerging, thus performing their ablutions.”
At that time, by means of his supernormal power, the World-Honored One manifested five hundred masses of glowing red charcoal on the opposite bank.
Then, those jaṭila brahmins, shivering with cold after emerging from the water, stood upon the bank and each approached a fire.
At that time, those Jaina ascetics with matted hair thought to themselves:

"This must certainly be a supernatural feat performed by that Great Śramaṇa; suddenly these five hundred fire-pits have appeared, smokeless and flameless, so that we may emerge from the cold water and warm ourselves by the fire."
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This Great Śramaṇa possesses great majestic power!
He possesses great supernormal powers!"

He was then able to manifest five hundred fire-hearths, free from smoke or flame, so that my five hundred disciples with conch-shell topknots might emerge from the cold water and sit by the warmth of the fires;
nevertheless, they still could not attain arhatship as I have now.
"At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he returned to that grove and stayed there, walking in meditation.
At that moment, those jaṭila brahmins, wishing to fetch water, each held a jar or carried a water-pot; yet, when they attempted to take up water, they were unable to grasp them."
At that time, those Śramaṇas with matted hair thought to themselves:
"This must surely have been done by that Great Śramaṇa, which has caused us to be unable to take up our jars and water-flasks."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Uruvilvā Kāśyapa and all five hundred of his brahmin companions with hair-tufts like conch shells, saying: "Kāśyapa!"
"Do you each wish to take water using jars, *kamaṇḍalus*,
and other such vessels? Kāśyapa replied,
"Excellent, Śramaṇa!"
"These five hundred śramaṇas with spiral-topknots wish to take water using their jars and water-pots.
After the Buddha had asked this, all five hundred śramaṇas with spiral-topknots were able to take up their jars and water-pots and obtain the water.
At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"How extraordinary, how extraordinary!
This great śramaṇa possesses such great power!"
He possesses great supernormal powers!
He is able to cause these five hundred Brahmāṇas with conch-shell topknots to obtain water when permitted to do so, and to fail to obtain it when not permitted;
nevertheless, they still have not attained Arhatship as I have now.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he returned to that forest and stayed there, walking in meditation.

At that moment, when it was previously the time for Uruvilvā Kāśyapa to perform his fire sacrifice, he would always sit atop seven *tāla* trees; however, when he later attempted to ascend those same seven *tāla* trees for his subsequent sacrifice, he was unable to climb them.
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"It is certain that it was this Great Śramaṇa who performed this supernatural feat; there is no doubt about it. He has caused me to be unable to ascend this tāla tree to offer sacrifice to the fire."
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa possesses great majestic power!
He possesses great supernormal powers!"
"It is indeed so; had you not permitted us to climb the tree, we would not have been able to ascend.
Nevertheless, we still do not possess the state of Arhat that you possess now."
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished eating, he returned to that grove and stayed there while walking in meditation.
At that moment, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa ascended seven *tāla* trees to perform a sacrifice; having ascended, he was unable to remain there in safety.
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa thought to himself:

"It is certain that it was this Great Śramaṇa who performed this supernatural feat; there is no doubt about it. He caused me to ascend these seven *tāla* trees to my former dwelling place, yet I could not remain there and desired to ascend further."
Then he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, Śramaṇa!
We pray that you will allow us to continue dwelling here at these seven tala trees and perform our fire sacrifices as before."
When the Buddha had finished speaking, Kāśyapa and the others immediately returned to their former positions, dwelling securely atop those seven tala trees.
At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This Great Śramaṇa possesses great majestic power!"
"You possess great supernormal powers!
You are indeed able to grant me permission to stay, so that I may stay, and to deny it, so that I may not;
nevertheless, even so, you have not yet attained Arhatship as I have now."
“At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he returned to that grove and stayed there walking in meditation.
At that moment, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, having finished his fire sacrifice, wished to cover it up to store it away, but he was unable to do so.”
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"It must certainly have been that śramaṇa Gautama who performed this supernatural feat, preventing us from covering the fire."
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, Śramaṇa!
We pray that you may allow us to cover this fire."
Having spoken these words, he was immediately able to cover the fire.
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This Great Śramaṇa possesses great supernatural power!
He possesses great supernormal powers!
He is thus able to cover what he intends to cover and not to cover what he does not intend;
nevertheless, he has still not attained arhatship as I have now.
At that time, having finished his meal, the World-Honored One returned to that old forest and stayed there, walking in meditation.
At that moment, when Kāśyapa was performing the fire sacrifice, the fire and the wooden kindling ran hither and thither, unable to remain still in one place.
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"It must certainly be that śramaṇa Gautama who has performed this supernatural feat, causing my sacrificial fire implements to run hither and thither as if driven by someone, unable to remain still."
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, Śramaṇa!
I pray that these sacrificial fire implements of mine may attain stable abiding."
At that time, the Buddha said to Kāśyapa,
"It shall be as you intend. Thereupon,
the sacrificial implements for the fire became immediately stabilized.
For this reason, Kāśyapa and the others thought to themselves:
"This Great Śramaṇa possesses great majesty!
He possesses great supernormal powers!"
"You have indeed granted me permission to dwell wherever I may stay with my sacrificial fire-vessels; had you not granted this, I would not have stayed.
Nevertheless, even so, I still cannot attain Arhatship as I do now."
“At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he returned to that grove and stayed there walking in meditation.
At that moment, suddenly and unseasonably, a great black cloud arose in the sky and a heavy downpour of rain fell; yet where the Buddha resided, there was no rain.”
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"I shall now cause this water to spread everywhere, yet within the water there shall appear dry ground where dust rises, manifesting a place for walking to and fro."
Having formed this thought, he immediately manifested the dry ground and dust as before, walking back and forth in meditation.
At that time, Kāśyapa had this thought:
"Since it is not the proper season, how is it that clouds have suddenly arisen in the sky out of season and a great rain has fallen?"
"The place where this great śramaṇa resides is likewise filled with a vast expanse of water.
Perhaps this śramaṇa has been submerged by the water, or perhaps he is no longer to be seen?"

Having formed this thought, he took many brahmins with conch-shell crests and others onto his boat, searching everywhere until he gradually reached the place where the Buddha was. Upon arriving at the Buddha’s location, he stood there in such a manner.
At that time, Kāśyapa saw that while there was water on both sides of the World-Honored One, only the center appeared as dry ground, where dust rose as he came and went, pacing back and forth.
Having seen this, he addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Śramaṇa!
Are you now dwelling here within this great body of water?"
The Buddha said,
"Stay here.
Having spoken these words, he soared into the air and immediately went to Kāśyapa’s boat.
"At that time, for this reason, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
'This Great Śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers!
He possesses great majestic authority! "
"Thus he is able to perform such a course of practice while in the water;
nevertheless, he has still not attained arhatship as I have now.
(The Mahāsāṃghikas speak thus:)
"The Tathāgata manifested these five hundred supernatural powers for the sake of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and his followers; yet at all times, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa thought to himself:
'This Great Śramaṇa possesses great majestic power!'"
“He possesses great supernormal powers!
Although his transformative arts and virtues are such as these, he has not yet attained arhatship, just as I have now.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
"This foolish person has for immeasurable time harbored such thoughts:
'This Great Śramaṇa possesses great majestic power!
He possesses great supernormal powers! "
"Nevertheless, I have not yet attained Arhatship as I do now.
Yet, I can now cause this Kāśyapa and his disciples to open the eye of wisdom and give rise to a mind of weary detachment."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Upatiṣya Kāśyapa, saying these words:
“Kāśyapa, you are not an arhat now, nor have you yet entered the path of an arhat. You truly lack the marks of an arhat; how much less could you have attained the fruit of arhatship?”
Upon hearing these words, at that moment, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa felt a sense of shame and awe; his body hair stood on end as he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying:
“Excellent! ”
“World-Honored One!
Grant me the going forth and confer upon me full ordination.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words to Upatiṣya Kāśyapa:

"O Mahākāśyapa! These five hundred brahmins with conch-shell crests dwell in reliance upon you and follow your practice of the Dharma. You should deliberate together with them on what is beneficial and what is harmful, inform them so that they may understand, and perform such deeds as accord with their inclinations."
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa immediately went to the place where the five hundred brahmin *śikhin* ascetics were, and upon arriving, he addressed them, saying:
"O brahmins and young students! You all..."
"From me you may take this dwelling place for your residence, as well as the hall where the fire-god is enshrined and the sacrificial vessels; use each according to your own inclinations.
As for me, I now wish to go to the Great Śramaṇa to practice the holy life (brahmacarya)."
At that time, those five hundred disciples, the Brahmans with spiral-topknots, spoke thus together to Uruvilvā Kāśyapa:
"Preceptor!..."

Ever since we saw that great śramaṇa Gautama, we have long cherished the desire to go before that great śramaṇa and practice the holy life; however, out of reverence and consideration for our preceptor’s mind, we did not speak.
"Upādhyāya, if you now wish to practice the holy life under that Great Śramaṇa, we too shall follow you there and rely upon his teaching."
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa and his disciples went to where the Buddha was; having arrived, they stood to one side.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa and the others, saying: "O brahmins!

You may cast away your deer-skin garments, your water-pots, staffs, and various topknots; let all your conch-shell crests, fire-offering vessels, and sundry implements be thrown entirely into the waters of the Nairañjanā River."
At that time, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We shall not disobey, exactly as the Great Virtuous Śramaṇa has instructed.
Then those brahmins took the deerskin garments they were wearing, as well as their various vessels and utensils, and went to the riverbank, casting them all into the water.
Having cast those various objects into the water, they made various sounds—some hissing with reversed *tsi-tsi* sounds—and followed along with the current.
When those śikhins saw these various wonders, their hearts were further filled with joy; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One..."
"May we, like you, leave the household life and receive the precepts.
At that time, the Buddha spoke to those brahmins, saying:
"O bhikṣus!..."
"Come and enter into the Dharma taught by me, practice the holy life (brahmacarya), and bring an end to all suffering.
At that moment, those five hundred elders went forth at his voice and immediately became fully ordained.

At that time, Nadi-Kāśyapa, the matted-hair ascetic, was practicing the path on the bank downstream of the Nairañjanā River; he saw their deer-skin garments and the implements and vessels used for fire worship drifting along with the current.
Having seen this, he was struck with dismay and his heart was filled with terror, whereupon he uttered these words:
"Alas! What a strange occurrence!
My elder brother has likely been defeated by bandits; otherwise, he must have been killed by someone at his dwelling."
"I should now go there to observe what calamity or strange portent has caused such a sudden change as this.

Having formed this thought, his younger brother Nadi-Kāśyapa first dispatched many brahmins with conch-shell crests to go ahead and investigate, instructing them to report whatever they encountered, whether good or bad.
"Examine it yourselves: what is so strange about that?
What is the matter?
Having received these instructions, the disciples went there to look and returned to report:
"Each of us is well and we serve the Gautama clan.
Then Nadi-Kāśyapa, surrounded on all sides by his three hundred disciples, went to the dwelling place of the elder Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa.
Upon arriving, he immediately saw the teacher Uruvilvā Kāśyapa and his disciples with their hair and beards shaved and wearing saffron robes.
Having seen them, his heart was not greatly pleased, and he spoke this verse to his elder brother Kāśyapa:
"O Venerable One, you have performed fire sacrifices in vain; In vain, moreover, have you practiced asceticism for nothing."
"Today, having cast off these ascetic practices, he is like a snake shedding its old skin.
Then, Nadi-Kāśyapa, the one with the matted hair, addressed his elder brother, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, saying:
"Is this one truly superior?"
At that time, the Elder Uruvilvā Kāśyapa replied, "This is indeed superior!
It would be better to practice this way; this practice is most wonderful."
At that time, Nadi-Kāśyapa, the one with the matted locks, addressed his three hundred disciples, the young brahmins with matted locks, saying:
"You young brahmins with matted locks!..."
"As for my residence, the springs and ponds, and all my belongings, you may dispose of them as you see fit;
I now wish to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of the Great Śramaṇa."
At that time, those three hundred disciples of the brahmin Nārada Jaṭila addressed their teacher, saying:
"Upādhyāya, if you now wish to go to that Great Śramaṇa to practice the holy life (brahmacarya), we too shall follow you and go together to his side to practice the holy life."
At that time, Nadi-Kāśyapa, the one with the matted locks, together with his disciples, went to where the Buddha was; having arrived at the Buddha’s location, they stood to one side.
At that time, the Buddha addressed those brahmins, saying:
"Can you now take the deer skins you wear upon your bodies, as well as the vessels and implements used for the fire sacrifice, and cast them into the waters of the Nairañjanā River, discarding them?"
Those brahmins spoke together to the Buddha, saying, "As the Śramaṇa has instructed, we dare not disobey.
Yet they proceeded with their preparations as before, immediately casting [the items] into the water; they made a splashing sound and were carried away by the current.

At that time, those jaṭila brahmins, seeing such rare and marvelous events, were filled with even greater joy; subsequently, those elder bhikṣus went forth at the appropriate time and immediately attained full ordination.

"At that time, Kāśyapa of the Matted Hair from Gayā was downstream by the river when he suddenly saw deer skins and the various implements for his fire-sacrifices being carried down by the current. Having seen this, great terror arose in his heart again, and he spoke these words:
'Alas! What a strange occurrence! "
"Could it be that my elder brother’s dwelling has been destroyed by bandits, though he himself was not killed?
I shall now go there to observe what calamity has occurred."
Having formed this thought, he first dispatched many brahmin ascetics with spiral-topknots to go there and observe in advance, instructing them:
"Report back on whether it is auspicious or inauspicious. You must investigate: what portents are there?"
"What were those matters?
The disciple returned and reported them exactly as he had been instructed.

At that time, Gayā-Kāśyapa of the Śikhin clan then personally led two hundred disciples, surrounding him on all sides, and went to where the elder Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and Nadī-Kāśyapa were. Upon arrival, he saw the two Kāśyapas with their topknots shaved and wearing saffron robes.
Having seen this, his heart was not greatly filled with joy, and he spoke these verses toward his two elder brothers, the Kāśyapas Uruvilvā and Nadī:
“Brothers, you formerly sacrificed in vain to the fire god, And likewise practiced asceticism in vain;
Today, having together cast these aside, It is just like a snake shedding its old skin.”
At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and the elder Nadī-Kāśyapa together replied to their younger brother, the brahmin Gayā-Kāśyapa, with these verses:
"In the past, we offered sacrifices to the fire god in vain; We also practiced asceticism in vain.
Now that we have been able to abandon this dharma, It is truly like a snake shedding its old skin."
At that time, Gayākāśyapa again asked Uruvilvākāśyapa and Nadīkāśyapa and the others, saying:
"Brothers, is it truly superior here?"
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa said:
"This place is truly excellent!
It would be better to practice this path; this path is most wonderful."
At that time, Gayākāśyapa spoke to his two hundred disciples, the brahmin māṇavas, saying:
"You, brahmin māṇavas!..."
"Regarding all the springs, ponds, and various furnishings in my dwelling, you may decide for yourself how they shall be disposed of;
I now wish to practice the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa."
At that time, those two hundred disciples of the brahmin Gaṇḍa-makuṭa, having addressed their teacher, the brahmin Gayā-kāśyapa, spoke as follows:

"Venerable Teacher, if you now wish to go to that Great Śramaṇa to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*), we too shall follow the Teacher; let us all go together at once to the side of the Great Śramaṇa to practice the holy life in common."

At that time, Kāśyapa of the Uṇṇā-jaṭa (the "Conch-shell Topknot") and his disciples went to where the Buddha was; having arrived at the Buddha's location, they stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Śramaṇa!"
"I and my disciples now wish to enter the dharma of the śramaṇas; all matters concerning this should be maintained accordingly.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those jaṭila brahmacārins, saying:
"If you are able to do as I have said, you should take your deerskin garments and all the utensils and implements for the fire-sacrifices, and cast them all away into the Nairañjanā River."
They replied, "As the Śramaṇa has instructed, we dare not disobey.

At that time, those jaṭila brahmins immediately took their deer skins and various ritual implements for the fire sacrifice and cast them all into the river. Having cast them into the river, their leather garments, water jars, and pots produced various sounds—*ṭi-ṭi*, *cang-gu*, and *hu-hu*—as they flowed downstream with the current.
"At that time, those jaṭila brahmins, having witnessed such rare and marvelous events, were further filled with joy and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'Excellent!'"
“World-Honored One!
Grant me the going forth and the full ordination.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying:
"O bhikṣus! Come and enter into my own teaching of the Dharma, practice the holy life (brahmacarya), and bring an end to all suffering.
At that time, those elders, in response to these words, went forth from the household life and immediately attained full ordination.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having stayed as long as he desired within the village of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, gradually proceeded toward the vicinity of Gayā City.

The Tathāgata stayed upon the summit of that Elephant Head Mountain with a retinue of one thousand bhikṣus; he then taught and transformed them by means of the three kinds of supernormal powers—namely, the power of the body, the power of speech, and the power of the mind—and disciplined them through these practices.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to manifest his supernormal powers—namely, making one body into many bodies and returning many bodies to one; disappearing from above and appearing below, disappearing from below and appearing above; disappearing in the east and appearing in the west, disappearing in the west and appearing in the east; disappearing in the south and appearing in the north, and disappearing in the north and appearing in the south; passing unimpeded through mountain precipices and stone walls—manifested these feats.
He enters the earth as if it were water and treads upon water as if it were solid ground; he rises from the earth into the air in the full lotus posture, just like a soaring bird.
From his body he emits smoke and flames like a great mass of fire, extinguishing fire by manifesting water and dispelling water by emitting fire.
These suns and moons possess such majestic power that he can touch, stroke, grasp, and hold them with his hand, even moving with sovereign ease as far as the Brahma Heaven.
This is the Tathāgata’s supernormal power manifested in his physical body.
"Regarding the manifestation of the supernormal power of speech: 'O bhikṣus!

You should now know that you must distinguish things in this way; you must not give rise to such distinctions; you should observe and contemplate in this way; and you must not contemplate or observe in this way.'"
"O bhikṣus! You should realize it in this way; do not realize it in that way. O bhikṣus!"
"You should practice in this way; do not practice in that way.
This is the Tathāgata manifesting the supernormal power of speech.
As for manifesting the supernormal power of mind: "O bhikṣus!..."
Now you should know this:

all these phenomena are ablaze. As for what is meant by "ablaze," the eye is ablaze, forms are ablaze, eye-consciousness is ablaze, eye-contact is ablaze, and the feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-pleasant-nor-painful—that arises conditioned by eye-contact is also ablaze.
By what does it blaze?
It blazes with the fire of desire; it blazes with the fire of hatred; it blazes with the fire of delusion.

I have thus spoken of the burning of the eye; likewise, the ear is burning, sounds are burning, and so on in brief until: the nose and odors are burning, the tongue and flavors are burning, the body and tangibles are burning, and the mind and mental phenomena are burning. Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is burning.
By what is it set ablaze?

It is by the fire of desire that the afflictions are set ablaze; by the fire of hatred that the afflictions are set ablaze; and by the fire of delusion that the afflictions are set ablaze. In this way, I have explained the defects of the sense organs—the ear, nose, tongue, and body—and their corresponding objects.

"Furthermore, if there is a person of great learning who is able to engage in such profound contemplation, they will become weary of the eye, weary of eye-consciousness, and weary of eye-contact. Regarding the feeling produced by eye-contact—whether it be painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—they will likewise become weary of it; this is weariness toward the eye."

“Furthermore, in this way, one becomes weary of and detached from the ear and sounds; and so on, briefly stated, one becomes weary of and detached from the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena.”
If there is feeling born of mental contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-pleasant-nor-painful—one becomes weary of and detached from it as well.
Once weary and detached, one is no longer stained by attachment; being unstained, one attains liberation.

Having attained liberation, there immediately arises within him such pure wisdom through which he knows for himself: "Birth and death have been severed; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence."
“This is the supernormal power (ṛddhi) produced by the intention of the Tathāgata.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was thus teaching the three kinds of supernormal powers, those one thousand bhikṣus, his followers, became free from outflows through the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and their minds attained liberation from all phenomena.
And there is a verse that says:
"The stream of all desires for birth and death has been severed; The holy life has been attained for one's own benefit;
All that was to be done has been fully accomplished; One shall no longer undergo future existence."

At that time, when those one thousand bhikṣus had heard this teaching from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they were no longer subject to conditioned existence within the outflows (āsravas). They immediately attained the excellent liberation of the inner mind, abandoned the dharma of the brahmins, and were called the Saṃgha of Śrāvakas.

Chapter 45: Upasena, Part One. *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Forty-five, Part One: Upasena. "At that time, the three Kāśyapa brothers had a nephew who was a *jaṭila* brahmacārin. This brahmacārin was named Upasena (translated in the Sui language as 'Supreme General'), and he dwelt upon a mountain called Asura. There, he constantly practiced the path of the rishis together with two hundred and fifty *jaṭila* brahmacārin disciples."

When he heard that his three uncles, the Kāśyapas, along with their disciples, had gone to that Great Śramaṇa and all renounced the world, shaving off their hair and beards, he was struck with alarm and became greatly displeased, saying aloud:
"How extraordinary, my uncles!"
"For many years he has sacrificed to the fire god, yet today he has suddenly entered the ranks of the śramaṇas to become their disciple.
I shall now go to that place and rebuke him: 'Why have you committed such an unwholesome act?'"
Making a gurgling sound from his throat, he went to where his three maternal uncles were; having arrived, he saw them with their hair and beards shaved off and wearing saffron robes.
Having seen him, he spoke this verse to his maternal uncles:
