"Uncles, you have vainly sacrificed to the fire for a hundred years, And likewise practiced those ascetic penances in vain.
Today we shall together abandon this dharma, Just as a snake sheds its old skin."
At that time, his three uncles, the Kāśyapas, together replied to their nephew Upasena in verse, saying:
"In the past, we offered sacrifices to the fire god in vain, And likewise practiced asceticism in vain;
Today we have abandoned this dharma, Just as a snake sheds its old skin."
At that time, having heard these verses, the general, the Śramaṇa with the conch-shell topknot, again questioned his three maternal uncles, saying:
"Is this one capable of victory?"
At that time, those three maternal uncles replied:
"This is indeed superior!
It would be better to perform this practice; this practice is most wonderful."
At that time, the military commander Śikhin, the brahmin, addressed his two hundred and fifty brahmin disciples, saying to them:
"O you brahmin youths, māṇavas!..."
"Regarding all the springs, ponds, and various furnishings in that residence of mine, you may take them as you see fit and dispose of them as you wish;
I now desire to practice the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa."
At that time, those two hundred and fifty hair-rolled ascetics (jaṭila) addressed Upasena the hair-rolled ascetic, saying:
"Preceptor, if you now wish to go to that Great Śramaṇa to practice the holy life (brahmacarya), we shall also follow the Preceptor and go together to his side to cultivate pure conduct."
At that time, the military commander Śaṅkhakuṇḍika, the brahmin, along with his disciples, went to where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Virtuous Śramaṇa!
"I now wish to lead all my disciples into the dharma of the śramaṇas; even regarding this matter, you should hold to it thus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those jaṭila brahmins, saying:
"If this is so, you should take your deerskin garments and your fire-offering implements and cast them aside to one side."
Those brahmins replied, "We shall not oppose the instructions of the śramaṇa.
They then went to their dwellings, took the implements for the fire sacrifice, and cast them aside.

"At that time, after the brahmin had discarded the sacrificial fire vessels, he returned to where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the Buddha's presence, he prostrated at the Buddha's feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'Excellent!'"
“World-Honored One!
Grant us the going forth and the full ordination.
The Buddha spoke to them as follows:
“Come, O bhikṣus!
Enter my well-expounded Dharma and practice the holy life (brahmacarya) for the sake of bringing an end to all suffering.
At these words, those two hundred and fifty elders went forth and immediately attained full ordination.
At that time, the World-Honored One further expounded the Dharma for those elders, once again instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them by means of the three kinds of supernormal powers as before.
At that time, they had completely exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) regarding unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and their minds attained liberation.

Then, the World-Honored One first gathered his assembly of bhikṣus—namely these one thousand two hundred and fifty people together—who had all gone forth from the life of a brahmin; they were all arhats who had fully realized their own benefit, attended upon the World-Honored One, and had personally witnessed and verified his teaching of the Dharma.
Furthermore, subsequently, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha,
saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
What roots of goodness did those disciples of the Jaṭila Brahmin plant in the past,
that today they have all been able to leave the household life, receive full ordination, and realize arhatship?
What karma did he perform in the past to receive this retribution now?

Furthermore, why is that elder Uruvilvā Kāśyapa alone, together with his five hundred brahmin disciples with conch-shell crests, the leader, the most wondrous, the most excellent, the highest, and the most venerable;
while Nadi Kāśyapa’s three hundred disciples are the leaders, the foremost, the most excellent, and the most wondrous?
Among the two hundred disciples of Gayākāśyapa, he was the foremost, the most excellent, the most sublime, and the most venerable.

Furthermore, what karma did the Elder Uruvilvākāśyapa create in the past, such that today, although he is so difficult to convert, he has been transformed by the various instructions of the World-Honored One, while all other brahmins have easily accepted conversion?
Having spoken these words, he remained silent.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
Listen with a sincere and attentive mind!
I recall that in the distant past, while still within this Jambudvīpa, there were a full thousand merchants. Among those merchants, there were three brothers, each serving as a leader of the caravan.

The first was named Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, who led five hundred merchants; the second was named Nadī-Kāśyapa, who likewise led three hundred merchants; and the third was named Gayā-Kāśyapa, who similarly led two hundred merchants.

"At that time, those three great merchant leaders and their merchants, desiring together to go into the sea to seek their livelihood, had completed the preparation of goods suitable for entering the ocean."

The value of these goods amounted to three hundred ten million gold coins: one hundred ten million were intended for his own provisions; one hundred ten million were intended for the other merchants to serve as their capital; and one hundred ten million were intended for miscellaneous expenses and the maintenance of the ships.
Having thus completed their preparations, they proceeded by stages until they reached the seashore.

Upon reaching the shore, they made offerings and sacrifices to the deity of the great ocean and prepared a ship. Furthermore, they hired five additional men at double the usual rate—namely, one skilled in managing and repairing the vessel, one who observes the four quarters, one who enters against the current, one who is an excellent swimmer, and one who sets and manages the sails.
Having thus obtained those five men, the three merchant leaders raised their voices and proclaimed:
"Who is able to enter the sea?
Having thus shouted this proclamation three times, they immediately boarded the ship and entered the sea together for the sake of seeking wealth.
Once they had reached the midst of the great ocean, they suddenly encountered a black wind. That wind blew their ship and cast it onto a sandbank in the sea, where it came to a standstill.
*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll 42;
*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll 43.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on Upasena, Part II:

"At that time, the merchant leader and his fellow traders, having reached the island in the sea, encountered various kinds of miscellaneous precious jewels. They gathered them up and filled their ships, then returned to the shore; having secured their treasures, they desired to return to their own country."

Along the way, he encountered a stupa; this stupa was a reliquary stupa for the World-Honored One Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. The stupa was dilapidated, its foundations and steps collapsed, and it was falling apart in every place.
Having seen this, the eldest merchant leader addressed the other two merchant leaders and the assembly of merchants, saying: "O you people!

If you know that we did not spare our own lives for the sake of seeking wealth when we entered the great ocean, and have now returned from that place having obtained profit, then we may now together perform the causes and conditions for wholesome karma that will benefit us in future lives."
As an ancient wise person said in a verse:
"The power of merit accomplishes great benefit; Because people obtain such benefit, negligence arises.
When there is negligence, there is no mind of upholding the precepts; By these causes and conditions, one falls into hell."
At that time, having spoken these verses, the merchant leader further addressed them, saying:
"You should know!
For this reason, we must now direct our minds together and gather as much wealth as each can afford to maintain this stūpa for the relics of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa."
At that time, those caravan leaders and the multitude of merchants together addressed the senior caravan leader, saying:
"O great and virtuous caravan leader!"
"If you collect the money, you should act as the master yourself and oversee the construction; we shall each contribute whatever amount of wealth we can according to our means.
Then, the senior merchant leader spoke these words:
"I am not fit to be the overseer."
Why is this? My affairs and conditions are many, and I am unable to repair this ruined stūpa. If I were to manage and restore this stūpa, it would interfere with and ruin my livelihood at home.
Those merchants and the two merchant leaders earnestly entreated him for a long time, requesting that he be sent to oversee the affairs.
Thereupon, those merchants quickly brought forth various amounts of money and goods and entrusted them to him.

"At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa repaired that stūpa; he himself constructed the first *kapota* (dome) and installed it upon it. Next was the second *kapota* by Nadi-Kāśyapa, and next was the third *kapota* by Gayā-Kāśyapa."

In this manner, they proceeded in succession with those merchants and their leaders to thoroughly attend to the stupa of the relics of Kāśyapa Tathāgata; all that was broken or collapsed was restored to its original state, making it as magnificent as when it was first built.
Having finished the meal, they made this aspiration:

"May we, in future ages, once again encounter such a World-Honored One! Having encountered him, may we swiftly realize and understand the teachings and instructions spoken by that World-Honored One. Furthermore, in all future lives and throughout every birth, may we never fall into the three evil realms or the four destinies."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “You should know!
Those three Kāśyapas and the thousand merchants are now these three elders and the one thousand bhikṣus.”
Furthermore, monks!
At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa had previously been earnestly entreated for a long duration by the merchants; only then did he finally consent to oversee the matter.
Due to that karma, it was only after a long time that they have now begun to receive my transformation before me.
At that time, the two merchant leaders Nadi-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa, along with the other merchants, briefly uttered these words:
"According to our means, quickly produce as much wealth as you can."
"By the retribution of this karma, he has today swiftly submitted to my transformation.

At that time, the eldest merchant leader, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, first made an offering upon the first dome of the stupa for the relics of the World-Honored One Kāśyapa Tathāgata; by the retribution of that karma, he has today become the foremost among these five hundred men, the most excellent, the most wondrous, and the very best."
Nadī-Kāśyapa was the second to receive the bowl; due to that karmic retribution, he now serves as the leader of three hundred brahmins and has attained the foremost position.
Gayā-Kāśyapa was the third to receive the bowl; due to that karmic retribution, he now serves as the leader of two hundred śikhin brahmins and has attained the foremost position.
"At that time, they made this aspiration:
'May we, in all future lives and throughout every birth, never fall into the evil realms or the hells.'"
"By the retribution of that karma, they did not enter the evil realms or even hell, but were constantly reborn among humans and devas, experiencing happiness.

Furthermore, when they together saw that the stupa containing the relics of Kāśyapa Buddha had fallen into ruin, they repaired it so that it was restored to its former state and made this vow in their hearts:
'May we, in future lives, once again encounter a World-Honored One such as this; having encountered him, may we quickly realize and understand whatever Dharma that World-Honored One preaches.'"
"Due to the retribution of that karma, he has now encountered me, immediately gone forth from home, received full ordination, and attained the fruit of Arhatship. At that time,
the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha,
saying, "How rare it is, World-Honored One!"
"How is it, World-Honored One?

Did you see that Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa had fallen into a wrong path, and did you employ expedient means, manifesting five hundred kinds of supernatural powers to transform him, before he finally attained the fruit of arhatship?"
Having spoken these words, he remained silent.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!

Not only today have I seen Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, who had fallen into a false path, emerge through courageous and diligent effort, having converted him by means of five hundred kinds of supernatural transformations.
"In his past lives, he also fell into wrong paths; my mind has labored diligently to transform and guide him, and I have succeeded.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying, "Excellent!"
World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of this matter?
We pray that you will explain it for us.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "You bhikṣus!
Listen with a sincere and attentive mind!"
I recall that in the past, there was a kingdom named Videha (translated in the Sui language as "Non-Upright Body").

Within that country, there was a Kṣatriya king named Aṅgada (translated in the Sui language as "Body-Portion"), who had been consecrated as king by coronation. He possessed great power, a vast multitude of troops, and an abundance of wealth and grain, such that his storehouses were overflowing.

"At that time, the king harbored wrong views. Once, on the fifteenth night of the month when the moon was full and its radiance shone brightly, the king summoned his ministers during the first watch of the night, and they all assembled together."

The first minister was named Vijaya (translated in the Sui language as "Difficult to Conquer"); the second chief minister was named Sumana (translated in the Sui language as "Good Intention"); and the third was named Aravada (translated in the Sui language as "Foremost Speech"). These three chief ministers were the most eminent leaders.
"At that time, the king again extensively summoned and assembled immeasurable great ministers and addressed them, saying:
'O you ministers!'"
"Each of you should speak from the depths of your own hearts regarding what means you might employ to pass this single night together in mutual entertainment so that we do not fall asleep.
At that time, the minister named Foremost spoke to the king, saying:
"Great King!..."

You should know that, according to my view, one must prepare the fourfold army; those kingdoms not yet subdued shall be brought under submission, and once they have been subdued, one shall govern and dwell there.
Then, the minister Subhadra again addressed the king, saying:
"Great King!

You should know that, according to my view, all enemies everywhere have now been completely subdued; there is nothing further to fear. It is now fitting that you enjoy the five desires to your heart's content and find joy therein."
At that time, the minister Duryodhana again addressed the king, saying:
"Great King!
You should know that the five desires are things that can always be obtained; what is so extraordinary about this? What is so rare?"
But, Great King!

If there should now be any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who is diligent, observant of the precepts, endowed with extensive learning and vast wisdom—if such a person is found, he should be venerated and served.
"Why is this? Because he awakens people.
At that time, the king replied to that minister, saying:

"Your single word is most excellent; this speech is truly beautiful. Therefore, you must now examine and observe with precision: where are the best śramaṇas and brahmins, who are diligent in their observance of the precepts, learned, and wise? I shall go there to serve and make offerings."
Then the former minister addressed the king, saying:

"Great King, if you require such a person, I now know where such a person may be found. In the Deer Park, there is a man of great diligence and vast learning named Nagna, of the Kāśyapa clan, who is able to speak many kinds of subtle and wonderful words. Your Majesty should now serve that man."

"At that time, the king prepared a magnificent carriage drawn by four excellent horses and sat upon it. He wore white garments and put on white necklaces; those to his left and right all likewise wore white robes. A white parasol was raised over him, he wore white leather sandals on his feet, and held a white fly-whisk adorned with white mani-jewels in his hand. With the majesty of a great king and the supernatural power of a great king, accompanied by his ministers leading and following before and behind, he proceeded to the side of the naked ascetic Kāśyapa."
Having arrived, he paid his respects and sat to one side to inquire about what he had not yet heard.
At that time, King Aṅga greeted the naked ascetic leader Kāśyapa, saying these words:
"Venerable sir, are your four great elements at ease?"
Are all the seasons harmonious and favorable?
Are your necessities for sustaining life fully provided?
Is it not difficult to obtain food and clothing, nor are you lacking in anything, and are you free from disturbances?
At that time, the naked ascetic Kāśyapa replied to King Aṅga, saying:
"Great King!
I now lack for nothing, and my body has attained peace and freedom from ailment.
Furthermore, Great King,
is your own person at ease in its movements and free from distress?
Have virtuous deeds and benefits increased?
Are the people within the realm prosperous and happy?
Is the King’s administration upright, impartial, and just?
At that time, after King Aṅgada had exchanged greetings with the naked ascetic Kāśyapa, he asked him concerning a point of doubt in his mind:
"Venerable One!..."

"In this world, there are various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who each proclaim their own teachings and practices. Among these, Venerable One, please explain for me in due order that which leads to the ultimate truth."
Having spoken these words, the naked ascetic Kāśyapa then replied to the king:
"Great King, listen well!
Regarding that which is most true within this, I shall now explain this true meaning. There is a verse herein, which those of dull faculties are unable to comprehend."
"In this world, those who are obscured and deluded, whether speaking truth, falsehood, or lies—
because they lack wisdom, they are unable to discern or understand the words they encounter."
All karmas of every variety do not exist; the retributions of good and evil likewise do not exist.
Even the bodies of yakṣas and others are not real, so how much less could there be the higher devas?
Furthermore, there are no parents or kin; this world and the next are both utterly severed.
Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas alike—all of them are entirely empty.
Even the teachers of the world are no more; who else could possibly be tamed?
When foolish people teach others to give, the wise, having heard it, do not follow their hearts.
If one is skilled at deceiving others to take their wealth, being truly foolish yet claiming to be wise, such a person will die when they ought to die;
having practiced giving, they shall reap no fruit thereafter.
This body is always connected as a whole; it is impossible to say that it is severed.
Whether it be fire, wind, earth, or water, whether in states of suffering, non-suffering, or pleasure—the seventh element is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); none of these can be killed.
Within the space between the body and the life-force, weapons operate from within;
worldly fools do not know this, and they say, "This one has been harmed and killed."
Such fear is called ignorance; one who undergoes it is a person of wisdom.
After passing through eighty-four thousand births, one finally attains liberation during the process of transmigration.
Only then can such afflictions be purified, at the conclusion of those eighty-four thousand births.
The cycle of transmigration proceeds without error or confusion, just as the tides of the ocean follow their fixed limits;
such is the sequence of these dharmas, which you, Great King, should now understand.
At that time, having heard the verse spoken, the former minister addressed the naked ascetic Kāśyapa, saying:
"So it is, so it is, O ascetic Kāśyapa!"
As the Venerable One has said. Why is this so?
Venerable Kāśyapa!
I know my past lives; I recall that in the past, while in the city of Kuśāmbī, I was once a butcher.
At that time, I slaughtered countless and boundless cattle, sheep, buffalo, pigs, goats, and horses. I killed them and sold them for money, using the proceeds to sustain my life.
"After I had committed such evil karma, I passed away from that life and have now been born into this family of a great general, possessing abundant wealth.
For this reason, I know that there is no retribution for good or evil deeds."

At that time, the chief minister of King Aṅga, named Duryodhana, was standing behind the king. Having heard these words, the minister wept with tears falling from his eyes; he sobbed and remained speechless.
At that time, King Aṅga said to his minister,
"For what reason are you now weeping so bitterly?
Viśākha replied:
"Great King!
You should know that the verses spoken by the ascetic Kāśyapa, as well as the words of the former minister, are entirely consistent with this principle and contain no error."
“‘Great King!

You should know that I also recall in the past, while in the city of Kauśāmbī, having been a householder who was capable of great renunciation and served as a lord of dāna, distributing all my wealth and possessions in common with others.’”
During the bright and dark fortnights, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days, they constantly observe the eightfold precepts of the fast and always diligently guard their body and speech.
"Having performed such pure deeds, I have now fallen into the womb of a lowly slave-girl and was born as a servant.
Great King!

You should know that for this reason, upon hearing the words of the naked ascetic Kāśyapa and the former minister, I wept with such overwhelming grief that I could not restrain myself; I also realized that there is no virtuous path in this world."
At that time, having heard these words from the naked ascetic Kāśyapa, King Aṅga rose from his seat and returned to his palace.
After that night had passed, he assembled all his ministers and officials and addressed them, saying:

"O you three! From this day forward, if there are matters of private misconduct or good and evil affairs, be careful not to consult me. I now dispatch these three great ministers—Duranjayasumanas, Pūrvokta, and the others—to these three men, who are clever and wise, shall judge affairs on my behalf."

When King Aṅga had spoken these words, he entered a palace named *Varṇa-śobhana* (Exquisite Color) and sat within it. There he remained for seven days, enjoying the pleasures of the five senses, dwelling in negligence, self-indulgence, and the unrestrained pursuit of his desires. After those seven days had passed...

At that time, King Aṅga had a daughter named Manoharā. Having dressed herself in various garments of many colors and adorned her body with various necklaces and ornaments made of the seven precious gems, she proceeded toward the Palace of Exquisite Colors and approached her father, the king.
Having arrived, she prostrated at the feet of her father, the king, and sat to one side, remaining silent. Then,
King Aṅga said to his daughter,
"Sumanā, my dear daughter!"
Have you ever gone into that grove of trees to play?
Within it there are many kinds of trees, and upon those trees are various flowers and fruits; furthermore, there are various birds singing—have you entered therein with a sense of delight?
"What do you crave?
Tell me, and I shall grant your wish.
Having spoken these words, he asked the woman what she required.
At that time, the maiden Manoharā addressed her father, the king, saying:
“Excellent, my lord!
My body and its necessities are now lacking nothing; I wish only to address one word to my lord. I pray, O Father King!”
"Listen to the girl’s counsel," he said,
and spoke these verses:
"O Father King, I now desire to practice giving To all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas."
"Whenever the fifteenth day of the moon arrives, I pray that you will give me the value of a thousand pieces of gold.
At that time, King Aṅga, having heard these words spoken by his daughter, immediately replied to the maiden Manoharā in verse, saying:
"Good daughter, listen now with a sincere heart; I have heard this from wise men:"
Though you may wish to bestow various kinds of wealth, all is empty and there will be no karmic fruit.
Why do you now give rise to this intention to deceive and delude the ignorant people of the world?
Since neither the present nor the future exist, why must you further exhaust yourself in such toil?
"O foolish woman, do you not now hear that Kāśyapa’s preaching of the Dharma is perfectly unerring?
Truly, there is no creator of karma nor a person who acts; there are only the fruits of good and evil for all humans and devas."
Yakṣas and spirits do not exist at all, nor do parents or kinsmen;
by briefly explaining eighty-four thousand births, such afflictions can thus be purified.
If eighty-four thousand eons have passed, the wandering in saṃsāra will finally be free from deluded mind;
just as the ocean tide follows its appointed time, that which has not yet arrived cannot be anticipated in the interim.
One should simply wait for the time to come with natural spontaneity—what use is there in forcibly creating worldly turmoil?
You should know what Kāśyapa has said: this matter is without falsehood and is true;
it holds for neither the present nor the future world. Do not now exhaust yourself in vain.
At that time, having heard these words spoken by her father, King Aṅga, the maiden Manoharā felt displeased in her heart and immediately addressed her father again in verse:
"O Father, you are now the king of this land; You ought to govern the world with the True Dharma.
Since your wicked ministers are sycophantic and devoid of sincerity, They further urge Your Majesty to serve a foolish teacher."
Kāśyapa and those three great ministers—what they have said is not true or correct.
Our father, the King, is a bad friend; now he falsely assumes the appearance of a wise friend, practicing a deviant path himself and leading others astray.
How can one distinguish such a lowly and ignorant person?
Now, instead of bestowing peace and happiness upon the King, you have conversely taught him to create unwholesome causes.
I have heard of such matters in the past, and now I see them with my own eyes:
because of ignorance one is born here, and later one again obtains an ignorant body.
Having emerged from the realm of darkness, one enters the realm of darkness again; thereafter, one returns once more to undergo the realm of darkness.
Since Kāśyapa is a person of delusion, he proclaims what accords with his own ignorant and confused mind.
As a king, you are the lord of men who governs the four quarters; you understand principles and have mastered worldly affairs.
Why, then, like those small children, do you enter upon the paths of false and inferior ways?
Following after mental sensations and associating with such people, one learns their ways and immediately gives rise to defiled attachment;
like an arrow already stained with blood, it enters the quiver and, as it is passed from hand to hand, becomes further smeared by them all.
The wise associate with deep self-restraint; they do not become intimate with evil companions or friends.
Although they themselves commit no sins, they constantly habituate themselves to those who do.
Through long familiarity and habitual practice, one’s own characteristics are formed; thereafter, one naturally encounters ill repute.
Therefore, just as with that archery target, the wise likewise fear being struck by transgression.
Do not associate with evil companions; always stay close to wise and virtuous friends.
Even if sentient beings have purified their physical karma over eighty-four thousand lifetimes, when they act as butchers killing many lives, or like hunters, archers, and fishermen.
Kāśyapa is just like those others, and those others are likewise the peers of Kāśyapa;
when these two are weighed against one another, they are of a single kind and equal, with no distinction of superior or inferior.
Thus, Kāśyapa, one who lacks the principle of non-substantiality leaves the home life in vain,
blinded by ignorance and delusion; clinging to this falsehood as the cause of purity, they exhaust eighty-four thousand lifetimes,
wandering in error and contrary to the right path, their minds confused by lack of wisdom and folly.
When sentient beings attain purity, they no longer undergo the eighty-four thousand sensations;
though thieves and bandits plunder and kill people and property, or commit evil acts and harbor enmity toward others,
they are no different from Kāśyapa, and Kāśyapa is likewise no different from them.
If sentient beings attain purity therein, how could there be eighty-four thousand births?
When such numbers of good and evil are taken up, whether superior, inferior, or middling, all are equal—
neither superior nor inferior, and furthermore, no differentiation arises.
If sentient beings attain pure cultivation, passing through eighty-four thousand places,
yet those people are foolish and lack wisdom, they are like Kāśyapa’s empty renunciation.
Just as a fiercely blazing fire completely consumes all sacrificial offerings, so too,
due to ignorance and folly, one burns away the entire mountain of merit.
The minister spoke these words, perceiving the future: "Though he committed many sins, there will be no retribution;
because he cultivated meritorious deeds in previous lives, he now experiences a heart of joy."
When a person commits various transgressions, they abandon merit and naturally incur calamity.
Like a boat that does not emerge from the water because it is so heavily laden that it sinks, no one can lift it out;
it remains submerged in the water, perpetually decaying.
Just as when a person repeatedly commits various sins, and because they do not cease committing them,
their transgressions become excessive and they thus sink into hell— O King, I am that very person you previously mentioned;
because the affliction of my sin has not yet matured, it will soon be known once that sin reaches its fruition.
When their transgressions ripen, they fall into those hells;
covered and obscured by various mossy growths, the weight of the grasses rises up on its own such that they cannot bear it—
just as a ship becomes increasingly heavy and rigid the longer it remains thus.
The same applies to the various sins one commits: gradually and over time, they cause one to sink deeper and the body becomes increasingly heavy.
Just as when one creates the causes of wholesome karma, one swiftly attains rebirth in the higher realms.
This present life is like a seed in the earth; once karmic offenses are exhausted, one gradually arises.
When the retribution for various virtuous deeds is to manifest, one is then spontaneously born in a place of wholesome fruit.
"Then, after the maiden Manoharā had spoken these verses, she addressed her father, the king, once more, saying:
'Father King, you should know!
I have reflected upon this and also recognize my past lives.'"

Why is this? I recall that in the past, during seven lifetimes within the city of Rājagṛha in the kingdom of Magadha, because I was led astray by evil associates, I committed many sinful deeds and engaged in perverse lust, violating the wives and concubines of others while enjoying pleasures like those of the gods.
"Great King!
You should know that at that time, I remained concealing the evil karma I had created, like fire covered by ashes.
Furthermore, Great King!"
After I had relinquished my body in that place, I was again born into a wealthy family in the village of Vajra.

Having been born there, I encountered a spiritual friend and, during the dark and light fortnights, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days, I purely observed the eightfold precepts of the fast and constantly maintained the moral discipline.
"Great King!
You should know that having performed wholesome karma there, it is like depositing various treasures and firmly sealing them within the realm of water, where they then remain stationary."
"Furthermore, Great King!
At that place as well, I abandoned my body and life; because there remained karma not yet exhausted from evil deeds committed due to past circumstances, I immediately fell into the Raurava Hell."
Remaining in that place for many thousands of years, I underwent extreme suffering and distress.
"Furthermore, Great King!
When my karmic retribution there was completely exhausted, I cast off that body and was immediately reborn within the land of Pinākuṭa, taking the form of a white ram."
"Once born there, there were princes who, either driving chariots or having saddled horses, would mount upon me.
'Furthermore, Great King!'"
Having cast off my body in that place, I was again born in the country of Devīra, where I took the body of a sheep.
Having cast off my body there, I received the body of an ox; having cast off that ox body, I went out into the mountain forests and received the body of a monkey.
"Furthermore, Great King!
Having cast off that monkey body there, I was reborn in that same kingdom of Vajra, where I again received a body that was neither male nor female."
When his karma there was exhausted, he cast off his body and was immediately reborn in the Nandana Grove of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where he served as an attendant to Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
"Furthermore, Great King!

"After I cast off my body in that place, because I had previously maintained the six monthly fast-day precepts until they were pure, I have today been reborn into the family of a great king, possessing vast wealth and lacking nothing."

Moreover, Great King, why do you not now observe for yourself these causes and conditions? From what source have you obtained such merit? Is it not because of the wholesome karma created in the past that you now receive this retribution in such a manner?

“At that time, while King Aṅgada was thus engaged in conversation with his daughter Manoharā, a certain celestial seer named Punarvasu (translated in the Sui language as ‘Non-Crying’) descended from the heavens to observe Jambudvīpa. He came directly above the palace of King Aṅgada, gradually descending through the air.”
At that time, the princess, seeing the celestial seer thus descending from above, rose from her seat, prepared a higher throne, and invited the celestial seer to sit upon it.

At that time, having sat down peacefully, the youth joyfully prostrated at the feet of the celestial sage, joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation, and addressed the celestial sage, saying:
"Venerable Celestial Sage!
"Is there indeed in this world the ripening of the fruits of good and evil karma?
Are there yakṣas and devas?
Are there parents?"
"Are there this world and the next, and are there śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas?
I pray only that you, O celestial sage, will explain this to me; for my father, the king, does not believe in these matters."
At that time, Mahādeva Upatiṣya immediately questioned King Aṅgada in return, saying:
"Great King, what do you think?"
"Do you now truly believe this matter in your heart or not?
The king immediately replied,
"This matter is indeed so."
The celestial seer spoke again:
"Great King!

You should know that the retributions of all good and evil deeds certainly exist; there are yakṣas and various devas, there are fathers and mothers, there are this world and the worlds beyond, and there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas. Great King, you must have faith that I have descended here from the heavens."
At that time, King Aṅgada said to the celestial seer:
"Venerable celestial seer!
If there is a future world, may you give me five hundred gold coins today; in a future life, I shall repay you with a full thousand."
Then, the celestial seer Nārada addressed the king with these verses:
"I now give five hundred coins to the King; you must know that the King’s person is bound by prohibitions.
If there were no virtuous deeds within the King’s heart, for what reason would he repay one thousand in the future?"
In this world there are people who act with deceit; where could one find such persons in the next world?
A wise person does not grant debts to them; for such people, it is difficult to recover what is owed.
Falling into hell where fierce fires blaze, or being devoured on all sides by various birds—how can you repay me in future lives?
Sharp knives slice through your body until it is no longer whole; as each joint is severed, pus and blood flow forth.
Suffering and distress have no respite for even a moment; how can you return my one thousand coins?
When you raise your hand to seize and strip away my sinews, hacking and mincing my body as if cutting sugarcane, with not a single joint remaining intact—how can you return my double the amount?
With a body like that of a fierce, black, greasy dog, he wanders everywhere, mangled and torn apart as he is devoured;
having no flesh or body remaining in hell, how can you demand double the payment in the future?
In that place there is a great iron trident;
Falling into hell again and again, one is impaled upon it with hands pointing downward. How can you give me a thousand coins?
In the hells there are many forests of sword-trees; on each sword-head are sixteen blades.
They pierce one through from above without a moment's rest—who can give me double the money?
In the Hell of the Ash River, the hot, boiling currents flow with the swiftness of the wind or a flying arrow;
entering therein, one undergoes agonizing suffering—how can you give me double the money?
In the hell where one swallows glowing iron balls, or again, where molten red copper is poured down—
amidst such agonizing torments as these, how can you give me double the money?
In hell there are hands like torrential rain, each emitting fierce, blazing flames;
they sever my limbs and joints without a moment’s pause—how can you ask me for double the money?
That place is terrifying, shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, where the light of the sun and moon does not reach;
how can those who dwell there, ignorant and deluded, pay me double the price?
Great King, abandon these unrighteous practices; I urge Your Majesty to perform deeds in accordance with the Dharma.
If the King should cultivate such habits, he will not fall into hell hereafter.
From all directions— east, west, south, and north— may śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who come seeking alms be fully satisfied by the King with food and drink, clothing, medicine, bedding, and dwellings.
Those who practice the holy life with diligence— their words are heeded by recluses and brahmins—
and they are able to rescue the king from his misfortunes, just as a parasol shields one from a heavy rain.
When the King performs such wholesome deeds, he is followed by many friends who accord with him;
they reach the joyful realm of the auspicious path, attaining the supreme power among all supernatural powers.
Just as an ox crossing water goes straight across the current, those who grasp its tail can likewise cross to safety.
All the world is likewise: following what is upright, one attains uprightness; following what is crooked, one attains crookedness.
Among all those who practice the Dharma among men, even ordinary people who train in conduct will all achieve excellence.
At that time, having heard these words, King Aṅga again addressed the celestial seer Nārada in verse:
“Great Brahmā, celestial seer, have compassion for me, Just as parents love their cherished child.
I pray only that you appear before me frequently, So that, upon seeing this wise man, I may behold what is virtuous.”

I only pray that the Venerable One will deliver me; I am submerged in the profoundly deep ocean of afflictions, and I now have no ground upon which to stand. May the Venerable One alone be my place of refuge.
I pray that the Great Brahmā Seer protect me; now I cover my face as if treading upon a pit.
The sufferings in hell are immeasurable and manifold; I shall now follow each word of the Honored One.
At that time, the great seer Nārada, the deva, again addressed King Aṅga in verse,
saying: “If you, O King, do not cease committing evil now, If you harbor hatred and envy toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas,
And if your inverted views of nihilism are not removed, Then I and you shall never see one another.”
If the King can practice the conduct of the True Dharma, serve śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas,
and diligently maintain the precepts, practice giving, and cultivate meditation, then I shall always be able to see you.
At that time, the great celestial seer Nārada preached the Dharma for King Aṅga, instructing him in right view.
Once his mind had been turned, the king was filled with joy; he prostrated himself before the celestial seer, joined his palms, and circumambulated him three times to the right.
Then, Nārada rose from his seat, took leave of King Aṅga, and returned to his original place.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!..."
Now you should know that the celestial seer Nārada at that time was none other than myself, Śākyamuni, seen here today;
and the king Aṅgada at that time was none other than the body of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa seen this very day.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!

In the past, I saw that Uruvilvā Kāśyapa was possessed by intense false views and had fallen into a perverted path; therefore, I aroused a mind of diligent effort to teach and transform him, leading him into the True Path."

It is the same today; seeing that he has fallen into error and entered a heterodox path, I have exerted the power of great diligence to manifest five hundred kinds of supernatural transformations for his sake, teaching and transforming him so that he may abide in unsurpassed bodhi, reach the state of fearlessness until the end of birth and death, and arrive at the shore of nirvāṇa.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume 43 and Volume 44.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
46. Chapter on the Gift of the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had stayed for a short while at Mount Elephant Head, he gradually intended to head toward Rājagṛha, traveling along as he went.
At that time, not long after leaving the village of Uruvilvā, he arrived at Rājagṛha; along the way, there was a grove belonging to an ancient seer named Dharmamegha.

Within that forest of Dharma, there was an old hermitage of a rishi where five hundred practitioners of asceticism constantly resided. They had all attained the five supernormal powers and were all advanced in years; having long cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*), their hair was white and thin, their teeth were missing, and their backs were hunched. Their bodies and skin were covered with many dark moles, their throats hung down like the dewlaps of oxen, and their countenances were parched and withered. Their frames were decayed and broken, requiring them to lean on staffs to walk; they gasped for breath and coughed, falling over as soon as they wished to move. When attempting to step forward, they could not take even a single stride; emaciated and withered, their sinews were shriveled and they possessed little more than skin and bone. All were a hundred years of age, utterly frail and incapable.
Because they had planted various roots of goodness in the past, they encountered a Buddha during this present single lifetime and immediately attained the stage of faith and practice;
yet, because they had not heard the Dharma, they did not enter nirvana, but remained within their caves, each sitting in meditation.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to transform those ascetic seers out of compassion for them, went to their dwelling place. Standing outside the entrance of their cave, he spoke this verse and addressed the seers, saying:

"Though a person may speak a hundred phrases of meaning, If their names, flavors, and characters do not accord with the text, It is better to speak a single phrase that excels a hundred thousand, Causing those who hear it to attain tranquil concentration."
If a person speaks a hundred verses that lack meaning and have discordant phrasing,
yet one speaks even a single verse as most supreme and honored, upon hearing it, one naturally attains tranquil concentration.
If a person is skillful in the art of combat and alone can subdue a hundred thousand men,
yet now can subdue their own self, this is called the true battle of the world.
If one fights a thousand battles in a single month, and in every battle wins a hundredfold over others,
yet can place faith in the Buddha, the World-Honored One, that victory shall surpass those sixteen times over.
If one fights a thousand times within a single month, and in every fight wins a hundredfold over others,
yet can take refuge with faith in the Dharma that is upright and true, one will surpass those [fighters] by sixteen parts.
If one fights a thousand battles in a single month, and wins a hundred times over others in each battle,
yet can place faith in the entire Saṅgha, one will surpass that person by sixteen parts.
If one fights a thousand times within a single month, and in each fight is defeated by an opponent a hundredfold,
yet can contemplate the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), one will surpass that opponent by sixteen parts.
Just as a small child learns month by month, eating only as much as fits on the tip of a blade of grass,
if a person places their faith in the Buddha, the Tathāgata, they shall surpass that [child] by sixteenfold.
If there are those who can have faith in the Dharma and the Sangha Jewel, as well as contemplate the suchness of the nature of phenomena—
those who take refuge in this way possess immeasurable faith, which surpasses that [previous faith] by sixteen times.
If one were to perform worldly fire sacrifices for a full hundred years,
yet at some point with a single-minded heart take refuge in the Triple Gem, that merit would be hundreds of thousands of millions of times superior.
Thus, even a hundred such instances could not be exhausted; the verbal karma cannot be fully described.
By means of that sincere and steadfast mind, one is able to obtain such supreme karmic rewards.
If a person were to spend a full hundred years in the forest making offerings to the fire god,
yet upon seeing one who is well-disciplined arrive, were able to renounce [their own practice] for a moment to provide him with offerings,
this would surpass that lifelong fire sacrifice, which, though complete in many ways, lasts only for a single lifetime.
If a person lives for a full hundred years, their precepts broken and their mind devoid of tranquility,
it would be better to live for but a single day while firmly maintaining patience and diligence.
If a person lives for a full hundred years with a mind constantly distracted by folly,
it is better to live for a single day possessing wisdom and meditative concentration than that long life.
If a person lives for a full hundred years, blind, deaf, and muddled, without hearing or seeing,
it would be better to live for a single day having seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma.
If a person lives for a full hundred years, dull-witted, muddled, and lacking discernment,
it would be better to live for a single day while clearly observing the course of birth and death.
If a person lives for a full hundred years, yet does not contemplate the verse on the impermanence of the world,
one who can realize that the body is not real is better off than that long life, even if they live but a single day.
If a person lives for a full hundred years, yet does not perceive the place of the world’s nectar,
one who is able to recognize that nectar is better off than that long life, even if they live but a single day.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these sublime verses, all those practitioners of asceticism, having heard these verses, each and every one of them realized the six supernormal powers.
At that time, those practitioners of asceticism emerged from their cave; having emerged, they prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Having each paid homage, they soared into the air from that place, relinquished their life-force, and entered parinirvāṇa, emitting water and fire from their bodies to cremate themselves.
Once the cremation was completed, those śarīras fell from the air, each descending upon the ground.
At that time, the World-Honored One collected the śarīras of those five hundred arhats, gathered them into a single mound, and immediately erected a stūpa.
At that time, there were bhikṣus therein who assisted the World-Honored One by providing mud and stone to build and repair the stūpa.
With his divine hands, whose fingers were joined by webs, the World-Honored One personally laid the courses; when the stūpa was completed, it was upright and beautiful.
The World-Honored One performed various rites at that Śāriputra stūpa.

Having finished these, he proceeded toward the kingdom of Magadha together with the bhikṣus; his retinue of disciples numbered a full thousand, all of whom were former followers of the jaṭila brahmins who had gone forth under him. In this manner, they gradually made their way to the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and resided within its Yaṣṭivana (Staff Forest). At that time, there was a separate stūpa in that forest named Suvihita (Well-Established).
And there is a verse that says:
"At that time, surrounded by the great assembly, the World-Honored One gradually arrived at the city of Rājagṛha.
Staying within the exquisite Daṇḍaka Grove, the Tathāgata intended to dwell there."
At that time, there was a minor king in the kingdom of Magadha named Bimbisāra, who had heard it said of others:
"The śramaṇa Gautama!..."

A scion of the Ikṣvāku lineage, having renounced his kin from the Śākya clan to leave the household life, has today come to Magadha to wander and teach; he is accompanied by a community of bhikṣus numbering a full thousand, all of whom were formerly elder brahmins with spiral-topknots who have likewise left the household life.
We have now arrived at the vicinity of Rājagṛha and are staying together at the Well-Situated Stūpa in the Veṇuvana grove.

That śramaṇa has been able to achieve great renown throughout the world; that Blessed One, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One, currently resides there teaching those with whom he has a karmic connection.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One, by means of your own supernormal powers, you are able to realize and know all within this world—including its devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas."

Having known this, he was able to declare: "Birth and death have been severed; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence in future lives."

And that Blessed One teaches the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its meaning is subtle and profound, perfectly complete, and utterly pure—thus he teaches the Dharma.
"Those who are Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas such as these—if anyone should wish to go and see them, that person is most excellent!
I too shall now go to where that Great Śramaṇa is, for the sake of seeing the World-Honored One."

At that time, Bimbisāra of Magadha immediately ordered a fine, well-adorned carriage to be prepared and sat upon it. Surrounded by the brahmins, elders, and householders of the kingdom, numbering a full twelve nayutas of people, he led the procession out from Rājagṛha and proceeded to where the Buddha was, desiring to see the Tathāgata.

At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a courtesan named Bhadrā. She was lovely and upright, a sight everyone delighted to behold; she was peerless in the world, and she possessed a profound mastery of singing, dancing, acting, and music.
She was fully endowed with all manner of performing arts and the sixty-four skills.

At that time, the courtesan heard it said among people: "There is a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, who has gone forth from the royal lineage," and so on, until she thought to herself: "I should now go to that śramaṇa."
At that time, after she had thus manifested herself and was about to go out the door, she thought again:
"I should now see the World-Honored One in the presence of the Great King Bimbisāra."
He further thought to himself:

"Moreover, since the great King Bimbisāra will travel to the presence of the śramaṇa with a great force of men, and there will be a great clamor from the vast multitude, I fear they will obstruct me and prevent me from proceeding. I should now go quickly by way of the collapsed wall and empty space where no people travel, so that I may first see the World-Honored One."
At that time, having formed this thought, she hired many people and addressed them, saying:
"Whoever can extract the most bricks from this wall and city, to him I shall give such a sum of money."
At that moment, those hired laborers broke down the wall in a single instant, and they obtained a path cleared of all tiles, stones, and thorns, made perfectly level.

At that time, the courtesan Ambapālī immediately had a magnificent carriage prepared; she mounted it and departed from her own home, traveling along a straight, level, and well-maintained road, intending to go to the Well-Established Stūpa in the Bamboo Grove to see the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and pay him homage with reverence.
At that time, the World-Honored One knew the thoughts in the mind of the courtesan Pāṭalī. Having known them, he immediately thought to himself:
"If this courtesan had come before me first, then King Bimbisāra, arriving later, would see this courtesan standing before me and would consequently give rise to suspicion and obstruction."
Having formed this thought, he immediately performed a supernatural feat (ṛddhi), causing that courtesan to no longer be able to proceed ahead of the king.
King Bimbisāra, wishing to arrive first, found his chariot suddenly come to a halt and unable to move forward.
At that time, the Great King Bimbisāra felt terror arise in his heart; despondent and with his hair standing on end, he thought to himself:
"What spirit or deity, or what calamity, is now creating an obstacle for me to cause this to happen?"
At that time, a certain deva dwelling there, knowing the mind of King Bimbisāra, remained hidden in mid-air and unmanifested, and addressed the king, saying:
"Great King!
"Do not give rise to fear now.
Great King!
You have no calamity, nor is there any portentous anomaly."
"Nevertheless, Great King!
In the city of Campā at such-and-such a place, you have imprisoned a certain person named so-and-so; release him immediately, and the chariot shall proceed."
At that time, having heard these words from the celestial deity, King Bimbisāra immediately dispatched a messenger to order the man’s release.

Once he had been released, wherever the road was passable for chariots, the king proceeded by carriage; where it was not passable, he entered the mountain forest on foot and went to where the Buddha was staying.
Having arrived at the place where the Buddha was, they prostrated themselves at his feet and sat down to one side.
At that time, all the people, householders, and elders of Magadha there likewise prostrated themselves and stood to one side.
Some engaged in polite conversation with the Buddha, and having finished their mutual consolations, each returned to sit to one side.
Others, moreover, stood before the World-Honored One and announced their own names and clans; having thus introduced themselves, they withdrew to sit to one side.
Furthermore, some people joined their palms toward the Buddha and sat to one side;
others remained silent before the Buddha and sat to one side.
At that time, all the people of the kingdom—the elders and householders—having sat to one side, thought to themselves:
"Today there is a great śramaṇa here, as well as Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, our national preceptor."
I do not yet know whether this śramaṇa Gautama is currently learning the holy life from Kāśyapa,
or whether Kāśyapa and the others are learning and practicing the holy life from the śramaṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of all the people, elders, and householders of Magadha, addressed the Elder Uruvilvā Kāśyapa with these verses:
“Kāśyapa, what circumstances have you perceived, That you previously practiced austerities by the river?
Tell me and the assembly your intention: Why have you abandoned those sacrificial rites?”
At that time, the Elder Brahmin Uruvilvā Kāśyapa immediately replied to the Buddha in verse:
“Form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental objects—these are the five desires sought by people in the world.
Such defiled attachments fill the heavens; it was for the sake of craving these things that I performed sacrifices.”
At that time, all the people, elders, householders, and brahmins of Magadha there thought to themselves:
"This great śramaṇa!..."
Each recited a verse, and that Uruvilvā Kāśyapa likewise recited a verse; yet these two men ultimately did not know which was the teacher and which was the disciple.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the people had formed such thoughts, again addressed Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa with a verse, saying:
"Regarding the dharmas of form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and so forth—Kāśyapa, among these, what do you delight in?"
"Whether in the heavens or among humans, that which your mind covets—answer my question.
At that time, the elder brahmin Uruvilvā Kāśyapa again replied with these verses:
"I behold the tranquil, unobstructed emptiness; it is signless, without hindrance, and cannot be clung to."
“In this immutable place there is no deception; it is here that the sacrifice delights my heart.
At that time, all the people, elders, and householders of Magadha in that region thought to themselves:
“This great śramaṇa!”
He himself recited two verses, and that Uruvilvā Kāśyapa also recited two verses; even now, we do not yet know which is the teacher and which is the disciple.

"In this way, all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions possess this same principle: if they do not cause the entire great assembly to give rise to a heart of joy and a sense of wonder, they do not preach the Dharma."
At that time, wishing to inspire a sense of joy and wonder in the great assembly, the World-Honored One addressed Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, saying: "Kāśyapa!
If you know the proper time now, you may manifest the dharmas of a superior person and display supernatural powers for all the people, elders, householders, and brahmins of that Magadha kingdom.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has instructed, I dare not disobey.”

At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa rose from his seat and immediately manifested supernatural powers, soaring through the air with ease. In mid-air, he sometimes walked back and forth, sometimes stood, sat, or lay down; smoke and flames issued from his body, and at other times he made himself invisible.

Having thus manifested various supernatural powers and displayed them everywhere, he descended from the air and stood upon the ground. Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, you are truly my teacher; I am now truly an unsurpassed śrāvaka disciple of the World-Honored One.”
And he spoke in verse:
"Having mastered the subtle and wondrous supernormal powers, I prostrate at the supreme feet of the World-Honored One.
My duties as a disciple are now complete; The World-Honored One is truly my teacher."
At that time, the many brahmins, elders, householders, and the common people of the kingdom of Magadha conceived this thought:
"Is this Uruvilvā Kāśyapa now a disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama, practicing the holy life under the śramaṇa?"
Having understood this, they turned toward the World-Honored One, giving rise to faith and a sense of wonder.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the great assembly had conceived thoughts of joy and wonder, immediately preached the Dharma to them in successive stages: namely, he taught the practice of generosity and the observance of precepts; he spoke of the causes and conditions for rebirth in heaven and the retribution of karma; he spoke of the matter of wearying detachment from the five desires; he spoke of the cause for the exhaustion of outflows and the total extinction of afflictions; and he praised renunciation as the means to protect and assist liberation.

The World-Honored One knew that the brahmins, elders, householders, and the great assembly of the kingdom of Magadha had all given rise to hearts of joy, hearts of gentleness, and hearts free from attachment.

At that time, the World-Honored One knew that the great assembly was ready to attain the Way; furthermore, all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know that among sentient beings there are some who attain the Dharma of the Way through praise. He then spoke appropriately for the great assembly concerning what are known as suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

When the Blessed One proclaimed this Dharma-characteristic to that great assembly, while they were seated there with Bimbisāra at their head, eleven nayutas of people besides him attained realization all at once.
(Furthermore, another teacher said:

"There were twelve nayutas of people who, having distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, exhausted the realm of afflictions, and attained purity of mind, gave rise to the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, realizing them as they truly are: that whatever phenomena may arise are all of the nature of cessation.")
Just as a clean cloth, free from dirt and grease and devoid of black stains, easily takes on whatever color it is dyed with;

even so, those Brahmins, householders, and common people of Magadha, sitting upon those seats, became free from dust and defilement, and realized that all phenomena, up to and including the entire mass of suffering, possess the nature of cessation. Thus they knew through direct realization.
“Furthermore, among them, there were another ten billion lay devotees (*upāsaka*) who received the *upāsaka* precepts.

At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha had seen the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), known the nature of phenomena, and entered the nature of phenomena. Within the nature of phenomena, he had transcended all doubts, penetrating through to unimpeded realization. Regarding all phenomena, his mind was no longer obstructed; he had attained fearlessness. Within the Dharma of the World-Honored One, he no longer followed others nor questioned others; regarding all phenomena, he attained such sovereign and unimpeded knowledge.
Then King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Tathāgata, World-Honored One!
In the past, when I was a youth living at home, I made five kinds of vows; today, I have fully accomplished them all.”
What are these five?
First, World-Honored One, when I was in my youth, I attained the throne early.
"This was my first vow, which has now been fulfilled.
My second vow was that after I had attained the throne, a Buddha would appear in the world while I was governing my realm."
This was my second heart’s vow, which has now been fulfilled.
My third vow was that once a Buddha had appeared in the world, I would make offerings to that Blessed One and cause him to rejoice.
"This is my third wish, and it has now been fulfilled.
My fourth wish was that the World-Honored One, with a heart of joy, would preach the Dharma for me."
This is my fourth heart-vow, which is now fulfilled.
My fifth vow is that the World-Honored One shall preach the Dharma for me, and that I may fully realize and know it all.
"This is my fifth heart-vow, which is now fulfilled.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
When I was formerly a youth living at home, I gave rise to this thought: 'Whatever I undertake, may I accomplish it all.'"
"O Unsurpassed World-Honored One, I have now attained my goal!
O Well-Gone One, I have now triumphed!

It is as if a person with a hunched body has been able to stretch it out; as if one who was fleeing and hiding has been able to emerge; as if a lost person has found the way; as if one in a dark place has obtained light; or as if a blind person has clearly seen all forms."
O Unsurpassed World-Honored One!
I am likewise so now.
Yet, the World-Honored One, through various skillful means, has preached the Dharma for me.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
From this day forth, I take refuge in the World-Honored One, take refuge in the Dharma Jewel, and take refuge in the Noble Sangha.
From this day forth, at all times, I shall practice the conduct of an upāsaka; may the World-Honored One know that I hold myself thus."
O Tathāgata, World-Honored One!

From this day forth, for as long as this life lasts, I vow not to kill any living being, but to protect the lives of all beings as if they were my own, serving as a place of refuge for all sentient beings.
"Having thus observed the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action,
I pray that the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus will accept my offering of a meal tomorrow.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted the invitation for King Bimbisāra of Magadha.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, knowing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation by remaining silent, addressed the Buddha,
saying: "Excellent,
World-Honored One!"
"Having mounted this chariot, I shall enter the city of Rājagṛha and personally pull this chariot myself.
After he had spoken these words, the Buddha said to the king:
"Excellent, Great King!"
I only pray, Great King,
that you may always enjoy peace and happiness.
I have no need for the chariot.
Then, King Bimbisāra rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the World-Honored One three times, and took his leave of the Buddha to depart.
Not long after King Bimbisāra had departed, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is marvelous, World-Honored One!
How is it that today the King of Magadha has offered a horse-drawn chariot to the World-Honored One for him to ride, yet then requested to walk himself?”
"What does this matter mean?
Having spoken these words, he remained silent.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"O bhikṣus! Listen with a sincere and attentive mind.
It is not only today that King Bimbisāra of Magadha has offered me his horse-drawn carriage for me to ride and to pull for me."
"It was likewise in the past; he has already bestowed such things upon me.
Then the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha again, saying, "We pray only that the World-Honored One [would explain this]!"
"Please explain to us what that matter was.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I recall that in the past, within the kingdom of Kāśī, there was a king named Sukhābhiprāya who ruled as a Dharma-king in accordance with the Dharma."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wishing to see that king, addressed the Deva Mātali (translated into Chinese as Wuzhuchu, "The Unattached One"), the Charioteer, saying:
"O Mātali, go to the kingdom of Kāśī and bring King Sumati to see me. Speak to him for me, saying these words:
'O virtuous Sumati!'"
"The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wish to see you; O Benevolent One, do not decline, for you must certainly come.
At that time, the celestial charioteer Mātali addressed Śakra, saying:
"As Your Majesty commands, I dare not disobey."

Having received these instructions, he prepared an excellent carriage, yoked with a team of a thousand horses, and once the adornments were complete, he immediately descended by flight to the land of Jambudvīpa and went before King Sumati of the kingdom of Kāśi.
Having arrived there, he remained suspended in the air and addressed King Subhavyūha in verse:
"O Benevolent One, you may now come and mount the chariot; This celestial vehicle is adorned beyond compare.
The gods of the heavens have been mindful of you— He is the king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven."
At that time, having heard this, King Sumati immediately mounted his chariot from the east;
this vehicle was most excellent and beyond compare, as he proceeded toward the Exalted and Victorious Heaven.
The devas saw the king approaching from afar; each rose to welcome him and addressed him:
"Welcome, O Dharma-king among men! Sit here together with Śakra, Lord of the Devas."
At that time, Śakra, the Great Heavenly King, seeing the king approaching from afar, rose immediately to meet him and addressed the king, saying:
"Now, O Sovereign Lord, you may dwell here; enjoy the majestic power of the gods."
"When you wish to stop, it shall remain for as long as you desire; it will serve your purposes at will and never fail you.
At that time, having resided for a long period in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven of the Thirty-three Gods, the king’s mind was not at ease, and he thought to himself:
"I now fear that my lifespan is diminishing."
Having formed this thought, he immediately addressed Śakra with these verses:
"In the past, when I first came, I delighted in the heavens; The music here was of subtle and wondrous sound.
Now I fear that my life will come to an end, And for this reason, I no longer find joy in the fruits of heaven."
At that time, Śakra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, immediately replied to King Sumati with these verses:
“O King, your lifespan has not yet diminished; The day of your death is still far off.
It is only because your present wholesome karma is slight That you do not find joy in the heavens.”
O Benevolent One, in the past you relied on your own power; now those karmic deeds are exhausted without remainder.
Since your mind was once deluded by sinful karma, it is for that reason that your heart finds no joy in the heavens.
Now, if you wish to receive celestial power, and experience celestial bliss as it was in former times—
as if within a sublime chariot, or like being amidst a bewildering and wondrous grove—
if you now form such a thought, you shall immediately attain mental joy and dwell in this heaven.
At that time, having heard this verse, King Sumati immediately addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying:
“Great and Virtuous Heavenly King!

From this place I shall go to the human realm, where I shall perform many meritorious deeds, practice giving, practice asceticism, perform virtuous acts, speak with much truthfulness, and observe the precepts of fasting.”
"Once I have performed these various wholesome deeds, I shall return once more to this celestial realm.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to that king:
"So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said."

"From this place you have departed today and shall go among humans; there you must perform many kinds of meritorious deeds and cultivate much wholesome karma, including practicing generosity and observing the precepts of fasting. Once you have completed such wholesome deeds, you shall return to the heavens."

“At that time, King Sumati dwelt in that heavenly realm for a long period. Subsequently, he returned to Jambudvīpa and arrived at his royal palace; however, all the court ladies, queens, princes, ministers, officials, and kinsmen within the palace had died, and not a single one remained.”
But when the king did not see those former attendants, his heart was unhappy; filled with sorrow and dejection, he spoke these verses:
"These were their old garments, Necklaces, bracelets, and earrings— Things they cherished throughout their lives and never gave to others.
Now that they are dead, the objects remain; where is their body?"
Such various articles of adornment—beds, mats, coverlets, pillows, and exquisite rugs;
gardens, groves, ponds, and fragrant mountains—are all suddenly abandoned here.
Since all the people are no longer seen, and all the palaces have become empty space,
with wife, children, and kinsmen entirely gone— how could my mind find joy in this?
Though one may be wise, noble, and exceedingly wealthy, born into a great family of such majestic virtue,
if the malevolent spirits who govern life do not protect them, they will be ground down and utterly dispersed.
Whether rich or noble, poor or lowly; whether wise or intelligent, or foolish and ignorant;
whether young, middle-aged, or old—when one reaches this end of time, the spirit of the Lord of Life cannot protect them; all are seized and made to perish.
Whether they be kṣatriyas or brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas or śūdras, noble or lowly,
or even those of the caṇḍāla or mātaṅga classes— when the time has come, one does not discriminate among them but leaves [the teaching] open to all.
All things are crushed and broken without exception,
like the swift and torrential currents of mountains and rivers uprooting the trees growing on perilous banks; so too it is with old age, sickness, and death,
which devour the life-faculties of all living beings.
The four guardian lords dwelling upon the four peaks, and the palaces of the thirty-three gods in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven—
though one might travel through them with playful joy for seven days and seven nights, the time would not suffice.
I dwell in that abode of Śakra, constantly facing the Heavenly King before me;
as for the other devas seen there, I always observe them in such a manner.
Now I shall perform only meritorious deeds: practicing generosity and the precepts, as well as diligence, patience, wisdom, and meditation;
I vow never again to seek the reward of royal sovereignty.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
If you wish to know who that King Sumati was at that time, it was none other than myself."
That Mātali, the Deva-charioteer, was none other than this King Magadhin.
At that time, he offered me a chariot and drew it for me;
now it is likewise, for he offers me a chariot and likewise desires to drive it himself. Such was his original vow.

At that time, King Bimbisāra returned to his own palace. Having arrived, during that night he prepared various kinds of sweet and delicious food and drink, all of which were abundant and sufficient—namely, foods to be chewed, sucked, swallowed, and licked—and when all such things had been completed:

After that night had passed, he swept and sprinkled the halls and pavilions, arranged the various seats, and immediately dispatched a messenger to the Buddha’s presence to announce that the time had come, saying:
"Excellent! [The time has arrived]."
“World-Honored One!
The time has arrived; the food we have prepared is now ready.

At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One donned his robes and took up his bowl, surrounded on all sides by a community of bhikṣus numbering a full thousand—all of whom were former followers of the jaṭila brahmins who had gone forth under him. With them as his attendants, he proceeded toward Rājagṛha.

At that time, Śakra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, immediately transformed himself by magical power into the form of a māṇava; he was upright and pleasing to behold, such that all people delighted in seeing him.

Upon his head he wore a crown of spiral locks, and his body was clad in yellow robes. In his left hand he held a golden water-pitcher, and in his right hand he grasped a staff adorned with various jewels. He walked in front of the Buddha and the great assembly of bhikṣus; as he walked, his feet remained four finger-widths above the ground, never touching the dust.
At that time, Śakra, in the body of a māṇava, spoke these verses: “The Tathāgata,
who has tamed himself and can tame others, Together with these one thousand former jaṭila ascetics,
With such a golden and wondrous body— The Unsurpassed World-Honored One now enters the city.”
Having attained tranquility himself, he can bring others to tranquility;
together with these one thousand former jaṭila ascetics, the World-Honored One of unsurpassed excellence, with this golden and wondrous body, now enters the city.
Having himself attained liberation, he is now able to deliver others;
together with these one thousand former jaṭila ascetics, the World-Honored One of unsurpassed excellence, with such a wondrous golden body, now enters the city.
Having attained liberation for himself, he is now able to liberate others;
together with these one thousand former jaṭila ascetics, the World-Honored One of unsurpassed excellence, with such a wondrous golden body, now enters the city.
He who can expound ten dharma-gates, endowed with the ten powers and the ten forms of invincibility,
surrounded on all sides by a thousand bhikṣus— the Unsurpassed World-Honored One now enters the city.
At that time, all the people within the city, seeing Śakra, the Lord of Devas, spoke these words:
"How rare, how rare!
This māṇava!"
He is exceedingly handsome, peerlessly lovely, and a sight that all people delight to behold.
Who is his attendant? Whom does he serve?
At that time, Śakra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, replied to those people in verse:
“The Buddhas are well able to subdue all things; They are the tranquil, unsurpassed, and most supreme Honored Ones.
Among the world of gods and humans, they are the Worthy Recipients (Arhats); I now serve as their attendant.”
The Great Being is able to subdue all things; there is no one who can surpass the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Among the world of devas and humans, he is the Worthy One (Arhat); I now serve as his attendant.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded with composed grace to the palace of King Bimbisāra. Having entered, he prepared a seat and sat down.

Then, seeing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the great assembly were all seated, King Bimbisāra took various kinds of delicacies and food with his own hands and offered them to the Buddha, the Saṃgha, and the rest of the great assembly. All were fully satisfied and ate to their heart's content; when the various offerings had been entirely consumed, they finished.
When the Buddha and the assembly of monks had finished their meal and had washed their hands and feet,
each took a small seat and sat before the Buddha.
At that time, after King Bimbisāra had taken his seat before the Buddha, he reflected thus:
"Where shall we have the Buddha stay today?
Let it not be too near nor too far from the city,
so that those who have gone forth may dwell in peace and practice the Path according to the Dharma."
