At that time, King Bimbisāra again thought to himself: "This Bamboo Grove is near the city walls;

it is convenient for coming and going, and one does not grow weary traveling to and fro. It is level and easy to traverse, a place beloved by all people. For those seeking spiritual benefit, it is easily attained without difficulty. Furthermore, there are few mosquitoes, gadflies, venomous snakes, vipers, or scorpions. By day it is tranquil, with no people passing to and fro; at night there is little noise. It is suitable as an araṇya (forest hermitage), yet close enough to the city and moats so that movement is unimpeded. It is fit to be a place for virtuous men to practice the Way."
"I should now offer this bamboo grove to the World-Honored One as a place for him to sit.
Having had this thought, King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Great Sage, World-Honored One!"
"This Bamboo Grove is neither too near nor too far from the city of Rājagṛha; it is even suitable for a virtuous person to cultivate the path.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will instruct me as to what dharma I should teach, so that I may offer this bamboo grove to the World-Honored One as a place for him to sit."
At that time, the Buddha addressed King Bimbisāra, saying:
"It is so, Great King!
If you wish to give me the bamboo grove, you should be permitted to give it to the Saṃgha of the Four Quarters."
Then King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying,
“As the World-Honored One has instructed.
Thereupon, King Bimbisāra rose from his seat, took a golden pitcher in his hand, offered water to the World-Honored One, and again addressed the Buddha:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!

This Bamboo Grove Monastery is close to the city and is fit for virtuous people to cultivate the Way; I now offer it as a gift to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the Saṃgha of the Universal Community.”
"After this offering, we pray only that the World-Honored One will accept and enjoy it out of compassion for us.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted it out of pity, and then spoke these words of blessing in verse:
"All trees and various groves and forests, as well as the construction of all bridges and such,
channels, ponds, wells, and springs provided for relief, and boats and ships coming and going to ferry across the multitudes."
Throughout the day and night, their merit and reward increase daily without ceasing;
so it is for those who practice the Dharma and uphold the precepts—through firm faith and reverence, they are reborn in heaven.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished offering his benediction to King Bimbisāra, he rose from his seat and returned to his own quarters.
Having arrived at his quarters, on account of these events, he assembled the great multitude. Once they were assembled, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "You bhikṣus!"
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to personally maintain their own groves.
(The Niśāya masters relate this as follows:
"This was on account of the acquisition of the Bamboo Grove.")
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll 44 and Scroll 45,
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
The Chapter on the Gift of the Bamboo Grove, Part Two.

At that time, within the great city of Rājagṛha, there was an elder named Kalandaka. He was immensely wealthy in the kingdom, possessing vast resources and abundant servants; his household was in every respect no different from the palace of Vaiśravaṇa in the north.
That site of the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove belonged to that elder himself; it was not far from the city and was fit to be a dwelling for virtuous people.
In that garden, there were various seekers of the Way who came and went and resided there; the name of that practitioner was Ajivika (translated in the Sui language as "Wrong Livelihood").
(The teacher Kāśyapīya spoke thus:
"At that time, the Four Great Kings of the Four Quarters addressed the yakṣas of blue bodies and others, saying:"

"Go quickly, all of you, into the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove and sweep it clean, removing all gravel, pebbles, thorns, filth, and mounds of earth; make it level and smooth, free of pits and hollows, and ensure it is perfectly pure, for today the World-Honored One intends to dwell there for the summer retreat."
At that time, the assembly of blue-colored yakṣas and others, having received such instructions through the majesty of those Four Great Heavenly Kings, immediately replied:
"As the Heavenly Kings have commanded."
He hurried to that grove, swept it clean, and made it entirely level, upright, and pure.

At that time, there was a seeker of the Way among the Ājīvikas who rose at dawn, when the morning star was about to appear. Seeing four blue-colored yakṣas coming to sweep and sprinkle the Bamboo Grove, he went up to them and asked:
“Elders, what are you doing?”
"Who are you? They replied, "O noble one!"
"We blue yakṣas have been dispatched by the Four Great Kings to this place to sweep and sprinkle the Bamboo Grove, even to making it level and smooth."
"The Tathāgata now wishes to observe the rains retreat here for one summer; for this reason, we have come today to prepare this place.
At that time, the ascetic Ajivika, having witnessed these events, rose early at dawn and went quickly to the great householder Kalandaka. Upon arrival, he said to Kalandaka:
"O great householder!"

Now, knowing that the time had come and the night was nearly spent as the morning star appeared, I saw four blue-colored yakṣas sweeping and tidying the Bamboo Grove Monastery. Having seen them, I went to their side and asked them:
"Venerable elders!..."
"Who are you? They replied to me, saying, "We are those blue yakṣas who have been dispatched by the Four Great Kings to this place; they sent us to sweep this Bamboo Grove and said to us:"
“Go to the Bamboo Grove Monastery and repair it until it is level and even; the World-Honored One now wishes to dwell here for the rains retreat.
For this reason, we have come to this place to clear away and prepare this bamboo grove.”
At that time, the ascetic Ājīvika said to the householder:

"Householder, you should now first offer the Bamboo Grove Park to the śramaṇa Gautama for his use; I fear that later King Bimbisāra of Magadha might seize that park and give it to the śramaṇa Gautama."
"At that time, fearing you will not obtain alms, you shall fail to gain this merit and will only suffer in vain.

When the wealthy householder Kalandaka heard these words from the ascetic Ajivika, he immediately set out for the Buddha’s dwelling; halfway along the half-yojana path, he encountered the World-Honored One.

The householder Kalandaka saw from afar that the World-Honored One was approaching—delightful and upright, a sight for all to rejoice in, his body adorned with the various marks of excellence, just as the void is adorned by the many stars.

Having seen this, he immediately conceived a mind of purity and a mind of joy toward the World-Honored One. He approached the Buddha, and upon reaching him, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; then, holding a golden pitcher in his hand, he poured pure water over the Buddha’s hands.
At that time, the householder spoke these words: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
I reside in Rājagṛha; my name is Kalandaka. I have a grove called Veṇuvana, not far from the city, which is suitable for virtuous people to dwell in.
"I now offer this grove to the World-Honored One; may the World-Honored One accept this grove from me out of compassion and pity.
At that time, the Buddha said to the elder:

"If there should be someone who makes an offering to the Buddha—whether it be a grove, or a house and land, or other clothing, or other wealth—and gives these things as a gift to the Buddha alone, then those objects shall become a stūpa among gods and humans, and others shall not be permitted to use them."
The Buddha told the householder:
"If you now offer that bamboo grove as a gift to the *cāturdīśa* [the Sangha of the four quarters], then in the future, the entire great assembly shall be able to make use of it."
"I exhort you to practice such earnest and respectful giving.
When the householder Kalandaka heard these words of the Buddha, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the World-Honored One has instructed, I shall not dare to disobey."
At that time, the elder addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I now offer this Bamboo Grove Garden to all the Saṃghas of the three periods of the future; may those who come use it as they please."
"I pray that you will accept this grove for your own use out of compassion for me.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the Bamboo Grove from the Elder Kalandaka out of a desire to show him compassion; he then spoke a verse of benediction, saying:
"The first line of the verse says: 'In a grove with various trees,' and so forth, summarized thus: one shall immediately attain rebirth in heaven."
This was the occasion of the Blessed One’s very first acceptance of a gift at the Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the Blessed One was staying within the Bamboo Grove of Kalanda in Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were former seers and brahmins who had worn matted locks.

Chapter 47: The因缘 (Causes and Conditions) of Mahākāśyapa, Part One. From the *Buddha-benxingji-jing* (The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds), Chapter Forty-seven, Part One: The Causes and Conditions of Mahākāśyapa. At that time, not far from and yet not distant from the great city of Rājagṛha, there was a village named New Establishment (*Navasthāpana*).
(Another teacher spoke thus:
"The Mahāsāṃghika.
He further stated: [text missing])

"In the great city of Rājagṛha, in the kingdom of Magadha, there was a village; that village was named Mahāśātāra (translated in the Sui language as 'Great Marshland'). In that place there was a brāhmaṇa village, and that village was also named Mahāśātāra."
Now, within that village, there was a great and wealthy Brahmin named Nyagrodhakalpa (translated in the Sui language as "Capable Tree").

That great householder was immensely rich and possessed vast wealth; he had many servants and attendants, such that his residence was no different from the palace of Vaiśravaṇa in the northern quarter.
That elder, a great brāhmaṇa, governed five hundred villages, directing their labor and receiving their obedience.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha possessed one thousand sets of plow-oxen for tilling the land; that brāhmaṇa possessed all but one set, falling short of the full number of one thousand.
Why was this? Fearing that King Bimbisāra would give rise to feelings of envy, they therefore reduced their numbers.
As for all the Brahmin’s domestic animals, their number was beyond reckoning; one could only know their quantity by counting the smoke and fire.

In that place where the gold and silver were stored, there were in total twenty-five pits. When the wife of that wealthy Brahmin went into the garden to play and look about, she sat down beneath a *piṇḍa-bhāra* tree.

At that time, the wife, who had previously been pregnant, gave birth beneath that tree to a young boy who was lovely, handsome, and pleasing to all who beheld him; he was peerless in the world, like a statue of gold.
At the moment that boy was first born, a wondrous celestial robe spontaneously emerged from that tree.
When the robe appeared, his parents saw it and thought to themselves:
"This celestial robe must have arisen because of this boy's merit."
Therefore, because of this auspicious sign, he was named Pippalāyana—which in the Sui language means "born beneath a tree.
From the time of his birth, the boy was given a name based on that tree, and thus he has been traditionally called Pippalāyana.

At that time, the parents assigned four types of nurses to the boy, namely: the nurse for holding him, the nurse for nursing him with milk, the nurse for taking him out to play, and the nurse for looking after and raising him. These four nurses nourished and bathed him, held and amused him, and provided him with milk and food, causing him to grow.

At that time, the parents of the youth Pipphalāyana had this only son; their heart of love and esteem was such that they would not permit him to leave for even a moment, for if they did not see him, their hearts immediately became unhappy.

At that time, due to the boy’s own roots of merit, after he had been nurtured for but a short while, he gradually began to grow; before long, he had attained wisdom, and as he grew somewhat larger, he was able to walk and run.

When his parents reached the point where he was eight years old from conception, they immediately conferred upon him the Brahmin precepts. Once he had received the precepts, they entrusted him with their family estate and various arts and crafts, as well as the rituals for sacrificial offerings, instructing him in them all. These included writing, painting, arithmetic, and seal-engraving; the four Vedas and various prophetic methods; worldly eloquence and discourse; the practice of carrying the staff; the methods of great incantations; the treatises of Chāndogya; various literary compositions; the five elements, the stars and constellations, calculations, and the principles of yin and yang; and the knowledge of time through water clocks.
Within a single day and night, there are such-and-such hours; thus it is inauspicious, and thus it is auspicious.

Furthermore, the youth knows the signs of earthquakes, the thundering roar of peals, and the cries of birds and beasts; he understands all transformations by observing the movements of flying and running creatures.

Furthermore, he was proficient in the arts of physiognomy, knowing the marks of men and women, the marks of the six domestic animals, and the conduct of ritual purification and cleanliness. He knew the methods for receiving water and the methods for receiving the ritual water-jar (*śīlākumbha*). He knew the methods for receiving ashes, and was skilled in chanting and singing. He clearly discerned the auspicious signs of prosperity and decline, and performed rites to avert calamities, exorcise evil influences, and sacrifice to the fire-gods, the great beings, and the various deities; in all these matters, he was fully accomplished.
Having already trained himself, he is further able to teach others; whether receiving things from others or giving things to others, he has mastered all such matters through his training.

Within the world, there is nothing he does not penetrate and no place he does not know. His sagely wisdom is swift and rapid; he is shrewd, intelligent, and brilliant, possessing quick-witted and extensive eloquence, with sharp faculties and great skill.
That youth was by nature upright and honest; he constantly felt weary of the world, understood that desire is impure, and gave rise to a mind of renunciation.

Because he had previously encountered various Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, he had planted roots of goodness under them, cultivated various merits until they were fully accomplished, and understood the characteristics of all food. His mind largely desired to enter the gate of Nirvana; he constantly sought liberation, abandoned all afflictions, and did not accept any conditioned existence in the world, nor did he accept birth, old age, sickness, or death. Through his past cultivation, he had rotted away all bonds of karma; by the power of this wisdom, he reached the stage of maturity as one who is to attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
At that time, when the parents of the youth Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja saw that he had gradually grown up and was capable of experiencing worldly desires, having recognized this, they said to him:
"O youth Bhāradvāja!"
"I wish to betroth a girl for my son to serve as his consort.
After he had spoken these words, the youth Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja said to his parents:
"O father and mother!"
"My heart finds no pleasure in taking a wife or keeping a concubine; my wish and delight lie in practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Then, the parents of the youth Yajña said to their son:
"O our beloved son, you must first procreate and establish a lineage in this world, and only thereafter may you practice the holy life as you please."
Why is this? This matter has been handed down through tradition, saying:
"If a person has no son and has no successor, that person shall ultimately never be reborn in the heavens."
Then the youth replied to his parents, saying:
"O father and mother!
I have no need now for the succession of worldly traditions, nor do I wish to continue the lineage hereafter; I shall practice the holy life."
Thus his parents addressed the youth Pilindavatsa for a second and even a third time, saying:
"Dear son, you must establish yourself in the world and take a wife."
"Why is this? We fear that our family line will be extinguished.

At that time, when the youth Piṣpalayana had been thus distressed by his parents up to three times, he immediately took Jāmbūnada gold and instructed a craftsman to fashion the form of a woman. Having completed it, he brought it to his parents, displayed it before them, and spoke to his parents as follows:
“Father and Mother!
I have no need to enjoy the pleasures of the five desires; I wish to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
If, Father and Mother, you must insist on taking a wife for me to establish a household, you must seek one whose complexion is like that of Jāmbūnada gold and whose form is likewise.”
At that time, having witnessed such events, the parents of the youth Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja were filled with great sorrow and distress; they were despondent and unhappy, and thought to themselves:
"Where can we find a woman whose form is like the color of Jambūnada gold?"
At that time, the great brahmin Kauruṭa sat upon the upper terrace, his heart heavy with displeasure, remaining there in silence.
Now, there was a brahmin who served as the family preceptor for that household; he was one who constantly came and went, visiting the home of that wealthy brahmin.
Then, after that preceptor brahmin had entered his house, he offered blessings to the wealthy brahmin, speaking these words:
"O great donor, master of almsgiving!"
"May you increase all your wealth and auspicious rewards, lacking in nothing; may your wives, concubines, and children also increase and multiply.
He then asked the family members once more, saying, "O my masters!"
"Where is he now?
The family members replied,
"O Great Brahmin!"
"My master is now upon the upper terrace; his heart is deeply despondent, and he dwells there sitting in silence, sorrowful and unhappy.
Then, that preceptor Brahmin went to the side of the wealthy Brahmin and spoke to him thus:
"May the Great Donor [be well]!"
"Is your household wealth increasing? How have you fared since last night?
When you lay down to sleep at night, has your food been digested?
Furthermore, did you enjoy yourself with your beloved during the night, playing together and experiencing pleasure to your heart's content?"
But that host, the wealthy brahmin, remained silent and gave no reply.
He asked again:
"For what reason do you now remain silent and give no reply?"
"I have been with you in this way since we were young, sharing both our sorrows and joys; why do you not speak with me now?
Then, the great Brahmin Kauruṭa related the preceding events in detail to his preceptor, the Brahmin, and having finished speaking, he said to that Brahmin:
"Where could I find such a woman as this, with a complexion like the color of Jāmbūnada gold?"
At that time, the gatekeeper brahmin replied to the great brahmin, saying these words:
"O Great Donor, wealthy brahmin!"
"Do not grieve! Do not suffer!
Since you have acted as my benefactor, providing me with all that I require—clothing, food, and all necessities—I shall seek for you such a daughter of Jambūnada gold."

"Do not let your mind be doubtful; I shall certainly find it. I require provisions for the journey as well as companions; you must seek these out and give them to me, so that together with them I may go forth and search in the four directions."
At that time, having heard these words, the wealthy Brahmin prepared everything exactly as requested and provided it along with his attendants.

Then, once the Brahmin teacher had received the various provisions and was sent on his way, [the wealthy Brahmin] immediately fashioned a four-colored divine parasol, adorned with every kind of ornament, and established it as a deity; before it, he performed various kinds of music, surrounding it from front and back.

There were some parasols whose bases were fashioned from gold, and the faces of their deities were made of silver, or crystal, or lapis lazuli; having had them made, he sent three of the parasols away to other regions, while he himself followed with one.
He addressed those people on the various other paths, saying:
"In whatever villages and districts you go, announce this to all the village women:
'This is a deity; which woman among you is able to provide offerings?'"
"If one makes offerings, whatever wishes that woman desires will be immediately fulfilled.

You all should observe: if among those women you see one who has become golden in color, you should ask her family name, clan, personal name, and place of residence, and you must quickly return to my side.
Having spoken thus, he departed immediately.

Then that preceptor, the great brāhmaṇa, took a parasol-deity for himself, placed it inside a bag along with provisions for his journey, and traveled to other regions—whether to districts, villages, hamlets, cities, royal palaces, or streets. To whatever place he entered, he would entertain that deity with vocal music; wherever he went, there were women who, upon hearing that music, all came forth to gather and observe.
At that time, seeing the women gathered together, the great brahmin took a divine image out from his bag, showed it to the women, and spoke these words:
"O you women!..."
Each person should make offerings to this deity; if there is a woman who can make offerings to this deity, whatever she has in her heart that she seeks or prays for shall immediately be accomplished.

At that time, all those women took various kinds of unguents, powdered incense, flower garlands, and scattered blossoms from their homes, intending to use them to make offerings to that deity; by such means, they gradually proceeded toward the city of Vaiśālī.

At that time, not far from the city of Vaiśālī, there was a large village named Karavika (translated in the Sui language as "Red-Yellow"). At that time, within that village, there lived a very wealthy and eminent Brahmin named Kapila (translated in the Sui language as "Yellow-Red").
That brahmin was wealthy and possessed abundant resources, with many servants and attendants; his household was in every respect no different from the palace of Vaiśravaṇa in the northern quarter.

That brahmin had a daughter named Bhadrākapilā (in the Sui language, "Virtuous Yellow-Hued Woman"). She was lovely, of exquisite and peerless beauty, a sight that all people delighted to behold; there was no one like her in the world. She was neither short nor tall, neither coarse nor slender, neither too pale nor too dark, neither purple nor blue. In the full bloom of her youth, she was fit to be a precious jade woman for the whole world.
At that time, in the city of Vaiśālī, there was a festival called "Kindling the Fire. During this festival, five hundred women gathered together, and the woman Bhadrā also came to join that assembly.

At that time, the great brahmin, the deity who carries the parasol, approached those women; having arrived, he took the deity out from his bag and manifested it before all those women, saying these words:
"O you women!..."

"This is a celestial deity, most supreme and most wondrous; each of you should offer worship and sacrifices to it. If there are women who make offerings to this deity, whatever heart's desires they may have shall all be fulfilled."
At that time, all those women each took various kinds of powdered incense, ointments, garlands, and scattered flowers, and quickly ran toward that deity, saying these words:
"We now make this offering to this divine deity."
Only that daughter Bhadrā alone refused to go near the deity; however, all her female companions forcibly embraced her and led her toward the deity, and she too arrived at that place.
By the power of her majestic radiance, that form of Jāmbūnada gold lost its brilliance and immediately forfeited its natural color.
At that moment, the woman Bhadrā exerted herself and freed herself from her companions, fled to her own home, and spoke thus to her parents:
"O mother! O father!"
"I pray that you do not give me to another person. Why is this?
I have no need for a husband at present; in my heart, I wish to practice the holy life (brahmacarya)."
At that time, her brothers said to Bhadrā: "Sister! We truly do not wish to be separated from you even for a moment;
yet, if we do not marry you off, it would be impossible for us to follow the path of propriety."

People may say that this woman’s brothers must harbor improper and illicit intentions toward her; for this reason, they are unwilling to marry her to another, fearing they might be implicated in such suspicion.
At that time, her brothers spoke again, saying: "Do not worry!
If we were to give you away to another, we would certainly demand a great deal of wealth from him; if that person cannot provide such a large sum, then you will naturally never leave your home."
Then, whenever anyone came to those brothers to seek their sister, they would say this:
"If anyone wishes to take our sister, he must gather fine gold until it is as large as the girl herself; only then shall we give her to him."
At that time, the great Brahmin who served as the gatekeeper for the woman he sought, carrying a walking staff with a figure of Jambu-river gold at its top, saw Bhadrā and asked the other women:
"Whose daughter is this?"
"In whose family was she born?
At that time, those women replied to the visiting brahmin, "In this place there is a most eminent and immensely wealthy great brahmin named Kapila; she is his daughter."
At that time, having heard these circumstances, the visiting brahmin, as the sun was about to set and at the hour of dusk, gradually arrived at the house of the wealthy brahmin Kāpiḷa.
Having arrived at his house, he asked for lodging, and the family members immediately granted permission, lending him a place to stay.
After that night had passed, on the following morning, the visiting brahmin went to the brahmin of Kapilavastu; having reached him, he stood before him and uttered this blessing:
"May this virtuous brahmin’s household always flourish and increase."
Having thus completed these prayers of aspiration, he sat down to one side.
Then Kapila asked that visiting brahmin:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Was it peaceful for you last night?
How have you been since yesterday?
At that time, the visiting brahmin replied with these words:
"Last night, I was exceedingly peaceful and at ease; I was happy and free from affliction.
At that time, the daughter Bhadrā of that household rose from her bed in the early morning, went to her father’s side, prostrated herself at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, the brahmin guest who was seeking a daughter addressed the brahmin Kapilabhu, saying these words:
"Excellent, O worthy one!"
"Whose daughter is she?
Kapila replied to the guest,
"She is my daughter."
That brahmin asked again:
"Venerable sir!
Is there anyone to whom this girl may be given?"
Kapila said, "This girl has not yet been promised to anyone else. Then,
the brahmin guest who had sought the girl addressed the host Kapila, saying:
"O Greatly Wealthy and Benevolent One!

In the kingdom of Magadha there is a village named Mahāsthālā; within that village there is another hamlet, also named Mahāsthālā. In that place there was a great brahmin named Nyagrodhakalpa, who was immensely wealthy and possessed of abundant riches."
He had a son named Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja Māṇava, who understood all meanings by himself and was also able to teach others; he had thoroughly mastered all three Vedas.

Furthermore, he was able to analyze and discern even a single word or half-phrase, a single verse or half-verse, from treatises such as the *Discourse on the Ten Names of a Single Matter*, the *Nirgrantha-yuga* treatise, and the treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) concerning past events.

"You have been granted the prophecy of worldly eloquence, mastery of the sixty types of treatises, and an understanding of all the essential marks of a Great Man; you lack nothing in any of the various arts.
Then, having spoken these words, that visiting brahmin addressed the host, saying:
"I now exhort you, O worthy one!"
"Give this girl to that māṇava to take as his wife.
At that time, the wealthy brāhmaṇa and his sons replied to the visiting brāhmaṇa,
saying, "Great brāhmaṇa!"
"If this girl is to be married, she demands a great deal of wealth; who would be able to take her?
The visiting brahmin asked the host, "How much wealth does she demand?"
They replied, "In accordance with this girl's appearance, we require such-and-such gold.
At that time, hearing them, the visiting brahmin took the image of the Jāmbūnada-golden girl out of his bag and showed it to her parents and brothers, after which he spoke these words:
"This form made of Jāmbūnada gold should be called this woman; you all should take it and give this woman to me.
At that time, her parents and brothers thought to themselves:
"People there must have heard that our daughter is so exceptionally beautiful that they have gathered a great quantity of Jāmbūnada gold to fashion a female figure of such a large size."
At that time, her parents and brothers spoke thus together:

"If we were to take this Jāmbūnada gold of such form now, without considering the amount of wealth in that family, nor being familiar with the customs, etiquette, and social status of that country, our daughter might suffer distress once she arrives at their home; therefore, we must now secretly send someone to privately observe that household."
Having thought this, he addressed the Brahmin who was seeking a daughter, saying:
"May you be well, O Great Brahmin!
I now wish to dispatch a messenger to observe what the family customs and practices of that house are like."
"Then, after deliberating, would it be appropriate to grant them?
At that time, the visiting great brahmin replied: "So be it!"
"You should observe this at your own discretion.
Then, having spoken these words, the visiting great brahmin took his leave of his host and returned to his own country. Upon arriving before the brahmin Nyagrodhakalpa, he addressed him, saying:

"O virtuous and eminent great brahmin, you should rejoice in your heart! I have found a girl whose complexion is like that of Jāmbūnada gold; she is exceedingly delightful, peerless in her beauty, and a joy for all to behold."
Then, that wealthy brahmin asked the brahmin who was seeking a daughter:
"Great brahmin! Where did you see this girl?"
That brahmin then replied to him, saying:

"Not far from that woman's house, departing from the city of Vaiśālī, there is a village named Kapila. Within it lives a wealthy brahmin named Kapila, and that brahmin has a daughter named Bhadrakapilā."
At that time, when the parents of Pippalāyana heard these matters, their hearts were filled with great joy; it pervaded their entire bodies such that they could not contain themselves.

At that time, the great brahmin Nyagrodha Kappa immediately established a series of stations starting from his own village and extending as far as the city of Vaiśālī; at intervals of half a yojana along the path, he stationed a herd of cattle and constructed guest houses, completing these arrangements at every location.
At that time, the great Brahmin Kapila addressed those cowherds, saying:
"Each of you should make such preparations as follows: if there should be anyone coming here from the city of Vaiśālī, you must welcome and provide for all their needs, ensuring they lack nothing."
At that time, the brothers of the maiden Bhadrā Bhalikā departed from their home and traveled toward Magadha, arriving at the city of Rājagṛha.
They encountered a herd of cattle at its first station, where the local people came forward to meet them with bowed bodies, saying:
"Welcome, sirs!"
"From which direction have you come from so far away?

He then led him into a guest house, provided various scented waters for him to bathe, and further anointed his body with various fragrances. He then gave him various priceless garments to wear, and further fashioned various excellent fragrant flowers into garlands to place upon his head.

Thereafter, he separately provided various kinds of sweet and delicious delicacies and foods, commanding him to eat them—namely, to sip, suck, chew, bite, taste, and drink—endowed with all manner of flavors, until he was fully satisfied.
After they had eaten their fill at their pleasure, he finally addressed them, saying:
"This place is our own cowshed; you may stay here for one night. Tomorrow morning, rise early and proceed as you wish."
Then those guests asked the cowherd,
"Whose cowshed is this?
The cowherd replied:

"This is the cowherd’s hut of the Brahmin Nyagrodhakappa; therefore, it has been established for you as a lodging for travelers. I fear that while traveling back and forth, you may become exhausted by fatigue, hunger, and thirst, and fail to obtain what you require."
The guest lay down to rest for one night and rose to depart the following morning.

In this manner, he successively encountered the dwellings of the second herd of oxen, and likewise the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh; they all came out to meet him and receive him, and further addressed him, saying:
"O virtuous ones!..."
“From where have you come so far?
Please stay for one night and sleep in peace; tomorrow you may go as you please.
Then those guests asked the host:
"How many such cowsheds are there?
The son of the cowherd replied,
"From that village of Mahāśāṭha until the city of Vaiśālī, one cowshed is placed at intervals of half a yojana."
At that time, having heard these words together, the brothers of the maiden Bhadrā Kapilā immediately thought to themselves:
"If even in his cowshed he possesses such a quantity, what need is there to mention his other wealth?"
"We must now turn back from here and return to our own homes; we shall give our sisters in marriage to that family to be their wives."
Then, those brothers immediately dispatched a messenger to inform that wealthy brahmin, saying:
"Come and take our sister as your new bride."
Having spoken these words, he returned from there.
At that time, the young Brahmin Piṇḍola heard from the messenger that a girl had been found who met his heart’s desire. Upon hearing this, he immediately thought to himself:
"I should now go in person to see whether she truly possesses such virtuous conduct and wisdom."
At that time, the youth Pipphalivana immediately went to his parents and, kneeling with his right knee on the ground, addressed them, saying: "Ambāṭṭha!"

"In my heart, I truly have no desire for the five sensual pleasures and wish only to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Yet, since my elders have now forcibly sought a spouse for me, I shall now go there myself to beg for alms in due order and observe whether she is truly as the messenger described."
Then his parents said to their son, "If you know the time is right, you should go yourself.
Thereupon the youth took his leave and departed; he went on alms-round by stages until he gradually reached the village of Kappilagāma.
At that time, there was a custom within that kingdom such that if any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa came to beg for food, a woman would take food from her own hand and go out to give it to that person.
At that time, the maiden Bhadrā immediately went out from her house with food and placed it into the hands of the guest, the young brahmin.
When Pipphalāyana saw her, he thought to himself:
"This must certainly be that very girl."
At that time, the girl, having personally served the meal to the māṇava with her own hands, prostrated at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then the māṇava asked the girl: "O virtuous lady!
"Is there a place for me to be married?
At that time, the girl immediately replied,
"O worthy māṇava!"

In the kingdom of Magadha there was a village named Mahākāpa; in that place there was a Brahmin settlement, and in that settlement there was a wealthy Brahmin named Nyagrodhakappa. He had a son named Pipphalāya, to whom my parents had betrothed me as a wife.
At that time, Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja replied to the maiden Bhadrā, saying:
"Good woman!
I have heard that the young man does not desire to engage in the five sensual pleasures within his heart, but wishes to cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya)."
At that time, the girl addressed the young brahmin, saying: "Great Brahmin!
Having now heard such words as these, I am exceedingly joyful; I have no need for the five desires, and I wish to practice the holy life."
"Today he has been granted to him; this is merely the worldly intention of my parents, for which I have no real use.
Now they force me to follow the ways of the world and become his wife."
At that time, having heard these words, the youth Pippalāya asked the girl:
"O virtuous lady!
Have you ever seen the young brahmin Pippalāya before?"
She replied, "O good māṇava!
I have never seen such a thing."
Then, the māṇava spoke again to her, saying: "O virtuous girl!
I am indeed that very same māṇava, Bimbisāra.
I truly have no need for the five sensual pleasures; my inner heart now aspires to practice the holy life (brahmacarya)."
"This matter is the intention of my parents and kinsmen; since they are truly my parents, they have compelled me to take you as my wife.
At that time, having heard these words, the maiden Bhadrā addressed the young brahmin, saying:
"Excellent, O noble Great Brahmin!"

Having received these words, I am filled with great joy. Since you surely do not desire the five worldly sensual pleasures, do not delay for long; you should take me quickly, lest those people of the world who lack the holy life seek me out.

At that time, having received these words, Piṇḍola Bharadvāja immediately turned back from that place and returned toward his home. Upon reaching his parents, he knelt on both knees and addressed them, saying: "Ambāṭṭa!"

"In truth, I have no use for the five worldly desires; I wish to cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya). Since you two venerable ones desire to take a wife for me, simply bring that wife here for me with all speed."

At that time, Bimbisāra’s parents, together with the great Brahmin Kāśyapa, entered into a formal agreement and exchanged the requisite dowry. They prepared various foods and delicacies, priceless necklaces, and exquisite jeweled garments according to his demands. Selecting an auspicious and favorable day, they took a great quantity of wealth and jewels and went there to welcome the daughter of Bhadrakāśyapa as a wife for their son.
Having invited them into the house, he spread two mats of *tāla* wood within a single room.
Once they were settled, the two of them remained in that one room, each keeping themselves withdrawn and not coming into physical contact with the other.
At that time, when Pippalāyana’s parents heard this matter, they thought to themselves:
"How can it be that those two persons, while in the same room, do not touch one another with defilement?"
He then employed another expedient, removing all but one pair of garments; since they were sleeping together, they ought naturally to have been joined.
Yet those two did not touch one another at all; while Pippalāyana remained fast asleep, the woman Bhadrā rose and began to walk up and down.
Whenever the maiden Bhadrā fell asleep, Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja would immediately resume his walking meditation.
In this manner, they spent years alternating their activities, never sleeping together.
