In the chapter on the causal conditions of Mahākāśyapa,
at that time, while Bhadrā was fast asleep and her husband had risen to practice walking meditation, a black snake living in that place intended to pass by.

At that time, as Bhadrayā was fast asleep, one of her hands hung down over the side of the bed. Seeing a black snake about to pass by there, and observing that Bhadrayā’s hand was hanging down, Piṣpalayana thought to himself, fearing that the black snake might bite her hand; he immediately wrapped his own garment around his arm and lifted Bhadrayā’s arm, placing it back upon the bed.

At that time, Bhadrā was awakened from her sleep by the touch of his arm; terror arose in her heart, she became sorrowful and unhappy, and with a mind full of doubt and wonder, she immediately addressed Pilindavatsa, saying:
"O virtuous and noble son!
"Virtuous One, did you not previously make this solemn vow with me, saying, 'I have no desire to indulge in the five sensual pleasures; I wish to cultivate the holy life'?
For what reason now [do you act otherwise]?"
"Pipphalāyana replied: 'It is so!'"
"I do not practice lust.
Bhadrā said: "Noble son!"
"If you do not harbor desire now, why did you suddenly touch my arm just now?
At that time, Pipphalivana replied truthfully:
"Just now a black snake passed by here. Seeing your arm hanging before the bed, I thought at that moment: 'I fear that snake might spit venom and bite you.'"
"At that time, I wrapped my hands in a cloth and supported your arm to place you upon the bed; truly, I did not intentionally touch you.
In this manner, those two persons lived together in one place for twelve years, remaining within the same room without ever touching one another.

After twelve years had passed, at a later time, the parents of Pipphalāya passed away. Since the family estate was extensive, they immediately set about managing it; Pipphalāya personally supervised the agricultural work outside the house, while Bhaddā attended to all the domestic affairs and means of livelihood within the home.
At that time, on one occasion, Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja spoke thus to Bhadrā:
"Virtuous and benevolent lady!
You should instruct [the servants] to press sesame oil; I now wish to give it to the cows and other animals to drink."
Bhadrā then replied to her husband:
“As the noble son instructs, I dare not disobey.
Having heard these instructions, she summoned her maidservants and said to them:
"Quickly press this sesame oil; the noble son wishes to give it to the cows to drink.
When the maidservant heard these words from Bhadrā, she took the sesame seeds and placed them in the sun to dry, whereupon she saw hundreds of thousands of wriggling insects.
Having seen this, they each said to one another:
"We shall incur immeasurable sins.
Or again, some said:
"What sin do we now know that we have committed?
This transgression belongs to Bhadrā, for she caused us to perform such deeds.
When Bhadrā heard these words from the female messengers, she immediately said to them:
"If there are such faults and transgressions as these, you must no longer press oil.

At that time, Bhadrā had her people clear away the sesame seeds, entered the inner room, closed the door, and sat in silent stillness with her head bowed, her heart filled with displeasure as she reflected.

Having finished inspecting the fields of the Pippala tree and returning from his tour, he saw various sentient beings undergoing immeasurable and manifold sufferings; he further beheld the oxen in distress, driven and herded about without a moment’s rest. Having seen this, he was filled with sorrow and distress;
lowering his head in silence, he reflected thus: "Alas, all you sentient beings!"
"Enduring such suffering and distress.
He returned to his home, his heart filled with great sorrow; his countenance was unhappy, and he sat with his head bowed in contemplation.
Seeing Bimbisāra thus distressed, with his head bowed in thought, Bhadrā approached him. Having reached his side, she addressed him, saying:
"Noble son! Why are you thus sorrowful?
With a heart that finds no joy, you sit with your head bowed."

"Venerable one, you should not now harbor such a thought: 'The Master assigned me, Bhaddāla, to have oil pressed for him, yet he did not have it pressed; because of this circumstance, my heart is unhappy.'"
He replied, "O virtuous and benevolent one!
It is not for such reasons that my heart is ill at ease and I stand here with my head bowed."

This morning, as I departed from here to inspect the farming operations, I saw various sentient beings undergoing all manner of suffering; whether coming or going, walking or standing, they could not find even a moment’s peace.
Furthermore, I saw various oxen engaged in all kinds of labor, never ceasing for a moment; having seen this, I thought to myself:
"Alas, alas!..."
"All sentient beings undergo such suffering.
For this reason, my heart is not at ease, and I remain here with my head bowed.
At that time, Bhadrā again replied to her husband:
"O virtuous and noble son!
I too now see such great calamities.
Her husband asked:
"O virtuous and benevolent one!
What affliction have you seen?
Bhaddā then proceeded to relate these circumstances in detail.
At that time, Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja spoke these words to the maiden Bhadrā:
"O virtuous and benevolent lady!

While dwelling within the household, it is difficult to practice the pure life without flaw, without transgression, without injury, and without harm; one can never, for the duration of a single lifetime and a single existence, fulfill one's heart’s desire and practice the holy life (brahmacarya)."
Bhadrā replied: "Noble son!
For this reason, the two of us shall together and with deliberation renounce our homes and go forth into homelessness."
At that time, Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja replied to Bhadrika, saying:
"Worthy and virtuous one!
You should stay here for now; I shall seek out a teacher. Once I have found one, I will inform you, and you may then leave the household life to become a renunciant."
At that time, Viśvāmitra immediately summoned all the male and female servants within his household and addressed them, saying:

"Whatever wealth or grain you may have belongs entirely to you; I release you all to freedom as free persons. I wish to leave the home life to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) out of a sense of weary detachment."
At that time, Pipphalāya took his own priceless white cotton robe and immediately fashioned it into a saṃghāṭī. He then requested a man to shave off his beard and hair, saying:
"If there is a great arhat in the world who has gone forth, I shall now follow him to go forth and practice the Way."
At that time, there was not a single arhat in the world, except for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, when the first light of dawn appeared, the World-Honored One realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Then, on that very day, when the night had passed and the sun had just begun to rise, Pippalāyana Kāśyapa also went forth into homelessness.
This Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja Kāśyapa was born into the lineage of Mahākāśyapa; therefore, he acquired the name Kāśyapa in the world.
Having gone forth, he proceeded by way of successive stages, begging for alms from house to house within the village.

Again, at another time, traveling by stages, he arrived at the kingdom of Magadha, passing through the villages of Magadha and reaching the great city of Rājagṛha at the village of Nataṭa. Along the way, he suddenly saw the Tathāgata at a certain shrine for a deity; at that time, this deity was named Bahuputra (Many Sons), who sat there, exceedingly handsome and upright in body, like the array of many constellations within the void of space.
Having seen this, Kāśyapa immediately attained purity and reached the state of non-dual perception:
"I shall now surely behold the Teacher;
I shall now surely behold the Bhagavān."
At this moment, I shall surely behold the All-Knowing One;
at this moment, I shall surely behold the World-Honored One, the All-Seeing One—I behold the World-Honored One;
I behold the One of Unimpeded Knowledge and Vision—I behold the World-Honored One.

Having thus attained a pure mind, Mahākāśyapa’s thoughts continued in succession without distraction through right mindfulness. Having completed his prostration at the feet of the World-Honored One, he knelt with his right knee on the ground before the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I am a disciple of the World-Honored One; I only pray that the World-Honored One will be my teacher, for I am a disciple of the World-Honored One.
Therefore, the commentator spoke in verse:
"He beheld the Buddha beneath the Many-Sons Tree, Resplendent like a golden image of brilliant radiance."
Within his heart, he gave rise to the aspiration for all-knowledge, and with palms joined in joy, he turned toward the World-Honored One.
In that grove, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and, with palms joined before the Honored One, spoke these words:
“I pray only that the World-Honored One be my teacher, like a lamp lit in the darkness to provide illumination.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa, saying: "Kāśyapa!
If there is a śrāvaka disciple who, having thus completed this single-minded right mindfulness, says, 'This is my teacher.'"
With such a mind, one honors and makes offerings;
yet that teacher, not knowing, claims to know, and not seeing, claims to see.
Because that person accepts these honors and offerings through such false speech, their head shall split into seven pieces.

However, Mahākāśyapa! Now I know what is real and speak of it as known; I see what is real and speak of it as seen. When I preach the Dharma for my śrāvaka disciples, I explain causes and conditions; it is not without cause or condition. It is not that there is no opening or closing [of the teachings], nor is it merely a matter of opening and closing; I also manifest supernormal powers. It is not that I only manifest supernormal powers, but there is also opening and closing; it is not that there is no opening and closing.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
At that time, I spoke of causes and conditions, and even included both permissions and prohibitions; it was not without permissions and prohibitions.
As I have taught, you should practice accordingly and must not contravene it."
If you comply with my words in this manner, then in future lives, throughout the long night, you will obtain that which benefits yourself and attain great peace and happiness.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
you should train yourself in this way.
Kāśyapa!"
If you wish to train in such practice, you should give rise to a mind of reverence, respect, shame, and remorse toward those who live the holy life, whether they be inferior, middling, or superior.
Kāśyapa!
"You should train yourself in this way.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
at that time you must constantly maintain right mindfulness and never abandon it for even a moment."
Kāśyapa! Regarding this matter, you should further train yourself.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
At that time, you should contemplate the characteristics of arising and ceasing within the five aggregates:

namely, "this is form, this is the arising of form, this is the cessation of form; this is feeling, this is perception, these are mental formations, this is consciousness, this is the arising of consciousness, and this is the cessation of consciousness."
“Kāśyapa!
In this regard, you should train yourself thus.

At that time, having received this instruction from the World-Honored One, the Elder Mahākāśyapa gave rise to this state of impurity and constantly subsisted on alms-food. After seven days had passed, on the eighth day, he attained wisdom as taught.
When the World-Honored One had thus instructed them, he rose from his seat. Thereupon, the Elder Mahākāśyapa attended upon and escorted the World-Honored One.

At that time, not long after the World-Honored One had set out on the road, he stopped by the roadside beneath a tree. Having reached that tree, the Elder Mahākāśyapa took the saṃghāṭī robe from his own body, folded it into four layers, spread it upon the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This seat has been prepared for the World-Honored One; out of compassion for me, the Buddha shall sit upon this seat.
Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One then sat upon that seat. Once seated, the Buddha addressed the Elder Mahākāśyapa, saying: "Kāśyapa!"
“Such a saṃghāṭī is extremely subtle, most excellent, and most soft.
Then the Elder Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Excellent, excellent!
World-Honored One!
Out of compassion for me, please accept this seat.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Mahākāśyapa, saying: "Kāśyapa,
are you able to wear the rag-robes that I have worn?"
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
I am able to take up the rag-robe worn by that Tathāgata.”
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately gave the coarse rag-robe to the Elder Mahākāśyapa, and the World-Honored One then accepted the exquisite garment worn by Mahākāśyapa.
(In this world, there are those who harbor doubts:
"Is it possible that the Blessed One, out of compassion for others, might demonstrate the matters of great virtue and merit by first renouncing wealth and power to accept coarse cloth and rag-robes?"
Regarding that which he doubts, one should simply say it was this śrāvaka disciple Mahākāśyapa.

Even when he was able to receive from the Tathāgata those coarse rag-robes, and until he attained the fruit of arhatship and lived out his entire lifespan, that elder Mahākāśyapa did not abandon this perception.
Therefore, the World-Honored One bestowed this prediction upon them: "O bhikṣus!
If you wish to know who among my śrāvaka disciples is one of few desires, contented, and fully endowed with the practice of dhūta austerities, it is the Elder Bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa."
At that time, the World-Honored One was once again staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: “Bhikṣus!

In the past, I, having departed from all desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, entered the first dhyāna; at that time, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa was also exactly like this.
“Having left behind all desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, born of seclusion, joy and happiness, I entered and dwelt in the first dhyāna.

At that time, with the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, and with internal clarity and mental unification, free from directed thought and evaluation, born of concentration, joy and happiness, I entered the second dhyāna.”
At that time, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa was likewise; he too stilled vitarka and vicāra, and so on, until he entered the practice of the second dhyāna. “O bhikṣus!

At that time, being detached from joy, I dwelt in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware; experiencing bodily bliss, I entered the third dhyāna, which the noble ones praise as "dwelling in bliss through the abandonment of all concerns."

This bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa was likewise; detached from joy, he dwelt in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing happiness with the body—of which the noble ones declare, "One who is equanimous and mindful dwells happily"—having abandoned all concerns, he abided in bliss and entered the practice of the third dhyāna.

“Monks! At that time, desiring to abandon all suffering and relinquish all pleasure, I first extinguished sorrow and joy, and entered the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by the purity of equanimity and mindfulness.”

This bhikṣu Kāśyapa was likewise: having abandoned both suffering and pleasure, and having previously stilled sorrow and joy, he entered the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity and pure mindfulness.

"O bhikṣus! At that time, with a mind of loving-kindness, I dwelt in meditative absorption pervading one direction; likewise the second, third, and fourth directions; and so above and below, throughout all places and the entire world, I dwelt in meditative absorption, suffusing everything with a mind of loving-kindness—vast, immeasurable, free from enmity, and devoid of malice."
At that time, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa was likewise; even unto the absence of resentment, he did not give rise to thoughts of malice, nor did his feelings of sorrow or joy differ in this regard.

“Monks! At that time, with a mind of equanimity, I pervaded one direction and dwelt in meditative absorption; likewise the second, third, and fourth directions; and so above and below, throughout all places and the entire world, I pervaded everything with a mind of equanimity and dwelt in meditative absorption—vast, immeasurable, free from enmity, and without malice.”
At that time, the bhikṣu Kāśyapa was also like this, even to the point of not causing harm. "O bhikṣus!

At that time, having transcended all perceptions of form, having extinguished all perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to or thinking of any perceptions of diversity, I dwelt in the perception of the sphere of infinite space and entered the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space."
At that time, the bhikṣu Kāśyapa was also like this: having transcended all perceptions of form, he entered the sphere of infinite space.
"O bhikṣus! [he said.]
At that time, having transcended the sphere of infinite space, I contemplated the sphere of infinite consciousness and entered the practice of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
At that same time, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa did likewise, even entering the practice of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
“Monks! At that time, having transcended all perceptions of consciousness and attending to the perception of nothingness, I entered the sphere of nothingness.”
"O monks! At that time, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa was likewise, even unto entering the practice of the sphere of nothingness."
“Monks! At that time, having transcended all perceptions of nothingness, I entered the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
At that same time, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa did likewise, even unto entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”
“Monks! At that time, I transcended all states of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa did exactly the same.”
"O bhikṣus!
At that time, I entered the practice of the eight liberations, entering and emerging from them in both forward and reverse order; having entered, I emerged; having emerged, I re-entered."
At that time, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa was also like this; he entered and then emerged, and having emerged, he entered again.
"O bhikṣus! [he said].
At that time, I entered the practice of the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*), entering and emerging from them in both forward and reverse order;
having entered, I emerged, and having emerged, I entered again. At that time, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa did likewise, even to the point of entering and then emerging, and emerging and then entering.
“Monks! At that time, I entered the practice of the ten universal bases (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*); having entered, I emerged; having emerged, I re-entered.
This bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa did exactly the same, even to the point of entering and then emerging, and emerging and then re-entering.”

“O Bhikṣus! At that time, I sported within various spheres of supernormal power (*ṛddhi-viṣaya*), namely: dividing one body into many bodies, and combining many bodies into a single body; entering from outside to inside, and exiting from inside to outside; descending from above to below, and ascending from below to above; passing unhindered through stone walls and mountain obstructions; and entering into and emerging from the earth as if it were water, no different.

It is like a flame that vanishes as soon as it appears; or like the sun and moon, which possess great majesty and great power, yet one can reach out and touch them with one's hand, attaining mastery over the body even as far as the Brahma Heaven.

"O bhikṣus! At that time, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa was also like this; he likewise sported with various supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), being able to manifest many bodies from a single body, and again to merge many bodies into one, until he attained mastery over his body as far as the Brahma-heaven."
"O bhikṣus! At that time, with the purified divine ear which surpasses that of humans, I clearly heard all the various sounds I heard, whether they were the voices of devas or the voices of humans."
At that time, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa was likewise; he too was able to employ the pure divine ear that surpasses the human ear, such that he heard everything completely and clearly.
“Monks! At that time, by means of the knowledge of others' minds, I knew the mental activities of other individuals (pudgala) and understood their thoughts exactly as they were.”
If there is a mind of aspiration, one knows the mind of aspiration as it truly is; if there is no mind of aspiration, one knows the absence of a mind of aspiration as it truly is.
Likewise, if there is a mind of aversion, one knows the mind of aversion as it truly is; if there is no mind of aversion, one knows the absence of a mind of aversion as it truly is.
When there is a mind with delusion, one knows as it truly is that there is a mind with delusion; when there is no mind with delusion, one knows as it truly is that there is no mind with delusion.

When there is a mind with attachment, one knows as it truly is that there is a mind with attachment; when there is no mind with attachment, one knows as it truly is that there is no mind with attachment.
He knows a conditioned mind as a conditioned mind, and an unconditioned mind as an unconditioned mind.

He knows a small mind as a small mind, a vast mind as a vast mind, a great mind as a great mind, a narrow mind as a narrow mind, a distracted mind as a distracted mind, an undistracted mind as an undistracted mind, an immeasurable mind as an immeasurable mind, a boundless mind as a boundless mind, a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind, an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind, a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind, an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind, a mind abiding in concentration as a mind abiding in concentration, a mind not abiding in concentration as a mind not abiding in concentration, a liberated mind as a liberated mind, and an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind; he knows them exactly as they are.
At that time, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa was likewise; by means of the knowledge of others' minds, he knew the mental activities of individuals and understood such thoughts exactly as they were.
Whether there is a mind with aspiration or a mind without aspiration, up to knowing as it truly is whether the mind is liberated or not liberated, one is able to know it as it truly is.

“Monks! At that time, I recollected various matters of past lives: whether one birth, or two, or three, or four, or five; or ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty; or a hundred, or a thousand; or a single eon of dissolution, or a single eon of formation; or having dissolved, remaining; or having remained, dissolving; or I knew immeasurable eons of dissolution and formation, having been formed and then dissolved, or having been dissolved and then formed.”
"In that place, I had such a name, such a clan, such a birth, such food, such pleasure, such pain, and such experiences."

Regarding the duration of their lifespans, I remember and know all their various past lives: how they died there and were born here, or died here and were born there; with such characteristics and such forms.

This bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa was likewise; with his pure divine eye, which surpasses that of gods and humans, he saw the events of past lives—whether one life or more—and he recollected and knew all such destinies, including their various characteristics and forms.

“Monks! At that time, with the purified divine eye, which surpasses that of humans and devas, I saw beings passing away from here and being reborn there—some beautiful, some ugly; some born into good realms, some born into evil realms—according to their karmic retributions. I even knew truly of these beings who were fully possessed of evil conduct of body, fully possessed of evil conduct of speech, and fully possessed of evil conduct of mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and were perverted: because this karma was accumulated and its causal conditions were fulfilled, at the breaking up of the body after death, they fell into the evil realms.”

These sentient beings, being fully endowed with good conduct of body, fully endowed with good conduct of speech, and fully endowed with good conduct of mind, do not revile the noble ones; because of their right view regarding the causal conditions of karma and phenomena, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in a happy destination.

By means of such a purified divine eye, surpassing that of humans and devas, he perceives beings as they truly are: dying in one place and being born in another; whether superior or inferior, beautiful or ugly; in good realms or evil realms—seeing and knowing all how they receive retribution according to their karma.
This bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa is likewise; he is able to know as it truly is and see as it truly is. "O bhikṣus!

At that time, my outflows being exhausted, within the state of being free from outflows, my mind attained liberation and my wisdom attained liberation. In this present life, with supernormal powers at my command, I realized the practice of peace and bliss, and uttered these words:"
"Birth and death have been severed; the holy life has been fulfilled; what was to be done has been accomplished;

there is no further existence. This bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa was also thus: having exhausted all outflows, up to and including having accomplished what was to be done, he shall not undergo further existence.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What wholesome karma did this elder Mahākāśyapa perform in the past, such that he was born into a wealthy and noble family, possessed of abundant resources, and even accomplished what was to be done?”
Your physical form is upright and handsome, a sight that all delight in beholding; you are peerless in this world, most supreme and most excellent, appearing like a golden statue.
What karmic causes did you create to further leave the household life, fulfill the multitude of precepts, and realize the fruit of Arhatship?
Furthermore, the Buddha gave this prediction:
"Among all the bhikṣus, the one who is foremost in having few desires, being content, and practicing the dhūta austerities is the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa."
After he had spoken these words, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!
I recall that in the distant past, there was a pratyekabuddha named Tagarasikhin who constantly resided in that city of Vārāṇasī."

At that time, in the region of Vārāṇasī, grain was so expensive and famine so severe that white bones covered the ground; many people had died, alms were difficult to obtain, and those who had left the household life could not even maintain their basic livelihood.

"At that time, when the sun was in the east, during the early morning hours, the Pratyekabuddha donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Vārāṇasī. He went from house to house for alms but received nothing; as before, he washed his bowl and departed with it empty."
At that time, there was a man in the city of Vārāṇasī whose family was impoverished and possessed little in the way of accumulated wealth.

This poor man saw the Pratyekabuddha Takkāriya approaching; his deportment was dignified and orderly, he walked looking at the ground, his movements were measured and appropriate, his countenance was serene and his gaze level, his demeanor was fully perfected, and his mind was established in right mindfulness.
At that time, the poor man, upon seeing the pratyekabuddha, attained purity of mind; having gradually approached him, he addressed the pratyekabuddha, saying:
"Excellent, Great Sage!"
"In this city, would it be possible for me to seek alms for food and drink?
The Venerable One replied,
"Excellent, O worthy one!"
"In this city, I have been unable to obtain alms.
Then that poor man said to the Pratyekabuddha,
"Excellent, Great Sage!
"Come to my home.

At that time, there was only one *śīrṣa* measure of millet rice in that house which had already been fully cooked; he then brought the Pratyekabuddha into the house, prepared a seat for him to sit upon, and offered the rice to him.
Now, all Pratyekabuddhas possess such a quality: they convert sentient beings through the power of supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi*), and not by means of other [mundane] powers.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha Tagara, having received food from that person, out of compassion for him, rose into the air and departed from that poor man’s house.

At that time, when the poor man saw that venerable Pratyekabuddha soaring through the air and departing, he was filled with such joy and exultation that his entire body and mind were suffused with it. With his ten fingers joined together in reverence upon his head, he prostrated himself in worship and made this aspiration:
"May I, in the future, encounter such a holy Pratyekabuddha, or one even more sublime;
and may I hear and retain the essential teachings spoken by that holy one, swiftly attaining realization and understanding."
"Furthermore, I vow that in birth after birth throughout all my lives, I shall not fall into the evil realms. "O Bhikṣus!

If you wish to know who that poor and suffering person in the city of Vārāṇasī was at that time—who invited the Pratyekabuddha Bhagavān Tagara to his home and offered him food—it was the Bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa."

At that time, because that poor man was able to give a single meal with a sincere heart to the Pratyekabuddha Mahāgara on the basis of his small savings, he was reborn a thousand times in the northern continent of Uttarakuru; thereafter, for immeasurable lifetimes, he was constantly reborn in return and forth among great Kṣatriya clans, Brāhmaṇa lineages, and wealthy householder families.
By the power of the causal conditions of this karmic retribution, at the time when Kāśyapa Buddha appeared in the world, he became King Kṛkī of Kāśi.
That King Kṛkī of Kāśi reverently honored and respected the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa for the duration of his entire life, after which he entered parinirvāṇa.

This King of Kāśī constructed a stūpa made of the seven precious substances for the Buddha’s relics; these seven precious substances were gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, amber, agate, and musaragalva. The interior of that precious stūpa was adorned with the seven jewels, while its exterior was faced with stone masonry. That stūpa was sublime in height, reaching one yojana, and half a yojana in width.
The prince was named Śabarīṅka (in the Sui language, "Clinging to Conditions"), who fashioned a parasol of the seven precious substances atop that stūpa to completely cover it.
[Furthermore, another teacher says:
"He constructed the eight parts of the stūpa and bestowed clothing, food and drink, and footwear upon the community of bhikṣus; having made these offerings, he made this aspiration: ]
"May I, in the future, encounter such a holy one as this; may I immediately comprehend and realize the Dharma that the holy one preaches.
Furthermore, may I not be born within the evil realms, and in whatever place I am born, may I obtain a body of golden hue."
Having performed these actions, he then requested his father the king for permission to renounce the household life, but his father did not grant it.
Later, after his father had passed away, the prince was finally able to go forth.

Having gone forth, he recited the scriptures and accomplished meditative concentration; at the end of his life there, he was reborn repeatedly among gods and humans. After wandering through such births for immeasurable ages, in his final body, he has now been born into the family of the Brahmin Nyagrodhakalpa.
His family was immensely wealthy, fully endowed with riches and treasures, such that there was not the slightest lack of anything he required.

Yet, because of the causal power of having constructed a parasol made of the seven precious gems as an offering and act of reverence over the stupa of the relics of Kāśyapa Buddha, Mahākāśyapa attained a golden body. Furthermore, at that time, he had made this aspiration:
"May I not be born in the evil realms."

By the power of the causal conditions of this karmic retribution, from that time forward, he has never fallen into the evil realms, but has always been born among gods and humans, experiencing immeasurable and boundless rewards of bliss.
At that time, he further made this aspiration:

"May I encounter this holy person in the future; having encountered him, may he not turn away from me, or may I surpass this holy person; and when he preaches the Dharma, may I understand it immediately upon hearing it."

"By the power of the causal conditions of that karmic retribution, he encountered my such teaching; having encountered me, he immediately went forth, became fully endowed with the various precepts, and realized the fruit of Arhatship."
"Among all my bhikṣus who have been granted this prediction, the one who is of few desires and contented is this very elder, the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa.
[Thus spoke the Buddha. "O bhikṣus!"

This is Mahākāśyapa; by the power of the causes and conditions of the meritorious karma he performed in the past, he was born into a wealthy Brahmin family where he lacked for nothing, his physical form was upright, most exquisite and supreme, resembling a golden image. Furthermore, he attained the life of a renunciant, fully maintained the various precepts, and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
"Therefore, I have bestowed this prediction:
the one who is foremost among those who practice the dhūta austerities with few desires and contentment is none other than the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa.
At that time, after a long interval, the World-Honored One again addressed Mahākāśyapa at another moment, speaking these words:

“Kāśyapa! You are now approaching the end; youth has already passed and old age has arrived. You should discard these coarse and worn-out rag-robes of *paṃsukūla* that you wear upon your body; you may now take my excellent and exquisite garments.”
Kāśyapa! Come here.

These robes, bestowed by the householder—fine, light, and soft, cut with a blade, sewn and worn upon the body—accept them; go to receive invitations from others, and always remain by the Buddha’s side, never departing from me.
Having spoken these words, at that time Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For a long night, while dwelling in an araṇya, I have also constantly praised the dharma of the araṇya.”
For a long night, I have lived by begging for alms, and I have likewise praised the merit of begging for alms.
For a long night, I have worn robes made of discarded rags, and I have also constantly extolled the virtues of such rag-robes.
Throughout the long night, I have not eaten at improper times, and I have likewise praised the practice of not eating at improper times.
Throughout the long night, I have practiced eating in a single sitting, and I have likewise praised the practice of eating in a single sitting.

Throughout the long night, I have partaken of a single morsel of food with measured intake, and I have likewise praised the practice of eating a single morsel as well as the method of measured eating.
For a long night, I have dwelt among burial mounds, and I have likewise praised the practice of dwelling among burial mounds.
For a long night, I have dwelt in the open air, and I have likewise praised the practice of dwelling in the open air.
Throughout the long night, I have dwelt beneath trees and likewise praised the practice of dwelling beneath trees.
Throughout the long night, I have practiced walking meditation and likewise praised the practice of walking meditation.
Throughout the long night, I have constantly sat without lying down, and I have likewise praised the practice of not lying down.
Throughout the long night, I have maintained only the three robes, and I have likewise praised the practice of maintaining the three robes.
Throughout the long night, I have had few desires and been content; I have also praised having few desires and being content.
Throughout the long night, I have delighted in tranquility; I have also praised the dharma of delighting in tranquility.
Throughout the long night, I have never delighted in speaking words that are unbeneficial, nor have I ever praised those who do not delight in such unbeneficial speech.
Throughout the long night, I have constantly practiced diligence, and I have likewise praised the dharma of constant diligence.
Throughout the long night, I have accomplished right mindfulness and have likewise praised the dharma for accomplishing right mindfulness.
Throughout the long night, I have accomplished right concentration and have likewise praised the dharma for accomplishing right concentration.
Throughout the long night, I have accomplished wisdom and have likewise praised the dharma of accomplishing wisdom.
Throughout the long night, I have constantly entered meditative concentration and have likewise praised the dharma of entering meditative concentration.
The Buddha addressed Kāśyapa, saying: "Kāśyapa!

For what benefit do you see that, throughout the long night, you personally practice the dharma of the araṇya, and likewise praise the practice of the araṇya; and even throughout the long night, you personally enter meditative concentration, and likewise praise the dharma of entering meditative concentration?"
Thereupon, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Because I see two kinds of benefit, I have for a long night dwelt in forest hermitages (araṇya), and I likewise praise those who practice in forest hermitages; furthermore, for a long night I have constantly entered meditative concentration (dhyāna), and I likewise praise those who constantly enter meditative concentration.”
What are these two?
First, that I now personally attain the dharma of peaceful and happy practice;
second, that out of compassion for sentient beings of future generations.
I only pray that future generations, upon seeing us, will learn from our conduct and speak thus:

"In past ages, there were elder senior *śrāvaka* bhikṣus who for a long night delighted in *āraṇya* dwellings, praised the practice of *āraṇya*, and even constantly entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), while likewise praising those who constantly entered meditative concentration."
"How shall we train ourselves in those practices, even to the point of entering meditative concentration ourselves and praising those who constantly enter meditative concentration?
"World-Honored One!

Seeing these two kinds of benefits, I have for a long night practiced in the forest hermitage (araṇya), and I likewise praise those who practice in the forest hermitage; even to the point of constantly entering meditative concentration, I likewise praise those who constantly enter meditative concentration."
The Buddha said to Mahākāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent,
Mahākāśyapa!”
"In a future age, you shall bring great benefit and great peace to many sentient beings, establishing immeasurable devas and humans in security and well-being.
Therefore, dwell now in forest hermitages (āraṇya) as you please; whenever you wish to see the Tathāgata, come to see him from time to time."
At that time, the bhikṣus asked the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
For what reason is this Elder Mahākāśyapa able to bring such great benefit to so many sentient beings?”
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed those bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!
This Mahākāśyapa has not only brought great benefit to many people in the present; in past ages as well, he brought great benefit to many."
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:

Indeed it is so, World-Honored One!”
"I pray that you will explain the causes and conditions.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!"
I recall that in the past, this Mahākāśyapa once served as Śakra, the King of Devas.

"At that time, Śakra, King of Devas, had this thought:"

[you should respond accordingly].

"Do you require a man?
Do you require a boy?

"To secure a man?
You should reply with these words:

To provide food for this lion king;

likewise, one hundred such evil persons daily must be provided to feed this lion—persons who commit theft, those who engage in sexual misconduct, those who speak falsehoods, those who use double-tongued speech, those who use harsh words, those who engage in frivolous chatter, those with excessive greed, those with excessive anger, or those with wrong views. Then the multitude of people followed behind the lion king, seeking food for him as they had done in the past when instructed by Śakra, without any difference.

"At that time, because they were terrified of the lion, that assembly felt remorse for their past killing of living beings; they ceased from stealing, likewise from sexual misconduct, and even up to the point of having no mind for wrong views, fully and completely maintaining and practicing the ten wholesome actions."
From each household, one person renounced the world to study the Path and practiced the four Brahma-vihāras; after their lives ended, they were reborn in the Brahma-heavens.
Among that assembly, those who merely observed the ten wholesome actions without renouncing the world were mostly reborn among humans and devas, wandering through the cycle of existence.

This Mahākāśyapa, at that time, through such skillful means, brought great benefit to many people; by the power of causes and conditions from past lives, he now likewise brings great benefit to the masses of people.
"O monks! This monk Mahākāśyapa shall, in the future world within the Dharma-teaching of the World-Honored One Maitreya, likewise bring great benefit to many people."

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!

Having reflected thus, he relinquished his life and entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

After he had attained *nirvāṇa*, the two mountains closed back together. Later, when Maitreya attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and extensively reveals the teachings of the Dharma, at that time, the World-Honored One Maitreya will call to mind these relics of Mahākāśyapa.

Do you wish to see the śrāvaka disciple of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is foremost among those who practice dhūta, being one of few desires and contentment—namely, Mahākāśyapa?
Those bhikṣus replied:

"At that time, Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded on all sides by an assembly of immeasurable thousands, arrived at that place."

"At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Maitreya was at that place, preaching the Dharma to the bhikṣus, and spoke these words:

“Kāśyapa the bhikṣu practices in this manner; I teach in this manner. You all should now practice as Kāśyapa the bhikṣu practices.

"Among that assembly, immeasurable thousands of beings shall attain the pure Dharma-eye within that teaching.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"O bhikṣus! I now exhort you: train yourselves like the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa;
may you all conduct yourselves as the bhikṣu Kāśyapa does."

Chapter 48: The Story of the Couple Bhadrā and Kapilā. In the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*, Chapter Forty-Eight: The Story of the Couple Bhadrā and Kapilā. At that time, the maiden Bhadrā-Kapilā, having failed to find a virtuous teacher, went to the heretical parivrājaka and left the household life to study the Way. Within that Dharma, he attained great renown and accomplished sovereign power.

He further thought to himself:

He immediately entered meditative concentration and observed her with the pure divine eye, which surpasses that of ordinary humans. "Excellent, sister!

'Excellent, sister!'"

"Excellent, sister!
"What would your teachers be like?

Then that bhikṣuṇī said to the female outsider Bhadrā Kapilā,

Why is this? Because of my ugliness, I could not obtain alms; however, in all places where I am born, I shall always be lovely and handsome, a sight for which all people long to gaze.

he asked, and he then seized the maidservant, binding her and beating her severely. At that, the maidservant immediately raised her voice and wailed loudly.

"O bhikṣus! What do you think?

At that time, those four deva sons said to Śakra, the Lord of Devas:

"Regarding the verse previously mentioned, we shall now speak it.

"In walking and sitting, he is constantly contemplative; in lying down and sleeping, he always finds no pleasure."
"When I am immersed in sleep, only then does my mind find release.
At that time, among those four heavenly sons, one heavenly son spoke again in verse:
"O Heavenly King, you are happy; you sleep in peace and security."
"Just like the sound of a battle drum, it constantly disturbs me.

"Just as when one shakes curd near the ear, it churns me without ceasing.
Then the third devaputra spoke again in verse:
"Shaking curd may happen at times; there is both urgency and haste."
"I am distracted by desire, appearing like the shimmering light of the sun.
At that time, the fourth devaputra spoke again in verse:
"May you all be at peace; you are skillful in composing these verses."
"I do not know for myself now, whether I shall live or whether I am to die.

"Fearing she might abandon the bliss of the celestial realm, we shall quickly bestow this maiden upon him in secret.

From that time forward, that maidservant did not fall into the evil realms; instead, she traveled back and forth among the realms of gods and humans, passing through immeasurable births. By the power of the causal conditions of this karmic retribution, in every place of birth, he did not fall into the three miserable paths; instead, he traveled back and forth among devas and humans, constantly experiencing happiness.
At that time, he further made this aspiration:
"In the future, may I encounter a teacher such as this or even one superior to him, and upon hearing the Dharma from him, may I be able to fully comprehend it."

By the power of the causal conditions of this karmic retribution, he has now encountered me, further attained the going forth, become fully endowed with the various precepts, and is likewise able to swiftly attain supernormal powers.
I have bestowed this prediction upon her:
"Among the assembly of śrāvakas, among the bhikṣuṇīs, she who has attained the foremost mastery of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives is the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrakāpilāyī."
"O bhikṣuṇīs! This Bhadrā Kapilā planted roots of merit in the past;

by the power of the causes and conditions of those roots of merit, this bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā Kapilā has now been born into a wealthy and noble family of great brāhmaṇas. She is handsome and pleasing to behold, and among my assembly of śrāvaka bhikṣuṇīs, she is the foremost in recollecting her past lives."
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is rare, Bhagavān!”
This bhikṣuṇī Bhadrakāpilā, having followed the Elder Mahākāśyapa and attained ordination, was well able to conform to the dharma of the renunciant life.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!
This bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā Kāpilāyanī did not only follow Mahākāśyapa into the homeless life in this present life; in past lives as well, she likewise followed him in going forth."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
what is this matter?”
"I pray that you will explain this for us.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I recall that in the past, there was a poor man who cultivated his fields."
At that time, the poor woman went out from her home to bring food to her husband.
Upon reaching the bank of a river, she saw a venerable Pratyekabuddha sitting cross-legged beneath a tree, his body upright and his mindfulness correct, with both body and mind unmoving.

At that time, the poor woman, upon seeing the pratyekabuddha, felt pure faith arise in her heart; she joined her ten fingers in palms-together salutation, bowed her head to his feet, and proceeded with reverent devotion.

Her husband was in the fields when he saw his wife from afar as she emerged from her house and entered the lower part of the riverbank; seeing no place for crossing, he immediately gave rise to this thought:
"Who is there on the other side?"
"With whom do you dwell?
You have not come even now; I am hungry and thirsty, and extremely exhausted, wishing to arrive as soon as possible.
Because of these words, the husband immediately gave rise to great anger and resentment; feeling dejected and unhappy, he took up his staff and turned toward her.
Having arrived at that place, he saw a pratyekabuddha sitting peacefully in meditative concentration; having seen him, he immediately thought to himself:
"It is certain beyond doubt that my wife has now engaged in worldly affairs with that śramaṇa."
At that time, the man gave rise to great resentment and struck the Pratyekabuddha Vāsiṣṭha with a staff.
Thereupon, the Pratyekabuddha immediately departed from the opposite bank and flew through the air by means of his supernormal powers.
At that time, the poor woman said to her husband:
"Alas! You have committed such a great sin!
The seer was without fault; for what reason did you cause him such needless distress?"
"Now this Great Sage is fully endowed with the virtue of precepts, practices the sublime Dharma, possesses great majestic power, and is possessed of great supernormal faculties.
At that time, after the poor man had struck the Pratyekabuddha, he immediately felt remorse. Having felt remorse, he said to his wife:
"Excellent, sister!
"You should now go forth together with me and practice the holy life (brahmacarya) in common. Why is this?
For my present transgressions cannot be extinguished by minor causes and conditions."
The wife immediately replied to her husband with these words:
"Excellent, noble son!
I dare not disobey your instruction."
"Now the two of us shall leave our homes and renounce the world.
At that time, those two renounced the world with one mind.
Having renounced the world, the two practiced and accomplished a mind of loving-kindness; when their lives ended, they were reborn in the Brahma realm.
"O bhikṣus! What do you think?
Was that poor man who, in those former times, was engaged in farming anyone else?"
This was the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa.

As for that poor woman who, while providing food for her husband, made offerings to a pratyekabuddha, thereby cultivating a heart of loving-kindness until she cast off her body and, at the end of her life, was reborn in the Brahma palace—could she have been anyone else?
She is none other than the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā Kāpilāyanī.
Because she followed her husband into the religious life at that time, she has likewise followed Mahākāśyapa into the religious life now, never having contravened the teaching.

Chapter 49: The Account of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Forty-nine, Part One: The Account of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. At that time, not far from the city of Rājagṛha in the kingdom of Magadha, there was a village settlement named Nālada.
In that village, there lived a very wealthy and great Brahmin named Dhanjaya—translated in the Sui language as "Jizhi"—who resided in that village.
(There is another teacher who says:
"That brāhmaṇa was named Dhanadatta, which in the Sui language means 'Bestower of Wealth'").
That brāhmaṇa was exceedingly wealthy and possessed vast riches, no different from Vaiśravaṇa himself.
That brahmin had eight sons: his first son was named Upatiṣya;
his second son was named Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
and his third son was named Cunda.
His fourth son was named Jambuka-haritabhadra;
his fifth son was named Chanda;
and the sixth was named Jambukāka.
The seventh is named Kauṇḍinya;
the eighth is named Sudarśana;
these are known as the eight sons.
Furthermore, there was a woman named Susīma who had left the household life to practice the path within the teachings of the Pāṣaṇḍa heretics.
The Mahāsāṃghika masters further said:

"That brahmin had seven sons; namely, the first was named Dharma, the second was named Sudharma, the third was named Upadharma, the fourth was named Tiṣya, the fifth was named Upatiṣya, the sixth was named Kharaskandha, and the seventh was named Upavarṣa—these were his seven sons."

Among those novices, Upatiṣya was the eldest of the brothers; he was highly proficient in recitation and study, and he also taught others. Regarding the four Vedas, there was nothing he did not understand; his mastery of recitation was complete, and he was skilled at explaining all other treatises, such as those of the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra and others, including their names, each of which he could explain. He was clear regarding past lives and adept at making fine distinctions.
He was unhindered in his thorough understanding of the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
He had mastered the *Vyākaraṇa* treatises within his heart, fully accomplished the sixty-four skills, and was well-versed in the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*).

At that time, the māṇava was by nature gentle and his mind was upright and virtuous. He constantly harbored compassion and felt deep revulsion for worldly affairs. He repented of his past transgressions; having encountered many Buddhas in the past, he had planted various roots of goodness, accomplished numerous deeds, and was skillfully able to cultivate himself. He always delighted in diligence, was moderate in eating, and turned away from afflictions toward Nirvāṇa. In accordance with principle and without obstruction, he loathed all states of existence. Having perfected his various practices and worn away his fetters, he reached the stage of maturity, with only one more birth remaining. Intelligent and subtle, he reflected with refined thought and clearly understood all dharmas.
The boy’s parents would consult him on all matters concerning their household affairs before they would undertake them.
At that time, not far from the great city of Rājagṛha, there was a village named Kūlika.

Within that village, there was a certain householder of the great Brahmin caste; he was a great householder who resided in that village, possessing vast wealth and abundance, such that his home was no different from the palace of King Vaiśravaṇa.

That brahmin fathered a son named Kūṭadanta, who was handsome in appearance and pleasing to all who beheld him. He mastered all treatises and scriptures and was able to teach them to others; he even attained proficiency in the marks of a great man.
The youth Upatiṣya was his close friend.

At that time, the two of them cherished one another, always harboring joy, with harmonious countenances and pleasant expressions; if they were separated for even a short while, they would experience great distress and sorrow.
Throughout their past thousand lifetimes, they were bound together by the ties of mutual affection.
As a verse says:
"Through the mutual perfuming of causes and effects in previous lives, The two minds have become increasingly intimate with one another."
Because of such feelings of affection, they were like lotuses born within the water.
Upatissa and Kolita, those two, cherished and respected one another;
if they did not see each other for even a short time, their hearts were filled with anxiety and they suffered in self-reproach.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume 47 [and] Volume 48,
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, Part Two:
At that time, not far from the great city of Rājagṛha, there was a mountain named Gijjhakūṭa.
On that mountain, there is always a great assembly convened at one time, and that assembly is named Cīrikūṭa;
furthermore, there is a mountain named Riśicīra, where an assembly is also constantly held, and that assembly is likewise named Riśicīra;
there is yet another mountain named Vaihāra.
In this way, Mount Pañcaśīrṣa and Mount Vipula each have a single assembly; these assemblies are also named after those mountains, such as Vipula and so forth. Such are those mountains.
Just as they had departed from Kuruha, they established assemblies according to the seasons; at those assembly sites, great multitudes gathered.

At that time, immeasurable thousands, immeasurable hundreds of thousands, and even up to billions of people assembled from all eight directions, traveling by various vehicles—namely, elephants, horses, chariots, and on foot—desiring to witness those assemblies.
At that time, all the people of Rājagṛha came forth; they went from Rājagṛha to the village of Nālada, which was half a yojana from the settlement of Kollāga.
At that time, the youth Tiṣya thought to himself:
"I should now go to the place of Cūḍapanthaka and visit him to observe; if I go there, I shall surely achieve one thing: namely, a sense of weary detachment from the world."

At that time, the youth Upatiṣya mounted a carriage drawn by four elephants and departed from the village of Nālada, proceeding to the site of the festival at the Śrīgupta Canal for the purpose of viewing it.
The youth Kolita also had this thought:
"I should now go to that great assembly at the Śrīgupta canal, until my mind gives rise to world-weariness."

Mounting the back of the elephant, he proceeded forward; meanwhile, the boy’s attendants entertained the people with songs and dances as they emerged from the village of Kukkuṭa and arrived at the site of the sacrifice on the Jīrṇaka-hrada for the purpose of viewing it.

At that time, those two men were handsome and dignified in appearance, capable of delighting the hearts of others; they were proficient in all arts and crafts, reaching a level of mastery such that they were fit to be leaders among the multitude.
At that time, high seats were arranged within that assembly; when those people arrived, they each ascended their respective high seats.
Then the youth Upatiṣya saw that great multitude performing various musical arts, playing music, singing, dancing, and enjoying themselves in playful sport.
Having seen this, he immediately thought:
"This is a rare and unprecedented occurrence.
How is it that these people, amidst such suffering and distress, within such defilement and impurity, and in the midst of old age and decay, can yet indulge in pleasure and negligence?"
Such is the defilement of disease, wherein there is no peace; such is the impurity of death, wherein life is not long-lasting.
Yet this great assembly conceives thoughts of pleasure, being heedless and self-indulgent, engaging in various songs and dances, performing manifold music, and indulging in all manner of amusements.
Then Upatisya, having observed the great assembly, thought to himself:
"After a hundred years have passed, not a single one of this great assembly will remain."

While he was reflecting thus, remorse arose within him and no joy or longing remained; he then rose slowly and calmly from his excellent seat, gradually departed from the assembly, and went to a secluded grove. Arriving beneath a tree, he sat down dejectedly, with his senses stilled, contemplating meditative concentration.
At that time, there was a performer in the assembly who, through his acrobatic feats, brought joy to the great multitude.
Seeing the great multitude laughing boisterously, the youth Kuṇāla immediately thought to himself:
"In a hundred years from now, will the jaw and cheekbones of this great multitude still be able to join together?"
Having had this thought, he was overcome with great sorrow and distress, and no longer felt any desire for pleasure; he rose from his seat and sought the youth Upatiṣya, thinking to himself:
"Where is the youth Upatiṣya now?"

Looking around in the four directions, he saw from afar the youth Upatiṣya sitting peacefully under a tree in that forest, lost in contemplation; his heart was not set on pleasure, his senses were stilled, and he was absorbed in meditative concentration.
Having looked back and seen him, he immediately went to him and said:
"For what reason now is your mind not joyful, as you sit here alone in contemplation?"
"Do you not now encounter any calamities, portents, or inauspicious misfortunes and sufferings?
He then spoke in verse:
"The sounds of drums and lutes, The voices of men and women singing..."
One should listen to this wondrous sound; why then not give rise to joy?
At this time one should rejoice; do not harbor grief or affliction.
This is a time for experiencing happiness; it is not the time to weep.
"Yet we listen to these sounds, which are like those produced by celestial jade maidens;
this assembly is like a celestial gathering—why, then, do our hearts not rejoice?
At that time, the youth Upatiṣya said to the youth Kolita:
"How marvelous, dear friend!
Do you see such a great assembly as this?
While they enjoy great delight through various sounds and songs, not a single person from this great assembly will remain after a hundred years have passed."
He then spoke these verses:
"Beings are greedy for sense objects, yet those objects cannot save them;
all things are impermanent and lack solidity—what pleasure can there be for the foolish?"
These sentient beings, their minds stained by attachment to the five desires, will before long fall into hell;
at the end of their lives, they shall become mere dust and ash.
Now, within my heart there is not a single joy; fear and sorrow increase most grievously.
Although your music possesses pleasure, in my view, the mind delights in the Dharma.

Gods, humans, asuras, and kinnaras may experience joy within their hearts for a long time, yet they cannot grow weary of it and escape it before their lives end; therefore, I ought to practice the Dharma.
At that time, the youth Kolita again said to the youth Upatiṣya: "Upatiṣya!
My own thought is also exactly like this."
He then spoke in verse:
"Those for whom suffering and pleasure are the same, and for whom sorrow and joy are likewise the same, are praised by the wise; now I am also the same as you."
"What your heart desires, my mind shall likewise follow;
I would rather die with you than live apart from you.
At that time, the youth Kuṇḍadhāna again asked the youth Upatiṣya:
"What shall we do now? Then the youth Upatiṣya replied to the youth Kolita, saying:
"Friend, if that is so, we should now leave the household life and seek the supreme nectar of immortality."
Then the youth Kolita replied to the youth Upatiṣya, saying:
"As you desire, so do I rejoice."
"Upatisya! Since we have now abandoned our homes, we ought to go from here and seek ordination.
Then the youth Upatisya said to the youth Kolita:
“Kulidā! You should know the time.
We are now well-known to the public; if our families do not permit it, who will ordain us?”
Fearing their parents, they felt apprehensive that obstacles might arise.
"We should now consult our parents," they said.
Thereupon, the two youths departed from the assembly and returned to their home.
At that time, the youth Upatiṣya went to his parents and said to them:
"Excellent, my parents!
My present intention is to desire to leave the household life; I only pray that you will grant me permission."
At that time, the parents deliberated in private:
"Now, within this household, who shall be the successor?
Who shall be the master of all our means of livelihood?"
"Thus it is, young man!
We hold you so dear that when you wish to leave us behind to go forth and seek the Way, what heart could I have to bear parting from you?"
Then, after the parents had deliberated together, they said to the youth Upatiṣya: "Young man! Although we have many sons today, we are especially fond of you.

Not seeing you for even a moment causes us great distress; we always delight in seeing you and do not wish to be parted from you. Since your birth, you have never undergone hardship. In our hearts, we would not wish to be parted from you even unto death; how much less, while we are still alive, would we ever let you go?"
"If you permit me to leave the household life, such a thing shall never happen.
Thus he requested twice, and even up to three times, yet he was not granted permission.
Having made these three requests and still not received consent, [he departed].
At that time, the youth Upatiṣya, having not received permission, went without drink or food for one day, and continued thus for as many as seven days.
At that time, the parents, all their relatives, and various acquaintances gathered together and said to the parents:
"Excellent, O Noble Ones!"

"You all should permit Upatissa to leave his home and go forth into homelessness. If he is allowed to leave his home and go forth, he will delight in that pursuit of the Way and find a path to survival;
if his life is preserved, why should you worry that you will not see him?"
"If he does not take pleasure in that assembly, he shall naturally return; do not let him meet his end before you.
At that time, the boy’s parents immediately said to him:
"If this is truly so, we now grant our permission."
At that time, the youth Kuṇḍadhāna went to his parents and said to them:
"Excellent, my parents!
I now wish to leave the home life and go forth; I only pray that you will grant me your permission!"

These parents of Kūṭadanta had only one son, whom they loved most deeply; they could not bear to part with him even for a moment, and if they did not see him for but a short while, they were filled with great sorrow.
At that time, the parents of the youth Kuṇḍadhāna had previously made a solemn vow within their household:
"All members of this family, great and small, must not fail to carry out whatever you have promised to do for the youth Kuṇḍadhāna."
"Whatever you command shall be obeyed.
Then, having understood that the time was right, they said to the youth Kuṇāla:
"Do as you wish; act according to your own inclination."
At that time, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner in the great city of Rājagṛha named Pāyāsi Vatsagotra, who resided in that city with five hundred followers.
At that time, the youths Upatiṣya and Kolita had no place of refuge and did not know where to go.

Thereupon, the two youths shaved their hair and beards and went forth as renunciants under Śāṇakavāsa (translated in the Sui period as "He Who Is Victorious Over Others"), a non-Buddhist teacher, to study the Way.

At that time, those two men were swift and sharp in thought and conduct, possessed few desires and were content, and their wisdom was profound and far-reaching. To them, Śāṇakavāsin—the son of Viśvāmitra, translated into Chinese as "Distinctive Staff"—then proceeded to explain his own spiritual arts, various skills, medical prescriptions and medicinal herbs, and the non-conceptual meditative concentration (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*).
When the two youths had heard this, within seven days and seven nights, they attained complete mastery.
Having attained such mastery, the two of them became teachers for the Pārivrajaka non-Buddhists and their five hundred followers.
At that time, those two men led the great assembly in such a sequence;
yet, despite this, their inner minds remained unsettled.
Then the youth Upatiṣya said to Kolita, the parivrājaka (a wanderer who has "distanced himself," as translated in the Sui period):
"Excellent, Kolita!"
"This dharma of Sañjaya Parivrājaka does not lead to the ultimate exhaustion of the limits of suffering.
Kūṭadanta! You should seek a true teacher together with me."
Then the youth Kolita Parivrājaka said to the youth Upatiṣya Parivrājaka:
"I do not disagree with what Upatiṣya has said."
"Nevertheless, we must not entirely abandon this teacher to seek another elsewhere.
Then those two men made a vow with one accord:
"If either of us should find a teacher superior to this one, who can explain to us the supreme path of the Deathless (amṛta), we shall certainly inform the other."

At that time, after the World-Honored One had converted twelve nayutas of sentient beings, including Bimbisāra and others, he resided within the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha together with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus, all of whom had shaved their heads, abandoned the household life, and gone forth into homelessness.
At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu named Upasena, whose deportment was dignified and composed; among all the bhikṣus, he was the foremost.
In the early morning, he put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha; within that city, he went from house to house for alms.
(The Mahāsāṃghika masters speak thus.)
Other masters further state:

"At that time, Aśvajit (translated in the Sui language as Mǎxīng), at the hour of dawn when the sun was in the east, put on his robes and took up his alms bowl to enter the city for alms. Within the city, he went from house to house begging for food, his deportment dignified and orderly, his movements measured and proper. Wearing his saṃghāṭī and nivāsana, he carried his utensils with perfect neatness. Skillfully restraining his sense faculties, he settled his mind and gazed outwardly while contemplating all phenomena, proceeding straight ahead with right mindfulness."
At that time, all the people of the great city of Rājagṛha who saw him with their own eyes discussed it among themselves, speaking in verse:
“Skilled in restraining the senses and consciousness, Always tranquil and composed in his movements, With a smile upon his face, he utters beautiful words;
He must surely be a scion of the Śākya clan.”

At that time, the youth Upatiṣya saw the elder monk Aśvajit begging for alms in succession through Rājagṛha. His deportment was dignified and orderly, his movements were measured and restrained; he wore his saṃghāṭī and undergarments properly, and his alms-bowl was held with perfect composure. He had skillfully subdued his sense faculties and sat with a tranquil mind, gazing intently as he contemplated all phenomena. Walking upright with right mindfulness, he recited this verse for the sake of the people.
At that time, Upatiṣya the parivrājaka had this thought:
"All those in the world who are arhats, all the noble ones, and those who have attained or are progressing toward the path."
"This Great Virtuous One should now be counted among them; I shall go to him to ask about my mental doubts.
At that time, the wanderer Upatiṣya further thought to himself:
"If I go to ask him, now is not the right time."
Why is this? It is because of begging for alms.
One who seeks the Dharma should abandon pride and ought to follow [the teacher] wherever he may go.
Having formed this thought, the parivrājaka Upatiṣya followed behind him, observing where he was going.
At that time, the bhikṣu Aśvajit, having finished his almsround in the great city of Rājagṛha, was carrying his food out of the city.

Then Upatiṣya the parivrājaka went to where the venerable Āśvajit bhikṣu was; having arrived, he exchanged greetings with the elder Āśvajit bhikṣu, and after conversing together, he withdrew to stand to one side.
Then Upatisya the parivrājaka said to the venerable Aśvajit bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!
Are you the true Teacher, or are you merely a disciple of another?"
When he had spoken these words, the Elder Aśvajit said to the parivrājaka Upatiṣya:
"There is another Great Teacher; I am a disciple of that other Honored One."
At that time, the parivrājaka Upatiṣya asked the venerable bhikṣu Aśvajit:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Who is your teacher?
Under whom did you go forth into homelessness? Whose Dharma and practice do you delight in?
At that time, when the World-Honored One had first attained perfect enlightenment, all people called him "Buddha," "Great Śramaṇa," and "Mahāśramaṇa"; these were the names by which he was known.
At that time, the venerable bhikṣu Aśvajit addressed the parivrājaka Upatiṣya, saying:
"Excellent, O worthy one!"
"There is a great śramaṇa!
He is a son of the Śākyas, who has gone forth from among the Śākya clan.
He is my teacher; it is by relying on him that I have gone forth, and I delight in his Dharma."
At that time, the parivrājaka Upatiṣya again addressed the venerable Aśvajit, saying:
"Excellent, O worthy one!"

"Is that Great Teacher of yours handsome and dignified in appearance, surpassing you? And as for his virtues and skills, are they also superior to yours? At that time, the Elder Aśvajit spoke these verses: [The Buddha] is indeed more beautiful than you; His countenance is serene and his body is upright. He is endowed with all supreme qualities; In every respect, he excels you. He is a field of merit for all beings; He is the one who brings peace to the world. He is the unsurpassed teacher of gods and men; He is the peerless one in the three realms. He is the Great Sage, the All-Knowing One; He is the one who has transcended birth and death. He is the one who has attained liberation; He is the one who has reached the further shore. He is the one who has extinguished all afflictions; He is the one who has realized the ultimate truth. He is the one who has crossed over the great flood; He is the one who has reached the dry land of nirvana. He is the one who has attained the state of peace; He is the one who has realized the state of bliss. He is the one who has attained the state of coolness; He is the one who has realized the state of tranquility. He is the one who has attained the state of purity; He is the one who has realized the state of stainlessness. He is the one who has attained the state of light; He is the one who has realized the state of illumination. He is the one who has attained the state of wisdom; He is the one who has realized the state of omniscience. He is the one who has attained the state of compassion; He is the one who has realized the state of universal love. He is the one who has attained the state of equanimity; He is the one who has realized the state of impartiality. He is the one who has attained the state of skillful means; He is the one who has realized the state of liberation. He is the one who has attained the state of power; He is the one who has realized the state of sovereignty. He is the one who has attained the state of fearlessness; He is the one who has realized the state of intrepidity. He is the one who has attained the state of self-mastery; He is the one who has realized the state of independence. He is the one who has attained the state of mastery over all phenomena; He is the one who has realized the state of non-attachment. He is the one who has attained the state of mastery over all minds; He is the one who has realized the state of non-obstruction. He is the one who has attained the state of mastery over all speech; He is the one who has realized the state of non-retrogression. He is the one who has attained the state of mastery over all actions; He is the one who has realized the state of non-defilement. He is the one who has attained the state of mastery over all dharmas; He is the one who has realized the state of non-duality. He is the one who has attained the state of mastery over all beings; He is the one who has realized the state of non-discrimination. He is the one who has attained the state of mastery over all worlds; He is the one who has realized the state of non-arising. He is the one who has attained the state of mastery over all Buddhas; He is the one who has realized the state of non-extinction. He is the one who has attained the state of mastery over all truths; He is the one who has realized the state of non-decline. He is the one who has attained the state of mastery over all paths; He is the one who has realized the state of non-reversion. He is the one who has attained the state of mastery over all fruits; He is the one who has realized the state of non-abiding. He is the one who has attained the state of mastery over all vehicles; He is the one who has realized the state of non-differentiation.
