"As a mustard seed compared to Mount Sumeru, A cow's footprint compared to the great ocean,
A mosquito and a gadfly compared to the Golden-Winged Bird— So it is between me and him.
Even if a śrāvaka were to cross to the other shore And achieve all the stages, they would still be but a disciple."
"He does not even enter into the reckoning among those Buddhas; his majestic virtue is distinct from that of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Nevertheless, my teacher is fully enlightened regarding the phenomena of the three periods of time and has attained unimpeded wisdom."
"O Venerable One!
My teacher has achieved success in all matters regarding all dharmas.
At that time, the parivrājaka Upatiṣya said to the venerable Aśvajit:
“O virtuous one!
What Dharma does your teacher teach?
On what matters does he discourse?”
He then spoke in verse:
"Beholding such majestic deportment, With body and mind so profoundly tranquil and settled, I am thus caught in a web of doubt;
I pray that you will explain this matter for me."
Do not grow weary now; my mind is entangled in a web of doubt.
What Dharma does your teacher preach?
I pray that you will explain it for me.
Seeing this brahmin, he rose with reverence and asked this question, replying:
"My teacher is of the great clan of the Ikṣvāku lineage; he is the All-Knowing One, unsurpassed, my supreme teacher."
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit said to Upatiṣya: "O worthy one!
I am young in years and my study of the Dharma is but shallow; I have little knowledge and little learning—how could I possibly explain it extensively?"
"I shall now speak briefly for your sake.
At that time, Upatiṣya said to Aśvajit:
"Excellent, Venerable One!"
To speak briefly, as I am now, I do not delight in much talk.
Thus he spoke in verse:
"I take only the True Principle; I do not delight in names and phrases."
"The wise cherish the true meaning; relying on that meaning, I practice.

At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit said to Upatiṣya, "O worthy one, my Great Teacher has taught the Dharma of Dependent Origination and expounded the path to liberation; such is the Dharma spoken by my Teacher in verse."
(The Mahāsāṃghika masters speak thus;
the Kāśyapīya masters, however, speak otherwise.
What is the meaning of this?
“O virtuous one! My Teacher has spoken this verse of the Dharma:
‘All phenomena arise from causes; all phenomena cease because of causes.’”
"Thus regarding cessation and arising, the śramaṇa has spoken thus.
At that time, the parivrājaka Upatiṣya was well-versed in the principles of letters and grammar.
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit was able to understand both the words and their meaning, and he was further able to grasp both the sense and the phrasing; how much more so, then, for others?
“Of all phenomena that arise from causes, those very phenomena cease along with their causes;
the cessation of causal conditions is itself the Path—thus has the Great Teacher taught.

At that time, when Upatiṣya the parivrājaka perceived this course of the Dharma, right there he became free from dust and stainless, exhausting all afflictions and attaining the pure Dharma-eye; he perceived and understood according to reality that all conditioned phenomena possess the nature of cessation.
Just as a clean cloth, free from stains and devoid of black grease, easily takes on dye;
even so, Upatisya the parivrājaka, observing this method of practice, right then and there became free from dust and removed from defilement, until he attained knowledge of things as they truly are.

When that parivrājaka Upatiṣya had thus observed those dharmas as they truly are, attained those dharmas, contemplated those dharmas, entered into those dharmas, and transcended those dharmas, he was no longer ensnared by doubt; the mind of "is" and "is not" was entirely extinguished, and having attained the ground of fearlessness, he no longer followed the teachings of others, but was naturally able to know the Dharma of the Tathāgata for himself.
Then he spoke these verses:
"Such a practice of the Dharma as that which I have attained—
For many kalpas and nayutas of eons, I have never before obtained this Dharma."

At that time, the parivrājaka Upatiṣya, having seen all dharmas, having attained all dharmas, and having attained the arising of wisdom, cast aside his triple staff, adjusted his robes, and approached the venerable Aśvajit. He prostrated at his feet; having paid homage, he rose again, circumambulated him three times to the right, and departed from there to go to the place where Kolita the parivrājaka was.
Having arrived, Kuṇḍadhāna the parivrājaka saw from afar Upatiṣya the parivrājaka, whose face was pure and whose countenance was radiant; having seen him, he said:
"Venerable Upatiṣya the parivrājaka!"
At this moment, your faculties are already purified, your skin is radiant, and your face is clear and bright.
Have you now realized the Deathless?
"Have you perhaps attained the path of the Deathless?
Then the parivrājaka Upatiṣya said to the parivrājaka Kolita:
"O worthy one!"
"I have encountered the supreme Dharma of the Deathless and attained the path to the Deathless.
Then Kuḍṛṭa replied to him,
"O Noble One!..."
"From whom did you obtain such nectar?
Then the parivrājaka Upatiṣya replied,
"O worthy one!"
"I obtained it from that Great Śramaṇa.
Kūṭadanta Pāyāsika spoke again:
"Venerable sir!"
"What matters does that great śramaṇa teach?
What Dharma does he discourse upon?
How have you now attained the supreme path of the nectar of immortality?"
At that time, Upatisya the parivrājaka spoke these verses to Kolita the parivrājaka:
“Whatever phenomena arise from causes, Those phenomena cease according to those causes.
The cessation of causes and conditions is the Path; Thus has the Great Teacher taught.”

At that time, having heard these verses, Kolita the parivrājaka immediately, in that very place, distanced himself from dust and left behind defilement; he exhausted all afflictions and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. He realized that all conditioned phenomena possess the characteristic of cessation, knowing them as they truly are and understanding them as they truly are.
It is like a clean cloth that is free from stains and devoid of black grime, easily taking on dye.
Having thus observed and known it as it truly is, he spoke these verses:
"Such is this practice of the Dharma, Just as I have now attained it."
"For many kalpas and nayutas, you have never before attained this Dharma.
Then, Kauṇḍinya addressed Upatiṣya the parivrājaka again in verse:
"Because you have encountered the nectar of immortality, your face and eyes are pure and radiant."
"You have praised and spoken of this Dharma; having heard it, one attains the pure eye.
At that time, Kauṇḍinya said to the parivrājaka Upatiṣya:
"Excellent, O worthy one!"
"Hurry, hurry! You should go from here to the Great Śramaṇa; you must practice the holy life there.
That Blessed Buddha is my teacher. Then, the parivrājaka Upatiṣya said to Kolita:
“O Benevolent One!
Today we must not let our gratitude go unrequited; we should go to our original teacher, Sañjaya. Why is this?
"He has done much for us and previously bestowed great kindness upon us; he rescued us and enabled us to go forth into homelessness. We ought to go and see him."
Furthermore, there are five hundred followers and associates who rely upon us and practice the Dharma;
we must inform them, and if they give their approval, we shall practice together as well.
At that time, Upatiṣya the parivrājaka, together with Kolita the parivrājaka, went to their teacher Sañjayin the parivrājaka; having arrived, they said to him:
"Excellent, O worthy one!"
"We now wish to go to the Great Śramaṇa, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Then, Sañjaya the Parivrājaka said to Upatiṣya the Parivrājaka and the others:
"O worthy ones!"
"You must not go there; I shall join you all in instructing and training this assembly.
A second time, Upatiṣya the parivrājaka spoke again to Sañjayin the parivrājaka, saying:
"Excellent, worthy sir!"
"We wish to go to the Great Śramaṇa, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Then, Sañjaya the Parivrājaka spoke again to Upatiṣya the Parivrājaka and the others, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
Do not go to that place; these disciples are entrusted to you. As for me, I shall now go alone to a secluded spot to indulge my desires without interference.
Thus, for the third time, Upatisya the parivrājaka, together with Kolita the parivrājaka and others, said to Sañjaya the parivrājaka:
"We do not wish to have these people as our disciples; we only wish to go quickly to that teacher, the Great Śramaṇa, and practice the holy life there."
"That great śramaṇa is my World-Honored One; he is my teacher.
Having spoken these words, he turned his back on Sañjaya right there and departed, never to return.
At that time, those five hundred followers of the Pāṣaṇḍika heretics had this thought:

"These two, Upatiṣya and Kolita, are both highly learned and knowledgeable, intelligent and discerning; yet we have spent many years laboring with diligent effort to study and recite the arts, incantations, and other such matters."
However, these two individuals, throughout seven days and seven nights, attained complete mastery.
They are not ordinary persons; such as they ought to understand how to seek the state of excellence.
If he seeks that which I also seek; if he practices those dharmas that I also shall practice; and if he cultivates that holy life (brahmacarya) that I also shall cultivate.
Having reflected thus, he immediately followed him.
Then, Sañjaya the Parivrājaka addressed that great assembly, saying:
"O you people!..."
"Do not go! Do not go!
Although he spoke these words to stop him, he could not detain or obstruct him, and so [the monk] departed.
At that time, Sañjaya the Parivrājaka thought to himself:
"This great assembly will surely abandon me now.

Because of this cause and condition of being forsaken by the assembly, he was overcome with great anguish and distress; immediately, he vomited a great quantity of hot blood from his mouth and passed away.
At that time, Upatisya the parivrājaka, together with Kolita the parivrājaka, leading five hundred followers, went to the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
You should be well aware of the proper time; within this courtyard, you must prepare clean seats."
Those bhikṣus replied to the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Indeed, we shall receive your instruction.”
Then the bhikṣus immediately prepared a pure seat for the World-Honored One within that courtyard, and the World-Honored One sat upon that seat.

At that time, the Elder Kauṇḍinya saw from afar those two, Upatisya and Kolita, surrounded on all sides by their assembly of non-Buddhist followers as they were approaching; he then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

Now these two, the wanderers Upatisya and Kolita, possess great skill and are widely learned and knowledgeable; regarding all paths and arts, they are free from the net of doubt, and their fame has spread far and wide throughout the four quarters.
"If they have now come before the World-Honored One, it is my opinion that, having measured these two men, they have surely come desiring to debate with the Buddha.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed the Elder Kauṇḍinya, saying: "Kauṇḍinya! You..."
"I now know the minds of those two men; they have come seeking victory, not for the sake of debate.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing from afar the circumstances of those two wandering mendicants, Upatisya and Kolita, spoke these verses:
"To see the noble ones is joy; To dwell together with them is likewise joy."
"Not seeing the multitude of deluded ones—this is what is called 'eternal bliss.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"O you bhikṣus!..."
“Did you see these two parivrājakas, one named Upatiṣya and the other named Kolita?
Then the bhikṣus replied to the Buddha, “We saw them.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha again addressed those bhikṣus, saying: “You bhikṣus!
Now these two individuals are each foremost among my śrāvaka disciples:
one is foremost in wisdom, and the other is foremost in supernormal powers.
And he spoke these verses:
"Seeing those two approaching from afar, surrounded by disciples and their retinue,
the Honored One with the Voice of Cloud-Thunder addressed the bhikṣus:"
"These two individuals, born as non-Buddhists, have now come to where my great assembly resides.
You bhikṣus should know: one is preeminent in wisdom, while the other is foremost in supernormal powers."
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
Among all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the entire past, there was none superior within this assembly of śrāvakas; nor will there be any such among those of the future."
Now these two shall likewise be so. O bhikṣus!
In future ages, among all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, there will be none superior to me regarding this pair of śrāvaka disciples.
"O bhikṣus! You may also prepare a seat; you should have him sit there.
And so it was said in verse:

"The two Bull-Kings have attained profound wisdom; having already abandoned all false paths, though they have not yet reached this great forest, the World-Honored One has bestowed a prediction of their future attainment upon them from afar."

Then the two men gradually approached, intending to reach that grove; seeing from afar the Elder Aśvajit walking to and fro while looking at the ground beneath a tree, they went to where he was, and having arrived, prostrated themselves and stood to one side.
Then Kauṇḍinya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!

How is it that these Upatisya and Kolita, who have abandoned their superior births, their lives of luxury, and their state of great learning, have now conceived the most supreme resolve, yet toward the Elder Aśvajit they have conceived the lowest of resolves?”
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed the Elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya:

"One who possesses wisdom, wherever that wisdom is attained, always gives rise to gratitude, maintaining mindfulness without forgetting it. If one receives even a small kindness, one constantly remembers it without loss; how much more so when the kindness is great?"
Kauṇḍinya! These Upatisya, Kolita, and their companions attained the purity of the Dharma-eye at Āśvapuyujita.
For this reason, he spoke these verses of Dharma:
"Regarding the Dharma taught by all Buddhas, whoever listens to it and understands it,
will give rise to reverence in that place, just as a brahmin tends to his sacred fire."
At that time, Upatisya the parivrājaka and his fellow parivrājakas went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt on their right knees, and said:
“Excellent!
World-Honored One!
We now wish to leave the household life and practice the Way before the World-Honored One.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will grant us this favor!
"Grant me permission to go forth and receive full ordination.
The Buddha said to him,
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!"
"Now that you have entered into my Dharma of self-realization and practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) in order to bring an end to all suffering.

Having spoken these words, those bhikṣus spontaneously had the three robes appear upon their bodies and each took up an earthen bowl; their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, appearing as if they were young boys who had first had their hair shaved seven days prior.
At that time, the elders immediately became ordained monks and were fully endowed with the multitude of precepts.
Then, the elder Upatiṣya sat on the Buddha’s right side, and the elder Kolita sat on the Buddha’s left side, each seated to one side.

However, from the time the Elder Upatiṣya went forth until only half a month had passed, he exhausted all fetters and outflows, manifested supernormal powers, attained the perfection of the knowledge of supernormal powers, and realized the fruit of Arhatship.

At that time, after staying for only seven days, Kūṭadanta exhausted all his fetters and outflows; he manifested supernormal powers, attained the perfection of the knowledge of supernormal powers, and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, the elder Upatiṣya, Kolita, and their followers gradually became five hundred in number; they all went forth from the household life and received full ordination.

At that time, the elder Upatisya’s mother was named Śārī (in the Sui language, "myna"); for this reason, he was called Śāriputra by the world—*putra* meaning "son" in the Sui language. As for the elder Maudgalyāyana, that was his clan name; for this reason, he was called Maudgalyāyana by the world.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One bestowed this prediction upon them, saying: "O bhikṣus!
Among my śrāvaka disciples, Śāriputra is foremost as one of great wisdom."
"Among those with supernormal powers, Maudgalyāyana is the foremost.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
What roots of goodness did those elders Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others plant in the past?
By virtue of what causes and conditions have they now been able to leave the household life, become fully endowed with the various precepts, and realize the fruit of arhatship?
The World-Honored One further declared:
"Among the śrāvakas of great wisdom, Śāriputra is supreme; among those with supernormal powers, Maudgalyāyana is the foremost.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

“O bhikṣus! I recall that in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there were two people: one was a brother and the other was a sister. The brother was named Subhūti (in the language of Sui, ‘Good Love’), and the sister was also named Subhūti.”
At that time, her elder brother, Shan'ai, left his home to become a renunciant; having done so, he immediately attained the path of a Pratyekabuddha.
Her younger sister, Shan'ai, went forth among the Parivrājaka non-Buddhist practitioners to study the Way.

At one time, his elder brother, the Venerable Prabhāsa, a Pratyekabuddha, went to the place where his sister, the heretic Prabhāvatī, was staying; having arrived there, he spread out a seat and sat down.

Her younger sister, Shan’ai (Subhadrā), prepared various delicacies and provisions for food; she personally served them with her own hands until he was fully satiated. When the meal was finished, she further took a knife and a needle and offered them to her elder brother, the Pratyekabuddha.
When that pratyekabuddha had finished eating, he took the knife and needle given as an offering by his sister Supriyā and flew away before her very eyes.

Her younger sister, Suvatsā, saw with her own eyes that venerable Pratyekabuddha soaring through the air; filled with such joy and exultation that it pervaded her entire body and mind, she could not contain herself and joined her ten fingers in palms-together salutation.
From afar, he paid respectful homage to that Pratyekabuddha and immediately made this vow:

"May I, in the future, encounter such a teacher as this one or even one superior to him; may I swiftly attain realization of the Dharma he teaches; may I not be born in the evil realms; and just as a sharp sword cuts through whatever it strikes, by the causal karma of this severing, may all my afflictions in future lives be utterly severed and destroyed."
"Furthermore, just as this needle can pierce through everything, may it enable me to thoroughly penetrate all afflictions in future lives. O bhikṣus!
At that time, was the non-Buddhist wanderer (parivrājaka) named Subhadra, who gave the pratyekabuddha a knife and a needle, anyone else?
He was none other than the bhikṣu Śāriputra.
"Furthermore, monks!
I recall that in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a merchant who constantly went out to the great ocean to catch conch shells for sale.
At that time, the merchant thought to himself:
"The work I have done until now to seek wealth for my own livelihood is a source of great suffering; today, I ought to perform meritorious deeds that will serve as causes for future lives."
At that time, there was a pratyekabuddha dwelling near the city of Vārāṇasī.

When the sun was in the east, during the early morning hours, the pratyekabuddha put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Vārāṇasī to beg for food from house to house within the city.

The conch-shell merchant saw from afar the arrival of the Venerable Pratyekabuddha, whose deportment was dignified and orderly, and whose movements were steady and composed; with a serene countenance and level gaze, he beheld him. Having seen this, his mind attained purity, and he immediately paid homage, inviting the Pratyekabuddha to his home, where he honored and made offerings to him, providing various delicacies and supplying all that was needed.

When the Pratyekabuddha had finished receiving the food offered by him, the Pratyekabuddha, as is the nature of such beings, did not preach the Dharma; he transformed sentient beings solely through his supernormal powers, and not by means of any other method.
When the Pratyekabuddha had finished receiving the food and other necessities provided by the merchant, out of compassion for him, he immediately soared from that place into the air.

At that time, the merchant, seeing from afar with his own eyes the Pratyekabuddha soaring through the air, was filled with such joy and exultation that it pervaded his entire body and mind; unable to contain himself, he joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation and prostrated from a distance toward the Pratyekabuddha, making this aspiration:

"May I, in the future, encounter this Teacher or one even more sublime, and may I swiftly comprehend the Dharma he preaches. In every place of rebirth, may I never fall into the evil realms. May I also attain what he has attained, becoming like this Noble One who flies through the air; may I likewise be so in the future."
"O bhikṣus! What do you think?
Was the person at that time who captured and sold snails for his livelihood, yet later made offerings to a pratyekabuddha, anyone other than this very person?"
"This is none other than the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana. "O bhikṣus!

Because these Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana planted those various roots of goodness in the past, they have now been able to leave the household life and realize the fruit of arhatship; I further bestow upon them this prediction:"
"Among my śrāvaka disciples, Śāriputra is the foremost in wisdom;
Maudgalyāyana is the foremost in supernormal powers.

At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!

How is it that Śāriputra was able to transform these five hundred parivrājaka disciples of Sañjayin—who had already fallen into the wilderness of false views and were practicing perverted conduct—and lead them to the presence of the Buddha? Having seen them, how did the Buddha teach them to abandon the wilderness of false views and its perilous difficulties, so that they might attain liberation from all suffering?”
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: “Bhikṣus!

This Śāriputra has not only today led five hundred disciples of Sañjaya, the parivrājakas, who had fallen into the vast wilderness of great false views and were practicing in delusion, back to my presence, enabling them to escape those false views, delusions, and inversions, and attain liberation from suffering and distress.”

In the past as well, he was leading these five hundred people when they fell into peril; at that time, Śāriputra also guided them to come to me, and I, at that moment, rescued them from their distress and freed them from all suffering.
The bhikṣus said:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain it for us."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"I recall that in the past there was a horse-king named Kiṃpila. His appearance was upright and handsome; his body was pure white, like crystal or snow, and like white silver. He was like the full, clear moon or like a *kuṇḍa* flower; his head was deep blue, he ran as fast as the wind, and his voice was like a wondrous drum."
At that time, there were five hundred merchants in Jambudvīpa.
Those merchants, wishing to enter the great ocean, prepared their provisions and took three hundred million pieces of various merchandise;

"Having already delivered Vatsa and the others, whom will you take now?
To those who speak thus, you should answer with this verse:
"The World-Honored One, the Great Being, takes people away in accordance with the Dharma."
"Since there is such practice in accordance with the Dharma, how could a wise person go against it?

At that time, when those bhikṣus, at the break of dawn while the sun was in the east, put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms, all who saw them spoke this verse and said to one another:
"This great śramaṇa has returned; having crossed the Southern Mountains, he has come here."
"Having already delivered Vāśa and the others, whom will he take away now?
At that time, the bhikṣus replied to the people with those very verses.
At that time, having heard these verses, those people reflected:
"In all cases where the śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, delivers people, he teaches them to practice according to the Dharma, not otherwise."
Therefore, this sound lasted for seven days; once the seven days had passed, it was entirely extinguished, and from that point on, it could no longer be heard anywhere.

Chapter Fifty-two: On the Rituals for Preaching the Dharma. In the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*, Chapter Fifty-two, Part One: At that time, there were also many non-Buddhist wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) who would regularly assemble every five days to preach the Dharma to others, and great crowds would gather to go to them and listen to their teachings.
For these reasons, the various non-Buddhist practitioners, such as the Pārivrajakas, obtained great offerings, honor, and respect.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha in the great city of Rājagṛha conceived deep and correct faith in the Buddha’s Dharma and thought to himself:
"Now these non-Buddhist Pārivrajakas gather constantly every five days to preach the Dharma to others; many people go there to listen and receive it."
For these reasons, the various non-Buddhist practitioners have gained great gains and offerings, and are held in high esteem, honored, and venerated by the world.
Now, I too shall assemble the various teachers and urge them to preach the Dharma every five days; I should personally attend those great assemblies.
Within that great assembly, when they see me arrive, all the people should gather together.
By such causes and conditions, my teacher shall obtain great offerings and be held in high esteem by the world.
Having reflected thus, he went to where the Buddha was and reported this matter in detail.
At that time, the World-Honored One, prompted by this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"You bhikṣus!..."
"I have now granted permission for you all to assemble in a great gathering every five days to preach the Dharma to others and discuss the meaning of the Dharma.
Then the bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
"World-Honored One!"
"What dharmas should be taught?
What dharmas should not be taught?
When the bhikṣus had asked this question, the Buddha addressed the great assembly of bhikṣus, saying:
"O you bhikṣus!

I have now agreed that every five days we shall assemble among ourselves to praise the virtues of the Buddha, the virtues of the Dharma, the virtues of the Saṅgha, and the virtues of faith; and so on, in brief, to praise the virtues of ethical conduct and extensive learning, to praise the practice of giving, the practice of wisdom, the practice of contentment, and the practice of few desires; to praise the discourse on the dhūta ascetic practices, to praise dwelling in seclusion away from villages and towns, to praise the practice of sublime conduct, to praise beneficial deeds, to praise the practice of diligence, to praise making offerings to parents and elders, to praise making offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, to praise making offerings to all spiritual friends, to praise the speaking of wholesome words, and to praise those who have tamed the gates of their sense faculties.

He praised those who moderate their food and drink; he praised those who reduce sleep during the first and last watches of the night; he praised the arising of right mindfulness; and he praised the practice of respectful service.
Praising the signs [of the Buddha] and inquiring about them; praising hearing and thereby attaining realization;

praising receiving the teacher’s instruction without contravening it and practicing it after having heard it; praising being able to possess correct knowledge after hearing the Dharma; and praising hearing the True Dharma and acting in accordance with that Dharma.

He praised the recollection of the Buddha, praised the recollection of the Dharma, praised the recollection of the Saṅgha, praised the recollection of the devas, praised the recollection of generosity, praised the recollection of cessation, and praised the recollection of ānāpāna.

He praised the mindfulness of the body, extolling the constant contemplation of the visualization of impurity; he praised the mindfulness of the perception of death, and praised the mindfulness that regards food as impure.

He extolled the perception of the world’s lack of delight, praised the perception of impermanence, praised the perceptions of suffering and emptiness, praised the perception of non-self, and extolled the perception of cessation, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of extinction.

Furthermore, he praised the contemplation of white bones, praised the contemplation of detached bones, praised the contemplation of bloated corpses, praised the contemplation of decaying corpses, praised the contemplation of half-eaten corpses, praised the contemplation of scattered corpses, praised the contemplation of half-burnt corpses, praised the contemplation of burnt and reddened corpses, and praised the contemplation of loathsome corpses.

One should also praise the mindfulness of all merits; one should also praise the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, and the seven factors of enlightenment; one should praise the doors of liberation and the various factors conducive to liberation; one should praise the eight bases of mastery and praise the three types of supernormal knowledge; and one should also praise and speak of the merits of the six superknowledges.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume 49 and Volume 50,
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on the Ritual for Preaching the Dharma, Part Two.
At that time, the bhikṣus had this thought:

“The Tathāgata has already granted permission for us to assemble in a great assembly every five days; we ought to extol and proclaim the merits of all Buddhas, and even praise and proclaim the merits of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and so forth.”
Those bhikṣus then gathered together every five days and, raising their voices in unison, praised the Buddha’s merits, even extolling such qualities as the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
At that time, people came from all directions to listen to the Dharma; meanwhile, there arose discussions and criticisms, and they spoke thus:
"How is it that our various teachers all utter the same sound when preaching the Dharma?"
"It is just like a group of young children who have not yet learned; when they chant together, there is no difference between them.
At that time, having heard these people speaking with such disparagement of the Way, the bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was and reported the matter as described above.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying these words: “Bhikṣus!

From this day forward, I establish a rule for my disciples: you must not praise the meaning of the Dharma with a single voice; rather, you should only invite those possessed of eloquence who are capable of expounding the Dharma.”

At that time, some bhikṣus invited those whose faculties were dull and obscured, who were deficient and leaking, and who were not complete in their observance of the precepts, to expound the Dharma. Consequently, the multitude further reviled them, speaking in various ways with displeasure, saying aloud:
"If even these teachers act in such a manner, how much more so those who are not teachers?"
At that time, having heard of this matter, the bhikṣus went in full to inform the Buddha.
Then the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: “O bhikṣus!

From this day forward, I decree for my disciples that they must not request those who are dull-witted and of obscured faculties, nor those whose precepts are deficient or incomplete, to preach the Dharma to them.
"From this day forward, if you are invited to preach the Dharma, you should invite those who are endowed with wondrous conduct and have achieved excellence among the assembly.
The Buddha further proclaimed this regulation:

"One should carefully select those who possess eloquence and knowledge of the Dharma, who are well-versed in the sequential and traditional exegesis of the Āgamas, and invite them to preach the Dharma—indeed, those within the assembly who understand the Āgamas most thoroughly."
The Buddha again addressed those bhikṣus, saying:

"It is not only those who understand the Āgama sūtras who must be requested to preach the Dharma; furthermore, those who understand the Sūtras as well as the Mātaṅga [texts], such persons should be requested to preach the Dharma for the assembly."

If, within the great assembly, there are bhikṣus who understand the Sūtras, understand the Vinaya, and understand the Matanga [Sūtra], and who, moreover, should be selected for their clarity of diction and their complete mastery of eloquence.

Furthermore, among the monks present in this assembly, those who have a thorough understanding of the written word, possess clear eloquence, and are fully endowed with these qualities—I shall now permit such monks to be appointed from the lower seats in due order to preach the Dharma for the sake of the community.

If the first one becomes exhausted, invite a second; if the second becomes exhausted, invite a third; if the third becomes exhausted, invite a fourth; if the fourth becomes exhausted, invite a fifth; and so on, until as many capable preachers of the Dharma as there may be have been invited in succession to preach the Dharma for the assembly.
There are bhikṣus who, when preaching the Dharma in the open air, suffer from either cold or heat; I permit the construction of a hall for them to preach the Dharma beneath.
Even if there is a hall, if it lacks four walls and is exposed, wind may blow dust and grass that defile the bhikṣus; I now authorize the erection of four walls to screen out such dust and grass.
At that time, when the bhikṣus were in the Dharma-hall, if the ground was uneven, they should use various kinds of hemp or grass, and apply mud to the floor to make it clean and level.
At that time, after the bhikṣus had finished plastering the earthen floor of the Dharma hall, they recited, practiced walking meditation, and soiled their feet with dust while in the hall;
[the Buddha] permitted the bhikṣus that they ought to wash their feet.
At that time, because the bhikṣus washed their feet repeatedly and their feet were sore, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"One should sprinkle fragrant water upon the ground to settle the dust."
Once the dust had been removed, the ground became dry and once again soiled their feet. Thereupon, the Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall permit you to smear the floor of the hall with cow dung mixed with scented water."
At that time, the water dried up and the cow dung crumbled away, so his feet were once again soiled.
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should take soft grass or perhaps hemp and other such materials to spread upon the ground."
At that time, the multitude, seeing that Dharma Master possessed such eloquence and was able to expound the Dharma so skillfully, immediately took fragrant flowers and scattered them over him.
However, the bhikṣus did not accept his teaching and instead gave rise to feelings of weariness and detachment.
Why is this? Because the Buddha has prohibited it, those who have left the household life must not carry or possess ointments, powdered incense, or various garlands of fragrant flowers.
When people heard of and saw this matter, they spoke in disparagement, saying:
"These bhikṣus, even with such offerings, are still unable to receive them; how much less so those who are superior?
Then, the bhikṣus went to the Buddha and reported these matters in full.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!

If there are lay donors who, with a joyful heart and for the sake of auspiciousness, take various kinds of incense, flowers, ointments, powdered incense, and floral garlands, and scatter them over the Dharma Master, you should accept them."
At that time, the lay donors and patrons brought various kinds of wealth, treasures, and monastic robes to offer to the Dharma Master.
These bhikṣus, filled with fear and shame, would not accept those things.
The people of the world speak disparagingly, saying:
"These śramaṇas, these sons of the Śākyas, cannot even bear such trifling things; how much less could they bear anything superior?"
At that time, having heard these matters, the bhikṣus went in full to inform the Buddha.
Then the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
If there are laypeople who offer various wealth, robes, and other items to a Dharma teacher for the sake of joy, I permit such giving;
if the teacher has need of them, I allow him to accept and take them;
if he does not have need of them, I permit him to return them.

At that time, when the Dharma was being taught, many of the bhikṣus took up large sections of the texts for recitation from memory; some could not complete them even after a month and wished to stop, while others, out of fear and shame, wished to recite them through to the end, yet their bodies and minds were utterly exhausted.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the Buddha.
Then, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"When preaching the Dharma to the assembly, you should know the proper time."
At that time, while the bhikṣus were preaching the Dharma, they expounded the meaning of the teachings with subtle and wondrous voices.
Then, there was a bhikṣu who, being terrified and ashamed, reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I now permit you to expound the Dharma with subtle and wondrous sounds.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus took up the essential meanings and flavors from various sūtras and explained them to others, not following the sequential order.
At that time, the bhikṣus, feeling shame and fear, and apprehensive that they might contravene the Sūtras and Vinaya, reported the matter to the Buddha in full detail.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"I permit you to select the essential meanings from among the various sūtras as convenient, and to arrange the phrasing and sentences to preach the Dharma for others; however, take only the central meaning and do not distort the original text of the sūtra."

Thereupon, when the Dharma Master preached the Dharma, the assembly gathered so densely that his voice could not be heard clearly, and he was unable to cause the multitude to feel affection, joy, and delight.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"I have now granted permission: within the great assembly, a high seat should be prepared; you should invite the Dharma Master to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma, so that the entire assembly may hear it."
On another occasion, when the assembly gathered, the crowd was even greater, yet the voices of the masters preaching the Dharma still could not reach everyone.
At that time, the bhikṣus again went to inform the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You must prepare a higher seat, double the previous size, so that the preacher may ascend it.
At that moment, the great assembly increased even further, yet the sound still did not reach them all.
Then the bhikṣus went again to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I have already granted permission: a bhikṣu may preach the Dharma while standing or walking, as circumstances permit."
At that time, the bhikṣus gathered within a single hall. There were two bhikṣus who were expounding the Dharma, and because they obstructed one another, they then constructed two halls.

Within those two halls, each preached the Dharma separately, yet they still obstructed one another; they led bhikṣus from this hall to that hall, and at the location of that hall, there were other bhikṣus who, in turn, invited and received them to come to this hall. Thus, they came and went in such a confused jumble that the assembly was thrown into disorder, and people either left or arrived, causing the Dharma activities to be interrupted.
Furthermore, some bhikṣus took no pleasure in hearing the exposition of this Dharma gate.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha in full detail. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, two persons shall not preach the Dharma in the same hall. Furthermore, two halls shall not be so close together as to cause their voices to overlap and interfere with one another. Nor shall those from one assembly go to another assembly, nor those from one group go to another group. Moreover, you must not increase the gates of unwholesome dharmas or take no pleasure in hearing the teaching; if anyone shows hatred or aversion toward it, they must be dealt with according to the Dharma."
At that time, there was no Dharma teacher among the assembly, so the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha in full detail.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If there is no Dharma teacher, you should invite one who can recite [the sūtras] to ascend the seat and recite them."
At that time, there was no one among the assembly who could recite the scriptures, so the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha in full.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"I now authorize you to recite them in succession; you may appoint those from the senior seats to recite in order, or appoint those from the junior seats to recite in order, even down to the recitation of a single four-line verse."
At that time, when the Dharma masters recited the sutras, they spoke of the Dharma as if it were secular songs; therefore, people disparaged and ridiculed them, saying:
"This way of preaching the Dharma is no different from the singing and chanting of us worldly people."
"How can a shramana with a shaved head preach the Dharma as if singing songs?
When the bhiksus heard these words, they reported the matter in full to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If there is a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma by relying on worldly songs and chants, there are five faults.
What are these five?
First, one becomes personally attached to the sound of the song;
second, others who hear it become attached without grasping its meaning;
third, by the emergence and submergence of the sounds, one loses the textual phrases.
Fourth, when worldly people hear of this, they will revile and disparage it;
fifth, when people of future generations hear of this matter, they will immediately follow worldly conduct and take it as their constant standard.
If there is a bhikṣu who relies upon secular songs to preach the Dharma, there are these five faults; therefore, one must not rely on secular songs and chants to preach the Dharma.
"O bhikṣus! Those among you who have not yet understood the aforementioned Dharma, whenever they dwell or travel, should first consult their upādhyāyas, ācāryas, and others."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who wished to travel to another city, town, or village. Then his upādhyāya, ācārya, and others said to that bhikṣu:
"In this manner, Elder!..."
"You need not go.
At that time, the bhikṣu did not heed these words and proceeded on his way.

On the road, he encountered bandits who seized him; they beat and trampled him with their hands and feet until he was grievously distressed, leaving him with nothing but the breath of life. They plundered his robes and bowl, and only then released him.
Then that bhikṣu, having returned to the saṃghārāma, informed the other bhikṣus and related this matter in detail.
At that time, the bhikṣus brought this report to the Buddha.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One summoned the assembly of monks and addressed them, saying: "O bhikṣus!
Did your upādhyāyas and ācāryas truly not permit you to travel to distant villages?"
At that time, the bhikṣus replied, “It is so;
indeed, it was not permitted.
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should all know that this was improper!
Since your preceptors and ācāryas did not grant permission, why did you go to another village on your own authority?
“O Bhikṣus! [the Buddha said.]
There is a cause and condition for this. Why is that?
I recall that in the past, within this Jambudvīpa, there were five hundred merchants. Among these merchants was a caravan leader named Maitreya, who served as their foremost guide.
Then all the merchants gathered together and deliberated among themselves, saying:
"We should now prepare provisions and the equipment for entering the sea, and go to that great ocean to seek wealth; we shall surely obtain various kinds of rare treasures and return to our homes."

These so-called mani-jewels, pearls, jade, coral, gold, and silver—such treasures as these have made our families immensely wealthy for seven generations; they have provided the means for our sustenance and the support of our kin, establishing a vast foundation of property.

"At that time, those five hundred merchants prepared all their requirements for entering the sea. They possessed three million [units] of goods; they set aside one million for provisions and supplies for the journey, gave another million to those merchants as capital stock, and reserved the third million for the repair of the ships and the wages of the shipmasters."

Having prepared these things, each person settled their mind and received the eightfold precepts of the fast; having received the fast, they each returned to their own homes and took leave of their parents, wives, children, and kinsmen.
At that time, Maitreya went to his mother’s quarters and consulted her in detail on this matter.
His mother was then on the upper terrace of the pavilion, having recently washed and combed her hair; she was observing the eightfold fast and maintaining a state of dharma and tranquility.
At that time, Maitreya went before his mother and spoke these words:
"Excellent, my parents!
I wish to enter the sea to seek various treasures; having reached that place, I shall return bringing all manner of goods."

That is to say, regarding mani-jewels, pearls, crystal, and even gold and silver: I wish for these treasures to remain in my household for seven generations, so that our resources may be inexhaustible and we may possess abundant wealth, thereby supporting our parents and our wives and children, while also using them for almsgiving and performing various meritorious deeds.
At that time, the mother of the merchant leader Maitreya said to him:
"My son, why must you now enter the great ocean?

Within your home, you are currently very wealthy and prosperous, with all necessities fully provided; there is nothing lacking for whatever may be required. For seven generations, it has been sufficient to sustain us and provide offerings, while also allowing you to practice generosity and perform various meritorious deeds."
Beloved son, beloved son!
Within the great ocean there are many terrors, namely the perils of surging waves and fierce winds, the fear of being bound by the makara fish and the sea deities, and the fear of rākṣasī women.
"O Compassionate Beloved Son!
The great ocean is full of such perils as these.

I am now old, and my decline has reached its twilight; if you, my beloved son, depart, it will be truly difficult for us to meet again. Although I still have a small remnant of life, the day of my death is very near."
Thus he spoke with earnest and urgent words a second and a third time.
Then Maitreya addressed his mother once more, saying:
"Excellent, O Mother!"

"I shall certainly go to the sea for the sake of seeking wealth; having reached that place and obtained various treasures, I hope to return with them—namely, mani-jewels, pearls, and even gold and silver—to bring back as offerings for my parents and teachers, to practice the giving of alms, and to extensively cultivate merit."
Having spoken these words, he was about to set out.
At that time, the mother of the merchant leader Maitreya rose from her seat, took hold of Maitreya, and said to him:
"My beloved son, Maitreya!"
"I do not permit you to go to the great ocean to seek wealth.
Why is this? Within my home now, there is abundant wealth and property; we lack for nothing."
At that time, Maitreya thought to himself:
"My mother now takes no pleasure in my benefit but intends my ruin; today she once again refuses to allow me to go to sea to seek wealth. Today, disaster and failure will surely befall me."

Due to these causes and conditions, he gave rise to anger; he then threw his mother to the ground, struck her on the head, and immediately left the house. Together with the merchants, he traveled until they reached the seashore.

Having reached the sea, they made offerings to the sea deity and prepared the ships. They hired five additional men for three times the usual wage; these five were known as the helmsman, the oarsman, the bailer, the diver, and the navigator. Having deliberated on what was appropriate, they boarded the vessels and entered the great ocean in search of wealth.
When those people reached the middle of the sea, their ship was wrecked; all five hundred merchants perished in the water, and only the compassionate merchant leader alone survived.

At that time, Maitreya caught a single plank from that wrecked ship; relying upon it, he moved his hands and feet, exerting all his physical strength, and driven by the force of the wind, he was carried across the ocean waves and landed on an island called Viśvabhūti-deva (translated in the Sui language as "The Island of Transformation").
At that time, Maitreya remained on that transformed island, sustaining his life for a short while by eating various fruits and medicinal herbs.

Later, as Maitreya wandered across the island, he reached its southern edge and saw a path; following that road, he traveled until he reached a low-lying ground, where he gazed afar and beheld a city of silver. That city was delightful, exquisite, and rare, such that those who beheld it could never tire of looking.

There were watchtowers and battlements for repelling the enemy, surrounded by moats and ditches; there were celestial railings and various jeweled palaces, as well as terraces, halls, and residences with projecting beams and galleries, all covered above with jeweled canopies and adorned with every kind of precious gem.
Various banners and canopies were suspended, and precious pillars were erected; incense tables and censers were set out, burning all manner of exquisite fragrances.

Surrounding the city were various gardens, groves, springs, ponds, and channels, all fully providing places for enjoyment. In the very center of that city stood a precious palace named "Joyful Delight" (*Nandana*); this palace was subtle and wondrous, composed of the seven treasures, namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, amber, and pearls.

At that time, four women emerged from the city; they were upright and lovely, such that onlookers could never tire of beholding them. Most excellent and most wonderful, their bodies were adorned with various necklaces and ornaments. They approached the Compassionate One and addressed him, saying:
"Welcome, O Compassionate One!"
How were you able to venture here to this city?
This city has no ruler; it is replete with all manner of things and lacks for nothing. Within this city, there is a jeweled palace named *Nandana* (Joy), composed of the seven precious gems.

We four daughters reside within this palace; rising early and retiring late, our intentions are pure, our speech is upright and kind, our appearance is graceful and charming, and our voices are harmonious and elegant.

Therefore, you may now enter this city, ascend the jeweled palace, and enjoy yourselves together; in a place where there are no men, you may experience sensual pleasures together, acting in harmony and dwelling there as you please.
"We shall provide you with all things and serve and honor you.

At that time, Maitreya entered the city and went to the Palace of Jewels where there were no men; together with those four women, he enjoyed himself at will with the pleasures of the five senses for several years, several hundred years, and even several thousand years, indulging his desires in delight.
At a later time, those four women said to the Compassionate One:
"Excellent, Noble Son!
You should remain here and not go toward other cities."
At that time, Maitreya immediately gave rise to doubt and uncertainty:
"How is it that this woman says to me:
'Noble son, you should now dwell in this city and not go toward any other city'?"

"I shall now secretly contravene this woman's wishes; while she sleeps, I will take this path to another place and travel east and west to investigate for myself, so as to ascertain what has occurred, whether it be good or evil."
"Once you have awakened to this knowledge, you should act in accordance with the Dharma.

At that time, Maitreya, while waiting for the woman to fall into a deep sleep, rose slowly and quietly, descended from the jeweled palace, and walked about. He exited through the eastern gate, circumambulated the city, and having completed the circuit, arrived at the southern side. There he saw a path; he followed it and proceeded forward by degrees.

Then, he again saw from afar a golden city, upright and lovely, extending all around, with various springs, ponds, and channels filled to the brim. Within that city was a jeweled palace named "Ever-Intoxicated," exquisite and beautiful to behold, constructed of the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, and so forth, up to musaragalva and pearls.

At that time, eight women emerged from that city; they were lovely and handsome, most excellent and exquisite, their bodies adorned with various necklaces and ornaments, as they approached the presence of the Compassionate Merchant Leader.
Having arrived, he said:
"Excellent, O Compassionate One!
How have you come from so far?"
Furthermore, Maitreya said:

"This city is entirely constructed of pure gold; all manner of things and resources are fully provided. In the center of the city is a jewel palace named 'Ever-Intoxicated,' made of the seven precious gems. We eight daughters rise early and sleep late."

"Furthermore, Maitreya also entered that city, ascended the jeweled palace, and together with those eight women—in a place where there were no men—he fully enjoyed the pleasures of the five desires and took delight with them."
Having dwelt for several years, or even several hundreds of thousands of years, according to his will,
that woman later addressed the Compassionate One,
saying: "Noble son, O Compassionate One!"
"Do not go from here to another city.

At that time, the Compassionate One was likewise startled and suspicious; he immediately stole out and traveled about, visiting various places, until he saw in the distance a city of crystal, lovely and beautiful, which those who beheld it could never tire of looking upon.
In the center of that city was a jeweled palace named Manojña (The Delightful), subtle and exquisite, constructed from the seven treasures, including gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and even pearls.

At that time, there were sixteen women in that city who came forth from the city; their countenances were so upright and beautiful that onlookers could never tire of beholding them. Adorned with various precious necklaces and ornaments, they likewise addressed Maitreya, saying:
"Welcome, O Maitreya!"
"How could you venture here?
He spoke again:
"O Compassionate One!"

This city is composed entirely of crystal and is replete with all manner of things. In the center of the city stands a jeweled palace named Manojña (The Delightful), which is likewise established from the seven precious gems.
"We sixteen women shall rise early and retire late; please remain as you were requested before.

At that time, Maitreya entered that city and ascended the jeweled palace. Together with the sixteen women, in a place where no men were present, he fully experienced sensual pleasures and enjoyed themselves, passing many years, even hundreds and thousands of years.
At that time, the women spoke again to Maitreya, saying, "Be careful not to go east or west.

Maitreya was also suspicious, so he departed from them and traveled onward. As he proceeded further, he saw in the distance a city of lapis lazuli, lovely and well-proportioned, with solid walls on all four sides, and everywhere filled with springs, ponds, flowing streams, and canals.
"At that time, there was a jeweled palace in that place called Brahma-Virtue (*Brahmaguṇa*), delightful and subtle, composed of the seven precious gems.

Furthermore, thirty-two maidens emerged from the city; they were upright, dignified, and pleasing, such that onlookers could never tire of beholding them. They were exquisite and extraordinary, their bodies adorned with various necklaces and ornaments.
They said to Maitreya: 'Welcome, Noble One!'"
"May you be able to travel far.
He further said,
"O Compassionate One!"

"This city is composed entirely of lapis lazuli and possesses every requisite object. My conduct is pure and free from transgression; I always act only after first offering a formal announcement. My mind is harmonious and kind, and my speech is elegant and refined. I have now come to consult you: I pray that you will enter this city, ascend the jeweled palace, and enjoy ourselves together, fully endowed with the five desires and experiencing pleasure in harmony. Whatever may be required, I shall provide and serve."

At that time, Maitreya entered that city and ascended the jeweled palace; together with those thirty-two women, in a place where no men were present, he fully experienced sensual pleasures for several years, even for several hundreds and thousands of years, dwelling there with a joyful mind.
"At that time, those thirty-two women again addressed the Compassionate One:
'Excellent, Noble Son!
You must now take care not to leave this city and go to another city.'"
At that time, Maitreya again gave rise to doubt and reflected thus:
"How is it that these women speak to me in this way, saying:
'Noble son, take care not to leave this city to go to another city'?"

"I should now wait for the time when the women are asleep, then follow this path and proceed slowly and calmly; whether it turns out well or ill, once I have arrived, I shall know; and having known and seen it, I shall act accordingly."

At that time, Maitrāyaṇī, while those women were fast asleep, rose slowly and quietly, descended from the palace, and departed. She went out through the eastern gate of the city, circled around it, and arrived at the southern side. There she saw a road; having seen it, she proceeded along it. After a short while, she saw in the distance an iron city, with gates on each of its four sides.
At that time, there was not a single person in that city—whether man or woman, boy or girl—who came out to welcome Maitreya; they heard only this sound:
"Who is hungry? Who is thirsty?"
Who is it that is naked?
Who is it that is running in haste?
Who is it that has come from afar and is exhausted by the journey?
"Whose vehicle am I riding?
At that time, the Compassionate One thought to himself:
"I have previously seen a silver city, and within that city, four women came out to welcome me."
Furthermore, when I went to the city of Gold, eight women came out from within that city to welcome me.
On another occasion, when I went to the city of Crystal, sixteen maidens came out to receive me.
At another time in the past, when I encountered the city of Vaiḍūrya, thirty-two women came out to welcome me.
Yet now, in this city, there is not a single person—whether man or woman, boy or girl—who comes to welcome me; I hear only such sounds as these, which are unpleasant to my mind:
"Who is hungry? "Who is thirsty? and so forth.
Who is thirsty? Who is naked?
Who is running in haste?
"Who is it that has come from a distant road, weary with fatigue?
Who is my rider?
Just as I am now, if I were to enter this city, I would immediately know who made this sound.
At that time, Maitreya entered the city; once he had entered, the four gates were immediately closed.
Then Maitreya, his heart filled with fear and the hair on his body standing on end, fled in every direction, saying:
"I am now defeated! I am now ruined!"
As he was fleeing from place to place, he saw a man with an iron wheel upon his head; the wheel was blazing red, resembling a fierce fire, its flames so intense as to be utterly terrifying.
He then went to that place and asked,
"O virtuous one! Who are you?"
"By whom was the wheel upon your head set in motion?
Why is it so fiercely blazing and terrifying, like a mass of fire?
At that time, the sinner replied:
"O virtuous one! Do you know me?
I am a merchant leader named Gopīta."
At that time, Maitreya asked him again:
"What sinful karma did you commit in the past?
By reason of having created those causes and conditions for sinful karma, this iron wheel—so fiercely blazing and so intensely hot—revolves above your head."
That person replied:

"In days past, out of anger, I struck and trampled my mother's head. Due to the causal conditions of such karmic offenses, I now endure this great iron wheel—so fiercely blazing and so brilliantly flaming—which revolves above my head."
At that time, Maitrī, having heard these words, wept and wailed piteously; she repented and reproached herself, reflecting upon her own karma, and spoke these words:
"Now I am imprisoned, like a deer caught in a cage."
“At that time, there was a yakṣa in that city who guarded it by name of Bhalluka; he was within that city.
Then that yakṣa took from the merchant leader Gopīda the flaming wheel of fire upon his head, and having taken it, placed it upon the head of the Compassionate One.”

"At that time, the iron wheel upon Maitraka’s head was exceedingly blazing and fierce; he experienced great suffering, being intensely scorched and intensely burned, such that the pain was unbearable."
Immediately, he addressed the yakṣa with these verses:
“Around the four gates of this city, There is always a blazing radiance that terrifies people.
I am now bound by such constraints, Just like deer trapped within a deep cage.”
Excellent! I beg you, O Yakṣa King, to explain why this wheel has been cast upon me;
blazing with fierce flames like a mass of fire, it shall now bring an end to my life.
I first passed through the Palace of Joyful Delight, Then entered the Palace of Constant Intoxication within the Golden City;
Next I passed the Place of Crystalline Intent, And finally traversed the one named Brahma-Virtue.
First I entered the Silver City and met four maidens, Later, arriving at the Golden Gate, I encountered eight more.
There were sixteen women in the city of Crystal, and thirty-two more in the city of Lapis Lazuli;
having encountered those and then these in succession, each subsequent encounter was even more excellent.
Having already met with such as these, why do you now encounter this wheel of terror?
Because of my greed and lack of contentment, I now encounter such bitter suffering and calamity;
what other karma did I commit in the past to meet with this iron wheel spinning upon my head?
Blazing and radiant like a mass of fire, it shall now sever my life and limb.
O King of Yakṣas, may you respond with compassion: for how many years must I endure this wheel?
At that time, the yakṣa who guarded the city spoke to Maitreya in verse:
"In former times, while your mother observed the pure precepts, you stepped upon her head with your feet.
By reason of such karmic causes and conditions, an iron wheel now turns upon your head."
Blazing like a mass of fierce fire, its brilliant radiance is most terrifying;
this wheel revolves above your head, causing your life and body to be severed again and again.
For sixty thousand years you shall remain fully satisfied, without ever lacking a single year;
this wheel shall always remain upon your head, and you may never doubt that this fact is so.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one who knows you well bestows benefit upon you, Yet you instead return that harm to them,
Then you shall later suffer such calamity."
One should not give evil to those who do not deserve it, nor should one further inflict sin upon those who have committed no crime;
such a person will later suffer calamities like these.
If one harbors a mind of compassion yet seeks out another's faults, or fails to repay kindness toward those who have shown grace, [they shall likewise suffer].
They will subsequently suffer such calamities as these.
Just as one who is compassionate may harbor malice, the power of karma drags them from afar and brings them near; the power of karma drags them from the near and leads them away.
The power of karma leads people everywhere; according to the deeds they have performed, they experience suffering or pleasure.
Neither on earth, nor in the sky, nor within the ocean, nor even among the mountain crags and rocks—nowhere at all is there a place where one can escape and not undergo the results of karma.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: “Bhikṣus,
what do you think?”
At that time, as for this person of loving-kindness, could they have been anyone else?
Do not harbor such a thought; it was none other than myself.

Because I wished to enter the sea at that time, I observed the eightfold precepts of the fast; by the power of the causal conditions of that karmic retribution, I encountered these four kinds of precious cities, wherein all things were fully provided and nothing was lacking.
Because he trampled his mother’s head due to the causes and conditions of an evil mind of hatred, he underwent the suffering of blazing great iron wheels for a full sixty thousand years.
"O bhikṣus! It is due to the retribution of karma;
it is not experienced by empty space. Rather, it is sentient beings who create good and evil karma, and they experience this retribution according to the causes and conditions of that karma."
Therefore, monks, you must undertake your practice:
purify your bodily actions, purify your verbal actions, and purify your mental actions. Monks!

If there is a bhikṣu who is himself ignorant and foolish, unable to distinguish between demerit and merit, or the wholesome and the unwholesome, he should consult his preceptors, teachers, and ācāryas before subsequently traveling through cities, towns, or villages. If he goes on his own authority without the permission of his preceptor or ācārya, he should be punished according to the Dharma for his lack of respect and lack of filial obedience.

Chapter 53: The Original Birthplace of Śikhin Buddha. *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Fifty-three, Part One: The Original Birthplace of Śikhin Buddha. At that time, the Bodhisattva was dwelling on the banks of the river Uruvilvā, practicing austerities. He sat and lay down as circumstances required, wearing tattered and old garments, using whatever vessels were at hand, and consuming only a single grain of food within a single day.
That is to say, a sesame seed, or a grain of non-glutinous rice, or a small bean, or a mung bean, or a large bean, or red non-glutinous rice, or a green bean.
At that time, King Śuddhodana sought the Bodhisattva but did not know his whereabouts; he questioned others, saying:
"Where does my son dwell now?"
"What activities is he engaged in?
Thereupon, on a certain day, he secretly dispatched a messenger to inquire as to where the Bodhisattva was walking or sitting, and addressed the messenger, saying:
"You must now go and find out where my son is staying and what he is doing."
"You should inform me of this.
Then the messengers, having received this decree, immediately addressed the king, saying:
"As the king has commanded, we dare not disobey your will."

He immediately set out on his search, traveling by stages until he gradually reached the dwelling place of Uruvilvā. There he saw the Bodhisattva practicing difficult and ascetic austerities; he then returned and reported this to King Śuddhodana, saying:
"How excellent, Great King!..."

Now this youth, residing at the place called Uruvilvā, practices difficult austerities; his dwelling is entirely suited to his needs, such that he consumes as little as a single green bean for his daily meal.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having heard these matters, felt despondent in his heart; filled with sorrow and distress, he was unhappy and immediately spoke these words:
"Alas, my son!"
“Your body is so weak; for what reason has it come to such a state?
Then, in the sixth year, the messengers took the news of the Bodhisattva’s well-being and hardships and went before the Great King, reporting the matters in succession.

At that time, Yaśodharā, the daughter of the Śākya clan, heard from various messengers that the youth was in a place of asceticism, practicing austerities, dwelling and moving about as was appropriate for his station, even consuming only a single green bean for his daily meal.
Having heard this matter, he immediately reflected:
"For me now to receive pleasure in such tranquility is truly not good. Why is this?
"Now that my husband is engaged in ascetic practice, I too ought to follow the way of a youth and perform these austerities.

Having thought this, Yaśodharā immediately removed her necklaces, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, *maṇi* gems, and all manner of precious jewels; she cast away the scented ointments, powdered incenses, and various flower garlands. She donned pure white garments and kept only a single topknot. She lay upon a common and wretched mat, eating coarse and bitter food just sufficient to sustain life—such that no ascetic practice of the world could surpass hers.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had attained enlightenment, Udāyin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare it is, World-Honored One!

When Yaśodharā saw the World-Honored One dwelling in the mountain forests practicing austerities, how was she able to so skillfully follow the World-Honored One in his ascetic practice that no other person among the world could equal her?"
The Buddha said to Udāyin: "Udāyin!

Yaśodharā, the daughter of the Śākya clan, has not only followed me in practicing great asceticism when I was in the mountain forests in this present life; in past lives as well, when I was in distress, she was likewise able to follow me into great suffering and hardship."
Then Udāyin said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One,
what is the matter?”
"I pray that you will explain this for me.
The Buddha told Udāyin:

"I recall that in the distant past, long ago, there was a secluded hermitage in the midst of mountains, forests, and ravines. There dwelt a king of deer who led a herd of deer, sustaining himself by eating grass."
While he was wandering through that area in succession, a hunter set up a wooden snare and ensnared the king of the deer.
At that time, the herd of deer each fled and scattered in different directions.
At that time, there was a doe who, seeing the deer king caught in a snare, stood still and did not flee.
Now, those deer were largely able to understand human speech, and so the doe immediately spoke a verse to the deer king, saying:
"O Deer King, you must exert yourself; Stir your feet and head with vigor!"
"This trap has been set to catch people; they have not yet arrived here.
At that time, the Deer King replied to his mother with these verses:
"Though I now exert my strength, I cannot pull out this trap."
Using hides to make the noose-ropes, they bind and constrain one ever more tightly.
May the subtle and wondrous mountain forests, with their sweet springs and lush grasses,
ensure that in future lives we never again suffer such calamity.
And there is a verse that says:
"At that time, those two deer, with tears flowing from their eyes of terror,
were distressed because the wicked hunter had arrived, brandishing his sword and weapons."

The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume 51.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
The Chapter on the Previous Birth of Śikhin, Part Two:
At that time, the deer king saw from afar a hunter approaching with a staff in hand. He immediately addressed the female deer in verse, saying:
"This is a hunter who has arrived, His body black as soot, wearing a deer-skin garment."
"Now you have surely come to flay my skin, cut off my limbs and joints, and carry me away.
At that time, the doe went out from afar to meet the hunter; gradually approaching him, she spoke this verse:
"Excellent, O hunter! You may now spread out the grass mat."
"First I shall break through your skin and flesh; only then will I kill the deer king.
At that time, the hunter asked the doe, "What kinship do you have with this deer king?"
At that time, the doe replied to the hunter, "This is my husband;
we hold one another in great love and respect. For this reason, I have formed this thought:
'May I not be separated from him with whom I am so dear.'"
"For this reason, you must kill me first, and only afterwards reach the king of deer.
At that time, the hunter thought to himself:
"This is a virtuous woman; how extraordinary, how extraordinary!"
"Such a great deed as this can be performed by this deer.
At that time, the hunter felt great joy toward the doe and immediately addressed her in verse:
"I have never heard, since my youth, That there are wild beasts capable of speaking human speech."
This matter is most rare in the world; how could my heart bear to give rise to a harmful intent?
Since I do not kill your body now, I shall likewise release your husband as well.
Having thus preserved your life and that of your spouse, I pray that you two may always remain together.
"At that time, the hunter went to the trap and released the deer king.
Seeing that the king was freed from his bonds, the female deer was filled with great joy; her whole body leaped for joy, and she could not contain herself."
Furthermore, he addressed the hunter with these verses:
“Excellent indeed is this great hunter! All those kinsmen who see you will rejoice;
Just as I rejoice at seeing my husband delivered from danger, My exultation and leaping for joy are likewise the same.”
The Buddha told Udāyin:
"You should know now!
As for that king of the deer, could he possibly have been anyone else?"
I myself was that person;
the doe at that time was none other than Yaśodharā.

At that time, Yaśodharā already followed me and underwent great suffering and hardship; how much more so today, when she can follow me in practicing great asceticism, performing deeds that no one else among the people of the world is able to perform?
"Because Rāhula was oppressed by his past karma, he remained in the womb for six years.
Yaśodharā, out of grief and distress on account of this Bodhisattva, did not adorn herself."
However, after six years had passed, the Tathāgata realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the messengers sent by King Śuddhodana to observe his movements saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, rising from his seat; they immediately went to King Śuddhodana’s presence, and having arrived at the king’s location, they addressed him, saying:
“Great King!...”
"You should know that the Prince has now completed his ascetic practices; his heart's desire is fulfilled, and he has already risen from his seat.
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he separately commanded two men, saying to them:
"You two must now go to where the Prince is. Upon reaching that place, you shall proclaim my words and inform the Prince:"
"Now that your ascetic practices have reached their culmination, you should come quickly to preside over the affairs of state and become a Wheel-Turning King, endowed with the seven treasures.

Then those two, having received the king's command, accepted it with their heads bowed in accordance with the royal decree. Carrying out the intent of this edict, they went to the Prince’s location, prostrated themselves at his feet, and standing to one side, addressed the Prince, saying:
"Excellent, O Noble Son!
King Śuddhodana commanded us two to go to the presence of the Noble Son and say to him:
"Now that your ascetic practices have reached their completion, you should come quickly to succeed me on the throne and become a Wheel-Turning King, with all the seven treasures fully provided."
At that time, having heard those two men speak these words, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“If a person has already been tamed, there is nothing in the world they cannot tame.
The realm of all Buddhas is boundless; it leaves no trace and has neither coming nor going.”
"If a person does not enter the net, craving has no place from which to arise;
the realm of all Buddhas is boundless, without trace, and without coming or going.

At that time, Yaśodharā, having heard within her palace that the Prince’s ascetic practices had reached their ultimate limit, still hoped that he would surely return before long to receive the royal throne, govern the state and the people, and become a Wheel-Turning King. She then formed this thought:
"If the Prince becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King, I shall become his foremost queen.
Having thought this, she was filled with such joy and exultation that it pervaded her entire body, and she could not contain herself.

Applying various kinds of fragrant unguents to his body, he adorns himself with various priceless precious robes and necklaces; he partakes of exquisite delicacies and sleeps upon jeweled couches and soft bedding—performing such acts as these, he awaits the Prince.
At that time, after six years had passed and Rāhula’s past karma was exhausted, Yaśodharā personally provided for him with various kinds of provisions, food, and drink.
For this reason, Rāhula was immediately born.
Once he was born, the women of the inner quarters immediately consulted together and addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
"How extraordinary, Great King!"
"Yaśodharā! She has now given birth to a son.
Upon hearing this, King Śuddhodana became greatly incensed and spoke these words:
