"Now, it has already been six years since my crown prince left his home to become a renunciant; how then could Yaśodharā have given birth to this son now?"
At that time, Devadatta, the son of the Śākyas, spoke these words: "This is my son.
King Śuddhodana’s anger redoubled; he summoned all the Śākya clansmen and, having assembled them, addressed them thus:
"You all should know!

Yaśodharā has neither protected the Prince, nor me, nor the Śākyas; she disregards her reputation and, acting according to her own whims, has brought disgrace upon our clan. What should we do now to punish her severely?"
At that time, the Śākyas all raised their voices with one accord and spoke thus:
"Yaśodharā! You who have brought disgrace upon our family—we must punish you severely according to the laws for disgracing the family."
At that time, there was a high minister within that assembly who spoke these words:
"One should shave his hair, beat him with a staff, and after beating him, brand him."
Again, another minister spoke these words:
"One should cut off his ears and excise his nose.
Yet another minister spoke thus:
"Blind him in both eyes.
Then another minister spoke thus:
"Impale him upon a wooden stake."
Again, another minister spoke thus:
"Throw it into an empty well.
Yet another minister spoke thus:
"Throw him into the fire!
Another minister spoke thus:
"Make him embrace a pillar of glowing, intensely hot iron."
Again, another minister spoke thus:
"Bind his hands and feet, and send a great herd of cattle to trample him to death.
Yet another minister spoke thus:
"Have him laid upon the ground and trampled by white elephants.
Another minister spoke thus:
"Saw him apart from head to foot."
Again, another minister spoke these words:
"Let him be dismembered limb by limb and divided into eight parts.
At that time, King Śuddhodana addressed his ministers, saying:
"I now command Yaśodharā and her son to both face execution.

At that time, the Tathāgata, having already attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, beheld Yaśodharā and her son in a state of peril; moved by the intensity of his compassion, he looked about in every direction.
At that time, the Deva Vaiśravaṇa was not far from the Buddha; knowing the Tathāgata’s intention, the Heavenly King immediately took a brush, ink, and *tāla* leaves, and went to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One wrote a letter with his own hand and addressed the king, saying:
"The son who has been born is my own offspring; I pray that you harbor no doubt."
At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa, having received this letter from the World-Honored One, immediately went to the assembly of King Śuddhodana and produced the letter from the king’s breast.
At that time, that writing bore both evidence and verification; having seen this proof, King Śuddhodana reflected that this writing was truly from the hand of my own son, Prince Siddhārtha.
At that time, King Śuddhodana and the great assembly, for this reason, felt a heart of joy toward Yaśodharā.

Yaśodharā, having heard it said that the Great King had issued an edict intending to kill her and her newborn son, went with great haste to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī for the sake of protecting her life, and spoke these words:
"How wonderful, O Noble Queen!
"I have no such fault; this son born to me is the heir to the Prince's lineage. It will not be long before you hear that the Prince has arrived, and once he has arrived, you shall know for yourself."
"To kill me now would be a false and unjust act.
When Mahāprajāpatī heard these words from Yaśodharā, her heart was filled with joy once more.
He immediately dispatched a messenger to invite King Śuddhodana to the interior of the Aśoka grove; having arrived at the grove, he addressed the king, saying:
"I pray only that Your Majesty..."
You should know that Yaśodharā, the daughter of the Śākya clan, has come before me and said this: "I am free from such fault;
the son I have borne is the biological heir of the Prince. If that Prince himself were to come here, he would know the truth of the matter for himself."
"Therefore, Great King! Do not do this.
You must wait until that Prince arrives, so that we may know for certain what the truth of this matter is.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having heard these words of Mahāprajāpatī which were so beneficial and meaningful, replied to her, saying:
"These words are reasonable. If it is as Your Majesty the Queen has said, we should remain here and wait for the Prince’s arrival;
otherwise, let us know what the true nature of this matter actually is."

"Nevertheless, because King Śuddhodana had not yet found joy in the Śākya maiden Yaśodharā, he provided her with only a small portion of clothing and other ornaments, and sent her away to be settled in a suitable residence."
At that time, Yaśodharā, the daughter of Śuddhodana, went again to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī; having arrived, she said to her:
"How excellent, O Noble Queen!"
I now wish to go within the garden to fulfill a minor vow previously promised to the devas with a brief offering; I do not yet know whether the Noble Queen will grant me her permission.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, together with the Śākya woman Yaśodharā, took Rāhula and prepared an extensive array of offerings; carrying various articles, they went to the abode of that deity.
The deity there is named Lūtilaka; the garden is named Lūtilaka after that deity.
Within that garden, during the time when the Bodhisattva was formerly a householder, he would constantly engage in massage and recreation within it.
Within that grove was a great rock where the Bodhisattva had sat and risen in days past.
At that time, Yaśodharā, the daughter of the Śākya clan, having placed Rāhula upon that rock to rest, later seized the rock and threw it into the water, then made this vow:
"I now take a solemn oath, which is true and not false: except for the Prince, there is no other man with whom I shall engage in mutual intimacy."
"The son born of me is truly the offspring of the Prince's own lineage.
If this be not false, let this great stone float upon the water without sinking."

At that time, by virtue of that solemn vow, the great rock immediately floated and remained upon the water; it neither sank nor submerged, just as a plantain leaf floats upon the surface of the water.

At that time, when the great assembly had seen and heard this, they were struck with wonder; they clamored and cheered in unending exultation, shouting and leaping about, singing and dancing, twirling their skirts and sleeves, and performing various kinds of music and entertainment.

At that time, when King Śuddhodana heard this news, he was filled with such joy and exultation that it pervaded his entire body, and he could not contain himself. He immediately ordered the city of Kapilavastu to be adorned, commanding that all thorns, gravel, stones, dust, filth, excrement, and other impurities be removed; furthermore, he had the ground sprinkled with fragrant water, swept, smeared, and polished, and incense burners were placed everywhere to burn the most exquisite perfumes.

Between the incense burners were various precious vases of diverse and wondrous colors; these vases were filled with scented water, within which fragrant flowers were placed. Between the incense burners and the vases, rows of plantain trees were further arranged.

Furthermore, various variegated silken streamers were suspended, and banners and pennants of diverse colors were erected; strings of pearls were interlaced everywhere, and nets of golden bells completely covered the area above.

Furthermore, he fashioned images of the sun, moon, and constellations, which were suspended in the air; jeweled flowers and tassels hung down everywhere, interspersed at various points with the tails of diverse wild oxen.

At that time, the city of Kapilavastu was adorned like a magical illusion, a mirage, or a city of the Gandharvas. Once it had been thus embellished, he took Rāhula and entered the city. He summoned the Śākya clansmen and their kinsmen, and they all gathered together. Having extensively prepared various kinds of wealth, food, drink, and necessities, the arrangements were finally complete; he then specially made further preparations for Rāhula.

On the day Yaśodharā gave birth to her child, Rāhu, the Asura King, seized the moon; having seized it for a mere moment, he released it. Therefore, the kinsmen of the Śākya clan gathered and deliberated, saying: "Since this boy was born at the very instant when Rāhu was devouring the moon, let him be named Rāhula. Thus he was given the name Rāhula.

Rāhula was lovely and handsome; all who saw him were filled with joy. His skin was yellowish-white like the color of pure gold, and the crown of his head was shaped like a parasol. His nose was high and prominent like that of a parrot, and his two arms were long and slender, hanging down past his knees. All his limbs and joints were without deficiency, and his sense faculties were complete and fully developed.
At that time, King Śuddhodana appointed four nurses for Rāhula. What were these four?
First, one to carry him;
second, one to wash him; third, one to feed him milk; and fourth, one to play with him.
These four nurses nurtured him according to the seasons, and before long, he was endowed with complete wisdom.

At that time, the World-Honored One was at Vārāṇasī turning the Great Wheel of Dharma; then, the various devas each informed one another, and the sound spread from one to another until it reached the summit of the Brahma world.

At that very time, King Śuddhodana heard that his son Siddhārtha had already realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; having attained awakening, he had gone to Vārāṇasī to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma and was preaching the teaching for gods and humans.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, with even greater mindfulness directed toward the World-Honored One, thought to himself:
"By what skillful means can I cause the Prince to take pity on his kinsmen and come quickly to this city of Kapilavastu?"
He further thought to himself:
"Whom should I dispatch as a messenger?
Who possesses the wisdom and strategy to understand this matter?"
He further thought to himself:
"This son of the state preceptor Udāyin, and next Chanda—these two have, since their childhood, always been with Siddhārtha, playing together in the dust and soil, and traveling about as companions."
"These two men are both capable of reaching the presence of Siddhārtha; I shall now dispatch them there as messengers.
At that time, King Śuddhodana summoned the state preceptor’s son, Udāyin, and Chandaka, and addressed them, saying:
"You two should know the proper time."

Now that the Prince has already attained the realization of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he has gone to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma, expounding all dharmas for the sake of devas and humans.
"You all should now go quickly to where Siddhārtha is and proclaim my command, conveying my intent:

'Now you, the Prince, having practiced difficult austerities to their ultimate limit, have fulfilled your heart's desire and have already realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; you have further turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.'"
Having already expounded the various dharmas for the sake of devas and humans, it is well, O Prince!
You may now come to the city of Kapilavastu out of compassion for all your kinsmen.
At that time, Udāyin, the son of the royal preceptor, together with Chandaka, addressed the King, saying: "Great King,
you should know that if Prince Siddhārtha does not return, we do not yet know what further plan we shall devise."
The King replied to them, saying,
"You need only listen to the Prince's instructions.
Then Udāyin, the son of the state preceptor, together with Chandaka, addressed the King, saying:
"As Your Majesty commands, we dare not disobey your decree.

Having received the king's command, they prostrated at his feet and each returned to their respective places. They took leave of their parents and kinsmen, and gradually journeyed toward the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva), the abode of the sages in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
Having arrived at that place, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!
We have now come here, dispatched by the Great King Śuddhodana who commanded us, saying:”
"Excellent, Prince!

You have now transcended through your ascetic practices; may you fulfill your heart's wish and achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, turn the Great Wheel of Dharma, and further expound all dharmas for the sake of devas and humans."
“Excellent, Prince!
You should now come to this city of Kapilavastu out of compassion for all your kinsmen.
When the World-Honored One heard these words, he spoke this verse:
"If a person has already been tamed, there is nothing in the world that cannot be subdued;
the realm of the Buddhas is boundless, traceless, and without coming or going.
If a person does not enter the net, craving has no place from which to arise."
"The realm of all Buddhas is boundless, Without trace, and without coming or going.
Then Udāyin, the son of the royal preceptor, together with Chandaka, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What should we do? The Buddha addressed them, saying:
"Are you able to train in this dharma of renunciation for my disciples?"
At that time, although the World-Honored One questioned them, those two had already harbored a longing for renunciation in the presence of the Buddha; therefore, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We both wish to take up the life of renunciation."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One immediately granted him permission to leave the household life and conferred upon him full ordination.

At that time, from the moment he first left home until he sat down again, the World-Honored One never once turned his face toward his birthplace, Kapilavastu. Furthermore, he had not yet converted his virtuous friends and acquaintances, the five bhikṣus, nor his close and dear companions such as the Elder Yaśoda, nor the four great wealthy elders who were eminent men born in the city of Vārāṇasī.
What are these four? First, Vimala; second, Subhūti; third, Pūrṇa; and fourth, Gavāmpati.
At that time, the Venerable Yaśoda had more than fifty fellow spiritual friends.
The Elder Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra also had a retinue of thirty-one people;
the Elder Mahākātyāyana further had eighty-four thousand followers;
and the Elder Sāviya also had an excellent group of disciples totaling thirty, with sixty virtuous companions traveling together.
Furthermore, there was the elder Nāvikasīnaṃyana, born in the village of Migayā.
At that time, there was also a brahmin who had two daughters:
the first was named Nandā and the second was named Bharā.
At that time, there was also a brahmin named Deva together with his wife,
as well as the elder Piṇḍola Kāśyapa and five hundred other ascetics with matted hair.
Furthermore, there was the elder Nadi-Kāśyapa, a brahmin with matted hair, together with three hundred followers;
and there was the elder Gaya-Kāśyapa, along with his assembly of two hundred followers, who were likewise brahmins with matted hair.
At that time, there was also the elder Upasena, accompanied by approximately two hundred and fifty people.
At that same time, there were also five hundred ascetic sages in a grove of trees, for whom the rain of Dharma was falling.
In the city of Rājagṛha, there were King Bimbisāra and his ministers, totaling ninety-two nayutas of people;
as well as the Elder Mahākāśyapa, the Elders Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others; and furthermore, five hundred disciples of the non-Buddhist teacher Sañjayī Vairaṭīputra.
After having thus transformed such a multitude of people, the World-Honored One finally turned his face toward his native land, the city of Kapilavastu.
At that time, Udāyin saw the Bhagavat turn his face and sit facing his place of birth, Kapilavastu; furthermore, the devas addressed the Elder Udāyin, saying:
"Excellent, O Venerable One!"
"Now you should request the Buddha, wishing that he come to his birthplace, the city of Kapilavastu, out of compassion for his kinsmen.

At that time, the Elder Udāyin, well-knowing the Tathāgata’s intention to depart, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, adjusted his robes, joined his palms toward the Buddha, bowed with a stooped body and lowered head, and spoke this verse:
"Just as various trees out of season, Desiring to bear fruit and flowers, must wait for their proper time,"
Out-of-season flowers and fruits lack their usual luster; O Honored One, you may now cross the Gaṅgā River.
The trees are covered in blossoms, and the flowers are in full bloom; their fragrance pervades the lands of the ten directions.
Now that the flowers have opened and are about to bear fruit, it is precisely the right time for the Honored One to return to his birthplace.

At this time, it is most wondrous and supreme; the waters of the springs and ponds are clear, fragrant, and pure, while a hundred birds in the groves utter exquisite songs—this is the season for all things that bring joy.
In the past, the Śākyas made this vow: "May I alone possess the entire earth.
Seeing that the Honored One has gone forth, they are filled with great anxiety and fear; their hearts are not at ease, and they are deeply dejected.
The World-Honored One’s retinue has long been anxious;
because the Venerable One has fathered Rāhula, we pray that you go there to resolve their doubts, for the great assembly thirsts with longing to see you.

The Tathāgata, mindful of his mother’s kindness in nurturing him, out of a heart of compassion for her, should see that the Great Holy Teacher has come from afar; he ought to rejoice and cast off all sorrow and affliction.
The Great King Śuddhodana of the Śākya clan made this sublime vow in the past:
"When shall I behold my son, with his golden-hued body, entering this city of Kapilavastu?"
At this time, it was neither hot nor cold; it could truly be called the Way of the World-Honored One’s experiencing of bliss.
Hundreds of millions of Śākyas gazed up and waited for him, just as those under the star Piṣṭa hope for the return of the moon.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Udāyin, saying: "Udāyin!
If it is so, you two should first go to the city of Kapilavastu and tell my kinsmen, the Śākyas, speaking these words:"
"Now the Prince has completed his ascetic practices; out of compassion for you all, he intends to come before long.
Having received the Buddha's command, Udāyin and Chandaka addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I dare not disobey.

He prostrated at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, took his leave, and departed. Traveling by stages, he gradually reached the Nyagrodha Grove near the city of Kapilavastu and stayed for a short while in that village.
At that time, King Śuddhodana prepared his carriage drawn by four horses and went out to that garden to inspect a suitable site.

From afar, King Śuddhodana saw the elder Chandaka and Udāyin with their hair and beards shaven, wearing saffron robes and holding alms bowls in their hands. Having seen them, he immediately addressed his ministers, saying:
"O you ministers!..."
"Who is this person?
Having shaved off his hair and beard, he wears dyed robes and holds an alms-bowl in his hand.
Then the ministers immediately replied to the king:
"These two are disciples of Prince Siddhārtha.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, harboring deep distress and feeling despondent and unhappy, spoke these words:
"My son was handsome, his appearance pleasing, such that onlookers never grew weary of him; he was like a statue of gold. Yet now, his body has become like this."
Disliking the sight of them, he said to his ministers, "You must surely put these two to death; do not let me see them.
Having spoken these words, he finally proceeded into the park.
At that time, the ministers thought to themselves:
"Of these two individuals, one is the son of the National Preceptor, and the other is the attendant of Prince Siddhārtha."
Having deliberated thus, they were unable to send them away.

When King Śuddhodana was wandering for recreation in the park and was about to depart, the ministers, fearing that the king might see those two elderly men and give rise to afflictions, consequently placed them within an empty-walled courtyard.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!

You should now quickly prepare your robes and bowls; I wish to travel and visit other kingdoms, cities, towns, and villages, and because I have compassion for all my kinsmen, I intend to go to my own birthplace, the city of Kapilavastu."

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!”
It is truly unprecedented!
World-Honored One, now is precisely the time for you to act; it is most refined and most sublime.
World-Honored One, that you now wish to travel and visit other kingdoms and cities is indeed the right moment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra!
If you now wish to hear this matter, I shall explain it for you.”

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śikhin, desiring to travel through his own birthplace and inspect the various cities and villages there, was at that time engaged in matters of exquisite and most delightful causes and conditions.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Now is precisely the right time.”

I pray that you will expound for the bhikṣus the account of how, in the past, Śikhin Tathāgata went to his own birthplace to tour the towns and cities, so that the bhikṣus, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, shall uphold it accordingly.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse concerning the matter of Śikhin Tathāgata’s journeying to and beholding his native land:
“Excellent and most wonderful, Śāriputra! You should now listen with a single mind To how, in days of yore, the Holy Tathāgata Śikhin In the past beheld the matters of his birthplace.”
To every village and settlement he reached, he went to visit the noble Tathāgata Śikhin;
in each place, sweet springs welled up, fully endowed with the eight meritorious qualities.
In every village and settlement he reached, he went to see the Great Holy Teacher Śikhin;
everywhere there were various flowering trees, their branches and leaves hanging down in lush profusion.
Beneath every forest tree where he arrived was the place where the Tathāgata Śikhin had dwelt;
those trees spontaneously rained down wondrous flowers, which spread across the ground until it was completely covered.
Beneath every tree and forest through which he passed, wherever the Tathāgata Śikhin dwelt,
sweet fruits fell spontaneously from the trees, and their branches and twigs drooped down in graceful curves.
There is a tree that men can reach, its flowers and fruits mingled in great abundance, truly pitiable;
yet for the Great Holy Teacher Śikhin Tathāgata, such things manifest through the flow of his responsive resonance.
If there is a tree that no one can reach, Wondrous flowers and sweet fruits fall of their own accord;
Such are the miraculous manifestations Of Śikhin, the Great Holy Teacher, as he flows through the world in response to beings.
The devas dwelling within the void rained down great and wondrous *kankara* flowers;
such were the miraculous manifestations that occurred when the Great Holy Teacher, the Tathāgata Śikhin, traveled through the world.
The devas dwelling within the void universally rained down a cool and wondrous rain of flowers;
such were the miraculous manifestations that occurred when the Great Holy Teacher, the Tathāgata Śikhin, appeared in response to the needs of beings.
The devas dwelling within the void rained down flowers called māndārava;
such were the miraculous manifestations that occurred when the Great Holy Teacher, the Tathāgata Śikhin, appeared in response to the needs of beings.
The devas dwell within the void, raining down flowers called pāriyātra;
such are the miraculous manifestations of the Great Holy Teacher, Śikhin Tathāgata, as he flows through the world in response to sentient beings.
The devas dwelling within the void rained down flowers called Vibhaga;
such were the manifestations of the Great Holy Teacher Śikhin Tathāgata as he traveled in response to the needs of beings.
The devas dwelling within the void rained down flowers called "Superior Fragrance";
such were the manifestations of the Great Sage Teacher Śikhin Tathāgata as he traveled through the world in response to the needs of beings.
The devas dwelling within the void rain down all manner of exquisite fragrant flowers;
such are the miraculous manifestations that occur when the Great Holy Teacher, the Tathāgata Śikhin, appears in response to the needs of beings.
The devas dwelling within the void rained down flowers called "Universally Pervading Fragrance";
such were the miraculous manifestations of Śikhin, the Great Holy Teacher Tathāgata, as he traveled in response to the needs of beings.
The devas dwelling within the void rained down various kinds of wondrous fragrant flowers;
such were the miraculous manifestations that occurred when the Great Holy Teacher, Tathāgata Śikhin, traveled abroad in response to the needs of beings.
The devas dwelling within the void rain down flowers of pure gold and wondrous colors;
such are the miraculous manifestations that occur when the Great Holy Teacher, Śikhin Tathāgata, appears in response to the needs of beings.
The devas dwelling within the void Rained down exquisite flowers of the seven precious gems;
Such were the miraculous manifestations Of Śikhin, the Great Sage and Tathāgata.
The devas dwell within the void, raining down flowers of pure, genuine gold;
such are the manifestations that flow forth in response to the great and holy teacher, Tathāgata Śikhin.
The devas dwelling within the void rained down exclusively flowers with jeweled stems;
such were the miraculous manifestations that occurred when the Great Holy Teacher, Tathāgata Śikhin, traveled through the world.
The devas dwelling within the void rained down exclusively petals of *utpala* flowers;
such were the miraculous manifestations that occurred when the Great Holy Teacher, Tathāgata Śikhin, traveled abroad in response to the needs of beings.
The devas dwelling within the void rain down pure, wondrous powders of sandalwood;
such are the miraculous manifestations that occur when the Great Holy Teacher, Śikhin Tathāgata, appears in response to the needs of beings.
The devas dwelling within the void rained down the wondrous powdered incense of red sandalwood;
such were the miraculous manifestations that occurred when the Great Holy Teacher, Śikhin Tathāgata, moved through the world in response to the needs of beings.
The devas dwelling within the void rained down exclusively powdered gośīrṣa-candana;
such were the miraculous manifestations that occurred when the Great Holy Teacher, Śikhin Tathāgata, traveled abroad in response to the needs of beings.
The devas dwelling within the void Perform various kinds of celestial music;
Such are the miraculous manifestations Of Śikhin, the Great Sage and Tathāgata, as he flows through the world in response to sentient beings.
A non-human being in the midst of the void Waves and plays with various kinds of wondrous celestial robes;
Such are the manifestations that occur When the Great Holy Teacher, Śikhin Tathāgata, responds to the call of sentient beings.
The devas followed along the Buddha’s path, carrying all kinds of exquisite incense and flowers;
those flowers, intermingled with various radiances, rained down upon the roads until they were knee-deep.
At that time, there was neither cold nor heat, and there were no mosquitoes, gadflies, or other harmful insects.
The Great Holy Teacher, Śikhin Tathāgata, moved through the world by means of such manifestations as these:
the entire great earth trembled, along with the vast oceans and all the mountains;
the Great Holy Teacher, Śikhin Tathāgata, moved through the world by means of such manifestations as these.
The entire great earth was universally harmonious and supple; Pure and free from any evil thorns or brambles.
Such were the miraculous manifestations Of Śikhin, the Great Holy Teacher Tathāgata, as he traveled through the world.
All mounds and ruins were leveled and filled; mountains, hills, and ridges became entirely smooth and even.
Such were the miraculous manifestations as the Great Holy Teacher, Śikhin Tathāgata, traveled through the world in response to sentient beings.
Of the Kṣatriya caste and of great majesty, numbering eighty-six thousand,
they followed Śikhin, the Great Holy Teacher, wherever he walked, stood, sat, or rose.
There were eighty-six thousand Brahmins of pure conduct,
who followed the Great Holy Teacher Śikhin wherever he went— whether walking, standing, sitting, or rising.
Eighty-six thousand great elders of noble wealth and majestic power followed Śikhin,
the Great Holy Teacher, wherever he went— whether walking, standing, sitting, or rising.
There were also various devas dwelling on earth, all adorned with exquisite and pure forms;
they followed the Great Holy Teacher Śikhin wherever he walked, stood, sat, or rose.
Furthermore, there were hosts of deities from the realm of empty space, all of great majesty and most sublime;
they followed the Great Holy Teacher, Śikhin Tathāgata, wherever he went—whether walking, standing, sitting, or rising.
The Four Great Heavenly Kings and their celestial hosts, endowed with supreme and wondrous forms and majestic virtue,
followed the Great Holy Teacher Śikhin wherever he went— whether walking, standing, sitting, or rising.
The Four Great Kings who protect the world, along with others of extraordinary majesty and power,
followed the Great Holy Teacher Śikhin in his walking, standing, sitting, and rising.
The assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, with their subtle and wondrous power, became even more distinguished;
they followed the Great Holy Teacher, Śikhin Tathāgata, wherever he walked, stood, sat, or rose.
Śakra, King of Devas atop Mount Sumeru, together with his kinsmen, friends, and retinue,
followed the Great Holy Teacher Śikhin wherever he went— whether walking, standing, sitting, or rising.
The Yāma devas of the Good Realm, with exquisite and pure complexions and great majesty,
followed the Great Holy Teacher Śikhin wherever he went— whether walking, standing, sitting, or rising.

The Tuṣita heaven of the devas of joy and bliss, with its majestic power and most subtle merit—there the Great Holy Teacher, Śikhin Tathāgata, followed [the Bodhisattva] in every movement: walking, standing, sitting, and rising.
Next, the gods of the Nirmāṇarati heaven and others, whose practiced virtues were increasingly subtle and wondrous,
followed the Great Holy Teacher Śikhin in his walking, standing, sitting, and rising.
The gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, Resplendent with majestic power and radiant light,
Followed the Great Holy Teacher, Tathāgata Śikhin, In every movement— walking, standing, sitting, and rising.
The various devas within the palace of Mahābrahmā, with their wondrous forms and majestic power, radiate increasing brilliance;
they follow the Great Holy Teacher Śikhin wherever he walks, stands, sits, or rises.
All the various classes of devas in the realm of form, as well as the nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas,
gandharvas, and asuras; the yakṣas, bhūtas, and rākṣasas,
along with the kiṃnaras and mahoragas— all have attained perfect and sublime majesty.
The Great Holy Teacher Śikhin Tathāgata follows them in every movement— walking, standing, sitting, and rising.
Among all the various classes of sentient beings in the world, whether they have been mentioned or not,
the Great Holy Teacher Śikhin Tathāgata follows them in every movement— walking, standing, sitting, and rising.
That Honored One, Śikhin, having practiced in this manner, tamed immeasurable multitudes of devas and humans;
as a Perfectly Awakened One, he entered Great Parinirvāṇa, forever severing all realms of existence and future rebirth.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed Śāriputra, saying: "You, Śāriputra!

When the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān named Śikhin first desired to go to his own birthplace, there were such immeasurable, subtle, wondrous, and rare deeds."
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll 51 and Scroll 52,
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Fifty-Four: The因缘 (Nidāna) of Udāyin, Part One.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed Śāriputra, saying: "You, Śāriputra!"
"I shall now set out on a journey through the lands; first, I intend to go to the sublime place where I was originally born, and I shall do so in this manner.
Then Śāriputra rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!"
"When will you wish to travel through the lands and observe the villages?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "You, Śāriputra!"
"In this month, once the half-month has passed and the *poṣadha* ceremony is concluded, I shall then set out to travel through the various lands.
At that time, having completed the half-month *poṣadha*, the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, journeyed through various countries.

At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at the city of Rājagṛha; having finished his meal, he turned back and stepped upon the threshold of the city gate with his foot. At that moment, the great earth shook in six ways—shaking and shaking again, surging and surging again.

At that time, Bimbisāra, the king of the country of Magadha, together with a great multitude of people, went to where the Buddha was; he followed the Buddha’s journey as they traveled through various countries and visited various villages.

At that time, in the void of space, immeasurable multitudes of devas numbering in the thousands of billions saw that the Buddha was about to travel through the lands; they all gathered together, their bodies filled with such joy and exultation that they could not contain themselves. From their mouths issued various subtle and wondrous sounds as they sang, whistled, and rejoiced; they called out and shouted aloud, twirling their skirts and waving their sleeves, while brushing and playing with their celestial robes.
Furthermore, they scattered celestial utpala flowers, kumuda flowers, padma flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers over the Buddha.
They also took various kinds of powdered incense, ointments, and fragrant flower garlands, scattering them over the Buddha as well, scattering them again and again after each initial offering.
At that time, wherever the Bhagavat traveled and observed the various kingdoms, all classes of beings paid him homage, revered him, and made offerings to him.

Wherever the Tathāgata goes, he obtains robes that are most excellent and sublime, as well as food, drink, medicinal decoctions, beds, mats, and bedding; such requisites are beyond measure, and his offerings and honors are exquisite and never lacking, while his fame spreads throughout the world.
Yet the Buddha does not give rise to defiled attachment toward this fame and gain, remaining like a lotus flower amidst turbid water.
At that time, the World-Honored One possessed such immeasurable majesty and virtue; among all worlds, his majesty and virtue were most supreme and preeminent.

At that time, the Blessed One—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—through his supernormal knowledge, fully realized and knew this world and the world beyond, including the realms of gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, as well as all other celestial and human spheres.
That Blessed One taught the Dharma to the world with words and meanings that were skillful, excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, causing all to be fully endowed with the pure Brahma-faring.

At that time, the Blessed One, knowing those sentient beings who were capable of being transformed, immediately transformed them; to those who should be established, he taught them how to establish themselves, so that they might achieve accomplishment according to their respective abodes. To those who should receive the Three Refuges, he bestowed the method of the Three Refuges; to those who should receive the Five Precepts, he bestowed the Five Precepts; to those who should receive the method of the Eightfold Fast (Uposatha), he bestowed the method of the Eightfold Fast; to those who should receive the Ten Wholesome Actions, he bestowed the method of the Ten Wholesome Actions; to those who should leave the household life, he caused them to go forth; and to those who should receive full ordination, he bestowed the complete precepts.
Proceeding in this manner by successive stages, he gradually advanced until he reached the grove at the city of Kapilavastu and stayed there.

At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at the city of Kapilavastu and dwelt within the Nyagrodha Grove, where he spoke in verse concerning the sublime and wondrous events of his travels through the lands:
"The Great Lion of the Śākya Tathāgata, Gautama of supreme majesty and virtue, ... "
He went to observe the cities and villages, all of which possessed vast and extraordinary signs.
Wherever he intended to go among the hamlets and settlements, he would see the Tathāgata, the Great Holy Teacher;
everywhere, the entire multitude of people came to welcome and honor him with reverence and solemnity.
Wherever he wished to go toward a village or settlement to visit the Tathāgata, the Great Holy Teacher,
all the various flowering trees would incline themselves toward the place where the World-Honored One was.
Wherever the World-Honored One stands or rests beneath any forest tree,
that tree naturally rains down its blossoms, spreading them across the ground until it is completely filled.
To every grove of trees where the World-Honored One dwells,
sweet fruits fall spontaneously from those trees, and their branches and leaves all droop down in graceful elegance.
There is a tree that men can reach, its flowers and fruits mingled together, truly pitiable;
yet for the Great Holy Teacher, the Tathāgata Gautama, such things manifest through his miraculous response as he wanders.
There are trees that no human can reach, yet wondrous flowers and sweet fruits fall of their own accord;
such are the miraculous responses to the wandering of Gautama, the valiant and great Sage Teacher.
The various devas dwell within the void, raining down flowers called *karkarava*;
such are the miraculous responses that accompany the travels of Gautama, the heroic and great Sage Teacher.
The devas dwelling within the void rain down flowers called mañjūṣaka;
such are the miraculous responses to the majestic power of the heroic and mighty Great Sage, Gautama.
The devas dwelling within the void rained down various kinds of wondrously colored flowers;
such was the response to the majestic power of the heroic and mighty Great World-Honored One, Gautama.
The devas dwelling within the void rain down flowers called māndārava;
such are the miraculous responses to the majestic virtue of the heroic and great sage, Gautama.
The devas dwelling within the void rain down flowers called Pāriyātra;
such are the miraculous responses that accompany the travels of Gautama, the valiant and great Holy One.
The devas dwelling within the void rained down flowers called Vibhaga;
such were the miraculous responses as the Great Holy Teacher, the Lion of the Gautamas, traveled along.
The devas dwelling within the void rain down flowers called "Superior Fragrance";
such are the miraculous responses that accompany the wandering of Gautama, the Lion among Men and the Honored One of Gods and Humans.
The devas dwelling in the midst of space rained down various kinds of wondrous fragrant flowers;
such were the miraculous responses as the Great Sage Gautama, the Eye of Gods and Men, traveled forth.
The devas dwelling within the void rained down flowers called "Universal Pervasive Fragrance";
such were the miraculous responses as the heroic and mighty Great Sage Gautama traveled.
The devas dwell within the void, raining down exquisite golden flowers;
such are the miraculous responses as the heroic and mighty Great Sage Teacher, Gautama, wanders forth.
The devas dwelling within the void rain down flowers of exquisite, wondrous jewel-hues;
such are the miraculous responses that accompany the travels of Gautama, the Great Holy Honored One of Ten Powers.
The devas in the midst of the void rain down flowers with exquisite colors and precious stems;
such are the miraculous responses as the heroic Gautama, the eye of gods and men, proceeds on his journey.
The devas dwelling within the void rain down exquisite utpala flowers;
such are the miraculous responses as the heroic and majestic Gautama, Teacher of Gods and Men, proceeds on his journey.
The devas dwelling in the midst of the void Rained down powdered incense of exquisite agallochum;
For Gautama, the Honored One among gods and men of the three realms, Such events were manifested through his majestic power and spiritual resonance.
The devas dwelling in the midst of the void Rained down the wondrous fragrant powder of red sandalwood;
For the Great Holy Teacher, the Lion of the Gautamas, Such phenomena manifested as he traveled.
The devas in the midst of the void rained down exquisite powdered incense of ox-head sandalwood;
such were the miraculous responses as the heroic and mighty Great World-Honored One, Gautama, journeyed forth.
The devas dwelling within the void Perform various kinds of celestial music;
Such are the miraculous responses To the wandering of the majestic and great Sage Gautama.
A non-human being in the midst of the void Waves and plays with various kinds of exquisite celestial robes;
For the Great Holy Teacher, the Lion of the Gautamas, Such events manifest through his wandering and spiritual resonance.
The devas followed along the path where the Buddha traveled, all holding various kinds of exquisite incense and flowers;
for that Great Sage, the God among Gods, they rained down flowers along the road until they reached his knees.
At that time, there was neither cold nor heat, nor were there various mosquitoes, gadflies, or other harmful insects.
The subtle and wondrous Great Sage, Honored One among gods, By his responsive resonance can summon such events as these.
The entire great earth becomes level and even, Mountains, hills, and mounds all become flat and smooth;
Gautama, the Great Sage endowed with the Ten Powers, Manifests such responses as he travels.
The entire great earth is exceedingly pure, Free from evil thorns and all brambles;
Such are the miraculous responses as the World-Honored One, Gautama, of majestic virtue, wanders through the world.
The entire great earth trembled gently, Along with the vast oceans and all the mountains;
Gautama, the Unsurpassed Honored One of the Three Realms, Manifests such signs through his spiritual resonance as he travels.
All the kṣatriyas and brāhmaṇas, as well as the vaiśyas and śūdras and others—
numbering in the tens of millions— constantly followed after the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there were sublime celestial beings dwelling on earth, possessing various forms, strength, and great majesty;
they followed the heroic and mighty Great World-Honored One, Gautama, whether he was walking, standing, sitting, or staying.
Furthermore, the four world-protecting Heavenly Kings, all of whom possess great majesty and are most supreme,
followed Gautama— the subtle and wondrous Great Holy Honored One— whether he was walking, standing, sitting, or staying still.
Śakra, king atop Mount Sumeru, and Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world— Gautama,
the wondrous and most supreme Honored One, is always followed by such as these.
Furthermore, the various devas of the desire realm, as well as those of the four dhyānas and so forth in the form realm,
constantly follow and attend upon the Great Holy Honored One, Gautama, who is majestic and awe-inspiring.
Furthermore, there were various nāgas and garuḍas, gandharvas and asuras,
as well as hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas, all of whom followed after the Tathāgata as he traveled.
All classes of sentient beings in the world, both those already mentioned and those not yet mentioned,
all follow the heroic and valiant Teacher Gautama as he travels through various lands and cities.
As the World-Honored One thus traveled, he converted immeasurable humans, devas, and others;
out of compassion for his kinsmen, he has now arrived at his native city of Kapilavastu.
At that time, the elder Udāyin and the elder Chandaka went together to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then the two elders addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
King Śuddhodana has never possessed faith; he harbors impure thoughts and even does not wish to see the bhikṣus.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing this matter, addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Bhikṣus! Who among you is able to go to King Śuddhodana, and having arrived, to instruct and transform him so that he may come to have faith and reverence?"
At that time, there was a bhikṣu among the assembly who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This elder Śāriputra here is capable of going to the place of King Śuddhodana, employing skillful means to instruct and transform him so that he may come to have faith and reverence.”
Then a certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana is capable of going to King Śuddhodana’s presence and, through skillful means, teaching and transforming him so that he may come to have faith and reverence.”
Then a certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This elder Mahākāśyapa here is capable of teaching and transforming him so that he may come to have faith and reverence.”
Then a certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Elder Mahākātyāyana here is capable of teaching and transforming him so that he may come to have faith and reverence.”
Then a certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Within this assembly, the Elder Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa is capable of teaching and transforming others so that they may develop faith and reverence."
Then a certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Within this assembly, Nadi-Kāśyapa is capable of teaching and transforming him so that he may come to have faith and reverence."
Then a certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This elder Upasena is capable of going to King Śuddhodana’s residence and, through skillful means, teaching and transforming him so that he may develop faith and reverence.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Udāyin, saying: "Udāyin!
Are you able now to go to King Śuddhodana’s residence, and having arrived there, to teach and transform him so that he may come to have faith and reverence?"
Then Udāyin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am now capable.”
The Buddha then addressed him, saying: "You, Udāyin!
Go now to King Śuddhodana and, through skillful means, instruct and transform him so that he may come to have faith and reverence."
At that time, having heard these words from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Elder Udāyin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So be it, World-Honored One!”
"As the Buddha has instructed, I dare not disobey.
Then, at the break of dawn when the sun had just begun to rise, Udāyin dressed, took up his bowl, and went toward the palace of King Śuddhodana.
Having arrived, he asked the gatekeeper:
"Venerable sir, you should know:
where is King Śuddhodana now?"
The man replied,
"The King is currently in the palace attending to royal affairs.
Thereupon, the Elder Udāyin went to King Śuddhodana’s location and stood silently to one side.
At that time, when the ministers on his left and right saw Udāyin standing to one side, they immediately addressed the guards at the four gates, saying:
"Go quickly and stop this renunciant; do not allow him to remain here and cause the King to see him and give rise to evil thoughts."
Upon hearing the minister’s command, the gatekeeper hurried to Udāyin’s side, intending to drive him out.

However, when the gatekeeper saw him, he realized for the first time that this was the son of the National Preceptor; having been his childhood companion since they were small boys playing together in the dust with Prince Siddhārtha, he could not bear to expel him and instead turned back.
Then the ministers questioned the gatekeepers, saying:
"Why do you not drive out such renunciants?
Thereupon, the gatekeepers replied to the ministers, saying:

"That man is the son of the National Preceptor; from birth, he has been a close friend and companion to Prince Siddhārtha, sharing the intimacy of childhood play. For this reason, we cannot bear to drive him away."

At that time, King Śuddhodana, having finished attending to his affairs in the palace hall, rose with the intention of returning to his private chambers; surrounded on all sides by his ministers, he was being led into the inner palace.
At that time, Udāyin went quickly and arrived directly at the place where King Śuddhodana was, grasping the king’s hand.
At that moment, King Śuddhodana remained silent and spoke no word, thinking to himself:
"If I speak now, I fear the gatekeepers will drive him away."
The gatekeeper then thought to himself:
"The ministers themselves should drive him away.
The ministers, in turn, thought to themselves:
"The people within the palace gates ought to block him.
The people within the palace gates then thought to themselves:
"This man was formerly King Śuddhodana, whom he always cherished; now he has returned and walks hand-in-hand with him once more."
At that time, because each person held such thoughts, there was not a single individual who could drive him away.
Then, King Śuddhodana gradually entered the palace, ascended the inner chamber, and sat upon the lion throne.
At that time, having seen King Śuddhodana enter the inner palace and ascend the throne hall, Udāyin also ascended the throne hall and stood before the king, not far from him.
When King Śuddhodana saw Udāyin standing before him at no great distance, he was immediately overcome with affliction and, uttering a faint voice, spoke these words:
"Alas! What suffering!"
"The appearance of my son is thus withered and emaciated; it is truly loathsome.
You all must quickly drive this renunciant away! Who permitted him to enter and come here?"
Then the ministers addressed him, saying:
"Great King! As we see it, this matter is not so."
"Great King, you ought not to drive this man out. Why is that?
This man is both the son of the National Preceptor and a childhood companion of Siddhārtha, with whom he played in the dust."
At that time, Udāyin spoke with words of compassion, so as not to wound King Śuddhodana’s heart, and he uttered these verses:
“For the sake of seeking grain, one plows and sows; Out of greed for treasures, one enters the sea.
My mind now comes here out of longing to dwell; I pray only that this matter may be swiftly accomplished.”
Such a path is ever auspicious and brings constant peace and security from all fears;
for those who wish to travel to various regions in search of profit, it will surely cause Gotama to achieve his goals.
Again and again people plow their fields; again and again they scatter seeds therein;
again and again the heavens send down sweet rain; again and again the five grains ripen within the realm.
The mendicant begs again and again, and the donor gives again and again;
by practicing dāna repeatedly in this world, one repeatedly obtains its fruit in the heavens.
Again and again the cow yields milk; Again and again the calf goes to its mother’s side;
Again and again the woman conceives in her womb; Again and again she gives birth and undergoes all manner of suffering.
Time and again corpses are carried to the charnel ground; Time and again kinsmen weep as they escort them away.
If one attains the Noble Path and there is no further existence, One will not undergo rebirth within the midst of afflictions.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having heard these words of compassion from Udāyin, still harbored a slight doubt and immediately asked Udāyin again:
"Venerable sir, under whom did you originally go forth? Who is your Great Teacher?"
Then Udāyin replied to King Śuddhodana with these verses:
"The father’s name is Śuddhodana; The noble mother who gave birth is named Māyā.
Having carried him in her womb for ten months, After his birth, the mother passed away and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
Thus has a Noble One been born into your family—a Great Virtue, a Great Sage, a God among Gods.
That family has been delivered for seven generations, and its fame spreads everywhere.
A man of stature is most rare among men; he is not subject to rebirth in any place.
When such a Great Sage is born, his family shall always enjoy great peace and happiness.
Of the Śākya clan, he is the most renowned kinsman; Born of honor, his body is adorned with a hundred merits.
Such a son of the Śākyas is supreme among the gods; I have gone forth under him as a renunciant.
At that time, King Śuddhodana again asked the Elder Udāyin:
"Excellent, Bhikṣu!
From whom did you truly receive the going-forth?"
Furthermore, does that teacher of men possess right faith and the ability to practice the holy life with a correct mind?
Does he delight in dwelling in an araṇya, in empty and secluded places beneath trees?
At that time, the Elder Udāyin replied to King Śuddhodana in verse, saying:
"To whom did the King ask about those who have gone forth? Those people, with right faith, practice the holy life;
Having no fixed abode and harboring no anxiety or fear, They always experience bliss beneath the trees."
Fearless amidst the voices of others like a lion, Unentangled by nets like a fierce wind, Teaching others while remaining self-learned, He uproots all terrors; his own body knows no fear.
King Śuddhodana again asked the Elder Udāyin:
"O Bhikṣu, where is he now?"
Udāyin replied, “As Your Majesty asks,
that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is now here in this city of Kapilavastu, in the Nyagrodha Grove.”
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought to himself,
"This Udāyin is indeed my son's disciple.
For this reason, he addressed his ministers, speaking these words:
"You may now invite this bhikṣu to sit comfortably in his place.
Having heard the king's command, the ministers said:
"Great King!"
"I dare not disobey.
He then invited the Elder Udāyin to be seated.
At that time, King Śuddhodana again commanded his ministers:
"Ministers, give this food to this bhikṣu.
Having received the command, the ministers immediately took pure water and gave it to Udāyin; once he had washed his hands, they then presented the meal to Udāyin.
At that time, having received this food, Udāyin did not eat it himself, wishing instead to offer it to the World-Honored One.
King Śuddhodana then asked the Elder Udāyin:
"Monk, for what reason do you not eat this food?"
Udāyin said, "This food was intended to be offered to the World-Honored One; therefore, it is not eaten.
At that time, King Śuddhodana’s heart was again filled with anguish, and as tears flowed down his face, he spoke these words:
"Alas, my son! Your body was so supple;
while formerly within the palace, you constantly experienced happiness and your person was free from all suffering. For what reason do you undergo such hardship today?"
"Only after the bhikṣu has gone begging and obtained food shall he then eat.
When King Śuddhodana had spoken these words, he wept with a sobbing throat and addressed Udāyin again, saying:
"Let the bhikṣu eat this food for now; I shall now go separately to fetch more food to bring to your teacher."
Then Udāyin again addressed the king, saying:
"It is so, Great King!
This food has already been prepared as an offering for the World-Honored One; among all sentient beings in this world, there is none who is able to digest it."
"Why is this? For that Blessed One possesses the most excellent conduct of precepts, the most excellent meditative concentration, and his wisdom is likewise supreme.
Then King Śuddhodana addressed his ministers, speaking these words:
"O you, take some more food now and give it to this bhikṣu; once he has eaten, quickly take this food and send it to that prince."
The ministers immediately brought other food for Udāyin.
When Udāyin had finished eating, he addressed the king, saying:
"It is thus, Great King!"
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—such kings and multitudes of people, immeasurable and boundless, all came to pay him homage.
"Nevertheless, Great King!
You too ought to go to that place.
Having spoken these words, he rose from his seat and intended to leave the palace.
Then King Śuddhodana again addressed the Elder Udāyin, saying:
"Venerable sir, when you previously arrived at Siddhārtha’s place, you spoke these words:
'I shall come to see you before long.'"
Udāyin replied, "I shall respectfully obey the King's command.
At that time, the Elder Udāyin took the food and departed from the city, proceeding to the interior of the Nyagrodha grove. Upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, he addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
King Śuddhodana has been instructed by me and has attained joy; he wishes to come and see the Buddha.
When Udāyin departed from the palace, in the brief interval that followed, King Śuddhodana issued a command to his ministers, speaking these words:
"You know the time; Prince Siddhārtha has already arrived at this city. What should we do now?
The ministers replied, "Excellent, Great King!"

"If other śramaṇas were to come to the King's presence, we would still have to provide them with offerings and provisions; how much more so for Prince Siddhārtha, who is no different from us in person—how could we remain at ease without showing him respect?"
“We have merely protected the Great King’s mind; we have not yet reached that place.
Then, King Śuddhodana issued a decree to sound the gongs and proclaim throughout the city so that all might know:
“I now wish to go to the place where Prince Siddhārtha went to observe it. You all must each prepare yourselves with full adornment and follow me. The teacher Kāśyapa spoke thus.
(The masters of the Mahāsāṃghika school further state this, saying:
"At that time, King Śuddhodana addressed Udāyin, speaking these words:
'As the Bhikṣu intends!'"")
"What kind of food do you wish to prepare for the crown prince?
Then Udāyin addressed the king, saying:
"It is thus, Great King!"
If one wishes to prepare food for the World-Honored One, one must prepare excellent, pure, sweet, fragrant, and clean delicacies; it is only such food as this that the World-Honored One partakes of.
At that time, King Śuddhodana commanded his ministers: "You must know this!
Quickly prepare various pure and fragrant foods for the Prince."
Having heard the king’s decree, the ministers addressed the king, saying:
"We shall comply with the Great King's instructions and dare not disobey.
Thereupon, they immediately prepared various kinds of delicacies—pure, fragrant, and delicious foods—and having thus completed the preparations, they presented them to Udāyin.
Having finished his own meal, Udāyin took the pure, fragrant, and clean food and delicacies prepared by the king, departed from the city of Kapilavastu, and proceeded to the Nyagrodha Grove.
Arriving at the place where that Buddha was, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have already instructed King Śuddhodana, causing his heart to rejoice, and he wishes to come and see the Buddha."
"First prepare such fragrant and delicious food and drink for me, and then offer it to the World-Honored One; I pray that the Buddha will accept this food in accordance with the Dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"

"How did the Elder Udāyin convert King Śuddhodana so that he was filled with joy, and furthermore, enabled him to prepare pure, fragrant, sweet, and delicious food and drink to offer to the World-Honored One?"
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!

It is not only today that Udāyin has gone to the residence of King Śuddhodana, completed his teaching there, and brought me sweet and delicious food; in the past as well, he once taught him until he was filled with joy and brought me sweet food."
Then the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
What is the matter?”
“We pray that you will explain such matters for us; we now wish and desire to hear them.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“I recall that in the distant past, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a king of crows named Sūphadala (translated in the Sui language as ‘Good Son’). He resided in that city of Vārāṇasī, living in harmonious community with eighty thousand crows.”
The virtuous son, King Crow, had a wife named Subhāṣitā (translated in the Sui language as "Virtuous Woman").
At that time, the crow-wife, together with the crow-king, engaged in sexual union and became pregnant.
At that time, the crow’s wife suddenly had this thought:
"May I obtain pure, fragrant, and clean food—such as that which the human king now eats.
Because the crow’s wife could not obtain the food she longed for, she rolled about in distress and confusion; her body became haggard and emaciated, trembling and unable to find peace.
When the virtuous son, King Eṇī, saw that his wife was writhing in distress, her body withered and haggard, emaciated and trembling so that she could not find peace, he asked his wife:
"Why now do you writhen upon the ground, your body withered and haggard, emaciated and trembling, unable to find peace?"
At that time, the crow’s wife replied to the Crow King, saying:
"Excellent, noble son!
I am now pregnant, and I have had this thought:"
"I wish to obtain pure and fragrant delicacies such as those eaten by the king.
Then the parrot, Son of Virtue, said to his wife:
"How extraordinary, O noble lady!"
"As for me today, where could I obtain such fragrant and delicious food?
The royal palace is deep and secluded; it cannot be reached. If I were to enter, I would surely lose my life at their hands."
His wife replied again to the king of crows,
"Noble son!
If you cannot now obtain such food and drink, my death is certain, and the child within my womb will likewise surely not survive."
The noble son, King Eṇī, spoke again to his wife:
"How strange, O virtuous one!
The day of your death must surely be approaching, that you now think of such a thing so difficult to obtain."
After the noble son, King Eṇī, had spoken these words, he remained there lost in thought, sorrowful and despondent, and further reflected:
"According to my wishes, such fragrant, pure, and clean food as that eaten by kings is truly difficult to obtain."

At that time, within the assembly of the crow king’s subjects, there was a certain crow who saw that the noble son of the crows was dwelling in a state of sorrow and unhappiness. Having witnessed this, he went to where the crow king was and addressed him, saying:
"How extraordinary, O Holy One!
"For what reason do you dwell here, lost in sorrowful reflection?
Then the noble son, King Kāka, related at length the causes and conditions of the preceding events.
The crow spoke again to the noble son, the king, saying:
"Excellent, noble son!
Do not grieve further; I can act as king to seek out for you those rare, fragrant, and delicious delicacies fit for a king's consumption.
At that time, the King of Crows again addressed that crow, speaking these words:
"Excellent, good friend!
If you have the power to accomplish such a task for me, I shall repay you for the merit of your deed.

At that time, the crow flew from the place where the king of crows resided into the void, reached the palace of Brahmadatta, and alighted upon a tree not far from the kitchen, observing the interior of King Brahmadatta’s dining quarters.

When the king’s meal was prepared, there was a woman who had fully arranged the various delicacies; as the time for the meal approached, she took silver vessels and filled them with that food and drink, intending to present them to the king.

At that time, the crow flew down from the tree and perched upon the woman’s head; it pecked at her nose, and as she suffered from the pain in her nose, she immediately overturned the food onto the ground.
At that time, the crow took the food and brought it to the crow king.
Once the crow king had received it, he immediately gave it to his virtuous wife, the female crow.
Having received it, she ate her fill at once; her body became peaceful and secure, and thus she gave birth.
At that time, the crow went there every day to snatch away their food and bring it to the king of crows.
When King Brahmadatta repeatedly witnessed this occurrence, he thought to himself:
"How strange! How extraordinary!"
"Why does this crow come so frequently and constantly to defile my food, and furthermore, wound my womenfolk with its beak and claws?
Unable to endure these matters, the king immediately ordered the netters and hunters to be summoned, saying to them, "You must go quickly to that place where the crow is and capture it alive."
Having heard the king’s command, the hunters replied to the king,
saying, "As the king has commanded, we dare not disobey his decree. The hunters went forth,
captured this bird with their nets, and bringing it alive, they presented it to King Brahmadatta.
Then King Brahmadatta said to his crow:
"For what reason do you repeatedly defile my food?
Furthermore, why do you wound my women with your beak and claws?"
At that time, the crow said to King Brahmadatta:
"Excellent, Great King!
Listen as I relate this matter to you, so as to bring joy to Your Majesty."
At that time, King Brahmadatta felt great joy in his heart and thought to himself:
"How extraordinary this matter is!
How is it that this crow can speak the language of humans?"
Having formed this thought, he said to the crow:
"Excellent, excellent!
You must explain the meaning of this matter to me so as to bring me joy."
At that time, the crow addressed King Brahmadatta in verse, saying:
“Great King, you should know that in Vārāṇasī there dwells a king of crows, constantly attended by a retinue of eighty thousand crows; they all abide by his commands.”
The queen of that king of crows has something she longs for; I have now told the Great King the reason for it.
What the crow’s wife yearns for is fragrant and delicious food—exactly like what the Great King eats.
For this reason, I come here again and again to snatch away the Great King’s fragrant and delicious food.
Now, for the sake of that king of crows, I have been brought here and bound by Your Majesty.
How excellent it would be if the Great Holy King, out of compassion and pity, would release me!
For the sake of my husband, the king of crows, I have frequently come to snatch away Your Majesty’s food.
I recall that from the time of this present life until now, I have never before committed such a deed;
having now received a single command from Your Majesty, I shall henceforth never do it again.
When King Brahmadatta had heard these words from the crow, joy arose in his heart, and he spoke thus:
"How extraordinary this is!"
“Even a human being cannot possess such a heart of love and respect for his lord as this crow does.
Having spoken these words, King Brahmadatta recited this verse:
“If there be such a great minister, He should be granted a heavy reward of food and stipend.”
"You must be like this fierce and courageous crow, who does not spare its own life for the sake of its master in seeking food.
After King Brahmadatta had spoken this verse, he addressed the crow again, saying:
"Excellent, you crow!"

From now on, I shall always come here to take fragrant and delicious food; if there should be anyone who obstructs you and refuses to give you food, inform me at once, and I myself will give you my own portion to take away.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should know! That king of crows was my very self."
The crow that stole food from the king at that time was none other than the bhikṣu Udāyin;
King Brahmadatta was none other than King Śuddhodana.
At that time, the bhikṣu Udāyin gladdened him and obtained food for my sake;
now it is likewise, for he has caused King Śuddhodana to feel joy and has again brought food for my sake.
Then, King Śuddhodana finally rang the bell and issued a command to all the people of the city of Kapilavastu:
"Not a single person shall go ahead to see Prince Siddhārtha. If you wish to see him, you must accompany me to do so."
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll 52;
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll 53.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Sui Dynasty.

In the latter part of the "Chapter on the Causes and Conditions of Udāyin," at that time, King Śuddhodana was surrounded by all the members of his own inner palace, both preceding and following him. He further led all the members of Prince Siddhārtha’s inner palace, as well as other external relatives, along with the young Śākya youths and their attendants;

he also led the fourfold army, the hundred officials, the great ministers, generals, and aides, as well as the householders, elders, and senior citizens of the cities, towns, and villages. Displaying the power of the Great King’s majesty and manifesting the sovereign spiritual virtue of the Great King, he was encircled on all sides—left, right, front, and back—by his great kinsmen and military hosts.

At that time, the Śākya clansmen and their followers, numbering ninety-nine thousand in all, together with the inhabitants of the city of Kapilavastu, went forth from the city as one body, desiring to see the Tathāgata.
The World-Honored One saw from afar King Śuddhodana approaching with his great assembly in full ceremonial attire, and he immediately thought:
"If I see him and do not rise to welcome and honor him, people will say of me:
'Is this truly one who has realized the fruit of the practice of the precepts!'"
"Why is it that upon seeing my father, I do not rise to greet him?
"If I were now to see my father and the great assembly and rise to go meet them, they would incur immeasurable sin;
yet if I were to maintain my dignified demeanor and remain here, they would feel no sense of reverence toward me."
The Tathāgata, having performed these three kinds of mental contemplations and having seen these three kinds of causes and conditions, and having deliberated upon these three meanings;

rose from his seat and, by means of his supernormal powers, ascended into the air. While in mid-air, he walked back and forth, stood, sat, lay down, or slept; his body emitted smoke or flames, and he manifested various such supernatural transformations, appearing and disappearing at will.

At that time, the city-protecting deities and gate-guarding deities of the city of Kapilavastu rose into the air before King Śuddhodana, proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
With these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"On the day the Tathāgata first went forth from home, The yakṣas and various deities opened the gate for him, And Vaiśravaṇa and others showed him the way;
The World-Honored One is a vessel of great merit."
When the Tathāgata was about to depart from the gate, he made this great vow:
"If I do not subdue the hosts of Māras, I shall never again enter this city."
His vow is now fulfilled; the World-Honored One has once again subdued all Māras, realized the unsurpassed path of Bodhi, and accomplished his former aspiration.
The Great Man, having appeared in the world for the sake of merit and already realized the path of unsurpassed Bodhi,
now returns to enter this city out of compassion for all his kinsmen.
At that time, King Śuddhodana saw from afar the World-Honored One soaring through the air by means of supernormal power, manifesting various miraculous transformations; he then thought to himself:
"I recall that in the past, Prince Siddhārtha left his home to renounce the world and has now become a great seer, possessing great majestic virtue and great supernormal powers."
After King Śuddhodana had formed this thought, he descended from his horse-drawn chariot to the ground and proceeded on foot toward the place where the Buddha was.
As King Śuddhodana drew gradually closer to the Buddha, the Buddha likewise descended slowly from the air.
When King Śuddhodana arrived at the place where the Buddha was staying, the Buddha immediately descended from the air to his original location.

Seeing that the Buddha’s head was bare of a celestial crown, with his beard and hair shaven and his body clad in saffron robes, King Śuddhodana fainted and fell to the ground out of love for his son. After a short while, he regained consciousness; rolling upon the ground, he wept and wailed, his tears streaming down to cover his face.

At that time, those ninety-nine thousand members of the Śākya clan, along with their internal and external retinues, were all likewise overcome by fainting and rolled upon the ground; they wailed and wept with tears streaming down their faces, suffering great agony through their distress, resentment, and vexation.
At that time, the great assembly spoke in verse:
"The Great King leads the multitude to the Buddha's side; The father beholds the World-Honored One but has not yet spoken with him.
The King wishes to address his son, yet finds no words; He wishes to speak to the bhikṣu, yet likewise cannot."
When the king beheld the Tathāgata’s marks of a śramaṇa, he felt shame beneath his own parasol;
crying out loudly, hot breath issued from his mouth, and in his confusion and distress, he fell to the ground, uttering various cries.

The Tathāgata remained silent and entered meditative absorption; seeing this, the king was consumed by grief and anxiety, like a thirsty man who has traveled from afar only to find that the water he sees from a distance has already dried up.
At that time, the World-Honored One again had this thought:
"These Śākyas possess great pride and are haughty and self-willed; if they were to prostrate themselves with their heads to the ground in salutation to me, they would immediately become weary."
Having formed this thought, he immediately ascended into the air to a height of one zhang above the ground.
He further thought:
"Now that I am at such a distance from the earth, these people ought to bow their bodies in prostration."
And there is a verse that says:
"The Buddha observed that the kings harbored pride, So he flew and stayed in the air at a height of one zhang;
Out of compassion for all the other people as well, The Buddha therefore remained suspended in mid-air."
At that time, King Śuddhodana rose from the ground, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and spoke these verses:
“I now pay triple homage to the Honored One of True Suchness; I have already paid homage at his feet since his birth.
Long ago, while he was in the palace, the physiognomists prophesied: ‘He shall sit beneath a tree, with its shade covering his body.’”
Now I see you practicing the foremost conduct, your face and features as pure as a blooming flower;
this brings great joy to my body and mind, and for this reason I now prostrate three times in return.

At that time, King Śuddhodana prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; thereafter, the members of the two palaces and their retinues followed in succession, bowing their heads to the ground in worship. Next, the various relatives from outside the royal family also prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. Furthermore, the young princes of the Śākya clan likewise prostrated. Then, the generals, soldiers, aides, civil officials, and great ministers on the left and right performed their salutations in order. Following them, eminent householders of great clans prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and in succession, wealthy elders and senior laymen also paid their respects.

However, although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses such profound and subtle dharmas, he feared that the great assembly had not yet given rise to a heart of joy and longing, nor had they yet conceived a sense of their rarity and extraordinariness; for this reason, he had not yet preached such a dharma.

At that time, wishing to inspire joy, faith, and reverence in the beings of that age, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal powers, flew up into the air. To the east, at a height of one *tāla* tree above the ground, he remained suspended in mid-air. Having established himself there, he further manifested various kinds of supernormal transformations: namely, dividing a single body into many bodies, or combining many bodies into a single body; moving horizontally from below without his feet touching the ground; ascending from below and descending from above; and passing through stone walls and mountain barriers without obstruction.

They enter the earth as if it were water, and tread upon water as if it were solid ground; remaining in mid-air, they sit cross-legged, peaceful and unmoving. They walk through the sky like soaring birds;

from their upper bodies they emit smoke, while from their lower bodies they issue fire, like a great mass of flames, and like the sun and moon, possessing great majesty and great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). Their majestic power blazes forth and their radiance is brilliant.
At times they touch the sun and moon with their hands; their bodies grow so vast as to reach the Brahma-heaven. They manifest such various kinds of supernormal transformations.

At that time, having performed these deeds, the World-Honored One further manifested such paired supernatural powers: namely, from one half of his body, smoke issued from the lower part, while from the other half of his body, fire issued from the upper part.
The Tathāgata may, moreover, emit smoke from the upper half of his body while emitting fire from the lower half;
or he may emit fire from his left side while releasing smoke from his right side, or emit fire from his right side while releasing smoke from his left side.

Furthermore, at times the Tathāgata causes smoke to issue from the lower half of his body while the upper half remains as it is; or again, he causes cool, clear water to issue from the upper half of his body while the lower half remains as it is.

Furthermore, at times the Tathāgata causes cool, clear water to issue from the lower half of his body while the upper half remains as it is; or he causes smoke to issue from the upper half of his body while the lower half remains as it is.
At times the Tathāgata emits smoke from his left side while cool, clear water issues from his right side;
in a moment, he may again emit smoke from his right side while cool, clear water issues from his left side.
