Furthermore, at times the Tathāgata emits blazing fire from the lower half of his body while emitting cool, clear water from the upper half; and again, he emits blazing fire from the upper half of his body while emitting clear, cool water from the lower half.
Furthermore, at times the Tathāgata emits fire from his left side and clear, cool water from his right side.
At other times, the Tathāgata emits fire from his left side and clear, cool water from his right side.
Alternatively, from the right side he emits clear, cool water, while from the left side he releases blazing flames.
At other times, the Tathāgata emits fire from his entire body, while from between his two eyes he emits clear, cool water.
Sometimes from between his eyes he emits blazing fire, or again from his entire body he radiates clear, cool water.
At times the Tathāgata manifests his lower body while his upper body remains invisible, as he preaches the Dharma.
At times, he manifests only the upper part of his body while the lower part remains unmanifest, and therein he preaches the Dharma.

Furthermore, at times the Tathāgata enters the fire-light samādhi, from all his pores emitting various kinds of light—namely, blue light, yellow light, red light, white light, crimson light, and crystal-colored light.
The Tathāgata may again mount into the air at a height of one tala tree above the ground and manifest supernormal powers;
or he may rise to a height of two tala trees, or three, four, five, or seven tala trees, remaining in mid-air to manifest supernormal powers.
That is to say, he manifested the miracle of making one body into many bodies, even emitting light of the color of crystal, displaying all manner of supernatural transformations.
At that time, the World-Honored One again produced a body from the south, rising into the air to the height of one *tāla* tree to the west, and performed various miraculous transformations.

The World-Honored One, having perhaps vanished from the western direction, rose into the air to the height of one *tāla* tree above the ground in the north; there, dwelling in mid-air, he performed various supernatural transformations, such as manifesting many bodies from a single body, and even emitting light of the color of crystal.

In this manner, it was so for each and every direction; they all traveled through the air at a height of seven *tāla* trees above the ground, simultaneously manifesting various supernatural transformations, such as dividing a single body into many bodies, up to emitting light the color of crystal.

At that time, the great assembly, seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, manifest such supernatural powers, immediately gave rise toward the Buddha to a mind of joy, faith, reverence, and wonder, and other such states of mind.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the great assembly had conceived a heart of faith, reverence, and longing, descended from the sky and sat upon a seat at the head of the assembly; he then preached the Dharma to the great assembly in successive order.

As for what is called the teaching of the Dharma: it is that sentient beings have dwelt for a long night amidst afflictions; hearing these words causes them to give rise to weary detachment (*nirveda*).

For this reason, one encourages the practice of giving, ethical discipline, diligence, and patience so that they may be born in favorable realms; one instructs them to practice weary detachment from sensual desires and outflows (*āsrava*) to emerge from affliction; furthermore, one praises the merit of leaving the household life and extols the Dharma of liberation as being such as this.

When the Tathāgata taught these dharmas, he knew that the great assembly had given rise to hearts of joy, hearts of exultation, supple and equanimous hearts, and hearts free from external distraction.
At that time, the World-Honored One also possessed the dharmas upheld by all Buddhas, namely the dharmas of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Thereupon, for the sake of that great assembly, the World-Honored One skillfully expounded, proclaimed, and manifested them.

At that time, that great assembly—consisting of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings—immediately upon their seats became free from dust and removed from defilement; they were no longer subject to afflictions, severed all fetters, attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, and all accumulated phenomena were entirely extinguished in their marks as they attained knowledge in accordance with reality.
It is like a pure, stainless garment that is capable of taking on various colors; once it takes on these colors, it immediately assumes their hue.

When this had been said, at that time the immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings in the great assembly, while still upon their seats, became free from dust and defilement, were no longer subject to afflictions, severed all fetters, attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, and even reached the cessation of all marks, attaining knowledge in accordance with reality.

Then that great assembly, having personally seen all dharmas, attained all dharmas, realized all dharmas, and entered into all dharmas, had transcended all doubts, extinguished all delusions, was free from further uncertainty, and had attained fearlessness.
The causes and conditions for my birth have all been extinguished.
Having realized this, I take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha, and receive the five precepts of an upāsaka.

King Śuddhodana, because he was shrouded by the net of afflictions for his beloved son, failed to attain the fruit [of his desire]. Sitting before the World-Honored One, with a voice of compassion, he wept and choked with sobs, speaking in verse:
“Where have you gone, abandoning that exquisite adornment Of the seven-jeweled crown you once wore upon your head?”
Furthermore, you have cast away the bright, pure jewel from your topknot; with your head bare and your form disfigured, you lack majesty.
Where did you also discard those exquisite garments of Kāśī from the past?
How can my beloved son wear such coarse, rag-like robes of refuse?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to King Śuddhodana in verse, saying:
“Great King, there is a land named Nyasa;
It was there that I laid aside my celestial crown, Desiring to eliminate the pride of the self, And wishing to realize those nectar-like words.”
For the sake of robes dyed in the colors of the saṃghāṭī, I have cast aside those garments of Kāśi;
now that the saṃghāṭī has been donned upon my body, I have realized unsurpassed, wondrous Bodhi.
Thereupon, King Śuddhodana again addressed the Tathāgata in verse:
"In the past, while in my palace, I sought a hundred vows, Vowing that I might have a son who would become a Wheel-Turning King.
Now I see him with shaven head, holding an alms-bowl in his hand; For me, tell me, what supreme attainment has your son achieved?"
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed King Śuddhodana in verse, saying:
"The Wheel-Turning King may gain ten thousand hearts, yet never find satiety; Though he may obtain a long life, he lacks true sovereignty.
My mind is sovereign and boundless; I wish my son were not such a deluded Wheel-Turning King."
At that time, King Śuddhodana again addressed the Buddha in verse, saying:
"You formerly wore sandals made of the seven precious gems; You slept upon various soft and supple bedding;
You dwelt in peace within palaces and towers; A white parasol was held over your head."
“Your feet are soft and pure like lotuses; how could you tread upon sand, thorns, pebbles, and gravel?
At that time, the World-Honored One again replied to Śuddhodana in verse:
“I am now the Honored One, the All-Knowing One; I am unstained by all phenomena, like a lotus.”
"All those who have already renounced possess no craving or attachment, just as I now am free from all afflictions.
At that time, King Śuddhodana again addressed the Buddha in verse, saying:
"In the past, within the palace, there were sandalwood and other woods, as well as various fragrances cool as the moon."
Use this at the appropriate time to rub your body; having rubbed it, your entire frame shall receive peace and comfort.
Now that the early summer heat is at its peak, how will you travel alone through the forests and thickets?
Formerly within the palace you possessed exquisite voices; now that the court ladies are gone, with whom will you find delight?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Śuddhodana with these verses:
"I possess a Dharma-pool of cool and refreshing water, A place of no sorrow praised by the wise.
Bathe your body in this jewel-pool of merit; Do not drown in the water, but reach the further shore."
King Śuddhodana again addressed the Buddha in verse, saying:
"In the palace of old you wore garments of Kāśī; Your body was perfumed with the scents of lotus and campaka.
With soft, layered flowers stored within your robes, You sat within the palace of the Śākyas, majestic and resplendent."
Now, this coarse hempen rag from a dust-heap, dyed here and there with tree bark, barely covers the body and is truly shameful;
do you, a great man, not feel revulsion for it?
At that time, the World-Honored One further replied to King Śuddhodana in verse, saying:
"Regarding clothing, bedding, food, drink, and the like, I formerly gave rise to craving for them all;
But as for exquisite, upright forms—the objects of sensual desire— Through right mindfulness, I have now relinquished them all."
King Śuddhodana again addressed the Buddha in verse, saying: "In the past, within your palace,
there were vessels of the seven precious gems, as well as trays and tables of gold and silver,
filled with various delicacies of sweet and savory flavors— foods fit for kings to eat according to their own desires."
Now that you have obtained food that is cold, hot, coarse, or astringent—neither exquisite nor palatable—how can you eat it?
Why do you not feel aversion toward such food, and why do you not give rise to thoughts of loathing or resentment?
The Buddha again replied to King Śuddhodana with these verses:
"It is heard that all the holy ones of the past, present, and future, Whether eating coarse,
astringent, or bitter food, Out of compassion for the world, did not find it loathsome."
King Śuddhodana again spoke in verse, saying:
"When you were formerly within my palace, You sat and lay upon exquisite, soft, and supple spreads, The most excellent in the world, beyond compare;
Reclining with pillows to your heart's content, there was nothing to be disliked."
Now, upon this coarse, rough, and hard ground, you spread only grass and tree leaves;
how is it that you lie down and sleep without aversion, your body so supple and unharmed?
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed King Śuddhodana in verse, saying:
"I have now attained the wisdom of all masteries, And am entirely liberated from all suffering and affliction.
To extract the thorns of all suffering and affliction, I do not feel aversion, out of compassion for the world."
King Śuddhodana again addressed the Buddha in verse, saying:
"In former days you delighted in your home, scattering various exquisite flowers upon the ground;
within the rooms, lamps shone brightly without the need for wind, as did those in the towers and all the windows."
Her body adorned with flower garlands and necklaces, the woman was as upright as a jade maiden;
her speech was sweet and charming, she followed his will, gazing up at him without distraction as she listened to her husband’s commands.
The Buddha again replied to King Śuddhodana in verse, saying:
"O King of the Śākyas, I have newly practiced these deeds: The subtle and wondrous Brahma-conducts within the heavens.
Having attained mastery over the mind in my practice, I go wherever I intend and perform them all."
King Śuddhodana again addressed the Buddha in verse, saying:
"With the sounds of drums, lutes, and harps, And exquisite songs, you were awakened from sleep;
Just as Śakra dwells among the gods, So too did you dwell in the palace in the past."
The Buddha again replied to King Śuddhodana in verse, saying:
"The Sūtra and Geya produce wondrous sounds; Through the liberation of *yathābhūta*, you have now awakened me.
I have companions who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*); Great King, I dwell among such a multitude."
King Śuddhodana again addressed the Buddha in verse, saying:

"You have subdued all the mountains and rivers of the great earth, And even renounced a thousand sons endowed with every desire And the exquisite seven treasures to come here; Why do you practice this life of a śramaṇa?"
The Buddha again replied to King Śuddhodana with these verses:
"Wisdom and samādhi are my vast earth; The thousands of dhyānas are my sons;
The seven factors of enlightenment are my jewels— Great King, know that I have attained them all."
King Śuddhodana further spoke in verse, saying:
"In the past, you drove a chariot yoked with well-trained horses, The chariot adorned with various precious gems;
A pure white parasol covered your body, And a clean fly-whisk with a handle of clear lapis lazuli."
The Buddha again replied to the king in verse:
“I take right effort as my team of four horses; Wisdom, reflection, and a sense of shame serve as my chariot.
With diligence as my swift steed upon which I ride, I mount it to enter the realm free from sorrow.”
King Śuddhodana spoke again in verse:
"In the past, when you were at home, you rode Kaṇṭhaka; His body was pure, white, and most excellent, Adorned with various jewels upon his saddle and bridle;
Riding this well-trained horse, you traveled wherever you pleased."
The Buddha again replied to the king in verse:
“Of all the various horses upon the great earth, And the countless men in the world who ride them— All of them are subject to impermanence;
Having observed this, I have mastered spiritual powers at will.”
King Śuddhodana further spoke in verse, saying:
"When you formerly dwelt within the palace, The halls and pavilions were no different from those of the heavens;
Guarded by hosts bearing swords, bows, and arrows, Your body was clad in armor of exquisite refinement."
Now you are in the forest without protection, in a place where yakṣas and rākṣasas are fearsome;
with various beasts crying out in the darkness of night, how can you give rise to such fearlessness?
The Buddha again replied to the king in verse:
“Whatever yakṣas or piśācas there may be, And all the various beasts that are fearsome,
Wandering through the darkness at night within the forest— They cannot move even a single hair on my body.”
Fearless amidst the voices of others like a lion, Like the wind that cannot be bound by ropes,
And like a lotus flower unsullied by water, I remain untainted by the turbidity of worldly dharmas.

At that time, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, the Elder Uruvilvākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Upasena, Mahākauṣṭhila, Cunda, Revata, and other such immeasurable multitudes sat to the left and right of the Buddha.

At that time, because of their ascetic practices, those virtuous ones lacked physical luster; their bodies were exhausted by toil, their forms were emaciated, their complexions lacked radiance, and their strength was meager, such that only sinews and skin remained to envelop their frames.
At that time, King Śuddhodana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As for these people who are now seated to the right of the World-Honored One, from where did they come to go forth into homelessness?”
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his golden arm toward King Śuddhodana, pointing to each of those bhikṣus one by one and calling out their names as he showed them to the king, saying:

"This is Śāriputra; this is Mahākāśyapa; this is Uruvilvākāśyapa; this is Nadīkāśyapa; this is Gayākāśyapa; this is Upasena; this is Revata; this is Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra—such as these, all of whom are of the great Brahmin clans of the kingdom of Magadha."
King Śuddhodana again asked the Buddha,
“Who is this person sitting now at the World-Honored One’s left side?
From where did he come to leave the household life and join the World-Honored One?”
The Buddha said to the king:
"This is Mahāmaudgalyāyana; this is Mahākātyāyana; this is Mahākauṣṭhila; this is Mahācunda. All such as these were also the sons of great clans from the villages, towns, and settlements of Magadha."
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he was despondent and unhappy, and he thought to himself:
"This son of mine is truly a youth of great lineage, a Kṣatriya; he is handsome and pleasing, such that those who behold him never tire of looking at him, like a golden image."
Since he is a youth of a great Kṣatriya clan, it is not appropriate for him to be surrounded by Brāhmaṇas on his left and right;
since he is a youth of a great Kṣatriya clan, he should instead be surrounded by those of a great Kṣatriya clan, as this accords with the law.

Having formed this thought, and desiring to accomplish such a matter, he rose from his seat and returned to his palace. Chapter 55: The因缘 (Causes and Conditions) of Upāli The Mahāsāṃghika-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya-mātṛkā:

The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Chapter Fifty-five, Part One: The Causes and Conditions of Upāli. At that time, not long after King Śuddhodana had returned to his palace, a youth named Upāli came from among his own retinue to the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the mother of the youth Upāli took her son Upāli by the hand and led him to present him to the Buddha, saying these words:
"This Upāli once shaved the hair and beard of the World-Honored One."
Then Upāli immediately shaved the beard and hair for the World-Honored One.
At that time, Upāli’s mother said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One:”
"Is the youth Upāli skilled at shaving the Buddha's hair and beard?
The Buddha said to Upāli’s mother,
"Although he is indeed skilled at shaving the hair and beard, his body is too low."
At that time, the mother of the youth Upāli said to Upāli:
"Upāli, you shall shave the hair and beard for the Tathāgata; do not lower your body too much, lest it disturb the mind of the Honored One."
At that time, Upāli immediately entered the first dhyāna.
Then Upāli’s mother spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“Is the youth Upāli skilled at shaving hair and beard?
The Buddha said to Upāli’s mother,
“Although he is indeed skilled at shaving hair and beard, his body is leaning too far back.”
At that time, the mother of the youth Upāli again addressed the youth Upāli, saying:
"You, Upāli! Do not lean your body back too far, lest it cause the Venerable One’s mind to become disturbed."
At that time, Upāli entered the second dhyāna.
Then Upāli’s mother spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Has the youth Upāli finished shaving his hair and beard well?
The Buddha said to the mother of the youth Upāli:
"Although he has indeed shaved his hair and beard well, he has merely taken slightly too many inhalations."
Then the mother of the youth Upāli said to Upāli:
"Shave the hair and beard for the Tathāgata, but do not let him inhale too deeply, lest it disturb the Venerable One's mind."
At that time, the youth Upāli immediately entered the third dhyāna.
Then the mother of the youth Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“Has the youth Upāli been well-trained in shaving the hair and beard?
The Buddha said to the mother of the youth Upāli:
“Although he is indeed skilled at shaving the hair and beard, his exhalations are somewhat too frequent.”
At that time, the mother of the youth Upāli spoke to Upāli, saying:
"Shave the hair and beard for the Tathāgata, but do not let him exhale too much so as to cause the Venerable One’s mind to become disturbed."
At that time, the youth Upāli immediately entered the fourth dhyāna.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!..."
"Quickly take the razor from Upāli's hand so that he does not fall to the ground. Why is this?
That youth has already entered the fourth dhyāna."
At that time, the mother of the youth Upāli took the sword from Upāli’s hand.
Then, King Śuddhodana entered the city of Kapilavastu and summoned all the Śākyas to assemble; in the courtyard of the great palace, he issued this command to them:

"You Śākyas should know that my prince Siddhārtha, had he not gone forth into homelessness, would certainly have become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin Rāja), and you Śākyas should have served him."
Why is this? Because that renunciant has already attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and is already able to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma; he is the most excellent among gods and humans.

Since he is a prince of the Kṣatriya caste, lovely and handsome like a golden image, whom all people delight to behold, yet he takes disciples from the Brāhmaṇa caste to surround him on all sides—this is truly not appropriate.
"Since he is a prince of the Kṣatriya Śākya clan, it would be well if he were surrounded by other Kṣatriyas of the Śākya clan.
Then, all the Śākyas addressed King Śuddhodana together, saying:
"Great King!"
"What should we do for you first now?
At that time, King Śuddhodana addressed the Śākyas, saying: "You Śākyas!..."
If one knows the proper time, one must ensure that at least one person from each family renounces the household life.
If there are five brothers among the Śākyas, three should be ordained and two remain at home;
if there are four, two should be ordained and two remain at home.
If there are three people, two have left the household life while one remains at home;
if there are two people, one has left the household life while one remains at home;
if there is only one person, do not allow them to leave the household life. Why is this?
"Do not allow our Śākya clan to be extinguished.
At that time, all the Śākyas again spoke together to Śuddhodana, saying:
"Great King, if this is so, you must clearly establish a formal covenant."
King Śuddhodana immediately assembled the Śākyas and asked them,
"Since my son has now gone forth into homelessness, who among you is able to follow him and go forth as well?"
"If you are able to follow me and leave the household life, you may each write down your own names to serve as a record.
At that time, the five hundred Śākya youths each wrote their own names with their own hands, all declaring that they were able to follow the Prince in leaving the household life.
At that time, five hundred young Śākya boys each untied the necklaces they were wearing and said to one another,
"Who is worthy to take our necklaces?"
Having deliberated thus, he further thought: "This Upāli!
For a long time in the past, he has diligently served us Śākyas; this Upāli is worthy of receiving the necklaces we have taken off."
At that time, the five hundred Śākya youths each removed their necklaces and gave them to Upāli.
Having made this entrustment, they returned together to their respective homes and consulted their parents.
At that time, Upāli immediately thought to himself:
"Since these Śākyas have now been able to renounce such precious jewels and necklaces, it would be improper for me to enjoy them.

Yet, these sons of the Śākyas possess great majesty and great spiritual power; since they have already cast aside their esteemed official positions and various treasures and still desire to leave the household life, why should I not do the same?"

At that time, the barber Upāli, seeing the Śākya youths each going to consult their parents, immediately set aside the necklace he had been given as a gift and went straight to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Having stood to one side, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent,
World-Honored One!"
"I only pray that you will grant me permission to follow the Buddha and leave the household life.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately granted him permission to leave the household life and receive full ordination.
Then those five hundred Śākya youths each went to their own homes, consulted with their parents, and returned once more to King Śuddhodana’s side, addressing him thus:
“Great King!
You may now take us to the presence of the World-Honored One; since he has gone forth into homelessness, we too should follow him and go forth.

Then King Śuddhodana, together with those five hundred Śākya youths, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. Once they were seated, King Śuddhodana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is well said that it is not fitting for a Great Virtuous One of the Kṣatriya caste to be surrounded by those of the Brāhmaṇa caste; indeed, this is truly inappropriate.”
Now, since the World-Honored One is of the Kṣatriya caste, it would be fitting if he were surrounded by other Kṣatriyas; this would be for the best.

Yet, within the Śākya clan, there are five hundred youths who wish to go forth from home and receive full ordination within the Dharma of the World-Honored One. We only pray that the World-Honored One will grant their request!
“Out of compassion, please grant us permission to go forth and receive full ordination.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had granted permission for those five hundred Śākyas to go forth and receive full ordination, he taught them the rules of decorum and addressed them, saying:
“You bhikṣus!”
"Let all come together to pay homage to the Elder Bhikṣu Upāli.

Then those five hundred bhikṣus first prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and thereafter bowed their heads in worship to the Elder Bhikṣu Upāli. Having completed their salutations, they sat down in order.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Great King!
You should now prostrate to the bhikṣu Upāli, and then proceed to pay homage to the five hundred bhikṣus in succession."
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, the Great King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
I dare not disobey.”

He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and then, having paid homage to the senior bhikṣu Upāli, he proceeded to pay homage to the five hundred bhikṣus in turn; having finished his salutations, he returned to his original seat.
At that time, the World-Honored One, his countenance serene and joyful, spoke these words:
"Now this member of the Śākya clan has already subdued the arrogance of the Śākyas."
"He has likewise crushed the arrogance of the Śākyas.
Then the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying,
"It is rare, World-Honored One!"
"Because of the World-Honored One, this Upāli has now gained the respect and prostrations of these five hundred Śākya bhikṣus as well as King Śuddhodana.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "O bhikṣus!..."
"Upāli, it is not only today that you have received this reverence and prostration from these five hundred bhikṣus, King Śuddhodana, and others because of me.
You, O bhikṣus!"
In a past life, Upāli likewise, on my account, once received prostrations from five hundred ministers and was also honored with salutations by that king named Brahmadatta.
Then the bhikṣus each addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is the meaning of this?
We pray only that the World-Honored One will [explain it].”
"Please explain to me in detail the original karma of these two.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I recall that in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there were two men who were close friends. They were poor and lowly, and had no reputation in the world."
At one time, that man took a measure of mung beans from his own house and left the city of Vārāṇasī to seek work as a laborer.

At that time, there was always a Pratyekabuddha who lived in and frequented that city of Vārāṇasī; in the early morning, the Pratyekabuddha put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.

Those two poor men saw from afar the arrival of the Venerable Pratyekabuddha, who proceeded with dignified and composed deportment, gazing straight ahead; he wore his saṃghāṭī robe in perfect symmetry and proportion, holding his alms bowl without wavering.
Having seen this, those people attained pure faith and felt a sense of courageous joy toward the Pratyekabuddha. They said to one another:

"Our poverty is entirely due to the fact that in the past we never encountered such a field of merit; or even when we did encounter it, we failed to show respect, make offerings, or attend upon him. Had we encountered such a supreme field of merit and had we respected and made offerings to it, we would not now be suffering such calamities as these—namely, living by constantly working for hire without any wealth."
"We should now take this one *droṇa* of mung beans and offer them to the seer; if he, out of compassion, accepts our gift, we shall immediately be liberated from this poverty and suffering."
Having formed this thought, he offered these mung beans to the Pratyekabuddha and spoke thus:
"I pray only that the Venerable One will give rise to a heart of compassion and accept this gift of mine."

At that time, out of compassion for those two people, the Pratyekabuddha accepted their offering. Although he had accepted the gift, it is the nature of all Pratyekabuddhas that when they wish to transform sentient beings, they employ only supernatural powers (ṛddhi) and have no other expedient means.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha, out of compassion for those two people, accepted their offering and immediately ascended into the air from that direction and departed.

From the "Chapter on the Causes and Conditions of Upāli":

"At that time, those two friends, seeing the Pratyekabuddha soaring through the air and traveling unimpeded, were filled with great joy; their entire bodies leaped for joy beyond restraint. Joining their ten fingers in palms-together salutation, they paid homage at the feet of the venerable Pratyekabuddha and made this aspiration:"

"May we, in future ages, always encounter such a teacher, or one even more excellent than him; and having heard the Dharma he preaches, may we quickly understand it and not be reborn in the evil realms."
Having made this vow, at that time another person separately requested a boon, saying:

"By the power of this merit, may I in future lives always be born into a family of great lineage as a Brahmin; may I be able to recite and uphold the four Vedas, as well as the sixty kinds of arts and crafts."
And there is a verse that says:
"Not merely by being upright and harboring right faith Is one named a supreme field of merit;
One must offer worship to the Buddha and the Sangha, As well as encounter a Pratyekabuddha."
"Subsequently, those two men passed away; one was reborn into a Kṣatriya family in the city of Vārāṇasī and immediately succeeded to the royal throne, being named Brahmadatta.
The second man was born into a pure and eminent Brāhmaṇa family, named Upagupta Māṇava, and became fully proficient in all the treatises."

At that time, the young brahmin Upaga had a wife named Manāvikā, who was beautiful and lovely to behold; those who gazed upon her never grew weary of it. She was most excellent and marvelous, peerless in the world, and held in the deep love and respect of the young brahmin Upaga; if she were not seen even for a moment, his heart would immediately become displeased.
"At that time, his wife Manāvikā, having become resentful due to some minor matter, subsequently ceased speaking with Upaga.
Then Upaga, distressed and vexed, thought to himself:
'Today my wife Manāvikā does not speak with me; the sound of her voice has been cut off in such a manner.'"
Later, when four months of the summer had passed and the autumn season arrived, his wife Mānavikā said to the young brahmin Upaga:
"Excellent, noble son!"
"You should now go to the marketplace and purchase the finest unguents, powdered incense, and various flowers.

Why is this? The fourth month of the autumn season has now arrived; all people are together enjoying the pleasures of the five senses, and we too must adorn our bodies and enjoy the pleasures of the five senses."
At that time, having heard these words, the young man Upaga was filled with such joy and exultation that it pervaded his entire body; unable to contain himself, he thought to himself:
"How unexpected it is that my wife Manāvikā should suddenly speak with me!"

Now Upaga possessed a single gold coin that he had previously lent to someone in another village. At midday, as the sun scorched the great earth and shimmering mirages blazed forth, the color of the ground appeared like that of a red cock; he left his house and set out for that village, intending to collect the debt.
Along that road, his mind was bound and oppressed by lustful thoughts, and he sang lewd songs aloud.
At that time, the palace of Brahmadatta was not far away.

While King Brahmadatta was in his pavilion, enjoying the cool breeze and dozing during the day after waking for a short while, he suddenly heard the sound of a man singing a lustful song, intoxicated by the five desires.
Upon hearing this, the king immediately gave rise once more to his original desire, and spoke in verse:
"Whether it be due to habitual tendencies from the past, Or perhaps because of circumstances that stir one's emotions,
This attachment to the defilement of sensual desire Is like a lotus flower arising from water."
At that time, when Brahmadatta heard that lewd song, he was suddenly struck with alarm and suspicion: "Who is this?
At this time of the midday sun's intense heat, they harbor a mind stained by desire and sing such a lewd song."

Having formed this thought, he saw from the window at midday, when the great earth was scorched by heat, that Upaka was walking and singing along the road; he immediately summoned a minister and commanded him, saying:
"Go quickly, seize that singer and bring him before me."
Having heard the command, the minister immediately replied to the king,
"I dare not disobey your decree.
He then went to that border region, seized Upaga, and spoke to him as follows:
"O māṇava! Go, go! The King summons you now.
At that time, Upaga felt terror arise within him; his hair stood on end, and filled with dejection and unhappiness, he thought to himself:
"Now who knows what offense I have committed against Brahmadatta that causes me such grief and distress?

At that time, the minister took Upaga and went directly to King Brahmadatta. Upon seeing him, the king immediately conceived a feeling of affection; having conceived this affection, he addressed the man with a verse:
“The midday sun blazes with intense heat, and the great earth is red like a crimson rooster;
you now indulge in lustful songs—how can you feel no distress at this?”
The sunlight shines everywhere with intense heat, and the sand upon the earth is melting and becoming even hotter;
yet you now indulge in lustful songs—how can you feel no distress at this?
At that time, the young brahmin Upaga replied to King Brahmadatta in verse:
“Great King, you are not now tormented by heat; how could the sun blazing from above reach you?
Only the gaining of profit and the loss of profit—this is the most grievous of all afflictions.”
Though the sunlight may blaze with great intensity, this is but the lowest among afflictions;
to engage in various worldly activities—this is called the greatest affliction.
Then King Brahmadatta again asked the young brahmin Upaga: "Young brahmin!
What business are you attending to now, that you are traveling along this path upon the scorching earth?"
At that time, Upaga related these matters in detail to King Brahmadatta.
Then, King Brahmadatta again addressed the young brahmin Upaga, saying:
"Young brahmin!..."
"Stop, stop! Do not go!
I shall give you two coins right now—these are Indian gold coins.
King Brahmadatta then immediately gave them to him.
At that time, having received the money from Brahmadatta, Upaga again addressed King Brahmadatta, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!"

"Although I have received these two coins granted by Your Majesty, I now petition the King for one more. Together with the previous two, I shall obtain three; I will then go to the village myself to fetch one coin, so that combined with what Your Majesty has granted, I shall possess four. Thus, I may join with Māṇavikā to celebrate the autumn festival and enjoy the pleasures of the five senses."
King Brahmadatta again addressed the young brahmin Upaga, saying:
"Stop! Do not go!
I shall now give you eight coins."
He then gave it to him.
Having received the eight coins, Upaga again addressed the king, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!"
I pray that you will grant me your favor.
I now request one more coin from the King so that they may become nine; then I shall go to the village and fetch one for myself, making them ten in total.
"By such causes and conditions, I was able to enjoy the fivefold sensual pleasures of the autumn festival together with Mānavikā.
Then King Brahmadatta again said to the young brahmin Upaga:
"Stop, stop! Do not go!"
"I shall now give you sixteen coins.
The king immediately gave him sixteen coins.
Having received the coins, he spoke again to the king, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!
I pray you grant me your favor.

I have already obtained sixteen coins from Your Majesty; now I consult you to request one more coin so that they may total seventeen. Then, going to a village, I shall take one coin for myself, making eighteen in all."
"By these causes and conditions, I immediately attained companionship with the Mānavikās and experienced the pleasures of the five senses.
At that time, Brahmadatta spoke to him again, saying: "O Mānava!
"Stop, stop! Do not go!
I shall now give you thirty-two coins.
Having accepted the coins, he again addressed the king, saying:
“Excellent, Great King!
I pray you grant me your favor.

I have already received thirty-two coins from Your Majesty; now I further petition Your Majesty for one more coin. I shall go to the village and fetch one coin myself, so that together they will total thirty-four. With these, I shall be able to provide for my maṇavika and enjoy the pleasures of the five senses during the autumn festival.”
At that time, Brahmadatta spoke to him again: "O māṇava!
Stop, stop! Do not go!"
"I shall now give you sixty-four coins.
At that time, Upaga accepted the money and again addressed the king, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!"
I pray that you will grant me your favor.

I have already obtained sixty-four coins from Your Majesty; now I beseech the King to grant me one more coin. I shall go again to that village settlement to obtain one coin for myself, so that together we may possess sixty-six coins. With these, I and the Māṇavikā shall enjoy the fivefold sensual pleasures during the autumn festival.
At that time, Brahmadatta spoke to him again: "O māṇava!
Stop, stop! Do not go!"
"I shall now give you one hundred coins.
Then Upaga, having received the hundred coins, spoke again to the king:
"Excellent, Great King!"
I pray that you will grant me your favor.

I have now obtained one hundred coins from the King; I now petition Your Majesty for one more coin. I shall go to the village and obtain another coin there, so that together we may possess one hundred and two coins. With these, I and Māṇavikā may enjoy the fivefold sensual pleasures of the autumn festival.
At that time, Brahmadatta again addressed him, saying: "O māṇava!
Stop, stop! Do not go!"
"I shall give you another village separately as a fief for your emolument.
However, because the brahmin was both acquisitive and greedy, he went repeatedly to the king's side; consequently, the king selected the very best village and granted it to him as a fief.
Having received the seal of office, he immediately applied himself with diligence, never declining labor or service; like a servant, he attended upon the king.
Rising before him and sleeping after him, his conduct was gentle and mild, and all his deeds were entirely in accord with the king’s wishes.
His conduct was upright and honest; he served the king in such a manner that the king never had cause for displeasure or reproach.

By these means, he won the king’s favor, causing King Brahmadatta to rejoice incessantly. Subsequently, the king further granted him half of the kingdom to rule alongside Upaga, and they shared half of the royal granaries and treasuries as well.
Having received such exceptional favor, that brahmin enjoyed the complete pleasures of the five senses without any deficiency.
In this manner, all his subsequent undertakings were successfully accomplished under the supervision of the king.
That brahmin came from his own home to the royal palace, and the king would constantly sleep with his head resting upon the brahmin’s lap.
On one occasion later, King Brahmadatta lay down with his head resting on Upaga’s lap and fell fast asleep.
At that time, having seen that the king was asleep, Upaga thought to himself:
"How can there be two kings in a single kingdom, both exercising sovereign power? Furthermore, it is not fitting for two people to share the contents of a single treasury."
"I should now seek out King Brahmadatta and take his life; if I can kill him, I shall alone seize the royal throne and rule.
Having formed this thought, as Upaka was about to take up his sword, he further reflected:

"This King Brahmadatta previously performed a great service for me by dividing half his kingdom with me to rule together, and he even shared half of all his treasuries and granaries. If I were to kill him now, it would be an act devoid of gratitude and righteousness."
A second time, he thought thus:
"How could two people dwell in one place and together govern the state and transform the people?
Furthermore, it is not fitting for two people to share a common treasury or wealth."
Thus it continued until, at the third thought, he repented, thinking:
"If I were to kill him, I would surely be committing an act of ungratefulness.
Then Upaga, having had this thought, raised his voice and wailed aloud.
At that time, King Brahmadatta, hearing this sound of weeping, suddenly awoke from his sleep; having awakened, he asked Upaga:
"Why are you now making such a loud noise?"
Then Upaga related the previous events in detail to King Brahmadatta.
At that time, King Brahmadatta did not believe that Upaga could have such a thing, and he said to him: "Upaga!..."
"You must certainly not have such a thing. You, Upaka!
Do not speak these words!"
Then Upaga immediately spoke again to King Brahmadatta, saying:
"Great King, you should now believe my words; it is true that I gave rise to such an evil thought."
At that time, Upaga reflected further and thought to himself:
"I have suddenly given rise to such an evil thought; what circumstance has caused this?"
Having contemplated this with right observation, he spoke these words:
"That I have given rise to such evil thoughts must surely be due to my pursuit of the five desires and for the sake of royal power."

I have no need to covet this royal throne, nor do I have any desire for the pleasures of the world; because of these matters, such an evil thought has arisen in me, and I must now renounce my home and go forth into homelessness.
He then addressed the king, saying: "Great King!
Know now that I intend to renounce my home and go forth into the homeless life."
Then King Brahmadatta said to Upaga:
"Do not speak such words!
Since I have already shared half the kingdom with you for you to rule and given you half the granaries and treasuries, I now regard you as my own heart and mind; there is no one like you."
"If you go forth into the homeless life, my heart and mind will certainly find no peace.
Upaga then spoke again to the king, saying,
"Excellent, Great King!"
"I pray that you will grant me permission to leave the home life and go forth.
I am now determined to go forth without doubt; do not create obstacles for my practice of the Dharma.
At that time, King Brahmadatta again addressed Upaga, saying:
"Act as you please, according to your own inclination.
At that time, there was a potter in the city of Vārāṇasī who had previously gone forth and practiced the conduct of a rishi, dwelling in dependence upon that city.
At that time, that seer possessed great majesty and virtue; having already attained the five supernormal powers, he was able to touch the orbs of the sun and moon with his hand.
Upaga then relied upon that seer and shaved off his hair and beard.

Having left the household life, he practiced with courageous diligence and immediately attained the four dhyānas; he further acquired the five supernormal powers and possessed great majestic power, such that he was even able to touch the orbs of the sun and moon with his hand.

When King Brahmadatta heard that Upaga had left the household life to become a renunciant, achieving the state of a Great Sage and possessing great majestic power—even such that he could touch the orbs of the sun and moon with his hand—he smiled upon hearing this. He entered the inner palace and, in the presence of his court ladies, spoke these verses:
“Upaga has practiced virtue for no long time, yet he has already obtained a profound fruit of benefit.
That Sage is truly excellent to have attained a human body and abandoned the five desires to practice the life of renunciation.”
At that time, having heard King Brahmadatta recite these verses, the women of the palace were all filled with sorrow and distress; they then spoke together to King Brahmadatta, saying:
"Great King!..."
You should know that in the past, this man made his living by selling goods, gambling, carrying a staff, and begging for alms.
Because the power and influence of a Brahmin were meager, he therefore left the household life.
"Great King!
Do not now follow that man’s example by abandoning your home and kingdom to go forth as a renunciant.
At that time, King Brahmadatta had a barber named Khaṇḍapāla, who had long been in favor with the heart of King Brahmadatta.
At that time, King Brahmadatta sought out and summoned the barber, commanding him, saying:
"Gaṅgapāla! Now, for my sake, shave and groom my beard and hair."
Having spoken these words, he immediately fell asleep.
At that time, the barber Khaṇḍapāla, seeing that the king was asleep, began to shave and groom the king’s beard and hair.
Having been treated in this manner, King Brahmadatta did not wake from his sleep.
When the king later awoke, he said to the barber Khaṇḍapāla, "I have already issued an order for you to shave and groom my beard and hair; why have you not done so?"
Having spoken these words, Khaṇḍapāla addressed King Brahmadatta:
"I have finished my work; it is only that Your Majesty was asleep and did not wake."
At that time, Brahmadatta took a mirror and looked at himself; seeing that his beard and hair had been groomed and finished, he was filled with joy. He then commanded Khaṇḍapāla:
"I grant you the most excellent village; furthermore, I shall provide you with whatever else you desire."
Then the barber Gaṅgapāla said to King Brahmadatta:
"I have consulted in detail with the members of the royal household; I shall report back to the King after that."
Having spoken these words, he paid his respects and departed.
The barber Khaṇḍapāla, who had previously entered and exited the royal palace without hindrance, immediately went into the palace and said to the women of the court:
"The King has already granted me the most excellent village as a fief; what do you, the queens and consorts, think of this?"
"May it be taken?
At that time, the queen consort addressed the Khaṇḍapāla, saying: "Khaṇḍapāla!"
"Why do you now seek to take the king's most excellent village?
We currently have sufficient gold, silver, and precious jewels to give to you; however, we have a matter to entrust to you—will you carry it out for us?"
The barber Khaṇḍapāla asked the palace women,
"What task do you queens have now that I should prepare for you?"
Then the queens immediately said to that barber:
"Recently, whenever the Great King enters the palace, he always recites a verse, speaking these words:
'Though Upa has practiced virtue for no long time, he has already attained the profound fruit of benefit.'"
"That seer has done well to have attained a human body, having renounced the five desires to practice the life of a renunciant.
"At that time, hearing this verse from the king, we immediately thought:
'We fear the Great King will relinquish his throne and go forth into homelessness.'"
“Excellent, excellent, Khaṇḍapāla!
Go to the king’s presence and ask him about the meaning of this verse; what is its significance?”
At that time, Khaṇḍapāla immediately went in haste to King Brahmadatta; having arrived, he said to him:
"Great King!
You promised me the most excellent village, but I no longer have need for such a boon."
I merely wish to know the verse that the King recites every time he enters the inner palace before his queens and consorts:
“Though one practices virtue for but a short while, The resulting benefit and retribution are profound.
How excellent is that seer who has attained a human body, Having renounced the five desires to leave the home life.”
“‘Excellent, Great King!
I pray that you will explain the meaning of this verse to me; what is its principle?
Now, from the Great King, I beg for such a boon.’”
At that time, King Brahmadatta said to the barber Khaṇḍapāla:

"I have heard that the young man Upaga has renounced half of his kingdom to seek the life of a renunciant; he has become a seer of great power, capable of touching the orbs of the sun and moon with his palm."
I am now intoxicated and deluded by the five desires and am greedily attached to them; for this reason, I now look up with envy at him and frequently enter the palace to recite these verses.
Then, the barber Gaṅgapāla entered the inner palace, approached the queens and consorts, and spoke these words:
"O queens and consorts!..."
"Do not worry that the Great King intends to renounce the world; the Great King will certainly not renounce the world.

When the queen and the other ladies of the court heard these words spoken by the barber Khaṇḍapāla, they were all filled with joy. Their hearts leaped with delight, and it pervaded their entire bodies so intensely that they could not contain themselves. Taking various necklaces and ornaments, they adorned their own persons and said to him: "Khaṇḍapāla!"
"I give all these necklaces of mine to you now; henceforth, do not perform any further karmic deeds for the sake of sustaining your life.
When Khaṇḍapāla saw this, he thought to himself:
"That Upaga has already renounced such a half-share of the kingdom to seek the homeless life, and now King Brahmadatta looks up to him with admiration."
"Why should I not now do this so that all the world may envy me?

Yet, if I were to comply with the wishes of these queens who offer me these various necklaces and ornaments, the outcome would surely be unwholesome. Therefore, I shall now renounce them and follow the path of renunciation."
Having had this thought, Aṅgapaḷa went to Brahmadatta and said to him:
"Great King,
if you grant me my previous request, I now desire to renounce the world and go forth."
Then King Brahmadatta asked him, saying, “Gaṅgapāla!
At whose side do you now intend to go forth into homelessness?”
Gaṅgapāla replied, "Great King!
I wish to go to Upaka and enter the homeless life."
Then King Brahmadatta addressed him, saying: "Gaṅgāpāla!
According to your view, act as you wish."
At that time, Gaṅgāpāla shaved off his own beard and hair and went to the hermitage of the seer Upaga, where he immediately left the household life.

Having become a renunciant, he applied himself with diligent effort and soon attained the four dhyānas and the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). He acquired great majestic power and great majesty, such that he was even able to touch the orbs of the sun and moon with his hand.

When King Brahmadatta heard that Aṅgāraparṇa had already left the household life, become a great ṛṣi, attained great majestic power, and was even able to touch the orbs of the sun and moon with his hand, he could not help but feel profound admiration and desired to see him.
He addressed his ministers, saying:
"O great ministers!
I now wish to go to that place where the rishi resides, so that we may meet with him."
Then the ministers addressed the king, saying:
"Great King, it is not so!
It is not fitting for Your Majesty to go in person to that man's place; we shall instead dispatch a messenger to summon that seer here."
Then King Brahmadatta replied to his ministers, saying: "O you!
Such a thing could not possibly be true now; do not speak such words."
"Since the beginning of antiquity, there has never been such a practice; yet there were sages who lacked self-mastery and had to be summoned by others.
For us now, it is in accordance with the Dharma that we go there ourselves."
"For what reason?
Those seers are great fields of merit, worthy of receiving offerings; we must go there in person.

At that time, King Brahmadatta, relying on his own majesty and virtue, prepared five hundred chariots fully adorned and surrounded by them, along with five hundred high ministers, departing from Vārāṇasī to go toward those seers, desiring to personally bring glory to that world.
"At that time, the seer Aṅgīrasa saw the king approaching from afar; when he arrived, he addressed the king:
'Welcome, Brahmadatta!
It is rare indeed that you have come from so far.'"
At that time, those five hundred ministers, harboring resentment and hatred toward Khaṇḍapāla, spoke these harsh and coarse words:
"You are of low birth, born of a courtesan; you are filthy and impure, constantly washing away grime and grease. How can you address the Great King by name today?"
Then King Brahmadatta stopped his minister and said, "Do not speak such words!
Such is the way of the sages: they call people by their names. However, this seer possesses ascetic conduct and great spiritual power."
Then King Brahmadatta spoke these verses to his ministers:

"Do not harbor resentment toward this seer; This seer has fully perfected his practice, For he is able to endure all manner of hardships, And has thus attained liberation from all suffering and fear."
Since his mind has already attained the relinquishing of all evils, he is neither a shaven-headed monk nor a potter.
Having practiced austerities for many kalpas, he has subdued me; therefore, he calls out my name.
Behold him who has now attained the power of patience; having subdued his faculties, he has realized the fruit of enlightenment.
"Attaining the respect and honor of gods and humans, you shall be the most excellent among gods and humans.

At that time, King Brahmadatta and the various court ladies within the palace first prostrated at the feet of the seer and withdrew to stand to one side. Thereupon, the five hundred ministers also prostrated at the feet of the seer; having finished their prostrations, they then prostrated at the feet of the seer Aṅgīrasa, and subsequently also prostrated at the feet of the potter.
Once King Brahmadatta had sat down on one side, he addressed the sages with words of comfort:
"Venerable ones,
is your physical well-being harmonious and secure?"
"Is your livelihood obtained without toil?
Are there no people to disturb you, O sages?
At that time, the sages replied to Brahmadatta, saying:
"Thus it is, Great King!
This matter must be endured. However, is your own person at peace and harmonious?
Are all your kinsmen, the various ministers, and the common people within the realm entirely secure and well?"
Having spoken these words, those seers preached the Dharma to King Brahmadatta, instructing and transforming him so that his mind was filled with joy and his merit increased.

At that time, King Brahmadatta, having received the teaching and transformation of those sages through their exposition of the Dharma, felt joy in his heart and increased his merit; he rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the sages, and returned to his own abode.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If you have any doubt in your minds as to who that Upaga was at that time, [listen closely]."
"Do not entertain any other thought;
it was I myself who was he. O bhikṣus!
Should there be any among you who harbor doubts as to who that seer, the barber Khaṇḍapāla, was at that time—"
Do not harbor any other thought; this Bhikṣu Upāli is that very person. "O Bhikṣus!
Should there be any among you who harbor doubts as to who that King Brahmadatta was at that time, [listen:]..."
"Do not entertain any other view; this is none other than King Śuddhodana. O bhikṣus!
Should there be any among you who harbor doubts as to who those five hundred great ministers were at that time,"
Do not harbor any other thought; they are none other than these five hundred bhikṣus here and now. Bhikṣus!
At that time, it was because of me that the bhikṣu Upāli also received the respectful prostrations of five hundred great ministers, as well as the homage of King Brahmadatta.
"Now it is likewise; furthermore, it is because of me that five hundred bhikṣus and King Śuddhodana have come to pay their respects.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "You bhikṣus!"
"If you wish to know who among my śrāvaka disciples is the foremost in upholding the Vinaya, it is the bhikṣu Upāli.
At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"What karma did Upāli perform in the past?"
Driven by the retribution of that karma, he was born into a lowly family of barbers.
What further karma did he perform?

Driven by the retribution of that karma, he was able to leave the household life, receive full ordination, attain the fruit of arhatship, and now has received from the Tathāgata this prophetic declaration:
“O bhikṣus, among my śrāvaka disciples, the one who is foremost in upholding the Vinaya is the bhikṣu Upāli.
When the bhikṣus had finished speaking these words, they went to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
What karma did that Elder Upāli perform in the past?
By virtue of what retribution was he born among the lowly class of barbers?
Furthermore, what karma did he perform?

By virtue of that karma, he left the household life, received full ordination, and attained the fruit of arhatship; he was then granted a prediction by the Tathāgata, who declared him the foremost among my śrāvaka disciples in upholding the Vinaya.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Bhikṣus, I recall that in the past, in this very city, there was a barber. He sought a wife from a barber's family of equal standing to his own, and after a short while, he fathered a son."
That barber soon fell ill; although he received medical treatment, he did not recover, and due to his illness, he eventually passed away.
After his death, the barber’s wife took the boy and entrusted him to her own brothers, saying to them:
"This boy is your nephew. I now entrust him to you; you must ensure that this boy learns his father’s ancestral craft."
When the barber had heard these words from his sister, he accepted the boy and proceeded to instruct him in his father’s ancestral craft.
This barber was constantly in the royal palace, held in high esteem by the king; he regularly shaved the hair and beard for the king and did not often go outside to perform such services for others.

At that time, the king commanded that a white elephant be provided for him to ride as he traveled east, west, south, and north; he also provided a golden case to hold his razor and other miscellaneous items, and issued this command:
"In times when there is no Buddha, there are pratyekabuddhas who, like rhinoceroses, wander alone. When you go forth, you shall bring benefit."
Just at that time, there was a pratyekabuddha whose head hair, beard, nails, and body hair were all grown long; he came to the barber and addressed him, saying:
"Excellent, O worthy one!"
"I pray that you will shave off my hair and beard.
Then the barber replied to the Pratyekabuddha, saying:
"Excellent, Great Sage!"
"If you so desire, I shall permit you to wait for tomorrow; come early at dawn, and I will certainly shave off your hair and beard, as a seer does.
When the venerable Pratyekabuddha seer heard these words, he departed immediately.
When that night had passed and it was time to rise in the early morning, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went back to the barber, saying these words:
"Excellent, O worthy one!"
"Now, please shave off my hair and beard.
Then, the barber again addressed that Pratyekabuddha,
saying, "Excellent, Great Sage!"
"If it must be so, I will wait until evening and then shave you, O Immortal.
Thus it continued until, when the sun had set, he spoke again:
"I will wait until the morning."
"If he comes in the early morning, I shall wait until the sun sets;
in this manner, even if he does not shave in the morning, nor does he shave in the evening.
Thus it was that whenever the young man saw this venerable Pratyekabuddha, whether arriving in the early morning or arriving at sunset, it was always the same day after day.
Having seen him, he said:
"O Pratyekabuddha, Honored Sage!
For what reason do you always come here, whether in the morning or in the late afternoon?"
Then the Pratyekabuddha related the preceding events in detail to the youth.
At that time, the youth said to the seer:
"My uncle would never have shaved his hair for the sake of becoming a seer."
Why is this? Because he has become arrogant, relying on his privileged status of moving freely within the royal palace.
I shall now shave the hair of this seer.
Then that youth immediately shaved the hair and beard of the seer.
At that time, the Venerable Pratyekabuddha Seer thought to himself:
"This youth has performed a great act of merit; I must now manifest and proclaim his meritorious deeds for him."
Having formed this thought, he addressed the youth, saying: "O youth!
If you know the right time, you must certainly take my hair and beard; you shall have great benefit in the future."
Having spoken these words, like a king of geese spreading its two wings, he suddenly soared upward by means of his supernormal powers and departed through the air.

At that time, the youth took the hair and beard shaved by the pratyekabuddha and placed them upon his shoulder. With a mind of pure faith toward the pratyekabuddha, he joined his ten fingers in homage at his crown, prostrated, and immediately made this vow:
"May I, in a future age, encounter such a pratyekabuddha or one even more sublime; and regarding whatever Dharma those World-Honored Ones preach, may I quickly and fully understand it all."
Furthermore, I pray that I may never again be born into the evil realms.

Moreover, I pray that in all future lives and throughout all successive births, I shall always become such a barber, so as to serve and make offerings to such noble beings for the sake of the field of merit.
"At that time, within the palace of that city, the king had ascended the throne to attend to affairs of state, surrounded on all sides by his great ministers and courtiers.
From afar, that entire assembly beheld the Pratyekabuddha soaring through the air."
Having seen this, the great assembly addressed the king, saying: "Great King!
Today there is a most auspicious occasion; you have well attained a human body, for now a field of merit has appeared in the world within our realm."
The king then looked up and, having immediately seen that Pratyekabuddha, addressed his ministers, saying:
"He who shaves the beard and hair of this Pratyekabuddha will obtain great fortune and prosperity."
At that time, the barber who tended the king’s hair and beard, being present by the king's side, addressed the king, saying:
"A seer such as this, I am capable of shaving; who else could do so?"
When the youth heard these words, he went immediately to the king’s side and said to him:
“Great King,
you should know that my uncle is now speaking empty words and idle talk.”
"My uncle originally did not shave that person's hair and beard; since this was but a minor matter, he still falsely claimed, 'I shaved the hair and beard of that seer.
To speak of who actually shaved them, it was I myself."
At that time, the barber who served the king rebuked the youth:
"Alas, you foolish man!
What power do you possess?"
"I am able to shave off his hair.
At that moment, the youth pulled out the hair of the Pratyekabuddha and displayed it to the great assembly, saying:
"This is the hair of the Rishi; behold it now as I hold it forth."
At that time, having seen such a sight, the king immediately became enraged and said to the barber who constantly tended his hair and beard:
"Alas, you foolish man!
"You possess such power over me; for what reason do you deceive me today?
Depart from this country at once and do not remain within my realm!
He then seized the white elephant upon which he rode, as well as the various implements for grooming his beard and hair, and granted the boy a fief of revenue, commanding him, saying:
"From this day forward, you shall constantly attend to my beard, hair, and nails.
Then the youth addressed the king,
saying, "As Your Majesty commands, I dare not disobey."
From that time forth, he constantly served as the king’s barber, tending to his beard, hair, nails, and so forth.
Upon the end of his life according to his worldly lifespan, by virtue of those merits, he did not fall into the evil realms in birth after birth.
Moving from the heavens to the human realm, and from the human realm back to the heavens, he traveled back and forth between these two places.
Later, at one time, he was reborn in the city of Vārāṇasī into the family of a barber; he was handsome and pleasing, such that those who beheld him never grew weary of looking.
That boy was raised by his parents, and as he grew up, his intellect gradually developed and his skills were perfected.

At that time, the World-Honored One Kāśyapa appeared in the world—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Great Teacher, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened One, One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.

At that time, Kāśyapa—the Blessed One, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—had already turned the wheel of Dharma and reversed the cycle of saṃsāra; he had received the vehicle of Dharma and fulfilled his original vows; he was the most preeminent in attaining fame and benefit, possessing the resolve of a supreme man; and having opened and manifested the lotuses of those to be converted, he established immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings upon the path of goodness.
At that time, he was practicing his cultivation based on the city of Vārāṇasī, dwelling in the Deer Park at the site formerly inhabited by seers, together with a community of twenty thousand bhikṣus.
At that time, the barber who shaved their hair and beards frequently went to that grove to shave the hair and beards of the bhikṣus.
However, when that young boy was first able to walk, he went with his father into the monastery grounds.
However, monks, when various teachings are being expounded or discussed, if one should happen to arrive at that time when the Vinaya is being preached, one may either hear it or not hear it.
At that time, the youth asked the bhikṣus:
"How is it that all these words are equally virtuous, yet I sometimes hear them and sometimes do not get to listen?"
"What is your intention?
Then the bhikṣus replied: "O youth!"
"Such teachings as these are the secret matters of the bhikṣus; those who have not received full ordination must not hear them at all.
When the youth heard this, his heart was filled with distress, and he thought:
"How can I wish that I might quickly attain renunciation so that I may be worthy to hear these excellent words?"

Later, the youth went to the Vinaya Master and requested to leave the household life; he received full ordination (*upasampadā*), recited and upheld the Vinaya under the guidance of the bhikṣus, and acted in accordance with the Dharma. Nevertheless, despite doing so, he was unable to realize supramundane wisdom.
However, at a later time, when he was afflicted by illness and confined to his bed, as he was about to pass away, he made this aspiration:
"Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, has a bodhisattva named Rakṣaprabha who has already received the prediction, saying:
'In the future, during an age with a lifespan of one hundred years, you shall become a Buddha, named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.'"

"I now pray that I may meet Śākyamuni in the future; if my wish is granted, I shall likewise seek ordination within his teaching. Having received full ordination, among all the disciples of that World-Honored One, may I be the foremost in upholding the Vinaya."
Just as this master and preceptor of mine is today the foremost among the disciples who uphold the Vinaya under Kāśyapa Buddha,
so too shall I, at that time within the Dharma-teachings of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, be the foremost among the disciples who uphold the Vinaya.

"From that time forward, after his life ended, he was reborn in the heavens; and up until today, in this final body, he has been conceived and born into the family of a barber in the city of Kapilavastu, named Upāli—he is that very person."

"O bhikṣus, if you have any doubt regarding that barber boy at that time, do not entertain any other thought; he was none other than the bhikṣu Upāli."
However, Upāli, in the past, after having shaved the hair and beard of a venerable pratyekabuddha, he made this aspiration:
"May I, in birth after birth throughout all my lives, whenever I obtain a human body, always be born into the family of a barber."
Furthermore, at that time, he made another vow, saying:
"May I not be born within the evil realms.

By the power of the karmic fruit of that vow, he was not born in the evil realms; from that time forth, he has transmigrated among gods and humans, experiencing much happiness, and has now attained his own benefit.
Furthermore, he makes this aspiration:

"May I, in future ages, always encounter such teachers as these, or even those superior to them; and regarding the Dharma taught by those teachers, may I quickly realize it and immediately attain understanding."
"Due to the retribution of this karma, he has now encountered me as his teacher; he has immediately left the household life, received full ordination, and realized the fruit of Arhatship."
Furthermore, while within the Dharma-teachings of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, he made this vow:

"May I, in that future age, encounter the Tathāgata Śākyamuni; may I not turn my back on his Dharma, but follow it by leaving the household life. If I am able to leave the household life, may I be the foremost among his disciples who uphold the Vinaya."
"By virtue of that karmic retribution, he has now gone forth in my Dharma; among all my disciples who uphold the Vinaya, he is the foremost."
"O bhikṣus! In a past life, Upāli performed such karma that he has now received the retribution of being born into the family of a barber.

Furthermore, by virtue of the causes and conditions of those aspirational karmic acts, he has now received the retribution of going forth in this way within my Dharma, receiving full ordination, and realizing the fruit of arhatship."

The Causes and Conditions of Rāhula The Mahāvastu-Avadāna: The Collection of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Chapter Fifty-Six, Part One Furthermore, on another occasion, King Śuddhodana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will accept the food and drink we have prepared for tomorrow morning.
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.

When King Śuddhodana saw that the World-Honored One had silently granted his consent, he rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, took his leave, and departed.

Having arrived at his own palace, he immediately prepared various kinds of exquisite food and drink that very night—namely, foods to be swallowed, chewed, sucked, and lapped—and having completed these preparations, he swept and arranged the grounds as the night passed into morning.
He immediately dispatched a messenger to inform the World-Honored One, saying:
"The time has now arrived; food and drink are prepared. We only pray that you will deign to come.

At that time, as the sun was in the east, the World-Honored One put on his robes and took up his bowl. Surrounded on all sides by the community of bhikṣus, with the Buddha at their head, he proceeded to the palace of King Śuddhodana.
Having arrived, he sat upon the Buddha’s prepared seat, and the community of bhikṣus each sat down in their respective order according to the Dharma.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, with the Buddha at the head, waited until the bhikṣu-saṃgha was seated in succession; then, with his own hands, he served all varieties of exquisite foods and drinks, providing for them until they were fully satisfied and allowed to eat to their heart’s content.

Having seen that the Buddha and the Sangha were satiated with food and drink, he washed and cleaned their bowls and placed them on a small seat set aside; then, withdrawing to one side and sitting down comfortably, King Śuddhodana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One..."
"Please instruct me.
Furthermore, I pray that the World-Honored One, the Sugata, will manifest his presence so that I may constantly obtain benefit and peace for a long night.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Śuddhodana with these words:
"Great King, if you know the proper time, you ought to abandon this matter of listening to the Dharma, nor need you come repeatedly to inquire after the bhikṣus."
"Before long, Your Majesty’s own body shall likewise attain its most supreme and wondrous fruit.

At that time, the World-Honored One, employing skillful means to instruct King Śuddhodana, expounded the Dharma to reveal the truth, causing him to understand and awaken, and having brought him joy, rose from his seat and returned to his original place.

At another time, King Śuddhodana, through Śāriputra, attained the purity of the Dharma-eye and simultaneously realized the fruit of Srotāpanna. Having already grasped all dharmas, realized all dharmas, entered into all dharmas, and crossed beyond all doubts, his mind was free from delusion and he had attained fearlessness. No longer questioning other aspects of the Dharma practice, having fully realized and known them for himself, he approached the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"Excellent!..."
“World-Honored One!
I pray only that you will deliver me, allowing me to leave the household life, enter the Way, and receive full ordination.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
“Will King Śuddhodana, having renounced his home and left the household life within this teaching, be further able to realize the supreme Dharma?

At that time, the World-Honored One, having reflected upon this, realized for himself that King Śuddhodana was certainly not destined to renounce his home and leave the household life, nor would he be able to realize the supreme Dharma.
Having understood this, he addressed him, saying: "Great King!
If you know the proper time today, simply remain in your own home and practice the giving of alms to cultivate meritorious karma."
On a later day, the Great Lady Mahāprajāpatī invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, providing them with food and drink until they were all fully satisfied.

On the third day, the consorts and their retinues within the first palace again invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, providing them with food and delicacies that were likewise entirely sufficient.
On the fourth day, the second palace again invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, providing them with various kinds of food of a hundred flavors, all of which were fully sufficient.

As for Rāhula, he was first born from his mother's womb six years after the Tathāgata had gone forth into homelessness; on the day the Tathāgata returned to his father’s home, Rāhula was six years of age.
At that time, when the Tathāgata arrived at the city of Kapilavastu, Rāhula’s mother thought to herself:
"In the past, because of this Rāhula, I was slandered by my kinsmen; now that the time has come, I ought to personally purify myself regarding that matter in order to clarify my own character."

For this reason, one must certainly invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to offer them food and drink, and also invite all their kinsmen and attendants, thereby making oneself clear [to them].

Having formed this thought, Yaśodharā prepared various kinds of exquisite food and drink that very night. Once everything was ready, she sent a messenger at the end of the night to inform the Buddha, saying:
"The food and drink have been prepared; may the World-Honored One know the time is right."
He also commanded all his kinsmen and attendants, instructing them to assemble and come to the invitation.

At that time, in the early morning when the sun was in the east, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and, surrounded by the bhikṣus with the Buddha at their head, proceeded toward the royal palace together with one thousand two hundred and fifty great bhikṣus. Upon arrival, they sat down in order upon the seats that had been prepared.
At that time, Rāhula’s mother prepared a large ball of joy separately, called Rāhula, placed it in his hand, and spoke these words: "You, Rāhula!"
"Go among the assembly of bhikṣus and give the joy-pills to whoever is your father.
Rāhula’s mother further addressed all her kinsmen, saying:
"This is Rāhula; he must now seek his father."
Then Rāhula, holding the *mṛdvīkā* (jujube) balls, surveyed all the bhikṣus and went straight to the Buddha’s side, addressing the Buddha:
“O Śramaṇa! [I have done so.]”
"How refreshing and cool it is!
So it is, O śramaṇa!
How refreshing and cool it is!"
At that time, King Śuddhodana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! How is this so?”
"Does Yaśodharā indeed have such faults as these?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Great King, do not harbor such doubts today."
Yaśodharā is free from such faults; Rāhula is truly my own son.
It was only because he was constrained by the conditions of past karma that he remained in the womb for six years.

At that time, King Śuddhodana and his retinue, hearing these words of the Buddha, were all filled with joy; their bodies leaped with such exuberance that they could not contain themselves. Each of them took various kinds of food, drink, and delicacies in their hands and offered them to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, ensuring they were fully satisfied.

Having eaten their fill at their pleasure, the Buddha and the great assembly washed their bowls and rinsed their hands; each taking a small seat, they circumambulated the Buddha on his left and right and withdrew to sit on one side.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, out of reverence for the Buddha, was unable to inquire extensively about the causes and conditions as described above; instead, he addressed the bhikṣus in the assembly, saying:
