"I pray, O Venerable Masters!..."
“May the World-Honored One please explain the karmic causes and conditions regarding Rāhula and Yaśodharā.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What karmic causes and conditions did this Rāhula create in the past?”
"By what karmic retribution did he remain in the womb for six years?
And what karma did Yaśodharā commit that she carried him in her womb for six years?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable eons, there was a king of the Brahmin caste named Manuṣyadeva (Human-Heaven). He begot two sons; the elder was named Sūrya (Sun), and the younger was named Candra (Moon)."
The crown prince constantly took no pleasure in the world and desired to renounce his home life.
Not long after this, the king, along with his subjects and the devas, reached the end of their allotted lifespan and passed away.
After his life had ended, his sons, Sūrya and Candra, vied with one another for the succession.
The elder son said,
"You should become king and govern the affairs of state."
The second son spoke again to him, saying:
"You should serve as king and govern the affairs of state.
Then the Prince of Day addressed the Prince of Moon, speaking these words once more:
"You shall certainly become king; I shall renounce my home and go forth into homelessness.
At that time, Prince Candra again addressed his elder brother, saying these words:
"Since you have grown up, the royal throne belongs to you; it is not fitting for me to receive it."
On that day, Prince Sūrya again addressed his younger brother, Prince Candra, saying:
"When one receives the royal throne, what dharma should be performed first?
Prince Candra replied to him in turn:
"First, issue the proclamation.
Then, Prince Divākara again asked him:
"If there were someone in the world who violates this proclamation, what punishment should they receive?"
The Prince Moon replied to him again, saying:
"Those whose crimes are most grave must certainly be punished with severe penalties.
The Prince Day then spoke again to his younger brother, the Prince Moon, saying:
"According to the principles of justice, it was I who ought to have obtained the kingship.
I now simply relinquish the throne to you; you shall become king, while I wish to renounce my home and go forth into the homeless life."
At that time, Prince Day handed over the royal throne to Prince Moon and subsequently abandoned his home to leave the household life and practice the Way.
All of Prince Day’s retinue followed him in leaving the household life as well.
At that time, the Rishi Divākara thought to himself:
"These people have gone forth under my guidance;
now that I am their teacher, I must diligently study and seek the path so that I may excel them."
Having formed this thought, he then made a vow:
"May this body of mine, from this day forward, never take anything for itself unless it is given by another—not even a single object, not even water or a tooth-stick."

At that time, the rishi once forgot his original resolve; when others did not offer him medicinal roots, stalks, or various fruits, he took them for himself to eat. Furthermore, once at night, being thirsty, he saw another’s water jar, mistook it for his own, and proceeded to drink from it, leaving his own jar aside.
At that time, the seer who was the original owner of the water jar saw that his own jar was empty and contained no water, and he asked:
"Who has taken the water from my jar?"
"This is merely a dwelling place for thieves; it was never a site inhabited by sages.
At that time, the sage who had taken water to drink saw his own water vessel full and set aside to one side, and he then addressed him, saying:
"Out of ignorance, I took your water to drink, thinking it was my own."
Then that seer said to the seer who had drunk the water:
"If you have indeed drunk it, how excellent! How wonderful!
At that time, the seer who had mistakenly drunk the water thought to himself:
"I have violated my former vow; this is unwholesome.
This is not the way of the sages.
How can I now eat these various medicinal roots and fruits myself without first giving them to those who do not receive them?"
"Or did he take water from another and drink it himself?

Because of these circumstances, he became despondent and unhappy; sorrow and affliction arose in his mind, and sitting crouched upon the ground, he contemplated with right mindfulness, grieving over this matter.
"At that time, the young brahmin disciples immediately went to where the Rishi Aditya was, prostrated at his feet, and served him according to the Dharma."
Then that seer said to his disciple, the māṇava:
"You youths! From this day forward, do not prostrate yourselves before me."
"Why is this? Because today I have become a thief.
Then those youths questioned the royal seer, speaking these words:
"What is the matter with Upata?
At that time, the royal seer Sūrya replied to those māṇavas, saying: "O youths!..."
"You must now know that I have not received the medicinal roots, fruits, and so forth from anyone else, nor have I taken water from another to drink for myself.
Having spoken these words, those youths immediately addressed the Rishi Sūrya again, saying:
"Teacher, do not speak such words now!"
"Whatever you eat and drink, all of it shall be *upādāya* (derived from) objects.
Then the Rishi Sūrya spoke again to those *māṇavas*:
"Do you know that I do not obtain things from others, but take them for myself?"
However, I have now taken grass, leaves, roots, fruits, and water for washing from no one else, yet I have drunk them myself; I have thus become a thief.
Therefore, you should punish me for my crime, treating me exactly as you would a common thief, without any distinction.
Then all the youths said to that seer:
"We do not dare to judge the offense of our preceptor.
Our preceptor’s younger brother has now become king; he currently governs this realm and rules it according to the Dharma. If you go to his borders, he will surely be able to punish the preceptor."

At that time, the royal seer went to where King Candra was. When King Candra heard of this matter and learned that King Sūrya intended to come to his side, he immediately prepared the fourfold army and went out beyond the city walls to welcome him.
When King Sūrya arrived, he prostrated at his feet.
Then, the seer King Sūrya stopped King Candra, saying:
"Do not prostrate at my feet."
Why is this? Because, Great King, I am now a thief.
"You must punish my crime just as you would a thief; do not treat me otherwise.
At that time, the king asked his elder brother, the Rishi Divākara, "O Holy One, what kind of thief have you become today?"
At that time, the seer replied to King Candra: "Great King,

you should know that when I was practicing the path in a secluded and pure forest, I did not obtain medicinal roots, stalks, or fruits from others, nor did I take water from others for my own drinking."
At that time, having heard these words, the king was filled with grievous distress and anguish; he sobbed and wept, his face covered in tears, and thought to himself:
"How can such a seer—one whose fundamental conduct and meritorious virtues have been pure from the start and who is free from any fault—be punished for an offense today?"
Having formed this thought, he replied to the royal seer:
"I have promised the various seers that I shall take fruits, medicinal roots, and even water for myself to eat and drink."
"Therefore, whatever the seer eats is entirely his own property.
The Great Seer is no thief, nor can he be punished.
At that time, the seer King Sun said to King Moon:
"Great King, you have only now consented to this matter; it was not so in the past.
The king spoke again, saying:
"When I first ascended the throne in the past, I immediately made this declaration:"
"I have given grass, wood, and water to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas for them to use and eat as they please.
Therefore, Great Seer,
he is truly not a thief.
"How shall I now punish the offense?
Then that royal seer spoke again to the king, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!"

"I have now committed an unwholesome deed; reflecting upon it myself, I cannot extinguish this transgression. Since I took and drank the water from another's bathing jar, Great King, you must punish me no differently than you would a thief."
“At that time, King Candra had a nephew who was present in that assembly, and that nephew addressed King Candra, saying:
‘Great King!’”
"I shall only settle the matter of this seer's transgressions; do not let him suffer in distress or resentment.
At that time, King Candra said to the seer, "If that is the case, enter my park and dwell there to practice the Way."
At that time, after King Candra had sent the seer into his garden, he immediately forgot about him and no longer thought of him again.
Only on the sixth day did he remember and call for his ministers and officials, saying:
"That seer was in the garden; has he gone out or not?"
At that time, the ministers said to King Candra, "That rishi has not yet left the park; he is still within the garden.

Then, King Candra granted a general amnesty to all prisoners throughout the world, even including the birds and beasts that fly and roam. He summoned the rishi specifically, provided him with various kinds of sweet and delicious food and drink, and addressed him, saying:
"O Great Sage! Please depart as you wish.
Having been dismissed, King Candra felt unhappy in his heart.
"I have already committed an offense against this seer; because of this seer, I shall surely incur sin and loss.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If there is any doubt in your minds as to who that royal seer named 'Sun' was at that time," [he continued: "Who was he?"
Do not entertain any other thought; it was I myself who was that person.
You bhikṣus, if you have any doubt as to who that king named Candra was at that time, [it was I].
Do not entertain any other thought: it was Rāhula who was that very person.

Because he once brought that seer into the garden and made him stay for six days, due to the retribution of that karma, he dwelt amidst the afflictions of birth and death and underwent immeasurable suffering;
and due to the remaining karma, he further remained in his mother’s womb for six years.
“O bhikṣus! I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable eons, there was a herd of cattle at a pasture.

The wife of the owner of those cattle took her daughter and went to the herd to milk them for curdled milk. She brought two vessels, both of which were filled to the brim; she sent her daughter to carry the larger vessel, while she herself carried the smaller one.”
When they reached the middle of the road, he said to his daughter: "Go quickly!
The path here is treacherous and full of terrors."
At that time, the girl said to her mother, "This vessel is very heavy; how can I possibly move quickly?
Her mother spoke thus a second and a third time:
"Go quickly! There is great terror upon this road.
At that time, the woman thought to herself:
"Why do you make me carry this largest vessel and further urge me to walk so quickly?
Because of this, the daughter became angry and said to her mother, "Mother, please take this milk vessel as well for a moment;
I wish to attend to the needs of nature for a short while."
The mother then took that large vessel, shouldered it, and set out; the daughter followed behind, walking slowly and steadily.
At that time, as the mother carried the heavy burden, she traveled for six *krośas*.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If you have any doubt in your minds as to whether that girl, out of a mind of anger, sent her mother to carry a heavy load for six krośas?"
Do not entertain any other thought; it was Yaśodharā, the daughter of the Śākya clan, who was she.

Because at that time she caused her mother to carry a heavy load for six *krośas* along the road, by the ripening of that karma, she experienced immeasurable suffering within the afflictions of birth and death;
and due to the remnants of that karma, she has now carried a fetus for six years in this life.
“O bhikṣus! All karmas are not experienced in vain; according to the good or evil one has created, one receives the results for oneself. Therefore, you bhikṣus!”
You must always abandon these evils of body, speech, and mind.
Why is this? Because you, O bhikṣus, create the causes and conditions for good and evil through body, speech, and mind.
Thus we clearly see such retributions for good and evil.
You, bhikṣus! You should train yourselves in this way in wholesome karma.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the subtle and wondrous Dharma to King Śuddhodana and the great assembly, causing them to rejoice; having completed this display, proclamation, and edification, he rose from his seat and returned to his original place.
At that time, Rāhula’s mother sent Rāhula toward his father to request his paternal inheritance.
As Rāhula followed the Buddha, walking and speaking, he said these words:
“I pray only that you, O Śramaṇa!”
"Grant me a fief, O Śramaṇa! Grant me a fief!
Then the World-Honored One took his own finger and gave it to Rāhula; having grasped the Buddha’s finger, Rāhula walked beside him.
At that time, the World-Honored One took Rāhula and went to a quiet grove; calling out from afar to the Elder Śāriputra, he said: "You, Śāriputra!"
"I shall cause Rāhula to leave the household life.
Then Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"As the World-Honored One has instructed."
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, he ordained Rāhula and allowed him to go forth.

At that time, when the World-Honored One was establishing the prohibitory precepts for the bhikṣus, Rāhula was filled with great joy; he subsequently received the prohibitory precepts and practiced them in accordance with the Dharma.
Why is this so? Because such is the nature of the Dharma-teachings: Śāriputra, relying upon the Buddha’s instructions and precepts, received and taught them.
At that time, there were sons of good family who all attained right faith and right view.

Why is this? Because they all desire to leave the household life to seek the unsurpassed path of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*); because they have benefited from seeing the Dharma realized within themselves; and having realized it for themselves, they personally declare:
"The outflows are exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
Rāhula was likewise; he personally realized his own mind and attained right liberation.
The World-Honored One then gave him a prediction, addressing the bhikṣus:
"You should know that among my śrāvaka disciples who uphold the precepts, Rāhula is the foremost. This is what the masters of the Mahāsāṃghika school say.
(Regarding this, the Kāśyapīyas have another version:
"At that time, King Śuddhodana, having prepared various foods, summoned all his courtiers and kinsmen within the palace and commanded them, saying:
'None of you now shall show Rāhula and tell him that Siddhārtha is your father.'"
"Why is this? I fear that once Rāhula hears of it, he will immediately follow his father and renounce the household life.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, during that very night, prepared various kinds of sweet and delicious foods—meals to be chewed, swallowed, sucked, and lapped. Having completed the preparations, when the night had passed and the early morning dawned, he arranged the seats and, taking Rāhula along with his attendants—both boys and girls—surrounded him on all sides and sent them together into the Aśoka Grove.
Thereupon, he dispatched a messenger to inform the Buddha, saying:
"The time for the meal has arrived and the food and drink are prepared; may the World-Honored One know that it is time.

At that time, as the sun was in the east, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and proceeded with the assembly of bhikṣus surrounding him on both sides. They went together to the palace of King Śuddhodana.
Having arrived, they sat down in order upon the seats that had been previously prepared.

At that time, Rāhula saw those young boys and girls wandering about and playing in disorder, while their nurses did not restrain them; as they laughed and played together, he then secretly departed from the Aśoka grove and gradually entered the royal palace.
He went to see the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus; having seen them, he prostrated himself in worship.

Having completed his prostrations, he immediately ascended the multi-storied pavilion. At that time, Rāhula’s mother was already on the pavilion; she saw the World-Honored One with his head and beard shaven and his body clad in the kāṣāya robe. Seeing this, she wept in sorrow and spoke in verse:
“The daughter-in-law of the Great King Śākya, Her name is known as Suddhodanī (Śuddhodana’s daughter),”
"Seeing such a form of renunciation as this, my heart was filled with sorrow and I was consumed by grief.
Then, Rāhula asked his mother:
"Noble Lady, why do you weep so bitterly?"
His mother replied to her son Rāhula, saying,
"The one with a golden-colored body among the assembly of śramaṇas is your father.
Then Rāhula spoke again to his mother, saying:
"O Noble One, since my birth, I have never before recalled such a thing of happiness as this.
Having spoken these words, he descended swiftly from the pavilion, approached the Buddha, and entered the folds of the Buddha’s robe to remain hidden there.
At that time, the bhikṣus were about to block him, but the Buddha said to them:
"Bhikṣus, do not block him again;
simply let him enter within my robe and stay there."

At that time, King Śuddhodana, seeing that the Buddha and the Saṃgha were seated in order, personally served them various kinds of pure and delicious delicacies—namely, foods to be chewed, eaten, sucked, and lapped—until they were all fully satiated and had eaten to their heart's content.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he washed his bowl and rinsed his hands; taking a small seat, he sat to one side and made this aspiration for the King, his father:
"Fire is supreme among sacrifices; Verses of praise are supreme among all recitations;
The king is supreme among men; The ocean is supreme among all flowing waters."
Among the stars, the moon is supreme; among all luminaries, the sun is supreme.
Throughout the zenith, the nadir, and the four directions, as well as among the multitudes of sentient beings—whether gods or humans—the Buddhas are supreme.
At that time, having completed these verses of benediction for King Śuddhodana, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and departed according to his circumstances.
"At that time, while King Śuddhodana was later inspecting affairs and traveling here and there, Rāhula had already followed the World-Honored One and gone outside the palace."
Having already departed from the palace, he wished to return and enter once more.
At that time, the World-Honored One personally extended his finger to Rāhula and had him grasp it.

Then Rāhula felt a sense of peace and joy in the upper part of his body, as if a rope were tied to the feet of a bird so that it could no longer leave; thus, having attached himself to the World-Honored One, he was led immediately to the Nyagrodha Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Rāhula, saying: "Rāhula,
are you able to follow me and go forth from the household life?"
Then Rāhula replied to the Buddha, saying, “It is truly so; I am able to go forth.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, speaking these words:
"O bhikṣus! At this time, I cause Rāhula to leave the household life and go forth.
I dispatch Śāriputra to serve as his preceptor."
At that time, the bhikṣus had this thought:
"In the past, the World-Honored One once told us, saying:
'If one is less than twenty years of age, one must not receive the full precepts of ordination.'"
"Rāhula is now only fifteen years old; should we follow the Buddha’s former instructions, or is there some other reason for this?
While they were reflecting thus, they took up the previous matter and reported it in full to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!
Those who leave the household life at fifteen may become śrāmaṇeras."
At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣus immediately ordained him and invited Śāriputra to serve as his preceptor.
Then, King Śuddhodana sent forth the World-Honored One, the community of bhikṣus, and their various attendants; only then, when he was about to sit down to eat, he spoke these words:
"You all should summon Rāhula here so that he may eat with me."
At that time, his attendants searched everywhere but were unable to find him at all; they returned to the king's presence and together addressed the king, saying:
"Great King!..."
"I now seek Rāhula, but do not know where he may be.
At that time, King Śuddhodana again addressed them, saying:
"Go to the Aśoka Grove and throughout the various palaces; search for him everywhere."

Then his attendants immediately went to the Aśoka grove and searched throughout the various palaces, but could not find him; they returned and informed the king, saying, "We went to those places and searched, but we did not see him."
At that time, King Śuddhodana spoke to him again, saying:
"Go quickly to the Nyagrodha Grove; perhaps the World-Honored One intends to cause him to leave the household life and depart in such a manner."

At that time, having heard this command from the king, the attendants immediately went to that Nyagrodha Grove and searched everywhere; they found Rāhula, who had already been sent by the World-Honored One to leave the household life.
Having seen this, he returned to the palace and addressed the King,
saying: "Great King,
you should know that Rāhula has already been permitted by the World-Honored One to go forth into homelessness."
Having heard this, the king fainted and fell to the ground; after a short while, he regained consciousness.
He went out from the city to the Nyagrodha Grove, approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In the past, during his days as a householder, various Brahmins skilled in the interpretation of signs had already bestowed this prophecy upon him:
"If he remains at home, he will certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
"Bhagavān!
Having now renounced the household life and gone forth, I thought upon seeing the Bhagavān after his renunciation that I would entrust the royal throne to Nanda;
yet later, the Bhagavān caused him to go forth as well."
Once he had gone forth, I again reflected that Ānanda should succeed him to the royal throne;
yet, because the World-Honored One had already allowed him to go forth, I desisted.
After he had gone forth, I again thought that Aniruddha should succeed him to the royal throne.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One permitted him to go forth from the household life.
After he had gone forth, I again thought that Bāvari should succeed to the royal throne;
yet the World-Honored One likewise permitted him to go forth as well.
"Now I hope to keep Rāhula back, intending to entrust him with the royal throne;
yet the World-Honored One intends to let him go forth into the religious life.
If the World-Honored One does so and causes Rāhula to leave the household life, will he not surely sever my royal lineage?"
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
Even so, my affection for my son pierces through my skin, flesh, sinews, bones, and even to my marrow.
Therefore, World-Honored One, from this day forward, please establish such a rule of instruction: [that no one shall ordain a child without the parents' consent]."
“O monks! There are those who have gone forth [into homelessness] after having been permitted by their parents; only then are they released.
At that time, the Buddha addressed King Śuddhodana:
"As Your Majesty intends, I shall not oppose it; I will certainly instruct him to perform such deeds.

Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One then addressed King Śuddhodana, expounding upon the principles of all dharmas, manifesting his teaching and transformation, causing the king to rejoice, augmenting his majestic power, and further inspiring him with joy.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having become joyful, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, took his leave, and departed to return to his palace.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying: "You bhikṣus,
you should know that among all beings, it is most difficult for a son to repay the kindness of his parents."
Why is this so? For their parents performed what is difficult to do;
they manifested them to the world, nurtured the various aggregates (skandhas), and caused the body to be nourished and matured through breastfeeding.
Therefore, you bhikṣus!

From this day forward, if there are sons or daughters of good family who seek to go forth from the household life, you must first require them to consult their parents, and only then grant permission.
"If you do not permit them to go forth as monastics, they must be dealt with according to the law.
From this day forward, I establish this regulation: whenever anyone comes to request ordination, you must first ask them:
'Are your parents still living?'"
If that person replies,
"My parents are currently alive," one should then ask further:
"Furthermore, have you obtained permission from your parents to go forth [into the religious life]?
(However, regarding these five teachers, there were differing accounts, some saying:
"Rāhula was born two years after the Bodhisattva had first gone forth; he practiced austerities for six years and only then attained enlightenment.")

Seven years after his attainment of enlightenment, he finally came toward the city of Kapilavastu; following this sequence, when the day of Rāhula’s renunciation was counted, it was exactly his fifteenth year.
[Thus it was said. (Or there are some masters who speak as follows:

"When Māyādevī saw that the Bodhisattva had abandoned his home and gone forth into homelessness, due to this cause and condition, she wept in grief and distress, and her eyes were ruined and lost their sight.")

However, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, having already realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, returned to the city of Kapilavastu only after twelve years had passed, desiring to manifest compassion toward his kinsmen.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, surrounded on all sides by his entire retinue within the palace, led the way and proceeded at the head of the procession.
At that time, there were also ninety-nine thousand people from the same clan who came together to see the Buddha.
Among them was Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī; she went to the place where the Buddha was in order to see her son, Rāhula.
At that time, the Tathāgata manifested the twin miraculous transformations.
Then, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, having heard others say:
"Now my son has manifested supernatural powers—namely, emitting flames from the lower part of his body and cold water from the upper part of his body."
Having heard this, joy and exultation filled his entire being, such that he could not contain himself; he went to where the Buddha was.
Upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, out of reverence for the Buddha, he took the water flowing from the Buddha’s body and sprinkled it over his own person and used it to wash his face.

At that time, the World-Honored One caused Mahāprajāpatī to give rise to compassion, which pervaded her entire body so that she experienced bliss; her impaired eyes were immediately restored to clarity, surpassing their state as they were before.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī’s faith and reverence toward the Buddha increased even further.
Then, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!"
Why is it that this Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, for the sake of the World-Honored One, has wept in sorrow and lost her sight?
And how is it that, because of the World-Honored One, she has regained her purity?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the community of bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
It was not only today that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has caused me such grief and weeping, losing her sight; she shall likewise regain her purity because of me."
"In a past life, he also grieved and wept for me, losing his sight; yet once again, because of me, his eyes have regained their clarity.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is this matter?
We pray that you will explain it for us.
*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll 55.
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Fifty-Six,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on the Causes and Conditions of Rāhula, Part Two.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
I recall that in the distant past, long ago, in the kingdom of Kāśī, there was a mountain near a certain village called Ujjengaka."

On the southern face of that mountain, there was a grove; in that garden were various trees numbering more than a hundred thousand, with flowers and fruits flourishing and branches and leaves spreading luxuriantly. When viewed from afar, it resembled a mass of blue clouds.

Within that garden, there were lotus ponds everywhere in great numbers, adorning the groves; those forests were tall and lofty, spacious and tranquil. Some teachers say that Mount Uruvilvā is near the city of Vārāṇasī.

At that time, there was a herd of elephants on that mountain. Within the herd, there was a female elephant who had given birth to a son; his physical form was upright and handsome, such that those who beheld him never grew weary of looking.

Now, that elephant calf was pure white in body, fully endowed with six tusks, and its head was entirely black like the head of an indragopaka insect; it supported itself upon seven limbs touching the ground.

That elephant cub, not long after being raised, became a great elephant-nāga; practicing in accordance with the Dharma and being filial toward his parents, he showed a heart of reverence when making offerings to them.
However, as for that elephant calf, whatever food and drink it had—whether grass, fruits, or roots—it would first offer to its parents to satisfy them, and only afterwards would it eat itself.
"At that time, on another occasion, the Elephant-Nāga was wandering here and there in search of grass, fruit, and various foods.
Some hunters suddenly saw this elephant and thought to themselves:
'This Elephant-Nāga is not one whom any other person is fit to ride; only King Brahmadatta is capable of riding him.'"
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to King Brahmadatta; upon arrival, he addressed him, saying:

"Great King, you should know that within a certain forest there is an elephant-nāga, handsome and pleasing to behold. Its body is pure white and it possesses six tusks; its head is black like the bird Indra-gopaka, and its seven limbs touch the ground, just as I have seen."
"That elephant is fit for Your Majesty to ride; if it pleases Your Majesty's heart, you may send someone to seize that elephant and bring it here to show it to you."
At that time, King Brahmadatta immediately summoned those skilled in taming elephants and commanded them, saying:
"I have heard it said that there is an elephant-nāga with six tusks, upright and lovely to behold; those who gaze upon him can never tire of it, and even its seven limbs all touch the ground."
"You must all go quickly to that place, seize that elephant-king, and bring him to me; do not delay so that he might escape.
At that time, all the elephant-trainers, hearing King Brahmadatta’s command, replied to him:
"As the King has commanded, we dare not disobey his instruction."
He immediately prepared various strong leather thongs and other such items, went to the elephant, and cast a spell upon it.
The elephant came of its own accord toward the man; he then seized it, bound the elephant with those leather ropes, and led it away to King Brahmadatta.
At that time, when King Brahmadatta saw from afar that they were approaching with the elephant-king, he immediately rose to meet them. Out of great joy, he spoke these words:
"How wonderful to have obtained such a sublime Great Vehicle! How wonderful to have obtained such a sublime Great Vehicle!"
At that time, King Brahmadatta personally nourished and fed him; whatever the elephant was capable of eating, he gave it all to him, personally supervising and providing every morsel of food himself.
Despite this, that elephant-king grew even more emaciated; he constantly groaned, cried out with loud calls, and wept with tears flowing, finding no moment’s rest.

At that time, King Brahmadatta, seeing that the elephant-king was emaciated and haggard, even to the point of weeping and shedding tears in such a manner, approached the elephant, joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation, and said to the elephant-king:

"I have provided you with all kinds of excellent food and drink as offerings; yet you remain emaciated, your flesh does not adhere to your body, your complexion and strength have diminished, and your frame is afflicted by wasting. As I observe you, my heart is not gladdened, for you do not experience joy."
My heart loves you; I have provided for and nurtured you, never abandoning you for even a moment.
Whatever you require, I shall now give it all to you to bring you joy; for what reason do you not feel happy or delighted?
At that time, the Elephant-Lord addressed King Brahmadatta, saying:
"I now submit these words to the Great King to bring him joy."
At that time, King Brahmadatta, hearing those words spoken by the elephant-king, gave rise to a heart of great wonder and joy, and further thought:
"How extraordinary this is!"
"This king of elephant-lords is able to speak the language of humans.
Having formed this thought, he addressed that elephant-lord, saying:
"O Elephant-Lord King!
"By speaking such words, you have brought me joy.
At that time, the Elephant-Lord addressed King Brahmadatta, saying:
"Great King!..."

"You should know that within that forest there dwell my parents, aged and infirm. Since the time before I was captured by the king, I do not recall ever having eaten anything first myself without first giving it to my parents; the same applies to water and drink—I would always give it to my parents first, and only then drink it myself."
I now reflect that while I receive the king’s provisions and all necessary supplies, lacking nothing as he sustains me,
my parents remain in that forest, left all alone and enduring great hardship and suffering.
"It is precisely because I have not seen my parents that I am thus sorrowful and unhappy.
When King Brahmadatta heard these words, he conceived a sense of unprecedented wonder and thought to himself:
"How extraordinary this is! How rare!"
"Inconceivable!
Even among humans it is difficult to find such a dharma; how is it that this elephant-nāga is like this?
Having formed this thought, he addressed the elephant-nāga with these words:
"O Great Elephant Dragon King!

I would rather cast this body and life of mine into a prison than, by means of such practice in accordance with the Dharma, the wondrous conduct of upholding the precepts, or filial piety toward my parents, dare to disturb or disrupt such matters."
At that time, Brahmadatta again addressed the elephant king, saying: "O Elephant King!
I now release you to go to your parents; together with them, provide for one another and enjoy happiness as you wish."
Then, as King Brahmadatta released the elephant-king, he spoke this verse:
"Go now in peace, O Elephant-King; Be filial and provide for your parents.
I would rather relinquish this life-force of mine Than cause you further disturbance."
At that time, Brahmadatta released the elephant-king. Having been set free, the elephant-king gradually made his way to that forest.
At that moment, the mother of the elephant-king, because she could not see her son, was filled with grief and distress; weeping and wailing, she lost the sight of both her eyes.
Because he had lost his sight, he ran hither and thither from his original place, wandering to other locations.
When the elephant-king first returned to that forest, he searched for his mother but could not find her whereabouts at all.
Because he could not see her, he cried out at the top of his voice.
At that moment, the mother elephant heard his cry and immediately recognized that the voice belonged to her own son.
She, too, then let out a cry and wailed in sorrowful lamentation.
Hearing his mother’s call, that elephant dragon king followed the sound and went to where she was.
Upon seeing his mother, the elephant dragon king approached a pond, stayed there to rest, and settled his mother upon the bank.

"At that time, the elephant-nāga entered the pond, filled his trunk with water, and emerged; filled with joy, his body and mind leaped with such exuberance that it pervaded his entire being, and he could not contain himself."
He went to his mother’s side, sprinkled water over her, and bathed her.
At that time, as his mother received the water held by her son and bathed her body, her eyes became clear and pure once more, surpassing their former state.
When the mother elephant saw her son, she asked him:
"From where have you come?
You have only returned today; it has been a long time since I have been able to see you."

Then, that elephant-king related everything to his mother: how King Brahmadatta had sent men to seize him and take him to the royal palace for the purpose of offering him as a gift, and how he had been released and returned home; he told his mother all of these matters in detail.
At that time, having heard these words, the mother elephant was filled with such joy and exultation that it pervaded her entire body, which she could not contain.
She cried out:

"My son, my son! Just as I am today able to sustain and care for you, and experience such joy and happiness, I pray that King Brahmadatta, together with his parents, wife, children, male and female attendants, all his kinsmen, ministers, officials, and all his assistants, may likewise sustain and care for one another, and experience this same happiness as I do today."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus,
if you have any doubt as to who this Elephant Nāga King was, listen."
"I am that very person. You bhikṣus!
If you have any doubt as to who that elephant mother was at that time, [it was I]."
Do not conceive a different view; this was none other than Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
At that time, she wept for me, her sorrowful tears flowing down as she endured great suffering until both her eyes were blinded; yet, because of me, she has now attained purity once again.

Now it is likewise: because Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī could not see me, she wailed and wept in grief, suffering from sorrow and affliction until her two eyes lost their sight; now, once again, through me, she has regained her clarity.
"O bhikṣus!

When the Tathāgata was formerly on the path of practice and had not yet attained Buddhahood, he still performed such benefits for sentient beings; how much more so now that he has already achieved anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi!"
Therefore, O bhikṣus!

If there is one who possesses wisdom, they should always maintain a mind of reverence and a sense of wonder toward the Buddha; likewise, they must also give rise to a mind of reverence toward the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
"You, bhikṣus! You should train yourselves in this way. Chapter 57:

The Circumstances of Nanda’s Renunciation *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Fifty-seven (Part One): The Circumstances of Nanda’s Renunciation At that time, the World-Honored One converted Nanda, the son of the Śākya clan, leading him to renounce his home and leave the household life. He repeatedly explained the causes and conditions for renunciation and further praised the causes and conditions for renunciation, saying these words:
"Come, Nanda! You shall go forth into homelessness.
After these words were spoken, the Śākya son Nanda addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I shall not go forth. Why is this? Because—”
With four kinds of offerings, I shall serve the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus for as long as I live, providing them with robes, bedding, food, and medicinal requisites.

In this manner, the World-Honored One exhorted Nanda a second and third time, praising the merit of leaving home and going forth into homelessness, even repeatedly explaining the circumstances of his own renunciation and commending him to do the same. Yet Nanda remained unwilling to go forth, continuing instead to speak of seeking robes, bedding, food, and medicine, and of providing for the Buddha and the Sangha with all his life.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished his meal following a short while, he took a single attendant and proceeded slowly toward the house of the Śākya youth Nanda.
At that time, however, the Śākya youth Nanda was on an upper story of a multi-storied pavilion, sitting together with Sundarī, looking out from the tower and strolling about.

At that time, Nanda was atop the multi-storied pavilion when he saw the World-Honored One from afar. As the Buddha approached his location, he quickly rose in alarm and descended from the upper story. He went to the side of the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Welcome, World-Honored One!
From where have you come so far?"
"I only pray that you will deign to enter my hall and chamber, ascend the seat, and sit.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the hall and chamber; having ascended and taken his seat, he comforted Nanda, and once his consolation was complete, he sat in silence.
At that time, Nanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I pray that you will now accept this offering here; I shall dispatch someone to prepare the various delicacies and food."
The Buddha told Nanda, “I have already finished eating; there is no need to prepare anything.
At that time, the Śākya youth Nanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now there is honeyed syrup; may I drink it at this improper time?
The Buddha told Nanda, "I shall do as you wish."
At that time, Nanda again addressed the Buddha, saying, "So be it,
World-Honored One! Thereupon,
Nanda took up the Buddha’s bowl, filled it with non-timely gruel, and offered it to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One did not accept it.
Then, the Śākya youth Nanda took the bowl and offered it to an attendant, but that attendant, in turn, would not accept it.

At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and returned with his attendants, intending to go back to his original location; the Śākya youth also followed him down from the multi-storied pavilion, carrying the honey-drink, wishing to follow the Buddha.

At that time, Sundarī, a woman of the Śākya clan, saw the Śākya Nanda carrying a full bowl of non-timely honey-drink and following behind the World-Honored One. While Sundarī was still finishing combing her hair, she called out to Nanda in a loud voice, saying:
"Noble son Nanda!"
"Where do you wish to go?
At that time, Nanda pointed to the bowl and said, "I wish to take this bowl to present it to the Tathāgata; upon reaching him, I shall return immediately."
Sundarī said: "Noble son, come quickly!
Do not remain there for long."

At that time, the World-Honored One departed from Nanda’s house; for the sake of Nanda, he walked back and forth through the streets and alleys, desiring that all the people within the city see Nanda carrying non-timely juice and following after the Buddha.
At that time, when the people saw this event, they said to one another:
"The World-Honored One must now cause Nanda to renounce his home and enter the religious life."
At that time, the World-Honored One went to the monastery and called a certain bhikṣu; he secretly made a sign with his fingers, instructing him to take the honey bowl from Nanda’s hand.
At that time, the bhikṣu understood the Buddha’s intention and immediately took the bowl from Nanda.
Then Nanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“World-Honored One!”
"I now take my leave of the Buddha, wishing to return home.
The Buddha told Nanda:
"Do not go back!"
At that time, Nanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As I reflect upon it now, I do not wish to leave the household life."
"Why is this? It is because I desire to provide for the Tathāgata and the Saṅgha with the four requisites throughout my entire life.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Nanda, speaking these words:

"This Jambudvīpa world is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth; it is broad in the north and narrow in the south, shaped like the box of a carriage. It is filled with arhats as densely as sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, hemp, or rice."
If there are sons or daughters of good family who, throughout their entire lives, provide these arhats with the four requisites without fail,
and after those arhats have entered parinirvāṇa, further continue to make offerings by erecting stūpas for their relics.
Upon each of those stupas, they offered banners, canopies, precious bells, and victory banners; furthermore, they made various offerings of incense, flowers, and diverse oil lamps.
"What do you think?
Are the merits of these sons and daughters of good family great or not?
Nanda replied:
"The merit obtained is exceedingly great.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Nanda:

"Suppose there were Arhats filling this Jambudvīpa, and someone were to provide them with the four requisites for the duration of their lives, including incense, flowers, and the lighting of oil lamps."
Furthermore, if there is another person who makes offerings to a single Buddha, the merit and karmic fruit thereof will be twice as superior as that [of the former]. "Moreover, Nanda!

If a person can enter the teachings of the Buddha-Dharma, even to the extent of going forth from home, and practices the dharma of pure brahmacarya for one day and one night, the karmic fruit of this will be many times greater than that."
"Therefore, Nanda!
You must certainly leave the household life; do not again greedily seek the pleasures of the five desires.
Furthermore, Nanda!"

All sensual desires offer little flavor but bring much suffering and affliction; all sensual desires are impermanent and thus should be reviled and abandoned. They are the root of great suffering, a great ulcer, a great evil thorn, a great calamitous bond, and a great torment. They possess the characteristic of diminution and the characteristic of destruction; they are impermanent and unstable, never pausing for even a moment. They are not solid, being precarious, fragile, and easily broken; they abound in fear, and are suffering, empty, and without self. You must now, with earnest attention, contemplate the faults and afflictions of sensual desires in this way.
"Nanda! You should now carefully contemplate the faults and perils of the five desires; do not be greedily attached to them.

At that time, although the World-Honored One spoke of these faults to Nanda, Nanda’s heart still did not desire or aspire to leave the household life. Out of mere respect for the Buddha, however, he looked up and down hesitantly and said:
“World-Honored One!
I shall go forth.
At that time, as the World-Honored One was walking in meditation, he made a sign with his finger to summon a bhikṣu; when the bhikṣu came, the Buddha spoke to him, saying:
"You should summon a barber.
Thereupon, that bhikṣu immediately summoned a barber from among the assembly; standing before Nanda, he held a razor in his hand, intending to shave Nanda's beard and hair.
At that time, Nanda clenched his fist toward the barber and spoke these words:
"By what power do you dare to shave my head?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, with right mindfulness and right intention, addressed Nanda, saying:
"Come, bhikṣu! Enter into my Dharma and practice the holy life (brahmacarya) for the sake of ending all suffering."
When the Tathāgata had spoken these words, Nanda’s hair and beard fell away of their own accord, just like those of a bhikṣu.

Seven days after his hair and beard were shorn, he naturally came to wear the saffron-colored robes, holding in his hand an alms bowl, a vessel used according to the Dharma; thus that elder immediately became a renunciant and received full ordination.

At that time, Nanda was lovely and handsome, a sight for all people to behold; he possessed thirty marks, complete and without deficiency. His body was golden in color, standing four finger-widths shorter than the Tathāgata’s. The *kāṣāya* robe he wore was identical in every respect to the Buddha’s own garment, with no difference between them.

Having performed this and taken it up, when various bhikṣus saw him approaching from afar, they all thought that Nanda was the World-Honored One; wishing to rise and welcome him, they did so until they realized he was not, whereupon they returned to their original seats.
For this reason, the bhikṣus felt resentment and suspicion, and spoke thus:
"How is it that the Elder Nanda wears and maintains robes identical in quality to those of the Buddha?"
Then, the bhikṣus went at once to inform the Buddha.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One immediately assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned Nanda, saying:
"Did you make robes such as the saṃghāṭī to be the same size as those of the Buddha, and do you maintain them as such?"
At that time, Nanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This is indeed so."
The Buddha said to Nanda,
"This is not in accordance with the Dharma.
Why do you now wear the saṃghāṭī robe of the same size as that of the Buddha, the World-Honored One?"
At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked Nanda; having thus instructed him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, none of you shall accept or wear robes made according to the measurements of the World-Honored One.
Should anyone violate this, they shall be punished according to the law."
At that time, Nanda thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One has already prohibited us from receiving and keeping robes according to his own measurements. From now on, whatever robes we make must be beaten and pressed to bring out a luster before they can be worn."

At that time, Nanda immediately put on those polished, mended robes, took up his alms bowl, applied collyrium to his eyes, adorned his body, and put on leather sandals. Holding a parasol in his left hand and his bowl in his right, he approached the Buddha and said, “World-Honored One!”
"I wish to enter the village to beg for food.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Nanda, saying these words:
"Are you not, indeed, a son of good family?"
"Out of faith, did you leave the home life to become a renunciant?
Nanda replied, "It is so,
World-Honored One!"
"It is indeed so.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Nanda, saying these words:
"Since you are a son of good family who has left home and gone forth with faith, for what reason do you press and polish the robes you wear until they emit a lustrous sheen?"

Furthermore, for what reason do you adorn your body, apply collyrium to your eyes, wear leather sandals on your feet, hold a parasol in one hand, and carry an alms bowl in the other, desiring to beg for food?
"Furthermore, Nanda!
If you dwell in an araṇya, sustain yourself by begging for alms, and wear robes made of discarded rags, this is indeed excellent."
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: "When shall I see Nanda,
Dwelling in seclusion and always begging for food, Having few desires and being content,
having abandoned all remnants, And delighting in the remoteness from all thoughts of desire?"
At that time, for this reason and on account of these circumstances, the World-Honored One assembled the bhikṣus and addressed them, saying: "O bhikṣus!..."
"From this day forward, you must no longer wear robes that emit light;
if anyone should possess such a robe, they shall be punished according to the law.
Furthermore, you must not apply seductive ointments to your eyes, nor wear exquisite leather sandals, nor carry light and delicate alms bowls."
"Furthermore, you must not enter cities or villages to beg for alms while holding a parasol;
if you do so, you shall all be dealt with according to the law.

At that time, although Nanda had been forbidden by the World-Honored One from wearing these polished robes, from applying collyrium to his eyes, from wearing fine leather sandals, from carrying light bowls, and from using a parasol, he still remembered the power and pleasures of the king and was unwilling to comply with these prohibitions.
He still remembered that Śākya woman Sundarī; dwelling on her beauty and desire, he failed to practice the holy life and wished to abandon his precepts to return to his own home.

For this reason, he constantly painted images of that woman Sundarī. Later, at one time, while in a secluded place in the forest hermitage, he would take either bricks, tiles, or wooden boards and paint this image of the Śākya woman Sundarī, spending an entire day gazing upon it in this manner.
When some bhikṣus saw this, resentment arose in their hearts, and they said to one another:
"Venerable Nanda!
How can you stay in an araṇya and spend the whole day looking at drawings of women, whether made of brick, tile, or wood?"
At that time, the bhikṣus took this matter to the Buddha to inform him.
Then, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the bhikṣus and, in the midst of the assembly, questioned Nanda, saying:
"Did you indeed stay in an araṇya, or take bricks, tiles, or wooden boards to draw the forms of women, looking at them all day long?"
Nanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Nanda, saying:
"To do such a thing as this is unwholesome.
How could an ordained bhikṣu paint the image of a woman and gaze upon it?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!

From this day forward, you must not paint the forms of women, whether real or imaginary, out of a mind attached to desire, nor shall you gaze upon them after having painted them. Should any among you intentionally paint and gaze upon them in such a manner, they shall incur an offense of transgressing the precepts."
On another occasion, the Elder Nanda was on duty in turn to guard the monastery. At that time, Nanda thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata will soon enter the village for alms; today, I shall be able to return home."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Nanda had such a thought, addressed the Elder Nanda, saying:
"If you wish to go, close the doors of all the rooms before you depart."
At that time, having spoken these words, the World-Honored One immediately entered the village to beg for food.
The Elder Nanda thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has already entered the village to beg for food; I shall now return to my home."
At that time, Nanda saw that the door to the World-Honored One’s chamber was not closed, and he thought to himself:
"I shall close this door before I return."
He immediately closed that door, but seeing that Śāriputra’s room door had opened again, he went back to close Śāriputra’s door.
Once he had closed that door, Maudgalyāyana’s room door opened again; he then immediately closed Maudgalyāyana’s room door as well.
Having closed that door, he saw that the door to Mahākāśyapa’s room was open again; he immediately went to close Mahākāśyapa’s door.
Having closed that door, he saw that the door to Mahākatyāyana’s room was open again; he immediately went to close Kaṭyāyana’s door as well.
Having closed that door, he saw that the door to Uruvilvā Kāśyapa’s room was open again; he immediately went to close the door to Uruvilvā Kāśyapa’s room.
Once he had closed that door, the door of Nadi-Kāśyapa’s room opened again; he then went back to close Nadi-Kāśyapa’s door.
Once he had closed that door, Gaya-Kāśyapa’s door opened again.
At that time, Nanda immediately closed the door of Gayā’s room.
Once he had closed it, the door of Upasena’s room opened again.
After closing that door, he saw that the door of Kṣulla’s room had opened once more.
Having closed that door, he saw the gate of Mahācaṇḍa open;
having closed that door, he saw the door of Revata’s cell open;
having closed that door, he saw the door of Upāliputra’s cell open.
In this sequence, once one gate was closed, the second opened; once the third was closed, the fourth opened. Seeing the gates opening and closing one after another, he thought to himself:
"What transgression could those bhikṣus possibly have committed that they would seize me for either opening or closing these gates?"
"I shall now return, for I fear that the World-Honored One will arrive before long.

Having formed this thought, as he was about to depart from within the Nigrodha grove, the World-Honored One immediately observed Nanda with his divine eye and saw that Nanda was about to leave the Nigrodha location.
Having seen this, the Tathāgata vanished from the city of Kapilavastu and immediately appeared there in the Nyagrodha Grove.
At that time, having seen the Buddha emerge from within that grove, Nanda immediately took refuge beneath a nyagrodha tree and sat there with his body concealed.
Then, by means of his supernormal power, the World-Honored One lifted that great tree and placed it in the air; seeing Nanda sitting there with his body hidden, he spoke these words:
"Nanda, you there! Now!"
"Where do you wish to go?
Then Nanda replied,
"World-Honored One!"

At this moment, I have again recalled the pleasures and sovereign ease of that royal throne, as well as Śrī Sundarī; for these reasons, I take no delight in practicing the holy life and desire to abandon the precepts to return to my own home.
On account of this matter, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Having already left the thicket and attained freedom from it, One emerges from the thicket only to enter it again.
O *pudgala*, observe this fact: Having been released from bondage, one is bound once more."
At that time, after the World-Honored One had taught those verses of the Dharma to Nanda, he further exhorted him, saying:
"Venerable Nanda!
You should apply your mind with earnestness; within my sovereign teaching of the Dharma, practice the holy life diligently in order to bring all suffering to an end."

The World-Honored One taught Nanda with the Dharma, yet Nanda still could not forget the pleasures of the five desires from his former life, nor the delightful joys of his position as a king; he continued to long for Śrī Sundarī, took no pleasure in practicing the holy life according to the True Dharma, and his heart desired to abandon the precepts and return to his home.
At that time, there was another great householder who wished to invite the World-Honored One to provide him with food and drink.
At that moment, Nanda was next in turn to guard the monastery. Then, Nanda thought to himself:
"Now that the World-Honored One is about to enter the village to accept this householder’s invitation for a meal, I shall return home."
At that time, the World-Honored One, foreseeing that Nanda was forming this thought, and having known it, immediately addressed Nanda, saying:
"Nanda, you who are here now!
"You must certainly know the proper time to sprinkle and sweep the grounds of the monastery, and ensure that all the water jars are filled with water.
Having spoken these words, he immediately went to the village to attend the invitation.
At that time, the Elder Nanda thought to himself:
"Now that the World-Honored One has already accepted an invitation and is going to the village, I may now go home myself."
Having formed this thought, he looked back and saw that the room where the Tathāgata resided was covered with much filth and dust.
Having seen this, he thought:
"I shall first go and sweep away that filth, and only then return home."
Having formed this thought, he took up a broom and went to sweep that room.
As he swept one side, the wind blew back, filling the floor with dust and grass, so that it had to be swept again.
At that time, Nanda again thought to himself:
"Let me stop sweeping for now; first I shall cause all the water jars of the Sangha to be filled with water, and only then go home."
Having had this thought, he took that water vessel, went to the place where there was water, filled it completely, and once the vessel was full, he turned it over.
At that time, Nanda thought to himself:
"Why should I bother to sweep the ground and prepare water? The Tathāgata will return before long; I may as well go quickly to my own home."
Having had this thought, he immediately returned from that Nyagrodha Grove, intending to go home.

At that time, the World-Honored One, staying at the house of the elder who had invited him, observed Nanda with his supramundane, purified divine eye as he was about to depart from that Nyagrodha Grove and head for home.

Having seen this, he immediately manifested a separate transformation body, vanished from the house of the elder, and in a mere instant, arrived within the Nigrodha grove and appeared before the Elder Nanda.

At that time, when Nanda saw from afar that the World-Honored One was approaching, he immediately climbed a large, high, and precipitous cliff, descended from its far side, and sat down in concealment at a secluded spot.
At that time, by means of his supernormal power, the World-Honored One caused that steep embankment to become as level as the palm of a hand.
Then, seeing him seated there, the World-Honored One addressed Nanda:
"What do you intend to do here now?"
At that time, Nanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “Bhagavān!
I have already given my word that I would return home with Sundarī; now I am thinking thus:”
"Let it not be that I am made to utter a falsehood.
For this reason, I now wish to go to that place.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Nanda:
"Why do you need to see Sundarī now?
Her body is thus merely skin wrapping over sinews and bones; within, it is completely filled with marrow, brain, pus, blood, feces, and urine—most loathsome, like a latrine."
Thus it is, Nanda; I have now spoken briefly: the impurity emitted by each and every sentient being in union with his wife exceeds the waters of the great ocean, yet they remain insatiable.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Having sought to leave the dense forest and already attained liberation, One escapes from the forest only to enter it again.
O *pudgala*, observe such as these: Having been freed from bondage, they fall back into bondage."
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeking to transform Nanda, preached the Dharma and instructed him, saying:
"Now, you, Nanda!
Within my sovereign teaching of the Dharma..."
"Delighting in play, he practices the pure holy life (brahmacarya) for the sake of extinguishing all suffering.

At that time, although Nanda had been taught through such skillful means by the World-Honored One, he still took no pleasure in practicing the holy life. Instead, he formed a faction with the group of six bhikṣus; they frequently went to his side from morning until night, engaging in conversation and discussion, speaking only of matters such as wrong livelihood and various evils.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing and knowing his conduct, thought to himself:

"This Nanda has now begun to emulate those six groups of bhikṣus; I fear he will damage his meritorious deeds and spiritual practice. I should sever his association with those people as a partisan faction."
Having formed this thought, he immediately addressed the Elder Nanda, saying: "Nanda, come!
I wish to enter the city of Kapilavastu together with you."
Nanda replied, "I shall do exactly as the Venerable One has instructed. Then,
the World-Honored One entered the city of Kapilavastu with Nanda, and having entered, they gradually arrived at a fishmonger's shop.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw within that shop, upon a straw mat, one hundred stinking, rotting dead fish placed upon that mat.
Having seen this, he addressed the Elder Nanda, saying these words:
"Nanda, come here!"
"Take this fish and spread it upon a handful of *kuśa* grass.
Then Nanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"As the World-Honored One has instructed."
Having spoken these words, he immediately went to that shop and, beneath the fish stall, pulled out a handful of foul-smelling rushes.
Having grasped them, the Buddha again addressed the Elder Nanda:
"Hold them for a short while, then place them back on the ground."
Nanda replied,
"As the World-Honored One has instructed," and immediately took hold of the grass and stayed there.
At that time, Nanda held those blades of grass for a short while and then placed them on the ground.
Then the Buddha again addressed Nanda, saying:
"Smell your own hand."
At that time, Nanda immediately smelled his hand.
Then the Buddha again addressed Nanda, saying:
"What scent is on your hand?"
The Elder Nanda replied,
“World-Honored One!
It has nothing but an impure, putrid stench.”
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll 56 and Scroll 57,
translated by the Sui Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta.
In the *Nanda-nidāna-parivarta*, Part Two,
at that time the Buddha addressed the Elder Nanda: "It is so, it is so."

If a person associates with evil companions, taking them as friends, and dwells together with them, even though they may follow one another's lead for a short time, later, because of being defiled and habituated by their evil karma, their evil reputation will spread far and wide.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as one who stands at a fish stall And grasps a handful of grass with his hand Will have that hand smell of fish,
So too it is with those who associate with evil friends."
At that time, the World-Honored One again went with the Elder Nanda to a perfume shop. Seeing various bundles of incense upon the shop, he addressed the Elder Nanda, saying: "Nanda!
"Come, take these parcels of incense from atop that building.
At that time, Nanda followed the Buddha's instruction and took the parcels of incense from atop that building.
The Buddha told Nanda:
"In the interval of a single *nāḍikā*, hold a bundle of incense and then place it on the ground.
At that time, having heard these words from the Buddha, the Elder Nanda held this incense in his hand for the duration of one *nāḍikā* and then placed it back upon the ground.
At that time, the Buddha said to the Elder Nanda,
"Now you should smell your own hand and observe it.
Having heard the Buddha’s words, Nanda immediately smelled his own hand.
The Buddha said to Nanda, "Smell this hand; what kind of odor does it have?
Nanda replied:
“World-Honored One!
The fragrance from his hands is subtle and immeasurable.
The Buddha told Nanda:

"It is so, it is so. If a person associates with virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), dwells constantly with them, conforms to their influence, and remains in close proximity, they will certainly attain widespread renown."
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one holds aloof wood incense (*agaru*) in hand, Or even calamus, musk, and the like, The fragrance will naturally permeate them in an instant;
So too it is with associating with virtuous friends."

At that time, the World-Honored One departed from the city of Kapilavastu and returned to his original dwelling. Having gathered the great assembly of bhikṣus for this purpose, he addressed the Elder Nanda, saying: “Nanda!
"You must not now draw near those six groups of bhikṣus, nor should you form close friendships with them. Why is this?

If there is anyone who draws near such evil associates—even if they become their friends, or at times serve one another, or follow after all of their activities—merely by being closely associated with such wicked people, one will incur an evil reputation that spreads throughout the world."
“Elder Nanda!

If you wish to seek out friends and spiritual teachers, you should associate with the bhikṣus Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Kātyāyana, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Upasena, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahāsodāyin, Revata, and other such bhikṣus.”
I exhort you to draw near to, follow, and serve them. Why is this?

If a person draws near to a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) and serves them with devotion, even if they have not yet realized the ultimate benefit, they will nonetheless obtain worldly renown and fame.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, spoke in verse:
"If a person associates with evil friends, They shall not gain a good reputation in this present life;
Because they have associated intimately with evil companions, In the future, they will likewise fall into the Avīci Hell."
If a person associates with virtuous friends and follows their deeds and conduct,
though they do not realize worldly benefits in the present, they shall in the future attain the cause for the exhaustion of suffering.

At that time, although the World-Honored One instructed Nanda with skillful words, Nanda still clung to the pleasures of sovereignty over his royal throne; he recalled the five objects of desire associated with Sundarī and remained without joy in the Buddha-dharma. He wished to abandon the holy life, wished to cast off the full precepts, and desired to return to the affairs of household life.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having known the mind of the elder Nanda, thought to himself:

"This Nanda’s afflictions are burning fiercely; how could a minor teaching suffice to destroy them? I must now employ a skillful means, just as in the world one uses fire to extinguish fire, or uses poison to counteract poison."

Having formed this thought, he took the hand of the Elder Nanda and departed from the Nyagrodha grove; by means of his supernormal power, he made his body vanish and suddenly appeared, standing upon Mount Gandhamādana.
At that time, because the mountain was buffeted by the wind, two trees rubbed against one another and immediately caught fire, burning the mountain and producing great columns of smoke and flames.

At that moment, there were many monkeys within the mountain, numbering five hundred; their fur was scorched by the fire, and they all remained on the ground, rubbing their bodies to extinguish the flames.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw a female, blind monkey within that troop who was likewise using her hands to extinguish the fire on her body.
Then, the Buddha addressed the Elder Nanda:
"Do you now see this female, blind monkey within that troop who is likewise using her hands to extinguish the fire on her body, as has been done?"
At that time, Nanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so; I have now seen it.”
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Elder Nanda, saying:
"What do you think?
Between your Sundarī, who is lovely and dignified, and this monkey—whom do you consider superior?"
At that time, Nanda turned toward the World-Honored One with a frown and a knit brow, remaining silent and saying nothing.
Then, the World-Honored One took Elder Nanda by the arm and, vanishing from Mount Gandhamādana, proceeded to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and appeared before the Pārijātaka tree.
At that time, beneath that tree there was a large rock named Vānamukhara (in the Sui language, "Yellowish-Brown"), which stood at that spot.

At that time, Śakra, King of the Devas, went into that garden to sport within it; the garden was named Ikāpuṇḍarīka. He was surrounded on all sides by five hundred palace ladies and court attendants, who performed songs and instrumental music.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw King Śakra in the Ikāpuṇḍarīka Garden, leading five hundred court ladies, enjoying themselves with joyful music and pleasure.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Nanda, saying:
"Do you now see these five hundred court ladies performing music and engaging in playful diversions?"
Nanda replied, "So it is,
World-Honored One!
I have now seen it."
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately addressed the Elder Nanda, saying:
"What do you think?
Is the Śākya maiden Sundarī more beautiful?"
“Are the five hundred maidens beautiful?
The Elder Nanda replied,
“World-Honored One!”

If one were to compare that blind female monkey of that time with Sundarī, she would not equal her even by a hundredfold, nor a thousandfold, nor even a hundred-thousandfold; indeed, no calculation in the world could reach it.

If one were to compare this woman, Sundarī, with these five hundred court ladies as I do now, she would not even equal them by a factor of a hundred, a thousand, or even a hundred thousand; it would exceed all that can be calculated by worldly mathematics.
"How can this now be illustrated by a simile?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Nanda:
"Do you now wish to enjoy yourself with these court ladies?"
At that time, Nanda was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, saying to the World-Honored One:
"World-Honored One!
According to my own wish, I truly desire to enjoy myself together with those five hundred maidens."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Nanda:

"You may not now enjoy yourself with those women with this ordinary body. If you wish to do so, you must, with a joyful heart, practice the holy life (brahmacarya) within my Dharma. I shall then grant you this promise:

'If you can now comply with this Dharma and practice pure conduct, then at the end of your life, when you cast off this body, you will surely receive the reward in a future existence by being born in this place and enjoying yourself together with these five hundred maidens.'"
At that time, having heard these words, Nanda was filled with such joy and exultation that it pervaded his entire body; unable to contain himself, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"From this day forth, within the Buddha-dharma, I shall joyfully practice the pure brahmacarya.
World-Honored One!
You have now granted me your promise; I truly desire that in a future age I may be born in this very place, together with these five hundred court ladies, to enjoy ourselves in mutual delight."
At that time, the World-Honored One again took the elder Nanda by the arm, vanished from the Heaven of the Thirty-three, and returned to his original dwelling place.
At that moment, Nanda thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has previously promised me that in a future life, I shall obtain those five hundred court ladies with whom I may enjoy myself."

"Therefore, Nanda, for this reason, you should exhaust your body and mind to practice the pure holy life with right mindfulness. Subdue your sense faculties, moderate your food and drink, and during the first and last watches of the night, rise to recite and walk in meditation. Be courageous and diligent, refraining from conversing or joking with others;

let your mind not be restless or deceitful, and let your speech not be frivolous. Generate energetic progress, maintain awareness of the four postures, delight in emptiness and stillness, close the gates of the senses, and achieve the most supreme and subtle right mindfulness."

At that time, when Nanda wished to contemplate the eastern direction, he stabilized his body and mind and filled his will with resolve; having established right mindfulness, he then began to contemplate the eastern direction.
When one contemplates in this manner, there is no sorrow or affliction, no darkness, and regarding unwholesome dharmas, there is never any leakage or confusion.
In this way, when one wishes to contemplate the south, west, north, the zenith, and the nadir, one likewise stabilizes body and mind, and the will becomes fully suffused.
When contemplating in this manner, there is no sorrow or affliction, no darkness, no further leakage into unwholesome dharmas, and no confusion.
At that time, some fellow bhikṣus who were traveling with Nanda said to him: "Venerable Nanda! Previously, you did not restrain your sense faculties; regarding food and drink, you knew no satiety.

You constantly sought out fine beds, mattresses, and bedding for peaceful sleep, never feeling weary or tired. At times you would joke and laugh, your mind was unstable, and you were cunning and deceitful in speech. You never applied yourself with diligence but were always indolent; you lacked right mindfulness and were prone to forgetfulness. Your deportment was deficient and flawed; you had neither dhyāna nor samādhi, and could not collect the mind. Your senses ran wild and dissolute, beyond what can be fully described."

How is it that now your faculties are so well-tamed, you are moderate in eating and drinking, you never sleep during the first or last watches of the night, you are free from frivolous play, you have restrained both body and mind, you do not engage in idle chatter, you are courageous and diligent, you possess right mindfulness and right effort, you have already attained meditative concentration, your mind does not leak away, and your faculties do not wander?
"Elder, for what reason have you become like this today?
At that time, Nanda addressed those fellow bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable elders!..."

"You should know that the World-Honored One intends to bestow upon me five hundred court ladies in a future life so that I may enjoy pleasures and delight; for this reason, I now diligently practice the holy life within this Dharma."
At that time, the bhikṣus who were Nanda’s close friends and companions, wishing to tease, mock, and ridicule him, said to one another:
"Venerable Nanda!..."
"Under the Blessed One, you work as a hired laborer seeking a future reward; therefore, you practice the holy life within the Dharma.
Elder Nanda!
Is it not simply for the sake of five hundred celestial maidens that you practice the holy life in the presence of the Buddha?"
At that time, because the elder Nanda’s friends and fellow bhikṣus had called him "the hired laborer" ever since then, they continued to address him by that name.

Then, seeing that Nanda was practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) for the sake of celestial maidens, the World-Honored One took him by the arm, led him out from that Nyagrodha grove, and vanished into the depths of the great hell.

At that time, the World-Honored One saw a copper cauldron with a fierce fire burning beneath it; the cauldron was glowing so red that it was indistinguishable from the fire itself, emitting great flames and blazing with intense, radiant heat.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One addressed Nanda:
"Go and ask these wardens of hell: 'For whom is this copper cauldron being heated and boiling over?'"
When the Venerable Nanda had heard these words of the Buddha, he addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I shall do exactly as the Buddha has instructed.”
