He immediately went to the side of those various hell-wardens and asked them:
"For whom is this great copper cauldron boiling so violently as it is now?"
At that time, the hell-wardens all replied to Nanda, saying these words:
"The Buddha has a younger brother born of his maternal aunt named Nanda; it is for that man's sake that this cauldron is being heated."
Nanda asked again,
"Have you not heard? In the past,
the Tathāgata promised a person that if they practice the holy life for the sake of five hundred celestial musicians and maidens, they shall later be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
The various hell-wardens said:
"So it is, so it is; we already know this.
However, we have further heard that after such a person has fallen from those Trāyastriṃśa Heavens, they are reborn here."
At that time, having heard these words, Nanda felt terror arise within him; the hair on his entire body stood on end, and he thought to himself:
"If I must undergo such suffering here in succession, I do not wish for the karmic fruit of such celestial maidens even now."
At that time, the World-Honored One took the elder Nanda by the arm and, from within the hell, made his body vanish, returning to the Nyagrodha Grove to emerge.
At that time, Nanda was constantly addressed by his fellow practitioners and kinsmen as "the Buddha’s hired laborer"; they mocked him, rebuked him, and ridiculed him with derisive jests.

Furthermore, seeing the hells, he was filled with shame and dread; immediately developing revulsion and detachment, he lamented and repented for himself. Seeking a secluded place, he practiced walking and sitting alone, never again being negligent, but instead exerting himself with fierce diligence.

"Whosoever among good sons, possessing right faith, leaves the home life for homelessness to seek the unsurpassed, pure holy life (brahmacarya), and having practiced it, attains in this very life the superknowledges (abhijñā) through personal realization, achieves the destruction of all taints (āsrava-kṣaya), and declares with his own mouth:
'Birth and death are ended; the holy life is established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further existence.'"
Having realized the fruit of arhatship, his mind attained liberation.
The Elder Nanda was likewise; only after realizing the fruit of arhatship did he go to where the Buddha was, prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, and withdraw to sit to one side.
At that time, the Elder Nanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I now renounce the favor granted by the World-Honored One in the past. When I formerly desired to receive the reward from the Tathāgata, it was solely for the sake of the five hundred celestial maidens;
this is why it was so. But now, World-Honored One!"
"I have attained liberation.
At that time, the Buddha told the Elder Nanda:
"It is not only today that I have first attained liberation from you; when you first uttered these words:"
"The holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished,
and there is no further existence. At that time,

the Elder Nanda and his fellow bhikṣus, not yet knowing that Nanda had attained the destruction of the outflows, continued to mock and deride him as they had on previous days when he had not yet destroyed the outflows, uttering such words:
“The Elder Nanda is serving as a hired laborer for the sake of reward in the presence of the Blessed One; he practices the holy life for the sake of those five hundred celestial nymphs.
At that time, the Blessed One thought to himself:
“These bhikṣus do not yet know that Nanda’s outflows are exhausted; they still rely on his former state when his outflows were not yet exhausted, and thus they continue to say:”
"The Elder Nanda is practicing the holy life for the sake of those five hundred celestial maidens.
I fear that they will incur much demerit.
Therefore, I shall now proclaim and manifest before the assembly the fact that the Elder Nanda has exhausted all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
At that time, for these reasons and on account of these matters, the World-Honored One assembled the entire community of bhikṣus. Once they had gathered, he addressed them, saying: "O bhikṣus!"
If anyone says there is a handsome man, it is the bhikṣu Nanda;
if one says there is one who is upright and fair, it is also the bhikṣu Nanda;
and as for one of great physical strength, the bhikṣu Nanda is likewise such a person.
"If one says there is someone whose body is delicate, soft, and weak, it is the bhikṣu Nanda.
If one says there is someone whose faculties are tranquil and not distracted, it is also the bhikṣu Nanda."
"If there is anyone who says that among all those who know moderation in food and drink, it is the bhikṣu Nanda;
and if there is anyone who says that among those who do not sleep during the first and last watches of the night, it is now also the bhikṣu Nanda."
"If one speaks of those born of pure lineage on both sides of three generations, it is this very Bhikṣu Nanda.
If anyone says they have attained the six supernormal powers, it is also this very Bhikṣu Nanda."
"If one asks who has attained the concentration of the eight liberations, it is also the bhikṣu Nanda.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the community of bhikṣus, saying: "You bhikṣus!..."
"Among my śrāvaka disciples, the bhikṣu Nanda is the foremost in having his faculties well-subdued.
At that time, the bhikṣus asked the Buddha,
"So it is, World-Honored One!"
What roots of merit did that Elder Bhikṣu Nanda possess in the past?
By virtue of those roots of merit, he was born into the Śākya clan as one of great wealth and nobility, possessing abundant resources, and his body was upright, handsome, and pleasing.
Today the World-Honored One has further declared:
"Among my śrāvaka disciples, he who is foremost in having his faculties fully subdued is none other than the bhikṣu Nanda."
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed those bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!

I recall that ninety-one kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One, who resided in the realm of King Bandhumat."
There was a city there named Bandhumatī; at that time, the Buddha resided in that city, together with six thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats.

At that time, there was a king named Bandhumat who made offerings to that Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, honoring and revering them with such things as clothing, bedding, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, and requisites for dwellings, none of which were lacking.
"At that time, in the city of Bandhumatī, there was a son of a certain brahmin family; that youth constructed a warm bathhouse and invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to bathe as an act of offering."

When that youth of the Brahmin caste saw the bhikṣus emerging from the warm chamber— their bodies pure, exceedingly fragrant and clean, and free from any foul odor—his heart was filled with joy. Thrill and rapture pervaded his entire being, such that he could not contain himself. He made this vow:
"May I, in a future life, always obtain a body as pure, stainless, and free from any stench as this; may my body be like that of these bhikṣu-saṃghas, pure, fragrant, and odorless."

Furthermore, at a later time, when Vipaśyin Buddha—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—had entered parinirvāṇa, King Bandhumat took four kinds of precious substances for the relics of that World-Honored One to construct a stūpa, namely: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
At that time, the son of the brahmin clan, having overseen and managed the construction, built that stūpa.
Once the stūpa was completed, he made this aspiration in his heart:

"May I, in future lives, always encounter such a World-Honored One; may I understand and fully realize all the teachings he proclaims; may I never turn my back on those teachings, and in birth after birth, may I never enter the evil realms."

After that youth passed away, he was constantly reborn in the heavens or among humans; in his final birth, he was born into the family of a great and wealthy householder. His parents raised him, and as he grew up in due time, his intelligence and wisdom gradually developed until they were fully perfected.
“At that time, there was always a pratyekabuddha in the boy’s family who served as his preceptor and frequently visited the home.

That pratyekabuddha was lovely and handsome, fully endowed with the thirty marks of a great man; and the boy constantly provided for that pratyekabuddha with the four requisites throughout his entire life, never lacking anything.”
Those pratyekabuddhas remained for the full duration of their lifespans and subsequently entered parinirvāṇa.

At that time, the elder, seeing that the pratyekabuddha had passed away and entered parinirvāṇa, took his body and performed the cremation according to the Dharma. He collected the relics and erected a stūpa to make offerings to them, coating it first with clay and then applying a further layer of lime over the top.
For the sake of adornment, they hung various kinds of precious beads and necklaces, making this aspiration:

"May I, in the future, always encounter such Pratyekabuddha World-Honored Ones; may I understand and comprehend the Dharma taught by those World-Honored Ones upon hearing it, never forgetting it, and may I never fall into the evil realms throughout all my successive births."

I also pray that my own body shall be upright and pleasing, bringing joy to all who see it; that it shall possess the thirty marks of a great man, complete and without deficiency, no different from those of such Great Sages.

After that elder had relinquished his body and passed away, he was never again born into the evil realms; instead, he was constantly reborn among humans and devas, wandering for a long time until he was later reborn in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, there was a king named Kṛkī (translated in the Sui language as "Emaciated"), who had a son.
During that period, a Buddha appeared in the world, named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Nevertheless, during that Blessed One’s lifetime and after his parinirvāṇa, King Kṛkin constructed stūpas and temples made entirely of the seven precious substances—namely, gold, silver, crystal, beryl, red pearls, coral, and agate.

Outside that jeweled stupa, it was further covered with layers of coarse bricks; the stupa rose to a height of one yojana, with a longitudinal and lateral extent of half a yojana each, for which an inscription was made, naming it Daśapūrṇaka (translated in the Sui period as "Ten Marks").
"At that time, the seven sons born to King Kṛkī all addressed the king, saying:
'Excellent, Great King!
You should know that we wish to each offer a great parasol upon the stūpas containing the relics of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, in order to cover those stūpas.'"
"Excellent, Great King!
We pray that you will grant us your hearing and permission.
The king spoke to them, saying:
"Follow your inclinations!
I now grant you permission to build.

At that time, each of those seven princes took one jewel and fashioned a parasol for it to cover the top of the stupa; some fashioned parasols of gold, some of silver, and others even of agate and so forth.
Among those seven sons, the second prince fashioned a golden parasol to cover the top of the stupa and made this vow in his heart:

"May I, in future lives, always encounter such a Venerable Pratyekabuddha; may I understand and realize the Dharma he preaches, never forgetting it; may I never fall into the evil realms throughout all my births and lifetimes; and in every place where I am born, may I obtain a body like this golden color."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "O bhikṣus!

If there are any among you who harbor doubts regarding that son of a brāhmaṇa in the city of Bandhumatī, who made offerings to that Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, bathing them in a heated chamber and making this aspiration in his heart:..."
"May I, in a future life, obtain a body as pure, stainless, fragrant, and clean as this assembly of bhikṣus.
Who was that youth who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin, constructed a stūpa and made offerings to it?
"You bhikṣus! Do not entertain other views; this is none other than the bhikṣu Nanda.
"You bhikṣus! [he continued].

If you have any doubt regarding that elder, who for his entire life made offerings to that Pratyekabuddha, and after his passing, further raised a stupa for his relics, making offerings by plastering and repairing it, adorning it with lime and various ornaments, and offering necklaces to that stupa while making this aspiration in his heart:

‘May I, in a future life, be as handsome and pleasing as this Pratyekabuddha, such that those who behold me never tire of looking, and may my body be endowed with the thirty marks of a great man, complete and without deficiency, just like this seer.’
"Who indeed was he?
You bhikṣus, do not entertain any other view; it was this very bhikṣu Nanda.
"You bhikṣus! [he continued.]

If you have any doubt regarding that second son of King Kṛkī of the city of Vārāṇasī, who fashioned a golden parasol to cover the stūpa for the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa—do not entertain any other view; this was none other than the bhikṣu Nanda.

"However, in the past, when Vipaśyin Buddha and his community of monks were present, this Nanda built a warm bathhouse for them and provided them with ritual bathing according to the Dharma. Because of that, he made this vow:
'May I, in a future life, obtain a body as pure, fragrant, and stainless as this, just like this monk who is pure and stainless.'"

Furthermore, he made offerings to the Honored Pratyekabuddhas; after those Honored Ones had passed into parinirvāṇa, he erected stūpas for their śarīras, coating them with clay and adorning them with lime, and further embellishing them with necklaces. With his heart, he made this vow:
"In a future life, may I be as handsome and as pleasing as this, possessing the thirty marks of a great man in their fullness without deficiency, just like these sages."

Furthermore, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, he constructed a stūpa for his relics, making a canopy of pure gold to cover its summit, and made this aspiration in his heart:
"May my body be eternally golden in color in every place where I am born in future lives."

"By virtue of those karmic conditions, he has now attained such a delightful, upright, and beautiful golden-hued body that one never tires of beholding it; furthermore, he is fully endowed with the thirty marks of a great man, all complete and without any deficiency."
"At that time, he further gave rise to this aspiration:
'May I, in future lives, not be born into the evil realms.
By virtue of that karmic retribution, he was never born within the evil realms, but always attained birth among the devas and humans."

Furthermore, at that time, when the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin was constructing a stūpa, he supervised and managed the work; thereafter, he further provided the Pratyekabuddhas with the four requisites for as long as he lived.
By the power of the causes and conditions of that karmic retribution, I have now been born into the family of the Śākyas.
Furthermore, at that time, I made this vow:

"May I, in future lives, always encounter such a World-Honored One, or one even more sublime than him; and having heard the Dharma teachings of that World-Honored One, may I quickly attain realization and understanding."

"By the power of the causal conditions of that karmic retribution, he has now encountered me; right here in my presence, he has received the going-forth and the full ordination. I further grant him a prediction of enlightenment and declare to the bhikṣus:
'If you wish to know who among my śrāvaka disciples is foremost in the mastery of the sense faculties, it is the bhikṣu Nanda.'"

“O bhikṣus! You must know that the bhikṣu Nanda cultivated such roots of goodness in the past; by virtue of those roots of goodness, he has now been born into a family of the Śākya clan, his body is golden in color, and he is endowed with the thirty marks of a great man. Having now gone forth and received full ordination, he has attained the fruit of arhatship and further received this prophecy, saying:
‘If you wish to know who among my śrāvaka disciples is foremost in the subduing of the sense faculties, it is the bhikṣu Nanda.’”

**Chapter 58: The Causes and Conditions of Bhadrika and Others** *The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Chapter Fifty-Eight (Part One): The Causes and Conditions of Bhadrika and Others. At that time, the Śākya youth Devadatta, seeing the five hundred Śākya youths and others leave their homes to enter the homeless life, conceived this thought:
"I too should now leave my home and enter the homeless life under the World-Honored One."
Having formed this thought, he went before his parents and spoke to them thus:
"Excellent, my parents!
I have now resolved to leave the home life for the sake of the Buddha; I pray that you will grant me your permission."
Having spoken these words, the parents then said to the Śākya youth Devadatta:
"We have now reflected thus:
'We must rely upon Devadatta, and Devadatta, in turn, must rely upon us.'"
"Since it is so, you may do as you please.

At that time, the youth Devadatta, wearing exquisite and priceless garments and riding a most excellent elephant, was about to depart from the city of Kapilavastu. As he reached the cheek of a city gate, his clothes were caught by a hook and torn to pieces.

At that time, a great Brahmin skilled in interpreting signs was standing nearby and witnessed this; having seen it, he predicted that whatever the boy intended to accomplish would certainly not succeed.
At that time, the youth Devadatta, having departed from the city, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray, World-Honored One!
"Release me so that I may go forth [into the homeless life].

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing Devadatta’s past and present deeds with right mindfulness, understood his mental conduct; having observed him, he addressed Devadatta, saying: "Devadatta!"

"You should now be careful not to leave home and go forth as a renunciant; rather, you should return home and practice the Way while living as a householder. Take your wealth and money to use for giving and to perform various meritorious deeds; there is no need for you to go forth within my Dharma."
At that time, after the youth Devadatta had been rebuked by the Buddha, he went to the elder Śāriputra and addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
"Let me go forth [into the homeless life].
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra addressed Devadatta, saying: "Devadatta!"
"Have you not already gone to the Buddha's presence before?
Devadatta replied, "Venerable One,
I have indeed already gone to the Buddha's presence."
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra said:
"Devadatta! What did the World-Honored One say to you?"
Devadatta said to Śāriputra:
"It is so, Noble One! The World-Honored One spoke thus to me:"
"Do not abandon your home to go forth into homelessness; rather, you should remain at home, practice giving, and perform various meritorious deeds.
If you were to go forth within my Dharma, it would be of no benefit to you."
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has now refused to allow him to go forth into the Dharma; if I were now to let him go forth, that would be unwholesome on my part."
Having reflected thus, he then addressed Devadatta, saying: "Devadatta!
Just as the World-Honored One has instructed, you must certainly perform this matter accordingly."

At that time, the youth Devadatta, having been sent away by Śāriputra, went again to the elder Maudgalyāyana. Upon arrival, he prostrated himself at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed him, saying:
"O Mahāmaudgalyāyana!"
"May the Noble One, I pray,
grant me the going forth!
At that time, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana then spoke again to Devadatta, saying these words:
“Devadatta! Have you ever previously gone to the Buddha’s side?
Devadatta replied to the Noble One:
"I have already gone to the Buddha's presence.
Thereupon, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately addressed Devadatta, saying:
"The World-Honored One has spoken to you; what is the purpose of your intent?"
Devadatta replied to him again, saying:
"The World-Honored One said to me:

'You must not leave your home and go forth into homelessness here; rather, you should practice the Way while remaining at home in accordance with the Dharma, making various meritorious deeds through the giving of wealth. There is no need for you to go forth within my teaching; if you do go forth, it will be of no benefit to you.'"
At that time, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana likewise replied to Devadatta, saying:
"As the World-Honored One has instructed!"
"You must certainly perform such a deed.
At that time, having been refused ordination by Maudgalyāyana, Devadatta went to the place of the Elder Mahākāśyapa; the details are as previously described, and he subsequently went to Kātyāyana.
Next, he went to the presence of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa; then he went to the presence of the Elder Nadī-Kāśyapa;
then he went to the presence of the Elder Gayākāśyapa, as well as to the presence of Mahākauṣṭhila and Mahāsubhadra, but was refused by them all.
Having been refused permission, he then approached the elder Upālipantaka, prostrated at Upālipantaka’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the young Śākya Devadatta again requested ordination from the Elder Upāliputra.
However, the Elder Upāliputra questioned him, saying: "Devadatta!..."
"You should go first to where the Buddha is.
Devadatta replied, "Noble One!"
"I arrived at the presence of the Buddha the other day.
At that time, the Elder Upāliputra spoke these words:
"When you went to the presence of the Buddha, what did he say to you?"
Devadatta spoke thus: "The World-Honored One said to me:

'You must not leave the household life to become a renunciant here; rather, you should practice the Way according to the Dharma while remaining at home, giving wealth in alms and performing various meritorious deeds. There is no need for you to renounce the world within my teaching; if you do so, it will be of no benefit to you.'"

at that time, the Elder Upāliputra thought to himself:

Having reflected thus, he immediately addressed Devadatta, saying:

Devadatta proceeded in this manner, going from place to place to where the venerable elder bhikṣus were; and those venerable elder bhikṣus all spoke to Devadatta, saying:
"Since the World-Honored One has spoken these words, you must certainly perform such an act."
At that time, having been refused entry everywhere Devadatta went, he returned riding his white elephant toward the city of Kapilavastu and back to his own home.
At that time, Ānanda, the Śākya youth, seeing that the five hundred Śākya youths and others had all gone forth into homelessness, thought to himself:
"On this very day, I too must leave my home and go before the Buddha to seek ordination."
Having reflected thus, he went before his parents and said to them:
"I now desire to leave the home life and go to the Buddha to become a renunciant; I only pray that you will grant me permission to do so."
At that time, Ānanda’s mother had originally harbored no pure mind toward the Buddha. Why was this?

When the World-Honored One was still a bodhisattva living at home, his mother saw the Bodhisattva’s towering merit and magnificent, radiant power; she consequently conceived a defiled mind toward him and uttered various heterodox and perverse words.

At that time, because the Bodhisattva considered her merely as his maternal aunt, he remained silent and gave no answer to these words; for this reason, she harbored no pure mind toward the Bodhisattva.
Because he lacked a pure heart, he never ceased his efforts to persuade his son Ānanda to leave the home life and become a renunciant.
At that time, Devadatta heard others say that Ānanda intended to leave the home life and become a renunciant, yet his parents would not permit him to do so.
Devadatta went to where Ānanda was and asked him, "Ānanda,
if you truly desire to leave the household life and go forth, have your parents ever refused to grant you permission?"
Ānanda replied,
“Devadatta! It is exactly as you have said.”
"I do not know what deed I must now perform to cause my parents to permit me to leave the home life and become a bhikṣu, receiving the full ordination.
At that time, the Śākya son Devadatta said to Ānanda:
"If you later learn that your parents have permitted you to abandon the home life and go forth, you must certainly let me know; I shall then go forth together with you at the same time."
Ānanda then replied to Devadatta, saying:
"I do not contradict what you have said.
At that time, Ānanda had this thought:
Thinking, "My parents will certainly not allow me to leave home and go forth into the homeless life," he took five hundred *paliṣaṃpaṇas* from his house and went secretly to the kingdom of Videha.
Now, in that village there was an elder who had been a close friend of the king during his youth; he entrusted these five hundred *paliṣpaṇas* to him and said:
"I now entrust this money to you as my provision for food. Whenever I come here needing food, you must certainly purchase it for me with this money."
"When you arrive, you need not ask me where I have come from; once I have reached this place, you will surely know that I have come for the sake of food.
Having spoken these words, he went to a secluded forest hermitage (*āraṇya*) and undertook the vow of silence. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he remained silent and spoke no word.

When it was time to eat, he would go silently to the house where he had left his money, sit quietly, and receive food and drink in silence; having finished eating, he would return and depart again in silence.
At that time, the people living in that village frequently saw the Śākya youth Ānanda walking, standing, coming, going, sitting, or lying down in silence; having seen him, they asked:
"Who is this venerable one?"
At that time, Ānanda did not speak a word in reply to those people, but returned as before, departing in silence.
Then those people said to one another,
"This seer must have come from the kingdom of Videha."
Having spoken these words, they established a name for him, calling him the Seer of the Videha Kingdom.

At that time, Ānanda’s parents heard people say this: that Ānanda had fled from there and gone to the cities and villages of the Videha Kingdom, where he had undertaken the vow of silence, practiced the conduct of a seer, and attained the state of a seer.
Having heard this, he immediately dispatched a messenger who went to him and said: "Son! Son!
If you are determined not to remain at home, simply come here and go forth into homelessness in the presence of my Śākya youth."
At that time, Ānanda immediately returned and went to speak to Devadatta of the Śākya clan, saying these words: "Devadatta!..."
"You should know now!
My parents have already granted me permission to go forth into homelessness.
Devadatta then asked Ānanda:
"Under whom do you now intend to go forth?
Ānanda replied,
"I now intend to go forth under the Buddha."
Devadatta spoke again:
"In the past, I went before the Buddha and requested to leave the household life, but the Buddha did not grant me permission to do so.
Ānanda spoke again:
"You should go to the noble Śāriputra and request ordination.
Devadatta spoke again, saying:
"That man will not grant me ordination either."
In this manner, it continued even unto Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākātyāyana, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Upasena, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahācunda, and Upāliputra.
"There are such great virtuous elders and monks who all refuse to permit my ordination.
Ānanda asked Devadatta again, saying these words: "Devadatta!"
"According to your intention, where do you wish to go?
Devadatta replied, "Ānanda!"
"The places I go shall not be known to others.
Ānanda spoke again:
"I, too, shall follow Devadatta’s intention in this regard."
At that time, there were many young Śākya youths of great power and influence, each family sending one son to renounce the world under the Buddha.

At that moment, in the city of Kapilavastu, there were two brothers; the younger was named Maṇiruta (formerly transcribed as Aniruddha), and the elder was named Mahānāma. Maṇiruta... [was the younger brother].

Having long planted roots of goodness and cultivated the treasury of liberation, they face toward nirvāṇa and turn their backs on afflictions; they do not wish to be born within any state of existence, but desire to attain the exhaustion of outflows while remaining in this world within the triple realm.
Because he had already accumulated a great mass of merit, he was born into that family of the Śākya clan.

From the time of his birth, the family’s livelihood gradually increased; that is to say, they possessed in abundance money, various grains such as rice and wheat, pearls, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and various jade ornaments, as well as gold and silver, and both two-legged and four-legged creatures.

Furthermore, five hundred hidden treasures beneath the earth spontaneously manifested; while he was reclining on his bed, resting and sleeping, the devas brought five hundred kinds of priceless jewels and placed them upon the bed.
The child’s kinsmen, witnessing such rare and extraordinary events, deliberated among themselves, saying:
"While this boy was asleep, the devas brought priceless jewels and covered him with them; therefore, we must give him the name Maṇiruta."

That boy was lovely and handsome, such that onlookers never grew weary of beholding him; his body was yellowish-white like the color of gold, his head was shaped like a parasol, his nose was high and full like a parrot’s beak, and his two arms were smooth and long, hanging down past his knees.
His body was proportionate in length and breadth, with equal proportions from top to bottom; his sense faculties were complete, lacking nothing.
Furthermore, his parents appointed four types of nurses to attend to him: namely, one to carry him, one to bathe him, one to feed him milk, and one to play with him.
The four nurses nurtured and attended to him, and as he gradually grew up, his wisdom was perfected.

Seeing him now able to walk and run about from east to west, and having reached the age of being fit for work, they instructed him in various domestic arts and crafts, namely: writing, arithmetic, and seal-making; music, song, and dance; jesting, laughter, and banter; the art of the jester and graceful, seductive movements; the crafting of *maṇi* jewels; dyeing and tailoring garments; compounding various perfumes; painting flowers, leaves, and various images; and games such as *weiqi*, *liubo*, and *chupu*, as well as the composition of literary works.

There were elephant acrobats, horse acrobats, and chariot acrobats; skills in archery; postures and deportment; feats of strength and displays of prowess; arts such as massage; and contests of leaping over beams and racing.

He trained elephants and threw stones; he cultivated gardens and orchards; he knew how to enter and exit with grace; he understood omens of good and ill fortune; he moved with subtle and secret precision; he could break through enemy ranks; he clenched his own fist so that others could not pry it open; when standing upright upon the ground, no one could push him over.
Shaving the head and combing the hair, wielding a blade to hack and chop, and drilling through materials;

splitting and cleaving wood and stone; hitting targets with unerring precision, even piercing a person’s limbs or joints down to a single hair; releasing arrows by following their sound; drawing the bowstring and pulling the bow.

Thus, he was thoroughly proficient and fully accomplished in all these arts; there was nothing he did not understand. His mental intelligence was profound and far-reaching, his spirit was swift, his deliberations were skillful, and he was shrewd and brilliant.

Then, at one time, that boy followed his father to supervise the agricultural work and the household provisions. Having arrived there, he became parched with thirst; because of his thirst, he went to the edge of a body of water and cupped his hands to drink, whereupon the water transformed into the exquisite flavor of celestial nectar (*divyā sudhā*).
At that time, his father forbade him from drinking and cried out:
"My son, my son! Do not drink this water!
I fear it may cause your body to become unwell."
At that time, the youth Maṇicūḍa, having tasted this water, said to his father:
"Venerable One!
This water is exceedingly sweet and delicious."
His father did not believe him.
Then the boy cupped water in his hands and offered it to his father, saying:
"Father, if you do not believe me, please taste this water."
The father then tasted this water and replied to his son,
"Although I was born within the royal palace, I have never before obtained such wondrously sweet and delicious water."
Having spoken these words, his heart was filled with joy at such an unprecedented occurrence, and he said aloud:
"How rare is my son! He possesses great merit;
from the moment of his birth, the food and drink he has prepared have been complete in color, fragrance, and flavor, surpassing those of others by twice as much."
At that time, when his elder brother Mahānāma saw or tasted that food and drink, he immediately conceived a spirit of envy and said aloud:
"Why is it that such fragrant and pure delicacies are given only to my younger brother and not to me?"
At that time, his mother, understanding these words, said to him:
"My son, my son!
Do you not know?"
"From the outset, whatever food and drink has been prepared by this Maṇilūta has always been ten times superior to that provided by others.
Mahānāma still did not believe him.
Furthermore, on one occasion, while Maṇicūḍa was sporting in a pleasure grove, he sent a messenger from within that garden to his mother to request food.
He instructed the messenger, saying:
"Go to my mother’s place and have her send some food here."
Then his mother placed the food on a tray, covered it with a cloth, first showed it to her eldest son Mahānāma, and subsequently sent a messenger to deliver that food to where Maṇibhadra was.
Maṇibhadra also looked at this food; its color and fragrance were twice as excellent as before, and it filled every vessel to the brim.
Even so, Mahānāman still did not believe it, and said aloud:
"Though I know what good or bad is brought from within the house, who knows that it was not prepared and sent from the houses of our kinsmen?"
Again, at another time, Maṇicūḍa was once more in the park, watching and enjoying himself, when he sent a messenger to inform his mother, saying:
"I pray you, send a messenger to bring food here."
At that time, his mother took various empty vessels, placed them upon a tray, covered them with a cloth, first showed them to her eldest son Mahānāma, and only then sent him on his way.
He further addressed him, saying, "You should observe for yourself and discern whether this is true or false.

Having heard these words, Mahānāma followed the vessel and went to the side of Maṇibhadra. Upon arriving, he saw that all kinds of food were there, replete with exquisite colors, fragrances, and flavors.
At that time, the Śākya son Mahānāma, having witnessed these events, felt joy arise in his heart and said:
"How rare! This has never been seen before; my younger brother possesses such great merit and virtue."
As Maṇicūḍa gradually grew up and reached the prime of his youth, his parents built for him three halls:
one intended for sitting during the winter, one for autumn and spring, and one for sitting during the summer.
Those intending to sit in meditation during winter should prepare only for warmth;
those intending to sit in summer should prepare only for coolness;
and those intending to sit in spring or autumn should prepare only for temperate comfort.
In the hall where he dwells, no other men are present; it is intended for him alone to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses, possessing them in full abundance and residing there at his own will.
At that time, the youth Mahānāma had this thought:
"Among the youths of the Śākya clan, those of great influence have each sent one member from their respective families to renounce the household life."
"In my household now there is no one who has gone forth; I alone ought to renounce the home and go forth.
If I do not do so, I must send my younger brother Maṇibhadra to go forth."
Having had this thought, Mahānāma immediately went to the side of the Śākya youth Maṇicūḍa, and upon arriving, he said to him: "Maṇicūḍa!"

"Among us Śākyas who possess power, each family has sent one person forth from home. Within our own household, there is no one who has gone forth. Now I reflect: either you shall go forth, or I shall go forth."
At that time, the Śākya Māṇicūḍa addressed his elder brother, the Śākya youth Mahānāma, saying: "Mahānāma!
Since you have gone forth yourself, I cannot go."
Mahānāma spoke again to him, saying: "Maṇicūḍa!
If it is so, I now entrust to you the affairs of my household.

As for the way of life, one first plows the land, then harrows it; next, one removes the tiles, stones, stumps, and thorns, and only then sows the seeds. Once the seeds have been sown, if there is no rain from heaven, one irrigates at the proper time, weeds according to the rules, and then waits for the harvest to ripen, reaping and processing it, and storing it in granaries and cellars."
Having done this, when the following year arrives, they proceed once again in the same manner, constructing them in succession year after year without ceasing.
At that time, the youth Maṇicūḍa addressed his elder brother, the Śākya youth Mahānāma, saying:
"If it is so, then our family's work will never come to an end, nor will there ever be a time when it is exhausted."
"Since such work must be done without end, when shall we ever be able to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses within these three halls?
Then, the youth Mahānāma spoke again to his younger brother Maṇilūta, saying: "Maṇilūta!"
The affairs of one's livelihood are, by their very nature, inexhaustible, and there is no end to them.
Our parents were likewise stingy regarding the enterprises established by their ancestors; they too passed away without ever seeing those tasks reach completion.
At that time, the youth Maṇilūta again spoke to his elder brother Mahānāma, saying:

"If one knows that karmic actions cannot be exhausted and does not know when they will end, my parents likewise were stingy regarding the ancestral karma of our lineage; not knowing when it would end, they met their deaths."
"This is indeed not false; as I now reflect, Mahānāma ought to remain at home to manage the household affairs, while I wish to leave the home life to renounce the world and practice the Way."
At that time, the youth Maṇicūḍa went before his parents and said to them:
"Father and Mother!
I wish to leave the household life and seek ordination in the presence of the Tathāgata; I pray that you will grant me permission to go forth in the presence of the Tathāgata."
At that time, the parents said to the young boy Maṇicūḍa, "You should know that we have only two sons;
we cherish both of you with great affection, never letting you leave our hearts. If we do not see you for even a moment, our minds are filled with sorrow and distress."
Even if I were to die, I would still hope not to be separated from you; how much more so while I am alive today—how could I possibly grant you permission to go forth into homelessness?
Thus he requested a second time, and even a third time, saying:
"I wish to leave the household life for homelessness within the Dharma of the Tathāgata; I pray that you, my parents, will grant me your permission."

"In the past, when the Bodhisattva had gone forth from his home and was practicing the holy life, King Śuddhodana, driven by grief and anxiety on account of the Bodhisattva, gathered the kinsmen and retinue of the Śākya clan and addressed them, saying: 'O kinsmen!'"

"You must know this: since my son Siddhārtha has already left the household life, I no longer wish to occupy the royal throne, nor do I wish to wear this celestial crown. Among you, who is able to assume the kingship? To him I shall entrust the realm and immediately confer the consecration and bestow the celestial crown."
At that time, there was among the assembly a young Śākya named Bhaṭṭikā, whose mother’s name was Kṛṣṇagautamī; he addressed the king, saying:
“I am able to accept this royal throne and the crown.”

At that time, King Śuddhodana and all the Śākya clansmen, together with their entire retinue, immediately entrusted the royal throne and the celestial crown to the Śākya youth Bhaṭṭikarika and consecrated him.
From that time forward, the Śākya youth Bāhrika became the King of the Śākyas; his various kinsmen and attendants were known as King Bāhrika of the Śākyas.
However, after that Śākya king, Bandhula (Pāṭalika), had ascended the throne and ruled according to the Dharma for twelve years,
the Śākya clansmen and their kinsmen made a solemn vow:

"Whoever among us attains the status of king by wearing the celestial crown upon his head, that person shall prepare for all the Śākya clansmen and kinsmen a banquet of food and drink consisting of a hundred flavors."

That king, in his youth, had been a companion to that Śākya Maṇicūḍa since they were children, playing together in the dust; when he prepared the assembly, he issued a verbal command to summon Maṇicūḍa, speaking these words: "Maṇicūḍa!"
"You assist me; first you must provide for all my kinsmen, and only after that shall I eat together with you.
Maṇilūta addressed King Bimbisāra of the Śākya clan, saying:
"As Your Majesty now commands, I dare not disobey."
Then those two, having together provided for all the Śākya kinsmen, ate their meal; after they had finished eating, they left Mahānāma Manibhadra to stay overnight in the palace.
At that time, King Prasenajit of the Śākyas, having passed that night, when the sky was about to dawn, personally asked Maṇicūḍa, saying:
"Maṇicūḍa, have you slept peacefully?"
Maṇilūta replied to the king, saying,
"While sleeping at night, I could not find peace.
The king asked again:
"Why is this so? Maṇiluta replied to the king once more:
"Last night my belly pained me, and I suffered from chills and fever."
The king asked again,
“Why is that so? Maṇicūḍa replied to the king once more:
"The food and drink there were of unwholesome flavor; for this reason, at that time, I suffered from abdominal pain.
When the mat upon which he lay was being woven, the weaver suffered from chills and fever; for this reason, I too contracted the disease of chills and fever."
Then King Prasenajit of the Śākyas summoned the food preparer and asked him:
"When you prepared the food of a hundred flavors, did any of those various tastes increase or decrease?"
"Is it for the sake of moderation?
The person who had prepared the food replied to the king,
saying, "It is so, Great King!"
The flavor was slightly excessive; the flavor was as if deficient.

At that time, I was preoccupied with my tasks and could not proceed as I wished; though I inspected every detail, my assistants did not understand how to apply their minds and mixed everything together indiscriminately.
At that time, King Prasenajit of the Śākyas again summoned the weaver and asked him:
"When you were weaving the bedding for me, why was it not done with such care?"
The weaver replied, “It is so, Great King!

While I was weaving, I was afflicted by a feverish illness. Furthermore, Your Majesty sent a messenger to urge me on; at that time, my fever had not yet subsided, yet fearing Your Majesty’s wrath, I wove in haste and delivered the cloth. For this reason, my weaving did not reach the standard of excellence.”
At that time, King Prasenajit of the Śākyas gave rise to a sense of wonder and a sense of the unprecedented, thinking:
"Such a matter as this is inconceivable."
He further thought:
"How rare, how rare! Māṇilūta!"
"Indeed, there is such supreme and wondrous wisdom.
At that time, King Śuddhodana of the Śākyas addressed the Śākya youth Maṇicūḍa, saying these words: "Maṇicūḍa!"
"From this day forward, regarding whatever you may require from me, do not come here yourself; simply send a messenger, and I shall not fail you."
At that time, the mother of the Śākya youth Maṇilūta thought to herself:

"This Śākya king is a dear childhood companion of my son, playing in the dust together since our youth; he is a like-minded and virtuous friend, so it is certain that this man will not renounce the world."
Having had this thought, he immediately called his son Maṇilūta and spoke these words: "Maṇilūta!
If that Śākya king Bimbisāra renounces the household life to become a monk, you should at that time likewise renounce the household life."
At that time, having heard these words, the young Śākya Maṇicūḍa went to where the Śākya king Bimbisāra was.

At that moment, King Bimbisāra had come out from his palace and was seated, watching a *nāṭaka*—translated in the Sui language as a musical performance for auspicious occasions—a festive assembly of joy and pleasure.
At that time, the Śākya youth Maṇicūḍa thought to himself:
"If I were now to enter the assembly of King Bandhumant of the Śākyas, I would surely obstruct others from watching the festivities and amusements."
Having formed this thought, he sat down at the threshold and waited for the Nāṭaka-Prītikara assembly to conclude before entering.

At that time, while King Śakra Vaidiśaka was watching the assembly in full enjoyment, there was a woman among them with a melodious voice who played the vīṇā. While she was playing, one string broke; the woman immediately repaired it, yet no one in the Nāṭaka-Prītikara assembly noticed it, except for King Śakra Vaidiśaka alone.
Maṇicūḍa, who was at the side of the gate, also knew of this matter.

At that time, seeing that the assembly of Nandika and Sunanda was about to conclude, the Śākya youth Maṇicūḍa went to where the Śākya king Bimbisāra was; having arrived, he placed his arms around the king’s neck, and then withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, King Śuddhodana addressed the Śākya youth Maṇicūḍa, saying: "Maṇicūḍa!
Did I not previously tell you that if you have any need, you should not come in person, but simply send a messenger to request it? I shall not fail you."
"How can you still dare to come here today?
Maṇilūta replied to the king, saying, "Bāhrika!"
"This matter is such that no one can be sent to accomplish it.
At that time, the King of the Śākyas again addressed the Śākya youth Maṇicūḍa, saying: "Maṇicūḍa!"
Regarding what was called "accomplishment," what is the nature of this matter?
Should it be achieved by you,
or should it be achieved by me?
Maṇicūḍa replied to the king once more:
"This matter is due to me, but it also concerns you.
Bimbisāra then spoke these words:
“If there is anything concerning me, you should attend to it immediately.
Maṇiluta then addressed the king again, saying:
“Great King!
"You should know that my intention is to renounce the household life and go forth; such a matter as this will certainly concern you.
Bodhika replied to the Śākya youth Maṇicūḍa, saying: "Maṇicūḍa!..."
If you now wish to leave the home life and become a renunciant, and if it necessarily involves me, I shall release you.
Do not harbor any doubt or hesitation toward me; if you wish to go forth, do so according to your own inclination.
At that time, the Śākya youth Maṇilūta addressed the Śākya king Bimbisāra, saying:
"You must now go forth with me into the homeless life."
Why is this? My parents previously said to me: "Maṇilūta!..."
"If that Śākyan king Bandhula renounces his home to go forth into homelessness, you too shall follow him and go forth.
Then the Śākyan youth Maṇicūḍa again saw the Śākyan king Bandhula in the great assembly making this truthful declaration: "Maṇicūḍa!"
"If you now wish to leave the household life and become a renunciant, and since this concerns me, I shall not oppose you; you may go as you please.
At that time, all the Śākyas likewise spoke the truth; therefore, they requested the King to renounce the world together with them.
At that time, the Śākya king Bimbisāra addressed the Śākya youth Maṇicūḍa, saying:
"If this must indeed be so, stay for seven years; once my household affairs are completed, after they are finished, I shall go forth from home with you."
At that time, the Śākya youth Maṇicūḍa again addressed the Śākya king Bimbisāra, saying these words: "Bimbisāra!
Do not speak such words.
I cannot wait until seven years have passed. Why is this so?
"Bhadrika! Who knows that during this long period of seven years, there might have been some obstacle to our renunciation?
Bhadrika then spoke again to the Śākya youth Maṇilūda, saying these words:
“Maṇilūta! Wait for me for six years while I attend to my household affairs; thereafter, we shall together leave the home life and go forth.”
Maṇilūta spoke again to the king, saying:
"Bhadrika! You must not speak such words now."
I, too, cannot wait for six years. Why is this?
Six years is a long time; who knows if we might encounter some obstacle to our renunciation in the interim?
Bhadrika spoke again to the young Śākya Maṇicūḍa, saying: "Maṇicūḍa!
If it must indeed be so, then wait and listen while I prepare my household affairs within five years."
Thus it continued for four years, three years, and two years, yet Maṇibhadra refused them all.
Then the king spoke again:
"If this is truly so, wait but one year while I settle my household affairs; only then shall I go forth with you."
Maṇiluta again addressed the king, saying: "Bhadrika!
I cannot wait even for a year."
"Why is this? A single year is a long time; who knows if some obstacle might befall you or me?
At that time, King Śuddhodana of the Śākyas again addressed the Śākya youth Mahānāman, speaking these words:
“Maṇicūḍa! If it must be so, then wait while I attend to my household affairs for six months. When this was said, Maṇicūḍa refused.
[The same was offered] for three months, two months, and one month; Maṇicūḍa refused them all.
At that time, King Bandhula of the Śākyas again addressed the Śākya youth Maṇicūḍa, saying: "Maṇicūḍa!
If this is indeed so, wait for me for seven days and seven nights while I attend to my household affairs; thereafter, we shall together leave the home-life and go forth."
Maṇicūḍa then addressed King Prasenajit of the Śākyas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Prasenajit!"
"Do as you wish; I shall wait for you until the end of seven days and seven nights.

At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the village of Anomiya. For those seven days and seven nights, the king attended to his domestic affairs, adorning himself with necklaces and ornaments, and went into the park to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses. It was just as when a man, wishing to go to another's house for a great banquet, bathes his hair and body, adorns himself with necklaces and fine clothing, and only then proceeds to the other's home; likewise, it was so with the Śākya king Bimbisāra, who wished to go into the park to roam and enjoy himself.

At that time, there was another Śākya youth named Bāhula (translated in the Sui language as Duomei), another Śākya youth named Kuṃbhīra, another youth named Nandika, another Śākya youth named Ānanda, and a Śākya youth named Devadatta; like those before them, they all adorned their bodies in the same manner as described above.

Those youths, having dressed themselves together in various garments and ornaments, and having taken along a skilled barber, set out from the city of Kapilavastu with their fourfold army and proceeded toward the village of Anomiya.

At that time, King Bimbisāra of the Śākya clan possessed an object valued at three hundred taels of gold: one hundred taels of gold was for the price of the garment, one hundred taels of gold for the necklace, and one hundred taels of gold for the adornment of the saddled horse.
The youth Maṇilūta was likewise so.

Among the Śākya youths—Vāyuva, Kuṃbhīra, Nandika, Ānanda, and Devadatta—and others such as these, each also possessed precious objects worth three hundred taels of gold, even enough to serve as the cost for the adornment of saddles and horses.
The value of the precious items belonging to those youths amounted to two thousand one hundred taels of gold.

At that time, those Śākya youths departed from the city of Kapilavastu; each dismounted from his horse, removed the necklaces and ornaments from their bodies, and offered them all to the barber who was shaving their hair, saying to him individually:

"These necklaces and ornaments are given to you as the foundation for your livelihood. You should accept and use them as the basis for your means of subsistence and profession; do not seek anything else."
Having entrusted the necklace, he proceeded toward the village of Anomiya.
At that time, the barber thought to himself:
"These Śākyas are fierce and powerful; they will say that I have led their youths away to flee here and there. For this reason, I fear they will come to persecute me."
"Since those youths have already spat out these things, how could I eat them?
I must not now accept these various jewels.

If they, being so exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, possessing such great power and influence, yet renounced immeasurable resources, wealth, and even the affairs of kingship to leave home and go forth as monastics—how much more so should I now follow their example?"
Having thought this, the barber took those necklaces and treasures and hung them upon a tree branch, thinking:
"Should anyone see these, let them take whatever they wish; I shall never be considered a thief."
Having thought this to himself, he went to where the Śākya youths were.
When those Śākya youths saw the barber approaching from afar, they said to him:
"Why have you not returned home today?"
Then the barber replied to the Śākya youths, saying: "O noble sons!
I have now privately formed this thought: "
"The Śākyas are powerful, possessing great majesty and mighty strength; yet you say, 'I am leading these Śākya youths away, fleeing east and west.'"
"For this reason, it would surely cause my body and life to be terrified and oppressed. "O youth!
Since you have already spat out this thing, how could I now possibly wish to eat it?"
"As I am now, I shall not accept these things. Why is this?
Even though the Śākyas are powerful and possess great might, they have nonetheless gone forth from home; how much more so should I now go forth?"
"For this reason, I shall not return home.
When the young Śākyas heard these words, they said to him, "It was well of you to think thus;
having formed such a resolve, you do not return to your home."
Why is this? As you have said, our Śākya clan is majestic and powerful; they will surely say:
"He has undoubtedly fled with my child."
"Since these words have been spoken, he will certainly come to threaten your life.

At that time, the Śākya youths and their peers, together with the barber, went to where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, they prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Now we pray that you grant us permission to leave our homes and go forth into homelessness, and that we may receive full ordination.
They further addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
If you wish to go forth with us, you must first deliver this barber; he should be ordained before you. Why is this?
This barber has served us diligently through the long night of our practice without ever failing us; therefore, we shall grant him the going forth and the full ordination first.

Since he has already gone forth [into homelessness], and will only later allow us to go forth and receive full ordination, we must first pay homage to this hair-cutter, rising to meet him, joining our palms in reverence, and manifesting respect toward him.
Why is this? We Śākyas are arrogant and haughty;
now, because of this man, we Śākyas have turned our minds away from and abandoned our hearts of arrogance.

At that time, the World-Honored One first ordained the barber, granting him full ordination; thereafter, he successively granted the Śākya king Bhadrika the going forth and full ordination, followed by each of the others in turn, who likewise received the going forth and full ordination.

At that time, Ānanda and Devadatta, the two of them still not having been permitted to leave the household life, returned from the presence of the World-Honored One to the foot of the Snowy Mountains.

At that time, at the foot of that mountain, there was an elder of the Vāseṭṭha clan named Saṃgha. This man had practiced the holy life, already abiding in the third fruit and having accomplished the four dhyānas; he constantly dwelt there, relying upon that Himavat mountain.
At that time, the Vātsīputrīya Saṃgha, seeing Ānanda and the other two approaching, went out to greet them and comforted them, saying:
"O Śākya youths!"
"For what reason have you come here?
At that time, the two men replied to him, saying,
"We have now come here because we desire to leave the household life and become renunciants."
“Excellent, Noble One!
We pray that you will deliver us and enable us to go forth into homelessness.

At that time, the Saṃgha of Vātsīputra did not examine the conduct of the youth Devadatta, nor did they test his wisdom; they immediately allowed the two men to leave their homes and go forth, and conferred upon them full ordination.
The Elder Ānanda, not long after his renunciation, while dwelling in seclusion and practicing meditation and reflection, had this thought:
"If my preceptor would now permit me to go to the Buddha’s presence, I too must see the World-Honored One for myself."

Then, having formed this thought, Ānanda rose from his dwelling in the early morning and went to where the Venerable Vyāsaṣṭha was. He prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and having stood to one side, he addressed the Elder Vyāsaṣṭha, saying:
"Venerable Upādhyāya!"
"I now wish to go and see the Buddha; will you grant me permission?
At that time, the Vātsīputrīya Saṃgha replied to Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda!..."

If you know the proper time now, go to the Buddha; having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, you should prostrate at my feet before the Buddha and convey my greetings to the World-Honored One, asking whether he has little illness and little affliction, and whether his body is at ease.
"I hope your daily activities are light and easy, and that your travels for teaching and guiding others do not diminish your virtue. Is your physical strength and vitality better than usual?
At that time, having heard these words from Upādāya, Ānanda replied to him, saying:
"As instructed by Upādāya, I dare not disobey his teaching."
He then prostrated at the feet of the Saṃgha of the Vāseṭṭhas, circumambulated them three times, took his leave, and departed.
*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll 58;
*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll 59.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of Central India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on the Causes and Conditions of Bhaṭṭika, Part Two.
At that time, the Elder Devadatta saw Ānanda heading toward the place where the Buddha was and said to him:
“Venerable Ānanda!
Where do you wish to go?
At that time, Ānanda replied to him, saying:
"I now wish to go and see the Buddha.
At that time, the Elder Devadatta replied to Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda!..."
"If it is indeed so for you now, wait a short while; I also wish to go consult my preceptor, and we shall go together to the place where the Buddha is."
At that time, Devadatta went to where the Saṃgha of Vāyaseṭṭha was, prostrated at their feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed them, saying:
"I now wish to go and see the Buddha; I only pray that the Venerable Ones will compassionately grant me permission."
At that time, the Elder Vātsīputra Saṃgha replied to Devadatta, saying: "If you know the proper time, go to the Buddha’s presence and convey my words for me:
prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and inquire after the World-Honored One, asking whether he is free from illness and affliction, and whether his body is at ease."
"Is your daily life light and easy? As you travel about to guide and transform others, does it not diminish your virtue?
Is your physical strength and vitality superior to your usual state?
Devadatta replied to those Bhārgava Śrāvakas, speaking these words:
“As the Venerable One has instructed, I dare not disobey.
He then prostrated himself, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew.

At that time, Ānanda accompanied the Elder Devadatta; the two of them set out from the foot of the Snowy Mountains and proceeded toward the Buddha’s dwelling. Upon arriving at the Buddha’s presence, they bowed their heads to his feet in salutation and stood to one side.
At that time, the Elder Devadatta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
In the past, I requested the Tathāgata for ordination, yet the Tathāgata did not grant me ordination. May the Tathāgata today allow me to attain ordination!"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Devadatta, saying these words: "Devadatta!
For what purpose did you go forth into homelessness?"
"I pray that once you have attained it, you will not turn your back upon it.
At that time, the bhikṣus all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"
In the past, the World-Honored One constantly taught Devadatta for his benefit; why has Devadatta now turned against the Buddha and become his enemy?
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
It is not only today that I have taught this man Devadatta for his benefit, yet he has instead treated me as an enemy."
"In past lives as well, it was just like this; though I taught them for their benefit, they instead bore me malice.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One!"
"What is the meaning of this?
We pray that you will explain it for us.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I recall that in the distant past, long ago, there lived beneath the Snowy Mountains two-headed birds who shared a single body."
One bird was named Kalavinka, and the other was named Upakalavinka.
Of these two birds, whenever one was asleep, the other remained awake.
While Karoṭa was once asleep, near his head there was a fruit tree named Mātulunga; its flowers fell and were blown by the wind until they reached the side of where he lay sleeping.
At that time, the other head thought to itself:
"Although I am now eating this flower alone, once it enters my belly, both heads shall simultaneously obtain color and strength, and both shall be relieved of hunger and thirst."
However, that waking head did not wake the sleeping head, nor did it inform him; instead, it silently ate those flowers.
Later, when the sleeping head awoke, his belly was full and he belched as the air came out, whereupon he spoke to the other head, saying:
"Where did you obtain this fragrant, delicious, and exquisite food to eat?"
"May my body be peaceful, secure, and well-satisfied; may the sound of my voice become sublime.
The head replied, "While you were asleep, not far from my side here, there was a tree bearing *mātuluṅga* flowers and fruits; at that time, a single flower fell down beside my head."
At that time, I thought to myself:
"I shall now eat these flowers alone; once they enter my belly, we shall all obtain physical beauty and strength, and together we shall be relieved of hunger and thirst."
"Therefore, at that time, I did not wake you, nor did I inform you, as I immediately ate these flowers.
When the head heard these words, he immediately gave rise to a mind of anger and resentment, thinking thus:
"Regarding the food he obtained, he did not inform me or call me to wake up, but instead ate it himself."
"If this is the case, from now on, regarding whatever food and drink I obtain, I shall no longer call out to the other head to wake him and inform him.
Then, at one time, as the two heads were traveling along, they suddenly encountered a poisonous flower. Thereupon, he thought:
"I shall eat this flower, wishing that both heads may die simultaneously."
Then he said to that Kālodayin, "You sleep now; I shall remain awake.
When Kālodayin heard these words from Upakālodayin, he immediately fell asleep.
That Upaka had just eaten poisonous flowers.
Once Upaka had woken up from his sleep, he coughed and spat out air; immediately perceiving this poisonous vapor, he addressed the head, saying:
"What kind of foul food did you eat when you woke up just now?"
It causes my body to find no peace, and my life is about to end.
Furthermore, it makes my speech coarse and harsh; whenever I wish to produce a sound, it is obstructed and impaired.
Thereupon, the head named Awakening replied to that head, saying:
"While you were asleep, I ate poisonous flowers; I vow that both heads shall die at the same time."
At that time, that head spoke to the other head, saying:
"How can what you have done be so hasty? Why have you committed such an act?"
Then he spoke in verse:
"When you were sleeping in the past, I ate exquisite flowers of sweet and delicious flavor;
The wind blew those flowers toward me, Yet you, on the contrary, gave rise to such great anger?"
May one never behold a fool; may one never even hear of dwelling with a fool.
To dwell with a fool brings no benefit; it harms oneself and harms others as well.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you have any doubt as to who that kalaviṅka bird was at that time, which fed upon beautiful flowers, do not entertain any other view; it was none other than myself."
At that time, the Upakalava bird that ate the poisonous flower was none other than this Devadatta.
Although I acted for his benefit at that time, he instead gave rise to anger.
"Now it is likewise; though my teaching is for their benefit, they instead treat me as an enemy.
At that time, having gone forth, the Elder Vāṣpa (Vadhalika) attained the three supernormal powers within those three months of the summer retreat;
Maṇicūḍa attained the divine eye.
The Elder Vāṣpa, the Elder Nigrodha, and the Elder Nandika—these individuals realized the fruit of Arhatship;
Ānanda further attained the fruit of Srotāpanna;
and Devadatta accomplished the mundane supernatural powers of an ordinary worldling.

At that time, the elder Vattika, having attained the fruit of arhatship, whether in a forest grove, or dwelling in a secluded chamber, or staying in the open air, or residing in the Jeta Grove, would constantly utter these words three times during the day and night:
"Aha! What happiness!"
Thus he recited it three times.
At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus approached the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

That elder Vāṣpa, son of Gopikā, took no pleasure in the Dharma of the Blessed One; he was neither joyful nor delighted. Constantly recollecting the pleasures of wealth and nobility from his former royal status, and because he was perpetually mindful of such matters, whether staying beneath a tree, in an empty room, or in the open air, he would cry out at the three periods of the day:
"Alas, what happiness!"—thus he spoke three times.
At that time, the World-Honored One called to a certain bhikṣu and addressed him, saying:
"Come, bhikṣu! You should go to the presence of the bhikṣu Pāṭaligāma and speak on my behalf, saying these words:"
“The World-Honored One calls for you. That bhikṣu replied,
“As you command, I shall not dare to disobey.”
He immediately went to where the elder Pāṭaligāma was, and upon arriving, he said to him: "Pāṭaligāma,
the World-Honored One calls for you."
At that time, having heard those words, the elder Vāṣpa approached the place where the Buddha was; having arrived, he prostrated himself at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Bhadrika, saying these words: "Bhadrika!
Is it true that you do not delight in practicing the holy life within my Dharma?"
Do you constantly remember the pleasures of your former royal throne?
Because of those memories, whether beneath a tree, in a secluded chamber, or in the open air, you cry out at the three times of day:
"Alas, what happiness!"
"Alas, how joyful! Is it not so?
At that time, the elder Vāṣpa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, Blessed One!
So it is, Bhadanta!
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"What benefit do you see that you stay beneath a tree and repeatedly utter these words at the three times of the day:
'O, what happiness!'"
"Alas, what happiness!
At that time, the elder Vattika addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
In the past, when I lived at home and governed the royal throne as a consecrated Kṣatriya, my palace was surrounded by sevenfold walls that protected us.

Furthermore, there was an elephant army guarded in seven layers, and likewise a cavalry army in seven layers; there were also chariot troops and infantry, each likewise in seven layers. All were clad in armor and held weapons of war, namely bows, arrows, swords, spears, lances, shields, great vajra-maces, large iron clubs, iron wheels with spikes, tridents, battle-axes, and various other such weapons. They surrounded me on all sides, and outside the wall there were further seven layers of moats filled with water.

Even with such protection and such shielding, if one hears various sounds in the night, fear arises in the mind, and one finds no peace; the hairs on the body stand on end, shame and remorse constantly arise, and the sense faculties become disturbed.

“World-Honored One, whether I am now beneath a tree, in a quiet room, or in the open air, when I hear the various sounds of predatory beasts at night, I feel no fear; my hair does not stand on end, I feel no shame or trepidation, and my faculties remain unaltered.”
Therefore, as I sit alone in constant contemplation, this thought arises in my mind:

"I have now attained a matter of great benefit; the World-Honored One is my Great Teacher, who has awakened to the Dharma himself and teaches it. Within that Dharma, I have gone forth into homelessness and practice the holy life (brahmacarya). Many prohibitions and precepts have been received by me, making me a practitioner of wondrous conduct."
"I have now well attained the means of livelihood and well attained the end of life.
Therefore, World-Honored One!

When I compare the pleasures of my former royal throne and the times of my wealth and nobility to the joy of today’s renunciation—the joy of sitting in seclusion, the joy of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), the joy of tranquil concentration, and the joy of the *śramaṇa*—by recollecting these things, whether under a tree, in a quiet room, or in the open air, I am content with little desire. Begging for food from others, my body hairs do not stand on end; I am like a mountain deer, my mind attains mastery, and whether sitting, lying down, going, or staying, I encounter no obstacles.
At the three times [of day], he cried out:
"Oh, what happiness!
Thus he proclaimed it three times.
At that time, the elder Vāṣpa stood before the Buddha and, in the presence of the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"In the past, I dwelt within the deep inner palace, Where sevenfold walls were exceedingly high and steep;
The watchtowers and battlements were strictly maintained, Along with sevenfold moats and trenches."
The military host and guards, bearing weapons, protect me day and night;
though I thus defend myself in various ways, my body and mind remain nonetheless restless.
Now that I stand before the World-Honored One, there is not a single person to protect me;
even when I am in a secluded place, or among trees and mountain forests,
none guard me as my fellow sons of the Buddha, the Vatsas, each protect one another.
In walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, one is always at peace; therefore, the mind has no攀緣 (pāra-yaṇa, objective attachments).
In the past, within my palace, I rode upon great elephants; my body was clothed in fine silks and exquisite garments;
I consumed fragrant rice and delicious meals, with soups and stews seasoned with various meats.
Now I sit and lie down as I please upon a spread of grass; in empty solitude, I wear robes of cast-off rags.
Having abandoned craving and uprooted the very foundation of suffering, I shall do as I wish wherever I go.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"If a person knows life and does not give rise to affliction, They likewise do not grieve over the end of life.
If one can be courageous and perceive the True Dharma, Though they fall into the sea of suffering, they will never fear."
The bhikṣu who has severed craving for existence, having completely abandoned all things,
with the afflictions of birth and death utterly extinguished— such a one shall have no further becoming.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
If you wish to know who among my śrāvaka disciples of noble and wealthy lineage has abandoned home for the homeless life as the foremost, it is this very bhikṣu Bhaṭṭika."
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What roots of goodness did this elder Vādiraka cultivate in days past?”
In this life, he was born into a great and noble family of the Śākya clan, possessing abundant wealth and property with nothing lacking.
What further karma did he perform that allowed him to inherit the Śākya lineage and ascend to the royal throne?
Furthermore, what karma did he perform such that he was able to leave the household life, receive full ordination, attain the fruit of arhatship,
and receive a prediction from the World-Honored One?
"O bhikṣus! Among my śrāvaka disciples, he who renounced his noble status and wealth to go forth into homelessness is foremost of all, namely, Bhadrika."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
I recall that in the distant past, there was a poor man who supported himself by begging. He traveled from one city to the city of Vārāṇasī."
Having arrived at that city, all the beggars who saw him rebuked him, saying:
"From where have you come, and why have you reached this place?"
Consequently, they barred him and would not permit him to wander about begging for alms.
At that time, seeing this obstruction, the man thought to himself:
"I have committed no offense against these people; why then do they obstruct me from begging?"

At that time, there was an elder in the city of Vārāṇasī who had lost a copper bowl. While the elder was searching for the copper bowl and could not find it anywhere, he traveled to another village in pursuit of it.

At that time, the beggar found that copper bowl among a heap of refuse; he hung it upon the tip of his staff and went into the city of Vārāṇasī, proceeding from street to street and from lane to lane, from one intersection to another, and from one corner to another, crying out these words:
"To whom does this copper bowl belong?"
"Let those who know it take it.
Thus, he traveled far and wide in all directions, searching for its owner but was unable to find him.
Since he could not find the owner, he went directly to present it to King Brahmadatta.

Eventually, the householder later heard that someone had found a copper bowl from within those excrement heaps, hung it upon the tip of a staff, and was entering the city of Vārāṇasī, going from street to street and lane to lane, crying out:
"To whom does this copper bowl belong?"
He traveled and inquired everywhere, but did not know where the master was located. Since he could not find the master, he entrusted [the child] to Brahmadatta.
Having heard this, he went to Brahmadatta’s side and, upon arrival, said:
"Great King!"
"You should know that the copper bowl which was offered by the beggar previously is my own property.
At that time, King Brahmadatta sent a messenger to summon the beggar and said to him:
"Regarding the copper bowl you delivered previously, this householder now claims it belongs to me; what is the truth of the matter?"
That man then addressed King Brahmadatta, saying:
"It is so, Great King!
Originally, I did not know whose property that copper bowl was."

Having found it amidst a heap of refuse, I immediately hung it upon the tip of my staff and brought it back into the city of Vārāṇasī. I went here and there in search of its owner but could not find him; since I could not obtain the owner, I have now brought it to offer to Your Majesty, for whatever use Your Majesty may see fit.
At that time, having heard those words, Brahmadatta was greatly delighted in his heart and addressed him, saying:
"O worthy one!
What kind of boon do you now wish to beg from me?"
"I shall give it to you;
as for that bronze bowl, I shall return it to the elder.
At that time, the man addressed King Brahmadatta, saying these words:
"Great King!
If you now truly desire to grant me my wish with joy, I pray that Your Majesty shall appoint all the beggars within this city of Vārāṇasī to have me as their king."
Then King Brahmadatta spoke again to him, saying:
"What use is it for you now to be king over that beggar?
You should instead request some other excellent boon—be it gold, or silver, or the most superior village in the kingdom to serve as a fief—and I shall grant it to you."
Then that beggar spoke again to the king, saying:
"If Your Majesty is pleased and would grant me a boon, I now desire only that which was previously requested."
The King then replied, "Do as you please; act according to your own will.
At that time, there were five hundred beggars residing together in that city of Vārāṇasī. The one who had made the vow summoned them all to assemble and addressed them, saying:
"I have now obtained the status of king among you; you must surely obey my commands.
Then the beggars asked the king, "How will you command us now?"
"What task shall you have me perform? Then that man said:
"All of you together, some shall take me and place me upon your shoulders, some shall take me and carry me on their backs, and all the rest shall serve as my attendants, surrounding me as we go."

When those five hundred beggars heard his words, they immediately followed his instructions; some carried [the goods] on litters, while others bore them upon their backs, traveling from place to place. Whenever they came across a location with food, drink, or seating, they would go there to beg; having begged, they would carry it back to a single spot to distribute and eat together, thus sustaining their lives for a long time through such means.
