At that time, there was a man eating a *mohutaka*—translated in the Sui language as "joy-pill"—in a secluded place. Then, the Beggar King seized that *mohutaka* from the man and, having taken it, ran away.
The king’s retinue of five hundred beggars pursued that king until they had gone a great distance; being utterly exhausted, once they were weary, they all turned back.

That beggar-king was strong and vigorous of body; he ran without fatigue until he had gone a great distance, whereupon he turned his head to look back, but the five hundred beggars were nowhere to be seen.
Having finished looking [for food], he entered a garden, took water to wash his hands, sat to one side, and intended to eat that food.
Before eating, a sense of regret arose within him:
"I have acted unskillfully."
"Why should I now take this food from that person?
Furthermore, why does he deceive my followers?
This food is so abundant that I could not possibly eat it all."
"If there are any noble ones within this world who, knowing my intention, wish to come here, I shall immediately share [my wealth] with them.
Having formed this thought, a Pratyekabuddha named Bhadra flew through the air from the sky and descended directly before that man, landing not far away.

When that person saw from afar that Pratyekabuddha, whose deportment was dignified and orderly, whose gait was even and steady, and whose movements were appropriate—neither slack nor hurried—he attained pure faith in his heart upon seeing him thus.
Having attained a pure mind, he formed this thought:

"Because of the poverty and low status I experienced in the past, as well as my current state, I have failed to encounter such a field of merit; toward such a person, I did not practice generosity, nor did I offer respect or worship.
Had I encountered such a field of merit in the past, I would not be suffering such exhaustion today, nor would I be forced to sustain my life by being oppressed by others."
"I now offer this mahuda food to the rishi; I do not yet know whether this rishi has accepted it or not.
If he should accept it, I pray that in the future I may be spared from this body of poverty, lowliness, and distress."
Having formed this thought, he immediately took this food, *mahuda*, and offered it to the seer.
Now, for Pratyekabuddhas, there is this law: they teach and transform sentient beings solely by manifesting supernatural powers, and have no other method.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha accepted the *mohutaka* food from him; out of compassion for this man, he rose into the air from that place and departed.

When the man saw the Pratyekabuddha World-Honored One ascending into the sky, joy and exultation filled his entire body such that he could not contain himself. With a heart full of joy, he joined his palms at his crown and prostrated from afar at the feet of the Pratyekabuddha World-Honored One. Having made this salutation, he made this vow in his mind:

"May I, in future lives, always encounter a World-Honored One such as this, or one even more sublime than him; and may I, upon hearing the Dharma taught by that World-Honored One, quickly attain realization and understanding."

Furthermore, I vow that in future ages, I shall be born into a family of great majesty and noble lineage, serving as a king to govern and transform the realm, and never again among those poor children.
He further made this vow:
"In birth after birth and life after life, may I never fall into the evil realms.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, speaking these words:
“O bhikṣus! If you have any doubt regarding that time, as to who was this king of beggars in the city of Vārāṇasī who gave a *muhūrtaka* meal to the Pratyekabuddha?”
Do not harbor any doubt; it was the bhikṣu Bhaṭṭika.

At that time, as a beggar king, he gave food to a pratyekabuddha named Mahuda. Due to the karmic fruit of that deed, he has now been born into the Śākya clan, a family of great wealth and nobility, such that his resources and possessions lack for nothing.
Furthermore, at that time, he made this aspiration:
"May I, in a future life, be born into a family of great majesty and noble lineage, and act as a king to transform and guide others."
"By the retribution of that karma, I have now attained the royal throne among the Śākyas.
Furthermore, at that time I made this vow:
'May I, in all future lives and throughout every birth, never fall into the evil realms.'"
"By virtue of that karmic retribution, he was never born or fallen into the evil realms; he was always reborn among humans and devas, wandering back and forth, and experienced much happiness."
Furthermore, at another time, he made this aspiration, saying:

"May I, in future lives, always encounter such Pratyekabuddha World-Honored Ones, or those even more excellent than these; and having heard the sutras and teachings spoken by those World-Honored Ones, may I quickly know and quickly understand them."
"Due to the retribution of that karma, he has now encountered me, been able to leave the household life, receive full ordination, and attain the fruit of arhatship.
I have further granted him this prediction:
'Among my śrāvaka disciples, the one who has left the household life from the most noble lineage is the bhikṣu Bāṣpalipta.'"

"O bhikṣus! Because Bodhika formerly created such roots of goodness through these causal conditions, and by virtue of having created such roots of goodness, he has now been born into a family of the Śākya clan of noble lineage, possessing great wealth and high status, such that his resources and possessions lack nothing."

Among the Śākyas, he obtained the succession to the royal throne; yet, having renounced that kingship, he went forth into homelessness, received full ordination, and attained the fruit of arhatship. Therefore, I bestow this prediction: among my śrāvaka disciples who have gone forth from noble families, the bhikṣu Bhaṭṭika is the foremost.

That elder Vattīkā, having attained the fruit of arhatship, constantly dwelt in forest hermitages, sustained his life by begging for alms, wore rag-robes made from refuse, remained in the sitting posture without lying down, used whatever seat was available, and maintained only the three robes without any further accumulation.
At one time, while residing in the city of Śrāvastī within a forest hermitage, that elder was unable to find any grass or leaves.

He immediately sought out dried white elephant dung, gathered it to form a mat, spread his sitting cloth upon it, sat down cross-legged with his body upright and straight, and thus attained right mindfulness.
After one night had passed,
at the time of dawn, the elder Vāṣpa put on his robes, took up his bowl, and intended to enter the city of Śrāvastī to go about for alms.
At that time, there were many beggars within the city who, having obtained food by begging, departed from the city; not far from the city, each wished to eat separately the food they had received.

At that time, the elder Vāṣpa saw from afar those alms-seekers begging for food in the city; having obtained their food and gone not far from the city, they sat down separately intending to eat. He then went to their side and stood there in silence.
At that time, all the beggars thought to themselves:
"This bhikṣu must surely have compassion for us; that is why he has come to beg for alms."
Having formed this thought, each of them took a small portion from their own food and gave it to the elder Vṛjiputra.

At that time, King Prasenajit of Kośala was riding a great white elephant named Puṇḍarīka; he departed from the city of Śrāvastī accompanied by a chief minister named Śrībhadra (translated into Chinese as "Virtuous Excellence").

At that time, the King of the kingdom of Kosala, Prasenajit, saw from afar Bodhirika begging for food from those beggars and eating it; he immediately addressed his minister Śrībhadra with these words: "Śrībhadra!..."
"What kind of bhikṣu is this?
He begs for food from a pauper and eats it!
At that time, the minister looked closely at Bāvari again and, knowing he was not mistaken, addressed the king, saying:
"Great King!
You should know that this is King Bāhulika of the Śākyas.
Thereupon, the king addressed his minister, saying:
"If this is so, drive the white elephant toward that Pāṭalika.
Having heard the king's command, Śrībhadra addressed the king,
saying, "As the king has commanded, I dare not disobey."
Having received the king’s command, he led this white elephant for the king to mount, and they proceeded toward the Elder Vaidehaka.

At that time, King Prasenajit of Kośala, not far from the Elder Vaidehaka’s dwelling, dismounted from his elephant, prostrated at the feet of the Elder Vaidehaka, and having paid homage, stood to one side.
At that time, King Prasenajit of Kośala addressed the Elder Vṛjiputra, saying:
"Venerable One!..."
"Why is it that you have now conceived such thoughts of poverty and lowliness, as to beg for food and eat from among such poor people?
At that time, the Elder Vāṣpa addressed King Prasenajit of Kośala, saying:
"Great King!"

I do not now beg from them because of poverty; I already possess the seven kinds of precious wealth. It is simply that my mind delights in begging food from the poor, and I also wish to cause those impoverished children to sever their state of destitution, which is why I beg from them.
"Great King!
You should know that I already possess eyes; it is only because I wish to open the eyes of those sentient beings who are shrouded in ignorance that I have come to beg from you.
Furthermore, Great King!"
I have now already been liberated from all fetters; however, for the sake of bringing liberation to those sentient beings bound by greed and hatred, I go forth to beg for food.
“Great King!
I have now already crossed to the other shore; it is only for the sake of pulling out and liberating those sentient beings who are submerged in the mire of afflictions that I beg from you.
Furthermore, Great King!”
"I have already attained the state of being free from illness; however, because I wish to cure those sentient beings who are afflicted by the disease of the defilements, I beg for it from them.
Then King Prasenajit of Kośala spoke again to Bhadrika, saying:
"Venerable One!..."

I too am poor and lack the seven kinds of wealth; I too dwell in obscurity within the darkness; I too am submerged in the mire of the afflictions; and I now likewise suffer from the disease of craving. O Noble One! I pray for your compassion!
"Out of compassion for me, I only wish that you would come to my home again and again.
At that time, the Elder Vāṣpa addressed King Prasenajit of Kośala, saying:
"O Great Virtuous Great King!"
"There is no need for this.
Having spoken these words, he left the king and departed.

Chapter 59: Maṇicūḍa The 59th Chapter on Maṇicūḍa from the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*. Furthermore, at another time, the World-Honored One was expounding the various Dharmas to the bhikṣus. At that moment, the Elder Maṇicūḍa fell asleep and did not wake.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maṇicūḍa, saying these words: "Maṇicūḍa!
Why do you sleep thus within this Dharma and its meaning? Regarding this matter, it is profoundly unwholesome for you."
"Arise! Do not sleep!

From that time forward, Maṇicūḍa no longer slept; because he had been deprived of sleep for so long, his physical eyes were impaired, and he could perceive the forms of the world only with his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
Among my śrāvaka disciples, the one who is foremost in pure brahmacarya is none other than Maṇicūḍa."
On another occasion, while Maṇicūḍa was repeatedly sewing the seams of various garments, he held five needles with his five fingers.
At that time, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana approached him and said to him: "Maṇicūḍa!"
"Come now, let us travel together.
Then, the Elder Maṇicūḍa replied to Maudgalyāyana:
"Elder Maudgalyāyana!"
"Wait, wait! Wait until my robe is finished.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana spoke again to the Elder Maṇicūḍa:
"If you now sew this with supernormal powers, may it be quickly accomplished; if you wish to accomplish it with your current intention, may it likewise be completed soon.
While Maṇicūḍa was sewing this garment, the needle and thread broke. At that time, the Elder Maṇicūḍa spoke to himself:
"Who in this world desires to perform meritorious deeds?"
"Lend me your needle.
At that time, the World-Honored One was alone in his chamber, sitting in meditation with a concentrated mind; he then heard these words spoken by Maṇicūḍa with his pure divine ear.

Having heard these words, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he vanished from his original location and went to the elder Maṇicūḍa; standing before him, he took the needle and pierced through it.
At that time, the Elder Maṇicūḍa asked,
"Who is threading my needle for me?
The Buddha told him:
“Maṇilūta! It was I who threaded the needle for you.
At that time, all the bhikṣus heard these words and said:
“The Blessed One is threading a needle with a thread for that Elder Maṇicūḍa.
Having heard these words, they each reflected:
“If even the Blessed One assists one who has not yet accomplished his task to aid his pure holy life, how much more so should we? Why do we remain silent and fail to help him?”
From that time forward, whenever the community of bhikṣus had any task to perform, they each assisted one another.
At that time, the bhikṣus, on account of this matter, went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
"World-Honored One!..."
What virtuous karma did that Elder Maṇicūḍa plant in days of yore,
such that he has now been able to go forth, receive full ordination, and attain the fruit of arhatship?
The World-Honored One further declared: "O Bhikṣus!
Among my śrāvaka disciples, he who has attained the pure divine eye as the foremost is this Elder, the Bhikṣu Maṇicūḍa."
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed all the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!

I recall that in the distant past, beyond incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
When that Buddha, the World-Honored One, was preaching the Dharma for the bhikṣus, he praised in various ways the matter of the divine eye.
At that time, there was the son of a householder named Mahādhana who came to that assembly, sat among the multitude, and listened to his teaching.
After that son of a householder had heard the Dharma, he reflected thus:
"Although I have not yet consulted my parents to leave the home life and go forth, I shall now cultivate various roots of goodness for the sake of attaining the divine eye in a future life."

Having formed this thought, he prepared oil and obtained one hundred *dou*. At the place of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, the Unsurpassed, Truly Realized, Perfectly Enlightened One, he lit lamps as an offering and made this vow:

"May I, in a future life, encounter such a Buddha; may I quickly attain realization and understanding when that Buddha preaches the Dharma; and among all the disciples of that World-Honored One who possess the divine eye, may I be the foremost."
He further made this vow:
"In birth after birth and life after life, may I never fall into the evil realms.

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān Dīpaṃkara addressed the son of a householder, Mahādhana, saying:

"In a future age there shall be a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles; among the śrāvaka disciples of that Blessed One who possess the divine eye, you shall be the foremost."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!
Perhaps some among you harbor doubts as to who that son of a wealthy householder named Mahādhana was at the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara."
"This is none other than Maṇibhadra.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"I recall that in the distant past, long ago, there was a thief who was traveling along a narrow path in the darkness of night, intending to commit a robbery. When he reached the midpoint of his journey, the lacing of his shoe broke."

"At that time, there was a stūpa containing the relics of a pratyekabuddha in that place. At that stūpa, there was a man who, seeking merit, offered worship and service by lighting a lamp; however, the oil for that lamp was about to run out and the flame was on the verge of extinguishing."
When the thief arrived there, he saw that the lamp was about to go out; wishing to repair the broken laces of his sandals, he added more oil and used the tip of an arrow to trim the wick.
At that time, the lamp flared up once more with bright intensity.
When the thief saw the light of the lamp, he went not far from it and continued sewing his shoe-strap.
Because of that light, he was able to see the stupa.
Having seen the stupa, his mind attained purity; having attained purity of mind, he made this aspiration:
"Whose stupa is this?"

May I, in a future life, encounter this very stūpa-body of the World-Honored One, or one even more excellent than him; and may I, having heard the Dharma taught by that World-Honored One, swiftly attain understanding and realization, becoming the foremost among all the śrāvaka disciples of that World-Honored One who possess the divine eye.
"Furthermore, I vow that in all future lives, birth after birth, I shall not fall into the evil realms.
*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll 59;
*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, Scroll 60.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on Maṇicūḍa, Part Two.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“O bhikṣus! At that time, who was the thief who increased the lamp-light before the stūpa of the Pratyekabuddha?
Do not harbor any doubt; it was the bhikṣu Maṇicūḍa.”

Maṇiluta, in the past, was the son of a great householder named Mahādhana; later, he became a thief, yet for the sake of a stūpa containing the relics of a pratyekabuddha, he added oil to the lamps and, with a pure mind, made this aspiration:
"May I not be born in the evil realms in future lives."

"By the retribution of that karma, he was never born into the evil realms throughout his lifetimes in the world, but constantly experienced pleasure by wandering between the heavens and the human realm.
At that time, he further made this aspiration:
'May I, in future lives, always encounter a World-Honored One such as this, or one even more sublime than him; and may I swiftly understand the Dharma taught by him.'"
"By the retribution of that karma, he has now encountered me, a World-Honored One such as this, and has further attained the going forth and received full ordination in my presence."
At that time, he further made this aspiration:
"May I be the foremost among all the disciples of that Blessed One who possess the divine eye."
"By the retribution of that karma, he is now, among my śrāvaka disciples within this Dharma, the foremost in possessing the divine eye.
You bhikṣus!..."
Maṇibhadra, in the past he planted such roots of merit; by the power of that karma, he has now been able to leave the household life, receive full ordination, and attain the fruit of arhatship.
"O monks! I further grant this prediction: among my śrāvaka disciples, Maṇicūḍa is the foremost.

On another occasion, while the World-Honored One was staying at the Deer Park in Ṛṣipatana, the ancient abode of seers near the city of Vārāṇasī, it rained. At that time, the Elder Ānanda approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Having stood to one side, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Today it is raining, and there is no food or drink. What plan should we make so that the bhikṣus may pass this day and night?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do not grieve, Maṇilūta Bhikṣu!
The power of your present merit is exceedingly strong; today, Bhikṣu, you shall surely pass through this day and night."
At that time, the Elder Maṇicūḍa approached the place where the Buddha was; having arrived, he prostrated himself at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Now, by accepting my humble offering—if you partake of my food—you will be able to sustain all the bhikṣus for one day and night.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently gave his consent.
At that time, the Elder Maṇicūḍa, in the early morning, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went into the city of Vārāṇasī.
Having entered the city, he had never before begged for alms, nor did he have any relatives or acquaintances there.
At that moment, five hundred cauldrons of food suddenly appeared before him.

Thereupon, the Elder Maṇicūḍa immediately took those five hundred cauldrons of food toward the Deer Park; having spread out the seats and completed the arrangements, he went to inform the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the time has come and the meal is prepared; we pray that you will deign to partake."

At that time, when the sun was in the east, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and together with the bhikṣus, came to the dining hall and sat down in order upon the seats that had been prepared.

At that time, the Elder Maṇicūḍa, seeing that the Buddha and the Saṅgha were seated in order, took the aforementioned food from five hundred cauldrons and offered it to the Buddha and the Saṅgha; after they had eaten their fill to their heart's content, he then ate himself.
When the meal was finished, he went together with the bhikṣus to the lecture hall, where he spread out a seat and sat down.
At that time, the Elder Maṇicūḍa, having sat down, addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable elders!..."
How rare, how rare!
Never before have we seen such a thing as this, wherein there is such great karmic fruit, such great merit, and such great majestic power.
Why is this so? Venerable elders!
I recall that in the distant past, long ago, there was a poor man in the city of Vārāṇasī who possessed no wealth and maintained no storehouse.
At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there lived a Pratyekabuddha named Vatsa who resided there.

During that period, grain was expensive in the city, and the people suffered from famine; many were destitute, and within and without the city, many died, leaving only white bones scattered in disarray everywhere.
At that time, it was difficult for renunciants to obtain almsfood; oppressed by hunger, they were unable to practice the Path.

During that period, in the early morning when the sun was in the east, that Pratyekabuddha put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered Vārāṇasī to beg for food in sequence. He traversed the entire city but obtained nothing at all; he washed his bowl as usual and returned out of the city.
At that time, seeing the venerable Pratyekabuddha Vāsiṣṭha approaching, I went up to him and said:
"Excellent, Great Sage!"
"Did you manage to obtain any alms while begging for food here?
That venerable one replied to me, saying:
"O worthy one!"
"Why is it that I cannot obtain alms-food now?
At that time, I again addressed that Honored One, speaking these words:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"If that is so, please come to my home.
At that time, there was only one *śīrṣa* measure of cooked millet in the house; I immediately summoned that Pratyekabuddha, invited him into the house, and offered him that millet rice as a gift.
At that time, after the Pratyekabuddha had accepted my offering, he departed as he pleased.
During that period, I went out beyond the city walls to gather firewood; not far from the Śītavana cemetery, I was collecting timber.
In that forest, there was a skeleton of white bones that suddenly rose up and embraced my neck.
At that time, wishing to free myself from that corpse, I exerted myself with great effort, yet I could not escape.
On that day, as the sun was setting in the west and was about to vanish, I took up a corpse and entered the city.
As I entered the city, those who saw me said to me:
"Ho! Why do you carry this skeletal corpse into the city?"
I replied to them, saying: "O people!
Although I now exert all my strength, I am utterly unable to release this corpse."
"If among you there are any capable of releasing it, you should release it for me.
Then those people together carefully grasped this skeletal corpse and pulled at it with all their might, hoping to free it, yet they were unable to do so.
At that time, I gradually approached my home, hoping to remove those white bones and corpses; however, those white bones all transformed into gold and naturally fell to the ground.
At that time, I had this thought:
"I cannot use this gold for myself alone.
Having had this thought, I immediately went to King Brahmadatta and said to him:
"Great King!
You should know that I have now discovered a hidden treasure in the earth; may Your Majesty accept it and use it as a national treasure.
At that time, King Brahmadatta summoned his attendants and commanded them, saying:
"You all must follow this man; whatever he points out for you to take, you shall all receive and bring it here.
At that time, having heard the king's command, his attendants immediately came with me to my house, where I then showed the gold to those messengers.
At that time, the messenger returned and saw the corpse with its white bones just as before; having seen this, he said to me:
"Alas, you foolish man!
Are you not mad?"
"Why do you carry that corpse and white bones, mistaking them for gold?
Then that messenger returned to the king's presence and related the previous events in detail.
At a later time, I again went to the king's side and said to him:
"Great King!
You should know that I have obtained a hidden treasure; this matter is indeed true and not false.
I only pray that Your Majesty will accept it at once."
Then King Brahmadatta went to his house in person and saw that the gold hoard was nothing but white bones, no different from how they originally were; he spoke to me again, saying:
"Alas, you foolish man!
"You are possessed by madness!
Why do you conceive the notion that this white-boned corpse is gold?
I then addressed King Brahmadatta once more, saying:
"Great King!
You should know that this is indeed gold, not the bones of a corpse.
Having spoken these words thus, he repeated them a second and a third time.
At that time, holding that gold in my hand, I made this vow:
"If this gold and treasure are to bring about the ripening of wholesome karma for me, may King Brahmadatta likewise behold it."
Having made this vow, King Brahmadatta looked upon this corpse and saw it no differently than I had seen the gold and jewels; he then said to me:
"Excellent, O worthy one!"
"What kind of causes and conditions for wholesome karma have you cultivated?
Whom have you served as a deity in the past?
Which deva have you made offerings to?"
"Whom did you worship that he was able to grant you such a boon?
At that time, I spoke these words to King Brahmadatta:
"Great King!
You should know that there was once a rishi whom I used to provide with food.
It must have been due to his supernatural power that I have obtained this retribution today."
Then King Brahmadatta said to me:
"Because you performed such virtuous deeds, you have obtained this retribution today.
No one can take away this retribution of yours; from this day forward, you need not harbor any doubts, but may use it as you please."
"O Venerable Elders!
At that time, by the very karma of giving a single meal to that Pratyekabuddha, I immediately obtained its fruit and retribution; whatever wealth and provisions I required were provided at will."

Precisely because he gave a single meal to that person, he was reborn seven times in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where he experienced its karmic rewards; there, in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, he became Śakra, King of the Gods. Furthermore, among human beings, he became a king, and subsequently attained the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), ruling over the four continents as the lord of the world. He protected the world, possessed the seven treasures in their entirety, and even brought all under his sway, governing and transforming them according to the Dharma.
By the karmic fruit of that single meal of almsgiving, upon the end of his life he was reborn in the heavens; descending from the heavens, he was born among humans;
and when his life there ended, he again attained rebirth in the heavens.
Such is the cycle of transmigration, never again mixed with inferior births.

In whatever place I am born, I always obtain the most excellent and sublime palaces; if born among humans, I am born into a noble and wealthy family, with abundant resources and lacking nothing whatsoever.
Just as I experience much happiness in my celestial body, it is likewise so when I descend to be born among humans.
"By virtue of the fruit of giving a single meal, I have now been born into the Śākya clan.

On the day of my birth, the devas descended from heaven and covered my body with five hundred precious robes; furthermore, five hundred hidden treasures beneath the earth spontaneously appeared—all of which was the fruit of the gift of that one meal."
My parents have constructed for me three kinds of palaces:
one suitable for sitting in summer, one suitable for sitting in winter, and one suitable for dwelling and sitting during the two seasons of spring and autumn.

By virtue of the causal conditions resulting from that gift of food, I was born into the Śākya clan; at that time, my family’s prosperity increased day by day, such that our granaries were overflowing with grain and rice, and we possessed immeasurable treasures—pearls, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, gold, silver, jade, and so forth—and lacked for nothing in terms of bipeds or quadrupeds.

Furthermore, as a result of the merit from giving food at that time, while I was in the garden, my mother, wishing to test me, prepared an empty vessel, covered it with her robe, and sent it to me. When she had reached halfway there, various foods and drinks provided by the devas completely filled the vessel.
He ate fragrant and delicious food and gained great physical strength.
Furthermore, by the power of the karmic fruit of his gift of food, he accompanied his father to oversee the farming work.
At that time, suffering from hunger and thirst, he went toward some water, cupped it in his hands intending to drink, and the water transformed into the wondrous nectar of the gods (*amṛta*).

Furthermore, because the fruit of ripening from having given a single meal to another has matured, as he now enters this city of Vārāṇasī, although he has never had a close acquaintance with me, five hundred cauldrons of food spontaneously appear before me.
I accepted that food and sent it into the forest, where I invited the Buddha and the Sangha to partake of this offering, ensuring that the entire assembly of monks was fully satisfied.
By virtue of that karmic retribution, I have lacked for nothing in the four requisites of life.
"Because of the karmic causes and conditions of my gift of food to him, I lacked nothing in terms of worldly pleasures;
now that I have gone forth, I am likewise fully endowed with the happiness of the renunciant life."

Because the karmic fruit of that gift of food has ripened, he has now severed birth and death and attained the power of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). All that was to be done has been accomplished; he shall not undergo further existence and has reached the state of fearlessness. Upon arriving at this place, he shall attain *nirvāṇa*. Having attained *nirvāṇa*, there is neither pleasure nor pain, which he realizes for himself by his own nature.
Venerable elders!

At that time, I did not recognize him as a Pratyekabuddha World-Honored One. Had I known for certain that he was a Pratyekabuddha, I would have immediately sought a superior fruit, sought great majestic power, and sought the unsurpassed, vast fruition.
At that time, after the Elder Maṇicūḍa had spoken these words, he further recited these verses:
"I recall my own thoughts of the past, When I lived in dependence upon Vārāṇasī;
My occupation was that of a woodcutter, And there I encountered the Venerable Vasittha."
Having seen [the Buddha], he gave him a single meal; therefore, he was born into the noble Śākya clan, named Nīloda.
He was skilled in vocal arts and capable of dancing, as well as clapping his hands, singing, chanting, and reciting, along with all other various crafts and skills.
I have now personally realized my past lives, as well as the places where I was born in former ages;
having gone to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, I was reborn there, returning and coming back seven times,
sometimes acting as the King of the Śakras and at other times within the palace of the Lord of the Vaśavartin Devas.
Everything was performed according to my will; thus did I govern and transform the various devas.
Furthermore, for seven successive lifetimes, I served as a lord of men, a consecrated Kṣatriya king.
Possessing sovereign power and great strength, I subdued all multitudes without employing the blade, weapons, or any martial implements.
Ruling the great earth according to the Dharma, there are many immeasurable treasures;
within my realm all is abundant and rich. Born into a family of great wealth, my resources increase beyond counting, making me the foremost among all people.
The five desires of the world are all fully provided for, And the seven treasures and various jewels are without lack;
All this is due to such karma performed by me, So that I have never been born within the evil realms.
Now that I have gone forth from the Śākya clan and attained the state of the nectar of the three liberations,
for what purpose did I go forth and abandon my household affairs to come here?
Precisely because I have obtained these benefits, I come to repay the kindness of the Buddha, the World-Honored One;
knowing that my faculties were now ripe, the World-Honored One expounded for me the Dharma of impermanence.
If there is a mind-made emanation body that, through supernormal powers, comes of its own accord to my presence,
and if there are doubts within my mind, may they all be resolved for me by it.
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is without discrimination; Please teach me, in turn, that non-discriminating Dharma.
Now that I have heard those true words, I shall joyfully accept and practice them according to the Dharma.
In this way, I shall attain the three liberations, And thereby repay the kindness of all Buddhas.
I do not now delight in this end of life, nor do I cherish this lifespan;
yet when the time for the karma I have received arrives, I shall relinquish my life with right mindfulness and reflection.
I know the places of birth and death in the future, and I also know the places where sentient beings come and go;
having known that they have ended their lives in this place, I also know the place to which they will go and be reborn.
In the Bamboo Grove village within the territory of Vaiśālī, I shall relinquish my life-span;
beneath that lush and flourishing grove, having exhausted all outflows, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure divine ear surpassing that of humans, heard the Elder Maṇicūḍa recounting these causes and conditions of past karma and how he had now obtained such a retribution in the present.
He further expounded upon this with sublime verses.
Having heard these matters, he praised them with joyful delight. Chapter Sixty:

The Circumstances of Ānanda The *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*, Chapter Sixty: The Circumstances of Ānanda Furthermore, at one time, the Elder Ānanda was exhorted and requested by those of great virtue who shared the holy life (brahmacarya), that he should serve the World-Honored One.

From that time forth, he has exerted himself with all his heart and strength, keeping his mental conduct harmonious and well-adjusted; everything spoken by the Tathāgata, he has fully received and upheld.

Whatever matters he has heard from the mouth of the Tathāgata—whether mundane or supramundane—he is able to receive and uphold them all, never forgetting or losing them. Should anyone come to inquire about their doubts, he is likewise able to cause that person’s mind to rejoice.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the multitude and addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
Among my śrāvaka disciples, the one who is most learned and possesses keen wisdom—and among my attendants, it is the bhikṣu Ānanda."
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What roots of goodness did the Elder Ānanda cultivate in the past?”

By virtue of those roots of goodness, he was born this life into a great and noble clan of the Śākya lineage, possessing vast wealth and abundant riches, with great power and influence, lacking nothing whatsoever.

Furthermore, by what karma did he now attain the going forth and receive full ordination, obtain all the noble dharmas, never forget or lose anything upon hearing matters mundane or supramundane, and, when people come to ask about their doubts, always be able to gladden their hearts?
The World-Honored One further gave this prediction to the bhikṣus:
"If one knows among my śrāvaka disciples who is foremost in being learned, possessing wisdom, and having a powerful memory that never forgets, it is this very bhikṣu Ānanda."
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I recall that in the distant past, in ages long gone, there was a king who ruled and transformed this very city of Vārāṇasī; his name was Brahmadatta."
At that time, the king fathered two sons: the first was named Nandika, and the second was named Vāṇu (which in the Sui language means "Moon").
Between these two sons, Nandika was the elder.

As for that eldest son, his nature was naturally disciplined and virtuous, upright and gentle; he possessed great compassion, feared all transgressions, and felt weary of and detached from craving and existence.

That prince saw that within the city he was oppressed by the affairs of kings, tormented by government officials, and subjected to endless slaughter; there were many who were imprisoned—namely, those bound with shackles, fetters, and manacles, confined in dungeons and prisons, their hands and feet severed, their ears and noses cut off, and their eyes gouged out.
Having witnessed this event, he then had this thought:
"When my father-king has passed away after a hundred years, how shall I govern the royal throne?"
Now that I know the use of such a kingship, what would I wish to do with it?
And as for my own life and body, I also know what use they are. Why is this so?
"Now I see that all these sentient beings have their bodies tormented by various kinds of suffering.
Just as I am now, it would be better for me to leave home, renounce the world, and cultivate the Way."
Having formed this thought, he went before his parents and said to them:
"Father and Mother!
I wish to leave the home life, renounce the world, and practice the Way."
At that time, the parents replied to their son, saying:
"Your body is our beloved child; you are never absent from our thoughts, and we can never look upon you enough. We would rather die than be parted from you."
"We shall never let you go as long as we have life and breath.
This was repeated a second time, whereupon the youth Nandimukha addressed his parents, saying:
"Parents, you should know!..."
"I shall now certainly renounce my home and go forth into homelessness; I only pray that my parents will, out of compassion, grant me permission.
Thus he requested his parents again and again, until they finally gave their consent for him to renounce his home and go forth, saying to him:
“You are my son; as you desire, so shall it be according to your will.

At that time, Prince Hṛṣṭendriya-Brahmadatta, having been permitted by his parents to leave the home life, on another day abandoned his household and shaved his hair. He practiced the path in successive stages and awakened to the state of a pratyekabuddha. He was able to perform deeds of supernatural transformation, emitting light and water, causing the heavens to revolve and the earth to shake, and summoning clouds and rain; all such matters he was fully capable of accomplishing.
That Pratyekabuddha thought to himself:
"For what purpose did I go forth into homelessness?
That purpose has now been accomplished; I have attained my own benefit, and what was to be done has been done."
"I should now go to my place of birth out of compassion for my parents, my kinsmen, and other sentient beings, so that they may become fields of merit.

At that time, the Pratyekabuddha Bhagavān Nandamūla traveled by stages until he reached Vārāṇasī; having arrived in that country, he took up residence within the Āmra grove belonging to his father, King Brahmadatta.
"At that time, Brahmadatta heard it said by others:
'The youth Nandika has become a great seer and has returned here to dwell within my realm.'"
"I should now go to the presence of Nandika, manifest myself before him, and inquire after his well-being to comfort him.
Then King Brahmadatta, with great power and majestic splendor, displaying his divine majesty, departed from the city, surrounded by the fourfold army in front and behind.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha Venerable Nandimukha saw his father approaching from afar and thought to himself:

"These people, King Brahmadatta and the others, possess great power and are arrogant and conceited. If I were to stand before them in my ordinary form, King Brahmadatta and the others would certainly not show me respect."

Having formed this thought, he soared into the void and manifested various supernatural transformations: sitting, lying down, and walking; emitting smoke from one half of his body while fire issued from the other half; emitting fire from the upper part of his body while water flowed from the lower part—thus he displayed these manifold supernormal powers.

At that time, King Brahmadatta’s ministers and officials, seeing that venerable and great holy Pratyekabuddha soaring through the air and manifesting various supernatural transformations, had this thought upon seeing him:
"Although our prince has renounced the royal throne and now attained the life of a renunciant, he has become a great sage, possessing great majesty and great supernormal powers."

At that moment, his heart was filled with great joy; he leaped for immeasurable delight, a feeling that pervaded his entire body so intensely that he could not contain it, and he went to where the Pratyekabuddha Nandamūla was.
As the king gradually advanced, the Buddha again descended from the sky; when the king reached that place, he was filled with joy and veneration.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha descended and stood upon the ground, immediately sitting upon the seat that had been spread out.
"At that time, Brahmadatta approached the Pratyekabuddha, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Once seated, the Pratyekabuddha briefly expounded the various Dharmas, causing the king to rejoice and leap for joy immeasurably, as he revealed these virtuous matters."
"At that time, having heard the Dharma from the Pratyekabuddha, the Great King was filled with joy and exultation, and addressed the Pratyekabuddha, saying:
'Excellent, O Great Seer!'"

"Now that you have accepted my invitation, please reside permanently in my home. For your sake, Venerable One, I shall construct a monastery with walking paths and meditation caves; I will provide the four requisites for your support, and whatever your heart desires, I shall provide it all."
"If you wish to have compassion for all sentient beings and desire to go among villages and towns to beg for alms, you may do as you please; I shall not obstruct you.
The Pratyekabuddha, the Honored One, accepted the King’s request in silence.

At that time, seeing that the venerable Prītimūla Pratyekabuddha had silently accepted his invitation, the king immediately prepared various articles of offering, including walking paths and meditation caves. He provided the four types of requisites, giving them all as gifts, and furnished everything else that was needed.
"At that time, the Pratyekabuddha hermit Nandendriya, out of compassion for all sentient beings, entered the city to beg for food; it was at such a moment that he entered the city."

Prince Candra went daily to the presence of the Pratyekabuddha Ṛṣi Nandamūla to serve and make offerings to him; whenever he had doubts regarding various dharmas, he would go from time to time to question that Pratyekabuddha.
That Pratyekabuddha, having been questioned by Prince Bāṇa, remained silent and did not answer;
he only emitted flames of light from his fingers.
At that time, Bāṇa thought to himself:
"This Pratyekabuddha possesses great supernatural powers, yet lacks eloquence.
At that time, the Venerable Pratyekabuddha Nandimukha addressed Bāṇa, saying: "Prince Bāṇa!"
"Come, renounce the household life! If you are now unwilling to renounce the household life, I know for certain that after your life ends, you will surely fall into the evil realms.
If you do renounce the household life, you too shall achieve the state of a Great Sage and possess great supernormal powers."
At that time, Bāṇa went to his parents and spoke to them thus:
"Excellent, my parents!
The seer Nandika has now gone forth from the household life; I too now wish to follow him and go forth. I only pray, my parents, [grant me your permission]."
"Have compassion and grant me your permission.
However, his parents did not grant their consent.
Nevertheless, Prince Bāṇa continued to go repeatedly to the place of the seer Nandika, where he served and made offerings to him.
That Pratyekabuddha spoke to Prince Bāṇa several more times, saying:
"You should renounce the household life.
Prince Bāṇa then replied to his elder brother:
"My parents will certainly not allow me to leave home and go forth into the religious life today; what can be done?
At that time, the facial complexion of Prince Bāṇa manifested signs indicating that he would surely meet his end within seven days.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha seer Nandimukha said to Bāṇa:
"Come, Bāṇa! You must certainly renounce the household life and go forth into homelessness."
"Why is this? The signs of your end have appeared; within seven days, you shall surely pass away.
At that time, Bāṇa went to his parents and said:
"Father and Mother!
I only pray that you will release me so that I may leave the home life and become a renunciant.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha Sthūlakoṣṭhila likewise went before his own parents and said:
"Father and Mother!
You should grant Vāṇu permission to go forth into the homeless life. Why is this?..."
Since these signs have appeared, he will certainly pass away within seven days.
For this reason, his parents will inevitably be separated from him.
Because this is certain, it would be better for him to leave the household life and meet his end within the Dharma, rather than allowing him to meet his end as a layman.
The parents replied:
"Prince Bāṇu will surely meet his end within seven days; if he parts from us, we shall now grant him permission to leave home and go forth into the religious life."

"At that time, Prince Bāṇa immediately shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and having gone forth into homelessness, for seven days he made offerings with reverence and served him who was Joyful-Root (Nandimukha)."
At that time, after the Pratyekabuddha had instructed him in the rules of decorum for six days, on the seventh day he knew with certainty that his life would end.

Out of compassion for him, he rose from his seat, soared into the air, and displayed various supernatural powers: walking, sitting, and lying down; emitting smoke and fire; and making himself invisible.

The seer Bāṇa, seeing that the Pratyekabuddha Nandimukha manifesting various supernatural transformations in the midst of the sky, was filled with joy and exultation upon seeing this; it pervaded his entire body so that he could not contain himself, and with palms joined, he prostrated himself before that Pratyekabuddha.
Having prostrated, he made this aspiration:
"In future lives, may I always encounter such Pratyekabuddhas, or those even more excellent than these; and having heard the Dharma they teach, may I fully comprehend and understand it all."
Furthermore, may I become an attendant to those holy ones and make offerings to them.

Moreover, may I attain all supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) in future lives, and may all my majestic power be equal to that of this Buddha; should anyone come to inquire about the meaning of the Dharma, may I explain it all for them and cause them to rejoice.
"Furthermore, I vow that in every birth and throughout all lifetimes, I shall not fall into the evil realms.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!..."
If there is any doubt in your mind as to whether, at that time, Prince Bāṇa made offerings to that venerable Pratyekabuddha for seven days and received his teaching?
Do not entertain any other thought; this is none other than the bhikṣu Ānanda.
At that time, because Prince Bāṇa made an offering to the pratyekabuddha Nandimūla with a joyful heart, by the ripening of that karma, he has now been born into the Śākya clan.
At that time, he made this aspiration:
"May I, throughout all my births and lifetimes, never fall into the evil realms.
By virtue of that karmic retribution, wherever he was born, he never fell into the evil realms; he was born only among humans and devas, wandering back and forth and experiencing great happiness.
At that time, he further made this vow:
"May I, in a future life, encounter such a teacher, a holy person, or one even more excellent than this; and may I, upon hearing the Dharma taught by him but once, immediately attain understanding."

"By the retribution of this karma, he has now encountered me as such a teacher; furthermore, in my presence, he has gone forth from the household life, received full ordination, and attained the various noble dharmas."
At that time, he made this aspiration:
"May I, in a future life, if I should encounter such a teacher, serve as his attendant and provide offerings to that noble one."
"By virtue of that karmic retribution, he has now become my attendant and serves me.
At that time, he also made this aspiration:
'In a future life, may I attain great supernormal powers and great majestic might.'"
"By virtue of that karmic retribution, I have now attained the status of such a Great Sage and acquired great majestic power.
At that time, I also made this vow:
'If anyone comes to ask about their doubts, I shall analyze and explain them all for them, causing their hearts to rejoice.'"
"By virtue of that karmic retribution, Ānanda,
today when someone comes to ask about the doubts in their mind, you resolve them all and cause their hearts to rejoice."
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
I recall that in the distant past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a great wealthy householder named Saṃsṛtadatta (translated in the Sui language as 'King's Peace')."
That elder was immensely wealthy and possessed abundant riches and many enterprises, no different from Vessavaṇa, the Heavenly King.
Every day, five hundred pratyekabuddhas would regularly come to his house to eat.

At that time, there was a pratyekabuddha whose almsbowl had a small, pointed base like the shape of a drop of cow’s milk; wherever he placed it—whether on grass or upon a bamboo screen—it would immediately tip over and could not remain stable.
At that time, the householder Saṃjaya had a daughter who was lovely, upright, and possessed of all the marks of femininity.
Seeing that the Pratyekabuddha’s bowl was tilted and would not stay upright, she immediately removed her own bracelets and offered them to the Pratyekabuddha, saying to him:
"I pray only that you, Great Seer!"
"Take this bracelet and place it beneath your bowl.
At that time, out of compassion, the seer took the bracelet and placed it under the bowl; consequently, the alms-bowl no longer tilted.

At that time, seeing that the bowl remained perfectly still upon her bracelet without tilting or falling, she was filled with such joy and exuberance that it pervaded her entire body, which she could not contain. She made this aspiration:
"Just as this seer’s bowl rests upon my bracelet without leaning or falling, may I in future lives likewise remember and retain everything I hear—whether mundane matters or supramundane ones."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!
If you have any doubt as to who that daughter of the householder was at that time, [listen well]."
Do not entertain any other view; this was none other than the bhikṣu Ānanda.
At that time, with a heart of joy, he removed his own armlets and offered them to the Venerable Pratyekabuddha, placing the almsbowl upon them so that it would not tip over.

Because of this, he made this aspiration: "Just as this seer placed the bowl upon these armlets without it falling, may I, in future lives, remember and retain everything I hear—whether worldly matters or supramundane matters—and never forget them."
"By virtue of those karmic conditions, everything I have heard since then has not been forgotten.
At another time, when the sun was in the eastern sky, the Elder Bhikṣu Ānanda put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.

Departing from that Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, and not yet having reached the city of Śrāvastī, along the way there was a great tree named Śiṃśapā; beneath its shade, many brāhmaṇas were resting.
When the brahmins saw Ānanda approaching from afar, they said to one another:
"You should know!
This is a disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama, who is the foremost among those who are wise and of great learning."
After these words were spoken, Ānanda arrived and said:
"Venerable sir!
Please observe this śiṃśapā tree; how many leaves does it have?"
At that time, Ānanda, having observed the tree, replied to him:
"The eastern branch has several hundred leaves and several thousand leaves; likewise, the southern, western, and northern branches all have several hundred leaves and several thousand leaves."
Having spoken these words, he immediately departed.
At that time, after Ānanda had left, those brahmins took up a hundred leaves and hid them to one side. When Ānanda returned, the brahmins then asked him again:
"Venerable Ānanda!..."
"You have come again; pray, look once more at this śiṃśapā tree and tell me how many leaves it has.
At that time, Ānanda looked up at the tree and immediately knew the hundreds of leaves that had been plucked and hidden by those brahmins. He then replied to the brahmins, saying:

"On the eastern branch there are several hundred leaves and several thousand leaves; likewise for the southern, western, and northern branches, there are also several hundred and several thousand leaves in total."
Having spoken these words, he immediately departed.
At that time, those brahmins were struck with wonder and amazement, and they said to one another:
"This śramaṇa is exceedingly clever and possesses great wisdom."
Due to these causes and conditions, the brahmins attained right faith in their hearts; having attained right faith, before long, they all left the household life and realized the fruit of arhatship.

At that time, there were also the Elder Pūrṇaśobha (translated in the Sui language as *Jǐngsù*, "Well-Constellation"), the Elder Gopila (translated in the Sui language as *Jiāolóng*, "Dragon"), and the Elder Nandika; these three men were known only for the circumstances of their renunciation, but the causes and conditions of their birth were unknown, nor was it known what karma they had performed in former times.
Someone asked,
"By what name should this sutra be called? He replied:
“The masters of the Mahāsāṃghika school call it the *Mahāvastu* (Great Matter).
The masters of the Sarvāstivāda school name this sūtra the *Mahāvyūha* (Great Array).”
"The Kāśyapīya school is called the 'Causes and Conditions for the Birth of the Buddha.
The Dharmaguptaka school is called the 'Original Conduct of Śākyamuni Buddha.
The Mahīśāsaka school is called the 'Root of the Vinaya Piṭaka.'"
The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Volume Sixty.
